A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CCFG research, with a revised title and expanded evaluation in v2. All 14 pages of v1 and 20 pages of v2, including appendices, equations, tables, and figures, support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original class-conditioned and text-conditioned experiments, including ImageNet class pairs, GenEval, DPGBench, PIE-Bench-Neg, and appendix sensitivity and failure analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original MNIST/CIFAR10 class-removal experiments, text-to-image comparisons, and a 10,000-caption COCO evaluation, with additional results in Appendix A.

results.title: ContrastiveCFG: Guiding Diffusion Sampling by Contrasting Positive and Negative Concepts

C1.justification: The central novelty claim shifts from pioneering Event Cloud representation to integrating polarity into structural decisions beyond input-level inclusion. The abstract, introduction, and conclusion explicitly broaden the scalability claim to high-resolution as well as long-sequence events. Despite the classification-focused new title, all three original task families remain part of the claimed contribution.

C2.justification: v2 develops explanations of structural polarity integration, local Spatial-FA versus long-range Temporal-FA processing, and explicit versus implicit temporal features. Appendices I and J explicitly discuss accuracy–computation and input-size–inference-speed tradeoffs, while Appendix E acknowledges SECNet's own scaling costs. These substantially qualify and explain v1's more general efficiency arguments.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies random downsampling, Min-Max normalization, learnable scaling, FFT tensor reshaping, and the FPGA platform and clock. Much existing architecture and training information merely moves to appendices. Conversely, v1's explicit DHP19 subject and two-front-camera details disappear, and the abstract changes from code 'is available' to 'will be available' at a different repository.

E1.justification: All nine original datasets and three task families remain. v2 adds THU E-ACT-50, a real 1280×800, 50-class action recognition benchmark, extending evaluation to higher-resolution event data within an existing task family.

E2.justification: v2 adds EDGCN to object classification and EVSTr and EventMamba to the action accuracy comparison. THU E-ACT-50 introduces HMAX SNN, Motion SNN, and EV-ACT comparisons. The replacement hardware benchmark adds methods including C3D, ResNext-50, EventLSTM, and EventMamba while dropping several former hardware comparators. EventMamba was already cited in v1 but was not evaluated in these comparisons.

E3.justification: v2 introduces a controlled FPGA comparison at 200 MHz, joint event-count/centroid sweeps, and cross-dataset average accuracy reporting. The server hardware benchmark switches from DVS128 Gesture to UCF101-DVS. Its Table 6 specifies filename-based partitioning, whereas Appendix D retains random 20% testing; the actual UCF101 split and whether retained results were rerun are therefore unclear. The stated optimizer, learning rate, and epoch budget remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds separate D-FPS, EF-KNN, and Spatial-FA removal tests, a six-dataset comparison against the convolutional ECNet variant, computational-cost breakdowns, event/centroid sensitivity measurements, and qualitative pose comparisons. The original event-count study is retained. The old joint grouping ablation reappears as 'Input P' with identical results, rather than constituting a new experiment.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. v2's new Average columns aggregate accuracies across datasets and do not provide uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: DailyDVS accuracy changes from 0.993 to 0.9965, while the five object-classification accuracies and DHP19 pose errors remain unchanged. New results include THU E-ACT-50 accuracy of 97.25 versus EV-ACT's 92.7, FPGA SFA latency of 1.97 ms versus MLP latencies of 31.51–125.96 ms, and extensive ablation and runtime entries. The hardware table's 229.7 FPS on DVS128 Gesture is replaced by 120 FPS on UCF101-DVS; these are different settings, not evidence of a same-setting slowdown.

M1.justification: The matched pipeline retains D-FPS, feature-based KNN, coordinate averaging, Spatial-FA, attention aggregation, Temporal-FA, residual blocks, and prediction heads. v2's stage-indexed equations restate v1's Algorithm 1. Newly specifying learnable scaling, random downsampling, and Min-Max normalization does not establish a change from v1's less explicit implementation.

P1.justification: The paper is extensively reframed around scalability, with a new title and network name, revised contribution statements, and an expanded architecture-first method description. Dataset details, implementation material, hardware discussion, and pseudocode are reorganized across the main text and appendices. Additional module explanations substantially expand the narrative beyond simple renaming.

P2.justification: Figure 1 changes from an accuracy–compute–throughput plot to a seven-dataset radar chart, and Figure 3 is rearranged and relabeled. New displays include the tensor-dimension diagram, computational-cost chart, pose visualizations, FPGA comparison, architecture comparison, and runtime and ablation tables. Existing tables gain average columns and revised structures, alongside a new document layout and single-column appendices.

R1.justification: v2 attributes Event Cloud representation to prior work and substantially expands positioning against EventNet and voxel methods through Appendix B and Table 11, emphasizing structural rather than input-only polarity use. References are added for high-resolution action recognition, EDGCN, EventLSTM, and other supporting work. EventMamba's preprint-to-publication update is the same cited work, not a new reference.

T1.justification: The Event Cloud definition, grouping and normalization mathematics, Fourier identities, conjugate-symmetry argument, and quadratic-versus-FFT complexity comparison are retained. Added stage indices and pipeline equations restate existing operations. The appendices supply conceptual explanations rather than new formal assumptions, theorems, or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the central efficiency contribution: the convolutional replacement study isolates Spatial-FA's accuracy–cost tradeoff, FPGA measurements test hardware benefits directly, and the high-resolution benchmark extends scalability evidence. These address important gaps in v1's support for its design. Conflicting UCF101 split descriptions, the weaker code-release statement, and overstated total-GMAC savings in Appendix I limit reproducibility and precision, but the targeted experimental and explanatory gains provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Event Cloud network, renamed from FECNet to SECNet. The architecture, equations, retained experiments, figures, and tables can be matched reliably. Both documents are readable, including v2's appendices A–L; v1 contains no appendix.

after.justification: v2 retains original network results and adds high-resolution action recognition, FPGA measurements, further ablations, runtime sweeps, and pose prediction examples.

before.justification: v1 reports original classification, action recognition, human pose estimation, runtime, and component and event-count ablation results for FECNet.

results.title: Scalable Event Cloud Network for Event-based Classification

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the main claims: stock augmentation broadens distributional DP's applicability, theoretical guarantees characterize solvable objectives, and DηN demonstrates practical feasibility. Important qualifications to those guarantees change in the technical discussion.

C2.justification: Section 5.7 removes v1's claimed discounted advantage using f(x)=exp(-|x|)-1 and instead states that the established discounted objective classes coincide. It distinguishes finite-horizon advantages involving integrability and non-expected utilities. V2 also explains why improvement can fail for nonstationary policies and sharpens the continuity conjectures in Section 9.1.

D1.justification: Appendix H.1 repairs the displayed quantile-regression loss by removing a spurious nested loss symbol and correcting its notation. Section 6 clarifies the distinction between QR-DQN's inputs and DηN's stock-augmented inputs. Hardware and hyperparameter disclosures remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both evaluate desired-return generation, risk-averse and risk-seeking behavior, and constraint tradeoffs in gridworlds, plus desired-return generation in Pong. No evaluated domain or task scenario is added or removed.

E2.justification: The empirical comparator membership is unchanged. DQN and QR-DQN remain methodological and architectural references, rather than newly evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: Discounts, episode limits, evaluation procedures, training budgets, and network configurations in Sections 7–8 and Appendix H are retained. The reorganized hyperparameter tables report the same settings.

E4.justification: Both retain the realizable-return follow-up evaluation, risk-level sweeps, constraint-weight comparison, and analyses of approximation errors and stock editing. No new empirical ablation, robustness test, or error analysis appears.

E5.justification: Both report 30 independent gridworld training runs, 12 Pong repetitions, and 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. Replacing 'seeds' with 'independent runs' in one passage does not change the documented statistical procedure.

E6.justification: Tables 2–6 retain their numerical results and confidence intervals, and Figures 6 and 8 retain their histograms. For example, the Pong target return of 4 still produces a mean return of 2.26 with interval (2.22, 2.28).

M1.justification: The stock update, distributional Bellman updates, DηN architecture, action selection, and stock-editing procedure are retained. Revised validity conditions concern the theory; correcting the malformed loss expression does not establish a different implemented learner.

P1.justification: Technical exposition is substantially rewritten and reorganized across the DP guarantee discussion, Section 6's DηN explanation, and Appendix F's proof narrative. V2 creates a dedicated prior-work subsection and a guarantees-summary appendix, alongside widespread language and notation cleanup.

P2.justification: V2 adds Table 11 summarizing guarantees. Existing figures and tables are retained with relocations, caption refinements, and limited structural edits, including combining optimizer and learning-rate rows in Tables 7 and 9. The overall visual format remains similar.

R1.justification: Section 4.5 reorganizes discussion previously concentrated in Section 5.2, explicitly positions the vector-valued extension, and revises the description of Moghimi and Ku from distributional value iteration to policy iteration with a more specific utility class. Tamar et al. (2015) is added; Bertsekas (2019) and Pflug and Pichler (2016) are removed.

T1.justification: Theorem 8 restricts initialization to stationary policies, and Lemma 15 replaces the earlier nonstationary-policy argument with an explicit one-step improvement condition. Lemma 12 introduces an affine scaling characterization of discount indifference; Theorem 20 adds moment and continuity conditions for reward reduction. Appendices B, C, and F substantially revise the supporting proofs, and Section 5.8 corrects the CVaR integration limits.

improvement.justification: Revisions to Lemma 15 and Appendix B address unjustified nonstationary-policy reasoning, while Theorem 20 and Appendix F supply missing conditions for reward reduction. Section 5.7 also withdraws an unsupported discounted separation from classic DP. These repairs substantially strengthen the central theoretical contribution while preserving the empirical evidence. A remaining drawback is Lemma 12's new strict alpha<1 requirement, which conflicts with discount indifference of the indicator utility retained in Appendix C.2.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same stock-augmented distributional dynamic programming framework and DηN agent. Text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are available for reliable comparison, including v2's new Appendix I.

after.justification: V2 retains these original gridworld and Pong experiments, numerical results, and return histograms.

before.justification: Sections 7–8 report original DηN experiments in gridworlds and Atari Pong, with numerical results in Tables 2–6 and return histograms in Figures 6 and 8.

results.title: Optimizing Return Distributions with Distributional Dynamic Programming

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction broaden the central performance claim from outperforming structural pruning to outperforming both pruning and MoE-construction techniques. Detailed analysis becomes an additional stated contribution. The original claims about uncovering experts without updating pretrained weights and jointly learning routing and expert configurations remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations linking the modest VO-routing benefit to small head dimensions and poor head-pruning performance to distorted attention features. It also discusses temperature robustness, recommends fewer than 16 experts, and qualifies comparable throughput by sufficiently large batch size. Existing interpretations of expert semantics and width allocation are retained.

D1.justification: The abstract adds a code-availability statement and repository address. New comparisons disclose training-token budgets and the matched-iteration fine-tuning setting for LLaMA-MoE. The detailed module configurations, optimizer settings, GPU allocations, and data-processing instructions already present in v1 remain substantially unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds evaluated BoolQ, SciQ, TruthfulQA, and MMLU benchmarks in Tables 5–6 and Figure 10, substantially broadening task coverage beyond the original language-modeling and five commonsense benchmarks. The original training datasets and evaluation coverage are retained.

E2.justification: Tables 4–6 add evaluated LLaMA-MoE, G-MoEfication, LLaMA-MoE-v2, and CMoE comparators, including multiple configurations and fine-tuned variants. This introduces a substantial direct MoE-construction comparison group. The original structural and semi-structured pruning comparators remain represented.

E3.justification: Alongside the retained zero-shot protocols, v2 introduces 32-shot BoolQ, 5-shot WinoGrande and MMLU, 25-shot ARC-c, and 10-shot HellaSwag evaluations. It also introduces throughput measurements at batch sizes 512, 1024, and 1536. These are additional evaluation designs; the original default 10,000-iteration training setup remains unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained loss, dataset, and expert-count analyses, Table 13 tests local embeddings, head pruning, removal of VO routing, and temperature sensitivity. Figure 4 adds aggregate expert-utilization analysis, Figure 10 examines the MMLU accuracy–parameter trade-off, and Table 15 examines throughput scaling with batch size.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run summaries, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The retained expert-width boxplots describe variation among experts rather than uncertainty across experimental runs.

E6.justification: Original benchmark values are retained, including LLaMA-2 rows relocated from Table 3 to Table 12. v2 adds substantial MoE, MMLU, ablation, and throughput results: Table 13 reports 56.07 for full ToMoE versus 44.99 for head pruning, and Table 15 reports 2360.38–2919.45 tokens/s across batch sizes. Section 4.3 also incorrectly redescribes the unchanged 3.14-point advantage over ModeGPT-Alpaca as '3.14 times'.

M1.justification: The core architecture, expert construction, routing, and frozen-weight training remain the same. However, Section 3.4 changes the load-balancing probability calculation from explicitly defined softmax in v1 to GSmax in v2 without explaining whether this represents a changed calculation or inconsistent notation. An actual loss modification cannot be established reliably.

P1.justification: v2 rewrites the abstract, condenses the introductory background, edits method explanations and notation, updates author information, and removes the Impact Statement. The main section sequence and much of the existing method and appendix prose remain intact.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from a two-column conference layout to a single-column journal layout with substantially different front matter and table placement. v2 adds comparison and ablation tables and new plots, moves part of Table 3 into appendix Table 12, and combines v1 Figures 5–6 into v2 Figure 6.

R1.justification: v2 expands positioning against contextual sparsity through Deja Vu, CATS, and structured-sparsity work, and broadens dense-to-MoE discussion and comparisons through MoEfication, generalized MoEfication, LLaMA-MoE-v2, and CMoE. This substantially expands the prior-work context for its unified expert-construction and router-training claim.

T1.justification: New Appendix F derives the effective query–key width from overlapping binary pruning masks, showing that it reaches the allocated width K only when the masks coincide. This adds a focused mathematical justification to the qualitative concern already stated in v1 Appendix A.2.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses an important gap in v1: a dense-to-MoE method was evaluated mainly against pruning. Direct MoE comparisons, component validation, and measured throughput materially strengthen the evidence for its contribution. These gains outweigh new reporting problems, although the broader superiority claim needs qualification: Table 6 reports 57.40 for ToMoE versus 59.61 and 59.31 for LLaMA-MoE-v2, with very different training-token budgets. Those results support an efficiency–accuracy trade-off.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ToMoE. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated results between v1's Appendices A–E and v2's Appendices A–F.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds MoE comparisons, additional benchmarks, component ablations, and inference-throughput measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original ToMoE perplexity and zero-shot evaluation results, loss and dataset ablations, and expert analyses in the main text and appendices.

results.title: ToMoE: Converting Dense Large Language Models to Mixture-of-Experts through Dynamic Structural Pruning

C1.justification: The central contributions remain formalizing critical-cache selection through output perturbation and improving existing eviction methods with the same algorithm. v2 refines the headline empirical claims to more than halving average compression loss and adds negligible-overhead and universal plug-and-play language.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations of alpha as a safeguard for sensitive architectures and of conservative but tighter perturbation bounds. It newly argues that code tasks are weak indicators of cache-eviction quality, explicitly excludes direct compatibility with attention-free eviction, and identifies multimodal applicability as untested. The limitations concerning fixed alpha and distance choice largely restate v1.

D1.justification: v2 newly provides a public-code access statement, FlashAttention-2 implementation information, A100 hardware details, and a fused Triton kernel description that avoids materializing projected values. It also documents the last-256-token approximation used for H2O. These are substantial additions to v1's existing pseudocode, hyperparameters, dataset specifications, and prompt templates.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates two needle-retrieval tasks and 16 LongBench datasets. v2 substantially expands synthetic coverage to 13 Ruler tasks, including word extraction, variable tracking, and additional retrieval variants, and adds three SCBench multi-turn QA tasks. LongBench and both compression scenarios remain represented.

E2.justification: SnapKV and AdaKV remain, while HeadKV becomes a third extensively evaluated host and comparator. v2 adds evaluated H2O, PyramidKV, DuoAttention, and OBCache comparisons in Figure 2 and Appendices B.1 and D.2. StreamingLLM, evaluated in v1, remains discussed but disappears from the reported comparisons.

E3.justification: v2 adds Qwen2.5-32B and substantial new protocols: SCBench contexts truncated to 100K with multiple dialogue turns, latency measurements across batch sizes and context lengths, and chunked prefilling at 128K. The distance-metric comparison changes from v1's needle-retrieval setting to 4K Ruler. Existing LongBench dataset definitions and primary selection hyperparameters are retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds controlled alpha sensitivity and first-stage removal experiments at 10% and 20% budgets, plus empirical comparison of theoretical bounds with actual perturbations. It revises the L1-versus-L2 analysis. Conversely, v1's later-token perturbation diagnostics and some lowest-budget assumption-validation panels are removed rather than merely relocated.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. Additional averages and sensitivity results in v2 do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive results for new tasks, models, comparators, efficiency measurements, and ablations. For example, its new SCBench comparison reports EN.QA scores of 15.71 for AdaKV and 22.14 with the proposed selection at 40% budget. Existing Llama LongBench scores largely persist. Some repeated results conflict: v2 Table 10 reverses the AdaKV-plus-method and HeadKV-plus-method LongBench scores relative to Table 2.

M1.justification: The two-stage selection procedure, attention-plus-projected-value scoring, and perturbation objective remain unchanged. HeadKV supplies another integration setting; chunked prefilling supplies an additional evaluation protocol. The newly described fused Triton kernel computes the existing metric rather than introducing a different selection rule.

P1.justification: v2 revises the title and abstract, rewrites the experimental narrative around Ruler and context-only compression, consolidates experimental settings, and moves proofs out of the main text. The appendices are extensively regrouped into proofs, extended experiments, analyses, and additional details, changing the document's organization substantially.

P2.justification: v2 adds introductory summary bars, dense Ruler task plots, efficiency charts, and numerous comparison and analysis tables. LongBench tables are expanded and consolidated, while perturbation displays are rearranged and reduced. The retained dataset and prompt-template tables are mostly relocated and renumbered rather than newly introduced.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning around offline budget allocation, multimodal compression, channel pruning, and inter-layer cache sharing. Appendices D.2 and D.4 explicitly distinguish the approach from OBCache and Wanda, and the introduction identifies DefensiveKV as a follow-up. These changes go beyond bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: Definition 3.1, Assumption 3.4, and the principal theorems retain their mathematical substance. Their proofs move to Appendix A, while v1 Theorem E.1 becomes v2 Theorem C.1 with the same relaxed-bound argument. The new bound-tightness experiment adds empirical evidence, not a new derivation.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important gaps in v1: alpha ablations directly test the first-stage safeguard, efficiency measurements and kernel details support practical feasibility, and multi-turn QA tests the previously motivating unknown-future-question scenario. Broader comparisons strengthen the empirical case. New reporting errors, including inconsistent alpha tables, swapped scores in Table 10, and reversed timings between Appendix B.6 and Table 6, weaken numerical reliability but do not outweigh these substantial validation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs are complete and readable, including their appendices. Despite the new CriticalKV title and substantial reorganization, the same problem formulation, algorithms, proofs, and retained experiments can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 reports original Ruler, LongBench, SCBench, efficiency, sensitivity, and perturbation results in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original Needle-in-a-Haystack and LongBench experiments on Llama and Mistral, together with empirical perturbation and distance-metric analyses.

results.title: CriticalKV: Optimizing KV Cache Eviction from an Output Perturbation Perspective

C1.justification: V1's abstract and Section 5 claim greedy optimality when the surrogate accurately learns the utility. V2 narrows this to approximation guarantees under sufficient conditions. It also expands the headline empirical contribution to large-scale LLM fine-tuning, while retaining the central sequential-selection and ADP interpretation.

C2.justification: V2 replaces claims of directly controlling curvature and validating quadratic decay with a qualitative substitutability-proxy interpretation. It explains that low MSE does not establish the uniform conditions required by its guarantee. New LLM qualifications disclose potential reference-label leakage and coverage saturation after only 1–5 selections, making most remaining selections depend on the similarity fallback.

D1.justification: V2 adds a public-code pointer, classical CPU and DVRL configuration disclosures, and graph-search implementation details. Appendix J.7 supplies extensive LLM data preparation, reference construction, embedding, LoRA, evaluation, hardware, and timing information, including distinguishing timed H100 runs from H200 headline runs. These substantially expand reproducibility documentation.

E1.justification: V2 adds instruction-selection and LLM fine-tuning coverage through DATE-LM, using Tulu 3 instruction data and evaluating MMLU, GSM8K, and BBH. These introduce knowledge and reasoning tasks beyond the retained eight classical datasets and synthetic substitutability experiment.

E2.justification: The nine classical comparison methods remain. V2 adds evaluated Linear and MLP predictors in the surrogate comparison (Table 3), and BM25, Rep-Sim, RDS+, Grad-Sim, and LESS in the LLM comparisons (Tables 6–7). These are substantive additions to the evaluated comparator sets.

E3.justification: V2 introduces a budget-500 protocol reporting mean accuracy across selection sizes 1–500. Its new LLM protocol selects 10,000 of 200,000 instructions, performs two-epoch LoRA training of Llama-3.1-8B, and uses task-specific zero-, eight-, and three-shot evaluation. It also introduces shared-subset surrogate-error comparisons with fitted-intercept controls. The original small-budget dataset splits are retained.

E4.justification: V2 adds direct analysis of surrogate prediction quality using training/test MAE and MSE (Table 3), plus seven embedding variants testing representation choice for BipCov (Table 8). Conversely, v1's six-level curvature plots are condensed to endpoint panels in v2 Figure 3, omitting the intermediate plotted evidence.

E5.justification: Classical per-dataset reporting remains mean and standard deviation over 20 runs. V2 specifies three fine-tuning seeds for its headline LLM comparison and distinguishes these results from single-seed baseline and embedding experiments. The aggregate Std Dev row from v1 Table 1 is omitted in v2 Table 9; no new significance-testing procedure is introduced.

E6.justification: V2 adds budget-500 results, surrogate errors, and LLM results, including BipCov's 63.89±0.34% average versus RDS+'s 62.88±0.25% in Table 6. In the matched small-budget tables, DVRL values change, including bbc-embeddings from 0.560 to 0.653, and aggregate averages are corrected, including Bipartite from 0.041 to 0.750. Most other per-dataset entries remain unchanged; the new settings do not establish improvements over v1 under identical conditions.

M1.justification: V2 adds the BipCov adaptation: an embedding-based top-L similarity graph, greedy reference coverage, and mean-similarity filling after coverage saturates (Appendix J.7). This substantially extends v1's fitted, label-matched distance-threshold graph procedure. Threshold fitting is also reported as minimizing MSE rather than the absolute error specified in v1 Algorithm 2; the core exact-DP selection algorithm remains equivalent.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, theory exposition, and experimental narrative are substantially rewritten. Preliminaries are reorganized around explicit assumptions, regression characterization is separated from policy equivalence, and detailed RQ1 discussion moves to Appendix M. The appendix structure is extensively reorganized, including moving the DP algorithm from Appendix B to Appendix L.

P2.justification: V1's full DP comparison curves are replaced by a compact summary table, and its six-setting curvature figures become a smaller endpoint display. V2 redraws the main selection curves with revised styling and adds tables for larger budgets, surrogate errors, regression formulations, computational costs, LLM comparisons, and embedding ablations. The retained detailed results table also changes its summary-row structure.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands positioning around semi-values, submodular optimization, optimization from samples, datamodel/DsDm surrogates, and efficient valuation methods. Appendix A adds many substantive citations and explicitly distinguishes the approach from GraphFilter. The earlier detailed ADP literature survey is also replaced.

T1.justification: V1's common efficiency-constrained regression argument is replaced by separate Shapley, Banzhaf, and Beta Shapley formulations and proofs, including centered features and parameter restrictions (v2 Appendices B–D). V1 Appendix G's exact greedy-optimality theorem is replaced by a conditional (1-epsilon)(1-1/e) approximation theorem in v2 Appendix H. Normalization assumptions and the distinction between optimal subsets and optimal sequence prefixes are also corrected or formalized.

improvement.justification: Replacing v1's exact greedy-optimality claim and common efficiency-constrained regression argument with appropriately qualified formulations and proofs substantially improves the central theoretical support. Corrected result summaries, utility diagnostics, and fuller experimental documentation further strengthen the paper. Some detailed original curves disappear, and the LLM evidence has disclosed leakage and coverage-saturation limitations, but these tradeoffs do not outweigh the substantial corrections.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same sequential data-valuation framework and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Retained experiments and reorganized theoretical material can be matched reliably.

after.justification: V2 retains original classical experiments and adds budget-500 evaluations, surrogate-prediction experiments, and LLM fine-tuning results and embedding ablations.

before.justification: V1 reports original selection experiments on eight datasets and controlled message-passing experiments examining data substitutability, including Figures 3–6 and Appendix J.

results.title: Unifying and Optimizing Data Values for Selection via Sequential Decision-Making

C1.justification: v1 centres its contribution on a benchmark impossible for contemporary models. v3 explicitly restricts impossibility to original release and adds a central claim of sustained difficulty over a year, supported by tracking 46 baselines and reporting remaining headroom. Human comparison also becomes a headline contribution.

C2.justification: v1 speculates about future saturation and higher-resolution inputs. v3 interprets observed progress, overlapping solved questions and hint benefits, while cautioning that outputs cannot identify the architectural causes of improvements (Appendix D.3). Appendix F adds substantive limitations concerning sampling variance, manual curation, overfitting and alignment with deployed tasks.

D1.justification: Appendices A, B.5 and D add curator/evaluator details, dataset-v2 API access dates and Nebius usage, and complete prompts and rules for error discovery, consolidation and assignment. Earlier inference prompts, hardware and hyperparameters are largely retained or relocated. Exact settings for the expanded post-release evaluations remain less fully documented.

E1.justification: The benchmark retains 100 main questions and 334 subquestions, but dataset v2 modifies 23% of main questions, including corrections to incorrect or ambiguous answers (Section 3.2; Appendix A.2). v3 also introduces a bounded test scenario supplying visual hints on 37 questions. The overall visual-question-answering coverage remains similar.

E2.justification: The original 20-model roster is retained, while Table 7 adds 26 post-release model/configuration entries, including Gemini 3 Pro, GPT-5.2 and Llama 4 variants. Section 5.2 adds a human comparator, and Table 3 additionally evaluates GPT-5.4 and Gemini 3.1 Pro in the error comparison.

E3.justification: v3 adds a post-release protocol reporting only pass@5 and pass∧5, a human evaluation using ten question subsets with five independently duplicated subsets, and a 37-question experiment varying hints from zero to three. Error-category discovery and assignment use different response samplings. These substantially expand the evaluation design.

E4.justification: v1 primarily provides qualitative failure examples. v3 adds quantitative classification into nine error categories, question-level correctness analysis, formatting/refusal analysis across models, and an intervention testing whether visual hints reduce failures (Figures 8, 10–12; Tables 3 and 8). The earlier appendix failure cases are largely retained.

E5.justification: v3 adds human-score standard deviations and correlation across duplicated question sets, plus 95% confidence intervals for formatting accuracy (Figure 12). The existing CLT standard errors for subquestions and five-sample model evaluations remain; the PDFs do not establish an increased repetition count for those retained evaluations.

E6.justification: Table 2 changes results following dataset revision: Gemini 2 Flash Thinking's pass@5 changes from 7% to 5%, and Claude 3.5 Sonnet v2's subquestion score from 24.30% to 25.50%. New results include Gemini 3 Pro's 19% pass@5, GPT-5.2's 6% pass∧5, human performance of 29.5% and quantified hint benefits. Revised-dataset scores are not same-setting performance gains or losses.

M1.justification: The benchmark construction process gains post-release community red teaming and further adversarial refinement (Section 3.2). Human question creation, adversarial filtering and subquestion decomposition remain the core procedure. Changing the initial pipeline from four steps to three merely combines feedback and initial evaluation.

P1.justification: v3 substantially reorganizes the narrative around pre-release and post-release evaluation, rewrites the abstract and conclusion, consolidates experimental setup, and moves inference and completion-token material into the appendix. The appendix is reorganized into construction, protocols, additional results, error analysis, failure cases and limitations.

P2.justification: v3 adds longitudinal, correctness-grid, hint and formatting plots, together with human, post-release and error-analysis tables. Figure 3 replaces two illustrative examples; Table 2 changes from full-width to a compact single-column display; the completion-token table moves to the appendix. Retained failure-case figures are also reformatted.

R1.justification: The difficult-visual-benchmark positioning remains. v3 adds a small-scale evaluations subsection citing FrontierScience, GDPval and FrontierCS, cites τ-bench for reliability, and introduces longitudinal comparisons with ARC-AGI-2 and HLE. Medical-benchmark and Visual Riddles discussions are removed, alongside additions of newer model references.

T1.justification: The accuracy, averaged subquestion accuracy and CLT standard-error definitions are retained. Renaming k/k reliability to pass∧k preserves the all-samples-correct criterion. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs, and v3 adds no substantive mathematical development.

improvement.justification: Community red teaming corrects incorrect or non-unique answers, addressing an important benchmark-validity weakness acknowledged in v3 (Section 3.2; Appendix A.2). Human evaluation, longitudinal tracking, quantified errors and hint interventions substantially strengthen evidence beyond v1's initial scores and qualitative examples. Post-release settings and human test timing remain incompletely documented, but the corrections and stronger validation establish a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ZeroBench and contain readable text, equations, tables, figures and appendices. Corresponding methods, evaluations and failure examples can be matched, while dataset revisions and new experiments are identifiable.

after.justification: v3 reports revised baseline results, additional model evaluations, a human study, quantitative error analysis, formatting evaluations and visual-hint experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of 20 LMMs, including main-question and subquestion scores, completion-token measurements and qualitative failure analyses.

results.title: ZeroBench: An Impossible Visual Benchmark for Contemporary Large Multimodal Models

C1.justification: The central contribution changes from DABUF's classifier-assisted gradient attribution to a theoretically motivated denoising framework applicable to both gradient and hidden-state attribution. v2's conclusion also newly claims that gradient-based approaches consistently produce the safest retrained models, changing the paper's practical takeaway.

C2.justification: v1 emphasizes noisy long responses and explains Ada3's filtering failures through indiscriminate semantic matching. v2 emphasizes high-variance nuisance dimensions, complementary denoising and selection, and gradient attribution's purported ability to capture training dynamics. Its homogeneous-injection, detection-taxonomy, and adversarial-attribution limitations remain substantively unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 adds the safety-judging rubric, fixed GPT-4o version 2024-11-20, score-5 ASR threshold, and DRA's selected dimension count of 30. Conversely, it replaces explicit jailbreak split descriptions with a benchmark reference and omits v1's specified jailbreak filtering budget and gradient-projection details. Most LoRA training hyperparameters and hardware information are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate jailbreak injection using UltraChat, ToxicChat, and XSTest-Response, and gender-bias detection and mitigation using Bias in Bios. v2's adoption of the DATE-LM setup does not introduce an additional dataset, domain, or task in the supplied evidence.

E2.justification: v2 adds RepSim to jailbreak comparisons. Its jailbreak retraining comparison retains Wildguard but removes OpenAI Moderation, Llama-Guard, and GradSafe. Gender-bias comparisons replace Ada3 with Wildguard, GradSim, and RepSim. Plain response-gradient attribution already appears in v1 Appendix B, so GradSim is not wholly new to the paper.

E3.justification: Detection evaluation drops the reported top-100 precision, recall, and F1 measures in favor of AUPRC. Gender-bias filtering increases from 100 to 500 removed samples. v2 also constructs targets by pooling unsafe or biased outputs across ten inference runs and references DATE-LM's official test splits instead of v1's explicit custom split description.

E4.justification: v1's token-level attribution and token-count analyses are removed. v2 adds raw-versus-denoised t-SNE visualizations, an empirical relationship between discriminability and AUPRC, and separate denoising and dimension-selection ablations in Appendices C–E. The target-size analysis is revised to compare GradSim with GradSim-DRA.

E5.justification: v2 newly reports ten-run inference averaging for ASR and gender-bias evaluations; this does not establish additional independently trained models. Target-size resampling increases from ten repetitions in v1 to fifty in v2, retaining mean and standard-deviation reporting. Main result tables still lack uncertainty intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: Primary numerical results are extensively replaced. For example, v1 Table 2 reports Llama DABUF AUPRC of 52.0%/74.1% on ToxicChat/XSTest-Response; v2 Table 1 reports 83.2%/81.5% for GradSim-DRA and 92.6%/98.6% for RepSim-DRA. Baseline scores, retraining outcomes, and gender-bias results also change. Revised methods and settings prevent interpreting these as matched performance gains.

M1.justification: v1's DABUF uses gradient cosine similarity and classifier-screened, human-verified training examples as jailbreak attribution targets. v2's DRA instead centers and whitens representations, then selects dimensions using a leave-target-out discriminability objective. It operates on gradients or hidden states and uses unsafe model outputs as targets. These changes substantially alter representation processing, scoring, and target construction.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, method exposition, results discussion, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around DRA. Related work is reorganized and the appendices are restructured. The gender-data construction and much of the training-details text are retained through relocation rather than newly introduced.

P2.justification: Results tables are substantially redesigned with backbone-specific method groups and improvement columns, while precision/recall/F1 tables disappear. v2 replaces the token-count plot with representation visualizations, redraws the target-size comparison, and adds a discriminability scatterplot, component-ablation table, and boxed safety rubric.

R1.justification: v2 substantially repositions the contribution within representation-based detection and signal detection theory, adding DATE-LM, LARF, RepSim, a data-attribution survey, and theoretical references. The broader standalone attribution survey in v1 is condensed, with several simulator, valuation, and game-theoretic references removed.

T1.justification: Beyond v1's gradient-influence and token-aggregation definitions, v2 introduces a signal-detection formulation, a discriminability objective, and Lemma 3.1's optimal linear-score derivation. It develops covariance-based whitening and a target-based dimension-selection surrogate, with assumptions about rare unsafe data and alignment between target and unsafe-data means.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the treatment of noisy attribution through an explicit denoising formulation, mathematical derivation, and controlled component ablations, addressing v1's reliance on manually verified training targets for jailbreaks. Specified safety judging and repeated inference also improve evaluation transparency. These gains outweigh lost setup details and an overbroad conclusion: v2 Table 6 favors RepSim-DRA over GradSim-DRA for Llama gender-bias mitigation, contradicting the claim that gradients consistently produce the safest models. Higher cross-version scores alone do not establish improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work on detecting and filtering unsafe training data. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial methodological revision.

after.justification: v2 reports original detection and retraining experiments for DRA, supplemented by representation visualizations, target-size experiments, and component ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original jailbreak-detection, retraining-safety, and gender-bias experiments, plus token-level and target-set-size analyses.

results.title: Detecting and Filtering Unsafe Training Data via Data Attribution with Denoised Representation

C1.justification: v1 foregrounds superiority in frozen and fine-tuned classification, best calibration and resource-saving multivariate adapters. v2 reframes the contributions around synthetic pre-training, tokenization and enhanced frozen-encoder inference, claiming competitiveness with strong dataset-specific methods as well as other foundation models. Calibration superiority and adapter development are no longer headline contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations linking intermediate-layer advantages to contrastive-objective overfitting, data scaling and complementary token information. It discusses normalization-dependent probing, cross-model complementarity and TabPFN's dataset-dependent strengths. New qualifications include self-ensembling not improving UCR-91 and reconstruction objectives potentially requiring another architecture. Earlier calibration interpretations and detailed adapter failure discussions are removed or substantially reduced.

D1.justification: v2 adds dataset characteristics, domain-split rules, preprocessing references, baseline package versions/checkpoint references, probing settings and explicit self-ensemble interpolation lengths. It also documents revised fine-tuning settings. Conversely, v1's explicit pre-training batch size of 2048, four-V100 hardware specification and evaluation hardware disclosure are absent. The main source-code link remains the same.

E1.justification: v1 pre-trains on seven million real time series; v2 uses CauKer synthetic data for its main model, retaining real-data pre-training as an ablation. UCR and UEA coverage remains, while Ego4D, HHAR, Military Press, CAP and PCL substantially expand evaluation, including held-out device, source and age scenarios. MotionSenseHAR and SharePriceIncrease disappear; Blink and EMOPain are retained within the new domain collections.

E2.justification: Beyond retained NuTime and MOMENT, v2 evaluates Catch22+, TabPFN, TabICL, TiRex, Chronos2, TiViT-H and TiConvNext, and includes published self-supervised and supervised comparisons on UCR-91 (Figure 1 and Table 17). UniTS and GPT4TS are no longer evaluated. Adapter comparisons retain PCA and Linear/LComb but remove SVD, random projection and variance-based selection.

E3.justification: v2 introduces a UCR-91 comparison using standardized features and logistic regression, while retaining 200-tree Random Forests for the broader benchmark breakdown. Its Mantis fine-tuning study uses 500 epochs, batch size 128 and a fixed learning rate, replacing v1's 100-epoch, batch-256 studies and their model-selection comparisons. New domain-held-out protocols and synthetic sample-size runtime experiments also change the evaluation design.

E4.justification: v2 expands the differential-branch ablation into tokenizer capacity controls, pooling/kernel/backbone comparisons, real-versus-synthetic pre-training, matched-update layer analyses, token aggregation, self-ensembling, loss, augmentation and predictor-normalization studies. It adds TabPFN subgroup analyses and domain-shift tests. Earlier scratch/head/full comparisons are replaced by different fine-tuning analyses; adapter analysis is narrowed, and calibration/reliability studies are removed.

E5.justification: v1 explicitly identifies benchmark results as averages over three seeds with standard deviations. v2 retains many ± entries but drops these explanations from the corresponding benchmark-table captions; three-seed/run statements remain for particular architecture and fine-tuning experiments. Its adapter Table 12 reports point estimates without v1 Table 2's uncertainty. There is no documented increase in runs or new significance-testing procedure.

E6.justification: Results are extensively replaced and supplemented. v1 Figure 3 reports 0.7816 accuracy over 159 datasets; v2 Table 1 reports 0.8195 on full UCR and 0.7420 on UEA-27, alongside new HAR/EEG, layer-selection, ensemble and fusion results. v1's calibration results, including uncalibrated Mantis ECE 0.1131, disappear. Changed models, dataset groupings and protocols prevent treating these aggregate differences as same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The multibranch tokenizer and contrastive objective remain, but v2 adopts RoPE, RMSNorm and SwiGLU and introduces intermediate-layer extraction, classification-token/mean-token concatenation, multiple-interpolation self-ensembling and cross-model embedding fusion (Sections 3.2–3.4 and Appendix B). These change the architecture and inference procedure. PCA and the earlier LComb adapter remain as PCA and Linear in Appendix C.2.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, experimental narrative and conclusion are extensively rewritten around frozen-encoder inference. Related Work becomes a separate section, preprocessing is integrated into the architecture description, and fine-tuning/adapters move into a reorganized appendix. Terminology is clarified, including the meaning of zero-shot feature extraction. These are substantial narrative and structural changes beyond renumbering.

P2.justification: The single-column technical report becomes a two-column conference paper. The architecture diagram is revised, calibration and earlier fine-tuning displays disappear, and new layer-by-epoch, token-aggregation, scaling and ensemble figures are introduced. Benchmark tables are redesigned around method families and domain collections, with substantially different appendix table structures.

R1.justification: v2 adds a dedicated Related Work section and substantially expands positioning around synthetic pre-training, forecasting/vision/tabular foundation models and intermediate representations, including CauKer, TiRex, Chronos2, Roschmann et al. and Skean et al. Adapters are now presented as following Benechehab et al. and Ilbert et al., rather than as a headline contribution. Much calibration-related literature is removed.

T1.justification: v2 Appendix B.5 adds a short mathematical calculation relating interpolation length to token receptive field, including its limiting fraction of 1/32. v1's formal confidence and calibration definitions disappear with the calibration study. The core contrastive formulation remains equivalent, and neither version develops a substantial theorem-and-proof framework.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the empirical basis for its design and generalization claims. Table 7 compares real and synthetic pre-training; Appendix B controls tokenizer capacity and separates training-update effects from data scale; Table 2 adds held-out-domain evaluations. These address important gaps in v1's architectural controls and transfer evidence, while broader baseline families strengthen comparisons. Calibration and broad cross-model fine-tuning evidence are lost, and some reproducibility and uncertainty reporting deteriorates. Nevertheless, the controlled analyses and stronger support for the refocused claims provide a substantial net quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Mantis, despite substantial revisions to its architecture, training and evaluation. Text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison, including v1 Appendices A–B and v2 Appendices A–D.

after.justification: v2 reports original benchmark evaluations, domain-shift experiments, runtime measurements and extensive ablations in Section 4 and Appendices B–D. These include original outcomes beyond the published baseline results it also reproduces.

before.justification: v1 reports original classification, fine-tuning, architecture-ablation, adapter, runtime and calibration experiments in Section 3 and Appendix B.

results.title: Mantis: Lightweight Foundation Model for Time Series Classification

C1.justification: The central parameter-free MMA contribution remains. V3 adds systematic attention analysis as an explicit contribution and frames the empirical claim across three backbones, reporting +6.2% rather than v1's +7.2% against CCA. The abstract and conclusion omit their earlier no-additional-training-cost claim, although related assertions remain elsewhere.

C2.justification: V3 adds substantive interpretations linking attention patterns to task-dependent grounding and reliance on parametric knowledge. It replaces v1's explanation that input-order changes may confuse DOT with an explanation emphasizing insufficient training, and interprets mask-access and newer-backbone results. The pretraining information-leakage limitation is retained in Appendix A.

D1.justification: V3 explicitly documents DOT's approximately four-day pretraining and two-day finetuning durations and describes NLTK-based token grouping and SAM-based region aggregation for new analyses. Most existing hyperparameters, hardware specifications, preprocessing instructions, prompts and code-access information remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same pretraining datasets, supervised-finetuning mixture and 12 benchmark evaluations. Blip3-OCR and the AKI-4B study remain in v3's appendices. New analyses reuse existing tasks and data; additional backbones change model configurations rather than task coverage.

E2.justification: V3 adds Mixed-Attention (MA, Xie et al., 2025) to the central matched comparison, including the retained Phi experiment, and to detailed appendix tables. Its full within-image attention supplies a substantive alternative attention design beyond causal attention and CCA. The separate AKI-4B comparator set remains unchanged.

E3.justification: Evaluation expands from Phi to LLaMA-3.2-3B and Qwen2.5-3B, with additional Qwen3-1.7B/8B configurations in Appendix E.2. New protocols include DOT finetuning for 10k instead of 5k steps and testing 0%, 10%, 30%, 50% and 100% image-to-text access. The original short-schedule and zero-shot settings remain.

E4.justification: V3 adds longer-training controls for DOT, mask-access sensitivity analysis, linguistic-category attention distributions, and a segmented-region attention case study (Section 4.4; Appendix E.1, E.3–E.4). These examine training-budget effects and MMA's behavior beyond v1's order ablations and qualitative examples, which are retained.

E5.justification: V3 Section 4.1 newly states that results average three random seeds; v1 supplies no corresponding run count. This establishes a reporting change, not an explicit increase in runs. Neither version reports dispersion, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: V3 adds extensive MA, additional-backbone and ablation results. Retained entries also change: Phi MMA's MMMU score is 37.3 in v1 Table 1 versus 39.4 in v3 Table 2; AKI-4B's reported RealWorldQA score changes from 58.9 to 62.9. Its revised POPE and CV-Bench2D summary scores conflict with retained detailed scores, so these revisions do not establish reliable performance gains.

M1.justification: The DOT sequence and MMA attention-mask rules remain unchanged: image tokens attend to question tokens during supervised finetuning, while generated responses use causal attention. Additional backbones and partial-mask ablations do not redefine the proposed method.

P1.justification: The experimental narrative is reorganized into separate DOT, MMA-comparison and attention-analysis sections. The AKI-4B comparison moves from Section 4.3 to Appendix B, limitations move to Appendix A, and the remaining appendices are substantially reorganized. Main-text framing shifts from the named AKI model toward MMA.

P2.justification: The main text changes to two-column formatting. V1's central comparison table is split and expanded into backbone-grouped Tables 1–2; detailed tables gain MA entries. V3 adds attention distributions, a heatmap, sparsity curves and additional experiment tables, while relocating the existing qualitative figures.

R1.justification: Related work adds a focused comparison with Show-o's mixed attention. New citations cover LLaMA, Qwen2.5, NLTK and SAM, and DeepSeek-VL gains a reference despite already appearing as a comparator in v1. The broader positioning around causal attention's cross-modal limitation remains.

T1.justification: Equations (1)–(6), including DOT ordering and the generalized cross-modal mask, retain the same mathematical content. No theorem, proof or substantive derivation is added; the new mask-size explanation elaborates the existing computational-cost claim.

improvement.justification: V1's broad architectural claims relied on one controlled backbone. V3 substantially strengthens their empirical basis through additional backbone comparisons, the MA comparator, and training-length and mask-sparsity controls (Table 2; Appendix E). Attention analyses also make the proposed mechanism more inspectable. These gains outweigh reporting weaknesses: revised AKI summary scores conflict with detailed tables, Figure 10 contradicts strict monotonicity on POPE, and three-seed means lack dispersion reporting.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DOT/MMA research, with matching authors, equations and experiments. Inspection of all pages, including appendices and rendered figures, supports a reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: V3 retains original experiments and adds backbone comparisons, training-length and mask-sparsity ablations, and attention analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original experiments on DOT, MMA and AKI-4B, including benchmark results in Tables 1–2 and detailed appendix results.

results.title: Seeing is Understanding: Unlocking Causal Attention into Modality-Mutual Attention for Multimodal LLMs

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion add variance reduction as a central theoretical contribution and MR-BMIA as an implemented extension benefiting from additional references. Validation claims expand to text datasets. The introductory example is corrected from 37.5% TPR and a 64% improvement on CIFAR-10 to 35.75% and 54% on CIFAR-100, consistent with Table 1.

C2.justification: v2 explains the different roles of posterior sampling and independent reference datasets, including persistent variation between model centers and diminishing returns from more references. v1's abundant-resource limitation and mixture-Laplace future work become an evaluated extension. Appendix F adds substantive warnings about non-Gaussian p-value calibration, suggests unevaluated held-out calibration, and distinguishes empirical attack power from mechanism-level privacy guarantees.

D1.justification: v2 adds a BMIA implementation-code link, PyTorch and RTX 4090/L40 hardware disclosures, and detailed storage/scalability accounting. However, v1 Appendix B's epoch budgets, learning-rate decay schedules, MLP layer widths and explicit RMIA population-set assignment are omitted rather than relocated. Most Laplace implementation details survive in Appendix G. These additions and removals substantially alter the available reproducibility information.

E1.justification: v2 adds five text-classification datasets: Emotion, TREC-6, 20 Newsgroups, DBpedia and AG News. It also evaluates references trained on CINIC-10 against CIFAR-10 targets, a distinct distribution-mismatch scenario from the retained experiment using CINIC-10 only for non-member queries. Original image, tabular and toy-regression coverage remains.

E2.justification: v2 Table 5 newly compares BatchEnsemble, Packed Ensemble, Masksembles, SWAG and MC Dropout with Laplace-based BMIA. Table 4 adds Attack-R, LiRA and RMIA to an architecture-mismatch evaluation previously showing only BMIA. Conversely, QMIA's Texas-100, Purchase-100 and ImageNet comparisons disappear; its CIFAR results remain in Table 2.

E3.justification: v2 introduces 64-reference comparisons, reference-count scaling through K=128, single-reference RMIA comparisons, and text evaluation using BERT, DistilBERT and TF-IDF/MLP models. The stated image/tabular weight decay changes from 0.0001 in v1 Appendix B to 0.0005 in v2 Section 4.1; this establishes a reported setting revision, not that experiments were rerun. The original dataset split proportions remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New analyses test alternative Bayesian approximations, reference-count scaling, reference-training distribution shift, and Gaussian assumptions through score histograms, QQ-plots and t-statistic distributions. Architecture-mismatch analysis gains baseline comparisons. The original sampling-size, Hessian, prior-tuning and predictive-distribution ablations remain, with several relocated or renumbered.

E5.justification: v2 Table 9 newly reports means and standard deviations across reference models trained on distinct data subsets. For example, CIFAR-10 TPR at 1% FPR is reported as mean 9.48% and standard deviation 0.63 percentage points. v1 lacks this variability reporting; v2 still does not specify the run count or seeds.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive text, multi-reference and supplementary results. Table 1 revises BMIA's CIFAR-10 TPRs from 2.28/8.87 to 2.84/9.48 at 0.1%/1% FPR, and RMIA with two references changes from 8.39 to 12.86 at 1% FPR on CIFAR-100. Several training-time entries also change. Table 3 newly reports MR-BMIA TPRs of 12.48% and 45.57% at 1% FPR on CIFAR-10/100. Changed methods/settings prevent interpreting these revisions as controlled before-and-after performance gains.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 changes the test-statistic denominator from sigma/sqrt(N) to sigma*sqrt(1+1/M), explicitly accounting for target-score variability. v2 also introduces MR-BMIA: multiple reference-model posteriors, separate intra/inter-model variance estimates and a Welch-Satterthwaite degrees-of-freedom approximation (Algorithm 2; Appendix C). These change the inference procedure substantially.

P1.justification: The paper is retitled and substantially rewrites its abstract, introduction, background and method exposition. The former motivation and conditional-attack theory move into appendices, while discussion material becomes structured ablation and robustness subsections. The narrative is reorganized around Bayesian sampling, variance reduction and the multi-reference extension.

P2.justification: v2 adds multiple comparison/result tables, normality diagnostics, a t-statistic plot and a log-scale ROC plot. v1's OOD table becomes Figure 2b with only two FPR thresholds, and its architecture-mismatch plot becomes Figure 2c. Existing toy and conditional-distribution illustrations move into appendices; retained Laplace-ablation plots are relaid out.

R1.justification: v2 expands recent MIA coverage, including recommender-system attacks, and substantially rewrites Bayesian-method positioning around post-hoc Laplace versus SWAG, MC Dropout and efficient ensembles. This replaces much of v1's variational-inference/MCMC overview. New discussions also connect the method to mixture Laplace approximations and hypothesis-testing privacy frameworks.

T1.justification: v2 adds the intra/inter-model variance decomposition, Proposition 3.1, power-monotonicity Theorem 3.2 and their proofs, a linear-regression comparison of posterior sampling and retraining, and multi-reference variance estimators. Existing conditional-attack propositions move to Appendix B; the conditional-TPR statement changes its quantile-term sign to agree with the retained proof. The single-reference test-variance derivation is also revised.

improvement.justification: v2 turns v1's multi-reference future-work limitation into a specified, evaluated method (Algorithm 2; Tables 3 and 7), accounts for target-score variance, and adds comparisons and diagnostics that directly test methodological choices and assumptions. These substantially strengthen the work's scope and evidential support. The gains outweigh omitted training schedules and an overbroad Theorem 3.2 statement: its proof requires alpha < 0.5 although the theorem claims alpha in (0,1).

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same BMIA research despite the changed title and substantial expansion. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices support comparison, including matching material moved from the main text into appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds text-dataset evaluations, multi-reference experiments, alternative Bayesian-method comparisons and distribution diagnostics.

before.justification: v1 reports original attack evaluations on image and tabular datasets, a toy regression experiment, robustness tests and Laplace-approximation ablations.

results.title: How does Bayesian Sampling help Membership Inference Attacks?

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion drop the efficient Nash-RS algorithm contribution and its advertised 60.55% win rate. The central probability claims expand to bounded non-uniform Luce preferences, and the contribution narrative shifts toward extending statistical bounds beyond the uniform setting.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly qualifies collapse comparisons by the vanishing-KL-regularization regime and describes impartial culture as restrictive. Section 3.4 tempers v1's algorithmic-fairness conclusion to an output-diversity interpretation. The reward-hacking hypothesis disappears, while the principal interpretation linking Condorcet structure to collapse remains.

D1.justification: V2 removes the Nash-RS code link, model and dataset access details, four-A800 hardware disclosure, sampling batch sizes, and Table 7's training hyperparameters. Appendix F instead documents the synthetic weight construction, parameter grid, and simulation count. Removing the code disclosure does not establish that the repository itself became unavailable.

E1.justification: The LLM alignment experiments using OpenRLHF/prompt-collection-v0.1 are removed. V2 adds synthetic Condorcet-winner evaluations under uniform and non-uniform Luce preferences, including preferential weighting of one response. The earlier three-response simplex Monte Carlo example remains.

E2.justification: V1 Tables 5–6 evaluate Nash-RS against the base model, PPO, and Online-IPO; these empirical comparisons disappear from v2. Retained theoretical comparisons between RLHF and NLHF do not replace the removed evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: V1's one-epoch LLM training on 2,048 prompts, evaluation on 512 held-out prompts, and reward/win-rate metrics are removed. V2 introduces a simulation protocol estimating a designated response's winning probability: m = 3–6, n = 100–300 or 200–400 depending on m, and varying Luce weights. These are new protocols, not revised scores under the earlier settings.

E4.justification: V1 Appendix F.1 analyzes reward-function stability across preference ratios, reference-policy probabilities, and regularization strengths; this analysis is removed. V2 instead tests the predicted Condorcet-probability decay across preference bias, voter counts, and response counts in Figures 3 and 7.

E5.justification: V2 Appendix F explicitly reports 1,000,000 simulation trials per configuration, whereas v1 provides no comparable replication count. This adds statistical estimation information for new experiments, without establishing increased repetitions of existing experiments. Neither version reports corresponding confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: V2 removes the LLM reward and win-rate results, including Table 5's mean rewards of -0.3859 for the base model and -0.1001 for Nash-RS. It adds simulated winning-probability curves for a designated response, compared with n^(-m/ceil(m/2)). These are different outcomes under new settings, not LLM performance improvements.

M1.justification: V2 removes the proposed policy-reward reformulation, Nash Rejection Sampling, implicit-reward computation, and associated PPO training procedure from v1 Section 4. These are substantive method removals. The response-set decomposition algorithm remains, renumbered from Algorithm 3 to Algorithm 1.

P1.justification: The contribution narrative is substantially rewritten around statistical theory. V1 Sections 3.6–3.7 become separate proof Sections 4–5, related-work material moves to Appendix A.2, and the appendices are reorganized around generalized proofs and simulations. This changes the paper's narrative structure beyond adding scientific content.

P2.justification: V1's comparison, result, and hyperparameter Tables 4–7 and reward-visualization Figure 5 are removed. V2 adds the rate-comparison and simulation displays in Figures 2, 3, and 7 and redraws Figure 1. Existing tournament diagrams are retained, renumbered, and consolidated onto one appendix page.

R1.justification: V2 newly credits Sauermann (2022) with the tight uniform-ranking result and positions its advance around non-uniform preferences. It adds substantial social-choice alignment context and removes Nash-RS's rejection-sampling novelty discussion. The DPO and game-based optimization discussion is largely relocated to Appendix A.2, not deleted.

T1.justification: V2 generalizes Theorems 3.2–3.3 from impartial culture to bounded Luce weights and adds Theorem 2.3 and Corollary 3.8 with supporting proofs. It corrects Definition 2.3's implication, revises Theorem 2.1's proof and assumptions, and handles the singleton case in Lemma B.3. V1's policy-reward theorems and their proofs are removed.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the central statistical argument by extending restrictive uniform-ranking bounds to bounded non-uniform preferences, correcting the reward-consistency definition and proof, and acknowledging the prior tight uniform result. Explicit applicability conditions and targeted simulations further support this argument. Removing Nash-RS and its LLM experiments reduces practical coverage, but the improvements to the central theory's formulation, generality, and positioning outweigh that loss.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their readable text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial changes in scope.

after.justification: V2 retains the Section 2.3 Monte Carlo finding and adds original Condorcet-winner simulations in Section 3.3, Appendix F, and Figures 3 and 7.

before.justification: V1 reports original Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct fine-tuning results in Section 4.4 and Tables 5–6, plus a Monte Carlo finding about cyclic preferences in Section 2.3.

results.title: Statistical Impossibility and Possibility of Aligning LLMs with Human Preferences: From Condorcet Paradox to Nash Equilibrium

C1.justification: The central contribution changes from dual-phase semantic disambiguation and fused layout masking to a composition-aware cross-attention variant using subject presence and relational alignment. The abstract and conclusion expand the main applicability claim to compositional image generation and foreground Wan results, while no longer foregrounding trajectory control. Training-free operation and model independence remain core claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations for IoU feedback, preservation of general video quality, context-dependent interpolation, and tolerance of imperfect layouts. Appendix F explains motion/size planning failures and why sparse keyframes help. Conversely, v1's explicit caveats about ambiguous prompts, precise trajectories, and frame-level temporal control disappear; the general dependence on backbone capabilities remains.

D1.justification: v2 adds architecture-specific adaptation instructions, baseline-result provenance, shared-layout information, API cost and latency, and a revised planning template. However, it removes v1's explicit sampler, denoising-step, guidance-scale, resolution, and frame-count table, as well as its project-page link. These substantially change reproducibility documentation; removal of the link does not establish that the resource became unavailable.

E1.justification: v2 adds compositional image generation on T2I-CompBench and dynamic-attribute evaluation within T2V-CompBench. VBench coverage expands from two object/spatial aspects to its full 16-dimension quality and semantics suite. v1's separate trajectory-control demonstration is no longer included, although v2 still discusses customizable layouts.

E2.justification: Table 1 replaces numerous comparators, including ZeroScope, Latte, and VideoRepair, with methods including Dreamina1.2, Kling-1.0, T2V-Turbo-V2, MAGI-1, and SkyReels-v2. LVD and ViCo remain; DreamRunner leaves the main benchmark comparison but remains in component comparisons. v2 additionally evaluates SEGA, ToMe, VideoGrain, and the image-generation comparators SiamLayout and HybridLayout.

E3.justification: T2V-CompBench changes from 100 to 200 prompts per category, and CogVideoX-2B is replaced by CogVideoX-5B alongside additional Wan configurations. v2 compares LVD, ViCo, and Comp-Attn on shared backbones, with shared layouts for LVD. It reports intervention during the first 20% of denoising, versus v1's 10% rule for DLFA, and changes hardware from A100 to H100. Layout planning changes from ChatGLM-4 with 13 planned keyframes to GPT-4o-mini with four keyframes and interpolation.

E4.justification: v2 revises component ablations and adds an explicit removal test for IoU guidance, a fixed-interpolation coefficient sweep, and a manual layout-error analysis covering 1,400 prompts. The interpolation sweep extends v1's direct Word Swap control rather than introducing an entirely unrelated comparison. Appendix F newly tests dense versus sparse layout planning and distinguishes motion and size errors.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or statistical significance tests. v2's layout-error frequencies are additional empirical outcomes, not uncertainty estimates for the reported generation results.

E6.justification: The benchmark and ablation results are substantially replaced and expanded. Newly reported within-v2 comparisons include Wan2.2's T2V-CompBench average increasing from 0.5742 to 0.6414 with Comp-Attn, FLUX's image-generation average from 0.5819 to 0.6131, and layout-error rates of 2.93% versus 1.14%. These are new comparisons, not matched v1-to-v2 performance gains; backbone and evaluation settings changed.

M1.justification: DLFA's union of prior and adaptive masks and restricted attention is replaced by LAM's additive attention biases, controlled by layout IoU. Adaptive layouts change from prior-size-based top-k thresholding to mean thresholding, and CogVideoX modulation targets only video-to-text attention. By contrast, SAD becoming SCI does not itself change the conditioning calculation: the saliency score complements the former confusion score, preserving the interpolation.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, related work, and substantial method and results passages are rewritten around the Present-and-Align narrative. SAD/DLFA terminology becomes SCI/LAM, the standalone Applications section disappears, and the supplement is reorganized into Appendices A–G. The changes constitute extensive narrative restructuring, beyond text added for new experiments.

P2.justification: The overview and architecture diagrams are redrawn, and the similarity and mask-fusion illustrations are replaced by attention-response and distribution analyses. The main comparison table is reorganized into backbone-specific groups, with separate VBench, image-generation, latency, and diagnostic tables. Appendix galleries are regrouped by model, and the layout prompt is redesigned as a planning/interpolation diagram.

R1.justification: Related work is repositioned around complementary shortcomings of layout control and inference-time optimization, extending the discussion from video to compositional visual generation. New substantive references include SEGA, Attend-and-Excite, ConceptAttention, Wan, autoregressive diffusion methods, and recent layout-to-image approaches. This changes the methodological context and novelty argument beyond bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: The attention formalization is substantially revised: v1's size-derived thresholds, mask unions, and supplementary block-mask equations are replaced by mean-threshold layouts and signed, IoU-weighted attention-bias definitions in v2 Equations 4–12. This changes the mathematical operator, not merely notation. The complementary confusion/saliency formulations remain equivalent, and neither version introduces theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the evidence supporting effectiveness and applicability: shared-backbone comparisons reduce confounding, full VBench evaluation checks quality tradeoffs, and targeted ablations plus the layout audit investigate mechanisms and failures that v1 leaves weakly tested. Image-generation experiments support the broader applicability claim. These gains outweigh the loss of explicit hyperparameters and remaining overstatements, such as the broad LAM-superiority interpretation despite VideoGrain's higher Interaction score in Table 6.

A1.justification: The PDFs describe successive versions of the same compositional generation work, renamed from MagicComp to Comp-Attn. Both main texts and appendices are readable, including equations, tables, and image-only figures, and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original video and image generation evaluations, component ablations, latency measurements, and a manual audit of generated layouts. Appendix B distinguishes reproduced experiments from externally sourced baseline scores.

before.justification: v1 reports original generated-video evaluations on T2V-CompBench and VBench, component ablations, inference timings, and qualitative demonstrations.

results.title: Comp-Attn: Present-and-Align Attention for Compositional Video Generation

C1.justification: V1 emphasizes compression improvements over MiniCache and compatibility with MLA. V2 expands the central contribution to selective reconstruction, multi-turn robustness, and practical latency reduction, claiming up to 4.23× generation throughput and approximately 30% higher throughput than ShadowKV. Its conclusion also broadens comparative accuracy claims to quantization and token-eviction methods.

C2.justification: V2 replaces v1's prospective system discussion with explanations of dense reconstruction's compute bottleneck, offloading's PCIe limits, and SR's efficiency tradeoffs. It adds interpretations of multi-turn eviction failures and window-size saturation. Long generation becomes an explicit unresolved limitation, whereas v1 suggested periodically recompressing generated tokens.
