E4.justification: New Tables 6–13 investigate component attribution, diversity preservation, teacher-checkpoint sensitivity, U-Net/autoencoder robustness, dynamic weighting, latent convergence and initialization stability. They also isolate PDE supervision across distillation backbones. These substantially extend the existing sampling-step, loss-weight, hard-constraint and diffusion-schedule ablations.

E5.justification: V2 Table 12 newly reports MSE variance across random initializations for PIDDM-ref and DiffusionPDE on three downstream tasks. V1 has no corresponding uncertainty analysis. V2 does not specify the initialization count or seeds, so this establishes new variance reporting rather than a documented increase in repeated runs.

E6.justification: V2 adds FPD entries in Table 1, consistency-model results, compute/quality results in Table 3 and extensive diagnostic results in Tables 6–13. Existing reconstruction coefficient-MSE entries change from 0.913 to 0.091 for RF-2 and 0.954 to 0.095 for DMD, in the same 10^-1 units (v1 Table 3; v2 Table 4). Most original benchmark values are retained; new budget-dependent results are not same-setting performance changes.

M1.justification: The core teacher training, physics-informed distillation and masked latent inference remain unchanged. V2 adds a consistency-model distillation variant and an optional dynamic PDE-loss weighting procedure using detached running residual magnitudes (Table 4 and Appendix G.1). These are limited procedural extensions.

P1.justification: Related Work moves from main Section 2 to Appendix A, reorganizing the narrative and appendix sequence. The abstract, contribution statements, method explanations and conclusion undergo substantial rewriting. V2 also changes citation style and adds an author, acknowledgements and an impact statement.

P2.justification: V2 substantially expands the evidence displays with new Table 3 and Tables 6–13, adds FPD rows to Table 1 and a consistency-model column to the former Table 3. Figure 4 is redrawn with standardized color scales, and several displays are relocated or reformatted. Figures 2, 3 and 5 retain their plotted content.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands positioning against inverse-problem diffusion methods, including DDRM, DDNM, LGD, DPG and approaches that reduce posterior approximation error. It credits earlier DPS discussion of Jensen's Gap and explicitly distinguishes PIDDM from Tee et al.'s similarly named Physics-Informed Distillation. These are substantive positioning changes beyond moving Related Work to Appendix A.

T1.justification: New Appendix B.3 introduces a low-rank Gaussian setting and Theorems B.1–B.2 with proofs addressing slow constrained-coordinate score learning and constraint-error reduction through distillation. V2 also revises the earlier score derivation and corrects reverse-SDE and posterior-mean expressions. This is substantial formal content beyond the original derivations.

improvement.justification: The compute comparison and supervision-removal controls, especially Tables 3 and 13, substantially strengthen evidence for efficiency and the specific contribution of physics supervision. Added distributional diagnostics address weaknesses of relying mainly on moments, while narrower theoretical and novelty claims improve credibility. The weakened loss-weight caveats and incomplete reporting of new protocols remain drawbacks, but the improved experimental attribution and claim calibration provide a substantial net gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe PIDDM and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices. Relocated sections and retained experiments can be matched reliably.

after.justification: V2 retains these empirical results and adds compute comparisons, distributional measurements and component, robustness and optimization experiments.

before.justification: V1 reports original PDE benchmark comparisons, downstream-task experiments, ablations and synthetic MoG demonstrations in the main text and appendices.

results.title: Physics-Informed Distillation of Diffusion Models for PDE-Constrained Generation

C1.justification: The central contributions remain a diagnostic symbolic-math benchmark, perturbation sensitivity, stronger-model robustness and hybrid tool-use benefits. v2 explicitly claims previously unexplored symbolic and equivalence perturbation categories and broadens the leading robustness group to include DeepSeek-R1. These refine novelty and claim scope without replacing the main thesis.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands interpretation and qualifications: equivalence variants are framed as diagnostic stress tests rather than representative problem distributions; input length is examined as an explanation; SymPy-favoring selection bias and dependence among variants are acknowledged. It also distinguishes seed-answer contamination from training on perturbation procedures and offers new explanations for frontier models' limited benefit from tools.

D1.justification: Appendix B replaces provider-level expenditure totals with per-model/setup costs and newly specifies exclusion of answers that fail both parsing routes, without establishing that exclusion handling changed. However, v1's temperature settings and named API intermediaries disappear. Code/data access links and the detailed numerical validation parameters were already available in v1.

E1.justification: Both versions already evaluate integrals, limits, differential equations, series and hypergeometrics; hypergeometrics appears in v1 Figure 7. v2 adds the all-ones Numeric-All-0 input condition and evaluation with the original seed question and answer supplied in context. These extend test scenarios within the retained mathematical domains.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds a full-benchmark SymPy baseline, extending CAS comparison beyond v1's case studies. It also adds code-enabled GPT-4o alongside its no-code evaluation and replaces Gemma-3-27b-it with Gemma-3n-e4b-it. These materially revise the evaluated comparator set.

E3.justification: The evaluation expands from 61 seeds and 17,092 questions to 100 seeds and 35,368 questions. Numeric-All includes the new zero-digit condition, and the variance subset expands from 50 two-digit variants per seed to 50 each at two and three digits. Section 4 adds seed-answer prompting experiments, and Figure 1 revises the reported tool-use prompts. Pass@1 and the existing numerical validation tolerance remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds contamination stress tests, comparisons addressing expression length as an alternative explanation, a robustness-versus-seed-accuracy analysis, topic-stratified analysis, and diagnostics of dependence among generated questions. These substantially broaden the questions investigated. The hybrid LLM–CAS case study is retained as Figure 7, previously Figure 6.

E5.justification: Figures 2–3 newly report Wald 95% confidence intervals. Appendix C.3 adds seed-clustered residual uncertainty, effective sample-size estimation, residual correlations and split-half checks. This substantially extends v1's variance summaries. The additional random coefficient variants are distinct questions, not evidence of repeated runs on identical prompts.

E6.justification: Results are extensively revised under the expanded benchmark. Table 2 reports DeepSeek-R1 at 44.5% overall in v1 and 78.3% in v2, joining the leading group. GPT-4.1's code/no-code totals change from 23.6/19.8 to 46.2/48.9, reversing its reported code advantage. v2 adds SymPy's 39.2% total and contamination and topic-level outcomes. These are results under changed conditions, not controlled cross-version performance gains.

M1.justification: The seed-perturbation generation framework and answer-validation pipeline remain unchanged: regex extraction, SymPy parsing with Gemini fallback, and symbolic or numerical verification. The detailed validation rules in v2 Section 2.2 already appeared in v1 Appendix B. Added parameter settings and diagnostic experiments do not establish a new benchmark algorithm.

P1.justification: The abstract and substantial portions of the introduction, methodology, results and discussion are rewritten. Validation details move from Appendix B into the main text, benchmark-error examples move into Appendix A.2, and Appendix C gains a structured sequence of analyses. This constitutes extensive narrative revision and reorganization.

P2.justification: The main text changes to a two-column layout, Figure 1 becomes vertically arranged, and Figures 2–3 are redrawn with error bars and revised legends. v2 adds a robustness scatterplot and cost/topic tables, converts the identity list into Table 3, and expands the heatmaps. The existing hybrid case is relocated and renumbered; variance-heatmap success/failure markers are removed.

R1.justification: v2 adds explicit positioning against neuro-symbolic data generation and a sharper novelty contrast with GSM-Symbolic. It adds discussion or citations involving PAL, AFlow, MathArena, RIMO and PutnamBench, while removing Omni-MATH. The existing positioning around university-level symbolic manipulation versus word problems remains central; publication and bibliography-format updates alone are not substantive additions.

T1.justification: Appendix C.3 introduces a substantial mathematical construction absent from v1: Jeffreys-smoothed leave-one-out difficulty estimates, calibrated logistic probabilities, residuals, a seed-clustered standard-error estimator with finite-cluster correction, and an IID-equivalent sample-size definition. The perturbation identities themselves are retained; no new theorem proving LLM reasoning ability is supplied.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the evidence supporting the benchmark's diagnostic claims. The systematic SymPy comparison, contamination and length checks, topic analysis, and treatment of seed dependence address important comparison and validity questions largely unexamined in v1. These gains outweigh the loss of temperature/provider details and the unreconciled v1 subgroup figures retained in Appendix A.3. The improvement comes from stronger scrutiny and qualification of the benchmark, not simply its increased size or changed scores.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ASyMOB by the same authors. Their main text, tables, figures, equations and complete Appendices A–C are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v2 reports original evaluations on the expanded benchmark, including model and SymPy results, a contamination experiment, and topic-level and statistical analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original model evaluations on ASyMOB, including Table 2 accuracies, perturbation and code-use experiments, CAS case studies, and appendix analyses.

results.title: ASyMOB: Algebraic Symbolic Mathematical Operations Benchmark

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution statement redefine the central analytical contribution: v1 claims a generalization of shifted-divergence analysis, whereas v2 claims a novel coupling construction that bypasses its inapplicable global-Lipschitz requirement. The overarching claims of convergent privacy, hybrid noise and benefits from multiple orthonormal directions remain.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly identifies the pointwise-versus-global Lipschitz obstruction that invalidates v1's proposed use of shifted-divergence reductions, and explains how coupling separates failure probability from privacy cost. It also adds a privacy-versus-computation interpretation of increasing K. The existing limitations on practical LLM applicability are retained in Appendix A.

D1.justification: The new Figure 2 supplies parameter annotations for an additional numerical accounting example. Existing Figure 1 settings move from Appendix A.3 to Appendix B without substantive changes. No accompanying solver implementation, code-access information or hardware details are added.

E1.justification: Numerical bound evaluation expands from the strongly convex illustration in Figure 1 to smooth, not necessarily convex losses in v2 Figure 2. This is a limited additional numerical scenario; no datasets or applied learning tasks are introduced.

E2.justification: The numerical comparisons retain standard composition and output perturbation as comparators, including in the new Figure 2. Newly cited Bao and Gupta works are discussed but not added as evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: Figure 1's settings are retained. New Figure 2 uses plots labeled RDP with alpha=2, d=100000, sigma=0.1 and eta=K=1000, while varying n. Its exact reporting is inconsistent: the caption says DP and n=1000/2000, whereas the plot titles say RDP and n=10000/2000.

E4.justification: Figure 2 adds a numerical illustration of nonconvex privacy-bound saturation and sensitivity to sample size. The utility analysis and comparison of orthonormal versus i.i.d. directions already existed in v1's appendices; their relocation is not a new ablation.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated runs, seeds, empirical confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. Changes to analytical failure-probability accounting belong to the theoretical guarantees.

E6.justification: Figure 1's numerical curves are retained. New Figure 2 reports optimized privacy-bound curves that plateau below standard composition and output perturbation at sufficiently large iteration counts. These are additional results under different conditions, not improved scores for the retained comparison.

M1.justification: Noisy-ZOGD retains its clipped two-point estimator, orthonormal directions, hybrid Gaussian noise and projection. The noise-mixing parameter beta is complemented between v1 Equation (3) and v2 Equation (4), preserving the same algorithm family. The new auxiliary process is a proof device.

P1.justification: The abstract and analytical narrative are substantially rewritten around coupling. The conclusion and limitations are combined in Appendix A, the appendices are reorganized into A–J, and the main proof exposition is replaced. Author affiliations and other front matter also change.

P2.justification: The main text and references change from a single-column layout to two columns, with revised typography, running headers and citation styling. v2 adds a full-page Figure 2 containing two logarithmic plots. Figure 1 is retained with resizing and a revised caption.

R1.justification: Section 4 adds Bao et al. (2025) on multiple public-state update directions and Gupta et al. (2024) on inherent privacy, positioning this work as answering Gupta's additive-noise amplification question. The DPZero citation changes to its later publication; it is not a new comparison method.

T1.justification: Theorem 3.2 changes from conditional RDP on a high-probability event to an explicit DP guarantee with separate privacy-conversion and coupling-failure terms. Its proof replaces shifted-divergence reductions with an auxiliary process, bounded shifts, total-variation control and Gaussian transcript composition. Appendix H adapts the minibatch guarantee, while most utility and i.i.d.-direction derivations are retained.

improvement.justification: The decisive gain is the replacement of v1's unjustified global-Lipschitz step with an explicit coupling and total-variation argument in Theorem 3.2, substantially strengthening the central theoretical contribution and clarifying failure accounting. Local probability/formula transcription errors remain, including in Appendix H, and Figure 2 has conflicting metric and sample-size labels. These defects limit precision but are narrower than the improvement to the central proof strategy.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with readable methods, equations, figures and complete appendices. Renumbered and relocated material can be matched reliably.

after.justification: The added Figure 2 also evaluates theoretical privacy bounds. The complete paper reports mathematical analysis and numerical illustrations, without original empirical training, simulation or data-analysis outcomes.

before.justification: Figure 1 and Appendix A.3 numerically evaluate theoretical privacy bounds. Neither the main text nor appendices report optimization experiments, simulated training outcomes or empirical data analysis.

results.title: Privacy Amplification in Differentially Private Zeroth-Order Optimization with Hidden States

C1.justification: The three principal contributions remain causal temporal mixing, cluster-aware embedding, and sequential anomaly scoring. v2 adds an explicit contribution claim about improved normal/anomalous representation separability and more precisely limits causality to temporal information flow. Boundary refinement receives greater prominence but was already described in v1.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations of mask scaling, parameter robustness, inference-time batch normalization, and causality within the input window. It discusses training contamination, correlation shifts, and computational tradeoffs, and explicitly excludes causal discovery and univariate detection. Conversely, v1's limitations concerning residual correlations from shared mixing/head layers and temporal-mixer expansion are omitted.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code repository link, a dedicated baseline/result-source table, a Gaussian-component-based recipe for restricting alpha search, and explicit training-versus-inference normalization details. These materially expand reproduction guidance. Most existing hardware, software, and training settings remain, although the explicit Windows 11 and one-causal-mixer disclosures from v1 are omitted.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate multivariate anomaly detection on SWaT, WADI, PSM, SMD, MSL, and SMAP. The added protocols and analyses use these same datasets. The correlation-shift analysis changes the training portion used for clustering, rather than introducing a new task, population, or test environment.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds TimesNet, xLSTMAD, CATCH, PatchAD, SimAD, SAT, OracleAD, PCA-Error, and CAROTS with its CAROTS+ variant, while removing GTA. These substantially broaden the evaluated comparator set. Online SensitiveHUE also becomes a comparator in the repeated-run and computational-cost evaluations in Tables 12–13.

E3.justification: v1 evaluates CCM-TAD on multi-entity datasets using separate models and concatenated predictions. v2 additionally evaluates pooled training and averaging entity-wise metrics, separating comparisons by protocol. It adds PR_AUC, VUS_PR, VUS_ROC, Aff_F1, R_F1, and detection-delay/false-alarm evaluation. Table 9 also replaces the general alpha search interval with restricted dataset-specific intervals for SWaT, WADI, and PSM.

E4.justification: The existing architectural and clustering-variant ablations are retained. v2 adds boundary-correction ablation, representation-separation measurements, gradient-based causality verification, sensitivity analyses for cluster count and scoring/model hyperparameters, causal-mask scaling comparisons, and clustering derived from partial versus complete training data. Sections 4.2 and Appendix J therefore test several previously unevaluated mechanisms and robustness questions.

E5.justification: v1 Appendix E reports means and sample standard deviations over three seeds. v2 Appendix I reports five-seed averages with ± quantities and adds uncertainty reporting for Online SensitiveHUE. The basic mean-plus-spread approach remains, although v2 does not explicitly identify the statistic represented by ±; additional metric rows mainly expand the results.

E6.justification: Table 2 revises CCM-TAD's WADI F1 from 0.733 to 0.761. Under the retained prediction-aggregation protocol, MSL, SMD, and SMAP entries change from 0.619/0.599/0.524 to 0.638/0.602/0.551. These are revised reported outcomes, with identical tuning not established. Numerous results are added for other protocols, metrics, analyses, and computational comparisons. The original modular and clustering-variant ablation scores remain unchanged, as do PSM correlation values despite their revised reduction-sign convention.

M1.justification: The clustering procedure, reconstruction architecture, causal mask, loss, and cumulative scoring mechanism are retained. Equation 17 changes the endpoint-search range from t_a < t <= t_b to t_a <= t <= t_b, allowing the detected segment's first point to be selected as its endpoint. This is a limited procedural correction.

P1.justification: The abstract, introductory contributions, related-work discussion, experimental narrative, and conclusion are extensively revised. Existing material is reorganized alongside dedicated appendix sections for baseline sources, metric definitions, training behavior, causal motivation, and online applicability. The restructuring and explanatory rewriting extend beyond merely inserting new results.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn to show the correlation-profile graph and cluster embeddings. v2 adds scoring illustrations, gradient heatmaps, distribution plots, sensitivity curves, and correlation graphs. Comparison tables are expanded and reorganized; for example, v1 Table 4 becomes the transposed v2 Table 5. The main text also changes from one-column to two-column layout.

R1.justification: v2 substantially broadens positioning through statistical change-point and classical anomaly-detection literature, the PCA-Error critique of complex models, and newer methods including OracleAD, CAROTS, and PatchAD. It explicitly distinguishes temporal masking from Granger causality and root-cause discovery, and adds references supporting the statistical analysis and expanded evaluation metrics.

T1.justification: New Appendix A derives an approximate null distribution and expectation for the log-p-value anomaly evidence, including a negative-drift condition around alpha < 1/e. It discusses approximate uniformity of normal p-values and temporal dependence. v1 contains the algorithmic equations but lacks this substantial probabilistic derivation.

improvement.justification: Separating multi-entity evaluation protocols makes Table 2 substantially more defensible than v1's mixed-protocol comparison. Broader baselines and metrics, boundary-correction ablation, gradient checks, and sensitivity analyses provide important tests of previously under-supported claims. Comparative repeated-run results and reproduction guidance further strengthen the paper. Some earlier limitations disappear and the new ± statistic is undefined, but these drawbacks do not outweigh the substantial gains in evaluation credibility and explanatory support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CCM-TAD research, with matching core architecture and benchmark datasets. Their main texts, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original benchmark experiments and reports additional protocol comparisons, ablations, sensitivity analyses, computational measurements, and repeated-run results.

before.justification: v1 reports original CCM-TAD experiments on six datasets, component and clustering ablations, and repeated-run results in the main text and appendices.

results.title: Cluster-Aware Causal Mixer for Online Anomaly Detection in Multivariate Time Series

C1.justification: The central contributions—instance-conditioned latent modeling, interacting MCMC with SA, and convergence guarantees—remain. V2 broadens the headline performance claim from RL-based methods to NCO/learning-based baselines and adds an explicit contribution concerning effectiveness under low inference budgets.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations of instance conditioning, stochastic latents, training-loss differences, gradient-computation costs, and the diffusion prior's additional training requirements. It substantially expands limitations concerning scaling, longer decoding horizons, and global constraints that masking cannot enforce. The augmented CVRP150 loss to EAS remains acknowledged in Appendix F.2.2, although the main text now makes a broader all-settings superiority claim.

D1.justification: V2 newly documents encoder soft-clipping, inference updates restricted to the decoder's final layer, explicit baseline functions, budget-selection procedures, and a common PyTorch evaluation implementation. It supplies diffusion-prior training and knapsack-generation details. Existing architecture settings and the code-access link are retained. Describing R=40 as both a radius and a diameter leaves that implementation detail unresolved.

E1.justification: V2 retains the original routing coverage and adds CVRP200 evaluation in Table 11 and 0/1 Knapsack50 and Knapsack100 experiments in Table 13, extending empirical coverage beyond routing. CVRP with time windows and job shop scheduling are outlined in Appendix A.3 but are not experimentally evaluated.

E2.justification: V2 adds ELG and CNF to the corresponding TSP/CVRP comparisons, HGS to the CVRP comparison, and Adam and SGLD to the existing inference-method comparison. Table 9 additionally evaluates Active Search + IL and AGFN (greedy). These are reported comparisons absent from v1, not merely new citations.

E3.justification: Reported training duration changes from 2000 epochs in v1 Appendix E.1 to 8000 in v2 Appendix F.1; v1 Figure 4 already reached 8000, so this does not demonstrate additional training. POMO computational budgets/runtimes are revised, including CVRP100 without augmentation from 10 to 40 minutes. New experiments introduce controlled latent-dimension/radius settings, a diffusion-prior training protocol, and specified knapsack sample counts and capacities.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's inference-method, particle-count, and update-frequency analyses, v2 tests cost-weighted versus POPPY training, instance-conditioned versus independent priors, COMPASS + LGS, deterministic versus stochastic latents, and encoder versus diffusion priors. Tables 6–8, 10, and 12 and Figure 7 also examine latent dimension and radius. The earlier particle-count and update-frequency analyses are retained.

E5.justification: V1 Figure 3 and v2 Figure 2 both report means over 10 inference runs, and the existing particle-count boxplots are retained. V2 does not introduce new seed reporting, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty-estimation procedures for the expanded results.

E6.justification: The original LGS benchmark scores for TSP/CVRP100–150 remain unchanged, while POMO scores are revised alongside computational budgets. Numerous results are added: Table 7 reports CVRP100 objectives of 15.641 for the instance-independent model versus 15.524 for the conditioned model; Table 11 reports LGS's CVRP200 gap of 1.289%; Table 13 reports knapsack objectives of 20.018 and 40.512. These are new comparisons, not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The reported training prescription changes materially: Equation (2) switches from +βH to −βH, while Appendix A revises the decoder entropy-gradient sign, adds entropy contributions to the encoder estimator, and changes baseline placement. V2 also introduces a separately trained diffusion-prior variant and a knapsack decoder adaptation. The core encoder-decoder and interacting MCMC/SA framework remains; these documentary changes do not establish that earlier experiments were rerun.

P1.justification: The seven-section main structure and much of the existing method and theory exposition are retained. V2 rewrites portions of the introduction and related work, expands explanatory passages, adds experiment subheadings, and reorganizes appendix subsections. The supplementary contents page is removed. These narrative edits accompany the larger scientific additions.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a two-column conference layout for the main text. The separate routing tables become a combined main comparison without augmentation, with expanded full comparisons in Appendix Tables 4–5. Existing figures are relocated, resized, or restyled; the latent visualization and inference curves exchange numbering. Tables 6–13 and the radius-sensitivity Figure 7 are new displays.

R1.justification: The new Extensive Related Work appendix positions the method against reward-guided sampling, diffusion fine-tuning, GFlowNets, and large-scale NCO approaches. Other additions connect the training objective to IWAE and best-of-many objectives and discuss newer generalization and memory-enhanced solvers. This substantially expands research positioning beyond v1's NCO and MCMC discussion.

T1.justification: V2 adds an importance-sampling derivation, Proposition A.1 and its gradient proof, an inference-gradient derivation, and a conditional proposal-symmetry argument. It makes compactness explicit in the theoretical setting and replaces the exponential Lyapunov drift arguments with whole-state minorization and V=1 in Appendices C and D. Assumptions 4 and 8 and the associated Jensen step change from squared to unsquared L2 norms.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses v1's missing validation of central design choices through component ablations, broader baselines, and non-routing evaluation. Corrected entropy/gradient expressions and explicit applicability limits also improve technical clarity. These gains outweigh remaining defects: the main text overstates performance across all settings despite the retained EAS win in Table 5, and Appendix A.4's new importance-sampling justification does not consistently reconcile normalized ratios with the summed training weights.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe LGS-Net and Latent Guided Sampling by the same authors. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial revisions and reformatting.

after.justification: V2 retains original routing results and reports additional component ablations, baseline comparisons, CVRP200 results, and knapsack experiments in Section 6 and Appendix F.

before.justification: V1 reports original TSP and CVRP benchmark results, inference-method comparisons, training curves, and particle-count and update-frequency analyses in Section 6 and Appendix E.

results.title: Latent Guided Sampling for Combinatorial Optimization

C1.justification: The central SADG, NPAS, AV Filter, and adaptive-attack contributions remain, including the headline accuracy and attack-success claims. V2 qualifies the conclusion's effectiveness-stealth argument by explicitly allowing influential signals to be present but computationally difficult to detect.

C2.justification: Remark 4.1 explicitly treats attention as an empirical proxy rather than a causal influence measure. V2 adds interpretations of length bias, reranker behavior, false positives, and the combined defense's accuracy limitations, and distinguishes detectable signals from efficient detection. The original majority-corruption, redundancy, and task-specificity limitations remain.

D1.justification: V2 documents Keyword fallback rules and the procedures for additional perplexity, prompting, and reranking baselines. It omits v1's explicit in-context-learning, greedy-decoding, and GPT-4o temperature-0.1 disclosures. The implementation link, software libraries, and A100/H100 hardware information are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate RQA, RQA-MC, NQ, and HotpotQA using the same Google Search and Wikipedia sources. Short-answer, multiple-choice, multi-hop, and response-targeted poisoning coverage is retained. The added LLMs and attack generators do not introduce a distinct task or data domain.

E2.justification: V2 adds evaluated Misinformation Attack, RAGParadox, and CorruptRAG attacks beyond PoisonedRAG and PIA (Table 9). It also directly compares perplexity filtering, vigilant prompting, and ColBERTv2- and T5-based filtering (Table 12), substantially expanding v1's Vanilla and Certified Robust RAG comparisons.

E3.justification: V2 adds Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B configurations, false-positive evaluation across four thresholds, and combined-defense testing. The original 100-query, top-10 setup remains. Its main text reports RQA-MC for lambda tuning, whereas Appendix D.1 retains RQA, leaving that particular setting inconsistent.

E4.justification: New analyses quantify maximum token attention and passage lengths (Tables 5-6), measure benign-set false positives across thresholds (Table 11), and test complementarity with Keyword (Table 15). The original attention example, adaptive-attack analysis, and corruption/threshold sensitivity plots are retained and relocated.

E5.justification: Both versions report means over five seeds, exempt costly adaptive attacks, and use one seed for the sensitivity sweeps. Both report the same maximum standard deviations: 2.32 for ACC, 3.78 for RACC, and 3.56 for ASR. No new uncertainty-reporting practice is introduced.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial model, attack, baseline, and diagnostic results, including approximately 0.24 default-threshold false-positive rate (Table 11) and 1.22% average ASR for the combined defense (Table 15). Shared main-table entries, Wikipedia results, and adaptive-attack outcomes are retained; these additions are not same-setting performance improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The NPAS calculation, AV Filter procedure, and adaptive-attack objective remain unchanged. Appendix D.7 adds a composed inference procedure that first filters passages with AV Filter and then applies Certified Robust RAG-Keyword to generate the answer.

P1.justification: V2 substantially rewrites and compresses the main exposition, changes the title, standardizes NPAS terminology, and introduces named assumptions and remarks. Full SADG details, adaptive-attack material, and sensitivity analyses move into reorganized appendices, with a dedicated attention-rationale appendix.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a two-column main layout, adds a notation table and several diagnostic/comparison tables, and expands the main results displays for additional models. Existing figures remain but are resized, relocated, renumbered, and sometimes relabeled; several formerly main-text displays move to the appendices.

R1.justification: V2 adds citations concerning RAGParadox, CorruptRAG, attention flow, reranking, and newer LLMs, while dropping GARAG, RankRAG, and HopRAG references. It organizes attacks into content and instruction poisoning and elaborates Certified Robust RAG tradeoffs, while preserving the central research positioning.

T1.justification: Section 3 introduces explicit formal assumptions, including agreement among uncorrupted passages and at least two benign passages supporting the answer, plus attention-access and response-targeting requirements. The SADG definition, advantage formula, and NPAS equations remain substantively unchanged. No new theorem or proof is supplied.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens assessment of comparative robustness and selectivity by directly testing additional defenses and attacks and measuring benign-set false positives, gaps in v1's evidence. Explicit assumptions and the noncausal-attention caveat also improve claim calibration. These gains outweigh localized reporting problems, including omitted decoding details and conflicting lambda-tuning descriptions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SADG, NPAS, and AV Filter research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison despite the changed title, formatting, and organization.

after.justification: Section 5 and the appendices retain original experiments and add model comparisons, attack evaluations, false-positive measurements, and combined-defense results.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix C report original QA experiments, corruption detection, adaptive-attack outcomes, runtime measurements, and sensitivity analyses.

results.title: Through the Stealth Lens: Attention-Aware Defenses Against Poisoning in RAG

C1.justification: The central scientific claims remain: adaptive preconditioner dynamics can independently trigger spikes, persistent second-moment decay sustains instability, and gradient-directional curvature predicts spikes better than maximum curvature alone. The five-stage mechanism and lower-beta2 mitigation idea already appear in v1; v2 emphasizes them and supplies broader supporting evidence.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly introduces the frozen-time approximation and timescale-separation justification, distinguishes positive-curvature overshooting from saddle escape, and explains why increasing beta1 offers limited protection. It also adds substantive qualifications about one-dimensional theoretical guarantees, stochastic minibatch prediction noise, and computational limits beyond roughly 200M parameters.

D1.justification: v2 adds the large-Transformer hyperparameter table, ViT/ResNet and Adafactor settings, and details about power-iteration counts and Hessian-vector-product costs. It newly states that code accompanies supplementary materials, without verifiable access in these PDFs. Conversely, v1's dedicated Fig. 4 setup, including initialization distributions and separate network widths, is removed.

E1.justification: v2 adds MNIST image classification (Fig. D7) and natural-language next-token training on a 100B-token SlimPajama split (Sec. 6.2). This substantially extends coverage beyond v1's function approximation, CIFAR-10, and synthetic sequence tasks. The earlier CIFAR-10 and anchor-task experiments remain in the appendices.

E2.justification: v2 extends the controlled quadratic-optimization comparisons with evaluated AdaGrad, RMSProp, and Adafactor experiments (Figs. D15–D17). These additions are confined to supplementary quadratic tests; GD and the existing maximum-eigenvalue and update-directional-curvature comparisons are retained.

E3.justification: New protocols include a 187M-parameter Transformer with batch size 512 and gradient clipping, ViT/ResNet18 evaluations, and momentum-free beta2 sweeps. Fig. 3 adds a coupled case with beta1=0.6 and beta2=0.5; the earlier case survives in Fig. D21. Fig. 4's reported width changes from 1,000 to 20, but inconsistent v1 descriptions and retained curves do not establish a rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds substantial mechanism checks: beta2 mitigation experiments in Transformers, a beta1=0 sweep isolating adaptive dynamics (Fig. D22), multiple unstable eigendirections (Fig. D18), a test of the rounding-error explanation (Fig. D20), and larger-learning-rate sensitivity (Fig. D21). Earlier epsilon/clipping interventions and spike-type case studies are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. Additional trajectories and decay fits in v2 do not introduce statistical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results, including MNIST spike trajectories, reduced spike frequency at lower beta2 in the 187M Transformer, and contrasting AdaGrad/RMSProp/Adafactor dynamics. These are newly reported experiments, not improvements over matched v1 runs. Retained findings, such as FNN threshold crossing at epoch 179, spike onset at 184, and recovery at 206, remain unchanged.

M1.justification: Adam's update, the preconditioned Hessian in Eq. (7), the gradient-directional predictor, and its sustained version remain unchanged. However, v2 adds an Adafactor-specific preconditioned-curvature construction incorporating its scaling and clipping factors (Fig. D17), a limited adaptation of the diagnostic.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, stability explanation, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around decoupling and explicit qualifications. The former five-phase subsection becomes a standalone section, CNN discussion moves into the appendix, and the appendices are reorganized with new disclosure sections. These are substantial narrative and structural revisions.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column main-text layout, redraws Fig. 3 to display moment–gradient coupling, adds an overshooting illustration and five-stage diagrams, and reorganizes Fig. 7. Numerous new experimental figures and a hyperparameter table accompany these changes. Earlier CNN plots are relocated rather than removed.

R1.justification: v2 adds central-flow research, recent Adam convergence/ODE studies, and language-model and reasoning-task references, while clarifying its relationship to adaptive Edge of Stability. It removes Cattaneo and Shigida's lower-beta2 citation. These update the positioning without replacing the existing related-work framework.

T1.justification: v2 adds a local GD descent proposition, an exact loss-increase criterion using a path-averaged Hessian (Theorem D.1), and a decaying-learning-rate instability theorem. It also revises the momentum stability statement to require positive directional curvature and substantially reworks the existing five-stage theorem with additional assumptions, transition definitions, and finiteness arguments.

improvement.justification: The decisive gain is stronger testing of the mechanism beyond v1's predominantly toy, synthetic, and small-image-subset experiments. Natural-language training, additional architectures, and controls for momentum and alternative explanations materially strengthen empirical support. Explicit approximation and applicability limits also improve interpretation. The removed Fig. 4 setup and remaining theoretical inconsistencies, including Theorem 5.1 omitting an assumption required by Appendix D.2, temper but do not outweigh these substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Adam loss-spike mechanism and retain identifiable equations, experiments, and figures. Their text, mathematical content, figures, and appendices are readable, allowing additions to be distinguished from relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds results for MNIST, SlimPajama language modeling, additional architectures and optimizers, and controlled sensitivity studies.

before.justification: v1 reports original quadratic-optimization experiments and neural-network training results for function approximation, CIFAR-10, and synthetic sequence tasks, including supplementary analyses.

results.title: Adaptive Preconditioners Trigger Loss Spikes in Adam

C1.justification: The abstract and contributions narrow the novelty claim from four transforms to three. Tu remains implemented but is now associated with prior OSTQuant work. The central accuracy–speed positioning, up-to-3.9× speedup, and comparison with a method up to 29% slower are retained.

C2.justification: v2 adds explicit architectural applicability conditions, explanations connecting residual outliers across blocks, and interpretations of FlatQuant's numerical instability and OSTQuant's failure to preserve function. It also discusses weaker reasoning performance relative to FlatQuant and inconsistent GPTQ benefits. Limitations expand to decoding-benchmark constraints, integer hardware support, and untested MoE and microscaling extensions.

D1.justification: v2 newly discloses frozen/shared teacher weights, per-block gradient checkpointing, OSTQuant reproduction sources, and more detailed timing and inversion procedures. Core calibration and parametrization details remain. Appendix D replaces v1's explicit learning rates with validation-based selection without listing all selected values, reducing specificity in that respect.

E1.justification: v2 adds actual evaluations on MMLU and GSM8K, extending task coverage beyond WikiText-2 and the six retained common-sense tasks (Appendix H, Table 17). MMLU also appears in new ablations. This substantially broadens the capabilities evaluated; Qwen-2.5 7B experiments were already present in v1's appendices.

E2.justification: OSTQuant joins the static and dynamic comparisons. Conversely, QuaRot and FlatQuant are removed specifically from the training-loss comparison (v1 Table 12 versus v2 Table 15), while remaining elsewhere. QuaRot-opt in v2's main table corresponds to the already optimized QuaRot baseline in v1.

E3.justification: v2 adds model configurations including Ministral 8B and Qwen-2.5 32B, GPTQ evaluations, and unquantized parameter-perturbation protocols. Qwen-32B uses 512-token training sequences and method-dependent training lengths. Appendix D specifies 2048-token dynamic evaluation, replacing v1's general 4096-token rule for non-Llama-2 models. The complete main-table W4A8KV4 comparison is replaced by more limited appendix comparisons.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained individual-transform and optimization ablations, v2 adds integrated component ablations (Table 3), activation-outlier visualization (Figure 2), the Ph hybrid study (Table 12), an Lp sensitivity sweep (Table 14), and Gaussian-perturbation tests (Figure 4 and Table 21). Appendix K additionally compares inversion and rotation costs. These investigate component contributions, mechanisms, numerical stability, and computational overhead.

E5.justification: v1 already reports three-seed activation studies and uncertainty for the Tu ablation. v2 substantially extends reporting with three-seed means and standard deviations for a main-result subset and new ablations, five-seed perturbation results, and repeated operation timings. Appendix D newly specifies three-seed medians for FPTQuant and OSTQuant dynamic results; this does not establish an increase from a documented earlier run count.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive reasoning, model, GPTQ, ablation, and timing results and revises retained entries. In Table 2, Llama-2 7B W4A4KV4 perplexity changes from 940 to 603 for FPTQuant and 951 to 106 for FlatQuant, although v2 Table 12 retains the old values. Dynamic Llama-3 8B FPTQuant perplexity changes from 7.17 to 7.67 alongside revised evaluation settings, so this is not a demonstrated same-setting deterioration.

M1.justification: The default six-transform design and two-stage optimization remain. v2 adds an evaluated FPTQuant+Ph variant incorporating FlatQuant's online query/key transform (Appendix F, Table 12). Reclassifying Tu as an existing transform does not remove it from the method.

P1.justification: v2 clarifies quantization and mergeability explanations, folds the standalone Tu subsection into Other transforms, reorganizes experimental setup, and subdivides the compute-resource appendix. It also separates the impact statement and changes citation style. Much of the original prose and the overall introduction–method–experiments–discussion sequence remain.

P2.justification: The main text and references change from single-column to two-column conference layout. Figure 1 is recolored, Table 1 is reorganized, and Table 2 changes its model columns and bit-width blocks. New diagnostic figures and multiple ablation, uncertainty, and timing tables substantially expand the visual presentation; retained figures are also resized and relocated.

R1.justification: v2 integrates OSTQuant into related work, credits its relationship to Tu, and critiques its function-preservation properties. It adds deployment and microscaling references while dropping several QAT citations and QuIP#. These are focused updates to prior-work coverage and attribution; the central expressivity-versus-cost positioning remains.

T1.justification: Theorem 3.1 and its Appendix C proof remain unchanged. Limited mathematical revisions include removing Wg from the output-side local-optimization sum (v1 Equation 10 versus v2 Equation 9) and refining block-Hadamard cost from O(n log n) to O(n log(n/K)) in the transform-cost table.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation through integrated component ablations, numerical-stability tests, broader model evaluation, and reasoning comparisons with seed-based uncertainty. These address important gaps in v1's evidence, while revised novelty attribution and applicability discussion improve precision. Unreconciled scores between Tables 2 and 12 weaken some comparisons, and reasoning results expose a larger FlatQuant advantage, but the added controlled evidence and clearer limitations provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe FPTQuant with the same authors, core transforms, and optimization framework. All 25 pages of v1 and 28 pages of v2, including appendices, are readable and support matching text, equations, tables, and figures across the revision.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds component ablations, reasoning evaluations, perturbation studies, and training-cost measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original quantization accuracy, inference benchmarks, and ablations, including Tables 1–2 and Appendices E–H.

results.title: FPTQuant: Function-Preserving Transforms for LLM Quantization

C1.justification: Both versions claim zero-shot 4D interaction generation through LLM-derived part affordances, improved realism and text alignment, and flexibility across multiple people or objects. V2's emphasis on explicit planning and interaction scaffolding preserves the meaning and scope of these contributions.

C2.justification: V2 interprets the new substitutions as evidence of robustness across foundation models and explicitly adds degenerate segmentation to potential failure sources. Appendix B newly characterizes the pipeline as unoptimized but practical for offline synthesis and discusses possible acceleration; the finger-articulation limitation remains.

D1.justification: V2 adds stagewise runtimes of 0.6, 5.7, 8.3, and 6.0 minutes in Table 7, extending v1's optimization-only timing disclosure. The hardware, iteration counts, alignment procedure, and full prompts are retained, while v1's explicit promise to release code and data upon publication is omitted.

E1.justification: Both versions use Sketchfab objects and BEHAVE scans and demonstrate single-person, multi-person, single-object, and multi-object interactions. BEHAVE already appears in v1 Appendix A; v2 expands its evaluation without introducing a new dataset, domain, or interaction family.

E2.justification: HOI-Diff and CHOIS remain the Sketchfab comparators. V2 additionally evaluates them on the retained BEHAVE benchmark in Table 6 and Figure 11, where v1 showed only HOI-PAGE examples, providing a bounded extension of comparator participation.

E3.justification: V2 adds part-contact evaluation using manually verified LLM-identified relations and distance thresholds of 1, 3, and 5 cm. It also specifies a quantitative BEHAVE protocol with 18 test objects, three prompts per object, and five variations per prompt, and adds Gemini and HunyuanVideo substitution experiments; the original main evaluation settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained fitting, contact, and motion-state ablations, v2 adds foundation-model sensitivity tests in Table 4, fine-grained contact analysis, a pipeline-stage case study in Figure 10, and runtime profiling in Table 7. These substantially broaden examination of component dependence, contact fidelity, and computational cost.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates and perceptual-study percentages without confidence intervals, significance tests, or error bars. The added experiments introduce no new uncertainty-estimation practice; BEHAVE's five generated variations follow the existing diversity-sampling approach.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 and the perceptual-study values remain unchanged, but Tables 4–7 add substantial results. For example, Table 5 reports 1 cm contact accuracy of 0.887 for HOI-PAGE versus 0.318 for HOI-Diff and 0.274 for CHOIS; Table 6 newly reports BEHAVE VideoCLIP scores of 0.220, 0.200, and 0.214, respectively. These are additional evaluations, not improvements over v1 under unchanged settings.

M1.justification: The PAG construction, segmentation, reference-video generation, alignment, and object-motion optimization procedures remain substantively unchanged. The appendix prompts also match; the new planning and grounding terminology reframes existing stages, while alternative foundation models are tested as experimental variants.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and method undergo extensive rewriting around interaction planning and grounding, with renamed and regrouped subsections and condensed mathematical exposition. The appendix is reorganized, author information and citation style change, and impact and writing-assistance disclosures are added.

P2.justification: V2 redraws the pipeline diagram, adds the intermediate-results visualization and Tables 4–7, and expands the BEHAVE illustration into a baseline comparison. Existing figures and tables are relocated or rearranged, and the appendix changes from two-column to full-width presentation alongside a new document layout.

R1.justification: V2 adds HIMO, TOUCH, and OpenHOI, acknowledging supervised multi-object and complementary hand-object synthesis research. It also elaborates the contrast with ZeroHOI, while retaining the broader positioning around zero-shot generation with explicit part-level structure.

T1.justification: Appendix A newly defines thresholded part-contact accuracy and contact distance averaged from minimum part distances across frames. The PAG definitions and optimization mathematics otherwise remain equivalent; condensed fitting-loss notation and renumbered equations introduce no new proof or theoretical guarantee.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens evidence for the central part-affordance claim: v1 measured contact globally and demonstrated BEHAVE only qualitatively, whereas v2 adds manually verified part-contact evaluation and quantitative BEHAVE baseline comparisons. Foundation-model sensitivity tests, intermediate outputs, and runtime profiling further clarify dependencies and practical costs. Uncertainty reporting remains limited, but the new evidence addresses important experimental gaps and supports a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe HOI-PAGE. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and Appendices A–B are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial rewriting and reformatting.

after.justification: V2 retains these original results and adds foundation-model robustness experiments, part-contact measurements, quantitative BEHAVE comparisons, and runtime measurements.

before.justification: V1 reports original generation experiments, quantitative comparisons, ablations, and a 30-participant perceptual study, with additional qualitative results in Appendix A.

results.title: HOI-PAGE: Zero-Shot Human-Object Interaction Generation with Part Affordance Guidance

C1.justification: The abstract and introductory contributions retain the same central dispersion, localization, averaging and scalability claims. The conclusion extends the claimed theoretical grounding to both deterministic and probabilistic analysis and explicitly claims robustness, supported by the newly presented resolution-transfer experiments.

C2.justification: V1 treats the 0.2-point averaging gain mainly as support for its design. V2 explains that value projection contributes more at standard resolution, while averaging matters increasingly at larger resolutions, and discusses how fine-tuning may alter dispersion. It also interprets measured dispersion differences between vision and language and sharpens limitations: practical token counts may not approach the asymptotic regime, and demonstrated applicability remains limited to vision.

D1.justification: V2 adds a source-code link and a supplemental-code statement, ADE20K implementation and optimizer settings, SEMA-S stage depths, and the batch size for 1024-squared inputs. Appendix D newly documents higher-resolution window size and distinct VMamba/SEMA fine-tuning recipes. These substantially expand reproducibility information without establishing that retained experiments changed.

E1.justification: V2 adds ADE20K semantic segmentation and evaluates models trained at 224 squared on larger-resolution inputs without fine-tuning, introducing a resolution-shift scenario. Appendix C also presents medical segmentation benchmarks, but explicitly as results reproduced from another work rather than new SEMA experiments.

E2.justification: Within ImageNet Table 2, v2 adds Flatten-CSwin-T and removes EfficientFormerV2-L and LRFormer-S. It also reports larger baseline variants and introduces ResNet-50 and DeiT-S + MLN in the ADE20K comparison. The principal comparator families remain; DefMamba-S matches v1's DefMamba entry rather than constituting a new tiny-scale comparator.

E3.justification: Evaluation expands from tiny models to T/S/B configurations, adds untuned resolution testing, extends classification to 1024 squared and measures latency through 2048 squared. ADE20K introduces single-scale and multi-scale mIoU evaluation. The stated ImageNet initial learning rate is corrected from 4×10^3 to 4×10^-3; this textual correction does not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 retains the original averaging ablation but adds a value-projection removal control and averaging ablations at 672 squared with and without fine-tuning (Tables 7–8). It also adds untuned resolution-robustness tests and quantitative analysis of pretrained MILA's dispersion coefficients. These substantially broaden investigation of which components help and under what conditions.

E5.justification: V2 newly discloses that most experiments use one run and that SEMA-T was consistent across an unspecified several runs. Runtime results average 1000 executions, and the dispersion analysis reports distribution means and standard deviations. Accuracy confidence intervals, exact repeat counts and seeds remain unspecified; an increase in training repetitions is not established.

E6.justification: V2 adds SEMA-S/B ImageNet accuracies of 84.6/85.4, ADE20K mIoU of 48.2/48.5, and new runtime, untuned-resolution, ablation and dispersion results. SEMA-T's 83.7 accuracy, previously reported fine-tuned accuracies and COCO AP values remain unchanged. Table 2 drops MILA-T's published 83.5 entry while retaining 83.3 without v1's retraining marker; SEMA's COCO FLOPs change from 277G to 275G.

M1.justification: The core window-attention-plus-averaging design and value projection remain. However, v1 Algorithm 2 applies RoPE to Qw, Kw and Vw, whereas v2 Appendix G applies it only to Qw and Kw. This changes the specified procedure; the PDFs do not establish whether the implementation changed or its description was corrected.

P1.justification: The experimental narrative is reorganized into task-specific discussions, the brief appendix ablation becomes an expanded main-text Section 6, and limitations move to Appendix A. Algorithms and MILA justification move into appendices, alongside new experiment-setting sections. This substantially changes document organization even though much introductory and related-work prose is retained.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a two-column main text and extensively restructures displays: ImageNet comparisons are grouped by model scale, Table 3 gains untuned results, and COCO's vertically stacked panels become side-by-side columns. New runtime, segmentation and ablation tables are added. Existing diagrams are retained and resized or relocated, while the paired main-text algorithms become one appendix algorithm.

R1.justification: V2 adds connections to multi-query attention and DeepSeek-V2 latent attention, discusses the cited USEMA medical adaptation, and adds references supporting new experiments and probability analysis. It removes references associated with CPE, EfficientFormerV2 and LRFormer. The central positioning relative to MILA, Swin and earlier dispersion research remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: V2 adds Proposition 3.5/B.4, a probabilistic dispersion statement under bounded covariance and sparse positive dependence, with a new proof. It revises the generalized-attention definition and deterministic proof, explicitly handling all queries and heads, and corrects attention formulas and the Mamba induction. V1's auxiliary dispersion lemma is incorporated into the revised proof rather than substantively discarded.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation of SEMA's central design: Tables 7–8 separate value-projection and averaging effects, Table 3 tests resolution transfer without retraining, and Tables 4 and 6 add measured speed and semantic-segmentation evidence. Expanded implementation details and code-access information improve reproducibility. These gains outweigh reporting weaknesses, including mostly single-run accuracy results and the new probabilistic proof's failure to justify its stated simultaneous guarantee over all sufficiently large sequence lengths.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SEMA research work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison across renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: V2 retains original experiments and adds ADE20K segmentation, runtime measurements, resolution-generalization tests and ablations. Appendix C separately identifies its medical-image results as reproduced from Dayag et al.

before.justification: V1 reports original ImageNet-1K classification, higher-resolution fine-tuning, COCO segmentation and averaging-ablation results.

results.title: SEMA: a Scalable and Efficient Mamba like Attention via Token Localization and Averaging

C1.justification: The central claims about GP-based generalization, adaptation, and uncertainty-guided active learning remain essentially unchanged. The contribution list explicitly extends the stated scope to closed-loop evaluation and simulation-to-real transfer. The conclusion drops v1's explicit nuScenes state-of-the-art claim while retaining the broader robustness claims.

C2.justification: v3 elaborates the existing mechanism explanation through comparisons with deterministic anchors, semantic interpretations of token subclusters, and higher long-tail variance interpreted as lower confidence. It also interprets the new kernel and codebook ablations. These refine the original explanation rather than replace it; substantial new limitations or failure-boundary discussion is absent.

D1.justification: v3 specifies the 256-dimensional basis tokens, adds Algorithm 2 documenting the existing unsupervised-adaptation procedure, and supplies budgets for the new transfer experiments. Original nuScenes hardware, staged training durations, and computational-cost measurements are retained. The additions remain limited, and Algorithm 2 inconsistently mentions standard trajectory losses despite its unsupervised setting.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates nuScenes, including city transfer, turning and long-tail scenarios, low light, and motion blur. v3 adds Bench2Drive, Bench2Drive-to-nuScenes transfer, NAVSIM v1, and DriveArena evaluations, substantially extending environmental and interactive-driving coverage. Snow and fog are also added.

E2.justification: v3 adds evaluated comparators including SSR, ORION, GenAD, and DriveTransformer in new experiments. Senna and DiMA join the retained cross-city and long-tail comparisons. Active learning gains MC Dropout and Deep Ensemble comparisons, while Table 14 compares GP planning against MLP, diffusion, and VAE heads.

E3.justification: New protocols include Bench2Drive training on 1,000 clips and evaluation on 220 routes, closed-loop driving and ability metrics, and 12-epoch source training followed by 12-epoch sim-to-real adaptation. NAVSIM and DriveArena introduce additional planning metrics. Corruption experiments now include supervised and unsupervised adaptation, and agent prediction adds minADE/minFDE. The original nuScenes protocol is retained.

E4.justification: The original loss ablation is retained as Table 11. New analyses test kernel choice, trajectory-codebook diversity, alternative planner heads, and stronger uncertainty-based sampling methods. Appendix H adds variance and embedding evolution during training and uncertainty comparisons across ordinary and long-tail scenes. Corruption robustness also gains adaptation analyses.

E5.justification: v3 first reports numerical GP predictive variances across scene categories and a variance-versus-training curve in Table 19 and Figure 5; v1 describes and uses this uncertainty without reporting those diagnostics. This expands model-uncertainty reporting, not uncertainty around benchmark performance: neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantial closed-loop, transfer, robustness, and ablation results. New Table 18 reports agent minADE/minFDE of 0.62/0.99 for SparseDrive-S versus 0.54/0.83 with RoCA regularization. Many original nuScenes results remain unchanged. Some retained cross-city entries change beyond rounding: VAD-Tiny unsupervised Singapore-to-Boston L2 changes from 0.951 in v1 Table 2 to 0.94 in v3 Table 3, without an explained setting change.

M1.justification: The codebook, GP architecture, and staged training procedure remain. However, the stated losses change: negative log-sigma terms become positive, and the negative agent-motion term in v1 Eq. 5 becomes positive in v3 Eq. 6. These are limited objective corrections; the PDFs do not establish corresponding implementation changes or reruns.

P1.justification: The narrative is substantially reorganized: closed-loop and transfer experiments lead the evaluation, standardized nuScenes evaluation moves into Appendix A, and earlier training, computation, and ablation appendices become its subsections. Related work is condensed, the problem formulation gains GP preliminaries, and several experimental explanations and the conclusion are rewritten.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from single-column to two-column presentation. Figure 1 gains explicit loss and supervision annotations; the t-SNE display is revised to annotated city panels and enlarged in the appendix. Numerous new tables, expanded comparator and corruption tables, and training-diagnostic plots substantially change the visual presentation. Existing qualitative examples are retained and relocated.

R1.justification: v3 substantially broadens the comparison landscape through newer driving models, simulation benchmarks, uncertainty-estimation approaches, and additional GP vision literature. Appendix B explicitly positions GP planning against alternative planner heads, while the active-learning discussion compares uncertainty approaches. Several earlier multitask-driving references disappear, although the central positioning of GP integration into autonomous driving remains.

T1.justification: The loss-sign corrections revise the mathematical content of the claimed Gaussian-likelihood objectives, rather than merely changing notation. The predictive-variance expression is also corrected. v3 adds standard GP background in Section 3.1 and Appendix C, but no new theorem, proof, or substantive theoretical guarantee.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses an important weakness of v1's deployment claims: reliance on open-loop nuScenes evidence. Closed-loop and cross-domain evaluations, stronger active-learning comparators, and targeted kernel, codebook, and planner-head ablations substantially strengthen empirical support. Corrected loss signs improve mathematical consistency. These gains outweigh localized reporting problems, including unexplained cross-city numerical changes and inconsistent unsupervised-adaptation pseudocode; benchmark uncertainty reporting remains limited.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe RoCA. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables, and rendered figures, support reliable comparison and identification of relocated material.

after.justification: v3 retains original nuScenes results and adds simulation, cross-domain, ablation, agent-prediction, and training-diagnostic results.

before.justification: v1 reports original nuScenes experiments covering planning, cross-city adaptation, active learning, image degradations, and loss ablations.

results.title: RoCA: Robust Cross-Domain End-to-End Autonomous Driving

C1.justification: The central claims about PBP correction, byte-level conversion, ensembling, and proxy-tuning remain. v3 adds an explicit claim of being first to combine exactness, efficiency, and compatibility with future-dependent pretokenization. Its contribution list qualifies distribution preservation by invalid-token probability mass, while the abstract drops v1's unqualified preservation wording.

C2.justification: v1 largely treats invalid-token mass as negligible. v3 distinguishes local from global validity and acknowledges contrary findings in Appendix D. It also explains beam failures, qualifies the cross-model efficiency comparison, and interprets byte-sampling slowdown relative to bytes per token. These substantially expand the discussion of assumptions and practical limitations.

D1.justification: v3 documents special-token mappings, digit-group handling, ignore_merges, normalization, added-token automata, and tested tokenizer families. It also discloses the independent 25-million-character samples underlying conversion factors. These substantially expand reproducibility information, although v3 omits the explicit ByteSampler repository link provided in v1.

E1.justification: v3 adds substantive code-completion evaluation using HumanEval Random Span with the suffix discarded, extending beyond v1's illustrative code examples. It also reports tokenizer-correctness testing on at least 1 GB of Pile fragments. The original English, Chinese, ensemble, and proxy-tuning task coverage remains.

E2.justification: v3 newly evaluates Beam Summing at beam sizes 1, 3, 10, and 128 in Tables 10–11; v1 mentions beam search but reports no such comparison. Existing comparator families largely remain. The corresponding Phan-method rows retain identical numerical results despite updated naming and attribution.

E3.justification: The original evaluation protocols largely remain, but Appendices E–F introduce substantial new designs: controlled latency workloads, shared-vLLM beam comparisons with losses restricted to jointly successful examples, prefix-only code evaluation using pass@1, and matched byte/token decoding settings. The new Phan timing comparison explicitly uses different 7B models, so it is not a same-model speed comparison.

E4.justification: v3 adds invalid-next-token masking analyses for OLMo2 1B and 7B, beam-width sensitivity and empty-beam failure analysis, tokenizer-correctness checks, and controlled comparisons of decoding transformations at byte versus token level. These examine assumptions, robustness, and decoding behavior that v1 did not experimentally investigate.

E5.justification: v1 reports point estimates without uncertainty intervals. v3 adds 95% confidence intervals to proxy-tuning results, bounds the ensemble confidence intervals, reports uncertainty summaries for new measurements, and specifies 30 runs per method for the standard-sampling timing comparison. This does not establish that the retained experiments were rerun.

E6.justification: Tables 9–15 add runtime, beam-failure, masking, code-completion, and decoding results, including ByteSampler versus naive pass@1 of 0.824 versus 0.565. Original ensemble, proxy-tuning, and character-accuracy point estimates remain unchanged. Normalized losses are corrected: for example, ByteSampler's English bits per character changes from 0.81 to 0.87 and Chinese from 3.23 to 3.43, with unchanged raw losses.

M1.justification: The core covering-tree, pairwise-pruning, and streaming procedures remain. Appendix F adds token-level sampling transformations before aggregation into byte probabilities; v1 Appendix E only discussed the mismatch between byte-level and token-level transformations. Other expanded tokenizer-handling passages primarily provide implementation documentation.

P1.justification: The introduction and method exposition are extensively rewritten and reorganized. v3 presents covering-tree definitions and applications before their properties and streaming implementation, replaces the introductory example, and restructures the appendices. Existing tree examples move from Appendix D to G, and advanced decoding moves from E to F.

P2.justification: v3 adopts a two-column main layout, rearranges existing diagrams, adds a next-byte probability illustration, and redesigns the comparison table. The BPE walkthrough table is replaced by pseudocode, seven experimental tables are added, and the retained example trees are relocated. These are substantial display changes beyond renumbering.

R1.justification: v3 substantially revises positioning around tokenizer compatibility and the assumptions of competing exact methods. It incorporates canonical-generation work by Chatzi and Vieira, conflicting evidence about invalid segmentations from Geh and Vieira, and self-distillation research. This changes the scientific comparison with prior work beyond bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: Appendix D adds compactness, pairwise-validity, and prefix-probability proofs beyond v1's informal arguments. It revises whole-sequence-validity conditioning to prompt-covering validity and explains local canonicalization under repeated sampling. Table 1 also changes Back Tokenization's CPU complexity from exponential to linear, although v3's prose still describes exponential overhead.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens support for central claims: v1's token-count efficiency evidence is supplemented with measured runtimes and a same-model overhead comparison, while invalid-token assumptions and boundary-sensitive code completion receive direct tests. The revised distribution analysis and uncertainty reporting improve interpretability. Repeated baseline labels in Table 14, inconsistent complexity descriptions, and omission of the code link weaken parts of the revision, but the overall evidential gains are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ByteSampler work. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable, and retained content can be matched across substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds runtime benchmarks, invalid-token analyses, tokenizer validation, and code-completion experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original inference-cost measurements, English and Chinese prediction experiments, and downstream ensemble and proxy-tuning results.

results.title: Sampling from Your Language Model One Byte at a Time

C1.justification: The central claims about harmful expert overtraining, difficult-example memorization and beneficial early stopping remain. v2 explicitly extends the headline scope across model scales and asserts a causal role for negative parameter interference. MoErging is reframed as an appendix extension while its substantive claim is retained.

C2.justification: v2 develops the previously hypothesized memorization mechanism into a stronger causal account involving idiosyncratic updates and parameter interference. It presents early stopping as a general principle and suggests one plateau-stage checkpoint may suffice. The conclusion removes v1's explicit limitations concerning small models, restricted method coverage and already-published adapters.

D1.justification: v2 adds a public-code access statement, early-stopping pseudocode and the previously unspecified 1e-7 stopping threshold. It supplies additional comparator tuning grids, model settings and analysis procedures. Appendix B also clarifies that tuning occurs separately for every duration and seed; this documents existing evaluation rather than establishing a changed protocol.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same eight vision classification datasets and seven NLP tasks. The additional ViT, BERT and T5 evaluations reuse this coverage, and MoErging remains in Appendix K. Randomly withholding examples introduces experimental controls within existing datasets.

E2.justification: v2 adds Iso-C, Iso-CTS and TSV-M to the evaluated merging methods in Figures 1–2. DARE also joins the NLP comparisons, where v1 Figure 2 evaluated only Average, Task Arithmetic and TIES, and the forgotten-example comparison expands to include DARE.

E3.justification: v2 adds ViT-L-14, BERT-Base, T5-Large and T5-3B configurations, language early-stopping protocols, and new memorization/interference measurements. Its randomized memorization experiment withholds 90 examples per training run across difficulty groups. The original dataset splits and raw-accuracy evaluation remain.

E4.justification: Section 4 and Appendices D–I add randomized example-inclusion analyses, early-versus-late prediction diagnostics, parameter-interference measurements, per-task breakdowns and model-scale sensitivity. These substantially extend the mechanism and generality checks. Existing pruning, LoRA-rank and MoErging analyses are retained, including material relocated to appendices.

E5.justification: Beyond v1's mean/standard-deviation reporting, v2 adds inclusion-conditioned memorization estimation using 40 seeded models per dataset and Pearson correlations with significance tests in Appendix H. Appendix I specifies aggregation across task pairs and seeds. Figure 2 reports three seeds instead of two; the PDFs do not establish how the underlying runs were updated.

E6.justification: v2 adds results for new comparators and model configurations, T5 early stopping, memorization and interference. Table 2 reports 77.0 ± 0.3% TIES accuracy for aggressive T5 early stopping. Retained forgotten-example shares also change, such as Task Arithmetic's hardest-bin share from 28.7% to 28.3%. Table 1's merging means and the MoErging table results are retained.

M1.justification: Section 5.2 adds a T5 early-stopping procedure using constant learning rates, validation intervals/patiences of (100, 5) or (50, 3), and best-validation-checkpoint selection. The existing vision warm-up/adaptive-decay strategy and MoErging procedure are retained; the added vision pseudocode primarily documents the existing method.

P1.justification: The title, introduction, mechanism narrative, early-stopping discussion, related work and conclusion are substantially revised. LoRA-rank analysis moves to Appendix G, and MoErging material is consolidated in Appendix K. Section 4 is organized around three observations, and Section 5 separates vision and language strategies.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column layout and substantially expands its displays. Figure 2 gains a model-scale panel, Table 1 gains an Experts column and result highlighting, and the forgotten-example display gains DARE. New diagnostic figures, tables and pseudocode accompany relocated rank/MoErging displays. Reversed FFT/LoRA panel descriptions in v1 captions are corrected.

R1.justification: v2 adds SVD-merging references, work on specialized fine-tuning procedures, and Zhou et al.'s task-vector/gradient analysis.
