Section 6 explains how studying standard fine-tuning complements these approaches, while two broad MoE-upcycling references disappear. The central positioning around expert training duration and data difficulty remains.

T1.justification: v2 introduces formal definitions for inclusion-conditioned memorization and parameter-interference diagnostics, including pruned support sets and a zero-mean assumption for its variance measure. These are limited formal additions supporting empirical analyses; no new theorem or proof is developed, and the original merging, LoRA and MoErging mathematics remain.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens v1's largely indirect memorization evidence through randomized example inclusion, broader comparator/model validation and NLP early-stopping experiments. Added code-access information and implementation detail improve reproducibility. The stronger causal account remains imperfect: Appendix I labels an uncentered second moment as variance, gives inconsistent pruning-threshold definitions, and states a 60-fold increase where Table 4 implies about 604-fold. These weaknesses limit the mechanism interpretation but do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical support and practical usefulness.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study, with matching authors, datasets and retained experiments. Text, figures, tables, equations and appendices are readable. The expanded and reorganized material in v2 supports a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds evaluations of further merging methods and models, randomized memorization experiments, interference analyses and NLP early stopping.

before.justification: v1 reports original vision and NLP experiments on expert training duration, model merging, LoRA rank, data difficulty, MoErging and early stopping.

results.title: From Memorization to Parameter Interference: How Overtraining Experts Harms Model Merging

C1.justification: The interaction-layer and ACDA contributions remain central. The abstract and introduction extend the performance claims to measured WiFi delays and competitors handling unobservable random delays, and the introduction now acknowledges DCAC's use of hindsight delay information.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive discussion of missing convergence guarantees, performance under independent delays, computational bottlenecks, bandwidth requirements, and delays outside the interaction layer. Section 5 also qualifies superiority under alternative CDA settings, stating that ACDA leads in 15 of 25 benchmarks when all evaluated configurations are considered.

D1.justification: V2 documents WiFi collection using 100000 packets, 8 ms intervals, and 12000-byte payloads; explicitly specifies prediction-length and buffer-horizon choices; and explains Dreamer/DCAC integration and runtime. It also adds an explicit code-archive access link. These substantially expand reproducibility information beyond v1's existing architecture and hyperparameter details.

E1.justification: The same five MuJoCo tasks remain, but v2 extends the three simulated delay processes with library and office WiFi recordings replayed in simulation. Appendix F additionally evaluates independent Poisson(3) and DCAC WiFi delays, substantially broadening the delay conditions tested.

E2.justification: Dreamer, implemented using Dreamerv3, and DCAC join the existing comparisons in Section 5 and Appendix E.1. DCAC was explicitly excluded in v1. BPQL with the MDA policy was already evaluated in v1 and is retained.

E3.justification: V2 adds noise sweeps, floor/ceiling average-delay CDA settings, measured-trace replay with 99th-percentile delay bounds, and observation-skipping rates. The original million-step training and ten-trajectory evaluation schedule remains. The new WiFi low-CDA captions specify h=4 in Figures 28–29, whereas Table 8 specifies 1, leaving that particular setting inconsistent.

E4.justification: V2 retains the original MDA and low-CDA ablations while substantially extending noise sensitivity, including comparisons across 0–25% noise. It adds average-delay CDA sensitivity, tests violations of temporal correlation, evaluates packet skipping, and analyzes computational costs in Appendices B.2, E.4, F, and G.

E5.justification: Appendix B.2 newly discloses VDPO's fixed environment-reset seed and explains zero standard deviations in noiseless evaluations. Both versions retain ten-trajectory evaluations and standard-deviation reporting; v2 does not add reported repetitions across independent training seeds or confidence intervals.

E6.justification: V2 adds extensive WiFi, independent-delay, noise, timing, and packet-skipping results. Original synthetic-delay benchmark and ablation scores are retained. Existing noise-study values also change: BPQL's HalfCheetah return at delay 3 without noise changes from 7839.43 in v1 Figure 9 to 8159.28 in v2 Table 3.

M1.justification: The principal interaction layer, memorized-action heuristic, latent model, and training objectives are retained. Appendix G.3 adds an evaluated packet-skipping adaptation that generates actions from selected observations and makes memorized-action prediction account for skipped packets.

P1.justification: The main section order and much of the original exposition remain. V2 polishes language, reorganizes related-work paragraphs, clarifies delay and clock terminology, and updates appendix navigation. The continuous-time appendix moves from F to H without a substantive rewrite.

P2.justification: The main text changes from a single-column layout to a two-column conference format. Figure 2 is substantially redrawn, Table 1 changes its rows and displayed delay conditions, and numerous new experimental displays are added. Appendix E.5 also consolidates previously displayed results into comparison tables.

R1.justification: V1 characterizes DCAC as requiring observable delays; v2 recognizes its handling of unobservable delays and shifts the distinction toward control over action execution. Related-work positioning also expands to offline delayed RL, action chunking, and measured network-delay correlation, substantially revising the novelty context.

T1.justification: The POMDP formalization, model objective, and continuous-time mathematics are retained. Appendix G adds limited computational-cost reasoning, including sequential work proportional to h+L and the packet-generation time derivation in Equation 35. No convergence proof is added.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses an important comparison gap by revising its characterization of DCAC and actually evaluating it alongside Dreamer. Measured WiFi-delay replay and tests of noise, delay assumptions, independence, and computational constraints substantially strengthen the evidence and clarify applicability. Reproducibility also improves. Some overstatement remains: the introduction's 'all except one' claim overlooks the new Office/Hopper exception in Table 14, but this does not outweigh the substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same interaction-layer and ACDA research, with readable text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Retained material can be matched reliably, including v1 Appendix F, which becomes v2 Appendix H.

after.justification: V2 retains those experiments and adds original WiFi-delay measurements, simulation results using those measurements, robustness experiments, and execution-time measurements.

before.justification: V1 reports original MuJoCo experiments comparing ACDA with baselines, plus noise-sensitivity and adaptation ablations in the appendices.

results.title: Adaptive Reinforcement Learning for Unobservable Random Delays

C1.justification: v3 elevates active R2-based GPZ localization and label-distribution-controlled training dynamics, termed Neural Vortex, into central contributions. It strengthens the transition claim to necessity for intrinsic resistance while describing the entropy increase through a lower bound. v1 primarily emphasizes favorable transition/decision splits and depth insufficiency. The headline fourfold-MSE and 66% resistance claims remain.

C2.justification: v3 revises the account of one-hot radius dynamics and qualifies sustained label-smoothing gradients as an overconfidence phenomenon that vanishes at the smoothed optimum. Appendix C acknowledges potentially vacuous absolute bounds. The discussion adds substantive deployment trade-offs, adverse-distribution limitations and cautious hypotheses for text Transformers; Appendix G explicitly limits Neural Vortex to an explanatory metaphor.

D1.justification: v3 replaces the code placeholder with a concrete repository URL and supplies locator pseudocode, detailed enhancement-module definitions, the CIFAR-10 super-resolution source, and the actual FaceScrub acquisition count of 43,149 images. It also documents preprocessing, LPIPS configuration and deployment measurement procedures. These disclosures do not establish that the retained experiments changed preprocessing or were rerun.

E1.justification: v3 Appendix H.7 and Table 10 add MNIST as a reconstruction target, using MNIST, EMNIST and KMNIST as auxiliary sources. In v1, MNIST appears only as auxiliary data for the Japanese-character target. The other target domains remain, and clarifying that KMNIST denotes Kuzushiji-49 does not establish a new dataset.

E2.justification: The attack comparator sets are retained: v1 Tables 3–5 correspond to v3 Tables 9, 3 and 4. The limited addition is Table 5's explicit comparison of the new automatic locator against empirically identified transition zones.

E3.justification: v3 adds SSIM and AlexNet-based LPIPS to MSE/PSNR evaluation, introduces ResNet-50 target configurations, and evaluates automatic localization. Appendix I adds a separate deployment protocol using batch-one inference, eight CPU threads, latency, memory, communication and RAPL energy measurements. The previously stated core dataset splits and optimizer settings are retained.

E4.justification: New analyses test dimension normalization and sampling, training-seed and label-smoothing stability of GPZ localization in Appendix D. Appendix H.5 adds ResNet-50 evidence separating depth from dimensional expansion, H.7 extends auxiliary-distribution analysis to an MNIST target, and Appendix I quantifies deployment trade-offs. The earlier attack-enhancement ablations remain.

E5.justification: v3 newly reports localization agreement across resampled evaluations (3/3, pairwise Jaccard 1.00) and consistency across independent training seeds, although the training-run count is unspecified. Appendix I reports mean/p95 latency over 200 timed passes and a 500-iteration energy window. These are limited additions, not evidence of increased replication for the retained attack results.

E6.justification: The MSE/PSNR values in v1 Tables 3–5 are retained in their corresponding v3 tables. Substantial new results include SSIM/LPIPS scores, ResNet-50 reconstruction outcomes, MNIST-target results, localization comparisons and deployment costs. For example, Table 11 newly reports VGG depth-26/30 mean latencies of 2.60/2.65 ms and payloads of 256/128 KB; these are added measurements, not before-to-after performance gains.

M1.justification: v3 introduces an automatic GPZ selection procedure absent from v1. Appendix D and Algorithm 1 compute class-wise radii, normalize by representation dimension, and use relative drops and a threshold to select the transition zone. This adds an operational partition-selection method; the existing feature-enhancement and inversion architectures are largely retained.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, theoretical narrative and discussion are extensively rewritten around GPZ localization and Neural Vortex. Related work, dataset descriptions, implementation material and face-result discussion move into reorganized appendices with a roadmap. This is substantial narrative restructuring beyond the added scientific content.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn, Figures 4–5 gain SSIM/LPIPS panels, and new localization, ResNet-50, MNIST and deployment displays are introduced. Existing final-output and face results are relocated, with the final-output table expanded and its misleading caption corrected. The document also changes its template and uses full-width appendix layouts.

R1.justification: v3 substantially expands positioning through comparisons with neural collapse, mutual-information regularization and estimation, and encrypted private inference, including Split HE and PRISM. The introduction and Appendix J explicitly frame intrinsic split selection as complementary to existing defenses and distinguish its evaluation from defense-versus-defense competition.

T1.justification: v1's purported entropy-gap bound becomes an explicitly defined gap between upper-bound surrogates in v3 Eq. 8. Eq. 9 adds label-entropy and finite-precision corrections, supported by new discretization/KL derivations in Appendices B–C. Appendices E–F correct label-smoothing normalization, revise gradient-alignment reasoning, add target-reshaping derivations, and replace the unconditional nonzero-gradient claim with bounds requiring overconfidence and suitable Jacobian projections.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses important weaknesses in v1's entropy-gap reasoning and unconditional label-smoothing gradient claim, and makes partition selection operational through a documented, evaluated locator. Perceptual metrics, implementation disclosures and measured deployment trade-offs substantially strengthen the paper's assessability and practical relevance. Broad necessity claims and some inconsistent gradient wording remain, but these residual weaknesses do not outweigh the theoretical corrections and stronger supporting evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same collaborative-inference partitioning study despite the changed title. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable, and retained experiments can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds ResNet-50 experiments, MNIST-target results, automatic partition-zone localization checks and deployment measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original reconstruction experiments across vision models, partition depths, label-smoothing conditions, attack enhancements and auxiliary datasets.

results.title: Partitioning for Intrinsic Model Inversion Resistance in Collaborative Inference

C1.justification: V1 claims exact handcrafted implementations and architectural routes to clustering variants, explicitly deferring learnability. V2’s abstract, contributions, and conclusion additionally claim that training produces a generalizable clustering algorithm outperforming Lloyd’s on new tasks. Compact model size is also foregrounded, expanding the contribution from constructive expressivity to learned clustering effectiveness.

C2.justification: V2 interprets learned attention sparsity and weight structure, explains sensitivity through loss smoothing, and attributes OpenML underperformance to training-distribution mismatch. Its limitations explicitly distinguish empirical learning from unproved generalization guarantees and state that transfer to larger cluster counts is unsupported. These replace v1’s broader deferral of learnability with substantive mechanisms and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: V2 adds a code repository link and a detailed training recipe: mixture-generation steps, normalization to the unit hypercube, loss temperatures, learning-rate decay, training budgets, and iterative inference instructions. OpenML sampling procedures are also documented. V1 provides prescribed weights and mentions PyTorch but lacks these training and access details.

E1.justification: Beyond v1’s synthetic numerical validation, v2 evaluates transfer to Cauchy, Laplace, Gumbel, and lognormal mixtures and 15 OpenML datasets (Appendix B.4). Appendix I additionally evaluates robust clustering and randomized k-medoids on 10 OpenML datasets; these algorithms were only developed theoretically in v1.

E2.justification: Lloyd’s remains the main comparator. V2 Table 4 adds an evaluated comparison between robust k-means and trimmed k-means, which v1 presented without experimental comparison. The k-means++ experiment changes initialization of the retained methods. PAM and CLARANS remain cited methods rather than evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: New learning experiments introduce 10,000 training steps, batches of 32 clustering tasks, 320 validation tasks, and synthetic evaluation over 20 clustering steps. V2 also tests k-means++ initialization and specifies OpenML subsampling to at most 1024 points and 32 features with 10 clustering steps. These are added protocols, not demonstrated changes to v1’s retained validation.

E4.justification: V1’s parameter-sensitivity analysis survives as v2 Figure 7. V2 adds embedding-dimension ablations, loss-temperature and training-convergence studies, distribution-transfer tests, learned-weight and attention-map analyses, and sensitivity to robust-clustering parameters and the medoid sampling gap (Figures 4–6, 8–10; Tables 4–5).

E5.justification: V1 explains error bars through variation across parameter settings. V2 adds training curves aggregated over 10 random trials with interquartile ribbons, min–max ranges over 320 test tasks, and mean±standard deviation over 40 OpenML trials. Tables 4–5 additionally disclose aggregation over 10 trials.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial results for the learned model and existing algorithm variants. Table 1 reports average log objectives of 5.0052 versus Lloyd’s 5.2636 on Gaussian tasks, but 3.3443 versus 3.2528 on Cauchy tasks. Table 2 favors Lloyd’s on all 15 OpenML datasets. Tables 4–5 add robust-clustering and medoid results. These are new comparisons, not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: V1 prescribes transformer weights and leaves learning for future work. V2 adds learning of Q/K/V matrices using a smoothed k-means loss and iterative reuse of a trained single-layer model, resetting auxiliary embeddings between clustering steps (Appendix B). The handcrafted constructions largely remain. Section 2.4 specifies a rectified-quadratic FFN, inconsistently with Appendix F’s retained ordinary-quadratic construction.

P1.justification: V2 retitles the paper and substantially rewrites the abstract, introduction, and discussion, adding explicit contributions and a separate conclusion. Box 1 becomes explanatory prose, the existing dot-product construction gains a main-text section, and the single Methods appendix is reorganized into thematic appendices with a contents page.

P2.justification: V2 adds learning and diagnostic Figures 4–6 and 8–10 and results Tables 1, 2, 4, and 5. V1 Figures 4–5 and Table 1 are relocated as v2 Figures 7 and 11 and Table 3, with an appendix-reference column added to the table. Figure 3 is redrawn, captions expand, and boxed presentation changes substantially.

R1.justification: V2 substantially reframes positioning around compact constructive expressivity relative to universal approximation and Turing-completeness results. It adds that literature, further in-context-learning references, and clustering-initialization references, while removing v1’s extended mechanistic-interpretability framing and RASP/ALTA comparison. The change exceeds bibliographic updates to retained works.

T1.justification: The central equivalence proofs are substantially retained, including v1’s dot-product construction in v2 Appendix F. Limited additions include the O(d+k) size corollary, the smoothed training objective and its limiting relation, and dot-product parameter invariance in Remark E.1. V2 also removes v1’s preliminary pairwise-similarity-to-k-means derivation.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses the learnability question explicitly left open in v1. Controlled learning comparisons, embedding ablations, and repeated-trial reporting establish practical capabilities, while Cauchy and OpenML failures clarify their boundaries. Added implementation details and the code link improve reproducibility. The unreconciled rectified-versus-ordinary quadratic FFN description is a weakness, but the gains in empirical support and understanding are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same transformer realization of clustering algorithms despite the title change. Their text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains numerical validation and adds original training, ablation, distribution-transfer, and OpenML experiments in Section 2.3 and Appendices B and I.

before.justification: Section 2.3 and Figures 3–4 report original numerical validation against Lloyd’s algorithm and experiments varying temperature, dimensionality, sample count, cluster count, and scaling.

results.title: Transformer Circuits Can Realize Clustering Algorithms

C1.justification: The abstract and central claims about loss embeddings, initialization robustness, supervised/unsupervised applicability, and linear-setting convergence remain. The introduction and conclusion extend the claimed practical advantages to sparse participation, stragglers, and low communication and computation overhead.

C2.justification: V1's categorical assertion that loss vectors reveal no client data becomes a qualified discussion of underexplored leakage and possible differential-privacy tradeoffs in v2 Appendix C. V2 also adds overhead and memory arguments, explains FedAvg's advantage under overlapping label distributions, and softens the unsupervised superiority statement to match the retained losses. The earlier explanation attributing client-count scaling benefits to longer loss vectors is removed.

D1.justification: V2 supplies a code-access URL for CLoVE and the self-implemented baselines, previously listed only as self-implemented. It adds an experiment-specific client/sample-count table, details Dirichlet allocation for the main label-skew experiments, and states default initialization. Hardware and Python/PyTorch versions remain unchanged. These are substantial documentation improvements, without establishing changes to every underlying experiment.

E1.justification: V2 adds FEMNIST classification with individual writers as clients and evaluates intermittent participation, including rounds with fewer participating clients than true clusters. These extend the represented client population and operating conditions. The original image, text, reconstruction, and synthetic regression coverage remains.

E2.justification: The main comparator set remains, with CFL renamed CFL-S. V2 adds FINCH versus k-means as a clustering-component comparison. IFCA curves disappear from the corresponding MNIST convergence plot, v1 Figure 5(a) versus v2 Figure 7, although IFCA remains in scalability tables. FedGWC is discussed but not experimentally compared.

E3.justification: The reported general batch size changes from 100 to 64. Convergence tables replace percentage of final ARI attained with absolute ARI at round 10. Added protocols include unknown-K initialization, stopping after three unchanged rounds, participation-dependent ARI evaluation, and scaling to 1000 clients versus 200 in v1's scaling plot. These reported changes do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix E adds analyses of unknown cluster counts, early stopping, partial participation, and FINCH versus k-means, and substantially expands scalability testing. These examine practical assumptions and component sensitivity beyond v1. The original initialization, matching, agglomerative-clustering, square-root-loss, and averaging analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions generally specify three seeds and mean plus standard deviation. However, v2 Appendix E.5 describes Table 18 as reporting mean and variance, without reconciling this with the general policy. It is unclear whether this introduces a different uncertainty statistic or is a wording error; no increased run count is established.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial results, including FEMNIST accuracy of 68.2 ± 1.3 and new cluster-count, stopping, participation, scaling, and FINCH results. Convergence entries also change: IFCA's reported first ARI ≥0.9 round for MNIST label skew 1 changes from 2.0 ± 0.0 to never reached. Most original accuracy and reconstruction-loss entries remain unchanged; changed metrics and settings preclude interpreting the revisions as same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: V1 requires a known cluster count and continues clustering throughout training. V2 Algorithms 1–2 introduce cluster-count selection using silhouette scores, stopping clustering after assignment stability, and assigning subsequent clients using saved models and centroids. These substantially extend the procedure; random client subsampling itself already existed in v1.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, main section sequence, and much existing prose remain. Revisions concentrate on the comparative introduction, method exposition, assumptions, and experimental setup. The main-text ablation summary is removed while its appendix content remains, and appendices are reorganized around the added algorithm and discussion sections.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a two-column conference layout for the main paper, redraws Figure 1 with an additional loss-vector illustration, and merges v1's image and text accuracy tables into Table 1. It adds protocol/result tables and participation plots, expands algorithm displays, and separates and redraws the original combined convergence figure. These substantially alter the visual presentation.

R1.justification: V2 adds FedGWC positioning in related work and Appendix C.3, plus FINCH, FEMNIST/LEAF, and matching references, while removing the UNEXT motivation. It also introduces explicit priority claims concerning extensive unsupervised evaluation and autoencoder clustering. Most of the existing literature discussion remains.

T1.justification: Theorems 4.1–4.2 and Appendix A's mathematical definitions, bounds, lemmas, and proofs are retained. The expanded assumptions and random, nearly orthogonal initialization explanation bring existing appendix material into the main exposition. No new theoretical guarantee is supplied for the added practical variants.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses important practical gaps in v1 through explicit procedures and experiments for unknown cluster counts, sparse participation, early stopping, and larger client populations. Code-access information and detailed experimental specifications improve reproducibility, while the revised privacy discussion corrects an overly categorical assurance. Cost savings still lack direct measurements, and batch-size and uncertainty-reporting ambiguities remain, but the gains in practical validation and transparency are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CLoVE research. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting.

after.justification: V2 retains original experimental results and adds FEMNIST, unknown-cluster-count, early-stopping, partial-participation, scalability, and FINCH comparisons.

before.justification: V1 reports original classification, reconstruction, mixed linear regression, initialization, scalability, and ablation experiments.

results.title: CLoVE: Personalized Federated Learning through Clustering of Loss Vector Embeddings

C1.justification: The task-dependent, means-to-an-end thesis and three principal value notions remain. The abstract and introduction shift the claimed contribution toward empirical estimators and demonstrated human-AI/mechanistic-interpretability evaluation, replacing v1's emphasis on general use-case formalization, including recourse and debugging.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations of contrasting deception/sentiment effects and SAE information saturation versus behavioral underuse. It discusses accounting for unobserved human private information. Conversely, v1 Section 5's explicit applicability limits concerning future-based and individualized decisions are removed.

D1.justification: V2 supplies task-specific data-construction and explanation procedures, clustering grids and tolerances, an 8,192-unit SAE, Qwen3-14B identification, and full prompt templates (Appendix F), replacing the housing implementation details. It also adds an OSF code/data access link.

E1.justification: The Ames housing experiment is removed. V2 evaluates cardiac dysfunction using MIMIC-IV/MIMIC-CXR, hotel-review deception, Amazon Books and Beer sentiment, and training-bias detection using Jigsaw toxic comments. These substantially broaden and replace the evaluated domains and tasks.

E2.justification: V1 evaluates SHAP alongside feature/model signal combinations. V2 adds evaluated comparisons involving LIME and factual/counterfactual medical examples, deception example/heatmap/random-heatmap conditions, expert/top-1/top-2/adaptive sentiment explanations, and SAE explanation variants with a no-explanation control.

E3.justification: V1's housing experiment uses an 80/20 split, linear simulated human predictions and MAPE. V2 introduces accuracy and biopsy-utility evaluations, retrospective human-study analyses, reconstructed deception explanations, rule-based clinical actions and Qwen3-14B simulated auditors. These are new evaluation designs, not same-setting reruns.

E4.justification: V1's housing signal-combination analysis is removed. V2 adds a focused SAE feature-count sensitivity analysis: theoretical value saturates around three features while behavioral effects continue increasing through five (Figure 3 and Table 2). Appendix D supplies formal robustness definitions rather than reported robustness experiments.

E5.justification: Both versions report 95% confidence intervals. V1 Figure 1 specifies t-distribution intervals, whereas v2 Figure 2 specifies bootstrap intervals with 1,000 resamples; v2 also reports treatment-effect intervals in Tables 1–2. This changes uncertainty estimation without documenting increased independent runs or seeds.

E6.justification: The housing results disappear and substantial new results are reported. Examples include medical theoretic value approximately 0.12, deception Heatmap treatment effect 0.10 [0.07, 0.13], and SAE-top-5 effect 0.04 [0.03, 0.05] (v2 Sections 3/5 and Tables 1–2). These are different-task findings, not performance improvements over v1.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 changes from repeatedly halving signal bins to jointly searching explanation and feature clusters, preserving garbling relationships and maximizing rational-agent payoff. Compared with v1 Appendix A, v2 Appendix C changes the estimator's objective, constraints and procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and related-work narrative are extensively rewritten. V2 reorganizes the framework around estimands, estimation and demonstrations, moves the existing proof and bounded-agent discussion into appendices, and changes terminology, title and author ordering.

P2.justification: The single-column main text becomes two-column with redesigned example boxes. The housing bar chart is removed; v2 adds a workflow diagram, embedded medical payoff plots, multipanel human-study/audit figures and two treatment-effect tables.

R1.justification: V2 adds explicit positioning against Chen et al.'s use-case-grounded simulations and connects the framework to pragmatic interpretability, mechanistic auditing and scoring-rule research. It substantially replaces v1's Alternative Views discussion, including cited critiques of conventional decision theory, rather than merely updating references.

T1.justification: V2 adds independent/contextual value decompositions and a Blackwell/V-shaped-scoring-rule robustness formulation (Appendix D). It replaces Gaussian-perturbed beliefs with stochastic-kernel garbling (Appendix E) and drops v1's coarsening approximation guarantee. The original no-additional-information proof is retained in Appendix B.

improvement.justification: V1 empirically illustrates the framework only through synthetic housing decisions. V2 substantially strengthens practical validation by relating theoretical benchmarks to observed human-study behavior, revising the estimator and supplying richer implementation details. Reconstructed deception explanations, simulated clinical/audit decisions and removal of broader applicability caveats limit the gains, but the framework's empirical grounding and usability improve substantially.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same decision-theoretic explanation-evaluation framework. Their text, equations, figures and appendices are readable and support comparison, including v1 Appendices A–B and v2 Appendices A–F.

after.justification: V2 reports medical-data experiments, original reanalyses of earlier human studies, and an alignment-audit experiment with simulated decision-makers (Sections 3–5 and Appendix F).

before.justification: V1 reports an original Ames housing analysis using XGBoost, SHAP and simulated human predictions, with numerical value estimates and confidence intervals (Examples 10/12 and Appendix B).

results.title: Explanations are a Means to an End: Decision Theoretic Explanation Evaluation

C1.justification: V1's central contribution concerns overcoming degradation in deep VGG-style networks. V3 adds residual-path timing as a third failure mechanism and claims successful ResNet18 training. It also makes incremental PC plus spiking precision central to its claim of backpropagation-comparable learning with operations local in space and time.

C2.justification: V3 adds explanations involving asynchronous residual feedback, incremental updates reducing the need for forward updates, and different BatchNorm-freezing effects in PC and iPC. Appendix D.2.3 proposes free relaxation to recompute initial predictions, qualifying the storage-related biological-plausibility limitation. New robustness and hyperparameter-transfer findings receive substantive interpretation.

D1.justification: V3 expands the pseudocode into explicit PC/iPC phases and documents ResNet blocks, channels, strides and relaxation ranges. Section 7 adds a promise to release code upon acceptance, without documenting an available release. Existing PCX, hardware, preprocessing and seed disclosures are largely retained.

E1.justification: The classification datasets remain CIFAR10, CIFAR100 and Tiny ImageNet. V3 adds corrupted-input evaluation using six corruption types at five intensities on CIFAR10 (Appendix D.2.2), extending input-condition coverage. ResNet additions concern architecture settings rather than new datasets.

E2.justification: V3 adds incremental PC, including centered-nudging comparisons in Figure 3, to the evaluated accuracy baselines and adds incremental-PC runtime comparisons in Table 7. The matched depth/nudging plot replaces decaying-precision variants with incremental-PC variants, although decay comparisons remain elsewhere.

E3.justification: The reported TPE search budget changes from 500 to 200 iterations (v1 Appendix A; v3 Appendix B). V3 adds ResNet configurations and relaxation-step ranges, corruption-calibration protocols, selective-layer forward-update controls and hyperparameter-transfer procedures. Its main benchmark also reports the best normalization configuration rather than separate normalization columns.

E4.justification: V3 adds auxiliary-neuron ablations, linear-decay comparisons, neural-divergence measurements and forward updates restricted to the last three layers (Tables 10–12). Corruption calibration, BatchNorm affine-parameter controls and hyperparameter importance/transfer studies substantially extend v1's component and energy analyses.

E5.justification: V3 introduces fANOVA-based statistical estimation of hyperparameter importance in Appendix E.1. Five-seed accuracy summaries and five-repetition timing measurements remain; the additional result rows do not establish an increase in repeated runs.

E6.justification: V3 adds extensive incremental-PC, ResNet and diagnostic results; Table 2 reports ResNet18/Tiny ImageNet top-1 accuracy of 57.83% for iPC plus spiking versus 58.18% for BP. Retained entries also change: non-BF VGG10/CIFAR100 S+F top-1 accuracy changes from 63.35 ± 0.12 to 69.08 ± 0.08 (v1 Table 1; v3 Table 8). This is a revised reported result, without evidence establishing a same-setting performance gain.

M1.justification: V3 introduces auxiliary neurons along residual connections to synchronize error propagation and extends the proposed training approach to incremental PC with within-inference weight updates (Section 4.2 and Algorithm 1). The original precision schedules, forward updates and BatchNorm freezing remain; decaying precision moves principally to Appendix D.1.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contribution list and conclusion are substantially rewritten. Methods are reorganized into algorithmic and structural contributions with embedded experiments, and the appendices are restructured into algorithm, settings, complexity, ablation and hyperparameter sections. Decaying precision and detailed benchmarks are relocated.

P2.justification: Figure 2 expands from four to seven panels, and Figure 4 combines a new residual-block diagram and auxiliary-neuron comparison with an expanded BatchNorm plot. Main benchmark tables are redesigned around additional architectures, while retained comparisons move to the appendix alongside numerous new diagnostic tables. These are substantial display and layout changes.

R1.justification: V3 adds references supporting incremental PC, incremental expectation-maximization, biological precision and free relaxation. Previously cited muPC receives an explicit comparison distinguishing its feedforward/MNIST scope, while several hardware and equilibrium-propagation references disappear. The broader PC/EP positioning remains recognizable.

T1.justification: V3 defines the Gap Ratio using initial-to-final neural-state divergence relative to layer update energy (Appendix D.2.1). It also removes v1's algebraic assertion that nudging can be reproduced by setting inverse output covariance to beta. The principal energy and precision equations remain, with no new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens v1's limited architectural validation and largely indirect mechanism evidence through residual-network interventions, incremental-PC comparisons, targeted forward-update controls and BatchNorm controls (Figure 4; Tables 10–12 and 16). Robustness and hyperparameter-transfer analyses further test applicability. These gains outweigh localized reporting problems, including the unexplained non-BF VGG10/CIFAR100 S+F top-5 discrepancy between Tables 8 and 15: 86.84% versus 88.66%.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same predictive-coding research. Their main text, appendices, equations, tables and figures are readable and support comparison despite substantial expansion and reorganization.

after.justification: V3 retains original experiments and adds incremental-PC and ResNet results, targeted ablations, corruption evaluations and hyperparameter analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original classification experiments, component ablations, energy measurements and training-time comparisons on CIFAR10, CIFAR100 and Tiny ImageNet.

results.title: Towards the Training of Deeper Predictive Coding Neural Networks

C1.justification: v2 adds flexible open-source baseline reimplementation as an explicit contribution and qualifies architectural generality as applicability to networks modularizable into a DAG of levels. The central representation-matching and neuron-saliency contributions remain.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands the applicability and cost interpretation: it distinguishes one-shot fusion from iterative federated learning, recommends local attribution estimation under skew, and argues that slower fusion can be offset by avoided fine-tuning. Data augmentation becomes an explicit mitigation for data dependence. v1's interpretation of its two distinct gradient-optimization regimes is removed.

D1.justification: Appendices E–F add linear regularization strengths, attribution-data and score-selection instructions, ResNet implementation provenance, and dataset-specific architecture and fine-tuning details. Fusion configurations are substantially revised. Conversely, v1's explicit base-training epoch schedule is replaced by training until convergence, reducing reproducibility detail in that respect.

E1.justification: v2 adds BloodMNIST blood-cell classification, Tiny-ImageNet fusion, ImageNet-1k task fusion, and teacher-to-student ResNet compression on CIFAR-100. The MNIST clustering example is replaced by a CIFAR-10 example. These substantially expand the represented domains and evaluated tasks.

E2.justification: v2 evaluates activation- and weight-based Transformer OTFusion in the ViT comparisons, previously absent because v1 could not adapt its implementation. ZipIt! enters the sharded VGG and ImageNet comparisons. Whole-model KD receives explicit comparison rows alongside the head-only comparator, described as last-layer KD in v1 and LP in v2.

E3.justification: CIFAR-100 ViTs change from patch size 8 and MLP width 384 to patch size 4 and MLP width 1536. ViT fusion budgets change from 7000 sharded/6000 full-dataset samples to 5000. Gradient configurations switch to AdamW with head weighting disabled, and fine-tuning settings change. Added experiments introduce compression and augmentation protocols; activation-based Transformer OTFusion uses 200 samples versus 5000 for the proposed methods.

E4.justification: v2 adds fusion-data-size and augmentation ablations, unequal-width fusion tests, compression-versus-KD comparisons, and an end-to-end runtime analysis. The three-MLP MNIST clustering illustration becomes a two-VGG CIFAR-10 analysis including DeepLIFT and adjusted Rand indices (Figure 3). These substantially broaden tests of sensitivity, mechanisms and applicability.

E5.justification: Four-way full-dataset ViT results change from three seeds with standard deviations in v1 to a single seed without dispersion in v2 Table 18. v2 also reports variability for its new end-to-end timing measurements. Most retained accuracy comparisons continue using means and standard deviations.

E6.justification: Many results are replaced or added. Two-way full-dataset CIFAR-100 KF-Gradient with uniform scores reports 72.7% zero-shot/73.9% fine-tuned in v1 Table 14 versus 63.0%/75.2% in v2 Table 18; changed settings prevent interpreting this as a controlled performance comparison. New benchmarks and analyses add substantial results, while v1's non-IID CIFAR-100 ViT tables and Conductance runtime entries disappear.

M1.justification: The grouping-and-fitting framework remains intact. v2 adds HF-Gradient, combining Hungarian matching with gradient-based fitting, whereas v1 considered only KF for the nonlinear gradient variant (v1 Section 4.3.2; v2 Section 4.2.2).

P1.justification: The paper is retitled and extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, motivation and experimental narrative. Sharded experiments precede non-IID experiments, appendix results are organized by architecture and dataset, and the broader-impact statement moves before the references. These exceed terminology or copyediting changes.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to two-column presentation, with substantial table restructuring and relocation. v2 adds an algorithm-capability matrix and numerous benchmark and analysis tables, replaces the clustering display with a four-panel figure, and redraws the landscape plots with different scales and styling.

R1.justification: The introduction adds positioning around linear mode connectivity, divergent learned features, baseline quality and reproducibility. Related work adds substantive ZipIt!, REPAIR and multi-teacher distillation discussion. The earlier pruning/correlation motivation and its supporting citations are removed; publication-year updates to retained works are merely bibliographic changes.

T1.justification: Theorem 2 now explicitly fixes all preceding levels and limits its guarantees to the current level. A new NP-hardness discussion explains the exclusion of joint optimization across levels. The decomposition, principal proofs and 9-plus-epsilon approximation bound otherwise remain substantially unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 directly benchmarks Transformer OTFusion, which v1 could not implement, and tests broad applicability through medical/ImageNet data, compression and robustness studies. This resolves important gaps in empirical support. Clearer theoretical assumptions and attribution instructions also help. These gains outweigh reduced replication for four-way ViT fusion and lost training-epoch details. Unequal fusion budgets still limit transformer comparisons, and blanket superiority remains overstated: KD beats KF-Gradient on four- and six-way sharded CIFAR-100 in Table 17.

A1.justification: Both PDFs are readable versions of the same neuron-centric model-fusion work, despite retitling. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original fusion experiments, additional medical and ImageNet evaluations, compression results, and robustness studies in Section 5 and Appendices F–G.

before.justification: v1 reports original VGG and ViT fusion experiments, a MNIST clustering analysis, and runtime measurements in Section 5 and Appendices F–G.

results.title: Model Fusion via Retrofitting

C1.justification: Beyond v1's existing asymptotic-consistency claim, v2 explicitly claims guarantees in both idealized and realistic settings as a main contribution. The abstract drops the physics-guided imputation and cross-frequency-resolution characterization and centers the contribution on consistency between imputation and structure recovery. Joint EM/ANM learning and empirical advantage remain central.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly limits the consistency result to an idealized estimator and explains that approximate back-projection and feature sparsity do not guarantee variable-level recovery. It clarifies the discrete-grid treatment of irregular observations and adds limitations concerning instantaneous effects, changing causal graphs and computation. Section 5.3 now acknowledges modest CausalRivers accuracy and competitors' better SHD or SID, replacing v1's broadly positive interpretation.

D1.justification: V2 supplies pseudocode, model-specific pruning procedures, three-layer imputation-network details, RFF implementation information, and dataset/method hyperparameters in Table 12. It also identifies the RTX 4090 hardware and baseline repository links. V1 provided mostly generic descriptions and unresolved appendix references. These are substantial new disclosures, without establishing that all corresponding settings changed.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates synthetic linear/nonlinear series and CausalRivers. V2 retains this coverage and adds NetSim simulated fMRI connectivity data and the Medical and PM25 domains of CausalTime (Appendix I.5, Tables 9–10), substantially broadening the evaluated domains.

E2.justification: Rhino+TimeMixer and AERCA+TimeMixer are newly evaluated in all three main comparison tables. The original PCMCI+TimeMixer, PCMCI+EM, DYNOTEARS variants with TimeMixer, and CUTS+ remain. These additions substantially expand the comparator set beyond the original four alternatives.

E3.justification: V2 adds SID evaluation to Tables 2–3 and SHD to the formerly F1-only CausalRivers comparison. New experiments introduce controlled sortability conditions, hyperparameter sweeps, and lag-order evaluations using temporally unrolled graphs with CUTS+ summary graphs shared across lags. These are additional evaluation designs; newly disclosed implementation settings do not establish changes to retained experimental procedures.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's missingness and graph-size comparisons, Appendix I adds a noise-injection ablation, controlled nonlinear-function and lag-order comparisons, sortability robustness tests, pruning visualizations, joint imputation/discovery trajectories, and hyperparameter sensitivity analysis. These directly investigate component necessity, optimization behavior and robustness that v1 did not experimentally isolate.

E5.justification: Figure 4 newly reports averages over multiple runs with standard-error bands. Both versions already provide mean-and-standard-deviation reporting for CausalRivers and suppress deviations in most other tables. Explicit run counts and seeds remain unspecified; the PDFs do not establish an increase in repetitions.

E6.justification: The original ReTimeCausal synthetic F1 and SHD entries are retained, but other results change. Table 2 revises PCMCI+EM's 50-variable SHD/F1 from 138/0.258 to 124/0.311. Table 3 revises ReTimeCausal's reported CausalRivers F1 at 20%/60% missingness from 0.471/0.436 to 0.463/0.414. V2 also adds baseline scores, metric entries and extensive appendix results, including CUTS+ outperforming ReTimeCausal on Medical at 20% missingness (0.667 versus 0.658).

M1.justification: The stated kernel regression model changes substantively: v1 Equations 3 and 5 predict kernel features phi(X) using p-by-p matrices, whereas v2 Equations 4 and 6 predict completed original variables from lagged kernel features using p-by-d matrices. This revises the prediction target and regression objective. The surrounding EM loop, noise injection, smoothing and pruning remain.

P1.justification: The abstract, motivation, problem setup and method explanations are extensively rewritten, especially the separation of neural imputation from kernel-based graph estimation. Related work is reorganized between Section 2 and Appendix A, and organized supporting sections replace dangling appendix references. The title, author information and inconsistent ReCausalTime naming also change.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to two-column layout. Tables 1–3 gain comparator rows and redesigned metric groupings, while Figures 1–2 receive revised graphics, legends and placement. V2 adds pruning heatmaps, a convergence plot with uncertainty shading, algorithm pseudocode, and notation, ablation, benchmark and hyperparameter tables.

R1.justification: Section 2 and Appendix A substantially expand positioning against continuous-time Neural Graphical Modeling and entropy-based summary-graph discovery, distinguishing discrete lag recovery and theoretical guarantees. V2 also incorporates Rhino, AERCA, CausalTime, sortability research and additional EM/kernel estimation theory. Existing related-work material is partly relocated rather than removed.

T1.justification: V1 states asymptotic consistency but supplies no referenced appendix proof. V2 adds a conditional proof of Proposition 4.1, a finite-sample/finite-iteration SHD bound in Theorem G.1, and computational complexity derivations. It also corrects the summary-graph definition, replaces invariant structural functions with invariant causal directions, adds faithfulness, and specifies additional regularity, tuning and local-convergence conditions.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses substantial weaknesses in the supplied v1: missing referenced proofs and algorithm descriptions, sparse implementation information, and little direct evidence for key design choices. Conditional theoretical arguments, reproducibility details, targeted ablations and broader comparisons make the work substantially easier to assess. Explicit qualifications and acknowledgment of unfavorable metrics improve the interpretation of results. The practical pipeline still lacks an unconditional recovery guarantee, and run counts remain unspecified, but these residual limitations do not outweigh the gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ReTimeCausal and share identifiable methods and experiments despite the title change. Text, equations, tables and figures are readable. The supplied v1.pdf ends with references despite referring to appendices; v2.pdf includes readable Appendices A–L.

after.justification: Tables 1–3 retain original experiments, while Appendix I adds benchmark evaluations, ablations, sensitivity tests and convergence observations.

before.justification: Tables 1–3 report original causal-discovery experiments on synthetic time series and a CausalRivers subgraph.

results.title: Causal Discovery for Irregularly Time Series with Consistency Guarantees

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction redefine the model contribution from a single ST-LLM centered on alignment and positional encoding to studying two complementary STLLM baselines. The conclusion attributes gains to point-cloud understanding generally instead of specifically the alignment module. The REA dataset and joint spatial-temporal reasoning claims remain central.

C2.justification: V1 argues that positional encoding is important for balanced reasoning; v2 finds little benefit and attributes this to REA emphasizing QA rather than explicit grounding. V2 adds scalability versus interpretability tradeoffs between the two architectures and interpretations of decoder adaptation and cross-dataset transfer. Appendix H's template-overfitting limitation remains unchanged.

D1.justification: Training documentation is substantially revised: v1 reports approximately 12 hours of pretraining plus 5 hours on REA, whereas v2 reports approximately 6 hours on REA. V2 updates the REA system prompt and hyperparameters, documents baseline token pooling and human verification, and adds an SQA3D judge prompt while removing ScanRefer instructions. The code/data access link remains unchanged.

E1.justification: The five REA tasks remain, but v2 adds zero-shot situated-QA evaluation on SQA3D, previously used for pretraining rather than reported evaluation. V2 describes REA training for its main models, replacing v1's additional ScanRefer, Nr3D, 3D-LLM, and SQA3D pretraining coverage.

E2.justification: V2 retains the three original off-the-shelf comparators and adds VideoLLaMA3. More substantially, Tables 1-2 and Appendix E add REA-finetuned LLaVA-Video and LLaVA-OneVision comparisons, including restricted spatial-token variants. These provide comparison methods absent from v1's reported experiments.

E3.justification: Reported settings change from staged 3D pretraining followed by REA finetuning to one REA epoch, from 32 to 1,024 alignment queries, and from 1 to 64 neighborhood samples for the direct point-cloud model. V2 also introduces token-budget controls, SQA3D semantic judging, and human-audit protocols. The REA split sizes and existing REA evaluation metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V1's alignment and positional-encoding ablations are substantially revised and extended with query-count and decoder-adaptation comparisons in v2's Appendix E. Appendix A adds human assessment of point-cloud and QA quality and a judge-human agreement study. The original qualitative examples and model/judge failure cases are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports training-run replication, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. V2's human-audit and judge-agreement percentages are additional validation results, not estimates of experimental uncertainty.

E6.justification: V1's overall judge accuracies of 34.55%/39.50% are retained in v2 Table 7 for the frozen 32-query aligner. V2 Table 2 newly reports 41.89%/46.50% for the differently configured, finetuned aligner; this is not a same-setting performance increase. Finetuned comparator scores, SQA3D results, and human-audit findings substantially expand the results, while the original off-the-shelf REA scores remain unchanged.

M1.justification: V1 freezes the LLM decoder; v2 adapts it with LoRA while training projectors and, for STLLM-Aligner, the alignment module. The main aligner also expands from 32 to 1,024 queries. STLLM-3D corresponds substantially to v1's Raw Pointcloud ablation, so its promotion and renaming alone do not constitute a new architecture.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution narrative, method explanation, and experimental discussion are extensively rewritten. Section 4's formulation/architecture/training subsections become a two-model presentation; training material is consolidated in Appendix D, ablations move into Appendix E, and Appendix A becomes a reliability assessment. This is substantial narrative and structural reorganization.

P2.justification: Figure 4 is redrawn to show both architectures and LoRA, replacing the original architecture and alignment-detail presentation. The main comparison tables expand, Table 2 changes orientation, and new SQA3D, human-audit, dataset-overview, and dataset-comparison tables appear. Typography and page layout also change throughout, while most scene illustrations and qualitative panels are retained.

R1.justification: V2 adds citations for LoRA and VideoLLaMA3 and a dataset comparison covering HD-EPIC and Nymeria alongside previously cited benchmarks. References associated with the removed pretraining and explicit Q-Former discussion disappear. Most related-work categories and the distinction from existing spatial/video methods remain intact; publication updates and deduplicated references are bibliographic changes.

T1.justification: The input definitions and underlying positional-ray construction remain substantively equivalent. V1's explicit positional-encoding equations are condensed into prose in v2, without a new theoretical result, proof, or substantive change to mathematical reasoning.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses an important weakness in v1: comparing a trained proposed model primarily against off-the-shelf competitors. REA-finetuned controls and token-budget/decoder analyses better separate architectural benefits from training benefits. SQA3D transfer tests and human reliability assessments further strengthen the evidence. Reporting flaws remain: Table 4 percentages conflict with the stated 20 samples per task, and Appendix E's query-count improvement claim conflicts with the Gemini results. These limit precision but do not outweigh the substantial improvement in comparative evaluation and validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same REA dataset and spatio-temporal LLM research. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices are readable, and corresponding content can be matched despite substantial revision.

after.justification: V2 reports original REA comparisons, SQA3D transfer results, model ablations, and human evaluations of dataset and judge reliability.

before.justification: V1 reports original REA benchmark results, component ablations, and qualitative successes and failures in Section 5 and Appendices A and F.

results.title: Spatio-Temporal LLM: Reasoning about Environments and Actions

C1.justification: The central diffusion-normalization and geometric-application claims remain. v2 omits v1's explicit novelty assertion that mass-preserving normalization had not been used on general discrete geometric structures and emphasizes fixed-scale geometry processing. Its conclusion also adds a claimed connection to reversible Markov kernels and entropy gradient flows.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive limitations concerning inaccurate mass estimates and reduced expressivity when signal amplification is useful. It explains LDDMM contraction through spectral degeneracy and interprets the XYZ ablation as evidence that engineered descriptors strongly drive benchmark performance. The absence of guaranteed convergence to a true Laplacian was already acknowledged in v1.

D1.justification: v2 newly provides a repository address for CPU/GPU implementations and documents timing scope, V100/CUDA 12.1, CPU models, PyTorch/PyKeOps and KNN configurations. v1 explicitly declined to report runtimes. Existing Q-DiffNet hyperparameters and training details are retained; mesh-derived WKS inputs were already disclosed in v1 Appendix H.

E1.justification: The principal tasks, representation families and FAUST/SCAPE/SHREC19 benchmarks are retained. v2 extends coverage within these geometric tasks through Sumner horse and cat examples, including a defective cat mesh, and Armadillo scenarios with perturbed masses and nonuniform sampling.

E2.justification: The main correspondence comparator set is unchanged. v2 adds actual runtime comparisons with CPU sparse-LU/implicit-Euler diffusion and GPU dense Cholesky and matrix-exponential implementations (Tables 1 and 3; Appendix F), which v1 discussed without reporting these timing comparisons.

E3.justification: v2 introduces substantial evaluation protocols: five-iteration timing benchmarks up to one million points, CPU KNN settings with 25 or 100 neighbors, multiplicative mass noise, nonuniform downsampling, spectral bandwidth variation, and aligned XYZ inputs. Chamfer distance and mean area distortion add quantitative evaluation metrics. Existing correspondence splits and training settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New analyses test mass-estimation sensitivity (Appendix D), spectral stability under sampling and bandwidth changes (G), and dependence on WKS versus XYZ features (J). Appendices H and I quantify previously qualitative flow and deformation behavior. The earlier SHREC19 correspondence visualization in v1 Figure 6b is removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, experimental seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The standard deviation in v2's mass-noise experiment controls the perturbation distribution; it is not uncertainty reporting for estimated performance.

E6.justification: The main correspondence scores are identical in v1 Figure 6a and v2 Table 2. Substantial new results include runtime tables, robustness curves, animal examples, Chamfer convergence and area distortion. Under the new XYZ setting, Table 4 reports SHREC19 errors of 7.68 for Q-DiffNet (Q-FM), 9.35 for DiffNet (PC), and 10.5 for ULRSSM (PC); these are additional results under different inputs, not improvements over the retained WKS scores.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1, the normalized operator, kernel formulas, Q-DiffNet architecture and losses, and normalized geodesic construction remain unchanged. The new XYZ ablation and KNN runtime configuration evaluate existing input and sparse-operator capabilities rather than revise the proposed method.

P1.justification: v2 substantially rewrites prose across the introduction, related work, theoretical exposition and results. It changes the title, adds a motivation passage and a dedicated Limitations section, and reorganizes the appendices. This extends beyond wording changes required to introduce the new experiments.

P2.justification: The main text changes to two columns, Figure 1 becomes an explanatory diagram, and new tables and analytical plots are added. The correspondence results become Table 2 without the former qualitative panel. Six eigenvector plates are consolidated into three denser figures; the sphere panel remains, although v2 Figure 13 incorrectly calls it a cube.

R1.justification: The main literature framework remains, but v2 refines its distinction from manifold-limit research and adds references including diffusion maps, Belkin's point-cloud Laplacian, Maas's Markov-chain gradient flows, Sumner's shapes and GreenCloud. Several earlier software and background references disappear. These are limited positioning and citation changes beyond the citation-style conversion.

T1.justification: v2 adds Proposition 4.6 and its Appendix D proof, bounding first-order relative scaling-factor error by half the relative mass perturbation and deriving the variation of Q. Appendix A also adds the converse logarithm/Metzler argument. The original normalization and refinement theorems are retained as Theorems 4.4 and 4.5.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for the paper's practical claims: v1 lacked measured runtime comparisons, relied on mesh-derived descriptors in correspondence tests, and illustrated flow and deformation benefits mainly qualitatively. The new timing studies, XYZ ablation, quantitative diagnostics and proved mass-stability bound address those gaps, while explicit limitations improve interpretation. Mixed-hardware timings require care, and compressed figures introduce presentation defects, but these drawbacks are outweighed by the stronger validation and reproducibility information.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Sinkhorn-normalized diffusion framework despite the changed title and format. All 33 pages of v1 and 32 pages of v2, including appendices, support comparison of the text, equations, figures and results.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical studies and adds runtime measurements, robustness experiments, quantitative flow and deformation diagnostics, and XYZ-input correspondence results.

before.justification: v1 reports original spectral-analysis experiments, particle flows, shape interpolation and shape-correspondence errors, with further experimental results in its appendices.

results.title: Sinkhorn Normalization of Diffusion Kernels

C1.justification: The central claims remain that retrieving high-return targets guides generative planning out of OOD or low-return regions without static augmentation, yielding competitive or superior offline-RL performance. The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain this contribution; the expanded experiments primarily provide additional support.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands interpretations concerning heterogeneous data quality, limited gains on expert data, target reachability, robustness to imperfect retrieval, and why long remaining trajectories provide useful planning anchors. It adds runtime tradeoffs and qualifications about experimental scope. Dependence on available high-return states remains, while v1's discussion of stochastic retrieval failures and global-planning extensions is dropped.

D1.justification: Beyond v1's brief implementation settings, v2 supplies training/inference pseudocode, U-Net and DiT specifications, expert-subset selection rules, domain-specific horizons, retrieval counts, runtime/memory measurements, and a code-access link (Appendices B-D). However, v1's explicit 20 denoising steps and four-layer step-network specification are not retained.

E1.justification: v2 retains the nine locomotion datasets and adds AntMaze navigation, Maze2D navigation, FrankaKitchen manipulation, and OGBench stitching/explore evaluations. It also evaluates distinct deployment scenarios involving shifted initial states and previously unseen maze regions (Section 5.2; Appendices D.5 and D.10).

E2.justification: In the shared locomotion comparison, v2 adds CQL, IQL, MOPO, MOReL, SER, DiffStitch, and DiffuserLite, while removing CEIL, ReDiffuser, and TT. Additional comparisons introduce direct retrieval combination (DRC) and the OGBench comparators GCBC, GCIVL, GCIQL, QRL, CRL, and HIQL (Tables 8 and 17).

E3.justification: v2 introduces controlled evaluation protocols using Random-dataset initializations, 0%/20% regional training coverage, and baselines trained on the same expert subset. New DL-RAD experiments use distinct planning horizons, while runtime studies compare per-step, full-rollout, and fixed-step costs and 1-step versus 10-step replanning. These are added experimental settings, not evidence that v1's experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The original component-ablation ideas remain under renamed labels, and the similarity-threshold sweep moves to Appendix D.4. v2 adds backbone and naive-retrieval controls, expert-subset controls, OOD stress tests, ranking and similarity-metric sensitivity, periodic replanning, and trajectory visualizations. v1's training-curve comparison and k=6/30/60/120 candidate-count sweep are removed.

E5.justification: Table 1 changes uncertainty reporting from standard deviations in v1 to standard errors in v2, while both specify three random seeds. The retained similarity-threshold results lose their uncertainty estimates (v1 Table 2 versus v2 Table 9). An increase in run count is not documented.

E6.justification: The nine original RAD task means are retained as D-RAD, but v2 adds extensive DL-RAD, navigation, manipulation, OGBench, OOD, ablation, and timing results. For example, DL-RAD has a newly reported locomotion average of 87.5. The DS locomotion average changes from 77.0 to 81.1 despite unchanged task scores, correcting the aggregate. New variants and settings do not establish a same-setting improvement of the original RAD.

M1.justification: v1 uses scalar step estimation trained with MSE and a state-action diffusion planner. v2 replaces step regression with classification and cross-entropy, adds the DiffuserLite-based DL-RAD variant with state-only generation and inverse dynamics, and describes an expert-filtered retrieval database instead of all dataset states (Sections 4.1-4.4). These change substantive components and procedures.

P1.justification: The related work, preliminaries, method, and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten and reorganized. Diffusion background precedes the problem definition; the method is organized around TS, SE, and PL; experiments follow explicit research questions; and retained parameter analysis moves into new appendices. Terminology and contribution presentation also change throughout.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column main-text layout, redraws Figures 1-2, and restructures Figure 3 with separate task panels, revised axes, and an added control. The training-curve figure is replaced by navigation rollouts, return-distribution plots are added, and Table 1 becomes a multidomain comparison. Numerous new tables and algorithm displays substantially alter presentation.

R1.justification: v2 substantially revises positioning around conservative offline RL, generative planning, and augmentation, adding discussion of DiffStitch and DiffuserLite while dropping treatments of works such as AWAC, BAIL, CRR, and COMBO. Appendix F explicitly distinguishes RAD's decision-time planning from DiffStitch's offline augmentation and explains their potential compatibility.

T1.justification: v2 adds Appendix E's chain-rule derivation that target conditioning cannot increase conditional trajectory entropy. It also corrects the return-to-go discount exponent from i to i-t in the problem definition. These provide a limited theoretical addition and correction; the entropy argument does not establish a policy-performance guarantee.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses v1's central evidential gap: OOD-generalization claims previously rested on ordinary locomotion evaluations. Direct distribution-shift tests, naive-retrieval and expert-subset controls, broader tasks, computational-cost measurements, and fuller implementation details substantially strengthen empirical support and reproducibility. Some original analyses and uncertainty estimates disappear, and Appendix E's entropy inequality alone does not justify improved prediction accuracy. These limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RAD research work. Their text, equations, tables, and figures support comparison. v1 ends with references and has no appendices; v2's Appendices A-F were included in the assessment.

after.justification: v2 reports original D-RAD and DL-RAD benchmark results, distribution-shift experiments, ablations, runtime measurements, and additional appendix evaluations.

before.justification: v1 reports original RAD results on nine locomotion datasets, component ablations, training curves, and retrieval-parameter experiments.

results.title: RAD: Retrieval High-quality Demonstrations to Enhance Decision-making

C1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and new conclusion broaden the contribution from neural posterior validation to general two-sample testing. v2 also elevates the budget-matched Multiple test from an alternative comparator to a central contribution with its own robustness claim, alongside the retained Uniform test.

C2.justification: v2 adds explicit M-closed versus M-open and global versus local applicability limits, distinguishes Uniform's finite-sample guarantee from Multiple's asymptotic validity, and discusses when Multiple outperforms Uniform. Appendix D adds practical guidance and failure conditions, although its language about certifying joint validity overstates what non-rejection establishes.

D1.justification: v2 substantially expands implementation documentation through CIFAR preprocessing, classifier architecture, optimization, corruption grids, DC settings, and method-specific sampling budgets. However, v1's explicit Gaussian observation distribution and covariance construction are omitted. The code-access link is retained rather than newly provided.

E1.justification: v2 adds CIFAR-10 blur, swirl, and noise detection and a PROBES-based gravitational-lensing inverse problem (Sections 5.2–5.3). The Gaussian perturbations and high-dimensional manifold experiment remain. Mean shift and mode collapse were already evaluated in v1; their changed placement is not new coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated Discriminative Calibration, AutoML, and MMDFuse comparisons to the Gaussian benchmark plots, alongside retained C2ST, SBC, and TARP baselines. These methods also appear in the new lensing comparison. Local C2ST is discussed but explicitly excluded from evaluation.

E3.justification: The Gaussian comparison panels switch from Conformal Uniform(200) to Uniform(50), although the broader calibration-size sweep remains. New protocols include image classification using frozen Inception features and 1,024 training images per source, and lensing experiments using 2,000 training samples per source with diffusion-score bias interpolation. These are substantial additions to the evaluation design.

E4.justification: v2 extends the robustness investigation to strong versus weak image classifiers and a lensing classifier-degradation sweep at fixed posterior bias (Figure 3 and Table 2b). These test whether robustness transfers beyond the original synthetic settings. The existing calibration-size ablations and Gaussian/manifold degradation analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Three-seed averaging remains unchanged. v2 adds reporting of 50 lensing replicates, a default of 64 image-evaluation replicates, and 100 bootstrap resamples for Discriminative Calibration. It does not establish increased repetitions for the retained Gaussian experiments.

E6.justification: v2 adds image and lensing outcomes and revises Gaussian comparison curves, including markedly lower plotted SBC/TARP power. New Table 2a reports 66% power for Uniform(50), 50% for Multiple, and 28% for C2ST at bias γ=0.60 and degradation β=0. The Gaussian Uniform comparisons also change calibration budget, so those differences are not same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The Uniform test still uses independent calibration sets followed by a KS test, and the Multiple test retains its shared-calibration statistic and variance estimator. The expanded theory and experiment-specific classifiers do not establish a change to the proposed testing procedures.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and results narrative are extensively rewritten around general two-sample testing. The original unified methods section is reorganized into separate preliminaries, Uniform, and Multiple sections; Gaussian descriptions move to the appendix, and a conclusion and practitioner guide are added.

P2.justification: The main text changes from a single-column to a two-column layout. v2 adds an image-results figure and tables for sampling budgets, lensing results, and corruption grids, while expanding Gaussian plot legends and comparator curves. Mean shift replaces mode collapse in the main figure; both remain in the appendix, and many existing plots are retained and renumbered.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning within classifier and kernel two-sample testing, adding discussion of DC, AutoML, MMDFuse, local C2ST, and earlier classifier-test theory. It also qualifies the SBC comparison using newer test quantities and relates its assumptions to ranking and margin-condition literature, beyond v1's narrower posterior-validation positioning.

T1.justification: The original Uniform-test robustness bound is retained, but v2 adds a conditional p-value variance lemma, a rare-ties assumption, and Theorem 4.2 on the Multiple statistic's oracle scaling and relative estimation-error gap. Appendix A.4 expands into Hoeffding decomposition, central-limit, tie-noise, null-validity, and robustness derivations.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses v1's limited empirical scope and comparator coverage through image and galaxy-based inverse-problem evaluations and broader baseline comparisons. Explicit sampling budgets and clearer applicability and validity limits substantially improve readers' ability to assess the methods. Some Gaussian reproducibility details are lost, and the practitioner guide overstates what non-rejection certifies, but these shortcomings do not outweigh the substantial strengthening of the comparative evidence and practical explanation.

A1.justification: Despite the changed title and broader scope, both PDFs describe the same conformal C2ST work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison and matching of retained material.

after.justification: v2 retains original simulation results and adds CIFAR-10 corruption experiments and a galaxy-based gravitational-lensing evaluation.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulation results for perturbed Gaussian posteriors, classifier degradation, calibration-size ablations, and high-dimensional manifold posteriors.

results.title: Conformal C2ST: Turning weak classifiers into strong two-sample tests

C1.justification: The central contributions remain a multi-expert, reasoning-assisted benchmark for fine-grained captioning and QA, and DATE for rewarding detailed, discriminative descriptions. The abstract and introduction retain this scientific scope; expanded validation and model comparisons support these contributions rather than redefine them.

C2.justification: Section 6.4 adds specific limitations concerning short clips, residual annotation errors, entity swaps and reduced DATE discrimination on homogeneous corpora. New discussions interpret expert-error independence, weighting stability, discriminability and hallucination behavior. These substantially extend v1's brief limitations and model-specialization discussion.

D1.justification: Appendix E adds computational details for embedding normalization, token exclusions, TF/DF accumulation and weighting. Appendix I extends prompt assignments to the added models and clarifies default versus overridden system prompts.
