The construction-model inventory, synthesis prompts and code/data access statement are substantially retained.

E1.justification: Both versions use approximately 20,000 ACAV100M clips across the same eight domains, with the same captioning and QA tasks. The external datasets in the embedding comparison are retained. New human audits and silence case studies examine existing MECAT coverage.

E2.justification: Tables 2 and 3 expand from 6 captioning and 4 QA models to 17 and 15. Audio Flamingo 3 replaces Audio Flamingo 2 in these evaluations, while additions include Phi-4-Multimodal, Baichuan models, MiMo-Audio, Step-Audio-2-mini, Qwen3 variants and Gemini models. Audio Flamingo 2 remains part of benchmark construction.

E3.justification: Appendix F introduces a 150-pair human preference protocol and a 700-sample audit involving 20 audio professionals and a five-level relevance scale. It also tests alternative caption aggregation weights and varying bootstrap sample sizes; Appendices J and K report separate similarity and discriminability measurements. These are added evaluation designs, not established reruns under changed settings for the original comparisons.

E4.justification: v3 adds direct annotation-quality validation, sensitivity to aggregation weights, DATE stability across sample sizes and alignment with human preferences in Appendix F. Appendix J examines similarity versus discriminability, and Appendix L adds two silent-segment hallucination cases. These substantially extend v1's metric examples, distribution plots and judge-reliability analysis.

E5.justification: The existing Fleiss' kappa results are retained, but v3 adds Wilson confidence intervals, Wilcoxon tests with Bonferroni correction, a Mann-Whitney comparison and effect sizes. Its bootstrap study reports 50 iterations per group and sampling ratio, confidence intervals, coefficients of variation and maximum deviations. These are new statistical procedures, not evidence of increased model-generation runs.

E6.justification: v3 adds extensive model and validation results, including Gemini-3-Pro's 53.1 caption score and Qwen3-Omni's 52.3 QA score. Retained models also have revised Table 2 aggregates despite unchanged component entries: Pengi changes from 30.6 to 29.4 and Qwen2.5-Omni 7B from 43.0 to 42.6. These are numerical revisions rather than demonstrated performance changes; corresponding retained QA scores remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The expert-model, DeepSeek-R1 reasoning and filtering pipeline is retained, as is DATE's combination of weighted semantic similarity and cross-sample discriminability. Appendix E specifies previously unspecified embedding-level TF-IDF calculations; the PDFs do not establish an underlying procedural replacement.

P1.justification: Much of the abstract, method description and prompt appendices is preserved. Editorial changes include expanded introductory motivation, numbered subsections, rewritten performance discussion, a shortened conclusion, consolidated references and new disclosure text. These are localized structural and language revisions around the expanded scientific content.

P2.justification: v3 redraws the overview figure, regroups the expert diagram and merges v1's Figures 5 and 6 into a recolored, multipanel Figure 5. The model tables expand substantially, Table 3 changes orientation, and numerous validation and analysis tables appear in the appendices. The document also adopts a different conference layout.

R1.justification: v3 adds references for newer evaluated models, WavCaps and MMAR, and replaces the unrelated defect-prediction FENSE reference with an audio-caption evaluation reference. The main positioning against coarse annotations, closed-ended QA and insufficiently discriminative metrics remains intact.

T1.justification: Appendix E adds formal definitions for semantic term frequency using squared embedding similarities and embedding-aware document frequency and IDF. v1 gives only generic TF-IDF factors. This is a limited mathematical specification of DATE's weighting component; the principal similarity, rank and harmonic-mean equations remain equivalent, with no new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: The human preference study and 700-sample expert audit address an important weakness in v1: the lack of direct human evidence for automatically generated caption quality. Statistical uncertainty, sensitivity analyses and explicit applicability limits substantially strengthen the paper's evidential foundation. Numerical inconsistencies remain, including Qwen3-Omni's pure-speech similarity of 41.0 in Table J.1 versus 34.1 in Table K.1, but these do not outweigh the substantial validation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MECAT benchmark and DATE metric. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains original evaluations and adds broader model comparisons, human annotation audits, weighting sensitivity, bootstrap analyses and hallucination case studies.

before.justification: v1 reports original model evaluations on MECAT-Caption and MECAT-QA, metric comparisons, embedding analyses and LLM-as-judge reliability results.

results.title: MECAT: A Multi-Experts Constructed Benchmark for Fine-Grained Audio Understanding Tasks

C1.justification: Section 1.1 expands the random-allocation contribution from a logarithmic approximation guarantee to an essentially tight characterization for RAND, plus near-proportionality under small items. The principal greedy-impossibility and MIV-assisted 1/n-PROP1 claims remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations of empirical fairness-welfare tradeoffs and benign versus adversarial instances. It also explains why MIV information obstructs standard lower-bound constructions and explicitly limits the new tightness result to RAND, leaving stronger general online algorithms possible.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-repository link in Section 5, footnote 8, and synthetic-data generation details, including interest probability 0.6, positive values in [0.8, 1], and the correlated-value formula. v1 already supplies the core pseudocode and proofs but no implementation link.

E1.justification: v1 has no empirical evaluation. v2 evaluates online allocation on four synthetic valuation families: uniform, dense binary-interest, correlated, and specialist instances. It also empirically tests adversarial sequences derived from the existing greedy counterexamples.

E2.justification: v2 introduces numerical comparisons of Algorithm 1 against Greedy-1, Greedy-2, and Greedy-3 in Section 5 and Figure 2. These strategies were defined and analyzed theoretically in v1, but were not empirically evaluated against Algorithm 1.

E3.justification: The new random-instance evaluation uses eight agents, forty goods, per-agent maximum-value normalization, realized PROP1 ratios, and utilitarian welfare normalized by the ex-post optimum. Separate adversarial tests use prefixes of roughly 500 goods. These are newly introduced protocols, not revisions to earlier experiments.

E4.justification: v2 adds focused stress tests of the three existing counterexample constructions, checking their finite-prefix effects on greedy fairness and comparing Algorithm 1 on the same prefixes. v1 provides only the mathematical constructions and proofs.

E5.justification: v2 introduces repeated-trial and uncertainty reporting throughout its new random-instance evaluation: 500 independent trials per family and 95% confidence intervals in Figure 2. v1 contains no empirical run counts or confidence intervals; this is not an increase from a previously reported run budget.

E6.justification: v2 adds the first empirical scores, reporting that Algorithm 1 achieves PROP1 on every sampled random instance. For example, on dense instances its welfare is 0.960 versus Greedy-1's 0.954, with PROP1 ratios 1 versus 0.423. New adversarial results also quantify greedy failures and Algorithm 1's performance.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 and the existing one-sided-error adaptation are retained. However, v2 adds preprocessing for bounded two-sided prediction errors: inflate predictions by 1/(1-rho), then apply the one-sided guarantee with epsilon = 2rho/(1+rho) (Section 5, footnote 7).

P1.justification: The introduction and contribution narrative are extensively rewritten around machine-learning allocation systems. General related-work material moves to a new Appendix A, the conclusion is rewritten, and the greedy proof sketch and potential-function explanation are substantially revised.

P2.justification: The main text changes from a single-column manuscript to a two-column conference layout with running headers and a full-width algorithm display. The unchanged Figure 1 is relocated and resized, while new Figure 2 introduces four fairness-welfare panels with legends and confidence intervals.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting the greedy strategies, including Plaut and Roughgarden (2018), and expands background coverage of online voting and learning-augmented algorithms. Some earlier EFX and temporal-fair-division references are removed. The central relationship to Neoh et al. (2025) and Zhou et al. (2023) remains.

T1.justification: v2 adds a matching limitation for RAND (Proposition 4.2) and a near-proportionality guarantee under a small-item condition (Theorem 4.3), with proofs in Appendix C. It also repairs greedy proof steps, changes the concentration-proof constant from 27/(128 log(n/delta)) to 3/(32 log(n/delta)), and corrects the displayed potential to match the retained algorithm.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens theoretical completeness and reliability by establishing RAND's tightness and small-item regime while correcting proof and formula errors in v1. The new simulations, confidence intervals, and adversarial stress tests provide useful evidence about fairness-welfare behavior that the theoretical guarantees alone do not establish. Although the empirical support remains limited to synthetic settings, the combined gains are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their text, equations, figures, and complete appendices are readable, and retained algorithms and proofs can be matched across renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: Section 5 reports original simulations on four synthetic instance families and finite adversarial counterexamples. Figure 2 presents fairness and welfare results with confidence intervals.

before.justification: v1 reports theoretical results and proofs, without original empirical outcomes. Figure 1 illustrates the potential function rather than an experiment.

results.title: Approximate Proportionality in Online Fair Division

C1.justification: The headline claim changes from state of the art on GIFT-ZS and Chronos-ZS to state of the art on full GIFT-Eval. For full GIFT-Eval, v1 only claimed leadership among models without test-data leakage and approximate parity with TiRex overall. v3 also makes end-to-end sampling-rate equivariance an explicit central contribution.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive explanations of fixed-decoder local errors, complex-state dependence, time-noise regularization and basis truncation. New limitations identify heuristic scale selection and absent native multivariate/covariate support; Appendix D discusses automatic-selection failures with short contexts. The theoretical discussion qualifies equivariance as approximate and assumption-dependent.

D1.justification: v3 adds a FlowState model-access link and extensive reproducibility information in Appendices C–D: dataset inventories, balancing and preprocessing, augmentation details, quantile loss, optimizer and training hyperparameters, seasonality-selection pseudocode, model dimensions, hardware and training times. Most of this information is absent from v1.

E1.justification: Coverage is substantially reworked: the separate Chronos-ZS evaluation disappears, and the resampling study switches from Loop Seattle traffic to ETT temperature data. v3 adds hourly-context-to-15-minute-target forecasting and synthetic sine-wave tests with seasonalities 8, 24 and 100. Full GIFT-Eval was already evaluated in v1.

E2.justification: The full GIFT-Eval comparison replaces TimesFM-2.0 and Chronos-bolt-b with TimesFM-2.5 and Chronos-2-Synth, adds Kairos-23M/50M, and drops TabPFN-TS and YingLong. Appendix A.1 introduces comparisons with LightGTS-mini, MOIRAI-L, iTransformer and PatchTST. The robustness experiment also changes its comparator membership.

E3.justification: Reported main-model context increases from 2048 to 4096 steps, base forecasting length changes from 24 to 6, and model sizes change from 2.6M/9.1M to 3M/10.6M/18.6M. Synthetic generation changes from KernelSynth to CauKer. v3 also introduces four-horizon MSE/MAE evaluation in Appendix A.1 and changes the resampling study's intervals and MAE normalization.

E4.justification: v3 substantially expands ablations to test output gating, real versus complex SSMs, selective step sizes, a fixed decoder, time noise, causal normalization and basis truncation. Appendices add decoder case studies, aligned/misaligned encoding comparisons, automatic scale selection and scale sensitivity. v1's CPM/MPI ablations are removed.

E5.justification: v1 provides no run-count or variability estimates. v3 Table 2 newly reports a three-seed baseline with MASE and CRPS standard deviations of 0.0007 and 0.0011. Appendix D.1's blanket statement that all experiments ran once with seed 0 conflicts with this account; repeated-run coverage beyond that baseline remains unclear.

E6.justification: Results are extensively replaced and expanded. Full GIFT-Eval reports FlowState(G)-9.1M at 0.738 MASE/0.508 CRPS in v1 Table 3, versus the newly configured FlowState-18.6M at 0.701/0.487 in v3 Table 1; this is not a controlled same-setting gain. Chronos-ZS results disappear, while standard-benchmark, expanded-ablation and scale-selection results are added.

M1.justification: The SSM encoder, functional basis decoder and parallel-forecast training remain central. v3 adds an explicit output gate to the SSM block equations and architecture diagram, and Appendix D.2.2 introduces an optional automatic seasonality/scale-selection procedure. These are localized procedural extensions.

P1.justification: v3 revises the title and sampling-rate terminology, numbers sections, separates parallel forecasting from the architecture section, and rewrites the experimental narrative. Much of the introduction, background and core-method explanation remains closely matched; the largest expansion consists of new scientific and technical material.

P2.justification: v3 updates the architecture diagram, replaces the robustness plot with different axes and normalization, restructures the benchmark and ablation tables, and adds mixed-rate forecasts, decoder case-study plots, encoding heatmaps, a sensitivity plot and technical tables. The original parallel-training schematic is retained as Figure 3. Appendices introduce a substantial single-column presentation.

R1.justification: v3 adds references and connections to Chronos-2, Kairos, LightGTS, CauKer, diagonal-SSM initialization and classical discretization theory. The broader positioning relative to transformers, MLPs, SSMs and HiPPO remains substantially intact.

T1.justification: v1 offers architectural equations and informal sampling-rate arguments. v3 Section 4 and Appendix B add formal approximate equivariance, input-Lipschitz and exponential-stability assumptions, a two-rate ZOH mismatch proposition and proof, decoder error bounds, and a conditional multilayer extension.

improvement.justification: v1's central sampling-rate argument was largely informal and its training documentation sparse. v3 substantially strengthens the paper through conditional error bounds, direct decoder ablations, scale-selection and sensitivity analyses, explicit limitations and detailed reproducibility information. Removed Chronos-ZS coverage, less explicit overlap safeguards and inconsistent seed reporting are drawbacks, but the stronger support for the central mechanism and improved documentation provide a substantial net gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe FlowState and retain the same core research identity. Text, equations, tables and figures support reliable comparison throughout. v1 ends after its references; v3 additionally contains Appendices A–D, which were inspected.

after.justification: v3 reports original benchmark results, expanded ablations, mixed-rate forecasting demonstrations, representation analyses and scale-selection experiments in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original FlowState evaluations on GIFT-ZS, full GIFT-Eval and Chronos-ZS, plus sampling-rate robustness experiments and component ablations.

results.title: FlowState: Sampling-Rate‑Equivariant Time‑Series Forecasting

C1.justification: v2 broadens the headline applicability claims to multiple model families, MHA architectures, and long-context tasks. The abstract and conclusion replace the earlier 1.1x average decoding and 1.13x end-to-end claims with up to 1.6x decoding acceleration over full attention and 1.72x sparse-kernel acceleration. The training-free unified-selection contribution remains.

C2.justification: v2 removes v1 Section 5's explicit discussion of fixed budgets and ratios, full-KV-cache memory costs, unoptimized index union, and extensions to MLA/MoE. It adds interpretations connecting kernel efficiency to reduced memory traffic and re-selection placement to semantic abstraction and attention stability (Appendices A.2 and A.5).

D1.justification: v2 documents SGLang/FlashInfer integration, identifies PG-19-mini for retrieval and layer selection, and summarizes model-specific re-selection layers in Table 10. v1's explicit disclosure that index aggregation uses PyTorch primitives disappears; this does not establish an implementation replacement. The code-access link remains unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds five LongBench tasks: MultiFieldQA, Qasper, HotpotQA, TriviaQA, and PassageRetrieval-en (Table 9), substantially broadening coverage beyond the retained reasoning benchmarks. Its extended long-context retrieval evaluation builds on Needle-in-the-Haystack diagnostics already present in v1.

E2.justification: StreamingLLM joins the Qwen reasoning-accuracy comparisons in v2 Figure 5, whereas v1 used it only in attention diagnostics. New retrieval comparisons evaluate H2O and TOVA alongside existing methods (Table 8), and Quest joins the decoding-latency comparison (Table 1).

E3.justification: Reasoning evaluation expands to Qwen3-14B and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, with additional non-reasoning GQA/MHA configurations and larger token budgets. Quest's reported block size changes from 64 to 32 for Qwen and 16 for DeepSeek. The Llama-3.1/A5000 timing setup is replaced by DeepSeek/A100 measurements and additional SGLang/A5000 tests.

E4.justification: v2 adds direct reasoning-accuracy ablations of re-selection placement, including no re-selection (Table 11), and recency-pattern analyses across GPQA/AIME-25 and token budgets (Figure 10). FLOP and memory-transfer profiling investigates the source of kernel efficiency. Earlier aggregation, recency-ratio, and generation-length analyses are largely retained or relocated.

E5.justification: Reported main-evaluation sampling increases from 16 to 64 traces per problem for AIME and from 8 to 16 for GPQA; MATH500 retains eight. Pass@1 remains the estimator, and no confidence intervals or significance tests are added. v2 Table 2 separately retains the older 16-trace generation-length analysis.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive model, budget, retrieval, LongBench, ablation, and efficiency results. Qwen3-8B/AIME-24 accuracy at 2K changes from 73.75 in v1 Table 2 to 73.00 in v2 Table 5 under increased sampling. Figure 6 newly reports up to 1.58x decoding and 1.72x kernel speedups under revised settings, rather than demonstrating a same-setting improvement over v1. The retained generation-length table changes only through rounding.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 preserves per-head top-k proposals, unified aggregation, proportional recency preservation, and reuse of selected indices across layers. CUSA renames and explains the existing mechanism; the additional model evaluations and kernel measurements do not establish a changed selection algorithm.

P1.justification: The title and terminology change, and the introduction, observations, and methodology are extensively rewritten around CUSA and global stability. Main-text ablations and locality discussions are reorganized into an expanded appendix, while the dedicated limitations section disappears and an impact statement is added.

P2.justification: The document switches from single-column to two-column layout. The method diagram is redrawn, the reasoning plot expands from eight to sixteen panels, and latency-accuracy plots are replaced by efficiency bar charts. Numerous tables and heatmaps are added; existing analyses are relocated or redisplayed, and detailed reasoning-baseline tables become compact LessIsMore/full-attention comparisons.

R1.justification: References supporting LongBench, LongChat, TOVA, SGLang, and PagedAttention are added, while MagicPIG, Twilight, and Hymba are removed with the future-work discussion. The related-work taxonomy and central positioning against head-local selection and training-dependent sparse attention remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The attention, subset-selection, and attention-recall formulations remain equivalent, as does the algorithm's mathematical structure. Neither version develops formal theorems or proofs; v2's expanded stability arguments are empirical and conceptual.

improvement.justification: v1's generality and efficiency claims relied mainly on two Qwen reasoning models and a separate Llama timing proxy. v2 substantially strengthens their validation through another reasoning family, MHA retrieval, LongBench, serving-stack measurements, memory profiling, and direct layer-placement ablations. These address important gaps in architectural generality, practical efficiency, and design justification. Removing explicit limitations and detailed baseline tables reduces transparency, but the targeted empirical additions provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe LessIsMore by the same authors. Their complete text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison despite the changed title and substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds model evaluations, long-context benchmarks, serving-stack measurements, kernel profiling, and layer-placement ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original reasoning accuracies, attention-recall analyses, ablations, and decoding-latency measurements in Section 4 and Appendix A.

results.title: Less Is More: Fast and Accurate Reasoning with Cross-Head Unified Sparse Attention

C1.justification: Both versions claim a three-factor explanation based on learnability, reliability, and completeness, and a low-cost estimator of downstream semi/self-supervised performance. V2 foregrounds quantitative estimation and assumptions, but retains the original theoretical unification and practical contribution.

C2.justification: V2 newly interprets synchronized semi/self-supervised outcomes as indicating limited dependence on training strategy. It attributes polarized performance to amplification of beneficial or harmful pretext-task effects during training and extends its applicability interpretation to distribution shift. These explanations are absent from v1; no substantive limitations discussion is added.

D1.justification: V2 newly identifies PyTorch/torchvision, four-A800 hardware, LAMDA-SSL and Lightly implementations, and the single-A800 convention for timing measurements. It specifies Euclidean prototype assignment more clearly, while shortening Table 1's augmentation calls. Most basic training hyperparameters were already documented in v1.

E1.justification: V2 retains CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and the same 115 augmentation-based pretext tasks, while adding ImageNet-200 and Office-31. Office-31 introduces a distinct distribution-shift scenario, using Amazon labeled data and DSLR/Webcam unlabeled data.

E2.justification: Table 4 adds an explicit resource-efficiency comparison against conventional full semi-supervised and self-supervised training plus validation. The seven named SSL algorithms in the robustness experiments supply target training outcomes rather than competing performance estimators; no alternative pretext-task selection estimator is introduced.

E3.justification: The original basic CIFAR protocol is retained. V2 adds protocols using native SSL algorithms, ResNet-50, an estimation budget of 50 unlabeled samples per labeled sample instead of 10, and separate tests with 10 epochs or a 1e-5 learning rate. It also introduces cross-domain sampling and a timed resource comparison.

E4.justification: V1 has no component ablations or systematic robustness analyses. V2 adds all individual and paired indicator combinations on CIFAR-10 in Tables 2–3, plus algorithm, backbone, distribution-shift, data-volume, and hyperparameter tests. Although the text promises CIFAR-100 and ImageNet-200 ablations, those results are absent from the supplied appendix.

E5.justification: V1 reports correlation coefficients without significance testing. V2's Hypothesis Testing section adds one-tailed correlation t-tests at alpha = 0.01, using 115 tasks, 113 degrees of freedom, and a reported critical correlation of 0.226. Neither version reports repeated-run variability or confidence intervals.

E6.justification: CIFAR-10 correlations remain 0.785/0.820 for semi/self-supervised learning. Reported CIFAR-100 correlations change from 0.717/0.724 to 0.905/0.950, but v2 Figure 3 duplicates the CIFAR-10 plot and Figure 4 has conflicting paradigm labels, limiting verification. Numerous new results include ImageNet-200 correlations of 0.675/0.678, Office-31's 0.674, ablation and robustness scores, and estimation time of 29.6 seconds versus 1547.3/1651.6 seconds for full training and validation.

M1.justification: The specified prototype-alignment procedure changes: v1 uses f_target to extract labeled embeddings, whereas v2 uses f_pretext for both class prototypes and unlabeled embeddings. This is a limited procedural correction; the three-factor estimator, successive filtering, and final product remain intact.

P1.justification: V2 substantially rewrites the title, abstract, introduction, and related work, and consistently shifts terminology toward assumptions and performance estimation. It reorganizes the related-work subsections, shortens the conclusion, moves future work into the supplementary material, and introduces an Impact Statement.

P2.justification: Scatterplots are redesigned from individually labeled points to operation colors and strength-dependent opacity with legends. Table 1 becomes a compact single-column display, and new ablation tables, a cost table, and extensive supplementary figures are added. CIFAR-100 presentation moves to the appendix, but Figure 3 incorrectly repeats Figure 1 and Figure 4 contains conflicting labels.

R1.justification: The related-work discussion substantially broadens from a dedicated neuro-symbolic treatment to knowledge-integrated learning and expands coverage of SSL assumptions, safety, and pretext misalignment. New references include Rigollet, Mey and Loog, Von Rueden and colleagues, and He and Li; several earlier handcrafted-pretext and shortcut references are removed. This changes research positioning beyond bibliographic maintenance.

T1.justification: Equation 1 changes the probabilistic factorization by retaining x in the reliability conditioning and both x and the knowledge-satisfaction events in the completeness conditioning. Optimization expressions also replace indicator-loss minima with argmin expressions using named task losses. The central three-factor error bound remains, without a new theorem or substantial proof expansion.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses v1's narrow empirical validation: Tables 2–3 test the contribution of each factor, experiments with established SSL algorithms and distribution shift test broader applicability, and Table 4 directly measures the claimed cost advantage. These gains provide substantially stronger support than v1's single-backbone, simplified-loss CIFAR experiments. Duplicated or conflicting CIFAR-100 figures, unresolved references, and missing promised ablations weaken particular results, but do not outweigh the broader validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same three-factor estimation framework and 115-pretext-task benchmark despite the changed title. All pages were readable, including v2's supplementary sections. The reporting inconsistencies identified below are document issues, not extraction gaps.

after.justification: V2 reports original benchmark results, component ablations, robustness experiments, and resource measurements in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: V1 reports original CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 experiments comparing estimated performance with actual semi/self-supervised performance, including scatterplots and Pearson correlations.

results.title: Quantitative Estimation of Target Task Performance from Unsupervised Pretext Task in Semi/Self-Supervised Learning

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes parallel TTS as a core innovation and advertises up to 7.8% performance improvement and 10.3% latency reduction. v3 centers protocol-constrained routing, verifiable evidence reuse, and interruption-consistent execution. It explicitly bounds training-free claims to integration/control and replaces broad superiority claims with competitive performance and low orchestration overhead.

C2.justification: v3 explains reuse through evidence identity and runtime policies, rather than mainly through controller reasoning and contextual memory. It adds substantive limitations: sparse sampling impairs fine-grained temporal counting, continuous temporal encoders may capture rapid dynamics better, and routing remains imperfect for ambiguous inputs. These qualifications are absent from v1's largely affirmative interpretation.

D1.justification: v3 newly discloses 8 A100 80GB GPUs, FP16 inference, deterministic decoding, and a 20-FPS/20-frame-batch video configuration. Appendices provide revised controller/generator prompts, mapping contracts, evidence-record examples, and persistence rules. These substantially improve technical specification, while the existing 7–15-word TTS segmentation guidance is retained.

E1.justification: v3 adds WorldSense evaluation, including audio localization, recognition, counting, and semantic/temporal tasks, plus sustained, mixed, and independent dialogue scenarios. v1's AI2D and InfoVQA evaluations disappear. MathVision, CC-OCR, and MMBench-CN remain named in v3's setup, so their missing scores alone do not establish removal of that coverage.

E2.justification: The principal model comparators are largely retained after table merging. However, M2-omni's MMBench-EN comparison is omitted: v1 Table 1 reports 80.70, whereas v3 Table 1 shows no result. The sequential and parallel-pipeline TTS comparators, and Claude 3.5 Sonnet's scored specialized-task comparisons, also disappear.

E3.justification: v3 introduces controlled memory-on/off comparisons and fixed-controller expert-pair swaps with matched ASR and frame-sampling settings. Its new latency analysis separates routing from expert computation, excludes network I/O, and specifies 100 sampled queries per benchmark. These additions change the evaluation design; newly disclosed settings for retained benchmarks do not establish that those experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v3 adds memory-reuse ablation across dialogue types, fixed-controller expert-swapping analysis, and a WorldSense task breakdown examining semantic reasoning versus temporal tracking. The Video-MME length analysis remains, while v1's TTS architecture speed/stability comparison is removed. Controller replacement is additionally discussed qualitatively without a detailed results table.

E5.justification: v3 newly specifies seed=42 but drops v1's TTS timing-variability report. Neither version provides repeated-run confidence intervals or significance tests. The seed disclosure does not establish an increase in experimental runs.

E6.justification: New results include 44.07% on WorldSense, 49% average expert-call reduction, 10.36% average routing overhead, and 72.31% Video-MME accuracy using the new Qwen3 expert pair. The latter is a new configuration, not a same-configuration improvement over v1. MMBench-EN 88.54%, MMStar 69.37%, MMMU 70.04%, and Figure 3's results remain unchanged; MMBench-CN scores, specialized-task results, and TTS measurements are removed.

M1.justification: v1's mixed control-token/content output becomes token-only planning followed by a separate response-generation call in v3. The reported memory procedure changes to exact evidence-key cache-or-call with a retained full store and compressed context view. Explicit validation, fallback, cancellation, and completed-output commit rules substantially revise the procedure (Section 3; Appendices A–D).

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, method, experimental discussion, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Related work expands from two to five thematic subsections, the method is reorganized into input/orchestration/output stages, and retained benchmark discussion is condensed. Appendices are substantially rewritten and expanded with an additional experimental-results section.

P2.justification: v3 replaces the earlier conceptual/workflow diagrams with a redrawn three-stage overview, merges the main comparison tables, and adds efficiency plots, an expert-swapping table, and a WorldSense breakdown. The specialized-task table and TTS plot disappear. Figure 3's underlying plot is retained, while the document adopts new typography, colored headings, and styled boxes.

R1.justification: v3 substantially repositions the contribution against existing training-free composition systems, including HuggingGPT, Visual Programming, ViperGPT, and ReAct. It adds structured-generation, agent-memory, and streaming-assistant literature and emphasizes protocol-enforced execution and verifiable reuse as its distinction. This replaces much of v1's broader trained-model and multi-agent survey.

T1.justification: v3 introduces formal evidence-key construction and an exact-key, piecewise cache-or-call rule in Equations (1)–(2), replacing v1's general input-output and modality-selection equations. These revise the mathematical specification of the procedure. Neither version contains substantive theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially addresses v1's underspecified procedure and weak support for memory efficiency and modularity through explicit execution contracts, disclosed inference settings, and Figure 2/Table 2 experiments. Positioning against existing training-free systems and concrete temporal/routing limitations also make the claims better calibrated. Specialized-task and TTS evidence is lost, and promised interruption measurements remain unreported, but the gains in specification, relevant evidence, and scientific framing outweigh these gaps.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with readable main texts and appendices supporting matched comparison. Although v1 Figure 4 extends beyond the page boundary, its embedded numerical values and accompanying discussion are recoverable.

after.justification: v3 retains original benchmark results and adds memory/latency measurements, expert-swapping results, and WorldSense evaluation, including the task breakdown in Appendix F.

before.justification: v1 reports original orchestration benchmark results, Video-MME backbone comparisons, and TTS speed and stability measurements in Tables 1–3 and Figures 3–4.

results.title: Training-Free Multimodal Large Language Model Orchestration

C1.justification: The main claims about a single linear program, regression and classification support, and less conservative prediction sets are retained. v2 additionally claims applicability to other set representations and explicitly presents ZCP as a replacement for multi-output CP across many applications (Introduction, Section 1.2, and Conclusions), modestly broadening its stated scope.

C2.justification: Section 4.2 adds explanations of when output versus parametric uncertainties are appropriate. Appendix B.1 newly warns that calibration-dependent QR placement weakens coverage guarantees and suggests separate placement data. The conclusion adds explicit convexity, central-symmetry, and linearity restrictions beyond the existing computational-cost, overfitting, and multimodality caveats.

D1.justification: Section 6 newly states that the methods are implemented in the MATLAB toolbox CORA and provides a toolbox access link. Existing architecture specifications, data-generation instructions, hyperparameters, and runtime results remain substantially unchanged.

E1.justification: Table 1 retains the same ten regression and four classification tasks. Appendix A retains the same synthetic generators, real-world datasets, and photovoltaic forecasting task; no additional evaluated domain or scenario appears.

E2.justification: The corresponding regression and classification comparisons still evaluate ZCP against CP and IPM. Appendix B retains the same uncertainty-placement, cost-function, and outlier-detection comparators. Newly cited conformal methods are discussed but not evaluated.

E3.justification: Table 2's analytical comparison now accounts for up to n_out*n_y discarded CP samples from dimensionwise calibration. Empirical splits, network sizes, and metrics remain unchanged. Figures 2 and 4 relabel the outlier sweep from 1–5 to 1–4, although Section 6 still states 0–5; this reporting inconsistency does not establish a rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix B retains the same placement sensitivity, regression and classification cost-function ablations, and outlier-detection comparison, with unchanged evidence in Figures 6–9 and Table 3. The illustrative prediction sets in Figures 3 and 5 also remain unchanged.

E5.justification: Both versions report averages across 30 trained networks and 95% bootstrap confidence intervals, including the appendix plots. No repeated-run, seed, significance-testing, or empirical uncertainty-estimation practice changes are documented.

E6.justification: Table 2 contains substantive recalculations beyond changing its display from coverage to epsilon. For RF1 with five outliers, v1 reports CP coverage 0.9665; v2 reports epsilon 0.1088, corresponding to coverage 0.8912 under revised outlier accounting. IPM/ZCP remains at coverage 0.9381, reversing the displayed guarantee ranking. Empirical plots and appendix timings are unchanged.

M1.justification: The three-stage ZCP construction, uncertainty placement, and objective remain. However, v2 corrects operative constraints: the classification containment sign, boundary-point slack signs and nonnegativity, and the MILP retained-sample inequality (Theorem 7; Propositions 8–10). These are repairs to existing optimization procedures; the PDFs do not establish changes to the experimental implementation.

P1.justification: The related-work and preliminary sections undergo substantial rewriting and reorganization, including numbered related-work subsections, reworked IPM/CP explanations, and a separate Scenario Approach section. The contributions, coverage discussion, and conclusion are also restructured, with limitations presented explicitly as bullets.

P2.justification: The same nine figures and three tables remain. Table captions move below their tables, Table 2's caption is reformulated around epsilon and explicit 90% confidence, Figure 1 labels are simplified, and Figures 2 and 4 change their outlier legends. Plot geometry and results displays otherwise remain unchanged apart from relocation and spacing.

R1.justification: Section 1.1 substantially expands the positioning around scenario theory and its connections to conformal prediction, adding works such as Calafiore and Campi, Coppola, and O'Sullivan, alongside additional multi-output approaches by Cini, Gray, Braun, and Tumu. The conclusion now distinguishes the method's IPM foundation from its shared practical goal with CP. Earlier citations, including Romano's quantile-regression work, are removed.

T1.justification: The new Section 2.3 formalizes convex scenario optimization, explicitly states nondegeneracy and unique-optimum assumptions, adds the expected-coverage bound in Equation 9, and connects it to CP marginal coverage. Joint-output coverage reasoning is revised. Corrections in Theorem 7 and Propositions 8–10 repair substantive mathematical constraints, rather than merely changing notation.

improvement.justification: v1's boundary-point LP permits unbounded slack, and its outlier MILPs allow all observations to be discarded; v2 corrects both, alongside classification containment. These repairs resolve serious defects in the published construction procedures. Explicit scenario assumptions, coverage reasoning, and implementation information further improve reliability and reproducibility. These gains outweigh remaining reporting inconsistencies: the outlier legends conflict with Section 6, and Table 2's RF1 values contradict the blanket claim that CP provides stronger guarantees.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Zono-Conformal Prediction work. The complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–B are readable and can be matched across revisions and relocations.

after.justification: v2 retains these original empirical evaluations, including the benchmark results and Appendix B ablations. Retained results qualify independently of whether experiments were rerun.

before.justification: v1 reports original regression and classification experiments, coverage and conservatism measurements, computation times, and appendix ablations.

results.title: Zono-Conformal Prediction: Zonotope-Based Uncertainty Quantification for Regression and Classification Tasks

C1.justification: The central contributions of scalable path-conditioned world generation and phase-coherent RF simulation remain. v2 removes the explicit first-time RF-imaging data-generation claim and adds a comparative claim that augmentation scales better than competing RF simulation methods. The new real-measurement/HFSS evidence primarily strengthens the existing signal-realism claim.

C2.justification: v2 adds a token-imbalance explanation for path overfitting and explicitly attributes gains to the proposed components rather than autoregression itself. It interprets sensitivity to material mismatch and the limited diffraction/refraction effects in tested setups, explains scene-generation failures, and expands applicability limitations and future directions to fine-grained interactions and real-data refinement.

D1.justification: v2 adds MotionLCM adaptation details, material-curation information, pipeline timing and hardware, ray counts, antenna configuration, CUDA acceleration, and real-measurement reconstruction details. Code and simulator availability changes from a promised release to a reported release. Conversely, v1's explicit Sionna/Mitsuba implementation and licensing paragraph, 60 cm clearance setting, and failed-path retry description disappear.

E1.justification: v2 adds direct signal-fidelity evaluation using newly collected radar-camera measurements of walking and daily activities against glass, drywall, brick, and metal backgrounds, plus multiple frequency configurations. It also adds HFSS validation across four scenes and four radar poses per scene. These substantially expand test scenarios beyond the retained motion, respiration, imaging, and activity-recognition evaluations.

E2.justification: v2 adds MotionLCM to motion-generation and timing comparisons, Standard RT to imaging augmentation, RF Genesis to activity-recognition augmentation, and HFSS to signal-fidelity comparisons. Standard ray tracing already appeared in v1's phase-coherence tests, but its participation in the downstream augmentation comparison is new. These additions are supported by reported results, not merely citations.

E3.justification: New evaluations introduce WHAM reconstruction of synchronized camera observations, range-time comparisons using PSNR and energy similarity, and a four-scene-by-four-radar-pose HFSS protocol with diffraction/refraction controls. v2 also adds skating, bone-length, collision, and generation-success measurements. The retained motion-training settings, downstream splits, and augmentation budgets do not show corresponding substantive revisions.

E4.justification: v2 adds a state-only removal ablation in Table 2 and pooling, independent-masking, and input-perturbation studies in Appendix Table 6. It also evaluates physical plausibility, scene-generation failures and collisions, frequency robustness, material misassignment, and the effect of enabling diffraction/refraction in HFSS. These substantially extend v1's component and masking-hyperparameter analyses.

E5.justification: Appendix A.2.2 newly specifies that component-runtime measurements are averaged over 10 runs. This is a limited addition of repeat-count information for a new analysis, not evidence that retained benchmarks received more runs. Neither version reports confidence intervals or formal significance tests for the main performance comparisons.

E6.justification: Existing motion-benchmark and downstream augmentation scores are retained, but v2 adds substantial results. Examples include 71.6% versus RF Genesis's 54.6% accuracy at 19× augmentation, 28.63 dB PSNR against collected signals, and HFSS agreement of 33.57 dB without diffraction/refraction versus 31.25 dB with them. New ablation, robustness, physical-plausibility, and runtime results further expand the evidence.

M1.justification: The state-aware transformer, path masking, motion tokenizer, A* planning, and spatial/temporal phase-coherent ray-tracing procedures remain substantively unchanged. The frequency-dependent material model and material-selection workflow already appear in v1 Figure 19. v2 adds material-curation and precomputation details without establishing a change to the underlying method.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and substantial explanatory passages are rewritten. Scene evaluation is folded into Section 4.1, the discussion becomes a standalone conclusion, limitations move to the appendix, and societal impacts move into the main document. The appendix gains a more detailed subsection hierarchy, substantially changing the narrative organization.

P2.justification: The main text and references change from a single-column layout to a two-column conference format. Figure 1 explicitly adds prompt and sensor-configuration inputs; retained figures are resized or rearranged. New baseline and ablation tables, a panoramic-imaging gallery, and real/HFSS comparison panels materially expand the displays. The Doppler figure expands to four timestamps.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially revises positioning around phase coherence and the constraints imposed by time-indexed trajectories. It incorporates CASTER, Chen et al.'s 2025 RF modeling work, MotionLCM, and newer scene-interaction methods. v1's emphasis on short-duration scene-motion datasets is replaced by discussion of missing text control and required temporal inputs. This exceeds bibliographic updating.

T1.justification: The motion-token probability model, channel impulse response, vertex-group path expansion, and frequency-dependent dielectric formulas remain mathematically equivalent. Indexing and notation are clarified, but no substantive theoretical derivation, assumption, theorem, or proof is added or revised.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important gaps in v1's validation through direct real-measurement/HFSS comparisons, material and frequency robustness checks, and competing-simulator augmentation results in Tables 3–4 and Appendix A.3.3. The isolated state ablation and alternative regularization studies also strengthen component attribution. These gains substantially improve support for fidelity, usefulness, and design choices, outweighing the loss of some implementation disclosures.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe WaveVerse, with the same authors, core framework, and retained experiments. The text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support comparison despite extensive reformatting and added evaluations.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds baseline comparisons, real-measurement and HFSS validation, robustness analyses, and runtime measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original motion-generation benchmarks and ablations, RF phase-coherence simulations, and downstream imaging and activity-recognition experiments in Section 4 and Appendix A.

results.title: Scalable RF Simulation in Generative 4D Worlds

C1.justification: v1's contribution statement and conclusion describe a projection enforcing the secant condition. v2 instead claims PSD construction with training that encourages approximate secant consistency. It also removes the faster-global-minimum claim and narrows the intended advantage to costly iterative objectives, substantially qualifying the central guarantees and scope.

C2.justification: v2 explains dimension-dependent loss summaries, interprets scalarization's differing effects on quadratics and HMR, and distinguishes four-step speed from best-error inference cost. Appendix D adds task-distribution dependence, possible retraining, and hyperparameter limitations. The earlier HMR caption's inference about better internalized 3D priors is removed.

D1.justification: v2 supplies a project/code URL where v1 only promises release upon acceptance. It newly documents tensor shapes, coordinate sharing and BatchNorm operations, Bernoulli confidence sampling, LBFGS without explicit line search, and timing scope. Most architecture tables, hardware information, and training hyperparameters were already present.

E1.justification: Both versions use random quadratics, the quadratic/Rosenbrock/Rastrigin benchmark suite, and AMASS-to-3DPW human mesh recovery. The added studies vary dimensions, hyperparameters, and training fractions within this retained coverage; they introduce no new dataset or task.

E2.justification: v2 Table 1 expands the HMR comparison with reported TRACE, WHAM (ViT), and PromptHMR results, explicitly identifying their different training-data scope. It also adds L-SR1 without the secant penalty to the HMR comparison. The analytic comparator set remains unchanged.

E3.justification: v2 adds systematic training/evaluation buffer sweeps, unroll-depth and secant-weight sweeps using a 50-step loss summary, separately meta-trained scalar/vector controls, and AMASS training fractions from 80% to 0.1%. These substantially expand experimental design within existing tasks; the retained benchmark settings are largely unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's projection and input/width ablations, v2 adds buffer robustness, cross-dimensional hyperparameter sensitivity, scalar versus coordinate-wise learning-rate comparisons, and data-efficiency studies. Section 5.2.2 also directly measures whether the training penalty improves secant consistency during HMR inference.

E5.justification: v2 explicitly documents four random seeds for the new quadratic studies and mean-plus-standard-deviation reporting in Table 3. Conversely, the retained input/width ablation loses all uncertainty values from v1 Table 3 to v2 Table 4. No increase in runs for the legacy results is established.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results, including sensitivity heatmaps, secant-residual trajectories, scalarization comparisons, and reduced-data HMR scores: 53.03 with 10% AMASS and 70.78 with 0.1%. The new no-secant HMR row reports 52.80. Headline results remain 51.58 for L-SR1, 51.74 at four steps, and 55.90 for LGD.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 and Figure 2 add the identity contribution to the direction, reconciling them with B0=I already specified in v1 Equation 7. Appendix B.2 introduces a separately trained scalarized learning-rate variant. The primary architecture and secant-penalized objective remain unchanged; PGSM mainly renames and clarifies the existing mechanism.

P1.justification: The abstract, motivation, mechanism explanation, experimental narrative, and conclusion are substantially rewritten. Learned projection becomes PGSM, performance-profile definitions move to Appendix C.2.2, HMR gains dedicated evaluation and diagnostic subsections, and Appendix B is reorganized into four analyses.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column main-text layout, revises the block diagram, separates the retained performance-profile panel into Figure 4, and adds heatmaps and a secant-residual plot. HMR curves gain another comparator, while Table 1 is substantially restructured around training scope and timing; model sizes move to Appendix A.

R1.justification: v2 adds Chen et al. (2022), Liao et al. (2023), and Metz et al. (2022, 2023), and distinguishes its mechanism from online learned preconditioning. These refine the existing learned-optimization positioning; bibliographic corrections and citation-style changes do not constitute additional research coverage.

T1.justification: Section 3.2 adds the mathematical qualification that coordinate-wise rate scaling can make the effective operator nonsymmetric, so the PSD argument alone does not guarantee descent. v2 also corrects QN/SR1 update indexing and relaxes the stated sufficient condition on B0 from positive definite to semidefinite. Appendix F retains the existing lemma and proof.

improvement.justification: v2 resolves an important mismatch between v1's claimed secant guarantees and its penalty-based method, explicitly qualifies descent reasoning, and adds direct mechanism diagnostics and controlled robustness studies. Clearer HMR timing and training-scope comparisons improve interpretation. Removing uncertainty from the retained input/width ablation is a localized regression, outweighed by the stronger validation and more defensible central claims.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe L-SR1 by the same authors. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds buffer sensitivity, learning-rate scalarization, reduced-data training, and inference-time secant-residual results.

before.justification: v1 reports original analytic optimization experiments, AMASS-trained human mesh recovery results on 3DPW, component ablations, and computational measurements.

results.title: L-SR1: Learned Symmetric-Rank-One Preconditioning

C1.justification: The principal accuracy, calibration, and fine-tuning claims remain stable. However, v2's conclusion removes v1's unqualified claim of providing uncertainty estimates 'at no additional computational cost,' while retaining the narrower claim of deterministic-model efficiency for predictive inference.

C2.justification: Appendix A.3 distinguishes symmetry-preserving weight sampling from activation sampling that breaks coupling between irreducible-representation coordinates, clarifying the MACE/UMA limitation. Appendix E substantially develops the efficiency interpretation by separating approximately doubled training cost from unchanged deterministic inference cost and additional sampling costs. Section 4.4 also interprets directly tested acquisition benefits.

D1.justification: v2 adds MATPES access information, acquisition details, training hyperparameters, and explicit validation-based checkpoint selection. Most existing implementation details survive in the appendices. Conversely, it removes the BLIP repository pointer and the explicit float32-high precision statement; this establishes lost documentation, not withdrawal of the repository.

E1.justification: v2 retains the charged-particle, ammonia, and silica experiments and adds MATPES PBE materials configurations with iterative active-learning fine-tuning. This substantially broadens the represented materials and tests uncertainty-driven data acquisition beyond the original fixed-dataset evaluations.

E2.justification: The new MATPES comparison introduces BLIP with random acquisition as a control for uncertainty-guided acquisition, alongside fine-tuning without BLIP. Comparator membership in the retained particle, ammonia, and silica experiments is unchanged.

E3.justification: The MATPES experiment introduces separate initial-training, acquisition-pool, validation, and test partitions, repeated 10% pool acquisition, and five 25-epoch stages with batch size 128 (Appendix B.3 and Table 5). This is a substantial new evaluation design; the original benchmark settings are largely retained.

E4.justification: Section 4.4 adds a controlled analysis of whether uncertainty-based acquisition improves upon random acquisition, including learning curves across acquisition stages. Appendix E and Table 6 additionally analyze parameter counts and training, deterministic-inference, and sampling costs, addressing efficiency claims previously supported mainly qualitatively.

E5.justification: The new MATPES study explicitly reports means and standard deviations over three random initializations, with Figure 4 averaging three independent runs. The original four-seed results and silica standard-error reporting remain unchanged; there is no evidence of increased repetitions for those experiments.

E6.justification: Original benchmark scores are retained. New MATPES results report energy/force MAEs of 91.13 meV/atom and 103.85 meV/Å for uncertainty-guided BLIP, versus 96.65 and 105.12 for random-acquisition BLIP. v2 also adds ammonia comparator correlations, including GMM's 0.904 versus BLIP's retained 0.863, and ORB v3 computational-cost results.

M1.justification: v2 adds an active-learning application procedure that repeatedly selects the top 10% of pool structures by predicted energy uncertainty and fine-tunes BLIP. The underlying Bayesian model and Algorithms 1–4 remain unchanged. The KL weighting and dropout conversion newly shown in the main text were already documented in v1's appendices.

P1.justification: v2 condenses the existing experimental setup paragraphs, separates MLIP uncertainty into Section 2.4, and moves the local-reparameterization explanation into Appendix A.3. It also removes the impact statement and acknowledgements. The overall narrative order and much of the original methods and results prose remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds an active-learning results table and learning-curve figure, plus a computational-cost table. It expands the ammonia uncertainty table with a correlation column and the hyperparameter table with MATPES settings. Existing figures are retained and relocated, and the ammonia tables exchange numbering; these moves do not represent new results.

R1.justification: New Section 2.4 substantially expands the previously brief MLIP uncertainty discussion to Bayesian uncertainty, active learning, ensemble calibration, and post-hoc calibration. Added references include Thaler, Jinnouchi, Pernot, and Hu, positioning BLIP against calibration limitations as well as ensemble costs. MATPES is newly cited, while Parr's DFT reference is removed.

T1.justification: New Appendix A.3 introduces formal assumptions, Proposition 1 and its proof for stochastic equivariant maps, and a corollary connecting the result to BLIP. v1 supplied only a qualitative symmetry discussion. The existing KL derivation and relocated local-reparameterization formulas are retained.

improvement.justification: v1 mainly inferred active-learning usefulness from uncertainty–error correlations and discussed symmetry and efficiency qualitatively. v2 adds a controlled three-run active-learning study, a formal equivariance proof, and explicit computational accounting, substantially strengthening these important foundations. Removing the code link and leaving 6% of MATPES data unexplained by the stated split fractions weaken reproducibility, but these limited drawbacks do not outweigh the gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe BLIPs by the same authors. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds original MATPES active-learning results in Section 4.4, Table 4, and Figure 4.

before.justification: v1 reports original charged-particle prediction experiments, BLIP training on ammonia, and ORB v3 fine-tuning on silica, including predictive accuracy and uncertainty results.

results.title: BLIPs: Bayesian Learned Interatomic Potentials

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution paragraph and conclusion retain the same central claims: CDFG-based self-supervised representations improve RTL area/delay estimation, and post-mapping knowledge distillation further improves performance. The expanded experiments support these existing claims without redefining the main contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations for rare-operator masking benefits, poorer sequential-circuit performance, differing area/delay generalization, LLM overfitting and partitioning errors. Section 4.5 and Appendix O newly qualify technology-node transfer, memory requirements and scalability. Appendix M explicitly acknowledges that partitioning has not been validated on designs exceeding 100,000 CDFG nodes.

D1.justification: Existing hyperparameters and hardware descriptions remain. v2 additionally discloses frozen LLM backbones, a 30M-parameter model, approximately 40 hours of single-GPU training and a 42 GB training footprint. It expands dataset provenance and replaces the anonymous code/data repository pointer with a named GitHub code link. These are incremental disclosures, not evidence of changed original training settings.

E1.justification: Section 4.6 adds 102 industrial RTL modules organized into 51 functionally equivalent pairs, extending evaluation to industrial designs and pairwise quality ranking. v2 also names RTLCoder, MGVerilog and generated RTL among dataset sources, but the unchanged 13,200-design count and statistics do not establish that the underlying training corpus changed.

E2.justification: Appendices J–K add substantively revised comparators: all three CodeV models receive textualized CDFGs, and CodeV-QW-7B is additionally evaluated with full fine-tuning. v2 also removes Graph-XGBoost specifically from the distillation comparison in Table 2, while retaining it in Table 1. These changes substantially broaden the tested LLM alternatives.

E3.justification: The original split, metrics and training configurations remain, but v2 introduces several additional protocols: training with 5%, 10% and 20% of labeled data; disjoint functional clusters formed using embeddings and k-means with k=50; training on the smallest 80% of designs; and industrial pairwise ranking. These supplement rather than replace the original evaluation.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's two pretraining-task ablations, v2 tests stratified masking, input versus embedding masking, positional encodings, GNN/Transformer components and edge-sampling sensitivity. It also adds circuit-type breakdowns, functional and size-shift tests, limited-data analysis, LLM adaptation analyses, partitioning experiments and runtime scaling. These address substantially more questions about mechanisms, robustness and applicability.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The new runtime averages and per-class accuracies do not introduce uncertainty estimation or repeated-run reporting.

E6.justification: Table 1 and the shared rows of Table 2 retain their numerical values; the Graph-XGBoost distillation results are removed. Numerous new results appear, including industrial area/delay ranking accuracies of 82.35%/88.23%, partitioned accuracies of 78.43%/88.23%, and fully fine-tuned CodeV-QW-7B validation R2 values of 0.2685/0.0923. These are additional conditions and variants, not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The core architecture, pretraining objectives and distillation procedure remain. However, Eq. 2 replaces adjacency A with (A+A^T)/2 in positional encoding. Appendix M also introduces an optional inference adaptation that partitions designs at register boundaries, sums predicted subcircuit areas and takes the maximum predicted delay.

P1.justification: The shared abstract, methodology and conclusion receive limited wording and terminology edits, while the original narrative order remains. v2 introduces numbered sections, lettered appendices, clearer cross-references, acknowledgments and an impact statement. Most expansion consists of new scientific material rather than extensive rewriting of retained content.

P2.justification: v2 adds limited-data, architectural-ablation, partitioning and runtime figures, plus extensive new result tables. v1's coarse-count table and fine-count histogram are combined into Figure 5, and its node-type table becomes Table 12. The conference template changes typography, headers and caption placement, while appendices switch to a full-width layout.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for RTLCoder, MGVerilog, text embeddings and k-means, while removing CraftRTL and PRIMAL. It also sharpens the distinction between CDFGs, DFGs and ASTs. The central positioning against hand-crafted graph features and token-based LLM representations remains; publication updates to retained references do not constitute new cited works.

T1.justification: Eq. 2 substantively revises the Laplacian definition by replacing A with (A+A^T)/2 while retaining the in-degree and out-degree normalization factors. This is a localized mathematical change rather than equivalent notation. The remaining objectives and metric formulas are retained, and no theorems or proofs are added.

improvement.justification: v1 mainly validates its claims through the original benchmark and two task-removal ablations. v2 substantially strengthens validation with architectural controls, functional and size shifts, additional LLM comparisons and industrial ranking, while making practical limitations explicit. These gains outweigh limited reporting flaws: uncertainty remains unreported, and Appendix N's 52.18 GB peak-memory value conflicts with Figure 9's 51.0 GB label. The improvement comes from stronger scrutiny and clearer applicability boundaries, not higher retained benchmark scores.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same StructRTL research. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, figures and tables, support reliable comparison despite substantial additions and reformatting in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds original industrial evaluations, architectural ablations, generalization tests, alternative LLM comparisons and runtime measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original pretraining results, area and delay prediction experiments, baseline comparisons and pretraining-task ablations on a 13,200-design dataset.

results.title: Beyond Tokens: Enhancing RTL Quality Estimation via Structural Graph Learning

C1.justification: v1's principal empirical claim concerns eight standard NLP benchmarks against NTP and MTP. v2 broadens its abstract, contributions, and conclusion to DS-MTP, nine benchmarks, math/code generation, and solving the hardest tested star graph where the comparators fail. The conclusion also acknowledges weaker speculative decoding.

C2.justification: v1's tentative interpretation of TOP as a regularizer is removed. v2 adds interpretations concerning DS-MTP overfitting, task-dependent lookahead windows, and stronger learning signals from higher TOP weighting. It also discusses decoding limitations and explicitly limits extrapolation to larger models and longer training.

D1.justification: v2 adds configuration provenance, continued-training hyperparameters in Table 10, detailed synthetic-experiment settings, and disclosure of two weeks per 7B model on eight H200 GPUs. The original configuration table largely moves to Appendix A, but its device-batch-size and gradient-accumulation rows are omitted. The code-access link is retained.

E1.justification: v2 retains FineWeb-Edu and the eight original benchmarks, adds MMLU, and introduces continued training on Stack-Edu Python and OpenMathInstruct-2 with HumanEval, MBPP, GSM8K, and MATH evaluation. It also adds synthetic star-graph pathfinding and decoding tests on wiki, books, code, and math texts.

E2.justification: DS-MTP changes from a cited, planned comparison in v1 to an evaluated baseline alongside NTP/MTP/TOP at all three sizes in Table 2. v2 also evaluates two- and four-head MTP and DS-MTP variants in the star-graph comparison, substantially extending comparator coverage.

E3.justification: Retained base-pretraining settings agree, while new experiments introduce continued-training budgets, few-shot math/code protocols, pass@16/32/64, graph train/test splits and different layer-matching controls, 5,000-snippet decoding evaluations, and configuration sweeps. The newly stated zero-shot setting for existing benchmarks documents their protocol without establishing a change to those evaluations.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's MTP-head loss illustration, v2 adds a TOP-versus-MTP loss comparison, tests lookahead across graph structures and head counts, and studies window size and loss weighting in Tables 7–8. Appendix B adds componentwise training trajectories used to examine behavior such as DS-MTP's weak downstream performance.

E5.justification: Neither version reports seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The additional loss trajectories are not identified as uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Shared NTP/MTP/TOP scores on the original eight benchmarks are unchanged. v2 adds extensive results in Tables 2–8 and Appendix B, including TOP's 100% accuracy on G(5,5) versus the best baseline's 19.5%. Generative results are mixed: for example, 7B TOP scores 20.40% on MATH versus NTP's 21.74%. These are new comparisons, not improvements to the original scores.

M1.justification: The core TOP target construction, auxiliary head, and default loss remain unchanged. Sections 5.4–5.5 add limited procedural extensions: speculative decoding using ordered TOP predictions validated by the NTP head, and unequal NTP/TOP loss-weight variants.

P1.justification: v2 reorganizes the introduction/background discussion, expands the explanation of Algorithm 1, subdivides the method and experiments, and moves training configurations into Appendix A. The early-preprint Future Additions ending is replaced by dedicated Related Work and Limitations sections and an expanded conclusion, substantially changing the narrative structure.

P2.justification: The main text changes from one to two columns. Figure 1 is redrawn, Figure 2 becomes a two-panel comparison, and Table 2 is transposed and replaces colored differences with bold best scores. Numerous new experimental tables, graph illustrations, and appendix loss plots substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v2 adds a substantial Related Work section covering masked and denoising objectives, retrieval-based training, and newer MTP approaches, including register tokens and continuous reasoning. New benchmark, dataset, and configuration-source citations further broaden the positioning beyond v1's concentrated NTP/MTP and learning-to-rank discussion.

T1.justification: v2 adds formal DS-MTP definitions in Equations 5–8 and a limited FLOP/parameter derivation in Section 4.2 and Table 1, replacing qualitative overhead discussion with explicit expressions. The central TOP mathematics remains unchanged, and no theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 resolves important gaps in v1: DS-MTP comparison, generative evaluation, and direct star-graph testing of the lookahead motivation were previously only planned. These experiments, sensitivity studies, and disclosed decoding failures substantially strengthen the evidence and clarify applicability. Mixed generative gains, unexplained DS-MTP weakness, and absent uncertainty reporting warrant caution about broad claims, but do not outweigh the substantial improvement in empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TOP research, with matching authors, core method, and retained experiments. All pages, equations, tables, and figures were readable. v1 has no appendices; v2's Appendices A and B were included in the comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds DS-MTP comparisons, math/code evaluations, star-graph experiments, speculative-decoding measurements, sensitivity studies, and appendix training curves.

before.justification: v1 reports original pretraining and benchmark results for 340M, 1.8B, and 7B models in Table 2, plus a 16M-model training-loss experiment in Figure 2.

results.title: Predicting the Order of Upcoming Tokens Improves Language Modeling

C1.justification: The central contribution remains target-agnostic calibration through frequency filtering and gradient rectification. V2 qualifies the ID-preservation claim as first-order, explicitly emphasizes avoiding a loss-balancing coefficient, and extends the advertised empirical scope to semantic shifts. These refine rather than replace the core contribution.

C2.justification: V2 substantially develops interpretations of asymmetric projection, late-training gradient conflicts, batch-size effects and filtering-ratio trade-offs. New Appendix F explicitly limits applicability to image classification under covariate shift, excludes unknown-class OOD detection, acknowledges weaker Office-Home gains and discusses training overhead. V1 lacks this substantive scope discussion.

D1.justification: V2 supplies detailed Soft-ECE bin statistics, temperature t=0.1 and numerical stabilization, separate gamma tables for training strategies, Office-Home settings and implementation information for added baselines. Appendix D.6 newly specifies RTX 4090 hardware, PyTorch/CUDA versions, mixed precision and measured training costs. The FGR code-access URL is retained.

E1.justification: V2 adds Office-Home classification across Art, Clipart, Product and Real-World domains, evaluated with held-out-domain testing. This substantially extends coverage to visual-style shifts beyond the retained CIFAR/Tiny-ImageNet corruptions and WILDS deployment shifts.

E2.justification: V2 Table 1 adds evaluated Mixup and AugMix comparisons. Tables 3–4 introduce Weighted Sum, and Table 4 compares against PCGrad and CAGrad as replacements for FGR's rectification rule. These expand both practical baseline coverage and comparisons with closely related optimization mechanisms.

E3.justification: The stated main synthetic protocol switches from head-only fine-tuning to training from scratch with delayed FGR activation; the earlier strategy remains in the appendix. V2 adds ACE and test NLL reporting, pretrained transformer evaluations and Office-Home leave-one-domain-out evaluation. Appendix D.1 reports selecting gamma using ID validation ECE, whereas v1 specifies the ID test set; this establishes a reported protocol revision, not independently verified reruns.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's component ablations, individual hyperparameter sweeps and training-strategy comparison, v2 adds real-world optimization ablations, alternative calibration losses, gradient-conflict dynamics, activation-epoch and batch-size sensitivity, joint filtering-parameter sweeps and feature-space Wasserstein analysis. These substantially expand tests of mechanism, robustness and practical trade-offs.

E5.justification: Both versions report averages over three runs. V2 newly specifies independent runs with different random seeds, without establishing an increased run count. V1's explicit seed 1 for dataset splitting is no longer supplied. V2 Figure 7 adds shaded bands but does not define their statistical interpretation.

E6.justification: V2 adds extensive DenseNet-121, Office-Home, transformer, ablation and runtime results; Office-Home shifted ECE for FGR is 20.41%. V1's ResNet-50 synthetic Table 1 results are retained in v2 Table 13, rather than replaced by same-setting gains. Existing entries also change, including iWildCam FGR CECE from 0.160% to 0.155%, while WILDS post-temperature-scaling CECE entries disappear.

M1.justification: The DCT-filtered training mixture, DFL main objective, Soft-ECE calibration objective and asymmetric conflict projection are retained. Warm-up training and head-only fine-tuning already appear in v1's appendix. V2's numerical stabilizer and expanded loss implementation document details without establishing a new algorithmic component.

P1.justification: V2 substantially rewrites the abstract, introduction, theoretical explanation and experimental narrative. It introduces numbered sections, promotes ablations into the main text, relocates ID evaluation and existing sensitivity material to the appendix, and reorganizes the appendices into more detailed subsections with explicit limitations.

P2.justification: V2 redraws the introductory illustration, expands reliability diagrams, revises Grad-CAM comparisons, merges the earlier component-ablation tables and restructures the main results table around ACE. It also adds numerous analytical displays, relocates retained tables and changes the appendix to a full-width layout. These are substantial display changes beyond renumbering.

R1.justification: The three-part calibration, distribution-shift and frequency-domain positioning remains. V2 adds references on evidential learning, vision-language adaptation and frequency shortcuts, and explicitly distinguishes FGR from PCGrad/CAGrad. References supporting the removed generalization argument disappear. This expands context and sharpens positioning without replacing the research framing.

T1.justification: V2 removes v1's Theorem 1 and Rademacher-based generalization proof, including the joint-risk-minimization interpretation and tighter-bound claim. Proposition 4.1 and Appendix E instead establish half-space projection, minimum Euclidean correction and first-order calibration preservation, explicitly ignoring the numerical stabilizer. This replaces the central theoretical argument.

improvement.justification: V2 replaces v1's unjustified equivalence between projection and joint-risk minimization with a directly relevant, qualified projection argument.
