Comparisons with generic gradient methods, broader evaluations, reported validation-based hyperparameter selection and explicit limitations substantially strengthen scientific support and transparency. Training descriptions remain inconsistent, notably the 200-epoch warm-up versus Tiny-ImageNet's 100-epoch schedule, but these unresolved details do not outweigh the theoretical correction and stronger empirical scrutiny.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FGR research work despite the changed title. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices support comparison, including matching results relocated between versions.

after.justification: V2 retains original experiments and reports additional Office-Home, transformer-backbone, ablation, sensitivity and computational results.

before.justification: V1 reports original calibration and accuracy experiments on synthetic corruptions and WILDS datasets, with component ablations, sensitivity analyses and training-strategy comparisons.

results.title: Target-Agnostic Calibration under Distribution Shift with Frequency-Aware Gradient Rectification

C1.justification: The central claim that scalable hierarchical learning outperforms flat agents remains. v3 narrows the billion-sample novelty claim to online hierarchical RL, changes the abstract's throughput claim from 25x to approximately 35x and its training scale from 20 to 30 billion frames, and foregrounds algorithmic contributions alongside systems engineering.

C2.justification: v3 adds explanations concerning option degeneracy, non-stationarity, state-dependent coordination, duration selection and sample-efficiency tradeoffs. Appendix A replaces the assumption of entirely supplied rewards with a qualified discussion of learned rewards and their limited generality. It also removes v1's substantive limitation that options cannot be interrupted mid-execution, although the described duration mechanism still selects lengths beforehand.

D1.justification: v3 supplies discriminator architecture, training loss, optimizer details and hyperparameter sweeps for SOL+DIAYN. It also adds network parameter counts, the discount factor, Cython implementation information, an overall training listing and expanded wrapper/trajectory documentation. Reported NetHack runtime is revised. These additions substantially improve implementation documentation; the existing code-release location and hardware platform remain.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate ZombieHorde and TreasureDash, NetHack with Monk, Ranger and Archaeologist, and PointMaze U-Maze, G-Maze, Medium and Large layouts. The additional-character results move to v3 Appendix E.1; they are not new coverage. Learned-reward experiments and ablations use retained environments.

E2.justification: v3 adds Hierarchical RLLib to the NLE throughput comparison (Table 1) and compares learned-reward SOL against handcoded SOL and APPO in Figure 5. Existing baselines remain. MOC gains a PointMaze curve, but its evaluation and outcomes were already reported in v1 Table 6.

E3.justification: Reported NetHack training increases from 20 billion steps in v1 Section 5.2 to 30 billion in v3 Section 5.1. Common MiniHack/NetHack settings change from batch size 57372 to 32768 and reward scaling 0.1 to 0.01; controller settings and sweep ranges also change. New analyses introduce evaluation-episode protocols and duration, option-quality and PPO-epoch controls. These reported revisions do not establish which retained curves were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's option-behavior analysis, v3 adds controlled tests of bootstrapping, fixed versus adaptive durations, duration-set size, reward scaling, redundant or useless options, and PPO update epochs (Appendices E.3–E.7). Appendix E.2 adds policy-overlap measurements and controller behavior conditioned on health and experience, substantially expanding mechanism and sensitivity analysis.

E5.justification: NetHack reporting changes from three seeds with one-standard-error shading in v1 Figure 4 to five seeds with two-standard-error shading in v3 Figures 3 and 9. v3 also reports uncertainty over 500 evaluation episodes for option returns. The main MiniHack and PointMaze comparisons retain two-standard-error shading over ten seeds.

E6.justification: v3 provides extended NetHack results under revised settings and new SOL+DIAYN results showing slower learning but similar final MiniHack performance to handcoded SOL. New ablations report component-removal degradation and task-dependent effects of additional PPO epochs. Table 10 adds policy-overlap values of 0.154, 0.018 and 0.388. Reported SOL throughput changes from approximately 42000 to 43000 steps/second; these are updated reports, not an established same-setting improvement.

M1.justification: v3 introduces SOL+DIAYN: an online discriminator learns to identify options, and its probabilities supply rewards for non-task options (Section 5.3 and Appendix B.3). This adds a substantive reward-learning component previously left as future work. SOL's shared network, option-switch bootstrapping and adaptive durations already existed in v1.

P1.justification: v3 substantially rewrites and reorganizes the method exposition, consolidates the MiniHack and NetHack experimental sections, relocates detailed definitions and multi-character discussion to appendices, and restructures limitations and impact material. These changes extend beyond the prose needed to introduce new experiments.

P2.justification: The main paper changes to a two-column layout. The throughput bar chart becomes a table; NetHack plots are reorganized into separate LLM and non-LLM comparisons; the G-Maze illustration moves to the appendix. v3 adds an architecture diagram and numerous diagnostic plots, and replaces the original behavior display with expanded bar charts and distributions.

R1.justification: Section 4 adds focused comparisons with Agent57 and Park et al.'s offline hierarchical scaling work. It revises the relationship to hierarchical PPO methods from special cases of SOL's objective to distinctions involving bootstrapping and duration selection. New references support the degeneracy and non-stationarity discussion, while the broader research positioning remains hierarchical RL at scale.

T1.justification: Section 3.1 corrects the bootstrap state's index from t+K in v1 to t+K+1 in v3, matching the displayed reward sum through K. The principal value and advantage definitions remain in the corresponding algorithm appendices. The new mechanism discussion does not introduce a theorem or formal proof framework.

improvement.justification: v1 leaves reward discovery entirely to future work and provides little controlled evidence about SOL's individual components. v3's learned-reward experiment and extensive ablations directly address these important gaps, while expanded implementation details and five-seed NetHack reporting strengthen reproducibility and empirical support. Automatic reward learning is demonstrated only on the two MiniHack tasks, and removing the interruption limitation weakens transparency, but these qualifications do not outweigh the substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Scalable Option Learning (SOL). Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable, and corresponding content can be matched despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v3 reports original benchmark results, throughput measurements, learned-reward experiments and extensive behavioral analyses and ablations in Appendix E.

before.justification: v1 reports original throughput measurements and agent-training results on MiniHack, NetHack and PointMaze, including additional PointMaze results in Appendix F.

results.title: Scalable Option Learning in High-Throughput Environments

C1.justification: The optimization-over-estimation thesis remains, but v2 makes objective-aware parametrization a central contribution in the abstract, introduction and conclusion. Its main prescription now combines preserving objective maximizers while reducing the effective action space with using PWLL objectives; v1 primarily advocated PWLL and lighter parametrizations.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive applicability limits: PWLL cannot replace value estimators for evaluation or policy selection, end-to-end neural training loses concavity guarantees, and poor logging coverage can yield suboptimal policies. It also explains the expressiveness–optimization tradeoff of support restriction and the excessive conservatism induced by strong pessimistic regularization.

D1.justification: Appendix E.1 newly documents sample counts, user-history splitting, SVD embeddings, trainable policy parameters, logging-policy construction, reward-model fitting and clustering. Defaults include logging support 100, temperature 1, 2,000 clusters and PC threshold 0.1. v2 also adds a code/artifact link. These are substantial disclosures absent from v1, without proving that retained experiments changed settings.

E1.justification: MovieLens, Twitch and GoodReads remain the real-data benchmarks. Coverage expands modestly through a three-action synthetic bandit in Section 3 and stochastic reward-noise/shift scenarios in Appendix E.4, without adding a new real-data domain.

E2.justification: Figures 10 and 14 add RegKL-LIN and explicit pessimistic comparators: PAC-Bayesian IPS, ES and LS, plus IPS with sample-variance penalization. POTEC is removed from the corresponding MSE comparison, and DM (Bayes) disappears with the old heavyweight/lightweight experiment. PC was already evaluated in v1's figures.

E3.justification: The original batch-size and learning-rate-schedule sweep remains. New experiments compare default Adam with tuned one-cycle optimization and introduce controlled sweeps over reward corruption, clipping thresholds, RegKL temperature, action-space size, cluster count, logging support and pessimism strength. These substantially expand evaluation design; Appendix E.1's newly disclosed defaults do not establish changes to the original runs.

E4.justification: v2 adds support-restriction comparisons, optimization-landscape visualization, MSE trajectories, reward-noise robustness, linear-versus-logarithmic objective controls, and sensitivity analyses for action count, clusters, logging support and pessimism. The heavyweight-versus-lightweight convergence ablation in v1 Figure 3 is removed, although both parametrizations remain documented.

E5.justification: v1 reports no seed counts or uncertainty bands. Appendix E.3 introduces five-seed mean reward and shaded standard deviations across three datasets and two optimizer configurations in Figures 7–8, substantially strengthening statistical reporting for the stability claim. This is newly reported repeated-run evidence, not an established increase in runs for retained figures.

E6.justification: New results show benefits from support restriction, lower seed variability for cLPI, and performance under noise, hyperparameter and pessimism sweeps. Figure 12 reports that POTEC can match cLPI on MovieLens with 1,000 clusters. The original batch-size/schedule results are retained, while heavyweight/lightweight results and POTEC's MSE entries are removed.

M1.justification: v2 introduces objective-aware support restriction as an explicit learning adaptation, including softmax policies restricted to the logging support and comparisons against unrestricted policies. It also changes RegKL's weighting function from exp(r/beta) - 1 to exp(r/beta). The existing PWLL framework and POTEC decomposition otherwise remain.

P1.justification: The introduction gains an explicit contribution list, the estimator discussion is reorganized into standard and large-scale objectives, and optimization and empirical explanations are extensively rewritten. v2 adopts oracle-policy terminology, replaces the lightweight-policy subsection with objective-aware parametrization, and adds structured related-work, proof, implementation and experimental appendices.

P2.justification: v2 adds landscape surfaces, support-comparison panels, uncertainty bands, numerous ablation figures and a dataset-statistics table. v1 Figure 1 becomes v2 Figure 2, while the MSE chart is rescaled after removing POTEC and the old heavyweight/lightweight figure disappears. The document also changes conference template and introduces full-width appendix layouts.

R1.justification: Section 3 explicitly relates PWLL to offline-RL weighted behavioral cloning, discussing AWAC, AWR, CRR and reward-weighted regression, and disclaims novel PWLL update rules. New Appendix A substantially expands research positioning across OPE, OPL, pessimism and online versus offline large-action methods.

T1.justification: Appendices B–C supply oracle-policy derivations and proofs that v1 omitted or explicitly deferred, including optimization plateaus, local maxima and PWLL concavity. v2 formalizes the effective action space and adds stochastic-gradient convergence bounds under bounded-feature and bounded-weight assumptions, including variance-dependent noise floors, in Appendix D.

improvement.justification: v1 explicitly deferred proofs and provided little experimental-construction or uncertainty information. v2 substantially addresses these gaps through Appendices B–D, five-seed stability comparisons, controlled robustness analyses and implementation details. Clearer novelty positioning and applicability limits further improve precision. These gains materially strengthen the paper's support and reproducibility, outweighing the loss of the original heavyweight/lightweight comparison and POTEC MSE entries.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching authors, title, central argument and recommendation benchmarks. Text, equations and figures are readable. v1 has no appendices; v2's Appendices A–E are available and included in the comparison.

after.justification: Section 4 and Appendix E report original benchmark experiments, repeated-seed results and robustness analyses. Section 3 also adds a synthetic optimization-landscape example.

before.justification: Section 4 and Figures 1–3 report original reward, estimation-error and policy-parametrization experiments on MovieLens, Twitch and GoodReads.

results.title: Off-Policy Learning in Large Action Spaces: Optimization Matters More Than Estimation

C1.justification: The central benchmark contribution and findings about VLM strengths, LLM weaknesses, and fragility remain. v3 explicitly claims first-benchmark status, foregrounds TSLM underperformance as a critique of prior claims, and qualifies TSLM advantages relative to comparably sized LLMs.

C2.justification: v3 adds explanations involving signal complexity, CoT reducing refusals and positional bias, and evaluator sensitivity to paraphrasing. Limitations now emphasize restricted TSLM coverage and residual evaluator variability. Its new claim of complete cross-evaluator ranking consistency overreaches: Tables 18–19 reverse GPT-4o-Text versus ChatTS for Gen→GT.

D1.justification: New Appendix H discloses API and Hugging Face endpoint use, batching, and NVIDIA A6000 deployment. Human-example selection is newly described as stratified sampling, and clinical preprocessing is documented. Code/data links and the 150-token generation cap were already present; underlying implementation changes are not established.

E1.justification: v3 adds NICU-HR: 36,679 clinically annotated neonatal heart-rate pairs, extending coverage beyond short financial sequences and synthetic signals to longer clinical recordings. It also evaluates degraded plot images, introducing a new input-quality scenario for VLMs.

E2.justification: GPT-5.4-mini and Gemini-3.0-Flash are added in both text and vision configurations, expanding the reported comparison suite from 13 to 17 configurations. Automatic generation comparisons expand from three models to sixteen in Table 3; the original comparators remain.

E3.justification: v3 introduces GPT-5 entailment judging, controlled plot downsampling and nearest-neighbor upsampling, and NICU-HR preprocessing with opposite-mortality-class distractors. These add substantive evaluation protocols. An automated SUSHI sample-size increase is not established: v1 Appendix F already reports 1,400 examples.

E4.justification: New analyses test VLM sensitivity to pixelation, performance across seven SUSHI signal classes, and CoT-associated changes in refusal rates and positional bias. These extend the existing perturbation, ChatTime-refusal, number-filtered NLI, and interpolation analyses rather than merely relocating them.

E5.justification: Both versions report three human annotators, 40 shared examples, 100 unique examples per annotator, and agreement coefficients exceeding 0.8. Neither adds repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance testing; evaluation across distractor strategies already existed in v1.

E6.justification: v3 adds extensive clinical-data, newer-model, generation, pixelation, and class-wise results. Most matched original scores remain unchanged. One verified revision is GPT-4o with LLMTime on TRUCE-Synthetic differentiation using Sentence-BERT distractors: accuracy changes from 0.832 in v1 Table 10 to 0.819 in v3 Table 12.

M1.justification: The core recognition, differentiation, and generation procedures, four negative-sampling strategies, and modality-specific input representations remain unchanged. No new model architecture, training objective, or prediction algorithm is introduced; the additions concern evaluation coverage and protocols.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contribution statements, results discussion, conclusion, and limitations undergo extensive rewriting. Terminology shifts toward structural properties, the experimental setup is reorganized, and appendices are expanded and restructured around literature, diagnostics, and implementation.

P2.justification: The main text changes to two-column layout. Tables expand and generation results split into automatic and human panels; dataset examples are reorganized with NICU-HR. Robustness plots are condensed in the main text and expanded in the appendix, alongside new literature, class-wise, and evaluator tables.

R1.justification: New Appendix A substantially expands positioning through benchmark comparisons, including MTBench, TADACap, CaTS-Bench, and QuAnTS, and a separate table explaining other models' incompatibility with BEDTime. These are literature and eligibility comparisons, not additional experimentally evaluated baselines.

T1.justification: The dataset notation, task definitions, and mathematical reasoning remain substantively unchanged. Neither version contains theoretical propositions or proofs, and v3 adds no new formal derivation.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially addresses v1's narrow real-world coverage by adding longer, clinically annotated heart-rate data. Broader model comparisons and new complexity, pixelation, and CoT diagnostics make the benchmark substantially more informative. Some new interpretations overreach, particularly the claimed ranking agreement contradicted by Tables 18–19, but this does not outweigh the substantial coverage and diagnostic gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same BEDTime benchmark. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial expansion and reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical evaluations and adds clinical-data results, additional models, generation evaluations, and diagnostic analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original model benchmarking, human evaluations of generated descriptions, and robustness experiments in Tables 2–3, Figures 2–3, and the appendices.

results.title: BEDTime: A Unified Benchmark for Automatically Describing Time Series

C1.justification: The central contribution broadens from a TabPFN-specific gradient-free RL framework to a general reduction from RL to regression foundation models. The abstract and introduction expand comparison claims to PPO/TRPO, and the conclusion asserts that advances in general-purpose regression models can translate into improved RL foundation models.

C2.justification: v2 explains undiscounted episode selection as preserving delayed successes, interprets backbone-dependent performance through differing priors, and recommends fewer FQI iterations despite convergence-based expectations. These extend the interpretation, while the principal limitations concerning low-dimensional evaluation, reward shaping, prior mismatch and quadratic context costs persist.

D1.justification: Appendix B adds PPO/TRPO implementation sources and optimization hyperparameters, and documents exploration phases and iteration control. Software versions, hardware, reward-shaping formulas and reward perturbation largely carry over. Configuration details for KNN and alternative backbones remain limited, and no new code or data access information is supplied.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate CartPole-v1, MountainCar-v0 and Acrobot-v1. v2 explicitly evaluates CartPole without reward shaping in Figure 6, but v1 already mentions preliminary sparse-reward experiments without identifying their environments. It is therefore unclear whether this adds a test scenario or reports previously explored coverage more fully.

E2.justification: The principal comparison expands from DQN alone to DQN, PPO and TRPO. Appendix D and Figure 10 additionally evaluate KNN, TabICL and TabFlex against the TabPFN implementation. The context-management comparator set is retained. Appendix A's descriptive comparison table does not establish experimental evaluation of its other listed methods.

E3.justification: The reported FQI budget changes from 60 iterations in v1 to approximately 10 in v2, using alpha=0.1, gamma=0.99 and K=alpha/(1-gamma). Fixed initial random batches of 200/200/128 transitions are replaced by one initial episode with epsilon=1. v2 also introduces normalized runtime/reward comparisons across context budgets and matched-hyperparameter backbone testing. These reported changes do not establish which retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds context-management comparisons across memory budgets and execution times, a controlled backbone comparison without reward shaping, and sensitivity to FQI iteration count. These investigate efficiency, prior dependence and iteration-related degradation beyond v1's analyses. The original exploration, gating and context-size ablations remain; moving exploration plots to Appendix C is not an added analysis.

E5.justification: v2 Figure 3 adds uncertainty bands to the context-management comparison that v1 Figure 2 displayed as lines alone. Their statistical meaning remains unspecified. The stated ten seeds for main comparisons and five seeds per ablation setting are retained; an increase in repeated runs is not established.

E6.justification: v2 adds results for the expanded comparator set, TabICL's advantage on unshaped CartPole, context-budget/runtime tradeoffs and the finding that alpha=0.1 performs best in the iteration ablation. Main MountainCar learning curves also change between v1 Figure 1 and v2 Figure 2. Given the revised reported settings, these curves do not establish a same-setting performance improvement.

M1.justification: The central Bellman-refitting procedure, epsilon-greedy interaction and high-return gate survive under the ICR-FQI/ICR-RL names. Changes are limited to additional TabICL/TabFlex backbone instantiations and the stated RV partitioning rule: v1 targets B/2 transitions per group, whereas v2 defines groups using median episode return. The broader regression-oracle framing does not establish a redesigned algorithm.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and concluding narrative are extensively rewritten around the regression-to-RL reduction. Methods are reorganized into ICR-FQI, online interaction and context engineering; prior mismatch moves into Discussion. Numbered sections and Appendices A-D replace the earlier structure, alongside the title and terminology changes.

P2.justification: The document switches from two columns to one and adds a framework diagram, comparison table and several experimental displays. Existing plots are enlarged or redrawn. The original four-panel ablation figure is split between Figures 7 and 9, including reuse of the context-size plot. These are substantial visual and organizational changes.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning around regression foundation models versus RL-specific pretraining. It adds discussions of ICQL and behavioral foundation models, a comparative properties table, and references supporting alternative backbones, FQI, representation learning and adaptation. The RL2 description changes from LSTM-based to GRU-based, and several earlier references are removed.

T1.justification: v2 introduces a formal risk-minimization definition of in-context regression and adds Bellman-contraction/convergence reasoning under expressivity and coverage conditions. The original Bellman updates remain, while prior-mismatch reasoning is condensed and relocated. Neither version supplies a new convergence proof for the proposed implementation.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical support beyond v1's DQN-only comparison. Policy-gradient and KNN comparisons, alternative backbones, iteration sensitivity and measured context/runtime tradeoffs address important gaps in comparative validity and the efficiency rationale. Clearer method organization also helps. These gains outweigh remaining weaknesses: evaluation remains concentrated on classic control, some new protocols and uncertainty bands are underexplained, and the broader foundation-model claims remain only partially tested.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work, despite the change from TabPFN-RL to ICR-RL. Their complete text, equations, figures and appendices are readable and support comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original control experiments, expanded baseline comparisons, resource analyses, backbone comparisons and ablations in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original classic-control experiments against DQN, context-truncation comparisons and hyperparameter ablations, with experimental details in its appendix.

results.title: ICR-RL: Deep Reinforcement Learning via In-Context-Regression

C1.justification: The central contributions remain a broad entanglement benchmark and a modular evaluation framework, with steering dependent on the method–model–target combination. V3's abstract and conclusion add specific claims about social-behavior vulnerability, morality degradation from refusal suppression, and opposing political shifts across models. These sharpen the empirical claims without replacing the central contribution.

C2.justification: V1's brief representation-geometry and shared-prompt-mechanism discussion becomes an extensive account of method-specific hypotheses and feature superposition, explicitly distinguished from causal findings (v3 Sections 4.2 and 5). V3 also adds substantive qualifications about refusal-direction asymmetry, conditional-gating failures, political-view scoring, judge reliability, and transfer to deployment settings.

D1.justification: V3 substantially expands v1's short implementation appendix with exact negative-answer and judge prompts, CAA/RepE templates, direction-extraction details, selected layers and coefficients, conditional thresholds, decoding settings, hardware, software, and compute estimates (Appendices B–F; Tables 5–13). These largely disclose previously unspecified details rather than demonstrate changes to the original procedures.

E1.justification: V3 adds a distinct long-context reasoning scenario using LongBench v2 and directly steers commonsense morality, which v1 explicitly treats only as an unsteered secondary task. These extend both input conditions and intervention objectives. The nine-perspective terminology otherwise largely reorganizes existing coverage rather than introducing nine new tasks.

E2.justification: Both versions evaluate DIM, ACE, CAA, PCA, and LAT against unsteered models. Standard, NoKL, and Conditional variants already appear in v1. The added evaluations retain this comparator set; the unavailable DIM refusal result on Gemma reflects failed KL filtering in a newly added model setting.

E3.justification: V3 expands the evaluated model configurations from two to five and replaces substring matching with likelihood scoring for TwinViews, restoring political-view evaluation for Llama. It revises the entanglement normalization and introduces a LongBench protocol using 180 examples, contexts up to 32k tokens, bf16, FlashAttention-2, and likelihood scoring. Most smaller dataset counts in Table 3 document v1's existing 20% subsampling, although refusal split counts also differ.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained KL-filter and conditional-steering comparisons, v3 adds model-scale consistency analysis, human validation of two automated judges, invalid-answer analysis, hyperparameter-selection summaries, and decomposition of harmful versus beneficial entanglement. These address reliability and interpretation questions not analyzed in v1 (Appendices E.2, E.6, G.1, G.3, and G.4).

E5.justification: V1's heatmap asterisks identify target datasets, not statistical significance. V3 introduces paired t-tests with FDR correction by steering objective and significance markers throughout the result heatmaps, plus Cohen's kappa estimates for human–judge agreement. These are substantial additions to statistical reporting, without establishing additional seeds or repeated experimental runs.

E6.justification: V3 adds extensive model, morality-steering, long-context, and validation results. For example, Figure 10 reports a 21.2-point morality improvement from PCA steering on Llama. Existing entries also change: Qwen's DIM refusal-steering morality delta changes from −10.7 points in v1 Figure 3 to −15.5 in v3 Figure 13, alongside a changed baseline. TwinViews results are replaced under revised scoring, so they are not same-protocol performance gains.

M1.justification: The evaluated direction-generation, grid-search, and intervention procedures remain the same for DIM, ACE, CAA, PCA, and LAT, including CAST conditional steering. V3 expands their mathematical and implementation descriptions. V1's optional COSMIC-selector paragraph disappears, but both versions use GridSearch in every evaluated method; its omission does not establish a procedural change.

P1.justification: The paper is extensively rewritten and reorganized: the title and benchmark terminology change, related work moves before the benchmark, detailed methodology and limitations move into appendices, and results are structured around explicit findings, tradeoffs, and scale consistency. A dedicated interpretive section replaces much briefer discussion.

P2.justification: V3 adopts a two-column main layout, replaces the dataset sunburst with a taxonomy-and-examples diagram, and introduces perspective-specific effectiveness, entanglement, and tradeoff plots. Heatmaps reorder columns, add morality-steering blocks and significance annotations, and expand to additional models. Numerous new tables present validation, hyperparameters, decomposition, errors, and long-context results.

R1.justification: V3 adds literature connecting entanglement to fine-tuning, RLHF, and sycophancy, including Hawkins et al. and Malmqvist, while removing discussion of LEACE, iterative nullspace projection, and Im and Li's steering evaluation. The central positioning relative to AxBench, EasyEdit2, and modular representation-steering frameworks remains substantially intact.

T1.justification: Equation 2 changes entanglement from sqrt(sum of squared shifts)/n to sqrt(sum of squared shifts/n), a mathematically different normalization. Appendix G.1 adds signed harmful and beneficial components with the identity Entanglement² = Harm² + Benef². These are limited mathematical additions and corrections; the expanded steering formulas mainly document existing procedures.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens the benchmark's evidential reliability and reproducibility. It addresses v1's TwinViews formatting confound, validates two automated judges, distinguishes harmful from beneficial drift, and supplies statistical testing and detailed implementation information. Broader model and context checks further test the findings' scope. DarkBench validation remains borrowed from prior work and seed-level variability is uncharacterized, but the revisions resolve several important measurement and documentation weaknesses.

A1.justification: Despite the rename from SteeringControl to SteeringSafety, both PDFs describe the same benchmark and modular steering framework. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V3 retains original steering evaluations and adds experiments on Gemma and smaller Qwen models, morality steering, long-context reasoning, and human agreement with automated judges.

before.justification: V1 reports original steering experiments on Qwen-2.5-7B and Llama-3.1-8B, including aggregate results in Figure 2 and dataset-level results under three steering settings in Figures 3–8.

results.title: SteeringSafety: Benchmarking Representation Steering in LLMs Across Safety Perspectives

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the controlled measurement contribution and the same principal claims: English preference, amplification for lower-resource languages and middle positions, query-language preference, and language sometimes outweighing relevance. Added experiments support these existing claims.

C2.justification: Section 5.2 replaces the interpretation of a specific semantic decision point with a vocabulary-space transition and explicitly acknowledges logit-lens limitations. v3 also adds ELI5 overlap and grounding concerns, cautions about non-parallel MIRACL comparisons, and interpretations addressing semantic-similarity and formatting confounds. The earlier explicit limitation to pairwise English comparisons is omitted.

D1.justification: v3 identifies the LaBSE encoder and o3 evaluator and documents sampling, translation, and retrieval choices for new experiments. The code/data repository pointer changes from linguistic_nepotism to lang_preference. Existing prompt templates and underlying model identifiers are retained; the new experiments do not receive comprehensive implementation or hardware specifications.

E1.justification: MIRACL was already evaluated in v1, but v3 extends coverage to naturally authored queries and evidence in eight target languages, beyond translated English examples. Appendix M additionally introduces NeuCLIR retrieval and full-report generation with Chinese, Persian, and Russian documents; Persian is new language coverage.

E2.justification: Appendix C.2 adds an o3-based, RAGAS-inspired relevance-and-faithfulness evaluator and quantitatively compares its retained statements with the original judge-plus-NLI pipeline. The original six evaluated language models remain unchanged.

E3.justification: The original experiments retain their settings, while new protocols include constrained decoding, matched-language contexts, and perplexity reporting. Appendix K evaluates 818 filtered English MIRACL statements and samples 100 native queries per target language. Appendix M retrieves three documents per language and evaluates generated reports using ARGUE sentence precision, nugget recall, and F1.

E4.justification: v3 adds substantial checks of measurement validity: alternative filtering evaluation, LaBSE semantic-similarity analysis, non-cited-document language controls, constrained decoding, translation-quality correlations, and a qualitative citation-error example. Native-language and end-to-end experiments further test generalization. The ContextCite and alternative-translation analyses already existed in v1.

E5.justification: Appendix J introduces statement-level and query-level Pearson correlation estimates with two-sided tests of zero correlation in Tables 16–17. Existing Bonferroni-corrected t-tests and human-study power and agreement reporting remain unchanged; no additional run counts, seeds, or confidence intervals are disclosed.

E6.justification: Matched original accuracy and translation tables retain their numerical results. New results include evaluator agreement F1 of 0.847, native-language MIRACL comparisons, robustness-control scores, and NeuCLIR F1 of 0.124 for all-English contexts versus 0.080, 0.065, and 0.096 for Chinese, Persian, and Russian variants. These are additional settings, not improvements over v1 under identical conditions. v1's full ContextCite Table 12, including Hit@3 and Score@3, is removed, although Figure 19 remains.

M1.justification: The original four-stage translation, report-generation, filtering, and citation-prediction pipeline is retained. Appendix G adds a supplementary constrained-decoding variant that restricts outputs to valid citation IDs, constituting a limited inference adaptation rather than a redesign of the main method.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and most prose are retained, with local clarifications, revised terminology, and removal of a duplicated layer-analysis paragraph. Appendix headings are expanded and reorganized, and impact and LLM-use statements are added. The additional scientific content does not amount to a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: The main text and references switch from a single-column manuscript to a two-column conference layout, substantially reflowing text and repositioning displays. Figure 4 receives revised legend notation, numerous new validation and results tables are introduced, and the full ContextCite table is removed. Most existing plotted graphics are retained.

R1.justification: Targeted references are added for LaBSE, ELI5 limitations, logit-lens qualifications, constrained decoding, COMET, NeuCLIR, and ARGUE. References to Cui, Dasigi, and Shrivastava are removed. The central positioning against prior language-preference measurements remains stable; numerous other bibliography changes concern publication metadata rather than different works.

T1.justification: The voting rule, citation-accuracy definition, language-gap definition, and ContextCite surrogate equation remain unchanged. Neither version contains theoretical proofs, and v3's additional standard evaluation metrics do not introduce new mathematical reasoning or formal guarantees.

improvement.justification: v1 already included human validation, ContextCite, and alternative-translation checks, but lacked tests on naturally authored multilingual inputs and retrieved full-report generation. v3 addresses those important generalization gaps through Appendices K and M and adds controls for measurement artifacts, substantially strengthening the evidence. Its more cautious logit-lens interpretation also improves scientific precision. Removal of the detailed ContextCite table and incomplete specifications for some new experiments reduce transparency, but these limited costs do not outweigh the validation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same linguistic-nepotism study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, references, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds evaluator comparisons, robustness controls, native-language MIRACL experiments, and NeuCLIR report-generation results.

before.justification: v1 reports original six-model experiments on ELI5 and MIRACL, a human annotation study, layer-wise analyses, ContextCite attribution results, and translation-system robustness experiments.

results.title: Linguistic Nepotism: Trading-off Quality for Language Preference in Multilingual RAG

C1.justification: The central contributions remain student-centered correction data, capability-matched SFT, and short-horizon RL with localized rewards. Both versions claim that a 7B student approaches a 72B teacher across 12 benchmarks. The revised title and abstract retain this scientific scope.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive qualifications about the conditional O(H) bound and dependence on teacher quality. It interprets hard-case improvements as strategy refinement and explains differences from PRM-style supervision, OPD, ReLIFT, and DPO. It also introduces the unresolved claim that deep-search data is absent from training despite listing WebWalker as a training source.

D1.justification: New Appendix E supplies the teacher's error-localization and correction prompts. v3 additionally documents the 10% hard-example allocation for RL, filtering of easy examples, Qwen3's non-thinking mode, reward-scale selection, and additional baseline settings. The code link points to a different repository. These substantially expand implementation disclosure; the earlier 35k seed total and GPU memory specification are omitted.

E1.justification: Both versions list the same training sources and mathematical reasoning, factual QA, and deep-search benchmarks, including GSM-Hard in the appendix. New comparisons and analyses reuse existing task coverage. v3's assertion that deep search is absent from training conflicts with its retained WebWalker training source and does not establish a coverage change.

E2.justification: v3 adds OPD, PRM-style step-reward GRPO, and ReLIFT in Table 8, plus DPO in Figure 5. It removes Qwen2.5-32B TIR from the eight-task comparison and removes student CoT Prompting, plain CoT Distillation, and Agent Prompting rows from the exact-match comparison. GRPO and ARPO are retained under clarified BC-prefixed names.

E3.justification: Reported WebWalker and xBench test sizes change from 100 and 200 to 200 and 100, respectively; the PDFs do not establish reruns. New comparisons specify a Qwen3-32B teacher for OPD, twice the training data for ReLIFT, and the same MPS data for DPO. Core metrics, training hyperparameters, and the eight-step limit remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 adds a same-data DPO comparison testing the value of RL, a manual audit of 50 previously hard-to-teach cases distinguishing strategy improvement from generation instability, and a representative verification case. It also reports intervention token costs and a small reward-scale search. Existing component ablations, intervention-frequency analysis, and SFT data-scaling experiments are retained.

E5.justification: v3 Table 1 newly states that AIME24 and AIME25 results are averaged over five runs. v1 gives no corresponding run count, so this establishes new reporting rather than an explicit increase in runs. Neither version supplies confidence intervals or significance tests for these comparisons.

E6.justification: Table 1 revises SCoRe-RL's AIME24/AIME25 scores from 36.7/26.7 to 38.0/28.7 and its reported average from 50.8 to 52.3, alongside newly stated five-run averaging. Table 8 adds averages of 24.2 for OPD, 25.5 for step-reward GRPO, and 26.7 for ReLIFT against SCoRe-RL's retained 30.5. DPO, case-analysis, and token-cost findings are added; some exact-match values change, and GAIA difficulty-level results are removed. These are reporting changes, not an established same-setting performance gain.

M1.justification: The stated auxiliary reward is refined: v1 rewards avoiding the original erroneous action, whereas v3's Rformat additionally requires correctly formatted output. The underlying BC initialization, student-generated trajectories, earliest-error correction, correction-based SFT, and short-horizon GRPO procedure remain intact.

P1.justification: v3 retitles and reorganizes the paper, moving Related Work before Background, expanding explanations of complete-trajectory review and correction validation, and separating ablations from hard-case analysis. The appendices are reorganized into five sections, with dedicated positioning and prompt sections. These changes materially reshape the narrative.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from single-column to two-column layout. Figure 1 is substantially redrawn; Table 1 is split between the main text and appendix; Table 2 removes GAIA subgroup columns; and the exact-match table is shortened. New displays include the hard-case example, additional baseline table, DPO chart, and two prompt figures.

R1.justification: Section 2 and new Appendix A substantially expand positioning against DAgger/HG-DAgger and distinguish SCoRe from LEMMA and process-reward approaches. New OPD, ReLIFT, cognitive-alignment, and DeepSeek-R1 references support additional comparisons and explanations. Numerous publication-metadata updates accompany these substantive additions.

T1.justification: The three compounding-error and rollout-variance bounds, their mathematical assumptions, and their proofs are preserved, moving from Appendix A to B. The new assumptions remark restates existing conditions and qualifies practical interpretation without changing the derivations.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked direct comparisons with several teacher-guided alternatives and did not provide the central MPS prompts. v3's Table 8, same-data DPO comparison, and full prompt templates substantially strengthen comparative validation and reproducibility. The manual case analysis, five-run AIME reporting, and explicit theoretical limitations further improve transparency. These gains outweigh the removed comparison detail, although unexplained test-size revisions and the contradictory deep-search training claim remain weaknesses.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SCoRe research despite the changed title and format. All 21 pages of v1 and 24 pages of v3, including figures, tables, equations, and appendices, support comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains original SCoRe experiments and adds teacher-guided baseline comparisons, a DPO comparison, and manual analysis of previously unsolved cases.

before.justification: v1 reports original SCoRe benchmark results, component ablations, training-data scaling experiments, and analysis of teacher interventions and hard examples.

results.title: Student-Centered Distillation Narrows the Agentic Gap Between Small and Large LLMs

C1.justification: Both versions claim scenario-specific specification alignment, a benchmark unifying safety and behavioral evaluation, benefits from TTD, and efficient ALIGN3 improvements. The abstract, introduction, and conclusion foreground SpecBench more strongly in v3, but retain the scientific scope and principal contribution claims.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive interpretations of stage ordering, evaluator-specific privacy judgments, adaptability to changed specifications, and natural-language prioritization. It documents concrete ALIGN3 failure conditions and limits its correctness conclusion to the focused Biochem/Health check. Section 6 also softens the causal interpretation of safe-versus-unsafe behavioral differences to a conjecture.

D1.justification: v3 supplies complete alternative specification texts in Appendix K, exact prioritization wording in Appendix L, and an application-extension workflow in Appendix G. Conversely, specification-construction resource examples shrink from nine links to four. Core implementation settings, original prompt templates, and the repository destination remain unchanged; the new correctness check lacks a detailed judging rubric and sample count.

E1.justification: The original five domains, 103 specifications, and 1,500 prompts remain. Appendix K adds evaluation under substantially rewritten safety and behavioral requirements across all five scenarios, including different output structures and operational constraints. Appendix L adds a prioritized cultural-diversity requirement in Child. These extend coverage to changing task requirements without introducing new source datasets.

E2.justification: v3 Table 6 extends the benchmark comparisons with GPT-5.4, Gemini-3.1-pro, DeepSeek-V3.2, and Kimi-K2.5. The original model comparisons and Table 2's Best-of-N, Self-Refine, TPO, ZeroThink, and MoreThink comparator set remain.

E3.justification: The reported human study expands from 300 responses and 6,180 specification judgments to 1,200 responses and 24,720 judgments. v3 also introduces a four-judge comparison over 12 models and a Gemini-3.1-pro correctness evaluation for Biochem and Health. The original benchmark splits, generation limits, and primary SAR evaluation settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained component-removal and alpha-sensitivity analyses, v3 adds three stage-order ablations, correctness checks, broader evaluator robustness and item-level agreement analyses, evolving-specification tests, and a prioritization case study. Additional failure cases explicitly examine ALIGN3, TPO, and Self-Refine limitations (Appendices F, K, L, and M).

E5.justification: Figure 5 newly reports standard-deviation bars across models. Appendix F.1 adds Kendall's concordance test across four judges, reporting W = 0.995 and its significance. v1 already contained rank correlations and p-values; v3 does not introduce seed-based performance uncertainty or confidence intervals.

E6.justification: The central results in Tables 1–2 are retained, but v3 adds numerous results for reordered stages, correctness, frontier models, evaluator agreement, and changed specifications. Table 5 reports vanilla/ALIGN3 correctness scores of 45.7/48.0 for Biochem and 66.3/70.7 for Health. Human agreement changes from kappa 0.84 and a 6.5% SAR gap to 0.86 and 6.1% under the larger sample, so these are revised study estimates rather than same-sample gains.

M1.justification: ALIGN3 retains behavior optimization, safety-guided refinement, and holistic specification audit, with substantively unchanged prompts. Newly tested step permutations are ablations, and specification prioritization is an experimental input variation; neither replaces the proposed procedure.

P1.justification: The narrative is substantially reorganized around the benchmark: Related Work moves from Section 2 to Section 7, and the abstract, introduction, contribution list, and conclusion are recast in benchmark-first order. Analysis prose is revised, and the appendix gains a reorganized contents structure and dedicated discussion, application, evolving-specification, and prioritization sections.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from a single-column preprint layout to a two-column conference layout. Table 2 changes from side-by-side model comparisons to stacked groups, Figure 5 is redrawn with error bars, and v3 adds evaluator plots, result tables, alternative-specification panels, and qualitative cases. Retained figures and tables are extensively resized and relocated.

R1.justification: v3 adds references including Claude's constitution, AILuminate, LLM-as-a-judge research, and R1 safety assessment, while removing some earlier citations such as WizardLM. Appendix B explicitly distinguishes concise, adaptable test-time specifications from training-based deliberative alignment, and Section 5 more directly positions ALIGN3 as a thinking-intervention method.

T1.justification: The specification-alignment formulation, SAR definition and derivation in Equations 1–4, Best-of-N formulation in Appendix A, and embedding-filtering algorithm are substantively unchanged. No new theorem, proof, or formal weighted-specification objective is introduced.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens benchmark validation beyond v1's smaller human study and two-evaluator comparison through expanded human assessment and four-judge testing (Appendices E and F.1). Changed-specification experiments directly test the claimed adaptability, while order ablations and explicit ALIGN3 failures make the method assessment more informative. The correctness study remains underspecified, and Figure 49 has conflicting Claude/Gemini labels, but these localized weaknesses do not outweigh the substantial gains in validation and diagnostic evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SpecBench and ALIGN3 research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting, renumbering, and additions.

after.justification: v3 retains the original empirical results and adds expanded human validation, evaluator comparisons, correctness checks, frontier-model evaluations, and specification-variation experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of 33 models, TTD comparisons, ablations, attack experiments, and a human evaluation study.

results.title: Reasoning over Boundaries: Enhancing Specification Alignment via Test-time Deliberation

C1.justification: The central claim of training-free, memory-bounded episodic caching with near-full-cache accuracy is retained. The abstract revises the headline accuracy advantage from up to 40% to 30% and peak-memory reduction from 3.5× to 3.7×, although v4's introduction still states 3.5×. The conclusion newly claims the first framework combining the three components and emphasizes on-device conversational AI.

C2.justification: v4 extends the earlier context-holistic explanation to argue that each episodic cache preserves dependencies across episodes, and interprets document-task results as evidence of broader applicability. It also develops conclusions about calibration-domain independence and harmful overconcentration of layer budgets. Future-work discussion expands to incremental cache updates, implicit preferences, information deletion, and persona consistency, while the earlier quantization proposal is dropped.

D1.justification: v1's detailed efficiency hardware disclosure—A100 GPUs, CPU model, and PCIe transfer configuration—is removed without an equivalent specification for v4's replacement experiment. Explicit allocation sharpness values for the retained LLaMA/Qwen2.5 experiments and the patched-prompt representative-count setting also disappear. v4 provides selected Qwen3 configurations and stage execution counts, but leaves the new episode-creation threshold unspecified and retains pseudocode that omits Stage 3b.

E1.justification: The three conversational benchmarks and BookSum calibration are retained. v4 additionally evaluates NarrativeQA, HotpotQA, MuSiQue, and QMSum from LongBench, extending coverage beyond conversational memory to document tasks. Calibration robustness also introduces SAMSum dialogue and RepoBench-P code samples alongside BookSum.

E2.justification: v4 adds evaluated OracleKV and RAG-2K baselines and a Full KV with prefix caching comparator for efficiency. RAG-Episodic corresponds to v1's RAG-like alternative rather than an entirely new comparator. The original compression baselines remain represented, but v1 Figure 4c's accuracy comparisons against PyramidKV and retrieval-head allocation disappear; their KL-divergence comparison remains.

E3.justification: v4 adds Qwen3-4B/8B configurations, source-count and centroid-similarity query stratification, and calibration comparisons using one versus 100 samples. The efficiency evaluation changes from 100 queries with 100K-token histories to a single-batch, 300-turn evaluation with 90K-token histories, an 8K cache, and 90 retrieval/write-back events. It also accounts for preparation costs and prefix caching. These are substantially different evaluation designs, not directly comparable timing measurements.

E4.justification: v4 adds targeted multi-episode reasoning tests, segmentation-unit and allocation-sharpness ablations, and robustness tests for initialization, generation sampling, calibration domain, and calibration size. Encoder and episode-count analyses are revised under Qwen3 settings. Conversely, v1's block-size, segmentation-window, and medoid-count sweep plots, direct allocation-strategy accuracy comparison, and episode-switch trajectory analysis are removed. The clustering visualization and internal-state sensitivity analysis are retained.

E5.justification: v4 Figure 9 explicitly reports standard-deviation error bars over five seeds for stochasticity and calibration experiments. v1 already reported input variability and five-run averaging for efficiency, but lacked this seed-based robustness reporting. The revised efficiency experiment no longer specifies the earlier five-run averaging. This changes uncertainty reporting locally rather than throughout the main benchmark results.

E6.justification: v4 adds substantial Qwen3, document-task, cross-episode, robustness, and efficiency results. Retained numerical results also change: EpiCache's LLaMA3.1-8B LoCoMo averages at 6K/8K are 49.3/52.2 in v1 Table A2 and 47.3/50.2 in v4 Table A4. The original Qwen and LongMemEval detailed tables retain their numerical entries. Some v4 Figure A4 LoCoMo points do not agree with Table A4. The new efficiency results replace measurements under different conditions and therefore do not establish a same-setting performance improvement.

M1.justification: v1 constructs a fixed episode bank and retrieves caches for answering queries. v4 Section 3.1 adds Stage 3b: appending newly generated KV pairs, writing updated caches back, creating episodes when centroid similarity falls below a threshold, and rebuilding oversized caches. This substantially extends the procedure to ongoing conversation maintenance. Renaming medoids to centroid-closest segments does not itself change their selection.

P1.justification: v4 extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, method explanation, experimental narrative, and related work. Experiments are reorganized around main results, analyses, and efficiency, while appendices are restructured and original results relocated. The title and main-text terminology also change, although substantial mathematical and appendix material remains recognizable.

P2.justification: v4 adopts a two-column main-text and reference layout, redraws Figure 3 to show cache updates, and introduces several new plots and tables. v1 Figure 5 moves to Figure A4 with plotted revisions, and its scalability Figure 6 becomes Figure A3. The original ablation grid and latency/episode-switch figure are removed, while efficiency is presented through a new stage-by-stage table.

R1.justification: v4 substantially expands positioning against conversational memory systems and newer cache-management approaches, including SECOM, reflective memory, TRIM-KV, Cartridges, FlowKV, ArkVale, and IceCache. It distinguishes training-free EpiCache from trained cache representations and discusses limitations of external memory banks. Earlier A2ATS and quantization discussions are removed. Publication updates for retained works such as KVzip and Ada-KV do not constitute new references.

T1.justification: The LongConvQA formulation, clustering mathematics, sensitivity definition, and budget-allocation derivation remain substantively equivalent. Removing the unused average-scoring alternative from Equation (3) and adjusting segment notation do not change the mathematical reasoning. Neither version supplies formal guarantees or proofs.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens validation of important assumptions that v1 supported mainly indirectly: retrieving one episode despite distributed evidence, stable calibration across domains and seeds, and efficiency after including preparation costs and prefix caching. The added comparisons and targeted analyses make the central empirical case considerably stronger. These gains outweigh the loss of some ablations and reproducibility details, although incomplete cache-update documentation and Figure A4/Table A4 inconsistencies remain meaningful weaknesses.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe EpiCache and provide readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. The retained method components and experiments can be matched despite substantial additions, restructuring, and renumbering.

after.justification: v4 retains original evaluations and adds Qwen3 experiments, document-task results, cross-episode analyses, robustness measurements, and a revised efficiency experiment.

before.justification: v1 reports original LongConvQA evaluations, component ablations, sensitivity analyses, and runtime measurements, including Figure 5, Figure A1, and Table A1.

results.title: EpiCache: Episodic KV Cache Management for Long-Term Conversation on Resource-Constrained Environments

C1.justification: v1 principally claims an effective, broadly applicable transition module with strong data efficiency and generalization. v2's abstract, contributions, and conclusion explicitly claim a systematic reformulation of base positioning and state-of-the-art performance against policy-aware and geometric alternatives, including inference-speed superiority. This strengthens the central comparative claims beyond the original effectiveness claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations for Mobi-π's benchmark performance, sequential error compounding, and PTV3's architectural mismatch. It newly discusses failures involving small objects, distant viewpoints, noisy sensing, and limited manipulation policies. The conclusion replaces v1's RGB-only and failed-rollout future directions with active-learning implications and positioning N2M as complementary to intrinsic policy improvement.

D1.justification: v2 adds collision-check implementation details, benchmark GPU/CPU specifications, Pinocchio-based baseline details, and collection/training/inference timing accounting that distinguishes assumed overheads from measurements. Appendix C.6 documents the sequential task's demonstrations, randomization, M=300 augmentation, 150 training epochs, and human participants. These substantially expand reproducibility information beyond v1's robot, sensor, and augmentation descriptions.

E1.justification: v2 extends evaluation to a real-world sequence requiring navigation, chip-box pickup, further navigation, and disposal into a trash bin (Section 6.2). This substantially extends task requirements beyond individual manipulation transitions. The original RoboCasa tasks and five real-world scenarios remain, with four qualitative scenarios moved to Appendix D.1.3.

E2.justification: Mobi-π changes from a cited alternative in v1 to an evaluated comparator in v2's Table 1. v2 also adds a Human-Intuition baseline for the sequential task. Reachability and Oracle remain; the new benchmark uses a more rigorous IK- and collision-based Reachability implementation. MoTo and MoManipVLA are not separately evaluated implementations.

E3.justification: v2 introduces a CloseDrawer benchmark using BC Transformer and Mobi-π's diffusion-policy checkpoint, with success, human-labor, and inference-time measures. It also introduces a randomized 20-trial sequential-task protocol, separate policy-training budgets, and controlled encoder/augmentation comparisons. These are added protocols; the original four-task applicability experiment retains its stated 300-trial evaluation.

E4.justification: The original viewpoint-augmentation ablation is expanded with an augmented-view-count sweep, positional/noise augmentation removals, pretrained-versus-untrained Point-BERT, and PointNet++/PTV3 comparisons (Appendix D.2, Figures 15–16). These test which design choices drive performance. Appendix D.4 additionally reports qualitative failure observations, without presenting a controlled failure-rate benchmark.

E5.justification: v1 presents point estimates without uncertainty displays. v2 adds error bars and shaded bands to simulation and ablation plots, reports ± values in Table 1, and specifies six independent experiments of 50 trials for the new benchmark. The dispersion measures and seed counts remain undefined; additional runs for the retained experiments are not established.

E6.justification: Table 1 newly reports N2M success of 0.55±0.07 under DP versus Mobi-π's 0.24±0.05, and inference times of 0.07±0.03 versus 273.52±13.06 seconds. Figure 8 adds 12/20 completed sequences for N2M, versus 3/20 for Reachability and 5/20 for Human. Several retained Figure 5 scores also change. The new benchmark results are distinct experiments, not version-to-version performance gains.

M1.justification: Both versions retain the Point-BERT–MLP Gaussian-mixture predictor, successful-rollout supervision, regularized likelihood loss, viewpoint augmentation, and collision-free pose sampling. v2 elaborates the existing collision-checking step and evaluates alternative encoders and augmentations as ablations; it does not establish a replacement of the proposed N2M procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract, introductory motivation, contributions, related work, and conclusion are substantially rewritten. v2 introduces a shared Experiment Settings section and organizes evaluation around six explicit questions. Earlier qualitative experiments and separate appendix analyses are consolidated under Appendix D, producing a broad narrative and structural revision.

P2.justification: v2 switches the main paper to two columns, combines v1's Figures 5 and 6 into Figure 5, and redraws plots with uncertainty displays. It adds the benchmark table, sequential-task Sankey diagrams, and expanded ablation panels, while relocating qualitative figures and reducing the main-text representation visualization. These are extensive display and layout changes.

R1.justification: v2 substantially rewrites research positioning around geometric methods versus policy-aware positioning, identifying Mobi-π as the sole existing policy-aware alternative. It removes much of v1's discussion of state-value, distributional-similarity, and learned-transition approaches. Added references and discussion include MoManipVLA, newer foundation/RL policies, and PointNet++; this exceeds a bibliographic refresh.

T1.justification: The Gaussian-mixture definition, likelihood objective, and three regularization terms in Equations 1–3 are mathematically unchanged apart from notation. Neither version provides formal theorems or proofs; v2's additional mechanism discussions are explanatory rather than new formal results.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked a direct policy-aware benchmark and offered limited design and failure analysis. v2's Table 1, sequential-task evaluation, expanded ablations, implementation details, and explicit failure conditions substantially strengthen validation and clarify applicability. These gains outweigh reporting weaknesses, including undefined uncertainty measures and describing the oracle as an upper bound despite Figure 5 showing N2M exceeding it.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same N2M research work. Their main text, equations, figures, results, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial restructuring in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds a comparative benchmark, a real-world sequential task with human comparisons, and additional ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original RoboCasa experiments, real-world Lamp Retrieval success rates, qualitative robot demonstrations, and a viewpoint-augmentation ablation.

results.title: N2M: Bridging Navigation and Manipulation by Learning Pose Preference from Rollout

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion qualify the theoretical minimization claim as applying to a KL approximation and emphasize diagnostic stress-testing for watermark designers. The central detector-free RL attack, data-efficiency contribution, and headline empirical advantage remain.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly distinguishes the KL certificate from the original semantic radius and explains its use by designers with detector statistics. New interpretations identify poor cross-watermark transfer and sensitivity to the watermark proxy, while discussing mixed-family training and harder semantic watermarks. These materially qualify v1's broad effectiveness narrative.

D1.justification: v2 announces code access through a repository link and adds the GPT-4o judging prompt, perplexity evaluator, Qwen3-8B reference-model exception and weights, and construction details for new experiments. Most existing Appendix C hyperparameters, software, hardware, and training-time disclosures are retained.

E1.justification: The original four corpora remain, while v2 adds C4 natural-text/continuation comparisons and evaluations against SemStamp, k-SemStamp, and the setting labelled RLWatermark/GAUSSMark. Unseen-key, cross-watermark, and mixed-watermark scenarios substantially expand the evaluated conditions beyond v1.

E2.justification: Appendix D.13 adds evaluated DPO attacks with 100 and 7,000 preference pairs, released DPO checkpoints, and watermark stealing (WS), including direct comparisons in Tables 16–19. WS was only discussed in v1. Think+SysP already appeared in v1's appendix, so its appearance in v2's main table is not a new comparator.

E3.justification: Mixed-key training changes from four keys, including the test key, to 100 distinct training keys with an unseen test key. New protocols include perplexity and GPT-4o judging, stronger KGW parameter settings, DPO training-budget controls, and mixed-watermark training with a separate validation set. These materially extend and revise the evaluation design.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's prompt, reasoning, training-size, weight-sensitivity, and generalization studies, v2 adds semantic-threshold sensitivity, certificate/removal correlation, proxy-model sensitivity, generator–attacker matching controls, cross-watermark transfer, mixed-watermark training, and human-distribution approximation analyses (Appendices D.8–D.16). These test important mechanisms and failure conditions previously unexamined.

E5.justification: Appendix D.9 and Table 12 newly report Pearson and Spearman correlation estimates between the certificate and removal rate. Neither version reports repeated-training-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests for attack-performance comparisons; the theoretical concentration bounds are separate from empirical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v2 adds Qwen3-8B RLCracker results, DPO/WS comparisons, quality scores, and robustness and transfer findings. Existing entries also change: Table 1's Qwen3-1.7B Think ESR on 1,500-token KGW selfhash changes from 76.3% to 66.3%. Mixed-key scores are replaced under changed conditions, while the headline 98.5% Unigram result remains.

M1.justification: The core GRPO and dual-KL attack remain. Appendix C.3 introduces an adaptation for Qwen3-8B using Qwen3-0.6B for KL rewards instead of the default attacker copy, and revises the written semantic-reward scaling from sigmoid(x) to 2 sigmoid(x)-1. These changes do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

P1.justification: The existing theoretical and methodological narrative is extensively rewritten with new explanatory headings and clearer distinctions between robustness notions. The title changes, Appendix A's LLM-use disclosure is replaced by extended related work, and the conclusion and impact discussion are reorganized. These exceed localized language editing.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to two-column layout, Table 1 is substantially expanded, and Figure 3's panels are rearranged side by side. New threshold-sensitivity and distribution figures, adaptive-comparison tables, and separate text-quality tables materially expand the visual presentation; numerous retained tables are relocated.

R1.justification: New Appendix A substantially expands discussion of token-replacement, smoothing, DPO, and random-walk attacks. Section 4.1 also positions the distributional radius against Diaa et al.'s earlier robustness definition. This broadens the comparison with prior adaptive attacks beyond v1's mainly paraphrasing and proxy-model discussion.

T1.justification: Sections 3–4 redefine the distributional certificate around an input-conditioned local paraphrase distribution and formalize the semantic radius using output support and an infimum. v1's single-shot evasion proposition and Pass@k corollary are removed. v2 adds Proposition B.3, a bounded-variable proof of sub-Gaussianity allowing dependent tokens, and a dependence example.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important validation gaps through direct adaptive-attack comparisons, unseen-key evaluation, stronger watermark targets, and quality checks beyond P-SP. Its transfer and proxy studies expose meaningful limitations, while the revised theory clarifies the certificate's scope and supports its concentration assumption. These provide substantial gains over v1. Some overstatements and reporting inconsistencies remain, including D.13's blanket superiority wording versus Table 18 and unexplained low XSIR judge scores in Table 22.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe RLCracker and provide readable text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Retained material can be matched across the substantial revision and reformatting.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds adaptive-attack comparisons, robustness tests, transfer studies, and text-quality and distribution analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original watermark-removal experiments, baseline comparisons, and sensitivity and generalization studies in Section 5 and Appendix D.

results.title: RLCracker: Evaluating the Worst-Case Vulnerability of LLM Watermarks with Adaptive RL Attacks

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contributions: a realistic human-grounded personalization benchmark, evaluation with diagnostic feedback, and systematic analyses of search-augmented personalization. The added experiments support these contributions without redefining their scope.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the oracle experiment as identifying history-based preference inference as the primary bottleneck and qualifies reasoning models' advantage by showing sensitivity to noisy evidence. Appendix A adds proprietary-evaluator limitations, rubric self-consistency concerns and an instruction-following explanation for backbone differences. Recall is also framed more precisely as gold-information coverage.

D1.justification: v2 substantially expands annotation documentation: cohort expertise and interests, compensation and withdrawal terms, privacy screening, annotation instructions, revision-based quality control, k=6, and construction/evaluation costs (Appendices B and C.5). It also provides a direct repository pointer. These are expanded disclosures rather than evidence that the retained dataset was reconstructed.

E1.justification: The 30 users, 2,870 sessions, 150 queries and four task types remain unchanged. v2 adds explicit gold-information-need and controlled noisy-evidence scenarios, changing evaluation input conditions within the existing benchmark. Expanded descriptions of annotator backgrounds do not establish a broader sampled population.

E2.justification: v2 adds GPT-oss-120B and Qwen3-235B-A22B-Thinking-2507 evaluator alternatives in Table 7 and compares Qwen-generated versus GPT-5-generated rubrics in Table 8. The six response-generation models, original evaluator baselines and retrieval comparison methods are retained.

E3.justification: New protocols provide gold information needs directly to four models, replace 0%, 30%, 50% or 70% of gold information with unrelated content for the Sonar pair, and vary evaluator backbones and rubric generators independently. These substantially extend the experimental controls; the original Table 4 settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's history-context, query-expansion and gold-information analyses, v2 tests evaluator generality across model families, sensitivity to the rubric generator, the gap between explicit preferences and history-based inference, and robustness to noisy evidence (Tables 6–9). The earlier qualitative case studies are retained.

E5.justification: v1 reports evaluator-validation point estimates without corresponding run counts or uncertainty. v2 reports three-run means and standard deviations in Table 3 and the new Tables 7–8, introducing uncertainty reporting for a central validation component. This does not establish that v1 used fewer repetitions.

E6.justification: Table 3's full-evaluator average Pearson/Spearman/feedback accuracy changes from 0.853/0.857/0.870 to 0.847/0.853/0.881 under newly reported three-run aggregation. Tables 6–9 add noise, evaluator, rubric and oracle results. Dataset averages are corrected from 73.48/24.34 to 71.77/23.90 search/chat sessions without changing individual user rows. Tables 4–5 retain their scores.

M1.justification: The benchmark construction, personalization evaluator, gold-claim recall calculation, profile construction and query-expansion procedures remain intact. Alternative evaluator backbones are tested within the existing framework. Newly specifying k=6 and clarifying prompts do not establish a changed proposed method.

P1.justification: v2 makes targeted wording and terminology edits, makes task formulation an unnumbered paragraph, and presents personalization before coverage in the evaluation description. It removes the appendix contents page and adds acknowledgements and an LLM-use disclosure. Most existing prose and the overall narrative sequence are retained.

P2.justification: The single-column preprint becomes a two-column conference paper with extensive figure and table reflow. Figure 2 rearranges evaluation components, Figure 4 changes from a two-by-two grid to vertically stacked plots, and Tables 6–9 are added. Table 3 incorporates uncertainty displays; existing appendix examples and prompts are largely reformatted and renumbered.

R1.justification: v2 adds MMLU-Pro, Humanity's Last Exam, IFEval and IFBench references to contextualize backbone capabilities, while removing earlier citations including VerifiNER, MT-RAIG and Panickssery et al. The principal positioning against existing personalization and search benchmarks in Section 2 and Table 1 remains unchanged.

T1.justification: The task definitions, evaluator formulation, gold-claim recall formula and Shannon diversity equations are substantively unchanged. Renaming factual coverage as gold information coverage does not alter its mathematical definition. Neither version introduces theoretical propositions or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the benchmark's central evaluator validation through alternative evaluator backbones, an independent rubric generator and repeated-run uncertainty reporting, addressing v1's reliance on a single proprietary evaluator configuration. Oracle and noise controls improve diagnostic evidence, while annotation disclosures improve transparency. Some new interpretations overreach: Appendix A.4 claims improvements across all criteria, although Gemini-2.5-Pro's oracle tone score is 80.53 versus 84.40 in Table 4. This limits that interpretation but does not outweigh the stronger validation.
