A1.justification: Both PDFs describe BESPOKE with the same authors, benchmark and evaluation framework. The main text, figures, tables, equations and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison after matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds evaluator-backbone, rubric-generator, explicit-preference and noisy-information experiments in Section 4 and Appendix A.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluator–human agreement measurements, six-model personalization experiments, history-retrieval results and gold-information experiments in Section 4.

results.title: BESPOKE: Benchmark for Search-Augmented Large Language Model Personalization via Diagnostic Feedback

C1.justification: The central unification and local-convergence contributions remain. v2 explicitly extends its empirical superiority claim to nudity, singles out closed-form Hellinger as consistently dominating MSE in the abstract, and recommends it as the default in the conclusion.

C2.justification: v2 adds a small-batch divergence-estimation explanation for variational artifacts and distinguishes per-sample weighting from batch-level learning-rate adjustment. It expands practical loss-selection advice and states GPU-related limits on architecture testing. The existing aggressive-erasure versus preservation interpretation remains central.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-repository link and substantially expands optimizer, learning-rate, updated-parameter, discriminator warm-up, batch-size and prompt-source information. It newly discloses the larger prompt set used for retained ablation tables. However, v1's DDIM sampler and 30/50 inference-step specification disappears; these documentation changes do not establish reruns.

E1.justification: v2 adds nudity removal using the I2P nudity subset and MMA-Diffusion prompts, adversarial nudity and artistic-style scenarios using Ring-A-Bell, and a broader set of artists for sequential erasure. The earlier three-concept sequence remains in Appendix C.3.

E2.justification: Beyond v1's MSE/Concept Ablation and divergence comparisons, v2 evaluates methods including ESD, SPM, UCE, MACE, RECE, SAFREE and SPEED, plus SLD in nudity experiments. Conversely, the corresponding 500-step comparison removes the MSE empty and MSE near rows from v1 Table 3 to v2 Table 14.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce SD 1.5, SD 2.1, SDXL, SD3 and FLUX configurations and distinct protocols: 800-step closed-form nudity unlearning, 250-step transformer experiments and 50 steps per artistic style. Nudity-generation rates, body-region counts and adversarial-prompt evaluations supplement the retained CS, CA and KID evaluations.

E4.justification: v2 adds tests of whether adversarial prompts recover erased nudity or Van Gogh style, including Tables 4 and 10 and Figure 14. It also adds body-region/gender breakdowns and a ten-style cumulative-erasure study. Earlier regularization and training-duration analyses remain, although some matching MSE anchor controls are removed.

E5.justification: Appendix C.1 newly states that main results are averaged over multiple random seeds. Neither version supplies seed counts, uncertainty intervals or significance tests. This is additional reporting, without evidence that the number of runs increased.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive model, multi-style and nudity/attack results; Table 4, for example, reports I2P rates of 0.063 for H-DMU and 0.120 for CAbl. Most earlier SD 1.4 values remain. Table 14 removes MSE-anchor results and changes Van Gogh KID from -0.007 to 0.007 when erasing Snoopy with Hellinger near and both regularizers.

M1.justification: The target-to-anchor framework, closed-form objectives and variational minimax procedure remain. H-DMU and P-DMU rename existing instances. v2 supplies derivations for the alpha-divergence family already proposed in v1; additional architectures and implementation disclosures do not establish a changed algorithm.

P1.justification: The abstract, results narrative and conclusion are extensively rewritten, and method-instance terminology is standardized. Sequential erasure is integrated into Section 5.3, while Appendix C is reorganized into dedicated architecture, multi-concept, nudity, robustness, comparison and ablation sections, redistributing existing explanations as well as accommodating additions.

P2.justification: The main paper changes to a two-column conference layout and adds numerous plots, image comparisons and tables with comparison highlighting. Existing Figures 1, 5 and 6 move to v2 Figures 16, 15 and 12; the earlier divergence-wheel diagram disappears. New alpha-gradient surfaces and nudity/robustness displays substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v2 adds discussion of GLoCE and references supporting newer models, adversarial benchmarks, SPEED and optimization comparisons. Its positioning of CAbl and DoCo as special cases, and its claim to a general f-divergence unlearning framework, remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendices B.1.1–B.1.2 add alpha-divergence definitions, Gaussian formulas, variance conditions and a general gradient derivation, previously only promised. The main convergence theorems remain, while v1's variational-reformulation justification in Eqs. 49–50 is removed. The new general loss also leaves handling of the sign-sensitive normalization between v2 Eqs. 48–49 unexplained for alpha greater than one.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for the framework's generality beyond v1's SD 1.4-centered evaluation through additional architectures, independent baselines, nudity/adversarial tests and quantitative multi-style erasure. Fuller implementation details also improve reproducibility. These gains outweigh the removed MSE-anchor controls, although the broad robustness claim conflicts with Table 4's Ring-A-Bell results and the new alpha objective has an unexplained sign-sensitive normalization in Eqs. 48–49.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same f-DMU research, with matching authors, core objectives and convergence theorems. Their text, equations, tables, figures and appendices support a reliable comparison despite substantial expansion and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds results for further model configurations, ten-style erasure, nudity removal and adversarial robustness in Section 5 and Appendix C.

before.justification: v1 reports original gradient measurements, qualitative generations, single- and multi-concept erasure experiments, and CS, CA and KID results in Section 5 and Appendix C.

C1.justification: The abstract broadens claimed superiority from existing LLM augmentation methods to both LLM-based and traditional augmentation, and explicitly claims token- and concept-level safety improvements. The central collaboration and expert-guidance distillation contributions remain unchanged.

C2.justification: V2 substantially expands interpretation through arguments about noisy-expert safety, evaluator independence, and efficiency relative to training-based augmentation. Appendix A.4 also identifies missed contextual or implicit clinical information as a concrete failure mode, extending v1’s more general discussion of detection calibration and domain expertise.

D1.justification: Appendix A.3 explicitly states selected settings of learning rate 4×10^-5, LoRA rank 16, and three epochs, where v1 provided sweeps and recommendations. Appendix A.5 adds the V100 hardware, backbone, timing scope, and normalization details. These are documentation additions, not evidence of changed retained experiments.

Table 12 also introduces an SFT comparator for the cost analysis, substantially broadening the alternatives evaluated.

E3.justification: V1 measures entity preservation and hallucination using the guidance extractor. V2 adds alternative NER evaluators, UMLS concept-level scoring, a three-clinician evaluation of 26 notes, and a controlled runtime comparison normalized to 300 notes. These substantially extend evaluation design without establishing that retained downstream experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds Medical-NER and BioMed-NER expert variants, evaluator-sensitivity comparisons (Tables 3 and 5), clinician-based validation and an omission case study (Appendix A.4, Figure 6), and cost analysis (Appendix A.5). The earlier generalist-size comparisons and hyperparameter sweeps remain.

E5.justification: Five-run means and standard errors and the statement about fixed seeds are retained. Appendix A.4 newly reports inter-annotator reliability using Fleiss’ Kappa for three clinicians: 0.437, 0.710, and 0.655 for readmission, mortality, and length-of-stay, respectively.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial baseline, concept-level, evaluator-robustness, clinician, and runtime results. For example, Table 11 reports proposed-method token PR/HR of 0.74/0.22 and concept PR/HR of 0.79/0.20; Table 12 reports 40.21 minutes versus 34.01 for Naive. Matching earlier downstream, ICD, distillation, and hyperparameter scores are retained.

M1.justification: The weak-expert extraction, constrained prompting, generalist rewriting, candidate filtering, and DPO distillation procedures are retained. The prompt adds semantic-level wording but retains verbatim-preservation instructions; this does not establish a procedural change.

P1.justification: V2 revises the abstract, reframes the problem as structure-aware augmentation, tightens experimental discussion, gives distillation its own subsection, and reorganizes the appendices. Author, affiliation, funding, and disclosure text also changes, but the main section sequence and substantial portions of the prose remain.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to two-column layout, with extensive rearrangement of displays. Existing explanatory figures and the ICD table move to the appendix, comparison tables expand, and new safety, evaluator, clinician, and cost tables plus a highlighted clinical case figure are added.

R1.justification: V2 adds focused references including Abdollahi et al. on medical substitution, Labrak et al. on BioMistral, and Xu et al. on knowledge-infused clinical generation, alongside additional background and cost citations. Positioning expands to these alternatives while retaining the existing related-work framework.

T1.justification: Section 4.2 adds definitions of expert recall r and constraint-violation probability ε, and a conditional corruption bound rε + (1-r)p_c, with improvement claimed when ε < p_c and r > 0. This is a limited analytical addition; the existing augmentation and PR/HR equations remain substantively unchanged.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the central safety evidence by reducing dependence on v1’s potentially circular single-extractor evaluation through alternative NER evaluators, concept-level scoring, and clinician annotations. Broader baselines and an explicit failure case further improve credibility. The small clinician sample and incompletely specified SFT cost comparison remain limitations, but the independent validation addresses an important weakness in v1.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same clinical text augmentation framework. All pages, including figures, tables, equations, and appendices, are readable, and retained material can be matched across renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: V2 retains these empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, alternative entity-extractor evaluations, clinician annotations, and runtime measurements.

before.justification: V1 reports original augmentation-quality measurements, downstream clinical prediction results, component comparisons, distillation experiments, and hyperparameter sweeps.

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes state-of-the-art results on two grounding benchmarks and adaptive cursor movement. v2 broadens the headline contributions to agentic performance, superior performance with matched backbones and less training data, and spatial-reasoning generalization beyond GUI images. The interactive-grounding contribution remains central.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning spatial transfer, latency–accuracy trade-offs, historical visual context mitigating cursor occlusion, and limitations to click-style grounding. Appendix J extends the existing crop limitation with the implications of 31% missing-target detection and 20% false positives, explaining why reliable recovery would require further training.

D1.justification: v2 substantially expands resource and evaluation documentation: 8K training samples, per-update and rollout timings, throughput, latency accounting for rendering and history encoding, same-hardware RegionFocus evaluation, and the exact target-presence prompt. The original optimizer settings, GPU configuration, rollout details and system prompts are retained.

E1.justification: v2 adds OSWorld-G and UI-Vision grounding, online OSWorld interaction, SpatialMQA and SPHERE spatial reasoning, and cropped-image target-presence classification. This substantially expands task and domain coverage beyond the retained ScreenSpot benchmarks and cursor-in-box test. Training sources remain Aria-UI and OS-Atlas.

E2.justification: The original ScreenSpot comparator sets are retained. v2 adds reported comparisons with GUI-Spotlight in Tables 2 and 7, RegionFocus in Table 10, Qwen3-VL models in Table 11, and o3 and GTA1-32B in the OSWorld comparison, substantially broadening the comparison methods.

E3.justification: v2 adds UI-TARS-1.5-7B and Qwen3-VL-2B-Thinking training configurations, o3-based online evaluation with explicit action budgets, timed inference comparisons and binary target-presence testing. The original training hyperparameters remain unchanged. OSWorld results use different action budgets across methods, so they are not equal-budget comparisons.

E4.justification: The original reward, thinking, focusing and training-dynamics analyses are retained. New analyses investigate spatial transfer beyond GUI images, training and inference efficiency, test-time compute trade-offs, applicability to Qwen3 backbones and detection of targets excluded by cropping. The original case studies are retained rather than newly added.

E5.justification: Neither version reports independent run or seed counts, confidence intervals, error bars or statistical significance tests. The added results continue point-estimate reporting. GRPO trajectory sampling and reward normalization do not constitute experimental uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: The original Qwen-based ScreenSpot results remain 93.9% and 56.5%. New results include 58.1% ScreenSpot-Pro accuracy with UI-TARS initialization, 57.1% OSWorld accuracy with o3 at 50 steps, 43.4% on SpatialMQA, and 55.0% ScreenSpot-Pro accuracy for GUI-CURSOR-2B. v2 also adds timing and crop-detection outcomes and replaces ScreenSpot-v2 text/icon breakdowns with platform averages.

M1.justification: The cursor-control procedure, history conditioning, GRPO objective, four trajectory penalties and cursor-centric focusing remain unchanged. Additional backbones use the retained procedure. Appendix L discusses dragging as a future extension rather than an implemented modification.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution summary and conclusion are selectively rewritten. Spatial discussion moves from Section 4 to Section 3.3, and implementation appendices are reorganized. The LLM-use disclosure is removed, while impact and acknowledgement sections are added. Most retained technical prose remains closely preserved.

P2.justification: The single-column preprint becomes a two-column conference paper. Existing figure panels are split or relocated, ScreenSpot-v2 table columns are consolidated, and new tables present agentic, spatial, efficiency and backbone comparisons. Original workflow graphics, plots and case-study images are retained within the redesigned layout.

R1.justification: Section 4 and Appendices G–H substantially expand positioning against iterative cropping and test-time scaling, discussing GUI-Spotlight, GUI-ARP, GUI-RC/RCPO and RegionFocus. Appendix L adds GUI-Drag. These comparisons clarify the distinction between learning cursor-based spatial alignment and narrowing image regions.

T1.justification: The bounding-box formulation, distance reward, penalty definitions and GRPO mathematics are retained, with equation renumbering and formatting changes. No substantive mathematical assumptions, derivations, theorems or proofs are added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's narrow evidence for practical utility and generality through online OSWorld evaluation, non-GUI spatial benchmarks and additional backbones. Appendices F and J quantify runtime trade-offs and crop-recovery limitations, making the method more assessable. These gains outweigh reduced ScreenSpot-v2 subgroup detail and a localized reporting inconsistency: Table 11 attributes 58.1%/65.6% to a Qwen-based model, whereas Tables 1–2 associate those results with UI-TARS initialization.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GUI-CURSOR research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and can be matched despite substantial reformatting and expanded evaluation.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds grounding benchmarks, online agent evaluation, spatial-reasoning tests, additional backbones, efficiency measurements and crop-failure analysis.

before.justification: v1 reports original GUI-CURSOR results on ScreenSpot-v2 and ScreenSpot-Pro, alongside ablations, training analyses and the cursor-in-box experiment.

C1.justification: The introduction strengthens existence from some radius to an interval and centers the contribution on stationary shifted-gradient dynamics despite a nonzero original gradient. It also narrows the empirical claims to evidence consistent with the mechanism and recasts switching from a proposed remedy into an established warm-start safeguard that mitigates the failure mode.

C2.justification: v2 replaces v1's broad claim that most modern networks are real-analytic with conditional statements about suitable deterministic networks. It explicitly treats loss slices as suggestive rather than certification and stochastic/ReLU observations as outside the formal guarantees. Section 3.1 also adds an acute-angle interpretation explaining the stability condition.

D1.justification: Appendix C.2 documents gradient accumulation across the training set, normalization, absent augmentation, and optimizer settings for the new full-batch CIFAR experiments. v2 additionally states that the 10% warm-start fraction was not tuned. Existing implementation details and the same repository access information are retained; the repository disclosure is relocated.

E1.justification: v2 adds CIFAR-10 image classification while retaining MNIST, CIFAR-100, and the synthetic example. Full-batch evaluation on the already included CIFAR-100 changes the protocol rather than adding another task or domain.

E2.justification: The method comparison remains SAM-only versus the same GD/SGD-to-SAM switching schedule. The new CIFAR experiments sweep standard SAM's radius, including zero; cited SAM variants are not added as evaluated competitors.

E3.justification: v2 introduces a separate full-batch CIFAR protocol with ResNet-18, 10,000 steps, learning rate 0.001, no augmentation, and radii from 0 to 2 in increments of 0.5. It also introduces GradRatio and LossGap diagnostics and reports original versus shifted losses and gradients. The earlier MNIST and stochastic CIFAR protocols remain intact.

E4.justification: Table 1 and Appendix C.2 add a substantial mechanism analysis testing whether shifted/unshifted mismatch persists in larger ReLU networks under deterministic training. Final-gradient measurements and paired loss trajectories across radii extend the evidence beyond the earlier small smooth-network example. Existing perturb-and-return, switching, and synthetic sensitivity analyses are retained.

E5.justification: v2 clarifies that thin trajectory curves represent individual seeds and bold curves represent means. For the stochastic trajectories, this corrects v1 Appendix C.2's description of standard-deviation shading; the actual panels are unchanged. Existing counts of 80, 5, and 16 seeds and the other mean/standard-deviation summaries remain unchanged.

E6.justification: v2 adds full-batch CIFAR loss and gradient results absent from v1. For example, Table 1 reports CIFAR-10 at radius 1.5 with original/shifted losses of 0.773/0.001 and gradient norms of 11.932/0.011. These are new-setting findings, not improvements over matched v1 results. Retained stochastic peak accuracies remain 77.05% for SAM-only and 77.49% for switching.

M1.justification: The normalized SAM perturbation, shifted-gradient update, and initial 10% GD/SGD phase followed by SAM are unchanged. Calling the switching strategy a warm-start and revising the mathematical definition of hallucinated minimizers do not change the training procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, theoretical explanations, experiments, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. The dynamical and manifold subsections and their proofs exchange order, the analyticity appendix moves, and references move after the appendices. These changes substantially reorganize retained content as well as accommodating additions.

P2.justification: v2 changes typography, headings, text width, and figure sizing and placement throughout. It removes v1 Figure 3's maximizer-set illustration, adds Table 1 and two CIFAR trajectory figures, and separates the final synthetic figure collections across pages. Most retained plot panels are unchanged, although captions and numbering are revised.

R1.justification: Section 1.1 substantially refocuses positioning on large-radius, discrete-time SAM and prior switching schedules. v2 specifically attributes warm-start precedents to Andriushchenko and Flammarion (2022) and disclaims proposing a new training recipe. It also removes substantial portions of the broader applications and flat-minima literature survey while retaining the central SAM theory references.

T1.justification: Definition 2.1 adds shifted-gradient stationarity as an explicit requirement. Both existence theorems now establish nontrivial radius intervals, supported by new Lemmas A.5 and A.10. The manifold theorem is recast under C2 regularity and explicit local preimage assumptions. v2 also corrects the Jacobian transpose, multiplier signs, and surrogate smoothness constant, adds a Hessian-norm sufficient stability condition, and revises the neural-network analyticity assumptions.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses central weaknesses by explicitly connecting the definition to SAM-update stationarity, correcting derivative and convergence-proof details, and supporting interval-of-radius existence with additional arguments. New deterministic CIFAR diagnostics strengthen the mechanistic evidence. More careful treatment of loss slices, analyticity, stochastic observations, and warm-start novelty improves the match between evidence and claims. Stochastic and nonsmooth convergence guarantees remain open, but the revisions substantially improve correctness and evidential support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SAM failure-mode study. All 24 pages of v1 and 27 pages of v2, including appendices, equations, figures, and the new table, support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds full-batch ResNet-18 experiments on CIFAR-10/100, reported in Table 1 and Figures 8–9.

before.justification: v1 reports original MNIST training experiments, repeated-seed radius sweeps, stochastic ResNet-18/CIFAR-100 experiments, and synthetic visualizations.

C1.justification: The central contributions—text-based empowerment estimation, a goal-agnostic capability proxy, and identification of influential actions—remain. v3 extends its expressly claimed applicability to realistic tool use and emphasizes a complementary role alongside task-success measures in the abstract and conclusion, modestly revising the scope and qualification of the claims.

C2.justification: v3 substantially clarifies failure conditions: task-irrelevant control during off-domain navigation, misleading diversity near floor performance in retail, and finite-sample estimator bias. Appendix I also replaces v1's broad robustness interpretation with explicit acknowledgment of substantial Hanoi degradation using retained results. New architectural analyses motivate LoRA and qualify unrestricted fine-tuning, materially improving the discussion of applicability.

D1.justification: v1 already provides pseudocode, prompts, optimizer settings, dimensions, and hardware information. v3 adds LoRA rank 8 and alpha 16, specifies partial tuning of the final two layers, and reports H100 memory overheads. It updates the advertised code location from an anonymous host to a named GitHub repository and corrects Gridworld and WebArena setup descriptions.

E1.justification: v3 adds tau-bench airline and retail customer-service tasks using structured function-calling tools, extending evaluation beyond textual games and web browsing (Section 5, Figure 8). Gridworld, Tower of Hanoi, the four WebArena domains, natural-language conversion, and the authentication scenario were already evaluated in v1.

E2.justification: New Appendix C.3 and Table 5 compare EELMA with five trajectory-derived alternatives: discounted visitation entropy, action entropy, normalized state coverage, trajectory length, and unique-state ratio. This substantially expands comparisons of the proposed capability metric. Direct estimation and the Gemini-2.5-Flash prompt-only estimator already appeared in v1 and remain.

E3.justification: v3 adds tau-bench evaluation on 50 airline and 115 retail tasks with three Qwen2.5 scales, and adds Qwen2.5-32B-it to WebArena. New baseline correlations pool 16 WebArena and six tau-bench model-domain points. Authentication reporting introduces within-trajectory averaging. Appendix B.2 revises the stated training schedule from approximately 10,000 steps to a 20,000-step maximum while retaining convergence near 10,000; this does not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendices K–L newly test sensitivity to three embedding models and four encoder-training strategies, examining accuracy, training collapse, and computational costs. Appendix G.2 adds analysis of off-domain WebArena navigation. These substantially extend v1's existing complexity, CoT, memory, linguistic-variation, and authentication analyses.

E5.justification: Authentication reporting now distinguishes trajectory-level averages from pooled action-level statistics and explicitly displays numerical ± uncertainties in Figure 9, although their type is unspecified. The action-level standard deviations and Welch tests remain in Figure 11. Three-seed WebArena reporting and five-replicate prompt-estimator comparisons are retained; additional runs are not established.

E6.justification: v3 adds Qwen WebArena outcomes, positive airline and inverted retail empowerment trends, and Table 5's baseline correlations, including EELMA values of 0.39 for WebArena and 0.71 for tau-bench. Tables 7–8 add encoder accuracy and training-collapse results. Authentication means change from 0.365/-0.127 in v1 Figure 8 to trajectory-level 0.268/-0.094 in v3 Figure 9; the original action-level values remain in v3 Figure 11, so this is reaggregation rather than a performance change.

M1.justification: The paired InfoNCE objectives and difference-of-scores estimator remain. v3 introduces LoRA encoder adaptation and recommends it as the default; Appendix D also changes the reported WebArena embedding model from Jina embeddings to E5-Mistral-7B and adds an encoder layer. These are bounded architectural adaptations within the retained estimation procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method explanation, and discussion are extensively rewritten. v3 separates the capability hypothesis more clearly, explains latent states versus observations, reorganizes contributions and appendix headings, moves existing multimodal and power-seeking discussion into Appendix M, and adds an Impact Statement. These are substantial narrative and structural revisions beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to two-column layout, with widespread resizing and relocation of figures and tables. v3 redraws the method overview and several plots, expands Figure 7 with Qwen, and revises the authentication display. New tool-use, off-domain navigation, encoder, and fine-tuning figures and comparison tables substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v3 adds targeted references for LoRA, tau-bench, E5-Mistral, online learning, and related empowerment training. Appendix M distinguishes semantic state-level empowerment from Ellis et al.'s token-level approach. The central positioning relative to empowerment and benchmark-based evaluation remains; publication-year and venue updates to retained references are bibliographic changes.

T1.justification: Section 3 revises the formal empowerment averaging and normalization, replacing gamma^t/(1-gamma) with geometric weights (1-gamma)gamma^k. It also replaces the asserted exact score-difference estimate with an approximation requiring a small expected residual difference and explicitly discusses finite-negative-sample bias. These materially revise the core mathematical definition and justification, while Appendix A's reward-bound lemmas and proofs largely persist.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses important validation gaps through comparisons with simpler metrics, evaluation in tool-use environments, and controlled encoder analyses. It also corrects overly broad interpretations of linguistic robustness and makes estimator bias and capability-proxy failures explicit. These substantially strengthen the evidence and clarify its limits. Reporting problems remain, including stale WebArena correlations in the prose and Figure 12's mismatch between state-level plots and trajectory-level captions, but they do not outweigh the stronger comparisons and more qualified conclusions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe EELMA and retain identifiable corresponding methods, experiments, and appendices. The complete text, equations, tables, and figures support comparison despite substantial rewriting, reformatting, and added appendices in v3.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds tau-bench evaluations, trajectory-metric comparisons, WebArena error analysis, and encoder and fine-tuning experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original Gridworld, Tower of Hanoi, and WebArena experiments, including empowerment estimates, task performance, authentication results, and appendix comparisons with natural-language conversion and a prompt-only estimator.

results.title: Estimating the Empowerment of Language Model Agents

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion narrow the claim from achieving or setting the state of the art to outperforming most existing methods. The central contribution remains an explicit part-correspondence prior that improves existing GCD methods without substantial architectural changes.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations concerning transfer beyond DINO, benefits beyond background suppression, and degradation from excessive part fragmentation. New failure analysis identifies ambiguous local appearance, informative global shape, and age-related variation. Limitations now discuss frozen PCA construction and patch-grid resolution, while CNN incompatibility is softened to reduced direct applicability. v1's detailed broader-impact discussion is replaced by a generic impact statement.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents baseline and PartCo training times, peak training memory of 8.6 versus 12.0 GB, and computational costs of 54.1 versus 62.6 GFLOPs in Table B. It specifies the CLIP ViT-B/16 image-only configuration. Existing optimizer settings, hardware, preprocessing information, label-construction timings, and project-page access remain substantially unchanged.

E1.justification: All eight image datasets are retained, including Oxford-Pet and Herbarium19 from v1's appendix. The limited expansion is an auxiliary evaluation of semantic part correspondence against CUB's visible annotated parts in v2 Table F. CLIP and additional host methods change model configurations rather than dataset coverage.

E2.justification: Tables 1 and 2 substantially expand the evaluated comparator set, adding methods including APL, PartGCD, DebGCD, SEAL, RLCD, and HypCD variants. Appendix Table D introduces CLIP comparisons with TextGCD, GET, CLIP-GCD, and CPT. Oxford-Pet and Herbarium19 comparisons also add FlipClass and SelEx, beyond v1's SimGCD comparison.

E3.justification: Existing dataset splits, category ACC evaluation, and stated core training settings remain unchanged. New experimental protocols include CLIP ViT-B/16 image-encoder evaluation, additional host-model configurations, a reported balancing-factor sweep over 0, 0.1, 0.35, 0.7, and 1.0, Hungarian matching against visible CUB part annotations before downsampling, and foreground-only training controls.

E4.justification: v2 adds balancing-factor sensitivity, quantitative part-label validation, third-order over-fragmentation analysis, a foreground-only control testing whether background suppression explains the gains, computational overhead analysis, and per-class success/failure studies. Existing projection-dimension, unsupervised-loss, SD-DINOv2, and unknown-category analyses are retained. The implicit/explicit SPTNet analysis moves from v1 Table 4 to appendix Table E.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, standard deviations, or significance tests. The added experiments continue reporting point estimates.

E6.justification: Existing PartCo-SimGCD and PartCo-SelEx scores in Tables 1 and 2 are retained, while extensive results are added. New CLIP average ACC is 65.3 for SimGCD versus 70.5 for PartCo-SimGCD; part-label matching reports 80.8 and 77.5 for first- and second-order labels. Added Hyp-SelEx ranks above PartCo-SelEx on SSB average ACC, 86.0 versus 85.5. Newly reported SPTNet Stanford-Cars ACC is inconsistent: 72.3 in Table 1 versus 72.5 in Table E.

M1.justification: The proposed PCA/k-means label construction, first- and second-order priors, part-feature pooling, projection head, correspondence losses, and inference procedure remain unchanged. Third-order labels are investigated as an ablation; the additional backbone and host-method experiments do not revise the main algorithm.

P1.justification: Most introductory and methodological prose and the main section sequence are retained. Targeted revisions affect claims, results discussion, related work, and conclusions. The supplement gains an overview and reorganized subsections; the implicit/explicit analysis moves there, and the broader-impact section is replaced by a main-text impact statement.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from a single-column preprint to a two-column conference layout. Tables 1 and 2 expand and gain venue columns, Figure 6 is redesigned around four host methods, and existing diagrams and plots are rearranged. New tables and figures display compute costs, CLIP results, part validation, third-order labels, controls, and failure cases; retained appendix visualizations are enlarged and relocated.

R1.justification: The comparison literature expands substantially, and positioning becomes more specific. Section 5 distinguishes PartCo's training-only correspondence supervision from APL's aggregated part representation and PartGCD's adaptive decomposition and regularization. Section 4.2 contrasts PartCo with HypCD's hyperbolic embeddings. Additional references support CLIP comparisons and proposed object-centric and feature-upsampling directions.

T1.justification: The formal problem assumptions, PCA and clustering definitions, and loss equations are retained. No theorem, proof, or substantive mathematical derivation is added. The new part-matching evaluation is empirical, and moving category ACC from a numbered equation to inline text does not change its definition.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important validation gaps: Tables F and I directly assess part semantics and isolate background suppression, Table D tests transfer beyond DINO, and new compute and failure analyses clarify practical costs and boundaries. Expanded comparisons also motivate more defensible performance claims. These substantially strengthen the evidence for PartCo. The new balancing-factor description conflicts with Equation 8, SPTNet scores disagree between Tables 1 and E, and impact discussion is reduced, but these drawbacks do not outweigh the added controlled validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PartCo research and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete supplementary material. Relocated and renumbered content can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds CLIP evaluations, annotated-part validation, foreground-only controls, computational measurements, and per-class success and failure results.

before.justification: v1 reports original GCD benchmark results, component ablations, alternative label-construction experiments, and unknown-category estimation experiments in the main text and appendix.

results.title: PartCo: Part-Level Correspondence Priors Enhance Category Discovery

C1.justification: v1 foregrounds dual scaling and matrix imbalance as a new quantization proxy. v4 makes prediction of input activation magnitudes from weight statistics, enabling calibration-free pseudo-activation-awareness, a central contribution. Its abstract and conclusion also add explicit zero-to-negligible inference-overhead claims, materially expanding the paper's main claims.

C2.justification: v1 interprets imbalance as a better optimization target than kurtosis. v4 develops a different mechanism explanation involving training updates, implicit activation importance and prevention of row-wise outliers, supported by weight-versus-activation reconstruction analyses. It also explains the no-overhead variant's scale-sharing constraints and resulting quality/overhead tradeoff, and acknowledges that calibration still provides additional information.

D1.justification: Algorithm 1 makes previously mentioned log-domain accumulation and clipping explicit, adding detailed scale bookkeeping and best-iterate recovery. v4 also documents PyTorch scaling around gemlite and adds supplementary-code and licensing disclosures in Appendix A.2. The existing GitHub access information remains; these are documentation improvements rather than evidence that every underlying implementation changed.

E1.justification: v4 newly uses Chinese Wikipedia and Python-code activation samples for cross-domain comparisons, plus Gaussian inputs and targets in a single-layer simulation (Figure 2). The principal WikiText2/C4, HellaSwag/PIQA/MMLU and AIME benchmark coverage remains.

E2.justification: v4 adds reported comparisons with CrossQuant (Table 16), QTIP and QuIP# (Table 17), and GGUF Q4_0/Q3_KS baselines (Table 9). QuIP# was already cited in v1 but lacked a reported comparison. These additions substantially broaden the comparator families beyond the retained quantization baselines.

E3.justification: New protocols include W4A8/G128 with context length 2048 for CrossQuant, context length 4096 for codebook comparisons, and gemlite, SGLang and llama.cpp inference measurements with specified batch sizes and workloads. v4 also adds Phi-2/3/4 and additional Llama configurations. These extend the evaluation design; the original headline benchmark settings remain.

E4.justification: v4 adds weight/activation correlation diagnostics, a single-layer Adam simulation, column-scaling kurtosis analysis, weight-versus-activation reconstruction comparisons, AWQ/ASINQ kurtosis analysis and the no-overhead quality tradeoff. Conversely, v1's direct kurtosis-versus-imbalance optimization experiment (Figure 2) and 1D-versus-2D tiling ablation (Figure 4b) are removed.

E5.justification: Both versions retain the same ten-run quantization-timing summaries, including the same ± values and distribution plot (v1 Table 7/Figure 5; v4 Table 10/Figure 8). The additions introduce no new seed counts, confidence intervals, significance tests or uncertainty-reporting practices.

E6.justification: All twelve v1 tables retain their numerical results after matching renumbered content. v4 adds substantial new results: Table 5 reports 0.8–1.8% kernel overhead, while Table 9 reports Qwen3-1.7B Q4_0 perplexity of 21.30 for GGUF versus 17.65 with SINQ preprocessing. Further mechanism, Phi and comparator results are added, while the removed optimization and tiling plots remove result entries.

M1.justification: The core dual-scaling, normalization and A-SINQ approach remains. v4 adds a no-overhead variant that shares input scales across appropriate layers and absorbs them into preceding layers, including use before GGUF quantization (Section 2.3.1). This is a bounded procedural extension; several details in the expanded log-space pseudocode were already described in v1.

P1.justification: v4 substantially rewrites the abstract, contribution list, Section 2.2.1 and conclusion around pseudo-activation-awareness. It also revises the calibration explanation, shortens the tiling discussion and reorganizes the appendices around new reproducibility, diagnostic and deployment sections. This changes the explanatory narrative substantially beyond adding experimental content.

P2.justification: The document changes from a single-column to a two-column layout with extensive resizing and relocation of displays. New mechanism figures replace v1 Figure 2, additional inference/comparison tables appear, and the tiling-ablation panel disappears. The large-model table moves from the main text (v1 Table 3) to the appendix (v4 Table 13), retaining its results.

R1.justification: The related-work organization and most comparisons remain. v4 adds citations to CrossQuant, QTIP, Adam, gemlite and SGLang, discusses codebook deployment restrictions, and positions SINQ against the assumption that activation-awareness requires calibration. The Sinkhorn–Knopp reference present in v1 is absent from v4.

T1.justification: v4 corrects the AWQ objective by removing the duplicated input-vector factor in v1 Equation 5 (v4 Equation 6). The matrix-imbalance definition and dual-scale parameterization remain mathematically equivalent. The new inverse-square-root relationship in Equation 4 is presented as an empirical observation, without a theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens the mechanism explanation and deployment evidence. Unlike v1's quantization timings and algebraic overhead discussion, it measures inference overhead at kernel and end-to-end levels and quantifies the no-overhead variant's quality tradeoff. New weight/activation diagnostics and broader comparisons make the main claims more assessable. These gains outweigh the loss of the direct kurtosis-optimization and tiling ablations, although uncertainty reporting remains limited.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SINQ research work. Their text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial revisions and reformatting.

after.justification: v4 retains those original experiments and adds weight/activation diagnostics, inference measurements, method-variant evaluations and further comparisons.

before.justification: v1 reports original perplexity, QA, reasoning, quantization-timing and ablation results in the main text and appendices.

results.title: SINQ: Sinkhorn-Normalized Quantization for Calibration-Free Low-Precision LLM Weights

C1.justification: The abstract qualifies superiority over baselines as 'comparable or superior' and adds an explicit FKL sample-efficiency versus RKL stability/asymptotic-performance trade-off. The central PMD-based diffusion-policy contribution, introduction's contribution list and concluding scope remain substantially unchanged.

C2.justification: New Section 5.4 and expanded Appendix E.3 provide substantive guidance on choosing FKL versus RKL. They explain rapid FKL exploitation, RKL's more gradual clipped updates, and temperature-dependent collapse, proposing loss of replay diversity as a mechanism. v3 also discusses autoregressive ordering mitigation and qualifies scalability comparisons that v1 described more categorically.

D1.justification: v3 documents DQN-Macro search grids, KL-constraint schedules and the trajectory interpretation of Atari batch sizes, and revises Football implementation parameters. Most architecture and DNA-processing details remain unchanged. Conversely, v1's explicit identification of the four Atari scaling-study games is omitted.

E1.justification: The enhancer-generation task, MinAtar and Atari benchmarks, and eight Football environments are retained. The added '11 vs 11 SM' comparison changes the training budget within an existing task, rather than introducing a new environment or task requirement.

E2.justification: Football Table 2 adds separately evaluated MAT and MAPPO baselines alongside the retained autoregressive comparator, substantially strengthening this comparison. MAT is distinguished by randomized agent ordering, rather than merely renaming the original comparator. The revised planner comparison also adds a standard RL-D2 reference in Figure 14.

E3.justification: Appendix D.4 changes Football training from 100M to 1B steps for 11 vs 11 and from 10M/100M to 500M elsewhere. Table 4 revises learning rates, rollout length, entropy weight and gradient clipping. v3 also adds matched-wall-time FKL/RKL batch-size comparisons, a 100M-step Football control, and Atari median/IQM metrics. The planner evaluation changes its sample range and tested planning lengths.

E4.justification: v3 adds FKL/RKL compute and sample-efficiency comparisons, DQN-Macro hyperparameter searches, and Atari/Football KL-constraint sensitivity studies that expose learning instability and collapse. The existing planner analysis is revised. MinAtar temperature tuning, on-policy diffusion and architecture ablations were already present in v1 and are retained.

E5.justification: MinAtar Table 1 changes the reported seed count from 3 to 20 and introduces bootstrap confidence limits. Football Table 2 newly specifies bootstrap intervals over 20 seeds. Appendix D.5 adds 50,000-iteration stratified bootstrapping for Atari aggregate statistics and performance differences; this does not establish an increased Atari run count.

E6.justification: MinAtar and Football table entries are revised, and numerous comparative and sensitivity results are added. Football's reported 11 vs 11 RKL score changes from 54.2 to 99.4 under revised budgets and hyperparameters, so this is not a same-setting gain. The new small-budget comparison reports FKL 68.5 versus RKL 0.0. The full per-game Atari Table 5 is unchanged.

M1.justification: Section 4.1 removes the optional ELBO-difference importance-ratio approximation presented in v1, retaining the existing augmented-MDP single-step ratio. The PMD framework, FKL/RKL objective families, on-policy diffusion learning and appendix planner algorithm remain substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much foundational prose are retained. v3 copyedits wording, repairs the malformed Zekri citation, clarifies that 'on-policy' refers to diffusion trajectories, adds a practitioner-guidance subsection and explanatory appendices, and updates author and affiliation text.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to two-column layout with running headers. v3 adds a framework flowchart and several analysis figures, merges v1 Figures 3 and 4 into Figure 5, expands comparison tables, and relocates Table 5 to the end. Existing plots are extensively resized, rearranged or redrawn, with improved labels and captions.

R1.justification: Section 2, Remark 1 and Appendix G add focused positioning against evolution strategies, genetic algorithms and the cross-entropy method, with supporting citations. MAPPO also gains a reference. The established positioning relative to discrete diffusion, PMD and online reinforcement learning is retained.

T1.justification: v3 corrects the PMD normalization in Eq. (3), removes the erroneous leading minus signs from the ELBO expressions in Eqs. (4) and (5), and makes the masking transition consistent with its cumulative schedule. It removes Appendix B.3's ELBO-ratio bias derivation. The principal FKL/RKL proofs and temperature-duality derivation remain.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially addresses v1's limited Football comparison and weak guidance on choosing FKL versus RKL through stronger baselines, expanded uncertainty reporting, controlled comparisons and explicit failure analyses. Mathematical corrections also improve technical clarity. These gains are tempered by conflicting new Atari aggregates: Figure 8 reports RL-D2 mean/IQM 34.7/5.5, while Table 6 reports 31.33/4.98. Despite that reporting flaw, the comparative validation and practical understanding improve substantially; higher Football scores under larger budgets are not themselves evidence of improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RL-D2 study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable matching across the revision.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and reports additional baseline comparisons, budget and hyperparameter studies, and statistical analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original DNA-generation, MinAtar, Atari and Google Research Football experiments, including performance, computational costs and appendix ablations.

results.title: Reinforcement Learning with Discrete Diffusion Policies for Combinatorial Action Spaces

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contributions: general-corpus pretraining with per-token latent thoughts, superiority to doubled-parameter models at matched inference cost, and benefits from longer latent-thought chains. Renaming and additional supporting studies do not redefine these headline claims.

C2.justification: V3 adds interpretations of latent thoughts as preliminary hypotheses followed by verification, test-time sampling as evidence of candidate diversity, and fixed-depth training as causing depth overfitting. It also explicitly discusses approximately 8× training FLOPs, doubled KV-cache storage and preservation of positional context capacity, materially expanding the account of mechanisms and trade-offs.

D1.justification: V3 supplies explicit code and model-checkpoint links, replacing v1's supplementary-code statement and promise of a future public repository. It additionally documents 73,047 GPU-hours on 64GB GPUs, training-FLOPs accounting, BFloat16 precision and the doubled-depth construction of the 2.8B comparator. External resource availability was not verified.

E1.justification: V3 adds GSM8K mathematical reasoning and TruthfulQA generative question answering, evaluated with test-time scaling strategies (Section 4.5 and Appendix C). These materially extend the original language-modeling, general downstream and instruction-following coverage. The larger-model ablations otherwise reuse existing datasets.

E2.justification: Figure 1 adds TinyLLaMA to the training-compute scaling comparison; v1's scaling panels compare against Pythia. Existing baseline families in the downstream and controlled LLaMA comparisons remain. The additional seven-step PonderLM condition changes its computational setting rather than introducing a new method family.

E3.justification: The reported Jacobi sampling range changes from {2, 3, 4} to {2, 3}, without establishing that retained experiments were rerun. New protocols include voting and Best-of-N with 1–10 samples, CoT comparisons, EM/ROUGE-L evaluation, LLaMA-410M ablations trained on 6B tokens, and a seven-step PonderLM condition with 8× inference FLOPs.

E4.justification: V3 substantially expands convergence diagnostics beyond v1's vanilla-model MSE curve, including agreement with sequential inference and fixed-versus-randomized iteration counts. Appendices G–J add larger-model thought-chain scaling, isolated representation/Jacobi/interleaving ablations, memory trade-offs and qualitative plus quantitative latent-decoding probes.

E5.justification: Figure 9 and Appendix D.2 add explicit log-linear estimation of convergence decay rates and corresponding R-squared statistics; v1's convergence analysis only plots MSE. Neither version reports repeated-training seed counts, confidence intervals or significance tests. Test-time sample counts are inference budgets, not repeated training runs.

E6.justification: Tables 2 and 4 and the relocated detailed downstream table retain their numerical results. Substantial new results include GSM8K CoT EM of 32.90% versus 24.26% for Standard CPT, and LLaMA-410M average accuracy increasing from 39.7% to 44.9% across zero to five latent thoughts. Additional comparator, convergence, ablation and decoding results extend the evidence rather than demonstrate same-setting gains over v1.

M1.justification: The proposed hidden-state feedback, token-thought interleaving, Jacobi updates, next-token loss and reused positional IDs remain unchanged. PonderLM-2 is a rename. The changed iteration-count range is a training-setting revision; the newly tested component variants are ablations.

P1.justification: V3 substantially rewrites method and evaluation explanations, converts baseline lists into consolidated prose, and reorganizes the efficiency discussion around training and inference costs. It standardizes PonderLM-2 terminology and restructures the appendices: v1's substantive Appendices D–E become A–B, while its declaration sections disappear. These changes extend beyond adding scientific results.

P2.justification: The document adopts a new visual template with colored headings, a shaded abstract and revised running headers. Figure 1 gains a training-FLOPs panel, Figure 2 gains a causal-dependency diagram, and the convergence display becomes a two-panel logarithmic analysis. Several new plots and tables accompany the added studies; retained displays are also relocated and reformatted.

R1.justification: Narayanan et al. (2021) is removed from the introduction and bibliography. The substantive positioning against Coconut, PonderLM, depth-sharing approaches and discrete thinking-token methods, including the taxonomy, remains largely unchanged.

T1.justification: Section 3.3 and Appendix D introduce a causal finite-step convergence argument, stabilization within at most T iterations, contraction-based geometric and posterior error bounds, and an argument for equivalence with sequential inference. V1 specifies the iteration but provides no corresponding theoretical development. The fast-rate bounds depend on a contraction assumption.

improvement.justification: V3 addresses important gaps in v1 through component-isolating ablations, stronger training-compute comparisons and diagnostics connecting parallel training to sequential inference. These additions substantially strengthen the evidence and cost transparency, while resource links improve reproducibility information. The fast-convergence argument remains conditional on contraction, which empirical fits alone do not establish, and repeated-run uncertainty remains absent. These limitations temper but do not outweigh the gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same latent-thought pretraining work, renamed PonderLM-2 in v3. Text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: V3 retains those empirical results and adds test-time scaling evaluations, convergence diagnostics, component ablations and latent-thought decoding analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original pretraining, downstream evaluation, continual-pretraining and ablation results, including additional architecture-scaling experiments in Appendix E.

results.title: PonderLM-2: Pretraining LLM with Latent Thoughts in Continuous Space

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: retrieval-guided rewriting with a frozen retriever, ranking rewards that counter score inflation, and improvements across five benchmarks with a stated average Recall@10 gain of 4.9%. The additional evidence does not redefine these core claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations that gains exceed what model scaling or shortening alone provides, discrete ranking rewards explain group-size stability, and retrieval feedback regularizes generation failures. It also advances stronger deployment-efficiency arguments. The earlier limitations concerning LLM knowledge, retriever capacity, and inference latency are retained.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies the default K = 8 and explicitly describes deployment as one LLM rewriting pass followed by retrieval. The advertised repository changes from Chinese0123456/GRAPE to mogulzhang/GRAPE. Optimizer, learning rate, training steps, batch size, and prompt templates were already documented in v1; their relocation is not a new disclosure.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate Flickr30k-CN, CVLUE, XM3600, Wikipedia, and CIRR, covering the same multilingual, long-form, and multimodal retrieval tasks. The new comparisons, controls, and failure audit concern retained data and tasks; no distinct new domain or test environment is established.

E2.justification: v2 Table 4 adds evaluated comparisons with PlugIR's noninteractive rewriting component, Claude-Sonnet-4.6, and GPT-5.4. Table 5 adds an explicitly prompted shortening baseline. These substantially extend v1's comparisons with vanilla CLIP and the frozen rewriting LLM; Table 1's comparator set is retained.

E3.justification: The new appendix experiments introduce matched-prompt baseline comparisons, a restriction of PlugIR to rewriting without interaction, forced-shortening controls, K = 2/4/8 configurations, and a manual audit of 100 randomly sampled queries. These substantially extend the evaluation design. Existing dataset splits, recall metrics, retriever sizes, and training budgets remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained data-efficiency, reward-comparison, and qualitative analyses, v2 tests whether shortening alone explains Wikipedia gains, examines sensitivity to group size, and quantifies generation failures through a manual audit. These address several substantive questions previously untested in v1.

E5.justification: Table 5 newly reports mean query lengths and their standard deviations, adding statistical characterization beyond v1's individual examples. These describe variation across queries, not uncertainty in retrieval performance. Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: Table 1 remains numerically unchanged, but v2 adds substantial results in Tables 4–6 and Appendix A.6. For example, Flickr-CN (1k) scores are 58.7/90.1 for GRAPE versus 56.2/91.3 for Claude-Sonnet-4.6, showing metric-dependent advantages. The Wikipedia shortening control scores 34.8/73.7 versus GRAPE's 43.7/82.8. The new audit reports 14% failures for the unoptimized LLM and 3% for GRAPE.

M1.justification: The frozen retriever, rewriting models, format and ranking rewards, group-normalized advantages, and regularized optimization objective remain unchanged. The newly stated default K = 8 documents an existing configuration; it does not establish a change to the proposed procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, reward explanation, ablation discussion, limitations, and conclusion undergo extensive rewriting. v2 adds an Impact Statement, reorganizes and expands the appendix, and moves training details into Section 4.1. It also corrects the title's GPRO typo to GRPO and revises the author and affiliation presentation.

P2.justification: v2 replaces the single-column main text with a two-column conference layout, including running headers and substantially resized and relocated displays. Figures 1–7 and Tables 1–3 retain their underlying content, while new Tables 4–6 present baseline comparisons, query-length statistics, and group-size sensitivity.

R1.justification: The related-work organization and principal research positioning are retained. v2 removes the Qwen2.5 technical report and Qwen2-VL citations and bibliography entries despite retaining those models. The new appendix comparisons additionally position retrieval-aligned optimization against larger language models, without substantially revising the literature discussion.

T1.justification: Appendix A.1 retains the affine-invariance derivation and adds a mathematical decomposition of image features into a shared corpus mean and a sample-specific component. It derives cancellation of the shared mean in pairwise ranking comparisons, providing a limited new analytical explanation of score inflation.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical credibility by addressing important gaps in v1: comparisons beyond the original frozen LLM, a control testing whether shortening explains gains, and quantitative robustness and failure analyses. Tables 4–6 provide evidence for retrieval-specific optimization while preserving the original results. Limited protocol detail and absent run-level uncertainty remain weaknesses, and the broad failure-suppression and efficiency claims exceed the direct evidence, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial improvement in experimental support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GRAPE study. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support comparison despite extensive reformatting and appendix expansion.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds baseline comparisons, query-length analysis, group-size sensitivity results, and a manual failure audit in Appendices A.3–A.6.

before.justification: v1 reports original retrieval experiments across five benchmarks, including Table 1, data-efficiency and reward comparisons, and per-language appendix results.

results.title: GRAPE: Let GRPO Supervise Query Rewriting by Ranking for Retrieval

C1.justification: The central contribution—amortized posterior correction using scarce calibration data and two flows—is retained. The abstract and introduction extend its stated scope explicitly to prior and noise misspecification, including uncertainty about which model component is wrong. This is a scope extension within the existing contribution.

C2.justification: v5 interprets ablations as supporting joint source/posterior adaptation, attributes RoPE's uniform SBC ranks to prior regularization, and discusses persistent Wind Tunnel miscalibration and SBC's inability to guarantee correctness. It also identifies ODE sampling costs and missing calibration-size bounds. These substantially expand v1's interpretation and limitations, although Appendix C reverses the dispersion interpretations of U-shaped and hump-shaped rank histograms.

D1.justification: v5 replaces the supplementary-ZIP disclosure with a repository link and adds the UMNN implementation reference, Pendulum noise scale, Gaussian seed-recovery instructions, explicit-Euler solver disclosure, default learning rate and clipping threshold, and detailed runtime breakdowns. This substantially improves documented reproducibility without demonstrating that previously unspecified settings changed.

E1.justification: The four original tasks remain, but Appendices D.3–D.4 add materially different test scenarios: controlled violations of conditional independence and prior misspecification in Gaussian and Wind Tunnel models. The latter includes training under a restricted [10,20] prior while targeting [0,45], substantially extending the parameter populations and mismatch conditions evaluated.

E2.justification: v1 explicitly excludes RoPE and compares against NPE and MFNPE. v5 adds RoPE to the main comparisons and evaluates NNPE and J-NPE in Appendix D.1, Figures 6–7. This substantially expands the evaluated comparator set.

E3.justification: Gaussian evaluation changes from joint-distribution jC2ST and Wasserstein metrics to conditional-posterior metrics averaged over three observations. v5 also introduces MMD, SBC using 1,000 pairs and 500 posterior draws per pair, a fixed-budget hyperparameter grid, and inference timing over 5,000 observations. These are substantive evaluation changes and new protocols.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's calibration-size comparisons and posterior examples, v5 tests joint versus sequential training, each transport separately, dependence on conditional independence, robustness to prior misspecification, and learning-rate/clipping sensitivity. Figures 10–13 additionally compare posteriors before and after correction. These directly investigate previously untested design choices and failure conditions.

E5.justification: The original five-calibration-set boxplots remain. Added analyses report means and standard deviations over three seeds or calibration draws, while SBC explicitly uses one training seed and displays 95% reference bands under uniform ranks. These extend statistical reporting without establishing an increase in the original experiments' run counts.

E6.justification: v5 adds extensive baseline, calibration, robustness, timing and sensitivity results. For example, Table 1 reports jC2ST 0.768 ± 0.041 for full FMCPE versus 0.864 ± 0.004 for TX-only at dependence strength α = 2. Gaussian scores use changed metrics, preventing direct version-to-version performance comparison, and v1's Gaussian MSE panel is absent. Wind Tunnel KDE curve assignments for NPE and MFNPE also swap between v1 Figure 5 and v5 Figure 8.

M1.justification: The two transports, simulation-informed source distribution, flow-matching losses, joint optimization, frozen posterior estimator and stop-gradient sampling procedure remain equivalent in Section 3 and Algorithms 1–2. The broader prior assumptions and additional implementation disclosures do not establish a changed FMCPE algorithm.

P1.justification: The title, abstract and introduction are substantially revised; the joint-training explanation is reorganized; and results gain separate comparison, ablation and timing discussions. The original two appendices are reorganized into dedicated sections covering conceptual background, setup, calibration, additional results, timing and sensitivity. These changes materially alter the narrative structure.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from single-column to two-column layout, and the overview moves to the first page. Benchmark plots gain comparators and revised Gaussian metric labels; existing posterior plots are relocated or revised. New SBC grids, correction visualizations, ablation and sensitivity plots, and numerical tables substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v5 substantially expands research positioning by distinguishing classical M-open/M-closed misspecification from recovery of physically meaningful parameters. It adds discussion of Bernardo and Smith, Bürkner et al., Nott et al. and newer robustness literature, and recognizes Senouf et al.'s inductive alternative to RoPE. MFNPE's publication update does not constitute a new cited method.

T1.justification: v5 relaxes the known-correct-prior premise to allow an approximate training prior qΘ. New Appendix A derives a Gaussian counterexample showing persistent physical-parameter bias despite an M-closed model, and Section 3.2 adds a conditional-independence condition for identifying qX|Y with pX|Y. The central transport derivations remain unchanged; no new correction-error guarantee is established.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked component ablations, excluded the closely related RoPE comparator, and provided only coarse computational-cost information. v5 directly addresses these gaps through broader comparisons, tests of both flows and joint training, prior-shift experiments, and measured runtime breakdowns. This substantially strengthens support for the method's design and practical applicability. The reversed SBC dispersion labels and overly broad clipping-robustness interpretation require correction, but these reporting problems do not outweigh the substantial evidential gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs present FMCPE with the same two-flow construction and four core benchmarks. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite the title change and substantial expansion.

after.justification: v5 retains original benchmark experiments and adds calibration diagnostics, component ablations, prior-misspecification experiments, timing measurements and hyperparameter studies.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on Gaussian, Pendulum, Wind Tunnel and Light Tunnel tasks, including quantitative comparisons and posterior visualizations in Figures 2–6.

results.title: Flow Matching Calibration for Simulation-Based Inference under Model Misspecification

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion expand the central performance claim from mathematical reasoning to robust cross-domain transfer after math-only training. On-demand consultation, assistance internalization and the approximately five-point mathematical advantage remain the original core claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning complementary expert capabilities, consultation timing beyond total call budget, transfer beyond mathematics and applicability across policy families. Appendix D discusses coding failures when expert capabilities are poorly matched. Appendix E additionally claims bounded noise sensitivity, although its described offline workflow tests do not directly establish robustness of EAPO training.

D1.justification: v2 documents exact alternative consultation rates, erroneous-trajectory selection and fallback rules, and an example uninformative guidance message. It also explicitly states a shared interaction budget for the existing parallelism comparison. Original hyperparameter tables, prompts, model/data access information and vLLM configuration remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds HumanEval, HLE, GPQA, MMLU, EvalPlus, HotpotQA and SimpleQA evaluations, extending coverage into coding, scientific reasoning and question answering. It also tests erroneous and uninformative expert-input scenarios. DAPO-Math training and the three original mathematical benchmarks remain.

E2.justification: The principal comparison methods in Table 1 remain unchanged. Appendix H adds a budget-matched fixed-rate consultation baseline and slower/faster annealing alternatives directly compared with default EAPO in Table 9, providing a focused extension of the comparator set.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce budget-matched schedule controls, selection of three erroneous expert trajectories from 32 samples, and replacement of guidance with fixed uninformative text. Additional configurations include Llama-8B experts, stronger offline experts and a Qwen3-8B policy. The original mathematical evaluation protocol and core training hyperparameters are retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds expert-pool homogeneity ablations, consultation-schedule sensitivity and budget controls, offline noisy-guidance and stronger-expert tests, and another policy-family evaluation. These substantially extend analysis of complementarity, consultation timing and dependence on model choice. Original training-dynamics analyses and case studies are retained, sometimes relocated.

E5.justification: Both versions describe 32 sampled answers and the same variance across per-problem mean scores. v2 adds no training-seed counts, independent-run uncertainty, confidence intervals or significance tests. Additional variance entries extend the existing reporting practice.

E6.justification: Original Tables 1–2 and Figure 3 retain their results. New results include non-math averages of 49.25 for EAPO versus 47.15 for self-exploratory RL, and Qwen3-8B averages of 49.98 versus 45.44. Schedule and expert-quality results are also added. Section 3.2 changes the stated distillation comparison from 20.83% to 24.80% without changing the underlying scores.

M1.justification: The proposed procedure retains learnable expert consultation, parallel queries, the same reward and objective, reciprocal consultation annealing and independent test-time reasoning. Alternative schedules and model configurations are evaluated as ablations; they do not replace the default method.

P1.justification: v2 polishes several introduction and explanatory paragraphs, clarifies notation, revises headings and moves consultation dynamics and offline collaboration discussion into appendices B–C. The main section sequence and most existing method, related-work and implementation prose remain recognizable; the revision primarily expands scientific content.

P2.justification: v2 adds seven result tables, groups Table 1 by method category and adds an average column to the relocated offline comparison. It also adjusts diagram typography and Figure 3's legend, enlarges the response-length plot, and moves the consultation-rate figure into Appendix B. These substantially expand and reorganize the displays.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for the seven new benchmarks and two Chen et al. works on long-horizon agents. The existing positioning against expert-guided distillation, hierarchical RL and self/social learning remains largely intact. The Policy Distillation publication-year update represents the same cited work.

T1.justification: Trajectory probabilities, rewards, optimization objectives and evaluation-statistic definitions remain substantively unchanged. v2 clarifies history indexing and symbols but adds no theoretical result, proof or substantive mathematical derivation. Alternative schedule formulas specify experimental settings.

improvement.justification: v1 leaves cross-task generalization as future work and lacks a control separating consultation timing from total consultation budget. v2 addresses these important gaps with math-only transfer evaluations, a budget-matched schedule comparison and another policy-family evaluation (Tables 4, 9 and 11). These substantially strengthen empirical support. Sparse non-math evaluation details and Appendix E's overextension of offline robustness evidence limit some new claims but do not outweigh the gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same EAPO research work. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations and appendices support comparison, including matching material moved from the main text into appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds non-math evaluations, consultation-schedule comparisons, expert-quality experiments and a Qwen3-8B policy evaluation.

before.justification: v1 reports original mathematical reasoning evaluations, policy/expert scaling experiments, parallelism ablations and training dynamics in Tables 1–3 and Figures 3–5.

results.title: EAPO: Enhancing Policy Optimization with On-Demand Expert Assistance

C1.justification: The principal claims about training-free schema reuse, the over-2,000-trajectory benchmark, and up-to-19.8% localization improvement remain. v2 removes the abstract's assertion that CORRECT substantially narrows the gap to human-level error recognition, modestly narrowing the claimed impact.

C2.justification: Section 6 and Appendix A.11 add substantive limitations concerning ambiguous decisive-error labels, potentially suboptimal semantic retrieval, and later salient errors overshadowing the earliest decisive error. Appendix A.8 discusses feedback dependence and possible automated validation. These considerably expand the explanation of applicability and failure conditions.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents SFT training splits, learning-rate and batch-size searches and selected values, cluster-count selection, encoder context limits, and per-turn truncation. Appendix A.9 supplies error-injection prompts, and the abstract adds a public-code link. These substantially improve reproducibility documentation without establishing that previously reported experiments changed.

E1.justification: The original WHO&WHEN and seven CORRECT-Error tasks remain. v2 adds error-category detection on ProgramDev+ChatDev and AG2+GSM8K, AgentErrorBench evaluations including ALFWorld and WebShop, and streaming adaptation and recovery scenarios. These substantially broaden task requirements and evaluated environments.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains LLM-as-a-Judge, fine-tuning, and naive ICL and adds MIPRO as an evaluated comparator. The new recovery experiment also compares CORRECT-selected restart steps against random restart steps.

E3.justification: New protocols evaluate incoming-domain cache fractions, truncation budgets, retrieval noise at fixed k=5, error-category recall, and restart success. Section 4.2 also changes the stated human-labeler count from three to conflicting counts of four and five; the actual revised study size and whether it was rerun remain unresolved.

E4.justification: v2 retains the original transfer, cache-size, schema-count, oracle, and self-detection analyses. It adds streaming adaptation, similarity/hotness sensitivity, context-truncation and retrieval-noise tests, targeted recovery, and a multi-error failure case explaining prediction of Step 12 instead of the annotated Step 4.

E5.justification: Section 5 changes the reported aggregate from average performance to median performance over five independent runs. The stated run count remains five; no new confidence intervals or significance-testing procedure is reported.

E6.justification: Table 1 revises several entries, including CORRECT's GPT-5 Human-Crafted Acc@1 from 37.8 to 32.3; aggregation also changes, so this does not establish a same-protocol performance decline. Table 2 remains unchanged. New results include AgentErrorBench scores, streaming and robustness measurements, and restart success of 20% versus 10% for random restarts.

M1.justification: The core schema extraction, retrieval-guided diagnosis, and cache-management pipeline remains. Appendix A.13 adds an explicit adaptation that prompts for an error category instead of a step index. Newly documented clustering and preprocessing details do not establish a redesign of the original pipeline.

P1.justification: Introduction and contribution passages are tightened, method explanations gain an algorithm walkthrough, and limitations, impact, and additional appendix headings are introduced.
