The original main-section progression and much of the existing narrative remain, with most expansion attributable to added scientific content.

P2.justification: The main text changes from one-column to two-column layout. Existing plots are regrouped into multipanel Figures 1 and 4–6, and the trajectory-length plot moves to Appendix A.2. Table 1 gains a comparator row, while new result tables and injection-prompt panels substantially expand the displays.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting MIPRO, production-agent motivation, LLaMAFactory, and AgentErrorBench. Appendix A.7 explicitly contrasts CORRECT with static human-curated MAST taxonomies, and A.8 discusses EcoAssistant. The central positioning around training-free schema reuse remains intact.

T1.justification: Section 3.1 adds a mathematical specification of silhouette scores and the cluster-count stopping condition S(K+1)-S(K)<epsilon. The decisive-error definition and retrieval equations remain unchanged, and no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v1's dynamic-deployment and near-zero-overhead claims had limited direct experimental support. v2 adds streaming, recovery, cost, and retrieval-robustness evaluations, substantially improves implementation documentation, and explains a concrete failure mechanism. These strengthen evidence and reproducibility beyond merely adding benchmark scores. Conflicting human-labeler counts and Table 1's new mislabeling of absolute point differences as relative improvements reduce reporting precision, but do not outweigh the substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CORRECT and CORRECT-Error. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and can be matched despite reformatting and substantial additions.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds streaming adaptation, recovery, robustness, cost, and cross-domain evaluations, including appendix results.

before.justification: v1 reports original error-localization experiments, schema ablations, and human evaluation of synthetic trajectories in Sections 4–5 and the appendix.

results.title: CORRECT: COndensed eRror RECognition via knowledge Transfer in multi-agent systems

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution statements retain the same central claims: efficient RKHS solution paths, conditional calibration using low-rank embeddings, and finite-sample coverage analysis. The headline empirical claims of roughly 30% shorter intervals and 40-fold speedup also remain.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly acknowledges possible coverage distortion from calibration-based tuning and recommends independent tuning when feasible. It develops the locality-versus-stability tradeoff, weak bounds in sparse regions, and limitations as regularization vanishes. It also distinguishes estimated-group from true-group coverage and newly attributes CondCP's conservative results to solver approximations.

D1.justification: New Appendix B.5 details bandwidth cross-validation followed by SIC-based regularization selection; v1 only briefly mentioned SIC. V2 also specifies a GIN predictor and absolute-residual scores for molecular experiments and a 30-hour CondCP timeout for arXiv. Hardware and code-access information remain essentially unchanged.

E1.justification: The real-world datasets and tasks remain unchanged; arXiv moves to Appendix D.2.1. New elbow-size experiments extend synthetic coverage to different Dirichlet distributions, including stronger covariate shift, and different clusterwise label-noise regimes (D.1.7).

E2.justification: SplitCP appears in v1's synthetic Figure 2 and Table 4 but is omitted from the corresponding linear-predictor Figure 2 and Table 1 in v2. It remains in other comparisons, including v2's neural-network Figure 5. CondCP, PCP, and RLCP remain comparators.

E3.justification: The stated synthetic training/calibration/test split changes from 400/400/200 to 600/300/100. V2 also adds a two-layer neural-network predictor, half-calibration holdout tuning controls, kernel-family comparisons, sample-size sweeps, and evaluation at 25 hyperparameter pairs. These substantially expand the evaluation protocols; the PDFs do not establish that retained results were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds analyses of sample-size dependence, kernel sensitivity, calibration reuse versus separate tuning, hyperparameter sensitivity, cutoff randomization, and elbow sizes and breakpoint counts (D.1.1 and D.1.3–D.1.7). These directly investigate robustness and computational behavior beyond v1's existing feature-map discussion and MRI embedding comparisons.

E5.justification: Figure 8 newly reports within-seed variability of randomized cutoffs, and D.1.7 specifies ten independent data generations for the elbow studies. Existing benchmark experiments retain their 50-run reporting. This does not establish increased repetition of the original experiments.

E6.justification: Substantial new outcomes cover neural-network prediction, kernels, tuning, and computational sensitivity. For example, v2 Table 5 reports marginal coverage of 0.893, 0.884, and 0.892 for RBF, Matérn, and IMQ. Synthetic RLCP runtime changes from 0.917±0.11 seconds in v1 Table 4 to 22.05±0.07 in v2 Table 1; revised splits prevent interpreting this as a same-setting change. Molecular, arXiv, and MRI table values are retained.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 changes hyperparameter tuning from calibration data to a separate, disjoint Dsplit. This revises the proposed procedure, while retaining the RKHS objective, embeddings, solution paths, and randomized cutoff. V2 explicitly states that its main experiments still tune on calibration data.

P1.justification: V2 polishes explanations, brings related-work discussion into the introduction, moves the arXiv discussion into the appendix, and introduces numbered synthetic-analysis subsections. Author ordering also changes. These reorganize parts of the narrative while preserving the overall main-text and Appendix A–D structure.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is substantially recomposed with fewer heatmaps, and the molecular coverage panels are divided between main-text Figure 4 and appendix Figure 12. The synthetic summary table gains predictor-specific columns, and multiple new diagnostic plots and sensitivity tables substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: V2 elaborates the connection to LARS and existing RKHS path algorithms and adds adaptive-tuning and kernel references, including Efron, Gauthier, Rasmussen–Williams, Stein, and Gorham–Mackey. Li et al.'s influence was already acknowledged in v1's appendix. Publication updates for retained conformal references do not introduce new comparison methods.

T1.justification: V2 replaces v1 Theorem 2's alignment-dependent formulation with an oracle theorem and a separate estimated-group Corollary C.3. It adds Lemma C.13's density-dependent, square-root-lambda coverage-gap bound and proof, changes the coverage-gap prefactor in equation 10, and revises path derivations and complexity reasoning. These are substantive mathematical revisions.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the treatment of central validity and efficiency questions. It distinguishes independently tuned guarantees from calibration reuse, tests that practical departure, separates oracle and estimated-group coverage, and supplies kernel and elbow-size sensitivity evidence absent from v1. These gains outweigh reduced synthetic baseline reporting. Important limitations remain: main experiments still reuse calibration data, and Algorithm 1's joint cross-validation description is not reconciled with Appendix B.5's CV/SIC procedure.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SpeedCP and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–D. The retained material and relocated experiments can be matched reliably.

after.justification: V2 retains these original experiments and adds neural-network predictor results and several sensitivity, tuning, and computational analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original synthetic simulations and experiments on molecular property prediction, arXiv citation prediction, and brain tumor MRI, including coverage, prediction-set size, and runtime.

results.title: SpeedCP: Fast Kernel-based Conditional Conformal Prediction

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same three methodological contributions and claims about training-free retrieval, competitive performance, model generality, preserved generative abilities, and unified RAG. The additional experiments support these claims without substantially redefining them.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive explanations of missed relational cues and visual-similarity bias, attributes multilingual degradation to translation noise and image-text language mismatches, and interprets computational savings through shared features and caches. These extend v1's largely general discussion of computational overhead and dependence on backbone capabilities; the original limitations paragraph remains.

D1.justification: V2 identifies Qwen3-14B as the translation model, describes vision-feature/shared-prefix cache reuse, and specifies the Qwen2.5-VL demo's supported retrieval inputs. V1 already stated that runnable supplemental code was provided, so Appendix J expands implementation documentation rather than establishing a newly available public release.

E1.justification: V2 adds Chinese and French MMEB evaluations and English–Chinese lexical probes, substantially broadening explicit language coverage. Appendix B.3 also adds standalone Flickr30K/COCO image-to-text and text-to-image retrieval evaluations, supplementing the retained MMEB, MMEB-V2, and LVBench coverage.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds UniME-V2 and explicit two-stage MM-Embed and LamRA comparisons; v1's corresponding MMEB entries covered the latter methods' embedding components. Some comparator configurations are omitted, including the MMEB E5-V 3B entry, although that configuration appears in v2's new standard retrieval comparison.

E3.justification: New protocols include translated MMEB with unchanged English prompts, standard retrieval with Recall@1/5/10 and top-20 reranking, and forward-pass latency and peak-memory measurements across MMEB. Table 2 also changes VLM2Vec's reported training-data size from 0.7M to 1.0M without changing its scores; this does not establish that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds synonym/antonym/random-pair controls for semantic separation in Figure 8, concrete failure cases in Figure 9, and computational comparisons and candidate-count tradeoffs in Tables 9–10. These substantially extend diagnosis beyond the retained component ablations and candidate-count accuracy curves.

E5.justification: Mean/standard-deviation reporting for the original lexical probes and averaging over three prompt rephrasings and swapped label orders are retained. The additional experiments do not introduce new seed counts, repeated-run reporting, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial results for embedding components, two-stage comparators, multilingual and standard retrieval, semantic controls, failures, and computational costs. For example, Table 7 reports FreeRet top-10 scores of 67.8/62.7/60.4 on English/Chinese/French MMEB. Existing full-pipeline backbone scores and LVBench results remain unchanged. Table 8's two identically labeled FreeRet rows have different scores, leaving their intended configurations ambiguous.

M1.justification: Both versions use final-MLP bypass, controlled embedding prompts, and multiple-choice reranking with the same relevance scoring. Shortened example prompts and newly documented cache reuse do not establish a change to the underlying procedure.

P1.justification: Section 4.2 is rewritten around embedding and reranking performance, several headings and passages are shortened, and the appendix is reorganized into named sections A–J. An impact statement and an additional author appear, while most existing introduction, method, discussion, and conclusion prose is retained.

P2.justification: The single-column preprint becomes a two-column conference-format main paper. Table 1 is reorganized by retrieval stage, backbone results move to Table 6, Figure 7's panels are rearranged, and new Figures 8–9 and Tables 7–10 substantially expand the displays.

R1.justification: V2 adds references for UniME-V2, Qwen3, COCO, and Flickr30K, and removes Huang et al.'s Facebook-search reference. The related-work categories and central positioning of training-free retrieval against supervised adaptation remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: V1 Appendix A.2 becomes v2 Appendix C, retaining the affine final-layer approximation, cross-entropy gradient, Lexicalization Alignment proof, projection corollary, and practical implication. Renumbering and the new empirical semantic controls do not introduce new formal reasoning.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses important weaknesses in v1's evidence: Table 1 separates embedding from full-pipeline performance and supplies matched top-10 two-stage comparisons, while the appendices test language generalization, strengthen semantic controls, document failures, and quantify inference costs. These substantially improve comparative validity and understanding of practical limits. Table 8's duplicate configuration labels and missing hardware details constrain parts of the new evidence, but do not outweigh these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe FreeRet and contain readable main text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices. Relocated material, including the backbone results and theoretical analysis, can be matched reliably.

after.justification: V2 retains those original experiments and adds multilingual evaluations, standard retrieval results, semantic controls, failure cases, and computational measurements.

before.justification: V1 reports original MMEB, MMEB-V2, and LVBench evaluations, component ablations, representation probes, and multimodal retrieval examples.

results.title: FreeRet: MLLMs as Training-Free Retrievers

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the same three contributions: the constrained symplectic AE, geometric HNN and jointly trained RO-HNN. The central claims of physically consistent, stable, generalizable prediction of high-dimensional dynamics remain; the added experiments provide broader support without redefining those claims.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly distinguishes nonsymplectic dissipative flow from preservation of the reduced force-field structure and discusses port/contact-Hamiltonian connections. It adds hypotheses explaining nonsymplectic-AE effects, RO-HNN versus RO-LNN accuracy, and Strang integration's performance under dissipation. The latent-dimension tradeoff emphasized in the conclusion was already discussed in v1 Appendix H.2.

D1.justification: V2 supplies a source-code link, detailed analytical cotangent-lift derivatives and intermediate-state handling, implementation/training specifications for the new baselines, and runtime hardware and measurement details. V1 already states that it uses analytical layerwise differentiation; the expanded Appendix E documents that implementation rather than establishing a new computational procedure. The linked resource's availability was not independently checked.

E1.justification: The same 15-DoF pendulum, 90-DoF vortex and 600-DoF cloth remain. V2 adds a limited observation-corruption scenario: training on pendulum observations with Gaussian noise at 5% and 10% scales, followed by evaluation on clean trajectories (Appendix I.1).

E2.justification: V2 adds HNKO comparisons on all three systems and geometric and black-box RO-LNN comparisons on cloth. It also adds nonsymplectic-AE variants for vortex and cloth, a black-box HNN cloth comparison, and analytic-FOM and AE-implementation timing comparators. The earlier SMG, weakly symplectic AE and HNN comparisons remain.

E3.justification: New protocols cover noise-corrupted training, full-model training with 1,000/3,000/6,000 samples, additional comparator architectures and budgets, and solver-step-size/runtime comparisons. V2 Appendix H.2.2 also corrects the reported vortex latent dimensions from 3/6 to 6/10 and AE widths from 32/64/128/600 to 32/48/64/90 relative to v1 Appendix G.2.2. These reported corrections do not establish that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds noise robustness, full RO-HNN sample-size sensitivity, learned pendulum latent-trajectory inspection, and nonsymplectic-AE ablations. The cloth study newly crosses AE structure with Strang versus Runge–Kutta integration (Figure 20), while Appendix J analyzes accuracy–runtime tradeoffs and analytical versus autodifferentiated lifts. V1's latent-HNN data-doubling, latent-dimension, joint-training and damping ablations are retained.

E5.justification: V1 already reports means and standard deviations over test trajectories. V2 Table 7 newly reports a sample-size study involving ten models trained from different random seeds, and Figure 2 adds explicitly identified median/quartile bands. This expands uncertainty reporting locally without establishing increased seed counts for the retained experiments.

E6.justification: Shared numerical entries in Tables 1–4 remain unchanged, and v1's runtime Table 5 reappears unchanged as v2 Table 9. Substantial new results include HNKO's 5-second pendulum position error of 1.32 ± 0.94, sample-size-dependent RO-HNN losses in Table 7, and cloth runtimes of 16.01 seconds for RO-HNN versus 255.24 seconds for the FOM under the listed fine-step Strang settings (Table 8). These are additional comparisons, not performance gains between versions.

M1.justification: The cotangent-lifted symplectic autoencoder, geometric Hamiltonian network, SPD mass/damping parametrizations, Strang integration and joint multi-step loss remain. Expanded implementation explanations and the dissipative-system proposition describe or justify the existing procedure; the added architectures serve as comparisons and ablations.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much of the original wording remain. Focused revisions expand the introduction, dissipative-model explanation and conclusion, move the original proofs into Appendix D, consolidate runtimes in Appendix J, and add a terminology guide and Impact Statement.

P2.justification: The main text changes from a single-column layout to a two-column conference format, with extensive resizing and relocation. Tables 1, 3 and 4 expand; cloth panels from v1 Figure 11 move into the expanded v2 Figure 5. New displays cover notation, noise, sample size, component ablations and runtimes, while some new boxplots redisplay existing comparisons.

R1.justification: V2 substantially broadens positioning to Hamiltonian graph networks and Koopman approaches, adding discussion of their assumptions and differences from reduced nonlinear dynamics. It also adds Poisson-system references and literature supporting the HNN/LNN interpretation, while retaining the original MOR lineage. The PINN discussion replaces Karniadakis et al. with Saqlain et al.; bibliographic updates to retained works are separate from these additions.

T1.justification: V2 adds Proposition 3.3/D.3 and a proof concerning preservation of forced, Rayleigh-damped structure under reduction, including derivation of the positive-semidefinite reduced damping matrix. The original projection and symplecticity proofs are retained in Appendix D. The new damping-force derivation nevertheless uses a positive force contribution where Equation 11 subtracts damping, leaving a sign inconsistency.

improvement.justification: V2 closes important validation gaps through Koopman/Lagrangian comparisons, noise and ten-seed sample-size studies, dissipative-component controls, and accuracy/runtime analyses. These substantially strengthen support for the geometry and scalability claims, while added implementation details improve reproducibility. The sign inconsistency in the new damping derivation limits the theoretical clarification, but does not outweigh the broader empirical and documentation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RO-HNN research, with matching authors, methods and three simulated systems. All 28 pages of v1 and 32 pages of v2, including equations, figures, tables and appendices, support comparison despite substantial reformatting and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains these original experiments and adds baseline comparisons, noise and sample-size studies, component ablations and runtime analyses in Section 4 and Appendices I–J.

before.justification: V1 reports original pendulum, particle-vortex and cloth simulations, prediction errors, architectural ablations and runtime measurements in Section 4 and Appendix H.

results.title: Learning Hamiltonian Dynamics at Scale: A Differential-Geometric Approach

C1.justification: The abstract and listed contributions retain the same central denoising and inference claims. The conclusion revises computational cost from roughly twice standard inference to at most twice, adding the qualified empirical claim that last-half-only use requires 50% additional computation.

C2.justification: v2 explains the regularization roles of a and b and acknowledges that their precise threshold relationship is undetermined. It interprets new corruption and trajectory results as evidence beyond Gaussian-noise removal or truncated sampling, and discusses unresolved adaptation to time-unconditioned and variance-preserving models.

D1.justification: v2 adds a MAD code-access link and documents the new synthetic pixel-removal construction, sample count, and reuse of training settings. Existing hardware and training disclosures remain. Conversely, Figure 1 loses its explicit mixture weights, means, and inference parameters, and several settings for the new natural-image experiments remain unspecified.

E1.justification: v2 adds CIFAR-10 with Gaussian corruption, FFHQ with Gaussian, shot/Poisson, and pixel-removal corruption, and synthetic shapes with 50% pixel removal. This substantially expands controlled noisy-training coverage beyond v1's synthetic corruption and Cryo-EM examples; the earlier clean-image demonstrations remain.

E2.justification: Standard-score inference remains the evaluated comparison method. Table 1 additionally measures noisy training data as a reference, not another method. Figure 18 inspects standard and extended inference trajectories; the cited training-time methods and posterior-sampling approaches are not added as evaluated comparators.

E3.justification: v2 introduces clean-reference FID evaluation using 10,000 images, including training-data controls, across six corruption conditions. It also specifies 100,000 training samples for the new synthetic pixel-removal experiment. Figure 1's reported mixture variances change from 0.2, 0.5, 1, 2, 4 to 2, 0.5, 0.25, 0.1, 0.05.

E4.justification: Figure 18 adds a qualitative trajectory diagnostic addressing whether truncated standard sampling could explain denoising. New non-Gaussian experiments provide targeted corruption-robustness checks, and the conclusion briefly reports successful last-half-only extended-score use. Existing hyperparameter sweeps are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Both versions describe consecutive random seeds for selected image grids, without reporting repeated-experiment uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. v2's 10,000-image FID sample size is an evaluation setting, not a new repeated-run or uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: v1 contains no FID table. v2 Table 1 adds six conditions, including standard/MAD FIDs of 319.42/189.51 for synthetic Gaussian corruption, 147.47/77.15 for CIFAR-10 Gaussian corruption, and 257.42/101.12 for FFHQ shot noise. New image grids and trajectory results accompany these newly reported evaluations.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 retains the same extended-score update, finite-difference approximation, and correction factor. However, v2's conclusion describes a limited scheduling variant that uses the extended score only during the last half of inference. Renaming the finite-difference parameter from δ to Δ does not change the method.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence remain. v2 expands parameter explanations, research positioning, the experimental overview, and the conclusion; adds a noisy CIFAR-10/FFHQ subsection; and reorganizes Appendix A.1–A.4 into Appendices A–D. These are localized expansions rather than a wholesale rewrite.

P2.justification: v2 adds Table 1 and six experimental figures, redraws Figure 1, rearranges Figure 2, and enlarges or trims several image grids. The former Figure 5 parameter sweep moves to appendix Figure 12. A presentation regression is Figure 11's top/middle caption wording, which mismatches its side-by-side data/generated panels.

R1.justification: v2 adds related work on manifold-score decomposition, inverse problems, ambient diffusion, time-unconditioned generation, and classifier-free guidance. It clarifies distinctions from training-time denoising and posterior sampling while retaining the original research positioning. Bibliographic updates to retained works do not constitute new research coverage.

T1.justification: Definition 3.1, Lemmas 3.2, 3.3, and A.1, their proofs, and the correction-factor derivation are retained. Section 3's new footnote adds a limited mathematical generalization: replacing 1+γ with 1+γ/v makes the Dirac extended score match the score of a variance-v Gaussian.

improvement.justification: v1 supports noisy-data generation mainly through visual synthetic and Cryo-EM examples. v2 adds controlled natural-image corruption experiments and clean-reference FIDs, substantially strengthening evidence for the central denoising claim; Figure 18 also probes the truncated-sampling explanation. Missing experimental settings, lost Figure 1 setup details, and a Figure 11 caption error temper reproducibility and presentation, but do not outweigh the substantial empirical improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MAD by the same authors. The complete main texts, equations, figures, and appendices support comparison, including matching material moved or renumbered in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds corrupted-image generation experiments, FID measurements in Table 1, and an inference-trajectory analysis.

before.justification: v1 reports original toy simulations, image-generation experiments, synthetic-data denoising, and Cryo-EM experiments, including appendix parameter sweeps.

results.title: MAD: Manifold Attracted Diffusion

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contribution: replacing softmax with an information-geometrically motivated hierarchical parameterization improves optimization and downstream performance while remaining compatible with existing training techniques. Added evidence does not redefine this contribution.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly limits diagonality to score space and explains that network parameters can remain coupled. It adds interpretations concerning optimizer independence, implementation robustness, and activation performance across latent configurations. Appendix A adds a coordinate-wise rescaling rationale, while the explicit explanation of high PPO variance in v1 is removed.

D1.justification: v2 supplies links to Catnat implementations in PyTorch and JAX, newly documents the retained VAE experiment's learning-rate grids and validation-based selection, and provides training schedules, batch size, split changes, and tuning grids for the additional implementation experiment. The original GSL and PPO technical details are retained.

E1.justification: Figure 1 adds a small three-class, uniform-target cross-entropy optimization demonstration. The substantive benchmark coverage remains graph learning, MNIST/Binary MNIST, and Breakout/Seaquest; the additional VAE optimizer and implementation tests do not report new benchmark datasets.

E2.justification: The graph-learning comparison expands from sigmoid versus natural activation to include softmax and sparsemax in Table 2. Sparsemax also joins the existing softmax and two Catnat variants in the main VAE comparison, Table 3. The PPO comparator set remains unchanged.

E3.justification: Appendix G adds VAE evaluation using SGD instead of Adam. Appendix H introduces a separate implementation experiment with 150-epoch search runs, 500-epoch final runs, batch size 128, a validation/test subdivision, learning-rate searches, and ELBO evaluation. These are added protocols; the original GSL and PPO settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New Appendices G and H test whether Catnat's advantages depend on the optimizer or VAE implementation, providing substantial robustness evidence absent from v1. Figure 1 additionally compares optimization landscapes and gradient-descent trajectories.

E5.justification: v2 adds Welch t-test significance criteria at p<0.05 to Tables 2–5 and newly specifies five trained models for the main VAE aggregate statistics in Appendix F.2. Both versions already report uncertainty values; the stated GSL and PPO repetition counts are unchanged.

E6.justification: Table 2 revises GSL results: at θ*=0.5, sigmoid MAE changes from 0.0191 to 0.0101. Sparsemax rows and Tables 5–6 add substantial results. Table 6 includes weaker natural-activation performance: at N=10, K=8, its ELBO is -122.7±33.4 versus softmax's -95.5±0.4. Existing softmax/Catnat values in Table 3 and all Table 4 returns remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The hierarchical binary construction, sigmoid and natural activations, and natural-activation settings C=0 and A=2π remain unchanged. The new analysis of the network-parameter Fisher matrix does not change Catnat's procedure.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much existing prose remain intact. v2 polishes wording, subdivides Section 4.2, adds an explanatory natural-gradient appendix, removes the standalone reproducibility and LLM-usage statements, and adds an impact statement.

P2.justification: The main text and references change from one-column to two-column presentation. v2 adds the landscape figure, combines v1 Figures 2 and 4 into Figure 4, expands comparison tables, and adds Tables 5–6. Captions and performance highlighting change; the original PPO hyperparameter table is retained as Table 7.

R1.justification: Section 3 newly relates Catnat to hierarchical classifiers by Morin and Bengio, Mnih and Hinton, and Beygelzimer et al. It identifies existing classifiers as special cases and distinguishes their computational motivation from Catnat's geometric motivation, materially clarifying the relationship to close prior work. Additional citations support sparsemax, the alternate VAE implementation, and Fisher-metric transformations.

T1.justification: Section 4.2.3 adds the derivation Gθ=JᵀGπJ and its Catnat specialization, identifying the removal of cross-score terms without guaranteeing a diagonal network-parameter FIM. Proposition 4.1, Theorem 4.2, Corollary 4.3, and their original proofs remain substantively unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation through additional parameterization baselines and explicit optimizer and implementation robustness tests. The score-space versus network-parameter distinction addresses an important ambiguity in the theoretical interpretation, while implementation links and tuning details improve reproducibility. Table 6's unstable natural-activation results still warrant qualification of broad superiority language, but these limitations do not outweigh the stronger evidence and clearer theoretical scope.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Catnat research. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated proofs and experimental details.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical studies and adds comparator results, VAE experiments with SGD, and experiments using another VAE implementation.

before.justification: v1 reports original graph-structure-learning simulations, categorical VAE experiments on MNIST and Binary MNIST, and PPO experiments on Breakout and Seaquest.

results.title: Beyond Softmax: A Natural Parameterization for Categorical Random Variables

C1.justification: The central query-circuit, NDF, BoN and sparse-recovery claims remain. The explanatory scope expands modestly through optional SAE-assisted interpretation in v2's introduction, whereas v1 explicitly placed node and edge interpretation outside scope in Section 3.1.

C2.justification: V2 introduces shared-mechanism and actionability interpretations, and expands the necessity/sufficiency interpretation of existing complement-circuit results. New limitations discuss incomplete or polysemantic SAE explanations, unavailable head-specific SAEs, and the remaining need for manual inspection and graph condensation.

D1.justification: V2 adds a project-page link and identifies the GPT-2 SAE suite, activation-recording procedure and top-five feature extraction used in the interpretation study. Earlier detailed benchmark settings and runtime disclosures remain. The PDFs alone do not establish the linked resources' availability.

E1.justification: Existing dataset coverage is retained. Gender Bias already appeared in v1 Appendix B.5, but v2 adds feature-level bias steering and semantic interpretation as distinct evaluation tasks on it, beyond the earlier circuit-construction comparison.

E2.justification: The original circuit-discovery baselines remain. The new steering experiment adds lowest-NDF circuit selection among ten candidates as a comparator for highest-NDF selection (Table 2). Circuit Tracing receives discussion but is not experimentally benchmarked.

E3.justification: V2 adds fidelity experiments using GPT-2 XL and Llama-3-8B-Instruct, overlap metrics and feature-ablation protocols. Steering evaluation selects 50 of 986 high-bias queries, uses 32 queries for paired comparisons, and separately compares 27 high-NDF against 23 low-NDF queries. Existing benchmark settings are retained.

E4.justification: New overlap, Jaccard and UpSet analyses investigate shared circuit mechanisms (Section 6.4; Appendix C.11). Gender-feature ablations and an SAE interpretation case study examine actionability and semantic content (Section 6.5; Appendices C.12–C.13). Earlier ablations and complement-circuit analyses remain.

E5.justification: Tables 2 and A7 newly report across-query means and standard deviations, paired Wilcoxon and unpaired Mann–Whitney tests, and Rosenthal's r and Cohen's d. Appendix C.11 specifies sampling seed 2025. These additions do not establish repeated-seed evaluation of the retained benchmarks.

E6.justification: Earlier result plots and runtime values are retained, while scaling, overlap and intervention results are added. Table 2 reports mean logit-bias reductions of 0.810 versus 0.234 for best versus worst circuits. One inconsistency remains: Appendix C.5 claims approximately 0.4 NDF at 5,000 edges, whereas Figure A14(c) shows approximately 0.28 there.

M1.justification: The BoN, iBoN and BoN-CSM discovery procedures remain unchanged. V2 adds an optional post-discovery SAE procedure for extracting described features from circuit activations and performing feature interventions (Section 6.5; Appendix C.12), extending the interpretation workflow.

P1.justification: Most core exposition and section order are retained. V2 revises the introduction and limitations, relocates pseudocode and runtime discussion into appendices, removes the supplementary contents page, adds an Impact Statement, and updates affiliation and correspondence information.

P2.justification: The main text and references change from single-column to two-column presentation, with extensive resizing and repositioning of displays. V2 adds steering tables, overlap plots and circuit visualizations, revises Figure 1's illustration, and relocates existing algorithms and the runtime table.

R1.justification: V2 develops the comparison with previously cited Circuit Tracing, explicitly acknowledging its instance-level explanations and describing complementarity with in-place circuits. It adds Gao et al. for the SAE suite and removes the Foote, Shaham and Bricken automated-interpretability references.

T1.justification: The circuit definitions, attribution equations, NDF definition and NDF–CMD relationship are retained; the latter moves from Appendix C to D. No new proof or substantive derivation is introduced. The new bias-threshold inequality specifies experimental selection.

improvement.justification: V1 principally demonstrated output recovery and left semantic interpretation outside scope. V2 substantially strengthens the evidence for useful explanations through paired feature interventions linking NDF to actionability, circuit-overlap analyses and larger-model evaluations. Selected samples, acknowledged SAE limitations and the Appendix C.5/Figure A14 numerical inconsistency constrain the conclusions, but the added validation addresses an important weakness in the earlier paper.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same query-circuit research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains those experiments and adds larger-model evaluations, circuit-overlap analyses and quantitative gender-feature interventions in Section 6 and Appendix C.

before.justification: V1 reports original circuit-discovery experiments, paraphrase ablations, runtime measurements and supplementary analyses in Section 6 and Appendix B.

results.title: Query Circuits: Explaining How Language Models Answer User Prompts

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes ERM thresholds, nuclear-norm bias, factorization, and learned spectra, leaving heavy tails for future work. v2 makes quantitative spectrum–generalization links, sequential spectral recovery, emergence, and power-law scaling laws central contributions in its abstract, introduction, and conclusion.

C2.justification: v2 develops an interpretation connecting spectral outliers to recovered features and decomposing error into overfitting, underfitting, approximation, and mismatch contributions. It explains scaling crossovers through successive feature recovery. It also explicitly qualifies the unproved extension beyond the original asymptotic regime and the decomposition's approximate validity away from small error.

D1.justification: Appendix G adds numerical prescriptions for plotting the error decomposition, including a bulk-mass correction and a mismatch approximation. Repository, solver, Monte Carlo, hardware, and CPU-time disclosures remain. v2 drops v1's stated regularization search range of 10^-6 to 10^-1 and explicit PyTorch implementation reference.

E1.justification: v2 expands evaluated coverage from Marchenko–Pastur targets to power-law target spectra, including gamma = 0.75 in Figure 4. This introduces a qualitatively different hierarchy of feature strengths and sequential-recovery scenario, while retaining the original synthetic sequence tasks.

E2.justification: The factorized versus non-factorized Frobenius-regularized comparison remains, moving from v1 Figure 3 to v2 Figure 2. The Bayes-optimal recovery-threshold reference also remains in v2 Figure 8 left. No additional comparator enters these comparisons.

E3.justification: The added power-law experiment introduces excess test error relative to its asymptotic value, lambda = 1/d, 1, sqrt(d), learning curves at d = 200, and spectra at d = 400 for n = 4,000 and 400,000. These extend the settings; matched Marchenko–Pastur experiments retain their protocols.

E4.justification: v2 adds direct replicon-condition evaluations in Figure 7 and quantitative error-component analyses and validation in Figures 3 and 8 right. These substantially extend stability and mechanism checks. Existing temperature, token-count, and task-equivalence analyses remain, while v1 Figure 1's rank-versus-sample analysis is removed.

E5.justification: v2 Figure 4 explicitly reports single-run power-law spectra, adding a repetition practice distinct from the 64-run spectral histograms in v1 Figure 1. Its learning curves use eight instances with standard-deviation bars. Retained experiments keep their run counts and uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v2 adds power-law learning curves, heavy-tailed learned spectra, numerical replicon values, and error-decomposition results. Figure 4 reports distinct decay regimes associated with target spectral decay and regularization. Matched original results are retained, apart from removed rank curves; these additions do not establish same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The centered, tied single-head attention architecture, squared-error objective with weight decay, factorized and direct parameterizations, and AMP procedure remain unchanged. The new spectral and scaling analyses introduce no new training or inference component.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, contribution list, and conclusion are substantially rewritten. Related work receives a dedicated subsection, proof material moves into Appendix B, and the main narrative separates error asymptotics, spectrum–generalization analysis, and scaling laws. These are extensive structural changes beyond adding scientific content.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redesigned without its rank panel; v1 Figure 2 moves to v2 Figure 6, and v1 Figure 3 is split across Figures 2 and 8. New error-decomposition graphics, power-law plots, a phase diagram, and replicon plots substantially expand and reorganize the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning around scaling laws and emergence beyond linear or lazy regimes, adding literature including Kaplan, Hoffmann, Wei, Schaeffer, and Defilippis and collaborators. It also connects its scaling rates to compressed sensing and LASSO minimax results, broadening the original attention and matrix-sensing positioning.

T1.justification: New Appendices E–F introduce Conjecture E.1 extending the asymptotic characterization beyond fixed sample ratios, derive error decompositions for sharp and flat minima, and develop power-law risk rates and their phase diagram. This is substantial new mathematical analysis; the original core result still has a proof sketch.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the connection between spectra and generalization through explicit error decompositions, conditional scaling derivations, and supporting simulations, addressing questions left speculative in v1. Direct replicon checks also strengthen support for an important assumption previously assessed indirectly. These gains outweigh the removed rank plot and reduced tuning disclosure. The broader asymptotic extension remains explicitly conjectural, so the improvement does not amount to a completed rigorous proof.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same tied-attention ERM study. Their readable main texts, figures, equations, and complete appendices permit reliable matching despite retitling, restructuring, and substantial additions.

after.justification: v2 retains original simulations and adds power-law-target learning curves and spectra in Figure 4, alongside numerical stability and error-decomposition evaluations.

before.justification: v1 reports original Adam simulations validating learning curves, learned spectra, parameterization comparisons, and temperature/token sensitivity in Figures 1–6.

results.title: Single-Head Attention in High Dimensions: A Theory of Generalization, Weights Spectra, and Scaling Laws

C1.justification: The central contribution remains scalable latent-space transformer GANs using MNG and width-aware learning rates. The abstract, introduction, and conclusion revise the quantified headline from FID 2.96 in 40 epochs with sixfold fewer epochs to FID 2.18 in 60 epochs with fourfold fewer epochs. The main contribution is retained while its performance and efficiency claim changes.

C2.justification: v2 adds an explanation of early-layer underuse through final-output-only supervision, interprets deterioration after removing REPA as discriminator feature erosion, and discusses training-cost tradeoffs. Appendices A.8, A.10–A.11, and A.16 qualify the preliminary text-conditioning extension, simplified mathematical argument, depth/batch generalization, and limited seed coverage. These substantially expand interpretation and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: v2 adds a project-page link, MM-GAT configuration details, alternative-tokenizer specifications, compute-accounting procedures, GPU benchmarking settings, and REPA overhead measurements. Training-resource disclosure is updated for the longer run. However, it removes v1 A.1's precise guidance recipe—strength 1.1 applied to the first 30% of blocks—and no longer clearly distinguishes guided and unguided headline results.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates class-conditional ImageNet-256 generation and latent interpolation. v2 adds ImageNet-512 generation, MS-COCO text-to-image generation, unconditional FFHQ-256 generation, and unsupervised and text-directed image editing using GANSpace and StyleCLIP. These substantially broaden the represented domains and task requirements.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds STARFlow and LightningDiT-XL/2 to the retained ImageNet comparisons. The new MS-COCO comparison in Table 8 introduces a substantial additional comparator set, including Frido, VQ-Diffusion, U-ViT variants, AttnGAN, DM-GAN, DF-GAN, XMC-GAN, and LAFITE.

E3.justification: The headline training budget increases from 40 to 60 epochs, with v2 A.1 setting the gradient-penalty coefficient to 10 for epochs 40–60 after the original 0.1 setting. Existing patch-size and ablation plots switch from FID-5K to FID-50K. v2 also introduces CLIP-FID, precision/recall, latency/memory evaluation, and a fourfold-batch-size experiment with doubled learning rate.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained PCA, block-removal, and component ablations, v2 tests early-layer input/output similarity and sensitivity to latent noise, compatibility with larger batches, alternative tokenizers, and seed variation. It also adds REPA ablation at another model size, removal of REPA during continued training, and a training-compute scaling fit. These address additional mechanism and robustness questions.

E5.justification: v1 does not report a seed-replication analysis. v2 A.16 reports individual FID-5K outcomes from three differently seeded, 10-epoch GAT-S/2 runs alongside the original result. This provides limited seed-sensitivity evidence, without confidence intervals or systematic uncertainty reporting for the main comparisons.

E6.justification: v1 Table 1 reports 40-epoch FID 3.02 without guidance and 2.96 with guidance; v2 reports 2.18 at 60 epochs under a revised training schedule, so this is not a same-setting improvement. Original 20-epoch capacity scores remain in v2 Table 5. Substantial new results include ImageNet-512 FID 4.04, MS-COCO FID 7.98, FFHQ FID 9.74, and additional diversity, resource, and robustness measurements.

M1.justification: The core GAT architecture, MNG procedure, width-aware learning-rate rule, and loss formulations remain. Appendix A.8 adds a localized MM-GAT adaptation: frozen CLIP word tokens enter through MM-DiT-style conditioning, while the sentence embedding supplies global conditioning. This changes the model's inputs and conditioning beyond merely testing it on another dataset.

P1.justification: v2 substantially edits the abstract, introductory and architectural explanations, experimental setup, and early-layer discussion. It separates early-layer diagnosis from component ablations, reorganizes the further-analysis narrative, and restructures the appendix into topical sections. These changes extend beyond inserting new experimental results.

P2.justification: The single-column preprint becomes a two-column main paper with revised table and caption formatting. Figure 3 gains a training-compute panel, ablation axes are redrawn, and numerous task, metric, cost, and editing displays are added. Existing material is also relocated or condensed: v1 Tables 2–3 become v2 Tables 4–5, and v1 Figure 8 becomes v2 Figure 12; some older sample galleries are removed.

R1.justification: Literature coverage expands substantially into text-conditioned generation, latent editing, gradient normalization, and batch-size scaling, with new references including CLIP, GANSpace, StyleCLIP, and STARFlow. v2 also drops the explicit first-time claim in Section 2.2 and the connection to equalized learning rates and Karras et al. (2017). Publication updates and duplicate entries for existing works do not constitute additional research.

T1.justification: v1 states the inverse-width learning-rate rule and its rationale. v2 A.10 adds explicit independent, unit-variance channel assumptions, a definition of functional update magnitude, and a linear-layer SGD derivation relating output changes to learning rate times width. This is limited mathematical support, explicitly presented without a full proof.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation beyond v1's ImageNet-256-centered evidence. Additional generation tasks, CLIP-FID and diversity metrics, targeted mechanism and robustness tests, and resource measurements better support generality and efficiency claims. The improved headline FID uses longer training and a changed penalty, so it is not decisive by itself. Lost guidance details and the incorrect MNG labeling of the learning-rate ablation in Table 6 weaken reproducibility, but the broader, more diagnostic evidence provides a clear substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Scalable GANs with Transformers and retain identifiable corresponding methods and experiments. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support a reliable comparison despite substantial expansion and reformatting.

after.justification: v2 retains original GAT experiments and adds results for higher-resolution generation, MS-COCO text-to-image generation, unconditional FFHQ generation, editing, and robustness analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original ImageNet-256 generation results, model-scaling experiments, component ablations, representation analyses, and generated examples in the main text and appendix.

results.title: Scalable GANs with Transformers

C1.justification: The three central DDPO–DSM, variance, and AWM contributions remain. The abstract and conclusion raise the headline speedup from 24× to 34×, while the introduction changes GenEval performance from matching Flow-GRPO to surpassing it. The contribution list also includes ImageReward.

C2.justification: v2 clarifies the oracle/population scope and practical discretization bias of the equivalence argument. It replaces discussion of logit-normal and weak-KL failures with interpretations supporting the revised defaults, and adds an interpretation of preserved diversity after 600 updates. The central explanation linking noisy targets to slower optimization remains.

D1.justification: Appendix F.1 documents both configurations systematically, adding previously unstated sampling noise and guidance settings, reference-model choices, the EMA schedule, and precise batch-use mechanics. Section 3 specifies batch-global advantage normalization. v1's explicit shared-noise/timestep disclosure for likelihood-ratio estimation disappears. The code-access information remains unchanged.

E1.justification: Coverage remains CIFAR-10/ImageNet-64 pretraining and compositional generation, text rendering, and human-preference alignment. ImageReward adds a reward/evaluation model within the existing preference-alignment task; the PDFs do not establish a new dataset, domain, or task requirement.

E2.justification: v2 Table 1 adds TempFlow-GRPO as a quantitative GenEval comparator, reporting 0.97 overall and 2.8× speedup. v1 only discusses it in related work. The other corresponding benchmark comparator sets remain.

E3.justification: The main configuration changes from Euler–Maruyama sampling, four training timesteps, mixed on/off-policy updates, and task-specific KL coefficients to SA-Solver, six Monte Carlo timesteps, on-policy updates, and KL coefficient 1. Appendix F.1 explicitly distinguishes the earlier and later sampling steps, noise levels, and guidance scales. New sampler controls are introduced, and GenEval ablations now report training steps instead of GPU hours.

E4.justification: v1's timestep-distribution, four-value KL, and previous-policy batch-reuse ablations are replaced by Monte Carlo count, EMA-rollout versus on-policy, and KL 1-versus-3 comparisons. v2 additionally tests ODE/SDE compatibility (Figure 8), measures conditional target variance (Table 6), and examines diversity after 600 RL steps (Figure 10). The original ablation plots are not retained in the appendices.

E5.justification: Figure 10 newly specifies four different initial-noise seeds per prompt for the qualitative diversity demonstration. This is limited seed reporting, rather than repeated-training-run uncertainty analysis; neither version provides benchmark confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: Under revised settings, v2 reports final GenEval 0.985 and 16.54× speedup to Flow-GRPO's score, versus v1's 0.95 and 8.02×. SD3.5M PickScore changes from 23.02 at 91.1 GPU hours to 23.11 at 27.56 hours; OCR changes from 0.89 at 17.6 hours to 0.92 at 21.76 hours. These are different-configuration results. Original tables survive as Tables 4–5, and FLUX table values remain unchanged. New ImageReward, variance, ablation, and diversity results expand the evidence.

M1.justification: The advantage-weighted DSM/FM framework remains. The later configuration changes loss weighting from w(t)=1 to w(t)=t, replaces the fixed reference model with an EMA reference, and adopts purely on-policy updates instead of mixed data reuse (Sections 3–4 and Appendix F.1). These refine the existing procedure.

P1.justification: Related work moves from the main text to Appendix E, bringing theory directly after the introduction. The DDPO exposition is extensively rewritten, notation and detailed-background sections are added, and the appendix is reorganized around proofs, related work, configurations, and additional experiments.

P2.justification: The single-column preprint becomes a two-column conference paper. Figure 1's panels are rearranged, the ablation figure is replaced, sampler and diversity figures are added, and notation and variance tables appear. Earlier benchmark tables move to the appendix, while Figure 9 combines retained curves with an added ImageReward panel.

R1.justification: Appendix E adds a substantive distinction between AWM's signed weights and classical RWR/AWR, plus discussion of continuous-time RL by Gao and Zhao. New citations support normalization and reference-model choices, while the LLaDA 1.5 citation is removed. Existing positioning against DDPO and FMPG largely remains.

T1.justification: v2 explicitly frames Theorem 2.1 as an oracle, fixed-time population-minimizer equivalence. Appendix C.3 adds a substantial derivation connecting advantage-weighted DDPO's local gradient to clean-target DSM without assuming advantage independence from noisy states. Appendix C.5 derives the EDM noisy-target objective. The original DSM equivalence and variance proofs largely remain.

improvement.justification: v1 motivates advantage-weighted RL largely through unweighted DSM results; v2 adds an explicit local-gradient derivation and clearer oracle assumptions (Section 2.3 and Appendix C.3). Direct variance measurements, sampler tests, revised ablations, and detailed configuration documentation substantially strengthen the central argument and reproducibility. These gains outweigh the removal of earlier ablations and remaining reporting inconsistencies, including Figure 1's 8× caption beside a 16.54× plot.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Advantage Weighted Matching by the same authors. Their readable main texts, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds revised-configuration benchmarks, sampler comparisons, direct target-variance measurements, and a qualitative diversity study.

before.justification: v1 reports original CIFAR-10/ImageNet-64 pretraining experiments and SD3.5M/FLUX reinforcement-learning results, including benchmark comparisons and ablations.

results.title: Advantage Weighted Matching: Aligning RL with Pretraining in Diffusion Models

C1.justification: The central adversary-free optimization, one-shot sampling and convergence claims remain. V2's new conclusion explicitly includes inpainting in its empirical claims and qualifies benchmark ambitions generally as demonstrating flexibility and supporting theory; v1 made the qualification about not targeting state-of-the-art performance specifically for STL10 super-resolution.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive interpretations of intrinsic-dimensional adaptation and kernel, neighborhood and batch-size tradeoffs. It acknowledges incomplete recovery of two-moons crescents, discusses distilled diffusion's competing PSNR/SSIM advantages, and clarifies that the experimental nearest-neighbor implementation is quadratic despite the near-linear computational possibility. These materially sharpen applicability and limitations.

D1.justification: V2 adds a code-access URL, default batch size 200, Gaussian bandwidth sqrt(p), manual neighborhood selection, brute-force nearest-neighbor implementation details, and architecture/package information for new flow and posterior experiments. These are additional disclosures; they do not establish changes to retained implementations. ResNet-18/PCA preprocessing and image-generator descriptions were already present in v1.

E1.justification: V2 adds two-moons posterior inference, FashionMNIST half-image inpainting, and synthetic conditional-regression scenarios addressing intrinsic dimensionality and kernel sensitivity. Circle evaluation also extends to low-density conditioning at X=4. MNIST, CelebA-HQ and STL10 were already evaluated in v1, including its appendices.

E2.justification: V2 adds two- and three-layer MAF conditional normalizing flows to circle comparisons, SNPE with MAF to the two-moons experiment, and distilled diffusion to the existing MNIST denoising comparison. These substantially extend the evaluated alternatives beyond v1's GCDS, WGAN and standard conditional diffusion.

E3.justification: Added studies introduce conditional-mean and conditional-standard-deviation MSE evaluation at fixed conditioning inputs, ambient dimensions from 25 to 500, and kernel, neighborhood and batch-size sweeps. The kernel study specifies 5,000 training samples. For the retained MNIST comparison, Table 1 removes FID and Inception Score while retaining PSNR, SSIM and timing.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained noise-level comparisons and training snapshots, v2 adds intrinsic-dimension sensitivity (Figure 9), low-density conditioning checks against flows (Figure 10), kernel-bandwidth and neighborhood-size ablations (Table 2), and batch-size effects with tail-region plots (Figure 18). These substantially expand robustness and practical sensitivity analysis.

E5.justification: V2 specifies that Table 2 averages MSE over 100 repetitions; v1 provides no comparable experimental repetition counts. Figure 9 also introduces shaded bands without defining their statistical meaning. This is limited new statistical reporting, not evidence that retained experiments received additional runs.

E6.justification: Table 1 adds distilled diffusion with PSNR 10.658, SSIM 0.508 and 0.00092 seconds/image; the shared diffusion and CGMMD entries retain their reported PSNR, SSIM and timings. FID and Inception Score results are removed. New figures and Table 2 report dimensionality, sensitivity, inpainting and flow-comparison findings, including SNPE capturing two-moons crescents more accurately than CGMMD.

M1.justification: The ECMMD objective, nearest-neighbor construction and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged. The new two-moons experiment introduces residual MLP and full-covariance Gaussian-mixture MDN generator variants with LayerNorm blocks (Appendix C.3.2), extending the model instantiations within the existing framework.

P1.justification: Much of the abstract, introduction, method exposition and appendix prose is retained. V2 adds a conclusion, acknowledgments and impact statement, moves the contents to the supplementary materials, shortens some headings and pseudocode, and updates author information. These are localized structural and editorial changes.

P2.justification: V2 retypesets the main text and references in two columns, resizes and rearranges existing figures, and moves the STL10 visualization into the main text. Table 1 gains a comparator row and loses two metric columns. New experimental plots, an inpainting montage and the four-panel sensitivity table substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: Appendix A expands the closest-prior-work discussion to DISCO Nets and MMD gradient-flow samplers, including Arbel, Hagemann, Hertrich and Galashov and colleagues. It explicitly distinguishes CGMMD from a flow-based approach addressing the same conditional-sampling problem through formulation, kernel flexibility and theoretical guarantees. This substantively expands research positioning beyond bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: Theorem 4.1 becomes Theorem 4.4, restricting k_n from o(n^gamma), 0<gamma<1, to o(sqrt(n)) and replacing the displayed nearest-neighbor term n^(-(1-gamma)/d) with n^(-1/(2d)), up to logarithms. Equation (4.3) changes expected characteristic-function integral convergence to convergence in probability. V2 also defines intrinsic covering dimension and claims corresponding dimensional adaptation. Appendix E revises concentration bounds and corrects event indicators.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses v1's limited comparator coverage and lack of systematic sensitivity evidence. The distilled-diffusion and flow comparisons, explicit two-moons failure case, and kernel/batch-size analyses make strengths, weaknesses and practical choices much better supported. Added code-access and implementation disclosures further help reproducibility. Removed FID/Inception Score results and undefined Figure 9 bands reduce reporting completeness, but these costs do not outweigh the stronger, more balanced empirical assessment.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CGMMD research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and Appendices A-H are readable and support comparison, including matching material across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds posterior-sampling, inpainting, intrinsic-dimension and sensitivity experiments.

before.justification: V1 reports original helix and circle simulations, image-generation experiments, and quantitative MNIST denoising comparisons in Table 1.

results.title: One-shot Conditional Sampling: MMD meets Nearest Neighbors

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution bullets retain the same central claims: inference-time alignment using an SFT/DPO pair without additional training, improved alignment across models and benchmarks, and useful synthetic preference data. The explicit SFT+DPO qualification in v2's conclusion matches the method's already-stated scope.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands mechanism explanations and applicability limits. It attributes smaller full-fine-tuning gains to internalized preference information, interprets second-iteration failures as favoring one synthetic-data round, and explains mixed PPO results through the absence of the DPO probability-gap structure. It also adds interpretations of filtering sensitivity and training-duration effects.

D1.justification: Core optimizer, DPO and LoRA hyperparameters are retained. v2 adds pseudocode, base-model and SFT-workflow information, matching OLMo checkpoint descriptions, GPU and parallel-execution details, and a named GitHub code location replacing the anonymous link. Some oracle base-model descriptions become less specific.

E1.justification: The six preference datasets and AlpacaEval remain the demonstrated task coverage. New studies vary models, training or evaluators within that coverage. The Ultrachat-to-Ultrafeedback relabeling does not establish a dataset replacement: v1 already references ultrafeedback_binarized, and the corresponding results are identical.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated contrastive-decoding baselines using external 1B and 3B Llama Instruct references in Table 3, and standard beam search across beam widths in Figure 8. These substantially expand comparisons beyond the retained greedy, Bo2 and EFT baselines. Standard beam search is distinct from the AAD beam variant already studied in v1.

E3.justification: The original training protocol remains, but substantial new evaluation designs appear: OLMo 7B/13B models with GPT-4-turbo judging over 805 prompts; 502 human judgments from 40 raters; full-fine-tuning data scaling over 800 held-out prompts; and PPO training for 20,000 episodes. These are added settings, not evidence that the original experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds alpha sensitivity, standard beam-width comparisons, training-duration sensitivity, data scaling under full fine-tuning, iterative-DPO tests on additional retained datasets, and PPO compatibility tests. These examine previously untested robustness and applicability questions. The earlier entropy-thresholded beam analysis is retained in Appendix A.4.

E5.justification: Figure 3 newly reports means and standard deviations across Skywork, Nectar and Argilla, describing cross-dataset variation rather than seed uncertainty. Table 5 adds Bradley-Terry Elo estimation from human judgments. Neither version specifies repeated-seed counts or significance tests.

E6.justification: The original main tables and full-fine-tuning table retain their numbers, while substantial new outcomes are reported. Human AAD win rates include 58.7% against greedy DPO and 73.5% against Bo2; OLMo AlpacaEval win rates against greedy DPO are 71.5% and 75.2%. New negative findings include second-iteration degradation in Table 9 and Skywork PPO reward 3.02 for AAD versus 10.4 for Bo2 in Table 10. Two qualitative Bo2 responses, previously identical to AAD's, are replaced in the Obi-Wan and Dark Knight examples.

M1.justification: AAD still greedily maximizes the DPO/SFT token log-probability ratio over candidates passing the same min-alpha filter. Algorithm 1 documents this existing procedure. The entropy-thresholded beam variant is also retained, moving into the appendix.

P1.justification: Most existing abstract, introduction and explanatory prose is preserved. Changes include localized method and caption rewrites, terminology and grammar corrections, an impact statement, and appendix reorganization that consolidates supplementary results and relocates the beam discussion. The main section sequence remains intact.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from a single-column to a two-column conference layout. v2 adds six tables, three figures and an algorithm box, restructures Table 2, expands the BoN plot with Nectar curves, and relocates several existing displays. These are substantial visual and layout changes beyond renumbering.

R1.justification: v2 adds Amulet to related work and references supporting the entropy formulation, OLMo models, Qwen3 and SFT workflow; it also removes the min-p citation and revises dataset/model references. The central positioning among training-time alignment, EFT, contrastive decoding and reward-guided search remains.

T1.justification: New Appendix A.1 introduces a token-level MDP, an effective regularized reward, soft Bellman relations and a derivation connecting the log ratio to human reward and value differences, substantially extending v1's argument. v2 also corrects the extra denominator logarithm in Equation (5) and the missing logarithm in rDPO. The new Equations (12)–(13), however, have an apparent entropy-sign inconsistency with Equation (11).

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the central method through human preferences, direct contrastive-decoding comparisons, OLMo evaluations and targeted filtering, training and efficiency studies. These address important gaps in v1's evidence and practical characterization. Reporting PPO failures and iterative-DPO degradation also improves applicability guidance. The new derivation's apparent entropy-sign error and inconsistent descriptions of Iter 1' temper the gains, but do not outweigh the stronger empirical support and clearer boundaries.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Alignment-Aware Decoding by the same authors. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable and can be matched despite substantial reformatting and added material.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds human judgments, OLMo evaluations, comparator experiments and supplementary sensitivity and applicability tests.

before.justification: v1 reports original alignment benchmark results, reward-model accuracies, and experiments on data scarcity, regularization, beam search and iterative DPO.

results.title: Alignment-Aware Decoding

C1.justification: The introduction replaces the claimed 9% accuracy improvement with a 14.65% average improvement, identified in Section 4.3 as the F1 margin over SIDA. It also removes the claim to be the first reinforcement-learning approach for deepfake detection and explainability. The central dataset, architecture and paragraph-level optimization contributions remain.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive interpretations of backbone representations, label-free versus supervised rewards, reasoning diversity and computational bottlenecks. It newly discusses sparse-artifact majority-vote failures in SiT, limits coverage to face-centric deepfakes, acknowledges dependence on Gemini annotations, and recommends decision-support use. These considerably expand the explanation of mechanisms and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: v3 documents paragraph separators, two-layer projector/classifier structures, component parameter counts, full fine-tuning, explicit split ratios and profiling settings. It adds the LLaVA implementation source and changes the stated code/data location from Anogibot/PRPO to tuanrpt/PRPO. These materially expand reproducibility information, although v1's exact ConvNeXT checkpoint reference is removed.

E1.justification: The same five DF-R5 generation domains and face-focused detection task are retained. Appendix B.1 adds evaluation under noise, blur, brightness and contrast changes, JPEG compression and rotation, modestly extending coverage to altered input conditions.

E2.justification: The original detector, MLLM, PPO and GRPO comparator sets are retained. Tables 9–11 add evaluated variants including LLaVA with PRPO, DX-LLaVA with a spatial ViT-L/14 backbone, and supervised PRPO using ground-truth rewards.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include controlled backbone/loss comparisons, reasoning-diversity analysis on 5,000 images, perturbation testing with 100 images per domain and 16 responses per image, and eight human evaluators each rating five images. Computational profiling introduces batch-size and generation-length controls. The newly specified 98%/1%/1% split documents an existing experiment rather than establishing a changed split.

E4.justification: v3 substantially expands diagnostic evidence: architecture and auxiliary-loss controls, supervised versus unsupervised rewards, alpha/beta sensitivity, perturbation tests, saliency and representation visualizations, reasoning overlap with Gemini, computational breakdowns and qualitative cases. These investigate component contributions, grounding, teacher imitation and practical behavior beyond v1's existing reward and RL-method ablations.

E5.justification: Appendix E.2 and Table 20 newly report means and standard deviations of iteration time, throughput and latency over the first ten adaptation iterations. This adds runtime variability reporting; detection scores and explanation ratings still lack reported seed-based uncertainty or confidence intervals.

E6.justification: The principal benchmark and GPT-4o rating tables are retained, but Table 3 corrects the language-loss-only model's precision from 70.40 to 98.26. Extensive new results include human averages of 4.630 for PRPO versus 4.220 for Gemini, perturbation accuracy falling from 96.00 to 65.28 under JPEG compression, and architecture, supervised-reward, diversity, sensitivity and timing results. These are newly reported comparisons, not improved scores for the retained benchmarks.

M1.justification: The stated optimization objective changes from adding the KL term in v1 Equation 7 to explicitly maximizing the PRPO surrogate minus the KL penalty in v3 Equation 12. This is a limited objective correction; the main architecture, paragraph rewards and PCR algorithms remain unchanged. The PDFs do not establish a corresponding implementation change or rerun.

P1.justification: Most existing abstract, introduction, method and results prose remains close to v1. v3 clarifies wording and notation, separates dataset and implementation subsections, adds cross-references, and groups the appendix into thematic sections. Much of the additional prose accompanies new scientific content rather than extensive rewriting of retained material.

P2.justification: The main text changes from a single-column preprint layout to two columns, with substantially resized and repositioned displays. New tables, saliency maps, embedding/confidence plots and qualitative comparison panels substantially expand the visual presentation. Retained material is also relocated: v1's detailed results table becomes Table 17, and its evaluation prompt becomes Figure 13.

R1.justification: v3 adds citations to Khan et al. and Nguyen et al. on deepfake detection and Simonyan et al. on saliency, while removing some references, including Foteinopoulou et al. It also withdraws the first-RL novelty claim. The broader related-work framing remains similar; publication and author metadata updates are not new research coverage.

T1.justification: v3 corrects the mathematical optimization specification by explicitly maximizing the PRPO surrogate with a negative KL penalty, replacing v1's positive-KL combined expression. Other equation changes largely expose intermediate notation or clarify embeddings; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens validation through controlled backbone/loss comparisons, human checks of explanation ratings, and analyses exposing corruption sensitivity, computational costs and failure conditions. These address important evidential gaps in v1; the corrected KL objective and added implementation details also improve reproducibility. The human study is small and does not justify calling GPT-4o unbiased, but this overstatement does not outweigh the substantial gains in evidence and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DF-R5, DX-LLaVA and PRPO research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices support comparison, including matching retained material across the substantial layout changes.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds architecture comparisons, human ratings, perturbation experiments, reasoning-diversity measurements and computational profiling.

before.justification: v1 reports original cross-domain detection results, GPT-4o explanation ratings, and reward and reinforcement-learning ablations in Tables 4–8.

results.title: PRPO: Paragraph-level Policy Optimization for Vision-Language Deepfake Detection

C1.justification: Both versions claim dual-prototype evidential WSI survival prediction, explicit aleatoric/epistemic uncertainty, feature-to-decision interpretability, and state-of-the-art discrimination/calibration across five cancer cohorts. v2 rephrases the abstract and contributions, but retains their substantive scope; the added evaluations primarily support existing claims.

C2.justification: v1's limitations emphasize careful prototype-count selection. v2 instead interprets sensitivity results as supporting robustness and adds concrete boundaries concerning sparse tumor content, stronger domain shifts, and the pilot nature of clinical validation. It also explains the poor ablation performance of component prototypes without prevalence-weighted evidence mixing and develops λ's interpretation as controlling prediction conservativeness.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-access link, explicitly states that GMM parameters remain fixed during evidential-network training, and provides validation/model-selection details and training-time information. Its configuration table is revised accordingly. Both versions already document initialization, baseline adaptations, optimizer settings, patch sampling, and A100 hardware.

E1.justification: v1 Appendix B.1 and v2 Appendix G.1 report the same BRCA, BLCA, LUAD, UCEC, and KIRC cohorts with identical patient and WSI counts. The added analyses reuse this coverage; CONCH changes the feature extractor, while additional pathologist-rated examples extend the existing interpretability evaluation.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated MC Dropout and Deep Ensemble comparators in Appendix K, Table 9 and Figure 7. The nine principal baselines are retained. DSMIL is not newly evaluated: it already appears in v1's result tables and Appendix B.2 despite its omission from the main baseline-list paragraph.

E3.justification: v2 replaces cohort-specific learning rates with 1e-4, changes DPsurv's training budget from 50 to 30 epochs and λ from 0.1 to 0.5, and selects K from {1,2,3,4} through validation/early stopping instead of the earlier cohort/fold-size choices. It newly specifies a 15% validation holdout and explicitly reports retraining baselines under the shared selection protocol. New protocols include fixed-configuration ablations, CONCH evaluation on UCEC, and a two-pathologist, 10-point coherence assessment.

E4.justification: v1 has qualitative interpretation examples but no component-ablation or hyperparameter-sensitivity experiments. v2 adds component ablations in Table 2, K/C/λ/α sensitivity tests in Tables 6–7, feature-extractor robustness in Table 3, additional interpretation examples and expert ratings in Appendix I, and a targeted analysis of the lowest-rated case in Appendix L.

E5.justification: Five-fold cross-validation and mean-with-±-dispersion reporting are retained.
