The new sensitivity tables explicitly label their dispersion as standard deviation, extending the existing reporting pattern to additional results. Neither version reports random seeds, additional repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: The principal result entries and several rankings change substantially. DPsurv's reported mean C-index, IBS, and IBLL change from 0.685, 0.288, and 0.862 in v1 Tables 1, 2, and 4 to 0.704, 0.310, and 0.824 in v2 Table 1. These are revised results under changed training/selection settings, not controlled performance gains. v2 also adds ablation, sensitivity, CONCH, runtime, expert-rating, and alternative-uncertainty results.

M1.justification: Equation 15 removes the precision and distance-decay regularization terms, ξR1 and ρR2, leaving the weighted survival likelihood objective. The patch-prototype GMM, component-prototype evidence fusion, mixture aggregation, and prediction procedures remain substantively unchanged.

P1.justification: v2 substantially rewrites and reorganizes the narrative: it condenses the introduction and main related work, adds a method overview, expands mechanism explanations, and restructures the appendices into dedicated terminology, theory, experimental, interpretation, and limitation sections. These changes extend well beyond inserting new experimental content.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from a single-column to a two-column layout. v1's separate C-index, IBS, and appendix IBLL tables are consolidated into v2 Table 1, and the configuration table is restructured. Numerous new tables and Figures 4–7 are added. Figures 1–3 retain the same graphics but are resized and repositioned.

R1.justification: Most related-work content is retained in v2 Appendix B. A new focused discussion distinguishes DPsurv's within-WSI component reasoning from Huang et al. (2024c)'s multimodal survival fusion. References are also updated through additions such as Lu et al. (2023) and several 2026 works, while some introductory citations are removed.

T1.justification: v2 Appendix D.1 adds a short proof of the previously stated survival-function bound. The GRFN derivations, mixture proof, EM updates, and GMM limiting argument are retained across relocation and notation changes. Newly numbered definitions/propositions and the numerical toy example mostly explain existing mathematics.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's lack of evidence isolating component contributions and prototype sensitivity through Table 2 and Appendix H. Additional uncertainty comparisons, extractor testing, expert ratings, and a concrete failure analysis strengthen support for the central claims and clarify applicability limits. Clearer method explanations and code-access information also help reproducibility. Changed training settings prevent interpreting the headline scores as controlled gains, and the clinical study remains preliminary, but the added controls and explicit qualifications provide a substantial overall quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DPsurv and provide readable text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices. Retained content can be matched despite substantial restructuring, supporting a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports revised survival-prediction results and additional original ablations, sensitivity tests, feature-extractor comparisons, runtime measurements, and pathologist coherence ratings.

before.justification: v1 reports original five-fold survival-prediction experiments on five TCGA cohorts, including C-index, IBS, IBLL, calibration plots, and pathological interpretation examples.

results.title: DPsurv: Dual-Prototype Evidential Fusion for Uncertainty-Aware and Interpretable Whole Slide Image Survival Prediction

C1.justification: The abstract and contributions broaden from perplexity and selected zero-shot advantages at 150M–772M to results through 1.9B, superiority using half the training-token budget, and competitive GSM8K reasoning. The introduction explicitly claims improvements across all zero-shot evaluations at half budget, substantially strengthening the empirical contribution.

C2.justification: v1's low-efficiency and unavailable-GSM8K limitations give way to claims of competitive practical cost and demonstrated reasoning applicability. v2 adds a hypothesis that removing attention masking makes fork decisions effectively random. It corrects the overforking interpretation to slight improvement while retaining the top-k gradient-bottleneck explanation in Appendix D.

D1.justification: v2 adds a JAX implementation link, detailed training mixtures and schedules, 1.9B architecture and batch settings, v4-32 TPU hardware, XLA kernels, and the torch.compile/H100 timing procedure. These substantially expand reproducibility information beyond v1's smaller-model PyTorch and H200 setup.

E1.justification: v2 adds FineWeb pretraining, a mid-training mixture including MMLU, SmolTalk, and GSM8K-aug, and evaluation on ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge, and GSM8K. This substantially extends training coverage and introduces science-question and mathematical-reasoning evaluations. The earlier OpenWebText, peS2o, downstream benchmarks, and CLUTTR case study remain.

E2.justification: New Tables 6–7 add evaluated control variants using rightmost-only output merging or no attention masking. The original scaling suite retains the regular transformer, Copy-3, and Copy-5 comparators. The added 1.9B benchmark table compares against the regular transformer only.

E3.justification: v2 introduces 1.9B experiments with 20B/40B-token checkpoints, a warmup-stable-decay training recipe, and 2B-token mid-training before GSM8K evaluation. It also adds H100 forward/backward timing with eight sequences and new ablation budget settings. These are added protocols; the earlier 150M–772M benchmark results and their 2.5B-token training regime are retained.

E4.justification: Appendix C adds controlled tests of whether averaging fork outputs and attenuating attention improve performance. Appendix B adds measured computational-cost comparisons. These address architectural components and practical efficiency beyond v1's existing overforking, attention, entropy, autoregression, and qualitative allocation analyses, which remain.

E5.justification: No new seed counts, repeated-run information, confidence intervals, or significance tests are documented. Existing attention and perplexity distribution plots remain, while the added benchmark, timing, and ablation tables report point estimates.

E6.justification: New Table 1 reports 1.9B perplexities of 12.68/12.09 at 20B/40B tokens versus 15.03 for the 40B-token baseline, and GSM8K scores of 31.50/32.10 versus 31.46. Tables 5–7 add timing and ablation outcomes. v1 Table 1 is numerically unchanged as v2 Table 2. The overforking finding is corrected from worse to slightly better without changing its values.

M1.justification: Section 2.5 adds a cheaper output procedure for the 1.9B model: score-weighted residuals are averaged before one vocabulary projection and softmax, rather than mixing separately decoded probability distributions. The core forking, attenuation, positional encoding, and dynamic-budget mechanisms remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and experimental narrative receive focused rewriting, while much of the methods, related work, and existing analysis prose remains. The standalone Limitations, acknowledgments, and LLM-use sections disappear; an Impact Statement and two new appendix sections are introduced.

P2.justification: The main text and references change from single-column to two-column layout, with extensive figure resizing and relocation. Four tables are added and architecture tables expanded. Figure 1 moves to the first page, Figures 4–5 exchange numbering, and Figure 7's panels change from vertical to horizontal arrangement.

R1.justification: v2 adds Quiet-STaR to related work, cites the softmax-bottleneck literature, and adds references supporting the new datasets and training recipe. The TinyGSM citation disappears with the old scale limitation. The central positioning against serial reasoning and fixed pause-token approaches remains.

T1.justification: v2 Equation 12 introduces a mathematically different output definition that averages residuals before decoding, supplementing the existing probability-mixture definition. The main forking and attenuation equations and partial-RoPE construction remain substantively unchanged. No new theorem or proof is provided.

improvement.justification: The larger-scale reasoning evaluations, measured computational costs, and component ablations substantially strengthen validation, addressing v1's acknowledged lack of GSM8K testing and practical timing evidence. These gains outweigh remaining weaknesses: the blanket half-budget superiority claim conflicts with ARC-Challenge results of 24.50 versus 26.17, and the small GSM8K advantage lacks uncertainty reporting. The improvement comes from testing applicability, cost, and architectural choices more directly.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Thoughtbubbles with the same authors and core architecture. The main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison across renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds 1.9B-model evaluations, GSM8K and ARC results, forward/backward timing measurements, and component ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original pretraining and zero-shot benchmark results, attention and computation-allocation analyses, autoregressive evaluations, and an appendix overforking experiment.

results.title: Thoughtbubbles: an Unsupervised Method for Parallel Thinking in Latent Space

C1.justification: v1 presents DecepChain primarily as a novel backdoor attack. v2 reframes the contribution as investigating and stress-testing deceptive behavior under full post-training control. Its abstract and contribution list additionally claim robustness against further fine-tuning and detection, extending the original effectiveness and stealthiness claims.

C2.justification: New Appendix A.1 discusses ambiguous definitions of deception, limited access to internal reasoning, mitigation challenges, dependence on naturally erroneous outputs, and model-scale hypotheses. Sections 3.1 and A.4 clarify applicability under full post-training control and explain detector failures through natural trigger wording and apparently consistent erroneous reasoning.

D1.justification: v2 Appendix A.4 newly documents four rollouts per training question, a 210-example SFT dataset example, 20 SFT epochs, 10 GSM8K GRPO epochs followed by one MATH epoch, and exclusion of MATH500 from training. It also supplies trigger lists, detector settings and prompts, and participant qualifications. These disclosures do not establish that the existing training budgets changed.

E1.justification: v2 adds GPQA-Main's expert multiple-choice scientific questions to the six retained quantitative benchmarks, testing transfer beyond the original task coverage. It also adds scenarios involving altered, repositioned, and previously unseen semantically related triggers (Table 4; Appendix A.5).

E2.justification: v2 introduces defense comparisons against ONION and Chain-of-Scrutiny (CoS), actually evaluated in Tables 5–6. The original main comparator set remains: GRPO w/o BD becomes BaseRL, SFT w/ BD becomes BadNet, and DTCoT and BadChain are retained. These renamings are not new baselines.

E3.justification: v2 adds Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct configurations, post-training controls, GPT-5 judging, modified judge prompts, detection metrics, and a three-minute human evaluation with five new participants. It also changes DeepSeek's stated trigger from '@@%%TRIGGER%%@@' to 'What do you think?' and explicitly clips RAS at zero.

E4.justification: New analyses test persistence after further GRPO, ordinary SFT, and targeted SFT; trigger perturbations; ONION/CoS resistance; judge-prompt sensitivity; GPT-5 evaluation; and longer human inspection (Section 4.4; Tables 8–10). The original component and hyperparameter ablations remain. Appendix examples also add Llama cases and replace DeepSeek outputs.

E5.justification: Both versions report aggregate scores without experimental seed information, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The additional participants and disclosed training-rollout count do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: The original Qwen results and component ablations are retained, while DeepSeek entries change alongside its trigger setting: MATH500 DecepChain ASRt changes from 94.72 to 93.24, not a same-setting comparison. Numerous results are added, including 14B RAS values of 95.99–100.00 and GPQA RAS values of 8.52–34.98 (Tables 11 and 13), plus robustness and judge evaluations.

M1.justification: The core procedure remains self-generated rollout collection, SFT, and curriculum GRPO with flipped rewards and pattern checking. The three-stage presentation separates data collection from SFT; filtering incorrect rollouts and balancing correct/incorrect examples were already documented in v1 Appendix A.3. The two pattern-checker algorithms are retained.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and method narrative are substantially revised around deceptive behavior rather than attack terminology. Data collection becomes a separate explanatory stage, a dedicated threat-model subsection is introduced, and the appendices are reorganized and expanded. These narrative changes extend beyond simply inserting experimental results.

P2.justification: The main text changes from a single-column preprint to a two-column proceedings layout. Figure 1 is substantially redrawn; Figures 2 and 4 are restyled; Figure 3 is resized and relocated. Tables 1–2 gain model blocks, the component table changes structure, and numerous new tables plus a CoS prompt figure are added.

R1.justification: v2 removes the broad standalone backdoor/VLM discussion and substantially repositions the work alongside studies of sleeper agents, emergent misalignment, sandbagging, and other hazardous model behaviors. It adds corresponding citations and references for evaluated defenses and GPQA. This changes research positioning beyond bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: v2 Equation 5 changes the formal RAS numerator from the clean-minus-triggered accuracy difference to its maximum with zero. This is a limited mathematical-definition revision. The SFT and GRPO formulations remain equivalent, and neither version provides theoretical guarantees or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation by testing alternative judge wording, GPT-5, longer human review, and resistance to further training and detection. Results on a 14B model and GPQA, substantially fuller training details, and explicit threat-model and observability limitations address important gaps in v1. The longer human comparison uses different participants and uncertainty remains unreported, limiting causal and statistical conclusions, but the added checks and clearer documentation provide substantial overall gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DecepChain work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial expansion and reformatting.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds model evaluations, scientific question answering, robustness experiments, alternative judges, and a longer human evaluation.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark experiments, LLM and human trust evaluations, component ablations, hyperparameter analyses, and generated-response examples.

results.title: DecepChain: Inducing Deceptive Reasoning in Large Language Models

C1.justification: The central contribution remains a compact per-block learned zeroth-order optimizer trained once per base model and reused across tasks and derivative checkpoints. The abstract and introduction retain the 82.1% loss-win and 2.5% average accuracy-improvement claims. New experiments primarily support the existing transfer claim.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations of mathematical transfer, meta-training-source robustness, and trajectory choice. It explicitly limits evaluation to the MeZO-style regime and leaves combinations with LoRA, quantization, and offloading for future work. The new assertion of consistently beating MeZO overstates Table 6, which contains one contrary SQuAD result.

D1.justification: Appendix C.8 newly specifies, for LLaMA-3.2-1B on COPA, resets every five epochs and 15 total training epochs, alongside tuning rationale and claimed checkpoint/script releases. v2 also discloses use of MeZO prompt templates. These document existing procedures rather than demonstrate changes to them.

E1.justification: v2 adds a distinct mathematical-reasoning setting: Qwen2.5-14B is fine-tuned on MetaMathQA and evaluated on GSM8K and MATH-500. This extends coverage to longer-solution reasoning tasks beyond the retained seven-task NLP suite.

E2.justification: New Tables 11–12 include first-order Adam in predictive-performance comparisons; v1 included first-order methods only in memory comparisons. Table 5 also supplies an untuned base-model reference. The original main-table comparator lineup remains unchanged.

E3.justification: Added protocols include 10,000-step MetaMathQA fine-tuning followed by separate math-benchmark testing, alternative meta-training sources, and SGD-versus-Adam trajectory controls with loss summarized over 4,000-step intervals. Existing main-experiment learning-rate grids, batch sizes, and step budgets are retained.

E4.justification: v2 substantially expands diagnostic evidence through meta-training-dataset ablations (Table 6), SGD-versus-Adam trajectory ablations (Tables 13–14), and test accuracy/F1 convergence curves (Figure 7). These supplement, rather than replace, the existing normalization, reset, sharing, learning-rate, and single-versus-multiple-dataset analyses.

E5.justification: Appendix C.8 newly announces fixed-seed reproduction scripts, providing limited seed-related information. This does not establish additional runs: neither version specifies repeated-run counts or numerical seeds, and Figure 2 retains the same smoothed-loss standard-deviation reporting.

E6.justification: All 280 numerical entries in Table 1 are unchanged. Substantial new results include GSM8K accuracy of 85.6 versus MeZO's 81.4 and MATH-500 accuracy of 54.6 versus 53.0, plus meta-training ablations, trajectory comparisons, first-order reference scores, and accuracy curves. These are additional results, not improvements over v1 under its original settings.

M1.justification: The per-block PertNN architecture, meta-objective, normalization, periodic resets, and gradient-stopping approximation are retained. Revised sampling equations align the main text with the multiplicative perturbation construction already documented in v1 Appendix B.3; they do not establish a different implemented optimizer.

P1.justification: The main section order and much of the prose remain intact. Local rewrites affect the abstract, motivation, transfer discussion, conclusion, and limitations; acknowledgments, an impact statement, and Appendices C.6–C.8 are added. Author-affiliation and heading text also change.

P2.justification: The single-column preprint becomes a two-column conference-style main paper, with extensively resized and rearranged tables and retypeset algorithms. Appendix plots move to the end. Six tables and Figure 7 are added; the original derivative-transfer and sharing tables are retained with exchanged numbering.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations for MetaMath, GSM8K, and the MATH-500 evaluation source: Yu et al., Cobbe et al., and Lightman et al. The established zeroth-order and learning-to-learn positioning remains largely intact. Sun et al. appears in the expanded main related-work discussion but was already cited in v1.

T1.justification: v2 repairs a covariance inconsistency in the main mathematical description: perturbations use u = Σz with covariance ΣΣᵀ, replacing the earlier square-root construction while retaining the Frobenius-norm normalization. This makes the stated second-moment identity consistent. Appendix D's assumptions, bounds, and proof are otherwise retained.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for the central reuse claim through transfer to mathematical reasoning and controls on meta-training data and trajectory choice. First-order accuracy references and concrete reset/training disclosures improve interpretation and reproducibility. These gains outweigh localized weaknesses: Table 6 contradicts the new uniform-superiority wording, and several added first-order-reference tables report ZO Fine-tuner scores differing from Table 1 without explaining the settings.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ZO Fine-tuner and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices A–D. Retained material can be matched despite substantial layout changes and table renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds mathematical-reasoning evaluations, meta-training and trajectory ablations, first-order accuracy comparisons, and accuracy curves.

before.justification: v1 reports original fine-tuning experiments across four LLMs and seven datasets, derivative-checkpoint transfer, ablations, and runtime and memory measurements.

results.title: Learning a Zeroth-Order Optimizer for Fine-Tuning LLMs

C1.justification: The central contributions remain discovery of a resolution-related feature direction, lightweight frozen-backbone VPFA, strong benchmark performance and broader applicability. V2's abstract explicitly mentions averaging, but this qualification already appears in v1's introduction. The contribution list and conclusion retain their substantive claims.

C2.justification: New Section 7 states that the analyses do not prove a universal one-dimensional direction, suggests a possibly low-rank, input-dependent subspace, and identifies limitations from missing identity information and untested real-world degradations. It positions VPFA as complementary to reconstruction methods. V2 also adds Grad-CAM mechanism interpretations and explicitly limits backbone comparisons to matched within-framework settings.

D1.justification: V2 revises feature-pair construction instructions, documents the Grad-CAM score and gradient target, and adds backbone and comparison-control information. Most implementation details remain unchanged, including dimensions, initialization, optimizer settings and code link. Hardware information moves from Appendix A.1 to Section 5.2 rather than being newly disclosed; alternative-head configurations remain described only as standard.

E1.justification: All result-bearing datasets and tasks are retained, including the appendix's MSMT17, MLRpro, RegDB and RSTPReid evaluations. Separate-resolution tests use already-covered downsampling levels. However, v2 removes DukeMTMC from one dataset list while retaining the MLR-DukeMTMC reference; neither version provides Duke-specific results. Whether this represents removed coverage or correction of an inconsistent description is unresolved.

E2.justification: V2 adds FiLM, Adapter and mean-vector offset comparisons in Table 9, plus original TransReID-DeiT and CLIP-ReID baselines in Table 8. These substantially broaden comparisons beyond v1's existing residual ablation and benchmark methods. Table 3 retains its comparator membership; changed Part Aligned and PyrNet citations are not method replacements.

E3.justification: V2 adds fixed 2×, 3× and 4× evaluations alongside mixed-resolution tests, additional backbone/framework configurations, and replacement-head comparisons with a shared training protocol and loss. Training-data preparation also changes from identity prototypes and identity-level shuffling to individual feature pairs and random shuffling. The stated 5,000-pair budget, optimizer, batch size and 120 epochs remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New analyses examine sensitivity to resolution severity, generalization across feature extractors, and whether simpler adaptation heads suffice (Appendix A.2, A.4–A.5). Section 5.8 adds similarity-based Grad-CAM cases investigating matching cues. Existing residual, width, depth, feature-distance, retrieval and cross-domain analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report the same ten random splits and averages for CUHK03, VIPeR and CAVIAR, and the same Pearson-correlation standard deviations. V2 adds no new seed counts, confidence intervals, significance tests or uncertainty-estimation procedures.

E6.justification: All eleven original tables retain their numerical results, but v2 adds substantial results in Tables 7–9. Examples include 4× Rank-1 of 93.6 versus 85.6 without VPFA, CLIP-ReID CNN Rank-1 of 90.6 versus 88.2, and FiLM/Adapter Rank-1 of 92.1/91.8 versus VPFA's 94.1. These are new comparisons, not version-to-version gains. Table 7 also shows a 2× Rank-5 decline from 98.2 to 97.8. Section 5.5 newly reports TransReID throughput of 80.80 samples/second.

M1.justification: V1 explicitly trains on identity-averaged LR–HR prototypes in Equation (2), Algorithm 1 and Section 5.2. V2 instead specifies individual image-pair features without identity averaging throughout Algorithm 1 and Sections 4.4 and 5.3. This substantially changes the reported training inputs and supervision, although the backbone, residual MLP and loss remain unchanged. The PDFs do not establish whether retained experiments were rerun.

P1.justification: V2 retitles the paper, rewrites the abstract and training passages, and expands comparator explanations while retaining most existing prose and the main scientific section sequence. It moves environment details into the main text, adds limitations, impact and acknowledgements sections, and removes the LLM-use disclosure.

P2.justification: The single-column preprint becomes a two-column conference-style main text. Figure 2 is substantially redesigned with training and inference diagrams; Grad-CAM Figure 4 and Tables 7–9 are added. Existing tables and t-SNE panels are rearranged, while the original retrieval figure and appendix tables are retained under new numbering.

R1.justification: V2 adds FiLM and Houlsby-style Adapter references and a focused discussion positioning VPFA against general feature adaptation. It adds Zhao et al. for Part Aligned, reattributes PyrNet to Martinel et al., and removes the Gong and Goodfellow references. The main ReID and cross-resolution related-work narrative remains largely unchanged.

T1.justification: V1's Equation (2), defining identity-averaged training prototypes, is removed from v2's formulation. The residual mapping, squared-error loss and law-of-cosines derivation remain equivalent. The new low-rank interpretation is not developed into a formal theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens methodological support: Tables 8–9 address v1's limited validation across backbones and against general feature-adaptation alternatives, while Section 7 meaningfully qualifies the interpretation of the correlation evidence. These gains improve the justification and scientific caution without relying on higher headline scores. Reproducibility remains imperfect: some added settings are underspecified, and the revised pairwise-training description is not reconciled with the unchanged legacy results.

A1.justification: Both complete, readable 17-page PDFs describe the same VPFA research. Text, equations, figures, tables and appendices can be matched despite the changed title, layout and added analyses.

after.justification: V2 retains these empirical results and adds separate-resolution evaluations, backbone comparisons, feature-adaptation baselines and Grad-CAM examples.

before.justification: V1 reports original retrieval experiments, feature-correlation analyses, ablations, efficiency measurements and appendix experiments on robustness, cross-modal retrieval and cross-dataset transfer.

results.title: Resolution as a Direction: Vector-Panning Feature Alignment for Cross-Resolution Re-Identification

C1.justification: The introduction and related work qualify the priority claim from 'first' to 'among the first' and emphasize consistency-driven streaming. The principal claims about AR-OSD, unbounded-length processing, MovieLQ, semantic consistency and up to 58-fold acceleration remain.

C2.justification: Appendix D attributes flow-loss failure to small training windows and argues that LR conditioning limits error accumulation. Appendix F adds substantive limitations concerning training scale, architectural redundancy and VAE/DiT priors. Appendix A also clarifies the single-shot experimental boundary and discusses scene-transition handling.

D1.justification: V2 adds Stage-II pseudocode, regularizer updates and timestep sampling, causal-VAE caching and streaming execution details, MovieLQ's ten-clip count, and metric implementations. Its access statement changes from forthcoming code to available code and models. Some ambiguity remains: Appendix A.2 describes overlapping chunks while Section 3.1 specifies non-overlapping chunks.

E1.justification: Both use REDS for training and UDM10, SPMCS, MVSR4x, VideoLQ and MovieLQ for evaluation. Additional resolution and sequence-length profiling extends experimental settings within the same task. Appendix A.3 describes multi-shot handling but supplies no corresponding evaluation results.

E2.justification: Appendix E adds evaluated comparisons against DLoraL and FlashVSR on UDM10 and VideoLQ, substantially extending comparison to relevant streaming approaches. DLoraL was only discussed in v1. The original comparator sets remain; Stream-DiffVSR is discussed but explicitly not evaluated.

E3.justification: The original training settings, scaling factor and benchmark metrics remain. New protocols include varying cache length with chunk size fixed, comparing causal and full attention across lengths and 720p/1080p resolutions, and evaluating five consecutive 200-frame MovieLQ intervals. These materially extend controlled and long-horizon evaluation without establishing reruns of the original experiments.

E4.justification: Table 4d adds removal of the temporal loss. Appendix D adds comparison with optical-flow supervision, isolated cache-length sensitivity, causal versus full-attention scaling, and temporal error-accumulation analysis. These directly test design choices and long-sequence reliability beyond v1's retained ablations.

E5.justification: Neither PDF reports repeated-run counts, evaluation seeds, confidence intervals, standard deviations or significance tests. The additional result tables retain point-estimate reporting.

E6.justification: Tables 1-2, original Table 3 timings and retained Table 4 values are unchanged. V2 adds substantial latency, scaling, ablation, segment-wise and comparator results. For example, Table 10 reports higher UDM10 DOVER for FlashVSR than InfVSR (0.7953 versus 0.7826), but lower warping error for InfVSR (1.95 versus 2.47). These are new comparisons, not improved scores for the retained InfVSR evaluation.

M1.justification: V1 keeps visual prompts constant across all chunks; v2 introduces threshold-based reference switching across adjacent chunks. Appendix A.3 also describes scene-cut cache resets and prompt updates. The AR-OSD backbone, rolling cache, principal losses and two-stage training design remain.

P1.justification: V2 retitles the paper, substantially rewrites the introduction around three consistency-focused themes, revises method explanations and removes the standalone one-step-diffusion discussion. It also introduces an organized appendix narrative and impact and acknowledgment sections.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to two-column layout. Figure 1 is replaced, the separate patch-supervision illustration is removed, and new streaming, dataset and comparison displays are added. V1 Figures 4-6 survive as v2 Figures 3-5. Table 3 gains columns, Table 4 gains a row, and Tables 5-10 are new.

R1.justification: V2 updates positioning around concurrent FlashVSR and Stream-DiffVSR, qualifies priority, removes the dedicated one-step-diffusion survey and adds contextual references. The principal relationship to T2V priors and autoregressive generation remains. Publication and bibliographic corrections to retained works are not additional research coverage.

T1.justification: Equations 1-6 retain the mathematical formulation; the gradient-subscript correction clarifies notation. Appendix formulas explain existing VBench metrics and a cited comparison loss. The error-accumulation discussion supplies intuition, without adding formal assumptions, derivations or proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially improves support for the central streaming claims: Appendices A-B explain execution and training, D tests scaling and long-video degradation, and E adds directly relevant streaming competitors with visible metric trade-offs. Concrete limitations further improve transparency. These address important gaps in v1's validation and reproducibility despite unchanged headline scores. Conflicting overlap descriptions and insufficiently reconciled efficiency settings remain, but the added evidence and documentation provide a clear overall gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe InfVSR despite the changed title and layout. All supplied text, equations, tables and figures support comparison. V1 ends with references; v2 includes readable Appendices A-G, which are included in this assessment.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds latency profiling, controlled ablations, long-sequence analyses and streaming-method comparisons in its appendices.

before.justification: V1 reports original super-resolution evaluations, runtime measurements, qualitative comparisons and component ablations in Section 4 and Tables 1-4.

results.title: InfVSR: Toward Consistency-Driven Streaming Generative Video Super-Resolution

C1.justification: The central contributions remain standardized PRM training across reward types, vectorized MAH-DPO, and controllable inference-time alignment. MAHALO names the existing framework. Cross-domain PRM transfer and reward-verifiability takeaways foregrounded in v2's introduction were already present in v1's findings; the new experiments strengthen support without redefining these core claims.

C2.justification: v2 substantially qualifies the interpretation of objective compatibility: average correlations conceal conflicting examples, and the Human Values ensemble no longer dominates both specialists under explicit conflict. It adds explanations contrasting head-level gradient isolation with shared-representation updates, interprets sensitivity to PRM quality, and acknowledges limits concerning scaling beyond five objectives and moderate human–judge agreement.

D1.justification: v2 clarifies that the frozen reference policy shares no parameters with the trainable policy and discloses equal objective weights and balanced sampling. It also supplies hardware and settings for the new computational benchmarks and construction details for added studies. Existing domain hyperparameters, system prompts and the code-access URL are retained.

E1.justification: The three domains and their objective types are retained. v2 adds a deliberately selected population of 7,500 Human Values preference pairs with opposing helpfulness and honesty preferences (Appendix E.2), extending coverage to an explicit conflict scenario. The five-head experiment reuses existing math and human-values tasks.

E2.justification: v2 adds DPO Soup to the Math and Human Values training comparisons in Table 1, and evaluates scalarized Multi-Objective PPO in Human Values in Table 19. These introduce parameter-merging and PPO comparator families beyond v1's SFT and DPO-based comparisons. Existing comparators are retained.

E3.justification: Original domain training settings and default decoding budgets are retained. New protocols include five-head joint training on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, alternative segmentation rules, probabilistic overrides of PRM selection, controlled latency/memory measurements, GPT-4o evaluation on 500 math problems, and three-annotator evaluation on 100 problems. These substantially expand the evaluation design rather than establish reruns of the original experiments.

E4.justification: v2 adds segmentation sensitivity and PRM-selection-noise studies, explicit objective-conflict tests, five-objective scaling, qualitative interaction examples, computational overhead comparisons, and cross-model/human validation (Section 6.4 and Appendices C, E and F). The original discount-factor, head-weight and hidden-state-versus-text analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report three-run averages and standard deviations; additional result rows do not establish increased replication. v2 adds human-majority/judge agreement analysis, including 77.0% agreement and Cohen's kappa of 0.45 in Appendix F.2. This introduces an agreement statistic without adding confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: Retained numerical entries in all eleven original tables are unchanged. v2 adds substantial results: MOPPO scores 0.6764/0.2921/0.1460 on helpfulness/honesty/truthfulness (Table 19), cached PRM-guided decoding achieves a reported 4.2-fold speedup (Table 6), and human-majority engagement ratings are 64% for Base versus 87% for MAH-DPO (Table 22). Conflict, scaling, segmentation and noise results are also new.

M1.justification: The formal ensemble rule changes from averaging head probabilities in v1 Equation 5 to applying softmax to weighted logits in v2 Equation 4. Since v1 already described logit ensembling in prose, this corrects an inconsistent specification without establishing an implementation change. The architecture, DPO objectives, PRM training and cache-based decoding remain substantively unchanged.

P1.justification: v2 extensively rewrites the introduction around practical takeaways, condenses background and findings, and introduces the MAHALO terminology. It moves gradient analysis and decoding details into reorganized appendices, relocates the ethics material, adds an impact statement, and moves system prompts to the end. This changes the narrative organization beyond accommodating new experiments.

P2.justification: The main text and references switch from a single-column preprint layout to a two-column conference layout. Existing figures and tables are resized and relocated, Algorithm 1 moves to Appendix C, and numerous tables display the new analyses. Appendix result tables are regrouped and prompt boxes reflow across different pages.

R1.justification: v2 adds a focused discussion of interference and data/gradient compatibility, citing Dong's SFT-composition work, Wu's Mixture-of-Skills, and Liang's 2025/2026 work. Safe RLHF is newly cited for the PPO comparison, while some background references are removed. The overall PRM and multi-objective positioning remains stable; numerous publication-metadata updates do not constitute new works.

T1.justification: The ensemble distribution is mathematically revised from a probability mixture to softmax of a logit mixture, which is not an equivalent expression. Otherwise, the PRM targets and DPO mathematics are retained. Gradient and computational analyses move to Appendices B.1 and C.1 without new proofs or substantive derivation changes.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important gaps in v1's support for its central claims: it tests explicitly conflicting preferences, broadens comparator families, measures computational costs, and independently validates engagement gains with GPT-4o and humans. These additions substantially strengthen empirical credibility and clarify applicability limits. Human agreement remains moderate, and v2 gives inconsistent Socratic PRM backbone descriptions in A.3 and F.1, but these weaknesses do not outweigh the substantial evidential gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research framework and retain matching methods, datasets and experiments. Their text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds baseline comparisons, conflict and robustness experiments, computational measurements, and independent model and human evaluations.

before.justification: v1 reports original training-time and decoding experiments on MATH, UltraFeedback and Socratic Mind, together with head-weight, discount-factor and decoding-continuity analyses.

results.title: Simultaneous Multi-objective Alignment Across Verifiable and Non-verifiable Rewards

C1.justification: The central contributions remain state-aware contrastive regularization, lightweight view-cutoff augmentation, and improved simulation and real-robot performance. v3's abstract highlights the overall 69.7% RoboCasa result already reported in v1; the additional experiments support the existing contributions.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive interpretations concerning preservation of scene information alongside task-progress alignment, stronger benefits for less constrained tasks, and applicability across action-modeling paradigms and state configurations. It also explains TCN's computational overhead. The earlier LIBERO batch-size explanation disappears, while the object-pose/contact-force limitation is retained.

D1.justification: v3 newly documents per-dimension state normalization, two A100-SXM4-80GB GPUs and 64 CPU cores, training times, and implementation details for TCN and KNN analyses. Existing checkpoint, dataset and main training instructions remain; v1's pseudocode is removed. These disclosures do not establish changed settings for the retained experiments.

E1.justification: v3 adds DexMimicGen evaluations involving bimanual Panda arms with Inspire Hands and a GR-1 humanoid, substantially broadening embodiment and state-space coverage (Appendix E.4). It also adds real-robot testing under darker lighting. RoboCasa-Kitchen, LIBERO and the previous real-robot scenarios remain.

E2.justification: v3 Table 1 adds reported comparisons with DreamGen, DUST, Video Policy, FLARE and HAMLET. Table 3 additionally evaluates single-view and multi-view TCN. Conversely, the plain InfoNCE comparator in v1's LIBERO Table 6 disappears, although the RoboCasa 300-demonstration InfoNCE ablation remains.

E3.justification: New evaluation procedures include DTW-aligned, 32-class task-phase prediction using KNN with k=5; TCN comparisons with a 0.2-second temporal margin; compute profiling; and sweeps over schedules, temperatures, projection dimensions and batch sizes. The previously stated RoboCasa/LIBERO training budgets and evaluation trial counts are retained.

E4.justification: v3 adds hyperparameter sensitivity studies, scene/task-phase representation probes, lighting robustness tests, architecture and state-configuration checks, and task-group analysis. These examine robustness, mechanisms and applicability beyond v1's analyses. The expanded plain-InfoNCE analysis in v1 Appendix D.1 is removed, while the original main design ablations and CKNNA analysis remain.

E5.justification: v3 Table 8 reports separate results for training seeds 0, 7 and 42, and Figures 4 and 6 introduce error bars on average success rates. v1 supplies neither. The error-bar definition is unspecified, and the new seed reporting does not establish how many runs underlay v1.

E6.justification: The principal RoboCasa and LIBERO results remain 69.7% and 96.4%. New results include TCN success rates of 50.0/50.3% versus RS-CL's 53.0%, π0-FAST+RS-CL results, and DexMimicGen baseline/RS-CL results of 52.7/57.3% and 68.9/73.1%. Additional low-data SigLIP2 and plain-InfoNCE results are omitted. New Table 12 introduces inconsistent pick-and-place baseline averages: 30.1/55.6%, versus 30.8/55.3% in Figure 4 and the retained task-level results.

M1.justification: v3 adds an autoregressive instantiation of RS-CL on π0-FAST, which predicts action tokens through next-token prediction instead of flow matching (Appendix E.3). The RS-CL formula, state-distance weighting, summarization token and view-cutoff mechanism remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and narrative remain, with language polishing and localized rewrites. Simulation and real-robot setup descriptions are separated, and appendix material is regrouped. The reproducibility and LLM-use statements are removed, while an impact statement is added.

P2.justification: The main text changes from a single-column preprint to a two-column conference layout. The original RoboCasa comparison is redistributed into an expanded leaderboard and demonstration-count chart. Real-robot figures are redesigned, the standalone close-lid comparison disappears, and new analysis tables, lighting examples and an annotated representation visualization substantially change the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v3 adds references including DreamGen, DUST, HAMLET, Video Policy, DexMimicGen and DROID, while dropping the original RoboBrain and Open X-Embodiment references. It sharpens the distinction from separate contrastive pretraining, but retains the same broad related-work organization and research positioning.

T1.justification: Equations 1–5 retain the same mathematical content, with equivalent notation and additional explanation. Neither version provides formal propositions or proofs, and v3 introduces no substantive theoretical derivation.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens evidence for the central efficiency and applicability claims through TCN comparisons, measured computational costs, quantitative representation probes, seed checks, and autoregressive and complex-embodiment tests. These address important validation gaps in v1. The gains outweigh lost auxiliary results and reporting defects, including undefined error bars, inconsistent Table 12 averages, and the claimed 1.25% training-time overhead when Table 6 implies approximately 1.86%.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RS-CL research. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, are readable and can be matched despite reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains original experimental results and adds TCN comparisons, representation probes, robustness studies and evaluations on additional robot embodiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original RoboCasa-Kitchen and LIBERO experiments, real-robot evaluations, representation analyses and ablations.

results.title: Contrastive Representation Regularization for Vision-Language-Action Models

C1.justification: The central claims about order-invariant neural EDAs, structural regularization, and sample-efficient optimization remain. V2 makes the methodological contributions more explicit in the introduction and extends the conclusion from synthetic-benchmark robustness to practical applicability supported by neural architecture search.

C2.justification: V2 substantially expands discussion of applicability and limitations. It explains short-budget weakness through the diversity/convergence tradeoff, attributes poor large-instance performance of the original generator to insufficient capacity, and discusses critic scale sensitivity and computational cost. It also interprets the shared-generator and Gibbs results, providing new explanations of when particular designs help or fail.

D1.justification: V2 documents the shared generator's two 100-neuron hidden layers, critic architecture and tuning grid, curriculum settings, and NAS encoding and invalid-configuration handling. Table 3 expands CPU/GPU timing information across sizes and methods; the reported single-instance n=128 CPU time changes from 9 to 11.5 minutes. These additions substantially expand implementation and resource information beyond v1's existing defaults and software/hardware descriptions.

E1.justification: V2 extends evaluation beyond the retained synthetic QUBO, NK, and NK3 problems to NAS-Bench-101 neural architecture search. Appendix O evaluates mixed binary/categorical architecture configurations, including invalid configurations, adding a substantially different application and search environment.

E2.justification: V2 removes the explicit one-flip Tabu Search comparator, reducing the stated main comparison suite from 504 to 503 competitors. It also adds targeted comparisons against critic-based and Gibbs-sampling alternatives in Appendices Q and S, and comparative timing against BOA and CMApara in Table 3. The original PBIL, MIMIC, BOA, and Nevergrad comparisons otherwise remain.

E3.justification: Original default settings remain, but v2 adds substantial experimental protocols: 1,000-evaluation comparisons, Fast-RL-EDA with population 5 and 100 training epochs, critic scaling-parameter searches, and epoch/Gibbs-iteration sweeps. A much larger NK experiment is also introduced; its size is inconsistently reported as 1,024 in Section 4.2/Figure 19 and 1,028 in Appendix R.

E4.justification: V1's dropout, interaction-graph, population-size, KL-penalty, and network-depth analyses are retained. V2 adds training-epoch sensitivity, short-budget and curriculum analyses, a critic ablation, parameter-sharing and scaling comparisons, and a Gibbs-sampling ablation. These test previously unexamined design choices and failure conditions.

E5.justification: The retained experiments still use 10 instances with 10 independent restarts, standard-deviation bands, and two-sample t-tests with the same thresholds. New experiments extend these reporting practices; changed significance markers and additional result rows do not establish a new statistical procedure or increased replication of existing experiments.

E6.justification: V2 adds extensive NAS, short-budget, runtime, critic, shared-generator, and Gibbs-sampling results. All 42 main-table RL-EDA scores remain unchanged, but rankings and significance markers change after Tabu's removal: NK with n=128, K=8 retains 0.7369 while moving from rank 2/505 to 1/504. Figure 2 also replaces the NK n=256 panel with n=128 results, rather than showing a same-setting improvement.

M1.justification: The original order-invariant GRPO procedure remains, with renamed permutation notation. However, Appendices P–S introduce substantive variants: a curriculum that gradually reduces input dropout, a shared neural generator, critic-based advantages, and Gibbs sampling instead of autoregressive generation. Parameter sharing was only suggested as a possible extension in v1.

P1.justification: V2 rewrites part of the introduction into an explicit contribution list, corrects the expansion of GRPO, and clarifies generation/training-order notation. It reorganizes reproducibility and end-matter statements and adds an LLM usage declaration. Most retained methodological and theoretical prose remains closely matched; the additional scientific sections do not amount to a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: V2 changes the main paper to a two-column conference layout and extensively reflows figures and tables. It adds a generation/training diagram, comparative runtime and variant-result tables, and NAS, epoch-sensitivity, curriculum, scaling, and Gibbs plots. Existing displays are also renamed, renumbered, or relocated; the NAS curve appears in both the main text and appendix.

R1.justification: The introduction newly distinguishes generation-order invariance from the solution-space symmetries used by Sym-NCO and POMO. V2 adds their citations and the NAS-Bench-101 reference, while removing several Tabu-related references and the structured-dropout citation. The broader positioning relative to EDAs, Bayesian optimization, and autoregressive models remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix E revises the combinatorial coefficients in the permutation-averaged likelihood and introduces the general subset weight (k-1)!(n-k)!/n!. It replaces the earlier claim that fully conditioned terms receive much smaller weights with a qualified statement about decreasing weights up to n/2. Appendix L.2 adds time and space complexity reasoning. The existing PPO derivations and convergence argument are substantially retained.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses important gaps in v1's validation: it adds an application beyond synthetic landscapes and directly investigates budget limitations, scalability, and alternative design choices. Appendices O–S and the comparative runtime table substantially improve assessment of practical usefulness and failure conditions. Removing the strong Tabu comparator weakens comparative coverage, and the large-instance size inconsistency remains, but the broader validation and diagnostic evidence provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RL-EDA research work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching renamed variants and renumbered appendices.

after.justification: V2 retains original experimental results and adds NAS-Bench-101 optimization, short-budget experiments, scaling tests, and additional method comparisons.

before.justification: V1 reports original optimization experiments on QUBO, NK, and NK3, including comparisons, ablations, and sensitivity analyses.

results.title: Black-Box Combinatorial Optimization with Order-Invariant Reinforcement Learning

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion expand the contribution to language-model guidance, including a claimed 21.99% judge-score improvement over Dream. The introduction also explicitly qualifies APS as sacrificing asymptotic correctness for tractable inference. The central image-restoration and stylization claims remain.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly distinguishes its surrogate-guided inference from asymptotically unbiased MCMC, discusses ignoring normalization gradients, and adds possible posterior bias as a limitation (Implications 3.2–3.4 and Appendix C.10). It also attributes language coherence improvements to reward-guided joint sampling. Earlier tokenizer, backbone, stylization and ethical limitations are largely retained.

D1.justification: v2 supplies language-inference hyperparameters and the complete 20-prompt benchmark. Existing code/data and hardware disclosures largely remain. Some documentation is lost or inconsistent: the prior-preservation rationale and specified garment fine-tuning objective disappear, while Appendix C.2 mentions an entropy term absent from Algorithm 1.

E1.justification: v2 extends the image-focused evaluation to 20 open-ended language prompts covering creative writing, lists and constrained generation (Section 4.4 and Table 10). It also evaluates FFHQ super-resolution under additional measurement-noise levels. The existing image datasets, fashion task and larger 1,000-image FFHQ evaluation remain.

E2.justification: The new language comparison evaluates LLaDA-8B-Instruct and Dream-7B-Instruct against Dream+APS (Table 4). The identical-prior image comparison expands from one G2D2 row in v1 Table 5 to original G2D2 and two perceptual-loss variants in v2 Table 7. Existing image and stylization comparators are retained.

E3.justification: v2 introduces a language evaluation using Qwen3-0.6B rewards and a separate Qwen3-8B judge, with 128 diffusion steps and a 128-token generation limit. Added experiments vary inner optimization steps over 0, 10, 50, 100 and 200, noise standard deviation from 0.01 to 0.05, and G2D2 perceptual-loss weights. Retained image benchmark splits, resolution handling and principal budgets remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's existing perceptual-loss sweep, component ablation and identical-prior comparison, v2 adds optimization-step sensitivity (Table 6), measurement-noise robustness (Table 9), and G2D2 perceptual-loss controls (Table 7). These test convergence, sensitivity to corrupted measurements and whether the comparator benefits from the auxiliary loss.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests for its empirical results. The added noise-standard-deviation sweep concerns input corruption, not statistical uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: v2 adds language scores, including Qwen3-8B judge scores of 3.7523 for Dream and 4.5775 for Dream+APS, plus optimization-step and noise-sweep results. The expanded identical-prior comparison reports original G2D2 at 25.33 PSNR, 0.706 SSIM and 0.353 LPIPS, replacing v1's single 25.46/0.717/0.350 row with several configurations; accompanying prose still quotes the older values. Main Tables 1–3, the perceptual-loss sweep, runtimes and 1,000-image FFHQ scores are unchanged.

M1.justification: v2 adds a language adaptation that replaces the image decoder/measurement-error combination with scalar Qwen3-0.6B reward guidance for Dream-7B-Instruct (Appendix C.1.4). The quantized-expectation and anchored-remasking core remains. Algorithm 1 corrects the reverse iteration order; removing its explicit prior-preservation loss matches v1's already-zero default rather than establishing a changed image objective.

P1.justification: v2 substantially reorganizes the narrative: preliminaries become Section 2, related work moves to Appendix A, garment inpainting moves entirely into the appendix, question answering becomes a main results section, and reproducibility moves to Appendix C.11. The abstract, conclusion and method exposition are also extensively revised.

P2.justification: The main text and references change from a single-column to a two-column layout, with extensive redistribution and resizing of retained displays. v2 adds a language panel to Figure 1, a new language-comparison Figure 5, and Tables 4, 6, 9 and 10; it expands the G2D2 table. The former garment Figure 5 survives as Figure 12 rather than being removed.

R1.justification: v2 adds references concerning Dream/Qwen, masked-diffusion parameterizations, policy-gradient methods and partition-function estimation, and relates APS to approximate classifier-free and Tweedie-based guidance. The principal positioning against G2D2, SGDD and continuous posterior samplers remains; the original related-work discussion largely moves to Appendix A.

T1.justification: v1's Equation 6 uses an unnormalized likelihood factor independent of the candidate next token. v2 introduces token-dependent likelihood expectations and normalization factors, carrying corresponding log-partition terms through both variational bounds and their Appendix B proofs. Appendix C.5.1 also adds a Taylor-based surrogate derivation, a local-smoothness assumption and computational-complexity analysis.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses a serious deficiency in the central theoretical formulation by introducing a normalized, token-dependent likelihood tilt and revising the bounds accordingly. Explicit approximation limits and new convergence, noise and comparator controls substantially strengthen the paper's validity and evidential support. These gains outweigh remaining reporting weaknesses: inconsistent G2D2 prose and loss documentation, and language claims supported only by a small automated evaluation without uncertainty estimates.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same APS research work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material across substantial relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains the original image experiments and adds language-generation results, optimization-step ablations and measurement-noise robustness experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original APS experiments on image restoration, stylization and garment inpainting, including quantitative benchmarks, ablations and runtime measurements.

results.title: Test-Time Anchoring for Discrete Diffusion Posterior Sampling

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution bullets, and conclusion retain the same central claims: self-supervised verifier labeling, applicability across NLP tasks, and improved efficiency–quality trade-offs. The new experiments support these existing claims rather than redefine them; the introduction's numerical headline also remains unchanged.

C2.justification: Section 4.2 changes the SelfJudge-F versus AutoJudge-R interpretation from 'much less' to 'similar' performance degradation for the four-task comparison. New discussion explains judge/alignment complementarity, practical throughput gains, and larger-scale labeling feasibility. Section 3.2 also newly asserts preservation of distributional guarantees, without supplying a corresponding proof.

D1.justification: v2 substantially expands implementation and resource documentation: a vLLM implementation, A100 GPU counts and tensor parallelism, task-specific draft lengths, and four H100 GPUs for 70B label generation. It specifies the 500/220/500 prompt composition and 53,318 labels for the larger model. These accompany new experiments; the original labeling thresholds, logistic-regression search, and data-processing instructions remain.

E1.justification: Training still uses GSM8K, LiveCodeBench, and Dolly15k; evaluation retains GSM8K, MATH-500, LiveCodeBench, MMLU, and CNN/DailyMail. LiveCodeBench results move to appendix Table 6 rather than disappear. The added model sizes and serving implementation do not introduce new data or tasks.

E2.justification: The original external comparators remain, including SD, Top-k, AutoJudge, and AutoJudge+ in their corresponding comparisons. New Table 9 adds Judge-only verification as a comparator against alignment-only SD and combined SelfJudge. AutoJudge is explicitly not evaluated in the new 70B task-performance comparison.

E3.justification: Sections 4.4–4.5 add Llama-3.1-70B/8B experiments and vLLM throughput evaluation, with draft lengths of 20/15 for GSM8K/MMLU and single-/four-way tensor parallelism. Table 1 changes its aggregate from five tasks to four by excluding coding. The summarization-table caption also corrects the reported draft model from 0.5B to 1B, matching the main setup without establishing a rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds a component ablation testing alignment-only, judge-only, and combined verification (Appendix D.2, Table 9), a per-stage inference-time breakdown, and 70B label-generation cost analysis with million-label projections (Appendix D.1, Table 8). The existing suffix-length, threshold-sensitivity, and qualitative analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The existing four-fold coding evaluation is unchanged, and the added experiments introduce no new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial numerical evidence for 70B performance, throughput, verification ablations, and generation costs. For example, new Table 3 reports GSM8K throughput of 137.37 tokens/sec for SelfJudge-F versus 111.21 for SD. Original per-task results remain unchanged, but removing coding from Table 1's aggregate changes AutoJudge-R from +1.96/-2.7 to +0.49/-1.4 and SelfJudge-F from +2.06/-1.0 to +2.17/-1.6; these are aggregation changes, not same-setting performance improvements.

M1.justification: The semantic-preservation labeling procedure, logistic-regression verifier, and combined judge/alignment acceptance rule remain unchanged. Section 3.2's parallel/OR description expresses the same acceptance condition as v1's judge verification followed by alignment fallback; no new algorithmic component is established.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main narrative order remain intact. Local revisions clarify combined verification, training-only access to suffix tokens, and use of one verifier across tasks. New experimental subsections, an Impact Statement, acknowledgements, and affiliation updates extend the document without extensively rewriting its existing narrative.

P2.justification: The main text and references change from single-column to two-column conference formatting, with substantially revised typography and float placement. Five genuinely new result tables are added, while coding results are separated from Table 1 into appendix Table 6. Existing figures retain their content but are resized or relocated, and retained appendix tables are reorganized.

R1.justification: The cited works and substantive positioning relative to speculative decoding, JudgeDecoding, and AutoJudge are retained. AutoJudge's reference changes from an arXiv entry to a NeurIPS publication entry for the same work; bibliography styling does not constitute new research positioning.

T1.justification: The semantic-preservation definition, autoregressive decomposition, and Bayes-factor formulation remain unchanged. E5.justification: Appendix G adds statistical comparison through RSA correlation estimates between models, absent from v1. This is a limited statistical-analysis addition; neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial Qwen3-VL, agentic, unseen-object, transfer, and RSA results. For example, Qwen3-VL CFV accuracy is reported as 45.1% versus 28.7% for four-shot ICL; these are newly reported conditions, not improvements over the same v1 setting. Some entries are inconsistent: v2 retains 16.8% for OpenFlamingo CFV in Section 4.4, but Figure 7 plots approximately 15%.

M1.justification: The procedure remains causal head selection, aggregation of head activations, last-token vector injection, vector-only fine-tuning, and probability-weighted composition. P1.justification: The title and terminology broaden, method paragraphs receive targeted rewrites, and the one-shot rationale is expanded. Appendices are reorganized, and an Impact Statement replaces the former closing disclosures. The main section sequence and method subsection organization remain intact.

Dataset examples are separated from results, main performance figures emphasize cross-model averages, and detailed results move to the appendix. New ICL and similarity tables and agentic and transfer plots accompany retained or resized diagrams and ablations.

R1.justification: v2 adds LLaVA and Qwen-family references and removes the separate CLIP and RedPajama references. Positioning relative to function vectors, visual task vectors, and multimodal mechanistic interpretability remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Equations 1–6 retain the same activation averages, vector construction, additive intervention, training objective, and composition weights. Notation and explanations change, but no substantive mathematical derivation, assumption, theorem, or proof is added.

improvement.justification: The second architecture, agentic tasks, and unseen-object and cross-dataset tests substantially address v1's explicit limitations in architectural and relational generality. They strengthen evidence that function vectors transfer beyond the original controlled setting. Reporting problems temper the gains: agentic split counts conflict, the OpenFlamingo analogy plot disagrees with its text, and Figure 15 does not support uniformly superior fine-tuned performance. These weaknesses limit precision but do not outweigh the substantial improvement in evidential coverage.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same function-vector framework and research work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison despite the expanded scope and changed title.

after.justification: v2 reports original results for OpenFlamingo and Qwen3-VL, including agentic relations, unseen objects, cross-dataset transfer, and representation similarity.

results.title: Multimodal Function Vectors for Visual Relations

C1.justification: v1 claims its improved matrix-vector algorithm for any kernel satisfying the KDE assumption; v2 restricts the new improvement to Gaussian and Laplacian kernels and uses BIMW21 for Exponential and Rational Quadratic kernels. The stated Gaussian eigenvalue runtime improves from ε^{-(3+2p)} to ε^{-(3+p)} dependence. Mixed-sign hardness is redefined for the modified matrix family, and empirical corroboration becomes an additional contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations of practical error floors, the suitability of linear precision scaling, and Nyström's limitations for high-accuracy eigenvalue estimation. Section 12.4 explains size-versus-accuracy tradeoffs and qualifies timing conclusions by application, hardware, and KDE implementation. Sections 6 and 10 also make the revised kernel applicability and hardness boundaries explicit.

D1.justification: v2 adds an empirical implementation description absent from v1: Python 3.9.7, Numba, an M1 MacBook Pro with 32 GB RAM, random-sampling KDE with ceil(1/ε^2) samples, and a practical BIMW21 matrix-vector implementation using groups differing by 1+ε. Section 12.3 identifies scikit-learn's Nyström implementation. These materially expand reproducibility information.

E1.justification: v1 contains no empirical dataset coverage. v2 introduces evaluations of matrix-vector products and top-eigenvalue approximation using MNIST, Forest CoverType, and CLIP embeddings of CIFAR10, principally with the Exponential kernel. These are new linear-algebra evaluations on three represented data domains.

E2.justification: Beyond v1's theoretical comparisons, v2 adds evaluated comparators: Nyström approximation in Section 12.3 and Figure 7, exact matrix-vector computation in Section 12.4 and Figure 8, and the BIMW21 Gaussian matrix-vector method in Section 12.5's query-count and implementation comparisons.

E3.justification: v2 introduces experimental protocols absent from v1: main sample sizes of 1,000 MNIST, 10,000 CoverType, and 500 CLIP points; Exponential-kernel bandwidth targeting mean kernel value 0.001; relative-error metrics; and reference eigenvalues obtained by exact power iteration to convergence. Additional protocols vary bandwidth, iteration count, and dataset size, including timing studies at 10,000–30,000 points.

E4.justification: Section 12 adds empirical sensitivity analyses of eigenvalue error versus matrix-vector precision, convergence versus iteration count, and sensitivity to kernel bandwidth (Figures 4–6 and 9). Figure 8 examines when approximation becomes faster than exact computation as size and precision vary. These practical analyses have no empirical counterparts in v1.

E5.justification: v2 Section 12.1 introduces systematic repeated-run reporting: all experiments are stated to run independently at least 20 times, with one standard deviation shaded in plots. v1 has no empirical repeated-run or uncertainty reporting. This establishes a new reporting practice across the added experimental section.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive concrete results, including approximately linear eigenvalue-error scaling in Figures 4 and 6 and noise-limited convergence in Figure 5. Section 12.4 and Figure 8 report MNIST matrix-vector speedups at ε=0.1 of approximately 1.5 times at n=10,000 and over four times at n=30,000 versus exact computation. These are newly reported outcomes; v1 supplies no empirical values for a before-and-after performance comparison.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 replaces v1's fine geometric buckets and rounded weights with powers-of-two buckets and a new coordinate transformation that encodes weights in Gaussian or Laplacian KDE queries. The bucket count changes from Θ(log(n/ε)/ε) to Θ(log(n/ε)), with revised error handling. Algorithm 3 also changes its written threshold from τ=mε^3/C to τ=C/(mε^3). The noisy power-iteration procedure itself is retained.

P1.justification: v2 substantially reorganizes the narrative around Gaussian-specific main results and a consolidated technical overview in Section 4. Open questions move from v1 Section 9 to v2 Section 5; general-kernel discussion and proofs appear in appendix Sections 6–11, followed by empirical Section 12. The introduction and algorithm explanations are extensively revised.

P2.justification: v2 adds seven figures containing experimental plots and computational-cost comparisons (Figures 4–10). Table 1 gains an improvement-factor column and Gaussian-specific presentation. Table 2 removes two summary rows, whose revised theorems remain in Section 10. Existing figures and Table 3 are relocated, and Algorithm 1's displayed procedure is substantially rewritten.

R1.justification: v2 adds practical KDE and Nyström literature, including KAP22, GM16, and WS00, together with dataset and software citations. The discussion extends positioning against additive-error methods, while the central comparison with BIMW21 and most of the theoretical literature remain. This is a focused expansion supporting the new experiments.

T1.justification: v2 adds transformation Lemma 7.1 and substantially revises the matrix-vector proof and stated ε dependence. The mixed-sign lower bounds also change mathematically: Theorem 2.6 and v2 Theorem 10.2 use a modified matrix with exp(-||x_i+x_j||_2^2) off-diagonal entries and unit diagonal, replacing v1's ordinary Gaussian construction. The reduction changes from A union -B to A union B and explicitly bounds within-set interactions.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially improves the support and delimitation of its claims. The revised mixed-sign construction explicitly handles within-set interactions missing from v1's argument, while the new weighted-KDE method has a clearer kernel-specific basis. Repeated-run experiments add useful evidence about accuracy, convergence, and practical runtime tradeoffs. Narrower applicability is a substantive tradeoff, but makes the claims more precise. Runtime statements and pseudocode still need reconciliation, including Lemma 7.4's stated exponent versus its proof; these shortcomings do not outweigh the substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their complete text, equations, algorithms, tables, figures, and appended material support comparison, including matching results across substantial reorganization and renumbering.

after.justification: Section 12 reports original accuracy and runtime experiments on MNIST, Forest CoverType, and CLIP embeddings of CIFAR10. Figures 4–9 show experimental outcomes, including sensitivity studies and baseline comparisons.

before.justification: v1 reports algorithms, theoretical bounds, proofs, and mathematical illustrations, but no original experimental, simulation, or data-analysis outcomes.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the larger-model results as evidence of favorable scaling and adds discussion of applications and media-manipulation risks. E5.justification: The uncertainty-reporting practice is unchanged. Existing shaded plot bands remain without newly supplied explanations, seed counts, repeated-run protocols, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The listening study still reports 18 participants completing 10 trials each.

New results include matched Frieren and LoVA comparisons, runtime measurements, and the 1.01B variant's FAD of 1.05 and DeSync of 0.486; these are added comparisons and configurations, not improvements to the unchanged original model results.

Explicit mask-sampling and shortcut-target descriptions document existing components; the larger-model experiment does not establish a new algorithm or architectural component.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section order are retained. Changes include localized methodological explanations, an expanded related-work subsection, a shorter conclusion, new impact and acknowledgment sections, and an Audio Conditioning appendix subsection. Figure references replace previously unhelpful references back to Section 4.1.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from a single-column preprint to a two-column conference layout. Table 1 expands and Tables 3–6 are added. Figure 1 gains color coding and an expanded caption; the turkey-conditioning example moves from main-text Figure 4 to appendix Figure 5, while the existing performance curves become Figure 4. Appendix figures are redistributed across pages.

This broadens related-work coverage while retaining the existing novelty framing. Updates to publication years and venues for previously cited works are bibliographic changes.

These address important comparative and efficiency-evidence gaps in v1. Those shortcomings do not outweigh the substantial validation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SALSA-V. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and corresponding methods, equations, tables, and figures can be matched despite reformatting and relocation.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds baseline comparisons, generation-time measurements, and evaluation of a 1.01B-parameter variant.

before.justification: v1 reports original generation benchmarks, model ablations, conditioning and duration analyses, qualitative examples, and an 18-participant listening study.

These issues do not outweigh the stronger experimental support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same meta-awareness reinforcement-learning framework, renamed from MASA to MAPR. The complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables, and figures, support comparison despite extensive revision.

Reported automobile mean widths change from 21.085 to 18.957 for SR and from 31.058 to 15.667 for OCID, alongside revised trajectories and findings. These are changed reported results, not established same-setting improvements. Many earlier tabulated values remain, including the original entries of v1 Table 1, now v2 Table 3.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 corrects the adaptive update from alpha_t + gamma(alpha − cov_t) to alpha_t + gamma(alpha − (1 − cov_t)). This aligns the pseudocode with the update already used in v1's proof; it does not establish an implementation change. The residual decomposition, interval constructions, FWER selection, and other adaptive components remain.

P1.justification: V2 changes the title, author/venue material, terminology, and numerous explanatory sentences. It introduces a Related Work section, revises the non-adaptive experimental narrative, and reorganizes Appendix D around guidance and comparisons. Most existing method exposition, proof text, and the overall methodological sequence remain recognizable.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a two-column conference layout for the main text, relocates the original main results table to Appendix Table 3 with a CC column, and foregrounds coverage–width plots. It adds multi-panel baseline and single-stage figures, expands existing plots with ECI, and changes legends, captions, sizing, and figure placement throughout.

R1.justification: A dedicated Related Work section substantially expands positioning beyond v1's brief overview.
