It introduces medical-imaging uncertainty-propagation work and identifies Gong et al.'s cascaded-module method as the closest comparison, distinguishing its decomposition from the proposed FWER and adaptive approach. Foundational and survey citations are added, and several older references are removed.

T1.justification: V1 Proposition 2 becomes Proposition 5.5 with component quantiles at 1 − alpha/2, correcting the existence proof's unsupported inference from a 1 − 2alpha endpoint to 1 − alpha coverage. The Hoeffding exponent is also revised. V2 removes v1 Proposition 6 and Lemma A.3 concerning finite-sample hidden-Markov bounds, while retaining the long-run guarantee and mixing extension.

improvement.justification: V2 corrects an important gap in the scaling-existence argument and the inconsistent adaptive pseudocode. The previously missing close CC comparison and new single-stage controls materially strengthen evaluation and research positioning, while grid guidance and code-access information improve reproducibility. Removing the hidden-Markov finite-sample bound narrows theoretical scope, and some revised results retain inconsistent setting labels. Nevertheless, the gains in mathematical consistency and empirical scrutiny provide substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same residual-decomposition conformal prediction framework, despite the changed title and formatting. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete Appendices A–D support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains original synthetic and real-world experiments and adds baseline comparisons, parameter sweeps, and single-stage controls in Section 8 and Appendix D.

before.justification: V1 reports original synthetic experiments and automobile and stock forecasting results in Section 7 and Appendix D, including coverage, interval widths, and ablations.

results.title: Decomposition-Based Modular Conformal Prediction for Two-Stage Modeling

C1.justification: The central fixed-budget interference–performance claim and claimed first explicit demonstration remain. V2 reframes FPE as a controlled mechanistic intervention, explicitly attributes gains to disjoint parameter allocation beyond width alone, and extends its applicability claim to jointly learned representations (Sections 2.2, 5.2, and 7).

C2.justification: V2 substantially expands interpretation and limitations: it discusses disjointness controls, feature demand growing with width, preliminary circuit evidence, small-model scope, and hardware-dependent speedups and activation overhead. Appendix A.5 also explicitly acknowledges that its independent-support analysis does not enforce FPE's disjointness constraint.

D1.justification: V2 supplies a code-availability link, detailed trainable-embedding and CNN specifications, baseline mask-sampling and inference procedures, and storage-cost discussion. Algorithm A3 explicitly documents pre-training, expansion, and continued training. These additions substantially expand implementation guidance; the linked resource itself was not accessed.

E1.justification: The Boolean task and four vision dataset families remain. V2 adds raw-image CIFAR-100 classification alongside frozen CLIP features and nested 40/60/80/100-class classification scenarios, expanding input conditions and task coverage within existing domains (Sections 5.2–5.3).

E2.justification: V2 introduces two substantive comparators absent from v1: non-disjoint FPE with a fixed random mask, and DropConnect with resampled training masks and dense scaled test-time weights. Figure A6 and Tables A14–A15 explicitly evaluate these alternatives against FPE.

E3.justification: V1 lists batch size 500 and N=W=1000; v2 specifies batch size 64 with 25 pre-training and 25 fine-tuning epochs, retaining long training for the illustrative example. FashionMNIST warmup changes from 20 to 25 epochs. New experiments introduce matched mask controls and collision/clustering metrics. These are reported protocol changes, without establishing which retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds disjointness and mask-resampling controls, edge-collision measurements, clause-recovery analyses, and clustered-Gram case studies (A.8.4–A.9). The expansion-factor sensitivity panel in v1 Figure 6d is replaced by a class-count/width analysis. Depth, dynamic-mask, and 2:4 sparsity analyses were already present and are retained.

E5.justification: The main vision comparisons and Figure 6 now report ten trials where v1 generally reported five; ImageNet-1k already used ten. SEM bars and p<0.05 reporting remain. These reported-count changes do not establish additional runs, and v2's blanket ten-trial statement conflicts with retained five- and 30-trial appendix captions.

E6.justification: V2 revises vision plots and adds substantial joint-learning, class-demand, comparator, and circuit results. For example, Table A14 reports 64.8% for non-disjoint FPE versus 65.8% for FPE at width eight; at width four, the values are 51.0% versus 50.9%. These comparisons are new, while the original illustrative accuracies and several appendix tables remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The core disjoint splitting and magnitude re-pruning procedure is retained, including the previously documented deeper-network and structured-sparsity variants. V2 adds model adaptations with a trainable Boolean embedding and a jointly trained CNN feeding the classifier; expansion still operates on the classifier (Section A.7.1).

P1.justification: V2 extensively rewrites the introduction and conclusion, adds an explicit contribution list and scope statement, reorganizes methodology, and separates theory, symbolic results, vision results, and related work into distinct sections. The narrative shifts toward using expansion to study interference.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from single-column to two-column layout. The framework diagram moves to Appendix A.1, main performance figures are condensed while fuller displays remain in the appendix, and numerous accuracy tables and new control/circuit plots are added. Retained plots are distinguished from newly reported evidence.

R1.justification: The new Related Work section substantively distinguishes FPE from sparse autoencoders and DropConnect and discusses compatibility with quantization and distillation. Citations expand accordingly, including Cunningham et al., Wan et al., and GPTQ. This extends research positioning beyond relocating v1's pruning, growth, and superposition discussion.

T1.justification: The clause-coverage bound and expected collision-reduction derivation in Appendix A.5 are unchanged. V2 adds a distinct edge-level collision-rate definition—the proportion of traced edges used by at least two clauses—in A.9, a limited mathematical definition accompanying the new empirical analysis.

improvement.justification: V1 lacked controls isolating disjointness and evidence from jointly learned visual representations. V2 substantially addresses both gaps through Appendix A.8.4 and Section 5.2, while adding more direct circuit diagnostics, implementation guidance, and clearer applicability limits. These additions materially strengthen the central argument. Inconsistent trial-count summaries and preliminary mechanistic evidence remain limitations, but do not outweigh the substantial improvement in experimental support and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FPE research. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds joint representation learning, class-count sweeps, DropConnect comparisons, and circuit analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original Boolean-DNF and vision-classification experiments, including accuracy, interference measurements, and deeper-network and sparsity experiments.

results.title: Expand Neurons, Not Parameters

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: tangential updates carry semantic structure, their amplification promotes local likelihood gain, and TAG improves generation without retraining or additional denoiser evaluations. Broader experiments support these claims without materially redefining the headline contribution.

C2.justification: v1 emphasizes excessive amplification disturbing radial calibration. v2 develops a thin-shell interpretation, explains adaptive scaling and heuristic windowing, and explicitly limits the theory to local first-order gain rather than complete trajectory behavior. It also acknowledges approximate manifold geometry, interprets compositional and video findings, and discusses the perceptual-quality/FID tradeoff on Qwen-Image and the preliminary nature of 3D evidence.

D1.justification: Appendix F adds substantial reproducibility information beyond v1's brief software statement and code snippets: package/CUDA versions, GPU configuration, pipeline integration, guidance layers, SEG blur and SSG swap parameters, metric implementations, resizing, reference sets, and execution details. These disclosures do not by themselves establish changed experiments. Some conditional hyperparameters remain unspecified.

E1.justification: v2 adds compositional generation on T2I-CompBench Spatial and Complex, text-to-video generation on VBench prompts, and a qualitative image-to-3D test with SV3D. ImageNet and COCO remain represented, although COCO replaces ImageNet as the reference dataset for the main unconditional comparisons. The new compositional requirements and output modalities substantially broaden coverage.

E2.justification: v2 newly evaluates APG and TCFG in Table 6, UniPC in Table 9, and Self-Swap Guidance in Table 13. APG and TCFG were previously discussed but not experimentally compared. The SAG comparison rows from v1 Table 1 disappear, while PAG, SEG, CFG, and DPM++ remain in revised comparisons.

E3.justification: Reported settings change substantially: unconditional PAG/SEG compatibility uses PNDM instead of DDIM, conditional compatibility moves from SD1.5 to SDXL, and unconditional SD2.1/SDXL sample counts increase from 10K to 30K. FID computation changes from pytorch-fid to torch-fidelity. v2 adds aesthetic, preference, CMMD, compositional, perceptual-quality, and video metrics, alongside new windowing and adaptive-scaling protocols. These changes prevent direct comparison of many cross-version scores.

E4.justification: v2 adds analyses of when TAG should operate along the trajectory and whether adaptive normalization reduces amplification sensitivity (Tables 11–12). Computational analysis expands from latency to FLOPs, memory, and overhead, while Appendix C adds prompt-specific object and action error comparisons. The qualitative amplification sweep remains, but v1's numerical unconditional amplification curve is removed.

E5.justification: v2 newly specifies per-image seeds 0–29,999 for unconditional generation and seed 0 for conditional generation; this does not establish additional independent repetitions. v1's CLIPScore ± reporting disappears, while v2 Table 9 introduces IS ± values without explaining their statistical meaning. The earlier statement that latency averages 100 consecutive runs is also absent.

E6.justification: Benchmark results are extensively replaced and expanded under revised conditions. New Table 6 reports TAGcfg/APG/TCFG FID values of 19.29/19.52/20.72, with APG leading CLIPScore. Table 7 reports improved Qwen-Image perceptual scores but worse FID, 57.53 to 59.84. The original full-window SD1.5/DDIM FID of 67.805 survives in Table 11, alongside a new restricted-window result of 63.870. These are added findings, not evidence of uniform same-setting improvement over v1.

M1.justification: The core radial/tangential projection remains unchanged. Section 6.1 adds timestep-windowed application and norm-adaptive conditional amplification, which v1 only contemplated as future work. The conditional implementation also separates the TAG coefficient from the CFG coefficient, aligning it with v1's pseudocode and resolving inconsistent documentation. These are limited extensions and corrections to the retained sampler.

P1.justification: The experimental narrative is extensively rewritten and divided into new subsections; discussion is expanded, and conclusions and limitations are combined. Implementation material moves from Appendix B to D, with broader experiments, detailed positioning, and experimental documentation organized into additional appendices. The motivation is expanded, the title shortened, and C-TAG renamed TAGcfg.

P2.justification: v2 changes the main paper from single-column to two-column layout and substantially restructures tables and figure placement. It adds a geometric schematic, video and 3D illustrations, extensive comparison galleries, and methodological comparison/settings tables. v1 Figure 9 is retained as v2 Figure 10; the qualitative amplification panels remain with revised labels, while their accompanying numerical plot is removed.

R1.justification: Appendix E and Table 15 substantially expand research positioning, comparing the projected quantities, subspaces, objectives, and costs of TAG, APG, TCFG, Characteristic Guidance, Perp-Neg, MPGD, and SDDM. Newly cited literature also supports the expanded benchmarks, models, metrics, and Gaussian-shell motivation. This goes well beyond bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: Theorem 4.1 and its Appendix A proof are substantially retained. v2 adds an explicit step-budget constraint to the local optimization in Equation 11 and corrects the main theorem's equality condition to match v1's appendix. The exact squared-norm identity explaining radial perturbation in v1 Equation 21 is removed.

improvement.justification: v1 supports hallucination reduction mainly through general image-quality metrics and selected examples. v2 substantially strengthens that evidence with targeted compositional tests and direct APG/TCFG comparisons (Tables 5–6), while fuller implementation documentation and explicit theoretical limitations make the work easier to assess. These gains outweigh lost CLIPScore dispersion and reduced-NFE comparison detail, although incomplete conditional settings and unexplained uncertainty estimates remain weaknesses.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TAG research, with matching authors, core algorithm, theorem, and retained illustrations. The main text and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial expansion and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 reports original image-generation, compositional-faithfulness, video, and sensitivity results, plus SSG, EDM2, and qualitative image-to-3D experiments in Appendix B.

before.justification: v1 reports original image-generation evaluations in Tables 1–5, synthetic branching-distribution experiments in Figure 3, ablations, and additional generated examples in Appendix C.

results.title: TAG: Tangential Amplifying Guidance for Hallucination-Resistant Sampling

C1.justification: The abstract and central coverage/efficiency contributions largely remain. However, v2's introduction and Discussion qualify adaptation as domain-level recalibration using a shared target-batch threshold and describe novelty more specifically as the combination of semantic embeddings, density-ratio weighting and regularized conformal prediction.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations based on conditional score smoothness and effective sample size. Its rewritten Discussion explicitly identifies the unlabeled target-batch requirement, transductive evaluation, limited baseline comparisons and the distinction between larger prediction sets and intrinsic LLM reliability. These materially sharpen applicability and failure conditions beyond v1's limitations.

D1.justification: V2 adds a code-availability link and documents computing and reusing one threshold after offline target-batch adaptation. Appendix C retains the same data/logit source, excluded indices, XGBoost hyperparameters, seed and hardware. Comparable implementation details for the newly tested alternative components remain limited.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same processed MMLU multiple-choice data: 17 subjects and 272 ordered calibration–test subject pairs. The added component ablations retain this coverage; temporal, stylistic and open-ended-generation scenarios remain proposed future work.

E2.justification: Standard CP remains the only external conformal comparator actually evaluated in the LAC and APS experiments. Weighted and nonexchangeable CP receive discussion but no new comparative results; alternative embeddings and classifiers are DS-CP component ablations.

E3.justification: V2 explicitly specifies λ=max_i w_i throughout the experiments, replacing v1's default λ=1 recommendation. It adds controlled regularization and component sweeps and a calibration-and-test bootstrap check. The underlying data, preprocessing, 16 LLMs, 90% target coverage and coverage/set-size metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained APS and paired-coverage analyses, Appendix B adds a six-value regularization sweep across all models and controlled embedding and classifier sensitivity studies on four LLMs. Figures 5–10 examine MiniLM/MPNet/E5 and XGBoost/MLP/logistic regression, substantially expanding evidence about which components drive coverage and efficiency.

E5.justification: V2 newly reports bootstrapping both calibration and test instances with replacement and qualitatively compares bootstrap means and medians with full-data coverage. It supplies no replicate count or confidence intervals. The fixed classifier seed is retained, and ablation minima/medians/maxima describe variation across subject pairs rather than repeated-run uncertainty.

E6.justification: The LAC distributions in Figures 1–3 and APS distributions, matched from v1 Figures 5–7 to v2 Figures 11–13, change alongside the revised regularizer; updated set-size histograms include full six-answer sets. New Figures 5–10 report the coverage-versus-size regularization tradeoff and broadly similar behavior across alternative components. These are revised and additional results, not same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: Section 3 and Algorithm 1 change the default regularizer from λ=1 to λ=max_i w_i, affecting the conformal threshold within the existing framework. Embedding, density-ratio estimation and weighted quantiles remain; explicit target-batch inputs and shared-threshold outputs clarify the previously described workflow.

P1.justification: V2 substantially rewrites the coverage exposition and Discussion, recasts Algorithm 1, and introduces a dedicated related-work section. It also standardizes source/target terminology, compacts notation and reorganizes explanations around regularizer selection and structured appendix ablations.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column presentation to a two-column conference layout, with formerly full-page figures reduced and embedded beside text. Six ablation figures are added, and retained APS displays are relocated and renumbered from Figures 5–7 to Figures 11–13. This substantially changes visual organization and figure legibility.

R1.justification: New Section 6 substantially expands comparisons with existing LLM conformal methods, including new citations to Ren et al., Cherian et al. and Wang et al.'s ConU. It explicitly positions DS-CP against exchangeability-dependent methods, heuristic similarity weighting and approaches requiring specified shift mechanisms. Publication-metadata updates to existing references are not counted as new works.

T1.justification: Section 4 replaces unconditional total-variation bounds multiplied by weight suprema with expectations involving total variation conditional on the learned weights. It revises the independence assumptions and lower-bound proof, adds embedding-space score-smoothness bounds and an effective-sample-size proposition, and develops their proofs in Appendix A.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses an important theory–practice mismatch: v1 recommends λ=1 although its bounds require λ≥max_i w_i, while v2's default satisfies that condition. The weight-conditioned coverage analysis, supporting ablations and explicit batch/transductive limitations substantially strengthen rigor and interpretability. These gains outweigh reduced figure legibility, although comparative baseline breadth and bootstrap documentation remain limited.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DS-CP work. Their main text, equations, figures and Appendices A–C are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial reformatting and additions.

after.justification: V2 reports the corresponding MMLU analyses, revised results, and additional regularization, embedding-model and classifier ablations in Appendix B.

before.justification: V1 reports original CP-versus-DS-CP coverage and prediction-set analyses across 272 MMLU subject pairs and 16 LLMs, including APS results in Appendix B. Reusing existing model logits does not remove the originality of these analyses.

results.title: Domain-Shift-Aware Conformal Prediction for Large Language Models

C1.justification: Both versions claim a first source-free forecasting framework combining invariant disentanglement, LLM proxy denoising and distillation. The introduction's claimed average MSE/MAE improvements of 10.7%/9.3% remain unchanged; v3 also states both figures in the abstract. Renaming and added supporting experiments do not redefine the central contribution.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive applicability boundaries: weak zero-shot performance without adaptation and foundation-model advantages on Traffic. It also explains denoising as correction of systematic forecasting shifts, interprets regularization and decomposition tradeoffs, and discusses severe negative transfer at a low masking percentile and the weaker Chronos-proxy results.

D1.justification: v3 supplies a code-repository link, separate IDFL pseudocode, previously unspecified defaults including kernel length 25, masking percentile 0.3, correction strength 1, seasonal ratio 20%, and additional loss weights. Table 3 newly reports training time, GPU memory and target-model parameter count. These are documentation additions, not evidence that retained experiments used different settings.

E1.justification: v3 adds evaluations on Exchange, Solar and PEMS03 in Appendix A.2.17, extending coverage to exchange-rate forecasting and additional solar-energy and traffic data. The original seven datasets and alternative-source transfer pairs are retained.

E2.justification: The original eleven forecasting baselines remain. v3 additionally evaluates Chronos, UniTS, MOIRAI and Moment in Table 2; ADvSKM, CoDATS and SASA in Table 9; and moving-average, wavelet and Gaussian denoising alternatives in Table 5.

E3.justification: The original splits, 30% target adaptation and forecasting horizons are retained. Added evaluation designs include source-only zero-shot inference, foundation-model comparisons explicitly using lookback 336 and horizon 96, controlled proxy replacements, extensive parameter grids, and training-time/memory measurements. These broaden the protocol without establishing changes to the retained experiments.

E4.justification: v1 ablates LLM, proxy denoising and distillation and studies target-data size and learning rate. v3 additionally ablates IDFL and gradient invariance, examines five loss weights plus correction strength, masking percentile and decomposition kernel length, compares alternative denoisers and a Chronos proxy, and adds optimization and zero-shot analyses.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, standard deviations or significance tests. The added tables and plots continue reporting point estimates without statistical uncertainty.

E6.justification: All 432 numerical results in Table 1 and all 72 in v1 Table 2, retained as v3 Table 4, are unchanged. v3 adds substantial new results: for example, Table 2 reports Traffic MSE of 0.368 for MOIRAI versus 0.452 for TimeID, while Table 7 reports Exchange MSE of 0.102 for TimeID versus 0.111 for PatchTST. New ablation, sensitivity, zero-shot and efficiency results further expand the evidence.

M1.justification: Section 3 retains the decomposition, invariant masking, Fourier supervision, gradient alignment, proxy correction, distillation and overall objective. The renaming, additional hyperparameter disclosures and IDFL pseudocode do not establish a changed proposed method; the Chronos proxy replacement is an experimental variant.

P1.justification: v3 changes the title and framework name, rewrites the abstract and makes local wording corrections. It reorganizes experimental setup into subsections, moves dataset/baseline descriptions into the main text and relocates invariant-feature visualization to the appendix. The original introduction, methodological exposition and overall section sequence remain largely intact.

P2.justification: The document changes from a single-column to a two-column layout, extensively resizing and rearranging displays. Ablation panels are expanded and regrouped, the invariant-feature visualization is relocated, and numerous new comparison tables, sensitivity plots, a training-loss plot and an additional algorithm display materially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v3 substantially expands references and comparative positioning around time-series foundation models and domain-adaptation methods. Whereas v1 explicitly excluded foundation-model comparisons, v3 compares against them and discusses single-source adaptation relative to broad pretraining, alongside new comparisons with ADvSKM, CoDATS and SASA.

T1.justification: The forecasting, invariant-feature and proxy-confidence definitions in Appendix A.1 are retained, as are the substantive mathematical arguments. Added standard MAE/MSE formulas and derivative-notation cleanup do not introduce new theory, assumptions or proofs.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses important validation gaps in v1 by directly testing the central IDFL and gradient-invariance components, adding stronger comparison families, and documenting failure conditions. Newly disclosed defaults, resource measurements and code-access information substantially improve auditability despite unchanged main benchmark scores. Some new protocols remain thinly specified, the added IDFL pseudocode has loss-notation inconsistencies, and statistical uncertainty remains absent, but the gains in component validation and applicability assessment are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research framework, renamed from TimePD to TimeID. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains these empirical results and adds original baseline comparisons, dataset evaluations, sensitivity analyses, zero-shot experiments and resource measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original forecasting comparisons, component ablations, sensitivity experiments and prediction visualizations in Section 4 and Appendix A.3.

results.title: Invariant Representation Learning for Source-Free Time Series Forecasting with LLM-Centric Proxy Denoising

C1.justification: v2 makes robust sliding-window difficulty estimation and its claimed correspondence with human problem-solving explicit central contributions, extending v1's entropy-triggered compression framing. It also broadens and quantifies the headline efficiency claim to 13%–49% token reductions across mathematics and GPQA. The overarching intra-response adaptive-reasoning claim remains.

C2.justification: v2 introduces interpretations concerning transferable thresholds, the benefits of segment-level confidence, difficulty-dependent switching, and the limited benefits of scaling concise-training data. It removes v1's interpretation that reasoning-length control resides primarily in MLPs. The explicit limitations concerning calibration, non-local dependencies, and an unlearned controller are also removed.

D1.justification: v2 adds Algorithm 1, prompt templates, decoding settings, vLLM serving information, SFTTrainer/DeepSpeed details, and a code-access link. Appendix B documents selecting the shortest correct response from ten teacher samples and changes reported hardware from four A100s to four H100s. Conversely, v1's explicit flexible-match answer-extraction rule is no longer documented.

E1.justification: The three mathematics evaluation benchmarks remain, while v2 adds GPQA-Diamond, HumanEval, LiveCodeBench, StrategyQA, and CommonsenseQA, extending evaluation to science, executable code, and commonsense reasoning. Default adapter training moves from GSM8K to DeepScaleR-40K; GSM8K remains in a training-data comparison that also includes OpenMathReasoning-300K.

E2.justification: v2 adds fixed concise-mode controls, O1-Pruner, and Thinkless. Its named-method comparison uses BeConcise (Renze and Guven) instead of v1's Prompt baseline (Han et al.), removes ConciseHint, and retains CoT-Valve, DEER, and NoWait. Unlike v1's comparisons across multiple backbones, the expanded named-baseline panel is reported only for Qwen3-8B.

E3.justification: The main evaluation adds DeepSeek-R1-7B and replaces QwQ-32B-Preview with QwQ-32B. Training changes from up to ten epochs to one, with LoRA rank/scaling changing from 2/8 to 32/64. v2 specifies a uniform 16,384-token cap and adds Pass@2–5 evaluation, controller controls, and measured latency protocols.

E4.justification: v2 adds explicit threshold/window ablations, random/reverse/keyword switching controls, alternative distribution-based signals, training-data comparisons, switching statistics, and latency analysis. v1's layerwise LoRA study and three-model budget-sweep plots are removed. The house-flipping case is retained in Appendix D, while other qualitative examples are replaced.

E5.justification: Five-independent-run averaging is retained; no increased run count is established. v2 adds small capped error bars to the latency plot in Figure 6, but does not define their statistical meaning. Accuracy tables continue to report means without uncertainty intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: Main numerical results are extensively replaced, and new benchmark, ablation, latency, and Pass@k results are added. For example, the Qwen3-8B/AIME24 MixReasoning entry changes from 64.33% and 10,738 tokens in v1 to 67.33% and 8,873 tokens in v2. These are results under revised methods and training, not controlled same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: Section 3.2 replaces single-token normalized entropy and backward/forward regeneration windows with sliding-window averages of negative top-k log-probabilities. v2 also introduces a minimum dwell time and one-window rollback. These substantially change the switching procedure, while retaining the LoRA-based mode-control framework and training objective.

P1.justification: The introduction is extensively rewritten around fast/slow reasoning and explicit contributions, and the method is reorganized around how and when to switch. Experiments are restructured into main results, baseline comparisons, ablations, and further analysis. The appendix is reorganized into algorithm, implementation, theoretical/empirical analysis, and qualitative-example sections.

P2.justification: v2 changes the main text to a two-column layout, restructures the main results into separate fixed-mode and named-baseline tables, and revises the controller schematic. It adds confidence visualizations, ablation displays, latency plots, and appendix tables. The retained house-flipping figure moves to the appendix, while the earlier budget-sweep and layerwise figures disappear.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning through dual-process cognition, confidence-based inference including DeepConf, and formal uncertainty measures. It also adds literature supporting the new datasets and serving implementation, while removing the earlier MLP-memory positioning and associated references. The broad distinctions from compression, hybrid reasoning, and speculation remain.

T1.justification: Beyond revised controller definitions, v2 adds Proposition C.1 and a proof characterizing confidence through reverse KL and establishing monotonicity under majorization at fixed top-k probability mass. Appendices C.2–C.3 add mathematical comparisons with alternative signals and an assumption-dependent switching-overhead bound; v1 has no corresponding proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important evidence gaps in v1 through direct switching-control comparisons, measured end-to-end latency, and evaluation beyond mathematics. Algorithm 1, the detailed training recipe, and the confidence-score proof substantially improve assessability and reproducibility. Removing explicit limitations and leaving accuracy uncertainty unquantified are drawbacks, but the stronger validation of the mechanism and practical efficiency provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MixReasoning and contain readable text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Retained material can be matched despite substantial methodological revisions and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 reports original benchmark results, controller and training-data ablations, switching behavior, and latency measurements. Its appendices add coding, commonsense, and Pass@k results.

before.justification: v1 reports original accuracy and token-use results on three mathematics benchmarks, budget sweeps, layerwise LoRA ablations, and qualitative examples.

results.title: MixReasoning: Switching Modes to Think

C1.justification: The introduction adds explicit reasoning annotations supporting reasoning-aware training and evaluation, and the abstract broadens benchmarking to multimodal foundation models. The central claims about de-anonymized observability data, difficult temporal dynamics, and the importance of absolute scale remain substantially unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations linking scale to fault discrimination and location inference, discusses optimization and reasoning-capacity tradeoffs, and expands forecasting mechanisms in Appendix H. It also asserts generalizability beyond the testbed and insensitivity to anomaly-duration priors. Appendix F.2 newly claims performance gains from reasoning training, although Tables 2–4 and 6 show lower scores for +Thinking than its non-thinking counterpart.

D1.justification: New appendices document trace-generation models, conditioning metadata, scoring weights, filtering, training stages, and LoRA settings. v2 also clarifies corpus counts, revises the sample schema, and discloses that forecasting includes normal and anomalous sequences. The printed direct dataset URL disappears while the code URL remains; this establishes an access-information change, not loss of dataset availability.

E1.justification: The limited extension is reasoning-supervised training and qualitative assessment of reasoning outputs for existing anomaly and network Q&A tasks. The underlying 5G scenarios, applications, KPIs, and fault coverage remain unchanged. Recasting existing anomaly tasks as Q&A and reporting windowed sample counts do not establish new measurement coverage.

E2.justification: Tables 2–4 and 6 add Toto+Qwen-3-4B and its +Thinking variant. Table 5 adds DLinear and per-KPI linear regression. Mantis without scaling and additional scale-aware variants provide further evaluated comparisons. The original comparator families are retained.

E3.justification: Section 4.1 changes the normal/anomalous evaluation ratio from 95/5 to 80/20 while retaining 1,000 samples. The reported training schedule changes from learning rate 0.0001, batch size 64, and 10 epochs to 0.001, 32, and 5 epochs. New multimodal training stages and scale controls are introduced. These documented revisions do not establish which retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 directly tests scale information through Mantis component removal and NME additions across five architectures and six tasks (Section 4.6, Table 7). Appendix F adds candidate-versus-selected trace-score analysis and diagnostic reasoning examples. The original forecasting failure examples are retained and relocated, rather than constituting new experiments.

E5.justification: Neither version reports benchmark uncertainty through repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The new trace-score distributions and quantiles describe candidate quality, rather than uncertainty in benchmark performance estimates.

E6.justification: Table 2 replaces scores under the revised class mix, including Mantis F1 changing from 0.711 to 0.800; this is not a same-setting gain. Table 4 changes FEDformer accuracy from 0.355 to 0.495 and Informer from 0.600 to 0.654, alongside revised reported training settings. Substantial new results cover multimodal models, classical forecasting baselines, scale ablations, and trace selection. Most retained Table 3 and language-model Table 6 results remain equivalent after rounding or percentage conversion.

M1.justification: v2 adds a reasoning-trace synthesis pipeline using metadata conditioning, rejection sampling, and composite scoring (Appendix F). It also introduces Toto+Qwen3-4B models with encoder pre-alignment, LoRA fine-tuning, and reasoning supervision, plus NME scale-encoding adaptations. These are procedural and architectural additions; the original measurement and synthetic-anomaly pipelines largely remain.

P1.justification: The main narrative is edited and condensed while retaining its overall organization. Q&A curation absorbs the separate statistics subsection, the closing discussion is reorganized, and forecasting discussion moves to Appendix H. Training details move from Appendix F to G after the new reasoning appendix; much of the original appendix prose remains intact.

P2.justification: v2 converts the main text and references from single-column to two-column presentation and extensively rearranges displays. Table 1 is restructured, benchmark tables gain rows, Figure 5 is revised, and Table 7 plus reasoning-quality Figures 17–18 are added. The original forecasting Figure 7 becomes Appendix H Figure 19.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting reasoning training, early fusion, anomaly prevalence, and specific telecommunications fault mechanisms, including Parker, Zhang, Chameleon, and ADBench. Some earlier references, including citations for retained time-series baselines, disappear. The principal positioning against anonymized and normalized observability datasets remains unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix F.1 adds mathematical definitions of the composite trace-selection score and its weighted reasoning and format components, including task-specific correctness scoring (Equations 1–3). Neither version provides theoretical guarantees or proofs, and the existing anomaly-generation mathematics is retained.

improvement.justification: v1 supported its central scale claim mainly through comparisons between different models; v2 adds direct component-removal and scale-addition controls, substantially strengthening that evidence. Trained multimodal comparisons and detailed reasoning-data procedures also improve the benchmark's usefulness and reproducibility. The reasoning contribution remains less convincing: validation uses the selection score itself, and Appendix F.2 claims gains despite lower +Thinking results. These weaknesses qualify the additions but do not outweigh the stronger experimental support for the paper's central contribution.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe TelecomTS, and their complete main texts, appendices, tables, figures, and equations support comparison. Retained material can be matched despite substantial layout changes and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical evaluations and adds multimodal model results, controlled scale ablations, and reasoning-trace analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original 5G measurements, synthetic anomaly generation, and model evaluations for detection, localization, root cause analysis, forecasting, and question answering.

results.title: TelecomTS: A Multi-Modal Observability Dataset for Time Series and Language Analysis

C1.justification: The abstract and three listed contributions retain hybrid co-evolution, experience-driven learning, mutual model benefits, and applicability beyond molecular design. The introduction adds an explicit fixed-budget qualification to the performance claim. The additional cross-domain experiments principally support extensibility already claimed in v1 rather than redefine the core contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations of docking as evidence against exploiting a single predictor, including the GSK3β trade-off. Appendices newly argue practical synthesizability, cost efficiency, and transferable similarity mechanisms. A limitations section identifies primarily molecular validation and leaves continuous and mixed-variable settings for future work. Some interpretations exceed the evidence, notably treating favorable SA scores as proof of a hard constraint.

D1.justification: v2 supplies a concrete code-repository address instead of only asserting anonymous code/data availability. New documentation includes a 5,000-candidate budget, 50/32 API/local configuration, eight A800 40GB GPUs, runtime and API costs, TDC/RDKit scoring information, task representations and normalization, and detailed 50% elite/50% Pareto selection with duplicate removal. These substantially expand implementation disclosure.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates five-objective molecular optimization initialized from ZINC. v2 retains this coverage and adds Circle Packing, multi-objective traveling salesman, and capacitated vehicle routing experiments, substantially broadening the represented domains and optimization requirements.

E2.justification: v2 Table 1 adds reported molecular comparisons with GB-GA, REINVENT, MoLLEO, GFlowNet, and DyMol alongside the retained internal comparisons. Table 2 adds GPT-4o plus Gemini as a two-API comparator. The new routing experiments evaluate Pymoo, AIDE, FunSearch, ReEvo, and AlphaEvolve; their earlier appearance as citations did not constitute these comparisons.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include initial-population versus final-top-10 docking, MOTSP with n=100, MOCVRP with n=100 and m=20, and packing with n=26 and 31. Table 2 introduces controlled sweeps of similarity quantiles, API/local allocation, and update intervals. The original molecular initialization and model identities remain unchanged; newly disclosed resource settings do not establish changes to the earlier experiments.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained evolution, output-distribution, and loss analyses, v2 adds similarity-strategy, call-allocation, update-frequency, and two-API ablations in Table 2. Figure 6 compares training with and without similarity filtering. Docking validation and appendix analyses of synthetic accessibility and computational cost address additional questions about evaluator dependence and practical usefulness.

E5.justification: Table 1 changes its stated aggregation from mean and standard deviation over ten runs to five runs, although the shared numerical entries remain unchanged. This is a definite reporting revision, but the PDFs do not explain whether it corrects the caption or reflects different runs. No new significance-testing procedure is introduced.

E6.justification: Shared Table 1 values are retained, including MCCE Top1 fitness 4.35±0.17 and HV 0.847±0.138. New baseline rows show GFlowNet HV 0.871±0.288, exceeding MCCE. Extensive new ablation, docking, packing, routing, accessibility, and cost results are reported; Table 5 places MCCE first on MOCVRP but third on MOTSP. The former Top100 fitness, Top1 AUC, and Top100 AUC entries are omitted.

M1.justification: The alternating frozen/local models, DPO objective, similarity bands, and fallback pair construction are retained. Appendix A9 newly details elite/Pareto population selection, while Table 9 specifies task-dependent similarities already allowed by the framework. These additions document implementation and instantiation without establishing a revision to the underlying method.

P1.justification: v2 retitles the paper, moves related work after experiments, removes the preliminary section, rewrites the main-results discussion and conclusion, and adds limitations and expanded appendix explanations. Separate ethics, reproducibility, and LLM-usage sections disappear, while impact and acknowledgements sections appear. The restructuring also introduces unresolved 'Table ??' references and retains a now-incorrect Section 4.3 pointer.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from single-column to two-column formatting, with extensive figure relocation and resizing. Table 1 is reorganized into internal and external comparisons with fewer metric columns. Eight additional tables and a new two-panel stability figure are introduced, and algorithms gain numbered formatting. Existing Figures 1–5 largely retain their visual content.

R1.justification: The collaboration discussion now acknowledges training-based prior systems, including CollabLLM, trained small-model orchestration, and Collab-RAG. It refines MCCE's positioning around shared-task co-evolution versus one-sided or function-specific adaptation. Additional molecular optimization, combinatorial benchmarking, and synthetic-accessibility literature broadens the research context; renamed references to the same works are not separate additions.

T1.justification: v2 removes v1 Section 3's formal preliminaries, including the expected-return objective, SFT loss, and GFlowNet probability and flow equations. The substantive MCCE equations and appendix DPO objective remain equivalent despite renumbering. Neither version supplies theoretical guarantees or proofs for MCCE.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's reliance on internal comparisons through external molecular baselines, targeted ablations, and orthogonal docking validation. Selection and resource documentation also materially improve auditability. These gains outweigh important unresolved weaknesses: unchanged results are relabeled from ten to five runs, several new baselines exceed MCCE's HV despite broad superiority claims, and the circle-packing score is not clearly reconciled with its stated objective.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MCCE research work despite the revised title and organization. All 16 pages of v1 and 19 pages of v2, including equations, tables, figures, and appendices, support comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original molecular experiments and adds baseline comparisons, ablations, docking results, combinatorial optimization results, and resource analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original molecular optimization experiments, model comparisons in Table 1, output-distribution analyses, and training and co-evolution curves.

results.title: MCCE: A Framework for Multi-LLM Collaborative Search in Discrete Spaces with Similarity-Filtered Preference Learning

C1.justification: The three-component contribution and headline accuracy and convergence claims remain substantially the same. V3 explicitly extends the introduction's superiority claim to DAPO and narrows the ICL novelty assertion from effectiveness within RL generally to effectiveness within RLVR training.

C2.justification: V3 adds substantive interpretations of correctness-gated shaping, context limits favoring shorter solutions, and training/test difficulty mismatch making test-time ICL unhelpful. It newly discusses limits on model scale and task diversity and possible teacher-generated exemplars. V1's case-specific interpretations of reasoning errors are removed.

D1.justification: V3 newly documents DAPO-Math-17k and DeepCoder training sources and sampling counts, corpus initialization, precomputed retrieval lookups, standard evaluation without ICL, and component timings. It also provides additional model settings and announces public code and datasets through an access link absent from v1.

E1.justification: The math and code task domains remain. Appendices D-F add evaluations with truncated demonstrations, weaker or random retrieval, and test-time ICL, extending input conditions within existing tasks. Newly identifying the training-data sources does not establish that the underlying training data changed.

E2.justification: V1 evaluates GRPO and GSPO. V3 adds three-component DAPO and TreePO Sampling to corresponding Qwen comparisons, and CurES in Appendix G. Table 5 also newly compares component ablations against DAPO and TreePO Sampling; these are evaluated comparators, not merely additional citations.

E3.justification: V3 adds Llama-3.2-3B with distinct generation and decoding settings, comparisons at k=4, 8, 16, and 32, and a latency experiment using batch size 64 and 256 rollouts per prompt. Figure 3a switches from pass@4 to pass@1. These extend evaluation protocols beyond the largely retained Qwen settings.

E4.justification: V3 adds an isolated rollout-planner ablation, allocator hyperparameter sensitivity, length-bias and truncation analyses, train-versus-test ICL controls, retrieval-quality experiments, and allocation-distribution diagnostics. Earlier AS/ICL ablations remain, but the two worked GSPO/XRPO reasoning comparisons in v1 Appendix B are removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports training-run counts, random seeds, significance tests, or benchmark confidence intervals. V3 retains the existing mean-and-standard-deviation reporting across hyperparameter settings and extends it to another sweep. Added length z-scores and percentiles describe response distributions rather than experimental uncertainty.

E6.justification: V3 adds extensive benchmark and analysis results, including Llama average pass@1 of 4.48 versus GRPO's 4.17 and measured training overhead of 4.7%. LCBv5 scores and case-study outcomes disappear. Most matched Qwen3 scores remain, but new Table 5 reports HMMT pass@1/cons@32 of 21.66/23.33, conflicting with 22.29/26.67 retained in Table 1.

M1.justification: The three core components and Equations (1)-(6) remain unchanged. However, Algorithm 1 changes its corpus-update comment from adding only correct, non-ICL rollouts to adding correct rollouts. V3 does not establish whether ICL-generated successes become eligible or whether this is merely abbreviated documentation.

P1.justification: V3 merges background and related work, moves motivation into the method section, substantially rewrites existing motivation and positioning paragraphs, and reorganizes the experimental narrative and appendices. The ICL-template material is retained in Appendix C, while the former case-study appendix is replaced by organized analytical sections.

P2.justification: The document changes from single-column to two-column layout, adds a framework schematic and allocation histogram, and splits and expands result tables. Existing convergence plots move from main-text Figure 2 to appendix Figure 5. The boxed reasoning examples disappear, and the ICL template is reformatted.

R1.justification: Related work expands substantially to adaptive allocation, replay, and agent/meta-RL approaches, including CurES, GVM-RAFT, Knapsack RL, TreePO, CEL, LaMer, and RePO. V3 more explicitly positions runtime rollout allocation against prompt selection and distinguishes single-turn RLVR seeding from replay and multi-turn adaptation.

T1.justification: Appendix B adds a limited latency model and derivation of large-budget and worst-case overhead behavior, absent from v1. The optimizer's existing mathematics remains unchanged. The new derivation's ceiling-to-fraction equalities in Equations (7)-(8) are not generally valid.

improvement.justification: V3 addresses important validation gaps through relevant adaptive-sampling competitors, an isolated planner ablation, controls for test-time ICL, and measured per-step overhead. Training-source and implementation disclosures also substantially improve reproducibility. These gains outweigh the removed LCBv5 scores and illustrative cases, although conflicting HMMT entries in Tables 1 and 5 and mathematical errors in Appendix B limit confidence in some additions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same XRPO research. All 19 pages of v1 and 15 pages of v3, including equations, figures, tables, and appendices, are readable and support comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: V3 retains original experimental results and adds model and baseline comparisons, latency measurements, and several controlled analyses of ICL and rollout allocation.

before.justification: V1 reports original math and code benchmark results, training-convergence measurements, component ablations, hyperparameter experiments, and reasoning case studies.

results.title: XRPO: Pushing the Limits of GRPO with Targeted Exploration and Exploitation

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same headline contributions: the small-surrogate-loss plus path-length bound, a Polyak-style learning rate, the convolutional Fenchel–Young extension, and tight dependence on F_T and P_T. The revised lower bound and additional experiments strengthen support for these retained claims.

C2.justification: Section 3.3 qualifies the previous assertion of strong adaptivity as an interval-wise guarantee akin to strongly adaptive bounds. Section 3 also newly notes that all known tasks admitting the required decoding satisfy Assumption 3.1, refining the discussion of applicability.

D1.justification: V2 adds MNIST normalization and sampling instructions and quantifies decoding cost through an epsilon-dependent oracle-call estimate in Section 3.4. Hardware information is retained. However, the numerical finite eta_0 used for the experiments is not specified after the initialization revision.

E1.justification: Appendix E expands from two-dimensional synthetic binary classification to also evaluate three-class MNIST image streams. Each MNIST segment uses a newly sampled set of three digits, adding real-image data and changing-class scenarios while retaining the synthetic label-flip scenarios.

E2.justification: Both versions compare Polyak-style learning rates against Constant and AdaGrad. V2 extends this same comparator set to MNIST without adding or removing comparison methods.

E3.justification: The added MNIST protocol specifies 784-dimensional normalized images and within-segment sampling with replacement. The 10,000-round horizon, diameter D = 20, and cumulative-mistake metric remain. V2 also removes v1's inconsistent explicit 1/(2 ln 2) expansion of alpha/M for Constant; the retained synthetic curves do not establish that those experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix E extends the existing sensitivity analysis over 1, 10, and 100 changes to MNIST's changing digit subsets. This adds evidence about learning-rate robustness as non-stationarity increases, while retaining the original synthetic analysis.

E5.justification: Both versions report means and 95% confidence intervals over 10 independent trials per configuration. MNIST uses the same reporting practice; no additional statistical procedure or increased repeat count is stated.

E6.justification: Figure 2(d–f) adds MNIST mistake trajectories: Polyak-style trails AdaGrad slightly with one change but performs better with 10 and 100 changes. These substantially extend the empirical evidence. The synthetic trajectories from v1 Figure 1 are retained in v2 Figure 2(a–c), rather than showing improved same-setting performance.

M1.justification: Section 3.4 changes Equation (5)'s initialization from eta_0 = infinity to any finite eta_0 >= alpha/M, which can cap early updates. The OGD update, decoding methods, and surrogate losses otherwise remain unchanged.

P1.justification: V2 copyedits the prose, refines introductory explanations, adds a contribution list and impact statement, and reorganizes Appendix E into setup, datasets, methods, and results. The main section sequence and Appendix A–G organization remain intact.

P2.justification: V2 adds a conceptual label-flip illustration as Figure 1 and incorporates the retained three synthetic panels into a six-panel Figure 2 with MNIST results. It also adjusts paragraph spacing, affiliation formatting, and reference presentation.

R1.justification: Section 2.3 replaces the suggestion that the decreasing-step OGD bound is new with attribution to Hall and Willett (2015). V2 also adds Polyak-stepsize literature, the MNIST reference, and a stability-based non-stationarity connection. The broader structured-prediction positioning remains.

T1.justification: Theorem 5.1 and Appendix G replace separate comparator constructions with a mixed-block construction establishing a joint Omega(F_T + P_T) lower bound for one comparator sequence. Appendix G also changes the domain from a sphere to a convex ball and corrects the smooth-hinge expression. Appendix D removes the erroneous W_{T+1} = W_T identification, and Appendix F.2 repairs the excess-risk identity using the mean label encoding.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens mathematical reliability through the corrected proof details and joint lower-bound construction in Theorem 5.1 and Appendices D, F.2, and G. MNIST experiments also address v1's reliance on a single synthetic setting, while revised attribution improves scholarly accuracy. These gains strengthen both the theoretical and empirical justification of the paper, despite the remaining unspecified experimental eta_0.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, and Appendices A–G are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: Appendix E retains the synthetic experiments and adds original MNIST experiments, with cumulative mistakes and confidence intervals.

before.justification: Appendix E reports original synthetic online-classification experiments comparing three learning rates under different label-flip frequencies.

results.title: Non-Stationary Online Structured Prediction with Surrogate Losses

C1.justification: The training-free planning claim remains, but v2 adds predicting TTGS utility without rollouts as a main contribution. Its introduction and conclusion explicitly contrast strong locomotion benefits with negligible manipulation gains and assert graceful fallback when favorable conditions fail. This materially extends the paper's contribution and applicability claims.

C2.justification: v2 develops explanations involving missing intermediate states, local metric consistency, graph disconnections, and replanning oscillations, and discusses dataset-access requirements and local execution failures. It also replaces v1's caution about suboptimal subgoals with stronger safe-fallback interpretations. Appendix F's assertion of no performance risk exceeds the evidence, including degradations reported in Table 4.

D1.justification: v2 substantially expands reproducibility information: learner implementation sources, training-goal sampling distributions, OTA integration details, clustering parameters, manual tuning and selection procedures, expanded hyperparameter tables, and per-environment runtime measurements with GPU/CPU specifications. These disclosures go well beyond v1's value mappings and compact hyperparameter appendix.

E1.justification: v2 adds manipulation evaluation on scene-play-v0, cube-triple-play-v0, puzzle-4x5-play-v0, and puzzle-4x6-play-v0 (Table 2). This extends the empirical scope beyond v1's locomotion and maze-navigation evaluations to substantially different goal-reaching tasks.

E2.justification: v2 adds SAW and OTA, each evaluated with and without TTGS, plus an L2-kNN landmark planner (Table 7). GAS and CompDiffuser remain. GAS's pointmaze comparisons move into the fixed-setting comparison in Table 5, while its two visual-humanoid comparisons from v1 are omitted.

E3.justification: New protocols include fixed-hyperparameter TTGS/GAS comparisons, kNN and graph-size sweeps, million-triplet global/local distance sampling, and threshold-triggered replanning. The 50-rollout evaluation convention remains. The reported HIQL pointmaze-giant-stitch setting changes from (tau,T)=(12,24) in v1 Table 4 to (24,48) in v2 Table 14; the retained score does not establish that the experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained waypoint, no-penalty, and threshold ablations, v2 adds hard-threshold connectivity tests, L2-kNN sensitivity, triangle-inequality measurements, manipulation geometry and hop-ratio analyses, fixed-parameter transfer, graph-size scaling, and replanning tests. Table 9 also quantifies the clustering comparison that v1 described only through preliminary findings.

E5.justification: Eight-seed mean-and-standard-deviation reporting is retained. v2 newly states that hyperparameter screening used one random seed and that fixed seeds do not fix OGBench start/goal positions (Appendices A and L). These are additional seed disclosures, not evidence of increased evaluation replication or new significance-testing procedures.

E6.justification: The original HIQL/GCIQL/QRL results remain unchanged across all 15 shared benchmark rows. v2 adds scores for 12 previously untabulated maze configurations, SAW/OTA, manipulation, and supplementary analyses. GAS's main humanoidmaze-giant-stitch result changes from 8.3±4.5 to 82.4±2.5 with changed result provenance; fixed-antmaze-setting results remain separately in Table 5, so this is not a same-setting performance gain.

M1.justification: The core graph construction, soft penalty, Dijkstra search, and adaptive execution algorithm remain unchanged. Appendix B adds an OTA-specific distance adapter that blends primitive-step and option-level estimates, while Section 4.3 introduces a separate rollout-free hop-ratio diagnostic. These are bounded extensions rather than a redesign of TTGS.

P1.justification: The abstract and substantial portions of the introduction, related work, limitations, and conclusion are rewritten. Experiments gain dedicated manipulation and prediction subsections, while retained appendix material is reorganized within a much broader appendix structure. The narrative revision extends beyond inserting new results.

P2.justification: The main text changes to a two-column conference layout. Figures 3 and 4 gain additional methods and an ablation, Figure 5 adds four geometry panels, and numerous experimental tables are introduced. The main comparison and hyperparameter tables gain rows and columns; v1's threshold-sweep table is retained as v2 Table 3.

R1.justification: Section 5 substantially expands distinctions among online and offline graph planners, discussing GSP, IM-DSG, Bagatella and Martius, motion planning, and TAMP, alongside newer GCRL methods. Appendix A additionally claims TTGS is the first purely offline, test-time method in this setting. This changes research positioning beyond bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: v2 adds the formal largest-hop-ratio definition, a hindsight-relabeling/TD derivation, and OTA option-to-step conversion and blending equations. It removes v1 Appendix C's explicit temporal-efficiency-filter formula. These are limited mathematical additions and removals; the principal value-to-distance identities remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses substantial validation gaps through direct connectivity and landmark-planner controls, manipulation applicability tests, and separate repository-result and fixed-setting GAS comparisons. Fuller implementation, tuning, and runtime documentation also improves reproducibility. These gains outweigh an important qualification: the new blanket safe-fallback/no-risk claims conflict with Table 4, where QRL on antmaze-medium-stitch scores 62.0% without TTGS versus 40.1% with it.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TTGS research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial expansion and reformatting.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and reports additional learner comparisons, manipulation results, and original diagnostic, connectivity, scaling, and replanning analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original OGBench evaluations of TTGS with HIQL, GCIQL, and QRL, including success rates, ablations, and hyperparameter sweeps.

results.title: Test-Time Graph Search for Goal-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning

C1.justification: The core local-MAP framework, unification and reconstruction-performance claims remain. v3 qualifies motivation by acknowledging posterior uncertainty, explicitly relates novelty to DMAP, and omits the surrogate-gradient contribution from the abstract and contribution list, although the conclusion retains it. Claimed wins become 43/60 under expanded comparisons, replacing v1's inconsistent 46/60 and 49/60 statements.

C2.justification: v3 substantially develops the interpretation of covariance assumptions and k as prior tempering. It introduces a reconstruction-fidelity versus distribution-similarity interpretation of FID and explanations of the new solver, budget and conditioning analyses. However, its discussion of a favorable HDR comparison with DMAP lacks a corresponding DMAP result in Table 1.

D1.justification: v3 adds a code-access link and baseline settings, including DMPlug's 1000 epochs and MMPS's 100 steps with N=5. Main hyperparameters and hardware information remain. It removes v1 Section 4.3's surrogate-gradient recipe despite retaining non-differentiable-task results, reducing standalone reproducibility without establishing that the implementation changed.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same ten FFHQ/ImageNet restoration tasks and the same inverse-scattering, CS-MRI and black-hole scenarios. The synthetic mixture example and qualitative cases are retained. Added experiments vary solvers, budgets or conditioning within existing coverage.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds evaluated DMPlug, MMPS, MGDM, MAP-GA and DMAP comparisons across relevant restoration tasks, retaining the previous comparators. DMPlug and DMAP-related work were already mentioned in v1, but their new table entries substantially expand actual comparisons, especially with the closest MAP-based predecessor.

E3.justification: v3 adds FID, switches Table 3's quality column from PSNR to LPIPS, and introduces protocols for solver comparisons, reduced computation and a k2 sweep at 20 NFEs. Existing datasets, image counts, noise settings, checkpoints and Table 4 hyperparameters remain. Table 9's 200-gradient-step reference conflicts with Table 4's 100, leaving that setting unresolved.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained Gaussian-deblurring step ablation, v3 adds analytical versus gradient-descent optimization for super-resolution and box inpainting (Table 8), nonlinear-deblurring budget sensitivity (Table 9), and measurement-conditioning strength including k2=0 (Table 10). These substantially extend analysis of solver accuracy, computational tradeoffs and dependence on measurements.

E5.justification: Table 1 retains nonlinear-task ± values but removes v1's explicit explanation that they are standard deviations. Best-of-four phase-retrieval selection and mean/standard-deviation reporting over 94 MRI cases remain. No new seed reporting, repeated-run counts or significance procedures are documented.

E6.justification: Table 1 adds substantial baseline and FID results, while Tables 8–10 add solver and sensitivity outcomes. Among retained Table 1 entries, LMAPS FFHQ box-inpainting PSNR changes from 25.17 to 25.02. Table 10 newly reports PSNR increasing from 10.514 at k2=0 to 27.695 at k2=1. Scientific-result Tables 2 and 5–7 are unchanged.

M1.justification: The local MAP objective and denoise–optimize–renoise procedure remain. Algorithm 4 makes a limited pseudocode correction, changing the transition covariance from σn−1 I to σ²n−1 I and explicitly returning optimized x′0. The analytical solution tested in v3 was already derived in v1; the PDFs do not establish a broader implementation change.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much existing prose remain, with focused revisions to the abstract, motivation, contributions, covariance explanation and related work. Section 4.3 is removed, appendices expand and are renumbered, and an Impact Statement is added. v3 also duplicates baseline and metric paragraphs under Section 5.2 before the actual results in Section 5.3.

P2.justification: v3 changes the main text and references to a two-column layout, extensively resizes and relocates displays, expands Table 1 with baseline rows and FID columns, and adds Tables 8–10. Figure 1 is revised and Figure 2 updates DAPS pseudocode. Existing experimental plots and qualitative reconstruction images are retained.

R1.justification: Xu et al. (2025), already cited in v1, becomes the explicitly closest prior work, DMAP, with clean-space versus latent-space distinctions developed throughout v3. Classical Bayesian inverse-problem references and MGDM, MMPS and FID citations are added. Figure 1 also removes ΠGDM from the depicted unification relationship.

T1.justification: Section 4.1 and new Appendix B replace heuristic covariance assertions with Gaussian covariance bounds and asymptotic expansions, plus a smooth-prior Laplace-isotropy proposition and proofs. Appendix C derives a tempered-posterior interpretation of k. Appendix A adds mathematical analysis of component-selection regions and probabilities.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses important weaknesses in v1's covariance justification and comparison with its closest MAP predecessor through assumption-specific proofs, explicit DMAP positioning and direct evaluation. FID and new ablations substantially strengthen assessment of performance and mechanism. Removing surrogate-gradient instructions, conflicting Table 9 step counts and unsupported DMAP/HDR discussion weaken reproducibility and precision, but the theoretical and comparative gains provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LMAPS work. All pages, including equations, figures, tables and appendices, are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting and additions.

after.justification: v3 retains original LMAPS results and adds analytical-solver comparisons, nonlinear-deblurring budget experiments and measurement-conditioning ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original LMAPS reconstruction results, a synthetic Gaussian-mixture comparison, optimization-step ablations and runtime measurements.

results.title: Local MAP Sampling for Diffusion Models

C1.justification: v1 broadly argues that reasoning mechanisms already exist in base models and that post-training, including distillation, chiefly teaches when to deploy them. v4 makes a training-paradigm distinction central: RL primarily teaches orchestration, whereas SFT-distillation introduces or modifies mechanisms. It also elevates constructive model diffing into an explicit principal contribution.

C2.justification: v4 develops a new explanation based on RL using the model's existing mechanisms versus SFT imitating potentially incompatible teacher mechanisms, with model scale affecting recoverability. It classifies QwQ as mixed SFT+RL rather than v1's RL contrast. New limitations address mathematical bias in taxonomies, thinking-model influence through the coefficient MLP, and optimization failure as an alternative explanation for low SFT recovery.

D1.justification: v4 documents training-mixture counts and exclusions, rollout generation settings, the MLP architecture, category-balanced loss, optimizer settings, checkpoint selection, and family-specific prompt templates. It also specifies benchmark decoding and grading practices that v1 leaves unclear. The cited code-access path changes from cot-interp to thinking-llms-interp. These substantially expand and revise the reproducibility information.

E1.justification: Category-vector training changes from MMLU-Pro reasoning traces to a mixture of MATH, Natural Reasoning, SciBench, and TheoremQA, substantially revising the represented training problems and sources. MMLU-Pro remains the taxonomy-discovery corpus. GSM8K and MATH500 remain evaluation tasks; the additional Hendrycks-MATH holdout expands sampling within existing mathematical coverage rather than establishing a new domain.

E2.justification: v4 adds four Open-Reasoner-Zero thinking models and their base counterparts to the reported base/hybrid/thinking comparisons while retaining the DeepSeek-R1-Distill and QwQ comparisons. The ablation comparator set also changes: Only-bias disappears, MLP-magnitude-only and random-position controls are added, and random-category and random-vector controls are retained with revised implementations.

E3.justification: Base/hybrid prompting explicitly changes from step-by-step chain-of-thought instructions to a minimal question–answer prompt. v4 adds a disjoint 1,000-question Hendrycks-MATH evaluation and validation-based checkpoint/run selection. Vector-training budgets and batch sizes change, and the selected R1-Qwen-1.5B taxonomy changes from 25 features to 15. These are substantive protocol revisions, not merely newly disclosed settings.

E4.justification: v4 adds training-loss comparisons, a five-seed SAE stability analysis, and human validation covering benchmark judges, taxonomy judges, and category labels. It replaces the QwQ-only MATH500 ablations with four controls on two ORZ sizes across two benchmarks. The qualitative steering example changes, and v1's narrower-sweep sensitivity results in Appendix C.3 are removed.

E5.justification: v1 already reports five taxonomy-title repetitions but gives point benchmark accuracies. v4 reports three thinking-model rollouts, three judge repetitions per rollout, and accuracy mean ± standard deviation; it also reports three independent vector-training fits, five SAE seeds, and dispersion in steering usage. Benchmark error bars describe rollout/judge variability, not variability across vector-training seeds, since one fit is selected.

E6.justification: Results are extensively replaced and expanded. For example, the Qwen2.5-32B/QwQ-32B hybrid has 84.4% MATH500 accuracy and 91% recovery in v1 Table 2, versus 66.3% and 14.3% in v4 Table 1. These use revised methods and settings and are not a controlled performance decline. New ORZ results, loss curves, human-agreement findings, and stability results support a substantially different empirical picture.

M1.justification: v1 trains category vectors from selected sentence completions, includes a general bias vector, and searches steering coefficients/windows using thinking-model perplexity. v4 instead jointly trains category vectors and a coefficient-predicting MLP on token-disagreement positions with category-balanced cross-entropy, then uses disagreement gating and predicted coefficients during generation. These substantially change training and inference, beyond the new constructive-model-diffing terminology.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Section 3 is reorganized around motivation, framework, training, heuristics, and evaluation; taxonomy exposition is restructured, related work gains thematic subdivisions, and a dedicated Discussion & Limitations section appears. Appendices are reorganized and expanded, while the earlier contents listing and standalone reproducibility statement disappear.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to two-column layout. Separate benchmark tables are consolidated into a grouped three-benchmark table; the taxonomy heatmap is redesigned and expanded; training-loss and ablation plots are added; and the qualitative example is replaced. Appendix taxonomy tables gain full description columns, while steering-usage prose becomes structured tables.

R1.justification: v4 substantially repositions the work relative to model diffing and crosscoders, adding discussion of Lindsey et al. and Minder et al. It also adds SAE-stability research, rank-1 LoRA findings, and concurrent steering approaches by Cheng et al. and Zhang et al. The earlier direct-base-steering novelty claim gives way to explicit distinctions based on constructive diffing and training-paradigm diagnosis.

T1.justification: The SAE equations and taxonomy-score definitions are substantially retained. The limited formal revision removes v1 Appendix C.1's activation-difference expression for a steering vector and introduces v4 Appendix E.2's category-vector matrix and nonnegative state-dependent intervention alpha(h_p, c) times V_c. Neither version provides theoretical guarantees or proofs; constructive model diffing is primarily an empirical framework.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens the investigation by directly comparing four RL-trained pairs with distilled and mixed models, replacing v1's broad post-training interpretation with a more differentiated account. Human validation addresses v1's explicitly unvalidated judges, while seed-stability tests, stronger component controls, and detailed implementation information improve credibility and reproducibility. Important limits remain: taxonomy-judge agreement is moderate overall, and low SFT recovery may reflect optimization limitations. Changed protocols also prevent interpreting the revised scores as controlled performance gains or losses. These qualifications do not outweigh the substantial evidential improvements.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work, with matching title, authors, and methodological foundations. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices support comparison despite substantial revisions.

after.justification: v4 reports original experiments across nine model pairs, including benchmark results, training-loss analyses, ablations, human validation, and SAE stability experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original SAE taxonomy evaluations, GSM8K and MATH500 experiments, steering ablations, and additional appendix results.

results.title: Base Models Know How to Reason, Thinking Models Learn When

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion retain the central claims of efficient, accurate and unbiased kernel approximation through walk stitching and flexible termination. The introduction expands the advertised downstream contribution to include image classification, modestly broadening the stated application scope.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive qualifications about comparing intra-graph and inter-graph kernels. Appendix B.2 attributes weaker performance on node-labeled graphs to ignoring node labels and proposes label-aware walks as future work. Appendix C additionally interprets GRFs++ as positional/structural information for transformers. The original walk-reuse bias qualification remains.
