D1.justification: Appendix D replaces v1's promised future code release with a reported open-source implementation and a concrete repository URL. V2 also documents the ViT mask strength, eight-dimensional GraphGPS projections and use of SciPy's Al Mohy implementation. Existing mesh identifiers, hardware disclosure and hyperparameter sweeps are retained; detailed training configurations for the new transformer experiments remain sparse.

E1.justification: V2 adds ImageNet and Places365 image classification, COLLAB and REDDIT-MULTI-12K graph classification, and supervised GraphGPS evaluations including PATTERN, CLUSTER and MNIST. CIFAR-10 and Peptides, previously used as sources of graphs for kernel estimation, also receive supervised prediction evaluations. These additions substantially broaden the tasks and represented data.

E2.justification: Comparisons expand beyond GRF and exact diffusion to 20 graph kernels and four GNNs across Tables 8-9, four additional clustering methods in Table 11, and Al Mohy's matrix-exponential algorithm in Table 10. ViT and Performer controls are added for the new applications. Appendix B.2 explicitly attributes the external kernel/GNN scores to Nikolentzos et al.; they are not documented as new baseline runs.

E3.justification: New protocols include ViT validation-set top-1 accuracy with degree-2 masks and mask strength 0.5, GraphGPS comparisons using a Performer backbone without default positional encoding, fixed-degree non-diffusion kernel tests, and runtime evaluation on meshes up to 35,300 vertices. The existing 10-fold graph-classification protocol and 80% mesh-normal masking remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix B.6 adds a substantial generality study across three non-diffusion kernels, including downstream classification using exp(W^2). Figure 6 and Table 1 add mesh-size scaling analyses against exact kernel computation. Earlier long-distance, termination-policy and walk-reuse analyses remain; v1 Figure 4 is incorporated into v2 Figure 5(a).

E5.justification: V2 Tables 8-9 newly report classification means with standard deviations, whereas v1 Figure 6 presented these comparisons without uncertainty. The existing ten repetitions for kernel experiments and 10-fold classification evaluation remain. No increased run count, new seed specification or significance-testing procedure is documented.

E6.justification: V2 adds extensive transformer, runtime, non-diffusion-kernel and baseline results. For example, Table 3 reports ImageNet top-1 accuracy of 80.10 for ViT and 80.31 for GRF++. Original clustering and mesh scores remain unchanged. A retained classification ranking changes: GRF++ exceeds exact diffusion on REDDIT-BINARY in v1 Figure 6, but falls below it in v2 Figure 4/Table 9, which reports 84.4 versus 85.6.

M1.justification: Alongside the retained GRFs++ estimator, v2 introduces substantive model adaptations: normalized grid-kernel masks added to ViT attention and projected, summed eight-dimensional GRFs++ representations for GraphGPS (Appendices B.5 and C). Section 2.2.2 also reverses the printed termination inequality from <= to >=; this does not establish that existing experiments were rerun.

P1.justification: V2 shortens the introductory contribution paragraph, adds explanatory transitions and edits terminology and algorithm notation. The main section sequence remains recognizable. Reproducibility moves from Section 6 to Appendix D, Author Contributions is removed, and an Impact Statement is added. Most retained methodological prose is not extensively rewritten.

P2.justification: The single-column preprint becomes a two-column main paper with substantially rearranged displays. V1 Figures 4-5 are combined into v2 Figure 5, and the classification chart is enlarged and expanded to twelve datasets. New baseline tables, runtime displays and non-diffusion plots substantially change the visual presentation, beyond renumbering or numerical updates.

R1.justification: V2 adds references for ViT, ImageNet, Places365, GraphGPS and the newly compared GNNs, and discusses relationships to inter-graph kernels and positional encodings. The original positioning within GRF research remains intact. The Dwivedi preprint-to-journal update and removal of the duplicate Beutel reference do not introduce different prior works.

T1.justification: Lemma 3.2 and Appendix A.2 replace E[X1^2] with E[X1^T X1] in the MSE formula and revise the proof's symmetry argument accordingly. Section 2.1 adds boundedness to the convergence assumption, and Section 2.2.1 restores the missing lambda^p factor in the diffusion modulation function. These correct existing mathematics without replacing the principal theoretical framework.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens evidence for generality and computational usefulness through non-diffusion tests, broader comparisons and direct mesh-runtime scaling against exact computation. It also repairs the MSE derivation, reports classification uncertainty and provides implementation access information. These address important gaps in v1. Benefits are qualified by sparse transformer training details, inconsistent kernel formulas between Section 4 and Appendix B.6, and Table 11's overstated '3 out of 5' claim despite six datasets and ties. These reporting weaknesses limit some additions but do not outweigh the improved mathematical accuracy and broader empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GRFs++ research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched despite substantial layout changes and added experiments.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds image classification, GraphGPS experiments, additional kernel evaluations and mesh-runtime measurements.

before.justification: V1 reports original kernel-approximation and timing experiments, graph classification, node clustering and mesh-normal prediction, including additional results in Appendix B.

results.title: Computationally-efficient Graph Modeling with Refined Graph Random Features

C1.justification: The checkpoint-recycling, sunk-cost, and large-scale efficiency claims are retained. v2's introduction adds a more specific claimed boundary near Chinchilla-optimal compute and explicitly claims consistent performance regardless of growth order, refining the scope of the original convergence and orthogonality claims.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands the explanations for effectiveness: stacking requires repairing norm discontinuities, small noise breaks symmetry while retaining knowledge, and optimizer/update divergence supports complementary growth directions. It also adds interpretations of routing saturation and capacity–compute coupling, and connects the applicability of interposition to an observed convergence boundary.

D1.justification: Table 9 newly itemizes total, active, and core parameter counts; Appendix E explains shared-parameter alignment for the new diagnostics. However, its 36-layer description conflicts with Table 9's 40 layers. v1's statement offering supplementary code fragments and promising framework release disappears; the PDFs do not establish an actual change in code availability.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same DCLM, FineWeb-Edu, Nemotron-CC-HQ, code, and synthetic training mixture, and evaluate MMLU and the same six QA benchmarks. The community-model norm analyses also retain their coverage. New experiments vary model configurations and training stages within this coverage.

E2.justification: v2 Figure 6 adds randomly initialized new experts to the existing width-initialization comparison. Appendix C adds top-4/128-expert and top-8/64-expert controls against joint expansion. These extend the existing growth-control comparisons while retaining the original scratch-training, stacking, and noise-scale comparators.

E3.justification: v2 adds fixed-step comparisons from 2k–8k checkpoints, growth factor k=4 with 80 layers, alternative routing configurations, and opposite growth orders at 12B, together with optimizer-state and weight-similarity measurements. The scalability description also changes 54 layers to 56 and four activated experts to six; six was already specified in v1's appendix, and these reporting revisions do not establish reruns.

E4.justification: Substantial new analyses test the convergence boundary for interposition, norm discontinuities, larger growth factors, knowledge inheritance versus random initialization, routing alternatives, and growth-order independence. Appendix E adds gradient-direction and cumulative-update analyses. The pre-/post-norm function-preservation experiment is retained and relocated, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Task/checkpoint averages remain distinct from uncertainty estimates, and the new cosine-similarity analyses do not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v2 adds early-checkpoint results in Tables 12–19 and findings for the new controls and orthogonality analyses; Table 8 reports cumulative-update cosine similarity declining from 0.630 to 0.418. Matched retained benchmark values remain unchanged, including the 70B accuracy of 64.17. v2 Table 38 omits 16 intermediate 17B per-task result rows present in v1 Table 23.

M1.justification: The proposed procedures remain interpositional layer duplication and expert/router duplication with small Gaussian perturbations, doubling both expert count and activated experts during width growth. The additional experiments test configurations and combinations of these existing procedures.

P1.justification: The paper is retitled, with substantial rewriting of the abstract, related work, methodological discussion, and scalability narrative. Contribution bullets are absorbed into the introduction, function-preservation discussion moves into the appendices, and standalone reproducibility and LLM-use statements are removed.

P2.justification: The main text and references switch to two-column layout, with extensively resized and regrouped figures and newly structured analytical tables. v1 Figure 5's stability panels become v2 Figure 16, while the scalability loss and accuracy displays are combined in v2 Figure 11. New boundary, routing, growth-factor, and optimization figures substantially expand the visual evidence.

R1.justification: v2 adds references including Switch Transformers, neural-ODE regularization, DeepNet, upcycling scaling laws, and OLMoE. It more explicitly distinguishes inherited routers and small perturbations from dense-to-MoE upcycling, while retaining the original broader research positioning.

T1.justification: Section 3.1 newly defines and derives the reference compute budget F_c ≈ 6N_a(20N_a), using activated parameters to obtain approximately 5.88×10^19 FLOPs for the smaller model. This is a limited analytical addition. The growth equations and pre-/post-norm mathematics remain equivalent, and no new formal proof of growth optimality or orthogonality is supplied.

improvement.justification: v2 directly tests important assumptions that v1 supported mainly through structural intuition and one sequential growth path. The convergence-boundary experiments, initialization/routing controls, and opposite-order growth tests substantially strengthen the empirical justification and practical guidance without relying on improved headline scores. Inconsistent layer descriptions and removal of the code-release statement weaken reproducibility, but do not outweigh these substantial evidential gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MoE checkpoint-growth study. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison despite the changed title and substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds early-growth comparisons, routing controls, growth-order experiments, and optimizer and weight analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original pretraining and growth experiments, downstream benchmark results, noise ablations, and growth-timing analyses, including detailed appendix tables.

results.title: Beyond Sunk Costs: Boosting LLM Pre-training Efficiency via Orthogonal Growth of Mixture-of-Experts

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion retain the central claims: pretrained-compatible G-Star uses lightweight learned error correction to improve few-step text/code generation and enhance a 7B model. The expanded contribution list principally restates compatibility, late-stage refinement, and frozen-head findings already present in v1.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations involving confidence calibration, synthetic-noise mismatch, and why conditioning refinement on the current state can impede correction. It revises the favorable interpretation of the one-block predictor and quantifies approximately 50% full-depth latency overhead. Cross-domain transfer interpretations and a limitation concerning unoptimized inference are added; the earlier insertion/deletion and separate-training limitations remain.

D1.justification: New disclosures include the OWT predictor's 50,000-step training recipe, hardware and training times, Dream's RMSNorm-plus-linear head and optimizer schedule, and detailed compute/memory accounting. Appendix G adds practical schedule and temperature guidance. These substantially expand reproducibility information; the supplementary-code availability statement is unchanged.

E1.justification: Appendix C.4 adds transfer evaluation of the OWT-trained error predictor on TinyStories, OpenWebMath, CNN/DailyMail, and The Stack's Python subset. This introduces explicit out-of-domain error-detection scenarios across stories, mathematics, news, and code. Existing OWT, Conala, Tulu 3, and seven downstream benchmark coverage is retained.

E2.justification: Figure 4 adds evaluated P2-planner, RDM, and DDPD comparisons beyond v1's MDLM/ReMDM comparisons. Separate ReMDM-conf and cap/rescale rows disappear from the main comparison, although cap/rescale remain in the appendix tuning analysis. The new timing comparison also includes GPT-2 small autoregressive baselines with and without KV caching.

E3.justification: The main OWT comparison introduces denoiser-temperature Pareto sweeps, with 512-step baselines against 128–512-step G-Star. New protocols include 10,000 examples per domain, classification accuracy/AUC-ROC, and batch-one H200 latency measurements. Dream predictor training is reported as Adam at 1e-4 for 10 epochs in v1, versus AdamW at 3e-4 for 70,000 steps in v2; this documentation change does not establish that evaluations were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds denoiser-temperature quality–diversity analysis, predictor-capacity Pareto comparisons, cross-domain robustness tests, and DDPD/P2 remasking case studies. The earlier activation-time, ReMDM tuning, loop-size, and predictor-temperature analyses remain, as do the original guided/unguided examples.

E5.justification: Table 4 newly reports latency as mean ± standard deviation. Existing shaded uncertainty bands in generation plots are retained. Neither version specifies seed counts for those plots, and v2 does not state the timing repetition count.

E6.justification: v2 adds temperature-sweep findings, out-of-domain AUC-ROC scores of 0.90–0.98, and timing results such as 3.43 ± 0.10 seconds for 128-step G-Star-loop12B,H. Many detailed OWT point results from v1 Table 1 disappear. Conala and all seven Dream benchmark scores remain identical; the new results do not demonstrate same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–2 retain the same star-shaped sampling, training on model-generated errors, classification objective, and targeted remasking procedure. The hybrid and loop schedules also remain. Expanded head descriptions and methodological explanations do not establish a changed algorithm or architecture.

P1.justification: The introduction, preliminaries, and Sections 4.4–4.5 are extensively rewritten. Appendices are reorganized around theory, computational overhead, implementation, examples, and practical guidance; the earlier standalone refinement example is incorporated into Appendix F. Terminology, author listing, publication header, and acknowledgements also change.

P2.justification: The main OWT score table is replaced by two Pareto panels. v2 adds robustness and timing tables, a schedule diagram, and DDPD/P2 trajectory plots. Existing figures are resized or relocated, the conceptual sampler diagram gains annotations, and the unchanged Dream and Conala tables exchange positions.

R1.justification: Sections 1–2 and Appendix B substantially expand positioning against confidence-based sampling, stochastic remasking, and trained refiners. v2 discusses concurrent Kim and Huang studies and explicitly distinguishes its pretrained-compatible formulation from Okhotin's original star-shaped framework. Additional references support the new transfer datasets and inference-acceleration discussion.

T1.justification: Appendix A.2 adds Proposition 1 and a proof of the previously asserted ReMDM equivalence; the VLB proof remains unchanged. Appendix D adds an NFE derivation. Local mathematical regressions accompany these additions: Equation (17) changes the mask coefficient so probabilities generally fail to normalize, and the defined guided-step fraction has the opposite sign to its numerical use.

improvement.justification: The broader comparator set and temperature-swept evaluation substantially strengthen v1's limited empirical comparison. Cross-domain tests, measured runtime costs, and previously missing OWT training details make effectiveness, transfer, and efficiency more assessable. These gains outweigh the loss of detailed OWT point results and the localized formula inconsistencies in Appendices A.2 and D, although those inconsistencies still require correction.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Guided Star-Shaped Masked Diffusion. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison, including relocated material.

after.justification: v2 retains original generation experiments and adds temperature-sweep comparisons, cross-domain error-prediction evaluations, and measured inference timings.

before.justification: v1 reports original OpenWebText experiments, sampling ablations, Conala code-generation results, and Dream-Instruct 7B benchmark evaluations.

results.title: Guided Star-Shaped Masked Diffusion

C1.justification: V1's broad claim to be the first framework jointly addressing interference and hidden spatial confounding is narrowed in v2's introduction to the nonparametric setting. The central contributions—using interference as a multi-cause signal, conditional identification and extending SpaCE—remain.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly acknowledges that unrestricted CVAEs need not identify suitable confounders and that spatial structure makes recovery plausible rather than guaranteed. It expands discussion of separability, benchmark violations of theoretical assumptions, competitive exposure-mapping baselines and failure under localized confounding or coupled spillovers. These substantially deepen v1's mostly general limitations discussion.

D1.justification: Most Appendix C implementation information is retained. V2 updates tuning ranges, specifies the 0.25<p<0.75 model-screening cutoff, documents perturbation recipes and the Arctic configuration, and changes the replication repository reference from Spatial-CI to Spatial-Deconfounder. Repository availability was not externally checked.

E1.justification: V2 retains the pollution–mortality and sulfate–PM2.5 benchmarks and adds a real Pan-Arctic radiation–sea-ice task in Appendix E.5. Appendices E.1–E.4 also introduce distinct treatment-coverage, localized-confounding, directional-interference and confounder-dependent spillover scenarios.

E2.justification: Corresponding benchmark comparisons in Tables 1–2 and 5–6 add GMERROR, DURBIN, E-MAP-SPATIAL and E-MAP-SPATIAL+. These substantially expand comparisons against methods capable of estimating spillovers. S2SLS-LAG1 was already present; its newly reported spillover estimates are additional results rather than a new comparator.

E3.justification: Table 4 changes C-VAE-SPATIAL+'s reported beta search from 1e-5–10 to 1e-8–10 and raises the treatment-smoothing lower bound to 1e-3 for PM2.5–mortality with rd=1. New protocols include 10–70% treatment coverage, calibrated confounder injection, eastward-only interference, a 5% radiation intervention and radius sweeps through 5. The original spatial validation split and standardized absolute-bias metric are retained.

E4.justification: V2 adds latent-reconstruction inspection in Figure 4, targeted assumption-violation tests in Tables 7–10, the Arctic case study and systematic hyperparameter/radius sensitivity plots in Figures 5–8. V1 already compared radii 0, 1 and 2; v2 removes its per-benchmark R=0 table entries while including R=0 in the narrower direct-effect sensitivity analyses.

E5.justification: V2 adds tabulated posterior-predictive p-values with uncertainty intervals; v1 described this diagnostic without reporting its numerical uncertainty. Both versions retain the 10-run, 95% confidence-interval reporting convention. There is no documented increase in replication counts or new significance-testing procedure.

E6.justification: Many existing scores are revised, and new comparator, diagnostic and robustness results are reported. In Table 1, the humidity-confounded PM2.5–mortality result at rd=R=1 changes from DIR/SPILL 0.05/0.31 to 0.02/0.02. In Table 2, sulfate–PM2.5 with OC and rd=R=1 changes from 0.04/0.05 to 0.09/0.12. These are revised reported results, not controlled improvements across unchanged settings.

M1.justification: The central CVAE/GMRF reconstruction, separate outcome model and plug-in effect estimation remain unchanged. V2 removes the optional single-network training variant with blocked outcome gradients described in v1's Remark 1. Expanded factorization explanations do not establish a redesigned core estimator.

P1.justification: V2 extensively rewrites the introduction, related-work discussion, methodological explanations, theoretical narrative and results interpretation. Limitations are integrated into the main discussion, the impact statement moves before the references, and the former final appendix is replaced by organized robustness subsections. The LLM-use disclosure is removed.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from a single-column preprint to a two-column conference layout, relocating and resizing existing figures and placing Tables 1–2 side by side. Results tables gain diagnostic columns and revised highlighting. Four robustness tables and five figures covering latent reconstruction and sensitivity analyses are added.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands positioning through new discussions of causal generative models and identifiable/network deconfounding in Appendices A.4–A.5. Added references include DeCaFlow, Intact-VAE, D'Amour's deconfounder critique and work on spatial-confounding scales. These additions qualify the identification and novelty arguments beyond bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: Section 5 replaces Assumption 4's cross-site ignorability formulation with an explicit exclusion of unobserved single-site confounders. Assumption 5 now separately requires an ignorable population substitute confounder and consistent recovery by the fitted model. Appendix B.3 adds a proved Lipschitz bound of 2L times expected proxy error for both effects; the original identification proof is largely retained.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens comparative validation through spillover-capable baselines and targeted failure tests, addressing important gaps in v1. Explicit recovery assumptions, non-identifiability caveats and the proxy-error bound also clarify the guarantees. Reporting inconsistencies remain: Appendix D's exclusivity claim contradicts its expanded baseline tables, and the claimed movement of sparsity-test p-values away from 0.5 is not supported by Table 7. These weaknesses temper, but do not outweigh, the substantial gains in validation and qualification.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Spatial Deconfounder work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial additions and reformatting in v2.

after.justification: Section 6 and Appendices D–E report original benchmark experiments, robustness tests, sensitivity analyses and an Arctic sea-ice case study.

before.justification: Section 6 and Appendix D report original semi-synthetic experiments estimating direct and spillover effects on modified SpaCE datasets.

results.title: Spatial Deconfounder: Interference-Aware Deconfounding for Spatial Causal Inference

C1.justification: The central bias diagnosis and RLER contribution remain. The abstract and introduction revise the claimed improvement over the best RLIR baseline from 13.6% to 6.2%, reflecting the stronger comparator rather than lower RLER performance. v2 also explicitly broadens its validation claim across model families and non-mathematical tasks.

C2.justification: The original interpretation of coupling and over-reward remains. v2 adds substantive qualifications about requiring reliable semantic verification beyond mathematics, explains diversity emerging from identical initializations, and discusses diminishing ensemble benefits when per-policy rollout counts shrink while memory grows. These refine applicability and practical tradeoffs without replacing the central explanation.

D1.justification: v2 adds Algorithm 1, defines confidence bounds through quantiles with defaults 0.20 and 0.60, specifies per-policy selection quota caps, discloses common ensemble initialization, and documents rollout/resource accounting. These substantially expand implementation and reproducibility information. The existing prompt is retained in Appendix D rather than newly introduced.

E1.justification: v2 adds WebInstruct-verified training and MMLU-Pro evaluation across 14 disciplines, substantially extending the tested coverage beyond arithmetic and competition mathematics. Big-Math was already used for data scaling in v1, so its appearance in a dedicated v2 experiment is not itself a newly introduced dataset.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds evaluated INTUITOR and Co-rewarding comparisons alongside the retained Judge, Self-Consistency, and Frequency baselines. E3.justification: The main Qwen2.5-Math-7B configuration remains, but v2 introduces Llama-3.2-3B, Llama-3.1-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct evaluations, verifier-based non-math training, and MMLU-Pro Pass@1 reporting. These investigate additional mechanisms and robustness questions rather than merely adding benchmark scores.

E5.justification: Table 8 newly reports checkpoint accuracy variance and specifies a window of ±5 checkpoints around the best checkpoint. This adds an explicit training-variability statistic. Neither version reports independent training-run counts, seed-based uncertainty estimates, or confidence intervals.

E6.justification: The retained Table 1 numerical entries are unchanged, including RLER's 37.5 Avg@8 and 52.8 Pass@8. v2 adds substantial baseline, cross-model, non-math, sensitivity, diversity, resource, and intervention results. For example, Table 7 reports MMLU-Pro Pass@1 of 55.12 for RLER and 54.82 for Co-rewarding. These are newly reported results, not an improvement in the retained headline RLER score.

M1.justification: The ensemble, GRPO, selection, and TIES-merging pipeline remains. However, Section 4.2 changes interpolation from (1-alpha)r_H + alpha r_S to (1-alpha)r_S + alpha r_H, retaining the confidence-based alpha definition; Algorithm 1 confirms the reversal. This is a localized but substantive reward-rule revision. The PDFs do not establish whether it corrects the description or changes the implementation.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, related work, and substantial portions of the method and results discussion are rewritten around the self-confirming-loop narrative. Explanations and terminology are extensively revised. The appendices are reorganized into an algorithmic workflow, expanded experimental sections, the retained proof, and the retained prompt.

P2.justification: The main text changes from a single-column layout to a two-column conference format, with figures resized and relocated, panel labels added, and captions expanded. The selection table formerly embedded in Figure 6 becomes Table 2. New experimental tables, Figures 8–9, and Algorithm 1 substantially expand the visual presentation; the original plot data are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for Llama, General-Reasoner/WebInstruct, and MMLU-Pro, and refines positioning relative to agreement-based, confidence-based, and lagged-policy reward methods. Co-reward's changed bibliographic title corresponds to the same previously cited work. The related-work framework is refined rather than substantially expanded.

T1.justification: The hard-versus-soft reward proof is retained, moving from Appendix A to Appendix C. Limited mathematical changes include removing Section 4.1's explicit convexity-based ensemble-margin inequality and introducing the relative compute proxy in Equation 15, with an assumed backward/forward FLOPs ratio. There is no substantial new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: Stronger evaluated baselines, additional backbones, broader task coverage, and targeted robustness/resource analyses substantially address v1's limited validation; pseudocode and explicit defaults also improve reproducibility. These gains outweigh reporting problems: the interpolation reversal is unexplained, Appendix B.1.1 retains a 14.1-point arithmetic gain although Table 3 implies 11.1 over INTUITOR, and Figure 9's 70% FP/0% FN panel conflicts with the described FP-only intervention. These issues qualify specific conclusions but do not negate the substantial overall improvement in empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RLER study. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable, and retained content can be matched across the changed title, layout, and appendix numbering.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds cross-model and non-mathematical evaluations, sensitivity studies, diversity measurements, and reward-error interventions.

before.justification: v1 reports original controlled arithmetic experiments, mathematical reasoning benchmark results, component ablations, and unlabeled-data scaling experiments.

results.title: Breaking the Self-Confirming Loop: Diagnosing and Mitigating Systemic Reward Bias in Self-Rewarding RL

C1.justification: The central contribution remains text-preserving, black-box provenance auditing with bounded false positives. v2 qualifies completeness around sufficiently large marked collections and limits robustness requirements to non-adversarial processing. Its abstract and conclusion replace v1's precise 100% TPR and failure-rate headlines with broader high-detection claims, while extending the stated marked-data fraction to 0.25%.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive qualifications about context-dependent invisibility, font/viewer dependence, chatbot filtering, and the distinction between excluding marked documents and erasing their marks. It interprets multiple watermarks as potentially strengthening memorization, whereas v1 emphasized mostly mild interference. Section 4.3 and Appendix D also introduce sampling and optimization noise as explanations for variability.

D1.justification: v2 newly identifies H100/H200 hardware and documents alphabet screening, pipeline reconstruction, tokenizer identifiers, PDF fonts/viewers, and chatbot test inputs. However, its exact expanded character list and several supporting artifacts are deferred until acceptance; v1 explicitly enumerated its four characters. v2 also qualifies the code-release claim with an acceptance-dependent release statement.

E1.justification: v2 adds CNN/DailyMail News, extending evaluation from blogs and poetry to longer news documents with multiple cue/reply chunks. Appendix E also adds distinct input-environment scenarios involving PDF viewers, websites, preprocessing pipelines, tokenizers, and chatbot interfaces. The six named cleaning pipelines are compatibility tests, not six additional fine-tuning datasets.

E2.justification: v1 discusses competing approaches without experimentally evaluating one. v2 Section 4.6 and Figure 5 evaluate Wei et al. (2024)'s homoglyph watermarking method under the 50-watermark setting across both models and all three datasets. Other approaches listed in Table 3 remain conceptual comparisons.

E3.justification: The multi-watermark experiment changes from 1,000 training documents and 4/8/12 watermarks to 5,000 documents and up to 50 watermarks. Its five-query document-success measure is replaced by single-query chunk-level regurgitation rates. v2 also changes the alphabet and sampled collections and introduces 200-word chunks for News. The LoRA, training, and generation settings in v1 Table IV and v2 Table 5 otherwise match.

E4.justification: Appendix E adds systematic character-preservation tests through PDF/web handling, six cleaning pipelines, ten tokenizers, and three chatbot interfaces, plus a tokenization comparison with emojis. v1 principally discussed these vulnerabilities and supplied a small ChatGPT example. The expanded multi-watermark sensitivity study and Appendix D also examine individual watermark trajectories and outliers.

E5.justification: v1 reports means and standard deviations over five verification runs. v2 reports 95% confidence intervals with aggregation over five watermarks and three prompts per chunk, and explicitly averages three ranking-test repetitions. The new baseline evaluation adds empirical Z-scores against 100 random sequences. These change statistical reporting and sampling structure; an increase in independent training seeds is not established.

E6.justification: The main numerical results are extensively replaced under revised settings. For example, Mistral/Poems at 50 marked documents has p=0.132 in v1 Table II and p=0.903 in v2 Table 1, with different alphabets and sampled documents. The ranking evaluation changes from reported 100% TPR with 18,810 counterfactual challenges to approximately 96.7% TPR with over 100,000, including a failed Mistral/News watermark. These are not matched-setting performance changes. News, baseline, and preservation results are newly reported.

M1.justification: The instantiated marking component changes from four specified invisible characters to a screened 121-character alphabet (Section 4.1 and Appendix E.1). The cue/reply construction, cyclic embedding, reply extraction, trusted attribution, and ranking algorithms remain substantively unchanged; moving Algorithms 1–3 into Appendix A and renaming cr to t do not introduce new procedures.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, problem formulation, experimental narrative, and related work are substantially rewritten and condensed. Existing algorithms and notation move into Appendix A, the legal-context discussion moves into an Impact Statement, and related work now precedes limitations. These are extensive narrative and structural revisions beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: v2 changes the document template and appendix layout, redraws Figure 1, and reorganizes the main plots into dataset panels with rate axes. The multi-watermark boxplots become line plots with confidence bands, supplemented by individual-watermark curves. New baseline and tokenization figures, comparison and preservation tables, and expanded ranking-table columns substantially change the visual presentation.

R1.justification: Related work is substantially refocused around provider-controlled watermarking versus data-owner provenance auditing and free-text generation. v2 adds discussions of Waterfall, DECOP, and WASA and introduces the capability comparison in Table 3. It removes the extensive lexical/syntactic/format-based taxonomy and associated discussions such as LexiMark, UniSpaCh, and Innamark.

T1.justification: v2 Section 3.1 and Appendix A.1 generalize v1's parameter-specific watermark-space calculation. They explicitly recognize overlap overcounting, treat the forbidden-cue count as an upper bound, and derive a lower bound on admissible watermarks. The ranking-test FPR bound and watermark-repetition derivation are retained.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's lack of an evaluated competitor and limited empirical support for practical robustness. The baseline comparison, longer-document evaluation, larger multi-watermark study, and Appendix E measurements strengthen the evidence while exposing deployment limitations. These gains outweigh remaining weaknesses: the expanded alphabet is not fully disclosed, and Section 4.2 overstates completeness by claiming miss probabilities below 0.01 for all 30-document settings when Table 1 reports 0.156 for Mistral/Blog1k.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same cue/reply watermarking framework for auditing LLM fine-tuning data. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including v1 Appendices A–C and v2 Appendices A–E.

after.justification: Section 4 reports original fine-tuning experiments, including News and a competing watermarking method. Appendices D–E report individual-watermark analyses and character-preservation experiments.

before.justification: Section IV reports original LLaMA and Mistral fine-tuning experiments on Blog1k and Poems, measuring regurgitation, dataset-size sensitivity, multi-watermark interference, and ranking-test outcomes.

results.title: Data Provenance Auditing of Fine-Tuned Large Language Models with a Text-Preserving Technique

C1.justification: The headline contribution expands from a 4B rephraser outperforming ReWire to a 1B rephraser, 70 times smaller than ReWire's generator, doubling its performance gains. Claims now encompass 2.8B pretraining models, with the reported improvement range changing from 4.7%-14.0% to 3.7%-14.5%. The 2-3 times organic-data-efficiency claim is retained.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations concerning low-quality-data recovery, recycled data complementing organic data, OLMo2 adaptability, and faithful recycling versus knowledge distillation through QA generation. Appendix A adds task-category interpretations. New qualifications acknowledge baseline-only variance estimation, untested transfer to other corpora, and residual generator bias.

D1.justification: v2 adds 2.8B training hyperparameters, the enhanced comparator prompt, OLMo2 compute costs, and threshold-selection rationale. It omits v1's explicit long-document splitting and concatenation instructions. The abstract's resource statement narrows from code, rephraser, and recycled data to code; the PDFs do not establish actual resource withdrawal.

E1.justification: Both versions use DCLM-RefinedWeb and the same 22 downstream tasks, listed in v1 Table 6 and v2 Table 12. The FLAN reference for the influence-reward experiment is also retained. Larger pools and quality-based subsets remain within existing coverage; FineWeb and RedPajama are proposed only for future validation.

E2.justification: v2 Table 3 adds reward-aware Prompting+ and SFT+ comparators and Nemotron-CC Diverse QA using Qwen3-30B-A3B. Figure 3 also adds WRAP and ProX to the existing token-budget comparison, which previously compared RePro only with organic data. These substantially broaden the evaluated alternatives.

E3.justification: v2 adds OLMo2-1B initialization and 2.8B pretraining with a 144B-token pool and 55.9B/84.7B training budgets. New protocols include a 115.2B-token compute-equalized organic baseline, matched-source and matched-rephraser ReWire comparisons, source-quality fractions, and sampling-parameter sweeps. The original smaller-model main settings are retained.

E4.justification: New analyses test excluding high-quality sources from recycling, the origins of selected recycled examples, recycled-only versus mixed training, and sensitivity to temperature and top-p. Appendix D adds quality-stratified examples and prompting cases. Earlier reward dynamics, reward-weight studies, and quality-selection analyses remain, sometimes relocated.

E5.justification: v1 provides no pretraining seed-variability estimates. v2 Appendix B.4 and Table 8 report three organic-pool sampling seeds, per-category and Core standard deviations, and comparisons against twice those deviations. This is limited to the 400M organic baseline; v2 explicitly states that the full recycling pipeline was not replicated across seeds.

E6.justification: The original Qwen3-4B main results remain, including Core scores of 0.21658 and 0.29929. v2 adds substantial results for new configurations and controls: at 2.8B/55.9B training tokens, OLMo2-based RePro scores 0.36691 versus 0.35390 for organic data. Figure 4 newly reports 63.5% low-quality-source recovery, versus 31.0%-42.5% for comparators.

M1.justification: The GRPO procedure, four reward functions, filtering and mixing pipeline, and default rephrasing prompt remain unchanged. OLMo2-1B is added as a base-model configuration using the same method; no new algorithmic component or architectural modification is described.

P1.justification: The evaluation narrative is substantially reorganized: training dynamics and distributional analyses are combined, operation analysis joins the source-quality discussion, and alternative reward analysis moves to the appendix. The appendices gain a contents guide, category discussion, regrouped experimental details, and subdivided case studies. The abstract, introduction, and conclusion are revised accordingly.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from single-column to two-column conference layout. Main tables expand, five additional numbered tables appear, and Figure 3 changes from a two-series horizontal chart to a five-series grouped vertical chart. A new four-panel source-quality figure and additional comparison boxes are added; retained figures are resized and relocated.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations to the OLMo2 report, The Synthetic Data Playbook, Rubrics as Rewards, and FineWeb, while removing Zhu and Hauff's BERT-based reward citation. These support localized additions about rephraser size, reward design, and future coverage; the central related-work positioning remains.

T1.justification: v2 Equations 11-12 introduce explicit definitions partitioning high-quality recycled examples by whether their organic sources were low- or high-quality. The existing recycling, reward, and GRPO mathematics is retained; no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the evidence through compute-equalized organic comparisons and matched-source/model ReWire controls, addressing important attribution gaps in v1. Stronger comparators, another rephraser family, and larger and longer pretraining runs further test the central conclusions. Uncertainty remains restricted to the 400M organic baseline despite broader main-text wording, and omitted long-document instructions modestly weaken reproducibility. These limitations do not outweigh the substantial improvement in experimental support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RePro study. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables, figures, prompts, and examples, are readable and support reliable comparison across the reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds another rephraser, 2.8B pretraining experiments, controlled comparisons, additional ablations, and baseline variance estimates.

before.justification: v1 reports original 400M and 1.4B pretraining results, reward ablations, efficiency measurements, and analyses of recycled data.

results.title: RePro: Training Language Models to Faithfully Recycle the Web for Pretraining

C1.justification: The central any-prior, multi-output, feed-forward reconstruction and state-of-the-art claims remain. Novelty is narrowed from v1's first systematic prior injection within dense multi-view frameworks to v2's claimed first unification of flexible inputs and comprehensive multi-task outputs, particularly in the introduction and Figure 2.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations of geometry–appearance training interference, acknowledges training-data scale as a contributor to rendering gains, and interprets depth normalization and noisy-prior sensitivity. Appendix F provides concrete resource boundaries and explains the Gaussian head's higher memory cost. The earlier dynamic-scene and driving limitations remain.

D1.justification: V1 promises a future release; v2 reports publicly available code and weights and supplies a repository URL. V2 adds training times of 42 and 28 hours, BF16, gradient checkpointing, Flash Attention v3, and detailed evaluation/resource settings. Conversely, v1's synthetic-only fine-tuning and progressive-resolution descriptions are omitted; this does not establish that those procedures were abandoned.

E1.justification: V2 adds MatrixCity city-scale novel-view synthesis and reconstruction under deliberately corrupted pose, intrinsics, and depth inputs (Appendices B.4 and D). These extend coverage to a new scene domain and explicit sensor/calibration-error conditions. The 15-dataset training mixture and earlier task coverage remain.

E2.justification: V2 adds actual comparisons with Pow3R adapted using Procrustes alignment and MapAnything (Figure 5), DepthSplat (Table 4), NoPoSplat (Table 11), and 3D-GS and Mip-Splatting on MatrixCity (Table 10). These substantially expand comparator coverage beyond the retained v1 comparisons.

E3.justification: New protocols include multi-resolution DL3DV evaluation at 8, 24, and 64 views, pose-free optimization for the DepthSplat comparison, and two-view evaluation using specified cropping and downsampling (Table 4 and Appendix B.5). V2 also introduces a matched 32,500-step training comparison and controlled prior perturbations. These are additional evaluation designs, not evidence that the retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained prior-embedding and rendering ablations, v2 tests joint versus decoupled training, prior dropout probabilities, noisy priors, depth addition versus concatenation, and normalized versus unnormalized depth (Tables 12–16). Appendix F additionally analyzes memory scaling, view limits, and latency. These directly examine previously untested design dependencies and practical robustness.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. V2's noise standard deviations specify perturbation settings, while median latency is a benchmark summary rather than an uncertainty estimate.

E6.justification: All eight v1 numerical tables retain their values; v1 Table 4 becomes v2 Table 9. V2 substantially expands results through Figure 5, Table 4, and Tables 10–19: for example, MatrixCity 200-view PSNR is 20.36 for WorldMirror versus 19.18 for AnySplat. The new rendering scores use additional protocols and should not be interpreted as same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: Prior fusion, losses, and decoupled training already appear in v1, including Appendix A.2. However, camera decoding changes in description from a transformer over camera tokens to an MLP over backbone features, and Gaussian colors from spherical-harmonic residuals to RGB residuals; v2 Appendix F.1 still mentions spherical harmonics. The PDFs do not establish whether these are architectural changes or revised descriptions.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and method narrative are extensively rewritten. Core components are renamed, Model Training becomes a separate main section, and task sequencing moves from the appendix into the method discussion. Evaluation details and surface reconstruction are reorganized into appendices, with acknowledgments and an impact statement added.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from single-column to two-column layout, with revised overview labels, larger displays, and colored table rankings. V2 adds a prior-guided comparison chart and numerous tables, relocates the original rendering table and prior-benefit plot, and moves surface reconstruction to the appendix. V1 Figure 11's additional rendering comparisons are removed.

R1.justification: V2 explicitly positions its fusion design against newly discussed MapAnything and OmniVGGT and adds a multi-task-learning discussion citing Kendall, Zamir, and Zhou. This revises the novelty boundary and contextualizes decoupled training. Several earlier references, including Dens3R and some generalizable-rendering works, are removed.

T1.justification: The substantive token-fusion, normalization, and training-loss mathematics remain equivalent, including Appendix A.1. Neither version contains formal theorems or proofs. V2's expanded design rationale and empirical analyses do not introduce new theoretical derivations.

improvement.justification: Direct prior-guided comparisons and controlled training, noise, and depth-design experiments address important gaps in v1's validation of its central choices (Figure 5 and Tables 12–16). Explicit rendering protocols and resource disclosures also make the evidence easier to assess and reproduce. Architectural descriptions remain ambiguous and universal-gain language overstates some mixed results, but the added, directly relevant validation provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe WorldMirror. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite extensive rewriting and reformatting.

after.justification: V2 retains these original results and adds comparative evaluations, controlled ablations, noisy-prior experiments, and computational measurements.

before.justification: V1 reports original WorldMirror reconstruction, pose, normal, depth, and rendering results, including ablations and appendix experiments.

results.title: WorldMirror: Universal 3D World Reconstruction with Any-Prior Prompting

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction newly present the released 12M FineRegion-CN training dataset as an explicit contribution. The principal claims about bilingual fine-grained alignment, TIC, the Chinese evaluation benchmarks, and performance across 29 datasets and eight tasks remain substantively unchanged.

C2.justification: Section 4.6 and Appendices D–E add interpretations that bilingual Stage II supervision benefits both languages and that architectural/objective choices contribute beyond training-data differences. These extend the explanation of gains without changing the paper's general conclusions. The stated future directions concerning longer inputs and explicit object relationships remain.

D1.justification: v3 explicitly reports releasing FineRegion-CN, supplies separate code and model/data access links, and identifies its annotation pipeline and training examples. It also discloses retrieval splits and the sequential loss-weight selection procedure and search ranges. Conversely, v1's Gemma tokenizer and 256K vocabulary specification disappear. Core hardware, optimizer, batch-size, epoch, and Cat-Seg settings remain documented and unchanged.

E1.justification: v3 adds V* fine-grained visual-reasoning evaluation to the LLaVA comparisons in Table 7. Other benchmark coverage and training-data populations are retained. FineRegion-CN corresponds to the earlier 12M in-house Chinese region-text entry, rather than establishing additional training coverage.

E2.justification: v3 adds CLOC to bounding-box classification and English image-level comparisons, and UMG-CLIP to English retrieval/classification and segmentation comparisons (Tables 2, 4, and 6). Appendix E additionally compares retrained SigLIP 2 and Chinese-CLIP under matched Stage II data, extending Chinese-CLIP comparisons to English and localization tasks. These substantially broaden the relevant comparisons.

E3.justification: New designs include English-only versus bilingual Stage II training from a shared Stage I checkpoint, and matched-data baseline retraining with Stage I omitted for every compared model (Appendices D–E). Appendix F adds sequential loss-weight sweeps evaluated through average task performance. Existing main training settings remain stable; newly named retrieval splits clarify previously unspecified details.

E4.justification: Beyond retaining the original CMR/TIC removal ablation, v3 adds analyses of bilingual-data effects, model/objective benefits under matched training data, and sensitivity to all four auxiliary-loss weights. Appendix H adds four English/Chinese phrase-set similarity comparisons involving SigLIP 2 and FG-CLIP 2 with and without TIC. The earlier dense-feature visualizations are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or statistical significance tests. The new hyperparameter figure averages across evaluation tasks, not repeated runs, and introduces no uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantial results in Tables C–D, the loss-weight and TIC analyses, and V* evaluation, where FG-CLIP 2 obtains 50.3 overall. Retained scores also change: ViT-L/16 ImageNet-1K accuracy changes from 83.1 to 83.0 for FG-CLIP 2 and from 82.8 to 83.1 for SigLIP 2, reversing their reported ranking (v1 Table 3; v3 Table 4). Several English and Chinese SigLIP 2 scores are revised without explanation. Stage II-only results concern separate conditions.

M1.justification: The SigLIP 2 architecture, 196-token input limit, adaptive resolution, dense self-attention/RoIAlign components, two-stage training, and five objectives remain unchanged. The combined loss is reordered and its coefficients reindexed without changing their effective weights. The dense-head explanation moves between subsections.

P1.justification: v3 locally rewrites the motivation and architecture descriptions, reorders TIC/CMR and the combined-objective presentation, updates terminology and appendix references, and adds an Impact Statement. Most existing prose and the main section sequence remain recognizable; the added scientific analyses do not amount to a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from a single-column layout to a two-column conference format. The original combined localization table is split, ablation columns are reordered, comparison tables are expanded, and Figure 1 receives a detailed caption. New displays include training examples, loss-weight bars, controlled-comparison tables, and TIC heatmaps. Earlier dense-alignment and BoxClass example figures are retained as Figures C and D.

R1.justification: v3 adds UMG-CLIP to related work and adds references for V* and previously evaluated multimodal benchmarks. The Gemma tokenizer and compute-optimal ViT references are removed alongside their associated architecture details. The central positioning around unified bilingual fine-grained alignment remains intact.

T1.justification: The TIC loss, CMR loss, and globally synchronized margin equations are unchanged mathematically. Reordering the combined objective and reindexing its coefficients preserve the same formulation. Neither version adds formal assumptions, theorems, proofs, or derivations.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens evidence for the central contribution. Compared with v1's loss-removal ablations, Appendices D–F directly examine bilingual-data effects, comparisons under matched Stage II data, and loss-weight sensitivity, addressing important attribution and tuning gaps. Additional relevant baselines and the documented training-data release improve usefulness. The retraining control excludes Stage I, some score revisions remain unexplained, and tokenizer detail is lost, but these limitations do not outweigh the stronger empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe FG-CLIP 2 and contain readable methods, equations, experiments, figures, tables, and appendices. Retained material can be matched across renumbering, relocation, and the changed page layout.

after.justification: v3 retains original model evaluations and adds V* results, bilingual-data ablations, retrained-baseline comparisons, loss-weight experiments, and TIC similarity analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original FG-CLIP 2 evaluations on retrieval, localization, classification, segmentation, and multimodal benchmarks, together with training-objective ablations and qualitative visualizations.

results.title: FG-CLIP 2: A Bilingual Fine-grained Vision-Language Alignment Model

C1.justification: Both retain the claim of fixed-memory processing beyond three hours at 1 FPS and 360p. However, v2 replaces the central HF-optimization contribution with long-span prediction, two-stage training and modality-aware reading. It adds a benchmark contribution and claims about acquiring procedural knowledge from past video experiences, replacing v1's Video-MME-centered headline with broader memory-learning claims.

C2.justification: v1 explains performance through HF's balance between reconstruction convergence and information flow. v2 instead emphasizes temporal regularization, sparse-sampling failures and recent-memory bias, supported by new case studies. It qualifies retention as preserving useful summaries and discusses prediction-span noise, deepstack overhead and memory-dependent saturation. The impact discussion also adds concerns specific to persistent memory, including privacy and forgetting.

D1.justification: v2 documents TTT layer dimensions, prediction-span settings, deepstack handling, per-GPU batch size, second-stage training time and ELViM collection/filtering/annotation procedures. v1's detailed HF/CG and Muon implementation guidance disappears. Whereas v1 promises future releases, v2 supplies a repository link and states that implementation code and ELViM questions accompany supplementary material; actual external availability cannot be verified from the PDFs.

E1.justification: v2 introduces ELViM, testing procedural recall after at least 30 minutes of intervening videos, and evaluates real-time, omni-modal and contextual tasks on StreamingBench. MLVU and the OVO-Bench evaluation in v1 Appendix B disappear. Video-MME, LVBench and VideoEvalPro remain, as do the named training-data sources.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated PEMF and K-means clustering comparators and replaces Qwen2.5-VL comparisons with Qwen3-VL-based comparisons. Evaluations of Video-LLaMA-3, Dispider, StreamMem, TTTMuon and LaCT disappear. Standard TTT, Mamba-2 and merging/discarding comparisons persist. AdaReTaKe changes from an enhancement of the non-streaming baseline to a competing reader applied to video-SALMONN S.

E3.justification: The backbone changes from Qwen2.5-VL 7B to Qwen3-VL 8B, and the audio-visual LLaVA training subset increases from about 13k to 100k videos. v2 adds a training epoch with a 2048-frame cap after the 1024-frame stage. Its main reading setup uses 32k stored tokens with 8k chunks instead of v1's 128k. It also standardizes comparison backbones/data and introduces delayed-replay, partial-video and runtime evaluation protocols.

E4.justification: v2 adds ablations of long-span prediction, second-stage training, deepstack placement and prediction span, plus temporal-distance analysis and open-ended ELViM case studies. Memory-size and frame-count sweeps are retained but redesigned. v1's curvature/CG convergence study and Muon-versus-HF information-flow analysis are removed, including their appendix evidence.

E5.justification: Neither version reports actual seed/run counts, confidence intervals, error bars or a specified significance-testing procedure. v1's promise to release seeds is not a report of experimental repetitions. v2's dataset and runtime statistics do not introduce repeated-run uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: The main audio-visual reading model reports Video-MME overall/long accuracies of 74.2/67.8 in v1 and 76.9/71.3 in v2. These are replacement results under changed backbones, training and memory settings, not an isolated same-setting gain. v2 adds ELViM results, including 46.7% versus 32.5% for video-SALMONN 2+, and extensive new ablation/runtime results; MLVU, OVO-Bench and optimizer-comparison results disappear.

M1.justification: v1's Hessian-free, conjugate-gradient TTT module becomes TTTMEM with an additional delayed-input prediction loss and one-step SGD updates. v2 adds two-stage training that freezes TTT parameters during the second stage, switches from Qwen2.5-VL to Qwen3-VL, and replaces the reader's selection procedure with recurrent, modality-masked KV selection that preserves interleaved text tokens.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, contribution statements and conclusion are substantially rewritten. The methodology and experimental narrative are reorganized around TTTMEM, two-stage training and a dedicated ELViM section. The appendices are restructured, and separate ethics/reproducibility sections become an impact statement and dispersed access disclosures.

P2.justification: v2 changes the main paper from single-column to two-column layout, redraws the architecture and TTT diagrams, and adds training and benchmark-construction diagrams. It replaces optimizer plots with revised memory/frame plots and temporal-distance analysis, adds illustrated examples and case studies, and substantially restructures the benchmark and ablation tables.

R1.justification: The positioning shifts from Hessian-free optimization to episodic procedural memory. v2 removes the associated HF/Muon literature, distinguishes its use of TTT from prior video-stream segmentation work, and contrasts ELViM with VideoMMMU. New references include Qwen3-VL, StreamForest, Cambrian-S and StreamingBench, supporting a substantially revised novelty and evaluation context.

T1.justification: v1's second-order/HF derivation, curvature-matrix definitions, token-weighted loss formulation and CG stopping reasoning in Section 3.2 and Appendix A are removed. v2 formally defines the delayed-input prediction objective and a different masked, recurrent KV-selection rule in Sections 3.1 and 3.3. Neither version supplies formal theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for useful long-term memory through a targeted delayed-recall benchmark, more consistently controlled streaming comparisons, temporal-retention ablations and measured runtime/memory costs. These address important gaps in v1's predominantly general-video and optimizer-focused evidence. The gains outweigh narrower retained benchmark coverage and reporting weaknesses, including ELViM merging accuracy of 38.5% in Table 1 versus 35.4% in Table 2 and the abstract's 15-point claim versus the table-supported 14.2 points. Uncertainty reporting remains absent, and higher cross-version scores alone do not establish improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe video-SALMONN S, with a shared streaming-memory framework and overlapping evaluations. All pages, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable. The substantial method and protocol revisions limit direct performance comparisons but do not prevent reliable document comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original benchmark evaluations, ELViM dataset analyses, component ablations, runtime measurements and qualitative experiments, including Appendices A-G.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark evaluations, component and optimizer ablations, memory-size experiments and inference analyses, including results in Appendices A-C.

results.title: video-SALMONN S: Memory-Enhanced Streaming Audio-Visual LLM

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: ODE-based unification, GTP, two practical adaptations, and strong D4RL performance balancing expressiveness and efficiency. Additional appendix evidence does not redefine these claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations about short sampling trajectories, excessive temperature concentrating weight on high-advantage samples, and observation representation as the main challenge for visual inputs. Appendix D.1 also identifies the simple advantage-weighted objective and training cost relative to SSCQL as limitations. These extend the existing explanation without replacing its central mechanism.

D1.justification: v2 replaces the supplementary-code/future-release statement with a public repository address and adds computational details: 2M updates, batch size 256, i9-14900KF/RTX 4090 hardware, and FQL's training/inference step distinction. However, the expanded timing section drops v1's explicit halfcheetah-medium-expert task and 100-trajectory averaging description; visual implementation details remain limited.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained D4RL Gym, AntMaze, and toy multi-goal evaluations, v2 adds OGBench single- and double-cube manipulation with state observations and corresponding pixel-observation tasks (Appendix D.2, Table 6). This substantially expands both task and input coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds FQL, QIPO-Diff, QIPO-OT, and SSCQL to reported D4RL comparisons (Table 5), and adds FQL to the computational comparison. Some FQL scores are explicitly sourced from the SSCQL paper. Original comparator sets remain; CAC and DQL correspond to the earlier C-AC and D-QL names.

E3.justification: New evaluations compare two versus five sampling steps, scheduled discretization versus fixed N=40, and sweeps of sampling horizon and advantage temperature. The expanded computational comparison specifies a shared 2M-step, batch-256 setup. Separately, Table 4 changes hopper-medium-expert's reported temperature from 0.5 to 5.0 without changing its main score or establishing that it was rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix D.3–D.6 adds sampling-step, timestep-scheduler, and temperature-sensitivity analyses, alongside an expanded training/inference efficiency comparison. These directly test previously underexamined efficiency and robustness choices. The original score-approximation, value-guidance, teacher-free-objective, and multi-goal analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Existing results retain their five-seed mean-and-standard-deviation reporting. The new visual evaluations specify four random seeds, while state-based cube results are described as averaged over five tasks. No increased run count for retained experiments or new significance-testing procedure is reported.

E6.justification: Main Tables 1–3 retain their results, but v2 adds substantial entries in Tables 5–9 and Figure 6. Examples include GTP's 45±10 on state-based cube-double, 89±3 on visual cube-single, a two-step Gym average of 88.7, and 107.4±4.5 with fixed N=40. These are newly reported conditions and comparisons, not demonstrated improvements over v1 under identical settings.

M1.justification: The flow-map policy, score approximation, advantage-weighted losses, critic update, sampling procedure, and dynamic timestep schedule remain unchanged. The visual evaluations disclose no new architectural component and explicitly retain the core policy-learning formulation.

P1.justification: v2 rewrites portions of Section 3, revises several headings and explanations, adds acknowledgements and an impact statement, and removes the contents page. Appendix D gains additional subsections, but the main section sequence and most existing prose remain recognizable.

P2.justification: The main text and references change from a single-column preprint layout to a two-column conference layout. v1's Appendix E illustration becomes v2's main-text Figure 1. New comparison and ablation tables, an expanded computational table, and a two-panel sensitivity figure substantially change the visual presentation; existing diagrams and analyses are also resized or relocated.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for FQL, QIPO, and SSCQL and discusses GTP relative to these newer generative-policy approaches. It removes the historical discussion and citations to Lange et al. (2012) and Haarnoja et al. (2017). The broader related-work organization and research positioning remain largely intact.

T1.justification: The ODE definitions, score-approximation theorem, advantage-weighted derivation, continuous-time identity, and Appendix B proofs retain their mathematical substance. Theorem and equation renumbering, including numbering the previously stated total actor loss, adds no formal result.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the central expressiveness–efficiency claim. OGBench state and visual tasks address v1's narrow benchmark coverage, while newer baselines and sampling, scheduling, sensitivity, and computational analyses test important previously underexamined choices. The unexplained temperature revision and incomplete visual/timing documentation remain weaknesses, but do not outweigh the broader and more informative empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Generative Trajectory Policies work. All 26 pages of each version, including equations, tables, figures, proofs, and appendices, support comparison. Relocated and renumbered material can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds OGBench state and visual evaluations, sampling and scheduling ablations, sensitivity analyses, and computational comparisons.

before.justification: v1 reports original D4RL behavior-cloning and offline-RL results, component ablations, timing measurements, and a multi-goal policy visualization.

results.title: Offline Reinforcement Learning with Generative Trajectory Policies

C1.justification: v4 modestly narrows the contribution framing from a new analytical framework for persistent interruptible agents to an evaluation setting, benchmark, and error taxonomy, explicitly emphasizing single-round experiments. The central claims about dynamic fragility, the three failure modes, and drops of up to 60% remain.

C2.justification: v4 adds substantive interpretations concerning memorization controls, prompt sensitivity, problem difficulty, and why compact reasoning does not eliminate interruption failures. It narrows the coding-fragility discussion particularly to Qwen3 and explains that the proprietary-API proxy cannot establish native-reasoning behavior. The limitations also clarify the diagnostic scope and requirements for future interruption-aware training.

D1.justification: v4 discloses the 1% remaining-context panic criterion, GPT-5 self-doubt classification, annotation sample counts, a paraphrased guidance prompt, and the dataset acceptance rate. It specifies an MIT license and replaces the dataset-collection link with a direct benchmark-dataset link. The original prompts and general hardware/hyperparameter descriptions largely remain.

E1.justification: Both versions use GSM8K, MATH500, AIME24/25, and LiveCodeBench-v6, including their augmented update-driven problems. The added controls, model evaluations, and annotation checks use this existing coverage; no additional application domain or benchmark task is evaluated.

E2.justification: v4 evaluates Chain of Draft against ordinary Qwen3-8B reasoning under all three interruption modes (Section 6.4); v1 only cites it. Appendix F.2 also adds evaluated DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama and Nemotron-3-Nano comparisons beyond the original model families, substantially expanding the comparative evidence.

E3.justification: v4 adds paragraph-boundary interruption experiments, an augmented-problem/no-update control, larger model configurations, and a GPT-5.4-Mini proxy with internal reasoning disabled. Human validation introduces two 50-sample checks and multiple panic thresholds. Appendix F.4 re-bins existing runs by absolute character length; it does not establish new fixed-token-budget experiments.

E4.justification: New analyses test guidance paraphrasing, possible benchmark memorization, interruption boundaries, and dependence on relative indexing. Appendix E adds panic-threshold sensitivity and human checks of panic and self-doubt labels. The original scaling, turn-role, and speedup analyses are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Appendix E newly reports coefficients of variation across panic thresholds and human agreement estimates for the automated labels. Both versions retain 16 AIME trials, single runs elsewhere, and bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals; v4 does not establish increased repeated-run counts or specify a new significance-testing procedure.

E6.justification: v4 adds extensive model, comparator, and robustness results, including 90% panic-label agreement and 88% self-doubt-label agreement in Appendix E. Section 6.4 newly reports AIME panic rates of 13.1% with Chain of Draft versus 3.8% with regular reasoning at position 0.3. Existing LiveCodeBench update-driven curves also change substantially in Figures 4, 6, and 8, without an explanation establishing whether these are corrections or reruns.

M1.justification: The hard, soft, and update-driven interruption procedures and the prompt-guidance intervention already appear in v1 and remain in v4. The paraphrase ablation, additional comparators, and proprietary-model proxy do not establish a revision to the proposed core method.

P1.justification: The overall narrative sequence and much existing prose remain. v4 revises the abstract, contribution bullets, experimental rationale, and conclusion; separates limitations from the conclusion; and adds an impact statement and human-validation appendix. These are localized editorial and structural changes rather than a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: v4 converts the main paper to a two-column conference layout, substantially resizing and relocating existing multi-panel figures. It adds baseline and robustness figures, extensive appendix plots, and two validation tables. The original appendix plots are matched to Figures F.23–F.27, with some revised displays and results.

R1.justification: v4 adds model and software references, including Nemotron-3-Nano, GPT-5.2, Gemini 3, SillyTavern, and text-generation-webui. It explicitly connects the study to Chain of Draft through evaluation, while retaining the overall positioning against efficient reasoning under static contexts.

T1.justification: The inference formalization, interruption-conditioned accuracy and length definitions, and necessary-update condition in Section 3 are retained. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs; the new operational labeling criteria and empirical analyses do not revise the mathematical framework.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens support for the central diagnoses: Appendix E validates previously insufficiently documented failure labels, while the new controls, interruption analyses, and Chain of Draft comparison address important alternative explanations left open in v1. Broader model evidence and explicit proxy limitations further improve credibility. Small validation samples, overgeneralization from one paraphrase, and crowded figures remain weaknesses, but the net evidential improvement is substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same interruption study. Their text, equations, figures, and complete appendices support comparison, including matching retained material across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v4 retains original experiments and adds comparator evaluations, robustness analyses, and human validation in Sections 6.3–6.4 and Appendices E–F.

before.justification: v1 reports original accuracy, output-length, interruption, and model-scaling experiments in Sections 4–6 and Appendix E.

results.title: Are Large Reasoning Models Interruptible?

C1.justification: The central claims about population versus proportional regimes and regularization scaling are retained. The introduction's third contribution now explicitly claims empirical applicability beyond the theoretical assumptions and to other regularizers. The abstract additionally attributes the over-parameterized benefit to reduced parameter-estimation variance.

C2.justification: v2 explains how conclusions depend on evaluating the untouched or shifted distribution and adds societal tradeoffs for both choices in the Impact Statement. It also adds feature-shift limitations, an informal Bayesian explanation, and interpretations of alternative-regularizer behavior. The shifted-risk summary in Section 5 omits the kappa >= 2 restrictions attached to some appendix sign results.

D1.justification: v2 documents use of whynot and Mofakhami et al.'s code and largest network, and specifies equal L1/L2 weighting for elastic net. The original preprocessing, feature table, and repository address remain. The single-laptop hardware disclosure is removed. Exact neural-network architecture and hyperparameter values are largely delegated to the cited setup rather than supplied locally.

E1.justification: Gaussian simulations, Housing, and LSAC are retained. Section 6 adds GiveMeSomeCredit binary classification with strategic modification of manipulable features, substantially extending coverage beyond regression with synthetic label shifts. The sub-Gaussian extension is theoretical, not an additional empirical dataset.

E2.justification: v1 evaluates ridge regularization only. v2 Appendix A evaluates dropout, Lasso, and elastic net on the same Housing and LSAC settings and compares their behavior with ridge in Figure 4. This adds three alternative regularization families; Mofakhami et al. supplies the neural-network setup rather than a separately evaluated competing algorithm.

E3.justification: The original ridge experiments retain their splits, sample sizes, and retraining settings. The added neural-network experiment introduces convergence-based dynamics, strategic feature-copying controlled by delta, regularization sweeps, and final test accuracy. Appendix A also adds controlled replacement of the regularizer within the retained regression settings.

E4.justification: Figures 6–8 newly test whether the observed behavior depends on using ridge by substituting three other regularizers. The neural-network experiment probes applicability beyond linear regression. Appendix G adds covariance heatmaps and examines departures from the simplified covariance structure used in the theory.

E5.justification: v2 newly specifies shared randomness across delta and lambda and repeated runs for the neural-network experiment, although the count is only described as 'several times'. Existing trial counts and one-standard-deviation reporting are retained. There is no documented increase in runs for the original experiments or new significance-testing procedure.
