E6.justification: Figures 1–4 retain their original results. v2 adds neural-network accuracy curves showing mitigation through L2 regularization, nine regression panels for alternative regularizers, and empirical covariance estimates. These are substantial new results under added methods and settings, not improved ridge scores under the original conditions. Figure 6(c)'s caption incorrectly says the optimal dropout rate increases, while the plotted optima move downward.

M1.justification: The central ridge estimator and repeated risk minimization procedure remain unchanged. v2 adds empirical training variants using dropout, Lasso, and elastic net, and applies L2 regularization to a neural-network classifier. These extend the instantiated procedures without replacing the central method.

P1.justification: The seven-section main narrative and much of its wording are retained. v2 makes targeted explanatory rewrites, removes the main-text proof sketch while retaining the full proof, reorganizes the appendices, and adds Impact and Conflict of Interest statements. Affiliations and publication headers change, and an unresolved '(??)' reference appears in Appendix E.

P2.justification: v2 replaces the single-column main text with a two-column conference layout and substantially rearranges figure placement. It retains Figures 1–4 and Table 1 while adding the neural-network plot, three multi-panel regularizer figures, and two covariance heatmaps. These constitute substantial visual and layout changes.

R1.justification: Related work expands to initial-distribution evaluation, label shifts, and difficulties learning performative effects in high dimensions. The novelty statement changes from model choice being unstudied to a claimed first use of high-dimensional statistical tools. New citations include Mofakhami, Clara, Demirel, Tsoy, and Bracale; Cheng and Montanari is removed. The main intellectual foundation remains intact.

T1.justification: The original principal results remain as Theorem 4.1, Corollary 4.2, and Theorems 5.1–5.2. New Appendix D provides a sub-Gaussian extension with additional coefficient and initialization assumptions and a weaker probability guarantee. New Appendix F defines risk against the shifted training distribution and derives its deterministic equivalent, optimal regularization, and risk-sign results. v2 also explicitly discusses applicability to non-diagonal performative matrices.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the paper by extending its Gaussian theory, analyzing an alternative evaluation distribution, and testing applicability beyond linear ridge regression. Appendix F makes the dependence of conclusions on the risk criterion explicit, while Figures 5–8 provide broader empirical support. These gains outweigh localized weaknesses: incomplete neural-network reproduction details, omitted conditions in the shifted-risk summary, and the incorrect dropout-direction caption in Figure 6(c).

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, Optimal Regularization for Performative Learning. Their complete text, equations, figures, table, and appendices are readable. The original results and proofs can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds neural-network classification results, alternative-regularizer experiments, and empirical covariance analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original Gaussian simulations and Housing and LSAC regression experiments in Figures 1–4, with experimental details in Appendix D.

results.title: Optimal Regularization for Performative Learning

C1.justification: v1 presents greedy meta-AFA as its algorithmic contribution. v2's introduction explicitly extends this contribution to both greedy and planning-based acquisition and claims the first demonstration of their joint meta-learning formulation across tasks. This broadens the central contribution while retaining the original claims about in-context adaptation and robustness.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations involving feature synergy, task-representation bottlenecks, prior mismatch, and IPW estimation variance. It explicitly qualifies natural-missingness results because both population and context–query distributions shift, and adds limitations concerning full cost-sensitive planning and scale. The adaptivity interpretation also changes: v1 Figure 13 emphasizes benefits for LOS and mortality, whereas v2 Figure 15 says such benefits are difficult to demonstrate.

D1.justification: v2 documents BNN-Plan generation, synthetic covariate sampling, planning-specific hyperparameters, CNP adaptation, and logistic-regression propensity estimation, and adds baseline runtimes in Table 3. The hardware and source-code link are retained. However, Section 4.3 says the predictor is held fixed while Appendix A.7.6 retains joint updates for default training, leaving a reproducibility ambiguity.

E1.justification: v2 adds fully synthetic classification tasks with generated covariates and varying feature dimensions, interaction-rich BNN-Plan tasks, and transfer from synthetic covariates to real-world tasks. It also evaluates MIMIC contexts containing natural missingness, introducing patient-population and missingness shifts beyond v1's complete-case data with injected missingness.

E2.justification: The original MLP, GDFS, DIME, and DQN comparisons remain. v2 additionally evaluates a CNP-like attention-pooling model and its test-time-tuned variant (Figure 18), REINFORCE gradient estimation (Figure 17), and offline and semi-offline IPW estimators (Table 5). These substantially broaden the evaluated comparison methods.

E3.justification: The reported MIMIC test pool changes from 10,000 to 3,000, baseline features from three to five, and acquirable features from ten to fifteen. Metabric drops the listed age baseline and abcb1 feature, and its missingness changes from MAR to MCAR (dataset descriptions and Table 2). New planning experiments control encoder/predictor freezing, temperature 0.5, and four Monte Carlo samples; gradient studies introduce reference-gradient and estimation-budget protocols.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's context-length, missingness-rate, and adaptive-versus-static analyses, v2 adds controlled feature-synergy/lookahead tests, informative-feature precision and recall, synthetic-prior transfer and fine-tuning, natural-missingness stress tests, gradient-estimator sensitivity, and CNP adaptation ablations (Figures 5 and 12–18; Table 5). These examine substantial additional questions about mechanisms and robustness.

E5.justification: v1 already reports standard errors across 200 tasks in Figure 3. v2 retains this practice and additionally reports means and standard deviations across 50 sampled tasks for gradient-estimation experiments (Figure 17 and Table 5). Neither version specifies repeated-training seed counts; the additions describe task-level variability.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial lookahead, transfer, gradient-estimation, and meta-learning results. For example, Table 5 newly reports pathwise one-step bias norm 0.068 ± 0.037 using four samples. Existing acquisition and uncertainty curves also change, especially for MIMIC under its revised setting; Table 1 changes LOS prevalence from 34.12% to 44.90% and mortality from 3.48% to 8.67%. These are revised-setting results, not directly comparable performance gains.

M1.justification: v1 optimizes a greedy one-step acquisition loss. v2 adds a k-step lookahead objective and optimization through sampled acquisition trajectories, with a one-step-lookahead policy evaluated experimentally (Section 4.2 and Appendix A.5). This substantially extends the acquisition procedure; straight-through Gumbel–Softmax itself already appeared in v1.

P1.justification: The introduction, problem formulation, method explanations, and results narrative are extensively rewritten. v2 separates test-time acquisition, meta-training, and architecture into Sections 4.1–4.3, introduces thematic results subsections, and reorganizes the appendices. It also replaces the separate ethics/reproducibility statements with revised end matter and removes the LLM-use section.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column main-text layout and redraws Figures 1 and 2. v1 Figure 3 is split between v2 Figures 3 and 9; v1 Figure 5 moves to Figure 11; and the two adaptivity figures merge into Figure 15. Numerous new analytical figures and runtime/gradient tables are added, and MIMIC plots and heatmaps expand to fifteen features.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning through CNP/MAML-style meta-learning, TabPFN and continued pretraining, and IPW policy-gradient comparisons. It adds relevant work including DIFA, Norcliffe et al., and an in-context RL survey, and introduces an explicit novelty claim spanning greedy and planning-based meta-AFA. Publication updates for retained works such as DIME are bibliographic changes rather than new research relationships.

T1.justification: v2 adds formal submodularity and adaptive-submodularity definitions and discusses their approximation guarantee (Appendix A.4), then derives a multi-step lookahead objective and gradient estimator (A.5). It also extends the blocked-policy optimality argument across missingness patterns and corrects the missing inner gradient in Equation 6. The original identification assumptions and greedy theorems remain.

improvement.justification: The controlled lookahead experiments, alternative meta-learning comparisons, gradient diagnostics, and synthetic-to-real and natural-missingness tests substantially strengthen evidence for design choices and applicability beyond v1's evaluations. Explicit qualifications about prior mismatch and distribution shifts also improve interpretation. Reporting weaknesses remain, including conflicting predictor-freezing descriptions and apparently duplicated GP log-loss/MSE panels in Figures 4 and 10, but the added controls and substantive validation provide a clear substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Learning-to-Measure and retain matching methods, experiments, and proofs. All pages and appendices were readable, and figures, tables, equations, and relocated material could be compared reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical evaluations and adds lookahead, synthetic-to-real transfer, natural-missingness, gradient-estimation, and alternative meta-learning experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic regression, tabular classification, and MNIST experiments, including uncertainty, acquisition-performance, and adaptivity analyses.

results.title: Learning-To-Measure: In-Context Active Feature Acquisition

C1.justification: The headline logarithmic-regret and linear-in-1/ε sample-complexity contributions remain. However, the abstract and contribution statements retreat from SOMG's regularization-independent square-root guarantee: v2 allows logarithmic β dependence and withdraws its unregularized Markov-game guarantee.

C2.justification: Sections 3.3 and 4.2 newly explain why changing equilibrium policies complicate covering-number bounds and introduce logarithmic regularization dependence. Appendix D.2 discusses conditions for extending beyond linear approximation. Appendix D.1 expands the already-present single-agent interpretation rather than introducing that reduction.

D1.justification: Explicit SOMG bonus-tuning prescriptions change, and the unregularized projection/bonus prescriptions are removed. A remaining inconsistency affects these instructions: v2 Lemma C.1 includes H inside η1's logarithm, whereas the prescription following Eq. (24) retains the earlier expression. No implementation resources are added.

E1.justification: Neither version uses datasets or executed evaluation tasks. Appendix D discusses theoretical extensions, not additional tested scenarios.

E2.justification: Neither version reports experimental baseline evaluations. Table 1's changed selection of published theoretical guarantees concerns research positioning rather than evaluated comparator membership.

E3.justification: Neither version reports experimental protocols, data splits, evaluation budgets, or testing procedures. Revised algorithm coefficients and theorem conditions are theoretical changes.

E4.justification: Neither version contains ablations, robustness experiments, sensitivity tests, or empirical case studies. The new appendix material consists of theoretical derivations and discussion.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated runs, seeds, or empirical uncertainty estimates. Changes to failure-probability allocation occur within mathematical concentration proofs and are assessed under T1.

E6.justification: No measured numerical results or experimental findings appear in either version. Changes to regret and sample-complexity bounds are theoretical revisions covered under T1.

M1.justification: OMG and SOMG retain their main procedures. SOMG's bonus coefficient gains H and regularization-dependent logarithmic factors. The explicit unregularized specialization in v1 Appendix C.6 is removed, while v2 Appendix D.2 sketches an adaptation using general-function uncertainty widths.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and most prose remain intact. v2 organizes technical challenges into bullets, adds explanatory passages and Appendix D, revises guarantee terminology, and makes localized wording and cross-reference corrections.

P2.justification: Table 1 is reformatted with revised rows and caption, including separate regularized/unregularized matrix-game entries for Yang et al. Algorithm 1 moves from page 8 to page 7. Other changes are principally equation formatting and pagination; neither version contains figures.

R1.justification: v2 adds Ye et al. (2023) and removes Boyd and Vandenberghe (2004). Table 1 drops the OMNI-VI and Nash-UCRL theoretical comparisons, although their works remain discussed. Appendix D adds more explicit connections to existing general-function techniques and single-agent bounds.

T1.justification: v1 Lemma C.10 treats a fixed opponent policy; v2 replaces this with an equilibrium-dependent MSE value-function argument and adds superoptimistic covering, KL-identity, and payoff-stability proofs in Lemmas C.11–C.13. Concentration proofs now allocate failure probability across the horizon. Theorem 3.1 adds H/min{1,β} inside logarithms and restricts both guarantees to β>0. The unregularized theorem and supporting proofs in v1 Appendix C.6 are removed. Appendix D.2 adds general-function assumptions and mathematical definitions.

improvement.justification: The decisive gain is stronger support for the central Markov-game analysis: v2 replaces v1's fixed-opponent covering argument with arguments accounting for changing equilibrium policies and superoptimistic values. It also exposes additional logarithmic dependencies and withdraws the unregularized guarantee. These changes substantially improve the rigor and calibration of this theoretical paper, despite narrower guarantees and a remaining η1 inconsistency between Eq. (24) and Lemma C.1.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same OMG/SOMG research. All pages, mathematical displays, Table 1, algorithms, and appendices are readable, allowing substantive changes to be distinguished from relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 remains theoretical. Its revised proofs and additional discussions introduce no original experimental, simulation, or data-analysis outcomes.

before.justification: v1 reports algorithms, theoretical guarantees, and proofs, including its appendices. Table 1 compares theoretical bounds; no original experimental or simulation outcomes are reported.

results.title: Achieving Logarithmic Regret in KL-Regularized Zero-Sum Markov Games

C1.justification: V1 presents preliminary evidence for flat-map modeling and promising state/trait decoding. V2 claims a multi-representation model family, the first open fMRI foundation-model benchmark suite, strong state-decoding superiority within that benchmark, and a central null finding for trait prediction. These materially expand and qualify the contributions stated in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations linking normalization to functional-state sensitivity and volume-based age prediction to possible structural cues. It discusses small clinical samples, excluded subcortical structures, missing model-specific nuisance regression, and preliminary UKBB preprocessing. Appendix C.2 explicitly acknowledges tension between its downstream scaling results and Figure 7c and proposes a training-schedule explanation.

D1.justification: V2 newly documents preprocessing versions and coordinate spaces, sequence adaptation, initialization and positional-encoding details, mixed precision, and expanded configuration tables (Appendix B). Appendix D adds total compute expenditure. V2 also provides separate CortexMAE and BRAINMARKS access information and advertises model availability, extending v1's code/data disclosure.

E1.justification: V2 adds ABIDE, ADHD-200, ADNI, and PPMI diagnosis tasks and HCP-A age/sex prediction. UKBB sex evaluation disappears, while UKBB becomes an additional pretraining source in Appendix C.2. HCP task decoding remains, but NSD changes from 41 caption labels to 24 filtered object categories, revising its task requirements.

E2.justification: V1 evaluates connectivity and patch-embedding baselines, while discussing prior models through published scores. V2 directly evaluates SwiFT, BrainLM, Brain-JEPA, BrainHarmonix-F, NeuroSTORM, and Brain-Semantoks alongside connectivity (Figure 8; Table 14). The patch-embedding comparator leaves the main benchmark; a related depth-zero probing analysis appears in Table 11c.

E3.justification: V2 revises HCP/NSD splits and sample counts and introduces logistic probes with balanced accuracy for trait prediction. Attentive-probe training changes from 20 epochs with learning-rate/weight-decay tuning to 4,000 steps, 49 learning rates, and early stopping (Table 8). The default temporal patch changes from 16 to 4 frames, and scaling experiments use revised data/model ranges.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's data/model-scale and temporal-patch studies, v2 tests masking, augmentation, reconstruction targets, normalization, subcortical coverage, sequence length, spatial patches, and decoder/probe depth. It also analyzes pretraining mixtures, UKBB versus HCP, learned position embeddings, and interpolation artifacts (Section 5.3; Appendix C).

E5.justification: V1 provides point estimates without repeated-run uncertainty. V2 reports eight pretraining repeats with means and standard deviations, 100 randomized trait-evaluation splits, significance thresholds, and error bars. Figure 7 explicitly reuses Table 2's standard deviations for scaling error bars; it does not establish repeated runs for every scaling configuration.

E6.justification: V1's best reported NSD accuracy is 21.0% on its 41-class task; v2 reports 31.0% mean accuracy for default CortexMAE-F on COCO24 (Table 2). These are different settings, not a direct performance gain. V2 additionally reports extensive representation rankings, clinical null findings, compute measurements, ablation outcomes, and UKBB pretraining results.

M1.justification: The original flat-map MAE continues as CortexMAE-F. V2 adds parcellation and sparse cortical-volume variants with distinct patch embeddings (Section 3). Appendix C.3 additionally introduces cross-register decoding and decoder edge masking, substantially extending the model family and training procedures.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method exposition, and conclusion are substantially rewritten. The narrative is reorganized into separate related-work, modeling, BRAINMARKS, and experimental sections, with substantially restructured appendices. Terminology changes from fm-MAE to the CortexMAE family accompany this broader editorial revision.

P2.justification: V2 switches to two-column layout, redraws the architecture diagram, rebuilds scaling displays, and adds conceptual, denoising, representation, benchmarking, and diagnostic figures plus numerous tables. The retained cortical surface/flat-map illustration moves from v1 Figure 6 to v2 Figure 9. V1's preprocessing schematic and 41-label example display are removed.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands research positioning through a dedicated related-work discussion of foundation models, trait prediction, and state decoding. New references include Brain-Harmony, Brain-Semantoks, studies questioning deep-learning advantages over simple baselines, and CrossMAE/register methods. The contribution is repositioned around controlled benchmarking and representation tradeoffs.

T1.justification: Neither version develops formal theorems, proofs, or theoretical derivations. The scaling laws remain empirical fits; v2's representation hypothesis and architectural motivations do not introduce formal theory.

improvement.justification: V1 lacked direct comparisons across input representations and relied on difficult-to-compare published scores for prior models. V2 substantially addresses these deficiencies with matched representation experiments, shared benchmark protocols, repeated-run reporting, and extensive sensitivity analyses. Clinical null results and explicit preprocessing/scaling qualifications make the conclusions more assessable. Small cohorts and limited pretraining diversity remain constraints, but the improvement in evidential support and reproducibility is substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same flat-map fMRI research. Their text, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite v2's substantial expansion and revised experiments.

after.justification: V2 reports original representation comparisons, BRAINMARKS evaluations, scaling experiments, and extensive ablations and supplementary analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original masked-reconstruction experiments, scaling analyses, and downstream classification results on HCP, UKBB, and NSD.

results.title: Scaling Vision Transformers for Functional MRI with Flat Maps

C1.justification: The conclusion narrows the claim from state-of-the-art performance on 41 tasks to performance on a majority of tasks, acknowledging exceptions. Headline framing changes from a Geo-Foundation Model to a spatial/location embedding model, while the central SMF, modality-flexibility and generalization contributions remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds task-dependent interpretations of fusion, suggesting that land-cover and coarse land-use tasks may not require fused representations. It discusses architectural robustness and training/inference cost tradeoffs, and makes applicability limits more specific to point- or postal-code-level urban data.

D1.justification: v2 specifies the satellite crop's 2240-by-2240-meter footprint, documents the additional architectural configurations, and provides detailed runtime measurements and their inference protocol. Existing implementation recipes and code, dataset and weight access information are retained; the reproducibility statement moves to Appendix B.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same PP2-M data, urban prediction tasks, geographic coverage and synthetic experiments. The added city-wise crime results concern cities already evaluated in v1.

E2.justification: Appendix D.7/Table 11 adds the 'Encoded Modalities' comparator, using concatenated modality-encoder features with linear predictors. The original GeoCLIP, SatCLIP, GAIR, GPS2Vec, CSP, PDFM and Identity comparisons are retained.

E3.justification: The existing splits, metrics, pretraining budgets and downstream tuning procedures remain unchanged. Added experiments introduce per-city scoring after joint training, controls varying coordinate concatenation and fusion architecture, and a batch-size-1 coordinate-encoding latency protocol.

E4.justification: v1's appendix analyses are retained as v2 Sections D.1–D.4. New Sections D.5–D.8 test raw-coordinate dependence, encoder architecture/depth/pooling, feature concatenation and pretraining stability. City-wise crime analysis and computational-cost analysis further extend the examination of robustness and practical behavior.

E5.justification: v1 already reports variability over five downstream MLP seeds. v2 extends uncertainty reporting to five independent UrbanFusion pretraining runs with different initializations and data orderings (Table 12). Table 15 also reports timing variability over 5,000 forward passes.

E6.justification: Original benchmark values are retained, but substantial new city-wise, ablation, pretraining-variability and runtime results appear. Table 11 reports concatenation versus UrbanFusion scores of 67.3 versus 65.6 for land-cover F1 and 62.6 versus 88.5 for crime R2. Table 15 newly reports UrbanFusion inference at 6.57 ms and training at 519.30 minutes.

M1.justification: The proposed encoders, Transformer fusion, complementary modality masking, contrastive alignment and latent reconstruction remain unchanged. The new LSTM, depth and pooling configurations are experimental ablations; they do not replace the proposed architecture.

P1.justification: The overall narrative remains recognizable, with targeted rewrites of the introduction, synthetic-experiment explanation and conclusion. Existing appendix details are explained more fully in Section 4.5, the reproducibility statement is relocated, the appendix contents page is removed, and disclosure/impact statements are added.

P2.justification: The single-column preprint becomes a two-column conference main text, extensively resizing and repositioning figures and tables. Figure 3's panels change from side-by-side to stacked. Six new tables present additional analyses, while existing figure content and matched benchmark tables are retained.

R1.justification: Related work expands to discuss UrbanCLIP, ReFound, GeoLink, urban region pretraining/prompting and FlexiReg, distinguishing their region-level approaches from UrbanFusion's location-level fusion. Supporting architecture citations are also added. Publication and author-name updates to existing references do not introduce new evaluated baselines.

T1.justification: The proxy-modality assumption, Lemma 1, PID definitions and InfoNCE/Barber–Agakov derivations are retained from v1 Appendix D in v2 Appendix E. Notational corrections and citation updates do not change the mathematical argument.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked a direct concatenated-feature control and pretraining-level stability evidence. v2 supplies both (Tables 11–12), alongside coordinate and architecture controls, substantially strengthening validation of the central fusion contribution. It also acknowledges tasks where fusion loses and documents its higher training cost. These additions improve the evidential basis and qualification of the conclusions without replacing the original benchmark evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same UrbanFusion/SMF study and contain readable main texts and complete appendices. Corresponding methods, equations, figures and tables can be matched despite substantial reformatting and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds architectural controls, feature-concatenation comparisons, independent pretraining runs, city-wise results and runtime measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original urban prediction experiments, cross-regional evaluations, synthetic information-preservation experiments and ablations.

results.title: UrbanFusion: Stochastic Multimodal Fusion for Contrastive Learning of Robust Spatial Representations

C1.justification: The abstract narrows the performance claim from consistently outperforming baseline methods to outperforming standard CSCNNs and matching state-of-the-art baselines. The title drops 'with Complete Kernel Basis.' The central contribution of input-conditioned equivariant kernels remains unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 introduces a locality-based explanation for differing fluid and electrodynamics rankings, discusses richer conditioning for scaling, and identifies unoptimized Clifford operations as a runtime bottleneck. It also expands applicability discussion and adds limitations concerning multivector field representations. The general completeness conjecture and masking limitations were already disclosed in v1.

D1.justification: v2 identifies the existing equivariance evaluation as single-layer testing on NS, specifies standard-normal sampling for the random-condition ablation, and documents single-A100 timing averaged over the test set. Appendix B's architecture, masking, normalization, optimizer, and training-hardware details are otherwise retained.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate Navier–Stokes, shallow-water forecasting with SWE-1 and SWE-5 setups, three-dimensional Maxwell equations, and relativistic Maxwell equations. Appendix C retains the same datasets and task requirements. The new ablation and timing study use existing coverage.

E2.justification: v2 evaluates Transolver on NS, MW3, and MW2, whereas v1 reports it only on SWE-1. CViT comparisons expand from SWE-5 to all four data-efficiency tasks. Tables 1 and 4 therefore substantially strengthen comparator coverage within existing experiments.

E3.justification: v2 adds an N=64 NS evaluation point, a SWE-1 conditioning comparison at N=256, and a GPU timing protocol. The reported equivariance-error denominator changes from the magnitude of a sum to the sum of separate norms in Equation 18, although the reported errors remain identical; a rerun is not established.

E4.justification: Appendix D.1 adds a direct test of conditioning choices: none, mean pooling, max pooling, and a fixed random multivector. Appendix D.2 adds comparative inference timing to test conditioning overhead. These address central design and efficiency questions beyond v1's existing scaling, equivariance, and qualitative-error analyses.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty bars. The new inference-time averages remain point estimates rather than repeated-run uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: New comparisons place Transolver ahead of C-CSCNN on electrodynamics: MW3 at N=512 gives 3.99e-4 versus 4.51e-4, and MW2 at N=2048 gives 0.17034 versus 0.2519. New conditioning and timing results are also reported, including 54.30 ms for C-CSCNN versus 53.83 ms for CSCNN. SWE-5 results remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The conditional convolution, equivariant kernel parameterization, mean-pooled conditioning, ResNet backbone, circular masking, and MW2 normalization are retained. Max-pooling and random conditioning appear as ablation variants; the proposed default method is unchanged.

P1.justification: v2 revises the title, abstract, introductory framing, and experimental narrative; separates Clifford-algebra background into its own subsection; and expands the conclusion with limitations and an impact statement. The overall section sequence and most method and proof prose remain recognizable and unchanged.

P2.justification: The document switches from one to two columns. The data-efficiency plots are consolidated into a four-panel Figure 2 focused on C-CSCNN versus CSCNN, while broader comparisons appear in Tables 1 and 4. Ablation and timing tables are added, and equivariance results move from a table into prose. Existing rollout, masking, and residual images are retained.

R1.justification: New references support discussion of equivariance at scale, robotics, control, vision, and physics applications, plus ConvNeXt and Flash Clifford as future improvements. The principal positioning relative to steerable CNNs, Clifford networks, and implicit kernels remains intact.

T1.justification: Section 3.2 adds an explicit Clifford-algebra defining relation and grade-dimension formula. The equivariance-error definition also changes mathematically through its denominator. The conditional-equivariance proofs, completeness conjecture, and Appendix A algebraic demonstrations otherwise retain their substance.

improvement.justification: The expanded comparisons resolve a material weakness in v1's empirical positioning: v2 evaluates stronger electrodynamics baselines and acknowledges Transolver's advantage. The conditioning ablation and measured overhead substantiate central design and efficiency arguments. These gains are substantial despite remaining reporting gaps, including the unexplained SWE-1 mean-pooling MSE difference between Table 1 (0.3137) and Table 3 (0.2982).

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Conditional Clifford-Steerable CNN work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–D are readable and support comparison despite the changed title and formatting.

after.justification: v2 retains original forecasting and equivariance results and adds baseline evaluations, a conditioning ablation, and inference-time measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original PDE forecasting experiments, model-scaling results, equivariance measurements, and qualitative prediction errors in Section 5 and Appendix D.

results.title: Conditional Clifford-Steerable CNNs for PDE Modeling

C1.justification: The central pipeline, compact-model, and frontier-performance claims remain unchanged, including the reported 7–14% gains. v2 adds an explicit open-source release commitment in the abstract and announces pipeline, 20B checkpoint, and evaluation-suite releases in the introduction.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations about teacher dependence, retrieval benefits, generalization across model families, and operational applicability. It newly identifies the 8k context limitation for malware analysis, discusses secure-coding degradation, and proposes dequantization overhead as an explanation for slower 8-bit inference. Some interpretations are overstated: CyberSOCEval gains are not uniform, and secure-code pass rates consistently trail the reference models.

D1.justification: v2 supplies access links for pipeline code, the 20B model, and evaluation data. Appendices K–L add GPU counts, training durations, gradient accumulation, sequence packing, and inference configurations and resource measurements. These materially expand reproducibility information, although Appendix K's effective batch size of 3 is not reconciled with Section 4.1's retained batch size of 3072.

E1.justification: v2 retains the original coverage and adds unseen threat-report-to-ATT&CK mapping, product-specific CVE reassessment, CyberSOCEval threat-intelligence reasoning, and secure-code autocomplete and instruction tasks (Section 5.2 and Appendix J). CyberSOCEval malware analysis is described but explicitly omitted from reported evaluation because of context-length requirements.

E2.justification: The original comparator sets are retained. v2 Table 8 adds broad comparisons with Phi-4, Mistral Small 3.2, Llama 4 Scout, and Mixtral 8x22B, and extends DeepSeek-V3 beyond its earlier frontier CTI comparison. Llama 4 Maverick also participates in the new CyberSOCEval comparison.

E3.justification: The original training recipe and zero-temperature CoT evaluation remain stated. New experiments introduce exact-match and Jaccard scoring for CyberSOCEval, normalized MAD with a missing-answer penalty for CVE reassessment, and static-analysis pass rates for generated code. Additional controls vary retrieval and reformatter choice, while inference measurements vary precision and batch size.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's dataset/reformatting comparisons, v2 adds search-removal ablations across model sizes and a controlled gpt-oss-120B versus Llama-4-Maverick reformatter comparison (Appendix G). It also adds unseen-report generalization tests, deployment performance analyses, and qualitative examples. The earlier checkpoint-initialization, judge, and quantization analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports seed-based variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The existing answer-order swaps and human-judge agreement reporting remain unchanged; the new experiments do not introduce uncertainty estimation or repeated-run counts.

E6.justification: All seven original tables retain their numerical contents. v2 adds substantial results: for example, the 4B average is 71.11 without search versus 72.68 with the full pipeline. New findings include lower secure-code pass rates and mixed CyberSOCEval outcomes: 8B accuracy is 38.61 versus its baseline's 42.86, despite higher Jaccard. A new discrepancy appears in Table 11, which reports full-pipeline 20B RCM as 84.7 rather than Table 1's retained 87.40.

M1.justification: The proposed expert-guided formatting, multi-step retrieval, answer enrichment, and CyberPal training procedure remain unchanged. Alternative reformatters and search removal are experimental variants, while sequence-packing information is newly disclosed implementation detail rather than an established method revision.

P1.justification: v2 locally rewrites the introduction and results discussion, separates ablations from judge evaluation, moves the existing cybersecurity-model comparison into Appendix E, and adds release and disclosure text. The overarching section sequence and most method, training, and retained appendix prose remain intact.

P2.justification: The main text changes from a single-column report to a two-column conference layout. v1's three-panel ablation Figure 5 is replaced by an expanded summary table, while its results remain documented. Existing displays are relocated or resized, and numerous comparison, practical-task, and efficiency tables plus two qualitative example figures are added.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for CyberSOCEval, secure-code evaluation, additional model families, and quantization latency. Its central positioning relative to SecKnowledge, ReAlign, Primus, and Foundation-Sec remains largely unchanged; bibliographic updates do not constitute new research positioning.

T1.justification: The task-partition formalization in Section 3.3.1 is unchanged. Added descriptions of standard evaluation metrics do not introduce substantive theoretical development; neither version supplies new propositions, proofs, or derivations.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence that v1 lacked for component attribution and practical applicability through retrieval/reformatter controls, operational tasks, and secure-coding evaluation. Release links and resource reporting also improve reproducibility. These gains outweigh introduced reporting weaknesses, particularly the conflicting 20B RCM score, overstated CyberSOCEval improvements, and understated secure-coding losses. Those weaknesses limit individual conclusions, but the expanded evidence makes the method's benefits and boundaries substantially more assessable.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CyberPal 2.0 models and SecKnowledge 2.0 pipeline. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material across extensive layout changes.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds component ablations, practical security evaluations, additional model comparisons, and training-time and inference measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original fine-tuning experiments, benchmark comparisons, ablations, expert-grounded judge evaluations, and quantization results in Section 5 and the appendices.

results.title: Toward Cybersecurity-Expert Small Language Models

C1.justification: The central claims about contextual degradation and its mitigation remain. The introduction adds an explicit scope qualification: the intended setting concerns benign protected content that users may legitimately supply again. This narrows the previously broader sensitive-or-outdated-information framing without redefining the central contribution.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands applicability and limitations discussion. Section 8 develops forgetting–contextual-utility trade-offs beyond v1's brief tuning qualifications and identifies benchmark, model-size and deployment limits. Section 4.2 distinguishes preserving original contextual behavior from improving absolute grounding, while the new robustness discussion addresses degradation under noisy and conflicting evidence.

D1.justification: v2 adds high-level preprocessing details for GPT-4o-mini-generated answers and contexts, identifies TOFU conflict sets as distractor sources, and explains potential caching of frozen-reference outputs. Existing optimizer, learning rate, batch size, hardware, prompt templates and convergence tolerances remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained TOFU coverage, v2 evaluates PISTOL's interconnected company-contract data under A_B and A_C removal scenarios. It also adds longer synthetic contexts and conflicting-evidence scenarios, substantially extending input conditions beyond the clean contexts and single paraphrase/reasoning example in v1.

E2.justification: Appendix A.8 and Table 9 add evaluated PDU and SimNPO comparisons and extend vanilla-versus-context-aware comparisons to DPO and GradDiff. DPO and GradDiff already appeared in v1's diagnostic evaluation but lacked these augmented comparisons. The original six-method diagnostic comparisons remain.

E3.justification: v2 adds token-level accuracy and ChrF, a human-label comparison using 120 sampled triples, GPT-4o-mini answer expansion for PISTOL, and systematic noisy/conflicting-context protocols including two to five distractors. These are additional evaluation designs; the original TOFU models, training budget and convergence-selection settings are retained.

E4.justification: v2 supplements the retained forget-ratio and context-weight ablations and single-example context study with systematic long/noisy-context tests, conflicting-evidence tests and distractor-count sensitivity analysis. Appendix A.2 additionally tests agreement between the LLM judge and human labels, addressing measurement reliability.

E5.justification: New Appendix A.2 specifies 5,000 bootstrap resamples and reports 95% confidence intervals for human–LLM agreement and Cohen's kappa. This adds uncertainty estimation for a limited validation study; the retained benchmark plots and their reporting are unchanged, and no increase in model-training repetitions is documented.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results in Tables 5 and 7–13. For example, new Table 7 reports PISTOL A_B contextual LLM-Judge scores of 0.25 versus 1.00 for vanilla versus context-aware RMU; Table 11 reports 0.010 versus 0.605 under noisy contexts. Main Table 2's absolute scores remain unchanged, but the Qwen3-8B UNDIAL contextual delta changes from +0.02 to +0.01. Table 1 also replaces RMU's qualitative output.

M1.justification: The three-term objective and KL alignment to the frozen original model remain unchanged. Applying this objective to additional unlearning methods introduces no documented new algorithmic component. Reference-output caching is discussed as a possibility, not an implemented procedural change.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion receive focused rewrites and terminology clarifications. Limitations and Impact Statement sections are added, and the appendix is expanded and renumbered. Most existing explanatory prose and the main Sections 1–7 sequence remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column conference layout for the main text and references, substantially resizing and relocating existing displays, including compact single-column case-study tables. It adds Tables 5 and 7–13. Existing plotted content is retained, so the visual revision primarily concerns layout and additional tables rather than redrawn results.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for PISTOL, PDU, SimNPO, Eldan and Russinovich, Zhai et al., and GDPR. It also corrects the TOFU attribution and removes the Llama 2 reference. The main positioning relative to parametric and prompt-based unlearning remains; several other reference changes are publication-metadata updates.

T1.justification: The general unlearning objective, context-aware KL objective and mathematical descriptions of GD, NPO and RMU are retained, with the latter moving from Appendix A.3 to A.5. No new theorem, proof, substantive derivation or formal assumption is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially reduces reliance on one benchmark, a single-example context-robustness check and an unvalidated LLM judge. PISTOL, systematic noisy/conflicting-context tests, additional comparisons and human-agreement validation strengthen the empirical support, while explicit limitations clarify trade-offs and applicability. The evidence remains bounded by synthetic benchmarks and models up to 8B, but the additions address important weaknesses in v1 and provide a clear overall quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same context-aware unlearning work. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and the methods, equations, figures and tables can be matched despite reformatting and appendix renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds PISTOL results, human evaluation of the judge, additional method comparisons and context robustness experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original TOFU experiments on Gemma-2B-IT and Qwen3-8B, including baseline comparisons, context-aware variants, ablations and qualitative examples.

results.title: Forget to Know, Remember to Use: Context-Aware Unlearning for Large Language Models

C1.justification: The central claims concerning language feedback, GP-guided optimization, sample efficiency, and textual priors remain. However, v1's conclusion claims successful application in multiple Meta A/B-testing campaigns; v2 replaces this with a belief that LILO suits such settings. Unstructured-output applicability becomes a listed contribution but was already asserted in v1 Section 1.1.

C2.justification: V2 qualifies feedback-efficiency comparisons by discussing unequal decision-maker workload and interprets eventual baseline overtaking through limitations of LLM in-context learning and convergence. It describes summarization as an initial illustration and explicitly identifies human evaluation as future work. Conversely, v1's warning about bias toward the LLM's own world knowledge is removed.

D1.justification: V2 supplies code-access information, specifies batched BoTorch acquisition implementations and categorical kernels, and documents new utility parameters, summarization protocols, algorithms, and prompts. These substantially expand reproducibility information. However, v1's disclosure of five LLM calls per labeling instance disappears without a replacement count; this omission does not establish an actual sampling change.

E1.justification: V2 retains the original four outcome-function families and adds categorical architecture optimization on NAS-Bench-201 with Edge and Research personas. It also evaluates CNN/DailyMail summarization with generated text as outcomes (Section 5.3.5 and Appendix F.8), substantially extending domain and task coverage. Images are discussed but not evaluated.

E2.justification: The four main baseline families remain; preferential BO is renamed preference BO. The matched feedback-acquisition comparison adds qPredES and separate batched and greedy EUBO entries (Table 2). The new summarization comparison includes random candidate acquisition alongside the quantitative BO baselines.

E3.justification: V2 adds 16-trial evaluations and changes the feedback-budget study from matched budgets of 1, 2, or 4 to one LILO message versus up to 16 quantitative responses. The reported area-prior selection changes from the top 5% to 10%. Summarization introduces five-trial protocols using three fresh or ten fixed training articles and 20 held-out articles. DTLZ2's corrected main-text dimensions already appeared in v1's appendix.

E4.justification: The input-GP/outcome-GP/random pair-selection ablation is replaced by sequential qEUBO versus random labeling under restricted budgets. V2 expands feedback-budget analyses and adds direct label-accuracy measurement, longer-horizon evaluation, UCB and Thompson-sampling sensitivity, and fixed versus sampled article studies. The LLM-choice ablation is retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Figure 3 changes the reported replication count from 30 to 32 while retaining 95% confidence intervals; the scalar-versus-pairwise study changes from 30 to 16 replications per environment. The retained LLM ablation still reports 30. Some v2 counts are inconsistent: Table 2 says 30 while Appendix F.3 says 32, and Figure 15's caption and main-text footnote also disagree.

E6.justification: V2 revises benchmark curves and Table 2 and adds substantial NAS, summarization, labeling-budget, and longer-horizon results. Summarization matches the strongest oracle-feedback baselines, while longer runs sometimes let quantitative baselines overtake LILO. Figure 13 adds mean label accuracy of approximately 84% initially and 89% finally; F.4's above-90% description does not match the plotted means. V1 Table 1 is retained unchanged as v2 Table 3. Revised settings preclude treating all score differences as same-setting gains.

M1.justification: V2 adopts input-space-only GP modeling as its main formulation; v1 fitted input- and outcome-space GPs, although it already discussed omitting the latter. More substantially, v1's one-shot pair selection using the previous GP becomes sequential labeling with random initialization, qEUBO selection, and GP refitting between chunks (v2 Algorithm 2). Question generation also drops the preselected outcome indices.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method exposition, baseline descriptions, and conclusion undergo extensive rewriting. Related work and background become separate sections, experimental subsections are reordered, and the appendices are reorganized into dedicated implementation, baseline, environment, related-work, and results sections with a contents page. The title also drops Interactive.

P2.justification: V2 introduces a two-column main layout, redraws the overview graphics, and replaces Figure 2 with a different conceptual illustration. Benchmark panels are expanded and rearranged, the scalar ablation becomes a standalone figure, and numerous analytical plots and a related-work table are added. Existing appendix tables and conversation examples are also relocated and reformatted.

R1.justification: V2 adds Handa et al. as a language-based preference-elicitation comparison and references supporting the new benchmarks, metrics, and acquisition analyses. References to Alamdari, Ye, and Muller are removed. Appendix E's comparison table systematizes the existing positioning around feedback format, search space, LLM role, and uncertainty, while retaining the central novelty argument.

T1.justification: V2 adds mathematical definitions for NAS utility, including sigmoid contributions, interactions, and penalties, and for summarization utility with weighted quality scores and a completion penalty (D.2 and F.8.2). Existing optimization and benchmark formulations remain. The added GP and EUBO background explains existing machinery; neither version supplies new theoretical guarantees or proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation of the central mechanism and its applicability: previously untested textual outcomes receive a held-out summarization evaluation, preference-label accuracy is measured directly, and feedback-budget, acquisition, and longer-horizon studies expose both strengths and limits. Expanded reproducibility information and clearer organization further improve assessability. These gains outweigh reporting inconsistencies, including Table 2's conflicting counts and Figure 13's overstated accuracy description. Reliance on simulated decision makers remains an important limitation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe LILO. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial revision and reorganization.

after.justification: Section 5 and Appendix F report original optimization experiments, including NAS-Bench-201, text summarization, preference-label accuracy, and additional ablations.

before.justification: Section 4 and Appendix C report original optimization experiments across eight environments, including baseline comparisons and method ablations.

results.title: LILO: Bayesian Optimization with Natural Language Feedback

C1.justification: The core denoising contribution and headline gains of 6.7 points in mathematics and 1.5 in code remain. The contribution list newly claims explicit gradient analysis and noise-estimation sample complexity. The conclusion distinguishes clean population-gradient recovery for Dr.GRPO from variance-adjusted correction for GRPO.

C2.justification: v3 replaces v1's claim of fully recovering noiseless GRPO through the estimated variance with an oracle-versus-consistent-plug-in distinction, and explicitly qualifies the practical improvement guarantee. It adds clipping-related applicability limits and interprets the calibration budget quantitatively. However, its new statement that mean-only correction degrades performance overgeneralizes Table 5: the AceMath row improves from 72.37% to 73.13%.

D1.justification: v3 explicitly documents the unclipped sequence-level training objective, describes calibration corruptions as numerical modifications or injected code bugs, and supplies the clipping ablation's settings. These expand documentation without establishing changes to the original implementations. Repository access, hardware, runtime, and most hyperparameters remain unchanged; detailed MATH-specific setup information is still absent.

E1.justification: v3 adds mathematical-reasoning evaluation on MATH under synthetic noise, while retaining GSM8K and APPS. This extends coverage within the existing mathematics domain rather than introducing another task family. The clipping experiment uses the existing GSM8K coverage.

E2.justification: The corresponding comparisons retain uncorrected GRPO/Dr.GRPO and the mean-only correction comparator where previously evaluated. Table 7's DAPO and PPO labels designate clipping settings within Dr.GRPO, not newly evaluated full baseline algorithms.

E3.justification: New experiments extend model configurations to Qwen3-1.7B, Llama-3.2-3B, and Qwen3-4B, and introduce a 50-step clipping evaluation crossing four clipping settings with three noise levels. These substantially extend the evaluation design. The original experiments retain their reported splits, metrics, 10-epoch budget, and five responses per prompt.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained noise-rate sensitivity and mean-versus-variance correction comparisons, Appendix C adds a controlled test of whether clipping substitutes for denoising. Table 7 examines no clipping, DAPO-style, PPO-style, and tight clipping, identifying a regime where correction's benefit is suppressed or reversed.

E5.justification: Section 6.2 newly quantifies calibration uncertainty using a 95% analytical bound of approximately 0.108 on the estimated signal-retention factor, corresponding to relative bounds of 23.5% and 18.4% for the two reward models. Both versions retain seed=1 disclosures without reporting across-run uncertainty for accuracy.

E6.justification: The accuracy values in v1 Tables 1-5 are retained in v3 Tables 1 and 3-6. New results include MATH performance, such as Qwen3-4B scoring 24.87% without correction versus 31.58% with correction at noise (0.3, 0.4), and the tight-clipping reversal of 34.36% versus 33.13% in Table 7. The main-text code reward-model false-negative rate is also corrected from 0.231 to 0.233, matching the earlier appendix.

M1.justification: The two-stage correction method remains, but Algorithm 1 corrects the GRPO normalizer from Z to sqrt(max(Z, epsilon)) and replaces the 1/(2N) flip-rate denominators with the corresponding class counts. These are consequential corrections to the specified procedure; the PDFs do not establish that the original experiments were rerun.

P1.justification: The introduction and conclusion are substantially rewritten, and explanatory transitions throughout the theory are revised. Related-work positioning moves into Background, reward-binarization details move to Appendix B, references move before the appendices, and separate limitations and impact sections appear. Author information and theorem numbering also change.

P2.justification: Document-wide reformatting changes typography, the title and affiliation block, headers, reference columns, and table placement. v3 adds boxed explanatory notes and two tables. Figure 1 retains the same graphic but receives an expanded caption; existing result tables are reformatted and relocated rather than replaced.

R1.justification: v3 adds citations to VerifyBench, One Token to Fool LLM-as-a-Judge, and the MATH dataset, while dropping Ziegler et al. The introduction emphasizes imperfect verifiers, but the positioning against upstream reward-model robustness remains. DISCO's changed author attribution and REINFORCE++'s updated title refer to retained works.

T1.justification: v3 adds Theorem 5.4 deriving gradient attenuation and corrected-gradient relationships, and Proposition 5.6 giving a finite-sample noise-estimation bound, with proofs in Appendix A. It also supplies an explicit attenuation-inequality derivation and corrects the surrogate appearing in the estimated-rate improvement bound. The fixed-point comparison itself already appeared in v1, despite its new corollary label.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially improves the reliability of the method description by correcting central normalization and flip-rate formulas and qualifying v1's exact GRPO-recovery assertion. The gradient and calibration analyses strengthen the supporting argument, while the clipping ablation tests practical applicability and exposes a failure condition. MATH results broaden validation. Incomplete MATH-specific documentation and the overgeneralized Table 5 interpretation remain weaknesses, but do not outweigh these substantive gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same noise-corrected GRPO work. All main-text and appendix pages are readable, and the methods, equations, figures, and tables can be matched reliably across versions.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds MATH experiments in Table 2 and a clipping ablation in Appendix C, Table 7.

before.justification: v1 reports original training and evaluation results on GSM8K and APPS under synthetic reward corruption and learned reward models in Tables 1-5.

results.title: Noise-corrected GRPO: From Noisy Rewards to Unbiased Gradients

C1.justification: The central contribution and superior-defense claims remain. v2 replaces v1's continuous-monitoring and edge-restoration language with explicit per-query detection and pruning, emphasizes training-free operation, and adds a quantified low-runtime-overhead claim to the introduction.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands interpretation: threshold choice trades removal of useful communication against missed attacks; combined-attack resilience is attributed to decomposed local judgments; and low overhead is attributed to inexpensive sentence-pair scoring. It also discusses incompatible attack combinations and introduces a Byzantine-threshold scope limitation. The existing explanation involving isolation of infected benign agents is retained.

D1.justification: New Appendix A.1 specifies synchronous three-round schedules, 15/12 temporal nodes, 20/10 review messages, and detailed feedback routing. v2 also supplies runtime information and updates the stated code location to the BPD repository, while removing the separate future-release reproducibility statement. Existing prompts and baseline configurations are retained; these are principally documentation refinements.

E1.justification: MMLU, Alpaca, SAMSum, and ChatDoctor remain unchanged. However, Sections 4.6–4.8 substantially extend the adversarial scenarios to corrupted scoring, attackers informed about topology and detector scores, and combined Harmful+Reframing and Suboptimal+Reframing attacks. These alter the evaluated threat conditions beyond v1's individual attacks and dynamic graphs.

E2.justification: G-Safeguard, AGENTXPOSED, Challenger, and Inspector retain their membership in corresponding comparisons. This includes the DeepSeek-V3 text-generation comparison, moved from v1 Table 13 to v2 Table 18. The new experiments introduce no new external defense baseline.

E3.justification: New evaluation protocols include score-sign manipulation, disclosure of system information to attackers, a threshold sweep from 1.3 to 1.7, runtime measurements, and scaling to 7/10 agents and five dialogue rounds. Appendix B.4 adds exact-match evaluation against human labels on 50 sampled items. The original benchmark settings remain; Appendix A.1 primarily clarifies their implementation.

E4.justification: The original backpropagation ablation is retained. v2 adds substantial analyses of threshold sensitivity, robustness to compromised scoring and informed or combined attacks, computational overhead and scaling, and agreement between human and LLM edge scores (Sections 4.5–4.9 and Appendices B.3–B.4).

E5.justification: Table 1 newly states that three experiments were conducted, and Tables 1–2 report means with one standard deviation instead of point estimates alone. This reporting remains confined to the main GPT-4o/MMLU comparisons. v1 provides no run count, so an increase in runs cannot be established.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 contain revised values: BPD's reported average answer accuracy changes from 86%/87% to 85.4%/87.5%, now with uncertainty. New system-aware attack results report 83%/85% answer accuracy and 81%/82% detection accuracy, alongside new threshold, combined-attack, timing, and scorer-alignment results. Other original tables retain their values after equivalent rescaling and renumbering.

M1.justification: The temporal DAG, ternary edge scoring, backward score averaging, agent-level deviation threshold, and outgoing-message pruning remain the same. Naming the method BPD, adding Algorithm 1, and expanding its mathematical description do not establish a different algorithm.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, related work, and method exposition are substantially rewritten. BPD becomes the consistent method name, the methodology gains named stages and a summary, and the experimental narrative is reorganized into more focused subsections. Appendix organization and closing statements also change.

P2.justification: The main text switches to a two-column layout, Figure 1 is extensively redrawn, and tables are rebuilt with separate structure/method grouping and percentage displays. v2 adds Algorithm 1, two threshold figures, and seven result tables. Retained appendix tables are renumbered, and the misleading caption of v1 Table 14 is corrected in v2 Table 19.

R1.justification: v2 adds the BLEURT reference by Sellam et al. and removes background references including Brown et al., Kushwaha et al., and Yu et al. Related work is reorganized into attack and defense categories while retaining the main local-versus-global positioning. Numerous other bibliography changes concern publication metadata rather than different works.

T1.justification: Section 3.3 adds a finite layerwise matrix-product expression for propagated scores and explicitly states uniqueness through a single backward pass on the DAG. It also specifies zero-outdegree handling and formalizes the PageRank comparison. Most remaining mathematics reformulates the existing recursion; no substantial theorem or proof framework is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of previously untested weaknesses: scorer corruption, informed and combined adversaries, scorer reliability, and computational cost. Uncertainty reporting and explicit MAS schedules also improve transparency. These address important evidential gaps in v1. Reporting remains imperfect: uncertainty covers only two tables, and the introduction's below-10% overhead claim conflicts with the 10.6% hierarchy overhead in Section 4.9. These limitations do not outweigh the substantial added validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same signed-graph defense for multi-agent systems. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–B are readable, and retained material can be matched across renaming, restructuring, and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds adaptive and combined attacks, threshold sensitivity, runtime measurements, scalability experiments, and human validation of edge scoring.

before.justification: v1 reports original GPT-4o and DeepSeek-V3 experiments measuring task performance and malicious-agent detection, including attack comparisons, dynamic graphs, and a backpropagation ablation.

results.title: Securing Multi-Agent Systems Against Corruptions via Node Contribution Backpropagation

C1.justification: The central contribution remains predictive context embeddings that improve autoregressive language modeling. v3 explicitly claims downstream advantages under equivalent parameter counts and foregrounds quantified parameter efficiency. Its conclusion drops v1's stronger assertion that no backbone architecture changes are required, retaining compatibility with token-level evaluation.

C2.justification: v3 explains the preferred 0/12 split through deeper decoder integration of context, adds interpretations distinguishing context modeling from extra parameters and MTP, and motivates mean pooling through comparable ablation performance. It also replaces v1's blanket numerical descriptions of downstream gains with more qualified scale-dependent discussion. These refine the existing interpretation without introducing substantial failure or limitation analysis.

D1.justification: Appendices 7.1–7.3 newly disclose GPT-2 AdamW betas, clipping and warmup, explicit Pythia hyperparameters, A100 80GB hardware, and approximately 3,594/5,375 GPU-hours for the 1B/1.4B models. Efficiency hardware and the pooling checkpoint are also specified. These substantially expand documentation without establishing changed main training settings. Existing access links remain; the relocated GPT-2 table drops its layer-count column.

E1.justification: v3 adds AlpacaEval 2.0 and LongBench's 0–4k subtasks, extending evaluation to longer-input single-document, multi-document, summarization, synthetic, and code/classification tasks. Existing training corpora and benchmarks remain. SciQ already appears in v1's result tables; correcting the prose's SIQA reference is not added coverage.

E2.justification: v3 adds GPT2-PM baselines to perplexity and downstream comparisons across all four GPT-2 scales, plus a four-token MTP comparator at GPT2-XL scale (Table 6). v1 mentions parameter matching in its cost discussion but provides no corresponding performance rows; MTP is discussed but not evaluated.

E3.justification: v3 revises the chunk-size ablation from the default predictor depth to depth adjusted with chunk size to approximately match FLOPs and memory. New protocols include dynamic NTK-aware RoPE interpolation for LongBench, ordinary and length-controlled AlpacaEval win rates, and pooling comparisons at a 30k-step checkpoint. Existing main pretraining budgets and zero-/five-shot settings remain.

E4.justification: v3 adds an aggregation-strategy ablation (Table 13), matched-training Pythia convergence comparisons (Figure 6), and measured throughput/latency analysis (Table 10). It also materially revises the chunk-size study. Earlier predictor-depth, encoder/decoder-split, block-size, and attention analyses are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Figure 1 changes the reported parameter-scaling fit from zero-offset power laws to power laws with additive floors of 13.1 and 13.0, revising the statistical model used to summarize scaling. Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: Original perplexity/downstream rows and MT-Bench averages remain unchanged. v3 adds PM/MTP results, AlpacaEval win rates of 54.48% and 54.01% length-controlled, LongBench scores of 23.32 versus 20.21, and appendix analysis results. Parameter savings change from 38% to 39%; the revised chunk experiment favors w=4 rather than w=2 under different controls. The earlier below-5% GPU-memory-overhead observation disappears. Table 6's ARC-Challenge value of 21.6 conflicts with 21.4 retained in Table 12.

M1.justification: The reported inference pseudocode changes: v1 invokes context prediction inside every token iteration, whereas v3 initializes it once and updates it at completed chunk boundaries, also revising boundary indexing. The encoder–predictor–decoder architecture, mean pooling, additive fusion, and cross-entropy objective remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method explanations, experimental discussion, and related work are extensively rewritten. Architecture components receive separate subsections, analysis becomes a standalone section, and complexity, training details, and full GPT-2 results move into an organized appendix. These are substantial narrative and structural revisions beyond adding experiments.

P2.justification: v3 introduces a main summary table, expands comparisons with PM rows, and adds benchmark, efficiency, hyperparameter, and pooling tables plus training curves. Figure 4 merges the earlier ablation and length plots and revises the chunk-size panel; Figure 1 is redrawn and repositioned. Full GPT-2 tables move to the appendix, where Tables 9 and 11 duplicate the same perplexity comparison.

R1.justification: v3 substantially reframes related work around modeling above versus below tokens. It adds discussions of DLCM, CALM, MegaByte, and JEPA applications while removing discussions including BlockFormer, SegFormer, and LongNet. The distinctions drawn against latent and hierarchical predecessors change substantively; bibliographic updates to retained works are not counted as new research.

T1.justification: v3 Table 10 extends the existing complexity analysis with separate inference orders, O(Td) for the token decoder and O((T/w)d) for the context predictor, and combined overhead expressions. The principal gradient derivations and training/memory orders are retained; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens experimental credibility by adding explicit parameter-matched performance controls and an MTP comparison, addressing important alternative explanations for v1's gains. LongBench, convergence and efficiency analyses broaden validation, while the appendix materially improves reproducibility. Missing run uncertainty, duplicated tables, and the inconsistent ARC-Challenge entry remain weaknesses, but they do not outweigh the stronger evidence supporting the central contribution.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ContextLM and retain matching architecture and core experiments. All pages are readable, including v3's Appendix 7.1–7.7; v1 ends with references and has no separate appendix.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds parameter-matched and MTP comparisons, AlpacaEval, LongBench, training curves, efficiency measurements, and pooling ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original GPT-2/Pythia training and downstream results, MT-Bench evaluations, architectural ablations, and attention analyses.

results.title: Context-level Language Modeling by Learning Predictive Context Embeddings

C1.justification: The central contributions and performance claims are retained. However, v2's conclusion newly claims, to the authors' knowledge, the first Video MLLM ability to generate explicit spatio-temporal reasoning evidence within a single model without external tools, making the novelty claim more explicit and stronger.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the new controls as evidence that predicted timestamps identify informative visual content, and discusses applicability to stronger backbones, camera-motion shifts and sparse frame sampling. It also identifies diminishing returns from denser sampling. The earlier limitations concerning complex videos, small objects, multistep reasoning and absent audio remain substantively unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies 16 evaluation frames for V-STAR and 64 for other video benchmarks, and details Qwen2.5-VL checks of sentence–crop semantic consistency. These expand documentation without establishing changes to earlier settings. Conversely, v1's explicit commitment to release code, datasets and checkpoints disappears; the project-page link remains, and actual resource availability cannot be determined from the PDFs.

E1.justification: v2 adds LongVideo-Reason-eval, STAR and CameraBench evaluations, extending coverage of long-range reasoning, situated reasoning and challenging camera-motion conditions. These are substantive additions to the evaluated data and scenarios; the reported training-data sources and composition remain unchanged.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds VideoLLaMA3-7B and InternVL-2.5-8B to the general-video comparison, although these model families already appeared in the V-STAR comparison. Tables 9–10 also introduce a text-only control and Qwen3-VL base-model comparisons. These extend the comparator set while retaining the original main comparison framework.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include a 150-question VideoMME subset with evidence-aligned versus equal-count random frame removal, Qwen3-VL configurations at 4B/8B/32B, and 16-versus-64-frame and AKS sampling comparisons. Training-objective and fixed-sigma controls add further experimental settings. These are additional protocols, rather than evidence that the original experiments were rerun under changed settings.

E4.justification: v2 adds direct tests of evidence informativeness, a control removing grounded SFT evidence and RL thinking rewards, camera-motion robustness analyses, and frame-sampling sensitivity. The temporal-proximity ablation gains a fixed sigma=1 control; the fixed sigma=4 row repeats the earlier no-adaptation scores. Figure 10 also adds an open-ended QA case study.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals or significance tests. The eight-response test-time voting procedure is unchanged and is an inference mechanism, not uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Retained main scores and voting results are unchanged, but v2 adds substantial results, including 69.4 on LongVideo-Reason-eval, 70.5 on STAR and 58.8 on CameraBench, plus Qwen3-VL and control results. Evidence removal yields 66.0 versus 68.0 for random removal, from 68.7. Newly included VideoLLaMA3 scores 22.2 on TVGBench, exceeding the unchanged proposed-model score of 20.8. Conversely, Table 3 removes detailed What/When/Where training-ablation entries.

M1.justification: The proposed cold-start SFT, GSPO optimization, adaptive temporal proximity, temporal gating and confidence-aware voting procedures are retained. Qwen3-VL applications and alternative frame sampling are evaluated configurations; the expanded consistency-checking description does not establish a change to the existing annotation pipeline.

P1.justification: v2 condenses the abstract, edits several introductory and methodological paragraphs, standardizes the name to Open-o3-Video and expands the appendix roadmap. It removes the Ethics, Reproducibility and LLM Usage statements. The main section sequence and much of the existing prose remain intact, so this is not a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: The experimental displays are substantially expanded and reorganized: Table 2 gains comparator rows and LRR/average columns, Table 3 is reduced to aggregate metrics, and the reward ablation becomes an Ada./Gat. matrix. New tables display evidence controls, sensitivity analyses and additional evaluations, while Figure 10 adds a qualitative example. Existing appendix figures are also relocated.

R1.justification: Section 2 and new Appendix A.2 substantially expand positioning against grounded and tool-assisted video reasoning, discussing STCAT, LRR, EgoMask, Conan, LongVT, VideoZoomer, VTimeCoT and STVG-o1. The comparison distinguishes native single-round video QA from iterative tool use and specialized grounding. This accompanies the stronger novelty statement and new model, benchmark and sampling citations.

T1.justification: The reward definitions and GSPO mathematics remain substantively equivalent. v2 introduces shorthand and reformats equations; its additional single-instance Gaussian reward formula restates the existing temporal reward. No new theorem, proof or substantive derivation is added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical support for the central grounding claim. Unlike v1's benchmark gains and illustrative examples alone, the added evidence-removal and text-only controls directly test evidence usefulness and grounded training, while backbone and camera-motion experiments address generalization. These gains outweigh the loss of detailed training-ablation scores and the release commitment. The evidence-removal study remains small and uncertainty reporting is still absent, limiting how strongly individual gains can be interpreted.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Open-o3 Video research framework. Their complete main texts and appendices, including tables, figures and equations, are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds evidence-removal controls, Qwen3-VL experiments, additional benchmark evaluations and sensitivity analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original model evaluations, training and reward ablations, data-mixture experiments, and confidence-aware voting results in Tables 1–7.

results.title: Open-o3-Video: Grounded Video Reasoning with Explicit Spatio-Temporal Evidence

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and principal conclusion retain the same contribution: training-free dynamic positional extrapolation without additional sampling overhead, with stronger benefits at higher resolutions. The added experiments broaden support without redefining these core claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds the interpretation that DyPE mitigates attention-entropy shift and preserves native-resolution attention behavior. It also identifies GPU memory as limiting video evaluation to 33 frames. The core spectral explanation remains unchanged, while v1's explicit qualification that FreeScale uses an older SDXL backbone is dropped.

D1.justification: Appendix C newly states that code will be released upon acceptance; this is a future commitment, not evidence of released code.
