The project link, L40S hardware, 28 sampling steps and existing hyperparameters remain. Added experiments identify specific models, including Wan2.1 1.3B and Qwen-Image-Edit-2509.

E1.justification: Appendix E adds video generation evaluated with VBench and multi-reference image editing through multi-concept composition. These substantially extend the previous image-generation tasks. DrawBench, Aesthetic-4K, ImageNet and panoramic generation remain; testing Qwen-Image on Aesthetic-4K does not itself add dataset coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated comparisons with DemoFusion, FreCaS, DiffuseHigh, I-Max, FLUX+BSRGAN, UltraPixel, Diffusion-4K and HiFlow, retaining FreeScale. TASR already appeared in v1 Appendix B, but v2 extends its participation to DrawBench, additional resolutions, the human study and FiTv2 comparisons.

E3.justification: New protocols include global and patch FID/IS comparisons at 2048 and 4096 square resolutions, 33-frame Wan2.1 video generation at 1280×720, and editing at 2656×2656. The human study expands from two to three comparison pairs per prompt while retaining 20 prompts and 50 raters. Appendix F introduces a native-resolution attention reference. Existing experiment settings are otherwise retained.

E4.justification: New Appendix F adds a focused diagnostic using 20 prompts to test whether high-resolution generation preserves native-resolution attention entropy, reporting timestep curves and mean absolute deviations. The existing scheduler ablations and resolution-limit analysis remain unchanged.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, generation seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests. The new entropy averages and mean absolute errors are diagnostic measurements, not added uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial baseline, Qwen-Image, video, editing and entropy results. Its new TASR human comparison reports DyPE preferences of 70.5%, 80.6% and 94.2%. Shared FLUX, FiTv2, ablation and panorama scores remain unchanged. FreeScale's earlier CLIP, ImageReward and aesthetics scores disappear, while its 4096-resolution FID of 259.24 is retained in the expanded comparison.

M1.justification: The core DyPE scheduler and dynamic positional-scaling rules remain unchanged in Eqs. 13–17. v2 additionally evaluates a DY-YaRN+HiFlow inference variant incorporating progressive refinement (Table 3 and Figure 14), a limited procedural extension whose integration details are not supplied.

P1.justification: Most foundational exposition is retained. v2 splits Section 4.1 into positional-extrapolation and general-baseline comparisons, adds an Impact Statement and Appendix F, makes local language and reference corrections, and removes video generation from the conclusion's future-work discussion.

P2.justification: The document changes from a single-column to a two-column layout with extensive resizing and relocation of displays. Tables gain comparator rows and new experimental panels; new figures cover Qwen-Image, video, editing, general baselines and entropy. Several formerly separate appendix figures are compressed together onto the final page.

R1.justification: Section 5 adds discussion of FreeU and FAM-Diffusion and distinguishes RIFLEx's temporal extrapolation from spatial resolution scaling. Additional references accompany the new baselines, models and benchmark; the Frequency-aware Diffusion Models and Improving Image Generation with Better Captions references are removed. The central positioning against static RoPE methods and Lumina-Next remains.

T1.justification: The Fourier-mixture formulation, PSD derivation, progression map, assumptions and scaling equations are retained, including the appendix formulas. The new entropy analysis supplies empirical measurements rather than a new mathematical derivation, theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: The broader comparisons materially address v1's limited evidence against non-positional-extrapolation approaches. Cross-model evaluations and the attention diagnostic further strengthen support for generality and the proposed mechanism. These gains outweigh remaining sparse patch-evaluation and HiFlow integration details and a new reporting inconsistency: the Impact Statement denies human-subject involvement despite the retained 50-rater study.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DyPE work. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite extensive layout changes.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds broader baseline comparisons, Qwen-Image experiments, video generation, image editing and attention-entropy measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original FLUX and FiTv2 experiments, a 50-rater human study, scheduler ablations, resolution scaling and panoramic generation results.

results.title: DyPE: Dynamic Position Extrapolation for Ultra High Resolution Diffusion

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the central contribution: plug-and-play segmented permutation improves block sparsity while preserving causal attention, maintaining near-full-attention quality and enabling up to 2.75× prefilling speedup. The additional benchmarks support these existing claims rather than redefine them.

C2.justification: v2 develops the interpretation that gains mainly arise from clustering globally important keys rather than local query-key alignment. It adds substantive boundaries: diagonal slash patterns can be disrupted, query-specific heads benefit little, and mean pooling struggles with UUID retrieval. It also interprets GQA sharing and memory/scaling tradeoffs, substantially qualifying v1's largely positive account.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents default GQA key/value replication, torch.gather-based permutation, BFloat16 memory estimates and CUDA-event profiling. The standalone reproducibility statement and explicit unchanged-decoding note from v1 are removed, while the repository link and core hyperparameter, Triton and hardware disclosures remain.

E1.justification: v2 retains LongBench and LongBenchv2 and adds RULER's controlled synthetic evaluation, including retrieval involving random UUID key-value pairs. Appendix B.1 also evaluates permutation proxies on NIAH and variable-tracing scenarios, substantially broadening the tested task requirements.

E2.justification: The main comparison methods remain Full Attention, MInference, FlexPrefill, XAttention and MeanPooling. New diagnostic comparisons in Section 2 and Appendix B introduce random permutation, greedy local key alignment, random-query scoring and average-query scoring as alternatives to the proposed last-block proxy.

E3.justification: New evaluation protocols include oracle block selection at fixed attention coverage, analysis of all 1,024 heads at 32K, block-size sweeps and Qwen3-8B/Qwen-2.5-14B-1M evaluations with specified tensor-parallel configurations. These substantially extend the experimental design; the original main settings of B=128, S=256 and threshold 0.9 remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds proxy sensitivity across tasks, layer/head analyses, failure-case visualizations, block-size ablation and shared-versus-independent GQA permutation experiments. It also adds memory-cost analysis and extends timing analysis. The original query/key, segment-size and XAttention-selection studies are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests. The new head-category percentages and averages describe empirical variation rather than introducing uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 and the original 2.75× headline speedup are unchanged. v2 adds substantial RULER, additional-model, proxy, head, timing and GQA results. In Table 3, Llama PBS-Attn+ scores 86.87 versus XAttention's 86.46 and full attention's 88.09; the prose incorrectly gives the corresponding gaps as 1.41 and 3.21 rather than 0.41 and 1.22.

M1.justification: The core segmented permutation, last-query-block scoring and Algorithms 1–2 remain unchanged. Appendix G adds an optional procedure that averages queries across GQA heads to compute a shared permutation. PBS-Attn+ uses the permutation-plus-XAttention combination already evaluated in v1 Appendix B.2.

P1.justification: v2 substantially reorganizes the narrative: preliminaries move to Appendix A, a motivation-and-analysis section takes their place, and the introduction, method explanation and ablation discussion are rewritten around structural consolidation. Related work is refocused, the ethics statement becomes a shorter impact statement, and the reproducibility and LLM-use statements are removed.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from single-column to two-column layout, with extensive resizing and relocation of existing displays. New tables and figures present RULER, proxy/head analyses, failure cases, additional models and GQA comparisons; the ablation figure gains a block-size panel. Table 5 redisplays existing density results as block counts.

R1.justification: Section 5 adds focused comparisons with Reformer and MMInference and cites Prism; RULER and Qwen3 references accompany the new evaluations. Broad long-context, linear-attention and state-space background is removed. The central positioning as attention restructuring orthogonal to block selection remains.

T1.justification: Section 2 introduces a formal critical-key set and budget-constrained block-selection objective. Appendix B defines absolute sparsity gain at fixed coverage, and the text adds complexity reasoning. The permutation lemmas, theorem and proofs are retained, with the proofs moved from Appendix A to Appendix C.

improvement.justification: v1 demonstrated practical gains but provided limited evidence about why permutation works and where it fails. v2 substantially addresses that gap through controlled proxy comparisons, systematic head analyses and explicit failure cases, while testing additional tasks and models and clarifying implementation costs. These gains strengthen the paper's explanatory and empirical support enough to outweigh localized reporting problems, including the RULER arithmetic mismatches with Table 3.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe PBS-Attn, and their main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices support reliable comparison. Retained material can be matched despite substantial reorganization and expanded appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds RULER evaluations, additional models, permutation diagnostics and GQA experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original LongBench and LongBenchv2 evaluations, prefilling speedups, permutation ablations and overhead measurements.

results.title: Sparser Block-Sparse Attention via Token Permutation

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion retain the central hallucination-mitigation, preserved general capability, and low-overhead claims, including the stated 20.7% maximum improvement. The introduction expands the ablation contribution from validating components to also establishing robustness to hyperparameter selection.

C2.justification: v3 interprets extraction-layer stability as evidence of a model-intrinsic property and attributes Qwen3-VL's relatively high CHAIR scores to detailed descriptions interacting with string matching. It also refines v1's broad query-quality limitation into failures involving image-irrelevant content, including retrieved documents, and identifies a missing evaluation scenario for such inputs.

D1.justification: v3 adds a code-availability statement and link, the exact LLM extraction prompt and word-to-token mapping, the COCO localization query template, and Qwen3-VL configuration details. These extend existing documentation; the original hardware, precision choices, scoring model, and decoding budgets remain documented.

E1.justification: v3 retains the original coverage and adds AMBER's existence, attribute, and relation hallucination tasks and MMBench's perception/reasoning evaluation. Appendix A also introduces MathVista's visual mathematics domain for saliency-layer robustness analysis, extending coverage beyond the original TextVQA analysis.

E2.justification: VCD is added to the LLaVA-1.5 7B and 13B comparisons in Tables 2–3 and to the latency comparison in Table 4. Greedy decoding, VAF, VAR, and Rel-Attn remain; comparisons on Qwen models still use only greedy decoding.

E3.justification: v3 substantially extends the evaluation design with Qwen3-VL 8B, controlled enhancement-layer range sweeps, and cross-dataset extraction-layer checks. Added benchmark evaluations reuse the main hyperparameters without retuning and introduce AMBER subscores and MMBench's CircularEval procedure. Existing benchmark splits, decoding budgets, and GPT-4.1 scoring settings are retained.

E4.justification: Beyond retaining component and enhancement-strength ablations, v3 tests extraction-layer stability across datasets and samples, enhancement-layer range sensitivity, and POS versus LLM word extraction. Appendix H adds saliency case studies for open-ended captioning and weather questions. These address several previously untested robustness and mechanism questions.

E5.justification: Appendix A newly reports five random seeds, each sampling 50 examples, for each of two models on TextVQA and MathVista, with individual-run values in Tables 8–11. Both versions already average five GPT-4.1 scoring repetitions for MMHal-Bench; confidence intervals and significance tests are not added.

E6.justification: Matched original benchmark and component-ablation scores are unchanged, but v3 adds substantial results for VCD, Qwen3-VL, new benchmarks, and robustness studies. Examples include Qwen3-VL MMHal-Bench hallucination rates of 28.3 for greedy decoding versus 26.4 for GIFT, and LLaVA-1.5 7B AMBER scores of 83.9 versus 87.2. Table 7 newly reports 52.6 hallucination rate for LLM extraction versus 57.3 for POS extraction.

M1.justification: The default GIFT procedure remains unchanged. Section 5.3 and Appendix F introduce an optional variant that prompts Qwen3-VL 8B to select visually grounded words instead of using POS tagging, changing the token-selection component. Token weighting and bypassing unnecessary saliency computation remain future proposals.

P1.justification: v3 tightens prose while retaining the overall narrative and much of the method explanation. The former Analyses section is redistributed into experimental results and Section 5.3 Ablations, appendices are reorganized, and an Impact Statement replaces the separate LLM-use disclosure. Author affiliation information also changes.

P2.justification: The single-column preprint becomes a two-column conference paper with extensively rearranged displays. Table 3 is transposed, the latency bar chart becomes Table 4, and model plots gain Qwen3-VL panels. New analysis tables and saliency examples are added; the retained qualitative examples are enlarged and redistributed across pages.

R1.justification: Related work adds citations to Sarkar et al., Wu et al., and Qiu et al.; new evaluations add MathVista, AMBER, and MMBench references. The spaCy bibliographic citation becomes a website footnote. GIFT's overall positioning against contrastive decoding, visual-input modification, and attention steering is retained.

T1.justification: The mathematical procedure in Equations 1–7 is retained. Moving min-max normalization from Equations 2–3 into accompanying prose and naming the positive attention increment are equivalent restatements. Neither version introduces theoretical guarantees or proofs.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses a substantive validation gap through extraction-layer checks across five seeds and two datasets, plus enhancement-layer sensitivity tests. Additional benchmarks evaluated without retuning, VCD and Qwen3-VL comparisons, and code/prompt documentation materially strengthen empirical support and reproducibility. The original overlap between tuning and evaluation samples remains, but the new robustness and transfer evidence substantially improves support for the conclusions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe GIFT, with matching core equations and experiments. The main text, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting.

after.justification: v3 retains these empirical results and adds model and baseline evaluations, layer-selection robustness experiments, token-extraction comparisons, and additional benchmark results.

before.justification: v1 reports original saliency-localization results, hallucination and general vision-language benchmarks, component ablations, sensitivity analyses, and latency measurements.

results.title: Capturing Gaze Shifts for Guidance: Cross-Modal Fusion Enhancement for VLM Hallucination Mitigation

C1.justification: The benchmark, four-skill framework, and knowledge-versus-reasoning gap remain central claims. v2 adds a fifth contribution and an abstract claim that training on QuArch transfers to practical memory design, improving design success and achieving up to 1.99 times better area efficiency. v1 presented downstream usefulness principally as motivation.

C2.justification: v2 expands interpretations concerning downstream applicability, specialized versus unfiltered SFT, and the trade-off between design success and best discovered area. It adds conclusions about judge self-preference and clarifies the benchmark's relationship to executable agentic evaluations. Revised failure analyses also remove misleading claims about endianness and bit indexing from v1 Appendix C.3.

D1.justification: Appendix B.1 newly documents gated access, encrypted solutions, permitted judge hosting, and private leaderboard evaluation. Appendices B.6, D.11, and D.12 add training-data selection, 676 SFT samples from 45 questions, Together AI usage, hyperparameters, teacher prompts, simulator constraints, and controller-search instructions absent from v1.

E1.justification: The original benchmark retains its question count, topic coverage, and modality totals. v2 additionally evaluates memory-hierarchy design for matrix multiplication and DRAM-controller configuration across four workloads, extending evaluation from answering questions to proposing and iteratively optimizing simulated designs.

E2.justification: The full model comparison retains the original 26 models and adds GPT-5.2, Gemini 3 Pro, Gemini 3 Flash, and Qwen3-VL-32B. The headline tables replace the earlier GPT-5 and Gemini 2.5 entries with newer models. Appendix B.9 also adds a Qwen3-VL-235B judge alongside Claude and Gemini.

E3.justification: Section 2.3 changes the reported skill-labeling procedure from LLM classification to expert primary and optional secondary labels, revising the evaluated skill subsets. New experiments introduce two SFT configurations, ten-turn design trials with explicit area and energy constraints, and forty-proposal DRAM searches. The original zero-shot QA grading framework remains.

E4.justification: v2 adds two downstream case studies, comparisons between fine-tuning configurations, and a reported unsuccessful unfiltered-training alternative. Appendix B.9 expands judge validation with cross-judge agreement, alternative-judge score tables, and self-judgment bias analysis. Several failure examples in Appendix C.3 and C.5 are replaced rather than merely relocated.

E5.justification: The existing three answer generations and majority judging remain unchanged. The added studies report twenty independent trials per model/configuration and ten runs per model/workload, respectively. Figure 15 introduces correlation and significance reporting, with r = 0.726 and p = 0.007; these additions concern the new studies.

E6.justification: Skill-based scores change alongside revised labels: GPT-5 reasoning accuracy is 72.4% in v1 Table 4 and 72.0% in v2 Table 6, without establishing a same-partition performance decline. New results include Gemma success increasing from 30% to 70% and Llama from 55% to 95% under three-epoch SFT, plus area-efficiency, controller-design, and expanded judge findings.

M1.justification: v2 introduces QuArch-based model training absent from v1: filtering memory-related questions, distilling answers and GPT-5.2 explanations, and fine-tuning Gemma and Llama for iterative simulator-guided design (Section 4.4, Appendix B.6 and D.11). This substantially extends the methodology beyond evaluating existing models; the original benchmark construction and primary judging procedure remain.

P1.justification: The main narrative sequence remains recognizable. v2 edits prose and terminology, standardizes headings and model names, moves contributor acknowledgments and ethics/reproducibility material, reorganizes appendix subsections, and adds scope explanations. Much of the retained methodological text and prompt content remains closely matched.

P2.justification: v2 converts the main text and references to a two-column conference layout, rearranges the skills-framework figure, redraws distribution plots, and adds an example montage and controller-design scatterplot. It introduces training and judge-analysis tables, converts v1's confusion-matrix figure into a table, and removes the redundant frontier-only modality table.

R1.justification: v2 adds educational-framework, distillation, simulation, and architecture-workflow references, including ABET/ACM, s1, ArchGym, and CacheMind. These support the expanded scope, while Section 5 largely retains the original positioning against software, hardware-implementation, and general QA benchmarks. Publication updates to existing references do not constitute new related work.

T1.justification: Changes are confined to worked benchmark mathematics. Appendix C replaces earlier paging and bit-arithmetic derivations with page-entry sizing and branch-penalty examples, and C.7.2 adds a refresh-utilization derivation yielding 800,000 rows per bank. No general theoretical results or proofs about QuArch are introduced.

improvement.justification: The downstream studies substantially strengthen evidence for QuArch's practical relevance beyond QA accuracy, with controls and implementation details absent from v1. v2 also replaces failure examples that labeled answers incorrect despite matching their supplied solutions. These gains are qualified by reporting inconsistencies: Table 14a totals 916 responses despite the stated 908, and Table 15 does not support the prose's self-bias percentages. Table 9 also shows that improved success and minimum area occur under different training configurations.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe QuArch and retain the 2,671-question benchmark. Their main text, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial additions and reformatting.

after.justification: v2 retains original benchmark evaluations, expands the evaluated models and judge analyses, and adds fine-tuning and simulator-based architecture-design experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of 26 models, skill and modality breakdowns, failure analyses, and human validation of LLM judging.

results.title: QuArch: A Benchmark for Evaluating LLM Reasoning in Computer Architecture

C1.justification: v1 primarily claims an interpretable framework for describing and comparing reasoning. v2 additionally claims latent-state detectability and effective planning-based inference control, emphasizing accuracy gains and sparse interventions. The abstract, contribution list and conclusion substantially broaden the contribution from analysis to active optimization.

C2.justification: v2 shifts interpretation toward planning, intervention efficiency and model-dependent transfer. It adds substantive limitations concerning correlation versus causation, knowledge gaps, classifier errors, sentence boundaries, taxonomy sensitivity and the need for a correctness signal (Appendix E), alongside hypotheses explaining limited gains in the small distilled model.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-availability link, encoder/classifier architecture and optimization settings, selected intervention layers, steering strengths and thresholds, and prompt-steering templates. The original sentence-annotation prompt and worked example remain in Appendices K and M; the paragraph-annotation prompt is removed.

E1.justification: v2 adds MATH-500 and GSM8K, extending mathematical evaluation beyond AIME25 to a broader math collection and grade-school word problems. Scientific question answering remains covered by GPQA Diamond. Its increased sample count is a protocol change, rather than a new domain.

E2.justification: v1 compares unsteered models and reasoning-effort settings. v2 evaluates Q-Value steering against default inference, Greedy and Weighted steering, plus Positive, Negative, Balanced and Cross-Model prompt guidance (Tables 1 and 5). These are substantial additions to the evaluated comparator set.

E3.justification: GPQA evaluation expands from the first 50 questions to 198, and dual sentence/paragraph analysis gives way to sentence-based control. v2 adds token/intervention metrics, classifier train/test splits, held-out steering-layer selection, and a DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B evaluation. These introduce substantial new evaluation settings.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's descriptive trajectory and granularity comparisons, v2 adds second-order tests of the Markov approximation, cross-model transfer, paired steering examples, diversity/fluency checks, rescue/harm analysis, boundary-detection diagnostics and steering-strength sensitivity (Figure 3; Appendices C, F, H–J).

E5.justification: Both versions specify seed 42 for the main experiments. v2 newly reports five seeds per problem and mean ± standard deviation for the diversity/fluency study (Appendix F), plus correlation significance in Appendix C. These additions are limited to supplementary analyses; main accuracy tables still lack uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive steering and diagnostic results; Table 1 newly reports GPT-L AIME25 accuracy of 56.67% with Q-Value steering versus 43.30% default. Unsteered AIME accuracies match v1 up to rounding, while GPQA scores use the expanded sample. v1's detailed sentence/paragraph FSM-length and state-frequency results are removed.

M1.justification: The six-state taxonomy is retained, but v2 adds an inference-control system absent from v1: outcome-conditioned transition rewards, learned state classifiers, contrastive transition vectors, Q-value planning, confidence-based intervention gating and orthogonal activation steering (Section 3). This substantially changes the proposed procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, methods, results, related work and conclusion are extensively rewritten around reasoning control. Detailed state descriptions move to Appendix A, limitations become an expanded Appendix E, and the earlier descriptive results/discussion narrative is replaced. Original annotation material is reorganized into Appendices K and M.

P2.justification: v1's frequency plots and sentence/paragraph transition displays are replaced by taxonomy, workflow and intervention-example figures. v2 adds advantage heatmaps and substantially redesigned comparison and diagnostic tables. The page template, typography and running headers also change throughout.

R1.justification: v2 repositions the contribution against local behavioral steering, particularly SEAL and the retained Venhoff work, and substantially expands discussion of reasoning-graph topology and cognitive foundations. New references include Minegishi, Matsutani, Xiong, Schoenfeld and Nelson; this exceeds bibliographic updates to retained works.

T1.justification: v2 introduces outcome-conditioned transition matrices, the transition-advantage reward and formal control objectives, with Appendix B deriving Q-value updates through a deterministic-MDP reduction. It also revises the FSM alphabet from generated text spans to an epsilon-only alphabet and restricts accepting states to closure.

improvement.justification: v2 turns controllability from a potential application in v1 into an explicitly specified, experimentally evaluated method. Tests of the Markov approximation, intervention harms and side effects substantially strengthen validation, while implementation details improve reproducibility documentation. Some superiority claims overreach the evidence—Table 5 shows prompt guidance outperforming Q-Value steering for QWEN on GSM8K—and main accuracies lack uncertainty estimates. These limitations temper, but do not outweigh, the substantial gains in practical validation and diagnostic support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs contain readable text, equations, figures, tables and appendices describing the same FSM research. The shared taxonomy and experiments can be matched despite v2's substantial extension into reasoning control.

after.justification: v2 reports original steering experiments across four benchmarks, supplemented by transfer, sensitivity, diversity, intervention-effectiveness and failure analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original model evaluations, annotated reasoning trajectories, state frequencies, transition probabilities and FSM lengths on AIME25 and GPQA Diamond.

results.title: Modeling Hierarchical Thinking in Large Reasoning Models

C1.justification: v1 leaves larger models and more complex tasks to future work; v2 claims demonstrated effectiveness up to 1.1B parameters and uses this to support large-scale pretraining. It also elevates mitigation of uniform-output degeneration to an explicit contribution, while retaining the original loss-simplification and generation-quality claims.

C2.justification: v2 develops a new mechanism explanation: negative gradients counter overly uniform predictions under heavy corruption, with an attractive/repulsive interpretation in Sections 4.2–4.3. It expands the likelihood-versus-generation discussion to ELBO bounds and downstream performance. Conversely, v1's discussion of direct NCE instability and sensitivity to negative-sample counts is removed.

D1.justification: v2 adds large-model architecture, tokenizer, optimizer and 16-H800 hardware details; zero-shot preprocessing instructions; CFG weight 1.1; and training/evaluation descriptions with pseudocode in Appendices B–C. Curriculum training is documented more explicitly without establishing a change to the original procedure. The small-model hyperparameters and repository link are retained.

E1.justification: v2 retains LM1B/OWT and adds SlimPajama pretraining; zero-shot perplexity evaluation on WikiText, LAMBADA, AG News, PubMed and ArXiv; and downstream evaluation on ARC-e, BoolQ, HellaSwag, OpenBookQA, PIQA, RACE and SIQA, plus LAMBADA next-word prediction. This substantially expands the represented domains and task requirements.

E2.justification: v1's reported comparisons use Duo. v2 Table 3 additionally compares against SEDD-Uniform, UDLM and PLAID, using their cited results, while Figure 3 includes an AR reference. Table 7 also compares guided variants, substantially broadening the comparison methods.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce 1.1B models, Llama-2 tokenization, 2,048-token contexts and batch size 256, alongside zero-shot likelihood and downstream evaluation protocols. Figures 2–3 add a matched-batch, 0.5-epoch cost comparison and an 8–1,024-step sampling sweep. The original 170M, one-million-step training setup remains.

E4.justification: v2 adds sampling-step sensitivity analysis (Figure 3), direct training-time and memory comparisons (Figure 2), and CFG-on/off and cross-method guidance analyses (Tables 1 and 7). These investigate efficiency and guidance beyond v1's loss comparisons. The four appendix generation examples are retained unchanged.

E5.justification: Neither version reports random seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, standard deviations or statistical significance tests. The additional experiments retain point-estimate reporting.

E6.justification: v1 Table 1 is preserved numerically as v2 Table 2, and the appendix samples are unchanged. v2 adds substantial results for efficiency, sampling budgets, zero-shot perplexity and downstream tasks. For example, Table 4 reports LAMBADA scores of 17.02, 26.53 and 31.75 for Duo, SDDLM and SDDLM-V1. These are newly reported evaluations, not improvements over matching v1 runs.

M1.justification: The central denoising and negative-sampling objectives are retained; the anti-uniform KL formulation reinterprets the existing SDDLM-V1 loss. v2 adds an auxiliary unsupervised classifier-free guidance procedure that rescales prompt-conditioned predictions against random-token-conditioned predictions for likelihood and generation (Section 4.4). It also introduces a larger model configuration using RMSNorm and SwiGLU.

P1.justification: The abstract and conclusion are substantially rewritten, the introduction gains an explicit contribution summary, and the former unified method discussion becomes four named subsections. Related work is subdivided, and the appendices are reorganized into derivations, hyperparameters, experimental details and retained generation examples.

P2.justification: v2 switches the main text and references from one to two columns, resizes and relocates retained figures and tables, and reformats the sample boxes. It adds cost and sampling-step figures, downstream and guidance tables, a large-model hyperparameter table and an algorithm block. These are substantial visual changes beyond renumbering.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning beyond the earlier diffusion-language-model discussion, adding denoising autoencoders, contrastive learning, representation alignment, CFG and recent USDM scaling research. Examples include Vincent et al., Chen et al. (2020), Xiang et al., Yu et al., Ho and Salimans, and von Rütte et al.; these additions support new conceptual connections.

T1.justification: v2 adds a short derivation connecting uniform-to-model KL divergence with the retained random-negative objective (Section 4.2 and Appendix A.1), plus an explicit attractive/repulsive gradient expression (Equation 10). This adds limited mathematical reasoning without new theorems or convergence guarantees.

improvement.justification: v1 demonstrates generation quality only for small models and leaves efficiency largely unmeasured and larger-scale applicability untested. v2 adds direct resource measurements, sampling-budget analysis, broader comparisons and 1.1B downstream evaluations, substantially strengthening the evidence for practical usefulness. Added implementation details also help assessment. Large-model training budgets and statistical uncertainty remain insufficiently documented, and the proposed uniform-collapse mechanism lacks a targeted ablation, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial empirical gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs are readable versions of the same work. Their equations, figures, tables and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching the retained experiments and generation examples.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds training-cost measurements, sampling-step comparisons, zero-shot evaluations and 1.1B-model results, including classifier-free guidance experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original LM1B and OpenWebText experiments, including generation metrics in Table 1, training curves in Figures 1–3 and generated examples in Appendix B.

results.title: Simple Denoising Diffusion Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract and contributions expand to Gaussian-splat representation learning and multi-symmetry Hamiltonian dynamics, making accuracy and parameter/compute efficiency central claims. The introduction now characterizes algebraic and jet-tagging performance as matching baselines, moderating earlier superiority language. Exact adjoint equivariance remains the central architectural claim.

C2.justification: New Section 6 explicitly distinguishes covariance congruence from GL(n) adjoint action, limiting their equivalence to orthogonal frame changes and identifying translation-related extensions. The unchanged sp(4) results no longer motivate superior numerical conditioning, and Appendix H.1 interprets jet-tagging differences more cautiously. New drone interpretations address reductive-component contributions and convolution versus attention.

D1.justification: Appendices K–L document Gaussian sampling, masking, optimizer schedules, pretraining/fine-tuning budgets, pendulum generation and model settings, and JAX HLO FLOP measurement. Appendix I adds tensor-baseline feature decomposition and temporal-graph construction, plus explicit relative-translation-error windows and stride. These substantially expand implementation information; newly disclosed details do not establish changes to retained experiments.

E1.justification: v2 adds ShapeSplat/ShapeNet Gaussian reconstruction pretraining, aligned and rotated ModelNet10 classification, and double-spring-pendulum Hamiltonian dynamics under O(2), SO(2), and D6. These introduce new data representations, tasks, and physical scenarios. The original algebraic, jet-tagging, and drone coverage is retained.

E2.justification: The drone comparison adds Tensor Field Networks, SE(3)-Transformer, and Lie Neurons, including covariance variants. The jet-tagging comparison adds CGENN and reproduced Lie Neurons results. Gaussian-MAE, EMLP-HNN, and MLP-HNN become comparators in the new experiments; these are actual reported comparisons, not citation additions alone.

E3.justification: New protocols include masked Gaussian reconstruction followed by classification fine-tuning, and pendulum training on a 500/500/500 split with 30-second rollout evaluation and computational measurements. Jet tagging adds a 224k-parameter ReLN configuration. Appendix I.5 also reverses the stated VN sign-fixing and handedness-enforcement order relative to v1; this is a reported preprocessing revision, without evidence that retained results were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds targeted drone ablations removing the central or semisimple contribution, directly testing the proposed reductive construction (Tables 3 and 13). It also adds Gaussian rotation-robustness tests, reconstruction convergence curves (Figure 8), and expanded trajectory case studies with additional baselines (Figure 7). v1's velocity/covariance/log-covariance analysis is retained.

E5.justification: Table 5 and Appendix L newly specify three independent random-seed trials and standard deviations for the pendulum results. Existing five-run classification reporting and jet-tagging uncertainty reporting are retained. Neither version establishes an increase in repeated runs for the retained experiments.

E6.justification: The original algebraic, drone, and 84k jet-tagging scores are retained. New results include ModelNet10 accuracies of 94.82% aligned and 95.15% rotated for ReLN versus 93.39% and 18.28% for Gaussian-MAE, pendulum errors and computational costs, and additional drone baselines/ablations. Table 11 adds a 224k ReLN rejection score of 2201±101; this is a new configuration, while the 84k result remains 1979±87.

M1.justification: The core bilinear form and ReLN layer rules remain unchanged. However, Section 5.3 and Appendix K introduce a substantial Gaussian-MAE adaptation with ReLN encoding/decoding, scalar-conditioned attention, central positional embeddings, and replacement of the classification token with global pooling. The reported jet-tagging message equation also adds the second particle's self-contraction.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and experimental interpretations are extensively rewritten. Jet tagging moves from the main experiments to Appendix H, a separate limitations section is introduced, and the theoretical appendices are reorganized. Layer explanations and notation are clarified, including removal of the duplicated ReLN-ReLU bullet.

P2.justification: v2 adds the Gaussian-MAE architecture diagram, reconstruction-learning curves, expanded trajectory plots, and Gaussian, pendulum, and complexity tables. The drone results are redesigned into a compact main table and fuller appendix table. The original group survey is expanded and relocated, jet-tagging displays move to the appendix, and Figure 4's case selection and caption change.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds substantive positioning against Gaussian-splat learning methods and Clifford/geometric-algebra architectures, including Ma, Lu, Zhang, Ye, Brehmer, Liu, and Filimoshina. It argues that coupled geometric attributes distinguish ReLN from Gaussian-learning approaches. Several earlier citations, including Battiloro, Eschmann, and Yu, are removed, while the central relationship to Lie Neurons and Vector Neurons is retained.

T1.justification: Appendix F introduces theoretical scaling under a fixed scalar-feature budget, deriving linear-layer cost C²/n² and bracket cost O(Cn), with a layerwise comparison. Appendix B adds explicit classical gl(n) Killing-form identities and a proof intertwining SO(3) vector and adjoint actions. The principal nondegeneracy, logarithmic-map, and output-equivariance proofs are retained under reorganized numbering.

improvement.justification: v1's uncertainty-processing evidence lacked tensor-based comparators and targeted tests of the reductive components. v2 addresses both weaknesses through TFN/SE(3)-Transformer comparisons and component ablations, while Section 6 clarifies an important equivariance boundary. Additional applications and implementation details substantially strengthen support and assessability. These gains outweigh remaining overclaims: Table 6 supports lower FLOPs and latency but reports more ReLN-HNN parameters than EMLP-HNN, and Section 5.3 still overstates GL(3) equivariance relative to the stated covariance limitation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ReLN research, with matching authors, core construction, and retained experiments. The complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial expansion and relocation.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds Gaussian-splat learning, double-pendulum experiments, additional baselines, and component ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original ReLN experiments on algebraic benchmarks, jet tagging, and simulated drone trajectory estimation, including comparisons and input ablations.

results.title: Equivariant Neural Networks for General Linear Symmetries on Lie Algebras

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: analytically selected scaling enables accumulated high-rank updates, avoids optimizer restarts, and improves convergence and performance across the same task families and model scale. Additional experiments support these claims without redefining them.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations relating update rank to task size/difficulty and contrasting HiRA's Euclidean and intrinsic ranks. Appendix D discusses adapter asymmetry, interval tradeoffs, and potentially fixing scaling schemes from known layer patterns. These extend the existing rationale; the computational and storage limitations remain.

D1.justification: Appendix C newly documents learning-rate search grids, method-specific rate scaling, ReLoRA restart/warmup schedules, and LoRA-GA initialization and gradient-sampling settings. Conversely, v2 removes v1's explicit statement that source code and reproduction scripts accompany the supplementary material. This is a disclosure change, not evidence that code was withdrawn.

E1.justification: Both versions use synthetic linear regression, the same eight GLUE tasks, eight commonsense tasks, and MetaMathQA training with GSM8K/MATH evaluation. The added analyses reuse this coverage without introducing new datasets, domains, or input scenarios.

E2.justification: v2 adds ReLoRA and LoRA-GA to the LLaMA2-7B and LLaMA3-8B comparisons in Table 2 and the overhead comparison in Figure 3. These methods were discussed but not evaluated in v1. ScaLoRA-I also joins the synthetic and RTE comparisons in Figures 1–2, substantially expanding comparator participation.

E3.justification: Existing benchmark training settings are retained. Added protocols include thresholded rank measurement at 0.005, stable-rank evaluation, and an ARC-c sweep over I = 1, 3, 10, 30, 100. Figure 1 extends the displayed optimization horizon from 100 to 200 iterations. Newly disclosed learning-rate grids do not establish changes to existing experiments.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's synthetic/RTE diagnostics and mathematical scalar-scaling ablation, v2 adds large-model rank and stable-rank comparisons in Table 3. Appendix D investigates scaling-factor deviations, the accuracy/loss/time tradeoff across scaling intervals, scalar-only performance across commonsense tasks, and task-dependent layer-scaling patterns.

E5.justification: v2 newly specifies cross-layer means and standard deviations for rank and stable-rank measurements in Table 3. The three-random-run GLUE reporting remains unchanged. No increase in repeated runs or new significance-testing procedure is documented; the corrected uncertainty value in Table 2 is a numerical change.

E6.justification: New baseline scores, rank measurements, trajectories, and ablation results substantially expand the reported outcomes. For example, Table 10 reports ARC-c accuracy decreasing from 65.61 at I = 1 to 63.33 at I = 100. Original GLUE/math scores and retained commonsense means remain unchanged, while Table 2 changes ScaLoRA-I's LLaMA2 ARC-c uncertainty from ±0.76 to ±1.44.

M1.justification: The scaling objectives, column-scaling solution, scalar fallback, moment transformations, and merge/update procedure remain unchanged. Algorithm 1 implements the same method. ScaLoRA-I and the scalar-only variant already appeared in v1; their additional evaluations do not introduce new method components.

P1.justification: Most prose and section order are retained. v2 condenses main-text scaling statements, moves the explicit scalar solution to Appendix A.2 and the norm-computation explanation from B to A.2, and adds Appendix D. It also updates affiliations, citation style, acknowledgements, and ethics wording, while removing the reproducibility statement.

P2.justification: v2 changes the main text and references from single-column to two-column presentation and substantially resizes and rearranges displays. Figures 1–3 gain curves or comparator bars, Table 2 gains baseline rows, and new Table 3, Tables 10–11, and Figures 4–5 present the added analyses. Retained tables are also renumbered.

R1.justification: v2 adds Zhu et al.'s work on adapter asymmetry and connects it to Appendix D.1. Section 3 also sharpens the distinction from ReLoRA's restart-based merging. ReLoRA and LoRA-GA were already cited in v1; their new experimental participation does not constitute new references.

T1.justification: Most theorems and proofs are retained or relocated. However, v1's Assumption 2 permits either gradient norm to vanish, whereas v2's Assumption 3.4 requires their product to be nonzero, despite retaining the earlier prose explanation. Appendix A.4 corrects a missing scalar factor and expands a moment derivation; Appendix B adds a relative-overhead bound when I scales with r.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important gaps in v1's empirical support through direct ReLoRA/LoRA-GA comparisons, large-model rank measurements, and controlled interval and column-scaling ablations (Tables 2–3 and 10–11). These substantially strengthen validation of the unchanged method's central design and efficiency claims. The removed code-availability disclosure and new assumption/prose inconsistency are drawbacks, but do not outweigh the stronger experimental evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ScaLoRA work. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including v2's added Appendix D.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds baseline comparisons, weight-rank measurements, and ablations in Section 4 and Appendix D.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic-regression simulations and fine-tuning experiments on GLUE, commonsense reasoning, and mathematical problem solving in Section 4.

results.title: ScaLoRA: Optimally Scaled Low-Rank Adaptation for Efficient High-Rank Fine-Tuning

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion retain the central claims about fast exhaustive approximate retrieval, constraint handling, and the benchmark contribution. Section 2 newly makes an explicit priority claim that APEX is the first application of factorization-based retrieval to virtual screening of combinatorial synthesis libraries.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the error decomposition as indicating largely independent error sources and identifies which component should be improved for different endpoints. It also discusses MET's weaker zero-shot transfer and possible fine-tuning, and explains the selectivity-versus-absolute-score tradeoff in counter-screening. These add substantial diagnostic interpretation absent from v1.

D1.justification: Appendix A.8 newly specifies MPNN layers, pooling, dimensions, parameter counts, Adam optimization, learning rate, iteration limit, the 80/20 surrogate split, and factorizer fine-tuning. Appendix A.3 and Table 2 document the existing 28 endpoints and their computation. These substantially improve implementation disclosure; the code, data, and weights pointers remain substantively unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds zero-shot evaluation on the commercial Enamine REAL 70B library, extending beyond v1's constructed BRICS libraries. Figure 2 additionally evaluates Wager CNS constraints, and Appendix A.11 introduces selective counter-screening and a composite five-target objective. The original five protein targets remain unchanged.

E2.justification: Thompson sampling and random/background comparisons remain. Figure 10 newly compares the unfactorized surrogate against APEX on retrieval across evaluation budgets; v1 compared these models only on endpoint regression accuracy. The numerous methods added to related work are not additional evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: New protocols include zero-shot transfer with a 100,000-compound Enamine background sample, recall sweeps across evaluation budgets, and Kendall's tau-b and Spearman's rho metrics. Counter-screening imposes median-score thresholds on four non-objective targets and evaluates 100 compounds after true-objective reranking. These substantially expand evaluation design; Appendix A.8's training details are disclosures, not established changes to prior settings.

E4.justification: v2 adds endpoint-wise surrogate/factorizer error decomposition, retrieval sensitivity to evaluation budget, and comparisons diagnosing the effect of factorization on recall. Zero-shot Enamine evaluation tests transfer across libraries, while Appendix A.11 examines selectivity and composite-objective behavior. These analyses go substantially beyond v1's regression and retrieval comparisons.

E5.justification: Figure 2C newly reports mean recall and standard deviation across the five targets. This quantifies between-target variation, not uncertainty across independent training runs. Table 1 retains averaging over five objective-specific runs; no increase in repeated runs or seeds is documented.

E6.justification: v2 adds Enamine accuracy, enrichment, and runtime results, plus Wager CNS, budget-sweep, error-decomposition, and counter-screening outcomes. Table 1 retains the BRICS timings and adds, for example, 202.4 seconds for GPU retrieval of one million Lipinski-constrained compounds from REAL 70B. Existing regression values also change: surrogate R-squared for n_unspecified_stereocenter is approximately 0.61 in v1 Figure 7 versus 0.04 in v2 Figure 6, without an explanation of the revision.

M1.justification: Both versions use the same noisy-embedding surrogate, frozen-embedding reconstruction by the hierarchical factorizer, additive synthon contributions, and GPU top-k procedure. The reformulated loss notation and newly disclosed architecture details do not establish an algorithm change.

P1.justification: The abstract, core data/method exposition, and conclusion are largely retained. Editorial changes concentrate on the introduction and Thompson-sampling explanation, insertion of dedicated related work, separation of enrichment and runtime discussions, and organization of the expanded appendix. Venue, affiliation, and disclosure text also changes.

P2.justification: v2 changes the main text from a single-column to a two-column layout, relocates the library-construction and enrichment figures to the appendix, and substantially reorganizes the recall and regression displays. It expands the runtime table, adds an endpoint-description table, and introduces error-decomposition, budget-sweep, and counter-screening figures.

R1.justification: A dedicated Related Work section substantially expands v1's brief positioning. It discusses surrogate and active-learning screening, protein–ligand representation methods such as ConPLex and DrugCLIP, synthesizable generative models, and factorization precedents. It newly articulates complementarity with representation-learning methods and explicit factorization-based novelty.

T1.justification: Appendix A.6 adds the prediction-error and expected-MSE decompositions in Equations 24–25, including the cross term and the approximation when it is negligible. Appendix A.1 adds an asymptotic encoder-cost claim. The original optimization and factorization mathematics remains substantively unchanged; these are limited theoretical additions.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses two important weaknesses of v1: validation confined to constructed BRICS libraries and sparse architecture/training documentation. Commercial-library zero-shot results strengthen evidence of applicability, while Appendix A.8 improves reproducibility and the new diagnostics clarify error sources and screening tradeoffs. These gains outweigh localized theoretical overstatement, notably Appendix A.1's unsupported characterization of encoding cost as logarithmic in library size.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same APEX research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison across renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: v2 retains original BRICS-library experiments and reports additional Enamine REAL evaluations, error analyses, budget-dependent retrieval results, and counter-screening experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original retrieval, docking-score enrichment, regression, runtime, and Thompson-sampling comparison results on its constructed combinatorial libraries.

results.title: APEX: Approximate-but-exhaustive search for ultra-large combinatorial synthesis libraries

C1.justification: The central dynamic-chunking idea persists, but v2 adds explicit model/hardware portability and long-context feasibility claims: GPU/CPU support, 100K-context LLaMA inference on a 24GB GPU, and up to 10× prefill speedup at 128K. These replace v1's emphasis on on-device Gemma inference, percentage memory reductions, and applicability to both prefill and decoding.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly limits its target to prefill-dominated workloads and defers decoding optimization. It adds interpretations of distributed-evidence preservation, routing-overhead tradeoffs, sequential batching under memory constraints, and window-size sensitivity. v1's discussion of unsuccessful Gemma context extension and future adaptive budget allocation is removed rather than relocated.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents separate predictor training per backbone, 10,000 training steps and approximately 8.89 hours for Gemma, detailed baseline allocations, CPU hardware/software, 128-token row/column tiles, and buffer/routing reuse. Algorithms 1–3 substantially expand execution details. These disclosures improve reproducibility; the newly stated training duration does not establish a changed training budget. The repository link is retained.

E1.justification: v2 expands the reported LongBench coverage from 11 datasets to 16, adding TREC, PassageCount, PassageRetrieval_en, LCC, and RepoBench-P, including synthetic and code tasks absent from v1's results. It also adds RULER, including distributed-information tasks QA-1, QA-2, and VT. The three boundary-predictor training datasets are retained.

E2.justification: The LongBench comparison expands beyond dense and Block Sparse attention to StreamingLLM and its variants, MInference, DuoAttention, SeerAttention, and Quest, with model-specific participation documented in v2 Table 1. StreamingLLM previously appeared only in supplementary comparisons. The earlier H2O and PyramidKV performance comparisons disappear. Block Sparse remains the same comparator despite its changed citation.

E3.justification: v2 introduces LLaMA and Qwen configurations, including 4-bit and BF16 evaluations, CPU measurements, and batch-size experiments. Fixed token budgets are replaced by density-based settings of 6.25%, 12.5%, and 25%; LongBench's Block Sparse block size changes from 256 to 128. Needle retrieval extends to much longer contexts, and new evaluations distinguish attention-kernel latency from end-to-end TTFT. These changes prevent direct cross-version performance comparisons.

E4.justification: v2 adds separate component-removal ablations in Table 4, systematic boundary-window and NMS sensitivity tests in Table 7, attention-recovery analyses, and routing-overhead breakdowns. Budget analysis expands into LongBench density sweeps. Conversely, v1's boundary-sharing variant and supplementary KV-capacity/generated-length sensitivity studies are removed.

E5.justification: v2 Figure 2 introduces shaded bands around recall curves, absent from v1's plots, but neither its caption nor the text defines their statistical meaning. Neither PDF specifies seeds, repeated-run counts, or confidence-interval procedures. Whether the new bands represent uncertainty estimates or another form of variation therefore remains unresolved.

E6.justification: v2 replaces or expands much of the reported result set under different models, budgets, and aggregation. New LLaMA LongBench averages are 31.8 for DHSA, 27.9 for Block Sparse, and 32.7 for dense attention (Table 1); corresponding 48K RULER scores are 71.5, 43.1, and 75.2 (Table 5). Table 9 adds average TTFT of 1.88 seconds versus 3.28 for dense FA2. These are newly reported comparisons, not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The reported execution procedure changes from explicit token-level similarity/mask construction in v1 to compact, budgeted key-index routing in v2. v2 adds tiled online-softmax execution alongside SDPA and replaces the explicit decode algorithm with a prefill-focused workflow using dense decoding in evaluation. The boundary predictor, soft-label loss, and square-root length normalization remain substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and evaluation narrative are extensively rewritten. v2 adds a motivation section, separates inference acceleration from the core method, and introduces dedicated related work. Much of v1 Appendix B survives in reorganized Appendix A subsections, while workflow material is redistributed and the standalone limitations section disappears.

P2.justification: The main text changes from one-column to two-column presentation. The framework diagram is redrawn around index routing, the boundary-predictor diagram moves into the main text, and LongBench tables change from individual-dataset columns to task-category panels across models. New recall, density, CPU, batching, and ablation displays replace much of the earlier memory/decoding presentation.

R1.justification: v2 adds a substantial Related Work section positioning DHSA among sparse attention, alternative long-context architectures, and memory-constrained inference systems. New references include DuoAttention, SeerAttention, Quest, FlashAttention, state-space models, quantization, and speculative decoding. Publication updates to retained works such as LongBench and StreamingLLM are bibliographic changes rather than new research relationships.

T1.justification: v1 contains method equations and a short complexity discussion but no comparable recall theory. v2 Appendix B adds semantic-segment and boundary-accuracy assumptions, a chunk-score stability lemma, and conditional recall bounds with proofs for DHSA and fixed block sparsity. It also expands the complexity analysis to account for chunk similarity and routing.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for DHSA's practical prefill benefits. Component ablations address v1's limited isolation of the proposed mechanisms, RULER tests distributed evidence beyond needle retrieval, and broader baseline comparisons plus end-to-end TTFT/overhead measurements make the efficiency claims more assessable. Backend algorithms and calibration details also improve reproducibility. Explicit peak-memory and decoding studies are lost, and the new shaded bands remain unexplained, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical support and technical clarity.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DHSA, with readable main texts, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices. Retained content can be matched despite the changed title and substantial restructuring.

after.justification: v2 reports original LongBench, Needle-in-a-Haystack, and RULER results, component ablations, sensitivity analyses, and GPU/CPU performance measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original Needle-in-a-Haystack and LongBench evaluations, alongside latency, memory, and KV-cache analyses in its main text and appendices.

results.title: Long-Context Modeling with Dynamic Hierarchical Sparse Attention for Memory-Constrained LLM Inference

C1.justification: The three principal contributions, headline performance gap and longitudinal-stagnation claim remain. v2 qualifies broad statements about complete-query assumptions and adds a conclusion that richer natural-language feedback alone does not close the performance gap. These refine the claims without redefining the paper’s central contribution.

C2.justification: v2 develops the earlier overconfidence diagnosis and brief model-specific caveats into a strategic-versus-tactical account: deciding when to interact versus identifying useful questions. It adds interpretations of response bandwidth and interaction utility, explains the diagnostic purpose of restricted replies, cautions against fine-grained rankings, and explicitly treats simulated feedback as an approximation to real users.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents Serper search with five organic results and a 30-second timeout, annotator qualifications and paraphrase checks, a candidate-refinement threshold, configuration details, and confidence parsing. Conversely, it removes v1’s grader identity, temperature, human spot-check statement and complete grading prompt. These substantially change reproducibility documentation; the code-access link remains.

E1.justification: Both versions use 210 ambiguous identification questions across nine domains, comprising 139 English and 71 Chinese instances. Added studies reuse these questions or their interaction records. The new agent and responder configurations change evaluation procedures within the retained task coverage.

E2.justification: Appendix B.3 adds evaluated comparisons with Doubao Deep Search and OpenAI Deep Research. These commercial systems are additional comparators, distinct from the retained 17-model suite, including Doubao-1.6. No original model comparator is removed.

E3.justification: v2 adds ten-round ask-only and free-form-response configurations, matched-responder comparisons on 50 questions, human validation of 100 interaction records by two annotators, and interaction-utility measurements on 50 questions. These substantially extend the evaluation design. The main ten-round configuration and stated sampling parameters remain unchanged; the additions do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The original configuration, scaling and forced-interaction analyses are retained. v2 adds tests of search removal, response-channel restrictions, responder sensitivity and human agreement, scaffold dependence, and interaction usefulness. Section 4.7 and Appendix C.2 additionally provide failure attribution and a case where clarification and search still produce Ice Hockey instead of Hornussen.

E5.justification: The original main-table standard deviations and three-trial responder sampling remain. v2 newly identifies three independent main runs and reports pairwise Kendall rank correlations with p-values in Table B2. Appendix B.2 adds Krippendorff’s alpha and Cohen’s kappa for simulator–human agreement. This substantially expands statistical validation without establishing an increase in run counts.

E6.justification: Original main-table values and the complete scaling/forced-interaction appendix results are unchanged. Substantial new results include GPT-5 accuracy of 25.24% with ask-only and 25.71% with askNL, commercial-system accuracies of 10.0% and 6.67%, and responder, agreement, ranking, utility and failure-attribution findings. These are additional results under their respective settings, not revisions demonstrating same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The target-distractor construction and core ReAct architecture remain. v2 introduces limited procedural variants: Answer+Interact removes search from the available actions, and askNL permits free-form responder answers instead of three-way responses (Sections 4.1 and 4.5). These extend the implementation without replacing the main method.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much original prose remain. Changes include localized abstract, introduction and conclusion rewrites, expanded explanations, an Impact Statement, and reorganization into Appendices A–C. Author and venue/header text are also updated; the revision is not a pervasive rewrite of the existing narrative.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column main-text layout, adds an interaction-workflow diagram and several tables, moves the original task example to Appendix A.1, expands the ablation table, transposes the scaling table and rearranges the dataset-statistics figure. The revised forced-interaction plot omits GPT-4o-mini, although its numerical results remain in Appendix C.1.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands coverage of earlier ambiguity and clarification research, including AmbigQA, ASQA and clarification-question studies. It repositions InteractComp as complementary through its search/ask/answer loop, rather than relying primarily on a general-conversation versus search distinction. It also adds connections to tip-of-the-tongue retrieval, real-user query datasets and agent-training research.

T1.justification: The construction mathematics and responder-state formulation are retained, with no new theoretical results or proofs. Appendix A.6 supplies the standard five-bin expected-calibration-error formula for the already-used metric; this is additional explanation rather than a theoretical contribution.

improvement.justification: v1 left important alternative explanations insufficiently tested, including restricted response bandwidth, simulator choice and the ReAct scaffold. v2 directly examines these issues and adds human validation and detailed failure analysis, substantially strengthening the benchmark’s empirical validity and diagnostic value. The broader clarification literature also improves its positioning. Removing grader details weakens reproducibility, but the added validation and explanation provide a clear, substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same InteractComp benchmark, with matching construction principles, dataset coverage and original experiments. Their text, figures, tables, equations and appendices are readable, and relocated material can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds interaction ablations, responder validation, commercial-system evaluations and analyses of failures, ranking consistency and interaction usefulness.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of 17 models, configuration ablations, round-budget experiments and forced-interaction results in Tables 2–4 and Appendix A.5.

results.title: InteractComp: Evaluating Search Agents With Ambiguous Queries

C1.justification: Both versions claim a unified gradient-flow sampling framework for existing DRO problems, sampler-based solvers, and recovery of WRM as a special case. v3 foregrounds non-convex neural-network applicability, but v1 already allowed non-concave losses and analyzed non-convex optimization. The underlying contribution scope remains.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive explanations of intermediate-flow selection under poor hyperparameters, facial-sample diversity and failure conditions, and CNN optimization behavior. It also discusses possible extensions beyond smoothness and leaves analysis of an SGDA-style variant to future work. The earlier WFR warm-start and RGO applicability limitations are retained.

D1.justification: v3 adds ResNet-18 architectural adaptations, optimizer and training hyperparameters, MLMC truncation settings, latent-sampler configurations, controlled ablation settings, and measured training times. These materially expand reproducibility information. The stated RTX A3000 hardware and code-access link are unchanged.

E1.justification: v3 adds MNIST digit classification, FFHQ latent-space facial-attribute sampling, and raw-image CIFAR-10 adversarial evaluation alongside the retained fixed-feature task. L∞ attacks supplement L2 evaluation. The earlier synthetic classification and least-squares coverage remains in Appendix D.

E2.justification: Corresponding retained experiments preserve their comparator membership, including WRM, Dual Sinkhorn DRO, SAA/ERM, and the relevant sampler variants. The new CNN comparisons reuse existing methods. Newly cited works, including Wang (2025), are not additional evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce end-to-end LeNet-5 training and ResNet-18 fine-tuning, distinct PGD attack grids, and controlled latent-space sampling. The ResNet-18 comparison specifies 20 epochs, batch size 256, eight particles, and 20 inner steps at stepsize 0.01. These are added protocols; the retained CIFAR-10 feature experiment still uses 10 epochs and 100 inner iterations.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained entropy and SVG-initialization analyses, v3 adds facial-sampling ablations over τ, ϵ, stepsize, and particle count, plus trajectories illustrating instability and convergence. Appendix D.3 adds CNN training-loss diagnostics and an MNIST τ-sensitivity comparison.

E5.justification: v1 reports no empirical run counts or uncertainty estimates. v3 introduces mean ± standard deviation robustness tables, explicitly reports five seeds for CIFAR-10 and five runs for convergence diagnostics, and supplies timing uncertainty. This does not establish that the retained experiments were rerun.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantial quantitative and qualitative results while retaining the earlier benchmark plots. For example, new Table 4 reports CIFAR-10 PGD-L∞ error at Δ=0.015 of 34.06±0.83% for WFR-DRO, 35.02±1.13% for WGF-DRO, 39.74±1.86% for Dual, and 86.35±1.57% for WRM. Timing, sensitivity, and facial-sampling findings are also new; these are not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The stated sampler procedures change substantially: WGF/WFR drift signs and WFR reaction signs are reversed; Algorithm 4 replaces weight-proportional rejuvenation with uniform selection excluding the dying particle; Algorithm 5 adds the negative 2τ/ϵ score factor and the missing stepsize multiplier. These affect actual update rules, although the PDFs do not establish corresponding code changes or reruns.

P1.justification: The introduction and discussion are substantially rewritten, and the main experimental narrative is rebuilt around CNNs and facial sampling. Earlier main-text experiments move into Appendix D, WFR details move into a dedicated Appendix B.1, and definitions, terminology, and explanations are reorganized.

P2.justification: v3 adds a framework diagram, facial trajectory and ablation panels, a CNN convergence plot, and six tables covering robustness, timing, and sensitivity. The eight earlier figures are retained but rearranged within Appendix D. Algorithm placement and the visual organization of the main text also change substantially.

R1.justification: v3 adds references supporting entropic JKO, nonsmooth ULA, PGD, and latent autoencoders, and acknowledges Wang (2025) for identifying a proof flaw. Comparisons with FlowDRO and iterative JKO approaches become more explicit, while the basic positioning as a complementary sampling framework remains.

T1.justification: The outer-iteration bound changes from O(ϵ_opt^-2) to O(ϵ_opt^-4), with an S-dependent stepsize; Appendix C.4 changes total accuracy dependence from ϵ_opt^-4 to ϵ_opt^-6. Proposition 4.2 revises assumptions and gives an expected gradient-error bound for sufficiently large N, with explicit particle-approximation error. Important inconsistencies persist or arise: Theorem 5.5 states dimension dependence d whereas C.4 derives d², and the revised main-text Gibbs exponent omits the 2τ factor retained in C.1.

improvement.justification: The new end-to-end evaluations, uncertainty reporting, and sensitivity/timing analyses substantially strengthen support for practical applicability beyond v1's toy and fixed-feature studies. Revised sampler updates and the variance-aware outer-loop rate also address important defects. These gains outweigh the revised theory's consistency problems, including conflicting target scaling between Section 3 and Appendix C.1 and conflicting dimension dependence between Theorem 5.5 and Appendix C.4. The theory should therefore not be regarded as fully repaired.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GF-DRO research. Their text, equations, figures, algorithms, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching material moved between sections.

after.justification: v3 retains those experiments and adds original MNIST and CIFAR-10 CNN evaluations, facial-image sampling examples, and supplementary diagnostics.

before.justification: v1 reports original classification, sampling, CIFAR-10 feature robustness, and uncertain least-squares experiments in Section 6 and Appendix D.

results.title: Gradient Flow Sampler-based Distributionally Robust Optimization

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the central claims of warm-up-enabled joint training, synergistic co-evolution, improved efficiency and stronger simulation and planning performance. The conclusion references additional backbone and scaling evidence without redefining the core contribution.

C2.justification: New discussion connects larger world models with stronger supervision for latent actions and interprets Wan2.1 results as evidence of architectural generality. Appendix D.5 distinguishes higher per-step costs from faster convergence, while C.3 acknowledges a sampling-speed/quality tradeoff. The existing collapse explanation and dependence-on-pretraining limitation remain.

D1.justification: v2 newly discloses eight NVIDIA H200 GPUs, per-step and total training times, planning-specific inference and candidate-count details, and the four LIBERO adaptation suites. It documents configurations for the added studies and replaces the supplementary-folder link with a project website for demos. Core implementation details in Appendix B remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Planning coverage expands from four to seven RoboDesk tasks by adding Push Red, Push Green and Push Blue. Flat Block and Push Drawer remain in Appendix C.3 despite disappearing from the main planning table. The training mixture and simulation datasets remain unchanged; naming the four LIBERO suites adds documentation rather than establishing new coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds previously published AdaWorld planning scores to Tables 3 and 4; v1 only compared its own two-stage and joint models there. Figure 9 also introduces the two-stage baseline into the qualitative action-transfer comparison. Longer-trained checkpoints extend the existing baseline's settings rather than introduce another method.

E3.justification: v2 adds a LAM30K+WM52K control, model-depth and batch-size sweeps with corresponding warm-up schedules, Wan2.1 training configurations, and planning comparisons using 50 versus 200 action candidates and longer-trained checkpoints. These substantially extend the experimental design. Appendix C.3 also specifies planning-only three-step unguided inference, whereas v1 supplies only the general ten-step guided inference setting.

E4.justification: New analyses test sensitivity to world-model capacity, training-data exposure, backbone choice, planning sample count and training budget. Appendix D.5 examines computational efficiency, and Figure 9 adds comparative action-transfer case studies. The original warm-up, co-evolution and downstream codebook analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Section 4.5 newly states that planning runs use five seeds. v1 describes 30 initial-goal pairs per task but does not disclose a seed count. This establishes additional reporting, not an increase in runs. Neither version reports confidence intervals, variability estimates or significance tests.

E6.justification: Original probing and simulation entries are retained, but planning scores are revised: Upright Block changes from 20.0%/37.78% to 22.00%/35.33% for two-stage/joint models. v2 adds extensive budget, scaling, Wan2.1, runtime and transfer-comparison results. These are newly reported or revised results, not uniform performance gains; planning averages also cover different task sets.

M1.justification: Appendix D.4 adds a Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B backbone instantiation using the same AdaLN conditioning and warm-up/joint-training procedure. This is a limited model extension; the original OpenSora architecture, latent-action components, objectives and training procedure in Section 3 and Appendix B remain unchanged.

P1.justification: v2 edits terminology and rewrites portions of related work, probing interpretation and evaluation explanations. Appendix D gains three subsections and additional cross-references. Most original prose and the main section hierarchy remain intact; the revision is primarily an empirical expansion.

P2.justification: v2 moves the original probing table into the appendix, expands and restructures planning tables, and adds scaling, backbone and timing tables.
