It adds a scaling plot and reworks the single transfer gallery into Figures 7–9, including baseline comparisons. Existing Figures 1–5 are retained with resizing or relocation.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds discussion or citations for UniSkill, Motus, AC-LAM, MVP-LAM, LAWM, FLAM and V-JEPA2-based latent-action modeling, and removes the MaskGIT reference. These sharpen distinctions involving skill discovery, fixed action labels and nongenerative dynamics models while retaining the original joint-training novelty position.

T1.justification: The world-model formulation and reconstruction objective in Equation 1 are unchanged. Neither version supplies formal theorems or proofs, and the added scaling and efficiency analyses are empirical.

improvement.justification: v1 supports efficiency mainly through training-step counts and tests only one backbone. v2 substantially strengthens that evidence with longer-trained controls, reported wall-clock costs, Wan2.1 validation and scaling studies, while expanding planning to all seven tasks. These address important validation gaps. Missing uncertainty estimates and coupled batch-size/warm-up changes still limit interpretation, but the broader controls and clearer reporting provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CoLA-World, with matching authors, core method and retained experiments. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and visually inspected figures, support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds scaling studies, Wan2.1 experiments, expanded planning evaluations and computational measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original linear-probing, video-prediction, visual-planning and action-transfer results, alongside training and codebook analyses.

results.title: Co-Evolving Latent Action World Models

C1.justification: V2 narrows the highlighted equilibrium guarantee to stability within the safe-policy set and makes LLM tool-use validation a principal contribution, claiming safety improvements in realistic, open-ended environments. Conversely, its abstract drops v1's explicit structural qualification on the autonomy-alignment claim, although Theorem 1 still requires the ask-burden assumption. These change the scope and qualification of central claims.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations for voluntary deferral without forced overrides, the need for multiple strategic learners, exploration-induced train/test differences, and asymmetric intervention rates. It explicitly acknowledges that both experimental players are LLMs and real-human validation remains future work. However, v1's detailed discussion of safe training sandboxes, stalled task progress under weak corrections, and enforcing the wrapper on powerful agents is largely removed.

D1.justification: Appendix B adds substantial implementation information beyond v1's tabular hyperparameters: the Claude-assisted MDP construction pipeline, risk and reward calibration, complete prompts, history truncation, Qwen model specification, LoRA rank, Tinker training interface, importance-sampling loss, and Adam settings. These materially improve documentation of how the new experiments were constructed and trained.

E1.justification: The 15-by-15 Four-Rooms environment with randomly introduced taboo states is replaced by 10-by-12 Lavaland with terrain-dependent costs and three lava barriers. V2 also adds 144 constructed MDPs derived from ToolEmu scenarios, introducing language-conditioned oversight across tool-use domains such as email, files, payments, and smart locks.

E2.justification: The frozen base-policy reference remains in the gridworld comparison. Appendix B.2 adds an always-ask/oversee comparator in a numerical smart-lock example, alongside always-play/trust and selective oversight. These are limited, worked expected-return comparisons; v2 does not add a systematic empirical comparison against alternative oversight algorithms.

E3.justification: The replacement gridworld changes base training and oversight learning from 10,000 to 5,000 episodes/iterations, overseeing cost from 0.05 to 0.1, and entropy coefficient from 0.005 to 0.01; evaluation uses 50 greedy rollouts per checkpoint. The new LLM protocol introduces a 114/30 train/test split, batches of 16 episodes, up to 200 iterations, and early stopping with patience 50.

E4.justification: V2 adds an empirical test of the identical-reward assumption in Appendix C, previously relaxed only theoretically. Agents share safety penalties but separately pay unequal asking and overseeing costs, producing different intervention rates while retaining zero reported violations. This directly extends robustness evidence beyond v1's shared-reward demonstration.

E5.justification: V1 supplies no explicit repeated-seed or uncertainty reporting. For the new LLM experiment, v2 reports ten runs with different random seeds, individual results and mean/standard-deviation rows in Table 1, and one-standard-deviation bands in Figures 5 and 7. This does not establish additional repetitions of v1's gridworld experiment.

E6.justification: Four-Rooms results, including the task-return comparison against the base policy's approximately 5.17 return, are replaced by Lavaland results reporting zero violations within 2,500 iterations and 28.2% intervention. New LLM results include Table 1's average test reward of 8.58 ± 1.33. These are new or replaced settings, not same-setting gains. V2's risky-ask mean is inconsistent: Table 1 prints 99.2%, while its listed runs average 99.4%, matching Section 5.2.

M1.justification: The binary oversight interface remains, but v2 adds an LLM implementation with independently trained LoRA adapters, text/history inputs, action-token outputs, and importance-weighted updates using normalized step rewards (Section 5.2, Appendix B.4). Its tool-use reward also includes terminal task payoffs, extending the safety-and-interaction-cost objective used for v1's tabular wrapper.

P1.justification: The introduction and concluding discussion are extensively rewritten. V1's separate shared-reward section is integrated into Section 4.2, related work is reorganized into four subsections, and the appendices are reordered, including moving the Off-Switch reduction from Appendix A to D. The prose also replaces the Superintelligence/SI terminology with AI.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is substantially redesigned, the gridworld illustrations are replaced, and Figure 3 changes from three panels to two, removing the environment-return panel. V2 adds MDP diagrams, LLM learning curves, uncertainty bands, a per-run results table, prompt boxes, and robustness figures. Figures 4 and 6 display the same smart-lock graph, so they are repeated presentation rather than independent evidence.

R1.justification: Related work is substantially revised, adding dedicated coverage of adversarial AI control and potential-game learning, including Benton, Bhatt, Phuong, Lindner, Ding, and Song. V2 more explicitly positions cooperative oversight allocation relative to external monitoring and preference inference. V1's shielding, safe-interruptibility, and learned-deferral discussion and associated citations are removed; publication updates to retained works are not counted as additions.

T1.justification: V1's Theorem 2 claims a sufficiently penalized global optimum is safe and an unrestricted Nash equilibrium. V2 replaces this with optimization over a formally defined safe-policy set and equilibrium against safety-preserving deviations. Appendix A.6 adds a violation-probability margin assumption and finite-penalty theorem. Path-monotonic alignment and the task-performance theorem also receive revised conditions; the existing Off-Switch reduction and earlier relaxation proofs are retained in reorganized appendices.

improvement.justification: The held-out, ten-seed LLM study, explicit uncertainty, unequal-incentive experiment, and detailed implementation appendix substantially strengthen evidence beyond v1's single tabular demonstration. The main safety theorem is also more carefully restricted. These gains outweigh important shortcomings: broader-than-supported abstract claims, removed practical limitations, and Appendix A.6's unresolved use of eventual violation probability to bound discounted penalties. The improvement principally concerns empirical support and transparency; the constructed-MDP experiments still leave real-human and open-ended deployment validation unestablished.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Oversight Game framework, with matching authors, title, interface, and core analysis. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable, allowing additions, revisions, and relocated material to be distinguished.

after.justification: Section 5 reports original Lavaland and LLM oversight experiments. Appendix B supplies results from ten training runs, and Appendix C reports an experiment with asymmetric incentives.

before.justification: Section 6 reports original Four-Rooms gridworld experiments, including learned policies, safety violations, task returns, and action rates in Figures 2–3.

results.title: The Oversight Game: Learning to Cooperatively Balance an AI Agent's Safety and Autonomy

C1.justification: The abstract increases claimed unconditional benchmark leadership from 7/10 to 8/10 metrics, consistent with the revised Table 1 comparison. The introduction explicitly claims the first generation-ready use of inertial-frame canonicalization for autoregressive 3D generation. The central method and class-conditional contribution claims remain.

C2.justification: v1 briefly treats degenerate frames as physically equivalent. v2 substantially develops the limitations of nonunique PCA frames and perturbation-induced axis flips, distinguishes practical robustness from theoretically perfect canonicalization, and discusses frame averaging as a possible extension. Appendix E interprets the new tests as supporting practical stability, while qualifying comparison between ablation and headline configurations.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-repository link and clarifies ascending eigenvalue ordering and RDKit canonical-SMILES serialization. It first discloses exclusion of nine QM9 molecules and one Drugs molecule with degenerate principal moments from training. These disclosures do not establish when the implementation choices changed; detailed training configurations remain absent.

E1.justification: QM9, GEOM-Drugs, B3LYP-1M, and the five class-conditional targets are retained. Appendix E.1 adds Gaussian-perturbed coordinate scenarios on QM9 and Drugs, extending coverage to noisy inputs without introducing another molecular domain.

E2.justification: EDM-Bridge gains an actual results row in Table 1; v1 named it in the baseline discussion but reported no corresponding results. E-NFs matches v1's EFN/ENF naming, while the B3LYP and class-conditional comparator sets remain EDM and Geo2Seq.

E3.justification: v2 substantially extends evaluation design with Gaussian perturbations from 10^-4 to 10^-7 angstroms, full-dataset degeneracy scans, and controlled loss and atom-ordering ablations. Table 1 explicitly identifies MiDi re-evaluation under the EDM protocol. Existing dataset splits remain unchanged; Appendix E acknowledges a different ablation configuration from the headline experiments without specifying its parameters.

E4.justification: New Appendix E tests anchor stability under coordinate perturbations, principal-moment degeneracy, diffusion loss versus direct L2 regression, and canonical versus raw atom ordering. v1 asserted that direct regression performed poorly but supplied none of these quantitative analyses. The existing CFG editing examples are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The new robustness frequencies and ablation tables provide point results without uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 revise multiple results: InertialAR's QM9 validity changes from 97.4% to 97.3%, Drugs validity from 96.8% to 98.0%, and B3LYP molecule stability from 24.2% to 24.7%. MiDi's results are replaced under its explicitly revised evaluation protocol. Tables 4–7 add robustness and ablation findings, including L2 validity of 24.7% versus 97.4% for diffusion loss. Table 3 is unchanged; these revisions do not establish uniform same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The canonicalization, axis-wise rotary encoding, Nyström features, hierarchical type/coordinate prediction, losses, and guidance procedure remain substantively unchanged. GeoRoPE becomes GeoPE, RoPE-3D becomes ManhattanPE, and Nyström encoding becomes EuclideanPE, with equivalent computational formulas. The ablated alternatives do not replace the proposed method.

P1.justification: v2 rewrites the abstract, contributions, canonicalization discussion, and conclusion, and changes encoding terminology throughout. The appendix narrative is substantially reorganized: related work gains a subsection, the positional-encoding and quaternion tutorials disappear, and empirical analyses replace them. An Impact Statement is added.

P2.justification: The main text and references switch to two columns. Table 1 gains a backbone column and protocol annotation, Table 3 uses class-grouped sections, and four analysis tables are added. Figure 1 is relabeled, Figure 2 changes from a horizontal strip to a grid, and the retained editing and class-mapping figures exchange numbering and placement. v1's complex-number Figure 8 is removed.

R1.justification: New Appendix A.2 positions the method relative to Frame Averaging and canonicalization-discontinuity research, citing Puny et al. and Dym et al.; Zhou et al. and Ni et al. add biological applications. Novelty is more explicitly located in autoregressive generation. References associated with the deleted positional-encoding tutorial are removed, while the main molecular-generation literature remains.

T1.justification: Section 3.1 now states distinct-principal-moment and deterministic-anchor assumptions. Appendix D reconciles v1's conflicting anchor conditions and revises the proof using separate initial and final anchor coordinates, replacing its erroneous rigidity explanation. Appendix C corrects the Nyström block-matrix expression. The formal positional-encoding and complex/quaternion derivations in v1 Appendices E–F are removed.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for the retained method by correcting inconsistencies in the frame-sign argument, stating its applicability conditions, and supplying previously missing component and robustness tests. The MiDi comparison also becomes more transparent. Important limitations remain: ablation configurations and uncertainty are insufficiently documented, and the broad robustness interpretation exceeds what tiny perturbations and an anchor-change proxy directly establish. These limits temper, but do not outweigh, the gains in mathematical clarity and empirical validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe InertialAR. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting and appendix changes.

after.justification: v2 retains original generation results and adds canonical-frame robustness analyses and component ablations in Appendix E.

before.justification: v1 reports original unconditional molecule-generation experiments on QM9, GEOM-Drugs, and B3LYP, plus class-conditional generation and editing results.

results.title: InertialAR: Autoregressive 3D Molecule Generation with Inertial Frames

C1.justification: The three principal techniques and 51.3% performance-gap reduction claim remain. v2 adds measured 1.67× speedup over FP8 as a headline contribution, whereas v1 explicitly lacked hardware efficiency evaluation. It also claims a currently optimal fully-FP4/RHT configuration and identifies oscillation as the dominant failure mode.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations connecting unsuccessful transfer from vision models to supervision density and training duration, and distinguishes high quantization error from dynamic oscillation (Section 6.1; Appendix C.3). It adds optimizer-compatibility interpretations and replaces the hardware-unavailability limitation with architecture/scale limits and an explicit qualification that full-model speedups cover forward/backward computation rather than complete training-system overhead.

D1.justification: v2 supplies a project-code link, OutControl calibration details such as accumulating activation norms for approximately 50 steps near 1% training progress, subset-tracking pseudocode and state/sharding information. It also documents CUDA kernels, CUDA 12.8, GPU models, FlashAttention-2, TransformerEngine RMSNorm and timing configurations. Code availability is stated in the PDF, not independently verified.

E1.justification: The pretraining corpus, language-model evaluation datasets and downstream task suite are retained. Muon experiments and larger Llama2-structured timing models extend optimizer, model and execution configurations without adding a documented dataset, language, domain or learning task.

E2.justification: Beyond the retained Quartet and NVIDIA accuracy baselines, v2 Table 12 evaluates Wang et al. (2025), Tseng et al. (2025), and FourOverSix. The first two were previously cited but not evaluated. TransformerEngine-FP8 becomes an evaluated efficiency comparator in Section 5.3 and Appendix G.

E3.justification: v2 introduces Muon experiments and extensive latency/throughput protocols across matrix dimensions, model sizes, batch sizes, sequence lengths and GPUs. It also revises the reported 150M/370M learning rate from 4e-4 to 3e-4 and Hadamard block size from 32 to 16. These revisions do not establish reruns. The headline 52B/107B/212B token counts already appeared in v1 Appendix A.

E4.justification: New analyses test OsciReset tracking subsets, oscillation thresholds and suppression starting times; examine overlap between oscillation and quantization error; assess Muon compatibility; and isolate finer weight-scaling overhead (Appendices C, D.2, F and G.1). Earlier block-scaling, rounding, OutControl, loss-decomposition and precision-switching analyses remain, often relocated.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. Averaging training perplexity over the final 50 steps is retained. New descriptive percentages and parameter sweeps do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 retain their numerical scores, but v2 adds substantial baseline, Muon, sensitivity, memory and efficiency results. Examples include 35.03 validation PPL with 5% tracking versus 34.95 with full tracking (Table 7), and a 1.67× Transformer-block speedup over TE-FP8 in the specified RTX5090 benchmark (Figure 5). The existing activation-only ΔPPL is corrected from +0.43 to +0.44.

M1.justification: The double-block quantization, backward RHT, weight-resetting and OutControl procedures are retained. v2 adds an optional OsciReset variant that tracks a sensitivity-selected subset, typically 5% of weights, instead of every weight (Section 3.2; Appendix C, Algorithm 3). The OutControl calibration description provides implementation detail rather than establishing a changed selection method.

P1.justification: The narrative is substantially reorganized: related work moves to Appendix A, tracking/training pseudocode to Appendix C, and detailed ablations to Appendix D. The abstract and introduction are revised, and the former combined conclusion/limitations section becomes separate discussion, conclusion and limitation subsections. An impact statement is added.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to two-column layout, with extensive resizing and relocation of displays. v1 Figures 1–2 merge into v2 Figure 1, existing analyses move into appendices, and new comparison, sensitivity, memory and timing tables accompany throughput and latency plots. These are substantial display changes beyond renumbering.

R1.justification: v2 adds Metis and FourOverSix to related work, along with optimization and implementation references. It more explicitly positions oscillation mitigation as complementary to representational-accuracy approaches. The established relationship to TetraJet, vision-model oscillation methods and outlier-control work remains; moving Related Works to Appendix A is structural.

T1.justification: v1 Section 5.1 includes an inconsistent Hadamard equality with an extra 1/sqrt(2) multiplying the Kronecker product of already normalized matrices. v2 Section 4.1 removes that equality and retains the correctly normalized block recursion. The gradient-unbiasedness reasoning remains; no new convergence theorem or proof is supplied.

improvement.justification: v1 explicitly could not test its central efficiency promise on NVFP4 hardware. v2 addresses that important gap with measured GPU results, including full-model forward/backward comparisons, and strengthens validation through additional baselines, robustness checks and implementation details. These are substantial gains despite unchanged headline accuracy scores. Accuracy evidence remains limited to small OLMo-2 models, complete training-system speedups remain unmeasured, and the new optimality language exceeds the demonstrated scope.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe TetraJet-v2. All 16 pages of v1 and 20 pages of v2, including appendices, are readable. Corresponding methods, equations, tables and figures can be matched despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds baseline comparisons, sensitivity tests, Muon experiments, memory measurements and GPU efficiency results.

before.justification: v1 reports original OLMo-2 pretraining, downstream evaluations, ablations, oscillation measurements and precision-switching experiments.

results.title: TetraJet-v2: Accurate NVFP4 Training for Large Language Models with Oscillation Suppression and Outlier Control

C1.justification: The central architecture, decoupled-training, and asynchronous-sampling contributions remain. V3 extends the abstract, introduction, and conclusion's transfer-learning claim to heterogeneous robot–human joint training, alongside retained action-free video pretraining, and updates the headline real-world gain for its expanded evaluation.

C2.justification: V3 adds substantive interpretations of heterogeneous transfer, semantic versus reconstructive embeddings, and benefits retained without vision denoising. Section 5.3 explains non-monotonic scaling through accumulated ODE approximation errors. Appendix A.11 newly identifies self-occlusion and reliance on current observations as failure conditions, qualifying v1's predominantly positive account of anticipatory control.

D1.justification: V3 adds benchmark-specific training budgets and hardware, mixed-data batching and hand-pose retargeting details, latency measurement conditions, and a project-page pointer. However, v1's Appendix A.6 training and sampling pseudocode is removed. Core optimizer, encoder, learning-rate, and original training-budget details remain available.

E1.justification: V3 adds LIBERO and CALVIN ABC-D evaluation, EgoDex human demonstrations within mixed robot–human training, and three Franka tasks involving cord insertion, erasing, and brushing. These substantially extend the represented data and task requirements beyond v1's simulation benchmarks, action-free video pretraining, and four real-world pick-and-place tasks.

E2.justification: Beyond GR00T-N1.5 and FLARE, v3 evaluates π0 and π0-FAST on RoboCasa/GR-1, PAD and VPP in selected demonstration regimes, and π0 on Franka. FLARE is added to the BridgeV2 pretraining comparison. LIBERO/CALVIN tables include further comparators, with results taken from other papers explicitly distinguished from locally reproduced experiments.

E3.justification: New protocols include heterogeneous training with batch size 512 for 60k steps, LIBERO/CALVIN training schedules, noisy-future-state conditioning evaluated by action MSE, and RTX 5090/TorchInductor latency benchmarking. Added real-world tasks introduce distinct scoring rules and 24-trial evaluations. Original training budgets remain. V3's GR-1 caption changes the task grouping to 18/6, while its appendix retains 16/8, leaving that description inconsistent.

E4.justification: V3 adds semantic-versus-VAE embedding ablations, action prediction under corrupted future observations, zero-vision-denoising evaluation, latency analysis, and an occlusion-related failure case. Existing architecture, noise, depth, loss-weight, and synchronous-sampling ablations remain. V1's qualitative DUST-versus-GR00T cup-grasp comparison is removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports training-seed counts, variation across repeated training runs, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Results remain point estimates; additional real-world trial counts describe evaluation sample sizes without introducing uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Retained benchmark and ablation scores match after percentage conversion. New results include LIBERO 96.2% for DUST and FLARE, CALVIN average chain lengths of 3.91 versus 3.75, and mixed-training improvement from 58.5% to 64.4%. The real-world average changes from 67.7% over four tasks to a reported 59.9% over seven, not a same-setting decline. V3's seven printed DUST scores actually average about 60.2%, leaving its aggregate unexplained.

M1.justification: The proposed dual-stream MMDiT architecture, independent modality noising, weighted flow-matching objective, and asynchronous Euler sampler remain unchanged. Heterogeneous-data training applies the existing framework; alternative embeddings and zero vision denoising are evaluated as ablations.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and world-modeling preliminaries receive substantial rewriting. Transfer learning is reorganized into joint-training and pretraining discussions, and the appendix structure changes considerably. Reproducibility and LLM-use statements are removed, while acknowledgements and an impact statement are added. The rewritten noise example also introduces endpoint notation inconsistent with the retained equations.

P2.justification: V3 changes the main text from single-column to two-column presentation and reworks architecture and sampling diagrams. Comparison tables gain rows and task columns, and new experiment tables and a latency plot are added. The real-world task illustration is relocated and revised, the cup-grasp comparison is removed, and retained rollout illustrations are redistributed.

R1.justification: V3 expands positioning to concurrent world-action models, including Cosmos Policy, Fast-WAM, and DreamZero, explicitly distinguishing their video-generation priors from VLA augmentation. It adds optical-flow policy work, MMDiT attribution, and a substantial set of references supporting new VLA comparisons, benchmarks, human data, and representation analyses.

T1.justification: The formal problem setup, interpolation definitions, flow-matching losses, and Euler updates in equations (1)–(5) are substantively retained. Neither version introduces original theorems or proofs. V3's dependency verification is empirical rather than a new formal result.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens evidence for the proposal: PAD/VPP comparisons test alternatives central to its motivation, while additional benchmarks, insertion/tool-use tasks, latency measurements, and targeted ablations address v1's limited coverage and unmeasured deployment trade-offs. The failure analysis clarifies applicability. Pseudocode removal, notation/task-count inconsistencies, and the Table 3 aggregation discrepancy weaken reproducibility and precision; uncertainty reporting remains absent. These drawbacks do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical support and diagnostic analysis.

A1.justification: Both PDFs present the same DUST research work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison despite reformatting, renumbering, and substantial additions.

after.justification: V3 retains original experiments and adds LIBERO/CALVIN evaluations, heterogeneous-data training, additional real-world tasks, latency measurements, and diagnostic analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original RoboCasa, GR-1, and Franka experiments, BridgeV2 transfer results, sampling experiments, and component ablations.

results.title: Dual-Stream Diffusion for World-Model Augmented Vision-Language-Action Model

C1.justification: The central framing shifts from mitigating overthinking and shortening outputs to structured parallel exploration and reliable trajectory selection. v2 replaces the headline emphasis on up to eight percentage points of accuracy improvement and shorter responses with approximately fourteen points of average improvement across broader evaluations, and adds the claim that smaller models outperform models ten times larger.

C2.justification: v2 introduces a GRPO training-bias explanation for length–accuracy anti-correlation and interprets low-entropy, high-varentropy tokens as meaningful reasoning decisions. It also adds explanations concerning confidence-selection failures, voting stability, cross-domain applicability, and accuracy per unit of compute. These substantially extend v1's overthinking-centered interpretation.

D1.justification: Appendices A and D newly document the 48-active-branch cap and branching-disablement rule, voting budget, varentropy threshold, and computing configuration, including four H200 GPUs, bfloat16, batch size, and CUDA version. This substantially expands implementation documentation, without establishing whether v1 already used an undocumented cap. Explicit decoding temperatures are lost; the code-access URL is retained.

E1.justification: v2 retains AIME2024 and AIME2025 and adds GPQA-Diamond and LiveBench-Reasoning. Evaluation therefore expands beyond competition mathematics to graduate-level science and logical, puzzle, and spatial reasoning (Section 4.1, Table 1).

E2.justification: v1 principally compares DTS with standard inference. v2 adds evaluated Self-Consistency and DeepConf-low/high baselines, a max-logit trajectory-selection comparator, and comparisons with DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B and QwQ-32B-Preview (Tables 1 and 3, Figure 5).

E3.justification: v2 adds Qwen3-0.6B and Phi4-mini-reasoning-4B, eight-trajectory voting comparisons, and length-normalized max-logit selection. Efficiency evaluation shifts from average response length to accuracy versus PFLOPs. The stated decoding setup also changes from explicit dataset-specific temperatures to model-recommended settings, without identifying exact replacement values.

E4.justification: v2 expands the length–accuracy analysis and adds controlled comparisons of trajectory-selection rules, branching criteria, and entropy thresholds (Table 3 and Appendix C). It replaces v1's single qualitative case with examples across models and tasks, including Appendix B. v1's shortest/longest/overall selection summary is removed.

E5.justification: Both versions retain five-seed mean accuracy using seeds 0–4 and 100 trajectories per problem for the diagnostic analysis. However, v2 replaces the per-run scatter and linear regression with length-group mean accuracy estimates and shaded bands in Figure 2. The bands' statistical meaning is not specified; additional runs or defined confidence intervals cannot be inferred.

E6.justification: For DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B on AIME2024, v1 Table 2 reports DTS accuracy of 60.67%, whereas v2 Table 1 reports 73.33% for DTS-Greedy and 78.67% for DTS-Stable under the revised method. Extensive benchmark, baseline, ablation, and compute results are added, while aggregate response-length results are removed. Shared AIME repetition rates remain equivalent after rounding.

M1.justification: v1 branches when entropy exceeds a threshold and returns the first completed trajectory. v2 replaces this with a joint high-varentropy, low-entropy criterion, retains first-completion selection as DTS-Greedy, and introduces DTS-Stable, which votes over completed trajectories. These substantially change exploration and answer selection (Section 3, Algorithm 1).

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around parallel thinking. The introduction adopts a question-led structure, stopping strategies receive a separate subsection, experiments are reorganized, and implementation information moves into newly organized appendices. These exceed local terminology or copyediting changes.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to two-column layout. v2 replaces the opening bar charts with a radar chart, separates and redraws the length-analysis and method figures, restructures the main results tables, and adds compute, selection, ablation, infrastructure, and case-study displays. The rectangle example is retained with updated annotations.

R1.justification: Research positioning shifts from efficient reasoning and tree-based search toward parallel and adaptive thinking. v2 adds discussion and citations for Self-Consistency, DeepConf, Best-of-N, length bias, and confidence calibration, while removing v1's discussion of Tree-of-Thoughts and planning-based search. This changes the substantive comparison with prior research.

T1.justification: v2 adds a formal varentropy-based decision-token definition and an abbreviated GRPO objective with a length-normalization argument (Sections 2.2 and 3.1). These are bounded mathematical additions; no formal theorem or proof establishing the claimed length–accuracy relationship or optimality is supplied.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation: relevant multi-trajectory baselines address v1's standard-inference-only comparison, broader tasks and model families better support generality, and selection and branching ablations test key design choices. These gains outweigh reporting regressions, including lost temperature specificity and Appendix C's prose reversing the criterion stated in Equation 2 and Table 4. The improvement rests on stronger comparative evidence, not simply higher reported scores.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DTS research, with identifiable shared methods and AIME experiments. All pages, figures, equations, and tables are readable, including v2 Appendices A–D; v1 contains no appendices.

after.justification: v2 reports original experiments across four models and four datasets, including baseline comparisons, selection analyses, computational comparisons, and appendix ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original stochastic-decoding analyses and DTS experiments measuring accuracy, response length, and repetition on AIME2024 and AIME2025.

results.title: DTS: Enhancing Large Reasoning Models via Decoding Tree Sketching

C1.justification: The central interactive three-agent contribution and headline accuracy claims remain. v2 qualifies novelty as making the workflow trainable and adds the claim that gains are not explained by parameter count or inference time alone. These refine and extend the retained core contribution.

C2.justification: v1 emphasizes indispensable components and strong synergy across benchmarks. v2 instead explains their unequal, complementary effects, particularly grounding's dependence on schema complexity and verification's larger contribution. It also adds substantial interpretations of interaction efficiency, parameter scaling, and deployment trade-offs, explicitly acknowledging the three-agent cost.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents 600/160 RL training steps, approximately 13 hours on four H800 GPUs, eight verification rounds, A6000/32-CPU profiling, and sequential deployment and memory details. Prompts and the code URL persist. The separate commitment to releasing code and models is omitted; actual resource availability cannot be inferred from that omission.

E1.justification: v2 retains BIRD, Spider, and Spider-DK and adds SParC evaluation in Appendix D. SParC introduces questions dependent on preceding conversational context, substantively extending coverage beyond the earlier single-question benchmarks.

E2.justification: v2 Table 1 adds Qwen3-coder-30B and removes the separate Qwen2.5-coder SFT/RL rows from v1 Table 2. Appendices F-G add reasoning-model comparisons, high-budget SQL-R1 voting, a three-model ensemble, and 14B/32B shared-model multitask baselines. The original trajectory-selection comparators remain.

E3.justification: New designs include approximately 22-second matched-budget comparisons, 64-sample voting, joint generation/validation budget sweeps, and model-size controls. Arctic-Text2SQL-R1's reported main-table size changes from 7B to 32B without changed scores. v2 also states RL batch size 64 while retaining 128 in Table 4, leaving that training setting unresolved rather than establishing a consistent rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds controlled component isolation, parameter-scaling and efficiency analyses, interaction-length distributions, schema-complexity analysis, and cases examining semantic and pagination errors. These substantially extend v1's component, turn-limit, candidate-count, and selection studies, which remain after relocation.

E5.justification: Neither version reports evaluation seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or formal significance tests. Newly specified inference sampling counts and average resource measurements do not constitute uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: The original BIRD-dev/Spider-test/Spider-DK scores remain 77.84/89.75/78.13%. New results include SParC accuracy of 85.78%, 78.62% for the scaled-generator configuration, and extensive cost and behavioral measurements. New Table 7 reports GPT-5 Spider accuracy as 77.10%, conflicting with 78.39% in both main tables; this is an unresolved reporting discrepancy, not an established performance decline.

M1.justification: Both versions use the same GRPO-trained Grounding and Generation agents, execution-based rewards, ReAct interaction loop, and SFT-trained probability-based Validation agent. The prompts and selection procedure are retained. Larger-model experiments and proposed deployment optimizations do not establish a revised core algorithm.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and contributions, component interpretation, conclusion, and ethics/impact discussion undergo substantial rewriting. Experimental headings and appendices are reorganized, including separating generation prompts from behavioral analysis. Author and affiliation information also changes.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column conference layout for the main text, removes v1's capability-comparison table, adds agent-count columns and numerous analytical tables, and introduces an accuracy-latency plot. Existing figures are relocated or redrawn; Figure 3 changes axis limits and expands its caption, while Figure 4 changes colors.

R1.justification: The four related-work themes remain largely intact. v2 adds a specific contrast with MSc-SQL, cites MTSQL-R1 and additional agent, benchmark, and model literature, and drops references including MetaGPT and SQLGlot. Positioning shifts toward trainable interaction, but the broader research context remains recognizable.

T1.justification: The trajectory and MDP definitions, GRPO objectives, reward functions, and probability-based selection rule retain their mathematical substance. Some equations become inline text or prose, but no new theorem, proof, or formal assumption is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important weaknesses in evaluating v1's results: it explicitly accounts for the three 7B agents, adds parameter- and time-budget controls, documents deployment costs, and replaces blanket component-synergy assertions with more qualified explanations. These substantially improve transparency and assessment of the contribution. Conflicting batch sizes and baseline scores, plus unsupported SFT-efficiency extrapolations, weaken some additions but do not outweigh the gains from the new controls and clearer practical limitations.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MARS-SQL, with matching core methodology and original benchmark results. The text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support comparison despite extensive additions and reorganization in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds SParC evaluation, resource profiling, scaling and budget comparisons, and behavioral analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original BIRD, Spider, and Spider-DK evaluations, component ablations, interaction-budget experiments, and trajectory-selection results.

results.title: MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Framework For Text-To-SQL

C1.justification: The abstract and central claims of a hyperparameter-free, unbiased, variance-reducing baseline remain substantially unchanged. v2's conclusion adds an explicit claim of applicability regardless of task difficulty or semantic heterogeneity, extending the stated generality of the contribution.

C2.justification: v2 develops new applicability interpretations: difficulty heterogeneity reduces selected shrinkage, while semantic mixing reduces the benefit without shifting the tested optimum. It also interprets RLHF results as extending applicability beyond binary verifiable rewards. Sections 3.2 and 5.3 explicitly distinguish the proposed rule from classical Gaussian James–Stein guarantees, which do not directly apply.

D1.justification: v2 adds multimodal hyperparameter/hardware configurations and identifies the RLHF reward model and training recipe. Existing implementation listings are retained, but micro-batch sizes disappear from the configuration tables. Qwen3 clipping becomes internally inconsistent: Section 4.1 specifies 0.25, while Appendix D.5 retains v1's 0.28.

E1.justification: v2 adds image-based Geometry3k reasoning and a six-dataset RLHF mixture evaluated on Arena-Hard-v0.1/v2.0 and Arena-Creative-Writing. Appendix C introduces mixed-difficulty and mixed-task scenarios, including KnK-9. Qwen2.5 math training is now reported as DAPO17k alone, replacing the stated DAPO17k-plus-MATH12k coverage.

E2.justification: The value-function MSE comparison changes from JS, RLOO, and BLOO in v1 Figure 6 to JS, RLOO, REINFORCE++, and ReMax in v2 Figure 9. The six-method GSM8k comparison remains intact. The new RLHF table also includes the original Llama model as a control.

E3.justification: The value-function reference estimate changes from 32 to 128 trajectories per question. New protocols include gradient-error estimation using 128 questions with 256 responses each, controlled heterogeneity experiments, multimodal training, and reward-model-based RLHF with win-rate evaluation. These are documented protocol additions or revisions; the PDFs do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's baseline-MSE and training-dynamics analyses, v2 adds direct gradient-error comparisons against a Monte Carlo reference in Appendix B.2. Appendix C tests difficulty heterogeneity through KnK mixtures and semantic heterogeneity through matched-pass-rate KnK/Countdown mixtures and shrinkage-coefficient sweeps, directly examining when cross-prompt pooling helps.

E5.justification: v1 Section 4.1 explicitly states that random seeds are fixed for the mathematical-reasoning comparisons; v2 omits this assurance. GSM8k retains the same five named seeds and individual-run results. No new confidence intervals or significance-testing procedure is introduced.

E6.justification: v2 adds multimodal, RLHF, gradient-error, and heterogeneity results. Table 1 reports JS RLHF win rates of 56.7/7.4/23.4%, versus RLOO's 55.3/5.6/20.2%. Figure 4 revises the Countdown curves, while Figure 3 removes Qwen3's AMC23 results. The GSM8k and KnK subset tables retain their numerical values.

M1.justification: The two-level leave-one-out means, estimated shrinkage coefficient, and resulting advantage calculation remain unchanged. v1 Equations 8–14 match v2 Equations 10–16, and Listing 1 is functionally equivalent. The added applications use the existing method.

P1.justification: The exposition is substantially condensed and rewritten, with terminology shifting toward 'shrinkage baseline.' Proofs move from Appendix B to A, the main-text MSE analysis moves to Appendix B, and experimental material is reorganized into Appendix D's implementation, results, task-description, and settings sections.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to two-column layout. Figure 1 is redrawn, numerous plots are recolored and rearranged, new experimental displays are added, and configuration tables use compact paired columns. The individual GSM8k-run plot is removed while its tabulated values remain, and the Qwen3 AMC23 panel disappears.

R1.justification: v2 expands the statistical positioning with empirical-Bayes, minimax, and admissibility literature, including Efron–Morris, Baranchik, Brown, and Berger, while explicitly distinguishing its estimator from classical James–Stein shrinkage. It also adds discussion of small-rollout LLM practice, newer RLVR methods such as GSPO, and multimodal/RLHF research supporting the expanded scope.

T1.justification: The core propositions, theorem, and proofs are retained after relocation. Limited mathematical changes include the displayed GRPO variance denominator changing from m−1 to m and an explicit Gaussian James–Stein estimator definition in v2 Section 5.3. Neither changes the proposed shrinkage formula.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical support for the central mechanism: Appendix B.2 directly measures gradient error, and Appendix C investigates previously untested dependence on difficulty and semantic heterogeneity. Multimodal and learned-reward RLHF experiments test meaningful applicability boundaries, while the Gaussian James–Stein qualification clarifies theoretical scope. These gains outweigh limited reporting regressions, particularly omitted micro-batch sizes and conflicting Qwen3 clipping values; the core theoretical proofs remain unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same shrinkage-baseline research. All 27 pages of v1 and 29 pages of v2, including equations, figures, tables, and appendices, support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds Geometry3k, RLHF, direct gradient-error measurements, and heterogeneity studies in Sections 4.3–4.4 and Appendices B–C.

before.justification: v1 reports original mathematical and logic-reasoning experiments, five-seed GSM8k comparisons, and baseline-error and gradient-variance measurements in Section 4 and Appendix A.

results.title: Shrinking the Variance: Shrinkage Baselines for Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards

C1.justification: The compact-representation, cognitive-decoding and diffusion-generation claims remain. However, v2 explicitly adds task-induced reconfiguration and its global and directional relationships with cognitive performance as a main contribution in the Introduction and Conclusion. This extends v1's demonstrated state classification into behavioral significance that its Conclusion largely reserved for future work.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly interprets spectral/topological covariation as preservation of information derived from the same FC matrix. It adds contrasting interpretations of diffuse task reconfiguration and gradient-directed variation in relation to cognition. Its limitations also newly address fixed node correspondence, dense-attention cost, preprocessing/template dependence and the need for broader external validation.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents parcellation construction, architecture dimensions, optimizer settings, learning-rate schedules, checkpoint selection, GRU/DDPM configurations and baseline adaptations. It also specifies the gradient-only 20% edge threshold, reports computational costs, and supplies a code-repository pointer and data-access instructions. These substantially improve documentation beyond v1's brief appendix; newly disclosed settings do not establish implementation changes.

E1.justification: v2 adds the BSNIP clinical cohort of 984 individuals, including healthy-control versus schizophrenia classification, and evaluates associations with task performance and composite cognition. HCP resting-state, working-memory and seven-task coverage are retained: the seven-task experiment already appeared in v1 Appendix B.

E2.justification: Beyond v1's GAE comparator, v2 Table 1 evaluates adapted Graphite, GRALE and GATE models, plus FC+UMAP and GraphMAE representation controls. These substantially broaden the actual reconstruction and latent-separability comparisons; Appendix D explains their adaptations.

E3.justification: The HCP split changes from 853/214 training/test subjects to 746/107/214 training/validation/test subjects, and working-memory decoding changes from SVM to logistic regression. v2 adds clinical cross-validation, multiple parcellation resolutions and controlled behavioral regressions. Latent-generation evaluation changes from training-distribution KS/covariance checks to held-out-test MMD and 1-NN comparisons, with additional matrix and spectral metrics.

E4.justification: v2 adds removal tests for gradient alignment, edge conditioning and decoder memory across 64/100/150-node parcellations (Table 2). It also adds gradient-count sensitivity, range-versus-quantile stability checks, a reduced-rank analysis of metric covariation, and behavioral analyses of task reconfiguration. These substantially extend v1's feature comparisons and descriptive latent-space analyses.

E5.justification: v1 reports KS p-values but does not specify repeated-run counts or reconstruction uncertainty. v2 newly reports four-seed means and standard deviations, variability across BSNIP folds, estimates across 50 generated subsamples, and FDR-adjusted behavioral tests. This establishes expanded statistical reporting, without establishing how many runs underlay v1.

E6.justification: Working-memory load accuracies change from 80%/86% without/with dynamics in v1 to 78.6%/89.7% in v2 under revised protocols, so these are not matched-setting gains. New results include BSNIP AUC 0.7370 ± 0.0483 (Table 1), a two-factor readout explaining R²=0.52, and extensive baseline, ablation, behavioral and generation results. Earlier radial-correlation and latent-covariance diagnostics are no longer reported.

M1.justification: The edge-conditioned encoder, attention pooling, memory decoder and latent DDPM remain. A bounded but substantive revision changes spatial reconstruction from both node features and connectivity, with weighted node/edge losses in v1 Equation 4 and Appendix A, to connectivity-only MSE in v2 Sections 2.1–2.3 and Appendix C. Neural-dynamics integration already produced results in v1; v2's detailed GRU specification does not establish that the extension itself is new.

P1.justification: The title, abstract and introduction are substantially rewritten, with explicit contributions and much fuller methodological explanations. Spectral-method material moves from the appendix into the main Methods, experiments gain a dedicated protocol section and reorganized analyses, and the conclusion gains limitations. The appendices are reorganized into five focused sections.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to two-column layout. v2 adds a framework schematic and two comparison tables, replaces reconstruction learning curves with uncertainty-bearing bar charts, and adds factor-loading, behavioral, alignment and stability displays. Generation figures are redesigned, while v1's seven-task confusion matrix and diffusion covariance/noising panels disappear.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning around graph-level versus node-level autoencoding, oversmoothing, threshold sensitivity and alternative forms of geometry-guided learning. Added discussions and citations cover Graphite, GRALE, GraphMAE, neural dynamics and cognitive reconfiguration. v1's connectome-constrained simulation motivation and associated Lappalainen and Suarez citations are removed.

T1.justification: v2 Section 2.1 adds the mathematical qualification that Procrustes rotations prevent uniquely associating original diffusion eigenvalues with individual aligned gradient axes, motivating coordinate-range measurement. The underlying diffusion-map construction and attention/DDPM mathematics remain, and neither version supplies theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's limited comparator coverage, missing repeated-run uncertainty and sparse implementation detail through broader baselines, component ablations, uncertainty reporting and detailed training documentation. Clinical and behavioral evidence, held-out latent-generation checks and explicit applicability limits strengthen the scientific case. Some earlier diagnostics are lost, and changed protocols prevent direct accuracy comparisons, but the gains in evidential support and reproducibility are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same brain-graph autoencoder and latent-diffusion work, despite retitling and substantial expansion. Their complete text, equations, figures, tables and appendices support comparison. Changed experimental settings limit direct performance comparisons, not document comparability.

after.justification: v2 reports original reconstruction, cognitive decoding, clinical classification, behavioral associations, generation and ablation results in Section 3, Tables 1–2 and the appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original connectivity reconstruction, cognitive-state classification and graph-generation results in Section 3, plus seven-task classification and latent-distribution analyses in Appendix B.

results.title: Geometry-Guided Generative Representation for Functional Brain Graphs

C1.justification: The central claims about fine-grained dual-mask merging and metadata-free bit-packing remain. The abstract and contribution list replace the 1.28× inference-speed claim with up to 1.80× end-to-end throughput, change the stated benchmark count from seven to nine, and drop the headline 45× compression-time claim.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations connecting throughput gains to shared weight access and their attenuation to uncompressed attention, and interprets router-aware ablations as showing little additional benefit from gating signals. It distinguishes the packing scheme's pairwise restriction from higher-sparsity merging with explicit metadata. Conversely, it removes v1's explicit conclusion warning about the roughly ten-point AIME25 accuracy loss.

D1.justification: v2 specifies Triton implementation and profiling, RTX5090/4090 hardware, benchmark matrix dimensions and batch configurations, and explicitly identifies Qwen3's reasoning mode. These refine implementation and evaluation documentation. The code-access link and established calibration, threshold and quantization details remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds HumanEval code generation on Qwen1.5-MoE (Appendix A.7, Table 8), a focused extension into coding. WikiText-2, the seven general benchmarks, GSM8K, Math-500 and AIME24/25 are retained; the mathematical reasoning evaluations were already present in v1.

E2.justification: v2 adds D2 to the Qwen1.5 and Qwen3 comparisons and HC-SMoE+AWQ to the quantization comparisons. New kernel benchmarks compare against cuBLAS. Conversely, the end-to-end efficiency comparison drops Wanda, NAEE and HC-SMoE, comparing only the full model with PuzzleMoE. Comparator coverage therefore changes substantially across accuracy, quantization and systems experiments.

E3.justification: The reported systems evaluation changes from A100 deployments with 1024/512 prefill/decode lengths to an eight-RTX5090 cluster with batch and sequence-length sweeps. New microbenchmarks vary matrix dimensions on RTX4090/5090. v2 also evaluates 37.5%, 66.7% and 75% sparsity and introduces HumanEval Pass@1. The existing C4 calibration size, sequence length and similarity threshold are retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds Gaussian weight-distribution checks, router-aware saliency ablations, higher-sparsity robustness tests and kernel/workload scaling analyses (Appendices A.1, A.2, A.5 and A.8). Existing calibration, grouping, threshold and merge-group-size analyses remain; several are relocated rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Both versions specify 16 random expert-grouping seeds and report means and standard deviations. The numerical contents of v1 Tables 11–14 and v2 Tables 13–16 match exactly. No new confidence intervals, significance tests or repeated-run reporting procedure is introduced.

E6.justification: HC-SMoE's Qwen3 average accuracy changes from 54.9/37.2 to 62.4/54.9 at 25%/50% sparsity (v1 Table 2; v2 Table 1), while PuzzleMoE's corresponding results remain unchanged. Added results include HumanEval Pass@1 of 45.1/39.6, higher-sparsity scores and kernel benchmarks. Compression timings also change, and earlier memory/speed results are replaced. The new 1.80× throughput maximum uses different settings from v1's 1.28× result.

M1.justification: v1 describes a custom CUDA GEMV kernel; v2 introduces a fused Triton decode-GEMM kernel that concatenates paired experts' inputs and accesses their packed weight tensor once to compute both outputs (Section 3.3.2, Figure 5). This substantially changes inference execution, while the dual-mask merging equations and bit-packing format remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method narrative and conclusion are extensively rewritten. A new motivation subsection brings existing appendix reasoning into the main text, selected ablations move to an expanded appendix, and an impact statement replaces neither the removed LLM-usage statement nor its purpose. The title changes from sparse to fine-grained expert merging.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to two-column layout. v2 redraws the merging diagram, adds a fused-kernel diagram, kernel and throughput plots, and weight-distribution histograms, and expands comparison tables. The original memory/speed panels disappear; existing similarity plots and several tables are relocated or redisplayed.

R1.justification: v2 removes the dense-model-merging subsection and its Localize-and-Stitch, LoRS-Merging and model-merging-survey references, while adding HumanEval and QLoRA citations. The principal positioning against expert dropping and coarse-grained expert merging remains intact.

T1.justification: The Gaussian similarity-probability derivation is retained from v1 Appendix B.2 in v2 Appendix A.6. However, the new informal Lemma 3.1 states the variance-independent formula without the near-equal-variance qualification attached to that simplification in both appendices. This introduces a limited discrepancy in the stated assumptions.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for the central inference contribution through cuBLAS comparisons on two GPU types and batch/sequence sweeps, addressing v1's limited isolation of kernel benefits. Coding evaluations, broader comparisons and expanded ablations also clarify applicability. These gains outweigh losing the earlier competitor memory/speed comparisons and explicit AIME25 limitation, although the new lemma's missing variance qualification reduces mathematical precision. The improvement rests on stronger validation, not a direct comparison of the differently measured speedup maxima.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe PuzzleMoE and contain readable main text, figures, tables, equations and appendices. Their methods and experiments can be matched reliably despite substantial reformatting, renumbering and additions.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds HumanEval evaluation, kernel benchmarks, throughput sweeps, weight-distribution analyses and expanded sparsity and saliency experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original compression experiments on four MoE models, downstream accuracy, perplexity, inference measurements, ablations and results across 16 expert-grouping seeds.

results.title: PuzzleMoE: Efficient Compression of Large Mixture-of-Experts Models via Sparse Expert Merging and Bit-packed inference

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution list add a scaling-law claim of approximately 3-5 times greater compute efficiency on LLAMA3 and DeepSeekV3, with advantages increasing at larger scales. This extends the central contribution beyond v1's GPT2 acceleration and zero/one-layer tradeoff claims, which remain.

C2.justification: Takeaway 2 replaces the categorical function-preservation-to-non-muP implication with a qualified warning that zero initialization can block feature learning. Section 4.2 newly motivates interpreting upper-bound differences as actual-loss differences, while Appendix C.3 discusses cheaper first-stage optimizers and possible further convergence with longer training.

D1.justification: Appendix B adds hidden/intermediate dimensions, attention-head counts, weight tying, and other architecture details for the new LLM experiments. However, v2 omits v1's explicit 120k-step control schedule details and the former nanoMoE expert-count and auxiliary-loss specification. The existing GPT2 and optimizer implementation descriptions largely remain.

E1.justification: Both versions train and evaluate language models on OpenWebText and image classifiers on ImageNet. The additional model architectures and scaling sweeps retain these data and task requirements.

E2.justification: v2 Figure 19 introduces standalone NSGD source-model comparisons and NSGD/AdamW-to-Muon-NSGD transitions against Muon-NSGD controls. v1 Appendix C.5 compared AdamW and Muon-NSGD across schedules. The shorter fixed-size baseline in v2 Section 3.4 already appeared in v1 Appendix C.1.

E3.justification: v2 adds four LLM architecture configurations, 16-layer expansion tests, and scaling experiments with specified model-size ranges and token-to-parameter ratios of 50 and 100. Figure 19 adds optimizer-switching protocols at different expansion times. Section 2 also revises the stated weight decay from 0.1 to 0.01, without establishing that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds scaling-law analyses and optimizer-switching ablations and extends initialization comparisons across additional architectures. It removes the ResNet initialization and ordering plots from v1 Figures 2 and 4. The shorter-training and single-stage-versus-multistage analyses are retained and moved into the main text.

E5.justification: New Figure 2 reports fitted power-law parameters and R-squared goodness-of-fit statistics, ranging from 0.991 to 0.999. Neither version reports seed counts, repeated-run variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: v2 adds scaling-law results, including LLAMA3 zero-layer and fixed-size exponents of -0.241 and -0.218, additional architecture convergence results, and optimizer-switching outcomes. It replaces nanoMoE results with DeepSeekV3 results and removes ResNet initialization/ordering results. The headline GPT2 curves and reported savings in Figure 1 are unchanged.

M1.justification: The expansion rules, Muon-NSGD updates, and Section 7 training recipe remain intact. Appendix C.3 adds an optional training variant that switches from NSGD or AdamW to Muon-NSGD at depth expansion; v1's optimizer comparisons kept the optimizer fixed.

P1.justification: v2 retitles the paper, edits the abstract and contributions, divides Section 4 into two subsections, and moves v1 Appendices C.1 and C.3 into Sections 3.4 and 6. The main section sequence and much of the exposition remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds scaling-law and optimizer-switching figures, expands the initialization display to five architecture panels, and removes ResNet panels. Several retained plots are substantially enlarged and rearranged, notably the schedule and loss-compute figures, while appendix controls move into the main text. Both tables retain their contents.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for the new architectures and their components, SOLAR depth upscaling, and the revised theoretical argument, including Defazio et al. (2023) and Bu et al. (2026). References to STEP, nanoMoE, OpenMoE, and ST-MoE are removed. The overall positioning against earlier progressive-training approaches remains similar.

T1.justification: Section 4 changes from bounding averaged-iterate loss using Jensen's inequality to bounding last-iterate loss with an additional schedule-dependent term attributed to Defazio et al. (2023). v1 Equation 4.5's explicit loss-gap inequality is replaced by an empirically motivated comparison of upper bounds in v2 Section 4.2. These substantially revise the central mathematical argument.

improvement.justification: Figures 2-3 substantially strengthen evidence that the approach transfers beyond GPT2/nanoMoE to newer dense and MoE architectures and clarify how compute efficiency varies with scale. The optimizer-switching study and more readable figures add practical value. The largest-scale savings rely on extrapolated fits, and some ResNet analyses and reproducibility details are lost, but the broader direct experimental support provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same zero/one-layer progressive-training work despite the changed title. All 20 pages of v1 and 25 pages of v2, including Appendices A-C, provide readable text, equations, tables, and figures sufficient for comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds results for LLAMA3, Qwen3, Mixtral, and DeepSeekV3, scaling-law fits, and optimizer-switching experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original GPT2 and nanoMoE training experiments on OpenWebText, ResNet experiments on ImageNet, and initialization, scheduling, and optimizer ablations.

results.title: Scaling depth capacity via zero/one-layer model expansion

C1.justification: The central empirical claims and three stated contributions remain. The abstract strengthens its policy recommendation from policies that promote developer transparency to policies that mandate it, a limited substantive change in the proposed response.

C2.justification: v2 interprets annotation disagreement as substantially item-specific, expands regional recruitment limitations, and adds concrete risks of superficial compliance, exclusionary evaluations and disproportionate reporting burdens on smaller or Global South developers. Existing explanations involving incentives, resources and disclosure barriers remain.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents search dates, screening counts and flow, annotator backgrounds, adjudication, cross-document scoring, ethics approval and interview-quote selection. Some earlier inclusion details are omitted, including the stated 2024-onward search restriction, without establishing an actual change in implementation. Code and dataset links remain the same.

E1.justification: Both versions examine foundation-model reporting across the same seven social-impact categories, provider regions, sectors and stakeholder groups. Additional reporting sources enlarge the sample within this coverage; no distinct new task, domain or target population is established.

E2.justification: Neither version evaluates competing algorithms against a proposed algorithm. The first-party/third-party and organizational comparison groups remain; the added regression variants are sensitivity checks of the study's own analysis.

E3.justification: Post-release sources increase from 183 to 248. The new reliability assessment independently double-annotates 20 release-time models across seven categories and 250 post-release items, adding a substantial validation design. Reported interview duration changes from approximately 30 minutes to 45–90 minutes, without establishing that interviews were repeated.

E4.justification: v2 adds checks using tighter priors, provider-level slopes, and annotator/item effects, testing dependence on modeling assumptions and annotation disagreement (Tables 11–12 and Appendix L.2). Appendix E also expands provider-specific release trajectories beyond v1's Google and Meta examples.

E5.justification: v1 explicitly reports no formal inter-annotator agreement. v2 adds ordinal Krippendorff's alpha, detailed disagreement rates, uncertainty for annotator/item variation, and leave-one-out model comparison with a standard error. Existing Bayesian interval reporting and the eight-chain, 4,000-warm-up/4,000-sampling configuration are retained.

E6.justification: Section 5's first-/third-party means change from 0.72/2.62 to 0.77/2.64, and labor-reporting prevalence changes from 12.12% to 8.06%. The openness–environment coefficient's reported 95% interval changes from [0.009, 1.414] to [-0.065, 1.280], now including zero (v1 Table 3; v2 Table 9). Numerous counts and coefficients are updated, and agreement, sensitivity and detailed provider results are added. These are revised analyses, not same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The scoring framework and principal hierarchical ordinal model are retained. Appendix L.2 adds fitted sensitivity variants with category-specific annotator intercepts and item-category effects, providing limited extensions to the statistical model rather than replacing the central method.

P1.justification: The abstract and substantial portions of the main-text prose and interview quotations are condensed or rewritten. Terminological footnotes become Appendix A, the appendix hierarchy is reorganized, and separate conflict-of-interest, impact, acknowledgement and author-contribution sections are introduced.

P2.justification: The main text and references change from single-column to two-column layout, and sector/region figures move to the appendix. v2 adds a category overview table, provider-by-release panels, summary-statistics tables, a source-selection flowchart and sensitivity tables, substantially changing the presentation beyond numerical updates or renumbering.

R1.justification: v2 adds Raji et al. (2022) on third-party oversight, Selbst (2021) on institutional incentives, and several model-usage studies; Hobbhahn (2025) is removed. The principal positioning relative to the Foundation Model Transparency Index and Solaiman et al.'s taxonomy remains unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix L.2 introduces mathematical specifications for annotator and item-category effects, assuming zero-mean normal distributions with separate variances. The principal likelihood, hierarchical constraints, time effects and prior equations otherwise remain equivalent despite renumbering; no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses an important weakness in v1: unquantified reliability of the subjective annotations underlying its conclusions. Agreement testing on 390 independently double-annotated items and sensitivity checks involving priors, provider slopes and annotator/item effects substantially strengthen the evidential basis. Screening documentation also improves traceability. These gains outweigh remaining inconsistencies, including Section 5's outdated academia coefficient of 1.53 versus Table 9's 1.348 and unresolved citations in Appendix G.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study of social-impact evaluation reporting. Their complete main texts, appendices, tables, equations and figures are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports updated analyses covering 248 post-release sources, retains the interviews, and adds original annotation-agreement and statistical sensitivity results.

before.justification: v1 reports original annotation and statistical analyses of 186 release-time reports and 183 post-release sources, complemented by ten stakeholder interviews.

results.title: Who Evaluates AI's Social Impacts? Mapping Coverage and Gaps in First and Third Party Evaluations

C1.justification: The central claims remain controllable diversity-quality improvement through inference-time base-aligned collaboration, a family of lightweight routers, and validation across diversity-quality spaces. Both abstracts retain the headline 21.3% improvement and human-evaluation support. Additional benchmarks strengthen support without redefining the core contribution.

C2.justification: v2 qualifies the optimistic efficiency discussion with approximately two forward passes in the worst case and explicit prototype overhead. It adds reasons for excluding learned routers and clearer scope limitations. The creativity discussion becomes preliminary and drops the earlier explanation of conflicting literature, while the principal switching and early-stopping interpretations remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds decoding pseudocode, explicitly discloses no top-k truncation and Diverse Beam Search settings of 20 beams, 10 groups, and penalty 1.0, and specifies hardware/software for timing. These are documentation additions, not demonstrated changes to earlier settings. Existing code/data links remain, with a project-page link added.

E1.justification: v2 retains the three original open-ended datasets and adds GSM8K mathematical reasoning, IFEval verifiable instruction constraints, MT-Bench multi-turn dialogue, and Artificial Hivemind chat queries. Mathematical correctness, explicit constraint satisfaction, and multi-turn interaction substantially expand the evaluated task requirements.

E2.justification: The original benchmark comparator sets are retained. v2 adds Min-p to the Artificial Hivemind comparison alongside Top-p, and evaluates Back Translation, Mix-of-Agents, and Multi-Agent Debate in the new runtime comparison. These are localized comparator additions, not replacements of the main comparisons.

E3.justification: New evaluations introduce GSM8K accuracy and Pass@10, IFEval strict/loose prompt- and instruction-level accuracy, and a Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct repetition test with BACO's threshold chosen to match Min-p quality. Runtime comparisons use a common A100 80 GB and HuggingFace implementation. These add substantial evaluation designs without establishing changes to the retained experiments.

E4.justification: v2 adds a repetition-distribution analysis examining low-similarity generations and a runtime, throughput, and memory analysis examining computational cost. The original router and model-pair ablations, switching-pattern analyses, early-stopping examples, and threshold case study remain unchanged after relocation.

E5.justification: The new runtime Table A6 introduces plus/minus reporting, such as BACO's 22.9 ± 4.5 seconds per sample. Neither the meaning of the dispersion term nor a repetition count is specified, so additional runs cannot be inferred. The retained experiments do not gain seed counts or confidence intervals.

E6.justification: Original main performance tables and appendix Tables A7-A11 retain their values. New results include GSM8K/IFEval trade-off curves, MT-Bench Coverage of 0.681 versus 0.320, and runtime measurements. Figure 5 reports 15% low-similarity generations for BACO versus 8% for Min-p at nearly matched rewards, 8.083 versus 8.079. Format/content agreement values of 0.166 and 0.244 are omitted from the retained human study.

M1.justification: The token-level collaboration framework, routing strategies, word-boundary switching, aligned first token, and aligned-controlled termination are retained. Algorithm 1 in v2 documents rules already described in v1 Section 3 and Appendix A; it does not establish a changed decoding procedure.

P1.justification: v2 substantially condenses and rewrites the introduction, method explanation, results, and discussion. Related work moves from Section 7 to Appendix A; creativity discussion joins human evaluation; narrative evaluation details receive a separate appendix. It also adds a limitations section and removes the standalone reproducibility and LLM-use statements.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from a single-column to a two-column layout, with extensive resizing and relocation of figures and tables. v2 adds verifiable-task plots, a repetition heatmap, and a runtime table. Existing discourse plots, contribution plots, and annotation screenshots are retained and repositioned rather than removed.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting the new benchmarks, Min-p comparison, and efficiency discussion, while removing parts of the creativity debate, including citations to Si et al. and Gupta and Pruthi. The related-work discussion is largely retained, and BACO's positioning against quality-focused token collaboration remains unchanged.

T1.justification: The collaboration equations, diversity definitions, normalization, Coverage and Dominance formulas, and narrative-diversity calculations are retained. The added pseudocode formalizes existing operational rules; no new theorem, proof, substantive mathematical assumption, or revised derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the evidence that diversity gains can coexist with verifiable correctness through GSM8K and IFEval, beyond v1's open-ended quality assessments. Table A6 also replaces qualitative efficiency assurances with measured latency, throughput, and memory costs, making practical trade-offs assessable. Pseudocode improves implementation clarity. Some new protocols remain underspecified and two human-agreement statistics are lost, but these drawbacks do not outweigh the stronger validation and cost transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same BACO research. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison, including the image-based annotation interfaces. Substantial reorganization does not prevent matching retained content.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds verifiable-task evaluations, multi-turn dialogue results, repetition-distribution measurements, and runtime and memory comparisons.

before.justification: v1 reports original generation experiments on NoveltyBench, WildChat, and Narrative-Discourse, router and model-pair comparisons, and human evaluations of quality, diversity, and creativity.

results.title: Optimizing Diversity and Quality through Base-Aligned Model Collaboration

C1.justification: V2 broadens high-level kernel-stability claims from LoRA fine-tuning to fine-tuning generally and explicitly claims an extension beyond earlier idealized NTK approximations. The central auxiliary-data selection contribution and headline benchmark gains remain, with stronger narrative emphasis on general-data domain adaptation.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive interpretations attributing gains to selection beyond extra updates, describing warm-up as a modest contribution, and explaining CoT's role in matching reasoning patterns.
