It also discusses stability under moderate training regimes, divergence at extreme learning rates, conditional theoretical assumptions, and the limited leakage evidence supplied by 3-gram overlap.

D1.justification: V2 adds an official repository link, implementation rules for the new baselines, and clarifications about shared initialization, shared CoT supervision and selection-only warm-up. It also documents float32 gradient storage and resource costs. The original LoRA hyperparameter table, hardware description and prompt templates are retained.

E1.justification: Appendix H.11 and Table 16 add agricultural irrigation QA (AgXQA), solar-cell QA (SCQA), open-ended climate QA (ClimaQA Freeform), and Kinyarwanda news classification (KINNEWS). These substantially extend domains, language coverage and answer formats beyond the retained eight tasks.

E2.justification: V2 adds Embedding and Gradient selection baselines to Table 1 for both backbones across all eight original tasks. These provide substantial direct comparisons against simpler similarity criteria; the original Base, Domain-Only, Random, DSIR, LESS and TSDS comparisons remain.

E3.justification: The original main training configuration remains. New protocols include DeepSeek-R1-1.5B and Hermes3-8B kernel diagnostics, IA3 and full fine-tuning, 50-epoch learning-rate/batch-size tests, and a 30-epoch domain-only control. Added tasks introduce F1, BERTScore and Rouge-L evaluations, while approximation checks introduce Spearman correlations.

E4.justification: Appendix H substantially expands validation through kernel stability tests, approximation and projection fidelity checks, compute-performance analysis, an approximately update-matched control, warm-up and selection-stage ablations, and a 3-gram overlap audit. V1's scaling studies and selected-sample case studies are retained.

E5.justification: V1 specifies a fixed projection seed but no repeated-run counts or variability estimates. V2 newly states that main results average three runs and reports means and standard deviations over three independent runs for kernel stability in Table 6. This disclosure does not establish an increased run count for retained results.

E6.justification: V2 adds extensive baseline, diagnostic, ablation and additional-task results while retaining NTK-Selector's main Table 1 scores. Qwen3-8B's LESS FPB score changes from 30.3 to 60.3 and its average from 69.9 to 73.7; the discussion still quotes the old 49.8-point decline. The original Figure 2b scatterplot and approximately 6% cross-term statement are replaced by distribution and rank-correlation evidence.

M1.justification: Section 4 and Algorithm 1 retain the same embedding pre-selection, warm-up, summed-output LoRA gradients, random projection, average NTK utility scoring and top-N selection. The new theoretical and experimental analyses do not establish a change to the proposed procedure.

P1.justification: The title, abstract and portions of the introduction and conclusion are rewritten. Appendix headings are reorganized, acknowledgements and an impact statement are added, and the standalone reproducibility statement and contents page disappear. The main section sequence and most retained technical prose remain stable.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a two-column main layout, redraws and relocates retained plots, expands Table 1, replaces Figure 2b, and adds Figures 6–8 and Tables 6–16. Existing prompt and case-study figures are resized and renumbered. The enlarged case-study figure on page 38 also loses its visible caption.

R1.justification: Appendix E explicitly identifies the approximation as a rescaled version of Mohamadi and Sutherland's pseudo-NTK and positions the contribution as extending it to pretrained finite-width LLMs. New discussions substantially expand connections to Tensor Programs, neural and linguistic collapse, and Jacobian spectral research, alongside citations supporting new experiments.

T1.justification: New Appendix E connects the approximation to pseudo-NTK, decomposes output gradients, introduces isotropic readout and structured backbone assumptions, and presents an O_p(d^(-1/2) + sqrt(r)/d) relative-error argument. The original stability theorem, its proof, the kernel expansion and kernel-regression derivations remain.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation of the unchanged method. Its approximately update-matched control reports 69.5 for domain-only training versus 76.6 for NTK-Selector (Table 12), addressing an important alternative explanation left open in v1. New baselines, component ablations, approximation checks, overlap analysis and broader task coverage further strengthen the evidence, while Appendix E clarifies assumptions and prior-work relationships. These gains outweigh reporting problems, notably the revised LESS score conflicting with the retained 49.8-point-drop discussion.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same NTK-Selector research despite the changed title and format. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices provide sufficient readable material for a reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains original experimental results and adds baseline comparisons, kernel diagnostics, ablations, overlap analysis and evaluations on four additional tasks.

before.justification: V1 reports original fine-tuning results across eight tasks, kernel measurements, sensitivity analyses and empirical NTK regression comparisons.

results.title: Mining Useful General Data for Low-Resource Domain Adaptation

C1.justification: V1 claims both XP parameterized by n and FPT parameterized by n+d for linear counterfactual satisfiability. V2's contribution summary and Figure 1 retain only the latter guarantee, substantially narrowing a main contribution. The probabilistic treewidth claims remain.

C2.justification: Section 6 adds an explicit open question about polynomial-time solvability of linear counterfactual satisfiability with constantly many variables. This qualifies the tractability landscape where v1 had claimed a solution; the existing marginalization and broader-applicability discussions remain.

D1.justification: Theorem 5 explicitly clarifies that LP variables are created per distinct bag, since different tree nodes may share a bag, and that parents of omitted empty leaves serve as leaves. These document construction details without establishing an algorithm change.

E1.justification: Neither version uses datasets or empirical training/evaluation tasks. The revised theoretical graph restriction in Theorem 9 is not an evaluated scenario.

E2.justification: Neither version evaluates comparison methods or baselines. References to other algorithms and complexity results remain theoretical context.

E3.justification: Neither version reports experimental protocols, data splits, evaluation metrics, training budgets, or testing procedures.

E4.justification: No ablations, robustness tests, or empirical supplementary analyses appear in either version. Example 6 retains the same illustrative LP construction and solution.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated runs, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or empirical uncertainty estimates. Model probabilities are mathematical quantities.

E6.justification: Neither version reports empirical result entries or measured performance. Example 6's numerical probabilities and LP solution are unchanged; the revised complexity bounds are theoretical.

M1.justification: The treewidth-based LP construction and counterfactual algorithm enumerating variable orders and response functions are retained. V2 corrects the complexity analysis and clarifies the construction without changing the algorithmic procedure.

P1.justification: V2 makes local wording and notation refinements throughout the preliminaries and proofs, names authors in related-work attributions, and revises the contribution summary and concluding discussion. The six-section organization and overall exposition remain.

P2.justification: Figure 1 removes the counterfactual XP-by-n label and adjusts the corresponding box. Problem-definition boxes and displayed LP constraints are reformatted, with associated page reflow. The existing worked-example diagrams are retained.

R1.justification: V1's citation to the Fenton, Neil, and Constantinou review of The Book of Why is replaced by Pearl and Mackenzie's book itself. Other bibliography changes largely update metadata or numbering; the broader research positioning is retained.

T1.justification: Theorem 11 corrects the response-function count from a bound of d^(n^2) to d^(d^n), increases the resulting runtime bound, and withdraws XP membership parameterized by n alone. Theorem 9 also replaces vertex-disjoint paths of length 2 with pairwise vertex-disjoint edges, aligning its statement with the retained reduction.

improvement.justification: V2 repairs a serious proof-to-claim mismatch in a central contribution: the corrected response-function count no longer supports v1's XP claim. Theorem 11, the contribution summary, Figure 1, and the new open question now reflect that limitation. Although the claimed tractability scope narrows, removing the unsupported guarantee substantially improves reliability. Theorem 9's statement is also brought into alignment with its construction.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same theoretical work and contain 19 readable pages, including proofs, diagrams, and references. Neither supplied PDF contains a separate appendix. The material supports a reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 remains a theoretical paper. Its revised proofs and retained worked example do not constitute empirical results.

before.justification: V1 presents theoretical algorithms, complexity proofs, and a worked LP example, but no original experimental, simulation, user-study, or data-analysis results.

results.title: Gateways to Tractability for Satisfiability in Pearl’s Causal Hierarchy

C1.justification: The central input claim changes from requiring a supplied 3D model to operating from a reference image without curated CAD at deployment. v3 replaces broad self-supervised/label-free claims with annotation-free, adaptation-free inference after offline training, and emphasizes variable-reference fusion and persistent drift verification. This substantially redefines the contribution's scope.

C2.justification: v3 explicitly limits zero-shot claims because object identities can overlap between training and testing. It also distinguishes CAD-assisted benchmark alignment from deployment, qualifies reconstruction fidelity, separates initialization costs from steady-state tracking, and discusses language quality, threshold calibration, and difficult object materials/shapes. These substantive applicability boundaries were largely absent from v1.

D1.justification: v3 adds the exact semantic prompt and postprocessing, descriptor caching, detailed optimizer groups and precision/batch settings, runtime software and hardware, ICP sampling, and TOM calibration/memory parameters. Appendix H also specifies probabilities and mask geometry for the already-existing YCB-Video stress test. The code-access pointer changes; external availability was not checked.

E1.justification: The five BOP segmentation benchmarks and LM-O/YCB-Video pose benchmarks remain. However, v3 adds SA-V to SOM training, no longer lists TYOL in the training mix, and evaluates reference-image reconstruction and pose estimation using reconstructed geometry. This substantially extends the training and input-scenario coverage beyond v1's supplied-model pipeline.

E2.justification: CosyPose is added to the supervised segmentation comparison in Table 2. New diagnostic experiments also compare temporal recovery against per-frame binary triggering and aligned reconstruction against unaligned/ground-truth geometry. The principal CNOS, FoundationPose, cosine-similarity, and TOM attention comparison sets otherwise remain.

E3.justification: The main segmentation comparison changes from the 16-rendered-view setup to one reference with language conditioning, with variable reference sampling during training. Appendix D revises the SOM optimization recipe, including learning rates and gradient clipping. v3 also explicitly reports pose scores as AUC, adds AUROC, and introduces controlled geometry and temporal-noise protocols. These reported changes do not establish that every retained experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: v3 adds reconstruction/alignment controls, reference-count-by-language ablations, component runtime profiling, and transient-noise tests of temporal recovery. Language, HSFA-depth, and backbone fine-tuning analyses already existed in v1. The HSFA-depth values and original ablation graphics are retained; notably, the fine-tuning graphic is relabeled from DINOv2 to DINOv3 without establishing a new run.

E5.justification: v1 provides limited timing spreads without corresponding run-count documentation. v3 introduces five-run/seed means and standard deviations for pose, segmentation, reconstruction, and verifier comparisons, plus ten-repeat runtime profiling. Baseline uncertainty remains largely unavailable. This is a substantial reporting expansion, not evidence that v1 necessarily used fewer runs.

E6.justification: Table 2 replaces SOM's 68.5 mean AP with 67.7 under the revised single-reference configuration, so this is not a same-setting performance decline. Table 1 changes YCB-Video AR from 0.74 to 73%, while tracking and classifier accuracy means are retained. Reconstruction, AUROC, reference-count, runtime, and temporal-noise results substantially expand the reported evidence.

M1.justification: v3 adds SAM3D reconstruction from reference images, replaces DINOv2 with DINOv3, and revises HSFA conditioning and the active segmentation losses. TOM retains BCE-based verification but adds EMA smoothing, three-frame persistence, and controlled FIFO memory updates. These change the input pipeline, learned components, and recovery procedure beyond renaming or implementation disclosure.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, method, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Experimental questions are reorganized from four to five, subsections become more structured, and dedicated limitations and expanded technical appendices reshape the narrative. The title, author information, and publication formatting also change.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is redrawn for image references and SAM3D, and a reconstruction-comparison figure is added. Tables gain uncertainty displays, AUROC, revised supervision groupings, and new reconstruction, runtime, reference-count, and temporal-noise displays. The conference layout changes throughout, while several original qualitative and ablation figures are retained and relocated.

R1.justification: Related work is reorganized around reference-conditioned segmentation, geometric priors, and tracking verification. New discussions include SAM3, DINOv3, SAM3D, Pos3R, Direct3D-S2, reconstruction methods, and energy-based scoring. HSFA is positioned more explicitly as a task-specific composition of established attention operations, substantially revising the novelty context.

T1.justification: v3 revises the mathematical normalization and loss definitions and adds a similarity-transform alignment objective and formal temporal detection/calibration rules in Appendices G–H. These are limited mathematical extensions without new theorems or proofs. Negating the existing verifier logit and restating standard metric formulas do not independently constitute substantial theoretical advances.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially improves scientific assessability by replacing v1's contradictory label-free training framing with explicit supervised offline training and narrower inference claims, adding uncertainty reporting and diagnostic controls, and documenting reproduction-critical procedures. These address important weaknesses in v1. Limitations remain: strong reconstructed-geometry results depend on CAD alignment for benchmarking, the DINO ablation graphic is reused under a changed backbone label, and Section 4.1 still claims exact oracle matching despite lower YCB-Video values in Table 1. The substantial gains in transparency and experimental support outweigh these unresolved issues.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe STORM, with clearly corresponding SOM, HSFA, TOM, and benchmark experiments despite substantial revisions. All pages, including appendices A–F in v1 and A–H in v3, are available and readable; text extraction and visual inspection support comparison.

after.justification: v3 reports original benchmark results and additional reconstruction, reference-count, runtime, and temporal-robustness experiments in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original segmentation, pose estimation, tracking recovery, and failure-classification results in Tables 1–4, plus ablations in Appendix E.

results.title: STORM: Segment, Track, and Object Re-Localization from a Single Image

C1.justification: The central contributions remain expressive circuit-based MTP, expressiveness–latency trade-offs and preservation of verifier quality. The framing now explicitly emphasises bytes, and the empirical contribution names two backbones. Introduction and conclusion replace EvaByte's 5.47×/1.22× headline gains with 5.15×/1.17× and add Llama's 2.24× gain over STP.

C2.justification: V2 explains why expressive circuits can help sampling more than greedy decoding and connects EvaByte's strong greedy FF performance to MTP pretraining. It qualifies LoRA benefits by backbone and prior training. A new Limitations section adds substantive discussion of language switching, batch-size applicability and large-vocabulary memory bottlenecks, extending the narrower qualifications in v1.

D1.justification: V1 describes code attached to the submission; v2 supplies a public code/checkpoint location and states that all model variants are released. Appendix E adds target-model architecture and precision details, while Appendices C and F.1 document the FLOP-counting tool and memory-measurement settings. These materially expand reproducibility information, although external availability was not checked.

E1.justification: Both versions fine-tune on the Tülu 3 SFT mix and evaluate generation on English validation prompts. Llama adds a model configuration, not new data or task coverage. The downstream benchmarks in v2 Table 4 are explicitly reproduced from EvaByte's authors rather than newly evaluated with MTPC.

E2.justification: The STP and fully factorised FF baselines remain, as do comparisons among CP, HMM and BTree. Added Llama and greedy-decoding results use these same comparison families. Hydra and EAGLE remain unevaluated, and the additional model names in v2 Table 4 belong to reproduced external results.

E3.justification: Evaluation expands from EvaByte 6.5B to include Llama 3.2 3B Byte, with different model dimensions and no MTP pretraining. Section 4.2 revises stated throughput from mean accepted tokens divided by mean latency to total generated tokens divided by total generation latency, excluding prefill. New memory profiling specifies cached generation of 1,024 tokens. These establish expanded settings and a reported metric revision, without establishing which retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The rank, window-size and LoRA analyses are expanded across backbones and reported decoding regimes, exposing when expressiveness helps. New Appendices C, F.1 and G analyse circuit/head computation, measured inference memory and vocabulary-dependent training-memory requirements. The earlier HMM-configuration and alternative-loss analyses remain in Appendices H and J.

E5.justification: Both versions describe three runs using different sets of 250 prompts, and L40S tables retain mean-plus-standard-deviation reporting. However, v2 Tables 19–20 omit the standard deviations present in the corresponding RTX 3090 results in v1 Tables 4–5. This is reduced uncertainty reporting; the PDFs do not establish fewer runs.

E6.justification: EvaByte results are revised throughout. For L40S sampling, the reported best configuration changes from BTree with n=16 and two LoRA layers at 219.1 tokens/s, 5.47× STP, to one layer at 203.1 tokens/s, 5.15× STP (v1 Table 3; v2 Table 9). New Llama results reach 87.7 tokens/s and 2.24× STP in Table 15. Greedy results also reveal FF outperforming expressive heads for EvaByte. These are revised and added results, not a controlled performance decline across versions given the changed metric definition.

M1.justification: The FF, CP, inhomogeneous HMM and BTree architectures, likelihood-based training, LoRA layer sharing and decoding procedures remain substantively unchanged. Algorithms 1–3 are retained. The Llama experiments reuse this framework; Appendix G discusses possible future memory-saving adaptations rather than changes to the evaluated method.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, experimental narrative and conclusion are extensively revised around byte-level prediction, two backbones and decoding-dependent findings. Related-work material is reorganised, a dedicated Limitations section appears, and the appendices gain a substantially different hierarchy. Acceptance terminology and metric explanations are also clarified.

P2.justification: The main paper switches to two columns. Figure 1 is redrawn and relocated, including correction of its latency unit from milliseconds to seconds. Main-text architecture and LoRA comparisons become plots in Figures 3–4, with detailed tables grouped in Appendices K–L. New complexity, model-detail and memory tables and Figures 5–7 substantially expand the presentation; the circuit diagram in Figure 2 is retained.

R1.justification: The extensive related-work taxonomy in v1 Appendix H is replaced by more focused positioning in v2's introduction and Appendix D, explaining the parallel-joint-prediction desiderata and exclusion of Hydra/EAGLE comparisons. V2 also credits Basharin et al. with reporting latency as well as acceptance, correcting v1's acceptance-only characterisation, and adds references on byteification, constrained generation and softmax scalability.

T1.justification: The circuit factorisations, smoothness/decomposability definition and tractability arguments are retained. Appendices D and G add explicit memory-scaling arguments, including O(nsd) versus O(sd) feature storage and snvr logit storage, together with a possible low-rank unembedding parameterisation. No substantial new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens evidence beyond the single MTP-pretrained EvaByte backbone by evaluating byte-level Llama and reporting greedy outcomes that expose limits of expressive heads. Memory analyses, clearer throughput accounting, explicit limitations and code/checkpoint access information improve assessability and reproducibility. Losing RTX 3090 standard deviations is a drawback, and Section 4.3 still overgeneralises CP benefits despite Table 10's contrary greedy EvaByte results. Nevertheless, the broader and better-qualified evidence provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MTPC research. Their text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite the revised title and substantial reorganisation.

after.justification: Section 4 and Appendices K–L report original EvaByte and byte-level Llama experiments. Appendix F.1 also reports inference-memory measurements.

before.justification: Section 4 and Appendix D report original EvaByte experiments measuring acceptance, latency and throughput, including circuit-rank, prediction-window and LoRA ablations.

results.title: Fast and Expressive Multi-Byte Prediction with Probabilistic Circuits

C1.justification: The central competitiveness guarantee is retained, but Section 1.1 strengthens the headline sample-complexity contribution from approximately n^8/ε^4 to n^5/ε^4, or n^3.5/ε^3 using adaptive data analysis, suppressing logarithmic factors. The abstract also adds numerical experiments as a contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations connecting convergence to update sparsity, precision and noisy CHECK estimates, and interprets empirical performance relative to worst-case guarantees. Its new Limitations section discusses dependence on a predetermined comparator class, large iteration counts and enumeration costs. These substantially extend v1's mainly theoretical discussion of initial predictor quality.

D1.justification: v2 documents the synthetic generation equation, Gaussian features and noise, standardization and sigmoid processing, predictor training, multiplier-grid construction and experimental budgets. It also supplies a GitHub link for evaluation code. v1 provides algorithmic pseudocode and oracle analysis but lacks this experimental reproducibility information.

E1.justification: v1 has no empirical coverage. v2 evaluates synthetic Best Action problems with 4, 16, 64 and 256 actions, and maximum matching on a complete 10-node graph. Both use quadratic data generation and a misspecified linear predictor. Rejection and matroid optimization remain theoretical extensions.

E2.justification: v2 introduces actual comparisons against the best policy in a family that rescales predictions before optimization, and against the optimal solver applied to the original predictor. Section 5 constructs the policy family from a discrete multiplier grid. v1 discusses an abstract comparator class but reports no evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: v2 introduces a complete experimental protocol: approximately 10,000 base-predictor training samples, 4,000 Monte Carlo evaluation samples, utility-gap, utility-improvement and MSE metrics, and sweeps over CHECK batch size and precision. Experiments use disjoint batches and a 1,024-iteration cap; Appendix A specifies continued checking after iterations without detected violations. No corresponding protocol exists in v1.

E4.justification: v2 adds sensitivity analyses of sample size, precision and action dimensionality in Figure 2, plus iteration-by-iteration MSE analysis in Appendix A. These examine convergence speed, sparse updates and behavior at extreme precision settings. v1 contains no empirical sensitivity or convergence analyses.

E5.justification: v2 newly reports averaging matching utility results over five seeds and identifies the appendix's matching MSE trace as a single-seed result. This adds limited repeated-run reporting, but no confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. v1 has no empirical statistical reporting.

E6.justification: v2 adds all empirical results. For example, Figure 2b shows positive matching utility gaps at ε=1/4 with 256 samples per CHECK call and at ε=1/8 with 1,024, under the 1,024-iteration protocol. Figure 3 adds MSE-reduction and convergence trajectories. These are newly reported outcomes, not performance changes relative to experiments in v1.

M1.justification: The projected boosting framework remains intact. v2 changes the matching calibration parameter from ε/(2m) to ε/(2√m), affecting the update step, and adds an optional exponential-mechanism implementation of CHECK that adaptively reuses data (Section 3.3). These are localized procedural refinements; the rewritten weight functions clarify the original intended construction.

P1.justification: v2 substantially rewrites and expands the introductory example, practical motivation, related-work discussion and weight-class explanation. It separates algorithm exposition from analysis, incorporates the former Technical Challenges discussion into the introduction, and extends the narrative with evaluation, limitations and an appendix.

P2.justification: The document changes from single-column to two-column layout, with reformatted equations, pseudocode, headings and references. The original pipeline diagram is retained and resized. New multi-panel Figures 2 and 3 present utility and convergence results, with Figure 3 placed in Appendix A.

R1.justification: v2 adds Zhao et al. (2021), explicitly distinguishes its benchmark from Zhao's and Kiyani's decision-calibration settings, and adds adaptive-data-analysis/privacy references by Dwork, Bassily, and McSherry and Talwar. The foundational positioning remains. Kiyani's 2025-to-2026 citation update refers to the same work.

T1.justification: v2 revises calibration normalization and reworks the convergence and sample-complexity proofs using matching sparsity. Ignoring logarithmic factors, Theorem 2's rn^6/ε^4 sample bound becomes rn^3/ε^4 in Theorem 3.3, which explicitly assumes a known MSE upper bound r. It also adds an adaptive-data-analysis bound and substantially revises the bounds for the Section 4 extensions.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially improves the paper through a sharper sparsity-based analysis, clearer formalization, and concrete evidence about utility and convergence that v1 lacked. Experimental construction details, a code link and explicit computational limitations make the approach easier to assess and reproduce. Validation remains limited to synthetic settings and lacks uncertainty intervals, but the combined gains in theoretical precision and empirical support are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same multicalibration-based matching framework, with corresponding algorithms and theorems identifiable across revisions. Text, equations and figures are readable throughout. v1 has no appendix; v2's Appendix A is included in the comparison.

after.justification: Section 5 reports original synthetic experiments for Best Action and Maximum Matching. Figure 2 presents utility results, and Appendix A's Figure 3 reports MSE trajectories.

before.justification: v1 contains theoretical guarantees, algorithms and an illustrative counterexample, but no original experimental, simulation or data-analysis results.

results.title: Multicalibration Yields Better Matchings

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contribution: a differentiable semantic and spatial VLM critic applicable to both optimization-based and native 3D generation. Claims about semantic alignment, geometric consistency and cross-paradigm novelty retain their scope.

C2.justification: Appendices B–C add interpretations concerning specific geometric checklists, complementary semantic/geometric signals and meaningful VLM-only optimization gradients. They also identify VLM memory consumption as a bottleneck and suggest smaller backbones or quantization. These refine the existing account; the main interpretations and limitations concerning long, detailed prompts remain.

D1.justification: Appendix A supplies two algorithms, Torch-based differentiable preprocessing, the reference-image/rasterization pipeline, and concrete settings such as 10,000–15,000 updates, learning rate 0.001, guidance decay from 10 to 0 and 512×512 rendering. It also documents baseline provenance and code/attachment access statements. These substantially expand reproducibility information without establishing that the underlying experiments changed.

E1.justification: The 110-prompt GPTEval3D benchmark and existing text- and image-conditioned 3D generation settings remain. Additional household-object and scene examples in Appendix D stay within this coverage; no new dataset or distinct task scenario is identified.

E2.justification: Table 1 removes Fantasia3D, Instant3D and Magic3D from the reported comparison. The other seven baselines, including DreamReward and DreamDPO, remain, and Table 2 retains CLAY and Hunyuan3D. This narrows the comparison without replacing its principal competitors.

E3.justification: Appendix C adds substantial evaluation designs: point-cloud ULIP/Uni3D text and image alignment, gradient/reward measurements at three optimization checkpoints, four guidance schedules, and SDS-only/VLM-only/combined comparisons using CLIP cosine similarity. Existing Elo and 50-step sampling protocols remain. Table 2 newly specifies 24 prompts, but the PDFs do not establish an increase in sample count.

E4.justification: v2 adds prompt-formulation comparisons, content-only versus geometry-only diagnostics, guidance-schedule ablations, VLM-only optimization controls, and computational profiling in Appendices B–C. These investigate critic complementarity, guidance timing, the contribution of SDS and computational cost. The original geometry-query/multiview ablation is retained as Figure 7, previously Figure 6.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, dispersion estimates or significance tests. The new appendix tables continue reporting point estimates without uncertainty analysis.

E6.justification: Shared entries in Tables 1–2 are numerically unchanged, while three Table 1 rows disappear. Tables 3–7 add substantive findings, including CLIP scores of 0.290 for SDS-only, 0.271 for VLM-only and 0.317 for combined VLM3D, alongside new ULIP/Uni3D results and visual examples. Table 3 reports 120 seconds for guided feed-forward generation, conflicting with the retained 60-second statement in Section 5.2.

M1.justification: The dual-criterion Yes/No log-odds critic, SDS objective, annealing strategy and test-time gradient guidance remain unchanged in Sections 4.1–4.3. Appendix A newly documents differentiable preprocessing, reference-image conditioning and implementation algorithms; it does not establish a revision to the existing method.

P1.justification: The original section sequence and most main-text prose remain closely matched. v2 makes limited wording and author-affiliation edits, adds impact and acknowledgment sections, and organizes supplementary material into Appendices A–D. The expansion primarily supplies technical content rather than extensively rewriting the original argument.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 3–7, a prompt-comparison Figure 6, four multiview galleries in Figures 8–11, algorithm blocks and boxed prompts. The original Figure 6 moves to the appendix as Figure 7 with its visual content retained. Conference formatting also changes headers, typography and page layout, while Table 1 has fewer rows.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for PaliGemma, RLHF, ULIP and Uni3D, and explicitly relates its reward optimization to RLHF. The Fantasia3D reference is removed. The main related-work organization and research positioning remain substantially unchanged; the switch to author–year citations is stylistic.

T1.justification: Appendix C newly defines the paper-specific Geometry Score as the equal-weight average of Chamfer, Hausdorff and symmetric point-to-mesh distances between normalized meshes. This is a limited mathematical-definition addition. The core diffusion and critic equations remain unchanged, with no new theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: The appendices substantially address v1's sparse implementation documentation and limited quantitative examination of design choices. Concrete algorithms and settings improve reproducibility, while query/schedule/VLM-only ablations and independent 3D-native metrics strengthen assessment of the critic. These gains outweigh the narrower Table 1 comparison. The improvement remains qualified by the unresolved 60-versus-120-second runtime inconsistency and continued lack of uncertainty reporting.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VLM3D work, with readable text, equations, tables and figures. v1 ends with references; v2 includes Appendices A–D. The supplied material supports reliable comparison, including matching relocated content.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds quantitative ablations, runtime and memory measurements, external 3D-native evaluations, and additional generated examples.

before.justification: v1 reports original VLM3D results on 110 GPTEval3D prompts, feed-forward generation results in Table 2, and qualitative sensitivity and ablation experiments.

results.title: Let Language Constrain Geometry: Vision–Language Models as Semantic and Spatial Critics for 3D Generation

C1.justification: v1 presents bivariate causal discovery and lists multivariate inference as future work. v2's abstract, contribution list, and conclusion explicitly extend the contribution to likelihood-based causal-graph discovery, while retaining the original skewness-robustness claims.

C2.justification: New discussions explain noise-family selection, robustness beyond the skew-normal tail range, and when KDE helps or harms causal scoring. Sections 5.3-5.4 add substantive scalability and misspecification limitations. Future-work boundaries now include interaction effects and multivariate independence-based inference rather than multivariate discovery generally.

D1.justification: v2 adds multivariate spline sizes, five-fold cross-validation, a 3,000-iteration ECM limit, PC's kernel independence test, implementation caching/parallelization notes, and KDE bandwidth selection. However, it omits v1's 40 initial and 20 additional Bayesian-optimization candidates, log-search range, and acquisition-function specification. Hardware and code-access information remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds multivariate causal-graph recovery on synthetic six- and ten-node LSNMs, substantially extending v1's bivariate direction-identification task. The original 13 established benchmarks and six grouped skew-noise benchmarks remain.

E2.justification: The new graph experiments compare SKEWD-MV against HOST, GraN-DAG++, and CAM. Section 6.1 also newly reports CAREFL evaluations on skewed LSNMs, Tübingen, and SIM benchmarks, although CAREFL is omitted from the main comparison tables. The original bivariate comparator set is retained.

E3.justification: v2 introduces 100 generated datasets per graph size, each with 1,000 observations, and evaluates SHD, SID, precision, recall, and F1 with estimated versus oracle equivalence classes. It specifies exclusions for five failed GraN-DAG++ runs and zero-precision/recall cases in baseline F1 averages. The reported ECM convergence window also changes from one to 25 iterations; this does not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix B.6 adds extensive Gaussian-versus-KDE marginal ablations across bivariate and multivariate experiments. The oracle-equivalence-class comparison additionally probes the contribution of graph-estimation errors. The existing ECM ablation and residual-independence case study are retained.

E5.justification: The original across-benchmark standard-deviation summaries remain unchanged. v2 adds no seed-based repetitions, uncertainty estimates, confidence intervals, or significance tests for comparative performance. Its additional graph tables report means without introducing an uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: All numerical entries in v1 Tables 1-8 match v2 Tables 1 and 3-9. Substantial new results cover CAREFL, graph recovery, and KDE variants. For example, v2 Table 2 reports SKEWD-MV mean SHD of 2.27 and 4.72 for six and ten nodes; Table 13 reports SIM accuracy of 76% with KDE versus 54% with Gaussian marginals. These are additional comparisons, not improvements to unchanged-version scores.

M1.justification: v2 extends the bivariate method to SKEWD-MV: multivariate additive spline models with covariate-specific penalties, PC-based estimation of a Markov equivalence class, and likelihood-based selection among its DAGs. It also introduces evaluated variants using KDE instead of Gaussian marginal densities.

P1.justification: v2 rewrites the abstract and introduction, converts the contributions to a list, moves Related Work before the method, and relocates Bayesian-optimization exposition to Appendix B. It substantially reorganizes the modeling, inference, experiments, and appendices into numbered subsections.

P2.justification: v2 adds graph-comparison and marginal-ablation displays in Tables 2 and 10-16, plus Algorithm 2. It adopts an ICML proceedings layout with running headers, revised typography, caption placement, and plot sizing. The original nine figures and eight result tables remain, with the tables partly renumbered.

R1.justification: Related work adds discussion of differentiable DAG learning and score matching, including Zheng et al., Lachapelle et al., and Rolland et al., alongside references supporting PC, additive models, and graph metrics. Several background references are removed, but the central positioning against symmetric-noise LSNM methods remains.

T1.justification: v2 adds Proposition 5.1 and its proof establishing equivalence of partial and full likelihood maximization within a Markov equivalence class. It formalizes multivariate LSNMs and additive-model penalties and adds the restricted-HNM conditions underlying prior multivariate identifiability results. The original marginal-likelihood proof and bivariate identifiability theorem remain.

improvement.justification: v1 leaves multivariate discovery and non-Gaussian marginals as future work. v2 supplies a graph algorithm with a supporting scoring proof and comparative experiments, while controlled KDE ablations replace speculation about marginal assumptions with evidence of both benefits and failures. This substantially strengthens applicability and understanding of limitations while preserving the original results. Validation remains confined to small synthetic graphs, and some optimization details disappear, but these drawbacks do not outweigh the gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SKEWD research work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A-C are readable and support matching retained content despite substantial additions and reorganization.

after.justification: Section 6 and Appendix B retain those experiments and add original multivariate graph-recovery results, CAREFL evaluations, and marginal-density ablations.

before.justification: Section 6 and Appendix B report original causal-discovery experiments on synthetic and established bivariate benchmarks, including an ECM ablation.

results.title: Skewness-Robust Causal Discovery in Location-Scale Noise Models

C1.justification: The abstract and contributions narrow the advertised corruption tolerance from O(T^(1/2)) and O(T^(1/3)) to O(T^(1/4)) and O(T^(1/7)) for FC-RCGP-UCB and A2-RCGP-UCB, respectively. The introduction now distinguishes empirical robustness at T^(1/3) from the weaker guarantees. The zero-cost robustness claim remains.

C2.justification: Sections 4.3 and 5.6 newly interpret the gap between empirical corruption tolerance and proven rates as suggesting a loose observability penalty. The discussion also explicitly identifies known corruption budgets and function bounds as theoretical limitations and discusses robustness to misspecifying them. The Tc=0 heuristic observation already appeared in v1's appendix.

D1.justification: V2 updates experimental configuration listings, explains the base-seed-plus-run-index convention, and discloses using the heuristic function bound sqrt(Bf*kappa)=1. Embedded code links change repository identifiers from RCGP-943C to RCGP-46DE. Hardware, software, execution instructions, and runtime descriptions are otherwise retained; external availability was not checked.

E1.justification: The three benchmark tasks remain unchanged, but the Lunar Lander corruption scenario changes from falsely high rewards of +1000 to falsely low rewards of -1000. This revises the adversarial observation conditions within existing task coverage.

E2.justification: GP-UCB, Student-t Process UCB, and DiagnosticsGP remain the evaluated comparators in the corresponding experiments. No comparator is added or removed.

E3.justification: CIFAR-10 changes from 150 to 140 BO iterations, 4 to 10 initial points, and 2 to 4 training epochs per evaluation. Lunar Lander changes from 800 to 300 iterations, 5 to 10 initial points, and 5 to 4 episodes per evaluation. The appendix's Forrester iteration setting also changes from 25 to 30, although its plots remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The Lunar Lander robustness test is revised to assess resistance to spuriously low rewards instead of deceptive high rewards, with replacement evidence in Figure 5. No separate component ablations or systematic parameter-sensitivity studies are added.

E5.justification: V1 describes CIFAR-10 using a shared random seed; v2 explicitly repeats it across ten seeds and reports means and standard errors. Lunar Lander also newly reports ten-seed aggregation and standard errors. This substantially extends uncertainty reporting beyond Forrester, whose ten-run reporting is retained.

E6.justification: Figures 4–5 contain replacement results under revised settings. The CIFAR-10 curves now place FC-RCGP and A2-RCGP nearly together. In Lunar Lander, Student-t and DiagnosticsGP finish below GP in mean cumulative regret, reversing their earlier ordering relative to GP, despite retained prose saying otherwise. These are not same-setting performance gains. Forrester results in Figures 1 and 3 are unchanged.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–2 replace the unobservable clean-data standard deviation in acquisition with the observable RCGP standard deviation multiplied by a new factor, Psi(Tc). The adaptive model's plateau width also incorporates this factor. These change the formal selection and weighting procedures, while retaining the underlying P-IMQ and anchor/adaptive architecture.

P1.justification: There are targeted rewrites of acquisition-function explanations, theoretical qualifications, and discussion, plus corrected cross-references and reorganized appendix subsections. The acknowledgments are removed. The main narrative sequence and much of the existing prose are retained.

P2.justification: The main text and references change from two columns to one, relocating figures and widening algorithm and theorem displays. Figures 4–5 are redrawn with uncertainty bands and revised axis ranges, and Appendix E adds Table 1. Figures 1–3 retain their original graphical content.

R1.justification: V2 adds Li and Luo (2026), distinguishing their tempered-posterior treatment of model misspecification from this work's outlier robustness. It removes the Byzantine-failure reference to Blanchard et al. (2017). The broader research positioning remains stable.

T1.justification: Appendix D adds variance-comparison and observable-confidence-bound Lemmas 5–7 and substantially revises both regret derivations. Assumption 3 becomes a high-probability function bound, and the analysis retains previously suppressed beta-prime dependence. The thinned-clean-data construction is removed. New Appendix E compares observable and ideal corruption budgets, while Appendix H derives a standard GP's sensitivity to a single corruption.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the central theoretical contribution by supplying an observable-variance bound and revising the algorithms and claims to account for its cost, addressing v1's dependence on unavailable clean-data variance. Ten-seed uncertainty reporting also strengthens both application evaluations. These gains outweigh reporting shortcomings: Appendix I retains stale variance-proxy reasoning, and Section 5.5 contradicts Figure 5's revised baseline ordering.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work and algorithms. Their main text, equations, figures, and complete appendices are readable and can be matched despite substantial revisions and reformatting.

after.justification: Section 5 retains original Forrester results and reports revised CIFAR-10 and Lunar Lander results, including averages and uncertainty across seeds.

before.justification: Section 5 reports original cumulative-regret experiments on Forrester, CIFAR-10 hyperparameter optimization, and Lunar Lander.

results.title: Robust Bayesian Optimisation with Unbounded Corruptions

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion replace the globally low-rank teacher premise with per-image low rank and substantial dataset-level subspace rotation. The claimed failure regime is narrowed to wide-to-narrow ViT compression, acknowledging successful representation transfer between comparable models. The two remedies and headline accuracy claims remain.

C2.justification: v1 explains failure through insufficient token bandwidth within a purported shared low-rank space. v2 interprets encoding mismatch as both orientation and bandwidth mismatch, explicitly acknowledging that fixed Lift cannot resolve subspace rotation and attributing input-dependent alignment capacity to WideLast. This materially changes the mechanism explanation and qualifies what each remedy addresses.

D1.justification: v2 documents the uncentered PCA computation and newly states that code and raw data accompany supplementary materials, whose availability cannot be verified from the PDFs. It omits v1's explicit LayerNorm-normalized MSE and detached-teacher specifications, minimum learning rate, cooldown, and logit-loss weight. These are documentation changes, not established implementation changes.

E1.justification: Both versions use ImageNet-1K for classification and ImageNet validation images for representation analysis. The additional DINO, DINOv2, MAE, and CLIP encoders are model configurations analyzed on the retained image data, not new evaluated datasets, multimodal tasks, or input domains.

E2.justification: Comparator membership in Tables 2–7 is unchanged: the same standalone baselines, SoftKD, MSE, SpectralKD, and listed combinations remain in corresponding experiments. Newly discussed methods such as OFA-KD and RSD are related work, not additional evaluated KD comparators.

E3.justification: v2 introduces a substantially different diagnostic protocol: pooling token features from 1,000 images to estimate an uncentered shared PCA basis and evaluating reconstruction under that fixed basis alongside per-image SVD. Representation-analysis configurations expand from six to fourteen models. The classification experiments retain their stated dataset, training budget, and accuracy metric.

E4.justification: The new SVD-versus-PCA analyses test whether per-image compressibility implies a compact shared subspace, while expanded cross-model diagnostics examine this behavior across pretraining regimes. These substantially revise the mechanistic evidence. v1's layer-wise and stage-wise rank profiles are removed; the classifier-head, projector-width, and loss-weight ablations remain unchanged.

E5.justification: v1 explicitly states that ViT-Huge (MAE) was checked on two random 1,000-image subsets; v2 omits this repeated-subset information. This is a reporting removal, not evidence that fewer checks were performed. Across-image SEP standard-deviation bands remain, and neither version reports repeated-training-run uncertainty for classification accuracies.

E6.justification: New results include CaiT-S24 shared-PCA dimensions of 302 and 359 at 95% and 99% energy for approximately 99% of images, alongside retained per-image SVD values of 61 and 121. Tables 1 and 8 add model results and spectral summaries, while depth-profile results disappear. All classification values in Tables 2–7 and overlapping endpoint SVD/SEP values are unchanged.

M1.justification: Section 3 retains the inference-retained linear projector and final-block widening, with the same combined classification, logit-distillation, and feature-loss objective. Strategy 1/2 are renamed Lift/WideLast. The new PCA diagnostic changes their rationale; omission of the explicit normalized-MSE formula does not establish a different implementation.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, representation analysis, contribution list, and conclusion undergo substantial rewriting around per-image versus shared geometry. Terminology becomes Lift/WideLast, a dedicated related-work appendix is introduced, and the diagnostic appendices are reorganized. Author-list and citation-style changes accompany this broader narrative revision.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to two-column layout. Figure 1 and the SVD appendix displays are redesigned around PCA spectra, shared reconstruction curves, and overlaid SVD/PCA histograms. Tables 1 and 8 gain substantial column and row structure; SEP displays expand to additional models while the original six-model panels are retained and rearranged.

R1.justification: The new five-part related-work appendix substantially positions the work against low-rank compression, explicit alignment, selective distillation, and teacher conditioning. Added discussions include GhostNet, Yu and Wu, OFA-KD, and RSD; the introduction also distinguishes CLIP representation transfer from compression. Numerous generic KD and language-model references are removed.

T1.justification: v2 corrects v1's inference that per-image SVD rank percentiles guarantee one shared low-dimensional projector. Sections 2.1–2.2 distinguish input-dependent factorizations from a fixed shared basis, acknowledge the token-count rank ceiling, and introduce channel second-moment and shared reconstruction-energy definitions. This changes foundational mathematical reasoning, not merely notation.

improvement.justification: v2 resolves a central weakness: v1 incorrectly inferred a shared compact projector from per-image SVD ranks. Sections 2.1–2.2 correct that reasoning, and new PCA evidence directly demonstrates the distinction, including 302 shared-PCA dimensions versus 61 per-image SVD dimensions for CaiT-S24 at 95% energy for approximately 99% of images. Cross-model diagnostics and narrower compression claims substantially strengthen the scientific argument. Some loss and training details are omitted, weakening reproducibility, but this limited loss is outweighed by the foundational correction and supporting evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ViT feature-distillation work and retain the same two student modifications and classification experiments. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial rewriting and reformatting.

after.justification: v2 retains those original classification results and reports additional shared-subspace PCA and cross-model representation analyses in Table 1, Figure 1, and Appendices B–C.

before.justification: v1 reports original ImageNet-1K distillation, ablation, and standalone-training results in Tables 2–7, plus original SVD and SEP analyses in the main text and Appendices A–B.

results.title: From Per-Image Low-Rank to Encoding Mismatch: Rethinking Feature Distillation in Vision Transformers

C1.justification: The central contributions—identifying weak foundation priors and strengthening them through instance guidance and Gaussian regularization—remain. v2's abstract and contribution list emphasize scientific few-shot applications more explicitly, and its new conclusion claims scientific performance often approaches domain-specific priors, extending v1's scientific-results framing of substantial remaining gaps.

C2.justification: v2 qualifies scientific performance as comparable to or better than DIP, replacing v1's large-margin superiority interpretation. It explains MRI limitations through inadequate guidance coverage, states why two InverseBench tasks are excluded, interprets learned weights and parameter sensitivity, and discusses speed–quality tradeoffs. It also newly treats no-reference metrics as secondary indicators and explains that choice.

D1.justification: v2 adds two algorithm listings, sigmoid time parameterization and initialization, explicit latent encoding, dimension-matching instructions, gradient checkpointing, black-hole measurement details, and a project-page link. These substantially improve implementation documentation without necessarily introducing new procedures. Some earlier information disappears, including calibration construction and D-Flow's initialization guidance scale.

E1.justification: v2 adds black-hole imaging using nonlinear VLBI measurements with non-additive noise, substantially extending scientific coverage beyond LIS and MRI. The three natural-image datasets and four restoration tasks remain. The higher-noise calibration experiment from v1 is absent.

E2.justification: The comparator roster remains DIP, D-Flow, FlowDPS, FlowChef, OT-ODE, PnP-Flow, and the quoted Red-Diff reference. Unprompted variants omitted from v2's main Table 3 remain in its appendix. The domain-specific comparison moves from v1 Table 4 to v2 Table 16; black-hole imaging extends the existing scientific comparator set.

E3.justification: New protocols include black-hole evaluation with 100 targets, five guidance images, and closure-consistency metrics, plus parameter sweeps and runtime/memory measurements. Retained settings also receive explicit revisions: DIP's optimizer changes from Adam to AdamW, and Appendix A.2 describes the regression run as FMPlug rather than FMPlug-W. These are reported setting changes, without proof that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained component ablation, v2 tests learned warm-start time versus blur severity, shell thickness, NFE, random initialization, and MRI guidance-set size. It also analyzes guidance-weight correlations and illustrates MRI guidance mismatch. These substantially expand mechanism and robustness evidence (Sections 4.2–4.3 and A.7). Conversely, v1's calibration ablation at two noise levels is removed.

E5.justification: v2 adds ten random initializations per image on a DIV2K subset and reports mean-plus-variability entries for four methods in Table 17; v1 has no corresponding uncertainty reporting. It also reports Pearson and Spearman correlations for MRI guidance weights. This statistical reporting is localized: principal benchmark tables still lack uncertainty, and the aggregation behind the quantities called variances is insufficiently specified.

E6.justification: Scientific results are substantially revised: FMPlug's LIS PSNR/SSIM changes from 31.83/0.97 to 34.65/0.91, while MRI SSIM changes from beating DIP, 0.48 versus 0.39, to trailing it, 0.52 versus 0.54. v2 adds black-hole results, including FMPlug PSNR 22.91, and numerous diagnostic results. These are revised reports, not established same-setting improvements. Restoration tables and the relocated domain-specific comparison retain their numerical values.

M1.justification: v2's stated method and complete algorithms omit v1's additional mean–variance calibration, which used 4000 generated samples and a fitted network (v1 Section 3.1). The central learned warm-start, Gaussian shell projection, and softmax-weighted few-shot guidance remain. The PDFs do not establish whether calibration was also removed from the computations underlying retained results.

P1.justification: Much of the original exposition remains, with wording edits and expanded scientific motivation. v2 separates implementation issues into Section 3.3, reorganizes appendix sections, moves the domain-specific comparison into Appendix A.5, and adds a conclusion and impact statement. These refine the existing narrative rather than comprehensively rewriting it.

P2.justification: v2 converts the main paper to a two-column layout, replaces the opening conceptual diagram, adds scientific-guidance illustrations and diagnostic tables, and expands qualitative comparisons with marked regions and enlarged crops. Main Table 3 is shortened while its full comparisons remain in the appendix. These are substantial display changes beyond renumbering and numerical updates.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting scientific data/computation constraints and discussion of no-reference metric reliability, including Bommasani, Chua, Chen, Antsiferova, Liao, and Rasheed. It removes the citation acknowledging the preliminary Wan et al. version. Positioning against the established FM inverse-problem methods otherwise remains largely unchanged.

T1.justification: v2 Appendix A.6 explicitly identifies the original scattering expression as nonlinear and introduces the first Born assumption and resulting linear equation. It also adds black-hole visibility and closure-measurement mathematics. The Gaussian concentration theorem and core shell argument remain unchanged; the added indicator-function expression merely restates the existing constraint.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the scientific few-shot contribution: black-hole imaging, guidance-count and weight analyses, sensitivity studies, and repeated initializations address applicability and mechanisms that v1 scarcely tested. Pseudocode, implementation explanations, MRI failure analysis, and efficiency measurements also make the work easier to assess and reproduce. Gains are tempered by lost calibration evidence, unexplained LIS/MRI score replacements, and an overbroad stability claim—Table 17 gives FlowChef lower LPIPS variability than FMPlug. Nevertheless, the added diagnostic evidence and clearer applicability boundaries provide a substantial net quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FMPlug research by the same authors. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison across the reorganized material.

after.justification: v2 retains original restoration experiments and reports revised scientific results, black-hole imaging, sensitivity studies, computational measurements, and repeated-initialization experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original image-restoration, image-regression, LIS, MRI, and ablation results. Its separately attributed Red-Diff reference scores do not affect this assessment.

results.title: Saving Foundation Flow-Matching Priors for Inverse Problems

C1.justification: The central contribution shifts from hierarchical UCB with learned profiling guidance to hardware-constrained contextual bandits with pruning and Lipschitz/covering-based efficiency claims. V2 foregrounds provable sample efficiency and structured selection outperforming LLM reasoning. V1's fewer-token efficiency claim is replaced by better performance per dollar, despite acknowledged higher per-iteration costs.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive explanations for preferring bandits over full reinforcement learning, budget-dependent clustering granularity, hardware-dependent strategy allocation, and profiling's larger contribution at the default budget. It also interprets raw profiling injection as potentially harmful and explains why removing the strategy set disables multiple dependent components. These substantially extend v1's clustering and dropout-based mechanism narrative.

D1.justification: Section 3.6 and Appendices A, C–H add exact profiling counters and CUDA feature APIs, code-hash caching, masking/UCB parameters, the complete six-strategy catalog, a 16,384-token output limit, the named evaluation subset, and benchmark/GEAK adaptation details. V1's logistic-training buffer, SGD, and synthetic warmup specifications disappear with the replaced component.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates 29 kernels restricted to L1–L2. V2 reports 183 kernels spanning L1–L5 and 13 functional categories, with harder attention, linear-attention/SSM, quantization, and fused-operation tasks documented in Table 1 and Appendix E. This substantially broadens computational patterns and task difficulty.

E2.justification: The agent comparison expands from GEAK alone to GEAK plus Best-of-N in the main benchmark and backend experiments. Appendix G and Table 9 additionally evaluate PyTorch eager execution, torch.compile with inductor, and max-autotune as reference execution methods.

E3.justification: Default/extended budgets change from 10/20 to 20/40 iterations. V2 adds H20 and additional LLM configurations, with GPT-5 replacing the reported GPT-5.1 backend. Correctness tolerances tighten from atol=1e-3 and rtol=1e-1 to both 1e-4. Fast@1 changes from >1.1 to >1.0, shape aggregation becomes a ratio of total runtimes, and correct-only/fallback reporting modes and 50-/30-kernel subset protocols are introduced.

E4.justification: V1's clustering visualization and worked dropout case study are removed. V2 adds explicit component and framework ablations, including profiling removal and LLM strategy selection, plus clustering sensitivity over K={1,2,3,5}, cross-hardware strategy analyses, and quantitative runtime/API-cost analyses. These directly investigate mechanisms and tradeoffs that v1 largely illustrated or asserted.

E5.justification: Timing estimation changes from the mean over 1,000 timed iterations to the median over a 1,000ms measurement window; warmup likewise changes from iteration counts to duration. Appendix E newly specifies seed 42 for subset sampling. Neither version reports independent optimization-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: The result set is substantially replaced and expanded. For example, v1 Table 2 reports RTX 4090/DeepSeek best-of-iteration-9 speedup of 9.78× and Fast@1 of 54%; v2 Table 1 reports 1.74× and 43.3% under changed coverage, budgets, method, and metrics, so this is not a same-setting regression. V2 additionally reports correctness, ablation, strategy, cost, and PyTorch comparison outcomes.

M1.justification: V1's additive, learned logistic profiling bonus is replaced by hardware-saturation masks restricting UCB selection and softmax selection within clusters. V2 profiles cluster representatives rather than every candidate, changes clustering features from six dimensions to five, and replaces signed improvement rewards with nonnegative clipped rewards. These materially change the optimization procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, formulation, methodology, and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten. Related work moves from Section 2 to Section 5, the method is reorganized around characterization, clustering, and constrained selection, and the single proof appendix becomes Appendices A–J. The title, author list, and running header also change.

P2.justification: V2 introduces a system overview diagram, runtime breakdown and cost plots, and redesigned difficulty/backend comparison and ablation tables. The scalability display adds clustering configurations, while v1's separate Fast@1 trajectories, clustering scatterplot, and dropout plot disappear. New appendix tables document configurations, strategies, subsets, PyTorch results, and hardware-specific statistics.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands positioning around profiling-based agents such as CudaForge and TritonForge, metric/clustering bandits, and hardware-aware compilation. It explicitly presents KernelBand as complementary to model fine-tuning and explains exclusions of other agents in Appendix F. V1's separate hierarchical-optimization discussion and several associated citations are removed.

T1.justification: V1's cluster-similarity/profiling-error regret argument is replaced by explicit hardware-gain boundedness and Lipschitz assumptions, an epsilon-optimality theorem, and an approximation/estimation decomposition in Appendix B. The bound changes from a linear cluster-strategy prefactor plus clustering/profiling errors to square-root dependence on cluster-strategy count plus a cluster-diameter approximation term. V1's asserted equivalence between cumulative reward maximization and minimum final latency is also removed.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens support for the paper: v1's narrow easy-task evaluation and illustrative case studies give way to harder tasks, explicit component ablations, additional comparison methods, and measured cost tradeoffs. Stricter correctness checks and detailed appendices improve credibility and reproducibility. These gains outweigh losing the worked case study, although independent-run uncertainty remains absent and Appendix E's claimed <1% category deviation conflicts with Table 7. The changed protocols do not establish a direct performance improvement over v1.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe KernelBand and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. The substantial algorithmic and experimental revisions can be reliably compared; differing evaluation settings limit direct performance comparisons, not document comparability.

after.justification: Section 4 and Appendices G–J report original benchmark comparisons, scaling and sensitivity experiments, component ablations, cost measurements, PyTorch comparisons, and hardware-specific strategy statistics.

before.justification: Section 5 reports original GPU kernel optimization experiments against GEAK, including performance trajectories, hardware/backend comparisons, clustering visualization, and a seeded_dropout case study.

results.title: KernelBand: Steering LLM-based Kernel Optimization via Hardware-Aware Multi-Armed Bandits

C1.justification: The three central contributions remain the horizon trade-off, plug-and-play MoH and consensus-based dynamic inference. The 99% LIBERO and 2.5× throughput claims remain; removing the former from the abstract does not remove it from the introduction and conclusion. Additional experiments support the existing claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations distinguishing horizon diversity from generic ensembling, attributes ATE degradation to cumulative drift, and interprets action errors and gating shifts. Appendices C and H discuss proposed pretraining use and threshold rationale. Section 4.4 explicitly clarifies that throughput measures executed actions per predicted chunk, rather than wall-clock speed.

D1.justification: v2 documents StarVLA's Qwen3-VL backbone and setup details for the added experiments. However, it removes v1's project link and the maximum-gradient-norm value of 1.0 from the hyperparameter table. These are documentation changes; they do not establish code withdrawal or changed gradient clipping.

E1.justification: v2 retains LIBERO, seven RoboTwin tasks and the three original real-world tasks, while adding five RoboCasa household tasks and diagonal towel folding. These additions extend evaluation environments and introduce deformable-object manipulation.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds StarVLA and its MoH variant while retaining the existing comparators, including GR00T-N1. New Table 5 evaluates CogACT's Adaptive Temporal Ensemble, both alone and combined with MoH, on π0 and π0.5. These introduce a distinct backbone comparison and a substantive competing fusion strategy.

E3.justification: New protocols include RoboCasa training with 200 demonstrations per task, 10-step execution and 150 evaluation rollouts per task, plus towel folding with 40 demonstrations and 20 rollouts. Additional analyses vary maximum horizon with ten branches fixed and measure first-five-action L1 error on LIBERO training data. The original experiments' stated protocols remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds an identical-horizon ensemble control, maximum-horizon sensitivity analysis, per-step action-error analysis, task-dependent gating statistics and within-rollout threshold analysis (Table 4 and Tables 8–11). These investigate alternative explanations and mechanisms beyond v1's retained density, fusion and balance-loss ablations. Existing failure cases are relocated, not newly added.

E5.justification: RoboCasa results in v2 Table 2 introduce means and standard deviations across three random seeds. This uncertainty-reporting practice is absent from v1, but remains limited to the new benchmark; the retained LIBERO setup still specifies one training run with a fixed seed.

E6.justification: Existing headline results, including 99.0% LIBERO success, are retained. New comparisons report baseline versus MoH averages of 95.9% versus 97.0% for StarVLA and 28.0% versus 31.4% on RoboCasa, plus 75% versus 90% for towel folding. v2 also adds ensemble, ATE, horizon-sensitivity, action-error, gating and threshold results.

M1.justification: Section 3 retains the same horizon truncation and masking, shared action transformer, linear gating, training losses and consensus-based dynamic inference. StarVLA is an additional application of the existing procedure; no MoH algorithm change is documented.

P1.justification: The abstract and real-world discussion are condensed, subsection headings are simplified, and latency, gating statistics and detailed rollout discussion move into dedicated appendix sections. Motivation and discussion passages are added, but the introduction and method narrative remain largely intact.

P2.justification: v2 adopts an ICML layout with running headers and single-column appendices, adds multiple result tables, and redesigns Table 1 with shading and improvement annotations. Latency and gating plots move to the appendix; the main rollout figure is shortened and annotated while its full sequence remains in the appendix.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to Qwen3-VL, StarVLA, RoboCasa365 and SimpleVLA-RL, and explicitly distinguishes MoH's within-planning-step horizon fusion from CogACT's temporal ensembling. The broader related-work narrative and novelty positioning remain largely unchanged.

T1.justification: Equations (1)–(17) retain the same mathematical definitions, objectives and derivations. No theorem, proof or revised formal assumption is introduced; the added mechanism and threshold discussions are empirical or conceptual.

improvement.justification: The additional backbone and harder-benchmark evaluations strengthen generality, while identical-horizon and ATE controls address important alternative explanations left unresolved in v1. RoboCasa uncertainty reporting and the explicit throughput definition improve evidential transparency. These substantial gains outweigh the limited loss of reproducibility information from removing the project link and gradient-clipping disclosure.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Mixture of Horizons in Action Chunking. Their complete text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds RoboCasa evaluations, StarVLA experiments, towel folding and further controlled analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original LIBERO and RoboTwin evaluations, ablations, dynamic-inference measurements and real-robot experiments, with additional analyses in the appendices.

results.title: Mixture of Horizons in Action Chunking

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion newly claim demonstrated accuracy and efficiency benefits for frontier-model problem solving on IMO 2025 and Apex. Investigating workflow cost inefficiency becomes an explicit contribution, while QiuZhen-Bench curation disappears from the principal contribution list despite the dataset being retained.

C2.justification: v2 develops fixed-granularity token wastage as a mechanism motivating progressive segmentation, treats benchmark annotation problems as a reliability boundary for frontier models, and discusses harmful refinements and possible geometric-intuition limitations in solving. Section 4.2 adds an explicit rigor-versus-efficiency argument for informal verification. Conversely, v1's class-balance qualification of pruning efficiency is removed.

D1.justification: v2 adds operational timing/cost and token-accounting information and changes the code link to THUNLP-MT/pverify. It removes the direct dataset link and v1's explicit QiuZhen recipe specifying random selection of 300 problems, GPT-5-mini generation, and GPT-5 progressive@3/6 labeling. Appendix extraction and verification prompts remain substantively unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds actual problem-solving evaluation on six IMO 2025 problems and twelve MathArena Apex 2025 problems, extending coverage beyond judging supplied proofs to generating and refining solutions. IMO-GradingBench, Hard2Verify, and QiuZhen-Bench remain.

E2.justification: The reported GPT-5-mini scaling comparison gains vertical-pessimistic curves in v2 Figure 4, absent from v1 Figure 1. The new solving comparison also includes direct generation without verification alongside workflows using pes@12 and prog@4/4. Existing majority-voting, single-pass, and long-CoT comparisons are retained.

E3.justification: v2 introduces final-iteration manual IMO scoring, per-iteration answer-accuracy evaluation on Apex, and cumulative token accounting including verification. It also adds Gemini 3 configurations, full-versus-300-sample IMO-GradingBench evaluation, and runtime measurements under equal concurrency. These substantially extend the evaluation design beyond the retained binary proof-classification protocol.

E4.justification: New analyses test whether the 300-sample subset represents full IMO-GradingBench performance (Table 1) and whether token savings translate into runtime and API-cost savings (Appendix A.1, Table 4). Scaling and false-negative analyses expand, including Gemini 3 Pro Preview. The six detailed appendix cases are retained rather than newly added.

E5.justification: v2 first reports three trials per Apex setting and displays their individual trajectories in Figure 7 to expose variability. v1 provides no comparable repeated-run reporting. This does not establish additional repetitions for the retained verification experiments; confidence intervals and significance tests are not introduced.

E6.justification: New IMO results report totals of 13/42, 17/42, and 22/42 for direct generation, pes@12, and prog@4/4, using 129K, 1,310K, and 985K equivalent tokens respectively (Table 3). These are new comparisons, not cross-version performance gains. GPT-5-mini's reviewed FN counts change from 5 critical/5 minor/3 nonsense to 10/6/4. Apex trajectories, Gemini 3 verification results, extended scaling curves, subset results, and operational efficiency measurements add substantial evidence.

M1.justification: Section 3.5 and Figure 6 add an iterative solution-generation, verification, and error-correction workflow, stopping on acceptance or an iteration limit. The three underlying verification algorithms and appendix prompts remain substantively unchanged. The minimum segmentation size explained in v2 was already shown in v1 Figure 2.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten, method explanations are reorganized, datasets and metrics are combined, and a preliminary-experiments subsection is introduced. Related work gains subsections, the conclusion is substantially rewritten, and acknowledgements and an impact statement are added. These changes exceed inserting the new experiments.

P2.justification: The main text and references switch from single-column to two-column layout. Separate model-specific efficiency figures become a combined dataset-organized figure with expanded axes and revised styling; benchmark charts are compressed and updated. New subset, solving, and efficiency tables and workflow/Apex figures are added, while retained diagrams and appendix boxes are relocated and reflowed.

R1.justification: Related work expands into informal and formal verification, with substantive discussion of verification costs and additions including DeepSeekMath-V2, DeepSeek-V3.2, Aristotle, and Seed-Prover 1.5.
