Simple pessimistic verification is explicitly positioned as a mainstream representative baseline, sharpening the emphasis on progressive decomposition. Earlier scoring-bias and self-inconsistency discussion is removed.

T1.justification: The balanced-F1 definition, verification-check bound, and mathematical reasoning within the six appendix examples remain substantively unchanged. Notation and typesetting differences introduce no new theorem, proof, assumption, or derivation.

improvement.justification: v1 left downstream solving benefits largely prospective and relied on verification labels that its own cases questioned. v2 substantially strengthens the evidence through direct solving tests with contest scoring and answer checks, subset-representativeness checks, and measured runtime/API costs. The small six- and twelve-problem solving sets and loss of QiuZhen reproducibility details limit the gains, but the new evidence addresses an important gap in practical validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same pessimistic-verification work. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting and added experiments.

after.justification: v2 retains original verification results and adds contest problem-solving experiments, subset comparisons, and runtime/API-cost measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original verification experiments on three benchmarks, scaling comparisons, and manual analyses of false negatives.

results.title: Pessimistic Verification for Open-Ended Math Questions

C1.justification: The central robustness–privacy trade-off and stability claims persist. The introduction replaces the guarantee that diversity prevents attack transfer with a claim of reduced transfer risk, and newly claims empirical extension to more complex neural architectures. These refine and broaden the retained thesis.

C2.justification: v2 distinguishes attacked-input disagreement from the clean-data proxy and explicitly disclaims guarantees against all adaptive attacks. It revises the reconstruction-versus-membership discussion, qualifies neural membership leakage as potentially nonmonotonic, explains simultaneous-attack limitations, and develops efficiency-limited versus privacy-limited disclosure regimes beyond v1's qualitative sweet-spot discussion.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-repository link, dataset row/feature counts, neural architecture and Rashomon-tolerance details, and attack configurations. It documents reuse of ten pretrained RashomonCBMs without additional training and an NVIDIA RTX A5000 for their evaluation. These substantially expand reproducibility information without implying changes to retained tree settings.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained six tabular datasets and synthetic distributions, v2 evaluates Iris, Seeds, and Wine, and adds image/concept classification on AwA2. It also introduces membership-inference evaluation and simultaneous attacks targeting multiple released trees, substantially broadening tasks and threat scenarios.

E2.justification: The existing tree-selection comparators are retained. v2 adds an explicit comparison between simultaneous multi-model attacks and Kantchelian et al.'s single-model attack in Figure 17, alongside reference-model accuracy and random-guessing controls in the new neural-network experiments.

E3.justification: The original TreeFARMS/DRAFT settings remain. New protocols include joint-region attack searches over up to ten trees, AWP-estimated neural Rashomon sets with specified relative loss tolerances, FGSM evaluations, and Yeom membership-inference error. AwA2 evaluation introduces ten pretrained models and ten-step PGD with an 8/255 budget and 2/255 step size.

E4.justification: v2 adds clean-versus-adversarial accuracy analysis, simultaneous-attack robustness tests, neural-network sensitivity to attack strength, and quantitative disclosure-knee/privacy-constraint analyses. These investigate additional robustness mechanisms and operational trade-offs; the earlier stability, sparsity, and sampling-strategy studies are retained.

E5.justification: Existing five-fold and five-run tree reporting remains. Figures 20–21 specify twenty seeded trials and standard deviations for new neural-network experiments, while Figure 23 adds linear-fit slopes and R-squared reporting. These are additional reporting procedures, not evidence of increased repetitions for the retained experiments.

E6.justification: The original tree and simulation results are retained, while v2 adds substantial simultaneous-attack, neural-network, membership-inference, and disclosure-selection results. Its new AwA2 Table 7 reports 43.95% source-model versus 61.68% transfer-target task accuracy, a 17.73-percentage-point recovery. These are newly reported evaluations, not matched-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The central Rashomon-set approach and existing tree-selection procedures remain. Section 6.4 and Appendices E.6–E.8 add an auxiliary disclosure procedure: choose the smaller of a privacy-constrained model count and a Kneedle-derived knee count. v1 only discussed a possible disclosure sweet spot.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and conclusion undergo substantial rewriting and compression, including replacement of the enumerated contribution list. v2 reorganizes the appendices, adds a results-navigation section and operationalization subsections, and revises terminology and explanatory passages throughout.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column conference layout for the main text and references, relocates the conceptual comparison table and KL plot, and recomposes main-text figures while retaining their fuller appendix versions. It adds numerous analysis plots and summary/result tables, including neural-network panels, AwA2 results, and annotated disclosure curves.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially updates the literature and positioning. It explicitly distinguishes this set-level analysis from Hsu et al. (2026)'s individual-model trustworthiness study and frames its defense perspective against Yao et al. (2025)'s attack-transferability analysis. Additional works cover concept-based networks, robustness definitions, and privacy attacks.

T1.justification: v1's one-feature rule-list vulnerability claim becomes Theorem 4.2 with conjunctive-antecedent and nonempty-leaf assumptions and a general l+I−1 attack budget. v2 also adds a total-variation version of the ensemble distribution bound and Theorem C.5 linking approximation gains to convex-hull diversity, and corrects an inequality in the distribution-shift proof.

improvement.justification: v2 repairs important theoretical weaknesses through the revised rule-list assumptions and corrected distribution-shift proof. Its simultaneous-attack and neural/image evaluations substantially strengthen evidence beyond v1's single-target tree experiments, while added implementation information improves reproducibility. The new disclosure guidance has a limitation: its illustrative 35% tolerance does not establish the statistical privacy assurance claimed in Appendix E.8. Nevertheless, the improvements to mathematical validity and empirical support are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Rashomon-set study. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite extensive reformatting and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains these results and adds original simultaneous-attack, neural-network, membership-inference, and AwA2 attack-transferability evaluations.

before.justification: v1 reports original decision-tree experiments on six datasets, simulations using five synthetic distributions, and appendix studies of stability, sampling strategies, and individual-model vulnerability.

results.title: The Double-Edged Nature of the Rashomon Set for Trustworthy Machine Learning

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: outcome-aware spectral learning addresses misalignment, admits theoretical error analysis, and works on synthetic, dSprites, and OPE benchmarks. The additional theory and experiments strengthen support without redefining these main claims.

C2.justification: v2 explains instability of the alignment estimator at large delta and shifts advice toward conservative alignment-based selection. Appendix E.7.2 qualifies compactness of the modified OPE operator as an assumption, replacing v1's categorical assertion. Appendix G explains why outcome-predictive features alone can fail to recover the structural function.

D1.justification: Appendix E newly supplies a reproduction-code repository location. Table 6 and Appendix G document the naive baseline's five-feature architecture and its tuning and rejection procedures. Existing architecture and OPE hyperparameter tables are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate synthetic IV regression, the heart and ellipse dSprites tasks, and Cartpole, Mountain Car, and Catch OPE. The added tuning and baseline studies reuse existing task coverage; their parameter grids and sample sizes concern experimental settings.

E2.justification: Appendix G adds an evaluated naive outcome-aware comparator that learns outcome-predictive Z-features and then predicts them from X. SpecIV, DFIV, and KIV remain in their original comparisons. Bruns-Smith's method is discussed but is not directly benchmarked.

E3.justification: Additional experiments evaluate automatic delta selection. Appendix G specifies 15,000 training and 5,000 evaluation samples, noise variance 0.2, and a post-hoc rejection rule for predictions whose standard deviation exceeds five times that of Y. These are additional protocols; the original benchmark settings are retained.

E4.justification: Appendix E.9 adds practical tests of alignment-based delta selection on synthetic and dSprites data. Appendix G adds a substantial investigation of whether simpler outcome-aware learning suffices, examining MSE tails and unstable-model rejection across parameter grids. The earlier alignment and rank-two perturbation analyses are retained.

E5.justification: The new baseline study explicitly reports median, 5th-percentile, and 95th-percentile MSEs and fitted-model counts. Existing dSprites run counts and the five-run OPE mean/standard-deviation reporting remain unchanged; the PDFs do not establish increased replication of those experiments.

E6.justification: New Figures 14–15 report alignment-selected prediction errors; Figures 17–19 report comparable naive-baseline median errors but heavier tails and frequent rejection, versus 9 rejected AugSpecIV fits out of 1,200. Figure 4 revises displayed alignment distributions. Figure 3 removes v1's h_new median MSE of 61.16 at delta = 3. These additions and revisions do not establish an across-version performance gain.

M1.justification: v2 introduces a conservative alignment-based selection rule: scan increasing delta values and accept an increase only when estimated alignment improves by at least 5% (Appendices E.9 and G). v1 discussed alignment-based tuning heuristically. The augmented losses, 2SLS estimator, OPE iteration, and higher-rank extension remain substantively unchanged.

P1.justification: Related Work moves from Section 5 to Section 2, the delta-selection discussion is reordered, and explanatory prose and notation are refined. v2 also adds impact and funding statements and updates affiliations and citation style. Most existing narrative is retained.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from a single-column manuscript to an ICML two-column layout. Existing plots are resized and reformatted, Figure 4's panels are reversed, and appendix displays are rearranged. Five new result figures and Table 6 are added; v1's rank-two Figure 14 is retained as v2's Figure 16.

R1.justification: v2 adds a substantive comparison with Bruns-Smith (2025), distinguishing representation learning, convergence conditions, and post-hoc checks. It also adds Bennett et al. (2025) and Shen et al. (2026) to the saddle-point literature. The overall positioning around SpecIV remains.

T1.justification: v2 corrects the claimed attained loss bound to use the rank-d truncated operator's squared Hilbert–Schmidt norm and states the augmented spectral-gap assumption. New Proposition A.4 proves a population excess-loss-to-operator-gap bound. Appendices B and E.9 add boundedness/compactness and alignment-conditioning derivations, while existing proofs receive algebraic corrections.

improvement.justification: The corrected loss optimum and new Proposition A.4 materially strengthen the theoretical connection between training loss and operator error. Appendices E.9 and G address important practical gaps through tests of delta selection and simpler outcome-aware alternatives, supported by new code-access information. These gains outweigh the loss of the high-delta numerical annotation, although end-to-end DNN optimization and generalization guarantees remain open.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Augmented Spectral Feature Learning work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite reformatting, reordering, and added material.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds delta-selection experiments and comparisons with a naive outcome-aware baseline in Appendices E.9 and G.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic IV, dSprites, and off-policy evaluation results, together with alignment, parameter-sensitivity, and higher-rank experiments in its appendices.

results.title: Outcome-Aware Spectral Feature Learning for Instrumental Variable Regression

C1.justification: The central first-order oracle, convergence-rate and drop-in-library contributions remain. v2 changes the highlighted interface property from objective-agnostic to solver-agnostic, and adds prominent abstract/conclusion claims of comparable convergence with improved runtime and memory scalability. The principal asymptotic rate is unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands interpretations involving canonicalization overhead, ill-conditioned KKT systems, tolerance stability, memory growth and batch overhead. It replaces v1's specific explanation for improved Sudoku loss with broader robustness/scaling interpretations. Appendix G also qualifies GPU advantages as task-dependent and identifies CvxpyLayer gradients as a proxy reference.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents solver backends, 2,048 synthetic samples with an 80/20 split, two-layer MLPs, Adam, dimensions, tolerances and an eight-core/384-GB allocation. These disclosures do not establish changes to previously unspecified settings. The earlier big-M/DPP implementation explanation is removed, and the code link changes from guaguakai/FFOLayer to GT-KOALA/FFOLayer.

E1.justification: v2 retains synthetic QP decision-focused learning and 9×9 Sudoku, and adds an SOCP task with a nonlinear norm constraint in Section 6.3. This substantially extends empirical coverage beyond linear constraints to the general-convex setting central to the paper.

E2.justification: BPQP and dQP become evaluated comparators in the retained QP/Sudoku experiments, alongside CvxpyLayer, QPTH and LPGD (v2 Figures 3–4). Alt-Diff appears in the conceptual comparison table but is explicitly excluded from reported experiments, so it is not counted as an added empirical baseline.

E3.justification: v1 reports primary LPGD results with tolerance 10^-12; v2 Section 7 instead reports matching the proposed method's tolerance, with the tightened setting examined separately in Figure 8. v2 also introduces dimension, batch-size and tolerance sweeps, CPU/GPU comparisons, and memory, gradient-error and throughput measurements.

E4.justification: v2 adds extensive analyses of problem-size scaling, memory components, approximate-gradient fidelity, batch efficiency, backward-solver tolerance and GPU alternatives (Figures 5–13). Figure 8 also expands v1's qualitative LPGD tolerance observation into a direct loss/runtime comparison.

E5.justification: Appendix G.1 newly states that each experiment uses ten random seeds, and Section 7 describes averaged timings; v1 specifies no run count. Neither version defines confidence intervals or significance tests. This is newly disclosed replication, not evidence that the number of runs increased.

E6.justification: The retained loss/runtime plots are revised, including LPGD results under a reported tolerance change. v2 adds SOCP, BPQP/dQP and diagnostic results, including nearly flat reported FFOCP memory versus sharply increasing CvxpyLayer memory in Figure 6. These are new or revised outcomes, not established same-setting performance gains across versions.

M1.justification: Both versions use the active-set Lagrangian surrogate, original and perturbed solves, finite-difference hypergradients and detached-gradient linearization. The solver-agnostic framing and simplification using zero unperturbed ghost multipliers clarify this existing procedure rather than introduce a new algorithm.

P1.justification: v2 extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, problem statement and method exposition, restructures Section 4 and refocuses Section 5. Proofs and general-convex discussion move into reorganized appendices, while a conclusion, acknowledgements, impact statement and dedicated experimental appendix reshape the document.

P2.justification: The main text changes to a two-column layout. v2 adds a method illustration and comparison table, redraws the main experiment plots with additional methods and three task panels, and introduces numerous diagnostic figures. The original code example is retained as Figure 2 rather than removed.

R1.justification: Section 2 and the new Table 1 substantially expand positioning against differentiable optimization layers, especially dQP, BPQP, LPGD and Alt-Diff, and claim a distinctive combination of solver independence, first-order information and finite-time guarantees. Additional differentiable-QP and software-framework references are introduced. The older nonconvex-bilevel survey is largely retained and relocated.

T1.justification: v2 qualifies active-set equivalence with differentiability and local active-set constancy (Theorem 4.5). Lemmas C.1 and E.1 add explicit finite-perturbation error derivations and their detached-gradient counterpart under regularity assumptions. v1 already claimed finite accuracy but relied on cited bounds and an asymptotic argument in Appendix D.2. The principal complexity, general-convex and smoothing results are retained.

improvement.justification: v1's scalability and general-convex claims had only two linearly constrained empirical demonstrations. v2 adds nonlinear SOCP evaluation, stronger comparators and controlled scaling, gradient-accuracy, tolerance and GPU studies, substantially strengthening the empirical basis and exposing tradeoffs. Clearer theorem conditions and experimental disclosures also help. Removed big-M documentation and inconsistent CPU/GPU memory labeling limit reproducibility, but do not outweigh these substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FFOLayer research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial rewriting and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 reports original results on synthetic decision-focused learning, Sudoku and SOCP, plus scaling, memory, gradient-accuracy and sensitivity experiments in Appendix G.

before.justification: v1 reports original training-loss and runtime experiments on synthetic decision-focused learning and Sudoku in Sections 6–7 and Figures 2–3.

results.title: A Fully First-Order Layer for Differentiable Optimization

C1.justification: The central contribution remains runtime-adaptive scheduling combined with dynamic batching for augmented inference. v3 emphasizes execution-state and cross-round awareness and revises headline performance claims: the abstract's goodput ranges of 4.7–33.1x and 3.3–13.2x become 6.5x and 4.7x, described as geometric means in the introduction.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive interpretations linking SSJF to GPU underutilization and InferCept to excessive CPU offloading, and explains degraded behavior at extreme beta values (Appendices D.3 and D.9). It also explicitly delineates the fixed-value, fixed-cost scope of its theoretical guarantee and leaves guarantees for online, evolving requests unresolved.

D1.justification: v3 newly specifies 50-token prediction buckets, the 110M-parameter predictor, execution off the critical path, default beta=5e-5, and MARS reimplementation with a shared prediction interface. Conversely, it removes v1's 70/30 and 60/40 predictor training/evaluation splits and explicit phase-cost calculations, replacing the latter with more abstract formulations. Reproducibility documentation changes substantially in both directions.

E1.justification: The underlying INFERCEPT-derived dataset, called Merge in v1, and ToolBench remain. v3 adds a distinct mixed serving scenario by disabling external calls for 50% of INFERCEPT requests while retaining their prompts and output lengths (Appendix D.1).

E2.justification: The main comparisons expand from vLLM and InferCept to include predicted-output-length SSJF. Appendix D.6 additionally evaluates a reimplementation of memory-based MARS on INFERCEPT and mixed workloads. These introduce substantially stronger scheduling comparators into reported evaluations.

E3.justification: v3 replaces OPT-13B on two A100 GPUs with Vicuna-13B and adds Llama-3-70B-Instruct on four A100 GPUs. It removes the fixed-2,000-request and relaxed-5x-SLO evaluations, introduces controlled prediction-noise and beta sweeps, and adds P99 TTFT for sensitivity analysis. It also specifies geometric-mean aggregation across settings; the primary latency SLOs remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 adds a scheduling-only ablation, separating its contribution from dynamic batching, plus prediction-error injection, beta sensitivity, scheduling-overhead scaling, and GPU/CPU memory-occupancy analyses (Section 6; Appendix D). The latency breakdown expands to baselines and external-call time. Burst testing remains but loses ToolBench coverage, and relaxed-SLO sensitivity results are removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The added latency percentiles and prediction-noise experiments measure performance and robustness; geometric-mean benchmark summaries do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: v3 revises existing results and adds SSJF/MARS, mixed-workload, 70B, and diagnostic results. For example, AugServe's reported OPT-13B/H800 goodput at 2 req/s and CV=1.5 changes from 1.15 in v1 Table 6 to 0.82 req/s in v3 Table 7. Fixed-2,000-request, relaxed-SLO, and TPOT result sets disappear. Changed methods and configurations preclude interpreting the revision as a uniform same-setting performance gain.

M1.justification: v1's phase-cost priority with an additive waiting-time adjustment becomes the descending value-density priority (1 + beta*w)/C in v3. Algorithm 1 also changes from explicit queue precedence to global ranking and greedy selection. The token budget now specifically counts reclaimable Swap/Discard contexts. These alter scheduling beyond renaming the retained prediction-and-feedback framework.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, motivation, design, evaluation, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. v3 introduces a separate Problem Formulation section, reorganizes the design narrative around state awareness, moves Related Work into Appendix C, and restructures the appendices into A–E. Author and terminology changes accompany this broader reorganization.

P2.justification: v3 combines v1 Figures 7–9 into a consolidated performance figure, adds lifecycle and system-architecture diagrams, converts the component ablation into a table, and introduces multiple diagnostic plots. Existing plots gain comparator series and revised axes or legends. The appendix changes from dense two-column presentation to full-width text, equations, tables, and figures.

R1.justification: v3 substantially sharpens positioning against MARS's per-round memory-based scheduling and newly cited BatchLLM's free-memory-based batching. v1 groups the MARS paper with length-based schedulers without this detailed distinction. Tool-agent references are also added. The substantive change concerns research positioning, beyond publication-metadata updates to retained references.

T1.justification: v1's proposition about longer requests finishing earlier is removed. v3 adds formal service-segment definitions, a constrained scheduling objective, and an integral space-time cost formulation. Appendix E supplies a new 1/2-approximation proof for simplified fixed-cost knapsack selection using greedy packing plus the best feasible singleton; it explicitly excludes a guarantee for the full online scheduling problem.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens validation of the scheduling contribution through SSJF and reimplemented MARS comparisons, an independent scheduling ablation, prediction-error tests, and mixed-workload and 70B evaluations. These address important gaps in v1's predominantly FCFS-based comparisons and untested prediction robustness. Removing predictor splits, explicit cost calculations, and some earlier evaluations weakens reproducibility and coverage, while the new proof remains narrowly scoped. Overall, the stronger comparative and diagnostic evidence provides a substantial net quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AugServe. Their complete text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial rewriting and reorganization.

after.justification: v3 reports original comparative experiments, ablations, prediction-error tests, overhead measurements, and additional workload evaluations in Section 6 and Appendix D.

before.justification: v1 reports original serving experiments, latency and goodput measurements, component ablations, and burst-arrival tests in Section 5 and Appendix B.

results.title: AugServe: Adaptive Request Scheduling for Augmented Large Language Model Inference Serving

C1.justification: The central claims identifying LLD-driven collapse and stabilizing training through selective likelihood preservation remain. The abstract updates the proposed contribution from response-level to action-level gating and raises the headline relative-improvement claims from 37.8%/32.0% to 45.2%/37.1%.

C2.justification: v2 adds an explanation of how response-level gating can over- or under-penalize individual actions and interprets GSPO/Llama findings as evidence of broader applicability. Appendix D adds turn-level hidden rewards as a concrete future direction. The main OOD-feedback, shared-prefix, and early-warning interpretations are largely retained or relocated.

D1.justification: v1 largely delegates implementation details to Search-R1. v2 Appendix B.2.1 supplies vLLM settings, sampling parameters, learning rate, KL/clipping coefficients, training rollout count, batch sizes, four-H100 hardware, sequence budgets, and the adaptive answer-weight formula. v2 also adds code and model access links. These substantially expand reproducibility information.

E1.justification: Both versions train on NQ or NQ+Hotpot and evaluate the same seven QA datasets using the same Wikipedia retrieval corpus. NQ-only experiments remain in v2's appendix. Added model, optimizer, and tool-round analyses use the existing search-QA coverage.

E2.justification: v2 Tables 1–2 add ZeroSearch, StepSearch, CriticSearch, and Tree-GRPO comparisons; Table 1 also adds Search-R1-GSPO. CoT, IRCoT, and SFT rows present in v1 are removed. The retained PPO/GRPO comparisons therefore sit within a substantially revised comparator set.

E3.justification: The reported default regularization weight changes from 0.1 to 0.2, with 0.3 for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. v2 adds Llama3.2-3B and GSPO configurations. Figure 8 replaces the Qwen7B-Base regularization sweep with a Qwen3B-Instruct NQ+Hotpot study including weight 0.2 and a longer displayed training horizon. Newly disclosed implementation settings are separate from these explicit changes.

E4.justification: v2 expands the token/response ablation into a systematic comparison including action gating (Table 3), adds tool-context-round diagnostics (Figure 6) and correct-versus-incorrect likelihood analysis (Figure 9a), and revises the regularization-strength study. Successful reasoning examples are replaced, while the failure cases are retained. v1's separate pre-collapse diagnostic plot is omitted.

E5.justification: v2 Figure 9a explicitly reports mean likelihood curves with standard-deviation bands; v1's shaded training plots do not specify variability this way. Neither version supplies repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The new plot does not establish that additional independent runs were performed.

E6.justification: Many results are added or replaced: the 7B-Base NQ+Hotpot LLDS average changes from 0.462 to 0.480 under revised gating and weights; v2 adds GSPO+LLDS at 0.451 and Llama GRPO/LLDS/MA averages of 0.212/0.374/0.427. Some earlier NQ-only results disappear. These are not clean same-setting gains between versions. v2's claimed 45.2% improvement also conflicts with Table 1's 0.440 versus 0.312, which implies approximately 41.0%.

M1.justification: v1 gates LLDS on whole-response likelihood decreases; v2 makes action-level gating the default and retains the earlier formulation as LLDS(response). LLDS-MA also changes from excluding answer tokens to applying an adaptive answer-token weight, specified in Section 5.5 and Appendix B.2.1. These change the regularization procedure.

P1.justification: The paper is retitled and extensively rewritten across the introduction, preliminaries, mechanism discussion, methods, results, and conclusion. Section 5 is reorganized, detailed related work and practical guidelines move into appendices, and NQ-only results are consolidated there. This is substantial narrative restructuring.

P2.justification: The main text changes from one to two columns, with widespread figure resizing and rearrangement. Training curves change from a 2-by-2 grid to one row; v2 adds a mechanism schematic, tool-context plot, and variant/Llama tables, combines likelihood and tool-use diagnostics, and replaces successful-example panels.

R1.justification: Sections 2 and B.1 substantially expand positioning against training–inference mismatch explanations and dense-reward methods, discussing StepSearch, CriticSearch, and TreeGRPO supervision or rollout costs. v2 also adds GSPO and hidden-reward references and more explicitly distinguishes its tool-integrated analysis from earlier single-turn LLD work.

T1.justification: Appendix A.2 adds formal Definition A.3, specifying expected likelihood decay, a representation-similarity condition, and self-amplifying decay. This extends the earlier informal death-spiral definition. The action-level and trajectory-level theorems and their proof structure remain substantially unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation and reproducibility: Table 3 directly tests gating granularity, relevant dense-reward comparisons and GSPO/Llama experiments probe applicability, and Appendix B.2 supplies previously missing implementation details. These address important evidential and disclosure gaps in v1. Reporting inconsistencies temper the improvement, particularly the erroneous 45.2% headline and Section 6.2's stale 0.430 versus Table 1's 0.440. Nevertheless, the additional targeted evidence and documentation provide a substantial net quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LLD/LLDS research. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, proofs, and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial rewriting and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 reports original training analyses and benchmark experiments, including additional gating ablations, GSPO experiments, and Llama results in Appendix B.

before.justification: v1 reports original Qwen experiments, training-dynamics measurements, regularization ablations, and generated reasoning examples in Sections 5–6 and the appendices.

results.title: On Group Relative Policy Optimization Collapse in Agent Search: The Lazy Likelihood-Displacement

C1.justification: v1's abstract and introduction claim a first unified framework capturing adverse selection, moral hazard and reputation. v2 narrows the headline contribution to a controlled AI-only market testbed emphasizing adverse selection, reputation and skill-investment tradeoffs. This changes the claimed economic scope, beyond wording alone. A broad novelty assertion nevertheless remains in v2 Appendix A.2.

C2.justification: v2 treats macroeconomic relationships as directional sanity checks rather than sufficient market fidelity and explicitly rejects quantitative forecasting. It qualifies training responses as mechanism-dependent, distinguishes observational trace associations from causal evidence, and interprets prompt-control results as supporting the specific reasoning decomposition. The earlier explanation that planning adds little is removed, and applicability and manipulation risks receive substantive discussion.

D1.justification: v2 supplies substantially fuller implementation information: matching and reputation pseudocode, job-generation distributions, skill initialization and noise, benchmark-feedback mechanics, observation/action examples, control prompts and configuration tables (Appendices B–C). It clarifies that the prompted termination hazard does not terminate simulations. However, v1's detailed metric formulas and token-accounting explanation are not retained.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates proxy-task markets. v2 describes CipherTask and OrderingTask and mentions interactive execution, but provides no clearly identifiable experimental configurations or results for those tasks. Its population-size and mechanism sweeps otherwise retain proxy-market tasks. Whether evaluated task coverage actually expanded is therefore uncertain.

E2.justification: Beyond the retained CoT, ReAct and policy baselines, v2 evaluates structure-only SSA, knowledge-only SSA and four alternative reasoning scaffolds (Tables 18–19). Fixed/FIXPL corresponds to Specialist/SPEC, rather than an entirely new comparator, although its documented policy changes. Greedy also changes from no voluntary training to probabilistic training.

E3.justification: Reported baseline settings change from reputation window 10, forgetting factor 0.85, Gumbel temperature 0 and LLM temperature 0.5 to 5, 0.5, 0.01 and 0.2 where supported (v1 Appendix G; v2 Appendix C). Trace evaluation switches from GPT-5 to Claude-Sonnet-4 and introduces anonymization and quantitative human validation. New prompt controls and scalability studies add evaluation designs. These reporting changes do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v1 already contains price-sensitivity, demand-shift, recession and component-ablation analyses. v2 adds tests separating reasoning structure from domain knowledge, alternative scaffold controls, robustness across scoring/reputation/learning/matching mechanisms, and scalability analyses up to 128 agents (Appendices D.3, D.6–D.7). The existing component ablation is also substantively revised.

E5.justification: v2 adds run-level bootstrap 95% confidence intervals, repeated judge sampling, quantified human agreement, model-adjusted reward associations and explicit main-effects ANOVA. Reported repetition counts also change, but remain inconsistent: the SSA summary specifies 25 markets while Table 11 specifies 10 runs; macroeconomic validation specifies 20 runs versus 50 simulations elsewhere. These discrepancies prevent inferring a definite increase in executed runs.

E6.justification: Headline rewards such as SSA's 633.5 and CoT's 419.4 are retained, but v2 adds extensive control, robustness, adaptation and scalability results. The planning ablation changes from little or no benefit in v1 to a positive 0.027 main effect with p < 0.0001 in v2 Table 17. Tables 18–19 add scaffold rankings, and Table 20 reports SSA/CoT reward ratios of 1.22–2.05. v1's token-usage results disappear.

M1.justification: The SSA reasoning scaffold and bid/train market loop remain. v2 extends the specified framework with interactive cipher/ordering execution using persistent task memory and hint-based learning (Appendix B.5). Contract-specific shared instructions also replace v1's differing payment instructions for SSA and its baselines. These changes are localized extensions and corrections.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and substantial portions of the methods and experimental narrative are rewritten. Economic-forces discussion moves into the appendix, and the former separate appendices are reorganized into background, implementation, experiments and results, with a contents page. The main narrative now explicitly separates diagnostic associations, prompting interventions and controlled explanations.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column main layout, resizes and relocates retained figures, and moves trace examples and the ablation display into the appendix. Figure 8 replaces contribution boxplots with present/absent bars. Performance tables are rebuilt into economic and behavioral panels, and substantial configuration, robustness, control and scalability tables are added.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning around metacognition/calibration, opponent modeling, planning, LLM economic actors and emerging agent marketplaces (Appendices A.1 and A.4). New connections include human-capital theory, Bayesian games and agent-economy infrastructure. The introduction also shifts from broad first-framework claims toward a more specifically situated economic testbed.

T1.justification: The formal objective changes from infinite-horizon discounted return in v1 Section 3.1 and Appendix E.5 to finite-horizon undiscounted cumulative reward in v2 Appendix B.3.7. This revises the stated horizon and discount assumptions, although both versions primarily evaluate fixed-length episodes. The underlying CES and Bayesian reputation framework remains, without new theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important evidential gaps through targeted prompt controls (Tables 18–19), mechanism robustness tests (Tables 12–13) and human validation of trace scoring (Appendix C.5). Fuller implementation documentation and narrower simulation claims also improve interpretability. Conflicting SSA run counts and prompt-control horizons—100 rounds in Appendix D.6 versus 50 in Table 18—remain material reproducibility flaws. Nevertheless, the added controlled evidence substantially strengthens support for the paper's central conclusions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AI-Work/SSA research, with matching authors, market framework and retained experiments despite the changed title. Text, equations, figures, tables and all appendices are readable and support comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds prompt-control experiments, mechanism robustness tests, scalability results and quantitative human validation of trace scoring.

before.justification: v1 reports original market simulations, LLM comparisons, SSA prompting experiments, capability ablations and trace–reward analyses in Sections 4–5 and the appendices.

results.title: When AI Agents Compete for Jobs: Strategic Capabilities and Economic Dynamics of AI Labour Markets

C1.justification: The central embedding and agent/group monitoring contributions remain. Section 4 additionally makes identification of aggregate causal effects through query design and natural experiments an explicit framework-level conclusion. Since v1 already argued for a causal interpretation of its pandemic findings, this is a limited extension.

C2.justification: v2 distinguishes detecting behavioral change from identifying its responsible component and explicitly discusses inflated false-positive rates in the retained real-data analysis. It adds interpretations of signal concentration and pipeline sensitivity, explains the latent interactions behind tweet histories, and distinguishes expected stateful drift from anomalous or consequential change.

D1.justification: v2 adds a repository link advertised as providing code, data, and replication scripts, and specifies cosine similarity as the existing retrieval criterion. It also documents new simulation parameters and embedding-model names, dimensions, and sources. The original prompts, hardware, and generation-time disclosures remain.

E1.justification: Appendices A.3.2 and B.1.2 add synthetic scenarios where temporal change affects only a subset of queries, extending evaluation from broadly distributed changes to sparse behavioral shifts. The real population, three query topics, and 2018–2024 coverage remain unchanged.

E2.justification: Figure 3 adds TDKPS-C to the comparisons, while its agent-count panel removes the oracle and DCorr curves shown in v1. Appendix D.3 introduces a random-tweet retrieval baseline. The existing group-level comparator set remains unchanged.

E3.justification: Added experiments introduce null-versus-alternative calibration comparisons, sparse-query designs with fixed or increasing total signal, and 200-permutation testing protocols. Appendix D evaluates four embedding configurations and retrieval depths of one to three tweets using rank agreement and retrieval-similarity measurements. These substantially expand evaluation design without establishing revisions to the original experiments' settings.

E4.justification: v2 adds calibration-versus-power analyses, separates signal sparsity from total signal strength, tests embedding-model and retrieval-depth sensitivity, evaluates retrieval against random tweets, and presents a query–tweet–response case study. These address several methodological and application-level questions absent from v1.

E5.justification: Beyond v1's trial counts and confidence bands, v2 reports standard errors from 100 Monte Carlo trials for calibration and 50 trials for sparsity (Tables 1–3). Retrieval quality also gains median and interquartile summaries. These are reporting additions for new analyses, not evidence of increased runs for the original experiments.

E6.justification: Figure 3 and Tables 1–3 add calibrated-test outcomes and sparse-signal findings. Tables 5–7 report embedding agreement of 0.992–0.998, retrieval-depth agreement of 0.812–0.874, and retrieval-quality differences. Figure 6B also changes existing results: Democrats' correlation changes from K=0.43, p=0.043 to K=0.51, p=0.017. The accompanying text retains the earlier values, creating an inconsistency.

M1.justification: Appendix B.1.1 adds TDKPS-C, which splits response replicates into independent basis-estimation and testing subsets and permutes only the testing subset. This is a genuine but localized procedural extension; the joint embedding framework and paired-energy group test remain unchanged.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized terminology and wording edits, expands the application explanation and discussion, and adds an Impact Statement and appendix subsections. Most existing prose and the overall narrative order remain; scientific additions account for much of the document's growth.

P2.justification: Seven new tables introduce calibration, sparsity, configuration, correlation, and retrieval-quality displays. Figure 3 is redrawn with calibrated-test curves, an expanded legend, and altered proportions. Figure 6 changes labels and its caption and removes numerical vertical-axis ticks from panel C. The other principal figures are retained.

R1.justification: Appendices A.3 and A.4 replace the Zhu and Ghodsi (2019) citation with the already cited 2006 scree-plot paper, and the separate 2019 reference disappears. The broader related-work positioning is retained; other reference changes primarily correct bibliographic metadata.

T1.justification: The embedding objective, original hypotheses and test formulas, SNR arguments, and complexity derivations are retained. The sample-splitting extension reuses the distance statistic and permutation p-value formula; its calibration explanation is qualitative. Formal error guarantees remain future work.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's acknowledged false-positive inflation by implementing and evaluating a calibrated alternative. Table 1 demonstrates near-nominal rejection rates with an explicit power tradeoff, while the new robustness analyses strengthen the evidence supporting the pipeline. These gains outweigh the reporting inconsistency introduced between Figure 6 and its text. Calibration still costs power, and the retained real-data analysis remains uncalibrated; the improvement does not establish general error guarantees or causal identification.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TDKPS research, with matching authors, framework, simulations, and digital-congressperson application. Their text, equations, figures, and appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical investigations and adds calibrated-test, signal-sparsity, embedding-model, retrieval-depth, and retrieval-quality results.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulation results on power and false-positive rates, plus analyses of 99 digital congresspersons across 14 timepoints (Figures 3–6).

results.title: Detecting Perspective Shifts in Multi-Agent Systems

C1.justification: The central claims about learning diffusion bridges through self-consistency without differentiating through trajectories remain. V2 adds an explicit contribution in the abstract and introduction concerning extension to general stochastic optimal control, developing what v1 discussed briefly in Appendix B.5. Stronger performance adjectives alone do not constitute a separate claim change.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations of dimensional scaling and SC2 as a more damped objective, and explicitly discusses possible fixed-point instability relative to NGDB. The molecular discussion adds substantive boundaries: single-mode paths, overdamped versus underdamped differences, and sensitivity of energy assessment to smoothing. These extend v1's existing ellipticity, simulation-cost and Jacobian-growth discussion.

D1.justification: V2 newly identifies JAX and NGDB's Brownian auxiliary process, and documents extensive molecular implementation details: AMBER14, OpenMM/DMFF, endpoint alignment, discretisation, guiding-drift modifications, training updates and hardware. Appendix G adds asset and license links for BEL, TPS-DPS, OpenMM and DMFF. These improve documentation without establishing that the retained experiments changed implementation.

E1.justification: V2 retains the original benchmark coverage and adds a Müller–Brown potential augmented with quadratic coordinates to 100 dimensions, plus transitions between C5 and C7ax conformations of the 22-atom alanine-dipeptide molecule. This substantially extends the evaluated input conditions and adds a real molecular system.

E2.justification: V2 adds evaluated BEL comparisons across the standard bridge problems and a guided-proposal MCMC reference for cell diffusion (Table 1, Figure 6 and Appendix E.4). Table 5 also adds published PIPS and TPS-DPS reference values, explicitly under different, underdamped dynamics. NGDB, SDB, FB and Doob's Lagrangian comparisons from v1 remain.

E3.justification: The added experiments introduce substantial protocols. The 100-dimensional test uses a larger network and 8,000 training steps, evaluating metrics only on the first two coordinates. Alanine uses 30,000 discretisation steps over 0.1 ps, different training budgets and hardware for CCDB and NGDB, and constrained/smoothed energy evaluation. The new drift-interpolation ablation also specifies its own learning rate and training budget; these are not revisions to all retained benchmarks.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained weighting-schedule and STL ablations, Appendix E.9 adds quantitative comparisons of general versus gradient-form neural parameterisations. Appendix E.10 tests intermediate auxiliary drifts across double-well barrier heights. The augmented Müller–Brown experiment additionally probes sensitivity to ambient dimensionality. These provide substantial new evidence about parameterisation, stability and scaling.

E5.justification: Matched quantitative comparisons retain mean and standard deviation over five runs, and the new ablation tables follow the same convention. No increase in repeated runs, new seed-reporting practice, confidence intervals or significance-testing procedure is established.

E6.justification: Most matched benchmark values remain unchanged, including the original Table 1 rows and two-dimensional Müller–Brown results. V2 adds BEL scores, further runtimes, molecular and 100-dimensional results, and new ablation entries. It also corrects the average-schedule double-well entry from 0.150±0.078 in v1 Table 3 to 0.148±0.073 in v2 Table 6. Results from the added settings do not establish same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The fixed-point bridge learner, backward target recursion, weighting schedules and STL adjustments are retained; SC1/SC2 largely correspond to v1's existing auxiliary-drift choices. For alanine, v2 introduces limited procedural adaptations: including the base drift, scaling and clipping the Brownian guide, and performing multiple gradient updates per simulated batch (Appendix E.6).

P1.justification: V2 extensively rewrites and expands the main explanation, separates loss construction from bridge parameterisation, and brings derivations, auxiliary-drift discussion and benchmark descriptions forward from the appendices. The appendices are reorganised into separate method, generalisation, proof, experiment and SOC sections. CCDB and SC1/SC2 terminology replaces much of the earlier naming.

P2.justification: The main text changes to two-column layout, and figures and tables are substantially reorganised. Table 1 moves into the main text and gains performance markers; the cell plots become an expanded comparator grid. New molecular panels, a SOC relationship diagram, and runtime and ablation tables appear. Existing figures are also merged, relocated or replaced, rather than all representing new scientific content.

R1.justification: The diffusion-bridge positioning is retained, while Appendix F substantially develops the relationship to adjoint matching, SOCM and unweighted SOCM. V2 also incorporates molecular transition-path research and newer adjoint-sampling work, including Holdijk, Seong, Havens, Liu and Choi. This broadens the substantive research context beyond a limited citation update.

T1.justification: V2 adds a broader matrix-based self-consistency relation in Appendix D.3 and formal SOC extensions with nonzero running costs, including Theorems F.1–F.2 and reparameterisation derivations. V1 Appendix B.5 only outlined these connections. V2 also corrects the OU control formula (v1 Equation 36; v2 Equation 78). The new SOC appendix contains an internal inconsistency: its positive-gradient terminal condition conflicts with its exp(-g) convention.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens evaluation of the retained method: BEL and guided-MCMC comparisons broaden validation, while parameterisation and auxiliary-drift ablations test stability claims that v1 supported less directly. Fuller runtime evidence, implementation details and explicit molecular limitations improve assessability. The gains are qualified by the restricted 100-dimensional evaluation, differing molecular comparison conditions, and the terminal-cost sign inconsistency in Appendix F. Nevertheless, the stronger comparative and diagnostic evidence, together with clearer exposition, provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Control Consistency Losses for Diffusion Bridges by the same authors. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial restructuring.

after.justification: V2 retains these original experiments and adds further comparisons, ablations, a 100-dimensional Müller–Brown experiment and alanine-dipeptide simulations. These original results are distinguishable from the borrowed reference values in Table 5.

before.justification: V1 reports original simulations and quantitative comparisons for Ornstein–Uhlenbeck, CIR, double-well, cell-diffusion and Müller–Brown bridges, including ablations in Appendix C.

results.title: Control Consistency Losses for Diffusion Bridges

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions, and conclusion retain the same central claims: RAD supplies diverse rationales, P2CL enables discrimination and correction, MCA aligns rationale representations, and MIND achieves strong benchmark performance. The shortened abstract and additional supporting experiments do not redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning unseen-error robustness, transfer across backbones and datasets, the suitability of margin loss over InfoNCE, and gains beyond stronger visual modules. New Appendix D qualifies applicability through RAD preparation costs, VQA-focused validation, fine-grained perceptual failures, and dependence on original rationale quality.

D1.justification: v2 explicitly identifies the caption generator as frozen, clarifies RAD prompt placeholders, and documents generator and judge identities for added evaluations. It also explicitly advertises data and code at the existing project link. Original T5 hyperparameters and hardware disclosures remain substantially unchanged.

E1.justification: The three datasets remain, but v2 substantially expands evaluation scenarios: Table 9 tests six injected reasoning-error conditions, including five unseen types, and Table 10 adds M3CoT-to-ScienceQA transfer. These introduce interference and distribution-shift conditions beyond the original evaluations.

E2.justification: ScienceQA Table 1 adds VaLiK and MemVerse, each with two model variants. New analyses also include untuned Qwen controls and InfoNCE alternatives. The original benchmark comparator sets are otherwise retained.

E3.justification: Added protocols include randomly sampling 100 examples per dataset for perturbations, evaluating 7B–9B Qwen backbones and cross-dataset transfer, and scoring rationales with Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B across four dimensions. Table 14 controls visual encoders and caption generators. These supplement rather than replace the original T5 settings.

E4.justification: v2 adds systematic interference robustness, backbone compatibility, cross-dataset generalization, quantitative rationale assessment, InfoNCE temperature comparisons, and matched visual/caption controls. Earlier component ablations, hyperparameter sweeps, and qualitative cases remain; their appendix renumbering is not new analysis.

E5.justification: Section 4.2 newly discloses a fixed training seed of 42. This does not establish additional runs. Neither version reports multi-seed uncertainty estimates or significance tests for MIND.

E6.justification: Existing MIND benchmark scores and ablations remain unchanged, including 92.29% on ScienceQA and 57.38% for MINDbase on M3CoT. Tables 9–11 and 13–14 add substantial results, including Qwen-based M3CoT accuracies of 85.85–88.65% and matched-module advantages of 3.82–4.50 percentage points. These are new experimental results, not increases in the original scores.

M1.justification: RAD generation, the two P2CL stages, and MCA retain their procedures and objectives. Applying MIND to Qwen backbones does not document a new method component. The Equation 7 correction aligns the formula with the negative-mining procedure already described in v1.

P1.justification: The abstract is condensed, grammar and affiliations are edited, and prompt templates move from Section 3.2 to Appendix A. Discussion and appendix headings are expanded and reorganized, but most existing prose and the main narrative order remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a different conference layout with running headers, revised front matter, and reformatted tables. Appendix prose changes to full-width layout, enlarging the retained ablation table and hyperparameter figure. Five new tables are added, while earlier qualitative figures are retained and renumbered.

R1.justification: v2 adds the cited VaLiK and MemVerse works associated with the new ScienceQA comparisons. The prompt-based versus learning-based related-work organization and principal novelty positioning remain unchanged. Most bibliography edits concern citation style and venue formatting.

T1.justification: Equation 7 corrects hard-negative selection: v1 incorrectly applies Top-k to positive similarities, whereas v2 uses negative similarities. This repairs the mathematical definition to match the existing prose. Other definitions and objectives remain unchanged; no new proofs are introduced.

improvement.justification: Table 14 reduces an important confound in v1’s headline comparisons by matching visual encoders and caption generators while retaining 3.82–4.50-point advantages. New robustness and transfer experiments directly strengthen evidence for the framework’s central correction and generalization claims. Quantitative rationale assessment, the equation correction, and explicit limitations further improve the paper. Single-seed reporting and limited implementation detail for new experiments remain weaknesses, but the overall evidential improvement is substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MIND framework. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite reformatting and added experiments.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds perturbation, model-transfer, cross-dataset, rationale-quality, loss-comparison, and controlled baseline experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original MIND evaluations on ScienceQA, A-OKVQA, and M3CoT, including component ablations, sensitivity experiments, and qualitative reasoning cases.

results.title: MIND: Multi-rationale INtegrated Discriminative Reasoning Framework for Multi-modal Large Models

C1.justification: The central simulator, dataset, one-to-many tutor, and relative-performance claims persist. v2 recasts the contribution around Theory-of-Mind-based alignment and adds a concrete claim of sub-five-second latency with up to ten students, extending its practical scalability claim.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations of reward hacking, safeguards, error remediation, and possible rubric transfer beyond medicine. New limitations address simulation realism, static-image-only perception, unmeasured long-term learning, and increasing latency, while explicitly restricting applicability to educational simulation.

D1.justification: A new reproducibility statement documents a commitment to release the full code and dataset. The setup explicitly identifies LLaVA as another backbone, whose variant already appeared in v1. Training hyperparameters, hardware, durations, and operational prompts are otherwise retained; the release commitment does not establish actual availability.

E1.justification: The existing clinical and VQA benchmarks remain. v2 adds controlled scenarios involving factual errors, premature diagnostic closure, and safety or ethical risks, and explicitly broadens human participants from undergraduates to a cohort spanning junior students through senior interns.

E2.justification: Matched experiments retain their comparator sets, and new analyses reuse existing tutor baselines. The setup's o1-to-o3 edit matches o3 already reported in v1's tables. Gemini 3 Pro and GPT-5 are additional judges, not competing tutors.

E3.justification: Expert evaluation expands from 50 to 100 dialogues, and the user study from three to 200 participants. New protocols re-score 100 cases using three judges and manually evaluate immediate next-turn error correction across 300 cases with four-student groups. Existing training settings and benchmark splits remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds judge-sensitivity testing, controlled misconception-correction experiments, and analysis of reward-hacking behaviors and veto activation during training. These address evaluator dependence and remediation effectiveness beyond the retained component ablations, student-model robustness tests, and scalability analysis.

E5.justification: Section 5.3 newly reports statistical significance against the strongest expert-evaluation baseline at p < 0.05, without specifying the test. Three-run means and standard deviations, and the reported agreement value of 0.79, were already present in v1.

E6.justification: Table 4 replaces human ratings under expanded samples, including the tutor's reported expert average changing from 8.64 to 8.73; this is not a same-setting gain. New results include cross-judge scores, 88.50% correction success versus GPT-4o's 81.53%, and declining veto activation. Main benchmark, ablation, and existing robustness scores remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The structured thinking tags, agent interaction and review procedures, SFT followed by GRPO, and three-axis reward with a safety veto are retained. The Theory-of-Mind terminology and reward-hacking discussion do not establish a new method component; corresponding appendix prompts remain substantively unchanged.

P1.justification: The title and tutor name change, the abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten, and method descriptions are compressed. Related work is reordered and revised, while reproducibility, ethics, limitations, and additional appendix sections reorganize the narrative. Most existing appendix prompts receive only punctuation edits.

P2.justification: The new opening Figure 1 combines alignment schematics with a redrawn version of the earlier scalability plot. v2 adds the judge-comparison table and error-correction chart, moves Algorithm 1 into the appendix, and rearranges existing displays. Most established figures and table structures are retained.

R1.justification: The research positioning shifts substantially toward limitations of dyadic alignment, pluralistic objectives, Theory of Mind, and context dilution. New references include Ouyang et al., Sorensen et al., and Rabinowitz et al.; related-work discussions sharpen distinctions from single-student, non-clinical tutoring systems.

T1.justification: The reward, veto, and GRPO equations are retained, with no new formal assumptions, derivations, or proofs. The added correction-success measure applies the standard corrected/total success-rate formula as an empirical evaluation metric.

improvement.justification: The broader human evaluation, independent-judge checks, and controlled misconception tests substantially address v1's weak real-user validation and limited testing of evaluator dependence and correction effectiveness. Explicit limitations also improve claim calibration. These gains outweigh reporting shortcomings: Figure 5 remains unchanged despite revised Table 4 scores, and the new significance and latency claims lack supporting test or timing details.

A1.justification: Both complete PDFs describe the same ClinEdu simulator, ClinTeach dataset, and tutor, renamed from MedTutor-R1 to ClinTutor-R1. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical evaluations and reports expanded human studies, judge-robustness results, and controlled error-correction experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulation and medical VQA evaluations, ablations, scalability tests, expert ratings, and a real-user study.

results.title: ClinTutor-R1: Advancing Scalable and Robust One-to-Many Alignment in Clinical Socratic Education

C1.justification: The central collapse diagnosis and ACE contribution remain. v2 qualifies the earlier claim of predicting collapse exactly as a sharp sufficient criterion with an ambiguous zero boundary, and states the constructive guarantee up to the final sampling timestep. The headline synthetic error-reduction claim changes from over 5× to approximately 4×.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly distinguishes endpoint Bayesian factorization from intermediate transport paths, attributes schedule-alignment failures to nonuniform temporal evolution, and interprets the new guidance controls as evidence for validity-preserving correction. It adds ACE-lite's speed-versus-bias tradeoff and clarifies that ACE cannot repair inaccurate or semantically misaligned experts.

D1.justification: v2 adds project/code access information and a reproducibility statement. It documents molecular atom-count/type restrictions, pretrained-model data provenance, bond reconstruction, guidance-specific B2 values, baseline settings, and fragment-linking implementation. Hardware and memory disclosures are also revised. Newly documented details do not establish that every underlying procedure changed.

E1.justification: v2 adds actual pocket-conditioned fragment-linking evaluation on 66 fragment pairs; v1 only formulated this task and left empirical validation to future work. Scaffold evaluation replaces the deliberately weak-binding and model-generated CrossDock subsets with eligible CrossDocked test ligands. Checkerboard and COCO-MIG task coverage remains.

E2.justification: DiffDec disappears from the scaffold comparison, while Delete and AutoFragDiff remain. v2 adds evaluated heuristic time-varying guidance schedules, the schedule-aligned FKC-TRP comparator, and FFLOM for fragment linking (Appendices C.3, E.6, and E.2). These substantially expand the alternatives tested.

E3.justification: Appendix C.2 changes molecular evaluation to 76 eligible test pairs and batch size 5 instead of 10. It adds QED, SA, and Lipinski metrics and revises docking aggregation, replacing standalone validity reporting. New parameter-grid and alignment protocols are specified. Image-runtime evaluation now reports A100 hardware for ACE/FKC instead of A6000.

E4.justification: v2 adds joint B1/B2 sensitivity grids, heuristic guidance-schedule controls, schedule-alignment analysis, and ACE-lite efficiency/performance comparisons. These test correction strength, whether time variation alone suffices, and resampling tradeoffs. The earlier ESS and single-bump analyses are retained, partly relocated, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: v2 adds molecular docking standard deviations across generated molecules and specifies three seeds for new scaffold-schedule comparisons and one for fragment linking. The main scaffold description omits v1's explicit two-seed averaging statement; this does not establish a reduction in runs. Five-seed synthetic uncertainty reporting remains.

E6.justification: Molecular Tables 3–4 are replaced: ACE at guidance 1.4 reports mean Vina −7.10 on v2's test cohort, versus −5.37 on v1's CrossDock-Weak cohort, which is not a comparable-setting gain. v2 adds fragment-linking, alignment, sensitivity, and ACE-lite results and revises image runtime/memory values. Original checkerboard Table 2 survives as Table C.2; COCO-MIG accuracy values remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The weighted Feynman–Kac sampler and Algorithms 1–2 remain essentially unchanged. v2 extends the quadratic bump with a piecewise-linear component, specifies corrections across covering coordinate subsets, and introduces ACE-lite without resampling. These are procedural extensions within the retained ACE framework.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method narrative, and discussion are extensively rewritten. v2 introduces a three-step method overview, a standalone related-work section, scope/limitations discussion, and reproducibility and impact statements. Appendix organization and author information also change, beyond simple renumbering.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column main layout, redraws the overview, replaces the main molecular illustration, restructures molecular tables, and adds parameter-grid, guidance-comparison, and runtime displays. Existing material is also relocated: v1 Figure 6 becomes Figure C.4, while the concentration illustration moves from the appendix into the main text.

R1.justification: Section 5 and Appendix D substantially expand positioning against prior time-dependent guidance, including Wang et al. (2024b) and Jin et al. (2026), distinguishing path-validity correction from empirical guidance schedules. Additional discussion covers time reparameterization, discrete/RL steering, and fragment-linking research. Bibliographic updates to retained works are separate presentation changes.

T1.justification: v2 adds the zero-criterion boundary counterexample, an explicit finite-score/wrong-endpoint example, and a partial-support correction corollary. It reformulates the bump theorem around a truncated sampling horizon and revises Proposition E.1's tail bounds and proof. The concentration result already existed in v1; its revision, rather than promotion into the main text, constitutes theoretical change.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens v1's limited molecular validation through a broader test cohort, actual fragment-linking experiments, and controls comparing alternative guidance and schedule alignment. Boundary-case analysis, the revised tail proof, and implementation/code disclosures improve rigor and reproducibility. These gains outweigh removal of DiffDec and standalone validity reporting, although single-seed fragment evaluation, incomplete main molecular seed reporting, and some text/table inconsistencies remain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ACE diffusion-steering work. Their complete main texts and appendices A–F are readable, and equations, tables, figures, and relocated material can be reliably matched.

after.justification: v2 reports original synthetic, scaffold-decoration, fragment-linking, and image-generation results, alongside additional sensitivity and comparison experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original checkerboard simulations, molecular scaffold-decoration experiments, and COCO-MIG image-generation results, including appendix experiments.

results.title: On the Collapse of Generative Paths: A Criterion and Correction for Diffusion Steering

C1.justification: The introduction qualifies the novelty claim as, to the authors' knowledge, the first end-to-end real-time streaming talking-head diffusion method on a single GPU. Contributions and conclusion now foreground information-theoretic alignment and kinematic constraints for ASD. The central streaming, speed and quality claims remain.

C2.justification: V2 substantially expands the mechanism explanation through mutual-information alignment and frequency-sensitive smoothness regularization. Appendix D interprets the new examples as evidence of stylistic and acoustic generalization. Appendix E adds previously absent concrete limitations: motion blur during rapid head movements and unclear dental details, attributed to training data and aggressive VAE compression.

D1.justification: Appendices A-C disclose extensive preprocessing, architecture, initialization and training details, including hierarchical Whisper features, cache dimensions, noise scheduling, dropout rates, loss temperature and weights, gradient accumulation, memory usage and approximately 400 GPU hours. Identity-disjoint splitting is newly specified, and Appendix F describes research-only access. These substantially expand reproducibility information without establishing that every disclosed component is newly introduced.

E1.justification: HDTF and MEAD remain the training and quantitative evaluation datasets. Appendix D adds limited qualitative coverage of stylized portraits and cross-actor driving, including cinematic speech with background noise and speech with natural reverberation.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains FantasyTalking, Hallo, EchoMimic, Sonic, AniPortrait, Ditto and AniTalker. Figure 4 retains its existing comparator subset. Appendix D introduces no new competing method; Full ASD and w/o ASD were already evaluated in Table 3.

E3.justification: Section 4.1 changes the reported student training length from 121 to 97 frames. Sections 4.3-4.4 change ablation and case-study length descriptions from 120 to 121 frames. Appendix D adds qualitative comparisons with fixed portrait/audio inputs and matched training settings. The main benchmark metrics, 121-frame evaluation and eight-step sampling remain; rerunning is not established.

E4.justification: Appendix D.1 adds a qualitative Full ASD versus w/o ASD comparison examining degradation on a stylized portrait. Appendix D.2 adds visual generalization checks across portrait styles and acoustic conditions. These supplement the retained caching and distillation ablations with a limited set of qualitative analyses.

E5.justification: Appendix C.6.3 newly discloses sharing a random seed between teacher and student to generate matched Gaussian noise. This adds seed-handling information only: neither version reports independent-run counts, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests.

E6.justification: REST's reported runtime changes from 4.421 to 4.416 seconds in Table 1 and Figure 4. Table 3 changes w/o Contrastive FVD from 211.881 to 219.881, reversing its ordering against Full ASD at 219.870. Figures 8-10 add qualitative outputs. Other benchmark scores remain unchanged; the revisions do not establish a same-setting performance improvement.

M1.justification: The architecture and caching/distillation framework remain. However, Eq. 21 now includes the positive pair in the contrastive denominator; Eq. 23 replaces a signed difference sum with mean squared teacher-student second-difference matching; and Eq. 24 introduces weights, specified as 0.2 each. Algorithm 1 also corrects chunk, timestep and cache indexing. These revise the documented procedure without establishing that the implementation or experiments were rerun.

P1.justification: V2 revises the abstract, contribution list and portions of the methods and conclusion, consistently introducing semi-autoregressive terminology. Extensive explanations of existing components are organized into cross-referenced appendices covering datasets, architecture, training, qualitative analysis, limitations and ethics. This substantially expands the document's explanatory structure.

P2.justification: Figures 5-7 add attention-pattern, SpeechAE and A2V-DiT diagrams. Figures 8-10 add an ASD ablation display and cross-actor generated-frame grids. These substantially expand the visual explanation and evidence; the original benchmark tables and Figures 1-4 largely retain their layouts.

R1.justification: The principal THG positioning remains, with MultiTalk added to Section 2.2. New references connect ASD to contrastive predictive coding and mutual-information bounds, while others document preprocessing and architectural components. The novelty positioning is also qualified by the single-GPU condition.

T1.justification: Appendices C.1-C.3 introduce substantial formal analysis absent from v1: mutual-information invariance, an InfoNCE lower-bound derivation, velocity/content smoothness equivalence, the spectral penalty 16 sin^4(omega/2), and loss-complementarity arguments. These add assumptions, theorems and proofs beyond the revised main-text loss equations.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially reduces v1's implementation ambiguity through detailed preprocessing, architecture and training disclosures, and repairs loss equations that did not match their stated teacher-student purpose. Additional qualitative checks and specific limitations improve assessability. The new theory is less conclusive than its wording suggests: Theorem C.2 assumes independent marginal negatives, whereas implementation uses same-sequence frames. Despite this qualification, the gains in methodological specification and transparency are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe REST and contain readable text, equations, tables and figures supporting comparison. V1 ends after its references; v2 additionally contains appendices A-G, which were included in the comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains the original quantitative experiments and adds qualitative ASD ablation and cross-actor generalization results in Appendix D.

before.justification: Section 4 reports original HDTF and MEAD experiments, component ablations and generated examples in Tables 1-3 and Figures 3-4.

results.title: REST: Diffusion-based Real-time End-to-end Streaming Talking Head Generation via ID-Context Caching and Asynchronous Streaming Distillation

C1.justification: The abstract and three principal contribution themes are retained. The contribution list and conclusion now explicitly qualify the transfer between softmax and linear attention as applying to centered Gaussian inputs, refining the earlier Gaussian-input wording.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive discussion of why explicit convergence rates require further problem-specific assumptions, interprets structured initialization as mainly technical, and discusses extension to singular covariances. Appendix A interprets anisotropy as making optimization harder and potentially requiring longer prompts, substantially expanding the applicability and limitations discussion.

D1.justification: Appendix A newly documents data generation, training hyperparameters, PyTorch initialization, comparator normalization, and implementation provenance. It reports a public code repository, laptop execution, and approximately 30 minutes per architecture/prompt-length run; v1 contains no corresponding experimental reproducibility information.

E1.justification: v1 studies regression distributions theoretically but performs no empirical evaluation. v2 evaluates synthetic noisy in-context linear regression with both isotropic Gaussian covariates and anisotropic covariates having covariance entries 0.5^|i-j|.

E2.justification: v2 establishes empirical comparisons absent from v1: normalized linear attention is compared with softmax attention, and Figures 2 and 6 additionally evaluate the L-Bayes-optimal estimator, described as appropriately tuned ridge regression.

E3.justification: The new experiments introduce concrete training and evaluation protocols: dimension 5, SGD with learning rate 0.001, 500,000 steps, batches of 128 prompts, and prompt-length sweeps. Measurements include output/gradient discrepancies, prediction risk at matched training and evaluation lengths, and distances between training trajectories.

E4.justification: v2 adds prompt-length sensitivity analyses of attention outputs, gradients, and parameter trajectories.
