V2 evaluates AME, APE, and policy paths using a three-dimensional Gaussian design, high-dimensional Gaussian and mixture designs, and stochastic treatment interventions. Appendix Q additionally analyzes monetary-policy shifts and equity returns using financial and macroeconomic data.

E2.justification: Riesz regression changes from cited methodology in v1 to an evaluated baseline in v2 Tables 2, 3, 6, and 7. Table 8 compares Time-SMR with and without joint training. Appendix Q describes a financial-data Riesz comparison, but its reported table and plotted results do not establish that comparison.

E3.justification: V2 introduces empirical protocols absent from v1: two-fold cross-fitting, common outcome-regression architectures, population Monte Carlo truths, and bias, MSE, and coverage metrics. Appendix Q adds monthly preprocessing, full-sample nuisance estimation without splitting, specified policy-shift grids, and horizons from one to twelve months.

E4.justification: V1 contains no empirical ablations or robustness analyses. V2 examines stability under high-dimensional sparse and multimodal dense designs, directly tests joint training in Appendix P.3, and compares estimated policy paths with their local linear approximation. These additions investigate component effects and failure behavior.

E5.justification: V2 introduces reporting across 200 simulation trials, empirical coverage of 95% intervals, and pointwise policy-path confidence bands. Appendix Q specifies Newey–West HAC standard errors and pointwise intervals without multiplicity adjustment. V1 contains no corresponding empirical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: V2 adds all empirical results. Tables 2–3 report Data-SMR/Time-SMR/Riesz MSEs of 0.161/0.637/10.076 for AME and 0.486/1.117/74.918 for APE. Tables 6–8 add different performance tradeoffs and ablation outcomes; Appendix Q adds horizon-dependent financial estimates. These are newly reported results, not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: V1 already contains denoising and time-score estimators. V2 adds joint data/time-score training, ratio calibration and clipping, and a cross-fitted policy-path estimator using known pushforward maps. It also corrects the stated time-derivative procedure: v1 differentiates through bridge samples, whereas v2 explicitly holds the sampled input fixed.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and methodological narrative are extensively rewritten around Data-SMR, Time-SMR, and policy paths. Existing ATE material moves to Appendix E, infinitesimal-classification discussion to Appendix M.1, and the Bregman proof to Appendix H. The reorganization is substantial beyond the addition of scientific content.

P2.justification: V2 introduces applicability and results tables, error boxplots, policy-path panels, and algorithm boxes absent from v1. These substantially change the presentation of the method and evidence. Some additions are defective: Figure 5 contains only a caption, and Table 9 extends beyond the page's right edge.

R1.justification: The introduction and new Appendix A substantially expand positioning across semiparametric efficiency, covariate balancing, score matching, and policy/local-projection analysis. Added references include Hyvarinen, Vincent, Oko et al., and Jorda, supporting relationships and theoretical claims beyond v1's shorter DRE-centered discussion.

T1.justification: V2 adds formal policy-path and pushforward constructions, conditional score-estimation rates, proofs, downstream error bounds, and smoothing-bias/DML conditions in Sections 7–8 and Appendices G–L. The earlier Bregman proof is retained in Appendix H. However, Theorem 6.1's endpoint sum conflicts with that signed proof, and Appendix E.2 reverses the control-ratio integration direction relative to v1.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses v1's unsupported empirical stability claims through comparisons that also reveal undercoverage and failure cases. It replaces the loose AME–APE connection with a defined policy-path construction and applicability conditions, while adding conditional theory and implementation guidance. These are substantial gains in evidence and precision. New formula inconsistencies in Theorem 6.1 and Appendix E.2, incomplete experimental specifications, and unfinished appendix displays temper the improvement but do not outweigh those gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ScoreMatchingRiesz work, with retained methods and proofs traceable across reorganization. All pages and appendices support comparison. V2 has display defects, including a caption-only Figure 5 and overflowing Table 9, but the table's embedded numerical text remains recoverable.

after.justification: V2 reports original simulations in Section 9 and Appendix P, including a joint-training ablation, and financial time-series estimates in Appendix Q, Table 9, and Figures 6–8.

before.justification: V1 presents methodological constructions, mathematical arguments, and a Bregman-objective proof in Appendix A, but no original experimental or data-analysis outcomes.

results.title: ScoreMatchingRiesz: Score Matching for Debiased Machine Learning and Policy Path Estimation

C1.justification: The central contributions remain the 500-prompt benchmark, unified objective and judge-based evaluation, and diagnosis of persistent realism and alignment failures. Evaluating 15 rather than 11 systems expands support without redefining these headline scientific claims.

C2.justification: v2 substantially qualifies and expands interpretation: closed-source superiority becomes dimension-dependent, audio failures involve semantic matching and temporal control as well as physical grounding, and causal attribution is explicitly restrained. It adds limitations concerning proprietary-judge version drift, cautions against relying on aggregate rankings, and discusses judge weaknesses revealed by calibration.

D1.justification: Appendix E.1 newly documents score normalization, hierarchical IF aggregation, and the NonSpeech penalty and default. Section 3.1 adds curation counts and rewriting statistics. These clarify existing procedures; generation resolutions, judge decoding, frame sampling, synchronization settings, prompt templates, and code/data destinations are retained.

E1.justification: The 500-prompt suite, comprising 400 rewritten and 100 video-inverted prompts, retains its domains and tasks. The new human studies use validation subsets, and the real-video calibration concerns reference material already described in v1 Appendix F.2; these do not establish new dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: Tables 2–3 expand from 11 to 15 systems by adding LTX-2, HunyuanVideo1.5 + Hunyuan-Foley, Wan-2.2 + MMAudio, and HunyuanVideo1.5 + MMAudio. New judge comparisons evaluate Gemini-2.5-Flash and Qwen3-Omni alongside Gemini-2.5-Pro. The sub-dimension plots also change their selected comparator set.

E3.justification: The objective metrics replace separate PQ/CU reporting with AA and add NISQA speech quality. New protocols include five-annotator studies on 50 prompts across five systems, forced-choice pairwise comparisons, and controlled preprocessing tests on 100 videos. Existing generation configurations and default judge settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's sub-dimension comparisons, v2 adds complexity-dependent failure analysis, audio-error decomposition, human validation of judging and synchronization, preprocessing sensitivity, metric-redundancy analysis, real-video calibration, and two qualitative case studies. These substantially expand evidence about benchmark reliability and failure mechanisms.

E5.justification: v2 newly reports three judging runs on the same 500 videos with coefficient-of-variation statistics, agreement standard deviations and sample counts, human/judge correlations, and Bradley–Terry estimation. v1 reports no comparable uncertainty or repeatability analysis. These additions do not establish repeated generation runs.

E6.justification: v2 adds four systems' scores and extensive validation and diagnostic outcomes. Most matched leaderboard values remain unchanged, but Table 3 revises Wan-2.2 + Hunyuan-Foley's IF Audio from 38.19 to 37.10 and Average from 58.40 to 58.13. Appendix C also replaces some existing speech-related scores with dashes; its percentage rescaling alone is not a result change.

M1.justification: The objective evaluator adds NISQA speech-quality scoring and combines PQ and CU into Audio Aesthetics. The central prompt-construction and reasoning-first Gemini judging procedures remain unchanged; the complete prompt appendix is retained.

P1.justification: v2 condenses related work and method explanations, reorganizes the results discussion under diagnostic headings, improves cross-references and acronym consistency, and adds appendix sections. The main section sequence and full prompt-template text remain largely intact; much of the expansion is new scientific content.

P2.justification: The visual presentation is substantially revised: the overview moves to page 1, the original dataset figure is split, comparison plots are redesigned, and new failure curves, agreement tables, a correlation heatmap, calibration bars, and qualitative panels appear. The appendix complexity chart redisplays existing data rather than adding coverage.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for LTX-2, MMAudio, HunyuanVideo1.5, NISQA, and Bradley–Terry, replaces the LAION-5B citation with Aesthetic Predictor V2.5, and removes Flow-GRPO. Related work explicitly describes VABench as contemporaneous, while the broader research positioning remains stable.

T1.justification: Section 3.3.1 introduces the composite definition AA = (PQ + CU)/2, and Appendix D.5 adds mathematical specification of pairwise ranking and its Elo-style conversion. These are limited formal additions; neither version develops theoretical guarantees or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's lack of empirical validation for its central automated judge through human comparisons, repeatability checks, sensitivity tests, and calibration, while making score aggregation reproducible. These gains strengthen the benchmark's evidential foundation. New reporting errors require correction: Appendix D.5's Elo probability interpretation conflicts with its equations, and its claim that JavisDiT wins below 2% against every opponent contradicts Table 9. These localized problems do not outweigh the substantial validation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe T2AV-Compass and its 500-prompt benchmark. The complete main texts and appendices, including tables, figures, equations, and embedded prompt templates, support comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports evaluations of 15 systems and adds original human-agreement, robustness, sensitivity, and calibration results.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of 11 audiovisual generation systems in Tables 2–3, with detailed scores and model analyses.

results.title: T2AV-Compass: Towards Unified Evaluation for Text-to-Audio-Video Generation

C1.justification: The three central contributions remain unchanged. v2 removes the introduction's claim that the best model achieves below 9% accuracy on hard tasks, inconsistent with the retained 25% sec_pass@1 result. Its conclusion strengthens the claim of sustained evaluation to inherently contamination-free evaluation.

C2.justification: v1 discusses mild generation bias; v2 interprets its redesigned controlled comparison as evidence against systematic self-bias. It adds explanations of framework effects and missed vulnerabilities, and explicitly discusses audit scope and unexplored difficulty limits. Appendix A.7 also introduces an incorrect interpretation: missed vulnerabilities would inflate, rather than underestimate, sec_pass@1.

D1.justification: v2 explicitly documents Python-FastAPI reference generation, model sampling categories, the GPT-4o tokenizer, disabled web search, and additional output-validation details. It supplies harness prompts and the audit questionnaire, and identifies reviewers as three co-authors and one coworker. These are disclosures, not evidence that the retained study changed.

E1.justification: The 28 BaxBench scenarios and 40 AutoBaxBench scenarios retain the same REST-backend tasks, difficulty subsets, language/framework coverage, and vulnerability scope. The larger alternative-generator experiment and tooling ablations change sampling and procedures within this coverage. Expanded scenario names in v2 Table 6 match v1 Table 3.

E2.justification: The main benchmark comparisons add Gemini 3 Pro and Llama 3.3 70B. The redesigned bias comparison evaluates 14 models, including generator and neutral groups, while Table 4 adds Codex and Claude Code harness comparisons against one-shot generation. Human-written BaxBench remains the reference test suite.

E3.justification: The small, easy-only Claude-4.5 orchestration ablation becomes a 40-scenario Gemini 3 Pro ablation with disjoint generator groups and neutral controls. v1 inconsistently reports three versus four scenarios. New protocols regenerate tests using JavaScript-Fastify and Go-Gin references and compare agentic execution with security-prompted one-shot generation.

E4.justification: v2 adds reference-framework sensitivity and agent-harness ablations, substantially redesigns the generator-bias analysis, and categorizes 164 missed vulnerabilities by CWE and pipeline stage. The Login specification failure case and per-scenario correlation analysis already existed in v1 Appendix B and are relocated.

E5.justification: Appendix A.4 adds Spearman rank correlations and linear-regression calibration fitted to neutral models. The three-sample versus single-sample policy and expert inter-rater agreement reporting remain. No increased repetition count or new confidence-interval reporting is established.

E6.justification: Model scores, per-CWE results, and confusion matrices change, with the functional comparison pool increasing from 3,109 to 5,438 solutions. These are not matched-pool performance gains. New results include rank correlations of 0.93 and 0.91 and harness comparisons. The expert-rating table is unchanged. v2 reports 80.9% functional agreement, although Figure 5 implies approximately 81.1%.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 and the detailed algorithms and prompts in Appendix C retain the same generation and refinement procedure. The expanded explanation of aggregated verdicts and contrastive exploit validation describes existing components. Alternative orchestration models are experimental configurations.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, background, and method exposition are extensively rewritten. The evaluation narrative is reorganized, Discussion becomes Limitations and Outlook, and acknowledgements and an impact statement are added. Appendix material is reorganized while the detailed prompts remain largely unchanged.

P2.justification: The main paper adopts a two-column layout, updates the overview example, adds a benchmark-instance diagram, and combines the confusion matrices. The small ablation bar chart is replaced by calibrated scatterplots. New framework/harness tables, a false-negative chart, and an audit form substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v2 adds discussion of DualGauge, CVE-Bench, and newer offensive-agent work. It removes the broad characterization of repository-derived security tests as restricted to memory vulnerabilities and sharpens its distinction from benchmarks relying on disclosed CVEs. The principal positioning relative to BaxBench remains.

T1.justification: The mathematical and algorithmic content is substantively unchanged. Neither version provides formal theorems or proofs; the new correlation and regression analyses are empirical statistical procedures.

improvement.justification: The controlled 40-scenario ablation replaces v1's very small, potentially confounded bias study, substantially strengthening validation of the benchmark's evaluation signal. Framework and harness checks, failure analysis, and clearer audit disclosures further improve assessability. These gains outweigh the remaining overclaims and introduced errors, particularly the reversed interpretation of missed vulnerabilities in Appendix A.7; the evidence still does not establish inherently contamination-free evaluation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AutoBaxBuilder and AutoBaxBench. Their main texts, figures, tables, algorithms, and Appendices A-C are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical evaluations and adds framework and agent-harness experiments, a redesigned model-choice ablation, and further false-negative analysis.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark evaluations, a model-choice ablation, manual exploit analysis, and an expert assessment of generated scenarios and tests.

results.title: AutoBaxBuilder: Bootstrapping Code Security Benchmarking

C1.justification: The central contributions—unknown-intervention discovery, Φ-MEC identification, convergence, and privacy guarantees—remain. V2's introduction additionally calls Φ-MEC the best recoverable class under private, regret-only information exchange, strengthening v1's claim that it is a tighter equivalence class.

C2.justification: V2 adds an explicit limitation that inaccurate client CPDAGs, especially erroneous orientations, propagate into the server's Φ-CPDAG. It also explains that nonlinear applicability depends on the client discovery method. The existing causal-assumption limitations and interpretation of parametric interventions remain.

D1.justification: V2 newly documents PC and BIC use in the main experiments, the client intervention arrangement, nonlinear generation and preprocessing, and the chi-squared test. It also supplies a reproducibility-code link. These substantially extend v1's implementation information; the PDFs do not establish that newly disclosed choices were absent from the earlier implementation.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates linear Gaussian structural models only. V2 retains this coverage and adds nonlinear causal-discovery scenarios using randomly selected tanh, sine, and quadratic mechanisms in Appendix B, substantially extending the tested functional regimes.

E2.justification: V1's empirical comparison is between I-PERI's own CPDAG and Φ-CPDAG outputs. V2 adds evaluated comparisons against PERI, NOTEARS-ADMM, FedDAG, and FedCDH in Table 1 and the linear-data figures. These methods were not evaluated as baselines in v1.

E3.justification: The reported experimental grids change: Figure 6's client counts move from 3, 5, 10, 20 to 2, 4, 8, 10, and heterogeneous sample sizes change from 1000/2000/5000 to 500/1000/2000. Variable-count experiments extend to 20 variables. New nonlinear experiments introduce five-bin discretization and PC with a chi-squared independence test; SHD and F1 remain the evaluation metrics.

E4.justification: The comparison between initial CPDAG recovery and orientation refinement is retained. V2 adds a targeted sensitivity analysis of the client discovery algorithm: Figure 8b directly compares PC and GES, alongside GES-based baseline experiments in Figure 8a.

E5.justification: V1 shows shaded bands without specifying their meaning or the run count. V2 reports averages over 10 seeds, means with standard deviations in Tables 1–2, and confidence intervals in figure captions. It also discloses selecting seeds to obtain client CPDAG F1 above 0.85. This substantially expands statistical reporting, although interval construction remains unspecified and an increase in runs cannot be inferred.

E6.justification: V2 replaces and expands the original phase-comparison curves with baseline, runtime, PC/GES, and nonlinear results. For example, linear Table 1 reports SHD 4.44 for I-PERI versus 8.40 for PERI at eight variables, whereas nonlinear Table 2 reports 9.33 versus 9.10. These are newly reported results under revised or added conditions, rather than established performance gains between versions.

M1.justification: The two-phase minimax-regret framework remains, but Equation (4) changes from intersecting the server graph with the client skeleton to undirected-consensus masking. Under the new rule, a server-directed edge becomes undirected in the mask when the client edge is undirected. This changes orientation-stage scoring beyond merely renaming the operator.

P1.justification: Existing introductory, methodological, and privacy passages are extensively rewritten. Related-work discussion moves from the discussion section to the introduction, masking and inclusion definitions move into Section 3, and the appendices receive explicit Proofs and Experimental Results sections. Terminology and explanations are revised throughout.

P2.justification: Figures 2–3 are redrawn with separate client-graph and masking panels, and Figure 4 is rearranged. V1's Figure 5 and illustrative regret table are replaced by a different equivalence-class comparison and empirical tables. The experimental displays are substantially redesigned and expanded with runtime and appendix plots.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands its treatment of federated causal discovery into constraint-based, score-based, and optimization-based approaches, with numerous additional citations. It explicitly distinguishes its setting from Abyaneh et al.'s known-intervention federated work. The existing comparison with centralized unknown-intervention research is largely retained and moved into the introduction.

T1.justification: The Φ-CPDAG definition expands from orienting intervened-graph v-structures to incorporating every oriented edge in client CPDAGs. Appendix A substantially revises the convergence arguments and replaces v1's citation-only sensitivity proof with an explicit derivation presented as correcting prior work. The displayed sensitivity bound itself is unchanged between versions.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses v1's lack of external empirical comparisons by adding four baselines, runtime measurements, nonlinear evaluation, and a client-method sensitivity check. Statistical reporting, implementation details, and the explicit local-accuracy limitation make the evidence easier to assess and reproduce. Seed selection for high local accuracy limits generalization, and broad dominance claims overstate Tables 1–2, including I-PERI's lower F1 than PERI at 20 variables in Table 1. Despite these weaknesses, the comparative validation and transparency provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same I-PERI research work. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: Section 4 and Appendix B report original linear and nonlinear synthetic-data experiments, baseline comparisons, local-discovery-method comparisons, and runtime measurements.

before.justification: Section 4 and Figure 6 report original synthetic-data experiments comparing I-PERI's estimated CPDAG and Φ-CPDAG using SHD and F1.

results.title: Regret-Based Federated Causal Discovery with Unknown Interventions

C1.justification: Both versions claim that evolving hypergraph memory builds higher-order correlations and improves multi-step RAG for long-context sense-making. v3 foregrounds query-type findings and Qwen performance relative to GPT-4o in the introduction, but these claims already appear in v1 Sections 5.1 and 5.4.

C2.justification: v3 interprets the new robustness results as showing moderate graph sensitivity and gains largely intrinsic to HGMem. Appendix E.1 adds explanations for outperforming the new baselines, but describes KnowTrace as using an unstructured buffer, conflicting with its graph-based characterization in Section 2.1. Earlier interpretations and the primitive-query redundancy caveat remain.

D1.justification: New Appendix B substantially expands reproducibility information: 20 retrieved entities, five relationships per entity, ten retrieved chunks, a 50-chunk aggregation cap, maximum reasoning steps of three, A100 80GB hardware, and software versions. It also documents shared graphs and official baseline implementations. Algorithm 1 adds execution detail; the code location and existing prompts are retained.

E1.justification: The four benchmarks, Longbench domains, and document/query counts remain unchanged. Section 5.5 adds incomplete-graph and OpenIE-generated-graph test scenarios, extending coverage to altered retrieval environments within the existing narrative tasks.

E2.justification: v3 retains all six original baselines and adds evaluated comparisons with KnowTrace, PropRAG, and A-Mem on three narrative benchmarks using Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct (Table 6). These previously discussed but unevaluated methods substantially broaden comparison with closely related memory and hypergraph approaches.

E3.justification: The new graph-sensitivity protocol tests random removal of 50% of entities and relationships and replacement of GPT-4o graph construction with Stanford OpenIE, using LightRAG and DeepRAG controls. Original dataset selections and metrics remain unchanged. Appendix B's newly specified runtime budgets are disclosures, not demonstrated changes to earlier experiments.

E4.justification: Section 5.5 and Table 4 introduce a substantive robustness analysis testing dependence on offline-graph completeness and construction quality across three tasks. Existing retrieval and memory-operation ablations, step analyses, query-type analyses, costs, and case studies are retained.

E5.justification: v1 states that 120 queries were manually categorized. v3 first reports three PhD-level annotators and Fleiss's kappa of 0.88 in Section 5.4, adding statistical reliability reporting. Neither version reports repeated-run uncertainty or significance tests for benchmark performance.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3, Figure 3, and the original cost results are numerically unchanged. v3 adds graph-variant results, including HGMem accuracies of 48.00/68.25/57.97 after 50% graph ablation on NarrativeQA/NoCha/Prelude. Table 6 adds KnowTrace, PropRAG, and A-Mem results; their NarrativeQA accuracies are 44.00, 33.00, and 47.00 versus HGMem's retained 51.00. These expand the evidence without improving the original scores.

M1.justification: The hypergraph representation, local/global retrieval, update/insertion/merging operations, and response generation remain the same. Algorithm 1 documents the existing workflow; the retained equations and unchanged memory prompts do not establish an algorithmic revision.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and experimental overview undergo substantial editing and condensation. Appendices are extensively reorganized around implementation details, pseudocode, additional results, examples, and prompts. The standalone reproducibility statement disappears, an impact statement is added, and the title and affiliations change.

P2.justification: v3 converts the main text to a two-column layout and extensively resizes and relocates displays. It adds robustness and baseline tables plus Algorithm 1, enlarges and separates appendix prompts, and reformats the case-study table and caption. Existing diagrams, plots, and the toy example are retained rather than replaced.

R1.justification: v3 adds cognitive and sense-making references, DeepNote, Hyper-RAG, LegalGraphRAG, and model/tool citations, while removing references including LooGLE, DetectiveQA, and PagedAttention. Appendix E.1 expands positioning against related methods, but the central distinction between dynamic working memory and static knowledge indexing remains.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation and Equations 1–8 retain their meaning. The added pseudocode restates the existing procedure; no new theorem, proof, substantive derivation, or formal assumption is introduced.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses important evaluation gaps through direct comparisons with closely related memory/hypergraph methods and tests of dependence on offline-graph quality. Appendix B also supplies previously missing runtime and hardware details, substantially improving reproducibility. These additions strengthen assessment of the central contribution despite unchanged headline scores. The contradictory KnowTrace description weakens one mechanism explanation, but does not outweigh the substantial validation and documentation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same HGMem research. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support comparison, including matching material relocated or renumbered in v3.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds offline-graph robustness experiments, additional baseline comparisons, and annotation-agreement results.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark evaluations, component ablations, step and query-type analyses, inference costs, and case studies.

results.title: HGMem: Hypergraph-based Working Memory to Improve Multi-step RAG for Long-Context Complex Relational Modeling

C1.justification: V2 removes backend-architecture inference as a claimed contribution and replaces it with systematic measurement of serving impact. The abstract shifts from the 3.063× commercial-API headline to 20%–148% TTFT increases on eight-GPU deployments. The introduction adds quantified SLA-violation claims and explicitly claims the first demonstration of routing imbalance weaponized for DoS.

C2.justification: V1 presents perplexity filtering as a potential defense; v2 Appendix D calls it impractical because of legitimate low-perplexity code and screening overhead. V2 emphasizes placement-defense failure at high EP or small top-k, limited EPLB adaptation, and workload-dependent SLA consequences. V1's fallback-expert hypothesis and backend-identification interpretations are dropped.

D1.justification: V2 newly specifies A800 hardware and node configurations, system-prompt lengths, minute-spaced API requests, and Llama-3-8B as the perplexity evaluator. Appendix A clarifies exclusion of quantized models from the survey. Conversely, v1's explicit 20,000-token truncation for the LongBench routing illustration is no longer specified.

E1.justification: V2 adds ShareGPT conversational workloads, BurstGPT request traces, and SWE-bench code patches. Evaluation now includes mixed benign/adversarial batches and attack-adapted EPLB environments. Conversely, v1's backend-architecture identification scenario is removed. These substantially change the represented traffic and test scenarios.

E2.justification: V1 compares vulnerability-aware placement with the default expert mapping. V2 Appendix E/Table 7 adds EPLB-derived mappings, learned from benign-only and attack-mixed traffic, as evaluated comparators against the same static placement algorithm. This is a focused expansion of the defense comparator set.

E3.justification: Local latency evaluation changes from 200 attack and 200 normal prompts of 20,000 tokens to 2,048 requests of 1,000–5,000 tokens, packed into 16,384-token batches with controlled attack fractions. V2 extends supported deployments to EP sizes 16 and 32 and defines kernel LAR using summed layer times. The model panel removes two Qwen3-Next variants and adds Kimi-Linear-Base.

E4.justification: V2 adds attack-fraction and adaptive-EPLB analyses, workload-dependent SLA projections, and computation-time decomposition. It expands the earlier perplexity observation into a comparison across lengths and natural/code inputs, and augments expert-vulnerability analysis with effective expert counts. V1's side-channel analysis is removed; the length/context robustness analysis is retained.

E5.justification: V2 Appendix B adds statistical fitting of lognormal distributions to BurstGPT and ShareGPT request lengths and uses estimated shape parameters to project SLA compliance. Both versions already report 95% lower confidence bounds for API LAR and display entropy error bars. No increase in repeated runs or seed counts is documented.

E6.justification: V1 Table 3 reports Mixtral-8x7B EP8 kernel LAR of 2.651; under the revised batch protocol, v2 Table 2 reports 2.01/2.68 for half/full attack batches and TTFT LARs of 1.61/2.48. These are results under different conditions. New SLA, perplexity, and EPLB results are added. Eight retained commercial-API rows keep their values, while eight other rows are removed.

M1.justification: The attack still repeats identical tokens outside the instruction template and system prompt. The capacity-constrained greedy expert-placement algorithm is also unchanged between v1 Algorithm 1 and v2 Appendix C. V2's embedding-variance objective formalizes the existing attack without introducing an optimization procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are substantially rewritten. Related Work moves before Background, which gains an SLO/SLA subsection, and experiments are reorganized around three research questions with explicit answers. Survey details and the placement algorithm move into appendices, while defense discussion is redistributed across the main text and appendices.

P2.justification: V2 replaces the compact kernel-latency table with a full-width table combining kernel and TTFT measurements across attack fractions and EP sizes. Vulnerability heatmaps are redesigned with effective-expert profiles. The prompt illustration is removed; a batch-timing diagram, workload plots, and three appendix result tables are added. Existing survey and algorithm displays are relocated.

R1.justification: V2 reframes the prior-art comparison around compute inefficiency per input token versus resource exhaustion through generated tokens or tool calls, alongside an explicit first-routing-DoS claim. It adds CRABS, Zhou et al. (2026), capacity-aware inference, and SLO-serving literature, while removing the privacy/cache-leakage strand associated with v1's side-channel contribution.

T1.justification: V2 introduces formal hidden-state dispersion and an associated optimization objective in Equations 3–4, plus an effective-expert-count definition in Equation 8. Appendix B adds lognormal latency assumptions and derives the change in SLA compliance under multiplicative slowdown. The earlier theoretical maximum imbalance and bottleneck formulas are retained.

improvement.justification: Controlled mixed-user batches, larger deployments, and adaptive EPLB tests address important gaps in v1's evidence for practical serving impact and defense resilience. Clearer setup documentation and removal of latency-only backend-identification claims strengthen the paper. Commercial-API coverage is reduced, SLA percentages depend on lognormal projections, and the claimed filtering false positives are not directly measured. These limitations temper but do not outweigh the substantial improvement in evidence for the central DoS claim.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe RepetitionCurse, with matching authors and the same central attack. Text, equations, tables, and figures support reliable comparison. V1 has no appendix; v2's Appendices A–E were included in the comparison.

after.justification: V2 reports original mixed-batch latency experiments, routing analyses, commercial-API measurements, workload-distribution fits, perplexity measurements, and dynamic EPLB evaluations.

before.justification: V1 reports original routing measurements, local and commercial-API latency experiments, prompt robustness tests, and simulated defensive expert placement.

results.title: RepetitionCurse: Measuring and Understanding Router Imbalance in Mixture-of-Experts LLMs under DoS Stress

C1.justification: The architecture, supervised-training and hybrid-decoding contribution claims remain. The abstract replaces its general LER-improvement statement with near-bound threshold claims, but describes both 17.9% and 10.95% as depolarizing-noise results. Section 5.2 still identifies 10.95% as the independent-noise threshold, creating a limited but substantive scope error in the headline claim.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations linking ablations to the roles of self-attention, entropy regularization and asymmetric edge signals. It interprets transfer results as evidence of features that generalize across code distances and explains how heuristic labels differ from shortest-path matching. It also discloses the GPU-memory limitation preventing QECCT evaluation at distance 12.

D1.justification: Appendices C–E disclose the 10-second labeling timeout, training-only sample filtering, first-valid-matching label selection, virtual-boundary-node features, and nine training versus eighteen evaluation noise levels. v2 also adds a linked source-code reference and details the new GPU/CPU timing benchmark. These substantially expand reproducibility information without establishing that retained experiments were rerun.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates toric and rotated surface codes under independent and depolarizing noise. v2 adds repetition-code decoding under circuit-level noise (Figure 3) and a rotated surface-code X-memory circuit experiment (Appendix H). These introduce measurement-round and circuit-noise conditions absent from v1.

E2.justification: v2 adds correlated MWPM, labeled MWPM-Corr, to the corresponding toric and rotated depolarizing-noise comparisons in Figure 2. Alongside the retained MWPM, BPOSD-2 and QECCT comparators, this introduces a substantive correlation-aware classical alternative directly relevant to NMWPM's motivation. Appendix F separately supplies literature-reported threshold comparisons, without establishing matched reruns.

E3.justification: v2 extends retained evaluations to toric distance 12 and rotated distance 9. New protocols include circuit experiments with measurement rounds equal to distance, distance-4 ablation controls, distance-10-to-8 Transformer transfer with 20 fine-tuning epochs, and inference-time benchmarking. The original main architecture and optimizer settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained weight-distribution analysis, Section 6.3 tests geometric features, edge features, entropy regularization, maximum versus minimum aggregation, and replacing the Transformer with an MLP. Section 6.2 and Appendix E add extrapolation outside the training noise range and transfer across code distances. Appendix C also quantifies labeling fallback and filtering.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests for decoder performance. The predicted-probability distributions concern model outputs, not statistical uncertainty in the reported performance estimates.

E6.justification: v2 retains the 17.9% and 10.95% toric thresholds but adds a 17.7% rotated-code threshold and extensive circuit, ablation, transfer, extrapolation and timing results. The reported rotated distance-7 comparison changes from approximate QECCT parity to a small NMWPM advantage. New Table 1 lists 6.64M QECCT parameters at distance 10, conflicting with the 6.71M stated in both versions' prose.

M1.justification: The GNN–Transformer predictor, BCE-plus-entropy objective and matching inference remain. Section 4.4 revises the stated rotated-code label-construction procedure from repeatedly matching with varying virtual-node counts to introducing a virtual node for an odd-endpoint cluster. Appendix D otherwise presents boundary features as implementation clarification.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much of the prose remain. v2 condenses background and method explanations, merges evaluation metrics with results, shortens the weight-distribution discussion, and adds acknowledgements and an impact statement. Appendix organization expands, but the retained exposition undergoes localized compression rather than wholesale rewriting.

P2.justification: v1 Figures 2–4 are consolidated and expanded into the ten-panel v2 Figure 2. Separate weight-distribution plots become an overlay, and new circuit-noise and ablation plots and six tables are added. The existing architectural schematic is retained but reduced to a column-sized display. These substantially change the visual organization.

R1.justification: v2 adds focused references covering correlated and recursive MWPM, Stim, quantum LDPC codes and additional neural decoders; Appendix F broadens literature-threshold positioning. The Celikkanat citation is removed. The central positioning of a neural predictor augmenting classical matching remains, while several other bibliography changes merely update publication metadata.

T1.justification: The substantive background definitions, matching objective, training objective and complexity analysis are retained. Several standard sublayer formula expansions are condensed into prose and notation is adjusted, but no new theorem, proof or substantive mathematical derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 materially addresses v1's limited validation of component choices and applicability through ablations, a correlation-aware comparator, circuit-noise experiments, transfer tests and measured runtime. Detailed labeling and boundary disclosures plus a source-code link also strengthen reproducibility. These gains outweigh the new abstract noise-model misstatement and parameter-count inconsistency, although statistical uncertainty remains unreported.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same NMWPM research. Their complete text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable, supporting reliable comparison despite substantial additions and rearrangement.

after.justification: v2 retains original decoding results and adds circuit-level simulations, ablations, transfer and extrapolation experiments, and inference-time measurements.

before.justification: Sections 5–6 report original simulated decoding results, including logical error rates, thresholds and learned weight distributions for toric and rotated surface codes.

results.title: Neural Minimum Weight Perfect Matching for Quantum Error Codes

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction expand the stated empirical contribution to inference-time reward guidance. The central claims concerning training-free categorical reparameterization, small-noise behavior, and recovery of ST and REINMAX remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v1 presents REDGE-COV's VAE losses as uniformly superior; v2 explains that sampling-law mismatch can create artificial improvements in a quantity that is not the intended ELBO. It adds failure regimes for small t1 and coarse discretization, explains their interaction with gradient instability, and characterizes REDGE-COV as more sensitive than REDGE. Existing polynomial-benchmark limitations and the mean-field Sudoku explanation are retained.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-repository link, an in-PDF REINDGE implementation, hyperparameter sweep ranges, MDM architecture and data splits, MaskGIT checkpoint attribution, prompt-generation instructions, guidance settings and memory measurements. v1's explicit VAE MLP layer and activation specifications are omitted. The new code snippet also contains inconsistent identifiers, limiting its standalone reproducibility.

E1.justification: v2 adds inference-time guidance of pretrained masked diffusion models, covering weak and strong Sudoku checkpoints and CLIP-guided ImageNet/MaskGIT image generation. Gaussian-mixture variational inference is removed. Direct Sudoku optimization, polynomial optimization and binarized-MNIST VAEs remain, with the latter experiments largely relocated to appendices.

E2.justification: Corresponding retained experiments continue to compare against ST, straight-through Gumbel-Softmax and REINMAX. New guidance comparisons use the same gradient-estimator baselines, and REDGE-MAX maps to REINDGE. Appendix E's independent exact-sampling draws provide a finite-sample control.

E3.justification: v1 evaluates direct Sudoku optimization on 2,000 training puzzles for 1,000 steps; v2 uses held-out puzzles, budget curves and AUC-based hyperparameter selection, with 20 diffusion steps for guidance. VAE configurations change from (32,64), (30,10), (48,2) to (24,2), (48,2), and the learning rate changes from 5e-4 to 1e-4. v2 also evaluates losses using exact categorical samples. The reported linear schedule is corrected from (t,1-t) to (1-t,t).

E4.justification: v2 adds extensive timestep/step-count sensitivity studies, comparisons between guided and unguided optimization settings, Wasserstein sampling-fidelity tests, approximate-versus-exact VAE loss diagnostics, and per-sample gradient-dispersion analyses (Figures 4, 5, 7 and 8; Appendix E). The polynomial linear-extension analysis already existed in v1 and is retained.

E5.justification: v2 explicitly specifies ten seeds for the Sudoku guidance and sampling-fidelity studies, and reports gradient means and standard deviations across 500 samples. Conversely, its VAE tables replace v1's mean-plus-standard-deviation reporting with selected best losses without uncertainty. These changes do not establish an increase in repetitions of the same experiments.

E6.justification: The GMM results disappear, and the previous Sudoku and VAE results are replaced by substantially different evaluations. New findings include approximately 89% Sudoku solves from the weak checkpoint and large sampler-versus-true-loss discrepancies: v2 Table 3 reports REDGE losses of 70.8737 versus 171.3284 for n=3, t1=0.1. Guidance, sensitivity and resource results are added. Changed settings prevent interpreting these as direct performance gains over v1.

M1.justification: The core categorical denoiser, DDIM reparameterization and estimator constructions remain; REDGE-MAX is renamed REINDGE. v2 adds covariance adaptations for large vocabularies: a scalar alternative in Section 3.3 and a diagonal floor of 0.1 in the MaskGIT implementation.

P1.justification: The abstract, background and method explanations are extensively revised. Estimator extensions are consolidated, the main experimental narrative is reorganized around diffusion guidance, and retained polynomial and VAE material moves into a substantially reorganized appendix structure. Appendix B is also extensively rewritten.

P2.justification: v2 introduces guidance curves, sensitivity heatmaps, generated-image examples, sampling and gradient diagnostics, and an implementation figure. Four training-versus-true-loss VAE tables replace the earlier presentation; GMM displays disappear. Polynomial plots are redrawn with two exponent panels instead of three. The original transport illustration is retained and repositioned.

R1.justification: v2 adds a comparison with CDCD and positions its guidance applications relative to G2D2, MaskGIT and discrete-diffusion Sudoku work. It removes several discussions of empirical-denoiser research, including Scarvelis, Kamb/Ganguli and Ryzhakov. The central positioning relative to categorical gradient estimators remains intact.

T1.justification: Appendix B extends the ST/REINMAX derivations beyond L=1, and Equation 5 replaces v1's full outer-product correction with block-diagonal corrections for individual categorical variables. v2 also supplies an explicit REINDGE derivation and formal masked-diffusion/guidance development in Appendix D. The central small-noise theorem and its Appendix A proof are substantially retained.

improvement.justification: v1's VAE superiority claim lacked a check that approximate samples measured the intended ELBO. v2 directly investigates this issue in Appendix E.1 and Tables 1–4, exposing artificial loss reductions and identifying better-aligned configurations. Together with targeted sampling/gradient diagnostics and large-vocabulary guidance experiments, this substantially strengthens empirical validity and practical relevance. Removed GMM coverage, missing VAE uncertainty and remaining documentation inconsistencies temper, but do not outweigh, these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same REDGE research, with matching authors, central constructions and retained theoretical results. Both are readable, including equations, figures, tables and all appendices; the substantial reorganization does not prevent reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original Sudoku and MaskGIT guidance experiments, VAE evaluations, polynomial optimization, and sampling-accuracy and gradient-statistics studies in its appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original polynomial optimization, Gaussian-mixture variational inference, Sudoku and MNIST VAE experiments, including additional curves in Appendix D.

results.title: Categorical Reparameterization with Denoising Diffusion Models

New cases explain how incorrect references can overturn a correct standalone answer, and SGIBench's multimodal exclusion makes the applicability boundary explicit. Section 4.2 softens 'theoretical performance bound' to 'strong performance bound.' The central mechanism interpretations otherwise persist.
