Table 7 supplies model sizes, release dates, and token prices. These are largely new disclosures, not established changes to existing runs; the original JiSi hyperparameters and access statement remain.

E1.justification: Appendix B and Table 6 add four SGIBench task families: Wet Experiment, Dry Experiment, Deep Research, and Idea Generation. These substantially extend the original nine-benchmark coverage into scientific workflows. The multimodal subset is explicitly excluded. OpenRouterBench becoming LLMRouterBench retains the same cited commit and does not itself establish changed coverage.

E2.justification: Table 1 newly evaluates Symbolic-MoE and Self-MoA across the nine original benchmarks; v1 only discussed these methods in related work. This substantially strengthens comparison with competing routing-and-aggregation and single-model aggregation approaches. The previously evaluated external comparators remain.

E3.justification: New studies introduce a performance-estimation deviation metric, correctness-based difficulty groups, and a support-set-size sweep holding three reference responses fixed. Appendix B also specifies retaining the original embedding bank while adding scientific-task data. Original splits and judges remain. Appendix D.3 names fixed MoA/voting trios, conflicting with the retained per-benchmark selection description; this is a reporting ambiguity, not evidence that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Table 5 expands the original full/router-only/no-switch comparisons into seven component configurations. Sections 4.4–4.6 add similarity-estimation, reference-filtering, and aggregator-selection analyses; Appendices E–F add three similarity cases and two aggregation-failure cases. The original model-selection distribution analysis is retained in Appendix A rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: The split seed remains 42, and Figure 5 retains its existing 95% confidence bands. No new experimental replication counts, uncertainty estimates, or significance tests are reported. Sampling within aggregation baselines is part of their inference procedure.

E6.justification: All 29 shared Table 1 rows and Table 2 cost entries are unchanged. New baseline averages are 66.89 for Symbolic-MoE and 66.52 for Self-MoA. New SGIBench results report JiSi at 27.76 versus Gemini-3-Pro at 26.00. Additional analyses include an ARS-only ablation scoring 64.87 versus 67.83 with all three components disabled. These are newly reported comparisons, not improvements to the retained main results.

M1.justification: The embedding bank, query-response-length scoring, support-set aggregator selection, and adaptive routing-aggregation switch retain the same procedure in Section 3. The new scientific-task experiments extend the bank with additional data without introducing a new algorithmic component.

P1.justification: The introduction, related work, methodological motivation, and conclusion are substantially condensed or rewritten. Evaluation details and the original model-selection analysis move into appendices, while three diagnostic subsections enter the main experimental narrative. Terminology shifts toward 'multi-LLM,' and the author list changes.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 3–7, the support-set-size plot, and five boxed case-study figures. Existing ablation results are regrouped into domain summaries within the expanded Table 5. The original selection-distribution figure moves to the appendix as Figure 7, and table captions and surrounding layouts are revised. The retained leaderboard, radar, and scaling plots preserve their results.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations to Chen et al.'s multi-LLM repeated-sampling work and Xu et al.'s SGIBench work, removes ZOOTER/Lu et al., and drops the extended positioning against SMACS's smaller-model validation. The OpenRouterBench-to-LLMRouterBench citation update represents the retained benchmark rather than a separate research lineage.

T1.justification: Section 4.4 introduces the formal deviation measure 100 ||g − v||₁ / M. Section 3.3 also corrects the fine-grained model-score vector's dimension from N to M. The principal inference equations otherwise retain their substance, and no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v1 provided limited component-level validation and sparse baseline implementation details. v2 substantially addresses these weaknesses through controlled mechanism studies, expanded ablations exposing an adverse component interaction, two relevant evaluated competitors, and detailed implementation reporting. Scientific-task results also broaden support for scalability. The inconsistent MoA/voting selection descriptions and loss of per-benchmark detail for the no-switch variant are drawbacks, but the gains in empirical support and reproducibility are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same JiSi framework. Their text, equations, tables, and figures support reliable comparison. All pages were inspected, including v2 Appendices A–F; v1 ends with references and has no appendix.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds evaluated baselines, component and mechanism studies, scientific-task evaluations, and qualitative cases.

before.justification: v1 reports original JiSi evaluations across nine benchmarks, baseline comparisons, cost measurements, component variants, and model-pool scaling experiments.

results.title: Beyond Gemini-3-Pro: Revisiting LLM Routing and Aggregation at Scale

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same headline contributions: additive separation of prior-dependent burn-in from long-run regret, a generalized elliptical-potential lemma, an unavoidable burn-in lower bound, and extension to strongly log-concave distributions.

C2.justification: Section 4 adds an explicit interpretation of the two lower-bound regimes and a prior-dependent horizon threshold for long-run near-optimality. The conclusion retains the same limitations concerning log-concavity, Bayesian regret, and a well-specified prior.

D1.justification: Neither version provides experimental implementation details, computational resources, hyperparameters, or code/data access information. The appendix revisions concern mathematical derivations.

E1.justification: Neither version uses datasets or empirical evaluation tasks. Changes to the theoretical action-set assumptions and covariance coverage belong to T1.

E2.justification: Neither version evaluates comparison algorithms experimentally. Discussions of Thompson sampling variants and UCB concern cited theoretical guarantees.

E3.justification: No experimental protocols, data splits, evaluation metrics, training budgets, or testing procedures are reported in either version.

E4.justification: Neither version contains empirical ablations, robustness tests, or error analyses. The added sharpness construction in Section 3 is a mathematical argument, assessed under T1.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated runs, seeds, empirical uncertainty estimates, or significance tests. Changes to concentration arguments are theoretical proof changes.

E6.justification: There are no empirical result entries or measured findings in either version. Revised regret bounds and mathematical constants are assessed under T1.

M1.justification: Both versions analyze the same Thompson sampling procedure: sample from the posterior and maximize the sampled linear reward. The corrected likelihood expression in Appendix B.1 repairs the analysis, rather than introducing a different inference procedure.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and most prose are retained. v2 makes localized copy edits, changes policy notation, adds explanatory passages and an Impact Statement, and divides Appendix A into two proof subsections. Author-affiliation and citation formatting also change.

P2.justification: The entire document adopts a different template, changing typography, the title and author arrangement, affiliation placement, heading styles, running headers, and page-number footers. Equations and references are reflowed, and the separate Supplementary Materials banner disappears. Neither version contains figures or tables.

R1.justification: The cited works remain the same. Section 4 locally strengthens the paper's positioning by replacing reliance on Rusmevichientong and Tsitsiklis (2010) for a particular scaled-identity prior with its own long-run guarantee for general positive-definite Gaussian covariance.

T1.justification: Theorem 6 strengthens the burn-in bound from a truncated eigenvalue sum to a sum over all eigenvalues weighted by min(i−1,T), broadens the action-set assumption, and adds a long-run lower bound for positive-definite Gaussian covariance matrices. Corollary 7 improves the short-horizon scaling from S r d^(-1/2) min(T,d)^2 to S r sqrt(d) min(T,d). Appendix A strengthens Lemma 10, corrects Lemma 12 and summation indices, and adds the second-bound proof in A.2. Section 3 adds a first-term sharpness construction. Further corrections affect Theorem 1's constants, Lemma 5's proof, and Appendix B.1's likelihood and concentration argument.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the theoretical support for near-optimality: it improves short-horizon lower bounds and supplies a general-covariance long-run bound with a dedicated proof, where v1 relied on a restricted prior result from earlier work. Corrections to Gaussian scaling, eigenvalue indexing, and the Appendix B likelihood also improve central derivations. Local formula inconsistencies remain, including an extra sigma in Section 2.1.3 and an undefined q in Section 3's new construction, but these shortcomings do not outweigh the substantial gains in theoretical scope and correctness.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with the same title, authors, principal results, and appendices A–B. All pages and mathematical content are readable, supporting a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 remains entirely theoretical, including its expanded lower-bound analysis and appendices. It reports no experiments, simulations, or data-analysis outcomes.

before.justification: v1 presents theoretical regret bounds, mathematical examples, and proofs. Neither the main text nor the appendices report original empirical results.

results.title: Prior Diffusiveness and Regret in the Linear-Gaussian Bandit

C1.justification: The central contribution expands from an AI-specific retrieval benchmark to a multidisciplinary dataset with 8,940 tasks and a much broader corpus. The three-level taxonomy and claim that existing retrieval systems struggle remain. The abstract also updates the claimed downstream benefit from 23.4% to 25.3%.

C2.justification: New Appendix A.4 discusses citation prestige bias, parsing noise, influence without explicit citations, and limited query diversity. Section 5.2 more explicitly distinguishes plausible narratives from connected citation chains, while Appendix B introduces explanations involving recency bias, semantic drift, and omitted structural milestones.

D1.justification: V2 adds SQLite indexing and 24-core CPU deployment information plus a structured curation and quality-assurance description. The release link changes from an anonymous site to a named GitHub repository, and the subfield inventory is referred there instead of reproduced. Existing Faiss parameters, A100 configuration, and substantive prompt content remain.

E1.justification: Coverage expands from an AI corpus of approximately 18.6 million papers across 177 subfields to a reported 269-million-paper corpus covering 2,640 subfields in biology, medicine, chemistry, physics, materials science, geology, and AI. The three relational task categories are retained.

E2.justification: Tables 1–3 retain the same eight retrieval systems, and Section 6 retains the same four survey-generation conditions. Appendix B presents cases involving existing model families. The new Table 5 compares benchmark designs rather than adding evaluated retrieval baselines.

E3.justification: Reported query counts increase from 354/600/133 to 2,640/4,200/2,100 for ego-centric, pair-wise, and path-wise tasks, while downstream survey evaluation expands from 20 to 40 queries. V2 also reports expert filtering of candidate paths, a new 200-context annotation-validation protocol, and a top-five DPO retrieval case. Core metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 adds a human validation study of GPT-5 citation-sentiment labels and two detailed failure analyses: disruptive-paper retrieval in DPO and reconstruction of the Neocognitron-to-Swin Transformer trajectory. Appendix B and Tables 7–8 provide model outputs and error analyses absent from v1.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without repeated-run or seed information, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The new human–GPT-5 agreement percentage is an annotation-validation result, without accompanying uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 update results throughout: best novelty/disruption recall changes from 1.42%/4.60% to 1.47%/4.71%. Survey results are replaced for the larger sample, and the reported review-quality benefit changes from 23.4% to 25.3%. V2 adds 98% sentiment agreement and case-study outputs. Changed coverage and sample sizes prevent interpreting these as same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: Section 5.1 revises the reported path-construction procedure: v1 selects the maximum-cumulative-citation BFS path as ground truth; v2 treats it as a candidate and applies expert coherence filtering before finalization. The retrieval systems and core scientometric components remain unchanged.

P1.justification: V2 retitles and renames the work, revises the abstract and introduction, and polishes terminology and grammar. Appendices are regrouped into supplementary details, case studies, and prompts. The main eight-section sequence and much of the technical exposition remain.

P2.justification: The main text changes from a single-column ICLR layout to a two-column ICML layout, with extensive figure and table resizing and relocation. V2 adds Figure 3 and Tables 5–8, and redesigns the survey chart with percentage annotations and a Relation-Augmented legend.

R1.justification: Appendix A.1 and Table 5 extend comparisons with LitSearch, PASA, and STARK to corpus scale and supervision signals. V2 adds citation-context and science-mapping references and removes several Shao/Xu references. The central positioning around scholarly relations beyond semantic or entity-based retrieval remains.

T1.justification: The novelty Z-score and tenth-percentile definition, disruption formula, and citation-weighted BFS rationale are retained. The added disruption illustration and construction discussion introduce no new mathematical definitions, derivations, theorems, or proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 materially strengthens benchmark credibility through the 200-context sentiment validation, explicit expert checking of candidate paths, and substantive limitations discussion. Broader disciplinary evaluation and concrete failure cases also improve applicability and interpretation. These gains outweigh documentation weaknesses, including Figure 5 retaining 133 queries despite the text reporting 2,100. The downstream benefit remains based on providing ground-truth paths, so it does not establish an equivalent gain from a deployed retrieval system.

A1.justification: Both PDFs are complete, readable versions of the same research work, renamed from SciNetBench to SciNet. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison despite expanded coverage and substantial reformatting.

after.justification: Tables 1–4 report retrieval and literature-review evaluations, including 40 downstream queries. Section 4.1 and Appendix B additionally report sentiment-label validation and retrieval case studies.

before.justification: Tables 1–3 report original evaluations of eight retrieval systems. Section 6 also reports automatic and human evaluations of literature reviews across 20 queries.

results.title: SciNet: Evaluating AI Agents in Relation-Aware Scientific Literature Retrieval

C1.justification: The central claims about inadequate benchmarks, realistic missingness protocols, and a competitive simple baseline remain. The abstract and fourth contribution shift emphasis from introducing GNNmim to adapting MIM, while explicitly extending competitiveness to naturally occurring missingness. The novelty claim is narrowed to graph node-level tasks under arbitrary missingness and distribution shifts.

C2.justification: v2 substantially develops explanations of embedding redundancy, the contribution of message passing relative to non-graph models, and applicability under unknown natural missingness. It adds qualifications about bound tightness and explicit task limitations. The earlier proposed future direction of graph-structure-dependent MNAR mechanisms is removed.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-repository link beyond the existing supplementary-material statement. Appendix E.1 documents RelBench architecture, optimizer, learning rate, batching, sampling, text preprocessing, hardware, checkpoint selection, and runtime measurement. Table 5 newly documents FP and PCFI backbone selections; this disclosure alone does not establish that earlier experiments were rerun.

E1.justification: v2 adds five tasks from REL-EVENT, REL-TRIAL, REL-ARXIV, and REL-F1, extending evaluation to large temporal relational graphs with naturally occurring missingness and to node regression. Table 54 also adds the reverse shift from U-MCAR training to MNAR testing. The original datasets and test scenarios remain.

E2.justification: The original comparator suite is retained. v2 adds evaluated comparisons against RDL on RelBench, MICE+GNN on four datasets, MLP+MIM and XGBoost on three datasets, and AE-GNN in the AIR representation experiment. These introduce substantial new comparison families.

E3.justification: New RelBench experiments use MAE or ROC-AUC, matched ten-epoch budgets without early stopping, validation-selected checkpoints, neighbor sampling, and a nearly complete control dataset. Additional protocols compare raw AIR features with 256-dimensional autoencoder embeddings and reverse the original missingness-shift direction. These are added protocols, not established reruns of the original experiments.

E4.justification: v2 adds reverse-shift robustness testing in Table 54, an empirical test of embedding redundancy in Appendix K, and non-graph comparisons testing the contribution of graph structure in Appendix L. The earlier scalability, inductive, and mask-augmentation analyses are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: The original five-run reporting remains. New RelBench experiments explicitly report means and standard deviations across three seeds, identified as 0, 1, and 2. Table 2 replaces individual KS-test p-values with their overall range, reducing statistical detail. Neither change establishes an increase in runs for existing experiments.

E6.justification: RelBench, reverse-shift, embedding, and additional-baseline results substantially expand the evidence. Some existing AIR values also change: FP under S-MCAR at missingness 0.99 changes from 0.350 in v1 Table 28 to 0.450 in v2 Table 29. Most original results remain identical. The new reverse-shift results include substantial GCNmf advantages over GNNmim on ELECTRIC.

M1.justification: The proposed procedure still concatenates missingness indicators with filled features and processes them through a GNN. RDLmim applies this same augmentation to the existing RDL pipeline, explicitly retaining its other components. No new missing-feature algorithm, learning objective, or inference procedure is specified.

P1.justification: The six-section narrative and much of the original prose remain. Targeted rewrites affect the abstract, introduction, results discussion, and conclusion; terminology changes include zero-padding to zero-filling. v2 adds Q4, an explicit limitations paragraph, and appendix sections without broadly reorganizing the existing argument.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from single-column to two-column layout, with resized and redrawn plots, revised legends, and a different heatmap palette. Dataset statistics are consolidated, Table 2 is transposed, and the backbone table is expanded. New RelBench, benchmark-audit, and reverse-shift tables and Figures 9–11 substantially extend the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v2 acknowledges earlier missingness-indicator applications through Cao et al. and Cini et al., narrowing its novelty positioning. It also substantially expands discussion and citations concerning learned embeddings, GraphLand, OGB, GraphBench, relational learning, and classical and non-graph baselines. These extend the research positioning beyond bibliographic corrections.

T1.justification: The main definitions, theorems, and proofs are retained. New Remark A.1 identifies conditions making steps of the information-loss bound tight, including injective deterministic labels, independent feature entries, and identical marginals. This adds mathematical reasoning without changing the bound itself.

improvement.justification: v1's practical relevance relied on artificially imposed missingness and synthetic scaling tests. v2 substantially strengthens that evidence with naturally missing relational classification and regression tasks, matched comparisons, and runtime measurements in Table 3. The reverse-shift, embedding, and non-graph analyses further test important robustness and benchmarking assumptions. These gains, supported by better reproducibility information and narrower novelty positioning, outweigh reduced p-value detail and limited discussion of unfavorable reverse-shift results.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds RelBench performance and runtime measurements, reverse-distribution-shift results, and embedding and additional-baseline experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original node-classification experiments, dataset analyses, distribution-shift tests, scalability measurements, and inductive and missingness-mask ablations.

results.title: Rethinking GNNs and Missing Features: Challenges, Evaluation and a Robust Solution

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and discussion now distinguish equilibrium testing in normal-form games from compliance testing against a specified policy in stochastic games. The introduction removes the claim of requiring no stationary distributions. These qualify the headline scope to better match the existing technical formulation; the principal monitoring and detection-power contributions remain.

C2.justification: v3 explains why population-game detections concentrate on compliant players with profitable deviations rather than identify the agents causing the imbalance. It also discusses screening's discarded-observation and missed-signal costs, and removes the earlier interpretation emphasizing permanently remembered threshold crossings. The main limitations paragraph remains unchanged.

D1.justification: Appendix H.2 documents the population payoff matrix, uniform and Rock-biased strategies, and screening implementation. Section 4.1 changes the code-repository address from betting-equilibrium to anytime-detection-deviation. Existing gridworld solver, smoothing, and environment details are retained.

E1.justification: Appendix H.2 adds population Rock-Paper-Scissors, extending normal-form evaluation beyond the original two-player game to interactions where a biased minority changes the incentives of a compliant majority. This introduces a distinct population and payoff environment; the original normal-form and two gridworld scenarios remain.

E2.justification: The new population comparison evaluates Split-FWER and Split-FDR alongside the unscreened FWER and FDR procedures. These screening-based comparators were absent from v1; the existing experiments retain their comparator sets.

E3.justification: Appendix H.2 introduces a 3000-round protocol and a separate 50-round screening phase selecting 10 of 60 hypotheses before testing on subsequent observations. Section 4.1 also changes the stated significance level from 0.05 to 0.2, matching Appendix H.1 in both versions; this correction does not establish that the existing experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: The population experiment adds controlled comparisons of screening versus no screening and a diagnostic analysis of which player-action hypotheses trigger detection. The existing betting-parameter sensitivity analysis, null-error checks, unknown-deviation robustness experiment, and gridworld case studies are retained.

E5.justification: v3 specifies 200 independent trials for the new population experiment. Existing repetition counts, including 300 normal-form runs and 150 Grid Soccer trials per deviation magnitude, and Figure 7's interquartile reporting remain unchanged. This is additional repetition information, not an increase in runs for existing experiments.

E6.justification: New Figure 8 reports population-game mean detection times of 2025, 1248, 1438, and 802 rounds for FWER, FDR, Split-FWER, and Split-FDR, respectively, alongside detection distributions and hypothesis-level findings. Figure 1 also changes the FDR mean from 1545 to 1546 while retaining FWER at 1765; the FDR procedure itself changed, so this is not a same-method performance comparison.

M1.justification: Algorithm 2 replaces historical threshold crossings with comparisons against current e-process values. Section 2 explicitly stops all processes together at the first nonempty rejection set, replacing the earlier procedure with permanently accumulating rejections. This changes a central inference procedure, while the underlying payoff and likelihood-ratio constructions remain.

P1.justification: The title changes, and selected passages in the abstract, FDR explanation, stochastic-game introduction, and discussion are rewritten. Notation explanations and an Impact Statement are added. The main section sequence and most appendix exposition remain intact, with a new H.2 subsection inserted before the stochastic experiments.

P2.justification: The main text changes from a single-column manuscript to a two-column conference layout, with extensively resized and repositioned displays and new running headers. Figure 8 adds a four-panel population comparison, Figure 5 updates stopping-time markers, and several axes adopt 'Supermartingale' terminology. Existing gameplay figures and tables are retained despite relocation and renumbering.

R1.justification: v3 removes Tavyrikov et al. (2025) and positions the revised FDR procedure as standard e-BH from Wang and Ramdas (2022) applied to jointly stopped e-values. Appendix A adds Velasco et al. (2025), explicitly acknowledging parallels with token-auditing estimators and detection bounds. Most related-work positioning remains unchanged.

T1.justification: Theorem 2.8 and Appendix C.5 replace the guarantee for historical-crossing rejection sets at arbitrary stopping times with a guarantee at the common first-alarm stopping time. The proof replaces conditioning Ville's inequality on the data-dependent rejection count with optional stopping, Fatou's lemma, and an e-BH inequality. Appendix D also revises the conditioning filtration and explicitly counts action-pair hypotheses.

improvement.justification: v3 repairs an important deficiency in the central FDR contribution: Algorithm 2 and Appendix C.5 replace historical-crossing decisions and an unjustified conditional application of Ville's inequality with current e-values at a common stopping time and a matching proof. Although the stated guarantee is narrower, it is better supported. The population experiment, screening comparisons, and clearer distinction between equilibrium testing and policy compliance further strengthen the evidence and precision.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same sequential monitoring framework, despite the changed title and layout. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–H support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains original simulation results and adds a population Rock-Paper-Scissors experiment comparing four detection procedures.

before.justification: Sections 4 and Appendix H report original simulations of normal-form games, Grid Soccer, and Predator-Prey, including detection times, empirical error rates, and sensitivity analyses.

results.title: Anytime Detection of Strategic Deviations in Multi-Agent Systems

C1.justification: v7 adds sparsity-induced preference for low-dimensional correlates as a central theoretical contribution. Its abstract and conclusion also narrow v1's broader claim that selected features predominantly represent linguistic correlates to a claim about what contrastive evidence establishes for individual monosemantic features in the studied settings.

C2.justification: v7 interprets linguistic cues and reasoning as coupled phenomena and explains their asymmetric representation through sparsity. It newly allows individual features mixing cues with reasoning and explicitly limits the theory to idealized decoding. Distributed-representation caveats already existed in v1. Conversely, v1's explicit discussion of the counterexample generator's limitations is removed.

D1.justification: v7 adds an explicit code-repository link, Llama Scope configuration and licensing information, and exact Gemma-2 layer numbers previously described only as middle layers. Most hyperparameters, batch sizes, hardware, runtime estimates, and steering-generation settings were already documented in v1.

E1.justification: Both versions use s1K-1.1, General Inquiry CoT, and Pile Uncopyrighted for feature analysis, and AIME 2024 and GPQA Diamond for steering. The added Llama experiments use existing tasks and datasets; paraphrase construction refines the existing semantic-invariance test.

E2.justification: The evaluated Cohen's d, ROC-AUC, and frequency-ratio selection comparisons and unsteered controls are retained. Frequency-ratio experiments already appear in v1 Appendix C despite inconsistent main-text descriptions. Llama-3.1-8B is an additional model being analyzed, not a competing evaluation method.

E3.justification: v7 introduces semantic-content controls through paraphrase-based false negatives and adds Llama-3.1-8B at layer 16 with a 32,768-feature SAE. The detailed case study switches from Gemma-3-4B layer 27/s1K to layer 22/General Inquiry CoT. Sections 5.1 and F.2 also replace reported truncation with chunking, although F.1 and Appendix H still specify truncation, leaving preprocessing inconsistent.

E4.justification: The central falsification evidence now directly probes whether activation survives meaning-preserving reformulation. v7 Appendix G replaces v1 Appendix F's case study with different features and paraphrase counterexamples; feature 4010, for example, retains the original arithmetic problems while changing wording. Existing ranking-sensitivity, injection-strategy, convergence, overlap, and steering analyses remain.

E5.justification: Both versions use the same injection t-tests, significance thresholds, Bonferroni-corrected Mann–Whitney filtering, and descriptive activation statistics. Neither adds repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, or uncertainty estimates across runs. Changed statistical values and classification counts are result changes.

E6.justification: Many Gemma-3 detection, injection, concentration, activation-magnitude, and overlap results change. The reported main-experiment injection range shifts from 59–94% to 45–90%; Table 2's Gemma-3-12B layer 22/s1K context-dependent count changes from 19 to 55. Main falsification counts rise from 196 to 248, still with zero genuine features. Llama results are added, while Table 5's steering scores are unchanged. These are revised results, not established same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The false-negative construction step changes: v1 Section 3.4 generates reasoning text avoiding a hypothesized pattern, whereas v7 Section 4.4 paraphrases the feature's own top-activating reasoning samples while preserving meaning. This is a substantive but localized refinement; contrastive selection, token-injection rules, and steering remain essentially unchanged.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, conclusion, limitations, and Appendix A are extensively rewritten. Theory now precedes methodology, methodological subsections are consolidated, and the explicit contribution list is removed. The separate potential-risks appendix disappears, while acknowledgements and an impact statement are added.

P2.justification: v7 adopts a different conference layout with running headers, changed typography and spacing, and table captions above tables. It adds the conceptual Figure 5 and Llama Table 6, redraws several empirical plots with changed distributions or axis ranges, and replaces the qualitative activation displays. These exceed simple renumbering or numerical table updates.

R1.justification: v7 expands the reasoning-interpretability literature with works including Fang, Dong, He, Li, and Zhang, and adds sparse-coding foundations. More substantively, Section 3 and Appendix A distinguish the proposed dimensionality mechanism from feature absorption, which v1 discussed as a possible explanation, and reposition the contribution around limits on monosemantic attribution.

T1.justification: v7 adds Section 3 and Appendix B, absent from v1: an orthonormal-dictionary model with a stable cue and Gaussian distributed variation, cue-retention lemmas, an exponential suppression bound for l1 decoding, a Top-K residual-energy bound, and detailed proofs. This adds a substantial formal foundation.

improvement.justification: v7 addresses an important weakness in v1: unrelated reasoning examples could fail to activate a feature because their content differed, whereas the revised paraphrase tests directly probe semantic invariance, with concrete examples in Appendix G. Narrower claims and explicit theoretical assumptions also make the interpretation more defensible. The new proofs provide a bounded explanatory mechanism rather than relying solely on empirical correlations. Conflicting chunking/truncation descriptions still limit reproducibility, but the stronger falsification design and better-scoped conclusions substantially improve the paper.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching material moved or renumbered in v7.

after.justification: v7 retains original empirical analyses, revises numerous results, and adds Llama-3.1-8B experiments in Appendix C.1.

before.justification: v1 reports original feature-detection, token-injection, LLM-guided falsification, and steering results in Tables 1–5 and its experimental appendices.

results.title: Do Sparse Autoencoders Identify Reasoning Features in Language Models?

C1.justification: The central contributions persist, but the cost-learning guarantee is moderated. v1's abstract describes a bound guaranteeing fair matchings from the learned cost on unseen data; v3 describes fairness deviation, and its contribution statement specifies finite-sample versus population deviation for costs in a parameterized family. This narrows the theoretical claim without changing the main theorem.

C2.justification: Section 4.3 changes an important interpretation: v1 calls cost learning more flexible, whereas v3 explains that parametric costs restrict attainable couplings and penalized OT is more flexible. v3 also clarifies the pointwise bound and adds specific limitations concerning individual fairness, downstream outcomes, normative target selection and simulated dating preferences (Conclusion, Impact Statement, D.3).

D1.justification: v1 promises future code release; v3 reports code availability and supplies repository access information. Appendix D adds initialization details and extensive dating-data filtering, compatibility, distance-construction and optimizer instructions. Some earlier neural-width and outer-iteration details are omitted, and v3 inconsistently reports 50 test Y samples in Section 5.1.4 versus 500 in D.2.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates only two-dimensional synthetic distributions. v3 adds a semi-synthetic dating task with compatibility restrictions and seven income groups (Section 5.2, D.3). It also replaces the three-group concentric-circle example with a two-group Gaussian-plus-circle scenario, materially changing represented data and matching conditions.

Vanilla OT also becomes a held-out fairness comparator in v3 Figure 4; previously its reported comparison concerned exact versus penalized transport. Penalized OT, Mahalanobis and MLP comparisons remain.

E3.justification: v3 replaces the synthetic antidiagonal fairness target with [[0.20,0.30],[0.28,0.22]], changes the default synthetic epsilon from 2 to 1, and revises sample sizes, penalty grids and neural configurations. Table 1 raises the reported conditional-gradient iteration cap from 10 to 2000. KL-divergence utility evaluation is dropped, and new sampling and convergence protocols are introduced.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's geometry/model comparisons and reuse timing, v3 adds explicit training-versus-test fairness analysis (Figure 4), an entropy-sweep control (Figure 3c), sample-size-dependent fairness after discrete matching (D.4), and FairSinkhorn versus Sinkhorn convergence analysis (D.5). These substantially expand the practical and diagnostic questions tested.

E5.justification: Both versions report 10 runs for the reuse experiment. v3 adds test-fairness boxplots in Figure 4 and a separate 30-run averaging procedure with shaded bands for discrete matching in D.4/Figure 7b. The bands' statistical definition is unspecified; they are not identified as confidence intervals.

E6.justification: Under revised settings, v1's reported penalized-OT advantage on both synthetic datasets becomes similar Gaussian tradeoffs but superior penalized OT on Circles; v3 reports that Mahalanobis cannot reduce Circles fairness loss below 10^-2 (Figure 3). New results cover dating-task tradeoffs, training/test fairness gaps, discrete sampling and convergence. These additions and replacements do not establish same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The core FairSinkhorn, penalized OT and bilevel formulations remain. v3 extends neural costs from a shared embedding to separate encoders for X and Y (Example 4.2), introduces learned feature-distance weights for dating data (D.3), and describes row-wise sampling for discrete matches (D.4). These are limited extensions within the existing framework.

P1.justification: The main text is extensively condensed and rewritten. Related work is split between Section 2 and an extended appendix, and experiments are reorganized into synthetic and dating sections. v1's duplicate Approaches and Metrics subsections are removed; v3 adds dedicated limitations and impact discussions and revises the explanatory narrative.

P2.justification: v3 adopts a two-column main layout, redraws Figure 1 as a broader overview, and combines/redesigns the synthetic comparison plots. v1's individual transport-plan heatmaps are removed; v3 uses group-level mass insets and adds fairness boxplots, dating/compatibility figures and convergence/sampling panels. This is substantial visual reorganization.

R1.justification: v3 substantially expands positioning relative to fairness-constrained bipartite matching and fair division (Section 2, Appendix A.2), including Castera et al. and Panda et al. It distinguishes feature-based representation, mass splitting and symmetry between populations. Structured-OT and inverse-OT references are also added, while much of v1's existing review is retained in Appendix A.

T1.justification: The principal assumptions, existence/uniqueness result and Theorems 4.2/4.4 are retained with largely unchanged proofs. v3 C.2 adds a derivation of the sample-complexity constants' epsilon and lambda dependence, including exp(lambda Ks Kw/epsilon). v1 Appendix A's explicit FairSinkhorn convergence guarantee is removed; v3 instead reports empirical convergence.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses important empirical gaps in a paper previously evaluated only on two-dimensional synthetic problems. The dating experiment, entropy control, held-out fairness comparisons and discrete-sampling/convergence checks substantially strengthen support for practical claims. More calibrated theoretical wording, corrected method comparisons and expanded reproducibility information also improve quality. Missing implementation details and conflicting test-set sizes remain, but do not outweigh these substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching central formulations and theorem sequences. Their main texts, figures, equations, implementation table and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 Section 5 and Appendix D report original synthetic and semi-synthetic dating experiments, held-out fairness measurements, discrete-matching experiments and solver-convergence results.

before.justification: v1 Sections 5.3–5.5 and Figures 2–7 report original Gaussian and circular-data experiments, fairness–cost tradeoffs and inference-time measurements.

results.title: Optimal Transport under Group Fairness Constraints

C1.justification: The central IHM, privacy, and prior-sketching-analysis contributions remain. The empirical summary in Section 4.3 is narrowed from outperforming both baselines on all tested instances to usually outperforming them.

C2.justification: V2 explains applicability through gX and the need for larger T and k in the extreme-eigenvalue regime. Section 6 now emphasizes spectral-spread costs, potentially large hidden logarithmic factors, and analysis allowing clipping, replacing the earlier emphasis on explicit T dependence and relaxing bounded-data assumptions.

D1.justification: Appendix H newly identifies sklearn.linear_model.LinearRegression as the non-private solver and revises the tuning recipe and inconsistent sketch-size expressions. Appendix K specifies the new synthetic generator, n=2^15, d=2^5, noise scale 0.01, and both parameter configurations. Hardware and code-access information remain unchanged.

E1.justification: The 33 real datasets and synthetic clipping scenario are retained. V2 adds an isotropic synthetic regression scenario with covariates uniformly distributed on a sphere and a nearly maximal minimum eigenvalue (Appendix K). Datasets newly highlighted in the main figures already appeared in v1.

E2.justification: DP-GD is removed from the two-iteration comparison: v1 Figure 6 includes it, whereas v2 Figure 7 compares only IHM, AdaSSP, and LinMix. The separate full benchmark comparison with DP-GD is retained, moving from Appendix J to Appendix M.

E3.justification: The reported metric changes from training MSE to normalized excess empirical risk. The clipping experiment changes n from 2^18 to 2^19 and response-noise scale from 0.1 to 0.2. The new extreme-eigenvalue experiment compares T=3 with sketch multiplier 6 against T=6 with multiplier 12. Appendix H also revises the documented calibration recipe while retaining the default T=3; these disclosures do not establish that all experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 Appendix K adds a targeted test of whether default iteration and sketch sizes suffice when the minimum eigenvalue approaches n/d. The existing clipping analysis is revised, while the analysis showing benefits from reducing T to 2 is retained under a different appendix label.

E5.justification: Appendix H corrects the stated 95% confidence-interval formula from 1.96 times standard deviation divided by the run count to division by its square root. Both versions report 500 independent trials. The PDFs do not establish increased replication or whether the earlier formula was only a documentation error.

E6.justification: Benchmark curves are reported in a different metric, and DP-GD curves also change beyond a common offset: its low-epsilon ranking on Concrete Slump changes between v1 Figure 4 and v2 Figure 8. Clipping frequencies change from 59%, 57%, 52%, 50% to 40%, 45%, 54%, 56% under revised settings. V2 Figure 6 adds results showing benefits from increasing T and k in the extreme-eigenvalue scenario. These are substantial revisions to reported evidence, not demonstrated across-version accuracy gains.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 retains the same initialization, private noise calibration, Hessian sketches, clipped noisy gradients, and updates. Omitting the regularization-gradient term in experiments is disclosed in both versions. Revised theoretical parameter choices do not introduce a new algorithm component.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method explanation, parameter discussion, and comparison narrative are extensively rewritten. V1's separate sketching-intuition subsections are redistributed into the proof outline and baseline discussion; propositions and notation move between the main text and appendices. V2 also reorganizes experimental appendices and adds an Impact Statement.

P2.justification: The main paper adopts a two-column conference layout. Benchmark panels are regrouped across main-text and appendix figures, axes change to excess empirical risk, and captions and legends are revised. V2 adds the extreme-eigenvalue figure and a parameter table, and corrects the duplicated Kin40k label to 3droad in the iteration analysis.

R1.justification: V2 adds references to Abadi et al. (2016), Bassily et al. (2014), and Liu et al. (2023), and removes the Hoerl–Kennard and Tikhonov references. The introduction more explicitly positions IHM against AdaSSP's failure-probability-dependent slack, while retaining the same principal intellectual foundations.

T1.justification: Theorem 1 and Appendix C substantially revise the utility analysis. V1 assumes a bounded regularized condition number and retains an explicit iteration-dependent error term. V2 derives sketch-size requirements involving the new spectral-spread quantity gX, optimizes the iteration count, and states a bound incorporating gX with logarithmic factors suppressed. This changes the guarantee's applicability and derivation, rather than merely its notation.

improvement.justification: Theorem 1 and Appendix C address v1's restrictive condition-number assumption by deriving explicit spectral-spread-dependent parameter requirements and an optimized guarantee. This materially broadens the theoretical treatment. The new stress test exposes a consequential limitation of default tuning, and the corrected confidence-interval formula improves statistical reporting. These gains outweigh reduced explicitness from suppressed logarithmic factors and remaining unexplained changes in some DP-GD curves; the revised plots alone do not establish better accuracy.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same IHM research work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison despite extensive reformatting and reorganization.

after.justification: Section 5 and Appendices I–M report original benchmark experiments and analyses, including revised clipping results and a new synthetic extreme-eigenvalue experiment.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendices I–L report original experiments on 33 real regression datasets, an iteration-count analysis, and a synthetic clipping experiment.

C1.justification: The central claims about curvature supervision, scalable HVP training, co-training, 55% phonon improvement and transfer to third-order properties remain. The v4 introduction adds the claim that PFT also benefits a stronger OMat24-pretrained model despite substantially more upstream data, modestly broadening the explicitly demonstrated scope.

C2.justification: v4 explains the Hessian-loss-weight tradeoff between curvature accuracy and energy/force/stress accuracy, and clarifies that conductivity depends on both second- and third-order force constants. The discussion explicitly qualifies applicability by higher-order autodifferentiation availability and predominantly near-equilibrium evaluation, acknowledging that successful MD checks leave broader off-equilibrium evaluation unresolved.

D1.justification: v4 adds JAX and PyTorch HVP code, the OAM training recipe, FeNNol/OpenEquivariance implementation information, and specific model and GPU configurations. It newly states that training uses 8,510 structures derived from 301,414 displacement calculations. Reported PFT costs change from 140/60 to 35/15 A100-hours with/without co-training, without explaining the reduction. The stated code, weights and data access location is unchanged.

E1.justification: v4 expands upstream training coverage beyond MPtrj by training Nequix OAM using OMat24 and subsampled Alexandria, incorporating substantially broader DFT configuration data. Appendix A.6 adds high-temperature molecular dynamics on five single-vacancy transition-metal systems from TM23, a distinct off-equilibrium test scenario. The existing phonon, conductivity, stability and elasticity coverage is retained.

E2.justification: v4 adds full-Hessian training as a direct comparator to stochastic HVP training in Appendix A.1 and introduces the stronger Nequix OAM reference in the main benchmarks. Table 1 adds displacement-only fine-tuning, previously compared only in Figure 3, and the PFT variant of MACE-MP-0. MACE-MP-0 itself and the original external baseline sets were already present.

E3.justification: v4 adds direct third-order force-constant MAE, five additional Matbench metrics, and protocols for OAM training, full-Hessian controls, backend benchmarking and 100-ps molecular dynamics. The reported PFT learning rate changes from 0.0003 to 0.0001, and the energy-comparison sample count changes from 9,959 to 9,868. These revisions do not establish that retained experiments were rerun. The original MDR test split and 95/5 training/validation division remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New analyses test stochastic HVP against full-Hessian training across three crystal symmetries, sensitivity to Hessian-loss weights of 10, 100 and 1000, molecular-dynamics stability, and PyTorch versus JAX computational costs. Additional architecture and pretraining-scale experiments examine generality. The original co-training ablation, energy-discrepancy analysis, elasticity evaluation and band-structure examples are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, statistical significance tests or uncertainty estimates for the experimental results. The added experiments retain point estimates and training curves without introducing an uncertainty-reporting procedure.

E6.justification: v4 adds substantial results, including third-order MAEs of 10.52 versus 8.35 meV/Å³ for Nequix MP versus PFT, and OAM conductivity errors of 0.267 versus 0.198 before and after PFT. It also adds MACE, displacement-only, sensitivity, efficiency and MD findings. Existing Nequix MP PFT conductivity error changes from 0.306 to 0.307 and stability F1 from 0.747 to 0.748; these are reported numerical revisions, not established same-setting improvements. Retained Table 1 phonon scores and appendix elasticity scores are unchanged.

M1.justification: Equation (4), used in the EFS/PFT objective, changes the stated force loss from the mean squared L2 norm to the mean L2 norm. The sampled-column Hessian loss, HVP computation and co-training algorithm remain unchanged. The PDFs do not establish whether this is an implementation change or a formula correction.

P1.justification: v4 corrects local grammatical errors, standardizes terminology and headings, and updates affiliation and conference text. It inserts a third-order-results subsection, additional appendix subsections and an Impact Statement. The abstract, contribution list and main background/method narrative remain largely intact.

P2.justification: v4 substantially redesigns Figure 3 around a larger Hessian-error panel, updates plot palettes and captions, and adds three appendix figures covering efficiency, sensitivity and backend costs. It adds third-order and OAM-training tables, expands benchmark tables, and makes the Matbench table full-width with additional metric columns. Existing energy-discrepancy and appendix band plots are relocated rather than newly introduced.

R1.justification: v4 adds references for OpenEquivariance, TM23, PyTorch and FeNNol, supporting the new implementations and experiments. Section 5 largely preserves the positioning relative to Hessian training, distillation and direct-Hessian prediction. The publication updates for Amin et al. and Fu et al. refer to existing cited works.

T1.justification: Equation (4) substantively revises the mathematical force-loss definition by removing the square on the L2 norm. The force-constant definitions, sampled-Hessian expectation and HVP identity remain unchanged. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v4 addresses important validation gaps in v1: direct third-order errors strengthen the transfer claim, MACE and OAM experiments test broader applicability, and full-Hessian controls substantiate computational advantages. Sensitivity analyses and implementation details also improve scrutiny and reproducibility. Unexplained loss/settings revisions and absent run-to-run uncertainty remain limitations, but the added evidence substantially strengthens the paper overall.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PFT research. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: v4 retains original empirical results and adds evaluations involving MACE, Nequix OAM, third-order force constants, computational efficiency, hyperparameter sensitivity and molecular-dynamics stability.

P1.justification: v4 moves the comprehensive benchmark results and granularity discussion from appendices into the main text, substantially rewrites the offloading narrative, removes the separate Limitations section, and reorganizes the appendices. The abstract, conclusion, related-work discussion, and title are also revised.

Architecture and training displays are separated, larger-model and ablation displays are added, and representation and gating plots are redrawn. The comprehensive benchmark table moves into the main text, Table 2 is transposed, and two panels from v1's six-panel representation figure are dropped.
