improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens v1's largely correlational mechanistic case with controlled anchor interventions, checks the validation-loss advantage at 1B scale, and examines normalization, gradient stability, and practical runtime costs. Benchmark-cell revisions also restore arithmetic consistency. Strong causal interpretations and the removal of several explicit limitations remain weaknesses, but the new mechanistic tests and cost evidence provide a substantial overall quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ExoFormer research. Their complete text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material relocated between the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v4 retains original experimental results and adds 1B-model training curves, anchor interventions, anchor-depth experiments, normalization tests, and gradient diagnostics.

before.justification: v1 reports original 450M-model training experiments, downstream benchmark scores, normalization and granularity comparisons, and representation analyses.

results.title: Attention Projection Mixing with Exogenous Anchors

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction replace v1's unqualified 'optimal, minimum-variance estimator' claim with an effective variance-reduced estimator, narrowing the headline optimality claim. The central contributions—posterior inference, unifying noise and gradient estimators, extending to flow policies, and strong continuous-control performance—remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds targeted interpretations: latent-space support satisfies the equivalence theorem's condition, proposal experiments suggest robustness, and soft-Q degradation may reflect numerical difficulty. It also qualifies toy superiority as a limited-computation finding because all variants can succeed with sufficient training. These refine the retained account of variance reduction and training stability.

D1.justification: Appendices E–F add an explicit sample-based coefficient estimator with ridge regularization, toy energy and proposal construction, metric settings, and detailed RL hyperparameters. Table 1 specifies architectures, learning rates, budgets, and candidate counts; v2 also identifies JAX, baseline implementation sources, hardware, and training times. These substantially improve documentation beyond v1's generic implementation statements.

E1.justification: The same eight continuous-control environments are retained. v2 adds a synthetic two-moon density-sampling task in Section 5.1; the additional RL analyses use existing environments rather than expanding the control-task coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds QVPO to the main eight-task comparison, SDAC and DIME on two retained environments in Appendix G.3, and iDEM in the new toy comparison. v1 cited some of these methods without evaluating them. QNE's presentation as MaxEntDP in the RL comparison is matched as the retained comparator, not counted as an addition.

E3.justification: The new toy protocol compares equal posterior sample counts with 20 RFM versus 100 diffusion inference steps and evaluates SWD, MMD2, and Sinkhorn distance. Appendix G adds controlled sweeps of Monte Carlo samples, action candidates, and flow steps, plus alternate-proposal and soft-Q configurations. These substantially expand the evaluation design.

E4.justification: v1 has no reported ablation or sensitivity experiments. v2 Appendix G tests estimated control-variate coefficients against fixed noise/gradient variants, compares proposal distributions and standard versus soft Q-functions, and studies sensitivity to sampling budgets and flow steps. The control-variate and proposal questions are examined in both RL and the toy task.

E5.justification: v1 Figure 1 reports means with 95% confidence intervals over five seeds; the corresponding v2 Figure 2 reports means with minimum-to-maximum ranges over five seeds. The uncertainty summary changes, with no reported increase in the seed count.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive results absent from v1: toy discrepancies, ablation and sensitivity findings, additional baseline curves, and runtime measurements. Figure 1 reports RFM SWD of 0.113 versus 0.1311 for iDEM and 0.1768 for QNE, using 20 versus 100 inference steps. Table 2 reports training times of 15 minutes for RFM, 33 for DQS, and 30 for MaxEntDP. These are new evaluations, not matched-setting gains over v1.

M1.justification: Section 4.4 changes the RL instantiation from direct action-space flow to an unconstrained latent flow mapped through tanh, incorporating the Jacobian into the target density and posterior score. Training interpolants now use policy-generated endpoints instead of replay-buffer actions. These alter the specified procedure, while the general RFM framework remains.

P1.justification: v2 reorganizes the introduction into explicit contributions, compresses main-text related work while moving its detailed discussion to Appendix A, and relocates proofs to Appendix C. Reverse score matching moves from Appendix A to D, algorithm material moves to Appendix E, and experiments acquire separate toy/RL sections and detailed appendices. This substantially changes the reading structure.

P2.justification: v2 switches the main text to a two-column conference layout, redraws the main RL figure with revised legends and an added comparator, and relocates the algorithm display to the appendix. It adds six figures covering toy samples and supplementary experiments, plus hyperparameter and runtime tables.

R1.justification: v2 adds discussion and citations for DIME, GenPO, GoRL, and entropy-regularized flow matching, and explicitly identifies the review's off-policy focus. The four-category organization and positioning around unifying noise-expectation and gradient-expectation methods remain. Publication metadata updates are not counted as new works.

T1.justification: The main equivalence theorems, Stein identities, asymptotic variance minimization results, and reverse-score-matching proofs are retained, largely relocated to Appendices C–D. v2 adds the tanh-transformed target density and corresponding posterior-score derivation. It removes v1 Remark 2's simplified optimal coefficients for proposals equal to the posterior.

improvement.justification: v2 resolves important weaknesses in v1's empirical support and reproducibility. Appendix G supplies controlled evidence for the central control-variate mechanism and practical design choices, while the toy experiment directly tests distribution fitting. Appendices E–F make the implementation substantially more reproducible, and the bounded-action formulation explicitly preserves the intended target density. Headline optimality claims are also better qualified. Switching confidence intervals to seed ranges changes the uncertainty information available, but the validation and procedural clarity provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Reverse Flow Matching work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable, and retained content can be matched across the substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 reports original continuous-control results, two-moon sampling results, runtime comparisons, sensitivity studies, and ablations in Sections 5 and Appendix G.

before.justification: v1 reports original learning curves on eight DeepMind Control Suite environments, evaluated over five seeds in Figure 1.

results.title: Reverse Flow Matching: A Unified Framework for Online Reinforcement Learning with Diffusion and Flow Policies

C1.justification: The abstract, three introductory contributions, and conclusion retain the same central claims about Imitation Shock, anchor-induced suppression, and T3S gains in AR and dLLM settings. The added experiments support these claims without materially redefining them.

C2.justification: V2 explains recovery through changing relative gradient magnitudes and directional conflict, and interprets selector robustness as resulting from anchors emerging early and other tokens remaining suppressed late. These refine the existing suppression mechanism and its practical implications; the principal interpretation and previously stated limitations remain.

D1.justification: V2 documents the concrete step-10 shortcut, the typical bottleneck window of steps 6–15, and the checkpoint choices used in its sensitivity study. Existing trace generation, filtering, and training details are retained in Appendix I, formerly Appendix E. No new hardware, runtime, or code-access information is supplied.

E1.justification: The represented datasets and task domains remain unchanged. BOBA, S1K, OpenThought3, code reasoning, and the downstream evaluation suites already appear in v1. The added 3K/100K experiments change sample counts, while the new code results concern an already represented domain.

E2.justification: V2 adds evaluated comparisons against GKD and SWITCH in Table 15 and Mix Distillation in Table 16. These substantially extend v1's comparisons with SFT, RRT, inverted T3S, and static-confidence masking. The existing main-table and dLLM comparator sets are retained.

E3.justification: V2 adds OpenThought3-3K and BOBA-100K training conditions, a Qwen3-32B teacher/Qwen3-8B student setting for tokenizer-sharing comparisons, and a selector-checkpoint sweep from steps 2 to 50. Existing main training recipes remain unchanged. Section 2.1 also changes bottleneck selection wording from validation to training accuracy, matching the existing formal definition; this does not establish that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New Figure 6 examines anchor/non-anchor gradient-norm ratios and directional conflict across training. Section 4.4 and Tables 7–8 test whether precise bottleneck identification is necessary through a fixed-step variant and checkpoint sensitivity analysis. These substantially extend the existing interventions, loss-transfer analysis, static-confidence controls, and dLLM threshold analysis.

E5.justification: Both versions report AIME scores averaged over 16 runs. V2 adds no new seed specification, repeated-run reporting practice, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: Existing benchmark tables retain their scores, but v2 adds substantial results in Figure 6 and Tables 7–8 and 14–18. For example, Table 15 reports AIME24/25 scores of 80.83/70.00 for T3S, 73.33/53.33 for GKD, and 75.83/66.67 for SWITCH. Table 18 reports LiveCodeBench scores of 61.41 for T3S versus 53.29 for SFT. These are newly reported comparisons, not improvements to corresponding v1 measurements.

M1.justification: Section 4.4 introduces T3S-simple, which selects tokens using checkpoint 10 instead of searching for the minimum-training-accuracy checkpoint. This is a limited procedural variant. The original AR masking objective and dLLM union-masking method remain unchanged, with the latter relocated to Appendix D.

P1.justification: The document is substantially reorganized: the method setup becomes an overview, detailed dLLM formulation and analysis move to Appendix D, and related work moves to Appendix B. Experimental discussion is regrouped, a bottleneck-robustness subsection is introduced, and acknowledgements and an impact statement are added. Most existing scientific prose remains recognizable.

P2.justification: V2 adds the gradient-dynamics figure and seven experimental tables. Table 4 changes from stacked model blocks to side-by-side model columns. Existing plots are restyled, table captions move above tables, boxed takeaways become inline text, and several figures and tables are relocated, including the dLLM efficiency and threshold tables.

R1.justification: V2 adds references for GKD, SWITCH, Mix Distillation, entropy-guided token dropout, and other related work. Appendix H.2 adds a positioning distinction concerning teacher-side token signals and tokenizer-sharing requirements. The existing related-work argument is largely preserved and moved to Appendix B.

T1.justification: The substantive bottleneck and token-set definitions, masked objectives, union-masking equations, and loss-transfer mathematics are retained. Moving dLLM equations to Appendix D and omitting the standard introductory AR factorization do not revise the mathematical reasoning. No new theorem, proof, or formal assumption is introduced.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens empirical support by addressing v1's untested dependence on precise bottleneck selection (Tables 7–8), adding established distillation comparators (Tables 15–16), and directly measuring gradient dynamics underlying the proposed mechanism (Figure 6). Earlier results and dLLM details are preserved. The terse protocols for new Appendix H experiments limit reproducibility and some generality conclusions, but the combined gains in comparative and mechanistic evidence are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Training-Trajectory-Aware Token Selection (T3S). Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, tables, and figures are readable and support reliable comparison after matching relocated material.

after.justification: V2 retains those original experiments and adds gradient measurements, selector robustness tests, scaling results, and additional distillation comparisons.

before.justification: V1 reports original distillation experiments, checkpoint interventions, token analyses, and AR/dLLM evaluations, including Tables 1–12.

results.title: Training-Trajectory-Aware Token Selection

C1.justification: The central analytic-invertibility, radial-efficiency, and mode-collapse claims persist. V2's conclusion adds claims about standard benchmarks and hybrid benefits, narrows artifact advantages to affine coupling on structured targets, and makes the coupling-flow smoothness guarantee conditional on smooth conditioner networks.

C2.justification: V1 describes bijection costs as negligible and makes broader coupling-artifact statements. V2 discusses application-dependent runtime overhead, acknowledges spline mitigation of folding, interprets UCI hybrid failures through overfitting, and explains derivative-accuracy benefits. These substantially develop the applicability boundaries and interpretation of the central advantages.

D1.justification: Appendix C adds CIFAR10 architecture and preprocessing details, including ActNorm, GELU conditioners, logit preprocessing, and deviations from published RealNVP. It also provides UCI-specific architectures and training settings. V2 newly mentions a tutorial notebook; the original numerical-stability and parameter-constraint details are retained.

E1.justification: Section 5.4 adds image density estimation on CIFAR10 and tabular density estimation on POWER, GAS, HEPMASS, MINIBOONE, and BSDS300. This substantially expands coverage beyond the retained synthetic distributions and lattice field theory.

E2.justification: V2 adds a rational-quadratic spline baseline to the existing phi4 comparison and a spline variant to the layerwise spiral visualization. The new scalar smoothness and runtime studies also compare against splines. These extend participation of an existing comparator family.

E3.justification: New protocols include CIFAR10 bits-per-dimension evaluation, dataset-specific UCI training, a controlled 20,000-step comparison of 42 cubic bijections against three 14-knot splines, derivative-error evaluation, and isolated GPU timing. The earlier training budgets in v1 Table 3 remain in v2 Table 5.

E4.justification: Appendix B.3 adds matched-density analyses of second-derivative accuracy and training-loss variability. Appendix B.5 extends the layerwise artifact analysis to spline coupling, and B.8 adds runtime scaling with stack count or knot count. Earlier radial, Fourier, and mode-collapse analyses are largely retained.

E5.justification: V2 newly specifies that retained training curves use medians pooled across six seeds within 15-step or 50-step windows (Figures 12 and 15). Six-seed mean/standard-deviation reporting and three-run phi4 median/interquartile reporting remain. An increase in run counts is not established.

E6.justification: V2 adds CIFAR10 results of 3.36–3.37 bpd, UCI likelihoods, Fourier-flow NLL values, spline phi4 results, derivative-error ratios, and timing measurements. Table 3 shows spline+ improving over the reproduced spline on POWER, GAS, and BSDS300 but worsening on HEPMASS and MINIBOONE. Most earlier plotted results are retained.

M1.justification: V2 introduces and evaluates the spline+ hybrid: stacked sinh-conjugation bijections followed by a rational-quadratic spline. The three original analytic families, radial architectures, and zero-mode construction remain; renaming cubic polynomial to cubic conjugation does not change that method.

P1.justification: V2 extensively condenses and rewrites the introduction, background, methods, and conclusion. Stacking and coupling move into the bijection section, radial flows become the focus of Section 4, and experimental explanations are redistributed across expanded appendices. Terminology is standardized around conjugation and stack count.

P2.justification: The main text changes to two columns with extensive figure resizing, recoloring, and relocation. The 1D summary becomes vertically stacked, and the Gaussian-mixture display becomes a 2-by-2 grid. V2 adds benchmark tables, derivative and runtime plots, and a spline panel to the layerwise visualization.

R1.justification: V2 removes references including Midgley et al.'s SE(3)-equivariant flows and Draxler et al.'s coupling-universality work. It explicitly positions analytic bijections as complementary to equivariant and manifold architectures and clarifies its discrete-flow scope. The principal affine, spline, and radial-flow positioning remains.

T1.justification: Section 3.1 replaces v1's broad polynomial-degree argument with a denominator-degree argument and a general linear-over-quadratic rational form. Section 4.2 changes the stated origin-derivative condition from unity to an angle-independent constant and supplies explicit corrective-sinh parameters. The main inverse and Jacobian derivations remain.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens evidence for general applicability and smoothness benefits through controlled UCI comparisons, matched-density derivative analysis, a spline physics baseline, and measured computational tradeoffs. These address important gaps in v1's predominantly synthetic/physics evaluation and qualitative smoothness arguments. CIFAR10's claimed matched-architecture gain remains confounded by architectural differences disclosed in Appendix C.6, but the other additions provide substantial independent improvements in evidential support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same analytic bijections and radial-flow framework. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across the extensive reorganization.

after.justification: V2 retains original experimental results and adds CIFAR10 and UCI evaluations, derivative-accuracy comparisons, and runtime measurements.

before.justification: V1 reports original training results on one-dimensional densities, two-dimensional spiral and Gaussian-mixture targets, and phi4 lattice field theory.

results.title: Analytic Bijections for Smooth and Interpretable Normalizing Flows

C1.justification: The introduction adds BridgeRemoval-Bench as an explicit contribution, expanding the work beyond its method contributions. The conclusion drops v1's specific claim concerning removal of unmasked shadows. The central bridge formulation, AMM, and visual-quality/temporal-consistency claims remain.

C2.justification: V4 introduces substantive interpretations of the removal-versus-background-fidelity trade-off across inference steps, explains why VBench may not measure successful object removal, and acknowledges failures on rapidly moving objects. V1's explanation of implicit shadow removal through broader contextual reasoning is removed.

D1.justification: V4 adds benchmark mask/caption construction details, L20X inference hardware, schedule-table precomputation, convolutional AMM details, and a project-page pointer. The main training disclosures—including backbone, clip length, resolutions, optimizer, schedule, training budget, and H100 hardware—were already present in v1.

E1.justification: V4 adds explicit evaluation on DAVIS and the new 150-video BridgeRemoval-Bench, comprising stock, generated, and social-media videos with varied orientations and object configurations. V1 provides selected qualitative examples without a defined evaluation dataset. The approximately 47,000-pair training collection remains unchanged.

E2.justification: V1 evaluates ROSE, VACE, and GenOmnimatte qualitatively. V4 retains these and adds Ditto, ICVE, and the Zi et al. (2025b) method labeled Senoria in Tables 1–2 and Senorita in Tables 5–6. All six participate in the new quantitative comparisons.

E3.justification: V4 introduces CLIP-T/F, unmasked-region PSNR/MSE/LPIPS, VBench, and runtime evaluation, plus a three-criterion, five-point user study with 24 participants and 1,440 evaluations. It also tests 10–50 inference steps. The previously stated training configuration and default 50-step inference setting are retained.

E4.justification: Appendix C adds an AMM on/off comparison for a bus occupying approximately 80% of the frame and an inference-step sensitivity study with numerical and visual evidence. Appendix E adds a comparative fast-motion failure case. V1 contains no corresponding ablations or explicit failure analysis.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests. V4's participant and rating counts describe its new study's sample size, without adding uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: V4 adds quantitative results absent from v1, including BridgeRemoval PSNR values of 28.2154 on DAVIS and 33.2394 on BridgeRemoval-Bench, and a user-study average of 4.57 versus GenOmnimatte's 3.57. Tables 4–6 add step-sensitivity and VBench results, while qualitative examples are replaced and expanded. These are newly reported evaluations, not matched-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: Section 4.4 replaces background-only multiplicative modulation with mask-conditioned spatial scale and shift, generated through a 3D convolution and separate 1×1×1 projections. Equation 13 also adds the missing normalization factor multiplying predicted velocity. These change the specified component and inference calculation; the backbone and bridge training objective remain.

P1.justification: The title, main section order, and most introductory and related-work prose are retained. V4 renames Section 4, revises explanatory passages, expands experimental subheadings and appendix cross-references, and updates the author block. Much of the additional prose documents new scientific material rather than restructuring the existing narrative.

P2.justification: V4 retains the framework diagram but replaces v1's three qualitative galleries and adds a user-study chart, AMM and inference-step visualizations, and a failure-case figure. Six tables and additional appendix algorithm panels substantially expand the presentation. Large qualitative figures no longer interrupt the reference list.

R1.justification: V4 adds references supporting the new comparators, benchmark metrics, FiLM modulation, and mathematical discussion, and explicitly identifies AMM's FiLM inspiration. The related-work discussion and central positioning against noise-initialized diffusion remain largely unchanged; several other reference edits merely update publication metadata.

T1.justification: V4 adds Appendix B's Gaussian bridge marginal derivation, analytic guidance term, and claimed equivalence between velocity and score matching; v1 contains no supplied proofs. Equation 13's inversion is also corrected. These are substantial mathematical additions, although the schedule reduction and score-matching equivalence remain incompletely justified.

improvement.justification: V1's broad performance claims rely on selected qualitative examples. V4 substantially strengthens their assessability through quantitative comparisons, additional baselines, a user study, component and step ablations, and explicit failure analysis. It also corrects Equation 13. The new theoretical appendix leaves important derivation gaps, and statistical uncertainty remains unreported, but the substantial improvement in empirical support and disclosure of limitations outweighs these weaknesses.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe BridgeRemoval, and their text, equations, figures, and tables are readable. The supplied v1 ends with references despite an appendix cross-reference; v4 includes Appendices A–F. The supplied contents support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: Sections 5.2–5.5 and Appendices C–E report original quantitative benchmarks, a user study, ablations, and qualitative failure cases.

before.justification: Section 5.1 and Figures 2–4 report original qualitative experiments comparing BridgeRemoval with GenOmnimatte, ROSE, and VACE, although no quantitative results are provided.

results.title: Learning Stochastic Bridges for Video Object Removal via Video-to-Video Translation

C1.justification: The abstract and three main contribution bullets retain the same central claims. The introduction and conclusion add applicability claims for autoregressive and nonlinear settings and three-object relations, while presenting the broader practical implications more cautiously.

C2.justification: The discussion newly distinguishes positional comparison from additive attribute factorization and simple role-conditioned codes. Added analyses explain incomplete transfer to three-object scenes and qualify the contributions of deeper layers. Appendix R explicitly limits its decomposition to first-layer analysis and acknowledges unresolved normalization coupling and validation.

D1.justification: Section 2.2 newly identifies AdamW. New Appendix B discloses A100/H100/H200 hardware, runtime and memory estimates, approximately 720 GPU-hours for main-text experiments, and upstream CLIP/grokking code provenance. These are additional disclosures, without evidence of a change to the original optimizer or computing setup.

E1.justification: Coverage expands from one- and two-object 1D scenes to horizontal relations in 4×4 images and three-object scenes requiring simultaneous recovery of multiple relations (Appendices K and N). Appendix O additionally evaluates complete-caption generation.

E2.justification: Comparison variants expand within retained settings. Table 2 adds an EP+PP+BP ablation, whereas v1 Figure 5(e) used combined EP+PE+PP and EP+PE+PP+BP removals; it also adds ablated comparators to the previously unablated bidirectional experiment. No external baseline suite is introduced.

E3.justification: Added experiments introduce substantive protocols: three-object training samples two configurations per triplet and evaluation measures top-1, mean correct relations in top-3, and complete top-3 recovery. Autoregressive evaluation requires free generation of the complete caption. The original 1D splits and retrieval criteria remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix M adds bidirectional attention-term ablations and wrong-ordering failure analysis. Appendix N tests transfer from two-object training and performs three-object ablations. Appendices K, O and R add mechanistic checks in 2D, autoregressive and LayerNorm-containing models, substantially extending the original analyses.

E5.justification: Existing descriptive means and standard deviations across examples or positions are retained. v2 adds no seed counts, repeated-run reporting, confidence intervals or described significance tests.

E6.justification: New results include 98% unseen-pair accuracy on 2D images and 94% complete-caption generation accuracy in the autoregressive setting. Table 2 reports bidirectional top-2 accuracy falling from 92% to 64% under EP ablation; Table 4 reports three-object complete-relation recovery falling from 82% to 28%. These extend the results under specified conditions; the original result curves are retained.

M1.justification: The original CLIP procedure remains, but Appendix O adds an autoregressive architecture with frozen visual token embeddings, an MLP connector and a decoder trained by next-token prediction. Appendix N also adapts three-object contrastive training by selecting one valid caption and masking the other valid captions from negatives.

P1.justification: Targeted rewrites expand the motivation, related work and conclusion, rename Section 8.2, and add an Impact Statement and appendix sections. The existing section sequence and most original exposition remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds four substantive multipanel figures (20, 22, 23 and 27) and three result tables (2–4). Numerous retained heatmaps have substantially higher resolution, improving legibility. Existing figures are relocated or renumbered, Figure 10 panel labels are corrected, and the existing mechanism-summary table becomes numbered Table 1.

R1.justification: The introduction and Sections 8–9 substantially expand positioning: encoder mechanisms are distinguished from downstream decoder improvements, and relational understanding from attribute factorization. Added discussions of Parascandolo, Uselis and mechanistic-interpretability work accompany a stronger claim that prior studies lack an ablation-supported spatial mechanism. Bibliographic publication updates are separate editorial changes.

T1.justification: Appendix R adds a bounded extension of the attention decomposition to LayerNorm: Equations 32–35 separate centered token, positional and bias contributions into nine terms, while acknowledging coupling through the normalization denominator. The existing positional-encoding and RoPE derivations remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the central mechanistic argument beyond the original two-object analysis. Bidirectional and three-object ablations directly test its causal relevance, while transfer failures clarify its boundaries. The 2D, autoregressive and preliminary LayerNorm analyses address previously open applicability questions; sharper figures and computing disclosures improve assessability. Natural-image applicability and run-to-run uncertainty remain unresolved, but the added evidence materially improves the paper.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study and provide readable main text, figures, equations and appendices. Existing material can be reliably matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds experiments on 2D images, three-object scenes, autoregressive generation and nonlinear-model attention.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic-data experiments, including generalization sweeps, attention ablations, RoPE experiments and head-pruning analyses.

results.title: Left–Right Symmetry Breaking in CLIP-Style Vision-Language Models Trained on Synthetic Spatial-Relation Data

C1.justification: The introduction and contribution list narrow 'lossless' or no-sacrifice acceleration to maintaining comparable task performance. The central contributions, greater-than-90% pruning and up-to-4× acceleration claims remain. This qualification is incomplete because the abstract still says 'without sacrificing performance'.

C2.justification: V2 interprets extreme-pruning failures as losing computations needed for fine corrections, explains sampler complementarity, and attributes severe observation-shift failures primarily to the underlying policy. Its new Limitations section identifies dependence on fixed budgets, representative training data and the evaluated policy/platform scope. These substantially expand applicability and mechanism discussion. The new Impact Statement nevertheless contradicts the physical experiments by describing all experiments as simulation.

D1.justification: V2 documents a front-view camera and 200 demonstrations per new physical task, and specifies the 100-step DDPM schedule used in its budget comparison. Most hardware, optimizer, training-split and hyperparameter information is relocated unchanged to Appendix A.3. Project and pretrained-checkpoint access information is retained.

E1.justification: V1's physical pick-and-release task is replaced by Stack Bowls, Insert Pen and Assembly Line in v2. Appendix A.11 adds simulation scenarios involving lighting, background tint, distractors and occlusion, plus physical hand-occlusion, laser-distraction and low-light scenarios. The original RoboMimic and Kitchen coverage remains.

E2.justification: V2 Table 5 adds DPM-Solver++ comparisons, evaluating DPM10 and DPM50 against DPM50+SAG. Existing simulation comparators and the comparator set in Figure 5 remain. 'Full Precision' becoming 'Full Computation' is a rename; additional CP step budgets change settings rather than comparator identity.

E3.justification: New protocols include 10/50-step DPM-Solver++ comparisons, success-rate evaluation at 80%, 91% and 97% pruning, and approximately compute-matched CP/SAG comparisons at effective budgets of 3, 9 and 20 steps. V2 also introduces controlled visual perturbations. Its replacement physical tasks use 200 demonstrations each, versus 150 for v1's former task. Retained simulation benchmark settings are unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained component ablations and training curves, v2 adds sampler compatibility, pruning-rate sensitivity, compute-matched comparisons, aggregate block-participation analysis and simulation/physical observation-robustness tests. These examine complementary acceleration, budget fairness, computation allocation and failure conditions absent from v1's analyses.

E5.justification: V2 Table 11 explicitly reports successes over 20 trials for each physical robustness condition, adding trial-repetition information. The three fixed simulation seeds and uncertainty entries in retained Tables 1–3 are unchanged. No increased repetition of retained experiments, new confidence intervals or significance tests is established.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3, existing latency values and per-task component-ablation results are retained, but substantial new results appear. V1 Figure 5's pick-and-release result of 54% success at 40.5 Hz is replaced by results on different physical tasks, including Assembly Line at 58% and 44.3 Hz; these are not same-setting improvements. New findings include average success of 85% at 91% pruning versus 51% at 97%, sampler/budget comparisons and zero successes under low light. The specific pruner-overhead figure of less than 0.3% FLOPs is removed.

M1.justification: The observation-conditioned pruner, architecture, fidelity and sparsity losses, shared caches and training/inference procedures remain unchanged. Equations 1–13 and Algorithms 1–2 retain their substance. The DPM-Solver++ experiment tests compatibility without introducing a new SAG component.

P1.justification: Most existing prose is retained. Related Work moves before Methodology, implementation details move into the appendix, and wording around caching, evaluation and the conclusion is refined. Author metadata and baseline terminology change, the LLM-use disclosure is removed, and new analysis, limitations and acknowledgment/impact sections are inserted.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a two-column main-text layout and extensively resizes and relocates displays. It merges the two ablation-table panels, replaces Figure 5's physical-task display, revises diagram labels and captions, and adds six tables plus block-participation Figures 14–15. Existing appendix plots are retained and rearranged.

R1.justification: V2 adds citations to DiTA and Test-time Sparsity for Extreme Fast Action Diffusion, while removing VGGT-DP and TS-DP. The broader positioning against static caching, block-wise reuse and distillation remains substantially unchanged; moving Related Work earlier does not itself change that positioning.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation, objectives and cache-update equations remain substantively identical. Neither version supplies formal theorems or proofs, and v2's additional experimental budget comparisons do not introduce a new theoretical result.

improvement.justification: V1 leaves pruning tolerance, compute-matched competitiveness and observation-shift behavior largely untested. V2 directly investigates these issues through its sensitivity study and Appendices A.5 and A.11, while broadening physical validation and explicitly documenting failure conditions. This substantially strengthens the evidence and clarifies applicability. Limited uncertainty reporting, the incompletely qualified abstract and the contradictory simulation-only Impact Statement temper the improvement but do not outweigh these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Sparse ActionGen. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable and can be matched despite reformatting, relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains original simulation results and reports additional physical-robot, sampler, pruning-budget and observation-robustness experiments.

before.justification: V1 reports original simulation benchmarks, component ablations, pruning analyses and a physical pick-and-release experiment.

results.title: Sparse ActionGen: Accelerating Diffusion Policy with Real-time Pruning

C1.justification: The abstract expands the empirical contribution from PPO/SAC to include DPC and TD-MPC, and the conclusion now cites learned DPC control. The introduction narrows coverage wording from all environments to all core environment classes. The central standalone, differentiable, multi-agent, 3D benchmark claim remains.

C2.justification: V2 interprets gradient-based policy learning through sample efficiency and explains its additional runtime through simulator backpropagation. It discloses DPC training degradation and limits demonstrated applicability to CylinderJet2D/RBC2D, shifting future work toward 3D gradient-based learning. Existing transfer interpretations and most practical limitations remain.

D1.justification: Appendix C adds substantial numerical documentation: mesh construction, resolutions, actuation periods, timesteps, CFL conditions, smoothing parameters, temperature limits, and observation windows. Appendix D newly specifies PPO/SAC layer widths, multi-agent implementation details, DPC settings, and a TD-MPC hyperparameter table. These disclosures materially improve reproducibility without establishing that previously unspecified settings changed.

E1.justification: The same four environment classes and 13 configurations remain. Policy training and control evaluation expand from easy Airfoil3D to medium and hard conditions at Reynolds numbers 3000 and 5000, with restricted algorithm participation. These configurations were already defined and runtime-profiled in v1; v2 adds their learned-control evaluation.

E2.justification: V2 replaces D-MPC with DPC in CylinderJet2D comparisons, adds TD-MPC to CylinderJet2D and CylinderRot2D, and adds DPC, TD-MPC, and a classical PD controller to RBC2D. These additions are verified in Tables 9–10 and Appendix E plots. PPO/SAC variants and TCF opposition control remain.

E3.justification: The gradient-controller evaluation changes from test-time D-MPC optimization to DPC policy training and testing, including 40-step rollouts and stopping easy-cylinder training at 10,000 instead of 50,000 steps. V2 also introduces PPO capacity controls, algorithm-level training-time comparisons, and a 10,000-step budget for the newly evaluated hard Airfoil3D case. The stated cylinder reward changes, but the PDFs do not establish whether existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New Appendix E.5 compares PPO policy/value networks with widths [64,64] and [256,256] on two tasks, testing whether capacity explains performance. Section 4.6 adds analysis of computational cost versus sample efficiency. Qualitative controller comparisons expand, while the existing grid-refinement, dimensional-transfer, and domain-transfer analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Reported replication increases from three to five seeds for 3D cylinder and easy 3D airfoil experiments. However, v2 Figure 33 specifies four seeds for hard Airfoil3D despite the general five-seed statement and Table 8. IQM reporting and the existing 95% confidence intervals with 2,000 bootstrap replications remain.

E6.justification: Substantial controller results and harder-airfoil outcomes are added, D-MPC results are replaced, and 3D cylinder estimates and aggregate profiles change. For example, RBC2D-easy's best listed heat-transfer improvement changes from MA-PPO's 20.015% in v1 Table 9 to TD-MPC's 31.650% in v2 Table 10; the MA-PPO entry is unchanged. Revised 3D estimates involve increased seed counts and should not be interpreted as same-setting algorithm improvements.

M1.justification: Appendix D.3 replaces v1's D-MPC action-sequence optimization at inference time with an adapted DPC policy that maps observations to actions and learns through differentiable rollouts with gradient clipping. This substantially changes the gradient-control procedure, rather than merely renaming it. FluidGym's core solver and interface architecture remain unchanged.

P1.justification: V2 rewrites the gradient-control discussion, separates multi-agent interaction into its own subsection, and adds runtime, numerical-setup, and ablation subsections. It also makes local terminology, indexing, affiliation, and publication-header edits. The overall narrative and main section structure remain recognizable.

P2.justification: V2 adds mesh diagrams, an algorithm-runtime figure, and the network-size ablation figure; expands Figure 5 with training curves; and enlarges several result displays. Appendix flow visualizations gain colorbars and informative captions and are rearranged more compactly. Table 4 gains timing columns, hyperparameter tables expand, and runtime-table column ordering is corrected.

R1.justification: V2 adds BEACON to Table 1 and discusses its standalone but nondifferentiable 2D scope. It adds positioning against MuJoCo, credits Beintema's pioneering RBC control work, and cites TD-MPC, advanced continuous-control methods, and PD control. The main novelty positioning remains; the Gym-TORAX publication update is bibliographic.

T1.justification: The cylinder reward definition changes from penalizing mean absolute lift to penalizing absolute mean lift in Section 3.2 and Appendix C. These expressions are mathematically inequivalent. The MDP definitions, governing equations, and solver mathematics otherwise remain essentially unchanged, with no new theoretical guarantees or proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation of the benchmark's differentiability through policy-learning experiments and broader classical/model-based comparisons, beyond v1's online gradient-control demonstration. The capacity check, runtime tradeoff analysis, and extensive numerical documentation improve the credibility and reproducibility of the benchmark. Stale airfoil-exclusion text, inconsistent hard-airfoil seed counts, and the unexplained printed DPC learning rate remain weaknesses, but do not outweigh these substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe FluidGym and provide readable main text, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–E. Corresponding content can be matched despite additions and renumbering. Internal reporting inconsistencies do not prevent comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains original experimental results and adds DPC, TD-MPC, and PD-controller evaluations, harder 3D airfoil results, algorithm runtime comparisons, and a network-size ablation.

before.justification: V1 reports original PPO/SAC experiments, D-MPC cylinder-control results, policy-transfer evaluations, runtime measurements, and numerical validation in Section 4 and Appendices B/E.

results.title: Plug-and-Play Benchmarking of Reinforcement Learning Algorithms for Large-Scale Flow Control

C1.justification: The central vision-shortcut diagnosis and Bayesian training contribution remain. v6's conclusion extends its empirical claim to LIBERO and physical pick-and-place and replaces v1's sweeping statement about standard methods failing completely with comparative improvement claims. Its introduction changes the headline SimplerEnv improvement from 11.3% to 8.8%, although the abstract and Section 4.1 retain 11.3%, creating an inconsistency.

C2.justification: v6 adds substantive interpretations connecting auxiliary-language controls and loss-weight ablations to action-relevant grounding, and interprets higher NLL/PPL as preserved task uncertainty. It distinguishes training-loss evidence from downstream execution and argues that physical-test benefits concern instruction following more than motor control. New limitations explicitly exclude validation of dexterous/contact-rich manipulation. The earlier multimodal-degradation and training-overhead caveats are retained, not newly introduced.

D1.justification: v6 discloses default λ=0.3 and β=0.1, explains query-embedding expansion and prior-feature detachment, and substantially documents physical experiments: Franka Research 3, RealSense D435, Polymetis, end-effector pose control, demonstrations per color/vegetable, held-out red blocks, and distractors. Table 8 identifies 20 OXE subsets, robot platforms, and episode counts. These materially expand reproducibility information beyond v1.

E1.justification: v6 adds physical Franka evaluations involving colored blocks, unseen colors, multiple target blocks, distractors, and four vegetables, plus broader OXE pretraining coverage described in Table 8. LIBERO already appeared in v1's pilot experiments, so its expanded results are not wholly new task coverage. RoboTwin was named and planned in v1 without reported experimental evidence; its omission does not establish removed evaluated coverage.

E2.justification: SimplerEnv Table 1 removes RT-1-X, Octo-Small, and OpenVLA and adds Magma. RoboCasa adds Isaac-GR00T N1.5. LIBERO expands from the vision-only/full-model pilot comparison to comparisons including OpenVLA, OpenVLA-OFT, π0, π0.5, QwenFAST, and QwenOFT (v6 Table 6). Appendix B.4 also introduces an auxiliary-language-prediction comparator.

E3.justification: SimplerEnv training changes from 40k steps on 16 GPUs to 50k on 8, retaining batch size 16 per device; RoboCasa follows these settings. The pilot description changes language masking from evaluation to training. These are reported protocol revisions, without establishing reruns. New protocols include physical-robot trials and a 40,000-sample NLL/PPL analysis; LIBERO additionally specifies Avg@500 evaluation.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's baseline/query/full-model ablation, v6 adds separate λ and β sweeps, including zero-weight controls, a 16–128 query-count study, and auxiliary language-prediction controls with qualitative examples. It also adds the LIBERO Goal NLL/PPL diagnostic and physical tests of unseen colors, multiple targets, and distractors. These investigate component contributions, mechanisms, and robustness previously untested in the reported evidence.

E5.justification: v6 Table 7 introduces NLL standard deviations of 0.55 and 0.54 for its diagnostic analysis. Existing Avg@480 and Avg@50 reporting remains. Neither version supplies training-seed variability, confidence intervals, or formal significance tests; the new standard deviations do not establish additional independent training runs.

E6.justification: The proposed method's SimplerEnv average remains 66.5%, but Table 1 revises OpenVLA-OFT from 23.4% to 41.8%, π0 from 27.1% to 53.1%, and QwenGR00T's eggplant score from 64.2% to 54.2%. RoboCasa's proposed-method average changes from 50.4% to 52.6% under revised reported settings. The full-model ablation changes from 63.5% to 66.5%. Extensive LIBERO, real-world, and diagnostic results are added. These updates do not establish same-setting improvements between versions.

M1.justification: The shared dual-branch architecture, 64 action queries, LLR and flow-matching objectives, and posterior-only inference remain. Section 3.3 newly specifies detaching prior-query features when optimizing the prior action loss. Because v1 does not specify this gradient path, the PDFs do not establish whether this changes the procedure or documents an existing implementation choice.

P1.justification: Beyond renaming the method, v6 substantially reorganizes the narrative: related work precedes discussion, detailed discussion moves to Appendix C, capability-preservation material moves into Appendix B.4, and limitations precede a rewritten conclusion. Method explanations are expanded, several sections are condensed or rewritten, and acknowledgements and an impact statement are added.

P2.justification: The main text and references switch from single-column to two-column layout. RoboCasa's full table becomes an appendix table with grouped averages, accompanied by a compact main-text summary. New tables and Figures 6–9 display controls, diagnostics, dataset composition, domain differences, and physical rollouts. Figure 5 is relocated to the appendix; the original principal diagrams and qualitative examples remain.

R1.justification: v1 positions Bayesian decomposition mainly against architectural or scaling approaches. v6 explicitly acknowledges BayesVLA as another Bayesian approach and distinguishes LangForce's single-stage training from its described frozen-prior, two-stage procedure. This materially refines positioning against a close predecessor. Related work also expands discussion of TwinBrainVLA, adds 3D-Mix and shortcut-learning literature, and removes Octo; StarVLA's bibliographic update represents the same work.

T1.justification: The conditional-information bound, Bayesian identities, LLR derivation, and flow-matching equations are mathematically retained. Appendix A is rewritten without a new derivation or proof. The world-model factorization moves from v1's discussion to v6 Appendix C. The NLL/PPL diagnostic adds empirical measurement and interpretation, not new formal theory.

improvement.justification: v6 substantially strengthens two weaknesses of v1: physical validation existed only as a plan, and component analysis could not distinguish the full objective from simpler language-retention training. Real-robot comparisons and the auxiliary-language, zero-weight, and query-count controls provide consequential new evidence, supported by much better implementation documentation. These gains outweigh remaining weaknesses: the introduction's 8.8% conflicts with 11.3% elsewhere, ablation prose still reports 63.5% despite Table 5's 66.5%, and higher NLL alone does not establish the claimed entropy mechanism. The improvement lies in stronger empirical scrutiny and reproducibility, not simply more results.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work, renamed from BayesianVLA to LangForce. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including v1 Appendix A and v6 Appendices A–C.

after.justification: v6 retains original simulation experiments and reports additional LIBERO comparisons, physical-robot experiments, diagnostic measurements, and ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original vision-only pilot experiments, SimplerEnv and RoboCasa evaluations, component ablations, and qualitative language-generation results.

results.title: LangForce: Bayesian Decomposition of Vision Language Action Models via Latent Action Queries

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims about learned attention priors, extrapolation, disentangled sinks, and compatibility with optimized attention kernels. The new experiments support those claims without materially redefining them.

C2.justification: Section 6 newly explains ALiBi's NIAH failures through fixed slopes suppressing distant needles, contrasting this with GOAT's adjustable prior margin. Table 4 attributes frequency-grid robustness to compensation by learned coefficients. Existing interpretations and qualifications otherwise remain substantially unchanged.

D1.justification: Section 4 newly specifies the geometric frequency schedule and base, sink-MLP activation and initialization, and normalized position inputs. Tables 8 and 10 provide substantial FineWeb and VQA reproduction details, including architectures, optimization, tokenization or visual codebooks, budgets, and checkpoint selection. The earlier C4/ImageNet configurations and repository link remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds language modeling on the FineWeb corpus and a distinct multimodal task: spatial questions about CIFAR-10 image arrangements, evaluated under unseen image-token scan orders. These extend the data and task coverage beyond the retained language, retrieval, genome, and ImageNet experiments.

E2.justification: The new spatial VQA comparison evaluates No PE alongside RoPE and GOAT (Table 9), adding a comparator absent from v1's reported experiments. Existing comparator memberships are retained. FineWeb reuses RoPE, while FLT is discussed only as related work, not evaluated.

E3.justification: New protocols include 1.23B-parameter FineWeb models trained at length 2048 and evaluated through 16k, plus spatial VQA with 50k training scenes, 10k test scenes, and validation-NLL checkpoint selection. Appendix I introduces controlled variations in mode count, frequency configuration, and initialization. The existing C4 and ImageNet setup tables retain their settings.

E4.justification: Appendix I adds quantitative tests of Fourier mode count, frequency base, learned frequencies, and initialization, plus learned-head structure and training-loss checkpoint analyses (Tables 3–7). These substantially extend v1's prior visualizations. Appendix K additionally tests spatial VQA under held-out scan orders.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Figure 4 retains averaging over three genome continuations. The new Table 6 standard deviation describes variation across attention heads, not uncertainty across repeated experimental runs.

E6.justification: Table 1 adds FineWeb results: GOAT/RoPE scores are 20.75/20.82 at 2k and 24.77/417.43 at 16k. Table 9 adds spatial VQA accuracy of 20.3% for GOAT, 17.2% for No PE, and 16.5% for RoPE. Tables 3–7 add ablation and analysis results. Existing Figures 1–5 retain their results; these additions are not revisions of earlier scores.

M1.justification: Section 4 adds an optional explicit first-token bias to the specified sink parameterization and describes mixed 2D image and 1D text positions for multimodal attention. The central Fourier-prior SDPA construction remains unchanged. ImageNet's 2D factorization already appeared in v1; its expanded explanation does not establish a changed implementation.

P1.justification: v2 expands selected method explanations, clarifies one-sided transport, corrects 'scaled' to 'unscaled' scores near Equation 1, and adds related-work and experimental appendix sections. It also updates the publication footer. Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained.

P2.justification: v2 adds a substantial set of table displays covering billion-parameter evaluation, ablations, spectral structure, convergence, and VQA results and settings. The five original figures retain their content and design, with resizing or relocation, including Figures 4 and 5. Existing training tables are retained and renumbered.

R1.justification: New Appendix A consolidates positioning against additive biases, rotary encodings, attention sinks, and transport interpretations. It adds Choromanski et al. (2024)'s FLT and distinguishes its linear-attention Fourier construction from GOAT's softmax SDPA realization. Most other comparisons and citations were already present.

T1.justification: Theorem 4 changes its stated key-only realization from two padded dimensions in v1 Appendix F.4 to one scalar dimension in v2 Appendix G.4, matching its existing proof. Section 4 adds explicit parameterization equations, although Equation 20 prints cosine–sine products inconsistent with the stated axis-wise extension of Equation 12. The principal EOT, stability, and classification proofs are retained.

improvement.justification: v1 offered little quantitative evidence about sensitivity to GOAT's design choices and no billion-parameter evaluation. v2 addresses these gaps with targeted ablations, optimization checkpoints, and the matched FineWeb comparison, substantially strengthening the empirical basis for its design and scalability claims. Spatial VQA and detailed setup tables further improve coverage and assessability. The new Equation 20 inconsistency and continued absence of run-level uncertainty limit confidence, but do not outweigh the substantial evidential gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GOAT research, with readable text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Existing material can be matched across pagination and appendix renumbering, supporting a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds FineWeb results, quantitative ablations, training analyses, and spatial VQA results.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on C4 language modeling, synthetic retrieval, genome modeling, ImageNet, and a synthetic copy-mixture task.

results.title: You Need Better Attention Priors

C1.justification: The three headline contributions—comprehensive functionality, computational accessibility, and community-supported reproducibility—and the abstract's seven-line, 39-fold speed, and 20-fold memory claims remain. Explicitly naming text and five-plus uncertainty methods summarizes capabilities already documented in v1; the new experiments chiefly support retained contributions.

C2.justification: v2 substantially broadens interpretation and applicability qualifications: it attributes laptop advantages to storage, memory bandwidth, and single-core throughput; adds hardware/OS sensitivity, absent governance/de-identification tooling, and uneven modality maturity as limitations; and explains the code-count tradeoff through task identifiers and object-oriented design. Existing interpretability, distribution-shift, and multimodal limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds an explicit code-archive link, a project-site pointer, laptop/storage specifications, and training settings for the new benchmarks. It removes the standalone Software and Data paragraph and PyHealth 2.0 pip-install instructions. The extensive existing implementation appendix is retained; detailed splits, sample counts, and repetition counts for the new benchmarks remain largely unspecified.

E1.justification: Appendix F adds actual evaluations on MIMIC-III mortality/readmission, eICU mortality/length-of-stay/readmission, Medical Transcriptions classification, TUAB abnormality detection, and TUEV event classification. These substantially extend evaluated populations and tasks beyond v1's MIMIC-IV processing and chest X-ray examples. The corresponding dataset catalogues already existed in v1.

E2.justification: The original Pandas, PyHealth 1.16, and MEDS comparisons remain. Appendix F adds quantitative comparisons among EHR models, CNN/ResNet-18/ViT-B/32, text-embedding variants, and BIOT/ContraWR/SPaRCNet/TFM-Tokenizer, together with attribution and conformal-prediction comparator sets. These are evaluated comparisons, not merely added citations or catalogue entries.

E3.justification: New modeling experiments use a stated 20-epoch AdamW protocol with learning rate 0.0001, default hyperparameters, and no tuning or pretraining. They introduce task-specific predictive and faithfulness metrics and a TUEV conformal evaluation at alpha = 0.1. Processing tests additionally cover two laptops at four and eight workers; existing workstation settings are retained.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained X-ray error case, v2 adds quantitative attribution-faithfulness analysis on a mortality Transformer (Table 21) and prediction-set reliability comparisons involving vanilla, KDE-adjusted, KMeans-adjusted, and neighborhood conformal methods (Table 22). Actual laptop tests also examine the previously asserted resource-constrained feasibility.

E5.justification: v2 Table 22 introduces mean and standard deviation over random sample splits for empirical coverage and prediction-set size. v1 reports point estimates without this variability reporting. The split count and seeds remain unspecified, and most other results still lack uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Existing workstation processing values remain unchanged. Table 3 adds, for example, MacBook results of 1,357 seconds and 7.43 GB at eight workers, while Tables 8–22 add extensive predictive and diagnostic results. Table 2 changes PyHealth 2.0 task code counts from 7/7/7 to 34/18/23 and PyHealth 1.16 from 24/7/7 to 27/14/16, altering rankings. Added hardware/model results are not same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The nine-module architecture, patient/event representation, task schemas, model interfaces, and three-stage Dask/Polars/LitData processing pipeline are retained. Appendix F adds evaluations of models and post-hoc methods without documenting a revision to the proposed toolkit procedure.

P1.justification: v2 adds a benchmark appendix, hardware discussion, and an explicit limitations paragraph, with localized abstract and wording edits. Later appendices are renumbered, the Software and Data heading disappears, and publication information changes. Most existing prose and the overall narrative structure remain intact.

P2.justification: Figure 3 is redrawn with logarithmic axes, laptop curves, and expanded hardware labels and caption. Appendix F adds a substantial set of organized benchmark tables; Table 3 gains laptop rows and Table 2 is relocated with revised explanatory formatting. Figures 5–6 receive redesigned panels while retaining their underlying examples and results.

R1.justification: CovariateLabel's attribution changes from Fannjiang et al. (2022) to Tibshirani et al. (2019) and Laghuvarapu et al. (2023), with corresponding bibliography changes. The PyHealth research-initiative newsletter citation is removed. Positioning relative to MEDS, MONAI, Zensols, and existing benchmarks is otherwise retained.

T1.justification: Neither version develops new theorems or proofs, and the mathematical descriptions of existing components and conformal guarantees are retained. Added evaluation metrics and the TUEV miscoverage setting do not introduce new formal definitions or derivations.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses an important evidence gap: actual 16 GB laptop measurements substantiate accessibility previously inferred from workstation tests, and Appendix F evaluates advertised modeling and reliability capabilities that v1 largely catalogued. Revised code-count comparisons and explicit hardware and component-maturity limitations make the account more balanced. Missing benchmark splits, sample counts, and repetition details still limit reproducibility, but the direct feasibility evidence and broader empirical scrutiny substantially strengthen the paper.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PyHealth 2.0 toolkit, and their text, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison. v2 inserts a Benchmark Results appendix; v1 Appendices F–K are retained as G–L rather than removed.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds laptop processing measurements and downstream modeling, interpretability, and uncertainty-quantification results in Appendix F.

before.justification: v1 reports original MIMIC-IV processing-time, memory, caching, and code-count comparisons, plus chest X-ray classification, conformal coverage, and interpretability results in Appendix E.

results.title: PyHealth 2.0: A Comprehensive Open-Source Toolkit for Accessible and Reproducible Clinical Deep Learning

C1.justification: The central EAAS, fused-attention, and linear-activation-memory contributions remain. The introduction revises the stated convolution-stage speedup from approximately 6x to 1.5x and adds stable AlphaFold-protein refinement as an explicit contribution. The abstract qualifies the 20x TFLOPS claim as 'up to 20x.'

C2.justification: v2 introduces substantial qualifications: Appendix D discusses an efficiency/expressivity trade-off, Appendix E explains why an edge-centric baseline can outperform the method at very low neighbor counts, and Appendix J discusses lower achieved TFLOPS than dense SDPA in terms of irregular access and precision. Section 5.2 newly attributes the dominant end-to-end gain to Triton, with EAAS providing an additional benefit.

D1.justification: Appendix I newly documents training schedules, conservative initialization from the direct checkpoint, losses, learning rates, and backbone hyperparameters. Section 5.4 supplies GROMACS 2025.3 and NVT/300 K simulation details. The code link changes from the e2formerv2 branch to main. Conversely, the throughput appendix drops v1's explicit PBC disabling, sparse-attention override, and other configuration overrides; this is lost documentation, not evidence that those settings changed.

E1.justification: Appendix G adds training and evaluation on OC20 S2EF-2M, extending coverage to catalysis. Section 5.4 adds a roughly 30,000-atom solvated protein initialized from an AlphaFold prediction, extending the existing water simulation to protein structural dynamics. SPICE, OMol25, and bulk-water coverage remain.

E2.justification: The tensor-product comparison adds cuEquivariance and OpenEquivariance alongside e3nn. The inference comparison removes ORB-v3, replaces MACE-0 with MACE-OMOL, and adds EscAIP-S. Appendix J adds fully dense SDPA alongside the previously represented masked baseline. The new OC20 comparison also includes GemNet-dT, GemNet-OC, and SCN.

E3.justification: The tensor-product benchmark changes from first-/second-order plots covering 100-1,000 operations to a specified tensor product evaluated over 1,000-32,000 operations. New protocols include conservative-model component toggles at 5,000/10,000 atoms, a fixed-size neighbor-density sweep, attention-width comparisons, and a 2 ns protein trajectory evaluated by TM-score. Newly disclosed training settings do not establish changed training protocols for retained benchmarks.

E4.justification: Table 4 adds an end-to-end ablation independently enabling EAAS and Triton, testing their respective throughput and memory contributions. Appendix E tests sensitivity to neighbor density, including very sparse graphs. Appendix J examines attention-width and execution-regime effects. The protein trajectory adds structural-stability analysis beyond the retained water RDF.

E5.justification: Timing repetitions remain 10 warmups followed by 50 measurements for Figure 1 and 10 warmups followed by 10 measurements for inference throughput. The added results introduce no new seed-reporting practice, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: Table 1 revises conservative SPICE aggregate energy/force MAE from 0.57/7.80 to 0.31/7.05. Table 2 changes conservative OMol25 total energy MAE from 2.09 to 1.16, while biomolecule energy MAE changes from 0.52 to 1.01. Direct inference throughput at 1,000 atoms changes from 140.0 to 58.33 steps/s. Numerous ablation, kernel, OC20, density, and protein results are added. These are reported revisions; the PDFs do not establish identical training/model configurations for attributing performance changes.

M1.justification: Section 4.2 revises the stated query/key construction: Equation (6) replaces concatenated equivariant projections with invariant inner products within each angular degree. EAAS, factorized message passing, and streaming softmax remain substantially unchanged. Appendix D presents its additional nonlinear scoring details as clarification, which alone does not establish another implementation change.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution summary, related work, and attention explanation undergo substantial rewriting. Experiments are reorganized to present predictive accuracy first, incorporating the former dataset subsection. The appendices are reorganized around retained material and new proof, analysis, and training sections, and an impact statement is added.

P2.justification: The original tensor-product plots are replaced by a multi-backend runtime table. New displays cover ablations, neighbor density, OC20, training configurations, and dense-attention comparisons. The water RDF becomes one panel alongside a new protein TM-score plot, and the inference table's comparator columns are redesigned. The architecture diagram and four-panel kernel benchmark are retained.

R1.justification: A new related-work subsection positions the method against Gaunt tensor products, tensor decomposition, expressivity/runtime research, cuEquivariance, and OpenEquivariance. Appendix D substantially expands comparisons with EquiformerV2/eSEN/eSCN through nonlinearities and computational costs. The taxonomy also changes: Allegro moves to tensor-product methods and ViSNet to scalar/vector methods. This exceeds bibliographic metadata updating.

T1.justification: New Appendix B proves the existing pole-sparsity lemma using associated Legendre polynomials. Section 4.2 revises the invariant query/key definition, and Appendices D-E add operation-cost decompositions and dominance conditions. The central EAAS re-indexing derivation and Proposition 4.3 proof are retained, moving from Appendix B to C.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the central efficiency evidence through optimized comparison backends and component ablations, addressing important validation gaps in v1. Neighbor-density limits and the newly supplied training configuration also improve interpretability and reproducibility. These gains outweigh remaining weaknesses: the OMol25 prose still claims 1.27 energy MAE while Table 2 reports 1.16, and removal of throughput preprocessing details weakens that benchmark's documentation. The improvement rests on stronger validation and documentation, rather than the changed accuracy scores.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same E2Former-V2 research. All main-text and appendix pages are readable, including equations, figures, and tables. Relocated material can be matched reliably across versions.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds component ablations, neighbor-density experiments, OC20 results, additional kernel comparisons, and a solvated-protein simulation.

before.justification: v1 reports original SPICE and OMol25 predictions, kernel and inference benchmarks, and bulk-water molecular dynamics results.

results.title: E2Former-V2: On-the-Fly Equivariant Attention  with Linear Activation Memory

C1.justification: The abstract and central method, alignment, and memory contributions are retained. The conclusion modestly qualifies their scope: theoretical superiority is described relative to isotropic ZO baselines, and empirical performance generally improves over the considered baselines.

C2.justification: v4 adds explanations of the rank-versus-sampling-dimension tradeoff, small absolute cosine similarities, and computational overhead, while qualifying LoRA comparisons and larger-model generalization. Section 4.2 revises LOZO's memory explanation to recognize seed regeneration. Appendix B.4 also introduces an unsupported interpretation: Qwen3-8B results are described as evidence beyond the Qwen3/Pangu model families.

D1.justification: v4 newly specifies Qwen3's smoothing parameter as 1e-7 and states that the ZO methods share a codebase. Pangu's BF16 precision and 1e-4 perturbation scale, rank 1, and K=3 were already documented. Conversely, v4 omits v1's detailed OS versions, system RAM, and NPU memory capacities. These are documentation changes, not established experimental reruns.

E1.justification: Appendix B.4 and Table 5 add OpenMathReasoning, extending evaluation into mathematical reasoning beyond the retained classification and QA benchmarks. The Pangu GPU-to-NPU scenario already appeared in v1 Appendix B; its appearance in v4's main text is not new coverage. Larger Qwen model sizes are setting changes.

E3.justification: v4 adds Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B configurations, throughput evaluation in steps per second, rank experiments at 1, 4, and 16, and power-iteration experiments at K=1, 3, and 5 with exact SVD as a control. The existing 20,000-step ZO and 1,000-step FO budgets and memory-sweep designs are retained.

E4.justification: New Appendix B.6-B.8 analyses measure computational overhead, test the rank-1 choice, and compare power iteration against exact SVD. Including LOZO in the new alignment diagnostic examines whether activation guidance contributes beyond low-rank perturbations alone. These substantially extend the retained structural, alignment, and memory analyses.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental repeated-run counts, run seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The new tables retain point-estimate reporting. Random seeds used to regenerate perturbations describe the algorithm, not experimental uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Existing Qwen3-0.6B and Pangu GPU/NPU per-task scores are unchanged, while v4 adds larger-model, LoRA, throughput, and ablation results. Table 5 reports OpenMath scores of 0.640/0.560/0.580 for AGZO/MeZO/LOZO. New results are not uniformly favorable: Qwen3-4B BoolQ scores are 0.820/0.823/0.822, respectively. The Pangu GPU average row is removed.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1 and 2 retain the same activation-subspace extraction, Gaussian factor sampling, forward finite-difference estimator, and parameter update. The default rank remains 1 and power-iteration count remains 3. Exact SVD and other ranks are evaluated as ablations, not adopted as a revised method.

P1.justification: The introduction and contribution list are rewritten and consolidated, the gradient derivation and theoretical exposition are substantially compressed, and several headings change. Pangu cross-platform discussion moves into the main text, while Appendix B is reorganized from Pangu-specific material into datasets, implementation details, and multiple experimental subsections.

P2.justification: v4 adds six tables covering larger models, LoRA, throughput, and ablations. The former appendix NPU table moves into the main text, Figure 1's panels are reordered and recaptioned, and retained tables are reformatted, including removal of the Pangu GPU average row. The existing alignment and memory plots retain their reported evidence.

R1.justification: v4 adds references including Bentbib and Kanber's block power method and original dataset papers. It also explicitly positions LoRA as a complementary adaptation approach. The central positioning of activation-informed perturbations against data-independent MeZO and LOZO remains unchanged.

T1.justification: Proposition 5.1 replaces differentiability and interchange assumptions with an L-Lipschitz-gradient assumption. Theorem A.3's proof adds the quadratic-growth justification for applying Stein's identity. The principal smoothing and cosine-alignment results remain, including v1 Theorem 5.7 as v4 Theorem 5.6; most other mathematical edits consolidate or relocate existing material.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens empirical scrutiny: v1 lacked direct rank and power-iteration ablations, measured computational costs, and end-to-end evaluations above 1B parameters. The new controls, throughput measurements, larger-model results, and LoRA comparison address those important validation gaps. Missing uncertainty estimates and sparse LoRA/OpenMath protocols limit confidence, and Appendix B.4's model-family claim is erroneous, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gain in evidence about AGZO's design choices and practical tradeoffs.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AGZO research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material moved between the appendix and main text.

after.justification: v4 retains original empirical results and adds larger-model evaluations, OpenMathReasoning results, a LoRA comparison, throughput measurements, and ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original fine-tuning results, gradient-structure and alignment diagnostics, memory measurements, and Pangu GPU-to-NPU evaluations.

results.title: AGZO: Activation-Guided Zeroth-Order Optimization for LLM Fine-Tuning

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution bullets, and conclusion retain the same scientific claims: training-free manifold-informed latent search, bounded KV memory, improved trajectory coverage with up to 13-point AUC gains and approximately 1.1–1.3× overhead, and poor scaling of hard geometric filtering. The added experiments support these claims without redefining them.

C2.justification: V3 substantially expands applicability and failure discussions. Section 5.3 identifies hidden-state access requirements and the limitation for closed-box APIs; Appendix A explains the fixed random interface’s perturbative role; Appendix H discusses over-regularization, candidate collapse, and loss of exact information under aggressive KV resets. It also interprets the newly tested chunk-length trade-off between control frequency and overhead.

D1.justification: Appendices A and C supply implementation information missing from v1’s unresolved appendix references: Gaussian initialization, normalized hidden states for bumpiness, proposal radius 0.05, score weights 0.5, prefix-cache reuse, batched rollouts, and explicit accounting for rollout and cache-rebuilding tokens. These materially improve reproducibility documentation without proving that previously used settings changed.

E1.justification: V3 adds evaluated instruction-following and generative-writing tasks through IFEval and the Literature & Arts subset of WritingBench (Appendix D.3, Table 12). This substantially broadens task coverage beyond v1’s retained mathematics and code-generation benchmarks.

E2.justification: V1 cites ToT and GoT but reports TGR-Token as its token-space control, without separate results for those methods. V3 directly evaluates ToT and GoT against TGR on AIME25 and HumanEval in Table 11, materially strengthening the comparator coverage for its central latent-versus-token search comparison. Existing main-table comparator sets remain unchanged.

E3.justification: V3 adds a controlled chunk-length experiment with S = 256, 512, and 1024 while holding L×S = 12288 fixed, latent-interface and rollout-strategy sweeps, and Self-BLEU@32 evaluation for the new pilot tasks.
