These introduce additional experimental designs and metrics. The retained main experiments keep their stated default settings; newly disclosed implementation details do not establish reruns.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained component ablations and rollout-depth/candidate-budget sensitivity plots, v3 adds chunk-length and latent-interface sensitivity tests, hard-filter feasibility measurements, selected-versus-rejected anchor diagnostics, quantitative collapse/cycling analyses, and overhead decomposition. Tables 4, 6, 8, 13, and 14 and Figure 7 substantially expand evidence about stability, mechanisms, and computational costs.

E5.justification: V1 already displays ±1σ uncertainty bands in Figure 4. V3 newly specifies three independent runs with seeds 42, 1234, and 3407, adds dispersion summaries in Table 13, and reports IQR across hyperparameter settings in Figure 13. This expands statistical documentation without establishing that the number of runs increased; the main result tables still lack uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: The numerical entries in Tables 1–3 remain unchanged. V3 adds extensive results across model scales, additional comparators, pilot tasks, sensitivity settings, and geometry/efficiency diagnostics. Examples include TGR AUCs of 78.6 on IFEval and 63.6 on WritingBench, and hard-filter acceptance of 28.5% at 1.7B versus less than 1.5% at 14B. These are newly reported results, not improvements over matched v1 measurements.

M1.justification: The default anchor sampling, geometric scoring, residual injection, and chunk-wise inference procedure remain unchanged. Appendices A.5 and C.9 add optional multiple-rollout scoring and top-two candidate reevaluation, evaluated in Table 8. These are limited procedural extensions; the expanded initialization and implementation descriptions do not establish a redesigned method.

P1.justification: The original section order and most main-text prose are retained. Changes include capitalization, affiliation and publication-header information, a conflict disclosure, resolved cross-references, short robustness and applicability additions, and an appendix roadmap. The substantial scientific additions do not entail extensive rewriting of the existing narrative.

P2.justification: V3 retains the original main tables and figures while adding Table 4, appendix Tables 5–14, Figures 6–13, and a fuller inference algorithm display. New visualizations include geometry distributions, scoring box plots, scaling profiles, throughput comparisons, and stability plots. This substantially expands the presentation of evidence, beyond page-count growth or numerical updates.

R1.justification: V3 adds citations for IFEval and WritingBench and briefly positions TGR as complementary to KV-cache compression and retention methods in Appendix B.2. The existing related-work sections and principal positioning against sampling, RL, and geometric approaches remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: V1 provides an acceptance-rate definition and qualitative scaling arguments. Appendix B adds explicit runtime and KV-memory derivations, including the approximate 1 + Ks/S forward-token multiplier, and a spherical-cap concentration heuristic for exponential acceptance decay. Appendix E formally specifies candidate-diversity statistics, including spectral-entropy effective set size. This substantially expands mathematical support, although the concentration argument is explicitly heuristic.

improvement.justification: V3 remedies an important deficiency in v1: implementation details and supporting analyses repeatedly referenced there were absent from the supplied paper. The appendices now provide substantial technical documentation, explicit derivations, controlled sensitivity tests, and direct ToT/GoT comparisons, improving reproducibility and scrutiny of the retained claims. Some additions remain weak: WritingBench’s pass criterion is unspecified, and Appendix G.1’s claimed successful example contains incorrect algebra. These temper confidence in those additions, while the overall gains in technical completeness and supporting validation remain substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TGR work, with matching methods and main experiments, and their supplied contents are readable. V1 ends after the references despite unresolved appendix references; v3 includes Appendices A–H. This is an identifiable difference in supplied content, not an extraction gap.

after.justification: V3 retains these original results and adds controlled sensitivity experiments, further baseline comparisons, open-ended evaluations, and quantitative geometry and efficiency analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original mathematical-reasoning and code-generation evaluations, component ablations, inference-scaling results, and comparisons across training stages in Section 4, Tables 1–3, and Figures 3–5.

results.title: The Geometric Reasoner: Manifold-Informed Latent Foresight Search for Long-Context Reasoning

C1.justification: The introduction narrows its optimizer contribution from developing an LM-based optimizer to employing one, and incorporates identifying time entanglement into the architectural contribution. The central TINN claim and abstract's approximately 4× error improvement and 10× convergence claims remain.

C2.justification: V2 interprets nearly rank-one parameter trajectories as support for compact temporal embeddings and argues from the precision controls that gains are not primarily precision artifacts. It also discusses stronger optimizers benefiting small TINNs and accumulated integration error in the separation method. These refine the existing mechanism explanation without replacing it.

D1.justification: V2 supplies model structures, iteration budgets or observation counts for added tasks and compact-PirateNet LM settings in Table 16; the original configuration tables are retained. It changes the listed repository owner from CYDai-nycu to CYDai-ml and adds a supplementary-code reproducibility statement. Actual code availability cannot be verified from the supplied PDFs.

E1.justification: V2 retains the original five forward PDE benchmarks and adds Kuramoto–Sivashinsky, two-dimensional flow mixing, three-dimensional Klein–Gordon and Navier–Stokes, inverse Burgers coefficient identification, and a transport-equation comparison. Appendices B.6–B.10 and E.1 substantially broaden the dynamics, dimensionality and task requirements evaluated.

E2.justification: V2 adds an evaluated HyperPINN-style comparator (Table 6), direct SPINN comparison (Table 7), and the previously only discussed space–time separation method (Section 2.2 and Appendix E.1). Compact PirateNet also joins the LM ablation in Tables 4 and 16, although larger PirateNet models already appeared elsewhere in v1.

E3.justification: The original main-experiment configurations, sampling counts and metrics are retained. New protocols include a common Adam learning-rate schedule across architectures, compact PirateNet under LM, controlled single/double-precision trials, small-model optimizer comparisons, and iteration/time-to-target-error measurements. New tasks additionally introduce ten-window training and inverse identification from 2,000 observations.

E4.justification: Appendix A.2 adds a KdV singular-value diagnostic testing whether fitted parameter trajectories are approximately rank one. Expanded architectural controls and Appendices E.2–E.6 examine compact versus full hypernetwork modulation, architecture versus training strategy, precision effects, convergence efficiency and optimizer dependence, substantially extending v1's ablations.

E5.justification: Five-seed experiments and mean/standard-deviation reporting already appear in v1 and are retained. V2 newly specifies that the previously claimed 10.55× and 2.30× speedups use seed 4 (Table 14). This qualifies their statistical scope; it does not establish increased replication or a new uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: Table 2 and retained ablation entries are unchanged, but v2 adds substantial results, including errors of 5.20E-05 for three-dimensional Klein–Gordon and 4.05E-04 for Navier–Stokes. New comparisons also show HyperPINN slightly outperforming TINN on Allen–Cahn (Table 6) and MLP outperforming TINN on Klein–Gordon under the common Adam protocol (Table 7). These are additional findings under new comparisons, not revised main-benchmark scores.

M1.justification: The core time embedding, affine parameter lift, physics-informed objective and LM algorithm remain unchanged. Limited procedural extensions include learning two unknown Burgers coefficients in Appendix B.10 and using ten time windows for Kuramoto–Sivashinsky in Appendix B.6.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and most existing prose remain. Changes include localized contribution and related-work revisions, widespread replacement of 'accuracy' with more explicit error terminology, updated publication information and cross-references, and new impact/reproducibility statements. Appendices are expanded and renumbered rather than comprehensively rewritten.

P2.justification: V2 adds solution/prediction/error panels for Kuramoto–Sivashinsky and flow mixing (Figures 7–8), diagnostic and comparison Tables 5–10 and 14, and PirateNet rows in the LM ablation displays. Figures 1–6 retain their original graphics, while existing tables are relocated or renumbered. The added visual evidence substantially expands the presentation.

R1.justification: V2 adds HyperPINN, PINN failure-mode and loss-landscape studies, and RoPINN, clarifying differences from full hypernetworks and compatibility with training improvements. These are focused positioning additions. Datar et al.'s change from a 2024 preprint to a 2026 publication refers to the same work.

T1.justification: Appendix A.1 adds spatial and mixed-derivative bounds for shallow networks with bounded activation derivatives, contrasting fixed and time-varying derivative envelopes. Appendix A.2 adds an affine-trajectory dimensionality argument. These extend the mathematical explanation, while Proposition 5.1 and the LM derivation remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the evidence for the architectural contribution through the HyperPINN comparison, additional architecture controls, precision checks and optimizer analyses, addressing important gaps in v1's comparisons. Broader PDE and inverse-problem tests also strengthen applicability evidence. Some new experiments remain incompletely specified, and Appendix E.6's Burgers Adam error conflicts with Table 10, but these reporting defects do not outweigh the substantial gains in experimental support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TINN research. Their text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices support comparison; the original appendices can be matched to their expanded and renumbered counterparts.

after.justification: V2 retains those original experiments and adds further PDE and inverse-problem results, a parameter-trajectory diagnostic, and additional controlled comparisons.

before.justification: V1 reports original neural PDE-solving experiments, including five benchmark comparisons in Table 2, architectural and optimizer ablations, and derivative-error and training-stability analyses.

results.title: TINNs: Time-Induced Neural Networks for Solving Time-Dependent PDEs

C1.justification: V1 emphasizes dimension-independent exact capacity and attributes practical limitations to learnability. V3 retains the exact Theta(k) claim but adds robust margin feasibility and LIMIT counterexamples as central contributions. Its principal geometric conclusion is narrowed to the absence of an exact-capacity obstruction, acknowledging a different normalized positive-margin regime.

C2.justification: V1 already mentions finite precision and the many required query maps. V3 adds substantive boundaries from normalized margins and conditioning, distinguishes exact witnesses from generalizing encoders, and explicitly states that its experiments do not refute positive-margin lower bounds. It also interprets the new tokenizer controls in terms of representation, feature allocation and optimization.

D1.justification: V1 includes executable simulation code with learning-rate scaling, scheduling, stopping and dimension-search details. V3 removes that listing and supplies a repository link instead. It adds token-sum pseudocode, tokenizer identification, observed-vocabulary allocation, repeated-token and chunking details, plus exported document/query vectors. The PDFs therefore gain new implementation information while losing self-contained simulation details.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates abstract synthetic top-2 subset retrieval. V3 retains that coverage and adds text-based LIMIT and LIMIT-small retrieval, introducing actual document/query tokenization and relevance evaluation rather than merely changing synthetic sample counts.

E2.justification: The WBNL fitted free-embedding reference is retained. V3 adds Promptriever Llama3 8B at dimension 4096 as the principal LIMIT comparator, using reported Recall@2 values of 0.030 and 0.543, and compares three token-sum variants. These are substantive new comparisons; the Promptriever scores are attributed to prior work rather than reported as reruns.

E3.justification: V3 adds Recall@2 evaluation with 1,000 queries per LIMIT dataset, dimensions 32–4096, and separate dimension-4 overfitting using known relevant documents. Its plotted centroid grid starts at m=10 rather than v1's m=5. The retained simulation still uses Adam and hinge loss; omission of v1's training schedule does not establish a changed training budget.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's centroid scaling analysis, v3 adds systematic tokenizer controls comparing handmade phrases, vanilla words and Qwen tokens across embedding dimensions. These test sensitivity to tokenization and available vocabulary knowledge. The separate cyclic-polytope overfit also checks whether the benchmark admits exact low-dimensional solutions.

E5.justification: V1 gives no explicit random seeds. Appendix C of v3 specifies seed 42+d for token-sum results, except seed 107 for full LIMIT vanilla at d=64. This adds seed disclosure, without establishing increased repeated runs or introducing confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests.

E6.justification: V3 adds extensive LIMIT results, including vanilla Recall@2 of 0.7060/0.9545 at d=4096 and reported cyclic-polytope Recall@2 of 1 on both datasets at d=4. Figure 1 also changes centroid dimensions from 7 to 8 at m=20 and from 23 to 24 at m=640. These are revised reported witnesses; identical optimization settings are not established.

M1.justification: V3 retains centroid optimization but adds label-unaware random token-sum retrieval: shared Gaussian token vectors are summed into document/query embeddings and ranked by inner product. It also implements deterministic squared-polynomial query construction for cyclic-polytope overfitting. These add substantive retrieval procedures beyond v1's optimized centroid experiment.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, discussions, related work and conclusion are extensively rewritten. V1's combined centroid-theory/simulation section becomes separate robust-theory and experimental sections. Appendices are reorganized into expanded proofs, theoretical comparisons, retrieval algorithms/results and embedding tables. These are substantial narrative changes beyond inserting new scientific content.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to two-column conference formatting. Figure 1's two panels become one redesigned plot with a cyclic-polytope series and witness terminology. V3 adds Figure 2, five experimental/vector tables and an algorithm display, while removing v1's theoretical summary table and long code listing; the summary table's mathematical content remains elsewhere.

R1.justification: V3 substantially revises its relationship to Weller's work by recognizing compatibility with positive-margin bounds. Section 6 and Appendix B replace v1's direct bound comparisons to Guo and hierarchical retrieval with qualified comparisons between different structured settings. Alon and Vershynin are added and Hornik is removed; Weller's publication update alone is not counted as a new work.

T1.justification: V3 adds normalized RMED/RMED-C definitions, packing bounds, the sharp margin ceiling m/sqrt(k(m-1)(m-k)), robust centroid proofs, and simplex/JL constructions. Appendix A.1 strengthens exact linear MED to min{2k,m-1}. Existing Euclidean and centroid proofs are revised, while the exact centroid bounds are retained. The new JL bound in Appendix A.3 has a displayed denominator inconsistent with its proof's inverse-square margin-slack dependence.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially improves the central argument by separating exact capacity from normalized-margin feasibility, strengthening the exact linear bound, revising proofs and correcting comparisons with structured retrieval theory. The tokenizer controls add evidence relevant to its narrowed empirical claim. These gains address important scope and rigor weaknesses in v1. They outweigh the loss of inline simulation code and the localized but substantive inconsistency between Appendix A.3's JL bound and its derivation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MED retrieval study. All 18 pages of v1 and 22 pages of v3, including proofs, experimental figures, tables and appendices, support comparison. The substantial expansion does not prevent matching retained content.

after.justification: Section 5 reports synthetic retrieval simulations and original LIMIT/LIMIT-small experiments, with numerical results in Figures 1–2 and Appendices C–D.

before.justification: Section 4.2 and Figure 1 report original centroid-embedding optimization simulations for synthetic top-2 retrieval; Appendix B supplies simulation code.

results.title: $\mathbb{R}^{2k}$ is Theoretically Large Enough for Embedding-based Top-$k$ Retrieval

C1.justification: The central contributions remain a modular closed-loop discovery benchmark and evidence that adaptive planning becomes more important as search difficulty increases. v2 emphasizes this finding in the abstract, but v1 already states it in the introduction and conclusion. The additional experiments support the existing claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning misleading surrogate scores, direct LLM structure proposals, reasoning depth, memory, structural context and transfer across chemical families. It also recommends matching component-training data to the reference set and warns of recall from larger generator training sets. Some new interpretations overreach: Table 5 shows mixed structural-context and reasoning-depth effects, while Table 6 contains planning policies below the random baseline.

D1.justification: Appendix C.4 adds implementation and checkpoint references for MatterGen and OMatG, including MatterGen's chemical_system checkpoint and guidance factor 2. Table 5 documents the added model and control configurations. Existing hardware, prompts, relaxation settings and code-access information remain; GPT-5.1 and StructureMatcher details were already disclosed in v1.

E1.justification: v2 retains the 30 intermetallic systems and adds 10 systems each from chalcogenides, halides and oxides, explicitly listed in Table 3 and evaluated in Appendix C.6/Table 6. This substantially broadens the chemical domains actually tested.

E2.justification: Tables 4–5 expand the evaluated comparison sets beyond Random/Chemeleon generators and GPT-5.1. OMatG is tested with Random, Diversity and LLM planners; MatterGen is tested with random selection. Additional orchestrators use Claude Sonnet 4.6, DeepSeek v3.2 and GPT-5.4 Nano.

E3.justification: Appendix B.4.7 revises reported filter application from all policies to the LLM orchestrator and MLIP-ranking policies; this does not establish that experiments were rerun. New ablations vary reasoning limits and history length, while MatterGen uses chemical-system conditioning. The underlying 50-query budget, five episodes per system, oracle and metrics are retained.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's pipeline-component, system-size and stability-threshold analyses, Appendices C.4–C.5 add generator and LLM comparisons and ablations of MLIP tools, generator tools, structural information, reasoning steps and history length. These substantially expand investigation of which components support agent performance.

E5.justification: Both versions report five independent episodes per system and standard errors of the mean. The added tables follow the existing uncertainty-reporting practice. No new repeated-run scheme, confidence-interval procedure or significance-testing method is documented.

E6.justification: Tables 4–6 add substantial generator, agent-ablation, LLM and chemical-family results. For example, Table 5 reports AUDC 0.48(2) without the MLIP tool versus 0.40(2) for the default agent. Figure 7 also changes the illustrated acquisition outcomes. Table 1's numerical differences are equivalent rounding, not demonstrated performance changes.

M1.justification: The MADE rollout, benchmark classes, diversity-planner equations and default LLM orchestration procedure remain unchanged. Additional generators, LLMs and component-removal configurations are evaluated within the existing framework; they do not introduce a redesigned proposed method.

P1.justification: Related Work moves from Section 4 to Section 2, with corresponding renumbering. The abstract is tightened, experimental cross-references are expanded, and affiliation, publication and acknowledgment text changes. Most existing prose and appendix explanations are retained, so this is a limited reorganization rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: v2 adds substantial comparison displays in Tables 4–6 and expands Table 3 into grouped chemistry-family columns. Figure 7 is redrawn with larger labels and a shared legend. The original Figures 1 and 2 exchange numbering and placement, and several other displays move while retaining their content.

R1.justification: v2 adds Höllmer et al. for OMatG and replaces the cited Settles 2011 work with the 2012 Active Learning book. The related-work arguments and Appendix A positioning remain essentially unchanged. Abhyankar's retitled conference publication corresponds to the previously cited preprint.

T1.justification: The discovery-policy definition, stability condition, optimization objective, metric formulas and diversity-planner equations are retained. No new theorem, proof, derivation or substantive mathematical revision appears.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's narrow empirical demonstration of benchmark generality by adding three chemical families, alternative generators and LLMs, and agent-component ablations. Tables 4–6 make dependence on chemistry, models and tools directly inspectable, while checkpoint details and the recall caveat improve transparency. Some new interpretations overstate the evidence, particularly reasoning-depth benefits and consistent planning gains, but these weaknesses do not outweigh the substantial expansion of evidence supporting and qualifying the benchmark.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MADE benchmark. All 22 pages of v1 and 25 pages of v2, including appendices, equations, tables and figures, are readable. Retained content can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds generator comparisons, agent ablations, alternative LLM evaluations and results on additional chemical families in Tables 4–6.

before.justification: v1 reports original computational discovery experiments across intermetallic systems, including policy comparisons, system-size and stability-threshold analyses, and discovery-diversity results in Table 1 and Appendix C.

results.title: MADE: Benchmark Environments for Closed-Loop Materials Discovery

C1.justification: The introduction adds computational efficiency to the encoder's stated contributions. The central claims about geometry-agnostic encoding, Gemma integration, spatial reasoning, targeted transcription, and localization performance retain their scope.

C2.justification: v1 says dynamic applications require future velocity/trajectory modeling; v2 removes that limitation and explains that independent 250-ms inference already supports moving-source localization. It also adds rationales for classification and token ordering, and attributes inference speed to transformer parallelism.

D1.justification: Unlike v1, v2 announces publicly released models and supplies a repository address. Appendix K documents the spatial-text baseline prompt, while Section 4.1 specifies profiling tools and GPU hardware. Android microphone-coordinate access guidance is also added. These substantially expand access and reproducibility documentation; repository contents are not established by the PDFs.

E1.justification: Section 4.1 adds LOCATA Task 3, featuring a moving human speaker and stationary microphone array, beyond the previously evaluated Tasks 1 and 2. Existing training datasets and the four synthetic/RSL2019 LLM tasks are retained.

E2.justification: Table 3 adds Gemma (2-stage), which receives PhaseCoder localization outputs as text, on both evaluation datasets. The new efficiency comparison also evaluates BAT's Spatial-AST in chunked and global modes alongside GI-DOAEnet. These substantially extend the comparisons beyond v1's encoder and spatially unaware LLM baselines.

E3.justification: v2 adds a computational evaluation using 10-second inputs, 2/4/8-channel configurations, memory/FLOP/latency measurements, and 250-ms versus 10-second Spatial-AST processing. It also introduces zero-shot evaluation with spatial coordinates sampled every 160 ms. Existing training budgets, decoding settings, and accuracy/WER protocols remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The moving-source robustness test and representative trajectory in Appendix E/Figure 4 are new. Existing microphone-count sensitivity results, UMAP projections, reasoning breakdowns, model-size findings, and transcription examples are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Mean/median WER reporting and the appendix's correct/total counts are retained without a new uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: v2 adds efficiency results, two Gemma cascade rows, and LOCATA moving-source MAE of 9.85 degrees. The cascade achieves 57.61% synthetic reasoning accuracy versus the unchanged fine-tuned model's 76.76%. Existing benchmark-table scores remain unchanged. v1's separate synthetic-summary statistics are replaced by discussion of the retained microphone-count results.

M1.justification: The encoder architecture, positional embeddings, classification losses, two-stage training, spatial-token integration, and Gemma LoRA procedure remain unchanged. Added explanations clarify existing choices; the new text-based cascade is a comparison baseline.

P1.justification: v2 copyedits the prose, expands several explanations, adds conflict-of-interest and impact statements, and reorganizes the appendices. The main section sequence and most of the explanatory narrative remain recognizable.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from single-column to two-column conference formatting. The task-definition table moves to Appendix D and is expanded, a computational table and trajectory figure are added, Table 3 gains baseline rows, and existing appendix figures and tables are substantially reflowed.

R1.justification: New Section 2.3 discusses SpatialSonic, ViSAGe, SALM, and SmartDJ, positioning universal spatial encoders as potential controls for generation and editing. Profiling-software references are also added. The existing localization and spatial-LLM positioning is retained.

T1.justification: The positional-embedding and loss definitions, coordinate transformations, and label-discretization equations in Appendices A–B are retained. No new theorem, proof, or substantive mathematical derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses an important weakness in v1's validation by adding an LLM baseline explicitly supplied with spatial information, with its prompt documented in Appendix K. The efficiency comparison and moving-source evaluation also test practical properties previously unsupported by measurements. Together these substantially strengthen the evidence for the approach while retaining the original results. Model-release documentation further improves reproducibility, although neither version provides repeated-run uncertainty estimates.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PhaseCoder/Gemma 3n research. Text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and can be matched despite reformatting and appendix reordering.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds computational-efficiency measurements, a spatial-text Gemma baseline, and moving-speaker localization results.

before.justification: v1 reports original encoder localization experiments, fine-tuned Gemma results on four spatial-audio tasks, and appendix analyses.

results.title: PhaseCoder: Microphone Geometry-Agnostic Spatial Audio Understanding for Multimodal LLMs

C1.justification: The introduction strengthens novelty positioning from an efficient edge inference engine to the first system accelerating mobile and edge MoE inference through lossless compression. The central system contributions and abstract's headline latency and throughput claims remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands interpretation of the gains: approximately 76% is attributed to the core system and 24% to cache management, with cache planning described as providing a moderate additional benefit. It interprets page-cache support as opportunistic, explains robustness through stable popularity ranks, discusses FineMoE's edge limitations, and explicitly identifies Jetson-only evaluation and separate-memory adaptation as future work.

D1.justification: v2 supplies a code-access URL, documents compressor-extension APIs, and discloses the existing ablation's 10 GB memory footprint and batch size 16. Appendix E.1 adds initialization costs and less than 1 GB additional buffering overhead. The main implementation stack and hardware specifications are retained; repository contents were not inspected.

E1.justification: The ShareGPT workload, three MoE models, and two Jetson configurations remain unchanged. v2 extends tested operating scenarios to background memory pressure and deliberately mismatched planning inputs. It adds no dataset, language, application domain, or evaluated hardware family.

E2.justification: Appendix E.3 newly evaluates FineMoE against ZipMoE on Qwen1.5-MoE across 5–30 GB memory footprints, reporting TTFT and TPOT in Tables 5–6. FineMoE's underlying work was already cited in v1 but was not evaluated there. Existing main comparators are retained.

E3.justification: v2 adds controlled evaluation designs: background RAM consumption of 0, 20, 24, 28, and 32 GB; planning-distribution smoothing with alpha from 0 to 1; and end-to-end compressor comparisons across memory budgets. These substantially extend the controls supporting performance attribution and robustness. The 10 GB memory footprint and batch size 16 newly stated for the existing cache ablation are disclosures, not demonstrated setting changes.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained cache-policy ablation, v2 adds quantitative component-gain attribution, OS page-cache isolation, sensitivity to inaccurate popularity estimates, expert-activation trace analysis, and end-to-end compressor sensitivity. Tables 1–2, 4, and 7 and Figures 11–12 investigate several previously untested explanations and robustness questions.

E5.justification: Both versions retain Figure 9's average curves and shaded ranges between the top and bottom 10% values. v2 adds no repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or revised uncertainty-estimation procedures.

E6.justification: Original benchmark outcomes are retained, while substantial new results appear in Tables 1–7. Table 2 reports 56.64% TTFT and 53.32% TPOT reductions versus MoE-Infinity under 32 GB background memory consumption. Table 4 reports 16.8% and 9.5% slowdowns at maximum planning perturbation. Initialization timings, FineMoE comparisons, and compressor-specific latencies are also newly reported.

M1.justification: The bit-field compression pipeline, cache-affinity scheduler, hierarchical cache management, and Algorithms 1–4 are retained. Compressor APIs receive additional documentation, while adaptation to separate CPU/GPU memory is proposed as future work; neither establishes an implemented method change.

P1.justification: The original narrative and method exposition largely remain intact. v2 corrects wording, clarifies passages in Appendix B, adds Discussion and Extended Results sections and acknowledgements, and moves Algorithm 4 alongside Appendix C. Author contribution and publication information are also updated.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the visual presentation with seven tables covering attribution, memory pressure, initialization, sensitivity, FineMoE, and compressors, plus Figures 11–12 showing memory-pressure contributions and activation distributions. Figures 1–10 are retained. Algorithm 4 is relocated, and the scheduling bound becomes a displayed, numbered equation.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations on quantization, edge computing, and scheduling, including Fu et al. and scheduling work by Davies et al. and Maiti et al. It also introduces explicit first-system positioning. FineMoE was already cited, and several other reference changes update metadata rather than introduce different works.

T1.justification: Appendix E.2 adds the formal perturbation definition F_tilde = (1-alpha)F + alpha E(F) for the sensitivity experiment. The existing scheduling approximation bound, maximum-entropy theorem, and proofs in Appendices A–D remain unchanged; their other edits concern explanation, placement, and equation numbering.

improvement.justification: v1 acknowledged page-cache benefits without isolating their contribution and did not empirically test inaccurate planning estimates. v2 addresses these important evidential gaps through memory-pressure controls and sensitivity experiments, while clarifying component contributions and adding a relevant comparator, deployment costs, and code-access information. This substantially strengthens support for the central efficiency claim. Run-count and uncertainty-reporting gaps remain, and broader hardware applicability is still untested.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ZipMoE, with matching methods, original experiments, and theoretical appendices. Text, equations, tables, and figures support reliable comparison. The relocated cache-planning algorithm and renumbered equations can be matched.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds memory-pressure experiments, planning sensitivity tests, initialization measurements, and further system comparisons in Section 5.1 and Appendix E.

before.justification: v1 reports original compression and hardware measurements, inference benchmarks on three MoE models, and cache-management ablations in Figures 1–4 and 7–10.

results.title: ZipMoE: Efficient On-Device MoE Serving via Lossless Compression and Cache-Affinity Scheduling

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution list retain the same framework, 41-model extraction claim, HHH and identity findings, and 18.4% defense reduction. The added conclusion paragraph about downstream attacks reiterates risks already raised in v1's introduction and discussion rather than introducing a new central capability claim.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly defines self-evolution as selection-policy adaptation over fixed, hand-designed skills and interprets the new ablations as evidence for adaptive selection. Its limitations now distinguish black-box consistency from accuracy and explain paraphrase-bounded fidelity. These are substantive qualifications within otherwise largely retained interpretations.

D1.justification: A new footnote announces a project repository containing code, data, and extracted ground-truth files; v1 lacks this project-access information. v2 also documents the new comparison prompt's length and source-prompt validation for two CLIs. The PDFs establish these disclosures, not the linked resources' accessibility.

E1.justification: Section 4.8 substantially extends deployment coverage beyond the original Claude Code case with evaluations on Gemini CLI, Codex CLI, Cursor Agent CLI, Perplexity Sonar, and Copilot CLI. These add native assistant environments and prompt configurations, including two systems with source-accessible reference prompts. Original coverage remains.

E2.justification: v2 directly evaluates PLeak, Raccoon, and Zhang et al.'s output-inversion method in Tables 5 and 8; v1 discussed these works without such comparisons. Tables 6–7 also introduce bare-agent, introspection-only, random-selection, and unguided controls. The original defense comparators remain.

E3.justification: New protocols include a four-model comparison using a known 1,168-token prompt and best ground-truth similarity at B=3, Sonnet 4 ablations at B=3/5/10, six-model agent evaluation at B=5, and production evaluation with UCB at B=15. These supplement the unchanged original B=20 setup rather than establish reruns under its conditions.

E4.justification: Tables 6–7 add substantive tests of skill selection, UCB, query budget, and full versus unguided agents. These directly examine the framework's contribution beyond simple requests and random exploration. Existing defense and threshold analyses remain, but v1's detailed convergence table is removed while its aggregate finding is retained.

E5.justification: Table 7 newly reports means and standard deviations over three seeds for the six-model agent comparison. v1 had no comparable across-seed uncertainty reporting. The existing convergence correlation and p-value remain unchanged; the new reporting does not establish increased replication of the original experiments.

E6.justification: Tables 5–8 add extensive results: for example, GPT-4o at B=3 scores 0.727 for JustAsk versus 0.701 for Raccoon, and production-system averages are 0.703 versus 0.606. The full agent outperforms the unguided agent on five of six targets but scores lower on Mistral Large. Original black-box and defense scores remain unchanged. v1 Table 7's per-turn convergence values disappear, although r=0.94 remains reported.

M1.justification: The core UCB procedure, default skill taxonomy, and Appendix B algorithm remain unchanged. v2 introduces an evaluated +Raccoon variant that adds Raccoon templates to the selectable skill pool (Section 4.8, Table 8), implementing an extension contemplated in v1. The fixed-taxonomy explanation in Section 3.1 clarifies the existing learner.

P1.justification: The related-work prose is condensed, and the method explanation, conclusion, and limitations receive localized revisions. Three experimental subsections and acknowledgements are added, alongside correspondence and bibliographic edits. Most existing prose and the appendix organization remain intact.

P2.justification: The empirical displays are substantially expanded with baseline, budget-ablation, uncertainty, and production-comparison tables (v2 Tables 5–8). v1's HHH summary and convergence tables are removed; the HHH values remain in prose. Figure 5 moves later, while the existing figures and overall visual style are preserved.

R1.justification: v2 adds Ma et al. (2025) on model and agent safety and Wu et al. (2026) on internal safety collapse. It further positions adaptive selection against fixed extraction strategies and describes incorporating prior templates. Changed author lists for PANDORA, RACE, ProxyPrompt, and other retained works are bibliographic updates rather than new cited research.

T1.justification: The UCB equation and update rule, Appendix B algorithm, and Appendix C similarity definitions remain unchanged. No new theorem, proof, substantive mathematical derivation, or formal assumption is introduced.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked direct evidence establishing the framework's value over simpler agents and prior extraction methods. v2's controlled comparisons, component and budget ablations, and repeated-seed evaluation address that central deficiency and expose conditions where the framework helps or fails. Clearer fidelity limitations also improve interpretation. Removing the convergence table reduces transparency, and reference prompts for the closed production systems remain underexplained, but the added controlled evidence substantially improves the paper overall.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same JustAsk study and provide readable text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–M. Sections and displays can be matched across renumbering, and the appendices retain their substantive content.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, component ablations, repeated-seed agent evaluations, and production-system extraction results in Tables 5–8.

before.justification: v1 reports original Claude Code extraction results, experiments on 41 black-box models, controlled defense evaluations, and extraction and identity analyses.

results.title: Just Ask: Curious Code Agents Reveal System Prompts in Frontier LLMs

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion retain the same contributions: separation between zero and one noisy string, equivalence across positive finite noise levels, and characterization of non-uniform noise-dependent generation. Theorems 2.14–2.17 in v1 correspond to 2.16–2.19 in v2 without changed claims.

C2.justification: The interpretations of the noiseless/noisy separation and the collapse across positive noise levels remain unchanged. Added proof intuition and the explicit phrase 'hierarchy collapses' explain existing conclusions without introducing new limitations or applicability claims.

D1.justification: No implementation, hyperparameter, hardware, runtime, or code/data-access information is added or revised. The additional technical material concerns mathematical reasoning rather than implementation or experimental reproducibility.

E1.justification: Neither version uses datasets or conducts training or evaluation tasks. Newly discussed generation settings appear only as related work.

E2.justification: Neither version evaluates comparison methods or empirical baselines. The additional citations in v2 do not constitute evaluated comparators.

E3.justification: Neither version contains experimental protocols, evaluation metrics, data splits, or training settings. The theoretical generation definitions retain the same noise allowance.

E4.justification: No empirical ablations, robustness tests, sensitivity analyses, or case studies appear in either version. The adversarial language constructions remain mathematical proofs.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated runs, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or statistical uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: There are no empirical result entries in either version. The principal mathematical bounds, separations, and equivalence conclusions are retained; changes to their supporting proofs are assessed under T1.

M1.justification: The generation procedures in Lemmas 3.1 and 4.1 and the construction in Algorithm 1 retain their steps. The revised partition construction in Lemma 3.2 repairs a mathematical proof rather than changing the generation method.

P1.justification: The title changes from 'Quantifying Noise in Language Generation' to 'Characterizing the Effect of Noise in Language Generation in the Limit.' V2 expands related-work prose and proof explanations and makes localized wording and notation corrections, while retaining the overall section order and narrative.

P2.justification: The displayed sequence of ordered lists in the separation proof changes from two lines to one, and the unchanged Algorithm 1 moves from midpage to a page top during reflow. The single-column design is retained, with no added figures or tables.

R1.justification: Section 1.1 substantially broadens its literature coverage with nine additional works, including mistake-bounded, agnostic, metric-space, replay, private, and contrastive generation and list identification. It also explicitly positions finite-noise results against the previously cited infinite-contamination work. Renamed citation keys and publication metadata updates are not counted as new works.

T1.justification: V2 substantially repairs Lemma 3.2: v1 used an arbitrary partition without establishing nonempty consistency sets, whereas v2 constructs a partition satisfying that necessary condition and justifies selecting a finite witness of the required size. V2 also adds monotonicity Lemmas 2.10 and 2.13, makes the noisy-closure-dimension definition more precise, and corrects the uniform-bound argument in Lemma 4.1 and the countability wording in Lemma 4.5. These strengthen proofs supporting the central characterization results.

improvement.justification: V2 repairs an important logical gap in Lemma 3.2, which underpins the main noise-equivalence and characterization results. V1 inferred a dimension bound from finite closure without ensuring the required nonempty consistency sets; v2 explicitly constructs a partition ensuring them. Together with the supporting monotonicity proofs and corrected quantifier arguments, this substantially improves mathematical reliability while preserving the headline conclusions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs are complete, readable versions of the same theoretical work despite the changed title. Their definitions, theorems, proofs, and algorithm match reliably. Neither PDF contains an appendix.

after.justification: V2 remains entirely theoretical. Its added lemmas, revised proofs, and expanded literature discussion introduce no original empirical results.

before.justification: V1 reports mathematical definitions, constructions, and proofs, with no original experimental, simulation, or data-analysis results. Empirical studies mentioned in the introduction are attributed to other work.

results.title: Characterizing the Effect of Noise in Language Generation in the Limit

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution list retain the same substantive claims about factorized reward modeling, improved mathematical and dialogue RLHF performance, and reduced length and sycophancy bias. The conclusion's revised invariance-motivated phrasing does not materially change those central claims.

C2.justification: v1 explicitly emphasizes the absence of causal-identification guarantees. v2 rewrites the limitations around conditional identifiability and interprets answer-edit sensitivity together with artifact invariance as support for causal decomposition. It also adds interpretations of model scalability, coefficient stability, judge agreement, and InfoRM's formatting-related accuracy collapse.

D1.justification: Appendix B adds last-nonpadding-token embedding extraction, full backbone fine-tuning, baseline configurations, judge decoding parameters, preference-data provenance, and code/data access pointers. Additional sections document sweep settings and model-size training costs. These materially expand reproducibility information without establishing changes to the original implementation.

E1.justification: The mathematical reasoning and dialogue datasets remain unchanged. Appendix I adds a distinct input scenario on the existing seven math benchmarks: changing final boxed answers from correct to wrong and vice versa while preserving the remaining response.

E2.justification: ODIN and MMD-based regularization, previously discussed but not evaluated, become actual comparators for length-bias mitigation and sycophantic-artifact robustness in Appendix F.1, Tables 11–12, and Figure 7. This substantially extends comparison against methods targeting the paper's central problem.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce five coefficient sweeps, 1.5B and 72B backbones alongside 7B, and DeepSeek-V3.2 and Kimi-k2.5 dialogue judges. Appendix I specifies 100 preference pairs per dataset per intervention direction and reward-change metrics. The original benchmark protocols are otherwise retained.

E4.justification: The original component ablations and examples are retained. New analyses test coefficient sensitivity, dependence on backbone size, robustness to judge choice, performance against artifact-specific mitigation, and sensitivity to controlled final-answer edits, substantially broadening the diagnostic evidence.

E5.justification: Tables 1–3 newly report means and standard deviations over three runs. Appendix F.5 adds 10,000 paired bootstrap resamples and 95% percentile confidence intervals for preference margins. v1 reports neither practice; this establishes additional reporting, not an explicit increase in run count.

E6.justification: The original main-table point estimates and ablation results are retained, while Tables 11–17 and Figures 7–8 add substantial results. For example, Table 11 reports math OOD accuracy of 83.2% for ODIN and 83.6% for MMD versus the retained 85.6% for CausalRM; Table 17 newly reports CausalRM's 86.1% and 86.6% intervention-direction consistency.

M1.justification: The factorized Gaussian encoder, causal reward head, reconstruction decoder, adversarial head with gradient reversal, and training objective remain unchanged. Algorithm 1 moves to Appendix A; the additional implementation disclosures do not establish a changed method.

P1.justification: The main narrative remains largely verbatim. v2 relocates Algorithm 1 and the existing derivation, reorganizes appendix sections, rewrites the limitations, adds acknowledgements, and makes limited wording and cross-reference edits. Most expansion consists of new scientific content rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is redrawn with colored branches and revised arrangement; Tables 1–3 gain uncertainty displays. Seven new tables and two new figures present the additional analyses. Existing qualitative examples are relocated and renumbered, rather than newly added.

R1.justification: v2 adds RewardBench and Ng et al. on guaranteed reward-model debiasing, while removing several identifiability references used in v1's limitations. The principal related-work discussion and positioning relative to InfoRM and artifact-specific approaches remain largely unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendices H and J add an identifiability definition, Theorem H.2, two lemmas, and proofs under invertible mixing, environment variability, representation invariance, and sufficiency assumptions. The earlier variational information-bottleneck derivation is retained and relocated from Appendix A to D.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for robustness through artifact-specific competitors, alternative judges, and controlled answer interventions, while filling important implementation and data-provenance gaps. A reporting flaw limits the statistical additions: Table 16 gives 42.9% average wins against Standard RM, whereas the six corresponding Table 3 entries average 52.5%, without explaining the discrepancy. Despite this localized inconsistency, the added diagnostic evidence and reproducibility information provide a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CausalRM work. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support comparison, including matching relocated derivations, ablations, and qualitative examples.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds artifact-specific comparisons, hyperparameter and model-size studies, alternative-judge evaluations, bootstrap analysis, and controlled answer-edit interventions.

before.justification: v1 reports original reward-model and downstream RLHF experiments on mathematical reasoning and dialogue, including bias tests, component ablations, and qualitative examples.

results.title: Factored Causal Representation Learning for Robust Reward Modeling in RLHF

C1.justification: The central claims about the optimization-inference mismatch, CAGE under unknown compression budgets, and the need for compression-aware evaluation remain. The abstract's replacement of robustness overestimation with incomplete exposure of vulnerabilities restates the same scientific claim.

C2.justification: Appendix E.9 adds a substantive applicability boundary, attributing limited black-box gains to difficulty transferring compression-alignment signals. E.10 interprets the optimizer and budget-sampling controls, while F.1 discusses stronger defenses alongside training and inference costs. The original Appendix G limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds a source-code access link, specifies the transfer surrogate and its PGD settings, documents resolution and encoder controls for RobustCLIP, and reports attack runtime. The original core hyperparameters and RTX 4090 hardware disclosure remain unchanged.

E1.justification: The original VQA-v2, TextVQA and GQA coverage remains. Appendix E.7 adds generative captioning on COCO, a different task despite COCO already supplying VQA-v2 images; E.11 adds driving-focused DriveQA. These substantially extend task and domain coverage.

E2.justification: Beyond the retained VEAttack comparison, v2 evaluates AttackVLM-ii and VT-Attack in Table 13 and an EOT budget-sampling baseline in Table 17. It also adds a Random selection control in Table 3 and RobustCLIP/FARE and DPS defense comparisons in Tables 20–21.

E3.justification: Original main settings remain, while new protocols include InternVL3-8B, 100-sample captioning evaluation with CIDEr, black-box encoder transfer using epsilon 16/255 and 100 PGD steps, APGD/MI-FGSM comparisons, and matched 224-by-224 standard/FARE victims. Section 5.3 also replaces CRA with its complement, CRD.

E4.justification: The original component, perturbation-budget, weighting, scoring and budget-prior ablations remain. New analyses test encoder transfer, budget sampling versus CAGE, optimizer dependence, computational cost, a random-selection defense control, and resilience against existing defenses.

E5.justification: Neither version reports seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals or significance tests. Additional result rows and average runtime measurements do not introduce a new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Main Table 2 and the retained Qwen, ablation and detection scores are unchanged, but v2 adds extensive results. For example, Table 7 reports 39.9% versus 33.4% robust accuracy for baseline versus CAGE on InternVL3/VisionZIP at 72 tokens; Table 14 reports captioning CIDEr of 0.1998 versus 0.1090 at 64 tokens. These are new comparisons, not improvements over v1 runs.

M1.justification: v2 corrects the specified RDA gradient flow: Section 4.3 changes the stopped-gradient distribution from p(s) to p(d), and Algorithm 1 explicitly detaches the distortion target. The remaining CAGE procedure is retained; the PDFs do not establish whether the implementation changed.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence remain. Local edits correct RDA wording, introduce CRD terminology, update correspondence and publication information, and add acknowledgements. Appendix D is reorganized for multiple LVLMs, and E/F gain experiment-specific subsections.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the tabular presentation across model, task, attack, transfer, optimizer, runtime and defense comparisons. Table 3 gains Random rows; v1 Table 11 moves into the main text as v2 Table 4; Figure 4 is redrawn for CRD with reversed token-budget ordering. Other figures are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds literature and discussion on robust encoders, DPS, encoder-based transfer and reasoning applications while retaining its original research positioning. VEAttack's updated publication citation refers to the same work, rather than a newly introduced research direction.

T1.justification: Section 5.3 revises the defined normalized metric from CRA = R/C to CRD = 1 - R/C, measuring degradation instead of retention. This limited mathematical-definition change adds no theorem or proof; the existing derivations and defense formulas remain.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation by addressing v1's reliance on one principal attack baseline and VQA tasks, testing alternative budget handling and optimizers, and documenting limited black-box transfer. Runtime and existing-defense comparisons improve practical assessment, while the RDA correction resolves an implementation ambiguity. Some added protocols remain underspecified and uncertainty estimates are absent, but the gains in evidential support and applicability assessment are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CAGE study. Their text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched reliably despite additions, renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original results on another LVLM, additional tasks, attack comparators, transfer, optimizers, runtime and existing defenses.

before.justification: v1 reports original attack evaluations on LLaVA and Qwen2.5-VL, component and hyperparameter ablations, and defense and detection experiments.

results.title: On the Adversarial Robustness of Large Vision-Language Models under Visual Token Compression

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same core contributions: representation-space information compression, standard and zero-shot regimes, and claimed utility and efficiency advantages. The conclusion's maximum speed-up changes from 754× to 757×, a numerical update without a substantive change in the claim.

C2.justification: New Section 5 explicitly restricts protection to black-box access, acknowledges recoverable information in the frozen encoder, and discusses permanent inference overhead and dependence on Neural Collapse. Appendix G interprets proxy degradation as a privacy–utility trade-off. Section 4.3 also replaces the interpretation that SISA fails to forget with successful forgetting constrained by retraining costs.

D1.justification: v2 adds split-selection details, specifies Gaussian corruption of proxy weights, and reports transformation inference overheads of 0.59 microseconds on CIFAR-10 and 1.09 on Tiny ImageNet. Existing hyperparameter Tables 3–11 and code-access information remain unchanged; corresponding settings for the newly added baselines and RMIA are not supplied.

E1.justification: Both versions use the six-class synthetic dataset, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet for the same class and random unlearning tasks. Appendix G perturbs internal proxy weights within this coverage; it introduces no new dataset, population, or input domain. LLM applications remain future work.

E2.justification: Tables 1–2 add evaluated Pretrained, Langevin Unlearning, AMUN, and NatMU comparators. Figures 4 and 6 also add the three new unlearning methods to efficiency comparisons. This substantially broadens the comparison set; the existing zero-shot comparators remain.

E3.justification: Section 4.3 and Table 2 replace the reported MIA privacy evaluation with RMIA. Appendix G introduces Neural Collapse diagnostics and a Gaussian proxy-noise protocol with sigma values 0, 0.1, 0.2, and 0.3. Existing dataset/model assignments and forget fractions remain unchanged; Appendix F still uses its original MIA AUC evaluation.

E4.justification: New Appendix G tests the central zero-shot proxy assumption using NC1, NC3, NC4, and classifier-versus-prototype accuracy gaps, then measures sensitivity to corrupted proxies in both unlearning tasks. These add substantial assumption-validation and robustness evidence beyond the unchanged beta/depth analyses in Section 4.5 and Appendix F.

E5.justification: v1 already reports plus/minus values but does not identify their meaning or benchmark run count. v2 specifies means and standard deviations across five random seeds, with fixed forgotten classes and different random-unlearning splits per seed. This is newly disclosed statistical information, not evidence that the number of runs increased.

E6.justification: Existing results change substantially: Table 1 revises SISA's Tiny ImageNet retain accuracy, forget accuracy, and CE from 58.9%, 58.2%, and 1.87 to 50.2%, 0.0%, and 3.05. Table 2 replaces privacy scores under RMIA, while Figure 4 revises reported speed-ups. New comparator rows, inference-overhead measurements, and Tables 12–14 add further results. Privacy scores across versions use different attacks and do not establish same-setting gains.

M1.justification: Algorithm 2 changes zero-shot retention weighting from the global class prior p(y=c) to the retain prior p(yr=c), adding its calculation. This corrects the pseudocode to match Equation 10 already present in v1; the architecture and main-text objectives remain unchanged, and an implementation change is not established.

P1.justification: Related-work and results paragraphs receive targeted rewrites, and new Limitations and Future Directions sections precede the renumbered conclusion. Appendix G and an evaluation-protocol paragraph are added, and the publication header changes. Most introductory, methodological, and retained appendix prose remains unchanged.

P2.justification: Tables 1–2 gain comparator rows, Figures 4 and 6 gain bars and revised ordering, and Appendix G adds Tables 12–14. Text and figure placement adjust to accommodate these additions. The overall visual design, conceptual figures, and existing sensitivity heatmaps are retained.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds substantive positioning against concept erasure and representation-editing research, including LEACE, kernelized rate-distortion, domain-adversarial representation erasure, and gradient-free forgetting. It distinguishes the proposed method through instance/class removal, tractable objectives, and zero-shot operation. The retain-access taxonomy also expands to incorporate Langevin, AMUN, and NatMU.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation, variational bounds, assumptions used in their derivations, and Appendix A proofs are unchanged. Algorithm 2 aligns its weighting with an existing equation; Appendix G supplies empirical diagnostics and interpretations rather than new formal bounds or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important weaknesses in v1 by explicitly acknowledging white-box vulnerability and directly testing the Neural Collapse assumption underlying zero-shot unlearning. Broader comparisons and clarified uncertainty further improve assessability. Missing new-baseline/RMIA settings and overstated robustness language remain drawbacks: Table 13 shows Tiny ImageNet forget accuracy rising from 1.1% to 6.0% despite claiming unaffected forgetting. Nevertheless, the scope clarification and new assumption tests substantially improve the paper's overall evidential grounding.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Representation Unlearning framework. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching retained appendices A–F and identifying the new Appendix G.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds evaluated baselines, Neural Collapse diagnostics, and experiments perturbing zero-shot proxies.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic-data experiments, class and random unlearning benchmarks, computational measurements, and hyperparameter analyses.

results.title: Representation Unlearning: Forgetting through Information Compression

C1.justification: The introduction recasts the theoretical contribution from a foundation to motivation, while Section 6 explicitly denies a formal identity and qualifies applicability by encoder geometry. The abstract and principal claims about the method, selective classification, OOD detection and curation remain largely unchanged; the conclusion still claims a rigorous link.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations connecting comparator rankings to density-modeling quality and attributes SigLIP weaknesses to its training objectives and texture-sensitive representations. Sections 6 and B.6 substantially expand theoretical and applicability limitations. The impact statement develops the existing rarity/fairness warning into recommendations for subgroup evaluation and human review.

D1.justification: V2 supplies a reproduction-code URL, explicit backbone identifiers and a new classification-protocol subsection specifying prompts, normalized cosine-similarity prediction and the absence of a trained classification head. It also resolves the residual-block documentation inconsistency. These are useful disclosures; the principal training hyperparameters and hardware specification remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use Conceptual Captions, DataComp and LAION proxies; the same six classification benchmarks; and ImageNet-1K, ImageNet-R and EuroSAT for OOD detection. Data-curation coverage is retained. Additional backbones change model configurations, not represented datasets or tasks.

E2.justification: V2 adds Embedding Norm, W-CLIP, Conformity and Gaussian Mixture Model comparisons to the existing MCDO and ProbVLM comparisons in Table 2 and the SigLIP table. These substantially broaden evaluation to density and geometry alternatives. MC-Dropout is the renamed MCDO comparator.

E3.justification: Appendix B.6 adds CLIP ViT-L/14 evaluations within the retained zero-shot protocol. It also specifies SigLIP2-256, whereas v1 names SigLIP ViT-B/16; equivalence of those configurations is not established. Existing metrics, proxy sample counts, training budgets and ablation settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The geometry/base-distribution, proxy-size and integration-step ablations retain their designs and results in Figure 3 and Tables 6–8. The dedicated OOD experiment and curation examples in Figures 4–5 are also retained. Expanded benchmark comparisons and explanatory discussion do not introduce a separate controlled analysis.

E5.justification: Both versions state that experiments use five different random seeds and report means with standard deviations. V2 extends the same reporting practice to additional comparisons; changed means and deviations do not establish a change in statistical procedures.

E6.justification: Many retained results change. For Conceptual Captions/CIFAR-100, Table 2 changes MCDO/REPVLM Acc@90 from 0.888/0.874 to 0.814/0.873, reversing their ordering. V2 adds four baseline result sets and CLIP ViT-L/14 results. The substantially revised SigLIP table includes negative REPVLM correlations on ImageNet-1K, but uncertain checkpoint equivalence prevents interpreting these as same-setting performance deterioration.

M1.justification: The conditional Riemannian flow, training objective, density-based score and inference algorithms remain unchanged. Appendix B.2 changes eight residual blocks to six, matching the six already specified in v1 Table 5; this resolves inconsistent documentation without establishing an architectural change.

P1.justification: The central theoretical and main-results narratives are substantially rewritten: Section 3.1 adopts labeled A1–A3 links, and Section 5.2 is reorganized around the expanded comparisons. Limitations and impact prose are expanded, while Appendix B gains a classification-protocol subsection and a restructured backbone discussion.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is replotted with seven methods instead of three. Table 2 and the matched SigLIP table expand accordingly, and a new CLIP ViT-L/14 table is added. Figure 1 is revised and resized, while several retained figures and tables move. These substantially alter the central evidence displays.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds a substantive density-and-geometry research strand covering whitened CLIP, conformity, embedding norms and modality gaps. Additional references contextualize local linearization, the unresolved density-preservation argument and generative-model failure analogies. This broadens the paper's positioning beyond probabilistic embeddings and sampling-based uncertainty methods.

T1.justification: Section 3.1 replaces claimed bidirectional relationships with an assumption-dependent chain. V2 explicitly rejects deriving pointwise Jacobian suppression from expectation-level optimality and removes the determinant/isometry density-preservation argument, treating proportional input and embedding densities as an empirical assumption. This substantially revises the central theoretical justification; Appendix A remains unchanged.

improvement.justification: V1 overstates the theoretical density–uncertainty connection and mainly compares against dropout and ProbVLM. V2 distinguishes assumptions from derivation, adds directly relevant density/geometry baselines, and reports backbone-dependent weaknesses with an applicability discussion. These changes substantially improve scientific credibility, supported by clearer reproducibility information. The retained 'rigorous link' conclusion and inconsistent SigLIP naming remain defects, but do not outweigh these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same REPVLM study. Their text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices support comparison, including matching relocated material and the renumbered SigLIP results.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical evaluations and reports additional baseline comparisons and CLIP ViT-L/14 results.

before.justification: V1 reports original selective-classification experiments, ablations, OOD detection and qualitative data-curation results, including supplementary SigLIP evaluations.

results.title: Epistemic Uncertainty Quantification for Pre-trained VLMs via Riemannian Flow Matching

C1.justification: The claimed local-SSL state of the art expands to include ImageNet. The introduction and Section 4 explicitly restrict BP parity to CIFAR-10, STL-10 and Tiny ImageNet, while the abstract adds ImageNet without similarly qualifying its parity sentence. The central theoretical and methodological contributions remain.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly discusses the remaining ImageNet gap and challenges of adapting local learning to residual connections. It adds the memory cost of fine spatial pooling and explains the activation-storage advantage of ideal local execution, while acknowledging that complete training with those ideal implementations was not performed.

D1.justification: V2 supplies a code-repository link and Algorithms 1–3 distinguishing ideal memory-saving execution from the implemented stop-gradient approach. It clarifies the existing pooled, concatenated linear readout and documents ImageNet architecture, adaptive pooling, optimizer schedule, hardware and training time. These substantially expand implementation and reproduction information.

E1.justification: V2 adds ImageNet representation learning and downstream classification to the retained CIFAR-10, STL-10 and Tiny ImageNet evaluations. This substantially extends the empirical coverage to a harder, higher-resolution benchmark; the MNIST simulations remain.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds SoftHebb (Journé et al., 2023) as a reported comparator, with CIFAR-10, STL-10 and ImageNet accuracies of 80.31, 76.23 and 27.3. The existing comparison methods are retained; the citation and table do not establish that SoftHebb was rerun.

E3.justification: The new ImageNet protocol uses eight convolutional layers with doubled VGG11 widths, 224-pixel inputs, batch size 256, and 100 epochs with LARS. Table 3 introduces an activation-memory and iteration-time evaluation at batch size 256. For the original three benchmarks, the stated training batch size changes from 32 to 128; the PDFs do not establish whether this corrects documentation or reflects rerunning experiments.

E4.justification: V1 defers resource-efficiency analysis to future work; v2 adds a substantive comparison of activation-memory requirements and iteration times for BP and ideal local implementations on STL-10 and ImageNet. It also tests the spatial-dependence and feedback ablations on ImageNet. The existing rank constraints, gradient-alignment analyses and training-stage plots are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions specify 95% confidence intervals from four random-seed simulations for Table 2 entries carrying uncertainty, and retain the existing figure uncertainty reporting. V2 introduces no new seed-count or statistical-testing procedure. Its added ImageNet scores have no reported confidence intervals.

E6.justification: New ImageNet accuracies are 42.55 for CLAPP++, 44.16 for CLAPP++DFB and 42.49 for CLAPP++both, versus 48.52 for BP-CLAPP++ and 55.19 for BP-InfoNCE. Thus DFB leads the local variants there, but a BP gap remains. Existing scores are retained, while Table 3 adds resource results. The new CIFAR-10 predictive-coding entry of 46.52 in Table 2 is unreconciled with 45.62 in the retained appendix comparison.

M1.justification: CLAPP++, CLAPP++DFB and the summed-loss CLAPP++both variant already appear in v1. V2 formalizes the existing spatial pooling and feedback construction and documents equivalent execution procedures; it does not establish a changed learning rule.

P1.justification: Section 3.3 receives a focused explanatory expansion, and the results and discussion receive targeted revisions. A new algorithm appendix precedes the retained appendix sequence. Grammar, affiliations, publication information and the erroneous template running header are updated, while most exposition and the overall narrative remain.

P2.justification: Table 2 gains ImageNet and spatial-dependence columns and a SoftHebb row. V2 adds the resource table, ImageNet architecture table and three algorithm displays. Figure 5 and the appendix figures are relocated, with caption refinements; existing plotted content is retained rather than replaced by new analyses.

R1.justification: V2 adds relevant references including SoftHebb, NoProp, scaling studies and VGG. Section 3.3 newly acknowledges related spatial pooling in Siddiqui et al.'s blockwise SSL, refining the mechanism's positioning. It also revises the Forward-forward objective description. The CPC reference's author/year update represents the same cited work, not a new one.

T1.justification: V2 adds Proposition 3.5 and its Appendix B.3 proof, constructing a spatially dependent feedback operator that can reproduce BP gradients in linear convolutional networks with unit pooling patches. It also explains why global pooling cannot generally do so. V1 supplied intuition and simulations for this case, rather than this formal existence result; its earlier theorems remain.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the spatial mechanism's theoretical justification and tests the central performance claim on ImageNet, revealing an important boundary to BP parity. The implementation documentation and qualified resource analysis also improve reproducibility and practical assessment. These gains outweigh the new predictive-coding numerical inconsistency and insufficiently qualified abstract wording. The resource savings remain estimates for ideal execution, rather than demonstrated savings over complete training runs.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CLAPP++ research, and their text, equations, figures, tables and appendices support reliable comparison. V1's appendices A–D correspond to v2's B–E; v2 adds an algorithm appendix and further theoretical and experimental material.

after.justification: V2 retains those original experiments and adds ImageNet classification results and resource-efficiency comparisons.

before.justification: V1 reports original gradient-alignment simulations, image-classification experiments in Table 2, and additional predictive-coding and ablation results in the appendices.

results.title: Can local learning match self-supervised backpropagation?

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction newly claim that learning 3D generation transfers back to perception and improves image-based 3D understanding. This adds a substantive claim while retaining the central unified captioning/generation contributions and conclusion.

C2.justification: Section 4.5 newly interprets the unchanged captioning comparison as generation-to-perception transfer and explicitly discusses shortcomings against non-MLLM generators. Section 4.7 adds scaling interpretations and explains decreasing training memory through smaller batches. Existing failure explanations and the main limitations section remain unchanged.

D1.justification: Section 4.1 newly identifies the held-out toys4k subset. Tables 4-5 document profiling budgets, batch and 3D-sample counts, memory, and timing. The existing implementation recipe is retained, and no code or data release information is added.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same source datasets and already demonstrate image- and text-conditioned 3D generation and object captioning. v2 identifies toys4k within Trellis-500K as the held-out subset, without establishing changed coverage. The appendix adds examples of existing tasks; user ratings add an evaluation procedure.

E2.justification: Table 1 and Figure 4 expand generation comparisons beyond SAR3D and ShapeLLM-Omni to Michelangelo, CraftsMan, Hunyuan3D-2.1, TRELLIS, and SAM3D. This substantially broadens the evaluated comparator set to non-MLLM systems. Captioning comparators in Table 2 remain unchanged.

E3.justification: v2 removes Uni3D evaluation and adds user-preference evaluation using 100 questionnaires and approximately 2,400 data points. New experiments vary VAE, MoT, backbone, and token counts; resource profiling spans 512-5120 tokens, with training measured on eight GPUs at 20,480 tokens per GPU. These are additional protocols, not replacements for the retained main training recipe.

E4.justification: New Section 4.7 and Table 3 investigate VAE capacity, MoT, backbone choice, and token-budget effects on generation quality. Tables 4-5 add training and inference resource-scaling analyses. These substantially extend the retained AdaLN, point-sampling, and failure-case analyses.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, variability estimates, or significance tests. v2's questionnaire and response counts describe study size; its statement about statistical meaningfulness does not introduce an uncertainty estimate or test.

E6.justification: Retained automatic scores in Table 1 and all captioning scores in Table 2 are unchanged. New comparisons report TRELLIS p-FID 7.36 versus CG-MLLM's 12.55, and SAM3D user preference 3.45 versus 3.32. Tables 3-5 add ablation and resource results, and Appendix A adds qualitative outputs. The three Uni3D scores are removed.
