M1.justification: Sections 3.1-3.5 retain the Qwen3-VL TokenAR/BlockAR architecture, frozen Hunyuan3D-2.1 VAE, masking and positional strategies, decoding, and staged training. Alternative backbones and components in v2 are ablation configurations, not changes to the proposed method.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and section order are retained. Changes include focused additions to the abstract, introduction, and discussion; a new ablation subsection, impact statement, acknowledgements, and appendix; expanded author information; and author-year citation formatting. There is no extensive narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to two-column ICML formatting, substantially relocating and resizing displays. Table 1 gains method groups and a different metric column, Figure 4 expands its comparisons, Tables 3-5 are added, and Appendix A introduces four galleries. Most other existing figures retain their content.

R1.justification: v2 adds the SAM 3D reference and removes Uni3D alongside its metric. It also explicitly positions performance relative to non-MLLM generators. The related-work survey and distinctions from earlier MoT architectures otherwise remain substantively unchanged.

T1.justification: The rectified-flow interpolation, velocity, loss, and inference equations in Section 2.2 remain equivalent. No formal definitions, assumptions, proofs, or derivations are added. The new scaling discussion interprets measurements rather than establishing a theoretical result.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's limited validation of architectural choices and efficiency through Table 3's component comparisons and Tables 4-5's resource measurements. The non-MLLM comparisons also provide important context and expose performance gaps, while the appendix supplies additional inspectable outputs. These gains outweigh the unexplained Uni3D removal and weaknesses in the new evidence interpretation: the user study is underdescribed, and the generation-to-perception claim lacks a control isolating that effect.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CG-MLLM research, with readable text, equations, tables, and figures supporting reliable comparison. The supplied v1 ends with references; v2 includes Appendix A and Figures 9-12, which were also inspected.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds user-preference scores, component ablations, resource measurements, and additional generated examples in Appendix A.

before.justification: v1 reports original generation and captioning results in Tables 1-2, qualitative outputs, and AdaLN and VAE reconstruction analyses in Figure 6.

results.title: CG-MLLM: Captioning and Generating 3D content via Multi-modal Large Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract and principal contributions remain substantially unchanged. The conclusion narrows 'consistently outperforms' to demonstrating empirical improvements and describes estimation of judge discrimination rather than unrestricted judge reliability. The introduction adds emphasis on gains with mixed-quality judge pools.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly distinguishes discrimination relative to the learned ranking from objective correctness. It adds substantive limitations concerning correlated judge errors, shared biases, and imbalanced or adaptive comparison designs. Appendix F.6 qualifies length effects as potentially confounded, while F.2 discusses the trade-off between judge diversity and comparisons per judge.

D1.justification: Previously referenced but absent appendices now provide algorithm pseudocode, gradients, simulation budgets and parameter construction, dataset counts, judge identities, decoding settings, and the complete judge prompt. v2 also identifies the excluded near-zero-discrimination judge and supplies a code/data access link. These substantially expand reproducibility documentation without establishing changes to all underlying settings.

E1.justification: The benchmark inventory remains MT-Bench, Chatbot Arena, UltraFeedback, and the in-house dataset. Appendix F.7 extends the tested input conditions to deliberately restricted connected comparison graphs, including a spanning-tree regime, without adding a new application domain.

E2.justification: Unweighted BTL remains the principal baseline. Appendix F.6 adds a direct internal comparison between the scalar model and its length-dependent extension. REM, GTR, and FTR remain discussed rather than empirically benchmarked.

E3.justification: New protocols include a six-lower/two-higher-quality judge pool assessed against a common weighted reference, tie-removal refits, and fixed-budget graph thinning (Section 5.4; Appendices F.4 and F.7). Appendix C.2 also describes spanning-tree seeding, qualifying v1's uniform-sampling account; the PDFs do not establish that retained simulations were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds substantial analyses of mixed judge quality, sensitivity to removing ties, length-dependent discrimination, and sparse comparison graphs. Appendices F.2 and F.5 additionally examine rank-based sample efficiency and judge discrimination across model sizes and datasets, extending v1's reported simulation, efficiency, and case-study evidence.

E5.justification: Both versions report 100 repetitions with interquartile bands for MSE, 500 replications for coverage, five repetitions for subsampling, and Wald confidence intervals. Additional interval rows and covariance derivations do not establish a changed uncertainty-reporting procedure.

E6.justification: The main benchmark tables and Figures 1–4 retain their results. New Section 5.4 reports weighted versus unweighted Pearson correlations of 0.9394 versus 0.8992 and Spearman correlations of 0.9212 versus 0.8316. Appendices add full rankings, judge estimates, tie-removal results, length-extension rank correlation of 0.9996, and sparse-graph results. These are additional findings, not improvements to retained same-setting scores.

M1.justification: The main scalar-discrimination BTL model and projected Adam procedure remain. Appendix F.6 adds an optional extension with gamma_k(z) = exp(alpha_k + beta_k z), using standardized question length and additional per-judge slope parameters with row-level gradients.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained. Local revisions clarify discrimination and estimation terminology, expand the conclusion, insert the judge-heterogeneity subsection, and add acknowledgments and an impact statement. The extensive supplementary scientific additions do not constitute a wholesale rewrite of the existing narrative.

P2.justification: v2 adds a main-text judge-scale table and substantial appendix displays: comparison heatmaps, a prompt template, full ranking tables, judge-discrimination plots, length-response curves, and sparse-graph results. The original four figures and benchmark tables remain, with relocation, reflow, and Chatbot Arena table renumbering.

R1.justification: v2 adds Newey and McFadden (1994) for the estimation proofs and explicitly contrasts FTR's overlapping judge/candidate pools with its own unrestricted pools. Other prominent reference changes are publication-metadata updates to already cited works.

T1.justification: Section 3 replaces uniform sampling with general full-support sampling and explicitly adds compact localization to Theorem 3.4. Appendix A supplies previously absent proofs and covariance derivations. Appendix F.6 adds an identifiability theorem and normalization corollary for the length-dependent extension.

improvement.justification: v1 deferred essential proofs and implementation details to appendices absent from the supplied PDF. v2 supplies that material, states important theoretical conditions, and adds targeted robustness evidence and substantive interpretive limits, substantially improving assessability and reproducibility. The gains are qualified by the mixed-quality study's internally fitted reference and the unresolved uniform-sampling versus spanning-tree description, but these limitations do not outweigh the improvements.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work and are readable throughout. v1 ends after the references despite citing appendices; v2 supplies Appendices A–F. Their inclusion can be assessed as added documentation without assuming that every documented experiment was newly conducted.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and reports additional mixed-quality judge, tie-handling, question-length, and sparse-graph analyses.

before.justification: Sections 4–5 report original simulation results, fitted benchmark rankings, and an in-house subsampling study, distinct from externally sourced benchmark scores.

results.title: A Judge-Aware Ranking Framework for Evaluating Large Language Models without Ground Truth

C1.justification: The two-reduction contribution and order-of-magnitude speed claim remain. v2 explicitly characterizes LEMUR as corpus-specific, adds fast-indexing and CPU/GPU-applicability claims in the introduction, and expands the stated main BEIR evaluation from six to eight datasets.

C2.justification: v2 introduces a substantive mechanism explanation: shared embedding geometry and feature expansion may matter more than highly training-specific representations, supported by the ELM experiment. It also explains the smaller visual-retrieval advantage through reranking costs and identifies corpus-dependent training as an obstacle to incremental indexing. These explanations and applicability qualifications were absent from v1.

D1.justification: v2 adds explicit query/indexing pseudocode, Gaussian sampling and scaling details for the ELM variant, and indexing-stage timings of 20, 70 and 198 minutes on the largest corpus. These improve implementation and resource documentation. Table 3's training hyperparameters, main hardware specification and repository access remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds three BEIR document/query collections: Touche-2020, TREC-Covid and FiQA-2018. ArguAna remains, but its ordinary benchmark evaluation is replaced by a distinct long-query scenario using 300 query vectors. Both corpus coverage and query-input conditions therefore expand; the other original collections and ViDoRe remain.

E2.justification: The main competitors remain MUVERA, IGP, DESSERT and PLAID. However, the ArguAna comparison in v1 Appendix C.1 includes IGP, whereas its replacement long-query comparison in v2 Appendix E includes only MUVERA, DESSERT and PLAID. Newly discussed methods such as WARP and BGE-M3 are not evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: v2 introduces nDCG@10 evaluation with 0.01 and 0.001 quality tolerances, plus query-averaged Pearson and Spearman correlation measurements. It specifies 300 vectors per ArguAna query and evaluates LateOn and mxbai-edge-colbert-v0-32m embeddings on SCIDOCS. The shared experiments retain the stated hardware, core training hyperparameters and recall/QPS protocol.

E4.justification: New analyses test preservation of relevance quality, agreement with exact MaxSim, long-query robustness and whether training the hidden layer is necessary. The dimension and training-data analyses are retained and expanded. Conversely, v1 Section 6.2 and Figure 3's exact-inference-versus-ANNS ablation is removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests or variability estimates. The added Pearson and Spearman correlations measure approximation quality rather than uncertainty.

E6.justification: Table 2 revises LEMUR QPS at at least 80% recall and k=100: NQ changes from 950 to 869, Quora from 6503 to 4068, and SCIDOCS from 3353 to 2591; corresponding baseline entries remain unchanged. Numerous dataset, embedding-model, nDCG, correlation and ELM results are added. ArguAna's replacement results use different query settings and cannot establish a same-setting performance change.

M1.justification: The principal MSE-trained MLP, frozen-feature OLS fitting, pooled-query search and MaxSim reranking remain unchanged. Appendix H.3 adds an ELM variant with fixed Gaussian hidden weights and only the output layer fitted, constituting a limited procedural adaptation.

P1.justification: Prose is extensively edited across the abstract, introduction, background, method and discussion. The abstract is shortened, scalable training moves before training-set selection, explanations are reorganized, and the appendices acquire a substantially revised structure. These changes extend beyond isolated wording corrections.

P2.justification: v2 adds two algorithm boxes, retrieval-quality and correlation tables, and long-query and ELM plots, while expanding benchmark plot grids. Quora and SCIDOCS model comparisons exchange main-text and appendix placement. The original exact-inference-versus-ANNS figure is removed, producing substantial changes to the displayed evidence and its arrangement.

R1.justification: New Section 5.2 positions LEMUR against TCT-ColBERT and BGE-M3, distinguishing corpus-specific search approximation from training general retrievers through distillation. Added discussion of WARP and further theoretical and retrieval literature substantially broadens the positioning beyond v1's emphasis on token pruning, MUVERA and storage reduction.

T1.justification: v2 adds Appendix B's universal-approximation assumption, Theorem B.1 and proof. On a compact token-embedding domain, the argument establishes an existential uniform token-score approximation and a query-level error bound of |X| times epsilon. v1 contains the algebraic search reduction but no corresponding approximation theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: v1 mainly establishes recall and throughput against MaxSim neighbors. v2 materially strengthens validation through relevance-based nDCG@10 evaluation, direct approximation diagnostics and long-query testing. The ELM analysis, explicit indexing costs, clearer distinction from distillation methods and incremental-indexing limitation improve scientific and practical assessability. Removing the exact-versus-ANNS ablation loses useful evidence, but the broader validation and clearer account of applicability provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LEMUR research. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial additions and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original retrieval experiments and adds retrieval-quality, correlation, long-query and random-feature results in Appendices C–H.

before.justification: v1 reports original retrieval experiments, baseline comparisons, embedding-dimension ablations and training-data analyses in Section 6 and Appendices B–D.

results.title: LEMUR: Learned Multi-Vector Retrieval

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's three contributions, and conclusion retain the same central claims: a general SMC optimization framework, analysis of idealized recursions and ESS, and effective reward tuning. The added experiments provide broader support for the existing generality claim without redefining those principal contributions.

C2.justification: v2 more explicitly limits standard SMC error arguments for particle-dependent targets and conditions the ESS interpretation on kernel choices. It acknowledges finite-sample covariance bias instead of claiming unbiasedness, and adds practical discussion of ULA instability, kernel-selection tradeoffs, and expected high-dimensional limitations of RWM.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-repository link and identifies personal-computer and Colab T4 hardware. It also supplies kernel-specific implementation information and detailed deblurring specifications, including image dimensions, corruption operators, initialization, step sizes, and the proxTV/Douglas–Rachford implementation. These substantially expand reproducibility information beyond v1.

E1.justification: v2 adds Bayesian image deblurring/MMLE using guitar and flower images, including stronger blur and noise conditions. It also adds the Vtight/Rtight scenario with a narrow reward region concentrated around one mode. The original Gaussian-mixture, two-moons, circles, blobs, and MNIST coverage remains.

E2.justification: The Langevin comparison set expands to include SOSMC-MALA, SOSMC-RWM, and SOSMC-HMC alongside SOSMC-ULA, ImpDiff, and SOUL. MYPGD is newly evaluated against SOSMC-MYULA for deblurring. Table 1 retains both Adam and SGD comparisons, including settings whose revised plots display only Adam.

E3.justification: New protocols include single-leapfrog, unit-mass HMC and deblurring with 20 particles, 3,000 iterations, controlled blur/noise conditions, and MSE/SSIM evaluation. Appendix G reports zero- and positive-KL regularization settings separately. Equation 26 also changes the Gaussian exponent denominator from sigma squared to twice sigma squared; this revises the reported specification without establishing that earlier experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds a substantial kernel-choice investigation, including the tight-reward stress test exposing SOSMC-ULA instability relative to Metropolis-corrected variants. Deblurring setups also examine different image content and increased corruption, supported by reconstruction metrics and enlarged image details. Existing regularization and fresh-sampling analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report ten-run Langevin summaries and describe the same confidence-interval and time-alignment procedure. Tables 1–2 newly tabulate terminal values with unspecified ± terms, but establish no different uncertainty procedure, increased run count, or significance testing. Additional numerical summaries are changes to results and presentation.

E6.justification: Langevin curves are revised and extended, while Tables 1–3 add terminal numerical results. New tight-reward findings show instability for ULA and stronger performance for Metropolis-corrected variants. In the new deblurring Setup A, Table 3 reports SOSMC-MYULA MSE 215.47 and SSIM 0.80 versus MYPGD's 312.71 and 0.74. These are newly reported comparisons; the 2D EBM and MNIST findings are largely retained.

M1.justification: The general SOSMC framework remains, but its concrete procedures expand substantially. Beyond v1's ULA implementation and suggested MALA option, v2 introduces evaluated RWM/HMC variants and proximal SOSMC-MYULA, incorporating acceptance steps, momentum dynamics, and proximal particle updates for nonsmooth potentials (Appendices A.2 and E.4).

P1.justification: Most original prose and section ordering remain. v2 polishes wording, terminology, and cross-references, subdivides Appendix A, and adds an Impact Statement and new experimental and derivational subsections. The expansion predominantly reflects added scientific material rather than wholesale narrative rewriting.

P2.justification: The main text and references switch to a two-column conference layout. Langevin plots are reorganized by optimizer, gain kernel curves, and relabel axes as NLL Proxy. New reward maps, deblurring reconstructions, enlarged image comparisons, and three quantitative tables substantially expand the displays. Retained 2D/MNIST figures are resized, moved, and renumbered.

R1.justification: Section 2.2 newly identifies Johansen et al. (2008) and Crucinio (2025) as close SMC-MMLE predecessors. Additional references support mean-field analysis, HMC, and proximal deblurring. The overall positioning remains a general framework encompassing specialized methods; the Carbone year update and consolidated Tieleman entries concern retained works.

T1.justification: v2 incorporates the initial weight G0 into Theorem 1, qualifies the ESS-divergence relationship, revises chi-square proof algebra, and corrects weight and reward-gradient signs. Appendix F.4 replaces the expectation-based surrogate argument with a weighted-particle formulation and restores the KL coefficient. Reversible-kernel, proximal-MMLE, and explicit gradient-representation derivations are added, while the idealized convergence rate remains.

improvement.justification: v1's broad framework was evaluated through ULA-based reward tuning; v2 tests alternative kernels and nonsmooth MMLE, including conditions that expose ULA's limitations. Corrections to the initial-weight identity, gradient signs, and surrogate derivation improve internal consistency, while new implementation and code-access information improves reproducibility. Together these substantially strengthen the paper's support and clarity. Finite-particle convergence remains future work, and deblurring results still lack uncertainty estimates.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SOSMC research, with matching authors, framework, and retained experiments. The complete main texts and appendices are readable, allowing reliable comparison despite substantial additions and reformatting.

after.justification: v2 retains original reward-tuning experiments and adds kernel comparisons and Bayesian image-deblurring results, documented in Sections 5.1 and 5.4 and Appendices E and G.

before.justification: Sections 5.1–5.3 and Appendix E report original Langevin reward-tuning, synthetic 2D energy-model, and MNIST experiments, including convergence curves and generated samples.

results.title: Efficient Stochastic Optimisation via Sequential Monte Carlo

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: augmenting Markovian CVaR policy optimization with quantile gradients to improve sample efficiency and risk-averse performance. The new proofs strengthen support without redefining these headline claims.

C2.justification: v3 adds a variance-based rationale for state-value advantages and explains consistent tie-breaking when optimal policies are nonunique. Section 3.3 newly interprets decaying ω as removing the VaR boost and asserts recovery of CVaR-PG's convergence properties. The unresolved convergence of the general Markovian learner remains acknowledged.

D1.justification: Algorithm 4 now explicitly applies the gradient-mixing weights that v1 omitted from its pseudocode, improving implementation clarity. The new tie-breaking note also clarifies policy execution. Appendix C's architectures, learning parameters, preprocessing details, and environment-access information remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same modified Maze, LunarLander, and InvertedPendulum tasks with identical noisy-reward regions and risk-averse behavioral requirements. No additional domains or test scenarios appear in the appendices.

E2.justification: The evaluated comparators remain REINFORCE, CVaR-PG, PCVaR-PG, RET-CAP, and MIX, with the same participation by task. MIX remains excluded from Maze, and unsuccessful PCVaR-PG results remain omitted from the LunarLander plots.

E3.justification: Sections 4 and Appendix C retain the same evaluation metrics, episode limits, risk levels, 20-trajectory update batches, network sizes, and hyperparameter tables. The numerical ω schedules are also unchanged; the weighting-specification correction is described under M1.

E4.justification: No ablations, sensitivity studies, robustness tests, or supplementary empirical analyses are added or removed. The new appendix material concerns theoretical guarantees rather than additional experiments.

E5.justification: Figures 2–3 report averages over 10 seeds with shaded standard errors in both versions. No new repeated-run information, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty-estimation procedures are introduced.

E6.justification: Figures 2–3 contain identical learning-curve graphics, and Sections 4.1–4.3 retain the same performance trends, rankings, and baseline failure findings. There are no new empirical result entries in the appendices.

M1.justification: Algorithm 4 corrects the stated policy update from g1 + g2 to (1−ω)g1 + ωg2. The objective also switches ω from weighting CVaR to weighting expected VaR. This is a limited correction to the reported update specification; the architecture, Bellman operators, risk-level tracking, and multi-step estimators remain unchanged. Implementation changes or reruns are not established.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained. Local explanations in Section 3 are expanded, acknowledgements and an impact statement are added, affiliation information changes, and references move from after the appendices to before them.

P2.justification: The single-column manuscript becomes a two-column conference-style main text and bibliography with running headers. Existing figures are resized and relocated, algorithms are reflowed, and Tables 1–3 are regrouped onto one page. The underlying figure graphics and table contents remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v3 adds references including Föllmer and Schied (2016), Agarwal et al. (2021), and Schulman et al. (2017), supporting CVaR equivalence, policy-gradient analysis, and the state-value rationale. A Langley (2000) bibliography entry is also added. The positioning relative to existing CVaR methods remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: New Appendices A.5–A.6 establish contraction and fixed-point results for policy evaluation, define a loss-induced risk measure, and prove monotone policy improvement under finite-action, bounded-reward, softmax-policy, and step-size conditions. These substantive guarantees were absent from v1. The earlier proofs are largely retained, with the Proposition 3.4 proof moved to A.7.

improvement.justification: v1 introduced VaR actor–critic updates without the policy-evaluation and policy-improvement guarantees supplied by v3's Appendices A.5–A.6. These additions substantially strengthen the mathematical foundation, while the corrected mixing weights resolve an important inconsistency in Algorithm 4. The improvement is primarily theoretical and documentary: empirical evidence is unchanged, and the conditional guarantees do not resolve convergence of the full Markovian learner.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CVaR-VaR research work. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, algorithms, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and their results in Figures 2–3.

before.justification: v1 reports original reinforcement-learning experiments in Maze, LunarLander, and InvertedPendulum, including return, risk-averse behavior, and CVaR learning curves.

results.title: Boosting CVaR Policy Optimization with Quantile Gradients

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution bullets, and conclusion retain the central claims: trajectory-free learning from instantaneous labels, joint instantaneous-force and finite-time prediction, and stable larger-timestep simulation at comparable computational cost. The expanded experiments support these existing contributions without redefining them.

C2.justification: v1 identifies alanine instability near 10 fs without a specific vibrational explanation; v4 proposes cancellation errors when integration steps coincide with 10–11 fs hydrogen vibrations (G.12). It also attributes Chignolin population bias to ScoreMD distillation, interprets BBA discrepancies through trapped MLFF rollouts, and adds temperature-robustness and chaotic-error-propagation interpretations.

D1.justification: v1 links code; v4 additionally states availability of model weights and self-contained JAX/PyTorch notebooks. New Appendices F.6–F.7 document data selection, coarse-graining and ScoreMD relabeling, architecture settings, cutoffs, batch sizes, epochs, hardware, and training times for the added systems.

E1.justification: Beyond v1's classical systems, MD17 molecules, and alanine dipeptide, v4 evaluates MD22 Ac-Ala3-NHMe with a missing conformational mode and coarse-grained Chignolin and BBA proteins. It also adds paracetamol evaluations across temperatures from 300 to 700 K, substantially broadening molecular coverage and testing conditions.

E2.justification: Appendix G.14 adds an evaluated trajectory-matching training objective, following TrajCast/FlashMD, for paracetamol and Ac-Ala3-NHMe (Tables 19–20). This directly tests an important comparison absent from v1. Existing VV, MLFF, ScoreMD, and SchNet/NequIP timing comparisons remain.

E3.justification: New protocols compare training objectives under force-evaluation budgets, generating trajectories at 0.5 fs and extracting state pairs separated by 7 fs. Protein evaluations introduce TICA projections and transition-probability comparisons; structural tables add HFM evaluation at 0.5 fs. The alanine total is corrected from 1 ms to 1 µs while ten 100 ns runs remain specified, indicating a reporting correction rather than demonstrated rerunning.

E4.justification: v4 adds temperature robustness tests, reference vibrational spectra investigating alanine instability, ethanol Lyapunov-time analysis, training-data-budget comparisons, and protein transition and individual-rollout analyses (G.10, G.12–G.17). These substantially extend v1's retained filter, timestep, sampling-distribution, and training-dynamics ablations.

E5.justification: G.5 explicitly identifies five distinct initial conditions for stability tests across all three thermostats, refining v1's replication description, which already reported five-run averages for related observables. The existing standard-deviation reporting remains; no increase in retained experiments' run counts or new confidence-interval or significance-testing procedure is established.

E6.justification: Retained large-timestep values in Table 1 are unchanged, but new 0.5 fs results and substantial additional findings appear. For example, Table 19 reports paracetamol PMF errors of 0.129 for HFM versus 5.772 for trajectory matching at 256 force evaluations, while trajectory matching slightly wins at 85k. Table 21 newly shows Chignolin transition JSD increasing from 8.11e-4 at 25 fs to 5.11e-2 at 45 fs.

M1.justification: The mean-flow objective, Algorithms 1–4, architectures in Appendix E, and coupled conservation filter remain unchanged. The new molecular applications use the existing framework; correcting 'endpoint-conditioned' to 'startpoint-conditioned' does not change the mathematical inputs or procedure.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and appendix organization remain recognizable, with localized wording corrections, added experimental subsections, and 'Broader Impact' renamed 'Impact Statement.' Most existing methodological prose is retained; the added scientific content does not constitute a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: Figure 8 becomes a full-width composite retaining alanine results and adding protein panels. v4 adds substantial displays for missing-mode recovery, temperature tests, trajectory-matching comparisons, transition matrices, and protein rollouts. Spectral panels are redrawn, and structural-observable tables gain explicit headers and 0.5 fs columns.

R1.justification: v4 explicitly credits Boffi et al.'s earlier flow-map framework, adds a PINN/Liouville-equation comparison, and cites additional relevant work such as Sabour et al. and the new datasets. The principal positioning remains intact; numerous publication-year and venue updates refer to already cited works.

T1.justification: The consistency derivation, sufficiency argument in Appendix C, and constrained-conservation derivation in B.3 are retained. Norm-symbol and parenthesis corrections are not substantive mathematical changes. The new Lyapunov and transition analyses provide empirical evidence rather than new formal results.

improvement.justification: v4 addresses v1's missing direct trajectory-training comparison and limited molecular coverage, while adding diagnostics of robustness and temporal fidelity and expanding reproducibility information. These substantially strengthen the empirical foundation. Local weaknesses remain: Table 19 qualifies the claimed uniform HFM advantage, Table 20 and Figure 28 disagree on an Ac-Ala3-NHMe budget, and Table 21 limits the claimed kinetic accuracy at 45 fs. These issues constrain the strongest interpretations but do not outweigh the gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Hamiltonian Flow Maps work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support matching retained material against the additions in v4.

after.justification: v4 retains those empirical results and adds Ac-Ala3-NHMe, coarse-grained protein simulations, trajectory-matching comparisons, and further diagnostic experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulations of classical mechanical systems, MD17 molecules, and alanine dipeptide, including quantitative comparisons and extensive ablations.

results.title: Learning Hamiltonian Flow Maps: Mean Flow Consistency for Large-Timestep Molecular Dynamics

C1.justification: V2's abstract consolidates the benchmark-specific accuracy claims into a general competitive-accuracy statement and drops the explicit claim of orders-of-magnitude energy savings. The central claims about parallel processing, scalable reservoirs, ESP, universality and computational efficiency remain.

C2.justification: V2 adds an oscillatory-dynamics explanation for complex eigenvalues and argues that faster hyperparameter search partly mitigates sensitivity. It acknowledges weaker LRA performance than several trained sequence models and qualifies S4 efficiency measurements because of different hardware. These additions refine the interpretation and applicability boundaries without replacing the main conclusions.

D1.justification: V2 adds a ParalESN code-availability link, an S4 implementation reference and architecture details, and an LRA dataset-size table. It explicitly identifies the provenance of LRA comparator results and revises the hardware disclosure. Most existing preprocessing, optimizer, readout and hyperparameter-search details remain unchanged.

E1.justification: V2 adds actual evaluation on four Long Range Arena tasks: Image, ListOps, Text and PathFinder (Appendices E.4 and G.5). These extend coverage to text, structured expressions and visual path reasoning. The original memory, forecasting, UEA/UCR and MNIST tasks remain.

E2.justification: S4 becomes an evaluated comparator on sMNIST and psMNIST in Table 4. The new LRA comparison additionally includes Reformer, BigBird, Linear Transformer, Performer, S5 and RWKV, using literature-derived comparator scores. The existing SCR and Structured RC comparison is retained, moving from v1 Table 9 to v2 Table 13.

E3.justification: Existing splits, the 24-hour Bayesian search budget and the 100-epoch training cap remain. V2 adds a two-layer S4 configuration with hidden size 172, evaluated on a different GPU, and an LRA comparison using published baseline scores. Appendix F.1 revises the reported V100 count from four to one; this does not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds deep-model hyperparameter sensitivity, including depth, concatenation and inter-layer settings (Figure 7), real-versus-complex ablations across memory and forecasting tasks (Tables 11–12), and a parameter-count analysis (Table 10). It also revises the shallow phase-sensitivity curve in Figure 6. The original structured-reservoir comparison remains.

E5.justification: The existing plus/minus reporting, sensitivity distributions and Figure 3 Wilcoxon comparison remain. Neither version specifies repeated-run counts or seeds. Added result rows do not introduce a new uncertainty-estimation or testing procedure; the new LRA table provides point estimates.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 and existing Table 4 entries retain their numerical results. New S4 entries lead the MNIST comparisons at 99.2% and 97.9%; new ablation, parameter-count and deep-sensitivity results substantially expand the evidence. Table 14 adds ParalESN's LRA results, averaging 63.7%. Figure 6 also changes the shallow theta_max sensitivity findings.

M1.justification: Section 3 retains the complex diagonal recurrence, initialization, dense first-layer and ring inter-layer input matrices, convolutional mixer and trained readout. The ring structure highlighted in v2's Figure 1 already appears in v1's Equation 5. The real-valued variant is introduced as an ablation control, without revising the proposed ParalESN procedure.

P1.justification: Prose is extensively revised across the abstract, method exposition, experimental discussion and appendices. Section 3 moves the scaling discussion before the equations; definitions now precede proofs through the C/D appendix swap; comparator descriptions are consolidated in Appendix F.2. These are substantial editorial changes beyond the added scientific content.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn to expose diagonal/ring structure and mixer operations. V2 adds the extensive deep-sensitivity Figure 7 and five tables covering LRA datasets, parameter counts, ablations and LRA results. Table 4 and Figure 5 gain S4, while Figure 6 and several table headers are reformatted. Existing tables are also relocated and renumbered.

R1.justification: New citations support diagonalizability and matrix bounds, complex-valued representations, LSTM attribution, LRA and RWKV. The principal positioning relative to RC, LRU and state-space models remains. Updates to existing S4, S5 and Verzelli references represent bibliographic changes rather than newly introduced prior work.

T1.justification: Proposition 4.2 changes from unrestricted exact equivalence to an almost-sure statement under i.i.d. entries with a density. V2 adds a substantive universality proof in Appendix D.3, including a filter-perturbation lemma and stochastic Lp extension, replacing v1's unsupported passage from approximate diagonalizability to exact equivalence. The ESP necessity argument also now addresses the unit-modulus boundary.

improvement.justification: The real-valued ablation, deep sensitivity study and LRA evaluation substantially strengthen and qualify the empirical case beyond v1's benchmarks. Revised equivalence assumptions and the perturbation analysis also address an important gap in v1's theory. Residual proof problems, notably Appendix D.3's incorrect geometric-series factor, and S4's different timing hardware limit these gains, but the stronger support for the central design and clearer applicability boundaries provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ParalESN research. Their main texts, figures, tables, equations and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching material across the reordered appendices.

after.justification: V2 retains those original results and adds S4 training results, real-valued ablations, deep-model sensitivity analyses and ParalESN results on Long Range Arena. The literature-derived LRA comparator scores are distinguished from the work's own results.

before.justification: V1 reports original memory, forecasting and classification experiments, computational measurements, and appendix sensitivity analyses.

results.title: ParalESN: Enabling parallel information processing in Reservoir Computing

C1.justification: v2 adds shared local spatial structure as a central explanatory contribution in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion. v1 chiefly explained robustness through Bayesian data dominance; v2 presents a joint explanation involving informative measurements and transferable local correlations. The central claim that weak priors can work in informative regimes is retained.

C2.justification: v2 explains reconstruction through measurement anchors and propagation through shared local structure, and suggests that scientific domains may share less transferable structure. It adds high-noise limitations and warns that favorable image-quality metrics can coexist with poorer physics-based performance, motivating task-specific losses. These materially refine applicability and mechanism interpretations.

D1.justification: v2 adds an authors' code-repository link, an explicit exponential-map formula, diagnostic and DRP setup details, and runtime/peak-memory measurements. Existing checkpoint identifiers, hardware, and main hyperparameters remain. The shortened ImageNet description omits v1's explicit validation-split statement, without establishing an actual split change.

E1.justification: v2 adds Linear Scattering and nonlinear Black Hole Imaging from InverseBench, substantially extending coverage beyond natural-image restoration. It also evaluates higher-noise scenarios. Existing natural-image tasks remain, while the compute comparison switches from FFHQ to CelebA-HQ.

E2.justification: Appendices C.3–C.4 add actual comparisons against DAPS and DiffPIR on inpainting, Gaussian deblurring, and 4× super-resolution, and Deep Random Projector on inpainting. The existing DPS, DMPlug, and DSG comparisons are retained.

E3.justification: New protocols include 3-versus-20-step sampling with 100 unconditional samples per setting, fixed-DPS prior swaps, three receiver configurations, and blur-PSNR evaluation. The compute study replaces v1's 100-/1000-step DPS curves extending to 10,000 evaluations with a 999–5000-NFE comparison using 333/1000 INO iterations and single/best-of-three/best-of-five DPS runs. Main restoration settings are otherwise largely retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds spatial-autocorrelation diagnostics to investigate retained structure, fixed-solver prior-swap experiments to examine domain mismatch separately, and sensitivity tests over Gaussian noise levels 0.01–1.0. These substantially expand the analysis beyond v1's retained optimizer ablations and box-inpainting/super-resolution failure studies.

E5.justification: v1 reports score-gap dispersion but only point estimates for reconstruction quality. v2 adds DRP PSNR/SSIM standard deviations in Table 9 and ± quantities for Black Hole Imaging in Table 11. The latter quantities and their replication basis are not defined, so they do not establish additional seeded runs or significance testing.

E6.justification: The original benchmark values are retained after renumbering, but substantial baseline, scientific-imaging, correlation, prior-mismatch, and noise results are added. For example, Table 16 reports that at noise 1.0, DPS reaches 22.42 PSNR versus 20.52 and 16.88 for in-domain and out-of-domain INO. The replaced compute results use different data and budgets and cannot establish a same-setting improvement over v1.

M1.justification: The initial-noise optimization objective, AdamSphere updates, and HoldoutTopK selection procedure remain unchanged in Section 2.1 and Appendix B. The added exponential-map formula documents an option already described in v1.

P1.justification: The abstract, introductory contribution account, Section 3 framing, and conclusion are substantially rewritten around two complementary mechanisms. Section 3 gains separate local-structure and failure discussions, Section 4.4 is condensed, Appendix C is reorganized, and an impact statement is added.

P2.justification: The main text changes from a single-column article to a two-column conference layout, substantially resizing and relocating figures and tables. v2 adds multiple diagnostic and benchmark tables plus a DRP visualization, and replaces v1's compute curves with Table 17. Most earlier qualitative panels retain their content despite resizing and renumbering; several inaccurate task captions are corrected.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations and discussion for Deep Random Projector, DAPS, and DiffPIR, broadening comparison with architectural priors and alternative diffusion solvers. Deng et al. and Karras et al. references are removed. Several other changed publication years merely update the same cited works.

T1.justification: Appendix C.8 introduces formal definitions of the distance-binned normalized autocorrelation and its sample-averaged profile, including the property Cx(0)=1. The posterior-consistency, Gaussian-mixture, concentration, and identifiability results and proofs in Section 3 and Appendix A remain substantively unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical credibility through stronger baselines and fixed-solver prior-swap controls, addressing v1's limited separation of solver and prior effects. Noise and scientific-imaging tests sharpen failure boundaries, while runtime and memory reporting clarify practical costs. The correlation evidence remains descriptive and some uncertainty details are unspecified, but the gains in validation, transparency, and calibrated guidance outweigh the narrower compute-budget coverage.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work, with matching algorithms, theoretical results, experiments, and appendices. Text extraction and visual inspection support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, spatial-correlation measurements, scientific inverse problems, prior-swap controls, and noise-sensitivity experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original image-restoration experiments, optimizer and early-stopping ablations, failure-mode tests, and synthetic posterior-concentration results.

results.title: Weak Diffusion Priors Can Still Achieve Strong Inverse-Problem Performance

C1.justification: The central contributions remain unified information-geometric molecular generation, evolving endpoints to prevent collapse, and improved geometric validity and scaffold recovery. Synchronization is emphasized more explicitly, but v1 already claimed joint uncertainty refinement and reduced modality mismatch.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations of Fisher-based modality weighting, collapse versus oversmoothing, and early molecular-prototype formation. It also acknowledges lower PB-Valid than MolPilot and explains why smoothing need not be tuned per protein. The limitation that geometric plausibility alone cannot deliver practical bioactivity discovery was already discussed in v1 Appendix H.1.2.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-availability link, identifies one A100 for the retained approximately 16-hour training time, and reports RTX 4090 sampling throughput. It clarifies hydrogen-only postprocessing and a shared metric pipeline, and changes Table 1's baseline-sample attribution from Qu et al. to Qiu et al.; this does not establish that experiments were rerun.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same CrossDock and MolGenBench coverage, including the existing seen/unseen target distinctions and BSD/CD38 cases. The new sampling and trajectory analyses do not introduce another dataset, population, or task.

E2.justification: The comparator membership in the existing benchmark tables is unchanged. New trajectory diagnostics reuse TargetDiff and MolCRAFT. Appendix F discusses MolPilot qualitatively but does not document a new matched numerical evaluation of it.

E3.justification: v2 adds 20- and 50-step evaluations alongside the retained 100-step default. Appendix J.4 evaluates validity and completeness at t = 0.3–0.6 and compares EvoEGF-Mol geometry at t = 0.6 with baseline outputs at t = 1.0. Existing dataset splits, sample counts, and principal benchmark protocols remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The new intermediate-state analysis tests when coherent molecular structures emerge, providing direct evidence relevant to synchronized refinement. Reduced-step ablations additionally test sampling robustness. Together these substantially extend the analysis beyond the existing endpoint-quality ablations, loss curves, and case studies.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Existing averages, medians, and strain-energy percentiles retain the same reporting practice.

E6.justification: Tables 1 and 4 change EvoEGF-Mol connectivity from 97.1% to 98.6%; existing MolGenBench and geometry results remain unchanged. New results include 85.8% and 92.0% PB-Valid at 20 and 50 steps, intermediate-state comparisons, and throughput of 1.5 molecules/second. Section 4.2 also replaces the incorrect best-Vina-Dock ranking with competitive performance, consistent with the unchanged table.

M1.justification: The architecture, evolving Gaussian and Dirichlet schedules, loss formulas, and iterative sampling procedure remain materially unchanged. Algorithms 1–2 clarify notation and explicitly expand the previously implicit bond update; the revised flow interpretation does not establish a different implemented method.

P1.justification: The abstract, substantial introductory passages, central method explanation, and two proof subsections are rewritten around synchronized parameter-space refinement and a qualified flow interpretation. Notation is standardized and the appendix narrative reorganized, although the main section order remains intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds two intermediate-state tables, expands Table 4 with sampling-step rows, and updates Figure 5 with a 50-step series and revised legend. Existing figures and tables largely retain their designs, with relocation and caption edits; the three final geometry-distribution figures are unchanged.

R1.justification: New Appendix F expands the previously brief MolPilot discussion into a comparison of optimized modality-specific schedules with analytic information-geometric paths, positioning the methods as complementary. Most bibliography changes update publication metadata for already cited works; the existing SLDM comparison is retained.

T1.justification: v1's explicit pseudoinverse sample-space velocity formula is replaced by density-tangent and Fisher-norm expressions plus a nonunique weighted-divergence/Poisson formulation with boundary conditions in v2 Appendix H.2. Appendix H.3 qualifies the earlier Fisher-flow-matching equivalence as a local parameter-space interpretation. New Appendix D derives a condition and Gaussian example distinguishing dynamic endpoints from scalar time reparameterization.

improvement.justification: The decisive gain is a substantial repair to the central theoretical justification: v2 replaces the asserted general sample-space velocity formula with a qualified divergence formulation and distinguishes the implemented parameter-refinement procedure from its local flow-matching interpretation. New trajectory and sampling analyses, corrected connectivity and docking-ranking statements, and implementation disclosures strengthen the supporting evidence. These improvements concern rigor and transparency; the principal benchmark outcomes and limitations in practical hit discovery remain largely unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe EvoEGF-Mol and contain readable main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices. Existing material can be matched across the appendix reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds reduced-sampling-step evaluations and comparisons of intermediate molecular states.

before.justification: v1 reports original CrossDock and MolGenBench evaluations, ablations, validation-loss curves, and molecular case studies.

results.title: EvoEGF-Mol: Evolving Exponential Geodesic Flow for Structure-based Drug Design

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction narrow broad hallucination and probability-calibration language toward reducing overconfident errors, improving answered-response reliability, and explicit abstention calibration. The abstract drops its calibration-improvement claim. The central contributions of advantage decoupling and dynamic uncertainty adjustment remain.

C2.justification: The new Metric Behavior Analysis acknowledges nonuniform accuracy/F1 gains and interprets them through limited remaining mathematical reasoning gains and chance-correct multiple-choice answers. Added discussions interpret uncertain-subset difficulty, NTF efficiency, and inference-time reliability/coverage tradeoffs. These substantially extend v1's explanations of the method's benefits and costs.

D1.justification: Appendix C newly specifies rule/string-based uncertainty recognition, treatment of nonconforming uncertainty expressions as definitive answers, and the absence of a learned reward model. Appendix D.3 discloses preprocessing that removes simple all-correct Qwen math examples. These disclosures do not establish that the retained experiments were rerun.

E1.justification: Appendix D.5 adds five multiple-choice AbstentionBench subsets: GPQA-Diamond-Abstain, Big-Bench-Disambiguate, MMLU-Math, MediQ, and MoralChoice. These introduce explicit should-abstain cases involving missing context, insufficient clinical information, and ambiguity, substantially extending the original answerable-question evaluations.

E2.justification: Comparator membership in the retained experiments is unchanged, including the DAPO comparison moved from Table 4 to Table 10. New evaluations reuse existing comparison methods; majority voting changes the inference protocol. The new GRPO-UC footnote clarifies its relationship to TruthRL/KnowRL without adding implementations of those methods.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce Qwen3-32B, controlled sweeps over w and rollout group size G, evaluation restricted to UCPO-uncertain cases, and aggregation using 1, 4, 8, or 16 responses. AbstentionBench adds total accuracy and abstention recall/precision metrics. The original main experimental settings remain as reported.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained component ablations and training curves, v2 adds performance sensitivity to w and G, tests whether UCPO-uncertain cases are difficult for GRPO, tracks homogeneous training groups to investigate NTF, and analyzes inference-time precision/coverage tradeoffs. These address several previously untested questions about uncertainty validity and robustness.

E5.justification: Both versions average three generated responses per evaluation instance. V2 additionally reports three independent UCPO training seeds, individual outcomes, and mean plus standard deviation in Table 6. This introduces training-variation reporting, but only for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on General Tasks.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 and the relocated DAPO table retain their numerical results. V2 adds substantial new results: Table 7 reports UCPO macro total accuracy/abstention recall of 58.60/60.52 versus 51.01/39.85 for GRPO-UC with reward 0.5; Table 8 adds Qwen3-32B results. Further additions cover sensitivity, uncertain subsets, seeds, filtering, and inference scaling.

M1.justification: The TAD, DURA, NTF, and low-resource training procedures remain unchanged. Appendix D.7 adds an inference adaptation, any-uncertain@n, which abstains whenever any sampled response expresses uncertainty and otherwise uses majority voting.

P1.justification: V2 makes targeted terminology and claim revisions, adds a baseline footnote, metric discussion, parameter-sensitivity section, and impact statement, and reorganizes the appendices. Much of the original prose and main section sequence remains; the expansion primarily introduces scientific content rather than extensively rewriting the existing narrative.

P2.justification: Tables 4–9 add distinct presentations for sensitivity, uncertain subsets, training seeds, abstention benchmarks, model size, and inference scaling. New Figure 10 displays raw and smoothed homogeneous-group ratios. Existing displays are retained and relocated, including v1 Table 4 becoming Table 10 and Figures 10–13 becoming Figures 11–14.

R1.justification: Section 5.2 adds positioning against inference-time confidence/semantic uncertainty estimation and RL-based numerical confidence calibration, with new citations including Malinin and Gales, Kuhn, and Damani. V2 also adds GDPO and benchmark-source references and clarifies GRPO-UC as a controlled abstraction of fixed-reward approaches.

T1.justification: New Appendix A derives uncertainty-suppression and aggregate-advantage conditions, analyzes the low-correctness regime, and establishes a unique interior zero of idealized DURA gain at fixed deterministic correctness. V1 lacked these derivations. However, the new equal-proportion zero-gain assertion in Section 4.5 conflicts with Equation (5), which approaches 1/6 for w=1 as the stabilizer vanishes.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens support for its central uncertainty-learning claims through explicit unanswerable-query evaluations, formal advantage analysis, and tests of parameter, seed, and model-scale robustness. It also narrows claims and better explains coverage costs. The new equilibrium misstatement in Section 4.5 is a concrete weakness, but its localized impact does not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical coverage and analytical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe UCPO and provide readable text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Retained material can be matched despite appendix expansion, relocation, and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds sensitivity, training-seed, unanswerable-query, larger-model, and inference-time experiments.

before.justification: V1 reports original UCPO experiments on mathematical reasoning and general knowledge, component ablations, training trajectories, and DAPO integration results.

results.title: UCPO: Uncertainty-Aware Policy Optimization

C1.justification: The central contributions and approximately 100× CIFAR-10 speedup claim remain. V2 narrows causal wording to group-removal counterfactual effects and recasts the conclusion around best or tied-best head-focused metrics. The conclusion also strengthens its general runtime claim from reduced cost to an order-of-magnitude reduction over LOGO.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly defines counterfactuals as operational model comparisons rather than structural causal counterfactuals. It interprets likelihood-oracle results as exposing weaker broader-ranking fidelity and adds substantive limitations concerning omitted density correction, absent approximation-error bounds, hierarchical or overlapping groups, and soft reweighting (Appendices D.5 and E). These substantially expand v1's qualifications.

D1.justification: V2 adds a GUDA code-repository link in the abstract and implementation details for the new likelihood evaluation, including batch size 64, 16 GPU shards, torchdiffeq, and solver tolerances of 10⁻⁵. It also revises the documented conditional-unlearning learning rate. Most existing implementation information is retained.

E1.justification: CIFAR-10 and UnlearnCanvas coverage is retained. Appendix D.6 adds an imperfect-grouping scenario by randomly reassigning 5% of CIFAR-10 group membership, extending evaluation beyond clean semantic groups.

E2.justification: V2 adds uniform style sampling and style-removed conditioning as evaluated comparison variants against AWSS in Table 3. The external comparator sets in the original main experiments remain unchanged.

E3.justification: V2 introduces supplementary evaluation against a PF-ODE likelihood oracle with aligned batching, a balanced 5% group-corruption protocol with retrained LOGO models, and controlled anchor comparisons. It also revises the stated conditional-unlearning learning rate from 1×10⁻⁶ to 2×10⁻⁶ in Appendices B.1 and C.2.2; the PDFs do not establish whether this reflects rerunning experiments.

E4.justification: Three substantive analyses are added: whether weighted retain-style anchors outperform simpler alternatives (B.1), whether ELBO attribution agrees with likelihood-based attribution (D.5), and whether attribution withstands noisy group membership (D.6). The earlier hyperparameter, aggregation, and qualitative analyses are retained.

E5.justification: The new PF-ODE analysis averages likelihood estimates over five independent Hutchinson seeds, synchronized across models. The noisy-partition experiment specifies seed 42. These add seed and stochastic-estimation reporting, but neither version reports confidence intervals or repeated-training uncertainty for the main comparisons.

E6.justification: Main-table accuracy values are retained, while substantial new results appear in Tables 3, 13, and 16. Anchor Top-1 scores are 0.456 for AWSS, 0.447 for uniform sampling, and 0.400 for style removal. Under the new likelihood oracle, GUDA leads DAS on Top-1 (0.645 versus 0.639), but trails on NDCG@3 (0.618 versus 0.630). Under noisy groups, GUDA achieves 0.673 Top-1 versus DAS's 0.666.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1, ELBO-difference attribution, preservation losses, ReTrack redirection, and conditional style-selection anchors are retained. The density-ratio correction changes the theoretical derivation; v2 explicitly states that the practical loss still omits this factor.

P1.justification: V2 makes targeted wording and terminology edits, expands related-work and theoretical explanations, corrects cross-references, and adds acknowledgements, a conflict disclosure, and a limitations appendix. The main section sequence and most existing prose remain intact.

P2.justification: V2 adds the anchor, likelihood-oracle, and noisy-partition tables; Table 13(a) also redisplays existing results. Existing figures are retained with label and annotation edits, including corrected style names. Tables and figures move through pagination while the overall document format remains stable.

R1.justification: Related work adds Datamodels (Ilyas et al., 2022) and music attribution through unlearning (Choi et al., 2025), explaining their relationship to GUDA. V2 more explicitly locates novelty in LOGOA, oracle validation, and conditional anchors while acknowledging ReTrack reuse. Numerous publication-metadata updates concern already cited works.

T1.justification: V1's Appendix A.1 claims an unbiased retain-only reformulation without the sampling density ratio. V2 inserts p_ret/p_for into Equation 15 and distinguishes that exact objective from the implemented approximation in Section 4.2.1. This substantively repairs the central mathematical justification. Appendix C.3.5 also corrects the truncated RBO range from [0,1] to [0,1−p^N].

improvement.justification: V2 repairs a central mathematical justification and distinguishes the implemented approximation from the exact objective. New anchor ablations, likelihood-oracle validation, and noisy-partition tests address important evidence gaps in v1, while expanded limitations improve interpretation. These substantially strengthen correctness and validation. Remaining reporting weaknesses include the unexplained learning-rate revision and the conclusion's broad order-of-magnitude speedup claim, since Table 2 supports only about 5.2× on UnlearnCanvas.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GUDA framework and main experiments. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching across revisions.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds anchor ablations, likelihood-oracle comparisons, and noisy-group experiments.

before.justification: V1 reports original attribution accuracy, runtime measurements, qualitative examples, and ablations on CIFAR-10 and UnlearnCanvas.

results.title: GUDA: Counterfactual Group-wise Training Data Attribution for Diffusion Models via Unlearning

C1.justification: The central contributions remain MCLP, its use in hybrid-reward RL, and the RP-TTS dataset. The conclusion broadens the claimed superiority from strong LALM baselines to both LALM and Instruct-TTS baselines. Human alignment receives greater prominence, but it was already claimed and investigated in v1.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations of semantic tokenization, fixed-transcript conditioning, and the ground-truth prediction direction. It replaces v1's interpretation of MOS as approaching ground-truth naturalness with an explicit stylistic-consistency interpretation, and explains the limitations of similarity proxies and single-turn comparisons. New limitations identify Mandarin-focused evaluation, restricted domains, and possible noise or bias from automatic annotations.

D1.justification: v1 promises a future dataset release; v2 reports public code and supplies a dataset access link. It identifies the scorer's Step-Audio-2 initialization and substantially expands training documentation, including optimizer parameters, clipping, sequence length, minimum learning rate, and RL iteration, batch, warmup, and decoding settings. Most additions disclose previously unspecified details rather than demonstrate changed experiments. Appendix A's construction prompts are retained.

E1.justification: Appendix B extends metric evaluation beyond Mandarin RP-TTS to English and Mandarin Genshin-Voice speech, using self-prompted and preceding-utterance-prompted zero-shot synthesis. This adds language coverage and distinct prompting scenarios. The renamed WenetSpeech-RP-TTS corpus and Appendix C subdivisions retain the original main evaluation coverage.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds four evaluated Instruct-TTS comparators: CosyVoice3, Higgs Audio V2, OV-InstructTTS, and Qwen3TTS, all without audio history. GPT-Audio, MiMo-Audio-7B-Instruct, and Step-Audio-2-mini remain, substantially broadening the comparison beyond general-purpose LALMs. Shortened MiMo labels do not identify a new baseline.

E3.justification: The evaluation drops Pinyin WER and adds CAM++ and Emo2Vec similarities. The MOS panel changes from 32 annotators with 30 valid responses to 50 with 48 valid responses, retaining 30 evaluation cases plus one quality-control case. SFT warmup is reported as 100 iterations instead of a 0.03 ratio, without establishing a rerun. Appendix B introduces a controlled self-versus-previous-prompt protocol using 1,000 samples per language from 20 speakers.

E4.justification: Table 3 extends the existing training-stage and reward ablations with human MOS and similarity metrics, directly testing perceptual benefits beyond MCLP. Appendix B adds cross-lingual prompting controls, while Appendix C analyzes dataset composition and performance by scene category, dialogue length, and speaker count. The original human–MCLP analysis and Figure 5 are retained and relocated, not newly introduced.

E5.justification: Both versions report 95% confidence intervals for MOS and the binned human–MCLP win rates. The correlation analysis retains 32 listeners and ten bins. New MOS rows follow the existing uncertainty-reporting practice; changed interval values and the larger subjective panel do not establish a new statistical estimation procedure. No seed or repeated-training-run reporting is added.

E6.justification: Tables 2–3 add baseline, similarity, and ablation MOS results; Tables 4–9 add cross-lingual outcomes and dataset/performance breakdowns. The proposed system's MOS changes from 3.646 ± 0.060 to 3.576 ± 0.045 under the revised listener panel, so this is not a same-setting performance decline. Shared CER and MCLP values remain unchanged, while Pinyin WER entries disappear. The retrieved-video count is corrected from 13,510 to 8,556, matching Table 1 in both versions.

M1.justification: The MCLP formula and conditioning, SFT objective, GRPO procedure, and gated MCLP-plus-CER reward remain unchanged. However, v1 describes scorer-training loss on TA4 tokens, defined as interleaved text and audio, whereas v2 specifies audio-token-only loss. The unchanged Figure 1 and expanded Section 4.1 do not establish whether this reflects an actual loss-mask change or corrected documentation.

P1.justification: The metric explanation and experimental narrative undergo substantial rewriting. Human–metric validation moves from the ablations into a dedicated subsection before the main results, and the ablations are reorganized around SFT, RL, and rewards. v2 also introduces a dedicated limitations section, standardizes CER terminology, and corrects the running title and author information.

P2.justification: Table 2 gains baseline-family grouping, additional rows, and revised metric columns; Table 3 gains similarity and MOS columns. Six new appendix tables display cross-lingual validation, dataset distributions, and stratified performance. These substantially expand and restructure the evidence presentation. The original five figures and dataset-pipeline table are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting Higgs Audio V2, emotion2vec, CAM++, and 3D-Speaker. Its broader positioning relative to controllable TTS, speech role-playing agents, and RL remains substantially unchanged. The PromptTTS 2 preprint-to-publication update identifies the same work and is not an added citation.

T1.justification: v2 removes the entire information-theoretic justification in Section 4.1, including v1 Equations 2–3 linking MCLP, conditional entropy, and mutual information under a small-KL assumption. Operational explanations replace this formal argument without a replacement derivation. The metric and optimization equations otherwise remain, with renumbering.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important empirical weaknesses: Table 2 adds relevant Instruct-TTS comparisons, and Table 3 provides human evidence for the central RL benefit, with SFT MOS 3.178 versus 3.576 after RL, reducing reliance on the optimized MCLP metric. Expanded implementation/access information and explicit limitations also improve reproducibility and interpretation. The formal mutual-information argument is withdrawn, scorer-loss wording remains ambiguous, and Appendix C has unreconciled training totals of 304,489 and 308,023. These shortcomings temper, but do not outweigh, the substantial improvement in support for the central empirical claims.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MCLP-based role-play TTS research. All pages, equations, figures, tables, and appendices were readable and could be matched across versions, with no material reading gaps.

after.justification: v2 retains and extends the original experiments, including additional baselines, human-rated ablations, cross-lingual metric validation, and stratified dataset analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original RP-TTS comparisons and reward ablations in Tables 2–3, subjective evaluations, and human–MCLP agreement analysis in Figure 5.

results.title: Evaluating and Rewarding LALMs for Expressive Role-Play TTS via Mean Continuation Log-Probability

C1.justification: V1 presents upper-bounding reconstruction residuals as a central theoretical contribution. V3 removes that broad claim and states maximality within a restricted class of stable scores instead. Its contribution list emphasizes mitigating cross-category/cross-region mismatches and comparisons with trained and training-free methods, while retaining the central RAD performance claim.

C2.justification: Appendix G shifts the explanation of low pixel F1 from background activations toward extreme anomaly-pixel imbalance and score-tail overlap. New discussions interpret backbone-controlled gains, unseen-normal memory coverage, hyperparameter robustness, and compression tradeoffs. V3 also removes the cross-dataset training/test-ratio argument for data efficiency from Section 5.2.

D1.justification: V3 explicitly specifies uniform fusion weights of 0.25 and official 3D-ADAM background filtering, and reports inference latency and memory requirements. Appendix A's preprocessing, retrieval parameters, software, hardware, and seed details remain unchanged, as does the code-access information. The new coreset variant lacks a detailed selection procedure.

E1.justification: V3 adds MVTec-AD2 evaluation in Appendix I and extends incremental-class evaluation to VisA, introducing macaroni1 alongside three fixed categories in Appendix L. This is a limited expansion within industrial anomaly detection; the original four benchmarks and RGB-only use of 3D-ADAM remain.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds GeneralAD to the standard comparisons. The 3D-ADAM comparison in Table A3 removes Uninet while retaining PatchCore and Dinomaly. The few-shot comparator membership remains unchanged; PatchCore is relocated and relabeled, not newly introduced.

E3.justification: The 3D-ADAM comparison upgrades Dinomaly to DINOv3 and expands reporting from two F1 metrics to seven metrics. V3 also introduces matched-backbone controls, explicit hyperparameter sweeps, FPR at 95% TPR evaluation, compression/latency comparisons, and VisA target-class scaling protocols. Background filtering is newly specified for 3D-ADAM; v1 does not establish its earlier filtering procedure.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained component ablations and encoder/scaling studies, v3 adds tests separating backbone strength from retrieval, sensitivity to K/radius/fusion weights, unseen-normal generalization, 3D-ADAM score distributions, memory compression, retrieval latency, and incremental-class transfer to VisA. These substantially broaden the questions examined.

E5.justification: Both versions retain the seed=1 and deterministic-CUDA statement in Appendix A, without adding repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The new score means and percentiles are distribution diagnostics rather than uncertainty estimates for experimental performance.

E6.justification: Table A3 replaces the 3D-ADAM results: RAD's image/pixel F1 changes from 92.6/32.5 to 96.4/46.4, and its image-level ranking changes. The upgraded comparator and newly specified filtering prevent interpreting this as an established same-setting gain. Substantial new results cover backbone controls, MVTec-AD2, sensitivity, false positives, efficiency, compression, and VisA scaling. Existing few-shot, scaling, encoder, and per-category scores are retained.

M1.justification: Section 5.6 introduces an evaluated coreset-compressed RAD variant, changing the stored feature memory. The main frozen-encoder, global retrieval, spatial conditioning, and multilayer cosine-scoring procedure remains unchanged. Explicit uniform fusion weights are newly disclosed rather than an established algorithm change.

P1.justification: The abstract, introductory motivation and contributions, spatial-conditioning explanation, Section 4, and Appendix G undergo substantial rewriting. Task-specific training terminology is adopted throughout. New efficiency sections and diagnostic appendices reshape the exposition, with the former per-category and visualization appendices moved from I/J to M/N.

P2.justification: V3 adds six tables displaying compression, score distributions, backbone controls, sensitivity, unseen-normal generalization, and VisA scaling. Table A3 is redesigned from two F1 columns to seven metrics; Table A1 reorders PatchCore, and per-category tables are packed more tightly. Existing plots and qualitative images are retained and repositioned.

R1.justification: V3 more explicitly positions RAD against existing training-free nearest-neighbor approaches and relabels PatchCore as training-free in Table A1. It adds references for deep nearest-neighbor detection, GeneralAD, MVTec-AD2, ImageNet, and two 3D anomaly-detection works. The extensive related-work review otherwise remains largely unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix D adds Theorem D.3, defining expected anomaly–normal separation and proving a near-optimality bound controlled by unseen-normal distance to memory under a finite-expectation assumption. V1 already contained empirical saturation, pointwise maximality, and non-expansiveness results, which are retained. Section 3.4 additionally derives retrieval-complexity bounds.

improvement.justification: V3 corrects an important overstatement by aligning the central theoretical claim with a restricted score class and adding a proved separation guarantee. Matched-backbone controls, unseen-normal and sensitivity tests, and measured resource tradeoffs substantially strengthen attribution and practical validation. The removed Uninet comparison and limited coreset implementation detail do not outweigh these gains; the improvement rests on stronger justification, not the higher replacement 3D-ADAM scores.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RAD research despite the refined title. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and can be matched reliably across revisions.

after.justification: V3 retains original empirical results and adds matched-backbone comparisons, sensitivity tests, unseen-normal analyses, efficiency measurements, and memory-compression results.

before.justification: V1 reports original RAD benchmark results, few-shot and data-scaling experiments, encoder comparisons, component ablations, and qualitative evaluations.

results.title: Is Task-Specific Training Necessary for Anomaly Detection?

C1.justification: The abstract and four principal contributions retain the same scientific claims: optimization-free rank approximation, monotonicity and lower bounds, convergence and sampling guarantees, slicing, and usefulness for generative learning. More specific transport/pretraining wording and additional evidence do not materially redefine these headline contributions.

C2.justification: Section 4.3 adds practical interpretation of K's approximation–sampling tradeoff and L's projection error. Table 1 explains empirical ratios above one, and C.5.2 qualifies feature-space discrepancies as representation-dependent. New discussions qualify efficiency by setting and acknowledge unfavorable dependence alternatives. Most of the existing limitations discussion is retained.

D1.justification: v2 documents logistic soft-CDF comparisons, interpolated quantiles, feature-space training components, testing settings, and generator/classifier architectures and optimization details. Appendix E distinguishes hard- and soft-rank runtime and memory costs. The anonymous code-and-data repository disclosure is replaced by a named GitHub code link; hardware information is unchanged.

E1.justification: CIFAR-10 replaces CelebA for image transport, and CIFAR-10-C adds realistic corruption-detection coverage. New experiments cover two-sample hypothesis testing, copula dependence alternatives, and generation of two-moons distributions with higher-dimensional extensions. The earlier estimation families, four transport toys, and MNIST remain.

E2.justification: The neural-KL and MNIST comparator sets are retained. New reported comparisons include Hotelling's T2, sliced optimal transport, MMD, and tuned MMD in Figures 12–13; C2ST in Figure 14; and sliced Wasserstein, MMD, and full assignment OT for generator training in Table 6.

E3.justification: New testing protocols include permutation calibration, with Figure 11 specifying N=M=2000, K=4, L=64, and 500 permutations. Appendix E adds shared-generator comparisons with external classifier-JS stopping criteria and a 3000-step budget. CO-RPT's rank schedule changes alongside the dataset replacement. Appendix C.1 corrects its random-projection description to coordinate-axis summation, matching v1's main text; this does not establish a rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds null-calibration checks, power-versus-runtime analyses across scale, shape, and dependence alternatives, and corruption-severity/sample-size analyses on CIFAR-10-C.
