Appendix E adds computational-cost and time-to-quality analyses. The earlier resolution, tail-behavior, and dimensionality analyses remain.

E5.justification: Existing 10-run mean-and-standard-deviation reporting is retained. New testing figures add rejection-rate standard errors over 100 repetitions and 95% binomial confidence intervals; Figure 14 specifies 10 independent C2ST trials per corruption–severity pair. These are additional reporting practices for new experiments, not increased run counts for retained benchmarks.

E6.justification: The numerical contents of v1 Tables 1–4 match v2 Tables 1, 3, 4, and 5. Newly reported outcomes include testing power and calibration, CIFAR-10 feature-training FID decreasing from roughly 380 to 41, and Table 6 timing results: at d=4, Rank takes 131.6 seconds versus SWD's 117.6. CelebA samples are replaced by CIFAR-10 samples; these are different-setting results.

M1.justification: The central rank/Bernstein estimator and transport constructions remain. Appendix C.5.2 adds generator training with rank-TV in discriminator feature space and a hybrid adversarial-loss variant; C.7 introduces permutation-calibrated testing using the chi-square specialization. Algorithm 1 also drops optional monotone-rank reordering. These are localized procedural extensions.

P1.justification: v2 clarifies empirical versus population notation, rewrites portions of the estimator and transport explanations, merges the concentration proposition into Theorem 2.6, subdivides the image appendix, and adds an impact statement. Affiliations and contribution notes change. Most existing prose and the overall narrative organization remain recognizable.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to two-column presentation, with extensive resizing and relocation of displays. v2 adds a notation table, a timing table, and Figures 11–16, replaces the Figure 5 image grid, and redisplays the transport snapshots. Existing numerical tables are retained and partly renumbered.

R1.justification: Targeted references are added for calibration, goodness-of-fit and two-sample testing, CIFAR benchmarks, and precision–recall divergences. Appendix C.6 newly distinguishes scalar PR-divergence approximation from direct PR-curve estimation. CelebA and some gradient-flow references disappear, while the central positioning as a generalization of earlier rank-based work remains.

T1.justification: v2 introduces atomless-reference assumptions and revises Theorem 3.3 to require Lipschitz f', allow zero limiting variance, and provide a positivity criterion. New Theorem 3.4 and Appendix B.9 establish oracle-reference asymptotic normality for growing resolution, with sqrt(N) << K_N << N under smoothness assumptions. Several existing proof terms and constants are also corrected.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens theoretical validity through explicit atomlessness and revised normality conditions, adds a proved resolution-selection result, and resolves the KL benchmark's conflicting protocol descriptions. Calibrated testing and external time-to-quality comparisons provide useful independent validation, including unfavorable cases. The new FID and timing results have limited repeated-run uncertainty reporting, and replacing CelebA is not a same-task performance gain, but these limitations do not outweigh the improvements in rigor and empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same rank-statistic f-divergence construction. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial reformatting and added material.

after.justification: v2 retains original estimation and MNIST results and reports additional CIFAR-10 generation, synthetic and image two-sample testing, and time-to-quality experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic divergence-estimation experiments, particle-transport demonstrations, CelebA samples, and MNIST training comparisons in Section 4 and Appendix C.

results.title: Approximating f -Divergences with Rank Statistics

C1.justification: The abstract revises the quantified detection-score advantage from 40% to 51.9%. The central contributions concerning cascaded tabular generation, mixed-type features, and a tighter transport bound remain unchanged, as does the conclusion's substantive scope.

C2.justification: V2 interprets the added train/test comparisons as evidence against overfitting and expands privacy cautions and the encoder-depth fidelity/privacy tradeoff. It corrects the direction of the DCR diversity interpretation and explains additional applications of informative missingness.

D1.justification: V2 adds an explicit TabCascade repository link, documents precision handling in Appendix A.2, and clarifies that encoders train on preprocessed numerical features in Appendix A.3.2. V1 already supplied substantial architecture, training, software, and hardware details; the new link does not establish when code first became available.

E1.justification: The same 12 datasets and complete-data and simulated-missingness scenarios remain, including missingness rates of 10%, 25%, and 50%. Added test-set metrics evaluate existing coverage rather than new datasets or tasks.

E2.justification: The evaluated baselines remain ARF, TVAE, CTGAN, TabDDPM, TabSyn, TabDiff, and CDTD. The ARF low-resolution substitution and other component comparisons were already present in v1.

E3.justification: V2 reports fixing a precision-related post-processing bug and specifies feature-specific rounding with synthetic and training-data precision capped at six decimal digits (Appendix A.2; Acknowledgements). It adds test-reference Shape, WD, JSD, and Trend evaluations, low-resolution JSD, and MIA evaluation across encoder depths. These materially revise evaluation while retaining the stated training budgets and split proportions.

E4.justification: V2 adds a train/test overfitting diagnostic in Section 5.3, directly evaluates low-resolution outputs using JSD in Table 23, and examines privacy across encoder depths in Table 24. These extend the existing ablation suite without changing its principal experimental questions.

E5.justification: V2 clarifies that aggregate uncertainties are standard deviations across 12 datasets and explicitly identifies single training runs with ten sampling seeds for complete-data and depth ablations. It also clarifies that training seeds affect data splits. The main three-training/ten-sampling-seed design already existed; no increase in repetitions is established.

E6.justification: Following the precision correction, Table 1 replaces TabCascade/CDTD detection means of 0.423/0.301 with 0.787/0.518; TabCascade's MIA mean changes from 0.959 to 0.935. Main and ablation results are extensively revised, with test-reference, low-resolution JSD, and depth-wise MIA entries added and some DCR ablation entries removed. These are revised evaluations under changed post-processing, not demonstrated same-setting model gains.

M1.justification: Section 4 and Algorithms 1 and 2 retain the cascade, DT/GMM encoders, CDTD low-resolution model, guided flow matching, learned schedules, and masking procedure. Rewritten discrete-state explanations and removed duplicate formulas do not change the proposed method.

P1.justification: Localized rewrites clarify discrete-state handling and low-resolution representations, rename Section 3 to Problem Statement and Motivation, and add acknowledgements. The main section sequence and most exposition remain, alongside limited publication-footer and bibliographic edits.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn, Figure 2a's legend and placement change, and Figure 23 moves onto its own page. Tables gain test-reference rows, four corresponding appendix tables are added, and selected ablation columns are reordered or replaced. The overall visual format remains.

R1.justification: V2 adds Daniels and Hogan (2008) and Molenberghs et al. (2014) for missing-data applications, and Yao et al. (2025) for DCR/privacy interpretation. It sharpens the distinction from image cascades. Other reference changes largely update publication metadata for existing works.

T1.justification: Appendix A.4 corrects the stated optimal DCR reference from 0.5 to Ntrain/(Ntrain + Ntest), approximately 0.778, with an explicit no-ties qualification. The transport-bound theorem and Appendix A.1 derivations and proofs otherwise remain substantively unchanged.

improvement.justification: The acknowledged precision bug compromised v1's central detection evaluation. V2 documents its correction and replaces affected results, while adding overfitting checks, clearer uncertainty reporting, and explicit code access. Resolving this central evaluation defect substantially strengthens empirical credibility. The limited loss of DCR ablation entries is outweighed by these gains and the added privacy analysis.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TabCascade research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices A.1-A.10 support reliable comparison despite revisions and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains original benchmark and ablation results, revises their evaluation, and adds test-set comparisons and further diagnostic results.

before.justification: V1 reports original synthetic-data generation experiments on 12 datasets, baseline comparisons, and component, missingness, and encoder ablations.

results.title: Cascaded Flow Matching for Heterogeneous Tabular Data with Mixed-Type Features

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions and conclusion retain the same claims about lower recoverability, improved secret encoding and mechanistic detection. The new experiments support and qualify these claims without redefining the headline contributions.

C2.justification: v2 distinguishes acceptable text quality from retained downstream capability and interprets mixed training as a partial mitigation. Appendices H–I add sampling and retokenization explanations and substantive limits involving exposure conditions, payload size, symbolic tasks and alphabet-search scaling. The hidden-state-access limitation was already acknowledged in v1.

D1.justification: v2 documents the mixed-training ratio, instruction-data source and reuse of Appendix D hyperparameters. Appendix H explicitly identifies greedy decoding as the main evaluation default and describes the retokenization pipeline. Existing implementation details and future code-release commitments are retained.

E1.justification: v2 adds downstream knowledge and commonsense evaluation on MMLU, ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag and WinoGrande, substantially extending coverage beyond secret transmission and detection. WikiText-103, helpful-instructions and Alpaca remain; mixed-motive training reuses the existing helpful-instructions source.

E2.justification: ASCII+Parity remains the attack baseline, and the same four encoding/bucketing combinations and base-model probe references are retained. The added studies reuse these comparison methods under new training and evaluation conditions.

E3.justification: v2 adds the 75/25 training mixture, capability degradation averaged across four benchmarks, and matched single-objective versus mixed-motive evaluations. Appendix H adds temperature 0.0 versus 0.7 testing and tokenization/decode/retokenization measurements across three text segments. Existing Wiki/TrojanStego hyperparameters and probe protocols are retained.

E4.justification: New analyses test whether benign instruction data mitigates capability loss, whether probe detection survives mixed-motive training, and whether sampling or retokenization disrupts transmission. These address substantial practical robustness questions absent from v1. The original OOD and XOR controls remain.

E5.justification: Appendix H.1 explicitly reports averaging three runs of 2,000 samples for the new temperature experiment. Existing classifier seeds, text-quality SEM reporting and probe confidence intervals remain unchanged. No increase in runs for retained experiments or new significance-testing procedure is established.

E6.justification: Original scores are retained, while Table 1 adds mixed-motive results, Table 3 adds capability losses, Figure 6 adds probe results, and Tables 7–8 add robustness outcomes. For example, v2 reports Llama-LoRA A+E exact match of 38% under mixed training versus the retained 30% under single-objective training, and Llama WikiText bucket-flip rates of 7.32% for parity versus 0.45% for embedding bucketing.

M1.justification: Section 6.5 introduces a mixed-motive training variant combining 75% steganographic examples with 25% ordinary instruction-tuning examples. This adapts the training procedure to preserve capabilities; the geometric encoding, bucketing, model architectures and probe methods remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The narrative gains Sections 6.5 and 7.4 and Appendices H–I, with limited edits to the XOR discussion, impact statement and terminology. Most existing prose and section order remain intact; the first-page publication footer also changes.

P2.justification: The evidence displays expand substantially: Table 1 gains mixed-motive rows and highlighting, Table 3 presents capability comparisons, Figure 6 presents mixed-motive probes, and Tables 7–8 present robustness results. Existing displays are retained and reflowed; the XOR table becomes Table 4, and Figure 5 only changes some TS labels to T.

R1.justification: v2 adds the benchmark references for MMLU, ARC, HellaSwag and WinoGrande. The related-work discussion and positioning relative to TrojanStego, inference-time steganography and mechanistic detection remain substantively unchanged.

T1.justification: Definition 3.1, the geometric constructions, Theorems 7.1–7.2 and their Appendix B proofs are unchanged. The added robustness and scaling discussions introduce no new formal derivation or theorem.

improvement.justification: v1 assessed text quality without measuring retained downstream capabilities. v2 addresses this important gap through capability benchmarks, a mixed-motive mitigation and verification that probe detection survives it (Sections 6.5 and 7.4). Appendix I also supplies meaningful applicability limits. The gains are substantial, although Table 7 needs correction: its near-invariant bit-accuracy claim conflicts with the Ministral Full E+E row's 3.1-point drop, and that row reports exact match exceeding bit accuracy. These localized inconsistencies weaken the temperature analysis but do not outweigh the broader validation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with readable text, equations, figures, tables and appendices. v2 retains Appendices A–G and adds H–I; renumbering and relocation can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds capability benchmarks, mixed-motive training, temperature robustness and retokenization results.

before.justification: v1 reports original model-training, payload-recoverability, generalization, text-quality and linear-probe experiments, including an XOR-masking control.

results.title: Hide and Seek in Embedding Space: Geometry-based Steganography and Detection in Large Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution list remove the explicit robustness claim while retaining claims of policy smoothness, competitive returns, and unchanged actor updates. The central contribution connecting critic geometry to policy sensitivity remains substantively unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly treats the losses as incentives rather than guarantees and adds a limitations section. The SAC discussion becomes more environment-dependent, including the near-tie on Ant. New interpretations address VFC approximation failures, critic-baseline collapse, component interactions, and Humanoid's deceptively smooth but unsuccessful baseline policy.

D1.justification: Appendix E.1 newly discloses the coordinate-search procedure, tuning order, MPR noise scale of 0.01, and curvature margin of 1.0. Additional analysis details specify autograd, SVD, eigenvalue computation, and log-based convergence measurement. The existing per-environment loss-weight tables and named hardware configurations are retained.

E1.justification: The original six continuous-control environments and observation-noise scenarios remain. Appendix N adds Humanoid-v5 under TD3, extending the existing locomotion coverage without introducing a new task family.

E2.justification: Appendix J adds evaluated SN-Critic and GP-Critic baselines on LunarLander and Walker, substantially extending comparison to competing critic-side regularizers. Appendix M adds CAPS+PAVE. Base, CAPS, GRAD, and ASAP remain in the principal comparisons.

E3.justification: v1 uses ReLU baselines against SiLU PAVE; v2 standardizes all methods to SiLU in the principal comparisons. Appendix A replaces finite-difference visualization with exact full mixed-Hessian spectral norms. New protocols include trajectory diagnostics, training checkpoints, full factorial ablation, and convergence measured against each method's own final performance.

E4.justification: v2 adds direct MPR/VFC proxy checks, exact Hessian and gradient-direction diagnostics, geometry tracking during training, critic-baseline failure analyses, and wall-clock analysis. Appendices K–M add sensitivity sweeps, all eight component combinations, and an actor-regularization combination test. The original incremental ablation and Pendulum sensitivity analysis are retained.

E5.justification: Tables 1–2 now explicitly identify standard deviations as across five seeds, and Appendix K identifies seeds 6–10 for its additional sensitivity experiments. Five-seed experiments and standard-deviation reporting already existed in v1; no increase in the principal experiments' run count or new significance-testing procedure is established.

E6.justification: PAVE's Table 1–2 results are identical, but comparator results, noise results, throughput, and learning curves change substantially. Under the revised activation setting, SAC Ant returns for ASAP change from 4642 to 5707, versus unchanged PAVE at 5706, removing its previous return advantage. Numerous diagnostic and ablation results are added; Humanoid reports returns of 309 for Base and 2894 for PAVE.

M1.justification: PAVE's Algorithm 1, three regularization losses, SiLU critic, and standard actor update remain unchanged. Exact Hessian computation is introduced for evaluation. Appendix M separately evaluates CAPS combined with PAVE as a supplementary combination analysis.

P1.justification: The title and affiliations change, related-work and results passages are edited, and theoretical remarks, limitations, and acknowledgments are introduced. The established introduction–theory–method narrative and much existing prose remain intact; the extensive new scientific material does not constitute a wholesale rewrite.

P2.justification: v2 adds numerous diagnostic, comparison, and ablation tables. Figures 1–3 are redrawn with revised norm labels and shared scales; Figure 1 switches from LunarLander to Walker. Learning curves are updated and redistributed, and appendix figures are relocated. The original sensitivity figure is retained.

R1.justification: Section 2.1 adds Zhao et al. (2023) and distinguishes action chunking from critic-level stabilization. Appendix J develops comparisons with previously cited critic-regularization approaches. Other reference changes largely correct metadata or update publication information; the overall research positioning remains.

T1.justification: The implicit-policy Jacobian lemma, Lipschitz bound, and principal derivations are retained. Section 5.3 corrects the inference that the trace-based penalty enforces an eigenvalue bound, acknowledging that it controls trace rather than individual eigenvalues. New remarks explicitly qualify applicability to boundary actions, nonunique optima, and critics lacking strict concavity.

improvement.justification: Standardizing activations removes an important confound in v1's comparisons. Correcting the trace-to-eigenvalue justification and adding direct mechanism checks, critic-side baselines, and factorial ablations substantially strengthen the paper's evidential foundation. Some new summaries overgeneralize—for example, the stated 14–47% baseline concavity range excludes Reacher's 100% in Table 15—but these shortcomings do not outweigh the improved experimental controls and theoretical qualifications.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PAVE research work. Their complete text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across revisions and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds proxy validation, Hessian measurements, critic-side comparisons, expanded ablations, convergence measurements, and Humanoid evaluation.

before.justification: v1 reports original TD3 and SAC experiments, observation-noise evaluations, component ablations, sensitivity analyses, and training-throughput measurements.

results.title: Stabilizing the Q-Gradient Field for Policy Smoothness in Actor-Critic Methods

C1.justification: v2 adds an explicit contribution that RN-D is algorithm-agnostic and benefits multiple on-policy algorithms, whereas v1 leaves evaluation beyond PPO to future work. Conversely, the abstract narrows its state-of-the-art claim to on-policy RL, and Section 7 explicitly disclaims superiority across all RL algorithms.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the new algorithm comparisons as evidence that benefits are not specific to PPO's surrogate. It adds an interpretation of runtime saturation with increasing bin count and explicitly identifies TRPO memory requirements as a barrier to matching the vision-based setup. Section 7 also qualifies the preferred bin count as task-dependent.

D1.justification: The abstract adds a code-repository address. Appendix B supplies new TRPO implementation details, including KL threshold 0.01, damping 0.1, ten conjugate-gradient iterations, and backtracking settings, and reports eight RTX 6000 Pro GPUs for TRPO/SPO. Runtime tables add concrete resource measurements. These substantially extend reproducibility information, although the new cross-benchmark GAE wording remains ambiguous.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same five Gym locomotion tasks, ten ManiSkill state tasks, and five ManiSkill RGB tasks. The added TRPO/SPO experiments reuse the state-based suites, and the runtime analysis uses existing tasks. Appendix D explicitly restricts RGB evaluation to PPO.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated TRPO- and SPO-based comparisons: Figure 1 compares their standard MLP-C implementations with RN-D, and Figures 10–11 also include RN-C and MLP-D under each algorithm. These algorithm-specific comparison suites were absent from v1. The original PPO comparator set and TD3/TD-MPC2 comparisons remain.

E3.justification: Appendix B.1 adds TRPO natural-gradient updates with a KL constraint, conjugate gradient, backtracking, and full-batch actor updates, plus SPO's softly regularized surrogate. Appendix C.5 introduces throughput measurements alongside runtime. The existing PPO hyperparameter table and training budgets are unchanged. The new GAE paragraph does not clearly reconcile its 0.99/0.95 values with the retained ManiSkill PPO values of 0.80/0.90.

E4.justification: New Appendix C.5 examines computational sensitivity to bin count on Humanoid-v4 and compares runtime across the four actor variants. This adds a focused overhead analysis. The existing gradient/SNR analysis, loss-swap ablation, actor-width sweep, and performance-versus-bin-count study are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions use five-seed reporting and 95% stratified bootstrap confidence intervals for learning curves; the three-seed TD-MPC2 disclosure also remains. New experiments extend the existing reporting practice without introducing different uncertainty estimation, significance testing, or an increased run count for retained experiments.

E6.justification: Figures 1 and 10–11 add aggregate and per-task TRPO/SPO results, showing higher aggregate performance for RN-D than MLP-C under both algorithms. New runtime tables report, for example, RN-D at 1.64 hours and 873.8 SPS versus RN-C at 1.75 hours and 811.1 SPS. Table 4 adds bin-count-dependent runtime results. Retained PPO curves and earlier ablation results are unchanged; the additions are not same-setting performance gains over v1.

M1.justification: The RN-D actor retains uniform per-dimension categorical discretization, pre-LayerNorm residual blocks, and the same output construction and critic design. TRPO and SPO provide additional optimization settings for evaluating this actor; no new RN-D architecture or parameterization component is introduced.

P1.justification: v2 shortens the title and running header, revises the abstract, expands the introduction, and makes localized revisions to the extended-study discussion and conclusion. It adds runtime discussion, implementation paragraphs, and funding acknowledgements. The principal section organization and most existing prose remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds a six-panel cross-algorithm overview, two substantial per-task figure grids for TRPO/SPO, and two distinct runtime tables, one repeated in the main text and appendix. Existing figures are retained and renumbered, with relocation and resizing. The new Figures 10–11 captions mention RGB variants despite Appendix D limiting those experiments to state observations.

R1.justification: Section 7 reframes TD3 and TD-MPC2 as representative off-policy efficiency comparisons rather than support for unrestricted state-of-the-art positioning. The cited-work set is otherwise retained. Changes to the SPO publication year/venue and other bibliography details do not introduce new research references.

T1.justification: Proposition 4.1, its assumptions and variance bounds, and the complete Appendix A proof are unchanged. The categorical/Gaussian likelihood derivations and Appendix C.2 loss-swap equations are also retained without substantive mathematical revision.

improvement.justification: v1's broad on-policy message relied on PPO experiments. The added TRPO/SPO evidence substantially strengthens that central generality claim, while the narrowed state-of-the-art wording improves its calibration. Runtime analysis, update details, and code-access information also improve practical assessability and reproducibility. These gains outweigh limited reporting problems: the new figure captions overstate RGB coverage, and the GAE settings are not clearly reconciled across benchmarks.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe RN-D and contain readable text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–D. The retained material can be matched reliably despite the shortened title, renumbering, and added experiments.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds TRPO/SPO experiments and runtime measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original PPO experiments on locomotion and manipulation tasks, including learning curves, gradient measurements, ablations, and off-policy comparisons.

results.title: RN-D: Discretized Categorical Actors for On-Policy Reinforcement Learning

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contribution statement, and conclusion now explicitly condition the monotonicity guarantee on non-interfering expansion. This qualifies the prominent claim using assumptions already present in v1's technical material. The central contribution of stable expansion through familiarization and routing memory remains.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning negative routing constraints, transferable agent knowledge, and amortized onboarding cost. It introduces substantive limitations involving environment drift, memory saturation, long expansion horizons, and budget-induced over-decomposition, and acknowledges the local scaling dip. Section 6 also adds a rationale for comparing against fixed three-agent strong-router configurations.

D1.justification: v2 supplies a code-access link, explicitly describes one-shot selection over finite memory candidates, and reports approximately $19.5 and 10–15 minutes per agent for onboarding. The detailed agent prompts and memory schemas are retained, as are the approximately 50 warm-up tasks and four rollouts per task.

E1.justification: Appendix D.2 adds standardized TaskCraft tasks as generic familiarization data for the non-customized warm-up control, extending the onboarding data beyond agent-conditioned synthesis. Evaluation remains on GAIA and HLE-MCQ; the larger pools and different router backbones are configuration changes.

E2.justification: Table 4 adds comparisons against variants without negative memory and without customized warm-up; Table 5 compares native and transferred memories. The original benchmark baseline roster remains. UniRoute, StageRoute, and EvoRoute receive discussion, but full implementations are not reported as evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: New designs include controlled component removal, direct Qwen-to-Gemini-3-Flash memory transfer, HLE expansion to 20 workers by adding ten Gemini-2.5-Pro-based agents, archived-plan replay on 100 HLE questions, and a 40-task GAIA variance subset. Tables 1 and 3 also redefine relative gains against same-count no-memory controls rather than the three-agent starting point. The original main evaluation settings are retained.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's malfunctioning-pool evaluation and case studies, v2 adds checks of non-interference and fallback compliance, component ablations, memory-transfer analysis, scaling beyond ten agents, and onboarding-cost analysis. Appendix D.7 additionally investigates the existing six-agent accuracy dip and attributes failures to tool-budget exhaustion.

E5.justification: v2 adds a limited uncertainty audit absent from v1: three independent seeds on 40 GAIA tasks, with accuracy standard deviations of 2.89, 1.44, and 2.89 percentage points at five, seven, and ten agents. Appendix C.2 also calls the 19/100 versus 21/100 replay difference nonsignificant without specifying a test. Full-benchmark uncertainty reporting remains absent.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results for the new analyses: at ten agents, Table 4 reports 55.2% for full MonoScale, 40.0% without negative memory, and 48.5% without customized warm-up; the new 20-agent HLE configuration reaches 23.4%. Table 2 changes the reported three-agent HLE accuracy from 11.60% to 11.70%. Core GAIA scores remain unchanged, and newly tabulated naive-scale-up overall scores already appeared in v1's Figure 1.

M1.justification: The frozen router, agent-conditioned task synthesis, success/failure memory construction, and conservative fallback remain unchanged. v2's practical-instantiation paragraph and Algorithm 1 explicitly document the existing candidate-selection procedure; they do not establish a new algorithm.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized rewrites to related work, theoretical exposition, results, and discussion, renames Section 6 to Discussion and Limitations, and inserts a procedural appendix. The main narrative order and extensive prompt, schema, proof, and case-study text remain largely intact.

P2.justification: Tables 1 and 3 gain separate matched no-memory and memory blocks; v2 adds ablation and transfer tables plus Algorithm 1. Several figures move, including Figure 1 from the first to the second page. Existing plots, illustration content, and case-study table designs are retained.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially expands positioning against UniRoute, StageRoute, and EvoRoute, distinguishing multi-step agent orchestration and reliability from model routing and cost–latency optimization. Fourteen cited works are added, extending coverage of agent risks, reusable skills, memory learning, and task synthesis.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions, assumptions, equations, and proofs are retained from v1's Appendix B in v2's Appendix C. Theorem 4.3 now explicitly names the existing non-interference and fallback assumptions, while Remark 4.4 explains their scope; neither introduces new mathematical substance.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical support for the central mechanism through controlled ablations that were absent from v1, supplemented by transfer and assumption checks. Explicit qualifications of the guarantee and analysis of the previously overlooked scaling dip improve scientific clarity. The small variance audit and overconfident predictability language in Section 6 remain weaknesses, but the stronger evidence and clearer applicability limits provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MonoScale and provide readable main text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices. Corresponding methods, proofs, agent configurations, memory schemas, and case studies can be matched across the appendix renumbering.

E6.justification: v2 adds MMR-V scores of 45.3% for RL and 44.7% for SFT+RL, alongside smaller-model, ablation and resource results. Existing 7B Video-o3 benchmark values are retained. P1.justification: Changes include localized related-work rewriting, expanded reward explanations, new experimental subsections, and moving efficiency analysis from Appendix E.4 into Section 5.5. Conference front matter, acknowledgements and an Impact Statement are added. Most existing prose and the main narrative structure remain intact.

P2.justification: The empirical displays are substantially expanded: Table 1 gains a benchmark column, comparator row and reproduction markers; the relocated efficiency table gains memory and token columns; and new Tables 7, 12, 13 and 15 present additional comparisons and analyses. Best-score highlighting is corrected in retained tables. Figures 1–15 retain their substantive content.

T1.justification: The attention-mask, reward, quota and over-turn optimization definitions in Equations 1–9 are retained. Added reward explanations do not introduce new mathematical assumptions, derivations, propositions or proofs.

Smaller-model, sparse-annotation and turn-distribution analyses substantiate generalization and efficiency more convincingly than v1. A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Video-o3 study. Their text, equations, tables, figures and Appendices A–J support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds MMR-V results, smaller-model evaluation, additional ablations and resource measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original video-QA and temporal-grounding results, component ablations, training curves, efficiency measurements and qualitative analyses.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution statements, and conclusion retain the same claims about historical repair reuse, inference without fine-tuning, cross-model improvements, and efficiency relative to the controlled forward-search baseline. The original limitations concerning Python-focused evaluation, sparse repair histories, and unreliable LLM judgments remain unchanged.

It also adds the no-plan control to the GPT-4o ablation. Existing benchmark settings, metrics, and MCTS budgets are retained.

Appendix B additionally analyzes resolved-issue overlap with four baselines. These extend the questions tested beyond the retained Guardian, MCTS, and exemplar-similarity analyses.

E5.justification: Appendix H newly states that sampling for the mini-SWE-agent experiment uses a fixed random seed, without supplying its value. The existing three-run Guardian stability analysis and McNemar tests are unchanged; no additional repeated-run or uncertainty estimates accompany the new comparisons.

E6.justification: Original benchmark, difficulty, Guardian, and cost results remain unchanged. V2 adds mini-SWE-agent results of 48/100 without ConRAD versus 58/100 with it, a no-plan Pass@1 of 32.0% versus BRD's retained 41.0%, and 10 uniquely resolved issues relative to four baselines. These supplement the principal results rather than revise them.

M1.justification: The retrieval, Exemplar Guardian, and backward reasoning distillation procedures remain unchanged. The Thought/Action/Observation integration used for mini-SWE-agent follows the integration already described in v1 Appendix C. Newly supplied prompts and explicit rejection fallback document the method rather than establish a procedural revision.

P1.justification: V2 rewrites the title, abstract, and introduction, standardizes the ConRAD name, and adds disclosure, acknowledgement, impact, and appendix sections. The main section sequence and most method and results prose remain intact.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to two-column layout, with substantial resizing and relocation of retained displays. V2 adds the mini-SWE-agent table, an overlap diagram, and extensive boxed prompt templates. The existing trajectory illustration is relocated and restyled as Figure 4.

R1.justification: V2 adds Gao et al. (2023) on in-context demonstrations and Li et al. (2025c) on model-aware in-context learning to support discussion of exemplar suitability. The broader related-work positioning remains unchanged; the APRMCTS/TSAPR reference retains the same arXiv identifier.

T1.justification: The outcome-conditioning expression, reasoning-plan definitions, exemplar tuple, and localization correctness criterion are retained. Neither version introduces theorems or proofs, and the added prompt rubrics are implementation documentation rather than new mathematical reasoning.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially improves reproducibility and empirical support. The prompt templates address a major documentation gap in this prompting-based method, while the no-plan control and mini-SWE-agent experiment address previously untested attribution and scaffold-generalization questions. The gains remain bounded: the new experiments use 100-issue subsets, lack additional uncertainty estimates, and leave the unmatched-budget MCTS comparison unresolved. Nevertheless, they materially strengthen the paper while preserving its original evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research framework, renamed from O-CRD to ConRAD. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains those original results and adds a mini-SWE-agent experiment, a no-plan ablation, and an analysis of resolved-issue overlaps.

before.justification: V1 reports original SWE-Bench Lite evaluations across three LLMs, component ablations, Guardian stability measurements, and inference-cost results.

results.title: From Historical Patches to Repair Plans: Outcome-Conditioned Reasoning for Repository-Level Program Repair

C1.justification: The abstract explicitly restricts the 3.52× throughput claim to large-batch settings. The central contributions—computational redundancy analysis, early-layer decodability prediction and training-free token eviction—and the conclusion's throughput maxima remain unchanged.

C2.justification: Section 5.2 changes the asserted safety-filter mechanism into a possible interpretation supported by indirect evidence, leaving causal validation to future work. The new Discussion and Appendix F substantially expand applicability limits and interpretation through low-batch slowdowns, remaining systems limitations, hyperparameter failure regimes and separation of framework effects from algorithmic gains.

D1.justification: Algorithm 1 and Appendix E consistently specify a cumulative arithmetic mean, resolving v1's contradictory references to an exponential moving average. v2 also identifies the H100-80G-PCIe hardware and LMDeploy implementation used in added comparisons. The existing code-access link is relocated, not newly supplied.

E1.justification: The mathematical reasoning, code generation, instruction-following and chat datasets and tasks are retained. New batch-size, GPU and hyperparameter experiments change settings within existing coverage rather than introducing new data populations or task requirements.

E3.justification: Appendix F adds substantial evaluation designs: batch size 1, throughput sweeps over expansion factors, a joint GSM8K accuracy–throughput sweep extending confidence thresholds to 0.5 and expansion factors to 2.1, H100 execution, and a shared-engine Fast-dLLM v2 comparison. The existing main-experiment protocols are retained.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's selection and cache ablations, v2 tests throughput sensitivity to expansion, the quality–speed tradeoff, low-concurrency limitations and hardware robustness. The additional shared-engine comparison also investigates how much the Fast-dLLM v2 throughput gap depends on framework differences.

E5.justification: Appendix F.1 in both versions states that results are averaged over two runs. Existing distribution summaries are retained, and v2 introduces no new seed information, confidence intervals, error bars or significance-testing procedures.

E6.justification: Main results are retained, but new results include batch-size-1 slowdowns in four of six cases, up to 2.33× throughput on H100 and up to 1.91× against the shared-engine comparator. The official Fast-dLLM v2 results also change: its WildChat throughput at batch size 256 rises from 257 to 284 tokens/s while FOCUS remains 2324. The reported maximum ratio consequently changes from 9.04× on WildChat to 8.35× on ShareGPT.

M1.justification: The importance-delta predictor, dynamic budgeting, token-retention constraints and neighbor-aware KV caching are retained. Algorithm 1's clarified cumulative arithmetic mean agrees with v1's existing Equations 17–19; it does not establish a changed averaging procedure.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and section order remain intact. v2 adds a Discussion section and appendix subsections, clarifies terminology and explanations, and updates author, publication and acknowledgement text. These are localized editorial and structural changes rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: The appendix gains Table 7, multi-panel sensitivity, H100 and shared-engine charts, and a joint accuracy–throughput scatterplot. These substantially expand the visual evidence. The original Fast-dLLM v2 Figure 15 is retained as Figure 18 with a clarified caption; most earlier displays remain.

R1.justification: The new Discussion adds Sparse-dLLM, d2Cache and LLaDA2.1, distinguishing FOCUS's query-token eviction from cache management and positioning token editing as complementary. The Chernoff reference is removed; other reference changes largely update publication metadata.

T1.justification: Appendix D.2 replaces Proposition D.1's Chernoff-style exponential bound with a Mills-ratio Gaussian-tail bound, adding the prefactor 1/((gamma−1)sqrt(2*pi)). The Gaussian assumptions, error event and gamma > 1 condition remain unchanged, making this a localized theoretical revision.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for the central efficiency claim: the shared-engine Fast-dLLM v2 comparison addresses framework confounding in v1, and the joint quality–throughput frontier directly tests the claimed tradeoff. Reporting low-batch failures and qualifying causal explanations also makes applicability clearer. These are substantive gains in evaluation rigor and claim calibration, although uncertainty reporting remains limited to two-run averages.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FOCUS research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices A–F are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds batch-size-1, hyperparameter-sensitivity, quality–throughput, H100 and controlled-baseline results in Appendix F.

before.justification: v1 reports original token-decoding analyses, generation-quality evaluations, throughput measurements and ablations in Sections 3 and 5 and the appendices.

results.title: FOCUS: DLLMs Know How to Tame Their Compute Bound

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims about condensation, model size, distillation, and dispersion training. C2.justification: V2 interprets the controlled study and layer ablation as stronger support for the proposed mechanism. It adds explanations for weaker alternative losses and suggests greater benefits on knowledge-heavy tasks than on WinoGrande. It also replaces deferred quadratic-cost optimization with discussion of manageable cost through token subsampling. These extend the retained interpretation without broadly redefining applicability.

D1.justification: V2 adds code-repository and project-page links, per-method A100 training hours and overhead ratios in Table 2, and configurations for the controlled experiment and Qwen3-1.7B in Table S1. Appendix A documents the revised gradient handling, and the main text discusses token subsampling. Together these substantially expand implementation, resource, and access information.

The ten downstream benchmarks and existing WikiText/C4 training coverage remain. PubMedQA, IMDb, and SQuAD were already described as used in v1; their new plots do not establish newly added coverage.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds evaluated noisy-embedding and active-forgetting comparators, inspired by Jain et al. (2024) and Chen et al. (2023), to the existing mid-training comparisons. This substantially broadens comparison beyond default training and the authors' three alternative loss formulations, which are retained.

E3.justification: V2 adds controlled MLP-width pre-training, Qwen3-1.7B mid-training, selective layer regularization, average ranks, and last-layer cosine metrics.
