E4.justification: V2 adds a model-size study holding depth, embedding dimension, and training conditions fixed (Figure 3), plus an early-versus-late-layer dispersion ablation (Table 3). Appendix C adds plotted evidence for previously described cross-corpus robustness and an alternative-metric analysis (Figures S2–S3). The original hyperparameter sweep remains as Table 4.

E5.justification: V1 reports benchmark point estimates without training-seed counts, standard deviations, or significance tests. V2 specifies three random seeds for mid-training and reports means, standard deviations, and Student's t-tests in Tables 2–3. This is substantial new statistical reporting, not evidence of an increase from a known v1 run count; pre-training results remain point estimates.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial result entries for new comparators, controlled models, and supplementary analyses. Newly mid-trained Qwen3-1.7B scores 55.68 with dispersion versus 54.57 with default training (Table 2); later-layer versus earlier-layer regularization scores 35.37 versus 34.96 (Table 3). Previously reported benchmark values are retained, including pre-training averages of 34.84 and 36.01.

M1.justification: Appendix A changes Algorithm 1 from ordinary epsilon-based clamping to a separate clamp threshold and a detached correction that preserves boundary gradients beyond the clamp instead of zeroing them. This changes the documented optimization procedure locally; the dispersion objective, architecture, and three alternative losses remain unchanged.

P1.justification: V2 merges the standalone preliminaries into Methods, nests the hyperparameter discussion within mid-training, subdivides Appendix C, and adds acknowledgements. It clarifies contextualized embeddings and corrects terminology and wording, including TrustfulQA to TruthfulQA. Most original prose and the overall narrative sequence remain.

P2.justification: V2 adds Figure 3, Figures S2–S3, and the layer-ablation Table 3. Table 2 is substantially redesigned with more rows, uncertainty, training-time, rank, and significance columns; Table S1 gains experimental columns. Figure 1 is redrawn, while several existing figures and tables are relocated or renumbered rather than newly introduced.

R1.justification: V2 adds relevant work by Li and Tokarchuk and explicitly distinguishes its layer-wise analysis and broad benchmark evaluation from concurrent dispersion work focused on perplexity. It also cites the new comparison methods and corrects TruthfulQA's attribution to Lin et al. (2022). These are focused additions to the existing positioning.

T1.justification: Definitions 1.1–1.2, the loss formulations, and the mathematical content of Appendices D–E are retained, including Propositions E.1–E.2 and their proofs. The additional cosine-similarity evaluation introduces no substantive new formal definition, theorem, or derivation.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the central empirical argument. The controlled model-size experiment and layer-placement ablation address weaknesses in attributing effects to condensation, while independent comparators and three-seed uncertainty reporting make the modest performance gains more assessable. Timing and access information also improve reproducibility. Some GPT2 comparisons remain nonsignificant and pre-training lacks uncertainty estimates, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in evidential support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work and contain readable main text, figures, tables, equations, and Appendices A–E. Corresponding content can be matched despite added experiments and reorganization.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds controlled model-size experiments, additional training comparisons, and layer-placement ablations, including Figure 3 and Tables 2–3.

before.justification: V1 reports original embedding-condensation measurements, mid-training and pre-training benchmark results, and hyperparameter ablations in Figures 2–4 and 6 and Tables 2–4.

results.title: Dispersion Loss Counteracts Embedding Condensation and Improves Generalization in Small Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution list retain the same central claims: a unit-dual-quaternion formulation, spectral initialization, feasible DQGPM refinement, recovery guarantees, and improved accuracy and efficiency over representative matrix methods. The revised technical qualifications do not materially rewrite these headline claims.

C2.justification: Appendix E newly explains the recovery guarantee's translation bounds, normalization nonsingularity, and leakage caused by changing alignments. Remark 3.3 adds an assumption of convergent iterates and revises the asymptotic interpretation. Appendix F explicitly limits its robustness interpretation by stating that arbitrary gross outliers would require reweighting or trimming. These substantially clarify applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: v2 adds an implementation-repository link and identifies gt.log as the source of 3DMatch relative transformations, with accompanying construction and evaluation instructions. The disclosed Python version, operating system, processor, and memory remain unchanged. Repository availability itself was not verified outside the PDFs.

E1.justification: v2 retains the synthetic and four Stanford object datasets and adds six indoor scenes from 3DMatch: Office1, Office2, Livingroom1, Livingroom2, Redkitchen, and Hotel3. Appendix F also adds Gaussian-mixture contamination scenarios, extending coverage beyond the original Gaussian perturbations.

E2.justification: SPEC, attributed to Doherty et al. (2022), is added to the synthetic accuracy/runtime comparisons and the Stanford quantitative and cross-sectional comparisons. EIG and SDR retain their existing roles, including SDR's exclusion from the main synthetic comparison. This extends the existing comparison framework with one additional spectral method.

E3.justification: Stanford perturbations change from (σt, σr) = (0.001, 1°) to (0.01, 10°), and some dense-graph missing rates change. The synthetic p = 0.08 setting is removed. New 3DMatch experiments use unperturbed gt.log transformations and score reconstructed relative motions on observed edges, unlike the existing aligned absolute-pose evaluation. Appendix F introduces mixture-contamination controls and a size sweep at p = 0.1.

E4.justification: New Appendix F tests sensitivity to both the proportion and severity of Gaussian-mixture outliers, then examines runtime as problem size increases. Figures 6–8 provide substantial new robustness and scalability analyses. The original sparsity comparisons and iteration-error plots remain; they are not new analyses.

E5.justification: v1's Table 2 explicitly reports 15% trimmed means because of EIG instability; v2 removes this disclosure. Both versions retain 100-trial averaging for the main synthetic and Stanford experiments and ± entries in Table 2. This changes statistical reporting, but does not establish additional runs or confirm whether trimming was actually discontinued.

E6.justification: Synthetic errors and runtimes are extensively revised: at p = 0.05 and noise (0.05, 5°), Table 2's DQGPM rotation error changes from 0.034 ± 0.051 to 0.132 ± 0.042. Stanford Table 4 is replaced under stronger perturbations. SPEC entries, 3DMatch Table 6, and Appendix F add substantial results. Changed settings and aggregation disclosure prevent interpreting these replacements as directly comparable performance gains or losses.

M1.justification: Algorithm 2 changes its specified initializer from the raw spectral eigenvector to its projection onto unit dual quaternions; Corollary 3.4 makes the corresponding change. The objective and iterative update remain unchanged. Since v1's experimental description already included projection, this establishes a limited correction to the stated procedure, without establishing an implementation change.

P1.justification: Most introductory exposition and the main section sequence are retained. Changes include local wording and notation corrections, a renamed Section 4.3, acknowledgements, an impact statement, and new appendix headings. The substantial scientific additions do not amount to a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: The main text is reformatted from one column to two, with extensive resizing and redistribution of tables and figures. The cross-sectional comparison moves from Table 5 to Table 3 and gains SPEC; other tables gain comparator rows. v2 adds 3DMatch Table 6, reconstruction Figures 4–5, and robustness/scaling Figures 6–8.

R1.justification: v2 adds Doherty et al. (2022) for SPEC and discusses concurrent work by Zhao et al. (2026) on anchoring matrix-based spectral estimators. The overall positioning around dual-quaternion recovery guarantees remains. Chen et al.'s change from a 2024 preprint to a 2025 publication represents the same cited work.

T1.justification: Theorem 3.2 replaces the previous dual-component bound with an aligned Euclidean residual analysis requiring bounded aligned translations, nondegenerate normalization inputs, and controlled alignment changes. Appendix D adds Lemmas D.4 and D.6 and their proofs, separating this analysis from the lexicographic inequality. Corollary 3.4's initialization bound changes, and proofs of Proposition 2.4 and the alignment lemma receive substantive treatment of degenerate cases.

improvement.justification: The decisive improvement is the separate dual-residual analysis and explicit conditions addressing v1's unsupported extraction of a dual-component bound from a lexicographic inequality (Theorem 3.2 and Appendices D–E). Added comparator, indoor-scene, robustness, and scaling evidence substantially improves empirical scrutiny. The guarantee is narrower, trimmed-mean reporting becomes less clear, and Appendix F's universal accuracy claim overstates Figure 7(c), where SPEC slightly leads at the largest outlier levels. These limitations temper, but do not outweigh, the substantial gains in rigor and assessability.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same dual-quaternion SE(3) synchronization work. The main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support comparison; retained material can be matched across the layout changes and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 reports revised synthetic and Stanford experiments, six 3DMatch scene evaluations, and additional contamination and scalability experiments in Appendix F.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic synchronization experiments and registration experiments on Bunny, Buddha, Dragon, and Armadillo, including errors, runtimes, and reconstructions.

results.title: Dual Quaternion SE(3) Synchronization with Recovery Guarantees

C1.justification: The DFS and distributed scheduling contributions remain. v2 adds the abstract claim of up to 1.70× throughput over sparse training and narrows v1's broad, consistently favorable performance language to prefix-sharing-heavy workloads. The conclusion also distinguishes the 8.31× training improvement from 2.28× end-to-end throughput.

C2.justification: v2 replaces the blanket quadratic-mask explanation with discussion of packed-tree training states, subtree splitting, and sparse-kernel utilization. Section 5.4 and Appendix B.2 establish a substantive applicability boundary: limited prefix reuse can expose traversal overhead and make DTA slower than dense training. These limitations were largely absent from v1.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-access link and four algorithms detailing traversal ordering, cache anchors, chunked backpropagation, and partitioning. It specifies default and large chunk sizes of 2048 and 4096, plus Sparse's FlexAttention implementation, 128-token block size, and 24K-token budget. These substantially improve implementation documentation.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates tau2-bench workloads. v2 Appendix B.2 adds GSM8K and AIME mathematical-reasoning workloads and a Modified Prefix scenario that removes the common global prompt from tau2-bench and retains leaf sequences, substantially extending coverage to weaker prefix sharing.

E2.justification: v2 Figure 5 adds FlexAttention-based Sparse and Sparse+CKPT comparisons across four model sizes, introducing evaluated prefix-reusing alternatives absent from v1. Existing dense and load-balancing comparators remain. Sparse is described as a proxy for packed-tree approaches, not a direct evaluation of Tree Training.

E3.justification: Section 5.1 and Table 1 change the stated RL algorithm from PPO to GRPO without explaining whether experiments were rerun. v2 also introduces a seven-allocation GPU sweep, low-compression tests with specified checkpointing conditions, compression metrics, and a 24K-token Sparse microbatch budget. The main 16K context and eight-H800 setup remain.

E4.justification: Appendix B adds analyses of rollout/training allocation sensitivity and performance under weak prefix sharing. Existing DFS, block-size, and distributed balancing ablations remain, but v2 no longer separately isolates Cut Tail. Memory analysis contracts from four model sizes in v1 Figure 5 to Qwen3-1.7B in v2 Figure 6.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, experimental seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. Both qualitatively acknowledge asynchronous-training nondeterminism without quantifying uncertainty.

E6.justification: v2 adds 1.52–1.70× throughput comparisons against Sparse+CKPT, allocation-sweep results in Table 2, and low-compression results in Table 3. The latter include DTA/AREAL throughput ratios of 0.58 on Modified Prefix and 0.62 on GSM8K for Qwen3-1.7B. The headline 8.31× training and 1.28×/2.28× end-to-end figures remain; the new results do not establish improvements over v1 under unchanged settings.

M1.justification: The stated chunk scheduling is revised: v1 Section 3.2 describes partial backpropagation followed by continued forward processing, whereas v2 Section 3.2 and Algorithm 3 specify right-to-left backpropagation over completed suffixes. The broader DFS prefix reuse and distributed partitioning design remains; most added pseudocode supplies implementation detail rather than new components.

P1.justification: The introduction, DFS and chunking explanations, optimization discussion, and evaluation narrative receive substantial rewriting. v2 reorganizes the optimization exposition, adds Section 5.4, and separates detailed algorithms and additional experiments into appendices, materially changing the document's structure and explanation.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column layout, adds a shared-prefix schematic, and relocates the existing DFS illustration to Figure 2. Throughput and load-balancing plots are redesigned with new legends and axis arrangements; memory panels are reduced. New algorithm displays and Tables 2–3 substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for FlexAttention, DeepSeekMath, GSM8K, and AIME, while removing the PPO reference. Section 2.2 more precisely relates Tree Training to the evaluated Sparse formulation. The broader RL-systems and tree-attention survey remains substantially intact.

T1.justification: v2 Appendix B.1 introduces an idealized pipeline-throughput model in Equation 3, and Section 3.2 adds explicit forward/backward operation-count reasoning. The original loss formulation, memory-depth argument, and contiguous-partitioning bound remain, without a new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: v1's broad efficiency claims relied on dense comparisons and a high-sharing workload. v2 substantially strengthens their assessment through a relevant sparse comparator, allocation sensitivity evidence, and tests revealing when DTA loses its advantage. Pseudocode and implementation settings also improve reproducibility. Reduced memory-ablation coverage and the unexplained PPO-to-GRPO reporting change are drawbacks, but the comparative evidence and clearer applicability boundaries provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AREAL-DTA and provide readable text, equations, figures, and tables. v1 ends with references; v2 includes additional Appendices A and B. The available material supports comparison throughout.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds sparse-baseline comparisons, GPU-allocation measurements, and low-compression workload results in Section 5 and Appendix B.

before.justification: v1 reports original RL reward curves, training throughput, GPU memory measurements, and distributed load-balancing ablations in Section 5.

results.title: AReaL-DTA: Dynamic Tree Attention for Efficient Reinforcement Learning of Large Language Models

C1.justification: The central contributions remain the multilingual public-health corpus and construction pipeline, the six-dimensional Public-Evaluator, and domain adaptation through Public-Model. The new clinical-gap experiments support the existing argument for specialized public-health evaluation. The abstract, contribution list and conclusion retain the same substantive research claims.

C2.justification: Appendix H adds substantive interpretations involving precision hallucination, demographic constraints being overridden by general priors, and plausible explanations masking factual errors. Appendix D.4 adds arguments about stylistic bias and the evaluator's size/stability tradeoff. The Impact Statement expands limitations to source harmonization and funding-related publication bias, beyond the retained geographic and linguistic caveats.

D1.justification: Appendices B-F supply previously missing generation and scoring prompts, detailed rubrics, response-source composition, arbitration instructions, inference hardware and settings, and LoRA/training configurations. The abstract adds code, evaluator and model release links. These substantially improve documented reproducibility, predominantly through disclosure rather than demonstrated reruns of retained experiments.

E1.justification: The corpus retains 280,210 instances, 15 domains, 17 languages and the same question formats. Public-health, clinical and general-science benchmark coverage is retained. The new clinical-gap and evaluator checks reuse already represented clinical/public-health data; appendix heatmaps disclose existing coverage. Additional datasets in Table 1 are related-work comparisons, not newly evaluated benchmarks.

E2.justification: v2 adds Medical_Model, AntAngelMed and BAICHUAN-M3 to a clinical/public-health comparison and a GPT-5 general-medical evaluator to the MedQA validation. DeepSeek-R1 and Kimi-k2-thinking are newly included specifically in evaluator Table 3. Table 7 additionally evaluates Qwen3.5-122B-A10B before and after SFT, substantially broadening the comparisons.

E3.justification: Added protocols include a 5:1 clinical training/test split for Medical_Model, assessment of 14,010 dataset items by 14 experts, and comparison of evaluators on 100 GPT-5 MedQA responses. Appendix B introduces 100-sample weighting experiments using Kendall's tau and top-10% overlap. These are additional designs; the original held-out benchmark and SFT evaluation sample sizes remain.

E4.justification: v2 adds human verification of dataset quality, sensitivity to perturbed versus uniform quality weights, an out-of-domain evaluator check, and interpolation analysis addressing the specialization/transfer tradeoff. Appendix H supplies three tobacco-domain failure cases and their scored responses. These substantially expand the diagnostic evidence beyond v1's retained scaling, SFT and perturbation analyses.

E5.justification: Tables 16 and 18 newly disclose training seed 42 for the evaluator and Public-Model. Appendix E specifies the agreement estimators and repeated-run calculations. The existing ten-run stability assessment is retained; neither an increased run count nor new confidence-interval reporting is established.

E6.justification: The main benchmark table is unchanged between v1 Table 4 and v2 Table 5. Substantial new results include the human quality score of 4.503/5, clinical and evaluator comparisons, weighting sensitivity, Qwen3.5 SFT results and full domain/language breakdowns. Table 10 newly reports interpolation scores of 6.512 on GlobalHealthAtlas and 7.545 on MMLU-pro. Table 7 also corrects the Qwen3-8B publichealth-qa decrement from 0.299 to 0.423.

M1.justification: Section 3.2.2 replaces v1's universal quality weights with format-specific weights: single-choice retains 0.45/0.25/0.20/0.10, while QA uses 0.25/0.35/0.25/0.15. Section 4.5 also introduces base/SFT checkpoint interpolation. These are limited procedural revisions; the core construction pipeline, six-dimensional evaluator and LoRA approach remain.

P1.justification: v2 adds an extensive explanatory structure in Appendices A-I, including complete procedural descriptions, scoring rubrics and supporting discussions where v1 had unresolved references. It also retitles the paper, revises the abstract and Impact Statement, expands author/affiliation information and repairs cross-references. The main section sequence remains largely unchanged.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the displays with clinical and evaluator comparison tables, sensitivity and configuration tables, dataset examples, distribution heatmaps and multilingual radar plots. The construction pipeline is redrawn and moved to Appendix B, and evaluator workflow displays are added. Existing benchmark tables and the scaling plot are largely retained and renumbered; dataset statistics move into Figure 1's caption.

R1.justification: Table 1 expands the resource comparison with HealthSearchQA, ApolloCorpora, MMedC and AfriMed-QA, with corresponding citations. Other citations are added, including Mega-RAG, while the related-work organization and central research gap remain largely unchanged. Numerous publication and bibliographic updates refer to already cited works.

T1.justification: v1 asserts theoretical guarantees but supplies no referenced proofs. v2 Appendix G adds a formal quality/noise assumption, a score-filtration risk theorem and proof, and Gaussian conditional-variance and arbitration derivations. This is substantial new formal content, separate from the added explanations of standard evaluation metrics.

improvement.justification: v1's reproducibility and reliability claims lacked the promised prompts, configurations and supporting appendices. v2 supplies these materials and adds a large human quality audit, weighting sensitivity tests and direct evaluator checks, substantially improving auditability and empirical support. Some inconsistencies remain, notably between Algorithm 1 and the appendix arbitration rules, while the theoretical guarantees depend on strong assumptions and approximations. These limitations temper the claims but do not outweigh the substantial documentation and validation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe GlobalHealthAtlas, Public-Evaluator and Public-Model, with directly matchable methods and experiments. All pages are readable. v1 ends after its references despite unresolved appendix references; v2 supplies Appendices A-I.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds clinical-model comparisons, human dataset assessment, evaluator validation, weighting sensitivity tests and checkpoint-interpolation results.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluator validation, multilingual benchmarking, fine-tuning ablations, data-scaling experiments, cross-domain transfer and input-perturbation results in Tables 3-9.

results.title: From Knowledge to Inference: Formalizing Specialized Public Health Reasoning on GlobalHealthAtlas

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions, and central conclusion retain the same claims about source-scarce compression, aligned hidden representations, and structure beyond scalar difficulty. Additional experiments support these claims. Extending beyond binary scoring is presented as future work rather than an established contribution.

C2.justification: New Section 6 explicitly discusses source hidden-state access and the untested scope of continuous-scoring benchmarks. The masking analysis identifies behaviorally distinctive missing sources as a failure boundary and qualifies pseudo-representations as an approximation. Appendix C.3 also adds explanations for the auxiliary baselines' source-scarce weaknesses.

D1.justification: Appendix C.5 newly documents forward-hook extraction, NVIDIA H20 96GB hardware, average compression time of 479.7 seconds, and hidden-state storage of 0.11–1.25GB. The default MLP widths are made explicit in prose, but were already illustrated in v1 Figure 2, so this does not establish an architectural change.

E1.justification: The five benchmarks and Appendix D model pools are retained. v3 adds a distinct partial-access scenario in which source hidden states are unavailable randomly or preferentially for behaviorally distinctive models. This simulates restricted access using existing models; it does not add actual proprietary-model evaluations or continuous-scoring tasks.

E2.justification: EffiEval and TailoredBench, previously discussed but not evaluated, become additional comparators across all five benchmarks and coreset budgets in Table 13 and Figures 4–5. Random, AnchorPoints, and GP-IRT remain; tinyBenchmarks (GP-IRT) is a clarified name for the existing comparator.

E3.justification: New protocols include controlled MLP variants, scalar-versus-vector extrapolation inputs, timing with and without hidden-state hooks, and random versus adversarial masking at 10%–50%. The reported temporal historical pool changes from the oldest 30% of models to the oldest 30 models, with ten sources sampled per trial. Retained temporal scores do not establish that this experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: New analyses test sensitivity to MLP width/depth, the choice of extrapolation features, and robustness to missing source representations, including adversarial removal and benchmark-specific sensitivity. These address additional component choices and failure conditions beyond v1's retained PCA, source-composition, source-count, and temporal analyses.

E5.justification: Appendix C.4 newly specifies 50 anchor selections within each of ten source combinations; it does not establish an increase in runs. The masking study separately reports variation across source combinations and across ten masking draws, explicitly cautioning that averaging draws reduces variance. Existing association-test formulas and significance values are retained, with clearer aggregation descriptions.

E6.justification: Existing main benchmark scores are retained, while substantial baseline, ablation, cost, and masking results are added. Table 8 reports average ranking correlation of 0.842 without masking versus 0.833 under random and 0.805 under adversarial 50% masking. Section 3.2 also changes the stated BBH Agreement gap from approximately 19 to 9 percentage points; the unchanged table values, 0.714 versus 0.631, imply 8.3 points.

M1.justification: The original alignment, consensus clustering, and ridge-extrapolation pipeline remains unchanged. Appendix C.14 adds an adaptation for partially inaccessible source representations: output-similarity-weighted mixtures of accessible embeddings replace masked embeddings during coreset selection.

P1.justification: v3 makes targeted method and statistical explanations clearer, corrects terminology and cross-references, adds a method-boundaries section, and moves the stability appendix earlier. Publication and author-footnote information also changes. Most existing exposition and the central narrative structure are retained.

P2.justification: New tables substantially expand the presentation of comparator results, computational costs, component ablations, and masking means and uncertainty. Figures 4–5 are redrawn with EffiEval and TailoredBench curves, expanded legends, and adjusted axes. Retained appendix tables also receive corrected budget labels and revised captions.

R1.justification: v3 adds hidden-representation citations to Burns et al., Gekhman et al., and Wang et al. (2025c), and revises the description of prior difficulty-estimation findings. The related-work taxonomy and primary novelty positioning remain. Most other reference changes update metadata for existing works.

T1.justification: New Equations 21–24 formally define output-similarity weights, pseudo-representations, the modified consensus embedding, and behavioral distinctness for adversarial masking. Existing mathematical development is retained; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses important gaps in v1 through direct comparisons with two relevant methods, measured computational overhead, and tests that expose limitations of partial hidden-state access. These additions substantially strengthen empirical support and practical interpretation while retaining the core results. Table 18 introduces a reporting ambiguity: its claimed five-benchmark average repeats the SEED-Bench scores. This limits that ablation's interpretation but does not outweigh the broader gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same REPCORE study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete Appendices A–D are readable and support reliable matching across additions, relocation, and renumbering.

after.justification: v3 retains these original results and adds evaluated baselines, architectural and extrapolation ablations, computational measurements, and hidden-state masking experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark-compression results on five benchmarks, including ranking correlations, estimation errors, representation analyses, and ablations.

results.title: Learning More from Less: Unlocking Internal Representations for Benchmark Compression

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims about targeted suppression, cross-domain transfer, task preservation, and failure under prolonged training. The additional experiments broaden support without redefining these core contributions.

C2.justification: The mechanistic interpretations and limitations remain unchanged, including the H1-H3 discussion, evidence favoring incomplete coverage at the blocking layer, and qualifications on activation-patching conclusions. The additional comparisons and model curves introduce findings rather than new mechanism explanations.

D1.justification: v2 identifies the additional models' SAE sources through EleutherAI and Arditi references and explains that discovery is repeated separately. It removes the original Goodfire SAE and Llama-3.1 resource references and the explicit KL-objective display. Shared hyperparameters and the code link remain, but new comparator configurations receive limited detail.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same Finance/Health experiments, six transfer domains, and core misalignment and final evaluation prompt suites. The additional model evaluations reuse this dataset and task coverage.

E2.justification: The external comparison expands beyond KL regularization to inoculation prompting, preventative steering, and test-time steering. Figure 7 includes linear-probe steering, while Figure 19 additionally displays SAE-based steering. Existing random-latent and Top-Delta controls are retained.

E3.justification: v2 adds full-pipeline evaluations on Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct and Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct, using model-matched SAEs and separately rediscovered latent sets. These substantially expand the tested model configurations; the original splits, metrics, and training defaults remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The latent-source, set-size, directionality, freezing, final-layer, reconstruction, and activation-patching analyses are retained. Matching Appendices D-F shows that their figures and findings are moved or renumbered, rather than newly added analyses.

E5.justification: Existing seed counts and uncertainty conventions are retained, including three-seed standard-deviation reporting and six-domain SEM reporting. The new model plots use the existing two-seed, six-domain SEM convention; no new statistical testing or uncertainty procedure is introduced.

E6.justification: Figures 7 and 19 add comparator results, and new Figures 20-21 report model-specific trade-offs. At lambda = 100,000, the latter show approximately 40% relative misalignment reduction for Llama-3.2-1B and 65% for Qwen-2.5-7B. These are additional settings and results, not improved scores for the original Llama-3.1 experiment.

M1.justification: The three-stage latent-discovery procedure and base-anchored, sign-aware blocking objective remain unchanged in Section 3 and Appendix A. The additional model experiments instantiate the existing method.

P1.justification: The title changes from 'by Blocking Causal Features' to 'via Latent Blocking.' Related-work, setup, and comparison paragraphs receive localized revisions, and acknowledgments and an impact statement are added. Most prose and the main section structure remain intact.

P2.justification: The document is extensively retypeset into an ICML format, changing typography, running headers, captions, spacing, and figure placement throughout. Figures 7 and 19 gain comparator series, Figure 19's axis range expands, and two model-replication figures are added. Most existing graphics and Table 1 retain their content.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds Wichers et al. on inoculation and Chen et al. on preventative steering, explicitly distinguishing BLOCK-EM from these interventions. SAE-source references are added, while the LoRA, Goodfire, and Llama-3.1 model references are removed. The broader research positioning is retained.

T1.justification: The SAE definitions, latent-selection scores, blocking-loss formulation, and patching mathematics remain substantively unchanged. Neither version supplies theoretical guarantees or proofs that are added or revised in the other.

improvement.justification: v1's external-defense comparison centers on KL regularization, and its experiments use one base model. v2 adds relevant prompting and steering comparisons plus model-specific replications on two further backbones, substantially strengthening evidence about comparative value and generality. Sparse configuration details and lost resource references limit reproducibility, but these documentation weaknesses do not outweigh the broader empirical validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same BLOCK-EM study. The main text and Appendices A-F are readable, and their equations, table, and figures can be matched despite reformatting and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds evaluations on two additional models and comparisons with prompting and steering baselines.

before.justification: v1 reports original fine-tuning experiments, cross-domain evaluations, latent-selection ablations, and activation-patching results in Sections 4-5 and Appendices C-F.

results.title: BLOCK-EM: Preventing Emergent Misalignment via Latent Blocking

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and principal conclusion retain the claims of posterior high-probability complexity guarantees, logarithmic slice overhead uniformly over partitions, and applicability without likelihood-specific assumptions. The new tightness result appears in Section 3 without redefining these headline claims.

C2.justification: Section 3 adds an explanation linking cluster splitting to smaller weights and narrower slice-variable supports. The conclusion redirects prospective extensions from general completely random measures toward general species-sampling processes. Existing interpretations of scalability and truncation limitations largely remain.

D1.justification: Algorithm 2 now explicitly identifies full-conditional sampling for occupied atoms, and Figure 4 newly documents thinning every two iterations; this disclosure alone does not establish that thinning changed. V2 also states that code accompanies supplementary material while retaining the same repository in a Software and data section.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate univariate Gaussian-mixture clustering using balanced three-cluster and perturbed-Zipf data. The Zipf scenario changes from 500 possible labels with probabilities proportional to c^-2 to 50 labels with probabilities proportional to c^-0.5, revising the represented cluster population within the retained task.

E2.justification: The balanced-cluster study retains the same six samplers, including both slice variants, both blocked Gibbs configurations, and both CRP variants. The Zipf study retains Slice versus BGS with L=10. The fixed-alpha experiments use these corresponding comparator sets.

E3.justification: Figure 4 changes its evaluation metric from Rand index to adjusted Rand index. Appendix B.3 adds alpha=1 controls alongside the existing Gamma-prior experiments and reports both clustering metrics. The stated sample-size grids, iteration budgets, burn-in, and initialization remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New Appendix B.3 tests sensitivity to fixing the concentration parameter at alpha=1 in both simulation settings. Existing co-clustering and cluster-count mixing analyses remain, with revised results; no broader robustness or ablation program is introduced.

E5.justification: Neither version reports independent-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Both use iteration averages and posterior-partition boxplots; the additional tables do not introduce a new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: The balanced-cluster runtime, ESS, and clustering plots change despite retaining their stated settings. Zipf results are replaced under the revised data distribution and, in Figure 4, a different metric. Figure 7 reverses the runtime ordering of Slice and BGS. Tables 2 and 3 add extensive fixed-alpha results, including Zipf ARI values of 0.646 for Slice and 0.352 for BGS at n=3000.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1 and 2 retain their sampling procedures. Renaming the stick-breaking variable and explicitly specifying the occupied atoms' full conditional are notation and documentation clarifications. Fixed-alpha experiments evaluate an existing model configuration.

P1.justification: V2 makes localized language and cross-reference corrections, adds descriptive corollary titles, and organizes Appendix A into numbered proof subsections with two previously embedded derivations presented as lemmas. Software and acknowledgments headings are added; the main narrative structure is retained.

P2.justification: V2 adds two detailed numerical tables and revises numerous empirical displays, including Figure 4's metric, axis, and caption, other plot scales, and co-clustering panels. Typography and caption formatting change throughout, the introduction moves onto the first page, and existing figures and Table 1 are repositioned.

R1.justification: V2 adds Canale et al. (2022) and Mena et al. (2025) to position prospective Pitman-Yor and species-sampling extensions. The broader positioning remains unchanged. The Balocchi reference is updated to its published form, rather than introducing a different work.

T1.justification: V2 adds Proposition 3.6 and its proof in Appendix A.6, establishing a logarithmic lower bound with positive probability under the singleton partition and ruling out a uniformly smaller-order overhead rate. Supporting Lemma A.3 is also added. Lemmas A.1 and A.2 reorganize derivations already present in v1; the earlier upper-bound results remain.

improvement.justification: Proposition 3.6 and Appendix A.6 resolve an important question left open in v1: the central logarithmic overhead rate is uniformly unimprovable. This substantially strengthens the theoretical characterization. Fixed-alpha controls add evidence aligned with the theory, and adjusted Rand scores make the imbalanced-clustering evaluation more informative. The revised Zipf results cannot establish same-setting performance gains, and independent-run uncertainty remains unreported.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, Complexity bounds for Dirichlet process slice samplers. Their main text, algorithms, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A and B are available and readable, supporting a reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 reports revised simulation outcomes in Section 5 and Appendix B, plus additional fixed-concentration experiments in Tables 2 and 3.

before.justification: V1 reports original Gaussian-mixture simulations, including runtime, effective sample size, clustering accuracy, and posterior co-clustering results in Section 5 and Appendix B.

results.title: Complexity Bounds for Dirichlet Process Slice Samplers

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the central zero-shot generalization, compositional search and parameter-recovery claims. The conclusion adds a claim that search overhead is competitive with gradient-based fine-tuning in the reported 1D/2D experiments, extending the claim of computational practicality.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands applicability and failure analysis. It interprets diffusion-estimation bias under missing physics, argues that sufficiently diverse coupled dictionaries can work without pure-physics training, and identifies the training recipe as complementary to search. It also qualifies short-window robustness by dynamics and adds search overhead and possible 3D bottlenecks to the limitations.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code repository link, detailed FNO architecture and training settings, A100 hardware information, and disclosures about dictionary selection and Navier–Stokes codebook use. These are targeted reproducibility additions. B.4's assertion that FNO budgets match MPP conflicts with its retained MPP description, so matching budgets cannot be confirmed.

E1.justification: The four primary PDE benchmarks remain. Coverage expands within advection–diffusion through an unseen Burgers-like perturbation and mixed-physics training followed by joint coefficient extrapolation (C.2–C.3). Both versions already contain seven main composition tasks; the revised task count is a textual correction.

E2.justification: FNO is added as an evaluated comparator in both composition and parameter-extrapolation comparisons, with results in Tables 1–2. MPP, Zebra, GEPS and direct DISCO remain. The added SINDy discussion does not constitute an evaluated baseline.

E3.justification: The main evaluation settings are retained, but substantial new protocols are introduced: seven perturbation strengths with 128 trajectories each and 84-step rollouts, mixed-training proportions, controlled retraining ablations, dictionary-size and fitting-window sweeps, and per-sample A100 timing (C.2–C.7). The GEPS adaptation budgets of 100/500/2000 steps were already documented in v1.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained operator-quality analysis and qualitative rollouts, v2 tests missing dictionary physics, entangled training operators, dependence on in-context conditioning and the codebook, sensitivity to dictionary size and observation length, and accuracy versus adaptation time. These directly investigate robustness, component contributions and practical efficiency.

E5.justification: Neither version supplies seed counts, confidence intervals, significance tests or comparable uncertainty estimates. The new trajectory counts describe evaluation samples, and GEPS optimization lengths do not establish additional independent repetitions.

E6.justification: Existing entries in Tables 1–3 are unchanged. v2 adds FNO scores and Tables 4–9, including Navier–Stokes error of 0.563 without the codebook versus 0.066 with it, and beam-search error rising from 0.055 to 0.797 as the unseen perturbation increases. These are new experimental comparisons, not changed performance under the original settings. Section 5.3 also corrects '5 out of 6' to '6 out of 7'.

M1.justification: The DISCO dictionary construction, search objective, uniform and beam searches, and Lie/Strang splitting procedures remain unchanged. The new training ablations test existing components; they do not replace the proposed method.

P1.justification: Most prose and the main section organization remain intact. Changes include targeted explanations and corrections, appendix subsections and cross-references, a clarification about compatible backbones, and updated affiliations, acknowledgements and publication text.

P2.justification: Tables 4–9 substantially expand the presentation with robustness, ablation, sensitivity and accuracy/time displays; Tables 1–2 gain FNO rows. The scaling-law plot moves and becomes Figure 4 instead of Figure 3, while Figure 2 and Table 3 receive clearer captions. Existing plot data and qualitative images are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds Sergeant-Perthuis et al. to the symmetry discussion and relates parameter recovery to SINDy, distinguishing learned-operator search from symbolic sparse regression. The added Li et al. 2021 reference describes the same FNO work already cited as Li et al. 2020, rather than a distinct research contribution.

T1.justification: The formal PDE-family setup, search objective, splitting formulas and stated accuracy orders are retained. No new theorem, proof or substantive theoretical derivation is added; the new perturbation equation specifies an empirical stress test.

improvement.justification: Appendices C.2–C.7 address central gaps in v1 concerning training restrictions, component contributions and adaptation cost. Coupled-only training still benefits from search (direct NRMSE 0.278 versus beam 0.190), while removing the Navier–Stokes codebook raises error from 0.066 to 0.563, clarifying an important dependency. Together with failure and runtime analyses, this substantially strengthens the empirical support and applicability boundaries. The new FNO/MPP budget inconsistency and continued absence of uncertainty estimates limit precision but do not outweigh these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same neural operator splitting work. Their text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched despite relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds robustness tests, mixed-physics training experiments, ablations, sensitivity studies and runtime measurements in Appendices C.2–C.7.

before.justification: v1 reports original PDE prediction experiments, parameter-recovery results, compute-scaling measurements and an operator-accuracy analysis in Section 5 and Appendices C–D.

results.title: Test-time Generalization for Physics through Neural Operator Splitting

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution statements and conclusion retain the same claims about architecture-preserving SLR induction, adaptive control, elastic deployment and embedding/LM-head asymmetry. The latter was already claimed in v1; its new experiment strengthens support without changing the core contribution.

C2.justification: v3 interprets the downstream results as evidence against abnormal task-performance collapse, explains update frequency through a regularization-versus-loss trade-off, and expands the rationale for excluding the LM head by default. These refine practical applicability and mechanisms while retaining the earlier central interpretations.

D1.justification: v3 adds a code-availability statement and repository address, identifies the downstream evaluation harness and default configurations, and specifies eight H100 80GB GPUs for timing. It also clarifies controller calibration and default LM-head exclusion. These are useful disclosures, without establishing changes to the retained experiments.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained C4 language-modeling evaluation, v3 Section 5.2 adds actual evaluations on MMLU, ARC-C, COPA, HellaSwag, BoolQ and PIQA. These substantially broaden coverage to knowledge, question answering, reading comprehension and several commonsense reasoning tasks.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains full-rank training, LoRA, ReLoRA, GaLore, LORO, CoLA, SLTrain and LOST. No comparator is added or removed in a matched experiment. The new downstream comparison reuses the existing vanilla baseline.

E3.justification: v3 introduces zero-shot accuracy evaluation using default lm-evaluation-harness configurations for the 1B models and the 646M compressed variant. Additional protocols include component-wise timing on eight H100 GPUs, a 60M LM-head penalty comparison, and a controlled 1B study of K/J = 5, 10 and 20 with J = 1. Existing pretraining settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix H adds direct evidence on whether LM-head structure can be induced without harming training loss.
