C1.justification: The abstract, contribution summary, and discussion qualify state-of-the-art accuracy as applying at larger or sufficient sampling budgets, narrowing v1's broader performance claims. Consistency, odd-only regression, and the explanation of paired sampling remain the central contributions.

C2.justification: v2 explains FFD's domain-dependent performance through interaction spectra and interprets the new sampling and proxy ablations. Its limitations explicitly discuss cubic scaling in the sampling budget, recommend capping interaction counts, and explain why paired sampling need not outperform independent sampling, substantially extending v1's brief coherence and correlation caveats.

D1.justification: v2 replaces the supplementary-code statement with a public repository link, specifies the default 100 LightGBM trees, and documents odd-target computation using m/2 regression rows and the affine solver shift. Exact boundary constraints, sampling-library information, and hardware were already disclosed in v1.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same eight value functions: DistilBERT, Estate, ViT16, Cancer, CG60, IL60, NHANES, and Crime. The added analyses use these retained tasks and domains without introducing new data coverage.

E2.justification: v2 newly evaluates FourierSHAP, FFD-RD, and its corrected variant in benchmark and runtime comparisons. Proxy, already evaluated in v1's plots, also enters Tables 1 and 3. PolySHAP-3 matches the earlier 3-PolySHAP rather than constituting a new comparator.

E3.justification: v2 adds paired/non-paired sampling crossed with all/odd interaction controls, tree-depth and tree-count sweeps, and SPEX spectral recovery with 100,000 queries. Tables 1 and 3 also revise reported budgets, including DistilBERT from 1,591 to 1,440. The main 30-instance evaluation, ground-truth construction, and MSE metric remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained runtime and interaction-count analyses, Section 5.4 and Appendices D.4–D.6 test the contributions of pairing and odd-only selection, sensitivity to proxy capacity, and interaction spectra underlying FFD performance differences. These substantially broaden examination of the method's mechanisms and robustness.

E5.justification: Existing MSE and runtime results retain median/IQR reporting, and Table 3 retains means and quartiles. However, v2's new Figure 16 includes error bars whose statistical meaning is unspecified. The PDFs therefore do not establish whether this introduces a different uncertainty-estimation practice.

E6.justification: Tables 1 and 3 replace OddSHAP values and several NHANES baseline scores, alongside substantial new comparator and analysis results. Estate OddSHAP mean MSE changes from 6.1e-5 to 5.1e-7, but its reported budget and support rule also change, preventing a same-setting improvement interpretation. New findings include FFD-RD outperforming OddSHAP on several tree-based benchmarks.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 changes the specified higher-order support size from ceil(m/eta) to ceil(m/eta)-d, counting the d linear terms within the regression-variable budget. The paired-sampling, GBT-screening, Fourier-regression pipeline and low-budget fallback remain intact.

P1.justification: The overall organization and much of the prose remain. v2 revises the introductory framing and discussion, expands regression explanations, moves Observation 3.1's proof to Appendix B, and adds experimental subsections. Affiliations, publication information, and bibliography formatting also receive localized edits.

P2.justification: Tables 1 and 3 gain comparator rows and reorder the synthetic-data columns; benchmark and runtime plots gain traces and legends. New Figures 5 and 13–16 display sampling ablations, proxy sensitivity, and spectra. The sparsity plots relabel their horizontal axis as regression variables, while existing displays are also relocated.

R1.justification: Section 3 now explicitly credits earlier odd-order dependence results, including newly cited Wendler and Zhou, and attributes basis equivalence to prior work. Appendix D.6 substantially develops the relationship between OddSHAP's adaptive screening and Zhou's fractional factorial designs, materially refining the positioning of the paper's central ideas.

T1.justification: Theorem 3.2 now distinguishes the decomposable vector space from affine boundary-constrained classes and explicitly assumes symmetric weights. Appendices B–C expand derivations and correct the regression sum and affine-projection description. Section 4 revises Fourier-extraction complexity from O(Ntrees*2^L*L) to O(Ntrees*4^L). These refine existing theory without adding a new principal theorem.

improvement.justification: The added FFD/FourierSHAP comparisons and direct component ablations address substantial gaps in v1's validation. v2 acknowledges competing-method wins, qualifies its headline accuracy claim, and improves mathematical precision, prior-work attribution, and implementation documentation. Figure 16's undefined error bars remain a reporting weakness, but the gains in evidential support and accuracy of positioning are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe An Odd Estimator for Shapley Values. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–D are readable and support reliable matching across the revision.

after.justification: The original empirical evaluation is retained and expanded with additional comparators, sampling and proxy-parameter ablations, and spectral-energy analysis.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix D report original evaluations on eight value functions, including estimation errors, runtimes, and interaction-sparsity ablations.

results.title: An Odd Estimator for Shapley Values

C1.justification: The abstract explicitly confines the analysis to Gaussian-mixture targets and perturbative stability, and drops v1's assertion that sufficiently decaying preconditioning is necessary. The introduction also removes the exception acknowledging earlier ALD guarantees under strong regularity. The principal contribution remains dimension-uniform continuous-time sampling guarantees.

C2.justification: V2 correctly interprets Theorem 3.1's condition as sufficient for its bound, expands the bias-versus-score-error tradeoff, and acknowledges covariance mismatch against the smoothed initialization rather than claiming only weight mismatch matters. Section 6 adds specific discrete-time high-frequency constraints limiting applicability.

D1.justification: Appendix D newly specifies the perturbation coefficient 0.05 and clarifies the distinction between the base smoothing matrix and its overall 2S=40 scale. Experiment-specific covariance and initialization descriptions are corrected and expanded. The step size, iteration budget, sample counts, and Colab resource disclosure remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate synthetic bimodal Gaussian-mixture sampling across increasing truncation dimensions, with exact scores and covariance-perturbed scores. No dataset, domain, or task scenario is added; the perturbation changes concern settings within retained coverage.

E2.justification: The comparator membership is unchanged: tailored versus flat spectra in Figures 1 and 3, and preconditioner spectra j^(-3.5) versus j^(-1) in Figure 4. Newly cited methods are not added as evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: Section 5.2 and Appendix D.5 change the covariance perturbation from proportional to j^(-3.5) to 0.05j^(-3). Appendix D also changes Figure 3's stated flat smoothing matrix from 40I to I under the retained 2S=40 schedule, and its initialization parameter tau_2 from 1 to 2, resolving conflicts with the main text. These reported corrections do not establish that every affected experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: The preconditioner robustness experiment under score error is revised for the new covariance perturbation, with corresponding replacement evidence in Figures 4 and 6. The question tested and the kNN sensitivity choices k=20,50,80 remain unchanged; Figure 5's sensitivity analysis is retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The retained kNN sensitivity comparisons do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Figures 4 and 6 replace the KL curves under the revised perturbation. For example, Figure 6's admissible-preconditioner estimate at d=75 is approximately 0.53 in v1's setup and 0.27 in v2's setup. The bounded-versus-growing trend remains, and Figures 1, 3, and 5 retain their results. These are different-setting results, not a demonstrated performance gain.

M1.justification: The Gaussian-smoothing ALD diffusion, diagonal preconditioning, linear annealing schedule, and Euler–Maruyama sampler are retained. V2 revises their theoretical analysis and adds spectral-design guidance without introducing a new sampling component or replacing the procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and much of Sections 2–6 are extensively rewritten for clearer scope and explanation. The appendix exposition is reorganized around a proof roadmap and named propositions and corollaries, incorporating the former B.4 material into the revised B.3.

P2.justification: All six figure roles are retained. Figure 2 is redesigned with clearer equation boxes and timeline annotations; captions, plot scales in Figures 4 and 6, and figure placement are revised. No new figure family or table is introduced.

R1.justification: The research positioning is substantially expanded: v2 identifies Guo et al. as the closest analysis, explains the shared path-space KL approach, and adds explicit connections to inaccurate-drift and function-space sampling literature. It also incorporates the newly cited discretization follow-up, Baldassari et al. (2026a), into its contribution and applicability discussion.

T1.justification: V2 substantially replaces v1's Appendix B.3–B.4 responsibility-error analysis with a centered decomposition, pairwise component-score differences, and an explicit bound involving D, R, and S_pair. New propositions and corollaries establish revised positivity, perturbation, and summability conditions. V2 also corrects score-error sign and normalization inconsistencies and derives a spectral balancing rule. Theorem 3.1's principal bound is retained.

improvement.justification: V1 leaves part of the combined responsibility-error bound informally specified and relies on restrictive individual-score moment bounds. V2 supplies an explicit pairwise-score bound, preserves perturbation cancellation, and proves consolidated sufficient conditions in Appendix B.3, materially strengthening a central stability argument. More careful claims and corrected experimental documentation add credibility. The revised KL curves use changed settings and do not themselves establish improved performance.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work and provide readable text, equations, figures, and Appendices A–D. The revised proofs and experiments can be matched reliably across versions.

after.justification: V2 retains original sampling simulations and reports revised score-perturbation results in Figures 4 and 6, alongside the retained experiments.

before.justification: V1 reports original Gaussian-mixture sampling simulations, including dimension-dependent step counts, empirical KL estimates, and kNN sensitivity results in Figures 1 and 3–6.

results.title: Dimension-Free Multimodal Sampling via Preconditioned Annealed Langevin Dynamics

C1.justification: The abstract and principal exact-characterization contributions remain unchanged. The introduction extends covariance/horizon scaling claims to variance as well as NSR and strengthens the motivation for exact evaluation. Its proportional initial-state-covariance wording for variance conflicts with the cubic dependence stated in Section 2.1.

C2.justification: The expanded discussion explains when exact baselines cancel small-covariance divergence, why approximation errors can preserve it, and how entropy regularization can help without guaranteeing stability. v3 also replaces the earlier universality suggestion with a narrower cross-system interpretation and explicitly leaves a general formal NSR–instability relationship open.

D1.justification: Appendix B newly supplies optimizer learning rates, batch sizes, two-layer MLPs with 64 hidden units and ReLU activations, and Monte Carlo time budgets. v1 specifies system equations and some horizons/covariances but omits most of these implementation choices. Much of this addition documents retained experiments rather than demonstrating altered implementations.

E1.justification: v3 adds Hopper-v4 and HalfCheetah-v4 locomotion experiments with MLP policies in Appendix B and Figure 10. These substantially broaden the evaluated environments beyond the retained low-dimensional control systems and pendulum task.

E2.justification: v3 adds direct REINFORCE–GPOMDP comparisons in Figure 8, empirical Monte Carlo versus exact calculations in Figure 9, and an exact-gradient Adam control for policy collapse in Figure 7. These substantially expand the comparison design beyond the retained GD, SGD, and Adam trajectory comparisons. PPO trains the new MuJoCo policies; it is not a head-to-head baseline.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include larger-batch and exact-gradient collapse controls, Monte Carlo accuracy evaluation with a ten-minute budget per iteration, and PPO experiments on MuJoCo. These are added protocols; newly listed hyperparameters for retained experiments do not establish that their settings changed.

E4.justification: Figure 7 adds controls testing whether sampling error causes collapse, together with policy log-standard-deviation and Adam-momentum diagnostics. Appendix B also tests sensitivity to the gradient estimator and the reliability of Monte Carlo variance/NSR estimates. v1 lacks these targeted analyses.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Gradient-estimator variance is the scientific quantity studied in both versions; the added Monte Carlo accuracy comparison does not introduce a new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Figures 1–6 retain their results. New findings include delayed collapse with larger batches, no collapse in the displayed exact-gradient Adam run, lower but similarly structured GPOMDP NSR, and substantial Monte Carlo estimation errors. New MuJoCo traces are also reported, although Figure 10 labels the HalfCheetah quantity 'Variance' while its caption describes NSR.

M1.justification: Appendix B extends the moment-evaluation framework to GPOMDP by replacing the full-trajectory return with quadratic reward-to-go terms. This is a limited procedural adaptation; the original REINFORCE estimators, Gaussian policies, and exact-moment procedures remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The abstract, main section sequence, and most mathematical exposition remain intact. Changes include local language corrections, reorganized related work, a retitled and expanded Discussion and Conclusions section, and insertion of an Additional Experiments appendix with corresponding proof renumbering.

P2.justification: v3 adds four substantial multipanel figures: collapse controls, comparative NSR heatmaps, Monte Carlo accuracy plots, and MuJoCo trajectories. Figure 7 also redisplays original collapse curves alongside new controls and diagnostics. Existing figures are resized or relocated while retaining their results.

R1.justification: Appendix A expands substantially beyond its short LQR/baseline discussion to cover policy-gradient variants, tabular and partially observed settings, estimator variability, and convergence dynamics. Added comparisons with Zhao et al. (2011) and Ilyas et al. (2018), among others, clarify the relationship to prior variance-scaling results and empirical gradient deterioration.

T1.justification: New Theorem 4 and Appendix F prove a positive probability of escaping any fixed ball for a scalar SGD update under specified noise-growth and continuity assumptions. Section 5 adds baseline-residual scaling arguments and an entropy-regularized stationary-covariance formula. The original principal moment calculations and proofs are retained.

improvement.justification: The collapse controls and Monte Carlo accuracy study address v1's weakly tested mechanism and motivation for exact evaluation, while Appendix B supplies important missing reproducibility details. The new theorem and expanded discussion strengthen and qualify the instability argument. These are substantial gains, despite remaining uncertainty-reporting gaps and new inconsistencies in variance-scaling prose and Figure 10's labeling.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their text, equations, figures, and complete appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v3 retains these experiments and adds policy-collapse controls, GPOMDP comparisons, Monte Carlo accuracy analyses, and MuJoCo experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original numerical experiments on linear and polynomial systems, optimizer trajectories, and Monte Carlo evaluations of neural policies on LQR and pendulum tasks.

results.title: Non-Uniform Noise-to-Signal Ratio in the REINFORCE Policy-Gradient Estimator

C1.justification: The central contribution and headline accuracy/speedup claims remain. V2 explicitly restricts the abstract's guarantee to new instances from the same distribution, corrects the benchmark count to six, and states in the conclusion that speedups exceed 60% on five of those six families.

C2.justification: V2 explains trajectory-level calibration versus repeated callback testing, discusses when an LSTM may be inadequate, and interprets calibration-size effects on reliability and runtime. Appendix D additionally acknowledges unavailable original generator parameters and the restriction of resampling studies to synthetic families. The original training-cost and distribution-matching limitations remain.

D1.justification: V2 newly specifies Gurobi 12 and MIPFocus=1 and documents the alternative predictors, perturbation mechanism, and resampling procedures. The original hardware, architecture, training duration, and code-access destination are retained. These disclosures do not establish that the original experiments were rerun.

E1.justification: Both versions already evaluate the same six problem families; the abstract's change from five to six does not represent a new dataset. Appendix D.1 adds shifted test distributions for CFLP, GISP, MIS, and MVC by perturbing continuous generator parameters.

E2.justification: Beyond the retained Gurobi/COPT termination baselines, Appendix C directly compares the LSTM against a conformally calibrated Linear predictor and CP UB rate heuristic. Appendix A.2 also adds separate evaluations of SCIP Feasibility Pump, RENS, and Simple Rounding, substantially expanding the evaluated alternatives.

E3.justification: New protocols test Gurobi MIPGap values of 1%, 2%, 5%, and 10%, generated datasets with 1000 training instances, controlled parameter perturbations, and calibration sizes of 5, 10, 20, and 100. These extend the evaluation design; the original benchmark splits and budgets are retained. Newly specified Gurobi version and MIPFocus information do not establish changes to the original experiments.

E4.justification: V2 adds convergence and prediction-error trajectories for 20 instances per family, statistics comparing discovery and certification of optimal solutions, simpler-predictor comparisons, solver-tolerance sensitivity, distribution-shift tests, and calibration-size sensitivity. These address predictor necessity and reliability questions largely untested in v1.

E5.justification: Mean and standard-deviation reporting already existed in v1. Appendix D newly specifies 100 independently sampled test sets for the shift study and 100 calibration-set resamples for the calibration study, including coverage variability in Table 16. No increased run count or new seed information is established for the retained benchmarks.

E6.justification: All 48 distinct original benchmark rows are retained unchanged, but substantial additional results appear in Tables 3–4 and 11–16. For example, Table 12 reports MIS runtimes of 11.7 seconds for LSTM versus 207.298 for Linear, while Table 14 reports OTS runtimes of 74.212 seconds for Gurobi at 1% tolerance versus 96.2 for LSTM. These are new comparisons, not demonstrated improvements over v1 under identical settings.

M1.justification: Section 4.1 changes the calibration-rank prescription from (n+1)/(c+1) >= 1-alpha to n/(c+1) >= 1-alpha, which can change the selected stopping threshold. The LSTM architecture, covariates, weighted loss, and overall training/calibration/deployment procedure remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The main section order and much of the prose remain intact. V2 makes focused terminology, notation, citation, and grammatical corrections, expands several explanations, and organizes the supplemental material into Appendices A–D, moving the original tabular results to Appendix B.

P2.justification: V2 substantially expands the visual evidence with the 24-panel convergence Figure 5 and new tables for convergence statistics, heuristics, predictor comparisons, tolerances, and sensitivity studies. Existing benchmark tables receive numbered captions, and the duplicated MVC table labeled Maximum vertex capacity is removed. Figures 1–4 are retained.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds work on learned presolving, GNN-guided predict-and-search, and Apollo-MILP, and expands the distinction from Clarke and Stellato's earlier heuristic-validation approach. The references also add SCIP and replace the Zhang optimizer citation with Kingma and Ba. Publication-year and venue updates largely concern already cited works.

T1.justification: V2 adds Theorem 5.3 and a proof giving coverage bounds under total-variation-bounded distribution shift. It also corrects the off-by-one bound in Lemma 4.2 and Theorem 4.1's proof, restores a factor of 2 inside Theorem 5.1's square-root terms, and changes the suboptimality definition to use the incumbent objective U rather than g.

improvement.justification: V2 corrects an important off-by-one error in the calibration argument and adds comparisons that directly test whether the learned predictor contributes beyond simpler calibrated rules. Repeated calibration studies and convergence analyses substantially strengthen the evidence for reliability and the proposed mechanism. Unexplained differences between Table 11's LSTM suboptimalities and Appendix B, plus incompletely specified regenerated datasets, limit some new evidence but do not outweigh these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same conformal early-stopping method by the same authors. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching v1 Appendix A to v2 Appendix B.

after.justification: V2 retains these experiments and adds original predictor comparisons, heuristic evaluations, convergence analyses, and distribution-shift and calibration-size experiments in Appendices A, C, and D.

before.justification: Section 6 and Appendix A report original experiments on six problem families, measuring runtime, suboptimality, explored nodes, and solution accuracy.

results.title: Conformal Prediction for Early Stopping in Mixed Integer Optimization

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction’s three contributions, and conclusion retain the same central claims: TABX provides efficient, configurable battle simulation and supports systematic studies of value learning, exploration, and generalization. The additional experiments support these existing contributions.

C2.justification: v2 introduces explanations linking UED difficulty to parameter dimensionality, health variation, and curriculum behavior. It qualifies the speed advantage by distinguishing recompilation overhead from simulation cost. A new limitations section identifies combat-only coverage and illustrative empirical insights, while the rewritten impact statement explicitly limits real-world combat interpretations.

D1.justification: The code pointer changes from an anonymous repository to the named GitHub repository. v2 also documents the two-team action/reward interface and how policies are trained for competitive evaluation. Most simulator implementation details, software and hardware disclosures, and hyperparameter Tables 5–8 are retained.

E1.justification: v2 adds evaluations on three matched SMAX scenarios: 2s3z, 5m_vs_6m, and 6h_vs_8z. It also introduces learned-policy opponents and UED evaluation across heuristic difficulty tiers from random to expert, substantially broadening the tested interaction conditions beyond v1.

E2.justification: SMAX, previously evaluated against TABX for throughput, becomes a comparator in the matched-scenario learning study in Appendix D. The existing MARL quartet, MAPPO/RND comparisons, and five UED methods remain unchanged.

E3.justification: Figure 4 and Appendix E extend the main MARL budgets from 20M steps, or 30M for ribbon/grid, to 50M or 100M. New protocols include matched SMAX configurations, throughput measurement without scenario resets, isolated attribute variation, and pairwise policy testing. Appendix E nevertheless retains a contradictory 30M-step sentence. v1 already contained a separate extended ribbon experiment.

E4.justification: v2 adds individual health, speed, and damage ablations in Figure 8; value-error/return correlation analysis in Appendix G; a fixed-configuration throughput control in Appendix H; and heuristic-tier robustness analysis in Appendix J.5. The earlier extended ribbon experiment and RND sensitivity analysis are retained, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: The five-seed mean and standard-error convention remains. v2 adds Pearson correlations and significance tests using eight scenario averages and 40 seed-level observations in Figure 25. Appendix J.5 reports three seeds for the new heuristic-tier experiment, despite the general five-seed statement. No increase in replication of existing experiments is established.

E6.justification: New results include matched-SMAX learning curves, competitive payoff matrices showing MAPPO strongest on average, poorer generalization under health-only variation, and correlations of -0.819 and -0.681. Figure 4 extends the main learning curves, while Figure 9 changes throughput curves and count labels; these do not establish same-setting performance gains. Tables 9–11 merely round earlier runtimes up to whole minutes.

M1.justification: Section 4 changes the stated action space from six actions with one rotation to seven with left/right rotations. However, Appendix A.2 remains unchanged and also lists a no-op action. The PDFs do not establish whether the procedure changed or its description was corrected; the remaining simulator mechanisms and baseline formulations are retained.

P1.justification: Most original prose and section order are preserved. Local expansions explain scenario design and generalization, add competitive evaluation and limitations sections, and introduce new appendix headings. The impact statement is rewritten, acknowledgements are added, and publication information is updated.

P2.justification: Figure 8 expands from two panels to five; Figure 4 receives longer training axes and revised displays; and Figure 9 changes scales and legends. New displays include matched learning curves, correlation plots, fixed-configuration throughput, competitive payoff heatmaps, and heuristic-tier results. Existing appendix figures and tables are also redistributed.

R1.justification: v2 adds PettingZoo by Terry et al. and MAgent by Zheng et al. It also strengthens positioning against SMAX by discussing distinct learning dynamics on matched scenarios. The overall related-work organization and benchmark comparison table remain.

T1.justification: The reward definition, PVL/MaxMC formulations, RND objective, and value-error estimation definition are retained. No new formal assumptions, theoretical results, proofs, or mathematical derivations are introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of TABX’s distinctiveness and practical tradeoffs through matched-SMAX learning comparisons and a throughput control separating simulation cost from recompilation. Attribute ablations and explicit limitations also make the generalization findings more informative. These gains outweigh remaining reporting problems, including contradictory training budgets in Appendix E and Appendix D’s approximately 2M-step crossover claim where Figure 21 indicates roughly 20M.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TABX simulator and provide readable main text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices. Retained material can be matched despite additions, relocation, and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds matched-scenario SMAX comparisons, attribute ablations, correlation analyses, competitive policy evaluations, and heuristic-opponent generalization results.

before.justification: v1 reports original MARL learning curves, exploration experiments, UED generalization results, value-estimation analyses, and throughput measurements.

results.title: TABX: A High-Throughput Sandbox Battle Simulator for Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same headline contributions: O(d log d) regret, O((C + 1)d log d) regret without knowing C, and an Omega(d) lower bound. The new appendices support and qualify these contributions without adding a new headline claim.

C2.justification: v1 describes distinct objective components as merely a technical convenience. v2 explicitly acknowledges that corruption detection requires distinctness because legitimate ties can also create cycles. Appendix D explains the uncorrupted exception. The conclusion additionally distinguishes this setting from inverse bandit learning, and Appendix C interprets the approximation-budget trend.

D1.justification: Beyond v1's general polynomial-time implementation discussion, Appendices A–C specify membership checks, interior-point initialization, approximation tolerances and failure probabilities, oracle costs, matroid greedy optimization, and experimental iteration budgets. v2 also supplies a code-repository link, substantially expanding implementation and reproducibility information.

E1.justification: v2 introduces the first empirical task coverage: synthetic online inverse optimization over time-varying uniform matroids, with changing item availability. v1 discusses uniform matroids theoretically but does not evaluate them experimentally.

E2.justification: Table 2 introduces actual empirical comparisons against ONS from Sakaue et al. (2025b) and OGD from Bärmann et al. (2020). Neither was experimentally evaluated in v1; its related-work table only compared theoretical bounds.

E3.justification: Appendix C establishes the first experimental protocol: d = 20 items, 10 unavailable each round, selection of 5 available items, and T = 5000. It measures regret and per-round runtime and tests centroid approximations with 100, 1000, and 10000 hit-and-run iterations. These are settings for a new experiment.

E4.justification: Table 2 adds a focused sensitivity analysis varying the hit-and-run iteration budget. It examines how approximation effort affects regret and computational cost. v1 contains no corresponding empirical analysis.

E5.justification: v2 introduces averages over five independent trials and 95% confidence intervals for regret in Table 2. This uncertainty-reporting practice is limited to the new synthetic experiment; v1 reports no empirical uncertainty.

E6.justification: Table 2 adds six empirical result rows. Mean regret is 1.640 for quadratic Algorithm 1 and 1.677, 1.491, and 1.201 for its centroid variant at increasing iteration budgets, versus 3.510 for ONS and 4.848 for OGD. Runtime results reveal increasing computational cost with approximation effort. v1 has no corresponding measurements.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–2 retain their steps. Appendix D adds an adaptation for uncorrupted feedback with tied objective components: contract strongly connected components and choose estimates constant within each component. The expanded centroid implementation details elaborate the approximation already contemplated in v1.

P1.justification: The main section order and most prose remain intact. v2 expands the lower-bound exposition, adds appendix cross-references and four appendix sections, and makes limited language, affiliation, equal-contribution, and acknowledgement edits.

P2.justification: v2 adds Table 2, adjusts the sizing and spacing of Figures 1–2 while retaining their examples, and moves Algorithm 2 from page 12 to page 11. Table 1 accommodates an additional citation, and surrounding text reflows; the overall presentation format is retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds Sakaue (2026) to the logarithmic-regret discussion, Guha et al. (2024) and Petriconi and Vernade (2024) for inverse bandit connections, and Shioura and Tanaka (2007) for oracle algorithms. These are focused additions; the central positioning around M-convexity and finite regret remains unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendices A–B add approximation-error, expected-regret, and explicit oracle-complexity derivations. Section 6 changes the randomized lower bound from R_T to E[R_T] and explicitly verifies the embedding preserves objectives and regret. Section 2.1 and Appendix D replace v1's blanket perturbation argument for ties with separate reasoning for uncorrupted and corrupted feedback.

improvement.justification: v2 corrects v1's overbroad treatment of ties and clarifies that the randomized lower bound is in expectation. Its explicit approximate-centroid regret argument, computational analysis, and expanded lower-bound reduction materially improve the theoretical contribution's reliability and checkability. The new experiment and code link provide additional, narrowly scoped empirical and reproducibility support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work, with matching core algorithms, theorems, and illustrations. All pages are readable, including v2's new Appendices A–D; v1 ends with references and has no appendices.

after.justification: Appendix C and Table 2 report an original synthetic experiment on time-varying uniform matroids, including regret, runtime, and confidence intervals.

before.justification: v1 presents theoretical bounds, proofs, and illustrative mathematical examples, but no original experimental, simulation, or data-analysis outcomes.

results.title: Finite and Corruption-Robust Regret Bounds in Online Inverse Linear Optimization under M-Convex Action Sets

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the same headline contributions: refined data- and variance-dependent guarantees for known-transition MDPs using global and policy optimization, supported by lower bounds. The new conclusion restates these contributions; the leading regret orders remain unchanged.

C2.justification: Section 4.2 replaces its blanket minimax-optimality statement with one restricted to first-order, second-order and variance-aware gap-independent bounds, aligning it with the path-length gap already acknowledged in v1 Section 6. The estimator discussion also explicitly qualifies optimism as applying to real episodes.

D1.justification: Section 2.2 newly specifies xi = 1/4 throughout the paper, whereas v1 leaves the step size within an interval. This supplies a concrete hyperparameter choice for the existing predictor, without establishing a different implementation or experiment.

E1.justification: Neither version uses empirical datasets or evaluated tasks. The revised stochastic MDP instances in Appendix G are mathematical lower-bound constructions, not additional evaluations.

E2.justification: Neither version evaluates comparison methods experimentally. Tables 1–3 compare theoretical guarantees for the same cited methods; the Dann et al. year-letter changes do not identify different methods.

E3.justification: No experimental protocols or evaluation settings are reported in either version. Changes to horizon requirements in Section 6 and Appendix G are theorem assumptions.

E4.justification: Neither version contains empirical ablations, robustness tests, error analyses or case studies. The appendices provide notation, related-work discussion and proofs.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated experiments, seeds, empirical confidence intervals or significance tests. Revisions to Appendix F's concentration arguments concern theoretical proofs.

E6.justification: There are no measured scores, rankings or observed outcomes in either version. Changes to symbolic regret guarantees are assessed under T1.

M1.justification: The OFTRL updates, optimistic estimators, log-barrier regularizers, loss shifting, dilated bonuses and virtual-episode mechanism are retained. The algorithms exchange numbers, and global-optimization pseudocode moves from Appendix D to Section 4; these are not procedural changes.

P1.justification: Targeted rewrites clarify the known-transition motivation and estimator discussion, and numerous mathematical cross-references are corrected. v2 adds a Conclusion and Impact Statement, introduces numbered subsections within Section 3, and relocates the global algorithm; most exposition and proof organization remain recognizable.

P2.justification: The main text and references switch from a single-column manuscript to a two-column conference layout with running headers and revised typography. Tables and algorithm blocks are resized or repositioned, including moving global-optimization pseudocode from the appendix into the main text. The four tables and two algorithms are retained.

R1.justification: The cited literature is retained, but Appendix G.1 now presents the base lower bound as an existing result rather than a generalized result. Table 1 also revises the displayed Jin et al. (2021) bound, restricting the minimum gap to suboptimal actions and dropping the additional HSA log(T) term.

T1.justification: Appendix G substantially revises the lower-bound argument: Lemma G.2 corrects the dependence on S and changes T ≥ A/(8H) to T ≥ SA/(8H), while Theorem G.6 replaces the variable-mean Bernoulli construction with scaled losses from a Bernoulli(1/2) base instance. Appendix E repairs the action-wise squared-error argument and bonus bounds. Theorems 5.2–5.3 sharpen the principal additive remainder from H^2 S^2 A log^2(T) to H^(5/2) S^(3/2) A log^2(T), with corresponding appendix revisions. These materially revise formal guarantees and their mathematical support.

improvement.justification: v2 repairs consequential gaps in the paper's central theoretical support. Appendix G corrects the state-count dependence and replaces the problematic small-variance construction with loss rescaling; Appendix E replaces an invalid action-wise inequality with a valid summed-action bound. These changes substantially improve confidence in the lower-bound and policy-optimization claims, alongside sharper remainder terms. The stronger horizon requirement narrows the stated lower-bound coverage but makes it better supported. The main benefit is mathematical reliability, beyond the extensive reformatting.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, equations, tables, algorithms and Appendices A–G support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting.

after.justification: v2 remains entirely theoretical. Neither the main text nor the appendices report experimental, simulation, user-study or data-analysis outcomes.

before.justification: v1 reports algorithms, analytical regret bounds and mathematical proofs, including in its appendices. Its comparison tables contain theoretical guarantees, not original empirical outcomes.

results.title: Data- and Variance-dependent Regret Bounds for Online Tabular MDPs

C1.justification: v2 makes freedom from CFL constraints, non-periodic applicability, and superior large-stride stability against flux-rate surrogates central abstract, introduction, and conclusion claims. v1 already claimed large-timestep capability, but did not make these explicit CFL and comparative-stability claims. Exact conservation and empirical rather than guaranteed dual-bound satisfaction remain central.

C2.justification: v1 suggests structural constraints make pushforward training largely unnecessary for shallow water; v2 interprets its revised ablation as showing a clear benefit. v2 also acknowledges a traffic-flow accuracy-versus-boundedness tradeoff from DCL, adds CFL-based explanations, and identifies lost resolution invariance and unvalidated multidimensional/mixed boundaries as limitations. Appendix E corrects the microstructure length-scale interpretation from the correlation's first zero crossing to its first minimum.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code URL, transport-head channel counts, the default epsilon value, ghost-cell implementation instructions, FluxGNN comparison controls, overlapping spinodal training-pair construction, scheduler details, and NVIDIA A800 timing hardware. These materially expand reproducibility information. Conversely, v1's detailed 100-rollout spinodal statistical-evaluation procedure is omitted, and resolution descriptions remain inconsistent.

E1.justification: The four PDE families remain, but v2 extends evaluation beyond periodic domains through a Dirichlet traffic-flow dataset covering steady inflow/outflow, shock formation, and congestion back-propagation with boundary-layer dynamics (Appendix D.3). This adds materially different boundary conditions and physical test scenarios. One-shot spinodal training already appeared in v1.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated comparisons with FluxGNN and the FluxGNN-D adaptation on Dirichlet traffic flow, including FluxGNN at both tested temporal strides (Table 5). These introduce a direct conservative flux-rate comparator absent from v1's experiments. Comparator membership in the retained periodic benchmarks is unchanged; CNN/ResNet labeling changes do not introduce another baseline.

E3.justification: Reported settings change substantially: convection–diffusion uses 16 instead of 32 channels and 300 instead of 100 epochs; shallow water changes from four blocks with kernel size 3 to six with kernel size 5, also using 300 epochs. Periodic traffic changes DCL weight from 0.1 to 1.0 and training to 300 epochs. v2 adds Dirichlet protocols at 10Δt and 50Δt. Appendix E changes the stated spinodal evaluation grid from 1024×1024 to 128×128. These revisions do not establish which experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds an epsilon sensitivity sweep for shallow-water momentum transport (Table 8), a periodic-only versus ghost-cell boundary-treatment comparison, a FluxGNN backbone/head modularity comparison, and large-stride stability testing (Table 5; Figures 10–11). These address robustness and component-necessity questions beyond v1's retained head, pressure-gating, pushforward, and receptive-field analyses.

E5.justification: v1 provides table entries with ± values without identifying a general training-seed protocol. v2 specifies mean and standard deviation over five independently trained seeds, except spinodal decomposition, explicitly described as a single training run. Its spinodal table consequently loses the earlier ± entries, and Figure 1 is identified as a representative seed. Figure 3's uncertainty over 100 rollouts already existed. An increase in training-run count cannot be inferred.

E6.justification: Most retained benchmark and ablation values are replaced. Examples include convection–diffusion L-head MAE changing from 1.82 to 1.36, shallow-water ResNet-LAP depth MAE from 3.12 to 1.75, and periodic traffic D-head MAE from 3.48 to 2.79, all ×10−3. Revised settings prevent interpreting these as same-setting gains. New Dirichlet results favor FluxGNN over FluxNet-D at 10Δt but favor FluxNet-D at 50Δt. Spinodal point estimates and speedups are retained.

M1.justification: v2 adds a non-periodic procedure using ghost cells, an interior/ghost identity input channel, replicate padding, and retention of interior updates (Section 3.6). The reported training objective changes from weighted multi-step L1 loss to one-step and final-step squared errors, with detached rollouts explicitly specified. The existing transport-head formulas remain substantially unchanged; describing their outputs as cumulative transport is principally clarification.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related-work discussion, method exposition, experimental interpretations, and conclusion undergo extensive rewriting. Appendices are reorganized into detailed numbered subsections, the LBM discussion moves into the method, and terminology becomes more consistent around cumulative transport and ResNet. These changes substantially revise the narrative beyond accommodating new experiments.

P2.justification: v2 adds the Dirichlet comparison and epsilon-sensitivity tables, a ghost-cell schematic, and two multi-panel rollout figures (Tables 5 and 8; Figures 9–11). Table 1 gains a channel-count column, captions and legends are revised, and the larger-stride receptive-field figures share a page. Existing shallow-water field images and spinodal visualizations are retained rather than newly generated evidence.

R1.justification: Research positioning shifts toward distinguishing cumulative transport from instantaneous flux-rate surrogates and their claimed CFL restrictions. v2 adds FluxGNN, Kim and Kang's numerical-flux work, additional conservation-correction research, and Jiao/Lan one-shot-learning references. Some earlier references disappear, including energy-based modeling. Updates of existing works from preprints to publications are bibliographic changes rather than new research coverage.

T1.justification: The existing conservation and capacity-bound arguments are largely retained. v2 supplements them with an open-domain mass-balance identity involving boundary transport (Equation 5) and the CFL-free argument in Remark 1. The separately presented U-head proof largely restates reasoning already present in v1; it does not constitute an entirely new guarantee.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation by testing the boundary extension left unresolved in v1 and adding a direct conservative-surrogate comparison that exposes both advantages and disadvantages across temporal strides. Explicit seed-based uncertainty, sensitivity testing, and implementation details make the evidence more assessable and reproducible. These gains exceed merely reporting better scores. They are tempered by CFL-stability claims broader than the tested settings support and unresolved spinodal resolution inconsistencies, but the overall evidential and explanatory improvement is substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FluxNet research. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–E are readable and support comparison, including matching retained material across renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and reports additional Dirichlet traffic-flow comparisons, large-stride evaluations, and sensitivity results.

before.justification: v1 reports original surrogate experiments on four PDE benchmarks, including accuracy, conservation, bound violations, ablations, microstructure statistics, and computational timing.

results.title: FluxNet: Learning Capacity-Constrained Local Transport Operators for Conservative and Bounded PDE Surrogates

C1.justification: The abstract and central claims about delayed analogy emergence and the two-component mechanism remain. Section 3.3 narrows the depth-scaling claim to fixed optimization settings, acknowledging recovery through tuning. The new conclusion explicitly extends the claimed empirical validation to a natural-language analogy benchmark.

C2.justification: v4 replaces the main text's inverse-depth-scaling interpretation with an optimization-dependent account. It also explains earlier linear decodability, warns that embedding norms influence Dirichlet energy, and expands the limitations discussion to acknowledge primarily correlational mechanistic evidence and partially tested real-world assumptions (Section 7; Appendices B and R-T).

D1.justification: v4 adds an implementation-code link in Section 3 and construction details for the new noise, multiple-functor, and implicit-query experiments. Appendix A's hardware, architecture, and default training tables are retained. Documentation improves modestly, although the new probes lack detailed training and evaluation split specifications.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates synthetic relational tasks and artificial LLM prompts. v4 adds natural-language analogy evaluation on E-KAR with Gemma-2-9B, plus scenarios with noisy structural correspondences, multiple categories and mappings, and implicit-functor queries (Appendices N-Q). These substantially broaden the represented domains and task requirements.

E2.justification: v1 uses logit-lens decoding without a learned-readout comparison. v4 Appendix R and Figure 25 directly compare it against a trained per-layer linear probe. This adds a diagnostic comparison method; the original Gemma and Llama model coverage is retained.

E3.justification: New protocols include a four-layer learning-rate sweep over 10^-5, 10^-4, and 10^-3; a fixed 100-entity comparison across two, four, and five categories; E-KAR source/candidate-pair measurements; and trained linear and bilinear probes. These substantially expand the evaluation design. The previously reported default architecture and training settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v4 adds targeted checks of optimization-related depth failure, imperfect structural correspondence, dependence on a single mapping and explicit functor cues, logit-lens readout limitations, embedding-norm effects, and bilinear relational structure (Appendices B and O-T). These extend the original sensitivity and geometric analyses and test several previously unresolved assumptions.

E5.justification: Both versions state in Section 2.2 that reported results are averaged over three random seeds. v4 provides no revised run-count statement or newly specified uncertainty-estimation or significance-testing procedure. Shaded result curves already appear in v1.

E6.justification: The original result plots and prompt-probability entries are retained, while v4 adds substantial new findings: deeper-model recovery with learning-rate tuning, E-KAR layer-wise trends, noisy and implicit-mapping performance, and probe results. Appendix T reports 81.1% bilinear-probe accuracy and a null-space ratio falling from 0.624 to 0.108. These are newly reported results, not same-setting gains over v1.

M1.justification: The core Transformer architecture and final-token cross-entropy objective are unchanged. Appendix Q adds a trained and evaluated variant that replaces explicit entity/functor queries with partial entity tuples. Appendix P extends the input formulation to multiple distinct functor tokens. These are limited procedural extensions.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and appendix discussions are retained with local editing and revised explanations. The limitations material from v1 Appendix L is reorganized and expanded into Section 7, followed by a new Conclusion and Impact Statement. The narrative changes are localized despite the substantial added experimental content.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from single-column to two-column layout, extensively resizing and relocating figures. v1 Figure 3 becomes v4 Figures 3-4, and v1 Figure 7 becomes Figures 8-9. Captions are expanded, and new appendix Figures 11 and 21-27 display the added analyses. Retained plots largely preserve their underlying content.

R1.justification: The main analogy and structure-mapping positioning remains. v4 adds references concerning grokking progress, synthetic-task interpretation, and causal interventions, including Nanda, Furuta, Noroozizadeh, Wang, and Wurgaft. It removes the McKenzie inverse-scaling reference and the introductory Qwen and Grok references. These are localized positioning changes.

T1.justification: The original task definitions and Dirichlet-energy derivation are retained, with Appendix F becoming Appendix G. Appendix T adds a bilinear relation score and a normalized null-space-ratio definition, ||Wf|| divided by the mean of ||We_i||. This is a limited mathematical addition; no new theorem or proof is supplied.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens the evidence and its interpretation. The depth-specific learning-rate control corrects an overbroad inverse-scaling interpretation, while E-KAR and relaxed-assumption experiments address important validity gaps. Readout and embedding-norm checks identify confounds, and the expanded limitations make the lack of causal validation explicit. New probe protocols remain sparsely documented, but the gains in experimental support and interpretive caution are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison. Retained material can be matched despite extensive reformatting and renumbering.

after.justification: v4 retains those original results and adds learning-rate controls, E-KAR evaluation, task variants, and representation-probing experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic-task training experiments, mechanistic measurements, and pretrained Gemma and Llama analyses, including supplementary experiments in its appendices.

results.title: Emergent Analogical Reasoning in Transformers

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list and conclusion retain the same central claims: OCR-style genomic modeling, six prompted tasks, improved prediction and efficient visual compression. The headline nearly 20-fold token reduction and 985-fold activated-parameter comparison remain unchanged. Additional supporting experiments do not redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: New Appendix B explicitly explains the visual layout as a computational interface without biologically grounded 2D geometry or annotation priors. Other additions argue against memorization and rice-specific pretraining as explanations, and identify limits involving long OCR spans, severe token bottlenecks and disrupted sequence continuity. These substantially expand the mechanism discussion and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: v2 adds front-page project and code links, a detailed rendering-configuration grid, and implementation descriptions such as adjacent-token pooling with tail handling. Table 2 relabels parameter counts as trainable, and Table S36 separately reports total inference parameters. Existing pretraining hyperparameters, hardware descriptions and baseline reproduction instructions are largely retained; linked repository contents cannot be established from the PDFs.

E1.justification: The biological corpora, nine eQTL tissues, five rice groups and two phenotype tasks remain unchanged. Beyond v1's rendering-resolution sweep, v2 adds input scenarios involving alternate fonts, layouts, fragment boundaries and downsampling with DNA content and layout held fixed (Section 4.7 and Appendix N).

E2.justification: Table 2 adds NT-v2-500M and GENERator-1.2B. Appendix A adds BiGRU/RNN, Performer/LinearAttn, Longformer/SparseAttn and two Transformer baselines. Appendix O additionally compares Caduceus and JanusDNA on RiceSubBench and adds Caduceus to RiceWGPB. These substantially broaden the evaluated comparator sets.

E3.justification: v2 adds chunked, frozen-backbone linear-probe evaluation for NT and GENERator; a shared-Transformer comparison with 10,000 tokens per representation; and a unified computational-cost protocol. It also introduces length-stratified OCR, token-pooling, contamination and representation-consistency evaluations, and tests HG38-pretrained models on rice. The original pretraining schedules and benchmark splits remain as stated.

E4.justification: New analyses test whether the advantage survives stronger sequence architectures, matched backbone/token budgets and a common pretraining source. Further additions examine contamination, OCR failure by retained length, token bottlenecks, rendering perturbations and representation consistency (Appendices A, I, K.1 and L–O). The original OCR, masked-span and Grad-CAM analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions retain seeded hashing for RiceSubBench and seed=42 for RiceWGPB. v2 adds no repeated-run counts, performance confidence intervals, significance tests or other uncertainty-estimation procedures.

E6.justification: Original benchmark scores remain unchanged, including OpticalDNA's 0.852/0.867 average eQTL AUROC. New results include NT/GENERator averages of 0.772/0.782, matched-budget 1D/2D AUROC of 0.558/0.626, token-bottleneck results ranging from 0.852 at 100 tokens to 0.776 at one token, and HG38-to-rice transfer results. v2 also adds extensive robustness, contamination and computational-cost measurements; these are additional results under their stated conditions.

M1.justification: The DNA rendering pipeline, visual encoder, projector, fusion module, document decoder, six pretraining tasks and training objective are retained. The new token-merging variants are experimental ablations; they do not replace the proposed OpticalDNA procedure.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and technical exposition are retained. v2 adds a motivation appendix, subdivides Appendix A, retitles Section 4.6, inserts robustness and transfer sections, condenses the impact statement and updates acknowledgements and front matter. These are limited editorial and organizational changes alongside the scientific additions.

P2.justification: v2 adds rendering, downsampling and transfer plots, a multi-panel representation-consistency heatmap, and numerous tables presenting new controls and analyses. Table 2 gains comparison columns, while Figure 3 corrects its legend from VisualDNA to OpticalDNA without changing its results. Existing displays are also repositioned. The new Figure 7 has an incorrect caption describing resolution-dependent eQTL results despite plotting rice transfer.

R1.justification: v2 adds the GENERator citation to Wu et al. (2025) and replaces the Consortium (2019) genome-reference citation with Schneider et al. (2017). The related-work sections and claimed novelty of the OCR-style genomic formulation remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The document and coordinate definitions, generative objective, curriculum formula, ROI metrics and Grad-CAM equations are retained. The added motivation and empirical analyses introduce no substantive new mathematical derivations, theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens assessment of the central representation claim through shared-backbone/token-budget controls, stronger baselines and pretraining-source controls that v1 lacked. Rendering, bottleneck and computational-cost analyses also expose practical strengths and failure regimes. These gains outweigh the added reporting problems, but the contamination assurance remains limited: Table S25 uses 11,253 and 16,569 RiceWGPB test sequences, whereas retained Table S23 lists only 21 and 26 test accessions, without reconciling the counts or units. Repeated-run uncertainty is still absent.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same OpticalDNA work. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, are readable and support comparison after matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds controlled comparisons, rendering robustness, token bottleneck, computational cost, contamination and cross-species transfer analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original eQTL prediction, rice classification, whole-genome phenotype prediction, OCR evaluations and ablation results.

results.title: Rethinking Genomic Modeling Through Optical Character Recognition

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion retain the central smoothing, accuracy, and efficiency claims. The introduction's empirical contribution now explicitly claims competitiveness with Mamba and specifies classification benchmarks. Temporal parallelization remains claimed in the surrounding prose despite removal of its separate contribution bullet.

C2.justification: v2 introduces substantive limitations concerning adaptive-solver dependence, bandwidth tuning, and loss of useful high-frequency information, including possible long-horizon forecasting degradation. It adds causal-window and latency qualifications, bandwidth trade-off discussion, and interpretations of head regularization, missingness robustness, smoothing-spline performance, and memory costs. These substantially expand the discussion of mechanisms and applicability.

D1.justification: v2 supplies Mamba configuration, forecasting normalization and causal refitting details, additional dataset-specific optimization settings, the head-regularization coefficient, and the smoothing-spline penalty formula. It also reports parameter counts, peak memory, and H100 profiling information. This substantially expands reproducibility documentation, although exact small-batch sizes are not supplied.

E1.justification: v2 adds ETTm1 forecasting, Speech Commands classification under missing observations, and 963-dimensional PEMS-SF classification. It also evaluates observation-drop scenarios on the three retained classification datasets. These substantially extend the tasks, domains, dimensionality, and input conditions beyond v1's coverage.

E2.justification: Mamba joins the retained three-dataset comparison in v2 Table 2, and a traditional Smoothing Spline baseline is evaluated in Table 10. The new forecasting comparison includes standard GRU, distinct from the existing GRU-D. Figure 10 also adds GRU-D and Mamba to the computational breakdown.

E3.justification: Appendix B.3 replaces v1's fixed 128-unit setup with reported parameter matching for Linear and Cubic baselines. The UWave Cubic table tolerance changes from 0.001 to 0.0001. New protocols include 24-step context/horizon forecasting, observation-drop sweeps, solver-order comparisons, and memory measurement. Figure 10 is now specified as H100 profiling with small batches. These are reported setting changes, not proof that every retained experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds head-diversity regularization tests, missing-observation robustness, solver-order sensitivity, memory/scalability analysis, and a comparison testing whether traditional smoothing alone explains the gains (Tables 3–10). The earlier noise, head-count, bandwidth, and single-path analyses remain; the additions address substantial new robustness and mechanism questions.

E5.justification: Both versions specify five independent random seeds in Appendix B.2 and report uncertainty using ± values and error bars. No changed run-count policy, confidence-interval procedure, or formal significance testing is documented.

E6.justification: v1 Table 1 becomes v2 Table 2 with replaced Linear/Cubic results under revised settings; CharacterTrajectories Cubic accuracy changes from 86.61% to 91.89%. The primary MVC GP accuracies remain unchanged, but added Mamba achieves 96.64% versus MVC GP's 95.07% on CharacterTrajectories. New results include ETTm1 MSE of 0.428 and extensive missingness, memory, regularization, solver, and scalability measurements.

M1.justification: The core smoothing, attention, convolutional feature extraction, and parallel integration procedures remain unchanged. v2 adds a forecasting adaptation using RevIN, context-only path construction, and a linear horizon predictor (Appendix B.6–B.7). It also tests an optional head-similarity penalty, without adopting it in the primary architecture.

P1.justification: Much of the existing abstract, introduction, method, results discussion, and conclusion is retained verbatim. Changes include localized explanatory edits, streamlined contribution bullets, new forecasting and limitations sections, Appendix C reorganization, and affiliation, disclosure, and acknowledgement additions. The revision is primarily scientific expansion rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: v2 adds forecasting Table 1 and Tables 3–10, while expanding the retained comparison as Table 2. Figure 5 replaces attention heatmaps with head curves aligned to original signals. Figure 10 changes its displayed comparisons, scales, and legend; the Pareto plots add Mamba, and several figures move. These are substantial display changes beyond numerical updates.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds localized positioning against GP adapters/GP-RNNs, interpolation and attention networks, and Mechanistic Neural Networks, alongside Mamba and additional GP/signature references. The central geometric-smoothing research gap remains unchanged. Publication updates for works such as DeNOTS and the clinical time-series benchmark do not represent new cited research.

T1.justification: Theorem 3.1, the spline estimates, Corollary 3.3, and Theorem 3.4 replace proportionality assertions with upper bounds up to constants. Appendix A explicitly carries solver-tolerance dependence through the smoothing and parallel-integration derivations. These revise existing mathematical claims; the derivative-bound argument, assumptions, and GP error comparison are otherwise retained.

improvement.justification: v2 materially addresses v1's limited validation and model-capacity confound through reported parameter matching, stronger comparators, forecasting and missingness tests, and explicit applicability limits. These changes substantially strengthen the evidence for when smoothing helps. Some conclusions remain overstated: Section 4.1 still claims consistent superiority although Table 2 places Mamba above MVC GP on CharacterTrajectories. That inconsistency limits the improvement but does not outweigh the stronger controls and broader, targeted validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same attentive-smoothing Neural CDE work. All pages, including Appendices A–C, are readable, and the methods, equations, figures, and retained experiments can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains original classification experiments and adds forecasting, missing-observation, memory, solver-order, regularization, and high-dimensional evaluation results.

before.justification: v1 reports original classification, timing, NFE, noise-robustness, and architectural-ablation results on three datasets in Section 4 and Appendix C.

results.title: Efficient Neural Controlled Differential Equations via Attentive Kernel Smoothing

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the claims of semi-supervised PPRM, unbiased risk estimation, anytime-valid error control, adaptive weighting, and faster harmful-shift detection across three application areas. Splitting adaptive weighting into its own contribution bullet and replacing false-alarm terminology with type-I error do not change those claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive qualifications: variance reduction must offset the normalization penalty for faster detection; fixed weighting can underperform SRM with poor predictors; and window length trades responsiveness to abrupt changes against stability under gradual changes. Appendix D also explains interpolation toward unsupervised monitoring and discusses computational-cost tradeoffs.

D1.justification: Appendix D.5 adds qualitative implementation guidance about lightweight coefficient estimation and online, offline, or self-predictor deployment, without runtime measurements. Conversely, Figure 3's caption no longer identifies Qwen2-VL-7B as its imputation model. This removes a documented configuration detail without establishing that the model actually changed.

E1.justification: The original image, QA, medical-domain, and wireless coverage is retained. v2 substantially expands evaluated conditions through stationary Bernoulli simulations, a no-shift LLM scenario, abrupt shifts in image and QA tasks, and intermittent-label image streams (Appendices A.4 and D). These are new scenarios rather than new named benchmarks.

E2.justification: The established SRM, URM, and ideal-PPRM comparators remain in the matched original experiments. Figure 12 expands image comparisons to include fixed-weight PPRM alongside adaptive PPRM, SRM, and ideal PPRM; v1's explicit fixed-versus-adaptive comparison was confined to the LLM experiment in Table 1.

E3.justification: Original defaults remain, including one labeled and 15 unlabeled samples per round and window length 60. Added experiments introduce a null-crossing evaluation with target delta_T = 0.15, stationary simulation with risk 0.5 and threshold 0.42, window-length and controlled predictor-accuracy sweeps, and label periods k = 1, 2, 3, 4. These substantially expand the evaluation design.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's predictor comparisons, adaptive-weight ablation, and non-monotonic shifts, v2 adds empirical false-alarm checks, theoretical-delay validation, window sensitivity, abrupt-shift tests, controlled poor-predictor analyses, weighting and variance diagnostics, and intermittent-label robustness tests (Figures 5, 6, and 10–14).

E5.justification: Section 5 changes the stated figure uncertainty summary from the full range across runs to mean plus or minus one standard deviation, called confidence intervals. v2 also describes averaging cumulative alarm indicators across independent null trials. Neither version specifies numerical run or seed counts, so an increase in repetitions is not established.

E6.justification: Table 1's values remain unchanged, including 519.08 versus 498.31 for fixed versus adaptive PPRM with Qwen2-VL-7B. Substantial new results include false-alarm curves below 0.15, simulated mean detection times of 91.74 for PPRM versus 231.96 for SRM in Figure 6, and window, predictor-quality, abrupt-shift, and intermittent-label findings. These are additional results, not demonstrated same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The main PPRM estimator and adaptive weighting procedure remain, but Appendix D.4 adds a hybrid procedure combining PPRM on labeled rounds with an unsupervised proxy bound on unlabeled rounds. Unlike v1's requirement for labels at every round, this extension supports intermittent labels and introduces a substantive additional monitoring component.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section order largely remain. v2 makes localized grammatical and terminology corrections, clarifies notation, reorganizes the contribution bullets, adds acknowledgements, and organizes new material into Appendices A.4 and D. The retained prose is not extensively rewritten.

P2.justification: v2 adds substantial diagnostic visualizations in Figures 5, 6, and 10–14 and revises existing axes, legends, label orientation, captions, and panel grouping. The earlier supplementary Figures 5–7 are retained as Figures 7–9; their renumbering is not an addition or removal. Table 1 retains its structure.

R1.justification: v2 adds Howard et al. (2020) to support the linear-boundary delay analysis and sharpens the distinction between persistent degradation monitoring and instantaneous-risk violations. Most other reference changes concern author names or publication metadata for already-cited works, rather than new research positioning.

T1.justification: Appendix A.4 adds stationary Bernoulli assumptions, estimator-variance and normalized detection-time derivations, and Proposition A.1's approximate delay-improvement condition. Appendix D.4 adds the intermittent-label risk decomposition and hybrid lower bound. Equations 26 and 38 also correct the covariance to pair true and surrogate losses on the same labeled input.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the evidence explaining when faster detection is credible: it checks false alarms, tests poor predictors and monitoring-window choices, and derives an explicit variance-versus-normalization tradeoff. These additions address important gaps in v1's largely benchmark-based support and expose failure conditions rather than merely adding favorable scores. The gains outweigh the limited documentation regression in Figure 3 and imprecise confidence-interval terminology. The delay analysis remains approximate, and experimental repetition counts remain unspecified.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PPRM research work. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, table, references, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite additions and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds empirical false-alarm evaluation, stationary simulations, sensitivity analyses, and intermittent-label experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original image-classification and LLM monitoring experiments in Section 5, plus MedGemma and wireless-channel experiments in Appendix C.

results.title: Prediction-Powered Risk Monitoring of Deployed Models for Detecting Harmful Distribution Shifts

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and concluding impact discussion retain the same central contributions: exact variational reformulation, simulation-free neural training, learning guarantees and competitive translation. Changing 'positive normalizer' to 'log-normalizer' aligns terminology with the existing formulation. The added experiments support the retained claims.

C2.justification: Section 6 adds substantive limitations concerning auxiliary-network expressiveness and restriction to quadratic costs. The new experimental discussion interprets the particle-count speed–quality trade-off and attributes the advantage over EgNOT to avoiding training-time simulation. Existing inference-sampling and numerical-instability limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds a VarEOT code-repository link and discloses clipping exponential arguments above 30 and gradients at norm 1. It also documents MSCI particle count/hardware and hardware allocation for timing comparisons. These are additional reproducibility disclosures; the PDFs do not establish that clipping was newly introduced. Some MSCI settings remain deferred to cited external work.

E1.justification: New Section 5.2 adds biological single-cell distribution interpolation on MSCI, covering four donors and trajectories from days 2 to 4 and 3 to 7 with intermediate-day evaluation. This substantially extends coverage beyond the retained synthetic example and face-translation tasks.

E2.justification: The new MSCI comparison includes Sinkhorn (Cuturi, 2013), Minimax (Gushchin et al., 2023) and IPF (Vargas et al., 2021), alongside the Langevin-based EgNOT comparator. These additional methods have reported comparison results, explicitly borrowed from Korotin et al. (2024). The original image comparisons retain LightSB and EgNOT.

E3.justification: The MSCI experiment introduces intermediate-distribution evaluation using energy distance, PCA dimensions 50/100/1000 and K=128. Appendix C.1 adds a timing protocol with 10,000 training iterations and K values from 32 to 512, using GPU execution for VarEOT/EgNOT and CPU execution for LightSB. Existing image splits, metrics and inference budgets are retained.

E4.justification: New Appendix C.1 and Table 4 examine how particle count K affects training time and FID, adding a focused computational sensitivity analysis. The existing epsilon-diversity and Langevin step-size/step-count analyses remain in Figures 6–7.

E5.justification: New Table 2 reports MSCI results averaged over two setups and five random seeds, with 95% confidence intervals. v1 provides no corresponding empirical uncertainty reporting. This is reporting for the added benchmark, not evidence of increased repetitions for the retained image experiments.

Table 4 adds timing/FID results, including 85 seconds/13.45 at K=32 and 409 seconds/9.575 at K=512. These are added results under their stated settings. All numerical scores in v1 Table 2, now v2 Table 3, are unchanged.

M1.justification: Algorithm 2 corrects the reported Langevin drift: v1 scales only the quadratic-cost gradient by 1/epsilon, whereas v2 scales the potential gradient as well, matching Equation (5). The accompanying inference density is corrected accordingly. The variational training objective and joint two-network procedure remain unchanged; the PDFs do not establish an implementation change or rerun.

P1.justification: Targeted rewrites clarify the learning-guarantee narrative, joint optimization and the distinction between simulation-free training and inference. Grammar and terminology are corrected, front matter is updated, acknowledgements are added, and experimental subsections are inserted and renumbered. The overall section and appendix organization remains intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds the MSCI and timing tables and relocates existing displays as the text expands. The original image-results table becomes Table 3 and corrects the A→Y label to A→C. Figures 1–7 retain their experimental content, with appendix figures redistributed across pages and minor caption edits.

R1.justification: v2 adds supporting literature on single-cell transport, energy distance, neural-network complexity and approximation, including Bunne et al., Koshizuka and Sato, Golowich et al., Maurer and Pinkus. Gottlieb et al. and Ledoux–Talagrand are removed with the replaced proof arguments. The central positioning against existing EOT/SB approaches is retained.

Proposition 3.4 now analyzes the joint empirical maximizer. Appendix A substantially revises contraction arguments, explicitly accounts for finite-K Gaussian sampling error, and replaces the approximation proof with a neural-network construction.

results.title: Variational Entropic Optimal Transport

C2.justification: v2 interprets the expanded results as supporting scaling with model size and test-time compute, and acknowledges that offline efficiency may sacrifice performance. The central shortcut-learning explanation remains.

E2.justification: Appendix C.8 and Table 10 add supervised distillation from Qwen3-235B-A22B (think) as an evaluated comparator. The original SFT, STaR and RLVR comparator memberships remain; applying existing baselines to the new domains does not itself constitute another comparator addition.
