The reported e1-verifiable RL settings change from 15 GRPO epochs plus 15 NuRL epochs to 5 plus 5, and rollout temperature changes from 0.6 to 1.0. New experiments also introduce Qwen3-14B and Llama configurations, a distillation comparison controlling tokens per example, and GPT-4o-mini grading for HealthBench.

E4.justification: The revision substantially extends capability and backbone analyses through Qwen3-14B scaling, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct failure testing and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B evaluation. Appendix C.7 adds a qualitative investigation of slow on-policy convergence, while Figure 16 revises the smaller-model analysis. Existing loss, sampling and deduplication analyses are retained.

E5.justification: The 128-sample pass@k estimation practice is retained. Neither version reports training-seed replication, confidence intervals, error bars or formal significance tests; the added experiments introduce no new uncertainty-reporting procedure.

E6.justification: RL results change in Figures 2, 6 and 14, and Figures 4 and 16 replace test-time results under revised evaluation conditions. Tables 2–5 and 10–12 add domain, distillation and backbone outcomes. These include HealthBench totals of 0.16 for both base and DAIL, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct pass@1 of 0.64 versus DAIL's 0.47. GPQA Table 1 and the contrastive-loss ablation values remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The main mixed-policy generation procedure and contrastive KL objective remain unchanged; 'privileged student' is renamed 'teacher'. Limited extensions appear in the exploratory on-policy DAIL variant in Appendix C.7 and HealthBench teacher conditioning on both expert solutions and grading rubrics in Appendix B.

P1.justification: The paper is retitled, consistently replaces 'privileged student' with 'teacher', and makes localized prose corrections and discussion revisions. It adds acknowledgments and a non-mathematics appendix, moving the previous Appendix B details to Appendix C. Most of the main narrative and section order remain intact.

P2.justification: Figure 4 expands to six panels with a Qwen3-14B row, and Figure 16 is redrawn, enlarged and relocated. New domain, distillation and backbone tables substantially expand the displays. Table 8 additionally tabulates Figure 2's results; it is a numerical redisplay rather than a separate experiment. Existing prompts and ablation displays are largely retained or relocated.

R1.justification: Section 4 adds Hübotter and Shenfeld's concurrent self-distillation work and repositions the already-cited Zhao work within that discussion. New benchmark citations and Shao et al.'s backbone-generalization motivation are added. These locally extend the positioning without replacing the existing related-work framework.

Some retained RL-failure language overstates the updated evidence—for example, Table 8 shows GRPO exceeding the base model on AIME pass@128—but the evaluation repair and broader empirical scrutiny provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DAIL research despite the changed title. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, figures and tables, are readable and support reliable matching across versions.

after.justification: The empirical studies are retained and revised, with additional non-mathematics evaluations, model configurations, distillation comparisons and exploratory experiments.

before.justification: Section 3 and Appendix B report original DAIL and baseline evaluations on mathematics and GPQA, including efficiency, ablation and generalization results.

results.title: Making Expert Reasoning Learnable with Self-Distillation

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion add a distinct claimed contribution: the first general training-loss lower-bound construction, supporting tightness in some regimes. v1 supplied upper bounds and recovered existing special-case tightness through ElasticNet; the original multidimensional learnability and LASSO claims remain.

C2.justification: Appendix D.2 newly interprets the lower bound as establishing unavoidable dependence and partial tightness in suitable constant-p regimes. Section 6.1 identifies exact inner minimization as restrictive, while the fixed-K footnote qualifies the prior-bound comparison. The general bilevel minimax question remains open.

D1.justification: Neither version provides experimental implementation settings, hardware, runtime measurements, or access instructions for its own code or data. The added proof constants and constructions are mathematical details, not implementation disclosures.

E1.justification: Neither version reports datasets actually used for empirical training or evaluation. Weighted group LASSO, weighted fused LASSO, and ElasticNet remain theoretical applications; the new lower-bound instances serve a proof.

E2.justification: Neither version evaluates comparison methods experimentally. Comparisons with Goldberg–Jerrum and Balcan et al. concern mathematical guarantees, not evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: Neither PDF specifies an empirical evaluation protocol. The added approximation tolerance and lower-bound construction define theoretical settings, not revised experimental budgets, metrics, or procedures.

E4.justification: Neither version contains empirical ablations, sensitivity tests, robustness studies, or error analyses. The approximate-minimization extension is a theorem, and the existing analytical application examples are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated experiments, seeds, confidence intervals, or statistical tests. The retained PAC probability statements are theoretical guarantees rather than empirical uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Neither version reports measured performance values, rankings, or experimental findings. The added asymptotic lower bound and approximation guarantee are mathematical contributions assessed under T1.

M1.justification: Section 6.1 adds a bilevel-loss variant that minimizes validation loss over an epsilon-optimal training set instead of exact training minimizers. This extends the loss formulation while retaining the FOL framework and existing LASSO objectives.

P1.justification: v2 adds upper/lower-bound subdivisions in Section 5 and Appendix D, Section 6.1, and acknowledgments, alongside scattered language corrections and affiliation updates. The overall narrative and section sequence remain substantially intact.

P2.justification: The template running header is replaced by the paper title, and the front matter gains conference publication formatting. Text and equations reflow around the additions. Figure 1 and its caption remain unchanged, and neither version contains tables.

R1.justification: v2 adds Balcan et al. (2024), Algorithm Configuration for Structured Pfaffian Settings, and positions the new lower bound relative to missing prior guarantees and Bartlett et al.'s bit-extraction technique. Nguyen and Nguyen's 2025-to-2026 citation change updates the same work rather than adding another.

T1.justification: v2 adds Theorem 5.2's Omega(p d log Delta_f) training-loss lower bound on unrestricted parameter domains, with a bit-extraction and stabilization proof in Appendix D.2. Proposition 6.2 adds a guarantee for epsilon-optimal inner solutions. Theorems 2.5 and 4.1 also explicitly fix the quantifier-block count K and revise complexity expressions, with corresponding changes in Appendix B.

improvement.justification: Theorem 5.2 and Appendix D.2 substantially strengthen v1's upper-bound account by supplying an original constructive lower bound and explaining unavoidable complexity factors. The approximation extension and explicit fixed-K qualification also improve applicability and precision. The general bilevel gap remains open, and Proposition 6.2 references Theorem 5.1 without clearly specifying the needed assumptions on the validation objective g. These limitations do not outweigh the substantial gain in theoretical completeness.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same theoretical work. The complete main texts, Figure 1, equations, and Appendices A–G are readable and support matching retained material and identifying additions.

after.justification: v2 remains theoretical. Its new lower-bound construction and approximate-minimization proposition are mathematical results; the constructed instances are proof witnesses, not empirical observations.

before.justification: v1 reports mathematical guarantees and proofs, including theoretical LASSO applications and an ElasticNet example in Appendix F.2. It contains no original experimental, simulation, or data-analysis outcomes.

results.title: Provably Data-driven Multiple Hyper-parameter Tuning with Structured Loss Function

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contributions and conclusion retain the same central claims: MentisOculi probes multi-step mental imagery, self-generated visuals provide no reliable reasoning advantage, and UMMs struggle with generation consistency and using visual evidence. The added experiments support these retained claims.

C2.justification: v2 develops a stronger interpretation of weak coupling between image and text reasoning, argues that greater model capability does not resolve it, and distinguishes MLLMs' oracle benefits from UMM limitations. New controls qualify the contribution of latent decoding and explanations based on input burden. Conversely, removing v1's datasheet deletes explicit boundaries against interpreting the benchmark as evidence about real-world perception or general intelligence.

D1.justification: Appendix G adds Latent Sketchpad's backbone, LoRA settings, training stages and losses, plus Mirage's text-only training details and model-specific retry information. v1's datasheet guidance on splits, licensing, distribution and maintenance disappears. The Gemini 2.5 endpoint entry changes from gemini-2.5-flash-image to gemini-2.5-flash, but the following sentence still specifies flash-image, leaving the actual configuration ambiguous.

E1.justification: The same five tasks and human population remain. However, Hinge Folding's task requirements change from 45-degree to 90-degree rotations, while a minimum-visible-area constraint replaces the exclusion of certain 180-degree rotations (Section 2, Appendix A and prompts). This revises one task's generated configurations and action space.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated comparisons with Latent Sketchpad, Emu 3.5 and Wan 2.6 (Figures 2–3), plus text-only fine-tuned controls for Mirage and Latent Sketchpad (Table 1). Gemini 3-I also joins the broader task and oracle comparisons where v1 principally evaluated Gemini 2.5-I.

E3.justification: Section 3.2 changes Rush Hour scoring from requiring a successful terminal state to accepting a trace containing a successful state. Appendix G.1 reports increasing Gemini 3-I's retry limit from three to nine and allowing fifteen attempts for Emu 3.5. New protocols include matched text-only fine-tuning controls, iterative oracle feedback and filtered-versus-unfiltered evaluation.

E4.justification: v2 adds controls testing whether latent gains arise from fine-tuning, whether oracle failures reflect simultaneous multi-image input, and whether excluding image-free responses affects accuracy (Table 1; Figures 14 and 24). It also adds direct image/text solution-disagreement analysis and MLLM oracle experiments (Figures 7 and 15), while expanding existing rollout diagnostics.

E5.justification: Both versions display uncertainty bars or bands and reference 95% confidence intervals in Appendix D.2. No new repeated-run, seed or uncertainty-estimation procedure is reported. Increased retries concern obtaining valid responses rather than estimating statistical uncertainty.

E6.justification: Substantial results are added for new comparators and controls. Table 1 reports Latent Sketchpad's Level 3 accuracy as 6.7% with latents versus 23.3% with text-only training; Table 2 newly reports overall omission rates of 28.9%, 0.9% and 27.2% for Emu 3.5, Gemini 2.5-I and Gemini 3-I. Figures 7 and 15 add modality-disagreement and MLLM oracle findings. Revised Hinge Folding scores concern changed task conditions.

M1.justification: The benchmark framework is retained, with localized procedural changes. Appendix A revises the Hinge Folding generator's rotation and visibility constraints, and Section 4.3 adapts the existing video action extractor to image-only UMM rollouts.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section order remain recognizable. Changes include targeted prose corrections, author-year citations, a corrected Form Board prompt heading, added analysis and conflict-of-interest sections, and appendix renumbering after inserting the latent-decoding section and removing the datasheet.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands and restructures the displays: comparator plots gain series, oracle plots use new groupings, and separate rollout diagnostics become multi-model grids. It adds disagreement, iterative-feedback, MLLM-oracle and filtering figures, two tables and Emu examples. Existing human and video figures are largely retained under new numbering.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations for Latent Sketchpad and Wan 2.6 and removes Gebru et al.'s datasheet reference alongside the datasheet. The broader related-work discussion and benchmark novelty positioning remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Neither version contains substantive theoretical propositions or proofs. The revisions concern empirical task construction, scoring and analysis rather than new mathematical derivations or formal guarantees.

improvement.justification: v1 could not isolate latent imagery's contribution from fine-tuning and based its oracle diagnosis mainly on Gemini 2.5-I. v2's text-only training controls, broader oracle comparisons, modality-disagreement analysis and feedback/filtering checks substantially strengthen the central empirical diagnosis. Removing the datasheet loses useful guidance, and inconsistent model descriptions weaken reproducibility, but these documentation regressions are outweighed by the improved controls and evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MentisOculi study. Their complete text, figures, tables and appendices support reliable comparison. Revised task and evaluation settings require care when comparing individual scores.

after.justification: v2 retains original model and human results and adds model comparisons, fine-tuning controls, oracle-feedback experiments and image/text disagreement analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original model evaluations on five visual reasoning tasks, diagnostic experiments and a five-participant human study.

results.title: MentisOculi: Revealing the Limits of Reasoning with Mental Imagery

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution list broaden the empirical generality claim from MoE models to dense and MoE architectures; the conclusion also includes multiple expansion stages. The central signal-preservation/symmetry-breaking contribution and the headline claim of up to 35% computational savings remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations connecting the residual training-loss gap to reduced compute and downstream generalization to loss-landscape geometry (Section 5.1). It interprets compute-matched gains as a larger scaling exponent (Section 5.5 and Appendix P), extends the RMS argument to post-normalization, and discusses iterative expansion's loss/compute tradeoff and further-stage limitations. These substantially extend v1's interpretation, although the claimed exponent improvement lacks a fitted scaling analysis.

D1.justification: v2 explicitly documents copy initialization for RMSNorm weights and supplies implementation recipes for the added dynamics baselines, including schedule remapping and accelerated decay. It also specifies the dense and iterative configurations. The original architecture, training hyperparameters, and hardware information in Tables 3-5 are retained, with the setup appendix moved from B to D.

E1.justification: The language-modeling task and the 12 downstream evaluation columns remain unchanged; v2's Tables 6-8 reuse the evaluations in Table 1. No new corpus, language, or domain is reported. Dense architectures, successive expansions, and compute matching change configurations and procedures within the retained task coverage.

E2.justification: Appendix K and Table 7 add evaluated dynamics-based comparators: Scaled Opt. + Remap LR, Uneven Splitting with 25%/50% Faster Decay LR, and FP-random + WN-Adapted LR. Table 7 also introduces downstream comparisons with previously loss-only heuristic baselines. Table 1's renamed Naive FP scaled baseline retains its original numerical results.

E3.justification: The original single expansion at 100B of 200B tokens is retained. v2 adds a dense configuration with intermediate size 4096 and a two-stage 256-to-512-to-1024 expansion at 50B and 100B tokens (Appendices N-O). Appendix P introduces comparisons at equal-FLOP points on training trajectories, substantially extending the original fixed-token evaluation design.

E4.justification: v2 adds a controlled RMSNorm copy-versus-random ablation (Appendix C), a four-configuration separation of RMS preservation and asymmetric strategies across three initialization pairs (Appendix I), and an analysis of immediate perturbation versus final loss (Appendix F). Iterative and compute-matched analyses further examine efficiency and composability. The original Muon tests and re-warmup sensitivity analysis are retained after relocation.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, experimental seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or a statistical uncertainty-estimation procedure. The added results continue the existing point-estimate and training-curve reporting practice.

E6.justification: The numerical results in Tables 1 and 2 remain unchanged, but v2 adds substantial ablation and comparator results in Tables 6-7, dense results in Table 8, and iterative and compute-matched findings. Table 8 reports downstream averages of 53.78 for SPARKLING, 53.39 for training from scratch, and 52.00 for naive expansion. Figure 14 reports a 0.0306 dense-model loss advantage at matched compute. These are additional comparisons, not improvements over v1 under changed settings.

M1.justification: Both versions use RMS-preserving rescaling, copy initialization, asymmetric optimizer-state reset, and asymmetric learning-rate re-warmup. v2 applies the same components to dense models and successive expansions. Its explicit RMSNorm initialization default clarifies implementation rather than establishing an algorithm change.

P1.justification: The six main sections and much of the original prose remain intact. v2 makes local language and terminology corrections, clarifies baseline names and defaults, expands Section 5 into five subsections, and reorganizes the appendices. Author information, citation style, acknowledgements, and an impact statement also change.

P2.justification: The single-column branded report becomes a two-column conference-format main text with different typography, headers, captions, and float placement. Retained figures are restyled or relocated, and configuration tables are arranged side by side. Three new tables and seven new figures display the added ablations, comparisons, and scaling analyses.

R1.justification: The distinct cited works are retained after matching publication updates and the consolidated OLMoE references. Sections 5.2 and Appendices K-L extend the positioning through explicit superiority claims over the dynamics-based approaches of Shen et al., Wang et al., and Yuan et al., previously discussed without these direct comparisons.

T1.justification: The RMS-preservation derivations, gradient-symmetry analysis, optimizer argument, scheduling equations, and Appendix A assumptions and derivations are mathematically retained. The added post-normalization, scaling, and iterative-expansion discussions provide qualitative arguments rather than new formal proofs or substantive revisions to the existing mathematics.

improvement.justification: The new component ablation and evaluated dynamics-based comparators address important gaps in evidence for combining RMS preservation with asymmetric optimization. Dense and iterative experiments strengthen applicability, while matched-FLOP comparisons complement v1's fixed-token efficiency argument. Together these substantially improve support for the central contribution. The new scaling-exponent interpretation exceeds what the plotted comparisons establish, and uncertainty reporting remains absent, but these limitations do not outweigh the stronger controlled empirical evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SPARKLING study. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting and appendix reordering.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds component ablations, prior-method comparisons, dense-model experiments, iterative expansion, and compute-matched analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original MoE training experiments, downstream evaluations, computational measurements, and ablations in Sections 3-5 and the appendices.

results.title: SPARKLING: Balancing Signal Preservation and Symmetry Breaking for Width-Progressive Learning

C1.justification: The framework, benchmark, and library-expansion contributions remain. However, the abstract, introduction, and conclusion narrow claims that the audit confirms hallucination minimization and that upstreaming validates general practical utility. V2 instead claims evidence for many valid residuals and selected curated outputs, presenting the work as a step toward AI-assisted library expansion.

C2.justification: V2 substantially qualifies the interpretation of the audits and library utility: solvability extrapolation becomes diagnostic, and human success is distinguished from closed-book model performance. It adds generation-model dependence, fixed-snapshot limitations, maintainer burden, and substantive curation requirements. Existing novelty and semantic-drift limitations are expanded, while claims about architecture-independent reasoning distillation are withdrawn.

D1.justification: V1 already provides detailed prompts and runtime settings. V2 adds proof-screen implementation rules, repository configuration and version-pinning information, approximate API costs, and precise PR identifiers, merge commits, file locations, and code for the three merged examples. These improve traceability without replacing the existing implementation documentation.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the 4,028-statement Mathlib folklore benchmark derived from 109 seed files across Foundational, Applied, and Abstract mathematics. The additional audits, sampling experiment, and prompt pilot do not establish new mathematical domains or task coverage.

E2.justification: The seven models in the main comparison remain unchanged. V2 additionally evaluates Goedel-Prover-V2-8B in Appendix C.3/Table 4; v1 evaluates the 32B variant only. The new 8B experiment is explicitly separate from the main Success@2 comparison.

E3.justification: V2 changes the success criterion by requiring proof-bypass screening. It adds 16 independent attempts without repair feedback for the 8B prover, a held-out audit sampling up to 20 residuals from each of five seeds, and two 160-candidate prompt conditions. The rejected-candidate audit is redescribed as seed-stratified. Initial generation plus two repairs was already defined in v1 Appendix C, so the clarified pseudocode does not establish a larger repair budget.

E4.justification: V2 adds a held-out audit testing whether residual provability generalizes beyond the original audit sample, and Appendix F tests whether explicitly requesting necessary hypotheses reduces missing-hypothesis failures. Appendix D also substantially revises the existing 31-case failure analysis from four categories to three. These extend the investigation of benchmark validity and generation failures.

E5.justification: V1 reports audit proportions without uncertainty estimates. V2 Appendix D adds a Wilson 95% confidence interval of 75.3-90.1% for the held-out audit and a per-seed mean of 83.7% with sample standard deviation 4.6%. This is a localized addition; repeated-run uncertainty for the main model scores remains unreported.

E6.justification: Table 3 and Figures 3-5 contain substantially revised results: overall GPT-Reasoning success changes from 22.32% to 19.39%, union success from 44.99% to 37.39%, and released proofs from 1,812 to 1,506. These accompany stricter acceptance rules, not a demonstrated same-protocol performance decline. New results include Goedel-8B solving 13/4,028 instances, humans proving 79/94 held-out residuals, and the prompt ablation. The failure-category counts also change.

M1.justification: The four-stage pipeline remains, but v2 adds a mandatory proof-bypass screen to proof acceptance in Section 3.2.4 and Algorithm 1. It rejects incomplete-proof placeholders and model-introduced axiom, constant, or opaque declarations after stripping comments. Appendix F also tests a hypotheses-first discovery prompt without adopting it as the main pipeline.

P1.justification: V2 extensively rewrites the abstract and substantial passages in the introduction, validity discussion, result interpretation, practical-impact section, conclusion, and impact statement. It consistently replaces agent terminology with module terminology, restructures Appendix D, and adds a cost subsection and Appendices E-F. The prose revision is broad despite retaining the main section sequence.

P2.justification: The overall layout and existing figure/table designs remain recognizable. V2 updates Figure 1 labels, relabels Table 1's 'Correct' column as 'Judge-accepted', revises plot axes, model labels, and captions, and relocates existing displays. It adds Tables 4-5 and three boxed proof listings without a wholesale visual redesign.

R1.justification: V2 adds Borkar (2009) for the Gronwall example and Gao et al. (2025) for semantic alignment, and replaces the generic GPT-5 system-card citation with two GPT-5.1-specific sources. The related-work discussion and positioning against lemma synthesis, proof-search systems, and existing benchmarks remain largely unchanged.

T1.justification: V1 describes merged lemma examples informally. V2 Appendix E supplies explicit mathematical statements and Lean proofs for gronwallBound_mono, restrict_const, and centralMoment_congr_ae. These are limited additions of formal mathematical content; no general theoretical guarantee for the pipeline is added.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses a central weakness in v1's error-only proof acceptance by screening incomplete proofs and introduced assumptions, with correspondingly revised results. The held-out audit, explicit merged proofs, and substantially better-qualified validity and utility claims strengthen the paper's credibility. Lower reported scores and a smaller proof library reflect stricter validation rather than poorer paper quality. Remaining limitations are more transparently acknowledged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MathlibLemma framework and benchmark. All pages, figures, tables, algorithms, and appendices are readable, including Appendices A-D in v1 and A-F in v2, supporting a reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical evaluations with revised results and adds a small-model Pass@16 evaluation, a held-out human audit, and a discovery-prompt ablation.

P1.justification: Editing is concentrated in the opening framing, related work, renamed memory section, component-specific ablation discussion, and cost discussion. Appendices are reorganized to accommodate additions, but the main section sequence and extensive method, prompt, and code passages remain stable.

P2.justification: v3 reorganizes separate component, search, and appendix sensitivity plots into a four-panel main ablation figure, and adds corresponding four-panel Medium/High figures. It adds the Claude comparison table and expands the cost table with budget-labelled columns. Existing overview, trajectory, reward, and originality displays are retained or relocated.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially expands positioning across automated research, budget-aware tool use, and agent memory. New citations include AI Scientist, PiFlow, Agent Laboratory, DeepScientist, and ExpeL. It adds specific distinctions between integrated MCTS rewards and external budget mechanisms, and between code-level reflection and high-level trajectory comparisons.

T1.justification: The problem definitions, optimization objectives, reward normalization, UCT expression, and update equations remain unchanged, including Equations 1–8. No new theorem, proof, formal assumption, or mathematical derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens evidence for the central architectural claims: the comparative-memory control isolates a previously untested component, harder-task and Claude experiments test generality, and the four-hour comparison addresses whether gains require higher spending. Explicit limitations improve calibration. The lesson audit still does not establish causal proof, and Section 5.2 retains an obsolete highest-Gold claim for standard MARS, but these reporting weaknesses do not outweigh the stronger experimental support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MARS framework. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v3 retains original experiments and adds comparative-memory controls, harder-task ablations, Claude evaluations, lesson audits, and reduced-budget results.

before.justification: v1 reports original MLE-Bench evaluations, component ablations, search analyses, lesson-utilization measurements, and computational costs.

results.title: MARS: Modular Agent with Reflective Search for Automated AI Research

C1.justification: The introduction explicitly elevates GAR to a contribution and reframes the theoretical contribution around nested training and near-optimal rank selection. The central train-once deployment and accuracy–cost claims in the abstract and conclusion remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations of knowledge transfer across budgets, clarifies the ranking-preservation interpretation already mentioned in v1 Appendix C.2, and discusses factorization memory/training overhead and compute-bound inference conditions. Existing limitations concerning data, optimization, and unevaluated adaptive routing remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-availability link, detailed pipeline and DP pseudocode, explicit GAR use across rank-based baselines, and RTX5090/torch.compile timing details. Conversely, v1 Appendix D.4's specific A100 node counts and training-duration estimates disappear. Core hyperparameter recipes remain.

E1.justification: The synthetic/MNIST, FineWebEdu, commonsense, ImageNet1K, and math/code training and evaluation coverage is retained. The added experiments examine rank-selection reliability and execution efficiency of existing operations rather than introducing new datasets or application tasks.

E2.justification: v2 Figure 5 adds LLM-PRUNER, LAYERSKIP, and independently trained FlexRank configurations to the Llama-3.2-1B comparison. This substantially broadens the evaluated comparators beyond the retained SVD/DataSVD/ACIP comparisons. v1's independent-model controls concerned different experiments.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include ten independently trained models receiving 10% each of the total training budget, exact-budget rank-selection diagnostics, and GPU forward-pass timing across active ranks. The existing NLP/CV training recipes and downstream zero-/few-shot settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New Appendix C.3/Figure 9 tests additive-probe ranking agreement, exact-budget selection success, and regret on failures. Figure 5 adds a matched-budget weight-sharing control, while Appendix D.4/Figure 10 tests practical GAR efficiency. The earlier GPT-2 ablations are retained.

E5.justification: Table 1 retains the same uncertainty values. v2 adds no reported seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Its new correlations, violation rates, and regret distributions are diagnostic evaluation results rather than changes to uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v2 adds comparison and runtime results in Figures 5 and 10. Figure 9 reports Spearman correlation 0.991, pairwise violations 3.70%, exact-budget matches 94.1%, and maximum relative regret 11.58%. Table 1's existing math/code results are unchanged.

M1.justification: The DataSVD initialization, nested DP rank selection, and distillation procedure are retained. GAR names and elaborates the identity-block inference reparametrization already described in v1 Section 3.5. Algorithms 1–3 add procedural documentation rather than establish a new method.

P1.justification: The introduction is condensed, contributions and method-stage descriptions are rewritten, Section 7 gains topical subsections, and an appendix contents page is added. Most section ordering, exposition, and proof text remain; the editing does not amount to a wholesale narrative restructuring.

P2.justification: v1 Figures 4–5 are merged into v2 Figure 4. New Figures 5, 9, and 10 and three algorithm displays substantially expand the presentation; other plots are redrawn, heatmaps relabeled, and tables relocated. Figure 4 incorrectly labels its retained relative parameter scale as absolute.

R1.justification: v2 adds LLM-PRUNER and concurrent work by Rauba and van der Schaar, explaining distinctions in decomposition, selection, and GAR. It removes the SPDY reference and revises its novelty positioning toward theoretical foundations. The updated Genzel reference describes the same ACIP work.

T1.justification: The main theorems and Appendix B proofs are retained. Section 3.5 corrects the gauge identity from (UG)(VG^-1)^T to (UG)(G^-1V^T), and Section 2.1 removes the expectation from the budget constraint. Appendix C.1 also introduces an apparent self-referential residual-definition typo.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for central rank-selection and deployment claims through direct ranking diagnostics, measured GPU efficiency, broader baselines, and matched-budget controls. Detailed pseudocode and code-access information also improve reproducibility. These gains outweigh the removal of training-resource estimates and the introduced labeling/notation errors, although the new validation remains limited to its reported settings.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe FlexRank and contain readable main text, figures, tables, equations, and Appendices A–D. The material supports a reliable comparison across the revision.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, rank-selection diagnostics, and GPU runtime measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic and MNIST experiments, language-model and vision evaluations, downstream adaptation results, and ablations.

results.title: FlexRank: Nested Low-Rank Knowledge Decomposition for Adaptive Model Deployment

C1.justification: The core claims remain: expected-reward RL is a first-order likelihood approximation, MaxRL interpolates toward maximum likelihood with compute, and experiments show better scaling and up to approximately 20× inference efficiency over GRPO. The abstract's one-line implementation emphasis was already stated in v1.

C2.justification: v2 qualifies baseline variance reduction as empirical rather than guaranteed, discusses collapse at small rollout/batch budgets, and interprets new solvability/perplexity evidence as capability expansion under finite compute. It also discusses nonnegative-reward applicability while leaving broader theory open. These substantially extend v1's interpretations of scaling, overfitting and prompt difficulty.

D1.justification: v2 supplements the existing project link with explicit code/script and pretrained-maze-checkpoint access instructions, maps the retained maze budgets to particular results, and documents new comparator and analysis recipes. It corrects the Qwen tokenizer description and aligns the GSM8K test-table label with the already stated Platinum dataset. Most original training and hardware details remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Appendix M.4 adds a maze scenario rewarding shorter trajectories with continuous rewards, extending the task beyond binary success. Existing datasets and mathematical benchmarks remain covered. GSM8K-Platinum and the four additional Qwen3 benchmarks were already used in v1.

E2.justification: Appendix L adds evaluated ZPD-style prompt weighting and Power Function weighting across ImageNet, maze, GSM8K and Qwen3 settings. PKPO, previously compared on maze and GSM8K, is newly compared against Qwen3-4B MaxRL with T=4, 8 and 16. The maze summary also drops RLOO and tabulates SELF, which was already plotted in v1.

E3.justification: New protocols include a controlled GSM8K rollout sweep, gradient-noise sampling designs, AIME trajectory/perplexity comparisons, and continuous-reward maze training with a 16M model, batch size 256, 16 rollouts and Mean/Best@32 metrics. Existing maze budgets are clarified rather than newly introduced. The reported Qwen prompt/tokenizer specification is corrected, without establishing that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds GSM8K rollout sensitivity and per-prompt distribution analyses, baseline-on/off gradient-variance tests, inverse-SNR analysis, and AIME per-problem solvability and perplexity studies. These test compute sensitivity, estimator stability and capability expansion. Earlier gradient-norm, training-dynamics and nonzero-success analyses are retained under reorganized appendices.

E5.justification: Appendix M.2 newly specifies covariance estimation from four sampled minibatches and inverse-SNR estimation using 64 gradient samples; Figure 30 adds trajectory-level perplexity distributions. These are localized statistical additions, not evidence of increased independent training runs. Neither version reports seed-level uncertainty for the main benchmark comparisons.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive baseline, sensitivity, variance and continuous-reward results. Table 10 newly reports 27/30 AIME problems solved by MaxRL versus 23/30 for both base and GRPO, with three exclusively solved problems. Retained maze Table 3 changes GRPO pass@1 from 43.6 to 39.6 and MaxRL pass@128 from 92.0 to 94.0; these are reporting changes, not demonstrated same-setting training gains. Main Qwen3 and majority-voting results remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The binary-reward objective family and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged. Appendix M.4 adds a limited extension to nonnegative rewards with positive expectation, optimizing log expected reward using mean-normalized advantages. The new N−1 characterization analyzes the existing estimator rather than changing its procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract and preliminaries are rewritten, main-text related work is streamlined, and appendices are substantially reorganized around individual experimental settings. A contents page, consolidated pass@k explanations and grouped Qwen3 results improve navigation. This is a substantial structural revision beyond simply adding scientific content.

P2.justification: Main-text comparison tables move to full-width appendix displays and gain pass@16 columns; the maze comparison plot gains a pass@16 panel. Numerous new baseline plots, distribution histograms, variance/SNR plots, a solvability table and a perplexity boxplot are added. Existing figures are also resized, relocated and regrouped.

R1.justification: Appendix B adds substantive relationships to Monte Carlo EM, forward-KL reward/advantage-weighted regression, success conditioning and PopArt, plus expanded discussion of difficulty-aware and risk-sensitive RL. This materially broadens research positioning beyond the relocation of existing related-work paragraphs and publication-metadata updates.

T1.justification: New Appendix D proves that Algorithm 1's dropped-baseline estimator targets truncation order N−1, distinguishing it from the retained order-N theorem for Equation 9. This substantially closes the theory-to-implementation gap. v2 also formulates the nonnegative-reward extension and corrects mathematical expressions, including the ImageNet policy-gradient loss sign and RLOO advantage.

improvement.justification: v2 resolves an important theoretical omission by proving the practical estimator's N−1 objective and supplies empirical checks for previously asserted variance reduction. Broader relevant baselines and targeted mechanism analyses substantially strengthen validation, while clearer organization and reproducibility details improve usability. Some inconsistencies remain, notably the binary-only conclusion alongside Appendix M.4, but they do not outweigh these substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Maximum Likelihood Reinforcement Learning (MaxRL). Their text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable, and retained content can be matched despite substantial appendix reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds baseline comparisons, gradient-variance analyses, capability analyses and a continuous-reward maze experiment.

before.justification: v1 reports original ImageNet, maze-navigation, GSM8K and Qwen3 mathematical-reasoning experiments, including additional benchmark results and training analyses in its appendices.

results.title: Maximum Likelihood Reinforcement Learning

C1.justification: The abstract and four headline contributions retain their scope. Section 6 adds more specific conclusions that selected vectors directly influence party-token generation and that forecasting gains are not explained by access to external party-position data alone, strengthening the attribution of the retained central claim.

C2.justification: v2 adds mechanism interpretations from the intervention and ICL controls, qualifies the layer range as a tunable default, notes uncertainty about sufficient prompt variation, and discusses multiclass probing as an untested extension. Its impact statement replaces generic language with specific profiling, political micro-targeting and bias concerns. The overall complementary-to-surveys interpretation remains unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 substantially improves documentation through persona-template construction and translation details, native-speaker verification, and multilingual probe prompts showing statement, answer, comment and shuffled party-list inputs (Table 3). It also documents new experimental settings and adds a concrete GitHub link with stated access to templates and harmonized data; v1 only says the code is available on GitHub.

E1.justification: The six election datasets, languages and persona attributes remain unchanged. v2 adds a distinct evaluation scenario using 1,280 persona-question pairs with non-political questions, such as choosing ice cream, while measuring party-token responses (Appendix B.5).

E2.justification: v2 retains the probability-based comparator and adds label-shuffled and random-weight probes, hard-label and soft-target regression baselines (Figure 6), no-scaling and matched random-vector controls (Figure 9), and ICL and random forecasting baselines (Figure 10). These substantially broaden the evaluated comparisons.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce alternative layer-window evaluations, a selectivity-gap metric, matched intervention conditions on identical prompts, and ICL contexts containing one example per party. Figure 6 specifies 4,000 training epochs and a 10% hold-out split for its comparisons. These are additional protocols; the existing forecasting settings and distance metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds substantial validation of probe specificity, sensitivity to layer-window selection, and targeted versus random interventions in non-political contexts (Appendices B.2 and B.5). It also reports inconsistent intervention effects without sign-inversion gating and tests whether supplying party-position information through ICL explains the forecasting advantage (B.6).

E5.justification: v2 adds significance markers to Figures 3 and 5, seeds 0-9 and standard deviations across configurations in Figure 6, permutation tests, one-sided sign-flip tests for layer selectivity, and paired t-tests for interventions. This substantially expands statistical reporting, without establishing increased runs for retained experiments. The tests underlying the new markers in Figures 3 and 5 are not identified.

E6.justification: v2 adds probe-control scores, layer-selectivity results, targeted intervention effects and ICL/random forecasting errors. Figure 6 reports approximately 0.99 macro-F1 for the probe, 0.33 for shuffled labels, 0.24 for random weights and 0.93 for hard-label regression. Soft-target regression is about 0.30, inconsistent with Section 5.1's general regression summary. The retained forecasting plots preserve their estimates.

M1.justification: The forecasting procedure remains unchanged: binary probes, the 0.5L-0.9L layer range, 2.5-IQR vector selection, sign-inversion filtering, activation aggregation and entropy gating are retained. The additional interventions validate existing components; the suggested multiclass head remains future work.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section order are retained. v2 makes targeted explanatory expansions, organizes Appendix B into six subsections, rewrites the impact statement, and updates heading capitalization, author order, affiliations and publication information. The expansion largely reflects added scientific content rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: v2 adds the probe-template Table 3 and four substantive displays: Figures 6, 7, 9 and 10. Figures 3 and 5 gain significance annotations, with Figure 3's horizontal scale extended to accommodate them. The original appendix Figures 6-7 and Table 3 are retained as Figures 8 and 11 and Table 4.

R1.justification: Section 3 newly credits the prompt-template structure to von der Heyde et al. and positions ten prompt variants as exceeding those used in cited comparable studies. The broader related-work argument remains stable. Publication updates, changed author/title metadata and removal of a duplicate reference do not establish new cited works.

T1.justification: Figure 7 introduces the selectivity-gap definition, Delta_sel = MacroF1_real - MacroF1_shuffle, for the new layer-window analysis. The forecasting mathematics, assumptions and Equations 1-17 remain unchanged; no new theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation that v1 lacked: probe controls, layer sensitivity, matched interventions and an information-supplying ICL comparator make the mechanistic explanation more assessable. Prompt documentation and a concrete code link also improve reproducibility. The gains outweigh reporting weaknesses, including the Figure 6 regression-summary discrepancy and underdocumented significance markers. The claim that external data cannot explain the advantage remains stronger than the one-example-per-party ICL comparison establishes.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same mechanistic forecasting study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and Appendices A-C support comparison, including matching retained material across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds probe comparisons, layer-window experiments, non-political interventions and in-context learning comparisons.

before.justification: v1 reports original probe performance and preference-estimation experiments across seven models and six national elections, including party, persona-attribute and entropy analyses.

results.title: Reading Between the Tokens: Improving Preference Predictions through Mechanistic Forecasting

C1.justification: The central claims remain that SSL ingredients can be mixed productively, unlabeled shifted data improves robustness, and Self-Seasoning learns mixtures without training labels. The abstract retains the +3.5%/+7% robustness claims; adding LeJEPA extends the supporting demonstration without redefining these contributions.

C2.justification: v2 interprets comparable Ratatouille accuracy as a practical advantage because Self-Soups avoid auxiliary labels. It also identifies a specific use case where seasoning outperforms fine-tuning: natural VTAB tasks with fewer than 500 training samples. The limitations paragraph remains unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 documents LeJEPA's lambda=0.02 and the revised few-shot search grids, batch-size rule, and held-out selection. It omits v1's explicit zero initialization and softmax parameterization of mixture weights. The entropy code and code/data access links are retained; repeating the code link in the abstract does not establish new availability.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same ImageNet evaluation variants, LAION-C, and 21 VTAB tasks with their corruption variants. Ratatouille uses four already represented VTAB datasets; the additional sample counts and augmentation configurations change protocols within retained coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds logit ensembles to the ImageNet comparisons, continued-SSL soups trained on the corresponding corruptions to Table 2, and an evaluated Ratatouille baseline in Table 5. The few-shot comparison adds full fine-tuning, replaces random-search seasoning with gradient-based labeled seasoning, and removes the best-ingredient comparator; stock and uniform-soup results remain in Appendix Table 9.

E3.justification: ImageNet experiments expand from three SSL algorithms to four with LeJEPA, and Section 4.1 evaluates 64 mixtures instead of 52. The revised few-shot study varies training size from 25 to 1,000, matches six-configuration tuning budgets, tunes Self-Seasoning's k and temperature, and reports held-out selection. Appendix A adds RandAugment and a doubled ingredient pool combining augmentation schemes.

E4.justification: New Appendix Tables 6–7 examine sensitivity to augmentation choice and increased ingredient diversity. Figure 4 and Table 9 add training-sample sensitivity analyses comparing seasoning with full fine-tuning across VTAB domains. The existing corruption evaluations and Franca connectivity analysis are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports seed-based repetitions, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The six runs per method in v2 are different hyperparameter configurations, rather than repeated runs for uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Figure 2 and Table 1 report revised results with four SSL ingredient types: uniform Self-Soup accuracy changes from 32.23/22.40 to 32.34/22.92 on IN-C/LAION-C under the changed configuration. v2 adds shifted-data comparator scores, Ratatouille results, augmentation results, and extensive few-shot results with revised mixture coefficients. Table 4 and the Franca curves retain their earlier results.

M1.justification: The supervised mixing option changes from v1's Instant Seasoning, which samples mixture weights and selects by labeled kNN accuracy, to cross-entropy-trained labeled seasoning in v2 Section 4.6. The central Self-Soup construction and entropy-based Self-Seasoning procedure remain unchanged.

P1.justification: Local revisions consolidate the seasoning explanation, rewrite the few-shot section, give the retained Franca analysis its own subsection, and reorganize the appendices. Most introductory and discussion prose is retained. Several stale references are introduced, including Table 7 references associated with Table 1 results and a Table 4 reference for the few-shot finding.

P2.justification: Figure 2 changes from triangular three-ingredient plots to square four-ingredient heatmaps. v2 adds few-shot curves, a Ratatouille table, augmentation tables, and comparator rows in existing tables. The seasoning presentation is reorganized into Figure 4 and Appendix Tables 8–9; the Franca figure is retained and renumbered.

R1.justification: v2 adds the LeJEPA citation and incorporates it as an SSL ingredient. The new Ratatouille experiment strengthens the existing positioning against supervised inter-training, while the related-work discussion otherwise remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The linear mode connectivity definition and Self-Soup equation are unchanged. New Equation 3 expresses the neighbor-entropy objective already described and implemented in v1 Appendix D; it adds mathematical exposition without a new derivation, assumption, or proof.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important comparison gaps: Table 2 adds baselines trained on the same corruptions, Table 5 directly evaluates Ratatouille, and the revised few-shot study compares seasoning with full fine-tuning under matched tuning budgets. Together with augmentation checks, these substantially strengthen evidence for the method's advantages and applicability. Stale cross-references and some lost initialization detail reduce clarity but do not outweigh these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Self-Soupervision research. Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, figures, and tables are readable and support comparison across the revised organization.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and reports additional ensemble, Ratatouille, augmentation, and few-shot comparisons in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original ImageNet robustness, VTAB transfer, Self-Seasoning, and Franca experiments, including quantitative results in Tables 1–5.

results.title: Self-Soupervision: Cooking Model Soups without Labels

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution statement, and conclusion retain the same central claims: geometry-matched GNS metrics, distributed variance estimation, and adaptive batching that preserves validation quality while reducing optimizer steps. The headline approximately 66% reduction remains unchanged.

C2.justification: Section 5.2 qualifies benefits from all optimizers to most, and Appendix D.2 identifies the CIFAR-10 MSGD exception. Appendix E explains nuclear-GNS overhead and identifies remaining implementation optimizations. However, D.2 retains a now-stale claim that Muon gives the largest step reduction: Table 11 reports 72.14% for signSGD versus 68.16% for Muon.

D1.justification: Appendix E substantially expands implementation documentation with layerwise FSDP pseudocode, explicit distributed collectives, gradient reconstruction, buffer requirements, and cost breakdowns. It also specifies profiling hardware, local batch sizes, measurement frequency, and averaging duration. These disclosures make the existing estimators substantially easier to implement and assess.

E1.justification: Both versions use C4 language modeling with 160M and 1B Llama 3 models, Imagewoof classification with SimpleViT, and CIFAR-10 classification with ResNet-18. The added sensitivity and timing experiments reuse this coverage.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds Euclidean-GNS comparisons for Signum, AdamW, specSGD, and Muon, substantially extending the direct comparison central to the geometry claim. The signSGD Euclidean comparison already existed in v1 Table 9. Table 4 additionally evaluates NormalizedSGD.

E3.justification: The CIFAR-10 step-reduction reference changes from batch 512 to 256, and Table 7 expands tolerance, learning-rate, and momentum searches and revises initial-batch settings. Imagewoof gains a batch-512 control. Appendix E introduces timing experiments with specified local batches and 1,000-step measurements. These are substantive reported protocol changes and additions.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained initial-batch, learning-rate-scaling, and seed analyses, v2 adds a tolerance-sensitivity study at theta values 0.5, 0.6, and 0.7 in Table 10. New Appendix E investigates estimator overhead at two model scales and analyzes compute, communication, and memory costs, substantially expanding practical-efficiency analysis.

E5.justification: v2 replaces point estimates with plus/minus summaries and specifies 10 seeds for the 1B results and 5 seeds for CIFAR-10. Imagewoof results first specify 5 seeds; the 160M experiments already reported 10 seeds. Earlier unspecified run counts prevent inferring an actual increase in runs.

E6.justification: v2 retains the principal 160M non-Euclidean results but adds Euclidean entries and revises the 1B and vision results. For example, Table 3 replaces signSGD's adaptive loss of 2.8411 with 2.9946 ± 0.0201. New timing results report 0.2–0.3% overhead for l1 GNS and 13.9–39.9% for nuclear GNS. Revised CIFAR-10 percentages use different reference batches and tuning, so they are not same-setting performance changes.

M1.justification: The GNS definitions, variance estimators, and Algorithm 1 retain the same adaptive-batching procedure, including moving averages, monotonic batch growth, and square-root learning-rate scaling. New Algorithms 2–3 document distributed implementations of the existing estimators.

P1.justification: v2 tightens introductory paragraphs, adds conflict-of-interest and impact statements, updates acknowledgements and bibliographic text, and appends the computational-cost section. The main narrative and section sequence remain largely intact; the added scientific material does not constitute extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: Several comparison tables gain columns or rows, and Tables 3–4 become full-width displays. v2 adds sensitivity, latency, and complexity tables plus two FSDP algorithm panels. Figure 1 has revised axis limits and geometric illustrations, while Figure 3 is relocated. These substantially expand and reorganize the evidence displays.

R1.justification: v2 adds Ahn et al.'s Dion paper as the source for distributed-collective notation in Appendix E. Most other reference changes update publication metadata or correct attribution for existing works, including Mann/Brown, without changing the central research positioning.

T1.justification: Theorems A.4–A.5 add O(1/K) bounds on averaged squared dual-gradient norms under gradient-scaled learning rates without requiring strong convexity, with corresponding proof extensions. Appendix B corrects the second derivative and inflection-point multiplier from 64/9 to 16/9. Appendix E adds complexity bounds. However, the revised A.4 telescoping line drops an expectation and incorrectly factors the quadratic penalty.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for the central geometry claim through broader Euclidean-GNS comparisons and improves empirical transparency through multi-seed reporting. Appendix E addresses previously unquantified implementation costs with measurements and detailed pseudocode, exposing meaningful nuclear-GNS overhead. The corrected CBS derivation also improves accuracy. These gains outweigh the localized new proof-editing error and stale CIFAR-10 commentary, although the timing measurements do not establish end-to-end training speedups.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including Appendix E added in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains original training results and reports additional comparisons, tolerance-sensitivity results, and measured GNS-estimation overhead.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix D report original language-model and image-classification experiments, including validation performance and optimizer-step reductions.

results.title: Adaptive Batch Sizes Using Non-Euclidean Gradient Noise Scales for Stochastic Sign and Spectral Descent

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions, and conclusion retain the same scientific claims about proactive clarification, curated supervision, sample-efficient fine-tuning, and improved CAD generation. The new evaluations support these claims without redefining their central scope.

C2.justification: v2 newly identifies missed simultaneous ambiguities and occasional incorrect incorporation of answers as ProCAD limitations. It interprets policy experiments as showing harmful under-clarification and diminishing returns from forced extra rounds, and adds arguments about human transfer and judge reliability. Section 3 also removes the speculative claim that decomposition mitigates reward hacking.

D1.justification: The abstract changes code and datasets from a promised future release to reported public availability. This is an access-status disclosure, although availability cannot be independently verified from the PDFs. Existing hardware, hyperparameters, training times, and full system prompts are retained; the prompt appendix changes from J to L.

E1.justification: Section 6.4 extends evaluation from LLM-simulated interaction to human-authored ambiguous prompts and human answers, using 100 examples from the existing CAD dataset. This introduces a substantively different interaction environment, while retaining the underlying geometry domain and original datasets.

E2.justification: Appendix K adds Claude Sonnet 4.5 variants using one-question-per-round, forced-follow-up, and single-question policies, evaluated alongside ProCAD and the existing all-at-once approach. The original model baseline sets remain unchanged; the human evaluation reuses Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, GPT-4o-mini, and Claude Sonnet 4.5.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include CAD-expert scoring of human interactions, a separate 100-example comparison of human and LLM judgments, and controlled policy experiments holding the clarifier and coder fixed. Appendix K introduces measured end-to-end latency and per-round ambiguity resolution. Existing training budgets, splits, and benchmark protocols are retained.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained qualitative examples, v2 adds systematic analysis of ProCAD's failures in Appendix J, controlled interaction-policy and round-level ablations in Appendix K, and human validation of automatic scoring in Section 6.4. These directly examine remaining errors, evaluation reliability, and the justification for batching clarification questions.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed/run counts, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The new human-agreement and failure percentages add point results, without introducing uncertainty estimation or repeated-run reporting.

E6.justification: Existing result tables retain their numerical values. New Table 6 reports mean CD multiplied by 10^3 of 1.28 for ProCAD versus 9.72 for Claude Sonnet 4.5 under the same human-evaluation setting and fixed ProCAD-coder; both have 12.2% invalidity. Tables 11–12 add policy-quality, latency, and round-level results. Appendix J adds failure statistics, and Section 6.4 reports over 96% human–LLM judgment agreement.

M1.justification: The two Qwen2.5-7B agents, data-construction pipeline, SFT objectives, and accept-or-batch-clarify procedure remain unchanged. Appendix K evaluates alternative interaction policies without changing the proposed ProCAD procedure.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and section ordering are retained. Changes include localized wording corrections, Section 6.4, new Appendices J–K, updated appendix navigation, and acknowledgments and impact statements. These are targeted insertions and edits rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column conference layout for the main text and references, with changed typography, running headers, and widespread resizing and repositioning of displays. It adds Tables 6, 11, and 12. The four existing figures retain their substantive content, while the original appendix tables are renumbered.

R1.justification: Appendix A adds Zhao et al. (2021a, 2021b, 2024), while Amodei et al. (2016) is removed with the reward-hacking discussion. The broader positioning remains intact. PR-CAD's updated authorship and date refer to the same previously cited work.

T1.justification: The MDP formulation, action space, reward, SFT objectives, and assumptions supporting the two-round policy remain unchanged. The added policy experiments provide empirical evidence rather than new mathematical derivations, assumptions, or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for the paper's central interaction claims. Section 6.4 addresses v1's reliance on simulated users through human-authored prompts, human answers, expert ratings, and validation of LLM judging. Appendices J–K expose ProCAD's own failure conditions and test the quality–latency rationale for its interaction policy. The human study remains limited to 100 source examples, and uncertainty and annotator reporting remain sparse, but the added validation and critical analysis materially improve the paper's credibility.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ProCAD study. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and can be matched despite substantial reformatting and appendix renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds human-interaction experiments, human validation of automatic judging, failure analysis, and interaction-policy ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original dataset evaluations, coding-agent experiments, and simulated clarification experiments in Sections 6.1–6.3 and Tables 1–5, with additional analyses in the appendices.

results.title: Clarify Before You Draw: Proactive Agents for Robust Text-to-CAD Generation

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the same contributions: comparative signals as control variates, an efficient asymptotically normal estimator, semantic regression for small samples, and validation on three benchmarks. The conclusion retains the proposed extensions to other auxiliary signals and metrics; its new applicability qualification is assessed under C2.

C2.justification: Remark 5.1 newly acknowledges finite-sample degradation with weak auxiliary signals and distinguishes variance reduction from pointwise dominance. The conclusion clarifies that precise estimation cannot repair benchmark invalidity. Section 5.3 also interprets the new checks as evidence against dependence on a particular auxiliary pipeline, subset, or rubric.

D1.justification: V2 provides a code-repository link and extensive implementation information unavailable in v1: a 32,768-token target limit, auxiliary limits of 8,192 or 2,048 tokens, explicit semantic-regression pseudocode, generation/judging/regression prompts, and a data example. These are newly documented details, not evidence that the original settings changed.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same Gaussian simulation setting and GPQA Diamond, AIME 2025, and GSM8K tasks. The added auxiliary-model, prompt, subset, and decoding experiments change procedures within this coverage, not the represented domains or tasks.

E2.justification: V2 adds a repeated-Y baseline using 12 target responses for five GPQA Diamond target models in Table 6. The naive estimator and simulation Oracle comparator remain. Alternative auxiliary models are configurations of the proposed approach, not additional competing estimators.

E3.justification: New Section 5.3 substantially expands evaluation design: an alternative GPT-5 mini/QwQ-32B auxiliary configuration, another AIME subset, an N=25 subset, and a correctness-only judging rubric. It also compares one response plus 11 comparisons against 12 target responses. Original Tables 1–3 retain their settings; newly disclosed appendix details do not establish reruns.

E4.justification: Tables 4, 5, 7, and 8 add explicit checks of sensitivity to auxiliary-model choice, subset selection, subset size, and judging criteria. Appendices B and C additionally make noise-sensitivity and sample-size analyses inspectable; v1 mentioned these analyses but omitted their referenced appendices.

E5.justification: V2 reports an additional AIME subset selected with a different random seed in Table 5, without identifying the seed value. The simulation's 100 independent trials are unchanged. Neither version reports empirical confidence intervals, standard errors, or significance tests for the real-world comparisons.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 are numerically identical, and Figure 2 retains the same plot. V2 adds results for the robustness conditions and repeated-Y baseline; Tables 1 and 6 support its finding that one-step estimates are closer to the reference accuracy in four of five models under both configurations. Figures 3–5 and Tables 9–11 supply additional supplementary results, not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The EIF, cross-fitted one-step estimator, and Monte Carlo correction in Algorithm 1 remain unchanged. V1 already describes using a fixed LLM semantic regressor without cross-fitting; v2's Algorithm 2 and prompting details document that variant rather than establish a new estimation procedure.

P1.justification: Most shared prose and the main section sequence remain intact. Changes include targeted clarification of the model specification and simulation indexing, wording corrections, updated cross-references, and the insertion of Section 5.3. Much of the added appendix length supplies scientific and implementation content rather than rewriting the existing narrative.

P2.justification: V2 replaces the single-column main text with a two-column conference layout and running headers, relocates Figure 1 to the opening page, and consolidates Tables 1–3 on one page. It also includes Tables 4–11, Figures 3–5, Algorithm 2, and boxed prompt templates. The original simulation graphic and table contents are retained.

R1.justification: V2 adds model-source references and a qualification about Bayesian methods' sensitivity to priors, while removing several citations, including Jin et al. 2025a/b and Xu et al. 2025. The central positioning around semiparametric efficiency remains. The Lu-to-Yan attribution update concerns the same survey and is bibliographic.

T1.justification: V2 supplies substantial mathematical material absent from the supplied v1: EIF projection, asymptotic-normality, variance-reduction, and orthogonality proofs in Appendix A, plus Gaussian derivations in Appendix B. These expand documented support rather than establish new theorem statements. Recasting Assumption 3.1 as Definition 3.1 preserves the same known-conditional-distribution model.

improvement.justification: Relative to the supplied v1, v2 resolves a substantial documentation gap by supplying referenced proofs, implementation details, and prompts, while adding targeted robustness checks and a repeated-decoding comparison. Its new limitations improve interpretation. The gains are qualified by absent real-world uncertainty intervals, a centering inconsistency in Appendix A.2, and Table 9's unsupported 18/20 improvement summary—the displayed estimates support 17/20. These issues temper the evidence but do not outweigh the substantial improvement in checkability and supporting evaluation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, and the supplied text, equations, tables, and figures are readable. However, v1 ends at the references and omits appendices it repeatedly cites; v2 includes Appendices A–D. This limits direct comparison of the earlier supplementary details.

after.justification: V2 retains those original results and reports additional robustness checks, repeated-decoding comparisons, and supplementary simulation and benchmark results.

before.justification: V1 reports original simulations in Figure 2 and evaluations of ten target models on GPQA Diamond, AIME 2025, and GSM8K in Tables 1–3.

results.title: Evaluating LLMs When They Do Not Know the Answer: Statistical Evaluation of Mathematical Reasoning via Comparative Signals

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the same contributions: combining entropic contraction with Markov exploration, controlling ULA bias, and constructing a practical importance-sampling approximation. The discussion preserves these central claims; the additional experiments provide broader supporting evidence without redefining the contribution.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly notes that bounded density ratios do not prevent finite-sample weight degeneracy, explains how an unsuitable projection family can collapse modes, and identifies practical lambda tuning as unresolved because admissible values depend on intractable expectations. It also adds interpretations of robustness to irrelevant dimensions and of BNN run-to-run variability.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-availability link and substantial implementation information for DiGS, the high-dimensional mixture, and the BNN experiment, including projection configurations, transition schedules, and evaluation procedures. Appendix E.5 supplies explicit cost formulas and identifies excluded costs. The original flow architecture, tensorized-mixture fitting details, and optional local move are retained rather than newly introduced.

E1.justification: v2 adds a four-mode mixture embedded in 200 dimensions with irrelevant Gaussian coordinates, a distinct scenario from the retained tensorized mixtures. Section 4.3 also adds synthetic Bayesian regression through a 550-parameter neural-network posterior, substantially extending evaluation beyond the previous mixture and two-dimensional geometry benchmarks.

E2.justification: DiGS is added to the existing RW, NUTS, and AIS comparisons on Dual Moons and Two Rings in Figure 5 and Table 2. The new BNN comparison evaluates MALA and DiGS against EM2C. MALA was previously mentioned as an available kernel, but was not an evaluated baseline.

E3.justification: For the existing two-dimensional benchmarks, NUTS maximum tree depth changes from 3 to 9; AIS changes from 40 temperatures and 1,000 transitions per temperature to 10 and 100, with proposal scale 2.0 instead of 1.0/0.9. RW is now described as N independent chains rather than one chain. Appendix E.5 introduces explicit evaluation-budget rules and extra iterations for lambda=1. New experiments introduce further configurations and held-out NLL evaluation. These are reported protocol changes, without independently establishing which experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix B.5 adds a focused robustness test isolating ambient dimensionality from the number of modes: four modes in 200 dimensions, assessed through a Wasserstein trajectory and final mode coverage. Existing mixing-parameter, exploration-kernel, and proposal-evolution analyses are largely retained; their relocation does not constitute new analysis.

E5.justification: The existing three-run mean ± standard deviation reporting remains. v2 additionally specifies ten runs for the BNN comparison and averages NLL over the final 20 iterations to reduce variability. This does not establish an increase in repetitions for the retained experiments.

E6.justification: v2 adds DiGS scores, the 200-dimensional results, and BNN NLL results: EM2C 0.1294 ± 0.0707, DiGS 0.2016 ± 0.0128, and MALA 0.2219 ± 0.0170. Existing AIS and NUTS results change; for example, Two Rings AIS SW2 changes from 0.65 ± 0.18 to 0.22 ± 0.18 under revised settings. Several appendix lambda=1 entries are revised or omitted. Main Table 1 and the existing two-dimensional EM2C scores remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The entropic mixture mapping and Algorithm 1 retain the same sampling, delayed weighting, resampling, and parametric projection procedure. The optional local move already appeared in v1 Appendix D.3. New kernel and Gaussian-mixture configurations instantiate existing components on additional benchmarks.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section sequence remain recognizable. v2 makes targeted explanatory rewrites, consolidates experimental details in Appendices B and C, reverses the order of two proof subsections, and moves the former implementation appendix from D to E while inserting BNN details. These are limited organizational and language changes alongside the new scientific material.

P2.justification: The main text and references change from one to two columns, with extensive resizing and relocation of figures. Gaussian-mixture tables are consolidated, resolving overlapping subtable content in v1 Table 4. Figure 5 and Table 2 gain DiGS columns; v2 adds the high-dimensional Figure 11, BNN Table 3, and budget Table 7. Several unchanged appendix figures are compressed onto shared pages.

R1.justification: Additional citations cover adaptive importance sampling and mirror descent, including Akyildiz and Míguez, Thin et al., and Bianchi et al.; baseline references include Chen et al. for DiGS, Hoffman and Gelman for NUTS, and Neal for AIS. Roberts and Tweedie is added for ULA. These expand attribution and comparison context without substantially changing the central research positioning.

T1.justification: Theorem 2 now explicitly requires 0 < gamma <= (2 C_LS L^2)^(-1), a restriction previously stated only in the supporting Proposition 3. v2 also corrects the GM25 mixture coefficient from 0.2 to 1/25. The central convergence results and appendix proofs otherwise remain substantively unchanged, with the intermediate result moved before the theorem proof.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the empirical support beyond v1's tensorized mixtures and two-dimensional targets through a 550-parameter posterior-inference comparison and a stronger DiGS baseline. The corrected theorem assumption, explicit practical limitations, code pointer, and expanded implementation details also improve precision and reproducibility. Budget matching remains approximate and excludes projection costs, so the revision strengthens the evidence without establishing equal-runtime superiority.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Entropic Mirror Monte Carlo, with matching authors, algorithm, and theoretical framework. The main text and complete appendices provide sufficient readable equations, tables, figures, and experimental details for comparison.

after.justification: The original experiments are retained, with additional results for a 200-dimensional Gaussian mixture and a 550-parameter Bayesian neural-network posterior, including comparisons against MALA and DiGS.

before.justification: Sections 4.1–4.2 and Appendices B–C report original sampling experiments on Gaussian mixtures, Dual Moons, and Two Rings, including quantitative results and proposal-evolution plots.

results.title: Entropic Mirror Monte Carlo

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the central claims: learned long-term KV importance, two-stage supervised/RL training, and stronger reasoning performance under reduced cache budgets. The additional evidence does not redefine these headline contributions.
