C2.justification: v2 explains how restricted multinomial sampling balances ranking errors against irreversible noisy evictions, interprets the new threshold and transfer results, and extends applicability discussions to larger models. Appendix A also qualifies the theoretical connection as a surrogate argument with local stability assumptions.

D1.justification: The abstract adds code-access information. Appendix E.1 newly reports training costs for DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B: approximately eight hours on two H800 GPUs for supervision and six hours on eight for RL. Appendix E.5 also explicitly identifies the main training maximum length as 32K.

E1.justification: v2 adds LongBench's long-input tasks, covering document QA, summarization, few-shot learning, synthetic tasks and code completion. Appendix E.4 also introduces science-domain training on SCP-116K followed by GPQA evaluation. These expand coverage beyond v1's retained training and evaluation tasks.

E2.justification: Matched comparisons retain their baseline membership. H2O, SnapKV and R-KV remain, while RPC, DuoAttention and G-KV were already compared in v1 Appendix E.5. The additional studies reuse existing comparison methods and reward variants.

E3.justification: New protocols include non-thinking, single-compression LongBench evaluation at a 1K budget; controlled entropy thresholds; training-length comparison at 8K versus 32K; and Qwen3-14B task evaluation plus 14B/32B diagnostic settings. The original experiments' stated settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New Appendices E.4, E.5 and E.7 test entropy-threshold sensitivity, reward choice across domains and models, transfer from shorter training sequences, and larger-model attention-loss and entropy behavior. These substantially extend v1's retained reward, input-feature, sampling and token-error analyses.

E5.justification: Section 4.1 still reports mean pass@1 over 32 independent evaluations. The added experiments introduce no new seed disclosures, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, error bars or significance-testing procedures.

E6.justification: Original matched results remain unchanged, but substantial new results appear. Table 7 reports LongBench averages of 38.95 for ForesightKV and 37.50 for SnapKV at 1K. Table 14 reports Qwen3-14B AIME2024 scores of 73.8 versus R-KV's 43.6 at 2K. Tables 10–12 and 15–16 add sensitivity, transfer and diagnostic findings.

M1.justification: v2 adds a task-specific inference adaptation: LongBench uses one compression after prefilling instead of repeated decoding-time eviction (Section 4.3). The scorer, Golden Eviction, ranking loss and GRPO remain unchanged. The sampling rewrite clarifies v1 Equation 2's negative-score rule and corrects the inconsistent description in Appendix B.2.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section sequence are largely retained. Local revisions expand the sampling explanation, reorganize Appendix A's argument, add experimental subsections and acknowledgments, and update publication and corresponding-author text.

P2.justification: The tabular presentation expands substantially with dedicated LongBench, sensitivity, length-transfer and larger-model displays in Tables 7, 10–12 and 14–16. Existing tables are redistributed and renumbered. All four figure graphics are retained, with Figure 3 relocated.

R1.justification: v2 adds the LongBench citation, Bai et al. (2024). The related-work discussion, existing references and positioning around jointly using supervised and reinforcement learning remain substantively unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix A retains Proposition A.1 but adds a substantive derivation connecting maximum future-block scores to an upper bound on cumulative evicted attention mass. New local Lipschitz assumptions connect attention perturbations to logit and token-loss changes, replacing v1's direct assertion that the single-query bound validates Golden Eviction.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for the retained method. Appendix A addresses the missing connection between the single-query bound and Golden Eviction's future-block surrogate, with explicit conditions for the loss argument. New long-input, larger-model, sensitivity and length-transfer experiments address important gaps in applicability and robustness evidence. Access and training-cost disclosures improve reproducibility. Uncertainty reporting remains limited, but the combined gains provide a clear overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ForesightKV research. Their main text, figures, tables, equations and Appendices A–E are readable and support reliable matching across additions, relocations and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds LongBench evaluations, sensitivity and length-transfer studies, and larger-model results.

before.justification: v1 reports original reasoning-benchmark evaluations, throughput measurements, reward and sampling ablations, and attention/token-error analyses.

results.title: ForesightKV: Optimizing KV Cache Eviction for Reasoning Models by Learning Long-Term Contribution

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same claims about reversible token selection, compatibility with dense and sparse attention, and improved accuracy-efficiency trade-offs, including the 3.23x headline speedup. Additional appendix evidence supports these retained contributions.

C2.justification: The new appendices explain recent-query scoring's advantage, justify the 0.5 layer-selection threshold, interpret prefill and decoding costs, and attribute the OrthoRank accuracy gap to scoring and per-head selection differences. These extend the existing interpretation. The original limitations paragraph moves unchanged from A.3 to A.7.

D1.justification: v2 specifies X-Attention settings S=16 and tau=0.9, OrthoRank pruning ratios, A6000 timing hardware, and a 128-token generation setting for the TPOT measurement. Core implementation descriptions and code/checkpoint links are unchanged. The main setup's A100-only statement is not updated to reflect the appendix hardware extension.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate RULER, InfiniteBench, LongBench, and Needle-in-a-Haystack. The additional experiments reuse existing long-context tasks and input lengths; no new dataset, domain, or task requirement is introduced.

E2.justification: v2 adds PyramidInfer to the token-eviction comparison in Table 5, evaluates SeerAttention and X-Attention with and without Token Sparse Attention in Table 12, and adds the non-eviction comparator OrthoRank in Table 13. These substantially broaden the evaluated comparator set.

E3.justification: Added protocols include equal-sized low/mid/high drift layer groups, a layer-selection threshold sweep, and full prefill latency measurements at 8K and 128K on A100 and A6000 GPUs. The new OrthoRank comparison matches prefill speedup because OrthoRank also skips FFN computation, extending evaluation beyond the existing attention-speedup comparisons.

E4.justification: Appendix A.3 adds recent-query scoring versus random-query and query-pooling alternatives, drift-group ablations on both models, and sensitivity to the layer-selection threshold (Tables 7–9). These substantially extend v1's retained drift correlation, token-coverage sweeps, overhead analysis, and dynamic-versus-fixed sparsity study.

E5.justification: Tables 10–11 newly report latency values with ± terms. Their statistical meaning and timing-run counts are unspecified, so additional repetitions cannot be inferred. The existing 200-run random layer-selection experiment remains unchanged.

E6.justification: Existing result entries in Tables 1–6 are retained, while v2 adds the PyramidInfer row and substantial results in Tables 7–13. Newly reported X-Attention comparisons give 2.72x versus 3.49x attention speedup and 83.39% versus 83.51% accuracy without/with Token Sparse Attention. Table 13 reports OrthoRank at 79.36% versus Token Sparse Attention at 87.02%, both at 1.27x prefill speedup.

M1.justification: Sections 2.2–2.4 and Algorithm 1 retain the same per-head QKV compression, output scattering and residual preservation, dynamic token coverage, and drift-based layer selection. The new scoring and layer-selection variants are experimental ablations, not revisions to the proposed method.

P1.justification: Changes include localized baseline descriptions, an Impact Statement, a proceedings footer, renaming A.2 to Additional Benchmarks, and organizing the expanded appendix into new subsections. The main narrative and section order remain largely unchanged.

P2.justification: Tables 7–13 add substantial displays for component ablations, threshold sensitivity, hardware timings, and baseline comparisons. Table 5 gains a PyramidInfer row and revised caption. Figure 7's heatmap layout is cleaned up and its erroneous latency caption is corrected; its results and Figures 1–6 are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds the OrthoRank citation and a focused architectural comparison distinguishing its hidden-state scoring and shared token set from per-head QKV selection. PyramidInfer, SeerAttention, and X-Attention were already cited in v1. The main related-work discussion otherwise remains unchanged.

T1.justification: The representation-drift definition, normalized drift rank and layer-selection rule in Equations 1–2, and coverage-selection mathematics in Algorithm 1 are unchanged. No new theorem, proof, or substantive derivation appears.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important validation gaps in v1: Tables 7–9 test key design choices, Tables 10–11 establish full prefill benefits while exposing short-context overhead, and Table 13 evaluates a relevant non-eviction competitor using matched prefill speedup. Together these substantially strengthen the method's empirical support and practical relevance. Undefined timing uncertainty and the unrevised A100-only setup statement limit reporting quality, but do not outweigh those gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Token Sparse Attention work. The complete main texts and appendices are readable, and corresponding methods, equations, figures, and tables can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds scoring and layer-selection ablations, full prefill measurements, and additional baseline comparisons in Appendices A.3–A.6.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark accuracy, attention timings, and ablations in Sections 2–3, plus LongBench and Needle-in-a-Haystack results in Appendix A.2.

results.title: Token Sparse Attention: Efficient Long-Context Inference with Interleaved Token Selection

C1.justification: The introduction strengthens the contribution statement from maintaining competitive accuracy and closing the compression gap to explicitly surpassing vanilla CoT performance. The central framework, gap-vanishing claim, throughput claim, and readability contribution remain essentially unchanged in the abstract and conclusion.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations that folded tokens provide denser reusable representations, restricted folding counts induce longer reasoning segments, and OOD results indicate compression behavior extending beyond mathematics. These extend the existing explanation of learned self-compression without replacing it or adding a substantive limitations discussion.

D1.justification: Appendices D and H document attention-map construction and the complete automated judge prompts, rubric, and output format. These support reproduction and interpretation of the new analyses. Core training hyperparameters, original synthesis/inference prompts, efficiency-test instructions, and the project repository disclosure remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Appendix B adds actual evaluations on ARC-Challenge and GPQA-Diamond for both backbones, extending coverage beyond mathematical reasoning to broader scientific and knowledge-intensive questions. The original training data and five benchmark comparisons in Table 1 are retained.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds evaluated H2O, LightThinker, and DeleThink comparisons for both backbones, including Cold-Start models using DeleThink generation. These methods previously appeared only in related work. The original comparison methods remain; Direct SFT is renamed Cold-Start in the setup.

E3.justification: v2 adds a separate DeepSeek-V3.2 judge evaluation on 1000 samples with a lenient coverage/readability rubric, peak-context and generation-length measurements, and an attention-scoring protocol. Appendix F tests 4/5/6 folding steps and 4k/6k/8k segment limits. The original training settings, Avg@32 evaluation, and 20-sample human assessment remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New analyses examine sensitivity to folding and segment-length limits, attention concentration, training dynamics of summary length and compression, and generalization under domain shift. Automated summary-quality assessment supplements the original human evaluation. The synthesis ablation and original readability case study are retained, with the latter moved to Appendix G.

E5.justification: Avg@32 sampling is retained, with no new seed information, independent-run counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The 1000 judge examples constitute a new evaluation sample, not additional repeated-run or uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Original accuracy, throughput, synthesis-ablation, and Mix-RL comparison values are retained. Substantial new results cover external baselines, OOD accuracy, peak context lengths, sensitivity, and attention dynamics. For example, Table 5 newly reports 82.5% ARC-C accuracy and 1172 peak tokens for 7B Mix-RL; Table 4 adds 15 failures among 1000 automated judgments.

M1.justification: The data synthesis procedure, summary-based context pruning, GRPO objective, three training regimes, and Appendix A generation algorithm remain unchanged. Additional folding limits are tested in ablations without changing the proposed default procedure.

P1.justification: The contribution bullets and selected related-work and synthesis passages are revised. New analysis subsections and appendices expand the structure, and the readability example moves to the appendix. Most existing prose and the overall narrative sequence remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the visual presentation with attention heatmaps, training-dynamics plots, folding-limit plots, judge-prompt panels, and new results tables. Table 1 gains comparator rows, Table 2 gains a peak-token column, and Figure 2 is redrawn with an explicit accuracy axis. The original readability example and timing plots are retained but relocated or renumbered.

R1.justification: v2 adds InftyThink, acknowledges similarity in data synthesis, and positions reinforcement learning and compression-gap elimination as distinctions. ARC and GPQA references accompany the new evaluations. The broader related-work discussion is retained; H2O, LightThinker, and DeleThink were already cited.

T1.justification: Appendix D introduces a mathematical definition of the attention heat score using head/layer averaging followed by averaging attention received from continuation tokens. This is a limited diagnostic definition; the original context definitions, optimization equations, and complexity reasoning remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical validation: external compression baselines address v1's reliance on internal training variants, while OOD tests and sensitivity/peak-context measurements directly examine generality and efficiency. These resolve important evidential gaps without changing the method or original results. The automated judge's lenient rubric provides limited evidence of strict faithfulness, and some new Table 1 difference annotations are incorrect, such as labeling 44.9 versus 52.2 a 7.5-point drop. These reporting weaknesses limit particular findings but do not outweigh the substantial validation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Accordion-Thinking work. All pages, including appendices, equations, tables, and figures, are readable and support comparison. Retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, out-of-distribution evaluations, sensitivity experiments, attention analysis, and automated summary assessment.

before.justification: v1 reports original mathematical reasoning experiments, training ablations, throughput measurements, and a human evaluation of summaries.

results.title: Accordion-Thinking: Self-Regulated Step Summaries for Efficient and Readable LLM Reasoning

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution bullets, and conclusion retain the same central claims: global geometric diagnostics inadequately predict binding, functional sensitivity provides complementary information, and objective design explains sensitivity differences. Expanded experiments and the revised encoder count strengthen the evidence without redefining these headline contributions.

C2.justification: v2 newly interprets initialization controls as evidence that training reduces functional rank and explains inter-model variation. It extends applicability to natural-image compositional evaluation within the CLIP-family scope. Appendix A.1 adds substantive cautions about off-manifold probes, the modest model sample and sparse objective families, and tasks where global geometry remains informative.

D1.justification: v2 expands checkpoint, source, and embedding-dimension documentation; newly specifies five power iterations; and adds A6000 timing comparisons in Appendix F. Appendix I resolves v1's conflicting 20-versus-100-image JER averaging descriptions in favor of 100, without establishing an actual sample-count increase. Code release remains planned in both versions.

E1.justification: v2 adds natural-image compositional evaluation on SugarCrepe: 7,511 image–caption trials covering seven addition, replacement, and swap subtypes. This substantially extends the original synthetic shape–position binding coverage. The synthetic binding and Same/Different tasks are retained.

E2.justification: Table 3 removes SimCLR and both I-JEPA entries and adds eight encoders, including MoCo v3, supervised ViT-B/L, and larger DINOv2, ConvNeXt, SigLIP, and EVA-CLIP variants. v2 also evaluates random-initialization comparators and linear CKA/Procrustes geometric comparators absent from v1.

E3.justification: Primary JER evaluation changes from Gaussian noise to ImageNet validation images, with noise retained as a control. New protocols include SugarCrepe caption ranking and scoring schemes, matched initialization comparisons, and pairwise geometry on 200 binding stimuli. Architectural controls change from parameter count to log parameter count. Section 3.1 also changes local-isotropy k from 16 to 32, although v2 Table 13 still lists 16.

E4.justification: New analyses test whether JER reflects training rather than initialization, whether its association survives natural-versus-noise inputs, and whether geometric diagnostics fail on matched noise inputs. SugarCrepe analyses control for ImageNet accuracy and architecture, while Appendix D tests inter-model shape distances. Existing readout, qualitative, and local-isotropy analyses remain.

E5.justification: v2 adds Mantel significance tests with 10,000 permutations and Spearman correlations. It removes the reported jackknife influence check in which 19/21 samples retained significance. Five-seed noise-JER means, standard deviations, confidence intervals, and regression LOO-CV remain; no increase in repeated-run counts is established.

E6.justification: Under the revised encoder suite and primary JER input domain, Table 2 replaces the JER–binding correlation of 0.65 with 0.69 and combined-predictor LOO-CV R² of 0.65 with 0.71. These are not same-setting gains; retained encoders' binding accuracies remain unchanged. Substantial new results include SugarCrepe correlation r=0.69, p=0.009, initialization calibration, shape-distance null results, noise controls, and computational costs.

M1.justification: v2 adds a null-calibrated diagnostic variant, ΔJER = JERtrained − JERnull, requiring measurements of trained and randomly initialized instances of the same architecture (Section 4.2 and Appendix C). The underlying Jacobian-spectrum estimator and original JER formula remain unchanged.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence remain intact. v2 adds contextual explanations, clarifies the Same/Different distinction and rank-collapse narrative, inserts natural-image validation before the retained readout analyses, and expands the appendix overview. Original appendices B–E become G–J rather than being removed.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the empirical displays with SugarCrepe, 26-model null-calibration, and computational-cost tables, plus compact shape-distance and noise-control tables. Tables 2 and 3 gain rows, and Figure 1 is updated for the revised results. Figures 2–6 retain their content despite relocation; the overall visual style remains stable.

R1.justification: v2 adds cognitive-science binding references, the SugarCrepe citation, and a focused discussion of inter-model representational similarity involving Kornblith, Williams, Bo, and Braun. This broadens the relevant comparison literature while retaining the original positioning around limitations of static geometric diagnostics.

T1.justification: Appendix C introduces the mathematical definition of the null-calibrated quantity ΔJER. The original JER definition, augmentation expansion, and objective-specific derivations are otherwise retained, with v1 Appendix B becoming v2 Appendix G. No new proof replaces the original theoretical account.

improvement.justification: v1's evidence relied on synthetic binding and noise-based JER. v2 substantially strengthens validity through natural-image JER, SugarCrepe validation, and initialization and matched-input controls that address generalization and confounding concerns. Added limitations and timing information improve interpretation and practical assessment. CLIP-only natural-image validation and reporting inconsistencies, such as the conflicting local-isotropy k settings, remain limitations but do not outweigh these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: v2 reports original evaluations of 26 encoders, retains the synthetic experiments, and adds SugarCrepe validation, initialization controls, and further diagnostic comparisons.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of 21 vision encoders, including synthetic binding results, geometric and Jacobian correlations, readout comparisons, and robustness analyses.

results.title: Global Geometry Is Not Enough for Vision Representations

C1.justification: The abstract and central contribution of dynamic, semantically conditioned LoRA unlearning remain stable. The introduction narrows the efficiency contribution to computational savings through a single training run in the multi-concept regime, dropping the earlier explicit memory-savings claim.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive limitations concerning keyword-driven suppression of benign cosmetics, animal, and medical prompts. It explains how mapping targets protect neighboring concepts, interprets adversarial resistance through pooled CLIP conditioning, and qualifies efficiency advantages as amortization across concepts. These materially expand the mechanism discussion and applicability boundaries beyond v1's largely positive interpretation.

D1.justification: Appendix B.1 adds training and inference hardware, wall-clock measurements, image resolution, and sampler details. Appendices E–F disclose ranks, loss weights, and mapping choices. Original prompt lists, the training configuration table, and the repository link remain. V2 removes the explicit MS-COCO-10k label from the celebrity results table, reducing sample-count documentation there.

E1.justification: V2 adds simultaneous removal of ten Imagenette classes and ImageNet-Confuse5 evaluation across five groups of visually similar erased and preserved classes. It also adds adversarial I2P prompts and benign prompts containing nudity-related language. These substantially broaden task requirements and test conditions beyond the retained object, nudity, and celebrity evaluations.

E2.justification: Stable Diffusion nudity Table 2 adds AdvUn, Receler, CPE, and STEREO. New comparisons include RACE for robustness and timing, SalUn/SPM/SP for multi-object erasure, ScaPre for fine-grained erasure, and static LoRA for inference timing. The external comparator sets in the retained Flux and celebrity tables remain unchanged.

E3.justification: New protocols include 95 adversarial prompts per attack, ResNet-50 and UQ benchmark evaluation, fine-grained preservation metrics, controlled runtime comparisons, and parameter sweeps. Celebrity evaluation drops the larger-encoder configuration. Appendix C.1 changes object-erasure sampling from 50 to 200 images per prompt, but Section 5.2 still states 50 and Table 1 is unchanged; this establishes a reported protocol revision, not a confirmed rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds UnlearnDiffAtk and Ring-A-Bell robustness tests, benign-context failure cases, runtime analyses, and ablations of LoRA rank, removal/retention loss weighting, and mapping targets versus empty prompts. Neighbor-probe examples test collateral suppression. These substantially extend v1's synonym examples, although its larger-encoder comparison is removed.

E5.justification: V2 Table 8 newly reports inference-time means and standard deviations over 100 generations. Figures 7–9 also disclose qualitative seed counts or identifiers. The main erasure benchmarks still lack repeated-training-run uncertainty estimates or significance tests; UQ's cross-method normalization is not such an uncertainty estimate.

E6.justification: Table 1 is unchanged. Reported UnHype NudeNet totals change from 18 to 8 on Stable Diffusion and 38 to 32 on Flux, alongside revised FID/CLIP values. The celebrity CLIP row changes from Acce/Accs/Ho of 11.72/87.48/87.88 to 0.46/86.35/92.48, while the NV-Embed-v2 row disappears. V2 also adds attack success rates of 0.00% and 1.05%, benchmark results, timings, and ablation outcomes; these additions are not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The NV-Embed-v2 celebrity-conditioning variant described and evaluated in v1 Section 5.4 is dropped; v2 retains the CLIP variant already evaluated in v1. This is a limited removal of a model variant. The hypernetwork trajectory formulation, removal and retention losses, LoRA placement, and Stable Diffusion/Flux inference procedures remain unchanged.

P1.justification: Localized rewrites clarify scalability, shorten inference explanations, and replace the celebrity encoder rationale. V2 adds experimental and appendix subsections, an impact statement, acknowledgements, and updated publication/affiliation text. Most existing exposition and the overall section order are retained; the added scientific material does not constitute a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: V2 adds substantial displays for adversarial performance, training/inference timing, new benchmarks, and ablations, plus Figures 7–12 showing failures and qualitative comparisons. Existing result tables gain highlighting and revised row structures. Figure 3 is relocated, and the training-prompt appendix is compacted; its retained prompt content is not newly added.

R1.justification: The related-work section and central positioning against static LoRA approaches are largely retained. Targeted additions cite adversarial methods and attacks, newer multi-concept work, and benchmark/evaluator sources, including STEREO, Ring-A-Bell, Li et al. (2025), and Deng et al. (2026). The discussion also qualifies the computational comparison with prior LoRA methods.

T1.justification: Appendix D introduces the mathematical definition of UQ through sigmoid-normalized erasure and quality scores and their harmonic mean; Appendix E specifies the new benchmark's Overall Acc measure. The underlying method equations and existing harmonic-mean metrics are retained. No theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens empirical scrutiny of the retained method: Section 5.5 and Appendices B.1 and D–F test adversarial recovery, computational cost, simultaneous erasure, fine-grained preservation, and component sensitivity that v1 did not establish. Concrete benign-context failures also make the limitations more informative. The new 50-versus-200 sampling contradiction and limited uncertainty reporting temper confidence, but the gains in validation and transparency are substantial independently of the higher reported scores.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe UnHype and retain matching methods, experiments, equations, and figures. All 14 pages of v1 and 23 pages of v2, including their appendices, support comparison. Internal reporting inconsistencies do not prevent identifying the changes.

after.justification: V2 retains original UnHype experiments and adds adversarial evaluations, runtime measurements, multi-concept benchmarks, ablations, and failure cases.

before.justification: Tables 1–4 report original UnHype experiments on object, nudity, and celebrity erasure, supported by qualitative examples and appendix evaluation protocols.

results.title: UnHype: CLIP-Guided Hypernetworks for Dynamic LoRA Unlearning

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: formalizing intent discovery, constructing a hierarchical user simulator, and training assistants to balance exploration and execution. Claims about performance, efficiency, generalization, and human satisfaction remain substantively unchanged; the additions supply further supporting evidence.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations of simulator robustness, hierarchy errors, and observed assumption violations. It explains how excessive diversity can disrupt technical-writing conventions and attributes discovery performance primarily to Rd while Re controls verbosity. Appendix B.10 explicitly qualifies this attribution because both reward variants inherit conversation contexts generated under the full reward.

D1.justification: v2 adds a title-page project link and concrete details for the new experiments, including alternative simulator model names, tangential probability 0.75, and reward-ablation preference relabeling with shared trajectories. Existing training hyperparameters, synthesis-cost information, simulator implementation description, and prompts are retained.

E1.justification: Appendix B.9 adds clarification-oriented document editing on 50 Medium articles and question answering on 400 AmbigNQ plus 400 NQ-Open questions. These extend evaluation beyond intent discovery in artifact creation to users with formed but unexpressed goals and ambiguous factual questions. The original domains, generalization tasks, and safety benchmarks remain.

E2.justification: Base, Prompted Base, and CollabLLM remain the external comparators, and the new independent benchmarks reuse that set. Table 11 adds a discovery-only offline-DPO variant as an internal ablation comparator against full-reward DPO, constituting a limited addition to comparison methods.

E3.justification: New protocols include controlled simulator ablations on 25 artifacts per domain, eight-turn document editing with character-level BLEU, and optional clarification followed by F1/answer-recall evaluation on 800 questions. Human validation uses 314 intent pairs and three raters per pair; conversation annotation combines LLM screening with manual verification. Section 6 also corrects the reported satisfaction cutoff from 7 to 8, without evidence of rerunning the user study.

E4.justification: v2 adds four simulator robustness tests: two alternative backbones, removal of single-dimension focus, and increased tangential probability. It also adds a reward-component ablation, human validation and error analysis of intent trees, and checks of monotonicity and dimension-switching assumptions in all 75 user-study conversations. These investigate central validity and mechanism questions absent from v1.

E5.justification: Appendix B.8 newly specifies that seeds are held fixed across simulator-ablation conditions. This is limited additional seed-control documentation. Three-trial averaging was already reported in v1; v2 does not establish increased repetitions for retained experiments or introduce confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: Main benchmark and retained appendix results are unchanged, but Tables 4–5 and 8–12 add substantial findings. These include BLEU 0.274 versus Base's 0.239, Ambig F1 0.202 versus CollabLLM's 0.197, and assumption violations in 4/75 and 11/75 conversations. Section 6 corrects Base's satisfaction percentage from 78% to 80% alongside the changed cutoff; the underlying Figure 5 is unchanged.

M1.justification: The proposed hierarchy construction, discovery-state updates, combined discovery and efficiency reward, and SFT/DPO/GRPO framework remain unchanged. Appendix A and the eleven prompts are unchanged. Alternative simulator configurations and discovery-only DPO are introduced as experimental ablations, without replacing the proposed procedure.

P1.justification: v2 tightens Section 2.3, makes scattered grammatical and cross-reference corrections, expands Section 5.3 with labeled paragraphs, and adds appendix subsections and acknowledgements. Conference front matter replaces the preprint notice. The established narrative and section organization remain largely intact.

P2.justification: New Tables 4–5 and 8–12 provide dedicated displays for hierarchy statistics and validation, simulator robustness, independent benchmarks, reward ablation, and assumption checks. This substantially expands the empirical presentation. Existing figures and tables are retained, with limited resizing, relocation, and renumbering rather than replacement.

R1.justification: The Almeda et al. (2024) DreamSheets reference is removed, and its related-work citation becomes an unresolved question mark. The remaining research positioning is largely unchanged. New evaluations engage more directly with the already-cited CollabLLM and clarification frameworks without redefining the paper's novelty.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation, hierarchy definition, state-transition equations, reward functions, and formal assumptions are retained. Section 2.3 rewrites their explanation, while Appendix C.1 empirically examines existing assumptions rather than changing them. No new theorem, proof, or substantive derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses a central validation gap: whether gains depend on its custom simulator and unverified intent hierarchies. Alternative simulators, independent benchmarks, human tree validation, and conversation-level assumption checks substantially strengthen the empirical foundation. The reward ablation transparently acknowledges shared trajectories. Some reporting defects remain or are introduced: Table 8's tangential column shows 53.7 versus the best baseline's 50.8, implying a 2.9-point gap rather than the printed 3.4. These limited defects do not outweigh the broader validation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DiscoverLLM with the same authors, core framework, and main experiments. Text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and can be matched across versions.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds simulator robustness experiments, independent benchmark evaluations, a reward ablation, human intent-tree validation, and analysis of the user-study conversations.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulated experiments across three domains, generalization and safety evaluations, and a 75-participant user study, including results in Appendices B–D.

results.title: DiscoverLLM: From Executing Intents to Discovering Them

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same contributions: disentangled alignment, tool-free global-to-local reasoning, data efficiency, and generalization to unseen table structures. New experiments support these existing claims without redefining the headline contributions.

C2.justification: V2 substantially expands interpretation of robustness and practical operation: it argues for data-scale stability, attributes gains to the framework rather than particular prompt wording, assesses self-revision reliability, and discusses why extra verification fails to help. Section 5.8 adds an accuracy–latency tradeoff interpretation and discusses REFOCUS's bounding-box dependency. The original limitations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: New Appendix H supplies the exact rephrased prompts and role prefixes. Table 8 specifies the shared Transformers backend and Qwen3-VL-8B implementations for REFOCUS and the proposed framework. Existing construction instructions, LoRA hyperparameters, and hardware disclosures remain unchanged. The existing repository disclosure moves to the abstract.

E1.justification: V2 newly reports VWTQ, VWTQ_syn, and VTabFact evaluations in Table 8, but does not explain how their represented data or visual conditions differ from the existing WTQ/TabFact coverage. A distinct coverage expansion cannot confidently be separated from another evaluation of existing task families. The original benchmark coverage is retained.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds RoT and DISCO+RoT comparisons. Table 8 newly evaluates the tool-assisted REFOCUS method against DISCO/Table-GLS and HIPPO, while Table 4 adds GPT-5.4-mini with and without Table-GLS. These substantially broaden the evaluated alternatives beyond v1's comparisons.

E3.justification: V2 adds 5K, 15K, and 20K alignment budgets, reasoning evaluations on Qwen3-VL-32B and GPT-5.4-mini, controlled prompt/revision variants, and assessment of 50 sampled instances by four raters. Table 8 introduces per-sample latency measurement using a common Transformers setting. Existing dataset counts and accuracy/F1 definitions remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's component ablations and layout analyses, v2 tests alignment-data sensitivity, rephrased and prefixed prompts, removal of revision within sub-table extraction, and additional evidence verification. It also adds human inspection of revision success and direct latency–accuracy analysis (Sections 5.6–5.8 and Table 14).

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. V2's four individual human-rating percentages are additional results; no uncertainty estimation or inter-rater agreement analysis is introduced.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial results in Tables 4, 6–8, and 14. Existing TabMCQ scores also change: Table 3's Gemma3n-DISCO direct-answering accuracy changes from 33.24 to 79.40, and Qwen3-DISCO/Table-GLS from 38.00 to 48.88. Corresponding averages, Figure 4, and appendix token counts change. The PDFs do not explain these revisions, so they cannot establish same-setting methodological gains.

M1.justification: Section 3 retains the same structure/global-content/local-content alignment objectives and three-stage Table-GLS procedure. The original prompts in Appendix C are unchanged. Revision removal, additional evidence checking, and alternative prompts are experimental variants, not changes to the proposed default method.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the section sequence are retained. V2 makes local wording corrections, adds Sections 5.6–5.8 and Appendix H, introduces acknowledgments, updates correspondence/publication information, and relocates the repository statement. These extend the document without extensively rewriting its existing narrative.

P2.justification: V2 adds separate tables for model extension, prompt sensitivity, revision analysis, and inference costs. It expands Table 2 and the complete understanding-results table, redraws Figure 4, and rearranges appendix displays. The non-tabular table moves from Table 4 to 5, and the token table from 10 to 15; the principal framework and case-study figures are retained.

R1.justification: V2 introduces RoT as a training-free row-wise reasoning alternative and adds several multimodal/reasoning references, including MUCAR and SAT, while removing the Flamingo citation. The main positioning against extensive supervised/reinforcement training and external-tool approaches is retained.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions, alignment losses, and inference formulations in Equations 1–7 are retained. Neither version contains additional theoretical propositions or proofs, and v2 introduces none.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens evidence for central robustness and efficiency claims. V1 lacked an isolated revision test and measured latency comparison with a tool-assisted competitor; Tables 7–8 address both, while prompt and data-size tests probe important alternative explanations. These gains improve the empirical justification of the unchanged method. Unexplained TabMCQ revisions and the continued absence of uncertainty reporting remain limitations.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DISCO/Table-GLS research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and can be matched despite additions, relocation, and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains original experiments and adds model comparisons, sensitivity tests, a human assessment of self-refinement, and measured inference-time results.

before.justification: V1 reports original table-understanding and reasoning experiments, component ablations, general-task evaluations, and appendix results, including Tables 1–4 and 10–11.

results.title: Decoupling Skeleton and Flesh: Efficient Multimodal Table Reasoning with  Disentangled Alignment and Structure-aware Guidance

C1.justification: The central claims about misalignment, staleness and basis rotation remain. V2 adds the stage-aware scheduling speedup to the introduction and extends the abstract's empirical claim from 1B-scale training to 3B-scale training with an 81.7% iteration reduction.

C2.justification: V2 adds an explanation linking early-stage misalignment to effective delay and motivating preferential basis updates. It interprets SOAP/Muon/Scion comparisons as distinguishing explicit alignment from preconditioning generally. It also discusses virtual-stage effects on absolute hardware timing and develops the memory tradeoffs of rotation variants beyond v1's qualitative discussion.

D1.justification: V2 adds a code-repository pointer, the 1.2% warmup and cosine schedule, and an explanation of multiple virtual stages sharing physical GPUs. It also documents Hessian estimation, stage-aware scheduling, 3B hyperparameters and partial training, and MoE configuration/source information. Warmup and virtual-stage details are newly disclosed, not established changes to existing runs.

E1.justification: Both versions use OpenWebText language modeling and the same quadratic and spiral toy objectives. The added 3B and MoE experiments change model configurations, while weight-stashing variants change training procedures; neither expands the represented data or task coverage.

E2.justification: V2 newly evaluates SOAP, Muon and Scion against basis rotation in Table 3, substantially broadening comparison beyond asynchronous-training baselines. PipeDream, PipeDream-LR, Nesterov and Delay Compensation remain. Figure 3's SGD-to-AdaSGD relabeling is not a comparator replacement: v1 Appendix B.1 already identifies AdaSGD.

E3.justification: V2 adds 3B training at P=32 with 82K reported iterations of a 250K-step schedule, a 100M eight-expert/top-2 MoE configuration, matched-budget scheduling controls, and Hessian-measurement protocols. It also relabels the retained no-stashing curves from PipeMare prediction to simply omitting stashing, reporting prediction separately in Figure 15. This establishes a reported setting revision, not that the retained experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds direct LLM update-oscillation and Hessian-norm measurements, uniform versus stage-aware versus reversed scheduling comparisons, and a quantitative memory-overhead analysis. It also separates no-stashing and weight-prediction robustness evidence. Existing approximation-fidelity, pipeline-depth and update-frequency analyses remain.

E5.justification: Appendix D.3 introduces randomized Hessian-norm estimation using 200 Cauchy vectors over 8,000 batches, adding a statistical estimation procedure absent from v1. Neither version reports repeated-training seed aggregates, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: Retained results include the 1B model's 76.8% iteration reduction. New results include a 29.2% stage-aware speedup, 81.7% and 46.8% iteration reductions in the added 3B and MoE settings, and Hessian-norm estimates of 0.5436 versus 0.1228. Table 3 adds SOAP/Muon/Scion slowdowns, but reverses the PipeDream-LR and Nesterov values relative to retained Figures 5 and 13; this inconsistency should not be interpreted as a verified ranking change.

M1.justification: V2 adds an optional stage-aware basis-refresh schedule that allocates more updates to stages with larger delays under a fixed total budget (Section 4.3 and Appendix I). The underlying Adam rotation procedure and four eigenbasis-estimation variants remain unchanged; algorithm reindexing and explicit arguments are clarifications.

P1.justification: The abstract, parts of the introduction and Section 2.1 are rewritten, Section 4.3 is locally reorganized, and explanatory appendices are added. Terminology, acknowledgements and publication information are updated. The overall narrative and most retained sections remain recognizable rather than undergoing wholesale restructuring.

P2.justification: V2 adds Figures 11, 15, 17, 20 and 21, a stage-aware panel in the efficiency figure, and memory and optimizer-comparison Tables 2 and 3. Existing plots are redistributed and renumbered, and Figure 3's legend is corrected to AdaSGD. These are substantial display additions beyond pagination changes.

R1.justification: V2 adds references supporting momentum analysis, training without stashing, Muon and Scion, and removes Arjevani et al. The established positioning relative to SOAP, GaLore and Hessian geometry largely remains. Abreu and Pan–Li bibliographic updates represent the same cited works.

T1.justification: Theorem 2.3 changes its delay factor from 1+τ to 1+dτ, with corresponding proof revisions. V2 adds stage-dependent-delay analysis and Theorem E.6, a momentum extension with an additional bounded-gradient assumption and Theorem E.8, and Appendix B's trajectory argument. The original basis-alignment theorem and its proof are retained.

improvement.justification: Direct LLM oscillation/Hessian measurements and SOAP/Muon/Scion comparisons address important validation gaps in v1. Clearer training and virtual-GPU documentation improves reproducibility, and the main convergence bound now explicitly includes dimension dependence. Table 3's inconsistent baseline labels and the partial 3B training results temper the evidence, but the stronger mechanism validation and transparency support a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same basis-rotation study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite additions and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains those experiments and adds original mechanism measurements, optimizer comparisons, stage-aware rotation experiments, and 3B and MoE training results.

before.justification: V1 reports original quadratic and spiral-loss experiments, OpenWebText language-model training, and pipeline-depth and rotation ablations in Sections 2 and 4 and Appendix F.

results.title: Mitigating Staleness in Asynchronous Pipeline Parallelism via Basis Rotation

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the same central claims: direct, model-agnostic, Neyman-orthogonal treatment-effect ranking, robustness to nuisance estimation errors, and empirical outperformance. The expanded conclusion reiterates these contributions and summarizes additional supporting experiments rather than redefining the core contribution.

C2.justification: Appendix A.1 newly explains that rankings alone cannot support decisions requiring treatment effects to exceed a numerical threshold. Appendix F.3.3 explicitly acknowledges that clipping modifies the ideal orthogonal objective. v2 also discusses low-heterogeneity benchmarks as less suitable for ranking and suggests that existing pair-dependent corrections explain the limited benefit of weighted sampling. These qualify and extend the retained interpretation.

D1.justification: The reported code location changes from an anonymous repository to an identified GitHub repository. v2 documents CRITEO's selective sampling, covariates, weighted binary losses, and evaluation details, and provides CATENets implementation pointers. Conversely, v1's explicit tree-ranker tuning grid and shared-nuisance-estimate statement are omitted. Common hardware, neural-network, optimizer, and hyperparameter-search details remain.

E1.justification: v2 retains the original synthetic, MovieLens, MIMIC-III, and CPS coverage, while adding CRITEO advertising data with observed binary website-visit outcomes and treatment-effect ranking on ACIC and IHDP. These substantially broaden evaluation beyond the original simulated treatment/outcome constructions.

E2.justification: The main T-learner, DR-learner, and plug-in ranker comparisons remain. The expanded synthetic comparison in v2 Table 12 retains the tree ranker and adds DR ranker, PairNet, and FlexTENet. DR ranker constructs pairwise targets from doubly robust pseudo outcomes and is distinct from the retained pointwise DR-learner.

E3.justification: The original main experimental settings are largely retained. v2 adds CRITEO confounded-training/randomized-testing procedures, AUUC evaluation, 10,000 training and 5,000 validation samples, and three test sizes. Appendix F.4 adds a separate CATENets-style implementation for the synthetic comparison, ACIC heterogeneity-based selection, the first 50 IHDP replications, and within-replication normalized AUTOC and win rates. These are additional or replaced experimental settings, not evidence that every retained experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained pair-count, nuisance-quality, and overlap analyses, v2 adds weighted versus uniform pair sampling, deliberately misspecified linear nuisance models, a nuisance-perturbation diagnostic for the clipped loss, and smoothing-parameter sensitivity across training sizes. Tables 10–11 and Figures 7–8 address practical robustness questions not tested in v1.

E5.justification: Five-seed means with standard deviations in tables and standard errors in performance plots remain the usual reporting practice. Appendix E.3 newly specifies that CRITEO test sets are redrawn for each seed, incorporating test-sample variation unlike the fixed test sets used previously. No increase in the retained experiments' run counts or new significance-testing procedure is reported.

E6.justification: New benchmark, baseline, and robustness outcomes substantially expand the results. Existing values also change: Table 3 revises Rank-Learner AUTOC from 0.94±0.21 to 1.00±0.19 at n=100 and from 1.30±0.03 to 1.31±0.01 at n=500; Table 4 revises DR-learner MIMIC-III AUTOC from 1.16 to 1.17. The expanded tree comparison replaces results under a different Rank-Learner configuration and removes its policy-value rows. New findings include highest relative AUTOC on both ACIC and IHDP, although IHDP overall win rate favors DR-learner, 42% versus 40%.

M1.justification: The core two-stage objective, orthogonal pseudo labels, and inference procedure remain unchanged. Appendix F.2.2 adds an evaluated variant that samples pairs proportionally to their correction weights instead of uniformly. Uniform sampling remains the main procedure, and label clipping was already present in v1.

P1.justification: Rewriting and reorganization concentrate on the experimental discussion and Appendices A, E, and F. Appendix F now groups material into main results, computational efficiency, robustness, and additional comparisons; the conclusion becomes an expanded numbered section. The abstract, main methodological narrative, and proof structure are largely retained.

P2.justification: v2 adds the CRITEO table and its appendix repeat, pair-sampling and misspecification tables, the ACIC/IHDP table, and two three-panel diagnostic figures. v1 Table 7 becomes the expanded, AUTOC-only Table 12 with additional comparator rows and second-best highlighting. Existing displays are also relocated, including Table 4 and the appendix subsampling and overlap figures.

R1.justification: v2 adds an uplift-modeling discussion in Appendix A.2, distinguishes budget-based ranking from threshold-based policies, and mentions orthogonal learning for preference-based LLM evaluation. References are added for these connections and the new benchmarks and baselines. The central positioning as the first model-agnostic orthogonal two-stage treatment-effect ranker remains unchanged.

T1.justification: The causal assumptions, Theorems 5.1–5.2, and derivations and proofs in Appendices B–D are substantively unchanged. Appendix F.3.3 introduces the mathematical definition of a finite-difference gradient-norm sensitivity diagnostic in Equation 137. This is a limited formal addition, not a new proof of orthogonality for the clipped objective.

improvement.justification: v1's validation centers on designed synthetic and semi-synthetic settings with limited comparators. v2 substantially strengthens empirical support through observed CRITEO outcomes, ACIC/IHDP, stronger neural baselines, and tests of misspecification, smoothing, and the implemented clipped loss. The new applicability qualifications also improve interpretation. These gains outweigh the loss of explicit tree-ranker tuning details, although ACIC selection and CATENets settings remain incompletely specified, and the clipping diagnostic does not establish exact orthogonality.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Rank-Learner: Orthogonal Ranking of Treatment Effects. Their complete main texts and Appendices A–F are readable, and corresponding methods, proofs, experiments, and displays can be matched despite additions and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds CRITEO, ACIC/IHDP, additional baseline comparisons, and several robustness and sensitivity experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic and semi-synthetic experiments, including ranking performance, nuisance estimation, pair subsampling, overlap sensitivity, and a tree-ranker comparison.

results.title: Rank-Learner: Orthogonal Ranking of Treatment Effects

C1.justification: The central contributions remain plausibility-based evaluation, a multiple-answer training resource, novel benchmark targets and effective fine-tuning. The introduction and conclusion update CREED to a 22.7M corpus with a verified subset and C3LM to a model family. The introduction also softens 'outperforming' the leading LLM baselines to achieving their performance.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly discusses circularity when ChemCensor supplies both training signals and evaluation, separating those models from the main comparison. Appendix N qualifies zero scores as missing reference support rather than definitive implausibility. The discussion adds explanations of reference-corpus bias and acknowledges conventional SSRS superiority; Appendix O nevertheless contains conflicting claims about LLM Top-K advantages.

D1.justification: Section 7 adds stated access links for code, datasets and models. Appendices D, G and H newly document RxnMapper, stereochemical and SEAr processing, SQLite storage, product-centric Parquet records and BRICS-based reasoning traces. Exact split-count reporting is removed, and conflicting GRPO settings leave part of the expanded training documentation unresolved.

E1.justification: Training expands from ChemCensor-positive reactions to the full enumerated CREED corpus, including previously excluded candidates; the filtered resource continues as revised CREED-CCV. Pistachio adds reference chemistry extending through 2023 for evaluation. The 100 URSA targets are unchanged, and USPTO-50K-test-mini is a subset of retained coverage rather than a new task.

E2.justification: v2 adds quantitative comparisons with LocalRetro, GLN, MEGAN, Chemformer, Graph2Edits, MHNreact, RetroKNN and R-SMILES in Tables 13-14. LocalRetro and RetroKNN previously appeared only in illustrative cases. LFM2 2.6B becomes an evaluated foundation baseline, while Kimi K2's full USPTO-50K-test results are withdrawn.

E3.justification: New protocols include 50,000-step LFM2 training, a USPTO-only control, evaluation on a random 497-target subset and expert assessment of 25 outputs from each of four models. Section 4.3 also changes reported GRPO group size from 16 to 8, temperature from 1.2 to 1 and KL weight from 0.05 to 0.1, although Appendix H retains the earlier settings.

E4.justification: Appendix M expands the retained Qwen comparisons with LFM2, filtering and reasoning ablations. Appendix N tests reference-database sensitivity using identical predictions, and Appendix R adds expert validation. Appendices C and E also add concrete exact-match failure cases and regioselectivity/stereoselectivity tests beyond v1's examples.

E5.justification: v1 provides benchmark point estimates without confidence intervals. Appendix Q and Table 16 introduce 95% intervals using 2,000 target-level bootstrap replicates for URSA and a normal approximation for USPTO. These quantify uncertainty across targets rather than repeated training runs. Some Table 16 point estimates disagree with Table 1.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive results for LFM2 variants, conventional models, the extended reference database, the miniature benchmark and expert agreement. Retained results also change: Kimi K2's reported URSA maximum CC becomes 1.12 rather than 0.00, and the relocated Qwen ChemCensor-reward result changes from 2.03 to 2.01. Changed training and scoring configurations limit direct performance comparisons.

M1.justification: v2 adds an LFM2-based C3LM branch and specifies a composite GRPO reward combining thinking-format compliance, SMILES validity and retrosynthesis correctness. ChemCensor filtering becomes optional in CREED construction, and the main models exclude ChemCensor filtering and rewards. The Qwen-based variants remain in Appendix M; expanded implementation explanations alone are not treated as new components.

P1.justification: The training and discussion narrative is substantially reorganized around LFM2 models and the separation of metric-dependent variants. Earlier Qwen experiments move into Appendix M, Appendix A becomes a model inventory, and the method and dataset appendices receive substantial explanatory rewrites. New validation appendices and an availability section further restructure the document.

P2.justification: v2 brings the two-benchmark bubble plot into full-width Figure 4, replaces Appendix A's plot with an inventory table, revises the pipeline diagrams and changes the error heatmap layout. It adds extensive case-study, sensitivity, baseline, confidence-interval and expert-annotation tables. The earlier CREED distribution plots and split-count table are removed.

R1.justification: v2 adds a brief conventional-SSRS subsection, discusses RetroTrim and cites supporting work on LFM2, additional conventional models, BRICS and reaction mapping. The Xu et al. ChemBench reference disappears. Most of the existing metrics and LLM literature review remains; publication updates to retained works do not constitute new research positioning.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions of maximum CC, deduplicated and zero-padded Top-K aggregation, and dataset diversity remain unchanged. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs. The added standard confidence-interval formula documents statistical estimation rather than a new theoretical result.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important weaknesses in v1 by separating direct ChemCensor-dependent training from the main comparison, adding strong conventional baselines and validating the metric against 100 expert judgments with 87% agreement. Reference-database sensitivity and uncertainty reporting further strengthen the evidence. Conflicting GRPO settings, mismatched statistical summaries and Appendix O's incorrect Top-K interpretation weaken reproducibility and reporting, but the new controls and independent validation still provide a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ChemCensor, CREED and C3LM research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching renamed models and relocated experiments.

after.justification: v2 reports original model experiments, expanded benchmark comparisons, reference-database sensitivity results and an expert evaluation of 100 model outputs.

before.justification: v1 reports original computational benchmarks and C3LM supervised and reinforcement learning experiments on URSA-expert-2026 and USPTO-50K-test.

results.title: When Single Answer Is Not Enough: Rethinking Single-Step Retrosynthesis Benchmarks for LLMs

C1.justification: The central claim of exact-gradient learning for arbitrary stationary non-conservative systems is retained. V2 characterizes Dyadic EP as an independent first-principles generalization of existing Dyadic Learning, and its conclusion expands the empirical claim from AEP on MNIST to both proposed algorithms across three datasets.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations concerning expressivity benefits from asymmetric connectivity and stabilization through input-induced diagonal Jacobian contributions. Appendix G.3 explicitly leaves a complete stability analysis outside scope and discusses residual oscillations and time averaging. Earlier hardware-implementation and temporal-memory limitations remain.

D1.justification: V2 retains the MNIST implementation information and substantially expands documentation through Tables 3–4 and Appendix G.6. Additions include CNN9 architecture, initialization, augmentation, optimizer and learning-rate schedule, weight averaging, target smoothing, and method-specific relaxation limits and stopping tolerances.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates handwritten-digit classification on MNIST only. V2 adds Fashion-MNIST apparel classification and CIFAR-10 natural-image classification in Sections 5.4–5.5, substantially broadening the represented data and domains.

E2.justification: V2 adds experimentally evaluated backpropagation comparisons: a Fashion-MNIST reference result in Table 1 and a direct CNN comparison in Table 2. V1 discusses backpropagation theoretically but evaluates only EP and VF against AEP. The new true-gradient reference substantially strengthens the comparator set.

E3.justification: Retained MNIST settings match. New protocols include matched-parameter comparisons across dynamics and connectivity, deeper Fashion-MNIST networks, a 40-epoch CIFAR-10 CNN evaluation, and output-variance measurement under constrained input projections. The stability experiment's budget is inconsistent: Table 3 lists 40 epochs, whereas Table 5 reports epoch 80.

E4.justification: V2 adds analyses of dynamics, connectivity and depth, plus an all-to-all MNIST stability control varying input-projection strength at fixed structural asymmetry. Appendix G.3 tests whether training suppresses oscillations independently of increasing input magnitude. These extend the retained asymmetry, learning-speed and Jacobian analyses.

E5.justification: Both versions already report means and standard deviations over ten runs for the retained MNIST experiments. V2 additionally specifies five seeds for CIFAR-10 and introduces a paired t-test comparing Dyadic EP with backpropagation, reporting p = 0.75. No increased run count is established for retained experiments.

E6.justification: The retained MNIST results match, including 92.7 ± 0.5% for AEP/AsymEP versus 64.3 ± 2.0% for VF in the feedforward experiment. V2 adds extensive results: Table 2 reports CIFAR-10 accuracies of 90.66 ± 0.25% for backpropagation, 90.69 ± 0.14% for Dyadic EP, 89.74 ± 0.14% for AsymEP and 10.00 ± 0.00% for VF. Fashion-MNIST and stability results are also newly reported.

M1.justification: The Asymmetric EP correction, Dyadic EP energy and dynamics, and parameter-update procedures remain unchanged. AEP is renamed AsymEP. The additional architectures and constrained-input experiments apply the existing algorithms under new experimental settings.

P1.justification: V2 renames AEP to AsymEP, tightens several explanatory passages, rewrites and relocates Out-of-Equilibrium Mechanics from Appendix E to C, and reorganizes subsequent appendices. It also adds an Impact Statement. The overall main-text narrative and organization remain largely intact.

P2.justification: V2 adds benchmark Tables 1–2 and appendix Tables 4–6, and expands v1's hyperparameter Table 1 into v2 Table 3 with a stability-experiment column. All seven original figures are retained with updated method labels and some relocation. The substantial addition of result and configuration displays goes beyond pagination changes.

R1.justification: V1 relates Dyadic EP primarily to Dual Propagation as a symmetric special case. V2 substantially revises this positioning by acknowledging Dyadic Learning and describing an independent generalization to arbitrary force fields, adding related works by Høier and Zach, Høier et al., and Nest and Høier. It also adds Millidge et al. and Osat and Golestanian, while removing Galley et al. (2014).

T1.justification: New Appendix E derives AsymEP as a first-order projection of Dyadic EP. Appendix G.3 adds spectral stability reasoning and derivatives for constrained input projections. The Dyadic gradient identity also changes from including an O(beta^3) remainder in v1 Eq. (69) to an exact expression justified by linearity in v2 Eq. (71).

improvement.justification: V2 addresses an important validation gap: v1 tested only shallow MNIST networks and did not directly evaluate Dyadic EP. The Fashion-MNIST comparisons, CNN9 CIFAR-10 evaluation against backpropagation, and constrained-input stability control provide substantially broader evidence, supported by added derivations and implementation details. The 40-versus-80-epoch inconsistency in Tables 3 and 5 limits reproducibility of the stability experiment, but does not outweigh these substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching renamed methods and reorganized appendices.

after.justification: V2 retains the MNIST experiments and adds original Fashion-MNIST and CIFAR-10 evaluations, plus constrained-input stability experiments in Appendix G.

before.justification: V1 reports original MNIST experiments comparing AEP, EP and VF under symmetric initialization, fixed asymmetry and feedforward connectivity, with additional analyses in Appendix F.

results.title: Equilibrium Propagation for Non-Conservative Systems

C1.justification: The abstract, three introduction contributions and conclusion retain the same central claims: adaptive token-level mixing of linear and softmax attention improves long-context modeling while reducing computational latency.

C2.justification: v2 interprets temporal routing and weight distributions as supporting context-dependent allocation and time-dependent mixing. It also interprets the Mamba2 experiment as evidence of architectural generality and explains the flexibility cost of larger chunks. Existing limitations and future directions remain.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents the default 64-token chunk size, softmax normalization of head-wise output weights, and cache/state updates and rollback during token generation. Hardware, optimizer settings, training budgets and the code-access location are retained.

E1.justification: Fineweb-Edu training and the original language-modeling, commonsense, retrieval, RULER and LongBench coverage remain. New comparisons and analyses reuse existing tasks and corpora, including PG19, NarrativeQA and CodeParrot.

E2.justification: New Appendix B/Table 5 evaluates NSA, MOBA, GDN with sliding-window attention, FlexPrefill, SnapKV, AdaKV and PyramidKV. Figure 7 adds FlexPrefill and SnapKV to latency comparisons. These substantially expand the evaluated alternatives beyond v1's original comparator set.

E3.justification: The new sparse-method comparison specifies 380M models, a 50% computational budget for sparse variants and a 1024-token GDN sliding window. Table 4 adds a 128-token chunk experiment. Original training budgets, context lengths and benchmark protocols remain; the default 64-token chunk size is newly disclosed.

E4.justification: Table 4 adds sigmoid versus linear output-weight activation and larger-chunk ablations. Section 5.2 and Appendix C.5 add temporal routing and output-weight analyses across three corpora, extending v1's aggregate token-distribution analysis substantially.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests or run-level uncertainty estimates. The additional results retain the existing point-estimate reporting practice.

E6.justification: Original table rows and plotted results are unchanged. New results include retrieval averages of 30.02, 30.57 and 27.85 for the added ablations versus 33.49 for the default, and 25.34 versus 19.25 for NAtS-L Mamba2 versus Mamba2. Table 5 adds sparse-baseline results, but its NAtS-L Hybrid NQ score of 20.72 differs unexplainedly from 16.53 in retained Table 6.

M1.justification: Appendix C.2 introduces and evaluates a NAtS-L variant combining softmax attention with Mamba2 instead of GDN. The original GDN-based architecture remains; expanded descriptions of its decoding and weight normalization do not establish a redesign.

P1.justification: v2 adds focused methodological explanations and analysis paragraphs, introduces Appendix B and subsection C.2, and updates conference front matter and bibliography metadata. Most original prose and the main section sequence remain.

P2.justification: v2 adds temporal-distribution Figures 6, 11 and 12, sparse-comparison latency Figure 7, and Tables 5 and 9, while expanding Table 4. Existing displays are retained and relocated, table captions move above tables, and Figure 1's legend changes from Inter-Chunk to Intra-Chunk.

R1.justification: Section 2 and new Appendix B substantially expand positioning through five families of sparse and hybrid attention, distinguishing fixed budgets, learned selection and approximation of full attention. Added works include FlexPrefill, AdaKV, PyramidKV, SeerAttention and AttentionPredictor. Publication updates to existing references do not constitute additional works.

T1.justification: Equation 22 explicitly defines softmax-normalized mixing weights, whereas v1 specified the weighted output combination and described weights only through linear projections. The new routing argmax restates existing highest-score selection; the original gradient and state-update derivations remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the central accuracy-efficiency argument by adding evaluations against relevant sparse-attention and KV-compression competitors missing from v1. Targeted ablations, the Mamba2 variant and decoding details also improve the evidence and assessability of the framework. Unexplained NQ discrepancies between Tables 5 and 6 weaken numerical consistency, but the broader comparative and diagnostic gains remain substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same NAtS-L research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across renumbering.

after.justification: The original empirical results remain, supplemented by sparse-attention comparisons, additional ablations, temporal analyses and a Mamba2-based variant.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix B report original language-model evaluations, retrieval and context-extrapolation results, latency measurements and ablations.

results.title: Neural Attention Search Linear: Towards Adaptive Token-Level Hybrid Attention Models

C1.justification: The abstract newly claims that EATcubic's favorable performance extends empirically to Negative Binomial latents and foregrounds GSM's broader applicability. The central contributions—systematic comparison, the cubic correction, and practical temperature-robustness guidance—remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the persistent ImageNet gap as structural and proposes implicit regularization to explain improved neural readout and limited-data behavior. It also qualifies that temperature robustness does not necessarily transfer to readout accuracy and identifies extreme-temperature instability for Negative Binomial models. These substantially expand the earlier interpretation and applicability discussion.

D1.justification: v2 supplies RGC processing/training instructions and basic setup details for the new appendix experiments, including previously unstated approximate original training/test counts. Conversely, Figure 12 omits the selected-temperature values shown in v1 Figure 15's legend. Code, data, and checkpoint access information is unchanged.

E1.justification: Beyond v1's van Hateren image patches and synthetic neural data, v2 evaluates ImageNet patches, recorded retinal ganglion-cell activity, and macaque V1 response prediction. The latter introduces a downstream neural-prediction task using pretrained features.

E2.justification: Matched experiments retain the same comparators: EATsigmoid, GSM, score-function estimation, and exact gradients where available. Added experiments reuse these methods or subsets of them. Newly cited alternative VAEs are not newly evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: Existing Appendix G protocols are retained, but added experiments introduce substantial settings: 40x40 inputs; RGC segmentation, a two-thirds training split, 30 epochs and 1-3 hidden neurons; fitted Negative Binomial dispersion with temperatures from 10^-6 to 0.5; frozen-feature linear readouts measured by explainable variance; and a 10,000-image training subset.

E4.justification: v2 adds limited-data overfitting analysis, Negative Binomial temperature sensitivity including extreme-temperature instability, and RGC robustness across hidden-neuron counts. These test additional failure conditions and applicability boundaries. The earlier firing-rate sweeps, Monte Carlo sensitivity analyses, and decoder visualizations are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Existing results retain 100-trial standard errors, 100-sample gradient uncertainty, and three-seed training standard deviations. No changed replication counts or statistical estimation procedures are documented. The added readout results include uncertainty values but do not establish a different reporting practice.

E6.justification: v2 adds RGC curves and Appendix H.3.1-H.3.4 outcomes. ImageNet ELBOs are -718.92 for exact gradients, -720.27 for EATcubic, and -755.40 for EATsigmoid. Macaque readout explainable variance is approximately 0.19, 0.22 +/- 0.01, and 0.24 +/- 0.01, respectively. These are newly reported experiments; original matched results are retained.

M1.justification: The proposed EATcubic procedure remains unchanged. The Gamma-Poisson adaptation already appeared in v1 Appendix H.3 and Algorithm 3. Corrections to GSM aggregation in Appendix C align it with v1's existing main-text formula; they do not establish a changed implemented method.

P1.justification: v2 revises introductory/background passages, expands the results roadmap, moves the dispersion discussion from H.3 to H.2, and organizes supplementary experiments into H.3.1-H.3.8. Author roles, affiliations, and acknowledgements are updated. Most core exposition and the main section sequence remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds RGC Figures 5 and 13, rearranges supplementary figure groups, and refines legends and page layout. For example, v1 Figures 13-15 become v2 Figures 10-12, with selected-temperature annotations removed from the last plot. Existing tables and most plot designs are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds positioning around metabolic costs and information geometry, references hybrid inference VAEs, and adds sources for neural datasets and explainable variance. The central novelty claim remains unchanged. Publication updates for Gumbel-Softmax/Concrete and the corrected wake-sleep bibliographic record refer to existing cited works.

T1.justification: Appendix C corrects Gumbel-noise indexing, restores category-weighted aggregation in Eq. (24) and Algorithm 2, and clarifies the zero-temperature limit. Appendix E corrects the Poisson exponential sign in Eq. (56). The moment proofs, gradient/Hessian derivations, and dispersion formulations otherwise remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v1's practical recommendations relied on small image patches and synthetic neural data. v2 supplies actual neural-recording validation and probes larger inputs, alternative latents, downstream prediction, and limited-data behavior, substantially strengthening and qualifying those recommendations. Appendix corrections also repair concrete mathematical errors. Several new experiments remain briefly documented, limiting reproducibility, but the broader validation and explicit failure conditions provide a substantial net quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same EATcubic comparison study. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A-H support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v2 retains these experiments and reports additional ImageNet, retinal-recording, Negative Binomial, macaque V1 readout, and limited-data results.

before.justification: v1 reports original sampling, gradient-quality, natural-image P-VAE, and synthetic POGLM experiments in Section 3 and Appendix H.

results.title: A hitchhiker's guide to Poisson gradient estimation

C1.justification: The modular DLL, distributional modeling and rollout-stability contributions remain.
