However, the abstract and conclusion narrow claims from meaningful epistemic uncertainty and well-calibrated rollout uncertainty to useful predictive uncertainty, and replace broad generalization language with more specific distributional-performance claims.

C2.justification: Section 3.3 and Appendix A.1 explicitly characterize underfitting-based epistemic uncertainty as heuristic and conditional stability as a regularity property, not a calibration guarantee. Section 5.3 adds backbone-dependent limitations and an explanation for DM's Kolmogorov advantage. Appendix C adds interpretations of rank, sampling-cost and data-efficiency tradeoffs.

D1.justification: V2 adds an explicit code-repository link, detailed U-Net and VAE specifications, optimizer and normalization details, and inverse-data generation instructions. These expand disclosure without establishing changes to retained implementations. Conversely, Appendix B.3 drops previously stated details including KS domain length, rollout integrator specifications and Kolmogorov viscosity and drag values.

E1.justification: V2 retains the four original forward-prediction benchmarks and adds a distinct Darcy inverse task: reconstructing a smooth log-Gaussian permeability field from sparse, noisy pressure observations. This extends task coverage beyond forward solution prediction and autoregressive forecasting.

E2.justification: The FNO, FNO-d, PNO, DM and LDM comparators remain in Tables 2–5. New Table 15 evaluates DeepONet-DLL against deterministic DeepONet and DeepONet-Dropout. Expanded descriptions of the existing PNO implementation do not establish a changed comparator.

E3.justification: Appendix C introduces rank, sampling-NFE and training-size sweeps, plus inverse evaluation on a 64×64 grid using 25 sensors with Gaussian noise of standard deviation 0.01. Appendix B.3 changes reported Burgers forcing modes from {1,2,3} to {1,3,5}. V1's diffusion horizon T=10 becomes T=1 with default NFE=10; rerunning experiments is not established. Darcy's revised source coefficients are algebraically equivalent to v1's mixture.

E4.justification: New Appendix C systematically examines coefficient-rank sensitivity, sampling-step sensitivity, training-data requirements and compatibility with DeepONet. These substantially extend v1's reconstruction comparison and qualitative analyses, which remain present.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-training run counts, training seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests. Predictive ensembles and spread metrics remain, while the new experimental tables also report point estimates without uncertainty across training runs.

E6.justification: Existing numerical entries in Tables 2–9 remain unchanged, but Tables 10–15 add substantial results on rank, NFE, dataset size and inverse reconstruction. For example, new Table 15 reports CRPS 0.121 and SSR 0.783 for DeepONet-DLL, versus 0.142 and 0.232 for DeepONet-Dropout. These are newly reported comparisons, not performance gains over v1 under matched settings.

M1.justification: Appendix C.4 adds a DeepONet adaptation using MLP output and conditioning encoders, whereas v1 implements these components through FNO. The central reconstruction objective, frozen operator encoder and coefficient-space flow-matching pipeline remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The abstract, uncertainty discussion, method explanations, experimental interpretation, related work, conclusion and theoretical appendix undergo extensive rewriting. A new ablation appendix is inserted, and the existing qualitative appendix moves from C to D. This is broad editorial restructuring beyond isolated wording changes.

P2.justification: Six new tables present rank, NFE, dataset-size and DeepONet comparisons, substantially expanding the experimental displays. Existing Figures 1–7 retain their graphical content, with relocation and caption revisions; Figure 2's caption now consistently describes velocity modeling and ODE sampling.

R1.justification: Section 6 substantially expands positioning through a new neural-process discussion and an explicit comparison with fixed-basis spectral diffusion. It also adds relevant work on flow-matching error bounds, wavelet diffusion, Bayesian FNO uncertainty and conformal prediction, clarifying DLL's relationship to these approaches.

T1.justification: Proposition 4.1 and Appendix A.2 replace centered conditional covariance with the uncentered second-moment operator and revise the optimal-subspace proof accordingly. Appendix A.1 revises the endpoint-stability argument and distinguishes marginal velocity from sample-level training targets, replacing v1's asserted error equality with a conditional-expectation inequality. These are substantive mathematical corrections.

improvement.justification: V2 repairs central mathematical justification gaps in Propositions 2.3 and 4.1, qualifies overstated uncertainty claims, and adds systematic sensitivity tests plus evidence of compatibility beyond FNO. These substantially strengthen correctness and empirical support. Some solver details are lost, and differences between main results and default-setting ablation scores remain unexplained, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantive gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DLL research work. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated qualitative results.

after.justification: V2 retains these empirical results and adds rank, sampling and dataset-size ablations, plus a DeepONet Darcy inverse-problem experiment in Appendix C.

before.justification: V1 reports original stochastic PDE experiments, deterministic rollout evaluations and encoder reconstruction results in Tables 2–7, with additional qualitative results in Appendix C.

results.title: Generative Neural Operators through Diffusion Last Layer

C1.justification: The abstract and discussion retain the principal contributions: fairness as bargaining, relative improvement as the KS solution, axiomatic justification, no-harm guarantees, and finite-sample convergence. The new introduction contribution list organizes these existing claims, while the ACS evidence supports the retained heterogeneous-predictability motivation.

C2.justification: New Appendix C substantially explains baseline dependence, interpretable defaults, and why pooled ERM or an existing Pareto compromise is generally unsuitable as the disagreement baseline. Remark 4.5 explicitly recommends choosing criteria by contextual axioms rather than universal preference for RI. Appendix G adds interpretations of demographic predictability differences and their persistence with additional features.

D1.justification: Appendix G supplies new reproducibility information: ACS access through folktables, employment filters, target transformation, feature encodings, weighted least-squares fitting, baseline and oracle construction, and frontier resolution. It also describes ERM warm-start and exponentiated group-weight updates, although numerical optimization hyperparameters and a held-out evaluation split are not specified.

E1.justification: v2 adds ACS log-income prediction for full-time, year-round employees across all 50 states, partitioned by sex and race. This introduces substantial real-data population and task coverage beyond v1's analytic examples; the theoretical regression, classification, and RKHS settings remain.

E2.justification: Figures 5, 8, and 10 introduce an empirical comparison of MMRI against ERM, Group DRO, MMV, MMR, and Nash. v1 compared MMR in its analytic example and other criteria schematically or axiomatically; ERM and Nash newly participate in reported performance comparisons.

E3.justification: The added ACS evaluation fits linear models with intercepts, group-specific oracles, and a constant-mean baseline, sweeping 10,001 group weights to construct frontiers. It evaluates single-feature and four-feature models using per-group RMSE, relative improvement, and oracle-gap ratios. These are new experimental protocols, not demonstrated reruns of an existing evaluation.

E4.justification: Appendix G adds six case studies examining how unequal predictability affects method allocations. Its single-feature versus four-feature comparison tests whether gap asymmetry persists with richer inputs. These provide empirical sensitivity and failure-mode analyses beyond v1's constructed illustrations.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. Table 2's new across-state ranges, medians, and proportions describe heterogeneity rather than uncertainty in performance estimates.

E6.justification: Figure 1 replaces the analytic MMR outcomes (−56%, 87%) and RI outcomes (69%, 69%) with ACS North Dakota outcomes of (−74%, 82%) and (57%, 57%), respectively; these are different settings, not performance changes under a common setting. Section 6 and Appendix G add extensive results, including gap ratios from 0.04 to 3.48 and only 27% near-symmetric configurations.

M1.justification: The relative-improvement objective, empirical estimator, and leximin refinement remain unchanged. Appendix G documents numerical implementations for the added experiments, without establishing a revision to the proposed method.

P1.justification: v2 adds an explicit contribution list, inserts an experimental section, expands baseline and figure explanations, and makes localized wording corrections. Existing sections and appendices largely retain their wording and ordering, with renumbering accommodating the additions.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn around the ACS example, and v2 adds Figure 5, Table 2, and the multi-panel empirical Figures 8–10. These substantially expand the visual presentation. Existing conceptual figures are retained, including v1 Figures 5–6 as v2 Figures 6–7.

R1.justification: v2 adds Zafar et al. (2017), distinguishing earlier bargaining-inspired preference fairness from its explicit bargaining formulation. It also adds Ding et al. (2021) and Korenman and Neumark (1991) for the empirical material and removes the CFPB credit-invisibility reference. The broader related-work structure remains.

T1.justification: The central axiom characterization changes substantively: Proposition 4.2 restricts individual monotonicity to expansions preserving other groups' optimal risks and replaces exchangeability-based symmetry with permutation equivariance. Proposition 4.4 and Table 1 are adjusted accordingly, including correcting egalitarian methods' IM entries. Theorem 5.4 tightens its condition from Δ/2 to Δ/4, matching the corrected 2ε0 denominator bound. Appendix D also removes unsupported strict-convexity and growth-bound assertions.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the central motivation with ACS evidence that unequal group predictability and problematic absolute-scale allocations occur in real data, extending v1's analytic illustrations. It also corrects an overstated monotonicity condition and a convergence-bound error, while explaining the consequential baseline choice. The experiments lack reported held-out validation and uncertainty estimates, but the gains in empirical grounding and theoretical precision are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with the same authors, relative-improvement framework, and principal theoretical results. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: Section 6 and Appendix G report original analyses of 2018 ACS income data across 50 states, including 400 partition–feature configurations and comparisons among fairness methods.

before.justification: v1 provides analytic population-risk illustrations, including Figures 1 and 4, but reports no experimental, sampled-simulation, or observed-data study. Section 5 develops an empirical estimator theoretically without reporting experimental outcomes.

results.title: Maximin Relative Improvement: Fair Learning as a Bargaining Problem

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contribution list, and conclusion retain the same scientific claims about deterministic branching, cached MCTS, and coding/mathematical reasoning performance. The additional experiments expand support without redefining the announced contributions.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands applicability and mechanism discussion: it replaces the exclusionary rationale for block diffusion with demonstrated compatibility, discusses memory-constrained deployment and incomplete-verifier robustness, and adds hypotheses about localized remasking and noisy intermediate-state rewards. Appendix A.7 explicitly qualifies the new comparisons because search formulations and reward interfaces differ.

D1.justification: v2 clarifies existing tokenizer conversion and the fixed generation window, and identifies math_verify for the retained MATH scores. New reproducibility information includes block size 4, additional model identities, single-H100 hardware for coding runtime measurements, GPU residency and CPU-offloading guidance, model memory and transfer times, and PRM invocation details.

E1.justification: LiveCodeBench, HumanEval+, MBPP+, and MATH remain the datasets and tasks. Appendix A.5 adds an incomplete-verifier scenario in which search receives reduced public-test feedback while evaluation still uses private tests. The additional model configurations do not introduce new task domains.

E2.justification: ReMDM and TReASURe, previously discussed only as related work, are now evaluated against UMF on LiveCodeBench and MATH respectively (Tables 12–13). This substantially extends direct comparison, including adding a MATH comparator where v1 reported UMF alone. Existing BoN, DTS*, Pair, and AB-MCTS comparisons remain.

E3.justification: New evaluation protocols include block-size-4 decoding, a three-model configuration at fixed NFE, public-test dropping, and runtime/memory measurement. Appendix A.6 also compares rule-based extraction and math_verify on identical MATH outputs. The retained main experiments keep their sample sizes and budgets; identifying math_verify for unchanged main scores does not establish that their evaluation procedure changed.

E4.justification: v2 substantially expands analysis beyond the original caching, action-type, and two-model ablations. It adds tokenizer-length drift measurement, three-model action-set analysis, runtime/memory and offloading analysis, public-test dropout robustness, and answer-extraction sensitivity. Table 3 also supplements cache-hit rates with saved-NFE measurements.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without documented repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or formal significance tests. The additional experiments do not introduce a new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Original main benchmark scores are retained, but substantial results are added. Tables 5 and 7 report three-model scores of 32/87/76 alongside unchanged two-model scores of 28/88/72. Table 6 reports block-decoding scores rising from 19% to 31% across budgets, and Table 10 reports 28/28/25/24% under increasing public-test dropout. Other additions include runtime/memory, alternative MATH extraction, and ReMDM/TReASURe results. These are additional configurations and evaluations, not revised scores for the original setting.

M1.justification: The main MCTS algorithm, deterministic actions, and caching remain unchanged. Appendix A.2 adds a targeted block-diffusion adaptation: actions remain fixed within each block, and search-node creation at mask-ratio checkpoints is deferred until the block boundary.

P1.justification: Localized rewrites clarify tokenizer handling, evaluation, and ablation interpretation; subsection capitalization is standardized. Appendix A is organized into A.1–A.7, but the main narrative and section order remain largely intact. The added scientific material does not constitute a wholesale rewrite.

P2.justification: Tables 6–13 substantially expand the presentation of compatibility, efficiency, robustness, verification, and comparator evidence, with some retained results redisplayed for comparison. Tables 3 and 5 gain information and expanded captions/structure. The existing case-study graphics are brought together and swap Figure 3/4 numbering; the original scaling plots are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds the Stable-DiffCoder citation and removes the Arriola et al. block-diffusion reference. Appendix A.7 adds focused positioning against ReMDM and TReASURe, while the main related-work narrative remains stable. The PG-DLM title/year update refers to the same cited work.

T1.justification: The formal state/action definitions, kernel-selection inequality in Equation (1), rollout-variance reasoning, and Appendix B remasking definitions are retained. No new theorem, proof, or substantive mathematical revision is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important gaps in v1's predominantly NFE-based validation by measuring actual runtime and memory, testing sensitivity to verifier availability and answer extraction, and demonstrating block-decoding compatibility. These additions materially strengthen assessment of practical efficiency and applicability while preserving the original evidence. The new baseline comparisons are explicitly qualified, although their configurations remain incompletely documented and statistical uncertainty remains unreported.

A1.justification: Both PDFs present the same UnMaskFork research. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and Appendices A–B are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v2 retains those results and adds original block-diffusion, three-model, runtime/memory, verifier-robustness, and baseline-comparison results.

before.justification: Section 6 and Appendix A report original coding and MATH evaluations, scaling curves, caching and action-set ablations, and a generation case study.

results.title: UnMaskFork: Test-Time Scaling for Masked Diffusion via Deterministic Action Branching

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion retain the same central claims: diagnosing projection failures, restoring subspace exploration with full-rank QHM, and approaching low-rank DDP performance with reduced communication. The added experiments support these existing contributions.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands interpretations of synchronization, outer-momentum interactions and computation-versus-memory tradeoffs. Its limitations explicitly acknowledge the missing convergence proof and untested longer training and larger scales. It removes v1's gradient-accumulation incompatibility statement and replaces the absence-of-empirical-efficiency discussion with timing analysis.

D1.justification: v2 clarifies fixed rank-ratio hyperparameter transfer and projected-gradient disposal, summarizes selected learning rates and QHM settings in Table 5, and supplies bandwidth and training-time information. These extend documentation of the existing framework; the architecture table, hardware allocation and core pseudocode remain unchanged.

E1.justification: SmolLM2 training and the five downstream tasks are retained. Appendix D.7 adds a modeled 10 Gbps communication environment alongside the experimental 100 Gbps setting, extending environmental coverage without adding datasets or language tasks.

E2.justification: v2 Appendix D.5 and Figure 12 introduce direct comparisons against tuned DiLoCo and DiLoCo with optimizer-state synchronization at both 16M and 125M scales. These substantively extend v1's evaluated DDP and full-rank adaptive-optimizer comparisons; DiLoCo previously appeared only in discussion.

E3.justification: v2 adds an equal-token batch-size comparison, outer-optimizer parameter sweeps, and communication-matched controls using either uniform synchronization or fixed parameter synchronization with adjusted state intervals. It also introduces timing evaluation. Figure 2a's stated model size changes from 125M to 16M, without evidence that this retained experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: New analyses test optimizer-state synchronization, server-momentum rotation, inner/outer momentum interactions, doubled batch sizes and matched communication budgets. The existing projection-signal analysis is expanded from a synchronization sweep to a joint worker-count and synchronization study in v2 Figure 15.

E5.justification: Neither version specifies repeated-run or seed counts, confidence-interval procedures or significance tests. The retained figures preserve their reporting practice; the added comparisons do not introduce a new uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: The original 720M Table 1 is unchanged, including perplexities 10.34 for low-rank DDP and 10.41 for LoRDO-Global. Substantial new results include DiLoCo perplexities of 34.38 and 33.65 without and with state synchronization at 16M, plus measured 100 Gbps training times of 24.23 hours for LoRDO-Global versus 28.96 for low-rank DDP.

M1.justification: The default algorithms and low-rank, QHM and error-feedback updates are unchanged. However, v2 Appendix D.4 adds an experimental Nesterov outer-optimizer variant with server-momentum rotation, whereas v1 deferred investigation of alternative outer optimizers.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main narrative remain intact. v2 moves limitations from Appendix A into Section 7, selectively expands explanations, revises appendix headings and cross-references, and updates affiliation, proceedings and bibliographic text.

P2.justification: v2 adds Figures 5 and 9–14 and Table 5. It replaces v1 Figure 8's training curves with the expanded heatmap presentation in Figure 15, substantially restructures the memory table, and redistributes figures around the expanded discussion.

R1.justification: v2 adds Yang (2021) and Yang et al. (2021) to support its scaling discussion and expands comparisons with DiLoCo and Muon. Most research positioning is retained; the MuLoCo and matrix-perturbation bibliography updates refer to works already cited in v1.

T1.justification: v2 adds mathematical arguments for CompleteP transfer under fixed width-to-rank ratios and worker averaging in Appendix F.1. It qualifies earlier full-rank aggregation reasoning, revises Table 3's memory accounting, and derives a memory advantage over Muon when r < p/3 for square matrices. No convergence proof is added.

improvement.justification: v1 relied heavily on analytical efficiency arguments and comparisons at fixed synchronization intervals. v2 adds tuned DiLoCo comparisons, equal-communication controls and measured timing, substantially strengthening practical validation. Clearer documentation and explicit limitations also help. The 10 Gbps timings remain modeled, and broad superiority wording in D.5–D.6 exceeds some rank-dependent results, but these qualifications do not outweigh the substantial gain in evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe LoRDO. Their complete main texts and appendices, including algorithms, equations, tables and figures, support reliable comparison after matching relocated and renumbered content.

after.justification: v2 retains these experiments and adds original batch-size, optimizer, communication-budget and timing comparisons.

before.justification: v1 reports original language-model training experiments at 16M, 125M and 720M scales, downstream evaluations and optimizer ablations.

results.title: LoRDO: Distributed Low-Rank Optimization with Infrequent Communication

C1.justification: The abstract and principal introduction/conclusion claims retain the rationality framework, extrinsic/intrinsic decomposition, Wasserstein/Rademacher control and three empirical hypotheses. The expanded conclusion presents prospective applications rather than newly established empirical contributions.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly distinguishes objective behavioural rationality from subjective-belief rationality and advantage functions, discusses unavailable optimal values, and expands economic and multi-agent applicability. Figure 5 adds a substantive termination/horizon explanation for Cliff Walking's nonmonotonic curves. Appendix E.2 also incorrectly calls Figure 6's retained gap–shift trend negative, despite its plotted increase.

D1.justification: V2 documents the new L2-strength settings and adds Algorithm 1 comments explaining transition tuples and probabilities. The DQN hyperparameter table, exact-value computation description and code-access link remain substantively unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate Taxi-v3 and Cliff Walking with action-randomised training environments and original deployment environments. The added analyses retain this coverage; the reward-shift extension is theoretical, without a new empirical task or environment.

E2.justification: The comparisons retain vanilla DQN, layer normalisation, L2 regularisation, weight normalisation and domain randomisation. The new L2-strength sweep varies an existing comparator's configuration rather than introducing another comparison method.

E3.justification: The main rational-risk evaluation changes from weighting states by the optimal policy's distribution to the evaluated policy's distribution. Section 5.2 also changes the reported H1/H2 training challenge from 25% to 10%; the earlier formulation and 25% setting are retained in Appendix E.2. V2 additionally introduces a five-strength L2 sweep.

E4.justification: Tables 1 and 7 add focused analyses of sensitivity to L2 strength and the relationship between reward and rational-risk gap. These extend the existing regularisation, domain-randomisation and environment-shift investigations. The earlier main analyses remain available as appendix special-case results.

E5.justification: Table 7 introduces Pearson correlation estimation for reward–risk associations. Both versions otherwise specify five independent runs and standard-deviation reporting; v2 does not establish an increased run count or introduce confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: V2 adds main curves under revised metrics/settings and new tabulated results. Its Table 1 reports Taxi gaps of 35.34±22.91 for DQN versus 15.07±5.71 with L2 strength 10^-3, and corresponding Cliff Walking values of 206.67±26.50 versus 150.13±18.08. These are within-v2 comparisons, not version-to-version gains. V1 Figures 1–3 survive as v2 Figures 4–6, while v1's supplementary reward-by-shift and empirical-risk curves are removed.

M1.justification: Definition 12 adds a practical measurement procedure using an approximate learned action-value function and its maximizing action, extending the earlier dependence on optimal action values. The DQN learner, regularisation interventions and transition-randomisation algorithm remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The main narrative structure is retained, with localized explanatory additions and editing. V2 removes Section 4.7, expands the conclusion into future-work directions, adds a corollary-proof appendix and reorganises the experimental appendix. Much of the existing prose remains unchanged.

P2.justification: The experimental presentation is substantially reorganised: new main Figures 1–3 accompany earlier figures relocated and enlarged as appendix Figures 4–6, with expanded captions. Two earlier supplementary figures disappear, two experimental tables are added, and the notation table is expanded. These changes go beyond renumbering or numerical replacement.

R1.justification: V2 adds positioning against Sunehag and Hutter's rationality axioms, value-alignment research, advantage functions and subjective-utility accounts. It removes the technical-novelty discussion contrasting supervised learning and static domain adaptation, along with the He and Zhang references used there. The overarching novelty position remains.

T1.justification: Definitions 7 and 9 change the state distribution defining expected risk. V2 corrects total variation, revises Assumptions 2–3, and changes the intrinsic-bound factors from sqrt(log|A|) to sqrt(2 log|A|) and log(H/delta) to log(4H/delta), with substantial Appendix B–C proof revisions. V1's expected-risk Corollary 4 is removed. New approximation-error and reward-shift bounds add 2H epsilon and H(H+1) phi terms, supported by a new proof appendix.

improvement.justification: V2 repairs important defects in the central theory, particularly the total-variation definition, policy-drift arithmetic and probability accounting, and removes v1's unsupported direct expected-risk corollary. The revised measurement scope and added sensitivity/correlation evidence substantially strengthen the paper. These gains outweigh the lost supplementary plots, although the new approximation-bound proof contains an unjustified absolute-value step and Appendix E.2 misstates Figure 6's trend.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same rationality-measurement framework. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and definitions, proofs, tables and figures can be matched across revisions and relocations.

after.justification: Section 5 and Appendix E report original DQN experiments, including revised main results, regularisation-strength comparisons and reward–risk correlations.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix D report original DQN experiments on Taxi-v3 and Cliff Walking, including reward, rational-risk and environment-shift results.

results.title: Rationality Measurement and Theory for Reinforcement Learning Agents

C1.justification: The principal dimension-dependent guarantees remain, but v2 removes the advertised fast-convergence contribution for bandit games from the abstract, introduction, and conclusion. It explicitly restricts environments and dynamic comparators to oblivious choices and adds a claim of first worst-case universal regret bounds in Section 5.2.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive applicability qualifications: adaptive environments remain unresolved, exp-concave losses pose additional difficulties, and the dynamic-regret guarantee retains an extra dimension factor relative to the worst-case benchmark. Remark 3 also explains how storing the latest coordinate-sign observation serves gradient variation differently from reservoir-based gradient-variance estimation.

D1.justification: Appendix E.1 newly specifies the number of dynamic-regret base learners, and explicit parameter recipes are revised, including the exploration radius for the nonsmooth algorithm in Appendix C.5. The practical binary-search construction already existed in v1; neither version provides code, hardware, or execution information.

E1.justification: Neither version uses datasets or empirically evaluated tasks. The removed game application and added universal-regret extension are theoretical analyses.

E2.justification: Neither version experimentally evaluates comparison methods. Table 1 retains the same analytical comparison with Chiang et al. (2013).

E3.justification: Neither PDF contains an empirical evaluation protocol. Revised algorithm parameters and theoretical assumptions do not represent changed experimental settings.

E4.justification: Neither version reports ablations, empirical robustness or sensitivity tests, error analyses, or experimental case studies.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental repetitions, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Changes to concentration bounds and estimator moments concern mathematical proofs.

E6.justification: Neither PDF reports experimental numerical or qualitative outcomes. Table 1's analytical bound entries are unchanged; revised theoretical guarantees and proof constants are covered under T1.

M1.justification: Appendix E.2 adds a separate worst-case universal ensemble combining Adapt-ML-Prod, bandit gradient descent, and a shared spherical two-point estimator. Retained procedures also change: Algorithm 1 uses shrinkage δ/r instead of δ/R, Table 2 changes the strongly convex step size from 2/(λ_i t) to 4/(λ_i t), and Eq. (E.7) restores a squared prediction-error term.

P1.justification: Sections 3.1 and 5 receive substantial explanatory rewriting, with guided derivations and fuller descriptions of the ensemble frameworks. Section 5 becomes two named subsections instead of three brief application items. Existing coupon-collector and Bregman-divergence material is brought forward from the appendices, alongside widespread language editing.

P2.justification: The two tables and six numbered algorithm boxes retain their basic designs, and neither version contains figures. v2 reformats Theorem 7 into a displayed case distinction, shifts algorithm boxes relative to nearby prose, and updates the publication footer, producing limited layout changes.

R1.justification: v2 expands contextual citations, including Motwani and Raghavan (1995), Gaillard et al. (2014), and additional dynamic and universal online-learning work. It sharpens the comparison with the Hazan–Kale estimator, while retaining the central positioning against Chiang et al. (2013).

T1.justification: Appendices A, C, D, and E substantially revise estimator bounds, sampling-gap arguments, and regret proofs. For example, the maximal expected squared estimator-optimism difference changes from 4dG² to 8dG² plus the retained remainder, and new Lemma 21 supplies a conditional-moment argument for universal regret. New Theorem 11 establishes worst-case universal bounds without smoothness, while v1's game Theorems 8 and 12 are removed. Obliviousness is made explicit, and the dynamic-regret definition now averages both queried losses.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important mathematical deficiencies: Algorithm 1 corrects feasible-domain shrinkage, Appendix A repairs moment and bias calculations, and Appendix E.2 strengthens the strongly convex universal-regret proof through new Lemma 21. Explicit obliviousness restrictions make applicability clearer. Although the game contribution is withdrawn and some bounds become more conservative, the improvements to feasibility, proof support, and claim precision provide a substantial net gain in rigor.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their text, equations, tables, algorithms, and complete appendices are readable, allowing revisions to be distinguished from relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 remains theoretical. Its additional universal-regret guarantee is supported by mathematical analysis, with no experiments, simulations, or data-analysis results.

before.justification: v1 reports algorithms, theoretical regret guarantees, and proofs, including its bandit-game application. Neither the main text nor appendices report original empirical results.

results.title: Improved Dimension Dependence for Bandit Convex Optimization with Gradient Variations

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same novelty, semantic-trigger, multi-entity-target, attack-success, and stealthiness claims. The conclusion also retains its claim of benign behavior under incomplete semantics. Additional experiments support or qualify existing claims without redefining the core contribution.

C2.justification: V3 adds explanations that excessive regularization overconstrains the trigger region and that stronger pruning suppresses the backdoor while damaging generation quality. Appendix A also distinguishes detection on triggered inputs from overall balanced-set accuracy. These qualify the evaluation while retaining the central semantic-generalization and stealthiness interpretation.

D1.justification: V3 adds a code-availability link, explicit prompts for the new evaluations, and clarification that fine-tuning robustness uses SDv1.5. Table 8 also discloses a twelfth paraphrase for the already-existing Figure 12 ablation; this is additional documentation, not evidence of a newly enlarged training trigger set.

E1.justification: V3 broadens semantic coverage through five additional trigger–target configurations and structured compositional and semantic-adjacent prompts (Tables 2, 5, 9–10). This extends the existing T2I backdoor task; MS-COCO utility data and Pokémon-caption fine-tuning data remain unchanged.

E2.justification: Pruning is newly evaluated as a model-level defense against SemBD in Section 5.6 and Table 6. The six attack baselines, four input-level detectors, and full/LoRA fine-tuning comparisons are retained.

E3.justification: V3 introduces category-based FTR and prompt-similarity evaluation, reporting 100 prompts per category, and a pruning-ratio sweep from 0.1 to 0.9. It also changes the stated evaluation-prompt generator from GPT-4 to GPT-5. The models, 800 optimization iterations, and 5,000-caption FID setup remain unchanged; the PDFs do not establish whether retained results were recomputed.

E4.justification: V3 adds quantitative tests of compositional trigger specificity and regularization versus FTR, stability across five trigger–target pairs, pruning sensitivity, and seed robustness. These substantially expand the questions tested beyond v1's existing qualitative regularization analysis, parameter and trigger-count ablations, target-design comparison, and fine-tuning robustness.

E5.justification: V1 provides no corresponding repeated-seed reporting. V3 Appendix D reports six specified seeds for each model, with individual metric values and means. This substantially expands repeatability reporting, without establishing that earlier experiments used fewer seeds. No confidence intervals or significance tests are added.

E6.justification: V3 adds extensive specificity, trigger–target, pruning, and seed results. For example, Table 3 reports FTR of 3.04% on SDv1.5 and 5.72% on SDXL at regularization strength 0.5; Table 6 reports zero ASR at pruning ratio 0.5. In retained Table 1, benign-model FID changes from 20.59 to 24.49, while other numerical scores remain unchanged apart from equivalent formatting.

M1.justification: Section 4 retains the same semantic trigger construction, substring regularization, multi-entity targets, projection editing, and training losses. The additional evaluations do not introduce a new method component.

P1.justification: V3 locally rewrites the abstract, introduction, and experimental discussion, reorders setup paragraphs, and reorganizes the empirical appendices. It adds acknowledgements, updates affiliations, fixes the placeholder running title, and corrects a figure reference. The overall main-section structure and method/proof exposition remain intact.

P2.justification: V3 adds eight tables and the multi-pair image grid in Figure 14, substantially expanding the experimental displays and rearranging their layout. Figures 1–13 are retained. V1 Tables 2–4 correspond to v3 Tables 4, 8, and 7, with the prompt table expanded and comparison tables gaining underlined emphasis.

R1.justification: V3 adds citations to Jiang et al.'s combinational attack, Guo et al.'s TrojanEdit, and Liu et al.'s pruning defense, and replaces the GPT-4 reference with a GPT-5 reference. The related-work organization and principal novelty positioning remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical objectives, semantic-stability analysis, and convergence argument are retained. V1 Appendices B–C correspond to v3 Appendices E–F with unchanged substantive assumptions, theorems, and derivations; differences are editorial and organizational.

improvement.justification: V3 addresses important gaps in v1's validation through quantitative trigger-specificity tests, evaluations across different semantic concepts, and explicit seed results. These substantially improve assessment of generality, repeatability, and failure conditions; pruning tests and fuller prompt documentation add useful support. Qualifications remain: Table 2's nonzero FTR conflicts with the retained blanket benign-behavior claim, and the new Table 3 ASR values are not reconciled with retained Figure 9.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SemBD research. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material moved or renumbered in v3.

after.justification: V3 retains original experimental results and adds trigger-specificity, trigger–target generalization, pruning, and random-seed evaluations.

before.justification: V1 reports original attack evaluations, defense comparisons, utility measurements, ablations, and fine-tuning robustness experiments.

results.title: Semantic-level Backdoor Attack against Text-to-Image Diffusion Models

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the module-inductive contribution, claimed superiority over 13 baselines, and headline 6.7% average improvement. The added experiments expand supporting evidence without materially redefining these central claims.

C2.justification: v2 clarifies that balanced modules and inducing points serve architectural purposes rather than representing biological sizes or entities. It qualifies Reactome enrichment as a partial external audit, interprets new coactivation and prior-removal results, and tempers the clustering comparison to complementary gains. The existing limitations discussion is retained under Section A.8.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-repository link, specifies shared trainable inducing points and separately sampled cells paired through latent mini-batch OT, and documents settings and resource use for scalability experiments. Core training configurations remain unchanged. Algorithm 1 loses its explicit input declaration, a small documentation regression.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates genetic perturbations on Norman and Replogle RPE1. v2 adds chemical-response prediction on ComboSciPlex and a distinct cross-cell-line scenario that trains on Replogle K562 and tests on held-out RPE1 perturbations (Section A.5). These substantially broaden intervention and transfer coverage.

E2.justification: Comparator membership in the retained genetic benchmark tables is unchanged. CPA becomes an evaluated baseline in the new ComboSciPlex comparison alongside scGPT, STATE, and CellFlow (v2 Table 4). scDFM is cited for split construction but is not reported as an evaluated comparator.

E3.justification: v2 adds discriminative cosine, energy-distance, and Wasserstein evaluations, specifying PCA-space calculations, Sinkhorn regularization, and averaging across perturbations. It also introduces drug-holdout and cross-cell-line testing designs and larger-gene-set configurations with changed model dimensions and batch sizes. Norman's stated split protocol changes from GEARS to scDFM, although split counts and main scores remain unchanged; this does not establish that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's clustering, encoder, loss, embedding, and hyperparameter ablations, v2 tests perturbation-adaptive clustering, removal of individual biological priors, alternative pooling, and larger gene sets. It also adds cross-module coactivation analyses, UMAP distribution case studies, and cross-cell-line robustness testing (Tables 5–6, 9–10, 18 and Figure 7). These substantially expand mechanism and robustness evidence.

E5.justification: The existing five-seed standard-deviation tables are retained. v2 additionally reports bootstrap positive rates for coactivation, means with standard errors across perturbations, paired Wilcoxon tests against CellFlow, and 95% confidence intervals for clustering/encoder comparisons (Tables 5, 14–15). This substantially expands uncertainty reporting without documenting an increase in the original seed count.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 retain their original genetic-benchmark values, while v2 adds substantial new results. Examples include ComboSciPlex rho-delta of 0.8671 for scBIG versus 0.8387 for CPA, and cross-cell-line MSE of 0.0324 versus CellFlow's 0.0377. Further additions cover distributional metrics, ablations, scalability, and coactivation. These are newly reported comparisons, not demonstrated performance improvements between versions.

M1.justification: The GRC–GCAE architecture, flow-matching backbone, and alignment losses remain unchanged. Section 3.4 adds a drug-specific adaptation using ChemBERTa molecular conditioning. The added descriptions of inducing points and mini-batch OT pairing clarify implementation without establishing a revision to the existing genetic-perturbation method.

P1.justification: v2 adds 'Single-Cell' to the title, updates author and affiliation presentation, adds acknowledgments, and introduces experimental and appendix subsections. Several explanations and captions are refined, but most existing prose and the overall narrative structure are retained rather than extensively rewritten.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the empirical displays with drug and transfer comparisons, coactivation, scalability, pooling, distributional metrics, and uncertainty tables, plus a new four-panel UMAP figure. The clustering-ablation table gains rows. Existing framework diagrams, enrichment heatmaps, and other plots are retained, with relocation and caption updates.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations including ChemBERTa, scDFM, protein-representation clustering, ProtChatGPT, and work on biomedical transformers and conditional image generation. These support new experimental choices and broaden context, while the central positioning against gene-wise representations and static biological graphs remains intact.

T1.justification: The method's mathematical objectives, assignment formulation, encoder equations, and existing metric definitions are retained. New Equations 16–18 state standard formulas for the added evaluation metrics; they do not introduce substantive theoretical reasoning, new formal assumptions, or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical support by addressing v1's acknowledged narrow evaluation scope through chemical perturbations and cross-cell-line transfer, while adding targeted component ablations, distributional validation, and statistical uncertainty. These gains directly support generalization and design choices. Some new protocols and uncertainty procedures remain sparsely documented, and Table 14's means are not reconciled with Table 1, but these reporting weaknesses do not outweigh the broader and more discriminating validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same scBIG research and contain readable main texts and appendices. Methods, equations, tables, and figures can be matched across additions, relocation, and renumbering, supporting a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds drug-perturbation prediction, cross-cell-line transfer, further ablations, distributional comparisons, and statistical analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original Norman and RPE1 prediction experiments, component ablations, biological analyses, efficiency measurements, and five-seed variability estimates.

results.title: Beyond Independent Genes: Learning Module-Inductive Representations for Single-Cell Gene Perturbation Prediction

C1.justification: The central hierarchical-gating, retrieval-quality, and HolisQA contributions remain. V2's conclusion modestly broadens the claimed applicability to organizing long contexts and long-term memory for LLMs and agents. Mentioning HolisQA in the abstract promotes a contribution already present in v1's introduction.

C2.justification: Section 7 newly identifies non-task-adaptive hierarchy construction and limited domain coverage as limitations. Appendix H.2 adds an interpretation linking filtering reliability to backbone capacity. Section 5.3 more explicitly explains the precision loss from structural expansion alone and relates gains over CausalRAG to graph heterogeneity.

D1.justification: V2 adds reported code and HolisQA access information, explicit Algorithm 1 function descriptions, the default hop decay of 0.7, expert-audit sampling and annotation details, and construction/query token, time, and cost breakdowns. Together these substantially expand practical reproducibility information. Appendix F.3 also removes v1's blanket statement that other baseline parameters use defaults.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same five standard QA datasets and five HolisQA domains. The added studies reuse existing coverage, mainly HolisQA-CompSci; gate perturbations and backbone substitutions change internal configurations rather than the represented data or QA tasks.

E2.justification: The benchmark comparator sets in Tables 3–4 are unchanged. Appendix E.1 adds evaluated Random and Semantic gate-construction comparators, alongside false-positive and false-negative gate variants, in the new Table 6 comparison.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include a 500-question gate comparison with matched gate counts, four six-value hyperparameter sweeps, cross-backbone filtering evaluation using Jaccard similarity, and cost/latency measurements normalized per 1K corpus tokens and per query. These substantially extend the evaluation protocol; the retained main benchmarks keep their stated backbone and metrics.

E4.justification: V2 extends the existing component ablations and gate on/off analysis with random-versus-semantic gate controls, 25% gate addition/removal tests, hyperparameter sensitivity, backbone stability, and quantified expert validation. Appendix D.2 also adds two cross-module retrieval cases. These address mechanism specificity, gate errors, reliability, and practical cost.

E5.justification: Appendix H.2 newly reports three filtering runs per backbone and mean pairwise Jaccard similarities. The expert audits also report inter-annotator agreement. Figure 13's existing 95% bootstrap confidence intervals are retained; no repeated-run uncertainty is added to the main benchmark tables.

E6.justification: Tables 3–4 and the existing ablation and scalability results retain their values. Substantial new results include gate-comparison F1 scores of 31.62 for Causal, 23.86 for Random, and 24.87 for Semantic; query cost and latency of $0.00049 and 0.801 seconds; and sensitivity, stability, and expert-audit outcomes. These are additional results, not improvements over v1 under unchanged settings.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 removes the score threshold tau and explicitly constructs undirected binary gates instead of scored directed gates. This is a limited specification correction: v1's Figure 9 already used binary judgments accepting either causal direction. The hierarchy, seeding, traversal, filtering, and generation stages remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The paper consistently adopts CausalRAG2, edits terminology and several explanatory paragraphs, and adds organizational headings for sensitivity, cost, limitations, and expanded appendices. The original narrative and most prose remain recognizable; the added scientific material does not constitute an extensive rewrite.

P2.justification: Tables 5, 6, 9, and 10 substantially extend the displayed evidence with cost comparisons, gate variants, a detailed cost/token breakdown, and four sensitivity blocks. Table 9 expands the Table 5 summary. Existing figures are largely retained, with naming updates and relocation, while the original graph-statistics tables are renumbered.

R1.justification: Appendix B.3 adds a broader positioning paragraph connecting the work to formal verification, uncertainty, typicality, and efficient AI systems, citing new works including VERGE, CausalGuard, and FORTE. The main RAG and causality positioning is retained; many other reference changes update metadata for already cited works.

T1.justification: Equation 1 changes the formal gate relation from directed pairs to unordered, non-self pairs. Appendix B.1 replaces the causal-transitivity justification for pruning with a reachability argument through parent gates and hierarchical edges. These revise the mathematical specification and reasoning without adding a substantial theorem or proof framework.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation of the central mechanism. V1's gate on/off study could not separate causal selection from generic extra connectivity; v2 adds matched-count random and semantic controls, gate perturbations, and quantified expert audits, alongside cost and stability evidence. These address an important evidential gap while preserving the main results. Validation remains concentrated in HolisQA-CompSci, and Table 10 leaves differing default-setting scores unexplained, but the gains in mechanism validation clearly outweigh these limitations.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same hierarchical causal-gating RAG framework and HolisQA benchmark, with HugRAG renamed CausalRAG2. The main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds gate-control comparisons, quantified expert validation, cost measurements, hyperparameter sweeps, and backbone stability results.

before.justification: V1 reports original benchmark results in Tables 3–4, component ablations, scalability experiments, and causal-gate retrieval measurements in Appendix E.

results.title: CausalRAG2: Hierarchical Causal Knowledge Graph Design for RAG

C1.justification: The two central methodological contributions and the abstract's headline gains remain unchanged. Introduction contribution (iv) broadens the claimed empirical scope from planning and ARC to 3B/7B models, scientific QA, and mathematics, accompanied by an explicit larger-model generalization claim.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations concerning IWU/RPS complementarity, order-dependent forgetting in sequential training, and how faster convergence offsets sampling overhead. Its new limitations paragraph explicitly restricts demonstrated robustness to the training-task mixture and identifies dependence on verifiable rewards, qualifications absent from v1.

D1.justification: v2 adds measured computational costs and documents model variants, training budgets, and lambda values for the new evaluations. The original optimizer, hardware, rollout, and sampler details remain; the existing code link merely moves to Appendix E. Full dataset and training specifications for the 7B experiments remain incomplete.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates Countdown, Zebra, and string-based ARC across difficulty levels. v2 retains this coverage and adds MATH and SciKnowEval scientific QA, covering biology, chemistry, physics, and materials science, including a heterogeneous mathematics/ARC/science mixture.

E2.justification: The original GRPO, SEC-GRPO, DAPO, and SEC-DAPO comparisons remain. v2 substantially expands comparison methods with sequential GRPO and DAPO under two task orderings (Figure 14), plus explicit IWU-only and uniform-weight RPS-only controls (Figures 10–11).

E3.justification: The original experiment settings are retained. New protocols include 150-step Qwen2.5-7B and OLMo-3-7B-Instruct training, selection of each OLMo method's best-worst-task checkpoint, sequential training for 240 steps per family under two orderings, and evaluation at a fixed 80-hour budget.

E4.justification: v1 already examines task-weight dynamics, RPS/AAS removal, and reward-only regularization. v2 adds component-isolation ablations across both original settings, detailed gradient-mixture diagnostics, sequential-order and forgetting analyses, and computational-overhead versus wall-clock convergence analysis. The retained RPS ablation also gains an ARC accuracy comparison.

E5.justification: Neither version reports independent-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests for the empirical comparisons. New runtime averages and training curves do not introduce repeated-run uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Original headline and regularization results are retained, while v2 adds substantial results. In the new Qwen2.5-7B experiment, MT-GRPO at lambda=0.2 reports 37.6% worst-task and 51.8% average accuracy versus DAPO's 25.0% and 58.3% (Figure 8). New OLMo results reach 45.8% worst-task accuracy (Figure 9), and the 80-hour comparison reports 53.6% versus DAPO's 43.2% (Table 1). These are newly reported comparisons, not version-to-version performance gains.

M1.justification: The stated robustness objective in Equation (5) changes from subtracting epsilon Omega(z) to adding it, with Omega also rescaled. This is a limited objective correction: the implemented GRPO loss, improvement-aware update, and Algorithms 1–2 retain their procedures.

P1.justification: Most existing exposition remains intact with local wording edits. Related Work moves from Section 7 to Appendix A, supplementary experiments receive dedicated subsections, and limitations and impact statements are added. Citation style, author presentation, and acknowledgments also change, while the core narrative structure remains recognizable.

P2.justification: v2 reformats the main text and references into two columns and substantially changes display placement and sizing. It adds evaluation, ablation, forgetting, and runtime figures plus Table 1. The old Figure 8 becomes an expanded Figure 16 with an ARC accuracy panel; the original regularization figures are retained as Figures 20–21.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting the expanded evaluation, including MATH, OLMo 3, and the Qwen2.5 technical report. The substantive positioning against distributionally robust optimization, multitask optimization, and GRPO research is largely retained in the relocated related-work section.

T1.justification: v1 Appendix B.1 is substantively corrected in v2 Appendix C.1: the Lagrangian signs and task-weight coefficients change, and the induced regularizer loses its factor K. v2 explicitly acknowledges that eliminating multipliers only establishes sum(z)=1; restricting z to the simplex produces a surrogate. This replaces v1's claimed equivalent reformulation and repairs central mathematical reasoning.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the paper by correcting the central Lagrangian argument and its equivalence claim, testing beyond the original model and synthetic task families, and adding component and sequential-training controls. The wall-clock analysis directly addresses whether extra sampling cost undermines the efficiency claim, while explicit limitations better bound applicability. Missing uncertainty estimates and incomplete 7B reproducibility details remain weaknesses, but the mathematical corrections and targeted empirical evidence provide a clear substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MT-GRPO. Their main text, equations, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support matching retained, revised, and added material.

after.justification: v2 retains these experiments and adds original 7B-model evaluations, component ablations, sequential-training comparisons, and runtime analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original Qwen2.5-3B post-training experiments on three-task and nine-task mixtures, including sampling and regularization ablations.

results.title: Multi-Task GRPO: Reliable LLM Reasoning Across Tasks

C1.justification: The central claim is narrowed from demonstrating synergy-dominated synthetic artifacts to providing suggestive evidence of structured redundancy-synergy patterns. Claims of consistent generalization become explicit improvements on 11 of 13 sets with codec/channel limitations. The abstract and conclusion distinguish overall gains from gains on the improved subset, while retaining the HyperPotter contribution.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly limits O-information to a diagnostic interpretation rather than a formal decomposition into pure redundancy or synergy. It acknowledges that removing components can improve codec-heavy results, proposes adapting the redundancy-synergy balance, and discusses efficiency, stability, and longer-input tradeoffs. The codec-masking hypothesis itself was already present in v1.

D1.justification: v2 supplies detailed HAGNN pseudocode, hyperparameter provenance, exact cluster configurations, checkpoint epochs, the 2,000-sample ITW selection disclosure, and operational details for new diagnostics and timing experiments. It specifies the cost-measurement hardware and batch sizes and replaces the anonymous code/model access reference with a GitHub repository reference.

E1.justification: Appendix D.2 adds evaluations on varied speech patterns using EmoFake, MLAAD with MAILABS, and SingFake, plus a fake-only MLAAD evaluation. This broadens the evaluated data and scenarios beyond the retained 13-set suite. PartialSpoof was already used in v1 and is not a newly introduced dataset.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds Wav2Vec2+VIB with and without HAR, distinguishing HAR's additional resynthesized training data. Table 7 also includes VIB's MLAAD accuracy, while Figure 3 introduces an architecture-matched untrained control. The original detection comparators remain.

E3.justification: v2 adds checkpoint-selection reruns using reported-disjoint, 2,000-sample PartialSpoof and ASVspoof5 development sets (Table 4), eight-second input evaluations (Table 16), accuracy for fake-only MLAAD, and new HOI and computational-cost evaluation procedures. The original four-second ASVspoof2019 LA training configuration remains the main setting.

E4.justification: New analyses test learned versus untrained O-information patterns, checkpoint-selection dependence, amplification transpose and normalization choices, FCM iteration sensitivity, computational scaling, and longer inputs. Table 9 also extends component ablations across all 13 original evaluation sets. Existing codec, SSL-front-end, convergence, and PartialSpoof analyses are retained.

E5.justification: v1 specifies seed 1234 and reports point estimates. v2 Table 15 reports both HyperPotter and baseline results for seeds 1234, 1111, and 4321 on five datasets, together with means and standard deviations. This introduces substantive repeated-run and uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: The original benchmark EER and F1 values remain unchanged, but substantial new results appear throughout the appendices. Examples include EmoFake EERs of 1.40% versus the baseline's 2.01%, and eight-second 21LA EERs of 2.04% versus 4.10%. The conclusion's former 15.32% average-gain figure is replaced with explicitly defined relative EER reductions of 12.68% across all 13 sets and 22.15% across the 11 improved sets.

M1.justification: The backbone, FCM hyperedges, relational amplification, prototype initialization, alignment stages, and EMA updates are retained. Algorithm 1 and expanded operator and greedy-alignment descriptions provide additional implementation documentation without establishing a change to the proposed method.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, information-theoretic exposition, amplification explanation, and conclusion receive substantive rewrites. Appendices A–I are reorganized into A–F with thematic subsections, and Discussion, Acknowledgements, and Impact Statement sections are added. This substantially revises the narrative and document organization.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from a single-column manuscript to a two-column conference layout. Retained figures are resized and relocated, while new trained/untrained heatmaps, an algorithm display, expanded comparison tables, and several new experimental tables substantially change the presentation. Existing appendix plots remain identifiable despite renumbering and relocation.

R1.justification: Targeted citations are added for VIB comparisons, HOI diagnostics, information-bottleneck motivation, incremental deepfake learning, and graph augmentation. Examples include Doan et al. (2024), Urbina-Rodriguez et al. (2026), and Pan et al. (2023). The overall related-work structure and hypergraph/prototype positioning remain.

T1.justification: Appendix F.2 adds time and memory complexity derivations, and Appendix B.3 defines centroid-based variables and label-relevant O-information gain. Section 5.3 replaces the optimal-permutation expression with an explicit greedy assignment formulation. These are bounded formal additions and corrections; the principal entropy, FCM, amplification, and EMA equations remain.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation that previously relied on ITW-based checkpoint selection and one reported seed. Alternative development-set experiments (Table 4), seed uncertainty (Table 15), trained/untrained HOI diagnostics, and detailed implementation and cost reporting address important evidential and reproducibility gaps. The revised headline claims also better reflect the retained results. The main scores still use ITW-based selection and the synergy interpretation remains suggestive, but the added controls and qualifications materially improve the paper's credibility.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe HyperPotter, with matching core methodology and identifiable correspondences across the main text and appendices. Text, equations, tables, and figures are readable and support a complete comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds development-set replacement experiments, additional benchmark evaluations, O-information diagnostics, seed comparisons, and computational-cost measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original HyperPotter evaluations, a retrained baseline, component ablations, codec-augmentation experiments, and representation analyses, including PartialSpoof case studies.

results.title: HyperPotter: Spell the Charm of High-Order Interactions in Audio Deepfake Detection

C1.justification: The abstracts and numbered contributions retain the same headline claims: noiseless exponential acceleration, superior noisy optimization scaling, implicit task alignment and matrix preconditioning, and the oracle-aligned SignGD comparison. Additional controls and refined formal conditions do not replace these core contributions.

C2.justification: Section 6.2 replaces the Hessian-centered explanation of TRA-SignGD with a one-dimensional logit-gap account and expands the explanation of vanilla SignGD's oscillations. Remark 4.3 interprets the NGD control. The new limitations discussion explicitly addresses orthogonal embeddings, zero initialization, the gap to practical transformers, omitted momentum, and exclusion of covariance-based preconditioners such as Shampoo and SOAP.

D1.justification: V2 newly discloses pretraining batch size 512, sequence length 2048, constant learning rates and the seven-rate sweep. It also specifies AdamW/full-Muon hyperparameters and random-initialization construction. These improve documentation without establishing changes to the retained LLM runs. Conversely, v1's explicit statement that MNIST Muon uses exact SVD without approximation is dropped.

E1.justification: The associative-memory, MNIST digits 1–9 and LLaMA pretraining tasks remain. Appendix G.3 adds empirical noiseless associative-memory evaluation alongside the previously evaluated noisy setting. Random initialization changes optimizer settings rather than dataset coverage.

E2.justification: The comparison set expands substantially: AdamW is added to both the numerical simulations and MNIST experiments, full Muon is added to the MNIST comparison, and normalized GD is evaluated against GD and Muon in Appendix G.3. These provide practical and normalization-based comparators absent from v1.

E3.justification: MNIST's stated learning rate changes from 0.01 to 0.005 and batch size from 64 to 128, while the architecture, 20 epochs and metrics remain. The K=1000, C=100 simulation is removed. New initialization tests use Gaussian matrices normalized to Frobenius norms 1 or 1000 and display loss over 100 steps.

E4.justification: Appendix G.3 adds a control testing whether global gradient normalization explains Muon's advantage. Appendix G.4 adds initialization robustness tests, with loss trajectories and task-space update heatmaps examining alignment beyond zero initialization. These directly investigate mechanism and assumption sensitivity. The earlier K=1000 size check is removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or error bars. The Gaussian standard deviation specified for v2's initialization experiment describes the initialization distribution, not statistical uncertainty.

E6.justification: New results cover AdamW, full Muon's lower MNIST loss and smaller accuracy gap than AdamW, NGD's slower and less balanced learning than Muon, and behavior under random initialization. MNIST curves are replaced under changed settings, so they do not establish same-setting improvements over v1. The K=1000 results disappear. Figure 2 retains the LLM scaling slopes of -0.66 for SGD and -1.13 for Muon.

M1.justification: The analyzed momentum-free Muon update, linear softmax memory model, cross-entropy objective and TRA-SignGD procedure are retained. Full Muon and normalized GD are added as experimental comparators; they do not revise the central method.

P1.justification: Focused rewriting affects the optimization-target and preconditioning explanations, and the conclusion becomes 'Conclusions and Limitations.' Supporting proofs are regrouped, including moving minimizer proofs into Appendix B. Acknowledgments, an impact statement and author-information updates are added. The main section sequence and much of the existing prose and proofs remain.

P2.justification: The main text and references change from a single-column layout to a two-column conference format. Figure 1 gains comparator curves and revised legends, with panel 1a changing from logarithmic to linear loss scaling. Figure 2 is resized into one column. The old K=1000 Figure 3 is removed; new figures show NGD comparisons, initialization losses and a large update-matrix heatmap grid.

R1.justification: V2 explicitly connects momentum-free Muon to SpecGD, adds NGD acceleration references and recent SignSGD/scaling-law work, and discusses Shampoo/SOAP as outside scope. Several earlier Hessian and logistic-regression references are removed. These refine the context while retaining the claimed first theoretical characterization of Muon's scaling laws.

T1.justification: Proposition 3.3 gains a necessary-and-sufficient characterization through diverging logit gaps, and Appendix B.3 replaces the scalar stability argument with a full Jacobian/eigenvalue proof. V1's all-time Lemma 6.1 becomes a proposition restricted to the noisy descent phase. Theorems 5.1–5.2 revise loss versus excess-risk statements; Appendix D retains the M^2 factor in the phase-end bound and qualifies the C-fold speedup for fixed M. The scaling assumption also changes from (log K)^(1/beta) much smaller than M to less than or equal to M.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially improves theoretical precision by restricting the overbroad all-time preconditioning statement, supplying a full stability proof and preserving the group-count dependence in the noisy comparison. The NGD and initialization controls strengthen evidence about mechanism and assumptions, while explicit limitations better calibrate applicability. Removing the K=1000 experiment and exact-SVD disclosure loses useful evidence and detail, but these losses are outweighed by the improvements to central arguments and their support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Muon associative-memory research. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, references and appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting and appendix renumbering.

after.justification: Section 7 retains original simulation, MNIST and pretraining results. Appendix G additionally reports normalized-GD comparisons and random-initialization experiments.

before.justification: Section 7 and Appendix I report original associative-memory simulations, imbalanced-MNIST experiments and LLaMA-style pretraining scaling results.

results.title: Muon in Associative Memory Learning: Training Dynamics and Scaling Laws

C1.justification: The abstract and central contributions remain largely stable. However, contribution 2 replaces the claim of optimal accuracy and efficiency with simple and effective estimation, and the new Discussion explicitly qualifies the ability to solve arbitrary reward-alignment problems.

C2.justification: v2 replaces the categorical posterior-versus-weighted efficiency comparison with reward-dependent importance-sampling reasoning and an open theoretical question. The new Discussion identifies large variance under poor prior coverage and errors inherited from imperfect distillation. New analyses also interpret reward hacking, Monte Carlo scaling, and excessive-noise failures.

D1.justification: v2 adds an experiment-code pointer, a FLUX checkpoint identifier, ImageNet architecture and initialization details, training configurations, sample counts, and NFE formulas. It also explains previously unspecified practical weighting, gradient normalization, and SANA score/velocity approximations. These disclosures substantially improve reproducibility without establishing changes to every retained experiment.

E1.justification: v2 adds ImageNet1k at 256×256, including class-conditional generation, 32× super-resolution, and prompt-guided generation of unusual compositions. It also adds UniGenBench++ evaluation. CIFAR-10, CelebA, and GenEval coverage is retained.

E2.justification: v2 substantially broadens direct comparisons: DPS participates in new posterior-guidance and SMC evaluations, while Flow Map Guidance is compared with Weighted Diamond Maps on FLUX and in SANA qualitative examples. Table 1 also adds HyperNoise, explicitly sourcing that result from Eyring et al. (2025).

E3.justification: New experiments introduce FLUX sampling configurations, ImageNet SiT/CFG settings, KID evaluation, held-out reward protocols, and explicit compute accounting across model sizes. The retained CIFAR/CelebA training description changes the outer-time range from [0.01, 1.0] to [0.01, 0.99]; this reported revision does not establish that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds FLUX sensitivity analyses for noise, guidance frequency, and Monte Carlo samples; ImageNet analyses of sample allocation and SMC particle tradeoffs; and a held-out reward test of reward hacking. Existing SANA ablations and CelebA robustness analyses are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Figures 7 and 10 newly specify shared initial-noise seeds across qualitative comparisons, and Appendix D.1.4 discloses shared noise across SMC particles. Neither version reports confidence intervals, significance tests, or variability across repeated experimental runs.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive ImageNet sampling, recovery, SMC, and prompt-alignment results, plus FLUX results reaching 0.785 on GenEval and 0.653 on UniGenBench++ in Figure 9. The original SANA mean GenEval score of 0.83 and CIFAR/CelebA FID table values remain unchanged. These are chiefly new-setting results, not demonstrated improvements over v1 under identical settings.

M1.justification: The two Diamond Map constructions remain. The stated distillation losses gain stop-gradient targets, Algorithm 2 adds ESS-triggered resampling and weight resets, and Algorithm 3 presents approximate, normalized guidance variants. The PDFs do not establish whether the newly documented practical heuristics changed the retained SANA experiments.

P1.justification: The experimental narrative is extensively rewritten into implementation, model-specific analysis, and compute-scaling discussions. Appendix D is reorganized into separate dataset, guidance, SMC, normalization, and model subsections, and a new Discussion closes the paper. Most introductory and core theoretical exposition remains recognizable.

P2.justification: v2 adds substantial comparison grids, ablation panels, and ImageNet tables, and expands Tables 1 and 2. It incorporates v1 Figure 6 into the three-panel Figure 9. Existing displays are also relocated: v1 Figures 5, 7, and 8 become v2 Figures 17, 11, and 12.

R1.justification: v2 adds references including Test-time Scaling of Diffusions with Flow Maps, Noise Hypernetworks, newer distillation methods, and the added datasets and benchmark. Section 6 removes the claim of being first to construct stochastic flow maps, while retaining most of the existing research positioning.

T1.justification: Appendix A.9 adds a formal extension to general stochastic proposal operators, including change-of-variables and Jacobian-determinant terms and alternative proposal examples. The central consistency results, DDPM transition result, and their original proofs are substantially retained.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's narrow empirical validation and sparse experimental documentation through ImageNet tests, FLUX and UniGenBench++ evaluations, direct guidance comparisons, and held-out reward analyses. Implementation disclosures and explicit variance and distillation limitations make the claims more assessable. Practical normalized guidance still differs from the proved estimator, and uncertainty reporting remains limited, but these gaps do not outweigh the substantial gains in evidence and reproducibility.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Diamond Maps research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–D are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial expansion and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds ImageNet, FLUX, UniGenBench++, and held-out reward evaluations in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original posterior-sampling, image-recovery, SMC, and SANA-Sprint alignment experiments, including FID results, GenEval scores, and ablations.

results.title: Diamond Maps: Efficient Reward Alignment via Stochastic Flow Maps

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contribution: lightweight diffusion drafting conditioned on target features enables fast, lossless speculative decoding. The headline claims of over 6× acceleration and up to 2.5× higher speedup than EAGLE-3 are unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations that lightweight adaptation preserves useful target-feature conditioning at longer contexts and that KV conditioning and parallel drafting make distinct contributions to speed. Appendix A.3 also argues that the additional projection and activation costs are modest. Existing interpretations and deployment tradeoffs remain.

D1.justification: Appendix A.3 newly specifies the shared RMSNorm projection, Q/K/V construction, bypassed computation and example memory requirements. The new experiments disclose fine-tuning sample and epoch counts and additional serving configurations. The original training recipe and code/model links remain unchanged.
