E1.justification: Section 5.4 adds training on LongAlign-10K and evaluation on LongBench's hotpotqa, qasper and gov_report datasets. This substantially extends the retained coverage to long-context scenarios, reaching 16K context for all three datasets and 32K for gov_report.

E2.justification: The original autoregressive and EAGLE-3 comparisons remain. Table 11 adds native MTP comparisons on three Qwen3.5 models, while Table 9 introduces EAGLE-3-5L, DFlash-AR and input-fusion/KV conditioning comparisons, substantially expanding the evaluated comparator set.

E3.justification: New protocols include fine-tuning Qwen3.5-27B's drafter on 1.6K samples for three epochs, context-length sweeps, and conditioning controls with five draft layers and block size eight. Appendix A.4 adds Qwen3.5, Qwen3-Coder-Next and GPT-OSS configurations, SGLang evaluations at concurrency eight, and vLLM evaluations at concurrency 1, 8, 16 and 32. Existing experimental settings are retained.

E4.justification: Section 5.5.5 adds a controlled comparison of KV injection versus input fusion under both autoregressive and diffusion drafting. Section 5.4 newly tests long-context degradation and recovery through fine-tuning. These address distinct mechanism and robustness questions beyond the retained depth, feature-count, block-size, loss-decay and anchor-sampling ablations.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests for its results. The added experiments continue the existing point-estimate reporting practice.

E6.justification: All nine original result tables retain their values after renumbering, and the original plotted results are unchanged. New Tables 4, 9, 11 and 12 substantially expand the findings. For example, v2 reports hotpotqa acceptance lengths of 3.61 versus 6.05 for base versus adapted drafters at 16K, and Qwen3.5-9B Math500 speedups of 1.7× for MTP versus 3.5× for DFlash. These are added experiments, not revised original scores.

M1.justification: The proposed parallel block-diffusion drafting, per-layer KV conditioning, random-anchor training and loss weighting remain unchanged. Appendix A.3 documents the existing mechanism more precisely; the added autoregressive and input-fusion variants serve as experimental controls.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main narrative structure are retained. v2 adds focused experimental and appendix subsections, broadens the serving-section title, and adds conflict-of-interest and impact statements. Acknowledgements, publication text and cross-references receive limited updates.

P2.justification: New Tables 4, 9, 11 and 12 introduce substantial displays for context adaptation, conditioning controls, MTP/model comparisons and vLLM concurrency. Existing tables are retained but renumbered and repositioned. All five original figures remain, with Figure 5 relocated and resized.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations for LongAlign, LongBench, vLLM/PagedAttention and the GPT-OSS model card. The related-work discussion and positioning relative to EAGLE, PARD and diffusion-based speculative decoding remain essentially unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix A.3 adds explicit mathematical definitions of the fused target features and layerwise Q/K/V construction, together with a parameter-memory calculation. This is a limited addition to the mathematical specification; the existing speedup analysis and loss-weight formula remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v1's conditioning argument relied on indirect depth and no-feature ablations; v2's matched-depth conditioning comparison directly strengthens the explanation of DFlash's advantage. Long-context adaptation tests, native-MTP comparisons and vLLM results substantially strengthen evidence for practical applicability, while Appendix A.3 clarifies the central mechanism and its costs. These gains improve validation and technical transparency without removing prior evidence, although uncertainty across runs remains unreported.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DFlash work. All main-text and appendix pages are readable, and corresponding methods, equations, tables and figures can be matched despite additions and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds long-context adaptation, conditioning ablations, additional model comparisons and vLLM measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original decoding speedups, throughput, acceptance lengths and ablation results, including the appendix experiments.

results.title: DFlash: Block Diffusion for Flash Speculative Decoding

C1.justification: The three-metric framework and central rank-instability thesis remain. v2 explicitly frames instability as persistence beyond earlier findings, foregrounds physical-time grounding and diagnostic decomposition as contributions, and states broader empirical generality. The abstract's ETA-specific headline is removed.

C2.justification: v1 speculates that SHOT-IM's objective explains its frozen accuracy; v2 attributes resilience to retained source running statistics, supported by Table 16. It also interprets contrasting batch- and layer-normalisation behaviour and adds substantive qualifications concerning hardware-specific rankings and default hyperparameters.

D1.justification: v2 supplies a direct code URL where v1 only referred to a supplementary repository, clarifies event-queue buffering and eviction, and identifies the Raspberry Pi 5 16 GB configuration. Core warmup, latency-calibration and frozen-BN implementation details were already present in v1.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates ImageNet-C only. Appendices C.7-C.8 in v2 add ImageNet-V2 natural distribution shifts, ImageNet-R artistic renditions and CIFAR-10-C corruptions, substantially broadening represented data and shift types while retaining image classification.

E3.justification: The original ResNet-50 settings remain, but v2 adds substantially different experimental configurations: ViT-B/16 with a 105.3 ms baseline and revised threshold/budget grids, and ResNet-18 CPU/GPU comparisons with budgets scaled to inference latency. The hardware comparison omits continuous evaluation; new buffering and normalisation controls also expand the evaluation design.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's pressure sweeps and utility decompositions, v2 directly compares buffered and unbuffered execution in Tables 8-9. Table 16 tests source-statistics retention and adaptation parameter scope using ETA and SHOT-IM variants. Hardware comparisons and expanded deficit profiles further investigate failure conditions.

E5.justification: Both versions already disclose single-seed experiments; v2 identifies seed 2025. It adds timing summaries with plus/minus entries in Table 9 and across-corruption standard deviations of rank correlations in Tables 25 and 45. These additions do not establish repeated-run uncertainty or significance testing.

E6.justification: With the enlarged ResNet-50 comparator set, offline winners change from ETA on all 15 corruptions to CMF on ten and DeYO on five; ETA's temporal wins change from 141/240 to 103/240 while its retained accuracy scores remain unchanged. v2 adds extensive results for the new configurations and ablations. Table 4 also replaces near-one covariance entries with near-zero values.

M1.justification: Tempora retains the same buffered discrete scheduler, hyperbolic delay discount and budget-exhaustion freezing procedure. Expanded simulation explanations and experimental variants do not establish a change to the proposed framework's core procedure.

P1.justification: The contribution block is reorganised from three empirical findings into framework scope, diagnosis and persistence. The temporal-pressure discussion and Discussion are substantially rewritten, Appendix B is reorganised, and Appendix C gains distinct architecture, dataset and hardware sections. These changes materially alter the narrative structure.

P2.justification: Figures 1 and 3 incorporate additional methods, with expanded ranks and legends, and v2 adds the ViT rank plot in Figure 5. New ablation, deficit and hardware comparison tables introduce substantial display changes; winner tables gain offline columns, and a large ViT decomposition uses landscape orientation.

R1.justification: Section 2 and Appendix B substantially revise positioning by explicitly crediting Ghunaim et al. and Alfarra et al. with earlier rank-instability observations, then distinguishing Tempora through physical-time constraints and diagnostic decomposition. New method, architecture and dataset references accompany this expanded relationship to prior research.

T1.justification: Equations (1)-(3), the batch-index recurrence and the insolvency reasoning are retained. Renaming the served-index set from P to Q and explaining properties of the existing hyperbolic function do not introduce new mathematical definitions, derivations or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's narrow empirical foundation and speculative explanation of frozen-model behaviour. Additional shifts, architectures and CPU hardware test applicability, while the buffering comparison and Table 16 ablation support protocol choices and a revised mechanism explanation. These gains outweigh presentation inconsistencies, notably Figure 5's 1-32 s budget labels conflicting with the 2.5-80 s grids in Tables 34 and 36. Single-seed and default-hyperparameter limitations remain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Tempora framework. All supplied pages, including equations, figures, tables and appendices, are readable and support reliable comparison despite the substantial expansion in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds comparator evaluations, controlled ablations, additional datasets, architectures and hardware experiments.

before.justification: Section 4 and Appendix C report original accuracy, latency and temporal-utility experiments for seven TTA methods on ImageNet-C.

results.title: Tempora: Characterising the Time-Contingent Utility of Online Test-Time Adaptation

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution statement broaden the demonstrated applicability from scratch-trained GPT models to pretrained modern MoEs adapted through continual pretraining, alongside additional reasoning tasks. Posttraining slimmability, explicitly left open in v1, becomes a demonstrated capability. The conclusion also replaces latency-scaling wording with a compute-quality claim.

C2.justification: v2 interprets continual pretraining as a practical adaptation route while explaining its trade-off against stronger full-pretraining frontiers. The remaining scale limitation becomes frontier-scale training from scratch. New discussion qualifies FLOPs-to-runtime generalization on memory-bound hardware, interprets routing stability across widths, and identifies width-dependent safety evaluation as a consideration.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-access URL, architectural and training-schedule details for the additional configurations in Table 3, Blackwell GPU information, and CPT initialization/corpus information. Existing optimizer, width-grid, calibration-budget, and gamma-optimization details remain unchanged; the additions supplement the original reproducibility information.

E1.justification: v2 adds evaluated zero-shot tasks on HellaSwag, PIQA, and Social IQA, extending coverage to multiple-choice completion, physical commonsense, and social commonsense reasoning (Table 2 and Appendix A.1). The original OpenWebText, WikiText-103, LAMBADA, and WSC coverage is retained.

E2.justification: Matched experiments retain vanilla MoE and the same uniform-width, normalized-probability, shared-gamma, and layer-wise-gamma comparisons. Added scale and task evaluations reuse these approaches. DeepSeek supplies a pretrained backbone; RoE and EMoE remain related-work citations rather than newly evaluated comparators.

E3.justification: New settings include GPT2-Large with 2.5B parameters and 50B training tokens, E64A8/E128A8 routing, and DeepSeek-V2-Lite adaptation. Appendix D introduces 0.5%/5% continued-training comparisons, while Appendices B.4–B.5 add runtime and routing-distribution measurement protocols. The original experiments' stated settings are retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds tests of whether FLOPs predict measured latency/throughput and whether width sampling preserves routing balance and expert-selection distributions (Figures 16–19). Figures 21–22 analyze adaptation budget and width-specific recovery during continual pretraining. Original ablations and routing-transfer analyses remain, including the E8A4 study relocated to Appendix C.

E5.justification: Figure 16 introduces fitted linear runtime-versus-FLOPs relationships, reporting coefficients and R-squared values. This adds statistical estimation, but neither version reports seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: New evaluations report 32.8% and 38.1% matched-perplexity FLOP reductions for GPT2-Large and adapted DeepSeek-V2-Lite, respectively (Figures 10 and 12). Table 2 adds reasoning scores, including HellaSwag accuracy of 0.335 for MoE versus 0.385 for MoSE. CPT and diagnostic findings are also added. The original Table 1 values and plotted results are retained.

M1.justification: v2 adds a continual-pretraining pathway that initializes from an existing non-slimmable MoE checkpoint and continues training under the MoSE objective (Section 2.3 and Appendix D). This extends the training workflow; the nested expert architecture, two-width objective, and inference allocation rules remain unchanged.

P1.justification: v2 adds Section 3.4, reorganizes supplementary material into Appendices B–D, moves the E8A4 discussion to Appendix C, and reorders the ablation and transfer discussions. It locally revises explanations, the abstract, limitations, impact statement, and conclusion, while retaining most original prose and the main section sequence.

P2.justification: v2 adds nine figures covering scale, adaptation, runtime, and routing diagnostics, adds the reasoning-results table, and expands the architecture table. All thirteen original graphics are retained with placement and numbering changes; notably, v1 Figure 7 becomes v2 Figure 20.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for the new reasoning benchmarks, DeepSeek-V3, Llama, and Medusa, and removes the adaptive-complexity hyperparameter-transfer reference. Positioning relative to slimmable networks, RoE, and EMoE remains essentially unchanged. DeepSeek-V2 authorship and the agent-paper publication updates concern retained works.

T1.justification: Section 2.4 corrects the description of the selected-expert set S(x): v1 specifies zero routing weights, whereas v2 correctly specifies nonzero weights, resolving the inconsistency with Equation 7. The numbered equations otherwise remain unchanged, and no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses v1's explicit open question about acquiring slimmability after pretraining through CPT and DeepSeek experiments. Measured runtime validation, routing diagnostics, and broader task and scale evaluations substantially strengthen the evidence for practical applicability while preserving the original results. CPT/runtime protocols remain incompletely specified and run-to-run uncertainty is absent, but these limitations do not outweigh the important empirical gaps addressed.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MoSE work. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched despite relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds larger-model evaluations, continual-pretraining experiments, reasoning benchmarks, and runtime and routing diagnostics.

before.justification: v1 reports original language-model training, downstream evaluation, inference-mode comparisons, and routing and width analyses in Section 3 and Appendix B.

results.title: MoSE: Mixture of Slimmable Experts for Efficient and Adaptive Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list and conclusion retain the same central claims: shared-universe alignment reduces the number of maps, GPA preserves geometry, and GCPA improves retrieval through consensus correction. The additional experiments support these claims without redefining them.

C2.justification: v2 extends the existing weak-consensus warning with interpretations of spectral concentration, candidate-model usefulness and corrector updates during sequential extension. Appendix G adds substantive applicability limits concerning incompatible task structure, PCA information loss and computational costs, alongside risks of transferring undesirable structure between models. This substantially develops the account of when and why alignment helps or fails.

D1.justification: v2 substantially expands experimental documentation through corruption recipes, feature-noise scaling, spectral preprocessing, sequential-update details and hardware/runtime/memory disclosures, including an NVIDIA RTX A6000 in Appendix A.6. However, the implementation repository link supplied in v1 Section 4.1 disappears, and the new lighter Flickr30k correction setting is not numerically specified.

E1.justification: v2 retains the original datasets and adds Flickr30k image-caption retrieval and ImageNet-1k class-prompt retrieval (Appendices A.5 and C.6). It also evaluates Flickr8k under corrupted training correspondences and noisy test embeddings, substantially extending the represented data and test conditions.

E2.justification: The principal NA, PW, GPA and GCCA comparisons are retained. Appendix C.6 additionally evaluates native CLIP-B/16 as a same-split Flickr30k reference, reporting R@1/R@5 of 0.863/0.976; this comparator role differs from CLIP's use as an aligned encoder or anchor in v1.

E3.justification: New protocols include sequential expansion from 10 to 20 models using 2,500 CIFAR-100 training samples, Flickr30k clean/noisy training conditions, Gaussian test-feature perturbations, and PCA-versus-padding controls. Flickr30k explicitly uses a lighter correction setting. For retained TED-MULTI experiments, descriptions change from all ordered pairs and six directed triad pairs to evaluated language pairs, without establishing that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained weak-link, correspondence-noise and trust-parameter analyses, v2 tests unsupported fragile pairs, continual addition, spectral changes, multimodal correspondence corruption, test-feature noise, CLIP-anchor dependence, dimensionality matching and candidate-model selection (Appendices A.1-A.2 and C.3-C.7). These address distinct questions about failure conditions, mechanisms and robustness.

E5.justification: v1 reports five k-means seeds and clustering standard deviations across models, but lacks uncertainty estimates for the principal retrieval results. Appendix A.7 adds 10-seed GCPA repetitions and 95% confidence intervals on three retrieval benchmarks, explicitly distinguishing deterministic GCCA estimates. Appendix A.6 also reports runtime averages over three fits.

E6.justification: Tables 1-3 retain their numerical values, while v2 adds substantial new results. Examples include Flickr30k clean R@1 of 0.640 for GCPA versus 0.626 for GCCA (Table 8), and a failure case at 50% Canny corruption where GPA reaches 0.719 versus GCPA's 0.643 (Table 4). Additional results quantify sequential extension, variability, spectral structure, computational costs and robustness; these are new findings rather than improvements to the original runs.

M1.justification: The core GPA construction, shared GCPA residual corrector, trust loss and inference mappings remain unchanged. Appendix A.2 adds incremental GCPA procedures: GCPA-ADD freezes the existing corrector, while GCPA-ADD-LIGHT updates the corrector after inserting a space while retaining existing GPA maps.

P1.justification: Most retained prose remains unchanged. v2 corrects retrieval subsection nesting, adds the Section 4.5 overview and limitations discussion, swaps the GCPA/GCCA algorithm appendices D and E, and expands acknowledgments. These are limited narrative and organizational changes rather than a wholesale rewrite.

P2.justification: The predominantly single-column document becomes a two-column layout, extensively resizing and relocating figures, tables and equations. Nine appendix tables are added. Figure 3 is redrawn with a percentage-scaled axis and numerical bar labels, while the other existing experimental plots are retained.

R1.justification: The related-work discussion and positioning against pairwise alignment and GCCA remain essentially unchanged. Supporting citations are added for new datasets and encoders, including Flickr30k, ImageNet, wav2vec 2.0 and ALBERT. Publication and bibliographic updates to retained works do not constitute new research positioning.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical credibility through retrieval confidence intervals, anchor and preprocessing controls, and explicit tests of harmful consensus and sequential extension. These address reliability and applicability questions left largely unresolved in v1, while the expanded interpretation explains important failure conditions. Removing the implementation link and leaving the lighter Flickr30k configuration unspecified weaken reproducibility, but these drawbacks are outweighed by the stronger validation and clearer applicability boundaries.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Multi-Way Representation Alignment. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial reformatting and expanded appendices.

results.title: VENOMREC: Cross-Modal Interactive Poisoning for Targeted Promotion in Multimodal LLM Recommender Systems

P1.justification: V3 copyedits the abstract and main text, rewrites the conclusion, adds acknowledgements, corrects the running header, and reorganizes appendix sections. P2.justification: V3 adds substantial comparative displays in Tables 5–8 and 10–12, including rollout diagnostics, latency comparisons, and the multidomain MME table. Existing appendix tables are relocated and renumbered, with associated layout changes. Figures 1–9 retain their graphical content.

It also explicitly relates SPARC to bottom-up divide-and-conquer approaches. results.title: SPARC: Separating Perception And Reasoning Circuits for Test-time Scaling of VLMs

P1.justification: V3 makes localized edits to the abstract, contributions, discussion, affiliations, and publication header. results.title: From Out-of-Distribution Detection to Hallucination Detection: A Geometric View

Appendix J adds perturbation and calibration-subsampling protocols.

improvement.justification: v1 supports practical applicability mainly through one COMPAS illustration despite relying on group calibration. v2 substantially addresses this gap with a calibration-error guarantee, targeted robustness experiments, and repeated held-out ACS evaluation with confidence intervals. COMPAS remains an illustrative constructed-score analysis with changed settings, but the additional evidence materially strengthens the unchanged method's reliability and practical relevance.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching the retained Appendices A–H.

results.title: Fair Decisions from Calibrated Scores: Achieving Optimal Classification While Satisfying Sufficiency

C1.justification: The central corpus, training-pipeline, and original performance claims remain. The introduction and conclusion extend the demonstrated contribution to transfer across model scale, programming languages, and inference paradigms, whereas v1 left agentic and broader model evaluation largely to future work.

Appendix D replaces the earlier untested-agent/single-scale discussion with an explicit limitation concerning broad edits excluded by the five-core-file filter, while retaining cross-architecture generalisation as future work.

Existing hyperparameters and processing specifications remain. The contribution statement changes 'we release' to 'we plan to release'; both appendices already describe a future release, so an actual availability change cannot be established.

E1.justification: v2 extends repository-repair evaluation beyond Python to Multi-SWE-bench Flash, covering C, C++, Go, Java, JavaScript, Rust, and TypeScript. It adds multilingual SFT using Multi-SWE-bench-RL and training/evaluation involving interactive OpenHands trajectories. The original benchmarks and multilingual mid-training corpus remain.

E2.justification: The additional comparisons include SWE-Gym and Lingma-SWE-GPT at 7B in Table 10 and an OpenHands-specific comparison against Qwen-Instruct, SFT-only, and SWE-Gym in Table 12. These extend existing comparator families and controls; the original Tables 6–7 retain their membership. SWE-Swiss is discussed but not included in reported comparisons.

E3.justification: New protocols include 7B models, 300 multilingual test instances with 9,331 multilingual SFT samples, and OpenHands v0.28 CodeActAgent with a 100-turn limit and empty-patch, looping, and turn metrics. Appendix A.7 adds similarity-stratified evaluation. The original 32B training and Agentless settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds controlled checks of transfer across model scale and inference frameworks, including agent failure diagnostics. Appendix A.7 newly investigates whether train-test similarity explains success, using similarity quintiles and manual inspection of the ten closest pairs. The original format, issue-linking, augmentation, forgetting, and sampling analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Appendix A.7 introduces a Pearson correlation and significance test between similarity and resolution outcome, reporting r = -0.061 and p = 0.184. Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, or confidence intervals for the main performance comparisons.

E6.justification: New results include 7B Pass@1 of 14.5%/20.4% on Lite/Verified, multilingual Pass@1 of 12.3%, OpenHands resolution of 20.7%/24.7%, and similarity-quintile outcomes. These are additional settings, not improvements over v1 under identical conditions. Original result tables remain unchanged; Section 3.2 corrects the SFT-only Lite value from 10.3% to 11.3%, matching Table 6 in both versions.

M1.justification: The core filtering, Search/Replace conversion, mid-training, and stepwise SFT procedures remain unchanged. Section 3.4 adds an agent variant trained on 491 successful OpenHands trajectories and executed through multi-turn CodeActAgent, a limited procedural adaptation beyond the original Agentless pipeline.

P1.justification: Most prose and the section hierarchy are retained. v2 adds Section 3.4, Appendix A.7, an appendix contents page, acknowledgments, and publication information; it locally rewrites the conclusion and discussion and corrects terminology and wording.

P2.justification: v2 adds four result tables covering scale, multilingual repair, agents, and similarity quintiles. Existing figures and tables retain their designs, with some relocation and renumbering; Algorithm 1 moves to the final page. These are localized additions and layout adjustments rather than a document-wide redesign.

R1.justification: v2 adds SWE-Swiss as complementary work combining SFT, reinforcement learning, and self-consistency. It also adds references supporting the contamination analysis, code embeddings, and FAISS. The broader positioning around PR-based mid-training remains unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical task formulations and Algorithm 1 are unchanged apart from presentation and spelling. v2 adds empirical similarity and correlation analysis, but no new formal assumptions, theoretical results, proofs, or substantive mathematical derivations.

improvement.justification: Section 3.4 substantially addresses v1's explicitly untested generality beyond a 32B model and Agentless inference, and tests multilingual repair rather than inferring it from multilingual training. Appendix A.7 adds evidence about contamination, while Appendix D states a concrete large-edit limitation. These changes strengthen the central argument's validity and applicability. The leakage audit does not prove contamination absent, and performance uncertainty remains unreported, but the overall evidential improvement is substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Clean-PR work. Their main text, tables, figures, algorithm, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including content relocated or renumbered in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds 7B, multilingual, OpenHands, and semantic leakage results in Tables 10–12 and 16.

before.justification: v1 reports original SWE-bench experiments, data-construction and augmentation ablations, and generalisation and sampling analyses in Tables 6–9 and Figures 2–3.

results.title: Pull Requests as a Training Signal for Repo-Level Code Editing

C1.justification: The abstract and principal contributions retain the same claim: language correlation and conditional-entropy statistics predict data-limited scaling exponents without free fitting parameters, supported by TinyStories and WikiText experiments. Additional evidence does not redefine this headline contribution.

C2.justification: v3 introduces an important qualification to the collapse interpretation: LLaMA's collapse appears sharper at β around 0.6–0.7 than at the independently measured 0.88 ± 0.06, despite compatible autoregressive scaling. It leaves this discrepancy unresolved and additionally distinguishes fitting-window uncertainty from statistical error and explains optimization/context constraints on exponent estimation.

D1.justification: v1 promises a future code release; v3 supplies a specific repository described as containing training code, data, and figure scripts. Appendices C and E additionally specify essential exponent-fitting windows and sampling grids, plus Mamba's architecture and optimization settings. These substantially improve documented reproducibility; repository contents were not independently inspected.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate next-token language modeling on TinyStories and WikiText-103. Additional architecture comparisons and exponent sweeps remain within this dataset and task coverage.

E2.justification: Figure 2 adds Mamba and infini-gram, labeled N-gram in the plot, to the retained GPT-2 APE, GPT-2 RoPE, and LLaMA comparison. This substantially broadens the entropy-independence test beyond transformer architectures to two different model families.

E3.justification: Section 4.2.3 and Appendix C.3 introduce empirical-exponent estimation from the lower envelope across context lengths, fitting its first m points for varying m. The retained experiments' tokenization, evaluation splits, model configurations, and optimization grids are unchanged; newly specified fitting windows do not establish that earlier experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's within-horizon decay analysis and architecture/context comparisons, v3 adds systematic β and γ sensitivity tests in Figures 8–12 and learning-curve fitting-window checks in Appendix C.3. These directly test the stability of the central validation and identify a LLaMA-specific collapse discrepancy.

E5.justification: v1 reports language-exponent point estimates without the uncertainty analysis introduced in v3. Section 4.2.3 and Appendix C add bootstrap errors for β and γ, propagated uncertainty for αD, and 95% bootstrap confidence intervals for empirical scaling exponents. These are estimation procedures, not evidence of additional independent training runs.

E6.justification: TinyStories γ changes from 0.34 to 0.325. New results include Mamba/infini-gram entropy curves, LLaMA autoregressive scaling in Figure 17, sensitivity findings, and the Appendix C.3 interval table; displayed T=64 results are omitted. The table's TinyStories intervals overlap the predicted interval even at m=11–12, although Section 4.2.3 highlights overlap only through ten points.

M1.justification: The prediction-horizon construction, scaling-exponent formula αD = γ/(2β), and underlying training approach remain unchanged. Added architectures serve as comparators; mathematical corrections and uncertainty analyses do not introduce a new proposed learning procedure.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and most existing prose are retained. Changes include localized explanations, a new error-estimates subsection, inserted sampling-noise and uncertainty appendices, conference front matter, and an Impact Statement; the original narrative is not extensively rewritten.

P2.justification: v3 adds uncertainty/sensitivity Figures 7–12 and an exponent-comparison table, merges v1 Figures 8–9 into Figure 14, and adds an autoregressive panel to the LLaMA figure. Legends, color scales, and supporting displays also change. T=64 panels disappear, although Figure 15's caption still lists that setting.

R1.justification: v3 connects conditional-entropy decay to Hilberg's hypothesis and prior entropy measurements, expands discussion of Zipf/quanta-based theories, and adds references for the new comparators and spectral detectability argument. These extend the existing positioning while preserving the claimed contribution relative to prior scaling-law theories.

T1.justification: New Appendix B derives the P^(-1/2) covariance-noise scale under independent-pair and fixed-vocabulary assumptions, using matrix concentration and singular-value bounds; v1 states this scale without that derivation. Appendix A also corrects the collapse derivation to retain H∞ and changes the telescoping sums' lower limit from 2 to 1.

improvement.justification: v1's central quantitative agreement relies heavily on point estimates and visual comparisons. v3 substantially improves its assessability through uncertainty estimates, fitting-window and collapse-sensitivity tests, and an explicit conditional derivation of the sampling-noise scale. Broader entropy comparisons and concrete reproducibility information strengthen that improvement. The unresolved LLaMA discrepancy and caption/table-summary inconsistencies limit the validation, but do not outweigh the substantial gains in evidential support and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching core theory and experiments. Their text, equations, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material across appendix moves and figure renumbering.

after.justification: v3 retains these original empirical results and adds non-transformer comparisons, exponent-sensitivity analyses, and fitted learning-curve confidence intervals.

before.justification: Sections 4–5 and Appendix B report original corpus statistics, transformer training results, scaling curves, and within-horizon learning analyses on TinyStories and WikiText.

results.title: Deriving Neural Scaling Laws from the Statistics of Natural Language

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction narrow the performance claim from outperforming existing foundation models to outperforming or matching them; the contribution list also drops 'significantly.' The central claims about integrating micro- and macro-structure, DGCL, and label efficiency remain.

C2.justification: V1's KISS hardware-shift explanation and generalization caution are replaced by an interpretation of robust cross-hardware performance. V2 adds demographic-bias interpretations, acknowledges demographic-shortcut risks in the Impact Statement, and identifies the hand-designed DGCL distance as a limitation. Appendix E's assertion that DGCL does not amplify bias is stronger than its subgroup evidence supports.

D1.justification: V2 adds a source-code/checkpoint availability statement and repository pointer, CFS/SOF channel and sampling information, and implementation details for the new comparisons, including augmentation settings and DINO momentum. Most original architecture, hardware, and training specifications remain intact; Table 9 corrects '120 epochs' to '120 patches.'

E1.justification: V2 adds CFS and SOF as cohorts excluded from pretraining for sleep staging and SDB segmentation, including an older, entirely female SOF population. CFS also extends few-shot evaluation to both tasks. The original pretraining corpus and existing downstream coverage remain.

E2.justification: LaBraM joins the SHHS1/KISS comparisons in Tables 1–2. New comparisons evaluate SimCLR and DINO pretraining, SleePyCo, SleepTransformer and DistillSleep-T for staging, and AIX for SDB segmentation (Tables 16–19). SleePyCo appears only in the SHHS1 comparison; the original main-table comparators are retained.

E3.justification: V2 adds LSTM-classifier evaluation alongside linear probing, CFS few-shot sample budgets, and architecture controls using batch size 32 with peak-memory measurement. Section 3.3 also changes the stated normalization from all signals to all except SpO2. This establishes a reported preprocessing revision, without establishing which experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained component and demographic-factor ablations, v2 adds a configuration without MAE, cycle-length sensitivity, Macro-Encoder architecture/memory comparisons, and alternative pretraining objectives. Table 4 extends the Macro-Encoder analysis to disease prediction, while Appendix E adds disease-performance comparisons across demographic subgroups.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. V2 continues reporting point estimates; demographic dispersion statistics follow the existing dataset-description practice.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 revise KISS staging accuracy/Macro-F1 from 62.8/60.6 to 71.0/70.0 and SDB accuracy/Macro-F1 from 81.8/75.4 to 85.5/78.0. Numerous external-cohort, LSTM, specialist, subgroup, and ablation results are added; the ISRUC accuracy curve is removed. Main SHHS1 and Table 3 results remain unchanged. The KISS revisions are not established same-setting gains: preprocessing wording changes, and unchanged Figure 11 still yields the earlier KISS scores.

M1.justification: The private/shared Micro-Encoder, bidirectional Mamba Macro-Encoder, hybrid reconstruction/contrastive objective, and DGCL procedure remain unchanged. Alternative architectures, pretraining objectives, and LSTM classifiers are evaluated as experimental alternatives rather than changes to the proposed foundation model.

P1.justification: Most method prose and the main section sequence are retained. Targeted passages are rewritten, Section 4.5 and acknowledgement/impact/conflict statements are added, and the former Appendix D material is reorganized across Appendices D–F. Author, affiliation, and publication-header text also changes.

P2.justification: V2 substantially expands the benchmark and dataset tables, adds columns or rows to existing analyses, and introduces Tables 11 and 14–19. Figure 5 changes from two ISRUC accuracy/F1 panels to three Macro-F1 panels covering ISRUC and CFS. Existing figures and appendix displays are also relocated.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially expands positioning beyond SleepFM and general time-series models to discuss SleepGPT, Sleep2Vec, OSF, LaBraM, and HiMAE. It more explicitly distinguishes SleepMaMi through its second-scale-to-full-night hierarchy. Additional references support the new cohorts, specialist comparisons, and DINO experiment.

T1.justification: The mathematical objectives and definitions in Equations 1–7 are substantively unchanged, and neither appendix adds proofs or theoretical results. Adding braces around the binary event indicator's values is a notation correction.

improvement.justification: The external CFS/SOF evaluations and controlled architecture, cycle-length, and pretraining comparisons address important gaps in v1's evidence for generalization and design choices. LSTM and specialist comparisons also reveal comparative limits, substantially improving the paper's evidential support. Material weaknesses remain: revised KISS tables conflict with unchanged Figure 11, and Appendix E overstates fairness despite Table 11 showing a larger absolute sex gap for SleepMaMi than Micro-only (0.015 versus 0.003).

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SleepMaMi research. The complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching material reorganized between appendices.

after.justification: Original empirical results are retained and expanded with CFS/SOF evaluations, demographic subgroup analyses, and additional controlled comparisons in Appendices E–F.

before.justification: Section 4 and Appendix D report original sleep staging, breathing-event segmentation, disease prediction, few-shot, and ablation results.

results.title: SleepMaMi: A Universal Sleep Foundation Model for Integrating Macro- and Micro-structures

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list, and conclusion retain the same substantive claims about drift robustness, GPU-native retrieval, near-full-attention quality, and decoding speedups. The added experiments broaden support without redefining these central contributions.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive qualifications about the SRHT approximation, the limited benefit of finer radius quantization, and CPU memory limiting batch scalability. It also explains prefill preprocessing costs. Conversely, the specific discussion of cached-activation privacy and misuse in v1's Impact Statement is replaced by a generic statement.

D1.justification: v3 adds a code-repository link, quantizer construction details, exact collision-tier cutoffs, deterministic tie handling, pseudocode, baseline budgets, and workload-selection instructions. It also discloses extending MagicPIG retrieval to decode-generated keys for long-generation comparisons; unchanged main results do not establish when that adaptation occurred. These substantially expand reproducibility information.

E1.justification: v3 adds RULER synthetic long-context evaluation at 128K, including multi-key retrieval tasks (Table 6). This substantially extends controlled retrieval coverage beyond the retained AIME25, MATH500, GPQA-Diamond, and LongBench-V2 evaluations.

E2.justification: Table 5 adds actual LongBench-V2 comparisons with Quest, ShadowKV, FreeKV, RetroInfer, SOCKET, and Twilight alongside the original PQCache and MagicPIG comparisons. Table 7 also expands latency comparisons with Quest, ShadowKV, RetroInfer, SOCKET, and Twilight. Several were previously cited without being evaluated.

E3.justification: The added RULER evaluation specifies Llama-3.1-8B at 128K context and a 128-token generation cap, with its configuration added to Table 1. The four original task configurations and main accuracy metrics remain unchanged. Newly supplied details about existing timing workloads do not establish that those experiments changed or were rerun.

E4.justification: v3 removes v1's explicit alpha-correction ablation finding of approximately 1.5–2.4 Recall@100 gains and the default configuration's 72.74% recall result. The drift ablation in Figure 10 and candidate-ratio sensitivity in Figure 9 remain. Six-tier collision explanations reappear in Appendix B rather than being removed.

E5.justification: Figure 10 retains the same average and standard-deviation reporting. Neither version supplies repeated-run counts, seed protocols, confidence intervals, or significance tests, and v3 introduces no new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Tables 2 and 3 are numerically unchanged, but Tables 5–7 substantially expand reported results. Table 6 reports RULER averages of 83.49 for ParisKV, 84.12 for full attention, and 80.29 for ShadowKV. Table 7 reports ShadowKV decoding faster than ParisKV at 128K: 18.76 versus 24.42 ms/token. These are added comparisons, not evidence of improved ParisKV performance between versions.

M1.justification: The normalization/rotation, analytic centroids, collision filtering, alignment-corrected 4-bit reranking, streaming updates, and UVA fetching remain unchanged. v3 documents quantizer construction and collision tiers more fully; six-tier scoring was already described in v1 Section 5.4. The expanded description does not establish a procedural revision.

P1.justification: v3 introduces extensive explanatory appendices, including a stepwise retrieval exposition and separately organized setup and efficiency discussions. It removes the standalone Design Space Exploration subsection while expanding some of its explanations in Appendix B, adds appendix cross-references, and sharply abbreviates the Impact Statement. Much of the original main-text prose remains intact.

P2.justification: v3 adds notation Table 4, comparison Tables 5–7, Algorithm 1, and TPOT Figure 11. It relocates Table 2 and compresses or rearranges the main experimental displays. The original figures are largely retained, so the substantial display changes come principally from the new appendix material.

R1.justification: Appendix A substantially expands positioning within approximate nearest-neighbor research, discussing graph, hashing, quantization, and hybrid search methods. Appendix B newly attributes the alignment-corrected estimator's inspiration to RaBitQ. v3 also adds recent evaluated baselines and distinguishes internal KV retrieval from external-corpus RAG.

T1.justification: Appendix B adds a proof sketch for the retained Beta-prior proposition and derives the coordinate-magnitude quantizer using Lloyd–Max updates. It explicitly qualifies applying Haar-based priors to SRHT as an approximation. The original proposition and reranking estimator remain unchanged; much of the additional estimator algebra restates existing mathematics.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially addresses v1's narrow comparison set and sparse reproducibility account through broader comparisons, controlled RULER evaluation, quantizer derivation, implementation details, and a code link. These additions make the empirical claims and procedure substantially easier to assess. The gains outweigh the loss of the alpha-correction ablation and localized documentation inconsistencies, including Table 4's incompatible D=256, B=16, and m=8 values.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ParisKV, with matching core methods, equations, and experiments. All pages and substantive displays support comparison. v1 ends with references; v3 includes additional appendices A–D.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds RULER evaluation, broader baseline comparisons, and additional latency results in its appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original reasoning and LongBench-V2 accuracy experiments, decoding efficiency measurements, retrieval analyses, and ablation results.

results.title: ParisKV: Fast and Drift-Robust KV-Cache Retrieval for Long-Context LLMs

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the same central contributions: two hyperbolic retrievers, hierarchy-preserving OEM pooling, up to 29% RAG gains, radial hierarchy encoding and parameter efficiency. New experiments support these existing claims. Removing the conclusion's speculative reference to future scalable and multimodal retrieval does not redefine the core contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations linking OEM's radial spread to reduced hubness and more navigable HNSW graphs, interprets excessive outward weighting as amplifying outliers, and uses MeSH errors to argue for specificity discrimination. Appendix D newly acknowledges approximately 48% HyTE-FH latency overhead and attributes it to unoptimized hyperbolic kernels. These materially expand the mechanism and efficiency discussion.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies the 16,384 pretraining batch size, OEM default p=1, a hard-negative mining reference, FAISS indexing and sign-flip instructions, timing configurations, and the MeSH construction recipe. It also replaces the anonymous code-access pointer with a named GitHub repository. These substantially expand reproducibility information; newly disclosed defaults do not establish changes to earlier experimental settings.

E1.justification: v2 adds MeSH/PubMed hierarchy-sensitive retrieval, requiring discrimination between target abstracts and ancestor, sibling and unrelated distractors. It also extends the reported use of MS MARCO from embedding-curvature analysis to ANN and hubness retrieval experiments. Existing training corpora, MTEB coverage and the five RAGBench datasets remain.

E2.justification: Table 3 adds Qwen-Embedding as a comparator alongside a Qwen-based HyTE-H instantiation. The pooling comparison expands from CLS versus OEM in v1 Table 4 to include Naive Pooling and Einstein Midpoint in v2 Table 7. Existing comparison methods are retained.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include 300 zero-shot MeSH queries at depths 3–6 with SpecHR, recall and MRR; ANN recall against exact neighbors on 100,000 MS MARCO passages and 6,980 queries; and latency for 32 queries on an H100. v2 also introduces an OEM exponent sweep and hubness measurement at k=10. The original MTEB and RAGBench protocols remain.

E4.justification: v2 substantially expands tests of the proposed mechanism: naive and Einstein pooling controls, sensitivity to the OEM exponent, MeSH errors separated by distractor type, and quantitative hubness analysis. These examine outward weighting, specificity errors and retrieval concentration beyond v1's CLS comparison and norm probe. The previous similarity-function and context-size ablations and Bixby case study are retained.

E5.justification: No repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests are added or revised. The existing hierarchy figure is unchanged, and the new tables report point estimates. Hubness skewness is an evaluation metric, not a new uncertainty-reporting procedure.

E6.justification: Principal existing scores are retained, while substantial new results appear. MeSH Recall@1 is 0.963 for HyTE-FH versus 0.810 for EucBERT; newly evaluated Einstein and naive pooling obtain MTEB means of 50.33 and 47.07 versus OEM's retained 56.41. Additional results cover Qwen variants, ANN recall, exponent sensitivity and hubness. Runtime measurements report 22.48 ms for HyTE-FH versus 15.21 ms for EucBERT per 32 queries. These are added comparisons, not demonstrated version-to-version performance gains.

M1.justification: The architectures and OEM pooling operator are retained, but Section 4.4 revises the stated training objectives. Stage 2 gains the missing InfoNCE denominator; Stage 3 replaces the multi-positive supervised expression with a single-positive objective using in-batch and mined hard negatives. These are changes to the written specification; the PDFs do not establish that the original experiments were retrained.

P1.justification: The training stages and ablation discussion receive localized rewrites, with new experimental subsections and a MeSH Appendix E that shifts Additional Results to Appendix F. Correspondence and publication-header text also change. Most introductory, architectural and theoretical prose remains intact, so this is not an extensive narrative reorganization.

P2.justification: v2 adds tables for ANN retrieval, MeSH scores and errors, empirical latency, exponent sensitivity and hubness. It expands the RAG comparison and pooling tables and redistributes existing tables across the revised layout. This substantially enlarges the visual presentation of evidence; Figures 1–4 remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds Oord et al. (2018) for InfoNCE and Nussbaum and Duderstadt (2025) for training and hard-negative mining, while removing Izacard et al. (2021). Appendix E additionally positions the diagnostic benchmark against a claimed gap in hierarchy-sensitive evaluation. The broader relationship to hyperbolic representation learning and existing RAG approaches is retained.

T1.justification: The original propositions, theorems and Appendix A proofs are unchanged. v2 adds an explicit Lorentz-to-MIPS sign-flip argument in Section 4.4 and defines SpecHR in Appendix E. The contrastive-loss equations are also substantively corrected or reformulated.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked direct empirical comparison with the Einstein midpoint and a retrieval diagnostic using known taxonomy levels. v2 supplies both, with sensitivity and hubness analyses that substantially strengthen evidence for its central pooling and hierarchy claims. Runtime measurements also expose practical costs. A material qualification is that the new HNSW explanation extends the query-document sign-flip identity to graph geometry without establishing that extension; this limits the secondary efficiency interpretation but does not outweigh the stronger central evaluation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same HypRAG research. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations and appendices are readable and can be matched across renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds MeSH retrieval, ANN, runtime, pooling-sensitivity, hubness and Qwen-based comparisons.

before.justification: v1 reports original MTEB and RAGBench evaluations, hierarchy probes, pooling and retrieval-context ablations, and a qualitative retrieval case study.

results.title: HypRAG: Hyperbolic Dense Retrieval for Retrieval Augmented Generation

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central claims: traditional metrics inadequately capture LLM difficulty, LM-CC measures semantic nonlinearity, and reducing it improves downstream performance. Shortened contribution bullets and additional supporting experiments do not materially redefine these claims.

C2.justification: V2 acknowledges that LM-CC does not always yield the strongest individual coefficient, hypothesizes that entropy-model capacity and calibration explain differences, and attributes ablation benefits to the hybrid hierarchy. Appendix E.3 adds a latency-versus-expressiveness tradeoff. The original semantic-nonlinearity interpretation and proposed applications remain.

D1.justification: V2 adds a source-code access URL, identifiers and links for additional entropy models, and disclosures about single-pass computation, mini-batching, and per-sample timing. Existing pseudocode, rewriting prompt, attempt count, temperature, and filtering details remain. Summarization dataset/scoring details and timing hardware are not supplied.

E1.justification: V2 adds evaluated code summarization in Tables 2, 4, and 6, extending task coverage beyond program repair, Python-to-C translation, and execution reasoning. The original xCodeEval and HumanEval tasks remain. The summarization dataset is not identified, although the added task coverage is explicit.

E2.justification: Table 5 introduces syntax-only and entropy-only decomposition variants as evaluated comparators against full LM-CC. The existing CC, HC, MI, CoC, and component-feature comparisons are retained. Additional entropy estimators and task-performing LLMs are experimental configurations rather than new competing complexity metrics.

E3.justification: Evaluation expands from CodeLlama alone to four entropy estimators and adds GPT-4o-mini and Qwen3.5-122B task performers alongside DeepSeek-V3. V2 also introduces decomposition controls and per-sample timing measurements. The original length-controlled correlation procedure, alpha and tau settings, and rewriting selection protocol remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New decomposition ablations test the contributions of entropy boundaries and syntax-guided structuring, addressing whether the hybrid construction is necessary (Table 5). V2 also adds analyses of dependence on entropy/task models and computational cost. The original weighting-factor ablation is preserved and relocated to Appendix E.2.

E5.justification: Both versions apply the same significance threshold and select the strongest significant grouped correlation across 9–11 groups (Appendix C). V2's significant-correlation ratios summarize additional outcomes without introducing a new uncertainty-estimation procedure. No new seed information, repeated-run protocol, confidence intervals, or significance tests are documented.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial correlation, decomposition-ablation, and timing results in Tables 2 and 4–6. The original three CodeLlama/DeepSeek-V3 correlation rows remain unchanged. Table 3's execution-reasoning original/rewritten scores change from 97.8%/98.3% to 94.1%/95.0%, and rewritten LM-CC changes from 9.4 to 9.3. These are revised reported results; no explanation or protocol revision establishes their cause.

M1.justification: The entropy-and-syntax segmentation, BFS hierarchy construction, and weighted aggregation of TotalBranch and TotalCompLevel remain unchanged. Equation 4 and Algorithm 1 are retained; additional entropy backbones and ablated variants expand evaluation without changing the proposed procedure.

P1.justification: V2 extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, method explanations, and experimental discussion. It moves the weighting-factor study and Implications section into appendices, shortens contribution statements, and adds acknowledgements and an impact statement. These constitute substantial language and narrative restructuring beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is redrawn with a separate perplexity-distribution plot and revised code/hierarchy panels. Table 2 gains entropy-model groupings and significance summaries, and Tables 4–6 are added. Figure 3 retains its plotted results but is enlarged and relocated to Appendix E.2.

R1.justification: V2 removes the AVATAR citation by Ahmad et al. and the DeepSeek-Coder reference by Guo et al., while retaining the main research positioning. Publication updates for works such as CodeMind and LongCodeZip concern matched existing works. Appendix E.2 more explicitly locates novelty in the LLM-aligned hierarchy rather than depth and branching themselves.

T1.justification: V2 adds a brief argument claiming O(n) token complexity from single-forward-pass entropy computation in Appendix E.3 and frames Assumption 3.2 around semantic rather than control-flow divergence. The principal equations, Theorem 3.3, Corollary 3.4, and Appendix B propositions and proofs are retained.

improvement.justification: V1 relies on one entropy estimator and one task-performing LLM and lacks controls separating entropy-based from syntax-based decomposition. V2's cross-model evaluations and decomposition ablations substantially strengthen evidence for portability and the hybrid design (Tables 2, 4, and 5). Code-access and cost reporting also improve practical assessability. The unspecified summarization protocol and unexplained Table 3 revisions limit reproducibility, but do not outweigh the substantial gains in validation of the central method.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LM-CC research. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching material relocated in v2.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds evaluations across models, code summarization, decomposition ablations, and computation-time measurements in Tables 2 and 4–6.

before.justification: V1 reports original complexity-performance correlations, code-rewriting experiments, and a weighting-factor ablation in Tables 1–3 and Figure 3.

results.title: Rethinking Code Complexity Through the Lens of Large Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion narrow the second headline finding from data-manifold rarity to local sparsity in representation space; the introduction explicitly identifies the theoretical density as that of the bridge mixture. The semantic-fidelity, memorization and KTS contributions remain.

C2.justification: Section 5.2 replaces the assertion that exact matching requires a terminal impulse with a conditional explanation based on how quickly the terminal gap closes. Section 6 and Appendix I add explanations of time-conditioned velocity rescaling, bounded perturbations and limited distributional change, using retained precision/recall results. New robustness and noise controls support additional interpretations of KTS's phase structure.

D1.justification: Section 6.2 newly spells out the nearest/second-nearest pixel-space gap ratio and the 10,000-sample memorization evaluation. Additional experiments document feature dimensions, checkpoint selection, noise controls and perturbation strengths. These expand reproducibility information without establishing changes to the retained training architecture or hyperparameters.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same three synthetic distributions, CIFAR-10, ImageNet-256 and CelebA experiments. New analyses reuse this coverage. Appendix F corrects 'four' synthetic datasets to 'three'; both versions actually describe and evaluate the same three.

E2.justification: Appendix I.4 and Table 11 add inference-time Gaussian velocity-noise injection at sigma=0.005 and 0.01 as comparators against FM and KTS on CelebA. Existing neural-versus-empirical FM and FM-versus-KTS comparisons remain.

E3.justification: New protocols include a 4,000-sample feature-space comparison, phase-boundary and schedule grids, solver/NFE/time-grid comparisons, neighborhood-size sweeps, and reintegration of 200 matched noise vectors. Section 5.3 also changes the stated midpoint budget from 100 steps to NFE=100; this establishes a reported setting revision, without establishing that the retained experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: v2 substantially extends the original alpha/beta ablations. Table 3 tests representation dependence; Tables 6–8 test phase boundaries, schedule functions and numerical settings; Appendices G/H test KPE ranking stability and neighborhood-size sensitivity. Table 11 tests whether generic noise perturbations reproduce KTS benefits.

E5.justification: Appendix G newly specifies seed 42 for the shared bank of 200 initial noise vectors. Existing mean/standard-deviation reporting, Bonferroni-corrected tests and effect sizes remain unchanged. No increased independent-run count or new confidence-interval reporting is established.

E6.justification: Original numerical Tables 1–4 are retained as v2 Tables 1, 2, 4 and 5. Tables 3 and 6–11 add substantial results, including minimum cross-configuration KPE rank correlation 0.9921. Table 11 reports noise injection at sigma=0.005 achieving FID 17.48 and memorization 35.31%, versus KTS 14.35 and 31.22%. These are added comparisons, not improvements over v1's matched KTS scores.

M1.justification: The KPE definition and proposed KTS procedure remain unchanged: velocity rescaling with linear early launch, exponential late damping, default phase boundary 0.6 and k=3. Alternative schedules are tested as ablations; they do not replace the proposed procedure.

P1.justification: v2 edits terminology, headings, explanatory paragraphs and notation, updates author/venue information and acknowledgements, and reorganizes some appendix introductions. The main section sequence and narrative remain recognizable; the largest expansions primarily document new scientific analyses.

P2.justification: Seven new numbered tables substantially expand the displayed evidence, including sensitivity comparisons and a solver-correlation matrix. Existing tables and Algorithm 1 are repositioned, and the visualization appendices move to J/K. Several retained figures are downsampled or rasterized, reducing fine-label clarity without adding new visual results.

R1.justification: v2 adds Lim (2025), 'On the hidden biases of flow matching samplers,' in Section 4.3 and Appendix A. Appendix C explicitly acknowledges the analogous derivation in Bertrand et al. (2025), already cited in v1. The broader research positioning remains.

T1.justification: Appendix I adds a spatial Lipschitz assumption and a proved Gronwall stability bound for KTS trajectory displacement. Appendix B makes nondegeneracy assumptions explicit and restricts the integrated energy bound to interior intervals under posterior dominance. Appendix D removes the additional divergence claim and argument following the terminal-gap lower bound. These materially extend and revise the theory.

improvement.justification: Tables 3 and 6–11 address important weaknesses in v1's evidence concerning representation choice, discretization, KTS schedules and generic perturbation alternatives. Together with narrower claims, revised Appendix B/D reasoning and the new stability proof, these substantially strengthen support for KPE and KTS. The full-trajectory assertion in Remark 4.3 remains inconsistent with the restricted Appendix B.4.2 bound, and some figures lose clarity, but these limitations do not outweigh the validation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same KPE/KTS research. Their main texts, equations, tables, figures and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching the original Appendix G/H visualizations to Appendix J/K in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds representation, numerical stability, schedule sensitivity and noise-injection comparisons.

before.justification: Sections 4–6 report original synthetic-data and image-generation experiments, including KPE correlations, training dynamics, and KTS quality and memorization results.

results.title: A Kinetic-Energy Perspective of Flow Matching

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction expand the contribution from 1.3B language-model validation to improvements across dense models, MoE, vision and diffusion, emphasizing compatibility with standard Pre-Norm recipes without architecture-specific tuning. They also temper the earlier categorical reconciliation and structural-impossibility claims.

C2.justification: New depth, pruning and warm-up interpretations provide more direct arguments for layer utilization and topology-specific robustness. v2 removes the explicit qualification about exhaustive learning-rate tuning for fair comparison. It also replaces v1's limitations concerning uneven downstream gains and massive activations with an appendix limitation about missing rigorous theoretical explanations and convergence guarantees.

D1.justification: Appendix Table 6 adds a full MoE configuration, including 24 layers, 96 experts, top-8 routing, scheduling and auxiliary-loss weights. v2 quantifies training-speed and memory overhead and updates aggregate compute from over 50,000 to over 60,000 A100 hours. Dense-model settings and code access remain unchanged, although the earlier explanation of gamma initialization is omitted.

E1.justification: v2 adds ImageNet image classification and image generation, plus C4 validation for layer-pruning analysis. FineWeb-Edu training and the existing language benchmark suite are retained. This substantially expands the represented data and task coverage.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds evaluated Peri-LN and SpanNorm baselines across all three existing 100B-token learning-rate regimes, including convergence and divergence outcomes. The previous comparators remain, substantially extending the normalization comparisons.

E3.justification: New protocols include approximately 390M-parameter models with four depth-width configurations trained for 12B tokens, and 15A2B MoE models trained for 100B tokens. v2 also introduces shortened/absent warm-up tests, individual-layer removal, and vision evaluation using Top-1 accuracy and FID. The original 1.3B settings are retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds fixed-parameter depth-width comparisons, direct layer-utilization tests through pruning, and warm-up stress tests separating topology robustness from residual scaling. Table 3 adds the Siamese ablation lacking both auxiliary mechanisms. The earlier sub-stream comparison is retained as appendix Table 4.

E5.justification: Neither version documents seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals or significance tests. Existing shaded training plots retain the same reporting practice; the additional results do not introduce statistical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: All 23 shared Table 1 rows retain their values. New results include MoE PPL of 7.92 for Pre-Norm versus 7.76 for SiameseNorm, DeiT-S accuracy of 79.8 versus 81.3, and DiT-L/4 FID of 45.21 versus 41.34. v2 also adds depth, pruning, warm-up, ablation and overhead findings, while dropping the earlier qualitative observation of increased massive activations.

M1.justification: The coupled streams, shared residual blocks, normalized-input mechanism and depth-wise scaling remain unchanged. Algorithm 1 restates the earlier forward equations. Applying the previously described construction to additional model families does not introduce a new method component.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and substantial theoretical and experimental prose are rewritten. Auxiliary mechanisms move into Section 3, topology and auxiliary ablations become separate subsections, and the sub-stream comparison moves to the appendix. The conclusion and limitations are separated, with funding and impact statements added.

P2.justification: Figure 2 expands into a full-width three-panel display with pruning results. Table 1 gains baselines and a MoE setting; new tables present depth/vision results and MoE configurations. Forward equations become Algorithm 1, the ablation table expands, and the earlier sub-stream table moves to the appendix.

R1.justification: v2 adds discussion and citations for SpanNorm, GatedNorm, MoE architectures and the new evaluation domains. It explicitly credits depth scaling and normalized input as established auxiliary mechanisms. The central positioning against ResiDual and Hyper-Connections remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The forward equations and Jacobian derivations are retained. However, Section 3 removes the deduction that subsuming component architectures makes their best performance a lower bound on SiameseNorm's achievable performance, and replaces the categorical prevention-of-vanishing-gradients assertion with a narrower identity-route statement. No new proof is supplied.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the paper's central evidence through direct pruning and warm-up tests, controlled depth comparisons, additional baselines and validation beyond one dense language-model family. These address important weaknesses in generality and mechanism support. Removing the massive-activation and uneven-gain caveats reduces transparency, and vision protocols remain terse, but the stronger validation and more restrained theoretical assertions provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SiameseNorm research. Their text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, MoE and vision experiments, depth studies, layer-pruning tests and warm-up stress tests.

before.justification: v1 reports original 1.3B language-model pretraining results, downstream evaluations, component ablations and analyses of training dynamics.

results.title: SiameseNorm: Breaking the Barrier to Reconciling Pre/Post-Norm

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the central claims about heuristic-oracle mismatch, global utility-based allocation, offline profiling, and 80% cache reduction with limited performance loss. Rewritten and consolidated contribution bullets do not materially redefine these claims.

C2.justification: The new Impact Statement identifies rare-context loss and mismatches in domain, context length or decoding settings as deployment limitations. Appendix F interprets the transfer experiment as reduced dependence on one profiling corpus and the integration results as support for a general allocation layer. Existing explanations of baseline failure modes largely remain.

D1.justification: V2 adds a Project Code link and specifies that the default profiling corpus is a Chinese novel disjoint from evaluation benchmarks. The 30-question count and principal hyperparameters were already in Appendix E. Conversely, Section 5.4 drops v1's explicit explanation of how the no-gap ablation allocates budget. Repository availability cannot be verified from the PDFs alone.

E1.justification: Appendix F.2 adds an English SAT reading excerpt as alternative profiling data, extending calibration-domain coverage beyond the generated novel. V2 identifies the existing default novel as Chinese; that disclosure does not establish replacement of the original corpus. LongBench and RULER evaluation-task coverage remains unchanged.

E2.justification: V2 retains Uniform, PyramidKV and AdaKV comparisons and adds evaluated comparisons with HeadKV using SnapKV and EA in Table 11, plus KVZip and CAKE in Table 12. These substantially broaden the comparator set. EA already appeared in v1's experiments; DefensiveKV is newly discussed but not evaluated.

E3.justification: The existing KVPress question-agnostic evaluation protocol is retained. Appendix F adds 90% compression settings beyond the existing 50% and 80% evaluations, varies calibration inputs, and introduces a fixed-budget HeadKV comparison. The numerical fixed budget is not specified, limiting reconstruction of that new comparison.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained optimality-gap ablation and allocation visualizations, Appendix F directly tests profiling-corpus dependence, extends compression sensitivity to 90%, and holds KVZip/CAKE metrics fixed while replacing their allocation. These additions materially broaden evidence about calibration robustness and dependence on the underlying metric.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals or significance tests. Averaging profiles over 30 calibration questions is already documented in v1 and does not constitute new run-level uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Existing benchmark scores in Tables 1–7 remain unchanged, but Appendix F adds substantial results. Table 9 newly reports 90%-compression scores of 44.29 and 44.69 for LU-KV with KeyDiff and SnapKV. Table 11 reports HeadKV versus LU-KV averages of 45.27 versus 46.37 with SnapKV and 45.34 versus 47.12 with EA. Calibration-transfer and KVZip/CAKE results are also added; these are new comparisons, not improvements to the original runs.

M1.justification: Section 4.2 and Appendix A.2 correct the specified convexification procedure: v1 applies PAVA to the raw loss sequence, whereas v2 projects marginal decreases and reconstructs the loss. This is a localized correction to the stated solver; the objective, greedy allocation and offline/online pipeline remain unchanged. The PDFs do not establish that the implementation or existing experiments changed.

P1.justification: V2 edits the abstract, introductory framing, contribution bullets and several methodological and experimental passages, while preserving the main narrative structure. It adds acknowledgements, an Impact Statement and Appendix F, and updates author affiliations and publication information. The existing manuscript is not extensively reorganized.

P2.justification: Appendix F substantially expands the result displays with tables covering compression sensitivity, calibration transfer, HeadKV and metric integration; Table 13 partly summarizes Table 12. V2 also relocates and expands the symbol table, revises captions, and replaces plotting labels such as 'mytest convex' with 'Our Method'. Existing benchmark tables and most plots retain their presentation.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds DefensiveKV and expands discussion of KVZip's reconstruction-based approach. HeadKV, CAKE and KVZip were already cited in v1. Most other reference changes update publication metadata, while the positioning around metric-specific global allocation remains unchanged.

T1.justification: Section 4.2 removes v1's unsupported inference of NP-hardness from non-convexity and acknowledges exact dynamic programming. Appendix A makes non-negativity and deterministic tie-breaking assumptions explicit, refines the inversion argument, and corrects the PAVA-based surrogate construction. The loss decomposition and greedy-optimality argument remain substantially intact.

improvement.justification: V2 strengthens central weaknesses in v1: it corrects the optimization account and adds direct tests of calibration dependence and comparisons with relevant previously unevaluated methods, especially HeadKV. These improve the technical credibility and empirical support for task-agnostic allocation, rather than merely increasing reported scores. The unspecified HeadKV budget and less explicit ablation description limit reproducibility, but the theoretical corrections and targeted evidence provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LU-KV research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support comparison; v2 retains Appendices A–E and adds Appendix F.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds compression sensitivity, calibration transfer, HeadKV comparisons and additional metric-integration results in Appendix F.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix B report original LongBench and RULER evaluations, allocation analyses, ablations, and memory and latency measurements.

results.title: Predicting Future Utility: Global Combinatorial Optimization for Task-Agnostic KV Cache Eviction

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution statements retain the same claims: efficient, accurate amortized discovery, training up to 500 nodes, inference up to 1,000 nodes, headline mAP of 99.6%/84.4%, and 4-13,000-fold speedups. Added evidence and limitations do not redefine the central contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations of failures under severe confounding, increasing sensitivity to prior quality, cycles under joint size/mechanism shift, and cases where SDCD has lower AID. It also proposes an optimization-based explanation for reduction benefits. The conclusion explicitly acknowledges missing real-world observational validation and generalization limits of simulated training.

D1.justification: Section 4.3 newly documents first reduction after k+1 blocks. Appendix C identifies SEA's Stage 1 public checkpoint and adds training costs of 48 GPU-hours for synthetic Stage 2 and 72 GPU-hours for SERGIO-GRN. CauScale's hardware, hyperparameters, training schedule and project-access information remain substantially unchanged.
