E1.justification: The synthetic SCM and SERGIO-GRN domains remain. v2 adds targeted synthetic scenarios with hidden common causes (Section 5.6) and purely observational inputs (Appendix F.3), extending input conditions without adding a new dataset domain.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains the same setting-specific comparator membership: CORR, INVCOV, FCI, NOTEARS, SDCD, DiffAN, AVICI and SEA-GIES. The new AID comparisons use existing baselines; the revised SEA checkpoint description concerns training settings rather than a new comparison method.

E3.justification: v2 adds AID evaluation with cycle-breaking, broader cyclicity assessment, hidden-node removal protocols, restricted prior-estimation sample counts and observational-only testing. Appendix C also replaces the statement that SEA was trained on the authors' data throughout with use of a public checkpoint for synthetic Stage 1. This is a reported protocol revision; rerunning the retained experiments is not established.

E4.justification: v2 adds analyses of cycle frequency and removal effects, robustness to hidden high-out-degree nodes, sensitivity to noisy graph priors, and performance without interventions (Section 5.3, Sections 5.6-5.7 and Appendix F.3). Figure 4 also revises graph-component ablation results. Existing pooling, distribution-shift and sample-size analyses are retained.

E5.justification: v1 reports averages over five independent test graphs without standard deviations. v2 systematically adds mean-plus-standard-deviation reporting for all main CauScale settings and the AID comparisons (Tables 5-6). The five-graph count is retained; additional training runs or seeds are not established.

E6.justification: Table 1 revises CauScale's SERGIO-GRN mAP from 71.4 to 54.0 at 100 nodes and 34.5 to 39.2 at 200 nodes; corresponding AUC values change from 95.1 to 90.5 and 90.3 to 90.8. Figure 4 changes ablation values, while new tables and Figure 7 add substantial cyclicity, AID, robustness and observational results. The SERGIO-GRN revisions are unexplained.

M1.justification: The core two-stream design and prediction head remain. v2 introduces iterative removal of the lowest-scoring edge in detected cycles as post-processing for acyclic outputs and AID evaluation (Section 5.3; Appendix F.1). The newly disclosed delay of the first reduction does not establish that the network was redesigned or retrained.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and section order remain. Local additions expand related work, explanations and limitations, introduce two robustness subsections and Appendices E-F, and update affiliations and acknowledgements. An added cross-reference is incorrect: Section 5.6 points to Table 7 rather than the confounding plot in Figure 7.

P2.justification: v2 adds the latent-confounding plot and five numbered tables covering cycles, prior errors, AID, uncertainty and observational results, plus complexity-analysis displays. Figure 2 swaps displayed row/column attention labels, and captions and placements change. The original pooling table and sample-size plot are retained as Table 3 and Figure 8.

R1.justification: Related work adds Granger/time-series approaches citing Gallagher, Tank, and Brown and Carlson, plus an explicit comparison with SEA's strategy. Henckel et al. is added for AID, and attribution of the decomposed prediction head changes from Lippe et al. to Wu et al. The overall research positioning remains stable.

T1.justification: New Appendix E derives forward-pass FLOP costs and supplies Proposition E.1 with a peak-inference-memory proof using m > n. Section 4.6 also revises the predicted sample-axis/node-axis compute fractions from 26.64%/38.75% to 36.60%/48.13%, accounting for the delayed first reduction.

improvement.justification: v1's central large-graph claim lacked uncertainty estimates and direct cyclicity checks at that scale. v2 adds these, AID evaluations and targeted robustness tests, substantially improving scrutiny of when discovery succeeds or fails. Expanded efficiency derivations and explicit limits on real-world applicability improve transparency. Unexplained SERGIO-GRN score revisions and inconsistencies involving Tables 1 and 6 and the retained sample-size plot remain, but the diagnostic and reporting gains outweigh these limitations.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CauScale with matching core methods and experiments. Their text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices (A-D in v1; A-F in v2) are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds cyclicity, causal-effect metrics, robustness experiments and observational-only evaluations (Tables 2, 4-7; Figure 7).

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on synthetic SCM and simulated gene-expression data, including accuracy, runtime, memory usage and ablations (Table 1; Figures 3-7).

results.title: CauScale: Neural Causal Discovery at Scale

C1.justification: The abstract's central task, benchmark, metric, and performance claims remain intact. The conclusion adds a demonstrated data-engine contribution: TimeChat-Captioner can supply supervision matching closed-source captioning APIs for downstream Omni-VideoLLMs, extending v1's more prospective supervision claims.

C2.justification: V3 adds substantive interpretations concerning judge dependence, human alignment, segmentation-granularity bias, and safeguards against over-segmentation. It qualifies five-system correlations as supportive rather than definitive and frames VideoQA results more precisely as evidence about caption quality. The existing context-window and long-video limitations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: The abstract changes resource availability from a future promise to a reported public release. Appendix E newly states that baselines use official checkpoints and recommended inference configurations. V3 documents LoRA use for the new student experiment, while the existing training hyperparameters, hardware, pixel limits, and prompt templates are retained.

E1.justification: The named benchmarks and original training sources remain unchanged. Section 5.5 adds training with captions for 18.7K additional videos but does not identify their source, domain, or relationship to the existing training pool. Whether these expand represented-data coverage or merely add samples is unresolved; the new metric-validation studies reuse OmniDCBench.

E2.justification: V3 newly evaluates CIDEr, METEOR, and SODAc against SodaM for human alignment (Table 7); v1 discussed these metrics without reporting this comparison. Figure 4 also introduces unfine-tuned and Gemini-caption-trained Qwen2.5-Omni-3B controls for the supervision experiment. Comparator membership in the original benchmark tables is unchanged.

E3.justification: New protocols include LoRA training of a 3B student on 18.7K captioned videos, evaluation with four LLM judges using fixed prompts and merging, and 129 blinded, randomized human comparisons by three experts. The original training settings remain unchanged. Table 2 and Section 5.3 clarify the existing caption-based QA protocol rather than establish a changed procedure.

E4.justification: V3 adds substantial validation of SodaM: sensitivity to judge choice, agreement with human preferences, and an ablation of DP merging (Section 5.6 and Appendix B). It also tests generated captions as student-training supervision. The earlier data-scale, reward, training-epoch, and qualitative analyses are retained.

E5.justification: V3 introduces Elo-based human preference analysis, Kendall's concordance, and system-level Pearson correlations with p-values. It explicitly distinguishes 122 non-tied comparisons from the five systems used for correlations. V1 contains no corresponding statistical validation; training-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, and seed reporting remain absent.

E6.justification: Original benchmark and appendix-ablation values are retained. New results include Daily-Omni accuracy of 44.9 using TimeChat captions, 44.4 using Gemini captions, and 7.9 without student fine-tuning (Figure 4). Tables 5–7 add merging results, alternative-judge scores, and human agreement reaching 77.9%, versus 47.5% for CIDEr, 55.7% for METEOR, and 60.7% for SODAc.

M1.justification: The Qwen2.5-Omni backbone, interleaved audiovisual inputs, SFT/GRPO training, four reward components, and SodaM procedure remain unchanged. The new LoRA student-training experiment evaluates caption utility without modifying TimeChat-Captioner.

P1.justification: Changes include a focused rewrite of Section 5.3, expanded and relocated baseline descriptions, a new experimental subsection and validation appendix, and author-affiliation, publication-header, and acknowledgement updates. Most existing prose and the overall narrative structure are retained.

P2.justification: V3 adds visual presentations of supervision utility and metric validation through Figure 4 and Tables 5–7. The existing qualitative comparison moves from the main text to the appendix as Figure 5, and Tables 2 and 4 receive clearer captions and labels. Existing diagrams and result-table contents are otherwise largely preserved.

R1.justification: V3 adds positioning around multi-shot understanding and generation through MMBench-Video and OneStory, cites AuroraCap for human evaluation and LoRA for student adaptation, and replaces the M-RoPE attribution to Qwen-VL with Qwen2-VL. The broader related-work organization and primary distinctions from earlier captioners remain stable.

T1.justification: The task definitions, SodaM alignment and merging equations, GRPO objective, and reward formulation are retained. The new metric-validation arguments are empirical; no new theorem, proof, substantive derivation, or revised mathematical definition is introduced.

improvement.justification: V1's headline findings depended on SodaM without direct human validation. V3 substantially strengthens that foundation through blinded human comparisons, competing metrics, alternative judges, and a merging ablation (Appendix B), while Figure 4 directly tests caption utility as training supervision. The human study remains small, the added training videos lack provenance, and claims that merging eliminates bias exceed the evidence. Nevertheless, the additions materially strengthen two central contributions while preserving the earlier results.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TimeChat-Captioner work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: V3 retains those results and adds student-training experiments, human preference evaluation, cross-judge validation, and a segment-merging ablation.

before.justification: V1 reports original captioning, caption-based VideoQA, temporal-grounding, and ablation results in Tables 1–6, including appendix experiments.

results.title: TimeChat-Captioner: Scripting Multi-Scene Videos with Time-Aware and Structural Audio-Visual Captions

C1.justification: Introduction contribution (2) adds an explicit claim that the neural vector-field representation supports symbolic-style interpretability through equilibria, Jacobians, stability, and phase-space geometry. The central claims about amortized inference, local representations, and rapid finetuning otherwise retain their scope.

C2.justification: v1's motion-capture explanation emphasizes discarded PCA information and induced memory; v2 distinguishes representation inadequacy from inference failure and uses finetuning evidence to support useful three-dimensional dynamics. The pendulum account changes from a weak sink to unstable spirals. v2 also discusses approximate-equilibrium residuals, context-dependent inference failures, and the lack of independent testing for evaluation-selected checkpoints.

D1.justification: Appendix D substantially expands reproducibility information with finetuning optimizer settings, learning rates, clipping, integrators, internal steps, checkpoint rules, task-specific configurations, and CPU timings. FHN gap handling and evaluation locations are specified, and the main text identifies the trajectory solver. The abstract changes the model/code/tutorial release status from forthcoming to available; this is a reported availability change.

E1.justification: Dataset families and prediction tasks are retained. Appendix F adds VDP/FHN context scenarios drawn from nearby Gaussian versus broader uniform initial-condition distributions, extending the state-space conditions represented in the inference inputs. The added Lotka–Volterra case study and ID/OOD breakdown use systems already covered by ODEBench.

E2.justification: Corresponding comparisons retain ODEFormer and the same seven classical baselines: BNeuralODE, NeuralODE, npODE, GPODE, ODE2VAE, LatentSDE, and GP-DNF. New FIM-ODE rows represent context and checkpoint-selection variants, rather than new external comparators.

E3.justification: The reported FHN setting changes from 25 sampled observations to 50, with v2 specifying 38 context and 12 withheld points. Appendix D introduces explicit test-MSE versus training-loss checkpoint selection and reports 300-epoch VDP finetuning instead of v1's general 200/800-epoch account. New evaluations specify context sampling, ID/OOD stratification, MSE summaries, and fixed-point diagnostics. These are reported protocol revisions; they do not establish which experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds quantitative equilibrium and stability diagnostics for pendulum, CDIMA, and Lotka–Volterra systems; ODEBench ID/OOD analyses; VDP/FHN context-size and initial-condition ablations; and checkpoint-selection sensitivity. Existing polynomial-degree, discretization, vector-field-quality, and dataset-scaling analyses are retained, largely moving from Appendix E to G.

E5.justification: The 100-trial noise-sensitivity analysis already existed in v1; v2 does not establish an increased repeat count. v2 foregrounds means and standard deviations in Table 4, adds error-distribution quantiles, and reports mean and standard deviation across ten training-selected checkpoints in Table 6. The latter measures checkpoint variability, not variation across independent training runs.

E6.justification: Table 4 changes FIM-ODE zero-shot MSEs from (0.89, 0.40, 0.33) to (0.90, 0.43, 0.40), and ODEFormer scores from (0.22, 0.45, 1.70) to (0.25, 0.60, 0.29). Finetuning and noise-summary results are replaced or expanded, alongside substantial new diagnostic and context-ablation results. Changed sampling and selection protocols prevent interpreting these as uniform same-setting gains. Main ODEBench and motion-capture score tables remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The polynomial prior, pretrained architecture, normalization, and vector-field loss remain unchanged. Appendix D revises low-data finetuning from v1's overlapping short-rollout formulation to full-trajectory single-shooting for VDP and FHN. Multiple-shooting remains for motion capture, making this a localized adaptation-procedure change.

P1.justification: Sections 5.1–5.3 undergo substantial narrative rewriting, and Appendix D replaces a compact general account with structured methodological and task-specific subsections. The additional experiments are reorganized into separate ODEBench, low-data, and synthetic-ablation appendices E–G. An Impact Statement, terminology edits, and author-order changes also appear.

P2.justification: Figure 2 expands from two to three systems and adds fixed-point annotations; Figure 3 adds motion-capture phase portraits. Table 4 gains a substantially revised row structure, and new tables display checkpoint comparisons, configurations, ID/OOD results, MSE distributions, stability diagnostics, and context ablations. Most earlier appendix graphics are retained and relocated.

R1.justification: v2 adds Bellot et al. and Wang et al. citations supporting the ODE/SDE identifiability distinction, plus a new pharmacokinetics reference. Mori and Zwanzig citations disappear with the revised motion-capture interpretation. The overall research positioning remains stable; matched preprint-to-publication updates are not new works.

T1.justification: The ODE background, existence and uniqueness statements, polynomial-prior mathematics, normalization derivations, and pretraining loss are retained. The added integration formula and Jacobian diagnostics document numerical procedures and empirical analyses; they introduce no substantive theoretical result or proof.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the paper's evidence and auditability: aggregate OOD claims gain disaggregated support, qualitative dynamical explanations gain quantitative diagnostics, and sparse finetuning documentation becomes explicit configurations and checkpoint-selection comparisons. Foregrounding noise averages also reduces reliance on favorable examples. The strongest low-data finetuning scores still use evaluation data for checkpoint selection, so independent superiority remains unestablished; the improvement rests on stronger analysis and transparency, not merely lower reported errors.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FIM-ODE research. The complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across reorganization and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical evaluations and adds fixed-point diagnostics, context-size experiments, checkpoint-selection comparisons, and disaggregated benchmark results.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic-ODE experiments, ODEBench evaluations, VDP forecasting, FHN imputation, motion-capture evaluations, and supplementary ablations.

results.title: Foundation Inference Models for Ordinary Differential Equations

C1.justification: The abstract and four principal contributions remain unchanged. The introduction and conclusion extend the empirical claim to long-context benchmarks and specifically claim successful memory extension through replacement of only eight layers in a pretrained 2.7B model. This modestly extends the practical scope of the existing conversion claim.

C2.justification: v3 adds an explanation for weaker from-scratch Palimpsa-D training and substantive applicability boundaries from RULER: shorter-context tracing losses, aggregation weaknesses, and mixed question answering. Appendix A.11 proposes different mechanisms for single-item and multiple-item retrieval. Its claim of consistent N-MK wins is overstated, however: Table 6 reports 21.8 versus the baseline's 24.6 at 8k.

D1.justification: v3 adds a code-repository pointer and documents the 2.7B base checkpoint, 64-layer architecture, width, vocabulary size, layer-selection procedure, training datasets, and three training stages. These substantially expand reproducibility information. Existing small-model hyperparameters and kernel details remain; the bscale initialization range added to Section 2.4 was already documented in v1's appendix.

E1.justification: v3 adds LongBench and RULER evaluation, covering long-context retrieval, tracing, aggregation, and question answering. Appendix A.10 also adds training on StackV2 code, SlimPajamas arxiv/book subsets, synthetic Needle-in-a-Haystack data, and LongAlpaca. This substantially extends the retained MQAR, FineWeb-Edu, and standard language-task coverage.

E2.justification: Corresponding experiments retain Gated Deltanet, Transformer++, non-metaplastic Palimpsa variants, and Simple GLA for throughput. The new 2.7B comparisons use the same Mamba2-equivalent Palimpsa-M without metaplasticity comparator. No distinct comparison method is introduced or removed.

E3.justification: v3 adds a 2.7B checkpoint pretrained on 300B tokens, followed by matched baseline/hybrid training with 10B continued-pretraining tokens, 5B context-extension tokens, and instruction tuning. It adds per-position NLL evaluation and RULER testing from 4k to 32k. The stated throughput configuration also changes from B=1, L=32 to B=16, L=2048; the unchanged plot does not establish that measurements were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained ablations and MQAR learning dynamics, v3 adds per-token WikiText NLL analysis of memory degradation (Figure 4), layer-wise memory-window diagnostics supporting selective replacement (Figure 6), and context-length sensitivity analysis on RULER. These substantially expand investigation of when and where metaplasticity helps.

E5.justification: The eight-seed MQAR reporting and standard-deviation displays are unchanged, and the new large-model results provide no additional run counts or significance tests. New Figure 4 contains shaded bands whose meaning and construction are undefined, preventing a reliable judgment about whether uncertainty-reporting procedures have expanded.

E6.justification: New results include 2.7B average accuracy of 59.22 versus 60.06 and LongBench overall scores of 19.3 versus 20.4 for baseline versus Palimpsa. RULER results are mixed: variable tracing scores are 59.6 versus 33.5 at 4k, but 14.9 versus 24.4 at 32k. The retained Table 2 changes the 170M fine-tuned Palimpsa-M average from 43.41 to 43.48; existing plots remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The Palimpsa recurrence and existing variants remain unchanged. Section 3.4 and Appendix A.10 introduce a targeted hybrid conversion: replace the eight Mamba2 layers with the largest median memory windows while retaining the other 56 layers. v1 only suggested future selective use of metaplasticity.

P1.justification: Most existing prose remains intact. v3 makes local paragraph and terminology edits, reorders the conclusion, adds Section 3.4, numbers previously unnumbered appendix sections, and corrects cross-references. It also replaces the template running header with the paper title.

P2.justification: v3 adds the NLL plot and layer-wise memory-window visualization, introduces LongBench/RULER tables, and expands Table 2 with a 2.7B block. Existing figures are retained but several are relocated or renumbered. The added plots and structured result displays substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v3 adds references for LongBench v2, RULER, and long-context training, and revises the Mesa derivation's attribution. Separate hypernetwork and FLA-library references disappear. The substantive positioning relative to Bayesian ICL, continual learning, Longhorn, and Mesanet remains largely unchanged; numerous other reference edits are publication-metadata updates.

T1.justification: v3 corrects Equation 1's predictive normalization, missing factors in the free-energy expression, and the Mesa matrix-multiplication order in Table 1 and Appendix A.4. Appendix A.3 adds an explicit Sherman-Morrison update and discusses its limitation under forgetting. These are localized mathematical corrections and extensions; the Palimpsa update remains unchanged.

improvement.justification: v1 supported long-context memory claims mainly through MQAR and standard language scores. v3 directly tests those claims with matched-training 2.7B comparisons, LongBench/RULER evaluations, and memory diagnostics, while exposing important task-dependent failures. Mathematical corrections and added reproducibility information further strengthen the paper. Undefined NLL bands and overstated retrieval-consistency prose limit interpretation, but the new direct validation substantially improves the evidence for the central claims.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Palimpsa study. Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, tables, and figures are readable and support reliable matching across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v3 retains these empirical results and adds original 2.7B-model evaluations, LongBench and RULER results, and memory diagnostics.

before.justification: v1 reports original MQAR experiments, language-model evaluations, metaplasticity ablations, learning-dynamics analyses, and inference-throughput measurements.

results.title: Learning to Remember, Learn, and Forget in Attention-Based Models

C1.justification: The introduction changes the contribution from a quantitative explanation of why reasoning improves generalization to a quantitative predictor of the extent of improvement. Related-work positioning makes a similar adjustment. This locally narrows the explanatory claim; the abstract and central correlation-based contribution remain unchanged.

C2.justification: V2 interprets incorrect chains as disrupting a coherent, compressible mapping and discusses cognitive tasks where No CoT succeeds. It adds an explanation for LongPPL's weaker correlations, qualifies PEFT estimates as potentially loose proxies, and cautions about model-family or dataset artifacts. The existing compression-based interpretation remains.

D1.justification: Appendix C and Table 6 add concrete task-generation ranges, split caps, and deduplication/decontamination instructions. Appendix D specifies LongPPL's K values and states that alpha and beta follow the cited settings. Existing LoRA implementation details, hyperparameter searches, and GSM dataset access information are retained.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates GSM8K and its mathematical stress-test variants. V2 adds algorithmic and cognitive Reasoning Gym tasks, covering six training task types and four held-out types, with easy and harder configurations (Section 4.5 and Appendix C). This substantially broadens the tested capabilities and environments.

E2.justification: Appendix D and Table 7 add LongPPL at K=64 and K=256 as evaluated predictors alongside ordinary perplexity and intrinsic dimensionality. The original GSM8K comparator metrics and 14 reasoning strategies remain. Reasoning Gym evaluates four existing strategies rather than introducing new reasoning methods.

E3.justification: The added Reasoning Gym protocol specifies an 80/20 split, caps of 3,000 training and 250 test examples per task, deduplication, decontamination, and geometric aggregation across ID, hard OOD, and held-out OOD evaluations. V2 also adds a 50%-incorrect training condition and two LongPPL configurations. Existing GSM8K settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New Table 5 tests sensitivity to training correctness by mixing incorrect chains into Short CoT and Gemma 27B CoT data. The Reasoning Gym experiments additionally test harder configurations and transfer to unseen task types. These extend the original threshold-sensitivity, distractor, and training-size analyses; relocating Figure 3 adds no new analysis.

E5.justification: Appendix C newly discloses fixed-seed generation of easy examples and a different seed for hard OOD examples. This adds seed-use information without reporting numerical seeds or additional training repetitions. Existing significance conventions remain unchanged, and the new results provide no repeated-run uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Original Tables 1–3 and detailed GSM8K scores are unchanged. New Table 4 reports intrinsic-dimension correlations of 1.00 in both Reasoning Gym categories, with Executed PoT best algorithmically and No CoT best cognitively. Table 5 reports Short CoT accuracy of 32.63% with correct training versus 20.61% with 50% incorrect chains. Table 7 adds LongPPL correlations of 0.60 and 0.62. These are additional experimental results, not improved scores under retained settings.

M1.justification: The LoRA rank/module sweep, configuration-selection algorithm, common-threshold measurement, and reasoning-generation procedures remain unchanged. The new experiments apply the existing framework; Appendix A.1 retains the same algorithm.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the overall narrative remain intact. V2 adds Section 4.5, appendix sections for Reasoning Gym and LongPPL, an explanatory subsection for Figure 3, conflict-of-interest and impact statements, and localized wording edits. Existing examples and detailed results are renumbered rather than rewritten.

P2.justification: New Tables 4–7 provide distinct displays for domain comparisons, correctness sensitivity, task configurations, and LongPPL results, substantially expanding the empirical presentation. Figure 3 moves from the main text to the appendix, and Figure 1's caption expands. Existing plots and GSM8K table structures are preserved.

R1.justification: V2 adds references supporting Reasoning Gym, LongPPL, high-entropy forking tokens, and compression bounds, including Stojanovski, Fang, Wang, Lotfi, and Shaw and colleagues. It modestly refines positioning toward prediction and qualified compression estimates. Publication and title updates to existing references do not constitute additional research coverage.

T1.justification: Section 6 newly states that layer-wise projection or PEFT estimates upper-bound intrinsic dimensionality and may give loose bounds relative to Kolmogorov complexity. This adds a theoretical qualification to the estimator. Section 2's mathematical definitions and equations remain unchanged, and no proof is added.

improvement.justification: V1's evidence is confined to GSM8K-derived mathematics. V2 substantially strengthens validation through different reasoning domains, including a cognitive setting where No CoT wins, and a direct correctness intervention (Tables 4–5). The added comparator and clearer predictive framing and proxy limitations further improve the paper. The new domain correlations involve only four strategies on Gemma-3 4B and lack repeated-run uncertainty, so their broader implications remain provisional.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable, allowing retained, relocated, and newly added material to be matched reliably.

after.justification: V2 retains those experiments and adds original Reasoning Gym evaluations, training-correctness experiments, and LongPPL comparisons.

before.justification: V1 reports original Gemma-3 1B and 4B experiments across 14 reasoning strategies, including GSM8K stress tests, intrinsic-dimension correlations, and threshold-sensitivity analyses.

results.title: Effective Reasoning Chains Reduce Intrinsic Dimensionality

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list and conclusion retain the same central claims: combining hard precedence with soft weights, recovering existing values, axiomatic characterization, scalable MCMC and priority sweeping. The added evidence does not redefine these headline contributions.

C2.justification: Section 6 and Appendices D/F add substantive applicability qualifications: utility evaluation versus sampling costs, dependence of proxy benefits on utility structure and fitting budget, and substantial memory overhead. They also explain why consequential DAG changes should alter attribution and frame edge sensitivity as guidance for validating the assumed graph.

D1.justification: v2 documents synthetic graph and utility construction, weighted dynamic programming, utility caching, simulation sampling settings, proxy/probability budgets and explicit perturbation edge lists. Runtime and memory measurements are newly provided. Existing generative-model and feature-classifier implementation details are retained in Appendices E–F.

E1.justification: v2 adds four synthetic poset families and sum-of-unanimity games under block-based and ordered-partition precedence structures. It also evaluates locally perturbed and disconnected Census Income DAGs. The original MNIST, CIFAR10 and Census Income application coverage remains.

E2.justification: The original SV, WSV and PSV comparator sets are unchanged. The new proxy-estimation experiment compares against direct Monte Carlo and includes a linear-only proxy alongside quadratic variants (Figure 10). Regression MSR and PolySHAP inform the adaptation but are not separately benchmarked.

E3.justification: The original application settings are retained. Appendix D introduces separate mixing, approximation-error and computational-cost protocols, including exact stationary references, ARE/AUCC metrics, player counts up to 8192 and controlled proxy budgets. Appendix F.4.2 adds specified edge-deletion, addition, cut and top-K tests with attribution and order-change metrics.

E4.justification: v2 retains the original priority sweeps and adds sampler-mixing analysis, estimation-error convergence, quadratic-term and fitting-budget ablations, and runtime/memory scaling. The new DAG-misspecification study tests local edge changes, disconnections and influential-edge subsets, substantially extending robustness analysis.

E5.justification: Appendix D.1.1 newly specifies 10,000 independent chains per mixing condition. The original application studies retain ten estimation seeds and mean/standard-deviation reporting. No new confidence-interval or significance-testing procedure is introduced.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 retain identical numerical results. New Figures 8–12 report mixing, approximation error, runtime and memory outcomes, including conditional benefits from the proxy estimator. Figure 19 adds DAG-sensitivity findings: most individual perturbations have small effects, while deleting marital-status→relationship produces an attribution shift of approximately 0.32.

M1.justification: The PASV distribution and original adjacent-swap sampler remain unchanged. Section 6.1 and Appendix D.2 add an optional estimation procedure combining a fitted quadratic utility proxy, pairwise-order probabilities and Monte Carlo residual correction. New Algorithm 2 also computes exact stationary pairwise probabilities through weighted dynamic programming.

P1.justification: Most existing prose remains essentially verbatim. v2 inserts a computational-cost/DAG-sensitivity section and dedicated proof/simulation appendices, separates the former experimental appendix into E and F, and updates headings, cross-references and the publication footer.

P2.justification: v2 adds six substantial multipanel figures covering mixing, estimation accuracy, runtime, memory and DAG sensitivity, together with an algorithm box and perturbation edge tables. Existing figures and numerical tables are retained; appendix figures are renumbered and some image grids are resized and reflowed.

R1.justification: v2 adds focused connections to Regression MSR, PolySHAP and regression-based KernelSHAP, plus references supporting poset counting, mixing experiments, synthetic benchmarks and the ROV proof. The original positioning of PASV relative to PSV and WSV remains unchanged.

T1.justification: v1 states the central theoretical results without their proofs. New Appendices B–C supply proofs for the axiomatization theorems, reduction propositions, limiting-weight propositions and acceptance-ratio lemma, together with auxiliary lemmas. Appendix D additionally develops weighted recursions and analytical expressions for benchmark and proxy values.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially improves auditability by supplying previously missing proofs and controlled evidence on computational scaling, estimator tradeoffs and local DAG misspecification. The new cost and memory results also make practical limitations clearer. These gains outweigh a dropped common factor in Appendix B.1's intermediate limit, which cancels after normalization, and optimistic wording about obtaining small errors from a few hundred permutations relative to Figure 9.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Priority-Aware Shapley Value work. Their text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable, and retained content can be matched across the expanded appendix structure.

after.justification: The original experiments remain, supplemented by synthetic mixing and estimation studies in Appendix D and DAG-perturbation experiments in Appendix F.4.2.

before.justification: Sections 5.1–5.2 and Appendix B report original data-valuation experiments on MNIST/CIFAR10 and feature-attribution experiments on Census Income, including repeated-run results.

results.title: Priority-Aware Shapley Value

C1.justification: The central contribution—conditioning selection and widening on remaining token budget—is unchanged. The abstract, introduction, and conclusion broaden the empirical claim from mathematical reasoning with sub-10B models to include a larger model and a complementary physics evaluation.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations concerning reward-dependent LiteSearch behavior, robustness near default hyperparameters, the contribution of dynamic widening beyond selection, and complementarity between early stopping and budget-guided search. It newly argues that shared PRM saturation preserves comparison fairness despite weakening selection signals. Appendix L explicitly states that no downstream models are trained, qualifying the retained data-synthesis interpretation.

D1.justification: v2 adds a BG-MCTS repository link and substantial technical documentation: UGPhysics sampling rules and category counts, rollout evaluation details, Qwen3's disabled reasoning mode, and beam-search and sensitivity configurations. Appendix E expands the retained PRM evaluation explanation, including previous judgments and per-prefix scoring of full solutions. The repository's actual contents or accessibility are not established by the PDFs.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates mathematical reasoning on MATH500 Level 5 and AIME24/25. v2 retains these and adds UGPhysics, extending evaluation to physics reasoning across 13 subjects and three problem types: laws application, mathematical derivation, and practical application.

E2.justification: The original comparator set is retained. Appendix I adds an actually evaluated beam-search baseline against BG-MCTS on MATH500 Level 5, with results in Table 8.

E3.justification: v2 adds Qwen3-32B with reasoning mode disabled and a distinct physics protocol: 120 sampled questions, five reference-checked rollouts per non-terminal node, majority-vote answer selection, and disabled LiteSearch early stopping. New appendix experiments introduce sensitivity sweeps and matched stopping controls. The displayed mathematical prompt also omits its former first example step; this documents a prompt difference without establishing that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained component ablations and tree analyses, v2 adds hyperparameter sensitivity, removal of the virtual generative node, a matched early-stopping experiment, and quantitative PRM-score diagnostics in Appendices G, H, J, and K. Removing the virtual node is distinct from v1's widening-annealing ablation. Appendix F.3 additionally examines LiteSearch's contrasting behavior on mathematics and physics.

E5.justification: The three-trial main results and two-run component ablations remain. Tables 6–8 newly identify sensitivity configurations, the no-generative-node variant, and beam search as single-run experiments, with some comparisons reusing averaged main results. No confidence intervals, significance tests, or seed lists are added; the PDFs do not establish increased replication of existing experiments.

E6.justification: The original two-model Table 1 scores and all Table 2 ablation scores are unchanged. v2 adds substantial results for Qwen3-32B, physics, and appendix controls; Qwen3-32B BG-MCTS reaches 0.784/0.801/0.809 on MATH500 at 10K/20K/30K tokens. New results include exceptions to uniform superiority: UGPhysics at 10K with Qwen2.5 gives 0.203 for BG-MCTS versus 0.211 for MCTS. Four missing decimal points in retained appendix precision entries are also corrected.

M1.justification: The BG-PUCT and virtual-child widening framework and Algorithm 1 are retained. The new physics adaptation uses reference-checked rollouts for node scoring and majority voting for final-answer selection instead of the mathematical experiments' PRM-based procedure. Appendix J also introduces an early-stopping BG-MCTS variant; these are limited procedural extensions.

P1.justification: Existing prose is extensively rewritten across the introduction, preliminaries, widening explanation, analyses, discussion, and appendices. Mathematical and physics evaluations receive separate subsections, and the data-synthesis discussion is reorganized into explicit single-solution and multiple-candidate settings. These changes extend beyond inserting new scientific content.

P2.justification: v2 adds a widening schematic, physics plots, and multiple diagnostic tables. Existing plots are reorganized into model panels with shared legends, Table 1 gains average columns and a Qwen3 block, and depth/width figures become larger grids. The main answered-node table drops precision columns, which remain in the appendix. Original qualitative tree examples are retained and renumbered.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations to UGPhysics, the Qwen3 technical report, and Komiyama et al.'s Best-of-infinity. The principal positioning against budget-agnostic tree search, LiteSearch, and prompt-based BATS remains, with an additional contrast to frontier-based beam search in Appendix I.

T1.justification: Section 3.2 adds a substantive qualification to the completion-bias definition: its contribution is set to zero for nodes already containing completed answers, whereas v1 states the correction without this exception. The principal equations and budget-redistribution algebra otherwise remain equivalent, and neither version contains theoretical guarantees or proofs.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked direct tests of larger-model generality, hyperparameter sensitivity, virtual-node removal, and matched early stopping. v2 substantially strengthens validation through Qwen3-32B experiments and targeted appendix controls, while improving methodological explanations and access information. These address important evidential gaps rather than merely increasing reported scores. Several controls remain single-run, physics evaluation requires reference answers, and broad superiority wording overlooks exceptions such as Table 3's 10K Qwen2.5 result. These limitations temper, but do not outweigh, the substantial gains in empirical support and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same BG-MCTS research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite extensive rewriting and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds Qwen3-32B and UGPhysics evaluations, beam-search comparisons, sensitivity tests, and further diagnostic experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original mathematical-reasoning experiments, baseline comparisons, component ablations, and search-tree analyses, including appendix results.

results.title: Aligning Tree-Search Policies with Fixed Token Budgets in Test-Time Scaling of LLMs

C1.justification: The introduction broadens the theoretical contribution from detecting speciation in high-dimensional Gaussian mixtures to detecting general class-structure speciation times. Section 2 explicitly includes classes not separated by first moments. The central empirical claims about semantic timing and guidance redistribution remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds the qualification that balancing priors can alter profile shape even when the characteristic transition window remains stable, and conditions the complement approximation on representative unconditional sampling (Appendix B). It interprets the SDXL example as supporting a link between prompt adherence and diagnostic interpretability. Section 6's original limitations are retained.

D1.justification: Appendix B adds explicit posterior-update equations and discloses Gaussian smoothing followed by interpolation for obtaining entropy derivatives. Appendix C newly reports GPU models, batch sizes and approximate profile-computation times, including SDXL. Existing sampler, schedule and main-experiment sample counts are retained.

E1.justification: v2 Figure 6 adds covariance-separated concentric Gaussians and a hierarchical mixture combining mean and covariance distinctions, extending the synthetic scenarios beyond mean-separated components. ImageNet and the existing text-prompt tasks remain; repeating the chair experiment with SDXL changes the model setting rather than task coverage.

E2.justification: New estimator-validation comparisons use ground-truth Gaussian-mixture entropy and intermediate estimators with natural priors, true complements and exact posteriors as references (Appendix B, Figures 7–8). The original unguided, limited-guidance and full-guidance comparisons retain their comparator set.

E3.justification: New protocols include 200-component mixture tests across dimensions 2, 8, 32 and 128, an EDM2-XS sample-count sweep with 200 integration steps, and a 25K-sample prior comparison. SDXL base 1.0 is also evaluated. The original EDM2-XS and SD 1.5 sampling settings and guidance-evaluation protocols remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix B adds systematic tests separating bias from prior balancing, complement approximation and posterior estimation, plus dimensional sensitivity and sample convergence (Figures 7–8). Appendix C adds an SDXL robustness case study. These substantially extend v1's qualitative discussion of estimator reliability.

E5.justification: v2 Figure 8 newly reports estimator standard deviations calculated using 20 seeds. v1 contains no corresponding repeated-seed uncertainty analysis. The existing median and interquartile summaries across ImageNet classes remain; the PDFs do not establish increased repetitions of the original experiments.

E6.justification: New results show covariance-driven and two-stage hierarchical entropy transitions, quantify approximation biases and convergence, and report smoother SDXL profiles with better qualitative prompt adherence (Figures 6–8 and 18). Figure 1a's toy curves are also revised. Original guidance scores are unchanged: v1 Tables 1–2 match v2 Tables 2–3, including limited-guidance optima of FID 3.55 and FDDINOv2 87.8.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 corrects the binary-entropy sign and moves final aggregation after both sampling branches. These are corrections to the stated procedure; posterior tracking, balanced priors and the unconditional-model approximation already appeared in v1.

P1.justification: Section 4 and Appendices A–B are extensively rewritten and reorganized around pairwise competition, score separation and estimator robustness. Implementation explanations move into Section 5.1, and Appendix C's narrative is substantially edited and reorganized. These changes extend beyond inserting new scientific material.

P2.justification: v2 adds a theory-summary table and Figures 6–8 and 18, redraws Figure 1a, reformats the guidance tables and rearranges generation montages. Three separate guidance-trajectory figures are consolidated into Figure 12, while retained Stable Diffusion examples and the failure case are relocated with expanded captions.

R1.justification: v2 adds Achilli et al. (2026) and explicitly connects the entropy diagnostic to its general class-structure speciation framework. This extends the prior connection to Biroli et al.; the broader information-theory and guided-diffusion positioning remains largely unchanged.

T1.justification: v2 substantially develops Appendix A with pairwise entropy-production derivations, explicit Gaussian probability bounds and partitioned-entropy identities. Sections 4.4 and A.4 extend the argument to proper/pure class decompositions and covariance-based separation. It also resolves the sign inconsistency between v1's main-text Eq. 8 and its appendix derivation.

improvement.justification: v1 relied on largely unquantified estimator approximations and a terse asymptotic argument. v2 corrects formula and pseudocode inconsistencies, strengthens the mathematical reasoning, and directly evaluates approximation bias and convergence with repeated-seed variability. These changes substantially improve support for the diagnostic's reliability and reproducibility despite unchanged guidance scores. The general-class extension remains asymptotic, and the added SDXL evidence is qualitative.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same entropy-based analysis of diffusion speciation. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v2 retains these results and adds synthetic class-structure experiments, estimator-bias and convergence analyses, and an SDXL experiment in its appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original Gaussian-mixture calculations, EDM2-XS and Stable Diffusion 1.5 experiments, generated examples and guidance evaluations in Section 5 and Appendix C.

results.title: The Entropic Signature of Class Speciation in Diffusion Models

C1.justification: The introduction expands the advertised theoretical scope from convex to convex and weakly convex problems. The conclusion also qualifies the stability advantage as a statement about convergence bounds. This materially broadens and refines the central theoretical contribution while retaining the original empirical claims.

C2.justification: Section 4.5 now exempts SPP from the assertion that the index expressions require no convexity, and Section 4.4 explicitly limits its benign-scaling takeaway to the convex case. Appendix B.2 adds an explanation reconciling negative Polyak-step results with large steps and inaccurate lower bounds.

D1.justification: The synthetic-data generation, dataset preprocessing, training details, gradient/loss logging, and data-access information are retained. Neither version provides additional implementation resources or hardware information relative to the other.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate CIFAR10, synthetic linear regression, and LIBSVM vowel/dna classification with the same scenarios. Appendix A.3's new quadratic specialization is theoretical, not an additional evaluated dataset or task.

E2.justification: Both compare SGD/SPS/NGN on CIFAR10 and logistic regression, and SGD/SPS/SPP on synthetic regression. Newly cited Muon and ScheduleFree work does not introduce evaluated comparators.

E3.justification: The learning-rate ranges, training horizons, warmup procedure, regression sizes, dataset splits, batch sizes, and plotted convex bound are retained. The new theoretical step-size restrictions do not change the reported experimental protocols.

E4.justification: The warmup, noise, batch-size, lower-bound, bound-parameter, training-horizon, and validation-loss analyses remain unchanged, including Figures 5, 7, and 9–11. The new quadratic specialization is a formal derivation assessed under T1.

E5.justification: Both versions approximate the expected stability index using three seeds with identical initialization and different data ordering. No additional uncertainty estimates, significance tests, or revised repeated-run practices are reported.

E6.justification: The corresponding plotted results and empirical findings are unchanged. For example, both report CIFAR10 SGD deterioration at learning rates of approximately 1 and above, SPS/NGN working well up to approximately 10, and synthetic-regression SGD failure around 0.03.

M1.justification: The model-based update and SGD, SPS, NGN, and SPP procedures are unchanged. The Lambert-W step in Appendix D already appears in v1. The weakly convex extension changes the analysis, not the optimization algorithms.

P1.justification: Most prose and the main section sequence are retained. v2 subdivides Section 3, expands the conclusion and Appendix A structure, adds an impact statement, removes the contents page, and makes local wording and cross-reference edits.

P2.justification: The single-column manuscript becomes a conference-format document with two-column main text and references, new typography and running headers, and extensively resized and repositioned figures. The same twelve figures and dataset table remain, but main-text plot panels are substantially smaller.

R1.justification: v2 adds Moreau (1965), Crawshaw et al. (2025), Defazio (2026), and Orabona and D'Orazio (2026), while removing Beck (2017). The conclusion discusses additional optimizer combinations, and Appendix B.2 addresses negative Polyak-step results. The main research positioning remains intact.

T1.justification: v2 adds weakly convex assumptions, Lemma 3.5, and the Moreau-envelope stationarity bound in Theorem 3.6, with proofs in Appendix A.1. Section 4 extends the applicability conditions and SPP bound, introducing a curvature-dependent factor and step-size restriction in Lemma 4.3. New Appendix A.3 derives specialized stability indices for interpolating quadratics. The original convex bounds remain.

improvement.justification: v1 connects the stability index to guarantees only for convex problems. v2 substantially extends that central connection through a proved weakly convex stationarity bound, explicit applicability conditions, and a revised SPP bound (Section 3.2 and Appendix A). These additions reduce an important theoretical limitation and improve the precision of the framework. The experiments remain unchanged and still use the convex bound; smaller main-text figures impose a readability cost, but the theoretical gains outweigh it.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same stability-index framework and optimization methods. Their text, equations, Figures 1–12, Table 1, and appendices A–E support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting and added theory.

after.justification: v2 retains these original training experiments and PEPit computations, including their plotted outcomes in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original ResNet20/CIFAR10, synthetic regression, and vowel/dna logistic-regression experiments in Section 5 and Appendix E, plus PEPit computations in Figure 2b.

results.title: Step-Size Stability in Stochastic Optimization: A Theoretical Perspective

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution bullets retain the central claims about update leakage, two-stage reconstruction and subspace camouflage. Original-output extraction was already asserted in v1; v2 supplies direct evidence for that goal. The conclusion's wording changes do not establish a different core contribution.

C2.justification: V2 removes v1's unresolved sequential-attack limitation and interprets the new cumulative-edit results positively. It adds decoy hallucination as a specific defense limitation while retaining candidate-pool dependence and concerns about long-term defense utility. Some new interpretations overreach: the claimed prompt-pool recall decline of at most 2% contradicts Table 14's larger zsRE declines.

D1.justification: V2 documents IMDb sampling, generation of 9,000 additional templates with Gemini 3.1 Pro, and the minimum-entropy baseline procedure. It clarifies pseudocode inputs and initialization and changes the advertised repository from EditingAtk.git to EditingAttack. Existing implementation settings remain largely unchanged; repository availability is not established by the PDFs.

E1.justification: The original benchmarks remain, but v2 adds evaluation of original-output extraction, cumulative sequential edits and factual knowledge about decoy subjects (Tables 3, 13 and 17). Candidate-pool experiments also introduce IMDb names and generated prompt templates, extending the represented candidate populations beyond the original libraries.

E2.justification: V2 adds a post-edit-only minimum-entropy baseline for prompt recovery, defined in Appendix E.1 and evaluated in Table 15. Table 16 additionally evaluates camouflage against the existing gray-box subject attack; v1's defense evaluation used the white-box attacker. Original subject-inference comparisons remain.

E3.justification: New protocols include 2–10 cumulative edits with N=100 and Top-(s×N) recall, subject pools from 2,000 to 10 million, and prompt pools from 1,000 to 10,000. V2 also introduces end-to-end recall and decoy True Fact Recall using rewrite/paraphrase prompts. These supplement the retained experimental settings rather than establish reruns of the original comparisons.

E4.justification: Appendix F adds subject- and prompt-pool sensitivity studies, sequential-edit robustness, defense testing against a gray-box attacker, and analysis of decoy hallucinations. These address substantial additional questions about scalability and defense side effects. The covariance and generic-template analyses already existed in v1.

E5.justification: Both versions state that results average five independent runs and retain existing uncertainty displays. However, v2's new Table 3 and Tables 12–17 report point estimates without the variability shown in v1's result tables. No increased run count or new statistical test is documented.

E6.justification: All ten original tables retain their numerical results after matching. V2 adds substantial outcomes: Table 3 reports CounterFact end-to-end Top-20 recall of 0.78, 0.74 and 0.81 for GPT-J, Llama-3 and Qwen-2.5, respectively; Tables 12–17 report the additional analyses and comparisons. The CounterFact utility plots also change the undefended reference rank from 1 to approximately 50.8 (v1 Figures 5/7; v2 Figures 4/6).

M1.justification: The spectral subject-inference procedure, relative-entropy prompt scoring and camouflage update remain unchanged. Algorithm 1's explicit initialization and Algorithm 3's added listing of P clarify existing operations. Querying the original model for recovered outputs was already described in v1.

P1.justification: Most prose and the main narrative remain intact. V2 moves limitations to Appendix A, separates implementation details from additional experiments, and gives defense theory its own appendix. It also makes localized language, cross-reference, pseudocode-documentation and publication-header edits.

P2.justification: V2 substantially expands the result displays with the end-to-end table and six appendix tables covering new evaluation questions. It relocates the covariance figure from the main text to Appendix F, reorders existing tables, resizes figures and adjusts CounterFact utility-plot axes. Existing figures are retained rather than replaced by new analyses.

R1.justification: Section 2 and Appendix B add Youssef et al. (2025), distinguishing reversal of model behavior from prompt/output reconstruction. Appendix B also adds Liu et al. (2026a, 2026b) on forward replay and locality evaluation. These are limited positioning additions, not newly evaluated external baselines.

T1.justification: V2 corrects the maximum-principal-angle definition and changes the upper bound in Equation 35 from max to min. It also repairs ROME normalization and missing or incorrect K/P factors in existing derivations, distinguishes edit keys from generic-template keys, and qualifies covariance convergence through matrix-concentration conditions. The existing theorem framework is retained.

improvement.justification: V2 resolves an important evidential gap: v1 explicitly omitted original-output recovery, whereas Table 3 directly evaluates end-to-end extraction. Larger candidate pools, sequential edits, a simple prompt baseline and decoy-factuality tests substantially strengthen validation and expose defense costs. Mathematical corrections improve reliability. Missing variability in new tables and overstated summaries remain weaknesses—for example, Table 14 reports a zsRE decline from 0.63 to 0.52 despite the claimed 2% maximum—but the added validation and corrected reasoning provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same KSTER attack and subspace camouflage defense. All 33 pages of v1 and 35 pages of v2, including figures, tables, equations and appendices, support comparison after matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: V2 retains those original experiments and adds end-to-end extraction, sequential editing, candidate-pool sensitivity, baseline comparisons and decoy-factuality results.

before.justification: V1 reports original attack and defense experiments across three language models, CounterFact and zsRE, alongside utility evaluations and appendix analyses.

results.title: Reverse-Engineering Model Editing on Language Models

C1.justification: The central contributions remain offline, per-head RL ranking with a budget-agnostic reward. The abstract, introduction, and conclusion extend the stated generalization scope explicitly to 128K contexts, or 32 times training length, and foreground passage retrieval alongside retained downstream tasks.

C2.justification: The explanation for supervised-ranking weaknesses changes from temperature and gradient problems to heavy-tailed importance distributions and magnitude-sensitive versus rank-only loss tradeoffs. v2 adds interpretations of head specialization, acknowledges attention as a task-utility proxy and the absence of an optimized end-to-end pipeline, and qualifies OASST2 superiority by noting LagKV's advantage at the smallest budgets.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-repository link and newly discloses trace-collection requirements: 4,649 OASST2 samples, under two hours on 56 GPUs, approximately 1.2 TB of traces, and 11 GB per head. It documents physical compaction and JudgeQ reimplementation with matched training data. These substantially improve reproducibility information without establishing changes to the retained training setup.

E1.justification: v2 adds RULER evaluation at 128K context length and LongBench passage retrieval in English and Chinese, substantially extending input-length, task, and language coverage. ARC-Challenge remains in Appendix A.7 rather than being removed; other original benchmarks are retained.

E2.justification: Appendix A.4 adds evaluated JudgeQ comparisons on RULER-128K, English/Chinese passage retrieval, and BoolQ. Section 4.2 adds pointwise regression, RankNet, ListNet, and weighted Soft-Sort alongside the existing Soft-Sort comparator, substantially broadening comparisons with learned approaches.

E3.justification: v1 evaluates single compression after prefill using attention-mask emulation. v2 retains that setting but introduces chunked prefill with repeated eviction and physical tensor compaction for long-context evaluations. It also revises the stated meaning of plotted -R^b from cumulative evicted importance to an individual rank's normalized AUC contribution.

E4.justification: The three-learning-rate Soft-Sort study is replaced by a comparison of five supervised objectives. New Appendices A.5-A.6 analyze importance-distribution heterogeneity, regression ranking errors, and agreement among 112 head-specific policies, adding substantial evidence about objective choice and specialization.

E5.justification: Figure 10 newly reports mean ranks with ±1 standard-deviation bands and variance across 112 heads on one sample. These describe inter-head variation, not uncertainty across training runs. The latency benchmark's averaging over 30 runs is unchanged.

E6.justification: v2 adds long-context, retrieval, JudgeQ, and head-analysis results. The replacement ablation finds Soft-Sort close to RL over most budgets, unlike v1's broadly poor surrogate results. BoolQ scores also change: KVP-S at 20 tokens rises from approximately 72% in v1 Figure 3 to 79% in v2 Figure 4, without an explained cause. Most original appendix curves remain unchanged.

M1.justification: Section 3.1.1 corrects the stated normalized training reward from R/R* to the negative cost ratio -C/C*. This changes the written optimization objective, while the per-head MLPs, inputs, Plackett-Luce/Gumbel sampling, and RLOO procedure remain. The PDFs do not establish corresponding implementation changes or retraining.

P1.justification: The overall section sequence and much existing prose remain. Targeted rewrites clarify reward definitions, compression protocols, generalization, and ablation explanations; the conclusion gains explicit limitations, an impact statement is added, and existing additional results move from Appendix A.4 to A.7.

P2.justification: v2 adds long-context, retrieval, JudgeQ, importance-distribution, rank-variance, and correlation displays. It redraws the supervised comparison, combines BoolQ and GovReport into Figure 4, and moves ARC-Challenge to the appendix. Existing Phi-4, qualitative, subtask, and per-head cost figures are largely retained and renumbered.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds LOCRET and JudgeQ and distinguishes their query requirements and training procedures from KVP. References for RankNet and ListNet are added, while the Nemhauser citation accompanying the removed hardness statement disappears. The broader related-work taxonomy and positioning remain.

T1.justification: Section 3 removes the claim of NP-hardness even for linear rewards and grounds nestedness in the additive reward rather than general task utility. Section 3.1.1 corrects reward normalization and derives the rank-weighted AUC expression, while redefining R^b. Proposition 1 and its appendix proof remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for the paper's central rationale: broader supervised comparisons reveal budget-dependent tradeoffs, while 128K and repeated-compaction tests address previously limited evidence for long-context use. Corrected mathematics, resource disclosures, and explicit limitations improve assessability. Unexplained BoolQ revisions, single-sample head diagnostics, and missing end-to-end latency measurements remain limitations, but do not outweigh these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same KVP research, with matching authors, core method, and retained experiments. Their main text, equations, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds RULER-128K, bilingual passage retrieval, JudgeQ comparisons, and analyses of supervised objectives and head specialization.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark evaluations, supervised-learning ablations, qualitative analyses, and latency measurements for KVP, including Qwen and Phi-4 experiments.

results.title: Learning to Evict from Key-Value Cache

C1.justification: The central contributions—aligning training masks with inference, preserving the posterior minimizer, and accelerating training—remain intact. v2 recalibrates the abstract's pretraining speedup from approximately 2.5× to 2.3× and extends the introductory empirical claims to a 4.0× ARM-initialized speedup and effective 7B post-training.

C2.justification: v1's limitation emphasizes reliance on synthetic TinyGSM data. v2 replaces this with limits on demonstrated training scales and inefficient single-epoch use. New discussion offers hypotheses for LoRA benefits, higher decoding confidence, and differing NELBO trends, and qualifies PAPL comparisons by generation-order sensitivity and a seed-specific failure. These substantially expand the interpretation and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: Section 4.5 and Table 2 add substantial Dream-Coder reproduction details, including data sources, LoRA rank, architecture, learning rate, epochs, hardware, batch size, and sampling temperatures. However, Section 4.5 specifies K=15 while Table 2 specifies K=6, leaving that setting unresolved. The repository target is unchanged: v1's generic 'Codebase link' already embeds the same URL printed in v2.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained Sudoku and TinyGSM/GSM8K coverage, Section 4.5 adds general code-generation fine-tuning using 700k pairs from opc-sft-stage-2-educational, KodCode-V1-SFT-4o, and OpenCodeInstruct. Evaluation on HumanEval and MBPP substantially broadens the represented data and task requirements.

E2.justification: v2 adds direct evaluations of PAPL, a related policy-aware training method absent from v1's comparisons. Figure 10 evaluates MDM+PAPL and PUMA+PAPL on both Sudoku and TinyGSM, including multiple PAPL reweighting strengths on Sudoku. Existing MDM and training-recipe comparisons remain.

E3.justification: Autoregressive initialization changes from 30k to 200k pretraining steps, and the reported Sudoku maximum length changes from 162 to 81. New experiments introduce frozen-backbone Dream-Coder fine-tuning with rank-128 LoRA, length-640 inputs, and Pass@1 evaluation every 2,000 steps. Appendix B.6 adds NELBO evaluation on 236k TinyGSM and 35k coding validation samples. These are reported protocol changes; the PDFs do not establish which retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 expands the scheduled-versus-fixed-K ablation into a comparison of multiple schedules and extends inference tests to confidence fast-forwarding, larger decoding batches, and nonzero temperatures, reporting accuracy and tokens per step. It also adds PAPL reweighting sensitivity tests and NELBO analyses on TinyGSM and Dream-Coder. Existing trajectory-stabilization and block-diffusion analyses are retained.

E5.justification: The three-seed TinyGSM protocol was already stated in v1. v2 adds explicit 95% confidence intervals in Figure 1 and the PAPL comparisons in Figure 10, whose caption also identifies a poorly performing seed. This improves uncertainty reporting without establishing an increased run count for the retained experiments.

E6.justification: Reported iteration speedups change from 2.5× to 2.3× for TinyGSM and 1.4× to 1.7× for Sudoku. The ARM-initialized speedup changes from 2.3× to 4.0× under the longer initialization budget, so this is not a same-setting gain. Throughput assignments switch from 3.41/3.78 to 3.78/3.41 iterations per second for MDM/PUMA. New coding, PAPL, policy-ablation, and NELBO results substantially expand the evidence; TinyGSM NELBO favors MDM at approximately 0.05 versus PUMA's 0.06.

M1.justification: PUMA retains teacher-forced chains, streaming minibatches, reuse of training logits, confidence fast-forwarding, and progressive chain-length scheduling. K is redefined from a stage count to an approximate per-stage token count. The new LoRA experiments apply the existing PUMA procedure; they do not introduce a new PUMA component.

P1.justification: Most foundational exposition and its ordering are retained. v2 makes wording and notation edits, promotes ablations to a separate subsection, inserts a Discussion section, expands Appendix B into named analysis subsections, and updates publication information and acknowledgments. The existing narrative is extended without extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: v2 adds coding, schedule-sweep, PAPL, and NELBO figures, a policy-ablation table, and a Dream-Coder column in the configuration table. Existing plots gain uncertainty bands or revised axes and legends, and the Sudoku illustration changes examples and marks prompt cells. The old trajectory Figure 7 becomes Figure 6, while the old four-panel Figure 6 becomes Figure 9 with a revised scheduling panel.

R1.justification: v2 adds substantive positioning against Planner Aware Path Learning (Peng et al., 2025b), distinguishing its policy-aware ELBO and loss reweighting from PUMA's changed masking distribution. This is a distinct work from the sampling paper already cited in v1. Section 5 also adds a conceptual connection to self-forcing, alongside references supporting the new coding experiments.

T1.justification: Appendix A.2 corrects the application of the weighted-cross-entropy lemma: v1 treats the time-dependent weight as a function of X alone, whereas v2 takes its conditional expectation over time given X. The principal propositions, assumptions, and sample-complexity argument remain unchanged. Appendix B.5 additionally formalizes the PAPL weighting objective.

improvement.justification: v1's empirical support centers on Sudoku and small-scale structured pretraining. v2 substantially strengthens validation through 7B LoRA code fine-tuning, direct PAPL comparisons, and broader sensitivity and NELBO analyses. Confidence intervals and targeted proof and throughput corrections improve assessability. Large-scale evidence remains limited to post-training, and conflicting Dream-Coder K values impair reproducibility, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gain in empirical support and research positioning.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PUMA framework and contain readable text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A and B. Retained material can be matched across the expanded experiments and renumbered displays.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds Dream-Coder fine-tuning evaluated on HumanEval and MBPP, PAPL comparisons, and further ablations and NELBO analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original Sudoku experiments, TinyGSM pretraining evaluated on GSM8K, and training-recipe and inference-policy ablations.

results.title: Stop Training for the Worst: Progressive Unmasking Accelerates Masked Diffusion Training

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the central contributions: lightweight adapters trained on interpretability artifacts improve frozen-model self-interpretation, transfer across settings and recover implicit bridge entities, with favorable scaling. Revised headline comparisons change the supporting evidence and emphasis, rather than these core capability claims.

C2.justification: Appendix K introduces a core-versus-periphery interpretation of why detection and generation prefer different labels and scales, and argues for multiple candidate descriptions. Section 3.4 explicitly discusses metric-dependent architecture tradeoffs. Appendix A.5 and Table 8 newly explain selection bias and limitations on comparing results produced by different scoring protocols.

D1.justification: V2 supplies additional scoring details, including Table 8's four-scale, one-trial procedure, Table 11's sample count and rescoring trials, and the 70B detection judge and activation-cache source. Appendix K provides adapter-specific grids and latent lookup instructions. Training hyperparameters and hardware disclosures remain, but v1's explicit code-and-trained-adapter release statement and link are removed.

E1.justification: Both versions cover Goodfire, Llama Scope and Gemma Scope SAE features, Wikipedia contrastive topics and TwoHopFact bridge entities. New comparisons and diagnostic analyses reuse this coverage. Adding detection F1 at 70B extends evaluation of the retained SAE-labeling task.

E2.justification: V2 adds two substantively different trained comparator families: rank-4 LoRA Activation Oracles on Wikipedia and Goodfire evaluations, and layer-specific linear probes trained with InfoNCE for bridge-entity detection (Sections 3.4 and 3.6). Existing baselines are retained.

E3.justification: Appendix A.5 replaces direct best-of-six SAE score reporting with candidate selection followed by independent rescoring, affecting Tables 2, 3 and 11 and Appendix I. V2 also adds 70B detection scoring using a 70B judge and Goodfire activation contexts, and a matched 1,000-latent ALL-CAPS comparison. Coverage and Wikipedia retrieval retain their earlier reporting protocols.

E4.justification: New Appendix K investigates disagreement between detection-optimal and generation-optimal labels, presenting five extreme cases per 70B adapter and scale analyses of the top twenty. Appendix I revises the format-versus-semantics analysis with matched rescoring and format-selection measurements, replacing the earlier four-lowest-scales comparison. Figure 7 also revises the training-data-size results; most existing ablations remain.

E5.justification: Independent selection and reporting seeds replace selection-biased maxima for the principal stochastic SAE metrics, substantially changing statistical estimation. Table 11 and the revised ALL-CAPS comparison newly report uncertainty estimates. Existing SEM, confidence-interval and paired-test practices remain; the changes do not establish additional training-seed replications.

E6.justification: Many SAE scores are replaced under the revised protocol. In Table 3, SA changes from 71.4% to 66.8% hit rate and SA+LR from 68.3% to 69.7%, reversing their ranking. The abstract's 71% versus 63% comparison corresponds to SA versus paraphrases, whereas 70% versus 50% corresponds to SA+LR versus repeated original labels. These are not comparable performance gains across versions. V2 also adds 70B F1, comparator and disagreement results, and revises Figure 7 and ALL-CAPS findings.

M1.justification: The frozen language model, adapter architectures, normalization, cross-entropy objective, layer-0 injection and multiscale generation remain unchanged. New inference explanations document existing operations; independent rescoring changes evaluation rather than the proposed adapter.

P1.justification: The introduction is extensively rewritten, methods gain dedicated inference and evaluation subsections, and the experimental narrative is reorganized around architecture and geometry before cross-dataset evaluation and scaling. Explanations are expanded throughout the main text, and Appendix K adds a substantial new discussion.

P2.justification: Table 3 gains a detection-F1 column, Table 18 adds paired-label examples, and Figure 7 is redrawn with revised vertical ranges. Several captions expand and figures and tables move with the reorganized text. Most displays and the overall two-column design are retained.

R1.justification: The bibliography is unchanged. However, v2 newly positions frozen adapters as empirically competitive with Activation Oracles and contrasts their free-form descriptions with fixed-entity linear probes. The broader positioning as complementary to language-model fine-tuning remains.

T1.justification: Appendix K newly defines a disagreement statistic combining detection-F1 and generation-hit-rate gaps between the two selected labels. This limited mathematical addition supports example ranking; the adapter mathematics remains unchanged, with no new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: V1 reports maxima from noisy candidate scores; v2 independently rescores selected labels, addressing a material source of inflation in the central SAE evidence. The new trained baselines and explicit analysis of metric-dependent labels further strengthen assessment of the method. Removal of the code/adapters link and retention of older protocols for coverage and cross-layer results are drawbacks, but the substantial improvement in evaluation reliability outweighs them.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study, with matching authors, methods and experiments. Text, equations, tables, figures and appendices support reliable comparison. V1 contains Appendices A–J; v2 retains these and adds Appendix K.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and reports revised SAE evaluations, new LoRA and linear-probe comparisons, and additional label-disagreement analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original adapter-training experiments, SAE feature-label evaluations, topic retrieval, model-scaling results and bridge-entity detection, together with appendix ablations.

results.title: Learning Self-Interpretation from Interpretability Artifacts: Training Lightweight Adapters on Vector-Label Pairs
