C1.justification: The abstract, contributions, and conclusion shift from broad score-guided planning, Bellman certificates, and sequential complexity to an offline-regression-plus-greedy guarantee. Faithful correspondence with syntactic provability and the learned prover's average truncated proof length become central claimed contributions.

C2.justification: V3 substantially sharpens applicability and interpretation: it distinguishes learned-policy occupancy from optimal proof length, explains candidate-retention requirements and instability when a prover leaves the covered region, and identifies oracle rollout labels and exact regression as idealizations. Its limitations explicitly separate the analyzed greedy pipeline from practical beam search, backtracking, repair, and multi-agent systems.

D1.justification: Neither version supplies an implementation, concrete hyperparameter configuration, hardware/runtime measurements, or code/data access information. The revised symbolic sampling and estimator specifications are methodological and theoretical changes.

E1.justification: Neither version actually trains or evaluates on datasets or benchmarks. References to miniF2F, LeanDojo, and other environments describe prior work, not experimental coverage.

E2.justification: Neither version evaluates comparison methods against its proposed framework. Added discussions of other theorem-proving systems are related work, not baseline comparisons.

E3.justification: Neither version reports an experimental evaluation protocol. Changes to sampling distributions, symbolic label budgets, and regression assumptions concern the theoretical learning model rather than executed experiments.

E4.justification: Neither version reports ablations, robustness tests, or empirical supplementary analyses. The easy/hard-instance discussions and scaling arguments are theoretical interpretations, not new tests.

E5.justification: Neither version reports empirical runs, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Their probability bounds and independent-label assumptions are mathematical statements rather than empirical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Neither version contains original empirical measurements, performance rankings, or observed result entries. Revised provability bounds and statistical rates are theoretical changes assessed under T1.

M1.justification: The analyzed learning procedure changes substantially. V1 specifies squared-loss empirical risk minimization in Theorem 6 and a net-based Lipschitz-extension estimator in Appendix F; v3 specifies depth-wise minimax absolute-error regression on sampled query pairs, followed by greedy selection within concentration sets (Assumption 3.1). Greedy scoring already existed, but the central training objective and estimator construction change.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, theoretical narrative, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around one principal learning guarantee. Eleven main sections become seven; related work enters the main text, proofs are consolidated in Appendix A, and truncation and representation-learning material move to appendices. Dedicated limitations, future-work, and impact passages are added.

P2.justification: V1's single-column presentation becomes a two-column main text and bibliography with single-column appendices, conference-style front matter, and running headers. V3 adds Figure 1, a diagram connecting natural-deduction and Lean proof steps to MDP components. Equations and theorem displays are extensively reformatted.

R1.justification: Most theorem-proving and test-time-scaling literature coverage is retained. V3 adds targeted positioning against Bourbaki, Amit et al.'s verifiability theory, and Sonoda et al.'s hierarchical-prover analysis, plus Lean 4 and cut-complexity references. Several anecdotal and sequential-complexity references from v1 are removed.

T1.justification: V3 specializes the stochastic-MDP framework to deterministic verifier dynamics, adds faithful-abstraction equivalence with syntactic provability (Proposition 2.2), and proves occupancy-weighted regret and conditional-success bounds. Its regression theorem uses explicit i.i.d. coverage and minimax-estimation assumptions. V1's adaptive-deviation result and detailed certificate and measure-compactness proofs are omitted, although certificate and truncation ideas remain in v3's appendices.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially improves the coherence of the central learning guarantee: v1's Theorem 6 specifies squared-loss regression, while Appendix F switches to a net-extension estimator and additional assumptions; v3 aligns its explicit minimax estimator, coverage assumptions, and proof. The detailed occupancy argument and explicit oracle-label and candidate-retention limitations further strengthen precision. The narrower planner scope and abbreviated certificate development reduce breadth, but the improved support for the main theoretical result outweighs those losses.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching title and authors. All 22 pages of v1 and 18 pages of v3, including their appendices, support comparison despite substantial rewriting and reorganization.

after.justification: V3 remains theoretical throughout the main text and appendices. Rollout sampling is an assumed learning model, Figure 1 is illustrative, and estimating the theoretical quantities from real traces is proposed as future work.

before.justification: V1 presents theoretical definitions, guarantees, proofs, and a literature review. Empirical successes discussed in Appendix A are attributed to other works; no original empirical results are reported.

results.title: Why Agentic Theorem Prover Works: A Statistical Provability Theory of Mathematical Reasoning Models

C1.justification: The central HARPO and unified-model contributions persist. v2 expands the reasoning claim to five named interpretability properties and recalibrates multitask superiority: the headline gain changes from +16.85% to +12.02%, while the discussion changes from best on nine tasks to top-two on eight tasks.

C2.justification: v2 interprets prediction agreement, brevity and human preferences through explicit XAI properties. It qualifies the proposed connection between balanced learning and transfer as requiring further investigation, and explains why SFT/BAM classifier heads preclude zero-shot evaluation. Conversely, it removes v1's substantive AUT qualification that improved precision comes with lower recall.

D1.justification: New Appendix D documents decoding parameters, tokenizer-based length measurement, paraphrase controls, annotator backgrounds, masking and annotation instructions. v2 also supplies a model/code repository link and states that these resources are released, replacing v1's post-review availability promise. Existing training hyperparameters and hardware disclosures are unchanged.

E1.justification: Table 2 expands held-out coverage from autism behavior recognition and speech emotion recognition to five contexts, adding in-the-wild depression recognition, social-media sentiment analysis and sarcasm incongruity recognition. The Human Behavior Atlas training coverage remains unchanged.

E2.justification: v2 Table 1 adds Gemma 4-E4B, OmniSapiens SFT, OmniSapiens BAM and EMAGRPO to the retained comparators. Gemma 4-E4B also joins the held-out comparison in Table 2. These additions substantially broaden both model and optimization comparisons.

E3.justification: v2 introduces systematic reasoning-evaluation protocols: answer agreement, paraphrase agreement, reasoning-token counts and masked pairwise human judgments. Appendix D specifies decoding configurations, a 512-token generation cap, fixed instruction paraphrases and three non-author annotators. The existing training budgets, checkpoint selection and predictive metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Section 4.3 adds stochastic-consistency and paraphrase-robustness tests, efficiency measurements and human assessments of specificity, coherence and concision. The original component ablations and HUM/SAR reasoning analyses are retained, although relocated. The detailed AUT overprediction, abstention and precision–recall analysis is removed.

E5.justification: v2 newly reports five independently sampled inference traces per input for consistency and average-token measurements (Table 3 and Appendix D). This concerns repeated inference, not additional training replications. Neither version reports training-run uncertainty, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: New results include OmniSapiens scores of 72.43, 58.47 and 69.27 on IDR, SMSA and SIR, plus automated and human reasoning outcomes in Tables 3–4. Retained per-task scores are unchanged. Expanded comparator sets change the model's average rank from 1.20 to 1.90 and HARPO's algorithm rank from 1.70 to 2.10; these are not same-setting performance declines. AUT diagnostic result entries are removed.

M1.justification: The Qwen2.5-Omni-7B backbone, task/sample advantage modulation, geometric centering, inertial smoothing, rewards and optimization objective are unchanged. Appendix A's Algorithm 1 differs only in its equation cross-reference; moving the model setup into Section 3 does not change the method.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contribution statement and conclusion are substantially rewritten around the model and its interpretability. Model setup moves from the experiments into Section 3; reasoning evaluation and algorithm analyses are reorganized; a new Appendix D shifts subsequent appendices. Affiliations, publication information and acknowledgements also change.

P2.justification: v2 adds two reasoning-evaluation tables and a boxed annotation guide, expands the main comparison and held-out tables, and enlarges the appendix comparison table. All seven figures are retained, but the main figures are reordered and relocated, including v1 Figures 1–2 becoming v2 Figures 4–5.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands its social-intelligence and interpretability positioning, adding foundations such as Baron-Cohen and Goleman and XAI evaluation literature including Langer, Nauta and Turbé. It also introduces EMAGRPO through Feng et al. as a multitask-balancing comparator. Several earlier motivation references disappear, although the core reinforcement-learning related-work discussion remains.

T1.justification: v2 Appendix D adds mathematical definitions of agreement across sampled predictions and agreement under paraphrasing, in Equations 13–14. The existing GRPO formulation and HARPO geometric-mean derivation remain unchanged, moving from Appendix D to Appendix E.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the empirical case by addressing limited held-out coverage and missing strong comparators, while adding documented automated and masked human reasoning evaluations. The broader comparison also appropriately reduces the headline multitask gain. These benefits outweigh the loss of the useful AUT recall qualification. Reporting weaknesses remain: human-study sample counts are unspecified, and some Table 4 win rates contradict Appendix D's formula—for example, 80.6% Tie+Win and 35.3% Tie imply about 70.0% wins excluding ties, rather than the reported 66.0%.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe OmniSapiens-7B 2.0 and HARPO. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations and appendices are readable and support reliable matching across the revision.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds held-out results, additional baseline evaluations, automated reasoning assessments and a human evaluation.

before.justification: v1 reports original HARPO training comparisons, held-out AUT and SER evaluations, component ablations and analyses of reasoning and training dynamics.

results.title: OmniSapiens: A Foundation Model for Social Behavior Processing via Heterogeneity-Aware Relative Policy Optimization

C1.justification: The introduction removes the claim that this is the first BG formulation incorporating machine-learning potentials as importance-sampling target energies. The main contributions—CG sampling, ESFM-based PMF learning, solvent-mediated accuracy, and computational savings—are otherwise retained.

C2.justification: Section 3.3 explicitly acknowledges learned-PMF approximation bias. Appendix B qualifies larger-peptide convergence as primarily covering the targeted dihedrals, and Table 5 cautions about cross-paper runtime comparability. Section 4.2 adds an interpretation of coarser mappings as improving ESS while generally reducing reweighted accuracy.

D1.justification: Appendices B–D substantially expand experimental documentation with larger-peptide simulation recipes, explicit flow/PMF training sample counts, and center-of-mass preprocessing. Hyperparameters and checkpoint-selection instructions are revised. Some earlier reproducibility information is removed, including the dipeptide box size and trajectory-recording stride; hardware, software, and code-access information remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds alanine tripeptide (42 atoms) and hexapeptide (72 atoms), extending molecular complexity beyond the retained Müller–Brown and 22-atom dipeptide systems. Tripeptide uses both CG mappings and hexapeptide uses Core Beta; evaluation focuses on selected dihedral pairs.

E2.justification: v2 Table 7 adds TarFlow and ECNF++ to the dipeptide accuracy/ESS comparison against the explicit-solvent reference. v1 compared accuracy with generalized Born baselines and included ECNF++ only in a runtime comparison. The new caption attributes the atomistic BG results to prior studies; it does not establish new baseline training.

E3.justification: Appendices C–D revise MB flow training from 2000 to 1000 epochs, dipeptide training batch size from 256 to 1024, ODE tolerances from 1e-4 to 1e-5, and PMF training from 250 to 300 epochs with changed decay and final-checkpoint selection. New peptide experiments introduce longer trajectories and targeted biasing protocols. Appendix B also replaces the stated implicit-solvent 2 fs/H-bond constraints with a blanket 0.5 fs/unconstrained setting. These are reported protocol revisions, not proof of reruns.

E4.justification: The clipping analysis expands from dipeptide to tripeptide and hexapeptide, with separate ablation tables and sensitivity curves for five system/mapping combinations (v2 Tables 7–9 and Figure 10). Resolution comparisons and structural diagnostics also extend to larger peptides. The short 10 ns unbiased-dipeptide sampling-failure illustration in v1 Figure 6b is removed.

E5.justification: Both versions report uncertainty values and specify ten independent MB data-generation trajectories. v2 changes table notation from ± values to parenthetical digits, but introduces no stated uncertainty-estimation procedure, model-run count, confidence interval, or significance test. The origins of the reported uncertainties remain unspecified.

E6.justification: Results are extensively revised and expanded. In Table 2, Heavy Atom dipeptide JS/PMF/ESS changes from 0.0075/0.2493/0.2325 to 0.0048/0.2005/0.5112. Unclipped dipeptide ESS changes from near-zero or unavailable values in v1 Table 6 to approximately 0.36–0.46 in v2 Table 7. Runtime values change, and larger-peptide and atomistic-baseline results are added. Changed protocols prevent interpreting these as controlled same-setting gains.

M1.justification: The ESFM-trained PMF, flow-matching proposal, importance reweighting, and 1% clipping procedure remain unchanged, as do the specified network architectures and Appendix F algorithms. Appendix C newly documents center-of-mass centering and noise, without establishing that this was a newly introduced procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, background, method exposition, simulation-free evaluation discussion, related work, and future-work paragraphs undergo extensive rewriting. Appendix G is reorganized around the expanded systems and analyses. These changes substantially revise the narrative and explanations while retaining the main section sequence.

P2.justification: Figures are extensively redrawn and regrouped: v1 Figures 3–4 become v2 Figure 2, the MB figure moves to Appendix G, and Ramachandran panels are consolidated and promoted into the main text. Dataset, runtime, and ablation tables expand across peptides. A new labeling inconsistency appears in v2 Figure 11, whose axes say phi despite its psi caption.

R1.justification: Section 5 adds constrained mean-force approaches and newer generative-sampling references, while explaining the relationship to already-cited Tamagnone et al. (2024) and Kohler et al. (2023). Future-work citations expand and the first-formulation novelty claim is removed, but the overall research positioning remains stable.

T1.justification: Equation (18) adds the 1/B normalization and explicitly defines ESS as a fraction in (0,1], correcting the mathematical definition to match fractional reporting. Propositions 1–3 and the Appendix A proofs are substantively unchanged.

improvement.justification: v1 supported its scalability argument mainly with a toy potential and dipeptide. The larger-peptide evaluations, direct atomistic-BG accuracy comparisons, and expanded resolution/clipping analyses substantially strengthen evidence for the central claims. Explicit PMF-bias and targeted-dihedral qualifications improve their interpretation. These gains outweigh reporting weaknesses: larger-system validation remains limited to selected dihedrals, and Appendix G.4 retains blanket clipping-benefit statements that conflict with the revised dipeptide results in Table 7.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Coarse-Grained Boltzmann Generators by the same authors. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–G are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching material moved between the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v2 reports original CG-BG evaluations on the retained systems and on alanine tripeptide and hexapeptide, with quantitative results and supplementary analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulations and CG-BG evaluations on the Müller–Brown potential and alanine dipeptide, including accuracy, runtime, and clipping experiments.

results.title: Coarse-Grained Boltzmann Generators

C1.justification: v1 centers its contributions on an efficient board-game algorithm and empirical component validation. v2's abstract, introduction, and conclusion make stability and convergence characterization central contributions and explicitly locate novelty in theoretical and empirical understanding of existing regularization ingredients. The principal efficiency claim remains.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations connecting efficiency to branching factors, architecture/computation tradeoffs, and alternative regularization results. It discusses multiplayer and infinite-horizon proof boundaries and possible stochastic/continuous-action extensions. The earlier spatial-complexity explanation for action-value learning and Retrace extension suggestion disappear; the asymptotic-performance caveat remains.

D1.justification: v2 describes the added shared-head and separate-network configurations and their computational implications. It removes v1's explicit n-step/lambda-return formulas and MLP-head description. Default hyperparameters, optimizer settings, parallelism, hardware information, and existing implementation/checkpoint references are otherwise retained.

E1.justification: v2 adds Matching Pennies, a simultaneous normal-form game, in Section 5.1. The five principal board games, 19x19 Go, and Count Up game are retained; Count Up moves from v1 Appendix L to v2 Appendix D. Stochastic and continuous-action environments are discussed but not evaluated.

E2.justification: Appendices I–J add evaluated Forward-KL, Entropy Reward, Discrete SAC, V-MPO, Munchausen DQN, and GRPO comparators. Table 2 also includes AlphaZero in the test-time MCTS comparison, whereas v1's corresponding 9x9 Go scaling experiment compared KLENT with Gumbel AlphaZero. The original principal baselines remain.

E3.justification: The original board-game protocols remain intact. Targeted additions include a five-game comparison using checkpoints trained with 800 million simulator evaluations and 800 test-time rollouts, a Matching Pennies regularization grid, and architecture controls including separate networks with approximately twice the computational cost.

E4.justification: v2 substantially expands diagnostic evidence: Figure 3 tests convergence boundaries, Figure 8 tracks policy-update KL divergence, Appendix H tests head/backbone sharing and an EMA variant, and Appendix I tests alternative regularization choices. Existing component ablations, hyperparameter sensitivity, rollout studies, and Count Up analyses are retained.

E5.justification: The new MCTS comparison in Table 2 explicitly reports means and standard errors. The existing learning curves and search-scaling experiments retain three-seed means and standard deviations. No increase in repeated-run counts or new significance-testing procedure is documented.

E6.justification: Principal learning curves and older appendix tables are retained, but substantial results are added. Table 2 reports MCTS average win rates of 32.2%, 53.6%, and 77.2% for AlphaZero, Gumbel AlphaZero, and KLENT. At 800 million evaluations, Tables 6–7 report 61%, 14%, 2%, and 3% for Forward-KL, Entropy Reward, Munchausen DQN, and GRPO, versus KLENT's retained 89%. Architecture and convergence findings are also added.

M1.justification: Section 4 and Algorithm 1 retain the analytical policy update, policy/action-value networks, lambda-return targets, joint loss, and self-play/fitting procedure. The new architecture and regularization variants are experimental alternatives; the proposed KLENT procedure is unchanged.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and conclusion are substantially rewritten. Related work and the problem setting are reorganized, value-learning exposition is compressed, and the appendices are reordered into four thematic parts with a contents list. These changes reshape the narrative beyond simply inserting new results.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column main-text layout, rearranges benchmark and ablation panels into horizontal rows, adds convergence and KL-divergence figures and comparison tables, and redraws Count Up results for the main text. The Go spatial illustration and ablation-configuration table disappear; existing branching-factor statistics are additionally displayed in Table 1.

R1.justification: v2 substantially repositions the work as extending regularized-policy and game-theoretic research, explicitly comparing its convergence condition with Sokota et al. It adds literature supporting Discrete SAC, V-MPO, Munchausen DQN, and GRPO comparisons, while trimming historical TD-learning and Q-learning discussion.

T1.justification: Beyond v1's analytical-update derivation and empirical equilibrium discussion, v2 adds Section 5 and Appendix C: local linear convergence under alpha(alpha + 2 beta) > ||R||_2^2/4, supporting Jacobian lemmas and proofs, a general-sum extension, and a bounded-horizon convergence argument. These constitute a substantial new theoretical component.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens v1's mainly empirical justification through conditional normal-form convergence analysis, targeted architecture and regularization tests, and broader MCTS comparisons. These additions better explain the design and test competing explanations for its efficiency. The finite-horizon proof presumes value-estimate convergence, new baseline configurations remain sparsely documented, and some method detail is lost, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in scientific support.

A1.justification: Despite the changed title, both PDFs describe KLENT and share the principal experiments. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds Matching Pennies simulations, architecture experiments, and additional algorithm comparisons.

before.justification: v1 reports original board-game experiments, component ablations, computational analyses, and Count Up game simulations in Section 5 and the appendices.

results.title: Revisiting Regularized Policy Optimization for Stable and Efficient Reinforcement Learning in Two-Player Games

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion expand the claimed applications from contamination detection to information retrieval and paraphrase detection. The theoretical contribution is qualified through revised conditional bounds and acknowledged non-decaying cases. The central claim of fast semantic search over trillion-scale corpora remains.

C2.justification: v2 acknowledges that the occurrence-ratio intuition underlying v1's theory fails empirically and discusses linguistic constraints and examples with r >= 1 (Section 4; Appendix M). It adds substantive explanations of beta-dependent ranking tradeoffs and insertion-related grammatical errors affecting quality judgments. The existing multiword-semantics and resource limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds GPT-5.4 judging and paraphrasing prompts, query-selection and exclusion instructions, and settings for the new evaluations. Appendix D documents hyperparameter rationales, while Appendix H explains frequently accessed versus example-retrieval index storage. Its proposed SSD/HDD configuration is deployment guidance, rather than a newly tested hardware setup.

E1.justification: v2 adds ORCAS search queries, information retrieval on TREC-COVID and SciFact, and source-document identification using GPT-5.4 paraphrases of FineWeb-Edu sentences. The existing seven-language corpus coverage and seven contamination benchmarks remain; v1's reference to six languages was inconsistent with its own Table 3.

E2.justification: BM25, previously discussed only as related work, becomes an evaluated comparator in retrieval and paraphrase detection (v2 Tables 17–18). The original comparisons with infini-gram, infini-gram mini, and SoftMatcha are retained.

E3.justification: New protocols include cold-cache controls, order-swapped GPT-5.4 judgments, manually prepared retrieval queries with precision/recall metrics, and 400 paraphrase-source tests. The pruning-latency sample increases from 400 to 2,000 queries. Reported English seven/eight-token proportions change from 7%/5% to 6%/6%, and cache clearing changes from CPU-cache terminology to OS page cache; these revisions do not establish reruns of all retained experiments.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's pruning ablations and output-size/threshold analysis, v2 adds smooth-minimum versus plain-minimum quality comparisons, beta sensitivity examples, cold/hot-cache robustness checks, and empirical validation of theoretical assumptions with and without insertions/deletions. Appendix K.3 also revises the existing pruning-latency analysis.

E5.justification: Appendix M newly reports log-shifted geometric means to reduce outlier influence. Appendix K.3 explicitly increases the query sample for more reliable p99 estimation. This concerns statistical estimation and query sampling, not additional independent runs; confidence intervals and significance tests remain absent.

E6.justification: v2 adds retrieval, quality-judgment, cache, real-query, and assumption-validation results. New paraphrase P@1 is 84.3% for Ours, versus 74.5% for SoftMatcha and 82.8% for BM25 (Table 18). The main 278.17 ms latency and contamination totals remain, while lookup growth changes from 2.27 to 2.30 per token. Under the expanded query sample, Figure 15 plots higher latency with all pruning techniques, contradicting the accompanying speedup claim.

M1.justification: The core suffix-array search, pruning techniques, similarity function, and adaptive thresholding remain. Appendix I adds document-scoring adaptations for downstream retrieval, including an explicitly tested IDF-weighted variant, Ours+IDF, for paraphrase source identification.

P1.justification: Related work moves partly to Appendix A, problem formulation becomes Section 2.2, and the method is reorganized into six subsections separating building blocks, pruning, indexing, similarity, and thresholding. The introduction and theoretical exposition are extensively rewritten, and the evaluation, application, and appendix structures are substantially reorganized.

P2.justification: v2 adopts the ICML layout, restructures Table 2, moves the suffix-array diagram from v1's Appendix H into main-text Figure 3, resizes the contamination figure, and redraws Figure 15. It adds tables for downstream applications, cache conditions, real queries, quality judgments, beta sensitivity, and assumption validation.

R1.justification: New citations support ORCAS, retrieval benchmarks, BM25, and query-length rationales. Earlier Heaps-law references to Baeza-Yates/Navarro and van Leijenhorst/van der Weide are removed. Table 2 refines lexical-semantic versus coarse-topic retrieval positioning, but the central relationship to SoftMatcha and the infini-gram systems remains.

T1.justification: v1 derives a constant query-length bound from its corpus-occurrence hypothesis and a moderate-gamma condition. v2 replaces this reasoning with explicit growth assumptions permitting r >= 1 and the bound A*a*(1-r^m)/(1-r), constant only when r < 1. It revises the corpus-size proof and adds conditional analysis of adaptive thresholding and additional pruning in Appendix N.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for practical usefulness through real-query, cold-cache, retrieval, and paraphrase evaluations, while exposing weaknesses in v1's occurrence-ratio rationale and making the theoretical conditions more explicit. Expanded experimental documentation and clearer organization improve assessability. Figure 15's contradiction with its pruning-speedup claim is a material regression, and geometric-mean checks do not fully validate expectation-based bounds. These limitations temper, but do not outweigh, the substantial gains in empirical support and theoretical transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SoftMatcha 2 research. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison across the substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds real-query evaluation, cache experiments, retrieval and paraphrase results, quality judgments, and empirical checks of theoretical assumptions.

before.justification: v1 reports original latency measurements, pruning ablations, multilingual search results, and manually verified benchmark-contamination findings.

results.title: SoftMatcha 2: A Fast and Soft Pattern Matcher for Trillion-Scale Corpora

C1.justification: The central claims remain a first benchmark for agentic game development, deterministic verification of multimodal tasks, persistent weaknesses in multimodal understanding, and benefits from visual feedback. Updated task counts, models, and performance examples change the supporting evidence without redefining these central contributions.

C2.justification: v2 drops v1's hypothesis that dynamically choosing between feedback mechanisms explains improved cost efficiency. It newly attributes lower full-set performance to multimodal variants, hypothesizes that Gemini 3 Pro's difficulty-split exception reflects stronger multimodal understanding, and interprets low transcript overlap as suggesting no systemic memorization. The new Impact Statement also explicitly bounds the tasks to using existing assets rather than creating assets.

D1.justification: v2 documents the new diagnostic procedures and supplies per-configuration median token consumption and costs in Table 4. It removes v1 Figure 6's disclosure that Gemini CLI costs were approximated using OpenHands, without explaining whether cost collection changed. Exact prompts in Appendices A–D and the public repository remain unchanged; the failure judge's identity and prompt are unspecified.

E1.justification: The main benchmark retains Godot 4 and the same four development skill categories; its larger task count does not establish a new development domain. Appendix J adds a distinct evaluation task: completing held-out tutorial transcripts to probe memorization.

E2.justification: Table 2 substantially revises the evaluated lineup: GPT-5.4 and GPT-5.4 Mini replace GPT-5.1-Codex-Max, Qwen3.5-397B replaces Qwen3-VL-235B, and Claude Opus 4.5 is removed. The OpenHands comparison also removes Claude Sonnet 4.5 while retaining Haiku 4.5, Gemini 3 Flash, and Kimi K2.5.

E3.justification: The evaluation changes from 115 base tasks plus 17 variants to 154 core tasks plus 179 variants. v2 adds core/full reporting and a human-labeled split of 131 easy and 202 hard tasks. New protocols include LLM classification of failures from four leading configurations and first-half-to-second-half continuation of 117 transcripts, scored with ROUGE-L and BLEU-4. The main pass@1 metric remains unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix H adds analyses of variant inclusion and human-rated multimodal difficulty; Appendix I supplements the existing qualitative failure discussion with quantified error categories; Appendix J adds a memorization probe. Feedback ablations are also revised: for example, Sonnet 4.5 loses its screenshot-only and video-only evaluations, while GPT-5.4 Mini receives both.

E5.justification: v1 Figure 6 reports a linear fit used to contextualize cost versus success; v2 removes that fitted statistical summary. Neither version reports repeated-run variability, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Appendix F retains the same mean, three-standard-deviation-filtered mean, median, and maximum reporting convention.

E6.justification: Results are extensively replaced and supplemented. With both feedback tools, Table 2 reports Gemini 3 Pro at 54.5% in v1 versus 53.8% in v2, and Sonnet 4.5 at 46.2% versus 34.8%; these use different task sets and are not same-setting performance declines. Tables 4–8 add subgroup scores, token and cost values, failure frequencies, and transcript-overlap scores. Task statistics also change. Appendix G's new GPT-5.4 attribution is uncertain because Figure 11 still labels the example GPT-Codex-5.1-Max.

M1.justification: The task-construction pipeline, deterministic Godot testing, screenshot MCP, and runtime-video feedback mechanisms remain unchanged. Appendices A–D contain identical construction, refinement, annotation, and agent prompts apart from formatting. Difficulty labeling extends evaluation rather than changing the proposed solving method.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and Appendices A–G are retained. v2 locally rewrites the abstract, results discussion, and conclusion, changes 'framework' terminology to 'harness,' adopts author–year citations, and adds acknowledgements, an Impact Statement, and Appendices H–J. Most construction, method, related-work, and prompt text remains closely matched.

P2.justification: v2 changes the main text to a two-column conference layout with running headers, resizes and relocates existing displays, stacks Figure 5's panels, and substantially redraws Figure 6 with model-family groupings and harness encodings. It adds Tables 4–8. The task-example figures and Figure 11's underlying graphic are retained rather than newly introduced.

R1.justification: v2 replaces the SlideChat pathology-image reference with SlideGen for the slide-generation comparison and adds BenchLM.ai as a source for the Design2Code comparison. The broader positioning relative to software benchmarks, computer-use agents, game playing, and specialized game-development systems remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Neither version develops formal theoretical results, proofs, or substantive mathematical derivations. The added empirical metrics and subgroup comparisons do not introduce new mathematical theory.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the benchmark's empirical validation beyond v1's category-level comparisons and illustrative failure case. Core/full and easy/hard analyses directly examine the intended multimodal challenge, quantified failure categories improve diagnostic value, and the transcript probe adds a limited contamination check. These address substantive validation gaps rather than merely increasing task counts. The unspecified failure judge and contradictory model attribution in Figure 11 limit reproducibility and consistency, but do not outweigh the added evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe GameDevBench and provide readable main text, tables, figures, and appendices. The retained sections and appendices can be matched despite substantial reformatting and additional evaluations in v2.

after.justification: v2 reports original evaluations on 333 tasks and additional core/full, difficulty, failure-pattern, and transcript-contamination results in Appendices H–J.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations on 132 game-development tasks, including agent success rates, feedback ablations, cost comparisons, and failure analysis.

results.title: GameDevBench: Evaluating Agentic Capabilities Through Game Development

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the three central contributions: stronger pretraining weight decay improves plasticity; minimizing pretraining loss need not optimize downstream performance; and representation, attention-rank, and overfitting effects offer potential mechanisms. The enlarged experiments strengthen support without redefining these contributions.

C2.justification: New Appendix A explicitly distinguishes correlational mechanisms from the experimentally isolated weight-decay effect and discusses sparse model configurations and untested regimes. Appendix D interprets observed stability costs. Its claim that upstream performance is unaffected is overbroad: the listed OLMo-2-1B-140x accuracy falls from 0.61 to 0.56 across decay settings.

D1.justification: v2 adds project-specific Models and Code links, a direct MMLUProCoT source reference, explicit OLMo checkpoint selection for fine-tuning, and detailed sample sizes, safety-training mixtures, and hyperparameter grids. These substantially extend v1's documentation of basic training recipes and hardware. The PDFs establish the presence of access links, not their external availability.

E1.justification: v2 adds fine-tuning on HellaSwag, Winogrande, PiQA, Arc-Easy, and Arc-Challenge, plus safety alignment using Alpaca and safety instructions with evaluation on I-MaliciousInstructions (Appendix C.3–C.4). The original six CoT tasks, pretraining corpora, and SST/AG News probing tasks remain.

E2.justification: v1's Table 3 includes only positive pretraining weight-decay values. v2 adds an explicit no-weight-decay control, λ = 0, for all five model groups and reports its results in appendix comparisons. The existing model families and positive-decay comparisons remain.

E3.justification: v2 introduces joint pretraining weight-decay/learning-rate sweeps and fine-tuning learning-rate/weight-decay/batch-size sweeps (Appendix E). New protocols include cloze accuracy, harmfulness scoring on 100 prompts with four safety-training sample sizes, and upstream evaluation before and after fine-tuning. The original CoT splits and default fine-tuning settings are retained.

E4.justification: New Appendix E tests whether the plasticity effect survives changes to other pretraining and fine-tuning hyperparameters, including selection of the best fine-tuning configuration. Appendix D adds stability–plasticity and upstream-performance analyses, while Appendix F.3 adds layer-wise parameter-norm analysis. The original probing, attention-rank, and leave-one-out analyses remain.

E5.justification: The new safety-alignment plots include error bars around mean harmfulness scores (Figures 12–16), but their statistical definition and run/seed counts are unspecified. The existing Pearson leave-one-out analysis is retained as Figure 10, formerly Figure 9.

E6.justification: v2 adds results for the new tasks, zero-decay controls, hyperparameter sweeps, stability trade-offs, and norm measurements. Existing results also change: the overall Greedy probing/downstream correlation is 0.93 in v1 Figure 15 and 0.87 in v2 Figure 25, alongside an expanded set of model variants. Figure 4(c)'s OLMo probing curves are also revised.

M1.justification: Both versions investigate AdamW pretraining weight decay followed by supervised fine-tuning using the same Llama-2 and OLMo-2 architectures. The added experiments do not introduce a new training algorithm, architecture, objective, or adaptation component.

P1.justification: v2 rewrites the abstract and portions of the methods and results, particularly Section 4.3, and reorganizes fine-tuning and evaluation material into task-based Appendix C. It adds discussion and analysis sections, while preserving the six-section main narrative and much of the original prose.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to a two-column conference layout. Numerous new experimental figures are added; v1 Figures 10–14 are consolidated into v2 Figure 24. Figure 6 is redesigned to display training loss, validation loss, and their gap, with additional revisions to panels, axes, legends, and captions elsewhere.

R1.justification: The main related-work section remains largely unchanged. v2 adds references for the new benchmarks and safety setup, vision-pretraining findings, and compositional generalization. Appendix A sharpens the comparison with Kobayashi et al. and expands the connection to the already-cited Lee et al. study.

T1.justification: The AdamW equations are rearranged and reindexed but express the same combined update. The attention-rank argument, training–validation gap, and 95%-singular-value pseudo-rank definition are retained. No new theorem, proof, or substantive mathematical derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence that the plasticity finding extends beyond CoT tasks and is robust to other training choices. Appendix E directly addresses v1's reliance on mostly fixed hyperparameters, while stability analyses, explicit mechanistic limitations, and project access links improve interpretation and reproducibility. Undefined safety error bars and Appendix D's overbroad upstream-performance interpretation are weaknesses, but they do not outweigh these substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same weight-decay and language-model-plasticity study. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison across the 28-page v1 and 32-page v2.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds commonsense and safety evaluations, hyperparameter sweeps, stability analyses, and parameter-norm measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original pretraining and fine-tuning experiments, linear probing, attention-rank measurements, and training–validation gap analyses in Sections 4–5 and the appendices.

results.title: Weight Decay Improves Language Model Plasticity

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contribution list and main conclusion retain the same claims about diffusion-native preference modeling, noise ensembling, competitive reward accuracy and efficient alignment. The new experiments supply additional support without redefining these core contributions.

C2.justification: Appendix C.3 explicitly distinguishes reuse of the formulation across backbones from transfer of trained rewards within compatible latent spaces. Appendix D.2 discusses requirements for untested broader applications. The conclusion removes the specific grid-artifact observation and instead references reward-hacking patterns already documented in v1.

D1.justification: v2 adds limited implementation descriptions for the comparison heads: direct pooling versus a lightweight transformer followed by pooling. The core hyperparameter tables, training and inference algorithms, hardware disclosure and project URL are unchanged; detailed implementation information for the added experiments remains limited.

E1.justification: Both versions use HPDv3 training data, the same four preference benchmarks and text-to-image alignment using Pick-a-Pic. Added SDXL and SD3.5-L experiments change model configurations within this coverage. Video, editing and audio-visual applications are discussed only as future extensions.

E2.justification: The main Table 1 comparator roster is unchanged. v2 additionally evaluates LRM-SDXL as an alignment comparator in Figure 5, whereas v1 compared it only on offline preference accuracy. Table 6 also introduces average-pooling and transformer-plus-pooling alternatives for the reward-head comparison.

E3.justification: v2 adds a controlled SDXL ReFL comparison holding the generator and optimization configuration fixed while changing rewards, and an experiment transferring an SD3.5-M reward to SD3.5-L. These new alignment curves extend through 200 steps, alongside new head configurations. This substantially expands the evaluation design; the original 150-step SD3.5-M experiment and benchmark protocols remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix C adds direct tests of reward-head aggregation, performance against LRM-SDXL with a matched backbone, and reuse of trained rewards across generators sharing a latent space. These address architectural dependence, backbone confounding and transferability. Earlier noise, layer-depth, uncertainty, Flow-GRPO and reward-hacking analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Appendix A retains the same 1,000 HPDv3 pairs, ten noise draws per pair, variation ratios, mean margins and score variances. The added experiments introduce no new seed reporting, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: v2 newly reports 71.55% average accuracy for DiNa-LRM on SDXL against 61.73% for LRM-SDXL (Table 5). Table 6 adds pooling-head averages of 71.03% and 71.14%, alongside the retained 71.49% Q-Former result. Figures 5–6 add SDXL alignment and SD3.5-L transfer findings. Original numerical results remain unchanged; these are additional results, not improvements to the original experimental runs.

M1.justification: Section 4 and Algorithms 1–2 retain the same noise-calibrated Thurstone formulation, fidelity loss, FiLM-conditioned gated Q-Former and multi-noise token ensembling. Additional backbone evaluations and alternative-head ablations do not revise the proposed default method.

P1.justification: v2 adds an appendix contents page, reorganizes Appendix C into four subsections, expands Appendix D and adds acknowledgements and cross-references. Most existing prose remains intact. Some reference edits introduce errors, including 'Table 5.3' and 'Appendix 3' where v1 correctly referenced Section 5.3 and Table 3.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the evidence displays with new SDXL and transfer plots (Figures 5–6), comparison and head-ablation tables (Tables 5–6), and an SDXL row in the backbone table. Existing figures and tables are retained but relocated or reformatted; v1 Figures 5–7 become v2 Figures 7–9.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting broader application discussion, including Reward Forcing, UniC and AnyTalker, plus a Visual-aware CoT citation in related work. The central positioning against algorithm-specific, step-level diffusion rewards remains unchanged. Publication and bibliographic updates to existing references do not constitute new related work.

T1.justification: The diffusion and flow-matching definitions, preference likelihoods, uncertainty calibration, loss, ensembling equations and appendix uncertainty formulas are unchanged. No new theorem, proof or substantive mathematical derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: v1's comparison with prior diffusion rewards used different backbones. v2's matched-SDXL accuracy and alignment comparisons substantially reduce this important confounding, while head ablations and shared-latent-space transfer provide direct evidence for architectural robustness and reward reuse. These additions materially strengthen the central empirical case and clarify its limits. Sparse implementation details for the new experiments and minor cross-reference errors temper, but do not outweigh, these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DiNa-LRM research work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds SDXL comparisons, reward-head ablations and an SD3.5-M-to-SD3.5-L reward-transfer experiment.

before.justification: v1 reports original preference-prediction experiments, architectural and noise-schedule ablations, uncertainty measurements, and ReFL and Flow-GRPO alignment results.

results.title: Beyond VLM-Based Rewards: Diffusion-Native Latent Reward Modeling

C1.justification: The abstract adds an explicit claim of favorable scaling behavior and narrows the first-architecture claim from adaptive mesh refinement generally to HR-adaptive simulations. The central claims about fused attention, mesh flexibility, super-resolution and cross-dataset learning remain.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the new scaling results as showing further growth potential and explains MINO's ATES memory failure through its mesh-dependent latent size. Appendix D emphasizes that APT's advantage is strongest in heterogeneous subsurface settings. The conclusion newly acknowledges that scaling was demonstrated for one physics type and leaves multiphysics pretraining and transfer fine-tuning untested.

D1.justification: Appendices C.1.2 and C.2.1 substantially expand implementation documentation for the added baselines, including widths, layers, tokens, graph hierarchy, optimizer settings and training budgets. v2 also specifies timing batch size and hardware and documents scaling configurations. Existing APT implementation descriptions and the promise to release code and created datasets upon publication remain.

E1.justification: New Appendix D adds Airfoil, Darcy and Elasticity evaluations, covering compressible flow, linear porous-medium flow and linear solid mechanics. This substantially extends task coverage beyond the retained subsurface and CarBench experiments. The scaling studies reuse ATES.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds Transolver, MINO, UPT and HOOD to the faulted CO2 comparison. Table 3 adds evaluated UPT and Transolver baselines on ATES and records an attempted MINO evaluation that exceeds memory capacity. These additions substantially broaden comparisons on existing tasks; the earlier comparators remain.

E3.justification: Section 4.5 introduces controlled experiments with 40k, 120k and 161k training samples and 0.8M, 17.5M and 69.4M parameters, reporting the best test loss during training. New baseline experiments specify additional training budgets and configurations. The faulted-CO2 timing protocol changes its reported GPU from A100 to H100, except HOOD on A100, and newly specifies batch size 340; these are not directly comparable timing conditions across versions.

E4.justification: Section 4.5 and Table 7 add data-size and model-capacity sensitivity studies, testing whether additional data and parameters continue improving ATES predictions. Section 4.3 also expands analysis of accuracy, latency and memory tradeoffs. Existing branch ablations, super-resolution tests, geological distribution-shift tests and qualitative cases are retained.

E5.justification: No changed run counts, seeds, uncertainty estimators, confidence intervals or significance procedures are documented. Table 9 newly reports 36M-model errors of 0.811/1.066; these are additional configuration results, not improvements to the unchanged 19M result.

M1.justification: Section 5.1 adds TITO+Struct, a conditioning variant combining Proteina structure embeddings with the amino-acid sequence without pLM embeddings. The underlying flow-matching objective, two-stage transformer architecture, and rollout procedures remain unchanged. PLaTITO-Big becoming PLaTITO-19M is a rename.

Changes include grammatical corrections, standardized notation, the PLaTITO-19M rename, updated cross-references, an Impact Statement, and new appendix subsections. P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the experimental displays with Tables 7–10 and Figures 11–12, adds rows to Table 1, and adds TITO+Struct columns to Figures 7–8. results.title: Protein Language Model Embeddings Improve Generalization of Implicit Transfer Operators

C1.justification: The abstract, first contribution, and conclusion replace the claimed large-mini-batch no-momentum guarantee with a full-batch-only guarantee and a failure counterexample at m = 2. This substantially narrows and redefines a central contribution; the other principal claims remain.

C2.justification: V1 describes the no-momentum batch condition as potentially conservative. V2 recognizes that it permits only full-batch training and explains that the counterexample does not characterize all stochastic dynamics. It also makes the batch–momentum trade-off more explicit and qualifies variance-reduction slowdown as a worst-case bound.

D1.justification: V2 documents the added MNIST experiment's class-balanced sampling, hidden width, sigmoid activation, cross-entropy loss, and parameter grids. These are localized reproducibility additions for a new experiment; the earlier algorithmic and experimental details are retained.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates synthetic Gaussian and orthogonal scale-skewed classification data. V2 retains these and adds MNIST digit classification, substantially extending coverage from constructed data to real images.

E2.justification: Comparator membership in the retained experiments is unchanged. The added MNIST comparison uses existing Spectral-SGD/Muon and variance-reduced variants; Figure 5 explicitly defines SGDM as Spectral-SGD with momentum, not an additional baseline.

E3.justification: The new MNIST protocol uses 1,000 balanced samples, a width-100 two-layer sigmoid network, batch sizes {10, 100, 500, 1000}, and momentum {0, 0.5, 0.9}. It tracks a margin normalized by the maximum layer spectral norm, introducing a substantially different evaluation design. Existing synthetic protocols remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Figure 5 extends batch-size and momentum sensitivity analysis, with and without variance reduction, to nonlinear MNIST training. This adds evidence about stability outside the synthetic linear setting while retaining the existing sensitivity analyses and per-sample case study.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or statistical tests. The added MNIST trajectories likewise have no reported uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Figure 5 adds the first real-data neural-network results: without momentum, batch size 10 retains a negative spectral margin while full-batch training reaches a positive margin; momentum and variance reduction mitigate this gap. These are substantial new results under new conditions. Figures 1–4 retain their plotted results.

M1.justification: The stochastic steepest-descent updates, momentum, SVRG-style estimator, and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged. The neural-network experiment applies existing optimizers; Appendix H.1 clarifies the canonical spectral direction already used rather than introducing a new update.

P1.justification: V2 locally rewrites Section 4.1, expands related-work and experimental discussion, revises appendix headings and the contents listing, and corrects wording and cross-references. Most prose and the overall document organization remain intact.

P2.justification: V2 adds the six-panel Figure 5 and adjusts caption formatting and figure placement. Figures 3 and 4 correct their stated geometries from ℓ2 to ℓ∞ and spectral, respectively. Figures 1–4 retain their plotted content.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds dedicated discussions of stochastic margin maximization and variance reduction, distinguishing the work from SGD, momentum SGD, and stochastic AdaGrad-Norm analyses and stating specific novelty claims. The no-momentum rate corollary is now explicitly attributed to Fan et al. (2025), materially revising its positioning.

T1.justification: V2 derives that Theorem 4.1's condition forces m = 1 because γ ≤ 2R, and adds Proposition 4.2 with its proof in Proposition D.6, establishing SignSGD failure on a separable two-sample dataset. Lemma H.1 also replaces equality of spectral and Frobenius argmax sets with a shared canonical direction. The momentum and variance-reduction bounds remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: V1 presents Theorem 4.1 as a meaningful large-mini-batch guarantee; v2 demonstrates that its assumptions force full-batch training and supplies a proved failure example. Correcting this central misstatement substantially improves scientific reliability. The Lemma H.1 correction and added MNIST evidence provide further benefits, although the nonlinear experiment remains qualitative support outside the linear theory.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, equations, figures, and appendices A–K are readable and support reliable matching despite additions and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains the original synthetic experiments and adds MNIST experiments with a two-layer neural network in Section 5 and Appendix K.1.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendices J–K report original synthetic classification experiments, including margin and directional-convergence results in Figures 1–4.

results.title: The Implicit Bias of Steepest Descent with Mini-batch Stochastic Gradient

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims about computational replacement, compact circuits, steering, and biological interpretability. The additional experiments support these claims without rewriting their headline scope.

C2.justification: v1 presents larger-model scaling as future work; v2 interprets 35M and windowed-CLT results as evidence of improved feasibility and an accuracy/compute tradeoff. It also adds global-functional-rule and circuit-stability interpretations, and explicitly identifies autoregressive and diffusion-model extensions as unresolved applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: v2 documents 35M latent dimensions and sparsity, newly discloses explicit LayerNorm in the 8M implementation and its omission for 35M, and supplies window width and additional evaluation settings. Appendix G.3 and Table 10 add NVIDIA RTX A6000 hardware information, parameter counts, and training-time estimates, including extrapolations for larger models. Code and visualizer access information is retained.

E1.justification: Both versions use UniRef50 training sequences, Swiss-Prot/InterPro family tasks, the same 12 ProteinGym assays, and the same seven steering assays. The new mutation-depth and stability analyses reuse existing coverage; larger backbones change model configurations rather than datasets or tasks.

Appendix A revises the reported auxiliary-loss setting from k_aux=floor(d_ESM/2) to 32, without establishing that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds GFP prediction analysis stratified by mutation depth, circuit-node overlap across family inputs and training folds, and a windowed-versus-standard CLT accuracy/cost comparison. These test functional consistency, circuit stability, and connectivity tradeoffs beyond v1's retained replacement-model ablations and biological case studies.

E5.justification: Appendix E.1 newly specifies that the mutation-depth analysis uses the circuit discovered with the first random seed. Existing cross-validation, steering-trial counts, and uncertainty-reporting practices are retained; the revision does not establish an increase in repeated runs.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results for ESM2-35M, windowed CLTs, mutation-depth retention, circuit overlap, and new steering comparators. For example, sequential 35M circuits achieve family F1 of 0.80 ± 0.12 and function Spearman correlation of 0.38 ± 0.19 (Appendix G). The original five tables and Figures 1–8 retain their results, while Section 3.1 changes the stated 8M function-circuit recovery from 74% to 76% without changing its reported correlation.

M1.justification: v2 introduces windowed CLTs, restricting each decoder to a width-w layer window instead of all preceding layers (Appendix G.3, Equation 14). This changes cross-layer connectivity and computational requirements; a width-four variant is trained and evaluated. The original circuit-discovery and steering procedures remain.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence remain intact. v2 adds focused discussion subsections and a scaling appendix, moves the SAE comparison from Appendix G to H, clarifies terminology, and updates the publication header and acknowledgments. This is a localized expansion rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: v2 adds mutation-depth Tables 3–4, comparator Tables 8–9, resource Table 10, and scaling/windowed-model Figures 15–16. Existing steering tables are renumbered, the SAE schematic becomes Figure 17, and appendix displays are redistributed and resized. The substantial change is new visual evidence, while Figures 1–8 and the interface screenshots are retained.

Equation 14 additionally defines the restricted decoder summation for windowed CLTs. These are localized mathematical changes; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's untested scalability limitation through actual ESM2-35M experiments and an evaluated windowed architecture that reduces parameters from 207M to 125M while retaining 82% versus 85% family-task performance. Broader comparators and circuit-stability checks strengthen validation. The gains remain substantial despite limitations: mutation-depth evidence uses one seed, larger-model timings are extrapolated, and Appendix G's latent-space percentages are inconsistent with its stated 12 × 4800 latent space.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ProtoMech research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching across revisions.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds ESM2-35M experiments, windowed-CLT evaluation, circuit-stability analyses, and additional steering comparisons.

before.justification: v1 reports original protein-family classification, function prediction, circuit discovery, steering experiments, and biological case studies.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same scientific claims: adversarial imitation for generative alignment, two optimization strategies, competitive results from 13K demonstrations, transfer to discrete images/video, and regularization against reward hacking. C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations of high-KL outliers as a source of PG instability, initialization dependence under policy–expert distribution shift, and differing data-scale effects on prompt-following and preference metrics. Its Impact Statement also introduces an explicit limitation concerning inheritance of expert-data biases and harmful content. These expand mechanisms and applicability boundaries beyond v1's retained discussion.

E2.justification: Comparator membership in the original experiments is unchanged, including RLHF-PD/PG, Online DPO, Reward Gradient, FPO, and the frontier-model comparisons. The masking comparison adds an 800-step condition against the original 400-step baseline. Existing benchmark protocols remain unchanged.

These address previously untested design choices and failure conditions while retaining the original analyses.

The four sampled reconstruction timesteps are part of an evaluation protocol, and the standard deviation in KL masking is an algorithmic quantity, not uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Tables 1–8 remain numerically unchanged. New Tables 9 and 12–16 add substantial results, including overall reconstruction PSNR 32.55/LPIPS 0.083, masked FAIL-PG UniGen 65.49 at 800 steps, data-scale scores, runtime measurements, initialization effects, and MMD/SWD distances. These are new measurements or conditions; the masking result is not a same-budget improvement over the retained 400-step result.

This changes the update procedure, while the original FAIL-PD/FAIL-PG algorithms and discriminator architectures are retained.

P1.justification: The main narrative remains largely verbatim, with a KL-masking pointer and updated appendix references. v2 adds appendix sections, acknowledgments, an Impact Statement, and conference publication information. Appendix G.1 introduces an incorrect Figure 4 reference for FAIL-PD and an unresolved 'Figure ??' reference for FAIL-PG.

P2.justification: Six new tables substantially expand the display of approximation, stabilization, scaling, timing, initialization, and distribution-distance evidence. Original Tables 1–8 and all five figures retain their content and designs; the two existing settings tables are renumbered, and the original visualization appendix moves later in the document.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations to Gretton et al. for MMD, Karras et al. for SWD, and Tschannen et al. for SigLIP 2. The main related-work discussion and research positioning remain unchanged; the Kurach reference is updated from its preprint to publication form.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked reconstruction-error validation of its central approximation and quantitative feature-space checks of expert-distribution alignment. v2 supplies both, alongside controlled initialization/data-scale studies and measured training costs, substantially strengthening support for design choices and revealing practical dependencies. KL masking also provides evidence of improved training stability. Unequal training budgets in that comparison, continued absence of uncertainty estimates, and new figure-reference errors limit the gains but do not outweigh the stronger methodological validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FAIL research work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds original approximation-error, KL-masking, data-scale, timing, initialization, and distribution-distance measurements in its appendices.

E5.justification: The existing five-seed mean-and-standard-deviation reporting and learning-curve uncertainty bands are retained. Table 4 applies this same practice to the added width configurations; no increased run count or new statistical estimation procedure is reported.

E6.justification: New Table 4 adds twelve width-sweep result rows. For example, width-128 Rational achieves 92.53 ± 1.47 normalized score on HalfCheetah, compared with 91.00 ± 3.41 for width-384 GELU. These are newly reported configurations, not improvements over matching v1 runs. P1.justification: v2 introduces a dedicated Related Work section, shortens the corresponding introduction passage, and makes localized explanatory and language corrections. It also adds equal-contribution and conference information. The overall narrative and appendix organization remain recognizable.

P2.justification: v1's separate IQL and TD3+BC tables become the two blocks of v2 Table 3, and the RL learning curves and activation snapshots are combined in Figure 3. v2 adds the width-sweep table, removes v1's pole-barrier Figure 7, and relocates retained displays. The remaining plots largely preserve their visual content.

R1.justification: The new Related Work section relocates existing application literature and adds positioning against algebraic/geometric and covering-number research, including Kileel, Grosdos, and Zhang–Kileel. Appendix A also adds Sasaki–Kanada and Borwein–Borwein sources for the AGM construction. These are focused additions rather than a redefinition of the paper's research position.

T1.justification: v2 substantially revises central mathematical support: it corrects the root-approximation proof's interval reasoning, repairs the Clenshaw recurrence and error analysis, and rewrites the lower-bound construction using the bounded target Rε(x)=ε/(x²+ε). The main theorem now explicitly allows tolerance-dependent targets, and the gated reduction is revised accordingly. Theorem A.4 also changes the pole equation from +π/2 to -π/2 and removes the nearest-pole characterization.

improvement.justification: Correcting the root-domain argument and Clenshaw output repairs substantive defects in constructions supporting the main approximation claims. The bounded, tolerance-dependent lower-bound example also improves the precision and substance of the theoretical comparison. Together with the controlled IQL width sweep and reconciled implementation details, these provide substantial gains in technical reliability and evidential support while retaining the original benchmark results.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same rational-neural-network study. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–G are readable and support comparison across section renumbering and relocated material.

after.justification: v2 retains these original empirical results and adds an IQL network-width experiment in Table 4.

before.justification: v1 reports original CIFAR-10 and Tiny ImageNet experiments, offline MuJoCo results, learned-activation analyses, and numerical convergence checks in Appendix A.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion add a headline claim that closed models show stronger robustness and reasoning consistency, interpreting the gap as an underdeveloped capability of open models rather than an inherent task limitation. The original accuracy–consistency tradeoff and augmentation/reward conclusions remain.

C2.justification: v3 explicitly distinguishes answer–reasoning consistency from internal causal faithfulness. It adds interpretations of semantic versus formatting effects, conservative judge bias relative to humans, and closed-model conflict resolution. Appendix C.4 also limits the grounding experiment to a proof of concept rather than a full grounding-faithfulness evaluation.

D1.justification: v3 adds exact closed-model prompt templates, examples explaining augmentation of the existing general-VQA datasets, grounding perturbation instructions and human sampling/labeling details. E1.justification: v3 retains the original spatial/general-VQA benchmarks and training datasets, but adds RefCOCOg referring-expression localization, extending evaluation to bounding-box prediction. Appendix C.1 also adds evaluation scenarios with correct auxiliary text and uninformative captions.

New analyses examine model-family generalization, directional localization errors and human validation of the judge (C.3–C.6). Appendix E adds closed-model conflict-resolution and hallucination cases. Earlier abstention and reward analyses remain.

E5.justification: v1 already reports across-dataset standard deviations and inter-judge kappa statistics. v3 extends reliability estimation to human annotations, including Krippendorff's alpha and agreement against human majority labels (Tables 11–14). It does not add explicit RL run counts or confidence intervals; the seed-variability caveat is retained.

On newly evaluated RefCOCOg, SpaceR has relative mean-IoU drops of 39% under Wrong-Caption and 80% under Wrong-Think (Table 10). Human–Qwen3 agreement is 91.8%, with kappa 0.813 (Table 13). M1.justification: The GRPO training, rewards, augmentation probabilities and consistency judge are retained. Appendix C.4 adds a procedural adaptation of perturbation construction: misleading directions are derived by reversing the gold bounding box's spatial direction, instead of selecting an incorrect answer option.

P1.justification: v3 separates open- and closed-model evaluation, adds an appendix contents page, clarifies terminology and rewrites the conclusion. Most existing prose and the main section sequence remain intact; the expansion does not constitute a wholesale narrative reorganization.

P2.justification: The main perturbation plots are redrawn to include closed models and revised legends. New control, consistency and InternVL plots, grounding/human-study tables and illustrated traces substantially expand the displays. Older figures are largely retained and relocated. Figure 3 introduces a caption that reverses the open/closed line styles shown in its legend.

R1.justification: Related work adds discussion of VLM-R3, CertainlyUncertain and Parcalabescu and Frank, while the introduction cites Jacovi and Goldberg to distinguish faithfulness concepts. Sources for the new models and grounding dataset are added. The overall positioning as a diagnostic study of RL-with-CoT remains.

T1.justification: Appendix C.4 introduces a quantitative definition of directional follow rate: the fraction of examples whose perturbed predicted box center shifts toward the injected direction relative to its default prediction. This is a limited new metric definition; no theorem, proof or substantial theoretical framework is added.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the study's validity: semantic controls address a prompt-format confound, human annotations independently validate the automated consistency judge, and another model family plus localization test generality. Explicitly limiting faithfulness to consistency also reduces interpretive ambiguity. Different prefix control and answer filtering limit the new open/closed comparison, but these caveats and minor presentation errors do not outweigh the stronger support for the central findings.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study. Their main texts, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable, and retained content can be matched across renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds closed-model comparisons, control experiments, grounding evaluations and a human annotation study.

before.justification: v1 reports original perturbation evaluations, consistency analyses and controlled RL finetuning experiments in Sections 2–3 and the appendices.

results.title: On Robustness and Chain-of-Thought Consistency of RL-Finetuned VLMs

C1.justification: The abstract and introductory contributions retain their original scope. V2 adds RQ3 and a conclusion claim that patient/facility anchors and judge evaluations establish stronger explanation-axis separation and clearer explanations than standard explanation baselines.

C2.justification: V2 interprets the new comparisons as support for label-domain factorization beyond sparsity alone. Appendix K argues that the residual is actively used in facility-sensitive predictions and discusses threshold-dependent calibration. Appendix J.5 specifically limits its anchors and judging rubric to grounding and auditability rather than causal correctness.

D1.justification: Appendix I.2 adds a code-repository pointer. Appendix J.5 documents attribution targets, candidate-code ranking and truncation, and judging rubrics. Existing architecture, hyperparameters, optimizer, training schedule and hardware disclosures remain unchanged; the repository's actual availability is not established by the PDFs.

E1.justification: Both versions use eICU and OCHIN for diagnosis and heart-failure prediction, retaining the geographic, temporal and five specialty-facility transfer settings. The added explanation assessments and ablations reuse the existing OCHIN facility setting.

E2.justification: V2 introduces an evaluated explanation-comparison suite comprising SHAP, Integrated Gradients and regular SAE in Section 4.4 and Figure 3. Regular SAE also becomes the comparator in the paired judge study. The existing predictive baseline sets remain unchanged.

E3.justification: Section 4.4 and Appendix J.5 add matched candidate-code budgets, patient-relevance and facility-specificity anchors, LAD/DAD/QCE metrics, and anonymized randomized explanation judging: 300 LLM cases and 25 cases assessed by two medically trained humans. Appendix K adds fixed-head residual masking and a threshold sweep. Existing prediction protocols are retained.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's component ablations, probes and patient cases, v2 tests explanation grounding against external anchors and judge preferences. Appendix K adds interventions testing whether residual information affects predictions, code-level masking examples, and sensitivity to the explanation threshold.

E5.justification: The retained prediction tables continue reporting the same means and standard errors. V2 adds no seed counts, repeated-run information, confidence intervals, significance tests or judge-agreement estimates; the new evaluation results are point estimates.

E6.justification: Existing prediction and probe values remain unchanged. New Figure 3 reports ExtraCare versus SAE LAD of 47% versus 36%, DAD of 42% versus 40%, and QCE of 32% versus 37%. Table 3 reports 68% LLM and 64% human preference for ExtraCare over SAE. Appendix K adds masking and threshold results, including Mental Health R@5 falling from 79.9 to 66.3 when the residual is masked.

M1.justification: The encoder, sparse autoencoder, dictionary-induced projection, losses and prediction procedure remain unchanged, as does Algorithm 1. Residual masking in Appendix K is an evaluation intervention, not a revision of the proposed method.

P1.justification: V2 makes local grammar edits, updates the running title, corresponding author and acknowledgments, and inserts RQ3, Section 4.4, Appendix J.5 and Appendix K. The existing narrative and section order are largely preserved rather than extensively rewritten.

P2.justification: V2 substantially expands the visual presentation of explanation validation through Figures 3 and 5 and Tables 3, 9 and 10. Figure 1 is redrawn, and Table 2 switches runner-up highlighting from blue text to gray shading. Existing result displays are retained, with several relocated or renumbered.

R1.justification: V2 adds references supporting SHAP/IG comparisons, recent clinical interpretability work and the information-theoretic discussion, and replaces the OCHIN source citations. The overall research positioning remains stable. BUA's bibliographic update and the retitled Hu domain-discovery work do not represent new comparison methods.

T1.justification: The original assumptions, projection definitions, proposition, lemma and proofs are retained. Appendix J.5 adds mathematical definitions for patient relevance, facility specificity and LAD/DAD/QCE in Equations 18–22, extending the formal evaluation framework without changing the method's theory.
