improvement.justification: V1's central transparency claim relied mainly on illustrative patient cases and representation probes. V2 addresses that validation gap with explanation comparators, patient-record and prevalence anchors, randomized anonymized judgments, and functional residual and threshold tests in Section 4.4 and Appendices J.5–K. These materially strengthen support for the paper's central contribution. The small human study and missing uncertainty estimates and judge-model details still limit conclusiveness.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ExtraCare research. Their text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered content.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds explanation comparisons, LLM and human evaluations, residual-masking experiments and threshold sensitivity results.

before.justification: V1 reports original eICU and OCHIN prediction experiments, component ablations, representation probes and patient-level explanation analyses.

results.title: Exploring Accurate and Transparent Domain Adaptation in Predictive Healthcare via Concept-Grounded Orthogonal Inference

C1.justification: The abstract's central transfer, representation, and exploration claims remain. However, the introduction now explicitly claims robustness to environmental geometry, option definition, and absence of preconstructed options. The discussion replaces v1's pre-exposure restriction with demonstrated operation using online option construction, materially broadening claimed applicability.

C2.justification: v2 interprets HSR representations and GPI policy composition as complementary, explains weak covering-option performance through restricted initiation sets and sparse rewards, and discusses stability beyond a modest option budget. It also qualifies online option construction as heuristic with unresolved theoretical foundations. These substantially extend interpretation and applicability boundaries while retaining the original topological explanation.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-repository access statement, online-option initialisation and update pseudocode, and the reward-discovery implementation used for GPI comparisons. Existing transfer and exploration hyperparameters remain. Numerical warm-up and option-refresh intervals are not supplied, so the additional reproducibility documentation remains incomplete.

E1.justification: Transfer evaluation expands beyond the canonical four-room environment to an asymmetric four-room layout with barriers, a Loop maze, a Corridor maze, and a Multi-pairwise-bottleneck maze (v2 Figure S3). These test materially different environmental geometries and connectivity structures. The original transfer and procedural-maze exploration scenarios remain.

E2.justification: Section 4.3 and Figure 5 add an actual SR-GPI comparison, evaluating policy composition with one-hot, HSR-row, and HSR-NMF representations against linear Q-learning. v1 discussed successor-feature research but did not evaluate this comparator family. The original representation and exploration baselines are retained.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include withholding the target reward vector until first goal discovery before switching to GPI, testing agents without preconstructed options, and varying option budgets across 4, 8, 16, and 32. Figure S6 adds a 10,000-action coverage analysis; the retained main exploration figure still reports 100,000-action coverage. These are added protocols, not demonstrated reruns of the original experiments.

E4.justification: v2 substantially expands robustness analysis: Figure S3 tests dependence on environmental topology; Figure S4 compares eigenoptions, covering options, random target options, and option counts; Figure 2i-l and Figure S6 test transfer and exploration with online-discovered options. These address dependencies that v1's representation and offline-versus-online analyses did not test.

E5.justification: Mean ± standard error reporting and the 20-seed default remain, while several added experiments explicitly use 10 seeds. Figure S6 introduces two-way ANOVA interaction tests. Figure 5 describes a paired t-test but reports df = 18 for 10 seeds, leaving the exact test unclear. There is no evidence that retained experiments used fewer runs.

E6.justification: Substantial new results include online-option transfer benefits (Figure 2l, p = 0.026), no significant difference between one-hot SR-GPI and HSR-NMF Q-learning (Figure 5c, p = 0.199), and benefits from combining GPI with HSR-row/NMF (p = 0.003/0.007). New appendix results report robustness across geometries and stabilisation beyond eight options. These supplement largely unchanged original results.

M1.justification: v2 introduces online option construction in Appendix B.2 and Algorithm S2: agents begin without options, learn a primitive-action SR, construct eigenoptions after warm-up, and periodically refresh them while learning HSR. v1 assumed pre-acquired options and left iterative discovery to future work. This substantially extends the procedure while retaining the underlying HSR/NMF framework.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the overall narrative remain. v2 adds a GPI results subsection, organises Appendix B into subsections, inserts GPI implementation details, and locally rewrites related work and discussion. Typographical corrections, acknowledgements, and conference-header changes accompany these additions, without a wholesale language or structural rewrite.

P2.justification: Figure 2 expands from eight to twelve panels, and v2 adds a GPI schematic/comparison figure, topology and option-sensitivity figures, an online-exploration figure, and another algorithm display. These substantially expand the visual presentation. The original exploration Figure 5 becomes Figure 6, and the original spectral Figure S3 becomes Figure S5; neither is removed.

R1.justification: The relationship to successor-feature/GPI research is substantively revised: v1 emphasised its allegedly shared diffusion limitations, whereas v2 positions GPI as complementary algorithmic machinery and studies combinations with HSR. Carvalho et al. (2023) is added to this discussion, alongside new predictive-map connections citing Yu et al. (2020) and Piray and Daw (2021).

T1.justification: v2 removes the leading discount factor from the main-text termination-kernel formula, matching v1's appendix expression. Appendix A changes the intra-option occupancy sum from ending at τ to τ−1, restores discounted continuation terms, explicitly conditions on termination states, and revises the contraction argument. These are mathematical revisions within the existing framework; Theorem 3.1's conclusion is retained.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important weaknesses in v1: dependence on pre-acquired options, narrow transfer validation, and the absence of an evaluated GPI comparator. Online-option experiments and Figures S3-S6 substantially strengthen the empirical support, while the GPI comparison clarifies HSR's contribution relative to prior methods. The online procedure remains heuristic, some implementation settings are unspecified, and Figure 5's statistical reporting is inconsistent, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Hierarchical Successor Representation for Robust Transfer. Their main text, equations, figures, algorithms, and appendices are readable and support comparison. Retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds experiments on online option construction, generalised policy improvement, alternative maze geometries, and option sensitivity.

before.justification: v1 reports original grid-world transfer experiments, representation analyses, and procedurally generated maze exploration results, including supplementary experiments.

results.title: Hierarchical Successor Representation for Robust Transfer

C1.justification: The central task-family synthesis contribution is retained. The abstract and conclusion extend the training-utility claim to token-matched and external-seed settings and highlight category-selective improvements. Section 6 additionally makes an explicit near-thousand-family novelty claim.

C2.justification: v2 replaces the explanation that complexity forces System 2 behavior with a selective-gains hypothesis and acknowledges limits of AST-based novelty measures. New limitations and audit discussion address seed dependence, restricted model coverage, missing gate ablations, survivorship bias, and prompt–code mismatches. Appendix N attributes roughly half the step-matched advantage to additional tokens.

D1.justification: Appendix M documents the new experiment's GPT-5.4 backend, two refinement iterations, difficulty levels, instance counts, and reuse of existing training hyperparameters. Appendices L/N document audit inputs and token-log comparisons. Core implementation details and prompts remain intact; the conclusion now explicitly states release of both framework and datasets.

E1.justification: v2 adds evolution and training on 30 external English-only Enigmata puzzle types, extending beyond the original Chinese seed distribution; Enigmata previously served as an evaluation benchmark. It also adds KORBench evaluation across five reasoning categories. Removed benchmark mentions lack corresponding v1 results, so they do not establish dropped evaluations.

E2.justification: The Seed/Evolve controls, mathematical-data mixtures, ARC mixture, and Qwen3 baselines are retained. The new Enigmata experiment extends the same Seed/Evolve comparison to another dataset; GPT-5.4 serves as a synthesis backend, not a competing baseline.

E3.justification: v2 introduces token-matched comparisons, nearly size-matched Enigmata training, length-normalized reflection measurements, and a human-audit protocol. Appendix B also replaces v1's mathematics pass@64/pass@8 specifications with pass@1 estimated using 64/8 samples. This substantially revises reported evaluation settings, without establishing that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New analyses examine compute-budget confounding, reflection frequency after length normalization, category-selective KORBench/BBH gains, and failures in 100 human-audited task families. These materially extend the retained subsampling, difficulty, complexity, and pipeline analyses. A gate-by-gate training ablation remains absent.

E5.justification: Appendix I retains the same 2,000-iteration bootstrap analysis and 95% confidence intervals. v2 adds no training-seed replication information, significance testing, or uncertainty-estimation procedure; the new benchmark and audit results are point estimates.

E6.justification: Original Table 2 numerical entries are retained. New results include Enigmata-trained BBH scores of 61.8 versus 67.3, KORBench overall scores of 43.0 versus 51.0, token-matched macro accuracy of 0.2312 versus 0.2480, and 85/100 audited families deemed usable. The new BBH breakdown in Section 5.3 reports 59.4 versus 69.3 without reconciling these figures with Table 2.

M1.justification: The CKPro agent hierarchy, generator–validator evolution, consensus verification, blind review, and refinement loop are retained. The executable prompt templates and training procedure are unchanged; revised checker and solver descriptions clarify the existing method.

P1.justification: Targeted rewrites affect the abstract, conclusion, validation description, and mechanism discussion, alongside terminology cleanup and additional cross-references. New limitations, impact, and experimental sections extend the existing organization; most established sections and prompt appendices remain substantially intact.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the displays with token-budget and efficiency plots, KORBench and audit tables, and an Enigmata block in Table 2. It redesigns the overview and evaluation-metric table and merges the former complexity-distribution and pattern-coverage figures. Some appendix plots redisplay existing analyses rather than add evidence.

R1.justification: v2 adds 'ARC is a vision problem!', replaces the Reinforce++ citation with OpenRLHF, and removes CRUXEval. Related work adds limited novelty and verification-focused positioning. Numerous other bibliography edits concern the same works' authorship or publication metadata.

T1.justification: Task-family definitions, unique-answer assumptions, gating and consensus mathematics, the pass@k estimator, and the KL formula remain substantively unchanged. Revised indices, state arguments, and complexity symbols clarify notation; no new theorem, proof, or derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens assessment of the central training-utility claim through external English-seed experiments and token-matched controls, addressing limitations of v1's step-matched, original-seed evidence. The human audit and explicit limitations also make reliability and applicability more assessable. Unreconciled BBH figures and the absence of fully compute-matched and gate-ablation experiments remain concerns, but the added controls and candid failure analysis provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SSLogic research. Their full text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated prompt templates and renumbered analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains these results and adds external Enigmata training experiments, KORBench evaluation, token-budget analyses, and a human audit.

before.justification: v1 reports original RL training results, controlled Seed/Evolve comparisons, difficulty and code-complexity analyses, and pipeline diagnostics.

results.title: Scaling the Scaling Logic: Agentic Meta-Synthesis of Logic Reasoning

C1.justification: The abstract, principal contributions, and conclusion retain their central claims. The introduction changes its specific claim of better calibration from comparison with Kuleshov et al.'s PIT method to Song et al.'s parametric recalibration approach.

C2.justification: New Section 7 explicitly discusses cubic calibration-set complexity, difficulties comparing complex distributions, insufficient feature-conditional calibration, and loss of continuous-density structure. Added appendix discussions explain the two-stage modeling rationale and implementation-dependent runtime. Appendix D also introduces an interpretation of comparable conformal coverage that understates the naval exceptions in Figure 4.

D1.justification: Section 6.3 newly documents five-fold regularization selection and its CKME objective. Added experiments disclose kernel/grid tuning, NVIDIA A100 hardware, and 1000-sample inverse-CDF representation for PIT timing. The code reference changes from recalibration_experiment to recalibration_icml2026. These are documentation and access-reference additions, without evidence that the original method changed.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same nine UCI regression datasets, Bike Sharing, and bimodal synthetic dataset. The added interval and computational evaluations reuse this regression coverage or vary representation sample counts without introducing new data populations or input scenarios.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated comparisons against Chernozhukov et al.'s split conformal prediction in Appendix D, unrecalibrated kernelized distribution regression in Appendix F, and a naive Gaussian-type kernel implementation in Appendix E. The original PIT, GPBETA, None(T), and None(T+C) comparisons remain.

E3.justification: New protocols evaluate nominal 95% intervals using coverage, relative width, and interval–PIT distance correlation; normalize direct-kernel comparisons to that baseline's CRPS; and measure runtime. Figure 5 fixes 300 predictions while varying distribution samples from 500 to 5000. The original benchmark splits and evaluation procedures remain; the newly disclosed regularization tuning does not establish a rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix E adds an EDK efficiency ablation across representation sizes, Appendix F investigates whether direct kernel regression removes the need for separate recalibration, and Appendix G analyzes runtime against PIT. Appendix D additionally examines prediction-dependent error cancellation through distance correlation.

E5.justification: Figure 5 newly specifies at least 25 timing trials per configuration. The original benchmark's 20 repetitions and standard-deviation reporting are retained; the PDFs do not establish increased repetition of those original experiments.

E6.justification: Table 1's numerical values and all seven original plots are retained, with the detailed plots renumbered 8–11. New Figures 4–7 report interval quality, direct-kernel performance, and runtime findings. These include substantially faster EDK computation and severe naval undercoverage: roughly 25–30% for recalibrated GDN, MDN, and BNN versus approximately 95% for conformal prediction.

M1.justification: The distribution kernel, CKME coefficient calculation, and simplex projection producing weighted empirical predictions remain unchanged. New Algorithms 1–2 summarize existing steps; v1's pre-image procedure in Appendix B is retained in v2 Appendix C.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main narrative order remain intact. Local editing, algorithm summaries, a dedicated limitations section, impact and acknowledgement text, and revised appendix organization improve exposition without extensive rewriting of the retained material.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a conference layout with different typography, first-page structure, and running headers, and adds two algorithm boxes and four substantive figures. Existing plots are resized or relocated. Figure 2 and Table 1 captions correct 'test set' to 'train set,' and Figure 2 gains explanatory discussion.

R1.justification: Related work expands substantially to classification calibration, multicalibration, local calibration, conformal prediction, and grouping loss. Section 4 and Appendix B acknowledge quantitative equivalence with Kull and Flach's grouping loss, materially refining the positioning of the decomposition and emphasizing its information-theoretic interpretation.

T1.justification: New Appendix B establishes the connection to grouping loss and adds Proposition B.1 with a proof equating expected-score minimization with entropy minimization subject to auto-calibration under realizability. Remark 5.3 newly states a compact-metric target-space requirement. The original principal results and Appendix A proofs are retained.

improvement.justification: The direct-kernel comparison and timing studies address important gaps in v1's empirical justification of the two-stage design and efficiency claims. Appendix B strengthens theoretical positioning, while tuning disclosures and explicit limitations improve reproducibility and applicability guidance. A material weakness is Appendix D's broad coverage-comparability claim despite severe naval undercoverage in Figure 4. The substantial gains in validation and transparency outweigh that overstatement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work and provide readable text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices. The original proofs, pre-image discussion, and benchmark results can be matched across the appendix reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds conformal-prediction comparisons, direct kernel-regression comparisons, and runtime experiments in Appendices D–G.

before.justification: v1 reports original regression experiments across eleven datasets and four base models, including CRPS scores and calibration-test results in Table 1 and Figures 1–7.

results.title: Nonparametric Distribution Regression Re-calibration

C1.justification: The central geometric-asymmetry and label-efficiency contributions remain. v3 explicitly adds generation and reproduction code to its release contribution. Its conclusion replaces the claim of F1 above 90% 'across all models' with F1 above 90% on SOCRATES-300K, although the abstract retains broader wording.

C2.justification: v3 interprets Fisher-direction differences as evidence of prompt-specific geometry and explains encoder/judge robustness and CoQA behavior. Appendix E explicitly prioritizes the structural finding over the propagator because standard classifiers perform similarly. It also adds interpretations of conservative annotation errors, limited small-sample significance, and the restricted comparability of external detector baselines.

D1.justification: v3 supplies a dataset DOI and repository references for dataset generation and result reproduction, whereas v1 only announces dataset release. It also documents baseline adaptations, CoQA model identifiers and generation/labeling settings, and the stratified selection of the existing human-validation sample. These substantially expand reproducibility information; linked resources were not accessed.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates the authors' time-sensitive factual-question corpus, renamed SOCRATES-300K in v3 without changing its coverage. v3 Appendix D adds CoQA-89K, generated from 199 conversational question-answer prompts, substantially extending evaluation beyond the original temporal-event questions.

E2.justification: v3 adds evaluated SelfCheckGPT (NLI), SemanticEntropy, and INSIDE comparisons in Table 4, plus an INSIDE re-execution on CoQA. Appendix E adds Euclidean/cosine centroid classifiers, Linear Regression, SVM, and kNN-5. The earlier Fisher-versus-UMAP/wPCA/EP comparison remains in Appendix F.

E3.justification: The original generation settings and 2/3–1/3 evaluation splits remain. New protocols include CoQA generation with three models, 150 responses per prompt, temperature 0.5, top-p 0.99, top-k 5, and ROUGE-L-based labels. External baselines introduce response subsampling, NLI clustering, and an SBERT-based INSIDE proxy; classifier ablations compare Fisher and original embedding spaces.

E4.justification: v3 adds encoder ablations, Fisher-direction similarity across prompts/models, response-set-size sensitivity, and classifier-replacement controls. Appendix A.2 adds disagreement categories and examples, inspection of 441 unknown responses, and a Gemini judge comparison. The existing stemming analysis also gains an embedding-similarity check. These investigate several previously untested robustness and mechanism questions.

E5.justification: Existing split counts, training subsampling, mean/std reporting, and 100-permutation null comparisons are retained. The new response-set-size analysis specifies 20 repeated subsamples and reports Wasserstein permutation-significance rates separately from merely exceeding the mean null distance (Figure 7). This extends statistical assessment without establishing additional runs for the original experiments.

E6.justification: Matched original tables retain their values, including 87.2% accuracy and 90.7% F1 in Table 2. Substantial new results include CoQA averages of 98.1% accuracy and 97.1% F1 under its distinct settings (Table 12). Table 13 newly reports Fisher-space F1 of 91.4% for Linear Regression versus 90.5% for APORIA-LP, alongside new baseline, robustness, and annotation findings.

M1.justification: The regularized Fisher projection and Wasserstein-based label-assignment procedure remain unchanged in Sections 3.3–3.4. APORIA and APORIA-LP name the existing framework and propagator; alternative encoders and classifiers are evaluated as ablations rather than incorporated into a revised method.

P1.justification: v3 rewrites the abstract, introduces consistent framework/dataset names, adds descriptive paragraph headings, and reorganizes appendix subsections. It also corrects the running header and updates author/publication information. The main six-section narrative and most existing methodological exposition remain, making the editorial reworking more limited than the experimental expansion.

P2.justification: v3 adds six substantive tables covering encoders, detectors, annotation disagreements, CoQA, and classifiers, plus new response-size and CoQA figures. Figure 9 augments the retained training-size plot with numerical summaries, and annotation examples receive boxed displays. Existing plots and tables are largely retained and relocated, rather than replaced with new results.

R1.justification: Related work adds INSIDE and expands its relationship to SemanticEntropy, SelfCheckGPT, and the dataset motivation. New citations also support CoQA, ROUGE, and broader background. The overall research positioning remains; changes to HEMM's author ordering and several publication records concern already-cited works.

T1.justification: The Wasserstein definition, Fisher objective, regularized scatter matrix, projection, and classification rule are retained. Neither the renamed framework nor the additional empirical analyses introduce a new formal derivation, theorem, or proof.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially addresses v1's limited validation of dataset generality, encoder dependence, annotation reliability, and classifier necessity. The CoQA evaluation and added controls clarify both the geometric finding and its boundaries, while explicit resource references improve reproducibility. These gains outweigh shortcomings: detector comparisons remain proxies, Table 3's default-encoder F1 is unexplained relative to Table 2, and Table 11 contains inconsistent totals. The improvement rests on stronger scrutiny and broader evidence, rather than higher reported scores alone.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same geometric hallucination study. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched despite renaming and reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds CoQA experiments, external baselines, classifier and encoder ablations, and further annotation and sensitivity analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original response-generation experiments, human annotation validation, geometric analyses, label-propagation results, and appendix ablations.

results.title: A Geometric Analysis of Small-sized Language Model Hallucinations

C1.justification: The abstract and introductory contributions retain the same central claims. The conclusion corrects the detector-training outcome list from three to four by including blatant deception, aligning it with the existing taxonomy.

C2.justification: V2 refines the mechanism discussion by linking evasion strategies to probe extraction and interpreting non-deception controls as evidence of deception-specific drift. It adds a narrow-task explanation for absent emergent misalignment. Section 6 replaces the untested-beyond-coding limitation with untested large-scale RL and richer action spaces.

D1.justification: Appendix H adds GPU counts, epoch information, a probe-filter fallback and configurations for new experiments. It discloses a multi-GPU gradient bug producing realized batch sizes of 4 and 1 for the larger models. Appendix Q supplies the classification prompt and manual-validation information, although its few-shot examples are omitted.

E1.justification: Appendix O adds restaurant-invitation generation with a cuisine-biased LLM judge and a cuisine-content probe, substantially extending evaluation beyond coding. Appendix P adds Python-code and docstring detection tasks. The original MBPP and deception datasets remain.

E2.justification: Table 16 changes its included probe comparisons from all three probe datasets to Simple and Diverse Deception only, excluding the MBPP-probe baseline from that aggregate. MBPP remains evaluated elsewhere, and the principal comparison methods are retained.

E3.justification: Table 12 revises the reported learning rate from 1e-4 to 5e-5 and default KL coefficient from 0.01 to 1e-4. Appendix H revises effective-batch reporting following a gradient bug. Added protocols include 500-step training and the Food-Sycophancy judge-based evaluation. These reported revisions do not establish that all original experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds deception-threshold sensitivity, non-deception feature controls, mean-pooled probe evasion examples, 500-step stability testing and detector training without the code-length penalty (Appendices N, P, S, T and V). These directly test dependencies and alternative explanations left unresolved in v1.

E5.justification: The three-seed main protocol, mean/standard-deviation reporting, standard-error plots and Appendix L significance tests remain. Added results extend existing reporting practices, including the ten-seed no-code-length-penalty design already present in v1 Table 5; no new uncertainty-estimation procedure is introduced.

E6.justification: V2 adds Food-Sycophancy outcomes, non-deception-probe stability, 500-step trajectories, 5/6 mean-pooled runs yielding obfuscated policies, and 10/10 honest no-length-penalty detector runs for each of two models. Table 16 replaces counts using a different model/probe pool, so changes are not same-setting gains. Section 5.2 also corrects Strategic Honesty from 26.9% to 26.5%.

M1.justification: The probe-penalized, KL-regularized objective, GRPO/LoRA training and linear-probe framework remain unchanged. The new task and additional extraction experiments apply existing procedures; expanded implementation disclosures do not establish a new algorithm.

P1.justification: The main seven-section narrative and abstract are retained. V2 makes targeted language, terminology and cross-reference corrections, adds acknowledgements and reorganizes back matter. V1 Appendix M's larger-model discussion is retained within the expanded Appendix R.

P2.justification: V2 substantially expands the displays with sensitivity, task, control, prompt and ablation tables plus extended-training curves. Figure 12 becomes a four-model comparison retaining the earlier Llama-70B results, and Figure 14 disaggregates the atlas. Existing figures are also relocated and Figure 6's model panels reordered.

R1.justification: New Appendix M explicitly contrasts the study's absence of emergent misalignment with the previously cited MacDiarmid and Denison studies. The cited-work set otherwise remains stable; updated years, venues and titles largely reflect publication metadata changes.

T1.justification: The objective decomposition and Appendix D policy-gradient claim, proof and derivations are retained. Removing the extraneous argmax from Equation 2 is a notation correction, not a substantive theoretical revision.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens evidence for the central findings by testing dependencies on coding, probe extraction, training duration and the code-length incentive. Particularly valuable are the non-coding experiment and ten-seed demonstrations of detector benefits without a code-length penalty. Threshold checks and implementation disclosures also improve auditability. The new judge setup and bug-fix validation remain incompletely documented, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Obfuscation Atlas study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds Food-Sycophancy experiments, probe-stability controls and further robustness evaluations.

before.justification: V1 reports original RLVR experiments on four models, deception-probe evaluations, ablations and model-belief analyses.

results.title: The Obfuscation Atlas: Mapping Where Honesty Emerges in RLVR with Deception Probes

C1.justification: The abstract and two introductory contributions retain the semi-analytical solver and tractable state-space analysis claims. The conclusion adds claimed advantages concerning continuous invariant-set geometry and universal approximation guarantees relative to discrete-time RNNs, modestly extending the central positioning.

C2.justification: V2 explains SINDy's function-library advantage and Latent ODE/Neural CDE rollout failures, connects LIF switching boundaries to resets, and interprets the cortical reconstruction as bistable. It also qualifies numerical and scaling limitations using new evidence and discusses initialization-dependent missed equilibria/cycles and the restriction to shallow architectures.

D1.justification: V2 adds a code-repository pointer, Latent ODE/Neural CDE tuning grids, explicit eigenvalue and perturbation thresholds in Appendix D.2, heartbeat selection/preprocessing instructions, and CPU/core information for cycle detection. These substantially expand reproducibility information; the perturbation strategy itself was already disclosed in v1.

E1.justification: V2 retains the original benchmarks and adds forecasting of irregular PhysioNet heart-rate series from ten subjects (Section 4.5, Appendix F.4), plus reconstruction of a stochastic Izhikevich neuron (Figure 6, Table 7). These substantially extend real-data coverage, task requirements and process-noise conditions.

E2.justification: V1 compares against discrete PLRNNs and Neural ODEs using Euler, RK4 and Tsit5. V2 additionally evaluates SINDy, Latent ODE and Neural CDE on the retained Lorenz, LIF and cortical-recording benchmarks (Tables 1, 3 and 4), substantially broadening the comparison methods.

E3.justification: V1 Table 4 explicitly evaluates cortical recordings in the original one-dimensional space; v2 Appendix G.1 specifies three-dimensional, noise-perturbed embeddings for neuron Dstsp evaluations. V2 also adds Lorenz prediction horizons, heartbeat forecasting with an 80/20 split, and sampling/perturbation sweeps. Its new Neural CDE comparison uses data-driven testing rather than autonomous rollout (Section 4.2).

E4.justification: V2 adds cycle-detection sensitivity to crossing-coordinate and flight-time initialization (Figure 7), expanded runtime scaling (Figure 8), ill-conditioning frequencies (Figure 9), a process-noise case study (Figure 6), and LIF sampling-density sensitivity (Table 7). These substantially extend v1's illustrative cycle examples and limited runtime comparison across P.

E5.justification: V2 adds 100-run initialization trials, 100-trajectory prediction summaries, a Wilcoxon comparison across heartbeat subjects and explicitly one-sided tests in Section 4.4. Table 3 describes 4/10 and 2/10 Euler runs as excluded rather than surviving. Prediction-time aggregation remains inconsistent: Table 1 specifies median/MAD, whereas Appendix G.3 specifies mean/standard deviation.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial benchmark, comparator, prediction-horizon and robustness results. Izhikevich results favor cPLRNN on Dstsp but standard PLRNN on DH (Table 7). Retained Lorenz P=10 cPLRNN Dstsp changes from 0.35±0.14 to 0.37±0.14, and Table 2 timings change. Revised neuron Dstsp values accompany changed evaluation conditions and do not establish comparable performance gains or losses.

M1.justification: The cPLRNN dynamics, interval-Newton switching solver, implicit differentiation, sparse teacher forcing and equilibrium/cycle detection procedures remain. Appendix D.2 and Algorithm 3 detail the matrix-perturbation and gradient-discard fallback already described in v1 Appendix A. The mathematical corrections do not establish a changed implementation or new method component.

P1.justification: Most existing exposition and the main section order are retained. V2 makes local language, terminology and cross-reference corrections, updates front matter, and adds Section 4.5 and supporting appendix subsections. The narrative changes are focused expansions rather than extensive rewriting or reorganization.

P2.justification: V2 adds Figures 3 and 6–9 and Tables 7–8, and restructures the Lorenz presentation: the earlier multi-P table becomes Table 9, while Table 1 adds comparators and prediction horizons. Figure 2 gains switching markers and a revised state-space projection. Existing appendix illustrations become Figures 4–5, with limited display corrections.

R1.justification: The main related-work taxonomy and novelty framing remain. V2 adds cited positioning around SINDy, PhysioNet, causal Neural CDE interpolation, neuronal bistability, numerical continuation and continuous-time approximation guarantees, including Brunton et al. (2016), Morrill et al. (2021), and Sagodi and Park (2026).

T1.justification: Equation 12 removes the erroneous constant bias term from the time derivative. Appendix D corrects the readout matrix to the appropriate N-by-M shape, and Equation 16 corrects the initial interval bound. The principal assumptions, cycle constraints and Appendix H theory remain substantially unchanged.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation of the method's practical claims through genuinely irregular real-data forecasting, stochastic-neuron reconstruction, and direct tests of scaling, conditioning and cycle-detection sensitivity. Correcting Equation 12 and adding implementation details and code-access information further improve correctness and reproducibility. Unequal rollout conditions for new baselines and inconsistent prediction-statistic descriptions limit some comparisons, but the added evidence addresses important gaps in v1.

A1.justification: Both PDFs present the same cPLRNN research, with readable text, equations, figures, tables and appendices. The core material and appendices A–H can be matched reliably; v2 adds further material, including appendices I–J.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical evaluations and adds heartbeat forecasting, stochastic Izhikevich-neuron experiments, and numerical robustness and scaling analyses (Section 4.5, appendices I–J).

before.justification: V1 reports original model-training comparisons on Lorenz-63, LIF simulations and cortical-neuron recordings, alongside recovered equilibria and limit cycles (Figures 1–2, Tables 1–4).

results.title: Continuous-Time Piecewise-Linear Recurrent Neural Networks

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same contributions: attention-output and mass matching, efficient subproblems, and an improved compaction cost–quality frontier. The added benchmarks supply evidence for these claims without redefining the central contribution.

C2.justification: Appendix G newly characterizes information-loss failures as graceful and low-risk, states incompatibility with multi-head latent attention, discusses GQA/tensor-parallel compatibility, and explains a background compaction arrangement intended to hide latency. These extend applicability and deployment interpretations without dedicated supporting evaluations.

D1.justification: Appendix B.3 adds KVMerger implementation information, including cosine-similarity clustering, Gaussian-weighted merging, and use of default parameters. v2 identifies the source of RULER tasks and borrowed scores and corrects Algorithm 3's loop-bound documentation. Existing code-access information and core implementation settings remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds QASPER generative QA over research papers, RULER retrieval/tracing/aggregation tasks, and LongBench v2 evaluation covering code, tables, multilingual documents, and structured contexts. These substantially broaden task and domain coverage beyond the retained QuALITY, LongHealth, and AIME evaluations.

E2.justification: KVMerger becomes an evaluated comparator on QuALITY, QASPER, and LongBench v2. RULER Table 11 adds comparisons with AdaKV, SnapKV, Finch, KeyDiff, TOVA, and PyramidKV using explicitly attributed leaderboard scores alongside original KVzip runs. This substantially expands the comparison set.

E3.justification: New protocols include token-level F1 on QASPER, screening LongBench v2 for 47 contexts answered correctly with context but incorrectly without it before reevaluating all methods, and RULER testing of AM-HighestAttnKeys-fast at 5% and 12.5% retained cache. Appendix B.2 also revises the Cartridges subset count from 360 to 357 questions, without establishing a rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix G.1 adds a brief qualitative failure-mode assessment: extreme compaction tends to lose specific information while preserving coherence. This is an unquantified observation, not a dedicated robustness experiment. Existing component ablations, query/head-budget analyses, and online AIME experiments are retained.

E5.justification: Head-sensitivity plots retain standard-error reporting, and the AIME table still averages four runs. The new benchmark tables provide point estimates without introducing seed counts, confidence intervals, significance tests, or new uncertainty-estimation practices.

E6.justification: Tables 1, 2, 10, and 11 add substantial benchmark and comparator results. For example, newly reported Llama RULER accuracy at 5% cache is 83.3% for AM-HighestAttnKeys-fast versus 46.6% for KVzip. QuALITY full-context accuracy changes from 71.5% to 71.1% in the summarization-combination table and from 72.1% to 71.1% in Appendix B.2. Existing plots are retained.

M1.justification: The objectives, key-selection variants, bias/value fitting, head allocation, and chunked/online compaction procedures are retained. Algorithm 3 corrects its loop bound to match the previously stated iteration count and returned iterate; this does not establish a different compaction method.

P1.justification: v2 adds Section 4.2, Appendix F.4, and Appendix G, clarifies Section 2, and makes terminology, cross-reference, grammatical, and publication-footer edits. Most existing prose and the overall narrative structure are retained.

P2.justification: v2 adds a compaction schematic as Figure 2 and substantial comparison displays for QASPER, LongBench v2, KVMerger on QuALITY, and RULER. The baseline-configuration table gains a KVMerger row. Existing plots are retained, with renumbering and some relocation rather than redrawing.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations for QASPER, LongBench v2, and RULER and explicitly contrasts Attention Matching with KVMerger's local merging. Wang et al. was already cited in v1; its new evaluated-baseline role expands positioning modestly without changing the overall novelty argument.

T1.justification: The attention-matching equations, least-squares formulation, and Appendix A mass-preservation derivation are unchanged. Section 2 clarifies concatenated sequence lengths and illustrates the existing formulation without adding mathematical results or assumptions.

improvement.justification: v1's empirical case relied mainly on two multiple-choice datasets. v2 substantially strengthens it through generative QA and retrieval evaluations and a token-merging comparator, testing whether compaction preserves information beyond answer selection. LongBench v2 remains limited to a selected 47-context subset, and Appendix G's instruction-following and latency assurances lack dedicated tests. These limitations temper the new claims but do not outweigh the substantial gain in empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Fast KV Compaction via Attention Matching. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison across renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original QASPER, LongBench v2, RULER, and KVMerger evaluations. Some additional RULER comparator scores are explicitly attributed to a leaderboard.

before.justification: v1 reports original QuALITY and LongHealth experiments, timing measurements, component ablations, and an online-compaction experiment on AIME 2025 in Appendix F.3.

results.title: Fast KV Compaction via Attention Matching

C1.justification: Both versions retain the central claims that CGP improves frozen representation evaluation, that its guidance produces a stronger BAT audio SSL model, and that standardized implementations improve reproducibility. The abstract and conclusion preserve these claims; v2's broader experiments and expanded explanations strengthen their supporting context.

C2.justification: Section 6 replaces v1's emphasis on anticipated benefits from further hyperparameter tuning with a more specific attribution of AS-2M reproduction gaps to training sampling. v2 also adds substantive qualifications concerning non-prototype probes' dependence on layer normalization, Head2Toe's Lasso/convergence sensitivity, and VQT's inability to train on cached features.

D1.justification: v1 promises code upon acceptance or request; v2 reports an open-source release and supplies a repository address covering BAT and baseline evaluation. It also expands configuration documentation, clarifies attention-gate persistence, and specifies the timing environment, including PyTorch 2.8.0, CUDA 12.8, and an RTX A6000. These substantially improve documented implementation and access information.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates AudioSet, ESC-50, and Speech Commands classification. v2 retains these and adds BirdSet HSN bird classification under distribution shift, DCASE2016 Task 2 sound event detection, and LibriSpeech speech transcription, substantially extending domains and task requirements.

E2.justification: v2 adds BEATs as an evaluated backbone alongside EAT and SSLAM. Table 5 also evaluates VQT and Head2Toe, previously discussed without experimental comparisons, and adds linear convex gated probing. ProtoBin, previously compared on EAT/SSLAM in Table 1, now participates in the main BAT benchmark comparison.

E3.justification: v2 explicitly refines final-benchmark settings. Comparing v1 Table 6 with v2 Table 7, AS-2M finetuning changes from 400k to 200k steps, AudioSet probing uses asymmetric BCE, and ESC-50 changes from CE to BCE. The reported AS-2M training count also changes from 1,932,574 to 1,912,024. New temporal-task protocols and ViT-Small evaluation further expand the experimental design; these disclosures do not establish that every retained experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds an explicit distribution-shift evaluation on HSN and a comparative analysis of probe latency, memory, parameters, and computation in Appendix D. Appendix F expands layer-weight analysis from v1's two classification datasets to six datasets and four backbones. The original frontend, target-selection, and decoder ablations remain.

E5.justification: v1 reports point estimates. v2 introduces ± values for ESC-50 performance in Table 5 and latency in Table 10. Their statistical meaning and run or seed counts are unspecified, so the PDFs support newly reported uncertainty but not an inferred increase in repeated runs.

E6.justification: Tables 1–4 retain their numerical results, but Table 5 changes extensively under revised settings: BAT's AS-2M CGP mAP is 42.90 in v1 and 45.03 in v2. The reported ESC-50 finding also reverses: CGP exceeds finetuning in v1 but trails it in v2. These are not controlled same-setting gains or losses. Tables 6, 9, and 10 add ASR, BAT-S, and computational results.

M1.justification: Equation (7) changes the stated local regression loss normalization from all N tokens to the masked-token count |Im|. BAT's principal components and CGP's aggregation/prototype procedure remain intact. The PDFs establish a revision to the written objective, without establishing whether the implementation changed.

P1.justification: The seven main sections retain their order and most methodological exposition. v2 edits terminology and tense, corrects 'CGB' to 'CGP', revises the contribution list and conclusion, reorganizes the appendices, and adds author-contribution and acknowledgement text. These refine the existing narrative without replacing its overall structure.

P2.justification: Table 5 is substantially redesigned around probing methods, backbones, and multiple metrics. Figure 1 clarifies the pooling diagram, and Figure 6 changes from two line-chart panels to a 24-panel layer-weight display. New ASR, smaller-model, and computational-cost tables, together with expanded configuration tables, substantially alter the presentation.

R1.justification: The positioning relative to D2V2, EAT/SSLAM, and prototype probing is retained. v2 adds references for DCASE, LibriSpeech, asymmetric loss, and additional bioacoustics work, while removing the BEANS future-work citation. Numerous other reference edits update bibliographic metadata for already discussed work.

T1.justification: Equation (7) replaces division by N with division by |Im|, mathematically changing the local-loss definition because only masked tokens enter the sum. The remaining formal development is essentially retained; neither version introduces theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the paper's broad claims through direct comparisons with additional probing methods and BEATs, evaluations beyond classification, and measured computational costs. Expanded implementation information and reported code availability also improve assessability. Undefined ± statistics, conflicting pretraining warmup descriptions, and an overbroad claim that CGP beats all probes despite the ESC-50 exception remain weaknesses. Nevertheless, the added experimental scrutiny addresses important limitations of v1's evidential coverage.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same BAT/CGP research. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across the expanded appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds detection, bird classification, speech recognition, smaller-model results, and measured computational costs in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original baseline reproductions, BAT component ablations, downstream benchmark results, and layer-wise representation analyses in Sections 4–6 and Appendix D.

results.title: BAT: Better Audio Transformer Guided by Convex Gated Probing

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same scientific claims: STING exposes greater illicit assistance, lower-resource languages do not consistently increase success, survival analysis characterizes attack efficiency, and reasoning and defenses have mixed effects. The additional experiments support these claims without redefining them.

C2.justification: v3 replaces the low-refusal-recall discussion about potentially underestimated ASR with an interpretation that judge noise is unlikely to explain language findings. It adds the interpretation that strategist quality is the main bottleneck in the tested ablation and extends defense-tradeoff interpretations to Omni-Moderation and additional targets. Existing broader interpretations and impact qualifications remain.

D1.justification: The introduction newly states a code release and supplies a repository location; repository contents cannot be verified from the PDFs. New analyses identify replacement-agent models and budgets, the multilingual-e5-small embedder, and moderation inputs. Existing hardware details, default hyperparameters, algorithm, and prompt templates are retained.

E1.justification: Section 6.1 expands human judge-validation coverage from Urdu and Telugu conversations to all seven study languages. The underlying AgentHarm task coverage, benign tasks, 44 base behaviors with 176 prompt variants, and overall seven-language attack suite remain unchanged.

E2.justification: Section 7.3 and Table 5 add OpenAI's Omni-Moderation as an evaluated defense alongside PromptGuard and the Safety Prompt. The single-turn and X-Teaming attack baselines remain unchanged. The additional target-model defense experiments retain the existing PromptGuard/Safety Prompt comparator set.

E3.justification: v3 substantially extends evaluation design with phase-separation scoring, staged agent-model substitutions at Smax=5, native-language planning, token/embedding comparisons, and filtering both attacker messages and target responses. Human-validation samples increase from 83 refusal and 56 intent judgments to 570 and 260, respectively. The original Section 5.1 experimental setup is retained.

E4.justification: New Appendices A.4-A.5 test decomposition quality and sensitivity to strategist, attacker, and evaluator strength. A.8.1-A.8.2 examine English-plan dependence and cross-language divergence. Expanded judge validation, Omni-Moderation testing, and defense transfer to GPT-5.1 and Gemini 3 Flash provide substantial additional robustness and diagnostic evidence.

E5.justification: Bootstrap 95% confidence intervals, Greenwood/log-log discovery-curve intervals, and Cox hazard-ratio reporting remain unchanged. No new seed, repeated-run, or uncertainty-estimation procedures are documented. The larger human-validation samples change evaluation design; the added appendix analyses generally report point estimates.

E6.justification: Original benchmark tables and figure results are retained, but substantial new results appear in Tables 6, 7, 10, 11, 13 and expanded Table 5. Examples include average AHS of 69.7% versus 58.8% after weakening all STING agents, native-language planning differences within 2.2 percentage points, and approximately 10% mean harmful-AHS reduction with Omni-Moderation. Judge precision/recall changes from 0.96/0.71 to 0.98/0.93 for refusals and 1.00/0.97 to 0.99/0.94 for intent on different validation samples, not matched-sample accuracy gains.

M1.justification: The four-agent STING procedure, phase progression, feedback, and success criteria remain unchanged. Algorithm 1 and the strategist, attacker, and evaluator prompt templates are identical. Alternative agent models and planning languages are experimental variations rather than a revision of the proposed algorithm.

P1.justification: Localized edits expand the RMJD explanation, related work, validation discussion, and defense narrative. New appendix subsections reorganize multilingual analyses and renumber subsequent sections; acknowledgements and the equal-contribution footnote are updated. The main narrative is largely retained rather than extensively rewritten.

P2.justification: v3 substantially extends the tabular presentation with dedicated displays for phase separation, agent-model ablations, native-language planning, linguistic divergence, and defense transfer (Tables 6, 7, 10, 11, 13). Table 5 gains Omni-Moderation rows and a revised caption. Existing figures are unchanged images, although several figures and tables move.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds HAICOSYSTEM as an existing multi-turn agent-safety exception and distinguishes its broad safety simulation from budgeted red-teaming. References for Omni-Moderation and multilingual E5 are also added. The remaining research positioning is substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix A.4 introduces a quantitative definition of phase separation: the fraction of phase pairs with non-overlapping invoked-tool sets, averaged across behaviors and strategies. The reachability formulation, RMJD definition, Cox model, and Kaplan-Meier derivations remain unchanged; the expanded RMJD explanation does not change its mathematics.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the evidence behind the central multilingual findings: limited Urdu/Telugu judge checks become a larger seven-language audit, and native-language planning tests address dependence on English strategies. Component ablations clarify which agents drive effectiveness, while additional defense evaluations test generality beyond Qwen3-Next. These additions address important validation gaps without changing the established headline results. Pooled judge reporting and mostly point-only new appendix results leave uncertainty, but the gains in evidential support are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same STING research. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and equations, tables, figures, and relocated material can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v3 retains those original results and adds strategist evaluation, component-model ablations, multilingual diagnostics, and additional defense experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original AgentHarm experiments, multilingual evaluations, judge validation, and reasoning, tool-knowledge, and defense ablations.

results.title: Helpful to a Fault: Measuring Illicit Assistance in Multi-Turn, Multilingual LLM Agents

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the same central contributions and headline claims: the QHFlow2 architecture, direct energy/force benchmarking, improved Hamiltonian accuracy, NequIP-level force accuracy, and favorable scaling. New supporting experiments do not redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: v2 explains the energy–force error gap and why global Hamiltonian MAE can misrepresent downstream accuracy. It interprets large-molecule failures through orbital ill-conditioning and explicitly acknowledges that one-shot forces need not be conservative. These substantially refine the mechanism discussion and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: v2 adds implementation disclosures about the single-Fock-build evaluation, B3LYP(VWN5) convention, SCF post-processing and H200 hardware, and two-H200/DDP training for ∇2DFT. The core architecture/training tables, software disclosures, and code-access information remain largely unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds training and evaluation on drug-like molecules in ∇2DFT and zero-shot evaluation on PubChemQH molecules with 45–98 atoms. Geometry optimization and local potential-energy-surface evaluation also extend the task coverage beyond the retained snapshot-prediction benchmarks.

E2.justification: v2 adds QHNetV2 to the QH9 comparisons in Table 2, trained eSEN baselines on rMD17 in Table 19, and xTB/MMFF comparators for geometry optimization in Table 25. HELM, SchNOrb, and PhiSNet were already compared in v1 Table 12; their appearance on ∇2DFT is an extension of coverage.

E3.justification: The reported SCF tolerance changes from 10^-13 in v1 E.4 to 10^-9 in v2 G.3. New protocols include a 1,920-GPU-hour ∇2DFT training cap, finite-difference force checks on 10 geometries per molecule, and BFGS optimization and Hessian evaluations with specified stopping thresholds and displacement steps.

E4.justification: v2 adds readout-degree and prediction-target ablations, large-molecule extrapolation, empirical error-scaling fits, analytic-versus-finite-difference force checks, orbital-subspace error decomposition, and geometry/PES diagnostics. These investigate substantial new questions. The original bond-stretching analysis is retained as G.10, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: v2 introduces numerical ± summaries in Tables 23, 26, and 27 and fitted exponents with R² values in Table 22. The meaning of the ± quantities is not specified, and no increased training-run or seed count is established. The existing statement about fixing random seeds remains unchanged.

E6.justification: Most existing MD/QH9 scores remain unchanged, but v2 adds extensive results, including ∇2DFT accuracy, large-molecule failures, force-consistency measurements, and local PES errors. Figure 4 also changes: QHFlow2-l's SCF cycle ratio moves from 52.8% to 47.4%. Because the reported convergence tolerance changes, this is not a demonstrated same-setting improvement.

M1.justification: The proposed SO(2) backbone, two-stage pair update, residual flow-matching formulation, priors, and training/sampling algorithms remain unchanged. The density-only and joint-output variants in G.11 are experimental alternatives; they do not replace the default Hamiltonian-prediction method.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained. v2 rewrites the conclusion and bond-stretching discussion, adds explanatory cross-references, moves SCF documentation from E.4 to G.3, and updates publication and acknowledgement text. The extensive new scientific material does not constitute a wholesale rewrite.

P2.justification: v2 adds twelve tables displaying new evaluations and analyses and expands Table 2 with QHNetV2 rows. Figure 4 is relocated and resized, Figure 6's reversed left/right caption is corrected, and the retained Figure 8 is integrated into a different appendix layout.

R1.justification: The new discussion in Section 3.3 and Appendix D.3 substantially expands positioning against HELM and QHNetV2, distinguishing their backbones, Hamiltonian readouts, pair refinement, and downstream energy evaluation. QHNetV2 is newly cited, while several ancillary reactivity references are removed.

T1.justification: G.8 adds a perturbative derivation of second-order energy error versus first-order force error, with particle-number conservation and nondegenerate/gapped-orbital conditions. It also formalizes integrated density error and molecular-orbital block decomposition. These additions go beyond v1's retained DFT and equivariance background.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation beyond v1's snapshot accuracy and scaling results. Force-consistency and local PES tests in Tables 23–27 address practical-use questions, while Table 21 and the conservative-force caveat make important failure boundaries explicit. The added comparisons and chemical coverage further strengthen the evidence. Some new documentation needs correction: Equation 27 does not reconcile its exchange-correlation potential expression with the energy definitions in Equations 23–25, and the ± summaries are undefined. These weaknesses do not outweigh the substantial gains in validation and qualification of the central claims.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe QHFlow2 and retain corresponding methods, benchmarks, and results. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds benchmark evaluations, force-consistency tests, geometry optimization, and further analyses in Appendix G.

before.justification: v1 reports original Hamiltonian, energy, and force evaluations, scaling experiments, ablations, SCF convergence tests, and bond-stretching analyses.

results.title: Machine Learning Hamiltonians are Accurate Energy-Force Predictors

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: defining NLQ4TSDB, introducing NLQTSBench, and proposing Sonar-TS's Search-Then-Verify framework. Expanded evidence and revised wording do not materially redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: Appendix D adds substantive limitations concerning synthetic data and authentic user queries, symbolic information loss, and the scalability of a fixed Experience set. Appendix C adds explanations of backbone and alphabet sensitivity, acknowledges moderate retrieval recall, and discusses computational tradeoffs. Section 6.3 also newly interprets the feature-table ablation as evidence about generic SQL-plus-Python agents.

D1.justification: v2 adds code-access information and states that configurations and operators are released. It newly documents the independent 110-query Experience bootstrap set, Lite's 100/200/200 task composition, and more explicit injection calibration details. Conversely, it omits v1's specification that report-outlier scoring uses F1 with a four-hour tolerance; this is lost documentation, not evidence of a changed implementation.

E1.justification: Benchmark construction expands from CausalRivers backgrounds alone to CausalRivers, ETTm1, and SMD backgrounds in v2 Section 4.2 and Appendix A.2. This materially broadens the represented source data, while retaining the nine full-benchmark tasks and three Lite tasks.

E2.justification: The main accuracy baselines remain unchanged; Omini-SQL is corrected to Omni-SQL. The matched ablation comparison adds a w/o Self-Correction variant in v2 Table 5, and Table 11 newly compares system overhead against MAC-SQL. The Qwen models are Sonar-TS backbone variants.

E3.justification: The full evaluation expands from 831 to 1,153 queries with revised task counts. New experiments vary Qwen backbone sizes and SAX alphabets and measure retrieval recall, candidates, latency, tokens, and storage. Appendix A also changes the stated injection constraint from SNR > 1.0 to 1.0 < SNR < 1.5 and corrects timestamp acceptance from strict < to <=; these reported revisions do not establish that every retained experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained component ablations and longest-plateau case study, v2 adds a self-correction ablation, backbone and SAX-alphabet sensitivity studies, intermediate Search-stage effectiveness analysis, and system-overhead analysis. These investigate robustness, configuration dependence, retrieval bottlenecks, and computational tradeoffs absent from v1.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests for the experimental results. The additional v2 experiments continue reporting point estimates.

E6.justification: Sonar-TS's full-benchmark scores change, including its average from 0.6168 to 0.6144, under different benchmark compositions. Baseline and existing ablation averages also change even where their task scores remain identical; Lite results are unchanged. Substantial new results include the 0.5930 self-correction ablation average, retrieval recalls of 0.5482 and 0.4713, and approximately 22-second Sonar-TS latency versus 15 seconds for MAC-SQL.

M1.justification: The SQL/SAX search, Python verification operators, self-correction, and prompt templates are retained. However, v1 describes continuously evolving Experiences within online querying, whereas v2 explicitly prohibits query-time updates and constructs Experiences offline. The PDFs do not clearly establish whether this changes the implemented procedure or clarifies the existing cold-start mechanism.

P1.justification: v2 substantially rewrites the benchmark, method, experimental discussion, and construction appendix. It moves Related Work before the benchmark, expands problem formulation into a problem-and-challenges section, reorganizes Appendix A around templates and construction, and adds dedicated experimental and limitations appendices.

P2.justification: v2 adds capability, metric-mapping, Lite-composition, sensitivity, retrieval, and overhead tables. It relocates and condenses the benchmark-statistics and operator tables, expands the ablation table, and converts the existing appendix Experience snapshot into Figure 4. The principal diagrams and case-study graphic are largely retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds a time-series similarity-search discussion citing KV-Match and MS-Index and distinguishes query-by-example from query-by-language. It also adds ETTm1/SMD source citations and removes the Cai and Naqvi references. The existing Text-to-SQL/TSQA positioning remains; publication updates for retained works are bibliographic changes.

T1.justification: v2 Section 5.5 introduces an asymptotic online-cost expression and accompanying scalability argument absent from v1. Appendix A.3 also corrects the timestamp success condition to permit exact matches when tolerance is zero. The core task formulation and SAX equations remain unchanged, and no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially improves empirical breadth and auditability through broader benchmark backgrounds, targeted sensitivity and ablation studies, and explicit retrieval and cost measurements. The independent Experience-initialization disclosure, code-access information, and substantive limitations address important reporting gaps in v1. Lost report-outlier scoring detail and an incompletely justified worst-case scalability argument remain drawbacks, but they do not outweigh these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Sonar-TS and NLQTSBench. All pages, including figures, tables, equations, and appendices, were readable and support comparison across the reorganized sections.

after.justification: v2 reports original benchmark evaluations and ablations in Tables 4–5, plus backbone sensitivity, SAX sensitivity, retrieval diagnostics, and computational costs in Appendix C.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark evaluations, component ablations, and a qualitative case study in Tables 1–2 and Figure 4.

results.title: Sonar-TS: Search-Then-Verify Natural Language Querying for Time Series Databases

C1.justification: The abstract, three introduction contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims: VIG measures visual dependence, identifies grounded tokens, and enables efficient selective training with improved grounding. The added experiments support these existing claims without redefining the central contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations concerning preserved linguistic competence and long-tail coverage, explaining these through unchanged text-only supervision, full input context, and selection by visual necessity. It also interprets the Qwen and VCD results as evidence of architectural generality and representation-level debiasing. The original computational-overhead limitation remains.

D1.justification: Appendix D adds the Open-Qwen2VL checkpoint reference, its selection threshold of 0.012, and training details including one epoch, batch size 128, learning rate 2e-5, AdamW, and ten-hour training time. Existing implementation disclosures are retained. Detailed text-only evaluation and POS-tagging instructions remain unspecified.

E1.justification: v2 adds MAmmoTH-VL instruction-training data and CV-Bench evaluation covering foundational 2D and 3D visual reasoning. It also introduces text-only evaluation on GSM8K, MMLU, HellaSwag, and TruthfulQA, substantially expanding the evaluated task requirements. Existing benchmark coverage is retained.

E2.justification: VCD is newly included in the VQAv2 textual-corruption comparison in Table E.1, although it already appeared in the general benchmark comparison. Table 3 also adds a vanilla Open-Qwen2VL 2B counterpart. The original VCD, PAI, VAR, and LACING comparisons in Table 4 remain unchanged.

E3.justification: v2 introduces a distinct Open-Qwen2VL 2B training configuration using a random 1M MAmmoTH-VL subset, with 701K samples retained. New evaluation procedures include combined accuracy across CV-Bench tasks, corpus-level POS aggregation, and category-retention analysis using 20%/60%/20% frequency tiers. These extend the experimental design; settings for retained experiments are unchanged.

E4.justification: New analyses examine VIG by POS category, preservation of text-only capabilities, retention of rare concepts and different training-task categories, and robustness relative to VCD under textual corruption. Appendix A adds five matched/partially matched/conflicting-image examples. The original selection-level and selection-ratio ablations are retained without substantive revision.

E5.justification: Neither version provides repeated-run or seed counts, significance tests, or defined confidence intervals. Existing distribution plots and attention bands retain their reporting practices; the added experiments do not introduce new uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results while preserving shared Table 3 values and all Table 4 scores. Newly reported Open-Qwen2VL results show 4.10B versus 2.42B active tokens and CV-Bench accuracy of 68.99 versus 70.01 for vanilla versus VIG training. Added results include text-only scores, POS and retention findings, qualitative VIG scores, and VCD's corruption-normalized score of 42.9 versus VIG's 54.1.

M1.justification: The blurred-image VIG calculation, top-p% sample selection, shared sample/token threshold, and loss masking with full answer context remain unchanged. Applying this procedure to Open-Qwen2VL adds an experimental configuration, not a new method component.

P1.justification: The title gains 'Focusing Where Vision Matters,' author and publication information changes, and new analysis paragraphs, an initial qualitative appendix, and an Impact Statement are added. Most existing prose, contribution statements, and section ordering remain intact rather than undergoing extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: The main text and references change from a single-column preprint to a two-column conference layout, relocating and resizing figures and tables throughout. Table 3 gains model rows and a CV-Bench column; Figure 2 gains CV-Bench. New displays include the POS plot, text-only and VCD tables, qualitative image grid, and two-panel retention figure.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for Open-Qwen2VL, MAmmoTH-VL, Cambrian-1/CV-Bench, and the four text-only benchmarks. It extends the empirical positioning against VCD under textual corruption. The related-work narrative and principal novelty positioning otherwise remain stable; citation-style and bibliographic corrections are presentation changes.

T1.justification: The VIG definition, cross-entropy/KL derivation, deterministic-supervision assumption, token decomposition, selection-set definitions, and CHAIR formulas remain mathematically unchanged. No new theorem, proof, or substantive derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: The Open-Qwen2VL/MAmmoTH-VL experiment substantially strengthens generalization evidence beyond v1's closely related LLaVA/ShareGPT4V models. Corpus-level token and retention analyses, plus the VCD corruption comparison, address important questions about selection behavior and robustness. These gains strengthen the empirical case, although unexplained identical 7B/13B text-only rows in Tables 5 and E.2 weaken that evidence, and the earlier main/appendix ablation discrepancies persist in Tables 6 and F.1.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VIG method and selective-training study. All 20 pages of v1 and 22 pages of v2, including their appendices, are readable and support comparison despite substantial reformatting.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds another model and training dataset, additional benchmarks, and new diagnostic analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark experiments, VIG analyses, attention and textual-corruption evaluations, qualitative examples, and selection ablations.

results.title: Focusing Where Vision Matters: Selective Training for Large Vision Language Models via Visual Information Gain

C1.justification: The central claims about efficient PLD accounting and Gaussian privacy–utility advantages remain. Section 1.1 now explicitly restricts the displayed runtime expression to Gaussian mechanisms and includes its sigma dependence; the technical overview also claims the tighter general-k reduction.

C2.justification: v2 explains that the favorable Gaussian comparison does not extend uniformly to Laplace mechanisms: Poisson can be better in higher-privacy regimes. It leaves a general characterization open, qualifies arbitrary-noise applicability by requiring a constructible dominating PLD realization, and explains unresolved comparisons caused by computationally limited bound precision.

D1.justification: Appendix C substantially improves implementation documentation through explicit indexing, endpoint handling, distribution-mixture semantics and disclosure of combined subsampling/re-discretization. Tables 1–2 provide configurations and numerical bounds for the new diagnostic. The code reference changes from RA_PLD to PLD_accounting and adds a package-index link; these are documented access changes, not independently verified availability.

E1.justification: v2 extends evaluation beyond Gaussian mechanisms to Laplace mechanisms and exercises all four combinations of two consecutive Poisson/random-allocation schemes. The Criteo-derived accounting settings, Bernoulli mean-estimation task and PREAMBLE application remain; no new real-data training experiment is reported.

E2.justification: The main Poisson, Feldman–Shenfeld, Dong et al., Monte Carlo and Chua lower-bound comparisons remain. v2 adds comparisons among four nested sampling combinations in Figure 15 and removes the separate comparison against the analytic second-order RDP reference in v1 Figure 9. Newly cited 2026 accounting methods are not added as plotted baselines.

E3.justification: Runtime evaluation changes from runtime versus discretization and step count to runtime versus the computed epsilon-bound gap. The reported FFT comparison changes from sigma=1, delta=10^-6 to sigma=3, delta=10^-10, retaining t=1000. New evaluations specify one versus 100 compositions and additional parameter grids; these do not establish same-setting performance changes.

E4.justification: Appendix D substantially expands sensitivity and applicability analysis through Gaussian parameter-grid comparisons, Laplace/Gaussian comparisons and nested-sampling tests. The second-order RDP diagnostic in v1 Figure 9 is removed, while v2 Figure 14 and Tables 1–2 directly examine how discretization relates to the gap between upper and lower epsilon bounds.

E5.justification: v2 Figure 4 newly reports runtime averages over 10 runs with standard-deviation shading; v1 provides neither that run count nor runtime variability. Both versions retain the Monte Carlo setup of one million importance samples and 95% confidence. The PDFs do not establish an increase in runtime repetitions.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive privacy-bound results for Laplace mechanisms, parameter grids, nested sampling and discretization gaps, while removing the second-order RDP results. Retained results also change: at epsilon=0.1, allocation PLD noise values in the mean-estimation experiment change from 1.89 to 1.88 for d=1 and from 59.68 to 59.56 for d=1000 (v1 Figure 4; v2 Figure 5).

M1.justification: The exp-PLD convolution framework remains, but the general-k reduction now mixes floor(t/k) and ceiling(t/k) allocations. Algorithm 1 computes the dual from the original input before discretization, rather than from its discretized approximation. Appendix C also corrects self-convolution control flow and rounding directions. These refine the documented procedure without replacing the approach.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized grammar and terminology edits, expands explanations, moves PREAMBLE ahead of runtime and utility discussion, and adds descriptive Appendix D subheadings. Most introductory, methodological and concluding prose retains its original structure.

P2.justification: Figures are broadly redrawn with revised colors, legends, typography and annotations. The runtime display is redesigned, new heatmaps and diagnostic tables are introduced, and several figures are relocated. Appendix C also switches some algorithms to side-by-side layouts. These changes extend well beyond numerical updates or renumbering.

R1.justification: v2 adds Dong and Ganesh (2026), Schuchardt and Kalinin (2026), and Dong and Özgür (2026), positioning the work against newer dynamic-programming accounting and asymptotic sampling analyses.
