Other changed citation years and venues largely update existing works rather than introduce new research relationships.

T1.justification: The main theoretical framework remains, with a tighter floor/ceiling reduction and proof in Lemma 2.8. v2 removes the discrete-only restriction on PLD realizations, specifies subsampling support and admissible parameters, and revises the probability-mass interpretation. Appendix B corrects Claim B.2 to use dual infinity masses and repairs endpoint and complexity derivations.

improvement.justification: v2 resolves important specification errors in v1, including misplaced self-convolution squaring, reversed convolution rounding and problematic dual construction for lower bounds. Corrected mathematical statements, fuller implementation guidance and direct discretization checks materially strengthen reliability and reproducibility. The Laplace evaluations clarify applicability boundaries. These gains outweigh the loss of the separate second-order RDP diagnostic.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work by Feldman and Shenfeld. The main text, equations, figures and Appendices A–D are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v2 retains original numerical and simulation results and adds Laplace-mechanism evaluations, broader parameter sweeps and nested-sampling comparisons.

before.justification: v1 reports original numerical privacy-accounting results, measured runtimes and simulated mean-estimation errors in Section 5 and Appendix D.

results.title: Efficient privacy loss accounting for subsampling and random allocation

C1.justification: The main contribution and competitive-performance claims remain. The abstract and introduction replace 'surpassing 70%' with approximately 70%, and the introduction replaces exceeding 90% below 50 samples with approximately 90%, matching the retained results more closely. The introduction also removes the claim that additional language scoring effectively costs only O(|Lambda|).

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands explanations and applicability limits. It attributes low-data performance to vocabulary structure and generative modeling, recommends a broadly multilingual trained vocabulary over convenience reuse, and discusses weaknesses under heavy corruption, non-Latin scripts and very low-resource GlotLID-C conditions. New length-bias interpretations and proposed scaling remedies further extend the discussion.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies a 1e-12 token-probability floor, the selected fastText minimum-count setting, and 1,000 samples per language for base-tokenizer learning in the timing experiment. It also reports comparative training times. These improve implementation documentation without establishing changes to the earlier experiments; the code-release information is retained.

E1.justification: The six benchmark datasets and language-identification tasks are retained. Appendix B.2 adds a distinct input-corruption scenario using character replacements on WiLI at rates up to 50%. The script and resource breakdowns analyze the existing GlotLID-C population.

E2.justification: The fastText, CLD3 and GlotLID-M comparisons remain. Section 6 newly compares dialect-group scores with reported DSL-ML 2024 shared-task systems, including French macro-F1 of 0.534 versus 0.385. These additional comparators are unnamed, and reruns or matched evaluation splits are not documented.

E3.justification: The original splits and headline training budgets are retained, but the evaluation design expands substantially. Additions include DeepSeek3.2 and Qwen3 vocabulary configurations, a specified stochastic corruption protocol, fastText epoch/minimum-count sweeps, comparative timing on the same hardware, and a 500,000-sample normalization experiment with an unnormalized rescoring control.

E4.justification: v2 adds tests of Viterbi versus marginalization, character-noise robustness, fastText hyperparameter sensitivity, and performance by script and resource tier. It also investigates segmentation-length bias and tests whether length normalization helps. These substantially extend v1's sample-efficiency, input-length and vocabulary analyses.

E5.justification: Figure 1 and Table 6 retain identical mean-plus-standard-deviation reporting, without adding seed or repeated-run counts. v2 calls the marginalization gain statistically insignificant but supplies no identified test, interval or uncertainty-estimation procedure; this is an added result characterization rather than a documented statistical-method change.

E6.justification: Existing result rows in Tables 1-8 are retained, while additional tokenizer rows and Tables 9-18 substantially expand the findings. Examples include macro-F1 of 0.396 versus 0.678 for UniLID and fastText under 50% corruption, and accuracy falling from 0.960 to 0.885 with length normalization on the 500,000-sample subset. These are new comparisons, not improvements to the retained scores.

M1.justification: The default shared-vocabulary, per-language EM and Viterbi classification procedure remains unchanged. v2 adds limited experimental inference variants: exact marginalization in Appendix B.1 and length-normalized scoring in Appendix E.3. Neither replaces the default; the newly disclosed probability floor does not itself establish a change to the earlier implementation.

P1.justification: The main sequence of Sections 1-8 remains intact. v2 makes targeted abstract and introduction edits, condenses dataset and baseline descriptions, revises parts of the results and discussion, and organizes additional analyses into appendix subsections. The new scientific content does not amount to a wholesale narrative reorganization.

P2.justification: Visual reporting expands substantially through Tables 9-18, covering decoding, corruption, tuning, timing and performance breakdowns. Tables 1 and 8 gain tokenizer rows. Figure 1 and the existing table structures are largely retained, while the new tables introduce substantial additional appendix layouts.

R1.justification: v2 adds Ng and Jordan (2001) to support the generative-versus-discriminative sample-efficiency explanation and Ren et al. (2022) in the low-resource discussion. It also explicitly positions results against shared-task submissions. Most related work remains unchanged; the corrected Land and Pinter identifier is only a bibliographic correction.

T1.justification: Section 4 corrects the inference complexity from O(|Lambda| + N*T_max) to O(|Lambda|*N*b + N*T_max), and corrects the maximum branching factor from N*T_max to T_max. It also adds complexity comparisons with fastText and CLD3. The underlying generative model and EM mathematics remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation: previously untested inference choices and unsupported comparative timing claims receive direct evidence, while new analyses expose important noise, script and length-related limitations. Corrected complexity and moderated sample-efficiency claims improve accuracy. Reporting remains imperfect: Section 6 gives GlotLID-C latency as 0.274 ms versus 0.307 ms in Table 12, and statistical insignificance is asserted without a stated test. These weaknesses limit individual conclusions but do not outweigh the substantial improvement in validation and characterization of applicability.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same UniLID research. All 14 pages of v1 and 17 pages of v2, including appendices A-B and A-E respectively, are readable; their text, equations, figures and tables support comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original decoding, corruption, hyperparameter, timing and error-analysis results in Tables 9-18.

before.justification: v1 reports original language-identification experiments, including benchmark comparisons, dialect identification, sample-efficiency studies and vocabulary ablations in Tables 1-8 and Figure 1.

results.title: What Language is This? Ask Your Tokenizer.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contributions, and conclusion replace the central claim of a tractable event-prior KL upper bound with an IVP representation or regularizer. The introduction also shifts graph claims from cross-channel influence toward temporal ordering and alignment. These narrow important theoretical and mechanistic claims, while annotation-free recovery and superior classification claims remain.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly limits ERGs to sensor-space timing summaries, excluding source-level causal, anatomical, or synaptic interpretations, and identifies the event-prior term as a regularizer rather than an exact path-measure KL. It also explains baseline boundary-output limitations and Cohort B variability. Its new channel-representativeness discussion requires qualification: Table 9 supports generally higher HC frequencies, but AD–MCI ordering is mixed.

D1.justification: V2 adds a code-access URL, explicit auxiliary-weight sweep values, and updated regularizer pseudocode. Most architectural and optimization details in Appendix F are unchanged. Conversely, v1's explicit most-recent-event definition of cross-channel lags in Section 4.6 is no longer specified as precisely.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same three synthetic frequency bands and EEG cohorts A and B, with the same participant groups. The added timing, weight-sensitivity, and channel analyses concern existing data and tasks; reporting more of the already-used 19 channels does not expand dataset coverage.

E2.justification: Tables 1 and 2 retain NODE, ODE-RNN, and STRODE for synthetic comparisons and EEGNet, LCADNet, LSTM, ATCNet, ADFormer, and LEAD for EEG classification. The new runtime comparison uses the existing computational-comparison methods. Newly discussed point-process models are not evaluated.

E3.justification: V2 adds one-factor sweeps of three auxiliary weights on Cohort A while holding the remaining protocol fixed, and introduces per-window forward time as an evaluation metric. Existing subject splits, two-second windowing, normalization, aggregation, training budget, and classification metrics remain unchanged. Detailed runtime measurement conditions are not supplied.

E4.justification: Appendix E.5 adds systematic sensitivity studies for dLIF, ERG, and IVP-KL weights, extending the existing prior-removal ablation to regularization-strength robustness. Appendix E.6 additionally tests whether the four plotted frequency patterns represent all 19 channels. These substantially expand the supplementary analyses; the original prior ablation remains numerically unchanged.

E5.justification: Both versions retain mean and standard deviation across five test folds and the synthetic event-rate intervals obtained through nonparametric resampling. The new runtime table also uses mean and standard deviation, without introducing a new uncertainty procedure or specifying repetition counts. No seed information or significance tests are added.

E6.justification: Tables 3, 8, and 9 add substantial results on runtime, regularization sensitivity, and channel-wide frequency patterns. Examples include LERD's 9.209 ms mean forward time and ERG-weight sweep accuracies ranging from 63.73% to 75.03%. Fifteen previously unreported channels extend Figure 2; HC is highest in 18/19, with T4 an exception. All original benchmark, ablation, computational-cost, and supplementary diagnostic-metric values remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The architecture and EPDE/MELP/ERG procedures remain largely unchanged, but the specified training regularizer changes. Section 4.3 and Algorithm 4 replace v1's U_epsilon upper-bound surrogate with a finite-horizon IVP integral using a normalized first-event prior. This revises one auxiliary loss; the PDFs do not establish that the retained experiments were rerun.

P1.justification: V2 makes targeted rewrites to the abstract, problem formulation, method explanations, visualizations, and conclusion. It relocates some theoretical setup, adds appendix subsections and acknowledgments, and updates author order, affiliations, and publication information. The overall main-section and appendix organization remains recognizable.

P2.justification: V2 adds runtime, sensitivity, and channel-frequency tables. Figure 4 retains the same plots but enlarges and rearranges them from two rows of three panels to three rows of two, pairing methods by frequency band. Other figures and retained tables largely preserve their displays despite relocation and renumbering.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds mechanistic Bayesian reasoning as context, citing additional Bayesian event/graph models, and contrasts LERD with observed-event point-process methods such as Smith and Brown and Truccolo et al. This expands the rationale for its annotation-free positioning while retaining the existing supervised-EEG and latent-dynamics literature structure.

T1.justification: Theorem 4.1 and Appendix B replace the claimed upper bound with a normalized finite-horizon KL representation, correcting the change-of-variable integrand and integration endpoints and stating an integrability assumption. V1's Corollary A.2 becomes A.3: general sub-Gaussian, zero-centered concentration is replaced by Gaussian concentration around the expected perturbation, with explicit bias and a revised matrix bound. Appendix D supplies a substantially revised proof.

improvement.justification: V2 repairs two central mathematical deficiencies: the incorrectly constructed finite-window KL bound and the uncentered concentration claim for nonlinear graph perturbations. The replacement results and explicit limits on causal and path-KL interpretations substantially improve soundness. Sensitivity tests and full-channel reporting also improve transparency without changing classification scores. Some lag-construction detail is lost and runtime documentation remains incomplete, but these limited drawbacks do not outweigh the corrections to the paper's theoretical foundations.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LERD study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–F are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: V2 retains these original results and adds measured inference times, auxiliary-weight sensitivity results, and additional channel-frequency summaries.

before.justification: V1 reports original synthetic event-recovery experiments, classification on two EEG cohorts, prior ablations, and analyses of inferred frequencies and graphs.

results.title: LERD: Latent Event-Relational Dynamics for Neurodegenerative Classification

C1.justification: The central claims about dense pretraining enabling flexible sparse inference remain intact. The abstract and introduction extend the accuracy-scaling claim from 2.6B to 7.6B parameters and advertise approximately one point of accuracy loss with 64-fold attention FLOP and KV-cache reductions.

C2.justification: v3 adds hypotheses explaining NoPE performance through shorter effective attention spans and limited RepoBench scaling through insufficient code data. It qualifies multi-dilation adaptation by the enormous hybrid-configuration space and expands proposed byte-level and parallel-reasoning applications. The central recurrence and sparsification interpretations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v3 supplies a code URL, documents the 7.6B model's dimensions and optimization hyperparameters, and clarifies adaptation learning rates in Appendix A.1. Conversely, it omits v1 Section 5.1's explicit instruction to always select the first and most recent blocks in top-k attention.

E1.justification: Both versions use FineWeb-Edu, PG19, the same six commonsense tasks, LongBench and RULER NIAH tasks. The PG19 experiment remains in v3 Table 11. Larger models and additional attention configurations do not introduce new dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: v3 adds GQA/MQA comparisons (Figure 5), SnapKV and StreamingLLM to the NIAH comparison (Table 7), and Mamba2/GatedDeltaNet to the retained LongBench comparison (Table 5). Table 20 also introduces literature-reported Griffin/Pythia comparisons. Quest/MoBA comparisons already existed in v1.

E3.justification: v3 adds 7.6B-model training on 100B tokens, FLOPs-matched GQA/MQA configurations, a 1024-KV-entry NIAH comparison and a head-hit analysis over 500 examples. Appendix A.1 revises the reported smaller-model adaptation rate from an example of 2e-5 to 0.1 times the original learning rate, explicitly retaining earlier results; this does not establish rerunning them.

E4.justification: New analyses test whether recurrence improves block-selection hit rates (Table 9), whether one adaptation stage can cover multiple dilations (Table 10), whether positional encoding is necessary (Table 13), and whether dilation complements top-k attention (Table 19). Existing component, recurrence-placement and adaptation-curve analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals or significance tests. The new 500-example head analysis specifies a sample size, not uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantial comparator and analysis results, plus 7.6B accuracy results: Table 8 reports commonsense averages of 64.4 for dense inference and 63.1 at D=64. Earlier 1.5B and latency results are retained, while v1 Table 13's detailed 2.6B commonsense results disappear. New Table 9 reports attention accuracy of 57.4 where Table 17 retains 63.2 for the same stated NIAH-MK-2 setting, an unexplained mismatch.

M1.justification: The full-sequence recurrence and active recurrence learning architecture remain unchanged. v3 adds procedural variants: joint adaptation across seven dilations (Table 10) and combined top-k/dilated inference, attending fully within selected blocks and using compressed representations elsewhere (Table 19).

P1.justification: The introduction, contribution list and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten. Efficiency and top-k discussions are reordered, positioning receives its own subsection, and the former appendices B–D are consolidated into experimental subsections. Existing design explanations and adaptation discussion also move between the main text and appendix.

P2.justification: v3 adds the GQA/MQA plot and multiple comparison and analysis tables, expands the scaling plot with a 7.6B curve and attention reference markers, and adds baseline rows to Table 5. Adaptation curves move into the main text, retained appendix tables are rearranged and compacted, and the detailed 2.6B table is removed.

R1.justification: New Section 5.3 and Table 6 substantially expand positioning against GQA/MQA, KV-cache eviction and other efficiency approaches, distinguishing their computational, storage and access properties. Additional citations contextualize NoPE, retrieval heads and larger-model comparisons. The Rae/PG19 citation disappears although the PG19 experiment remains.

T1.justification: The recurrence and dilated-attention equations and underlying mathematical formulation are retained. v3 adds empirical analyses and conceptual hypotheses, but no new formal assumptions, theorems, proofs or substantive mathematical derivations.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses important evaluation gaps: v1 provided 7B-scale throughput without corresponding accuracy evidence and lacked GQA/MQA and SnapKV comparisons. The new scaling results and controlled comparisons substantially strengthen support for the central efficiency–accuracy argument, while head-hit analysis tests the previously speculative block-scoring explanation. Removing detailed 2.6B results and introducing the unexplained Table 9/Table 17 accuracy mismatch weaken reporting, but these drawbacks do not outweigh the substantive improvement in validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RAT+ research. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains original experiments and adds 7.6B-model accuracy results, comparator evaluations and supplementary analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original pretraining, adaptation, downstream accuracy, ablation and efficiency experiments, including additional results in its appendices.

results.title: RAT+: Train Dense, Infer Sparse - Recurrence Augmented Attention for Dilated Inference

C1.justification: The introduction strengthens its specific headline overlap-localization result from 13.13° to 4.11°. The central contributions—JAEGER, SpatialSceneQA, and Neural IV—and the qualitative claims in the abstract and conclusion retain their scope.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations attributing benefits to structured representation and alignment, and explicitly limits FOA superiority to the studied comparison. It qualifies real-world transfer as a sanity check and contextualizes near-ceiling reasoning through harder scenarios and limited training. The rewritten Impact Statement adds concrete limitations concerning real acoustics, sensors, synchronization, and calibration.

D1.justification: The abstract changes from promising release upon acceptance to stating that code, checkpoints, and datasets are available at a specified GitHub repository; that availability was not externally verified. New appendices also document SimpleFuse's depth and waveform processing and the BAT branch substitution. Existing main-model hyperparameters and hardware details remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds evaluation on real STARSS23 recordings, restricted to approximately stationary single-speaker clips, extending the previously simulated coverage. Appendix D also introduces reasoning with four to six visible candidates beyond the original two-to-three-candidate scenarios.

E2.justification: The original Table 2 comparators remain. v2 adds SimpleFuse, which receives the same RGB-D and FOA inputs, and JAEGER (BAT), a matched-pipeline binaural comparator distinct from the existing standalone BAT baseline. These introduce substantive controls for architectural and representation advantages.

E3.justification: New protocols include pretrained-versus-scratch evaluation on 753 STARSS23 clips totaling 3.84 hours, separate median elevation and azimuth errors, matched-input and matched-pipeline comparisons, and training with 160 examples per harder candidate setting. The original experiments' stated splits, metrics, and training budgets are unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendices A–D add substantial analyses of simulation-to-real transfer, structured fusion versus simple input concatenation, FOA versus binaural representations, and sensitivity to more visual distractors. The original cross-scenario, depth, component, and asset-diversity analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, error bars, or formal significance tests. Existing mean/median reporting and the discussion of varying asset-generation seeds are unchanged.

E6.justification: Table 2 revises overlap DoA errors from 16.09° to 6.44° for Classical IV and from 13.13° to 4.11° for Neural IV. Table 3 also changes 22.06° to 19.25° and 16.36° to 14.85°, respectively. No explanation establishes whether these are corrections or reruns. Tables 6–9 add substantial results, including Neural IV accuracies of 95.0%, 77.5%, and 72.5% with four, five, and six candidates; these use a different training setting from the original benchmark.

M1.justification: The primary JAEGER architecture and Neural IV procedure remain unchanged. Appendix C introduces a limited architectural adaptation for comparison: JAEGER (BAT) replaces the FOA spatial branch with BAT Spatial-AST binaural embeddings while retaining the Qwen audio features.

P1.justification: v2 rewrites the Impact Statement, updates the resource sentence and publication footer, and inserts four appendix sections before the reordered original material. The main scientific narrative and method explanations remain largely verbatim.

P2.justification: v2 adds four compact appendix tables with captions. Table 4 moves between columns, and the unchanged Figure 4 moves to a separate final page. Existing illustrations and table structures are otherwise retained, with local text reflow rather than a broad visual redesign.

R1.justification: The cited-work set and related-work positioning are retained. STARSS23 and BAT were already cited in v1. The Hear You Are reference gains an OpenReview address and submission metadata, without changing the referenced work or its positioning.

T1.justification: Equations 1–9 and their mathematical constructions are unchanged. The coordinate-system definitions move from Appendix B to Appendix E without substantive revision; no new theorem, proof, or derivation appears.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for the architectural contribution by adding the input-matched SimpleFuse and matched-pipeline binaural comparisons missing from v1. The transfer and harder-candidate studies also expose applicability boundaries, supported by explicit qualifications absent previously. These gains address important evaluation weaknesses rather than merely increasing reported performance. The real-world study remains limited, harder-task training differs from the original benchmark, and the revised overlap scores remain unexplained, but the added controls and clearer limitations provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same JAEGER and SpatialSceneQA research. Text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and comparable; the original appendix material is retained and relocated in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds real-world transfer, architectural comparisons, and harder reasoning results in Tables 6–9.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulated localization, visual grounding, reasoning, and ablation results in Tables 2–5.

results.title: JAEGER: Joint 3D Audio-Visual Grounding and Reasoning in Simulated Physical Environments

C1.justification: The central claim that learnable order dynamics improve insertion-based generation remains. v2 extends the claimed benefits to fragment-constrained generation, explicitly claims meaningful molecular ordering, and quantifies headline quality gains as 17.5 and 6.7 percentage points. The methodological contribution is not fundamentally redefined.

C2.justification: v2 adds a structure-before-chemistry interpretation of molecular ordering, a sharper explanation of schedule instability, and an explicit correlation-versus-causation qualification for graph analysis. Its new discussion addresses shared-backbone scaling, idle sampling steps, and SAFE representation redundancy. Appendix F.2.3 also explains the decision to omit FCD.

D1.justification: The sparse molecule setup in v1 is expanded into detailed dataset, decoding, and metric documentation. v2 specifies canonical-SMILES conversion, fragment and salt handling, deduplication, fingerprint diversity, QED/SA thresholds, and PyTDC components, and adds implementation-library and dataset access references. These disclosures do not establish changes to previously used processing.

E1.justification: v2 adds four fragment-constrained molecular tasks: linker design, motif extension, scaffold decoration, and superstructure generation, using fragments from ten reference drugs. These introduce conditional completion requirements beyond v1's unconditional molecule generation. Star-graph coverage and SAFE training data are retained.

E2.justification: The corresponding graph and de novo experiments retain their comparator sets. The new constrained experiments extend comparison with SAFE-GPT/ARM, MDM, and FlexMDM; they do not introduce a distinct comparison method. Additional FlexMDM decoding configurations change settings rather than comparator identity.

E3.justification: The added constrained evaluation introduces fixed fragment-prefix completion, unchanged de novo checkpoints, 1024 sampling steps, and one completion per conditional input. v2 also adds unfiltered graph-order evaluation. Within retained experiments, the tabulated nucleus-sampling sweep drops p=0.2 and explicitly expands FlexMDM settings; the principal training budgets remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds molecular generation-time analysis across seven semantic token categories, supported by trajectories and Table 9. Appendix G.1.2 also tests whether graph-order conclusions survive removing the exact-match filter. Existing shared/separate-backbone and frozen/trainable-rate ablations remain.

E5.justification: v1 reports plus/minus values without specifying run counts. v2 identifies five de novo evaluation runs with different seeds and adds significance reporting for token-category timing, although the test is unspecified. Constrained-generation reporting is inconsistent: Table 3 says five runs, while Table 7 and Appendix F.2.4 say three. An increase in runs is not established.

E6.justification: De novo molecule scores are extensively revised: the medium-auxiliary, p=0.5, no-confidence row reports quality of 46.9% in v1 versus 79.5% in v2. The PDFs do not explain the broad score revisions, so these are reported replacements rather than established methodological gains. Constrained-generation and molecular-order results are added, while graph exact-match and token-accuracy scores remain unchanged.

M1.justification: LFlexMDM is renamed LoFlexMDM. The Kumaraswamy schedules, projected rate-matching objective, regularization, leave-one-out gradient estimator, backbone alternatives, and tau-leaping sampler are retained. Constrained generation evaluates existing checkpoints without introducing a new model component.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are substantially rewritten, related work moves after the experiments and new Discussion section, and the appendices gain a motivation section and reorganized experimental documentation. Model terminology is standardized around LoFlexMDM. These changes substantially alter the narrative beyond adding experimental content.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn with an explicit generator architecture panel. Graph displays are consolidated, and the retained loss plot is confined to the appendix. New constrained-result tables, molecular timing and trajectory figures, and filtered/unfiltered correlation panels substantially expand and reorganize the visual presentation.

R1.justification: The extended related work is substantially refocused: the learned-noise/image-diffusion discussion is removed, while insertion models, padding limitations, and learned generation order receive revised treatment. New references include Ding et al., the insertion-CTMC framework, Rainbow Padding, and molecular evaluation literature. v2 also explicitly positions the approach as applicable across three generation settings.

T1.justification: Section 2 corrects the likelihood-bound statement from minimizing to maximizing a lower bound, and Section 3 corrects the worked drop-token projection example. The six propositions, their proofs, the terminal-KL bound, and the main schedule and gradient derivations are otherwise retained.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation by testing fragment-constrained transfer, checking graph-order conclusions beyond successful trajectories, and directly analyzing molecular ordering. Detailed metric documentation also addresses important reproducibility gaps in v1. These gains outweigh reporting weaknesses, including inconsistent constrained-run counts and a headline 17.5-point comparison using FlexMDM quality of 62.0%, although Appendix Table 10 reports 63.2% under another decoding setting. The unexplained score revisions themselves do not establish improved paper quality.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, proofs, tables, and figures, are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original graph and molecule experiments and adds fragment-constrained generation results and further generation-order analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original graph-traversal and de novo molecule-generation experiments, including model ablations and generation-order analyses.

results.title: Insertion Based Sequence Generation with Learnable Order Dynamics

C1.justification: The three central contributions—exact factorization, advantageous graph partitioning, and L2G-Net—remain intact. v2's abstract explicitly claims scalability beyond standard GFT feasibility, and its introduction extends the claimed empirical applicability to inductive tasks and larger transductive graphs. These refine the contribution's reach without replacing its central premise.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations of task-dependent learned filters, positional encodings as complementary, and the tradeoff between per-epoch cost and convergence time. It explicitly recommends polynomial filters or message passing when linear complexity is essential, discusses dynamic and signed graphs, and leaves directed graphs for future work. These materially expand mechanism explanations and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: Appendix C and Table 8 provide hyperparameters for six added datasets, including hierarchy depths, learning rates, dropout, and training steps. v2 also discloses a 10^-12 deflation threshold and memory precision. Conversely, it omits v1's filter-bank counts and learnable-center formulation; those omissions do not establish that the corresponding mechanisms were removed.

E1.justification: Alongside the retained synthetic experiments and four heterophilous datasets, v2 evaluates peptides-func and peptides-struct as inductive molecular graph prediction tasks and Paris, Shanghai, Los Angeles, and London as much larger transductive graphs. These substantially expand task, domain, and scale coverage.

E2.justification: The original heterophily accuracy comparison retains its comparator set. New comparisons introduce methods including Specformer, Graph ViT, GRIT, and S2GCN on peptides, and SGFormer, GCNII, and DropEdge on City-Networks (Tables 13–14). Tables 10–11 also add training-time comparisons against GCN, ChebNet, and Polynormer.

E3.justification: v2 adds unsparsified peptide evaluation using AP and MAE, deeper City-Networks hierarchies with stated cut sparsification, 64-bit memory comparisons, and training-time comparisons with matched depth and hidden dimensions for selected baselines. The reported Tolokers filter basis changes from RBF to B-spline; this does not establish that the retained experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds impulse-response locality analysis (Figure 2), eigengap diagnostics concerning deflation (Figure 7), learned-filter analysis (Figure 9), and peptide comparisons with and without positional encodings. It extends the existing Minesweeper Grad-CAM analysis to the other three heterophilous datasets (Figure 10). These investigate mechanisms and behavior beyond additional benchmark scores.

E5.justification: City-Networks results explicitly report means and standard deviations over four random seeds. The original ten-partition heterophily reporting, three-run synthetic timing summaries, and attribution confidence-interval practice are retained. There is no reported increase in replication for the original experiments.

E6.justification: v2 adds peptide and city scores, memory requirements, training times, and diagnostic findings. Examples include peptide AP 72.14 and MAE 0.2479, and London factorization time 144.22 minutes; the corresponding ED runtime is projected because ED runs out of memory. The retained Amazon-ratings result changes from 53.41±1.34 to 53.39±0.58; other original accuracy and decomposition-time entries remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The factorization algorithms and core hierarchical spectral layer remain unchanged. v2 adds an inductive adaptation sharing filter banks across subgraphs at the same level and evaluates positional-encoding variants. It also specifies B-spline filters for every dataset, whereas v1 explicitly used RBF filters for Tolokers.

P1.justification: v2 extensively revises the introduction and explanatory narrative, moves related work from Section 2.3 to Appendix B, and reorganizes experiments around separate transductive, inductive, locality, and memory discussions. It adds dedicated expressiveness and intuition appendices and broadly replaces 'interface' terminology with 'cut'.

P2.justification: v2 adds a positioning table, multiple benchmark and efficiency tables, and figures for impulse propagation, eigengaps, a barbell graph, learned filters, and additional attribution curves. The hyperparameter table gains hierarchy levels and loses bank-count and basis columns. Original runtime, parameter-performance, and Minesweeper attribution graphics are retained and renumbered; Figure 1 receives a visual refinement.

R1.justification: The expanded related work in Appendix B adds substantive positioning against hybrid spatial-spectral GNNs and classical and HSS divide-and-conquer eigensolvers, including Cuppen, Gu and Eisenstat, and Ou and Xia. It reframes positional encodings as complementary and removes v1's assertion that optimizing earlier GFT factorizations is NP-hard. These exceed citation metadata updates.

T1.justification: Theorem 5.1 and Appendix G add a strict-containment argument comparing L2G-Net with global spectral filters, including a two-node counterexample. Theorem 4.1 changes the cut-size bound from O(n log n/epsilon^2) to O(epsilon^-2) and the construction cost from O(n log n) to O(|E| log n). Appendix F also revises the merging-complexity derivation and discusses quadratic-cost matrix products.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important gaps in v1 by testing unsparsified inductive molecular tasks and much larger, sparsified city graphs, directly examining previously untested applicability and scalability. Added efficiency and locality analyses make practical benefits and costs substantially more assessable. The stronger Theorem 4.1 bound lacks a corresponding new supporting derivation, and some filter specifications are lost, but these weaknesses do not outweigh the substantial gains in direct validation, research positioning, and explicit applicability limits.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe L2G-Net by the same authors. The complete main texts, figures, tables, algorithms, equations, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial additions and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds molecular and City-Networks evaluations, timing and memory results, and spectral and attribution diagnostics.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic runtime experiments, L2G-Net results on four heterophilous datasets, and a Minesweeper attribution analysis.

results.title: L2G-NET: Local to Global Spectral Graph Neural Networks via Cauchy Factorizations

C1.justification: The central claims remain that sparse perturbation-conditioned context and signal–noise separation mitigate mean collapse and improve DEG-aware prediction. v2 names the expanded benchmarks and highlights a 28% improvement already reported in v1 Table 3; the core contribution and conclusion are unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning graph coverage versus density, robustness to DEG definitions, and recovery of cell-specific pathways. It also identifies cross-cell-line limitations: simple mean and linear predictors can outperform AdaPert, with discussion of conserved perturbation effects and cell-state variation. These materially expand the mechanism explanations and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: v2 adds inference details including a four-layer GATv2 with concatenated skip connections, clarifies semantic embedding construction, and documents new graph and threshold settings. Conversely, it removes v1 Appendix E's training/model-selection description and Table 8's TxPert hyperparameter search space, including optimization budgets and validation-based selection information.

E1.justification: Evaluation expands from K562 and RPE1 to include JURKAT and HEPG2. Appendix C also introduces a distinct transfer scenario: training on RPE1, HEPG2, and JURKAT while holding out K562 as an unseen cellular context.

E2.justification: The original six main baselines remain, but v2 Tables 9–12 add Context Mean, Linear-GenePT, Linear-OneHot, scGPT, and Geneformer to the reported comparisons. The new cross-cell-line comparison also includes Perturb Mean, substantially broadening the controls beyond v1's comparator set.

E3.justification: v2 adds cross-cell-line testing, MAE-based evaluation, and the Systema protocol with perturbation/control references, top-20-gene scores, and centroid accuracy. Appendix A/Table 5 changes reported effect-size grouping from fixed DEG-percentage bins to within-dataset DEG-count tertiles. Appendix D additionally specifies and sweeps FDR/LFC thresholds. These are substantive reported protocol changes, without establishing that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendices D–G add DEG-definition sensitivity, graph-source and density ablations, fixed versus adaptive neighborhood comparisons, attention-threshold sensitivity, and DEG/non-DEG error analysis. Pathway validation expands to 272 K562 perturbations and pathway-specific rankings. The original loss/context ablations and HIRA case study are retained.

E5.justification: v2 newly specifies BH-adjusted Wilcoxon testing for DEG identification and 300 permutations for GSEA, extending statistical-procedure documentation. Existing mean-plus-standard-deviation reporting remains unchanged; neither version provides explicit training seed counts, and v2 does not establish an increase in repeated runs.

E6.justification: Main Tables 1–3 remain unchanged, but v2 adds extensive benchmark, transfer, Systema, ablation, and pathway results. For example, new Table 13 reports transfer Pearson correlation of 0.4601 for AdaPert, versus 0.5149 for Linear-GenePT and 0.6501 for Perturb Mean. Some appendix values differ from retained main results without reconciliation, such as K562 TxPert Pearson correlation of 0.5879 versus 0.580. v1 Table 10's RPE1 DES@100 and significant-gene Spearman entries are omitted.

M1.justification: The perturbation-conditioned subgraph selection, context aggregation, and three-term training objective remain unchanged in Equations 5–21. v2 clarifies GPT-4o versus text-embedding roles and documents inference architecture; these disclosures do not establish a changed underlying method.

P1.justification: The appendices are substantially reorganized: baseline and metric descriptions are consolidated under Experiment Settings, related work moves from C to H, and pathway discussion is consolidated within expanded case studies. v2 adds an appendix contents list, rewrites the abstract and portions of the introduction/data exposition, and adds Impact Statement and Acknowledgments sections.

P2.justification: v2 adds an inference schematic, benchmark and Systema charts/tables, threshold heatmaps, graph comparisons, error boxplots, and pathway-ranking displays. Original distribution Figures 7–8 are combined into Figure 6, and the HIRA display is retained as Figure 28. Dataset tables are expanded and restructured, while the hyperparameter table is removed.

R1.justification: v2 adds application citations including Kim et al. (2024), Ishikawa et al. (2023), and Gonzalez et al. (2025), while removing Dunefsky et al. (2024) and Feng et al. (2024). The data-driven versus knowledge-driven taxonomy and positioning of AdaPert remain essentially unchanged.

T1.justification: The numbered mathematical formulation and metric equations, Equations 1–30, are retained. v2 adds empirical evaluation procedures but no new theorem, proof, substantive derivation, or formal assumption.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the empirical foundation through simple mean/linear controls, fixed-neighborhood comparisons, DEG-threshold robustness tests, and pathway validation across 272 perturbations instead of relying on the HIRA example alone. The transfer study also exposes an important applicability limitation. These additions address significant gaps in v1's evidence for the proposed mechanism and biological utility. Removal of tuning details and unreconciled main/appendix results weaken reproducibility, but the broader, more diagnostic evidence provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AdaPert research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable, allowing retained, relocated, and newly added material to be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds evaluations on JURKAT and HEPG2, cross-cell-line transfer, graph and DEG-threshold analyses, and broader pathway experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original K562 and RPE1 prediction experiments, component ablations, regularization sensitivity, and HIRA pathway analysis.

results.title: Learning Adaptive Perturbation-Conditioned Contexts for Robust Transcriptional Response Prediction

C1.justification: The central efficiency and predictive-performance contributions remain. The abstract, introduction, and conclusion now restrict comparable implicit Bayesianness to the tested one-at-a-time streaming protocol. The conclusion additionally highlights context ordering, without redefining the main contribution.

C2.justification: V2 substantially qualifies interpretation through the teacher-forced consistency scope, finite-sampling effects in ordering diagnostics, architecture differences affecting TNP-A runtime comparisons, and attention-dependent memory tradeoffs. Section 5.1 also explicitly discusses CNP outperforming vanilla incTNP and TNP-D in factorised temperature forecasting, including a possible underfitting explanation.

D1.justification: Appendix E.3.1 substantially expands reproducibility of the central KL diagnostic by specifying teacher-forced densities, canonical reordering of mixture parameters, and the estimator. Further disclosures cover filtering, random ordering, comparator parameter differences, and memory measurements using 16-bit floats and specified PyTorch backends. Core training details and code access remain available.

E1.justification: Both versions cover RBF and mixed-kernel GP regression, synthetic tabular data, the same four UCI datasets, and HadISD interpolation and forecasting. The 24-hour evaluation and kernel-distribution shifts already appear in v1. New diagnostics reuse this coverage with different ordering, aggregation, or computational settings.

E2.justification: V2 includes TNP-A in Table 1(b)'s static AR runtime comparison, reporting cost ratios of 1.04 for GP and 0.81 for temperature. Its predictive scores already appeared in v1 Table 2(b), and its streaming runtimes were already compared in Appendix E.2. Other baseline families are retained.

E3.justification: Added evaluation designs include gradient-noise measurements using 80,000 samples, context-permutation diagnostics, aggregation over K=1,2,10,100 orderings, and memory measurements comparing attention backends up to one million context points. Existing benchmark settings remain stable; the expanded teacher-forcing description documents the retained KL experiment rather than establishing a protocol change.

E4.justification: V2 adds unfiltered hyperparameter outcomes and measured gradient noise (Appendix E.1.3), AR target-order sensitivity (E.5), memory scaling (G), and extensive context-order, greedy-ordering, and aggregation analyses (H). These directly investigate robustness and computational tradeoffs. V1's distribution-shift analysis is retained as Appendix I.

E5.justification: Appendix B newly states that results generally use one training run and seed per model. Table 1 also specifies ties within one SEM. SEM reporting and Monte Carlo averaging already existed; the new disclosure does not establish additional independent training runs.

E6.justification: Tables 2 and 3 retain their numerical results, but substantial new findings concern gradient noise, ordering, aggregation, memory, and TNP-A timing. For example, Table 8 reports a +0.0053 log-likelihood gain for incTNP-Seq on GP(64) when increasing aggregation from one to 100 orderings. Figure 21 shows higher incTNP memory use with FlashAttention despite linear scaling.

M1.justification: The core incTNP and incTNP-Seq procedures remain intact, but Appendix H adds substantive methodological extensions: greedy variance-based context ordering (Algorithm 2), incTNP-Prior with a learned token supporting empty contexts, and prediction aggregation across context permutations. These change training or inference procedures.

P1.justification: V2 selectively clarifies background, experimental interpretation, and conclusions; subdivides appendix discussions; updates affiliations and publication information; and adds an Impact Statement. Most existing prose and the overall introduction-background-method-experiments-conclusion structure remain, so the scientific additions do not constitute wholesale narrative rewriting.

P2.justification: V2 adds substantial visual material for unfiltered outcomes, gradient noise, ordering sensitivity, memory, and aggregation, including Figures 12–13, 19, 21–26 and Tables 6–8. Table 1 gains TNP-A columns and explicit SEM-based highlighting. Existing streaming and distribution-shift figures are retained with relocation and renumbering.

R1.justification: V2 adds Burt et al. (2020) to motivate variance-based ordering and Feng et al. (2024) for constant-memory alternatives, while removing Katharopoulos et al. (2020). The main positioning against existing NP and streaming methods remains. Consolidating duplicate Hollmann references does not remove a distinct cited work.

T1.justification: V2 adds Proposition 4.2 for conditional regression with i.i.d. inputs and Proposition C.1 extending the decomposition to non-i.i.d. inputs, with proofs. Appendix G derives transient, persistent, and total memory costs, while Appendix H defines a context-permutation KL diagnostic. These substantially extend v1's exchangeability and runtime analysis.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses important gaps in v1's assessment of sacrificed context-order invariance and KV-cache memory costs through direct diagnostics and measurements. Conditional-regression proofs, a reproducible KL-estimator description, and narrower consistency claims substantially strengthen justification and transparency. The new analysis exposes higher memory use with FlashAttention, and single-seed evidence still limits robustness conclusions, but these limitations are now clearer without weakening the retained benchmark evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Incremental Transformer Neural Processes. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: V2 retains these empirical results and adds original gradient-noise, memory, ordering-sensitivity, and prediction-aggregation analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original GP regression, synthetic and real-world tabular, and HadISD temperature experiments, including predictive accuracy, runtime, consistency, and distribution-shift results.

results.title: Incremental Transformer Neural Processes

C1.justification: The central contributions remain a three-regime, solver-verifiable induction benchmark and the finding that compact solutions generalize better. The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion expand the claimed evaluation scope to include symbolic synthesis alongside prompted models, without redefining the research question.

C2.justification: v3 develops universal-to-existential collapse as an explanation of structural failures, distinguishes GPT-5.4's FullObs/CI compactness gains from increased EC bloat, and interprets unified versus specialized symbolic search. It also corrects the equality-use discussion and adds specific limitations concerning bounded symbolic search, absent compactness-prompt ablations, and the limited renaming pilot.

D1.justification: v1's Software and Data statement postpones artifact release; v3 provides repository access information and states that datasets, code, cached outputs, and analysis artifacts are available. Appendix A documents symbolic encodings and search bounds, while Appendix C.1 adds target-pool construction steps, eligibility counts, and selection/reuse rules for the existing benchmark.

E1.justification: The original FullObs/CI/EC tasks, bands, and dataset sizes remain. Appendix B.6 adds a limited input-perturbation scenario: consistently renamed predicates and objects on 30 paired instances, ten per task.

E2.justification: v3 adds GPT-5.4, Gemini 3.5 Flash, DeepSeek4Pro, and Grok4.3 to the model comparison. Table 2 and Appendix A additionally introduce z3-prenex + rescue across the tasks, the FullObs-specific z3-ad-mix portfolio, and ilasp-frag for FullObs and CI, substantially broadening comparison beyond prompted models.

E3.justification: New evaluations introduce a 30-minute-per-instance symbolic search protocol and a paired 30-instance renaming design. GPT-5.2's reported reasoning setting changes from 64k to med (v1 Table 23; v3 Table 29), without establishing reruns. EC best-completion diagnostic totals also change from 199–200 to 135–137 predictions (Tables 19 and 25), without explaining the smaller sample.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained family, lift-hard, equality, and bloat analyses, v3 adds systematic tests of existential versus mixed quantification, premise-only occurrences of x, helper-like relational structure, and universal-to-existential collapse (Appendix B.5). It also adds the renaming pilot, model/problem fixed-effects controls, and new paired and failure case studies in Appendix D.

E5.justification: v3 adds fixed-effects regression coefficients, standard errors, and p-values controlling for model and problem (Tables 4 and 26). Confidence intervals and paired-comparison p-values already existed, but v1 Table 20's explicit specification of 95% percentile-bootstrap intervals, 2,000 resamples, and one-sided binomial tests is omitted.

E6.justification: Substantial new results include 65.9% FullObs accuracy for z3-ad-mix, 100% EC success for the unified Z3 baseline, and 93.5% EC validity for GPT-5.4. Existing results also change: Opus 4.6 FullObs accuracy changes from 22.1% to 23.7%, and Grok4 coverage from 67.2% to 89.3%. Held-out estimates, error profiles, and example outputs are revised; EC diagnostic values involve changed samples.

M1.justification: The core task semantics, listed formula templates, distractor/trap generation, existential completion, and AST-based scoring are retained. Expanded target-pool documentation does not establish a changed generator. The newly introduced symbolic solvers serve as comparison methods.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, setup, results, limitations, conclusion, and appendix explanations are extensively rewritten. Evaluation and experiments are merged into Section 5, the appendices are reorganized, and terminology shifts toward input worlds and instance-correct solutions. Unresolved figure references in v1 are repaired.

P2.justification: v3 adds FullObs and CI generalization plots previously absent despite textual references, plus symbolic, structural-analysis, renaming, and target-pool tables. Existing charts gain model series and revised legends, tables are expanded and relocated, and qualitative-example tables are redesigned with separate prediction and gold-formula columns.

R1.justification: v3 adds ABD and PROOFGRID citations and explains their respective relationships to concept synthesis through default–exception abduction and formal deductive reasoning. The established ILP, synthesis, and reasoning-benchmark literature is largely retained, with positioning adjusted to include symbolic comparisons.

T1.justification: The finite-structure definitions and FullObs, CI, and EC correctness conditions in Equations 1–5 retain their mathematical meaning. New semantic examples and target-pool explanations elaborate the existing formalism; no new theorem, proof, or substantive mathematical derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: Table 2 and Appendix A resolve v1's important lack of symbolic calibration, making benchmark difficulty substantially easier to assess. Structural analyses, robustness evidence, and detailed generation/access documentation strengthen interpretation and reproducibility information. These gains outweigh the unexplained smaller EC diagnostic sample, omitted bootstrap details, and the disagreement between FullObs prose and Table 4.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same INDUCTION benchmark. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial rewriting and reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains and updates those evaluations and reports original symbolic-baseline results, structural analyses, and a paired symbol-renaming experiment.

before.justification: v1 reports original model evaluations on 375 FullObs, 200 CI, and 200 EC problems, including held-out generalization and appendix error analyses.

results.title: INDUCTION: Finite-Structure Concept Synthesis in First-Order Logic

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: context-conditioned evolutionary modeling, a first-order approximation guarantee, SHM-corrected VEP, and guided antibody optimization. The additional experiments support these claims without redefining their scientific scope.

C2.justification: v4 replaces speculation that ESM2 helps mouse-antibody generalization with an interpretation emphasizing the evolutionary training objective. It adds explanations for failure at extreme branch lengths and expands the discussion of limited paired-chain training data. The principal limitations concerning approximation error and absent indels remain unchanged.

D1.justification: A new Reproducibility Statement supplies a COSINE code-and-data repository location. v4 also documents PRISM scoring modes, classical-model fitting details, and why the retained FLAb snapshot differs from another study's version. The original COSINE training hyperparameters, hardware, and preprocessing instructions remain intact; repository availability was not externally verified.

E1.justification: v4 adds training and evaluation on approximately 15,000 TrRosetta general-protein family alignments, extending coverage beyond antibodies and synthetic codons (C.6). It also adds two Petersen MAGMA-seq binding assays with distinct antibodies, antigens, and assay technology (C.8). Existing coverage is retained.

E2.justification: v4 adds PRISM to the existing Spearman and Pearson VEP comparisons. It introduces a WAG-style model fitted on the antibody training transitions and fitted WAG and LG+G4 comparators for TrRosetta (Tables S2–S3). The CDR optimization comparator set was already present in v1 and remains unchanged.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include six VEP branch lengths from 0.01 to 10, an 8M randomly initialized model versus the ESM2-initialized model, and runtime sweeps over sequence length and sampling steps (C.9–C.12). The classical-model comparisons introduce matched-data fitting controls. Existing main VEP settings, data snapshots, and CDR optimization budgets remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v4 substantially expands analysis of context dependence, branch-length sensitivity, dependence on pretrained initialization, and computational scaling (C.5, C.9, C.10, C.12). These address distinct questions about the source and robustness of performance. The SHM correction, paired-chain, SNR-weighting, and exact-versus-Taylor guidance analyses already existed in v1.

E5.justification: Both versions retain three replicates per synthetic epistasis level, five tree simulations per guidance setting, and the 15-sample exact-versus-Taylor comparison with identical two-sided t-tests. v4 introduces no new repeated-run, confidence-interval, or uncertainty-estimation practice; its branch-length sensitivity range is not statistical uncertainty.

E6.justification: v4 adds substantial results for new comparators, datasets, ablations, and runtime tests. Examples include TrRosetta test NLL of 1.027 versus 1.200 for WAG and 1.168 for LG+G4, and Petersen correlations of 0.504 and 0.328. Existing Table 1 scores are retained. Figure S4 updates Gillespie/matrix-exponential win fractions from 48.8%/40.2% to 52.0%/38.8% and plotted correlations from 0.62/0.53 to 0.64/0.56, although its caption retains the old correlations.

M1.justification: The COSINE rate parameterization, training objective, SHM-corrected selection score, and Guided Gillespie procedure remain unchanged, including Equations (2), (5), and (9) and Algorithms S1–S3. The new 8M model is an experimental ablation, not a replacement of the main model.

P1.justification: v4 locally rewrites related work, the CDR optimization discussion, and the impact statement, adds a reproducibility section, and expands the appendix organization. Most original prose and the overall background–method–experiments–conclusion structure are retained; the added scientific material does not amount to a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: v4 adds six result tables and a branch-length sensitivity plot, expands existing VEP tables with PRISM, and redraws Figure S4 with revised axes and labels. It promotes v1 Table S4 to main-text Table 2 with a fuller caption and enlarges and rearranges the additional-antibody plots from Figure S8 into Figure S9. These are substantial display changes beyond renumbering.

R1.justification: Section 3 substantially expands positioning against germline-aware antibody models, including Im et al. and PRISM, and adds evolutionary translation work by Koehl et al. New Appendix A.4 distinguishes COSINE's biological transition modeling from discrete flow matching, citing Gat and Campbell. Shanker et al. is removed. Publication updates to existing references are not new research coverage.

T1.justification: The first-order approximation bound, Gillespie exactness lemma, mutation-selection derivation, and Appendix D proofs are unchanged. The added discussion of discrete flow matching and standard classical-model parameterization does not introduce a new theoretical result or revise the existing reasoning.

improvement.justification: The new context-independent controls, branch-length sensitivity study, and backbone ablation address important gaps in v1's evidence for the source and robustness of COSINE's performance (C.5, C.9–C.10). Additional antibody assays and general-protein evaluations substantially strengthen validation, while the code/data statement improves reproducibility information. The backbone comparison changes model size as well as initialization, and Figure S4 contains stale caption values, but these limitations do not outweigh the gains in empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same COSINE study. Their text, equations, figures, tables, algorithms, and Appendices A–D support a reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v4 retains these original experiments and adds general-protein evaluations, antibody binding assays, and further controls and sensitivity analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic-codon simulations, antibody transition modeling, variant-effect prediction, and guided antibody optimization experiments.

results.title: Conditionally Site-Independent Neural Evolution of Antibody Sequences

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list and conclusion retain the central claims: extending inverse distillation to discrete diffusion, establishing uniqueness, enabling stable gradients and achieving 4×–64× fewer sampling steps while preserving quality. The 128×/256× composed DCD comparisons already appear in v1 Figure 5.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations based on teacher-versus-fake advantages, sequence mixtures and uniform-process holding times, and interprets the new gradient ablations. Appendix D.2 newly acknowledges that the proof does not cover the experimental factorized sequence loss, a more specific limitation than v1's evaluation and scalability caveats.

D1.justification: v1's promise to publish code becomes a project-page announcement of code, checkpoints and tutorials. v2 Appendix E.2 documents conditional-data formatting, tokenizer, loss masking, optimizer settings, precision, four-GPU training, a 250,000-step budget and execution-based scoring. Explicit sampling pseudocode is also added.

E1.justification: v2 adds TinyGSM training and GSM8K evaluation for conditional generation of executable mathematical solutions (Section 5.2 and Appendix E.2). This substantially extends v1's unconditional OpenWebText evaluation. The original OpenWebText and SEDD coverage remains.

E2.justification: Beyond the retained teachers, SDTT and Duo-DCD, v2's OpenWebText comparisons include SDTT + Di4C2, DiDi-Instruct, D-MMD, ELF and FLM/FMLM (Figure 3 and Table 2). The new conditional comparison also includes autoregressive models and S-FLM. These are reported comparators, not merely additional citations.

E3.justification: v2 adds MAUVE and Gradient Moment evaluation, an 863M model setting, and a conditional protocol using 512-token sequences, clamped prompts, execution-based exact-match accuracy and 32/64/128 reverse steps. These extend the evaluation design; the previously documented small-model OpenWebText settings are largely retained.

E4.justification: Appendix F.4 adds controlled comparisons of SUBS versus Gumbel/Argmax updates, full versus stop-gradient Duo updates, and Gaussian input noise for MDLM. Figures 14–15 and Table 4 investigate gradient stability and latent randomness, questions not experimentally isolated in v1.

E5.justification: v1 reports point estimates, whereas v2 introduces ± uncertainty terms for central IDLM GenPPL/entropy results and MAUVE comparisons in Figure 3 and Tables 2–3. Their meaning and repeated-run counts are unspecified, so additional runs or a particular uncertainty estimator cannot be inferred.

E6.justification: v2 adds conditional accuracies, 863M results, MAUVE/GM scores and ablation findings. Existing entries also change: 16-step SDTT GenPPL/entropy changes from 89.17/5.53 in v1 Table 1 to 61.34/5.36 in v2 Figure 3, without explaining the replacement. Appendix G also replaces full generations with shortened, partly reworded excerpts.

M1.justification: The inverse objective, alternating training, simplex relaxation, SUBS treatment and Gaussian reparameterization are retained. However, the printed MDLM objective gains a minus sign between v1 Equation (5) and v2 Equation (1), correcting its minimization formulation. The PDFs do not establish an implementation change.

P1.justification: The preliminaries and method explanation are extensively rewritten around masked and uniform diffusion. General SEDD material moves to Appendix A, related work moves into the main text, and a loss-intuition section and contents pages are added. The appendices are substantially reorganized and the qualitative material condensed.

P2.justification: v2 restructures the original quantitative table into comparison panels and separate tables with additional metric columns. It adds process and relaxation diagrams, a GenPPL–entropy plot and ablation plots, relocates existing SEDD and sampling-step figures, and replaces full-page sample listings with compact colored panels.

R1.justification: The broad acceleration survey in v1 Appendix A is replaced by a focused comparison in v2 Section 4, incorporating RSD, Di4C2, D-MMD, DiDi-Instruct and recent language flows. IDLM is now explicitly positioned through path-measure matching versus marginal matching and contrasted with consistency methods' factorization limitations.

T1.justification: v2 Appendix D corrects v1 Appendix C's interchange of optimization and expectation, keeping the optimization outside the population expectation. It adds explicit model-class/support assumptions and a gap-preservation lemma. It also restricts the sequence-level guarantee to the ideal full-sequence objective, explicitly excluding the practical factorized loss.

improvement.justification: Conditional accuracy, larger-model results and controlled ablations address important gaps in v1's evidence (Tables 1 and 3; Appendix F.4). The corrected proof and explicit restriction of its applicability also improve theoretical precision. Undefined uncertainty terms and partly rewritten qualitative excerpts reduce auditability, but the gains in empirical validation and mathematical clarity are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same IDLM research. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable, and relocated material, including the SEDD experiments, can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains original distillation results and adds conditional-generation accuracy, larger-model experiments and ablations in Tables 1 and 3 and Appendix F.4.

before.justification: v1 reports original IDLM distillation experiments on OpenWebText, including GenPPL, entropy and generated samples for SEDD, MDLM and Duo variants.

results.title: IDLM: Inverse-distilled Diffusion Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions and conclusion retain the same method, latent-alignment and efficiency claims, including approximately 6× decoding speedup, up to 96.9% reconstruction-performance retention and up to 36% pipeline acceleration. Added experiments support these existing claims.

C2.justification: New appendix discussions explain spatial generalization through convolutional structure, interpret component-specific resource savings, and discuss applicability to additional convolutional and transformer architectures. Appendix B.9 newly identifies failures involving tiny moving objects and dense faces, linking blur, flicker and detail loss to limited decoder capacity.

D1.justification: v2 documents implementation choices for added evaluations, including pretrained RAFT flow estimation from ground-truth frames and L1-based channel scoring from weights. Existing hardware, optimizer settings, loss coefficients, gradient masking, full prompts and code-access information are retained.

E1.justification: Appendix B.1 adds reconstruction evaluation on the DAVIS 2019 Challenge test set at 720p, extending coverage to complex motion, occlusions and fine details. Training data, UCF-101 and VBench coverage are retained. Higher-resolution latency testing already existed in v1.

E2.justification: Section 4.3 and Figure 11 add L1-norm channel pruning alongside the existing random-pruning comparator. New Table 7 also compares channel-pruning-only and operator-optimization-only variants. The principal LightVAE and Turbo-VAED comparator sets remain unchanged.

E3.justification: v2 adds RAFT-based warping error, parameter-count and peak-VRAM measurements, and protocols for DAVIS evaluation and Causal Forcing deployment with seven selected VBench dimensions. Additional backbone diagnostics are also reported. The existing training settings and original benchmark protocols remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The revision substantially expands diagnostic evidence: stronger pruning comparisons, component-specific resource ablations, DAVIS robustness testing, transfer to Causal Forcing, and SVD/operator-optimization analyses on HunyuanVideo and CogVideoX. The original resolution/frame-count study and training ablations are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests or uncertainty estimates for the experiments. The added SVD explained-variance results concern feature redundancy, not statistical uncertainty.

E6.justification: Original table values are retained, while substantial new results appear. Table 2 reports Wan warping errors of 0.018662 for Flash-VAED and 0.026640 for LightVAE. DAVIS Table 6 reports corresponding PSNR values of 32.03 and 27.92. Table 7 adds memory and parameter results; Table 8 adds Causal Forcing scores, including multi-view consistency of 0.318 versus the original decoder's 0.424. New pruning curves, qualitative examples and additional-backbone findings further expand the evidence.

M1.justification: Independence-aware pruning, stage-specific operator replacement, shortcut injection and three-phase distillation remain unchanged, including the losses and backbone-specific pruning configurations. Appendix B applies existing optimizations to additional backbones and discusses potential extensions without introducing a changed method.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are preserved. Changes include local wording and typo corrections, affiliation and acknowledgment updates, and expanded appendix organization. The original Appendix B.1–B.3 material is retained as B.6–B.8.

P2.justification: The document switches from a lab-branded format to an ICML layout, redesigning the opening page and rearranging or resizing existing displays. v2 adds four tables and two qualitative comparison figures, and redraws Figure 11 with an additional curve and revised axis ticks.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting DAVIS, temporal consistency, Causal Forcing and architectural/future-work discussion, while removing the Jetson technical brief and stereo-compression reference. The main related-work positioning remains stable. Publication updates and the retitled VLMQ reference concern retained works.

T1.justification: The method equations and Appendix A.1 computational-cost derivation are unchanged apart from numbering and formatting. New Equations 7–8 explain the adopted optical-flow warping metric; they do not introduce new theoretical reasoning, assumptions or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important validation gaps: temporal measurements directly examine coherence after operator replacement, DAVIS tests challenging reconstruction conditions, and L1 pruning provides a stronger comparator than random pruning alone. Resource ablations and specific failure conditions also make the efficiency-quality tradeoff more assessable. Causal Forcing coverage remains selective and reveals a multi-view consistency gap, but the revision substantially strengthens the evidence and qualification of the central claims.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Flash-VAED work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds temporal-consistency measurements, DAVIS reconstruction results, resource analyses and additional generalization experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original reconstruction and generation experiments, pruning and distillation ablations, and supplementary latency and scalability measurements.

results.title: Flash-VAED: Plug-and-Play VAE Decoders for Efficient Video Generation

C1.justification: The first history-aware HSM and MFAX contributions remain. However, v2 removes headline claims of state-of-the-art performance and first solving the partially observable macroeconomic game, emphasizing preservation of HSM convergence speed while learning history-dependent behavior.

C2.justification: v2 substantially qualifies applicability: public-history sufficiency is presented as an additional assumption and an approximation in applications, with private-history omission potentially suboptimal. It also explicitly acknowledges missing convergence guarantees and explains why lower gradient variance need not produce lower across-seed performance variance. These materially sharpen the interpretation and limitations of the unchanged experiments.

D1.justification: v2 explains that one shared GRU embedding is computed per timestep and broadcast across states, defines the recurrent reset mask, and explicitly supplies the Macroeconomics AR(1) noise equation whose parameters were already listed. It also replaces the direct repository pointer with a project-page and usage-example pointer. Architecture sizes and hyperparameter tables remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same partially observable Linear Quadratic, Beach Bar, and Macroeconomics environments. The new two-state counterexample in v2 Appendix A is a theoretical construction, not an additional experimental scenario.

E2.justification: The evaluated comparators remain SPG, IPPO, RIPPO, and M-OMD, with OpenSpiel and MFGLib retained in the library comparisons. v2 explains why AFP is excluded but does not evaluate it. Comparator membership in the retained figures and ablations is unchanged.

E3.justification: Appendix C.4 corrects Linear Quadratic's reported state count from 99 to 100 and its clipping boundary, removes a conflicting Beach Bar noise description, and adds principal wealth to consumption inside the Macroeconomics reward formula. These revise stated benchmark settings without establishing reruns. Evaluation metrics, hardware, budgets, and hyperparameter sweeps remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The SPG/RSPG memory comparison, ordinal-versus-categorical policy ablation in Figure 11, and supplementary policy and population visualizations are retained. The added counterexample supplies theoretical evidence rather than a new empirical ablation or robustness test.

E5.justification: Figure 2 retains the same uncertainty bands and reports 95% confidence intervals over 10 seeds in both versions. v2 shortens the caption but does not document additional runs, changed uncertainty estimation, or new statistical tests.

E6.justification: Table 1 adds explicit qualitative capability entries: all three libraries support analytic mean-field updates, while only MFAX is marked as supporting sample-based updates. Benchmark outcomes are unchanged: Table 2 retains its timing values, and Figures 2–11 retain identical graphics, rankings, and behavioral findings.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 gains an optional terminal-payoff initialization for the backward return, whereas v1 specifies zero initialization only. This is a limited correction to the stated procedure, consistent with the already-described terminal-reward environment. The recurrent policy, action parameterization, and blocking of gradients through mean-field transitions remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The main text is extensively rewritten and reorganized. Related Work moves before Preliminaries, the shared-observation argument is restructured around explicit assumptions, experimental subsections are consolidated, and Future Work becomes a separate section.
