Acknowledgements and revised author and affiliation text are also added.

P2.justification: The main text and references change from single-column to two-column layout, with substantial relocation of figures and tables. Figure 1 moves near the introduction, Figures 2 and 3 share a page, equation boxes are added, and Table 1 gains two capability columns. All eleven underlying figure graphics remain unchanged.

R1.justification: The related-work discussion substantially broadens its positioning to numerical solvers, common-noise theory, deep learning, and cooperative mean-field control, adding works such as Achdou and Capuzzo-Dolcetta and Carmona and colleagues. It explicitly acknowledges that model-free RL can incorporate recurrence, sharpening RSPG's distinction around exploiting known structure. These changes exceed the accompanying publication-year and bibliography corrections.

T1.justification: v1 Section 5.1 justifies restricting private history using shared observations alone. v2 introduces Assumption 6.1, requiring the public history and current individual state to contain the relevant aggregate-state information. New Appendix A proves that this condition is not automatic: full-history policies can obtain reward 1 while restricted policies obtain only 1/2. This materially corrects the theoretical scope of the policy reduction.

improvement.justification: The decisive improvement is correction of an important logical overreach: v1 treats shared observations as sufficient to discard private histories, whereas v2 states an additional informational assumption and demonstrates strict suboptimality without it in Appendix A. This substantially improves scientific validity and claim calibration. Clearer implementation details also help reproducibility, although the retained experiments do not validate the new assumption or establish reruns following the environment-formula corrections.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RSPG method and MFAX framework. All 26 pages of each version, including equations, figures, tables, and appendices, are available and readable; relocated content can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains these original benchmark results, timing measurements, and appendix ablations. Their retention from v1 does not change their empirical status.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on Linear Quadratic, Beach Bar, and Macroeconomics, library timing measurements in Table 2, and policy-representation ablations in Appendix C.4.

results.title: Recurrent Structural Policy Gradient for Partially Observable Mean Field Games

C1.justification: The central claims of unified generation through independent modality times and symmetry-aware ordering remain. V2 adds atom substitution through fixed known sites as an explicit introduction contribution. This extends the claimed capability without redefining the paper's central contribution.

C2.justification: V1's larger-unit-cell limitation is replaced by explicit exclusions of amorphous/disordered systems and a stability–novelty trade-off. V2 also adds explanations involving cation–anion ordering, transformer computational efficiency, and scaling. It interprets the new training controls as evidence against destructive task interference and for the importance of decoupled time axes.

D1.justification: V2 newly specifies fixed sinusoidal positional embeddings, lattice-length normalization by N^(1/3), and dataset-specific LogNormal parameters (Section 3.1; Table F.2). Table H.1 adds measured training and inference times with hardware and batch sizes. These improve documentation; the PDFs do not establish changes to the original implementation from these disclosures.

E1.justification: MP-20, MPTS-52, and the original three tasks remain. V2 introduces LeMat-Bulk as an evaluation reference and tests partially conditioned atom substitution on four MP-20 test crystals, fixing known species while generating masked species. These extend coverage within the existing inorganic-crystal domain.

E2.justification: The main DNG comparison adds MatterGen, PLaID++, standalone WyFormer variants, Crystal-GFN, CrystalFormer, DiffCSP, and LLaMat2/3-CIF; CDVAE, FlowMM, FlowLLM, OMatG, SGEquiDiff, and SGFM leave that table. FlowMM is also added to the ATG comparison in Table 3, and Table H.8 evaluates DNG-trained DiffCSP and FlowMM adapted to CSP.

E3.justification: The main DNG evaluation changes from 10,000 samples with CHGNet-based evaluation for MCFlow to 2,500 samples evaluated using three MLIPs and LeMat-Bulk hulls, with separate pre-relaxation conditions. Validity and matching rules change, percentages use all submitted structures, and metastability excludes stable structures. New protocols include METRe/cRMSE on original and polymorph-aware splits, filtered/unfiltered CSP, and 100 substitution samples per parent crystal.

E4.justification: V2 adds substantial tests of the central design choices: electronegativity versus atomic-number ordering and unrestricted permutation (H.4), CSP-only versus unified training (H.7), and coupled versus decoupled time axes (H.8). It also adds computational-cost analysis, evaluation-method sensitivity checks, and substitution case studies. The earlier guidance, permutation-space, scaling, and cumulative component analyses remain.

E5.justification: Table 2 newly reports means with standard deviations for formation energy, hull energy, and relaxation RMSD. Its caption specifies variation across 2,500 generated structures, averaged over three MLIPs. This adds distributional dispersion reporting, but does not establish repeated training runs or uncertainty across training seeds.

E6.justification: The main DNG results are replaced under different evaluation conditions, and multiple new result tables are added. Table 1 revises baseline scores: OMatG's MP-20 match rate changes from 61.88 to 63.75, with v2 specifying LinearODE, and CrystalFlow's single-sample MPTS-52 match rate changes from 22.71 to 21.00. Original MCFlow CSP and ATG entries largely remain unchanged; the new DNG numbers are not same-setting performance improvements.

M1.justification: V2 adds a limited inference adaptation for atom substitution: each atom-generation step overwrites known sites with their given types while sampling masked sites (Section 4.3). The core architecture, flow objectives, ordering, augmentation, and Algorithms 1–3 remain unchanged. Newly specified positional embeddings and prior parameters are implementation disclosures.

P1.justification: V2 tightens the abstract, consolidates contribution bullets, clarifies method explanations, revises experimental discussion, and reorganizes Appendix H around tables. It adds a conflict-of-interest disclosure and updates publication information. The overall section sequence and most methodological and background prose remain recognizable.

P2.justification: Table 2 is extensively redesigned with new metric columns and pre-relaxation groups. V2 adds the substitution table and six Appendix H tables, relocates existing displays, and consolidates Algorithms 2–3 onto one page. Existing template-CSP and MPTS-52 tables survive as H.3/H.6. Captions are revised, and the retained scaling plot loses its correlation-coefficient annotations.

R1.justification: Related work substantially expands to language-model and text-guided generation, hybrid pipelines, periodic Bayesian flows, Crystal-GFN, and Zatom-1, while removing several older generative-model citations. V2 also adds the LeMat and METRe evaluation foundations and claims structure-conditioned ATG was previously unstudied as a standalone generative task. These changes exceed bibliographic metadata updates.

T1.justification: The substantive flow equations, symmetry definitions, and mathematical development in Section 3 and Appendices A–B are retained. V2 clarifies notation and endpoint behavior. Its new cRMSE equation documents an adopted evaluation metric rather than introducing new theoretical reasoning or a proof.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens evidence for the central method. Table 2 and Appendix G replace heterogeneous DNG comparisons with a documented common protocol and model-consistent hulls. Tables H.4, H.7, and H.8 directly test ordering, unified training, and time decoupling, addressing important gaps in v1's support. Polymorph/filtering checks and explicit stability–novelty limitations further improve credibility. The changed DNG protocol prevents direct score comparisons, and sample dispersion does not quantify training variability, but these limits do not outweigh the stronger evaluation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MCFlow research. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–I are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: V2 retains original MCFlow results and adds LeMat-GenBench evaluations, atom-substitution experiments, computational measurements, and further controlled comparisons.

before.justification: V1 reports original MCFlow experiments on crystal structure prediction, de novo generation, and atom type generation, together with ablations and supplementary analyses.

results.title: Multimodal Crystal Flow: Any-to-Any Modality Generation for Unified Crystal Modeling

C1.justification: The introduction narrows previously unqualified posterior-uncertainty language to uncertainty in selected regions. The abstract and central contributions concerning nonlinear functional prediction, structured region selection, and theoretical guarantees otherwise retain their original scope.

C2.justification: v3 explicitly describes MAP PIPs as approximate selection scores and Laplace evidence as a practical surrogate. It qualifies exact support recovery under correlated predictors, discusses spline-resolution and richer-embedding limitations, and expands interpretation of ECG silver annotations. The new analyses also explain tuning tradeoffs and robustness boundaries.

D1.justification: v3 replaces the supplementary-material code statement with an explicit GitHub repository address and adds hardware specifications and runtime breakdowns. New analyses provide parameter grids and data-generation details. Most original architecture, optimizer, preprocessing, and dataset-access information is retained; repository availability was not independently checked.

E1.justification: The four real datasets and original simulation families remain. Appendices C.2–C.3 add SNR 2 and 3, an FGAM mean outside the assumed single-index structure, and Student-t errors with three degrees of freedom, substantially extending noise and misspecification coverage.

E2.justification: The five fitted baselines remain FNN, AdaFNN, cFuSIM, BFRS, and SLoS, including in the new stress comparisons. Appendix A.3/Table 3 adds an oracle F1-based choice of spline resolution as a reference for evaluating evidence-based selection. FGAM is a data-generating scenario, not an added baseline.

E3.justification: New protocols sweep spline resolution from 20 to 240, vary prior parameters and PIP thresholds, and measure runtime across sample sizes and observation-grid sizes. They introduce roughness, interval-length, and stability diagnostics. These supplement the retained main settings and data splits rather than establish that the original experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v3 adds evidence-selection diagnostics, spline-resolution and prior/threshold sensitivity, initialization stability, runtime scaling, and ECG resolution analysis (A.3–A.7 and D). Low-SNR, FGAM, and heavy-tailed-error tests additionally examine robustness beyond v1's main simulations.

E5.justification: v1 already reports 100 simulation replicates, distribution plots, and five fitting restarts. v3 retains these and adds mean/SD summaries for new 50-replicate studies, five-repeat runtime summaries, and a stability design with ten seeds within each of 50 datasets. This extends variability reporting without adding calibration or significance tests.

E6.justification: Existing result figures and Tables 1–2 are unchanged, but Tables 3–13 and Figure 6 add substantial findings. For example, Table 11 reports F1 0.944 under Student-t errors at SNR 10, while Table 9 shows some lower baseline RMSEs despite sBayFDNN's stronger F1. These are new-condition results, not demonstrated gains over v1.

M1.justification: Appendix A.2 and Algorithm 1 change final region selection from the restart with the lowest validation loss to thresholding PIPs averaged across restarts. Prediction averaging was already described in v1. The spline representation, network, priors, and MAP objective remain unchanged.

P1.justification: v3 adds Section 4.4 and acknowledgments, expands the conclusion, rewrites the evidence-score explanation, and organizes additional appendix analyses into subsections. Most existing prose and the overall narrative order remain, so this is a localized editorial expansion rather than extensive restructuring.

P2.justification: Tables 3–13 and the new seed-stability Figure 6 substantially expand the presentation of diagnostic, robustness, and runtime evidence. Algorithm 1 is reformatted and moved from the final page into Appendix A.2. Existing figures are retained, with appendix plots relocated and renumbered.

R1.justification: Related work adds localized functional PCA, functional generalized additive models, and nonlinear sparse models. Section 4.4 adds sparse Bayesian literature supporting MAP plug-in PIPs. These broaden context while retaining the original novelty positioning; publication metadata updates alone are not substantive additions.

T1.justification: Section 5's assumptions and theorems and Appendix B's proofs are unchanged substantively. Appendix A.4 adds limited mathematical definitions for newly evaluated diagnostics, including mean absolute successive PIP differences and minimum selected interval length divided by mesh size. No new theoretical guarantee is established.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially addresses v1's limited scrutiny of the tuning and optimization choices underlying region recovery, adding sensitivity, seed-stability, misspecification, and computational evidence. Its explicit qualifications of approximate inference and support identifiability also improve interpretation. These gains strengthen the paper despite unchanged core theory and main results; seed stability still does not establish posterior calibration, and the benefit of revised PIP aggregation is not demonstrated by the retained benchmarks.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same sBayFDNN research work. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v3 retains those original results and adds sensitivity, seed-stability, runtime, low-SNR, and model-misspecification experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original replicated simulations and evaluations on ECG, Tecator, Bike rental, and IHPC, including prediction and region-recovery results.

results.title: Sparse Bayesian Deep Functional Learning with Structured Region Selection

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: headwise chunking with GQA scheduling reduces attention memory while preserving throughput, with up to 87.5% intermediate-memory savings and Llama 3-8B contexts of 5M tokens on eight H100s and 8M on sixteen.

C2.justification: Section 6 newly explains when reduced CPU transfers or recomputation can convert memory savings into speed. Appendix D discusses floating-point differences from head reordering, while Appendix E explicitly discusses broader Transformer applicability and possible communication overlap. The original interpretation of long-context memory benefits remains.

D1.justification: Appendix A substantially expands implementation-level documentation of buffer allocation, aliasing, release, and backward accumulation. Additional disclosures cover the custom PyTorch operator supporting selective checkpointing, new experiment parameters, FSDP2, the CPU model, and FPDT's SwiGLU patch. The code link changes from the Together account to the author's account; these disclosures do not establish reruns of retained benchmarks.

E1.justification: Appendix D adds C4 training to evaluate loss convergence, extending v1's systems-performance evaluation to training behavior on a named dataset. The original model families and long-context coverage remain.

E2.justification: The original comparisons retain native PyTorch Ring Attention, USP Ring/Ulysses, and FPDT. New Table 5 additionally evaluates Ulysses with selective activation checkpointing against UPipe variants. Newly documenting FPDT's SwiGLU patch does not establish that the retained baseline experiments changed.

E3.justification: The added experiments introduce substantial evaluation protocols: fixed 3M-token batches with offloading stride K=7, selective checkpointing comparisons, and a batch-size sweep from 1 to 10 with CPU activation offloading disabled. Appendix D adds 1000 C4 training steps at 128K context, batch size 1, and learning rate 10^-5, recording loss every 100 steps.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained head-chunk-size ablation, Section 6 tests whether saved memory improves throughput through strided offloading, selective checkpointing, or larger batches. Appendix D adds a training-convergence check addressing numerical effects of head reordering. These substantially expand the questions experimentally investigated.

E5.justification: Appendix C newly cautions that the retained single-step runtime measurements have greater variance than the throughput measurements, especially at shorter contexts. This is a limited qualitative uncertainty disclosure; neither version reports run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or numerical variability estimates.

E6.justification: New Tables 4–6 and 10 add activation-policy, batch-size, and convergence results. For example, selective checkpointing raises UPipe throughput from 850.97 to 1056.77 tokens/second at 512K, and both methods reach loss 4.47 at step 1000. Figure 2 also revises memory values, including ALST attention memory from 37.5 to 33.0 GiB. The retained throughput, memory, and runtime tables have identical numerical entries.

M1.justification: The core headwise chunking and GQA scheduling algorithms remain unchanged. Section 6 adds optional procedural variants: strided activation offloading skips every Kth layer, while selective checkpointing retains attention outputs to avoid recomputation. The expanded buffer accounting does not establish a redesign of the original algorithm.

P1.justification: v2 tightens background, setup, and conclusion prose, adds an attention/GQA primer, consolidates implementation explanations, and reorganizes the appendices. Terminology and publication information are updated. The existing narrative and most methodological exposition remain recognizable; the scientific additions account for much of the expansion.

P2.justification: Four new empirical tables present the activation-policy, batch-size, and convergence studies. Existing theoretical tables use explicit normalized units, memory/runtime tables receive clearer column structures and highlighting, and figures are repositioned with revised captions and styling. This substantially expands the displayed evidence while retaining the original diagrams and benchmark plots.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations to LoongTrain, GLU Variants Improve Transformer, and the T5/C4 work, and removes the original PyTorch FSDP reference. It refines the communication-latency explanation and strengthens the stated relationship between its modified USP baseline and ALST, while retaining the overall research positioning.

T1.justification: The GQA memory factor is corrected, and Tables 2 and 7 substantively revise forward/backward accounting beyond changing units. For example, UPipe's normalized forward input-exchange term changes from 2+(gamma+1)/nu to 2+gamma/nu. New Appendix A derives buffer lifetimes, storage reuse, gradient accumulation, and stage-dependent backward peaks that v1 only tabulated.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important validation and explanation gaps: Appendix D supplies a previously absent training-convergence check, Section 6 tests practical uses of saved memory, and Appendix A derives substantially revised memory accounting. These additions strengthen confidence in the method and make its memory claims more auditable without replacing the original benchmark evidence. The convergence check remains limited to one model/dataset, and statistical uncertainty remains unquantified.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same UPipe work. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching retained material across renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: The original experiments remain, supplemented by activation-management and batch-size experiments in Section 6 and C4 training-loss measurements in Appendix D.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix A report original throughput, memory, runtime, and head-chunk-size experiments using Llama 3-8B and Qwen3-32B.

results.title: Untied Ulysses: Memory-Efficient Context Parallelism via Headwise Chunking

C1.justification: The abstracts, introductions, and closing synthesis retain the same central contribution: five explicit polynomial-memory extensions realizing selected SSM capabilities while preserving interpretability and online updates. The additional evaluations do not redefine that core contribution.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands applicability and mechanism discussion: it interprets language-modeling failures, examines why baseline architectures succeed or fail on recall, and discusses computational tradeoffs. Appendix F.3 explicitly acknowledges that Salience–Mamba differences cannot isolate scalar versus vector adaptivity without further ablations. Appendix F.2 also introduces the stronger, insufficiently established interpretation that continuous addressing is fundamentally mismatched to language prediction.

D1.justification: v2 supplies a code-access link absent from v1 and adds replication information for the baseline, scaling, and language-modeling experiments. Details include optimizer weight decay, learning-rate selection, early stopping, SSM timestep ranges, and Mamba timestep dimensionality. The original experiment descriptions largely remain intact.

E1.justification: v2 adds character-level language modeling on WikiText-2-raw in Section 3.6 and Appendix F, extending evaluation from synthetic mechanism demonstrations to natural-language data. The original synthetic task coverage is retained.

E2.justification: The selective-copying and associative-recall comparisons now include vanilla HiPPO, HiPPO with an MLP, LSTM, S4D, and Transformer configurations (Table 1). Language modeling adds evaluated LSTM, S4D, and Mamba comparisons (Table 4). Figure 4 also adds an Oracle Error reference curve absent from the corresponding v1 experiment.

E3.justification: New Appendix C.6 specifies 3,500 sequences with 70/15/15 splits, 4,000 optimization steps, validation-selected learning rates, parameter matching, and nearest-token accuracy. Follow-up experiments vary depth, positional embeddings, capacity, data, and optimization budgets. Appendix F introduces official language-modeling splits, perplexity evaluation, and validation-based early stopping. These are added evaluation designs, rather than established changes to the original illustrative experiments.

E4.justification: v2 adds associative-recall scaling and positional-embedding investigations (Table 3), a kernel/address-spacing diagnostic examining memory interference (Figure 6), and PCA/regression analysis comparing Salience and Mamba timestep signals (Appendix F.3). The original multiscale-variant analysis remains, with its figure renumbered from 6 to 7.

E5.justification: v2 Figure 1A first reports Volterra learning curves as mean ± SEM across five independent runs; v1 provides neither this run count nor that uncertainty statement. This establishes new reporting, not an increase from a known earlier run count. Reconstruction experiments retain their existing 64-trajectory SEM reporting.

E6.justification: New Table 1 reports 100.0% selective-copying accuracy for Salience HiPPO and 100.0% associative-recall accuracy for Associative Memory HiPPO. Table 3 adds scaling outcomes, including 99.7% recall for a two-layer Transformer with positional embeddings and doubled steps. Table 4 reports language-modeling perplexities of 6.80 for HiPPO+MLP, 7.52 for Salience, and 20.41 for Associative Memory, versus 5.54 for single-layer Mamba. Appendix F.3 adds 79% first-PC variance and regression R² values of 0.38 and 0.01. These are newly reported results, not cross-version performance gains.

M1.justification: The five extension procedures remain intact, but Appendix B corrects the specified base models: the Leg-T diagonal changes from +b_n b_k to -b_n b_k, and the Leg-S basis changes from L_n(exp(-tau)) to L_n(1-exp(-tau)). These are limited model-specification corrections; the PDFs do not establish corresponding implementation changes.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and section order are retained. v2 makes local language and terminology edits, expands the history-measure explanation, adds the new evaluation sections, and replaces the short Conclusion with a Discussion organized around performance, computational tradeoffs, and practitioner guidance.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the visual evidence with three new results tables and an associative-memory kernel heatmap. Figure 1 reverses panel order and adds uncertainty bands; Figure 4 adds an oracle curve and legend. Several retained figures move between columns or pages. The original systems table and multiscale appendix plot remain as Table 2 and Figure 7.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to Hochreiter and Schmidhuber for LSTM, Vaswani et al. for Transformers, and Merity et al. for WikiText-2. The existing HiPPO/SSM literature discussion and positioning around explicit, interpretable memory remain largely unchanged.

T1.justification: Section 3.2 explicitly transforms the input using f(phi^-1(t1)) and corrects the real-time history weighting to omega_1(phi(T)-phi(s))g(s), accounting for lag from the current time. Appendix B also corrects the Leg-T diagonal and Leg-S basis argument. The principal multiscale and forecasting derivations are retained.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical grounding: baseline and scaling comparisons address gaps in v1's synthetic demonstrations, while WikiText-2 exposes important transfer limitations. Corrected mathematical specifications, added uncertainty reporting, and a code-access link also improve assessability and reproducibility. These gains outweigh localized weaknesses, including Figure 6's 16-versus-32 coefficient discrepancy and claims of fundamental architectural mismatch that exceed the tested settings.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same HiPPO Zoo work. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison. Retained material can be matched despite relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds synthetic-task baseline and scaling results, WikiText-2 language-modeling results, and analysis of learned Salience and Mamba timestep signals.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic experiments on nonlinear system identification, selective copying, associative recall, variable-horizon reconstruction, and forecasting in Sections 3.1–3.5 and the appendices.

results.title: HiPPO Zoo: Explicit Memory Mechanisms for Interpretable State Space Models

C1.justification: The introduction removes the claim of biased estimators regardless of task, and the conclusion changes universal bias language to 'can be biased,' reflecting the revised theory. Conversely, the abstract and introduction strengthen the black-hole claim from matching state-of-the-art performance to setting a new state-of-the-art PSNR. Fast sampling approximations become an explicit contribution.

C2.justification: v2 retains computational-cost discussion but adds substantive qualifications: renoising is heuristic, measure-zero likelihood support can defeat the sampler, and likelihood-optimizing methods can outperform it on task metrics. Appendix I explains sparse global rewards and the motivation for tiled weighting, and explicitly limits super-resolution comparisons because priors and sampling budgets differ.

D1.justification: v2 announces a code-release URL and documents approximately 140,000 synthetic black-hole training images, the mean-flow model's architecture relationship to DDPM, image checkpoints, preprocessing, reward construction and inference budgets. It adds TITAN RTX timing information; v1's H100 runtime is not directly comparable. Some detail is lost: v1's explicit DDPM inner-step and candidate-count search grids are omitted.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates five Bayesian inference tasks and black-hole imaging. v2 retains these and adds 4× ImageNet super-resolution, including evaluation on a 1000-image SR3 list, and text-to-image generation with exact object-count constraints. These introduce distinct natural-image tasks beyond the original coverage.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds Langevin+Noisy Classifier, Langevin+REINFORCE, and MCMC No-U-Turn Sampler. New Table 5 compares super-resolution against published DPS, DDRM, RED-diff, C-ΠGDM, MPGD, RB-Modulation, and NDTM results. Figure 6 additionally compares prompt alignment with unguided generation and DPS. The original black-hole comparator set is retained.

E3.justification: The original Bayesian benchmark settings and Tables 3–4 are unchanged. v2 adds black-hole renoise configurations using 100 outer steps, alongside the retained 1000-step DDPM configuration, and introduces common-hardware timing and closure-phase/amplitude χ² evaluation. New image experiments specify super-resolution and prompt-alignment protocols, including 2048 candidates over eight steps for super-resolution and additional perceptual metrics.

E4.justification: v2 adds a Task 4 experiment separating estimator bias from variance as K increases (Appendix D, Figure 8), black-hole K-sensitivity analyses using PSNR and χ² (Figures 5 and 9), and DDPM-versus-renoise comparisons. Figure 10 adds a super-resolution trajectory and candidate-diversity case study. The original Gaussian variance analysis and black-hole qualitative comparisons are retained.

E5.justification: v2 newly reports 95% confidence intervals over 100 tasks in Figures 5 and 9 and specifies 100 repetitions for the new Task 4 bias/variance analysis. Existing table standard deviations and Appendix C's 100-call variance experiment remain. This extends uncertainty reporting without establishing increased repetitions for retained results.

E6.justification: All original Table 1 scores remain, but added baselines change some rankings: Langevin+REINFORCE scores 0.502 on Task 1 versus CBG's 0.505. Table 2 retains the original DDPM result, 26.10 (3.83) dB, and adds renoise results reaching 27.08 (3.74) at K=65536. New super-resolution results include 24.41 PSNR and 40.74 FID, alongside new qualitative findings. These are added configurations and experiments, not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The core estimators and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged, but v2 adds deterministic one-step denoise–renoise–denoise proposals in Section 5.3, Equation (21). Appendix I also introduces tile-local likelihood weighting and stitched updates for super-resolution. These change sampling and update procedures; the shortened DDPM inner loop already existed in v1.

P1.justification: v2 streamlines the introduction and related work, rewrites the black-hole experimental narrative, and moves computational discussion into a dedicated efficiency subsection. It also corrects terminology and affiliation text, updates equal-contribution marking and the publication footer, and renumbers expanded appendices. The overall section sequence and much original prose remain.

P2.justification: v2 adds plots for sample-count sensitivity and estimator bias/variance, natural-image comparisons, a super-resolution trajectory display, a renoise reconstruction grid, and Table 5. Table 2 gains timing and sampler-variant rows, while Table 1 expands and moves. Existing displays are retained: v1 Figure 5 becomes Figure 7, and Figures 6–7 become Figures 11–12.

R1.justification: v2 acknowledges Sun et al. (2024)'s related guidance-bias result and prior renoising methods, and adds references supporting mean-flow models, NUTS, image experiments and revised proofs. The existing comparison with Potaptchik et al. is extended to distinguish reuse of deterministic one-step models. These are focused attribution and positioning updates within the retained research framing.

T1.justification: Appendix A substantially revises the mathematics. Theorem 4.1 replaces its Lipschitz/Taylor argument with an explicit likelihood-maximizer reachability assumption and a new proof. The universal Gaussian-approximation Theorem 4.2 becomes a specific Gaussian-mixture counterexample. Theorem 4.3 gains a revised strict-Jensen proof and a prior-almost-sure constancy condition. These alter formal assumptions, scope and reasoning.

improvement.justification: The revised Appendix A addresses important proof and scope problems through explicit assumptions, a concrete counterexample and a strict-Jensen argument. v2 also addresses v1's principal practical bottleneck: its common-hardware Table 2 reports 26.10 dB in 2.9 minutes with renoising versus approximately 23 hours with DDPM. Added comparisons and analyses strengthen the evidence. Fast proposals remain heuristic, and super-resolution comparisons use different priors and budgets, so better image metrics do not establish posterior calibration. Nevertheless, the gains in theoretical reliability and practical usability are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Calibrated Test-Time Guidance for Bayesian Inference. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, support reliable comparison. Retained content can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds sampler comparisons, bias and variance analyses, quantitative ImageNet super-resolution results, and qualitative object-count prompt-alignment experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original results on five Bayesian inference tasks, 100 black-hole imaging instances, and a gradient-estimator variance experiment in Appendix C.

results.title: Calibrated Test-Time Guidance for Bayesian Inference

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contributions and conclusion retain the same claims about mutually beneficial assembly and generation, missing-part robustness, state-of-the-art assembly and the curated bone dataset. The added experiments support these existing claims without redefining the main contributions.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the new completion comparison as supporting joint over sequential reasoning and the fragment-count results as showing increasing value from holistic priors. Appendix A adds explanations for preprocessing and training choices. Existing failure mechanisms, applicability limitations and future-work discussion remain unchanged.

D1.justification: Appendices A–B substantially expand implementation documentation with point counts, normalization, PCA alignment, augmentation, FPS, network dimensions and parameter counts, pose tokens, optimizer scheduling, precision and fracture-loading procedures. These are primarily newly disclosed details. The original training budgets, hardware information and promise to release code and models remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use PartNeXt, Breaking Bad, MorphoSource and FRACTURA, covering assembly, generation, missing parts and optional reference images. The new generation measurements, fragment-count breakdown and anatomical statistics concern existing coverage rather than establishing a new dataset, population or task.

E2.justification: v2 adds SDFusion and MGPC as evaluated shape-completion baselines in Table 2, substantially extending comparison beyond assembly methods. It also quantifies the previously qualitative TripoSG comparison in Table 3. GARF, RPF and Assembler remain in the original assembly comparison.

E3.justification: New protocols include ground-truth alignment for completion baselines, randomly selected reference views for generation evaluation on 4,626 shapes, CD-L1/CD-L2, F-scores, EMD, decoding-failure measurement and PA stratification by fragment count. The original assembly settings remain unchanged; the relationship between the new 4,626-shape evaluation and Section 4.2's retained 3,903-shape evaluation is unexplained.

E4.justification: v2 adds systematic fragment-count robustness results in Table 5 and decoding-failure analysis in Table 3. Appendix A.4 reports qualitative findings from testing concatenated joint attention against bidirectional cross-attention, and Figure 8 adds reconstruction cases. The original component ablations and failure examples are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals or significance tests. The added decoding-failure frequencies are outcome measurements, without accompanying uncertainty estimates or a changed statistical reporting practice.

E6.justification: Table 1 and the original ablation scores remain unchanged. New results include completion CD-L1 values of 22.51 for SDFusion, 12.59 for MGPC and 9.39 for CRAG, in the displayed ×10−2 units; 25.0% decoding failures for TripoSG versus 0% for CRAG; and PA advantages over Assembler of 11.4 points at two parts and 22.8 at ten parts. These are newly reported comparisons, not performance improvements over v1 under unchanged settings.

M1.justification: The shared VAE, coupled assembly/generation branches, bidirectional adapters, flow objectives and two-stage training remain unchanged. Appendix A newly documents details such as QK normalization, per-part pose tokens and timestep sampling; the PDFs do not establish that these replace different choices used in v1.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained. Changes include a localized rewrite of the generation-evaluation discussion, added experimental subheadings and structured Appendices A–C, plus conference and acknowledgment formatting. The original narrative is not extensively reorganized.

P2.justification: v2 adds five tables covering completion, generation, fragment counts, dataset composition and architecture, plus Figure 8 with three new qualitative cases. The original ablation table becomes Table 4, and Figures 5–7 are repositioned. These additions substantially expand the visual and tabular presentation.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for SDFusion, MGPC, Marching Cubes and PCA, and explicitly compares CRAG with sequential assembly-then-completion approaches. Section 2 and the broader positioning relative to assembly and generative-model research remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix B.1 adds Equations 9–14 defining vertex projections, extremal thresholds and force-application regions for fracture simulation. This is a limited addition of mathematical specification. The core flow-matching equations remain unchanged, with no new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: v1 supported the generation side of its central contribution mainly through qualitative examples. v2 adds quantitative generation evidence, tests the important sequential-completion alternative and supplies substantial implementation and simulation details, addressing central validation and reproducibility gaps. The unexplained evaluation-set sizes and unspecified handling of failed meshes in aggregate quality metrics limit interpretation, but do not outweigh these substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CRAG and share the same core method and benchmark results. Both are readable throughout: v1 ends after its references, while v2 includes Appendices A–C. Text, figures, tables and equations support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds completion comparisons, generation-quality measurements, fragment-count analyses and additional qualitative examples in Tables 2, 3 and 5 and Figure 8.

before.justification: v1 reports original assembly experiments on PartNeXt and Breaking Bad in Table 1, component ablations in Table 2, and qualitative reconstruction and failure results in Figures 3–7.

results.title: CRAG: Can 3D Generative Models Help 3D Assembly?

C1.justification: The central contribution remains an algorithm-agnostic framework for dataset-level circuit stability. The abstract and contribution summary expand the explicitly claimed empirical validation to vision and language and revise headline benefits from up to 91% higher accuracy and 45% fewer neurons to 56% higher accuracy and 80% fewer components, distinguishing language compactness from vision accuracy gains.

C2.justification: Section 6 replaces the linear-runtime limitation with a caching-based account supported by approximately 2.4× ResNet overhead. New interpretations distinguish language accuracy plateaus from vision curves, attribute benefits beyond averaging to abstention, and identify concept-set size as a constraint on larger radii. Future-work boundaries shift from ViTs and language generally to larger language, multimodal, and sparse-activation models.

D1.justification: v3 newly documents vision discovery/evaluation overlap, 50 validation images per class, corruption severity, model sources, ViT hooks, language prompts and graph construction, certification pseudocode, caching, and runtime hardware (Appendices B–D). It replaces the promise of future code with a repository link, whose availability is not established by the PDFs. Newly disclosed vision settings do not establish experimental changes.

E1.justification: v3 retains ImageNet and the four vision OOD datasets and adds language evaluation on IOI, IOI-Hard, and Greater-Than. These introduce indirect-object and year-prediction tasks, with distinct OOD conditions involving object/place distractors, repeated question-and-answer detours, and pre-answer distractors (Appendix B.2).

E2.justification: The three vision comparators—relevance, activation, and rank top-K—remain. v3 adds evaluated EAP-IG baselines for language and a majority-vote comparator using the same 1,000 deletion samples for vision (Appendix F.5). The latter directly tests whether certification adds value beyond ensemble averaging.

E3.justification: New protocols include ViT-B/16 and GPT-2 Small evaluation, language splits of 100 discovery, 100 ID-test, and 100 OOD-test prompts, exact next-token accuracy, and task-specific certification-parameter sweeps. Additional experiments vary concept-set size and certified radius. The non-target-class oACC evaluation is removed; the main vision certification defaults remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 retains cross-distribution circuit-IoU analysis and adds independent-seed stability, radius-versus-data-size sensitivity, a matched-compute majority-vote control, runtime analysis, and expanded feature case studies (Appendices D–F). Conversely, v1 Appendix C's quantitative class-specificity analysis using non-target images is absent.

E5.justification: v1 reports certification confidence but no comparable empirical uncertainty or seed study. v3 Table 5 adds plus/minus uncertainty and paired class-level significance tests; Appendix F.2 reports 40 independent seeds and a 95% confidence interval for mean IoU. Appendix C.3 explicitly specifies Bonferroni family-wise error control. The certification sampling budget remains 1,000.

E6.justification: Retained results change: ResNet-101 relevance-based ImageNet peak cACC is 96% certified versus 86% baseline in v1 Table 1, versus 95% and 83% in v3 Table 1. v3 also adds language, ViT, runtime, and sensitivity results; language ID circuits match 100% baseline accuracy with substantially fewer edges. oACC results disappear. Revised vision numbers do not establish same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: Sections 3.1–3.3 extend the vertex-based formulation to edge masks, adding construction of circuits from certified edges and their incident vertices. The deletion sampling, inclusion probabilities, and threshold-and-abstain rule remain unchanged. This is a limited procedural extension of the existing wrapper.

P1.justification: The abstract, experimental setup, and results narrative are substantially rewritten around parallel vision/language comparisons and component-level terminology. Feature visualization becomes a separate main-text subsection, while the three-scorer comparison moves into the appendix. Appendices are reorganized into experimental setup, certification analysis, runtime, language results, and vision results.

P2.justification: v3 redraws the overview and pipeline figures, restructures Table 1 into a multimodal comparison, and simplifies the main vision curve grid. It adds language circuit diagrams, uncertainty tables, seed and radius plots, runtime displays, and feature panels. The original radius plot and structural-stability plot remain in revised presentations; the oACC table is removed.

R1.justification: v3 adds references supporting EAP/EAP-IG, Greater-Than, GPT-2, ViT, implementation libraries, and recent vision-transformer circuit work. The main positioning against dataset instability and input-level verification remains. The Anonymous-to-Hadad citation update and publication-metadata revisions identify retained work rather than new research relationships.

T1.justification: Theorem 3.1 and Appendix A change the certified neighborhood from edit distance < r to ≤ r, while definitions expand to edge components. Appendix C.2 adds a perfect-agreement sample-complexity analysis with simultaneous certification. The central radius formula and RS-Del proof strategy remain; the proof still concludes invariance of the non-abstaining smoothed label.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the previously CNN-only empirical case through language and ViT evaluation, a majority-vote control, seed uncertainty, and radius/data-size studies. Detailed estimation procedures and measured runtime also address important reproducibility and practicality gaps. Removing oACC weakens quantitative specificity evidence, and the pre-existing mismatch between the thresholded-output theorem and the non-abstaining-label proof remains. Nevertheless, the added empirical scrutiny and technical documentation provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Certified Circuits, with matching authors, framework, and identifiable retained experiments. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison.

after.justification: v3 reports original vision and language experiments, including circuit performance, seed stability, radius sensitivity, feature visualizations, and runtime measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original ResNet experiments measuring circuit accuracy, size, non-target-class accuracy, and structural stability on ImageNet and four OOD datasets.

results.title: Certified Circuits: Stability Guarantees for Mechanistic Circuits

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction's contribution list remain essentially unchanged. The discussion now makes the stopping-time dependence and minimum-loss scaling explicit, claims recovery of the stationary result, and adds label-noise applicability and an outlined nonlinear extension.

C2.justification: Section 5 and Appendix G add substantive interpretations of the sample-size/noise tradeoff and finite-size corrections. They identify conditions for the new scaling approximation, including α > 0, weak regularization, and dominant thermal noise, and explain why its stationary limit cannot generally be taken. v1 lacked this analysis of scaling behavior and applicability.

D1.justification: Captions provide configurations and integration steps for the added experiments, and the acknowledgements newly identify JURECA computing resources. Neither PDF supplies a code repository or a detailed reproduction workflow.

E1.justification: Appendix H and Figure 6 add an evaluated scenario with Gaussian noise on training labels, beyond v1's noiseless teacher. The synthetic Gaussian-feature regression domain remains; the nonlinear committee-machine extension is not experimentally evaluated.

E2.justification: Both versions compare theoretical predictions with direct simulations of the Langevin-trained model. v2's added scaling curves are predictions from its own approximations, and the Canatar comparison is an algebraic stationary-limit calculation. No additional competing method is experimentally evaluated.

E3.justification: New scaling experiments use N = 1000, P = 50–300, and dt = 0.005, and Figure 5 measures stopping-time minima across temperatures. In retained experiments, plotted legends add β = 1 and replace gβ = 1 with 0.5. These extend settings within the existing simulation framework.

E4.justification: New Figures 4–5 test asymptotic bias/variance scaling, finite-size corrections, and the temperature dependence of optimal stopping. Appendix H and Figure 6 additionally analyze sensitivity to static label noise. These substantially extend v1's analyses of dynamic noise and regularization.

E5.justification: Retained experiments still report averaging over 10^5 training-data realizations. New Figures 4 and 5 specify 10^2 and 5 × 10^3 realizations, respectively. These are additional experiment-specific replication counts, not evidence that retained experiments received more runs. No confidence intervals or significance tests are added.

E6.justification: v2 adds sample-size-dependent loss curves and minima, an approximately linear stopping-time-versus-β trend, and label-noise results showing earlier, higher-error minima with stronger noise. Retained plots also add β = 1 and replace the gβ = 1 result with 0.5. These are additional or differently configured results, not established same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The central linear regression model, Langevin training, and variational Gaussian framework remain. Appendix H extends the effective dynamics to static label noise. Appendix J formulates a nonlinear teacher-student model and its gradient dynamics, but leaves the disorder-averaged solution for future work.

P1.justification: Related work is reorganized into static and dynamic approaches, several passages are edited, and appendix explanations are expanded. A scaling-law section precedes the discussion. Most existing prose and derivations remain closely matched; the substantial scientific additions do not constitute a wholesale rewrite.

P2.justification: v1 Figures 2–3 are combined and redrawn as v2 Figure 2, with changed legends and plotting ranges. The regularization panels are reordered and relabeled. New Figures 4–6 add scaling curves, a minimum-loss inset, stopping-time points, and label-noise curves, substantially expanding the visual evidence.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially expands positioning within static and dynamic scaling-law research, adding discussions of Bordelon–Canatar–Pehlevan, Cui, Spigler, Defilippis, Atanasov, and Paquette and collaborators. It explicitly distinguishes identical teacher/student features and Langevin dynamics from down-projected models and finite-batch SGD. Appendix I adds a detailed connection to Canatar's stationary theory.

T1.justification: Section 5 and Appendix G add explicit bias/variance scaling laws, finite-size corrections, and t* = βα/[2(1+α)]. Appendices B–C add arguments concerning concentration and Gaussian exactness. New Appendices H–J derive label-noise dynamics, a stationary-limit connection, and a nonlinear model formulation. These substantially expand the mathematical substance.

improvement.justification: v1 promises analytical scaling and optimal-stopping results but mainly supplies dynamical equations and illustrative learning curves. v2 supplies explicit predictions, derivations, and targeted simulations in Section 5, Appendix G, and Figures 4–5, addressing an important gap in the central contribution. The tested label-noise extension adds further substance. These gains outweigh localized inconsistencies, including Figure 2's outdated caption and Appendix I's final stationary-loss formula dropping the factor 1/2 present in Equations 79–80.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same teacher-student regression work. Their text, equations, figures, and complete appendices are readable: Appendices A–F in v1 and A–J in v2. Internal caption inconsistencies do not prevent comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains simulation results and adds experiments on sample-size scaling, optimal stopping versus temperature, and static label noise, including Appendix H, Figure 6.

before.justification: Figures 1–4 report original numerical simulations of learning dynamics, generalization error, bias–variance decomposition, and regularization effects, compared with theoretical predictions.

results.title: Dynamics of neural scaling laws in random feature regression with powerlaw-distributed kernel eigenvalues

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion elevate a specifically identified, causally steerable routing circuit to a central contribution. v1 leaves the coexistence of shared representations and game-specific predictions unresolved; v2 claims to resolve it through localized conflict processing and emphasizes distinct mid-layer reweighting and early-selection regimes.

C2.justification: v2 introduces a mechanism in which the layer-4 MLP constructs conflict features and layer-5 components route them, and develops the contrast between NoMidFlip reweighting and DelFlank selection. Appendix C.1 adds an explanation of final-layer Iago intervention behavior. It also removes v1's explicit warning that rotational isomorphism alone cannot distinguish one shared representation from multiple similarly structured representations.

D1.justification: v2 specifies component intervention sites, last-token-output zeroing, and activation readout locations for the new circuit analysis. Appendix A's architecture, optimizer, learning rate, batch size, probe-training details, and code/model/data access information remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use Classic, NoMidFlip, DelFlank, and Iago, including the same pure/mixed training coverage and ambiguous-prefix scenarios. The added circuit experiments investigate existing game and prefix conditions rather than introducing new datasets or tasks.

E2.justification: The new circuit experiment compares full-circuit steering with routing-head-only steering and a runner-up layer-5 head using its own learned direction; Figure 6b labels the latter H0 control. Existing random-probe, one-hot-input, null-intervention, and matched/cross-probe comparisons are retained.

E3.justification: Section 5.4.2 adds a substantial component-level evaluation protocol: separate direction-learning and held-out steering sets, readouts before attention/after attention/after MLP, and last-token component ablations. New measurements include signed game-ID margins, unique-move branch preference, and wrong-game probability mass. Existing model-training and benchmark settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v1 localized effective NoMidFlip steering to layer 5. v2 adds component and individual-head ablations, tile-conflict projection analysis, steering-strength sensitivity, and controlled circuit steering. These tests investigate which components construct and route game identity and whether the localized circuit causally controls branch selection.

E5.justification: The added circuit analysis reports 1,000 bootstrap resamples for head-ranking stability and a Mann–Whitney test with a rank-biserial effect size. Existing confidence-interval reporting and Appendix A.4's fixed seed 42 and single model-training run are retained; the bootstrap does not establish additional training runs.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial circuit results, including Classic unique-move probability share changing from 0.48 to 0.68 or 0.01 under directional steering, and wrong-game mass increasing from 0.0001 to 0.0115 under ablation. All 12 Table 1 means and intervals and existing plotted results are retained. DelFlank accuracies of 77.4% and 75.8% are now correctly attributed in prose to layers 2 and 3, matching both versions' plots.

M1.justification: Section 5.4.2 extends the intervention procedure from residual-stream game-identity steering to learned component-specific directions applied jointly to the identified MLP–attention-head–MLP circuit. The game framework, transformer architecture, training, and original probing/alignment procedures remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The abstract, related-work opening, ambiguity/OOD discussion, and conclusion undergo extensive rewriting and condensation. Former Section 5.5 becomes 5.4.1 alongside the new mechanism subsection; v2 also adds Appendix C.1 and acknowledgments and edits publication information and terminology.

P2.justification: v2 adds a two-panel Figure 6 showing circuit readouts and controlled steering. Existing plots are retained, with some relocation/rescaling and subsequent renumbering; the DelFlank caption corrects layers 1–2 to 2–3. Table 1 is repositioned and its game-name capitalization standardized.

R1.justification: v2 adds Millière and Buckner, Mitchell, Schönemann, and Sikarwar et al., and removes Li et al. (2025) and Richens et al. It clarifies representational versus forward-dynamics meanings of world models while retaining the central positioning against vocabulary-only mOthello. Park et al.'s publication update represents the same work.

T1.justification: Section 3 corrects the stated move-set cardinality from '64 (or 65, including pass)' to 65 for the explicitly defined set containing all board positions and pass. The game-transition mathematics, Bayesian mixture derivation, and normalized-KL alpha score otherwise remain unchanged; no new theorem or proof appears.

improvement.justification: v1 explicitly leaves its central mechanistic puzzle unresolved after layer-level steering. v2's component ablations, matched head control, and held-out circuit steering provide substantially stronger causal evidence for a specific conflict-routing mechanism, materially strengthening the paper's explanatory contribution. Removing the useful Iago-isomorphism caveat weakens qualification, but the new controlled evidence provides a clear net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MetaOthello study. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–C support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds component-level circuit localization, ablation, and steering results in Section 5.4.2 and Figure 6.

before.justification: v1 reports original transformer-training results, probe measurements, representational alignment, and causal steering experiments in Table 1, Figures 2–6, and the appendices.

results.title: MetaOthello: A Controlled Study of Multiple World Models in Transformers

C1.justification: The abstract replaces the claimed theoretical guarantee of convergence to the exact data manifold with progressive agreement between data-consistency and prior variables. The efficiency discussion emphasizes inference efficiency. The central dual-feedback, SH, bias-reduction and superior-fidelity contributions remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds an SNR/geometry explanation for differing CT, knee and brain gains, interprets high-budget behavior and residual trajectories, and explains computational tradeoffs. It explicitly separates PSNR-versus-NFE evidence from formal optimization convergence, qualifies the supervised comparison's scope, and discusses SH applicability beyond dual-coupled solvers.

D1.justification: Appendix A.3 substantially expands baseline documentation with task-specific 10-slice validation, DAPS Langevin parameters and separate budget configurations, SITCOM optimization settings, and the MRI closed-form data-consistency implementation. Runtime hardware, batch size and memory details are added. The CT training recipe and code URL remain, although some new benchmark setups lack dataset/sample specifications.

E1.justification: v2 adds fastMRI brain reconstruction, AAPM and DeepLesion CT evaluation, and natural-image Gaussian deblurring, motion deblurring and 4x super-resolution. AbdomenCT-1K and fastMRI knee coverage remain; knee results move to Appendix B.1.

E2.justification: SITCOM joins the main quantitative comparison, and Appendix B.5 introduces the supervised ProCT comparator, substantially broadening comparison methods. The original four diffusion baselines remain in Table 3. Main CT qualitative panels replace DAPS with SITCOM, while DAPS remains evaluated elsewhere.

E3.justification: v2 adds recommended-budget comparisons: 100 NFEs for DDNM/DDS/DiffPIR, reported budgets of 5x200 for DAPS and 50x10 for SITCOM, and 50/100 NFEs for DC-PnPDP. The original uniform 50-NFE protocol remains in Table 3. New designs include a 200-slice brain subset, sweeps to 1000 NFEs, residual measurements and batch-10 runtime profiling.

E4.justification: The original component ablation and spectral diagnostic remain. v2 adds measurement-residual and dual-state trajectories, extends the budget analysis to examine high-budget plateaus, profiles runtime and memory, tests ProCT under in-domain/OOD conditions, and examines SH transfer to DDNM.

E5.justification: Unlike v1's point estimates, v2 Table 6 reports mean ± standard deviation for natural-image restoration. The aggregation unit, repeated-run counts and seeds are unspecified, so this establishes additional variability reporting, not additional independent runs.

E6.justification: v1 Table 1 is preserved numerically as v2 Table 3, and the component ablation is unchanged. v2 adds substantial results under its expanded protocols: Table 1 reports LACT PSNR 39.46 versus DiffPIR's 34.70 at 100 NFEs, and brain AF=10 PSNR 30.91 versus SITCOM's 28.67 under their reported budgets. Runtime, cross-dataset CT, natural-image and extended-budget findings are also new; these are not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The core DC-PnPDP updates and diffusion-prior architecture are retained. Appendix B.6 adds a procedural adaptation that inserts SH into DDNM by replacing its standard DDIM re-noising step, although the authors present this as a scope diagnostic.

P1.justification: v2 substantially reorganizes the empirical narrative into recommended-budget main results and controlled-budget appendix results, adds a dedicated Related Work section and structured diagnostic/discussion subsections, and rewrites the MRI and efficiency discussions. Much of the method and theoretical prose remains unchanged.

P2.justification: The main table gains budget columns and separate DC-PnPDP rows; the original table and knee figure move to the appendix. Main qualitative examples are replaced, Figure 4 is redrawn over a logarithmic budget range to 1000 NFEs, and new runtime, residual, ProCT and natural-image displays are added. Appendix CT panels are also replaced and include SITCOM.

R1.justification: The new Related Work section substantially expands positioning against PnP-ADMM convergence, adaptation and stochastic methods, plus concurrent diffusion/ADMM approaches. It explicitly distinguishes SH from AC-DC's Langevin correction, stochastic generative PnP, dual-ascent diffusion and colored re-noising. These are substantive additions beyond bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: The explanation of Eq. (13) corrects the Fourier normalization convention from a unitary DFT to an unnormalized FFT, making the stated HW scaling consistent. The spectral-consistency proposition and bootstrap/fixed-point assumptions, theorems and proofs otherwise retain their substance; appendices B–D become C–E.

improvement.justification: v1 supported efficiency mainly through uniform 50-NFE comparisons and a short budget sweep. v2 preserves that control while testing recommended and larger budgets, adding residual diagnostics and measured runtime, and clarifying positioning against closely related work. These changes substantially strengthen evidence for the central benefits. Some added experiments remain underspecified, Tables 1 and 3 contain unreconciled 50-NFE CT scores, and convergence claims remain incompletely qualified, but the overall gain in validation and transparency is substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DC-PnPDP work. Text, equations, tables, figures and all appendices are readable. Retained material can be matched despite substantial additions and relocation of the original main results.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and reports additional brain MRI, cross-dataset CT, natural-image restoration, residual and runtime results.

before.justification: v1 reports original CT and fastMRI knee reconstruction experiments, component ablations, spectral diagnostics and inference-budget results.

C1.justification: The central claims remain low-supervision alignment using a linear teacher, effective use of unpaired data, efficient KLOT differentiation and robustness across datasets and encoders. The contribution list and conclusion retain their scientific scope; the new experiments provide additional support.

C2.justification: v1 cautions that more encoder-pair observations are needed for firm conclusions; v2 presents mutual k-NN as a reliable diagnostic before alignment. v2 also substantially expands practical interpretations: teacher robustness is attributed to limited linear capacity and OT invariance, mismatched unpaired data are described as producing graceful degradation, and entropy/loss-weight choices receive mechanism-based explanations.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-repository link and documents the WavLM-Large speech encoder, corruption construction and additional hyperparameter searches. Most optimizer, architecture, hardware and baseline implementation details in Appendix A remain unchanged. The conflicting teacher-temperature values in Section 6.1 and Appendix A.1 reduce the clarity of the new guidance.

E1.justification: v2 adds SkyScript satellite-image/text retrieval and LibriSpeech speech/text retrieval, substantially extending the evaluated domains and modalities beyond v1's general image–text benchmarks. It also introduces synthetic-noise scenarios for unpaired embeddings while retaining the earlier dataset coverage.

E2.justification: Corresponding existing comparisons retain their comparator membership and baseline implementations, including Tables 4–6 and Appendix A.2. The added domain experiments reuse previously evaluated CCA, SAIL and STRUCTURE. UOT-RCL is newly cited but is not an evaluated baseline.

E3.justification: New protocols include SkyScript evaluation with 10k/30k test pools, LibriSpeech training with 1k pairs and 100k unpaired samples, weaker-encoder configurations, corruption sweeps and temperature searches using 500 Sinkhorn iterations. Section 6.1 reports teacher epsilon*=0.005, whereas v1 and the retained v2 Appendix A.1 specify 0.01. This leaves the actual default and whether retained experiments were rerun unresolved.

E4.justification: v2 adds teacher-pair corruption experiments, unpaired Gaussian-noise stress tests, loss-weight sensitivity across supervision/noise levels, and teacher/student temperature sweeps (Appendix B.2). It also adds Sinkhorn convergence analysis and extends encoder-similarity analysis to ResNet-50 and BERT. These substantially expand examination of robustness and design dependencies.

E5.justification: Both versions report spherical sliced Wasserstein distances as means and standard deviations over 20 seeds, using 100,000-sample subsets (v1 Appendix B.4/Figure 12; v2 Appendix B.3/Figure 15). No new run-count disclosure, significance test or uncertainty-estimation procedure is documented. Updated correlations are changes in results.

E6.justification: Existing benchmark tables retain their values, but substantial new results appear. v2 Table 7 reports SOTAlign SkyScript T2I/I2T R@10 of 27.3/27.4 and LibriSpeech S2T/T2S R@1 of 78.4/83.1. Table 8 reports 26.6 COCO MeanR@1 with 50% teacher-pair corruption versus 23.6 for SAIL. Expanded analyses report encoder-similarity correlation 0.95 instead of 0.83 and distribution-shift correlation -0.76 instead of -0.72.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 retains the same linear-teacher stage followed by alignment with supervised SigLIP and unpaired-data KLOT regularization. The corrected main-text gradient already appears correctly in v1's appendix; it does not establish an implementation change. The new modality experiments apply the existing framework.

P1.justification: Section 6 is reorganized into dedicated design-choice, supervision, data-source, encoder and benchmarking subsections, and Appendix B reorders distribution-shift and benchmarking material. Related work is tightened, local language is corrected, and affiliation/publication text is updated. Much of the existing prose and overall narrative is retained.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the experimental displays with convergence, sensitivity and satellite-retrieval plots plus new Tables 7–8. Distribution-shift and encoder-similarity plots are expanded and redrawn; the latter moves from v1 Appendix Figure 9 to v2 main-text Figure 7. Existing tables and several figures are also redistributed within the revised layout.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds UOT-RCL as prior OT-based frozen-encoder alignment addressing noisy labels and revises the CLIP background. References for the additional datasets and encoders are added. Positioning relative to OT-CLIP, S-CLIP, SUE and STRUCTURE remains substantially unchanged; the existing Assel/Monge Gap discussion moves from the appendix to Section 5.

T1.justification: Theorem 5.1, Equation 13, corrects the gradient denominator from teacher epsilon* to student epsilon, agreeing with Theorem C.4 and its proof already present in v1. Section 3.3 also corrects projection-matrix dimensions. The appendix's mathematical results and derivations otherwise remain substantively unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation by testing satellite and speech applications and examining teacher corruption, extreme unpaired-data mismatch and tuning sensitivity that v1 did not establish. These additions address important gaps in support for applicability and robustness. The corrected gradient statement and code-access information also help. The new inconsistency between teacher temperatures in Section 6.1 and Appendix A.1 limits reproducibility, but does not outweigh the substantial evidential gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SOTAlign work. Their main text, figures, tables, equations and Appendices A–C support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds satellite-image and speech retrieval, corruption experiments and hyperparameter sensitivity studies.

before.justification: v1 reports original retrieval and classification experiments, alignment ablations, supervision sweeps and gradient-computation efficiency measurements.

results.title: SOTAlign: Semi-Supervised Alignment of Unimodal Vision and Language Models via Optimal Transport

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion retain the central contributions and confidence-inflation warning. Section 2.1 explicitly extends the claimed independence to the underlying protein generator, and Section 2.2 adds a claim of physically plausible crystallographic ensembles. These are limited extensions of the existing contribution framing.

C2.justification: The new theory substantially qualifies optimization guarantees through biased surrogate gradients and conditional near-stationarity, rather than unconditional posterior ascent. V3 also adds interpretations concerning matched-compute advantages and sparse-restraint robustness. Section 5.3 newly describes ipSAE as largely unchanged, conflicting with the retained increases in Figure 13; this changes interpretation without reversing the plotted results.

D1.justification: Table 19 and Section C.2.1 add measured GPU memory and per-loop runtime information, and Table 17 identifies phenix.molprobity for structural validation. Relaxation documentation changes to AMBER99SB. Most hardware, software, preprocessing, optimizer, and hyperparameter details were already present in v1 and are retained after relocation.

E1.justification: V3 adds whole-protein density fitting without pre-modeled structures for 4NE4 and 5TEU, plus four larger NMR targets in Tables 19–20. These extend coverage within the existing modalities. The three X-ray targets omitted from some later tables still have cosine-similarity results in Table 11, so they are not entirely removed.

E2.justification: V3 evaluates ESMFlow, AFCluster, and BioEMU alongside the retained comparators for NMR and crystallographic benchmarks (Tables 5–6 and 14–16). AFCluster previously served as an MSA initialization tool, not an evaluated comparator. This substantially expands the comparison set; Boltz-2 is a tested backbone rather than a competing baseline.

E3.justification: V3 introduces matched 200/800-denoiser-call comparisons, controlled hyperparameter sweeps, NOE subsampling, Boltz-2 evaluations, and additional ESS, interface-quality, and geometry metrics. Relaxation is reported as AMBER99SB instead of AMBER99, without establishing that retained experiments were rerun. Table 9's default inverse temperature of 0.6 conflicts with the retained 1.68 setting in Section C.3.4.

E4.justification: New analyses examine hyperparameter sensitivity, annealing and energy smoothing, effective sample size, sparse-restraint geometric validity, MolProbity quality, and matched-compute performance (Tables 7–10, 17, and 20). Figures 10 and 14 add interface-accuracy diagnostics and transfer to Boltz-2. These substantially extend v1's convergence, seed-stability, and selected structural case studies.

E5.justification: V1 Table 8 already reports estimates with variability across five independent runs. V3 Figure 15 explicitly identifies the summaries as means and standard deviations, clarifying the uncertainty reporting. The run count remains five; the expanded target set does not establish an increase in repetitions or a new significance-testing procedure.

E6.justification: Core NMR Tables 3–4 are retained, but v3 adds extensive comparator, ablation, validity, runtime, and transfer results. Table 20 newly shows budget-dependent rankings: for 2B3W, Guidance/IT-Opt violation rates are 13.7%/14.4% at 200 calls and 13.7%/8.4% at 800 calls. R-factor and repeated-run entries for 4NPU, 3QDA, and 4RMW are removed, although their cosine scores remain.

M1.justification: The embedding updates, nested optimization, experimental objectives, ProteinEBM reweighting, and regularizers are retained. Algorithms 2–3 are unchanged. Boltz-2 applies the existing procedure, while the new surrogate objective is introduced for theoretical analysis rather than as a replacement empirical algorithm.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much of the prose remain intact. V3 makes localized language and terminology edits, adds acknowledgments and author-information changes, and moves implementation details earlier within the supplemental material. The substantial scientific additions do not amount to wholesale rewriting of the existing narrative.

P2.justification: V3 adds benchmark-summary violin plots, interface-metric bar plots, and Boltz-2 convergence plots. It moves v1 Figure 8 into the main text as Figure 7 and replaces the seed-stability table with a broader plotted comparison. Appendix figures are regrouped, numerous tables are added, and table captions and layouts are extensively reformatted.

R1.justification: V3 adds discussion of Richman et al.'s repulsive guidance and citations supporting biased-gradient analysis, BioEMU, DockQ, and MolProbity. Some background and benchmarking references are replaced. The principal positioning against coordinate-space guidance and MSA manipulation remains; publication updates to existing works do not constitute new research relationships.

T1.justification: New Appendix B defines a trajectory-averaged surrogate and displacement oracle, analyzes omitted-score and nested-drift bias, and introduces smoothness assumptions and variance bounds. Theorem B.8 supplies an O(1/K) stationarity bound with a bias/variance floor, followed by an expected-ascent corollary and proofs. V1 contains no corresponding convergence analysis.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens empirical scrutiny through broader baselines, controlled ablations, structural-validity checks, and matched-compute comparisons that v1 lacked. Runtime reporting and conditional theoretical analysis also make the method easier to assess. The conflicting temperature settings and ipSAE interpretation remain material weaknesses, but the added evidence meaningfully addresses important gaps in v1's validation and supports a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same IT-Optimization framework and share identifiable methods and experiments. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison; internal inconsistencies in v3 do not prevent matching the material.

after.justification: V3 retains those original experiments and adds baseline comparisons, ablations, structural-validity measurements, additional protein cases, and runtime and compute-budget results.

before.justification: Sections 5.1–5.3 and the appendices report original NMR restraint, crystallographic density, and protein-complex confidence optimization experiments.
