C1.justification: The central system and living-benchmark contributions remain intact. v4 corrects the headline code-reduction claim from 42% to 58%, consistent with the unchanged LOC totals, and qualifies the 82.5% reuse figure as a mean per-module share rather than a fraction of the entire integrated codebase.

C2.justification: v4 explicitly distinguishes ASR agreement from semantic fidelity, repository compression from fidelity, and attack effectiveness from budget efficiency. It adds interpretations of planner sensitivity and concrete limitations concerning manual framework extension, text-only black/gray-box coverage, and adversarial papers or repositories affecting the agents. These substantially qualify the system's applicability and evidence.

D1.justification: New disclosures include ABJ's gpt-4o-mini assist-model substitution, ReNeLLM's fixed 0.5 temperature, and stage-specific total and cached token usage. These document implementation choices and resource requirements without establishing changes between implementations. Existing interfaces, full agent prompts, and code-access information are retained.

E2.justification: v4 Table 5 adds evaluated pipeline comparators using Kimi-K2.5 separately as planner, coder, or auditor, plus variants without the planner or auditor. These are limited additions within the component study; existing attack and repository/no-repository comparison sets remain unchanged.

E3.justification: v4 adds several evaluation protocols: 15 ablation runs across three attacks, a three-sample Past Tense trace comparison, a 50-prompt SQL-structure check, an eight-criterion manual audit, and stratified token measurement across 12 attacks. Existing benchmark settings are retained. Section 4.3 also revises the reported reuse aggregation from an overall codebase fraction to a mean per-module share.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's repository, enhanced-refinement, and iteration-count analyses, v4 adds backend sensitivity and component-removal ablations, trace/mechanism verification, four manual semantic audits, core-versus-scaffolding LOC analysis, and attack effectiveness versus token-budget analysis. These directly examine architectural necessity, fidelity, compression, and efficiency.

E5.justification: Section 4.1 newly states that fixed seeds or deterministic settings are used when supported and acknowledges API nondeterminism. It supplies no specific seed values, repeated-run counts, or new confidence intervals. Figure 5's existing group standard deviations and correlation significance reporting are retained.

E6.justification: v4 adds substantial ablation, audit, LOC, and cost results, including GTA ASR of 46.0 with Kimi-Planner versus the 100.0 baseline. Table 1 is unchanged, while Figure 4 adds averages and changes GTA against GPT-OSS-120B from 27.7% to 22.9%. The newly reported 5.7-point mean absolute gap follows Table 1's displayed deltas, but those contain pre-existing arithmetic inconsistencies; the ASR columns imply approximately 5.91 points.

M1.justification: The three-component system, planner–coder–auditor workflow, bounded refinement, and evaluation harness remain unchanged, including Algorithm 1 and the appendix agent prompts. New backend substitutions and component removals are experimental ablations, not revisions to the proposed method.

P1.justification: v4 locally expands the paper-to-code discussion, adds a randomness paragraph, clarifies reuse wording, and extends future work. New analytical appendices are inserted and existing appendices renumbered, but the main narrative structure, method exposition, and full agent instructions are largely preserved.

P2.justification: v4 adds Tables 3–8 displaying token costs, ablations, traces, semantic scores, and core LOC, plus Figure 6's budget-effectiveness scatterplot. Figure 4 is redrawn with attack/model averages and reordered columns, and Figure 3's legend typo is corrected. This substantially expands the visual presentation of the evidence.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds reproducibility and peer-review context supported by Gundersen et al., Raff et al., and Aczel et al. This broadens the motivation modestly while retaining the same positioning around automated attack integration and standardized evaluation.

T1.justification: Appendix F.2 introduces a defined numerical semantic-fidelity score: eight criteria scored 0–2, N/A assigned 2, a fixed 16-point denominator, and explicit passing conditions. This is a limited scoring-definition addition. Existing auditor acceptance mathematics, invocation bounds, and runtime equations remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens evidence for the central design and fidelity claims through component ablations and checks beyond aggregate ASR. Cost analyses, corrected compression reporting, and explicit applicability and security limitations also improve assessability. Small selected audit samples, absent repeated-run uncertainty, and remaining numerical inconsistencies limit confidence, but do not outweigh these substantive gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Jailbreak Foundry and provide readable main text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices. Retained material can be matched reliably, including v1 Appendices E–H becoming v4 Appendices I–L.

after.justification: v4 retains these empirical results and adds agent ablations, trace and semantic audits, and token-cost measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original reproductions of 30 attacks, evaluation across 10 victim models, repository and refinement ablations, and engineering measurements.

results.title: Jailbreak Foundry: From Papers to Runnable Attacks for Reproducible Benchmarking

C1.justification: The central contributions remain sliding-window teacher alignment, decoupled global/local training heads, and fast long-video generation. The abstract now names human ratings and one-minute tests as supporting evidence, but retains the same scientific claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds concrete limitations involving action-state transitions and landmark revisitation, motivating stronger event planning and memory. It also qualifies the incomplete 60-second baseline coverage and cautions that LongLive's NFE is not directly comparable. The original interpretations of SFT, teacher alignment, and their combination remain.

D1.justification: Hardware, batching, sequence-parallelism settings, data preparation, and latent-boundary handling are retained and relocated into the main text. However, v2 omits the direct FastGen repository URL supplied in v1's references, while retaining the named codebase and project website; this slightly reduces access information.

E1.justification: v2 adds a 60-second generation scenario requiring sustained coherence beyond the retained 30-second evaluation. The training sources—Sekai, MiraData, and collected internet videos—and the underlying text-to-video task remain unchanged.

E2.justification: LongLive is added as an evaluated comparator in Table 1 and Figure 4; v1 cited it but did not include it in those comparisons. All previously evaluated comparators remain.

E3.justification: Appendix C introduces a human-evaluation protocol: 31 participants view randomized sets, comprising 25 sets at 30 seconds and 15 at 60 seconds, and rate quality, consistency, and static artifacts. Appendix B adds 60-second automatic evaluation restricted to available rollout/context-extension baselines. The original 200-prompt, 30-second evaluation remains unchanged.

E4.justification: The component ablations in Table 2 remain unchanged. Appendix B adds a focused horizon stress test examining whether fidelity and temporal evolution persist at 60 seconds, while the user study supplies targeted static-artifact ratings relevant to motion collapse.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without generation seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. v2's participant count and averaged human ratings describe the new study rather than introducing uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: All existing numerical entries in Tables 1–2 are unchanged, but Table 1 gains LongLive results. New Table 3 reports 60-second outcomes, including 0.9297 dynamic degree and 73.08 VLM consistency for the proposed method. Table 4 adds human ratings showing its highest overall quality and global consistency at both horizons. These are additional results, not same-setting performance improvements.

M1.justification: The shared encoder, separate flow-matching and distribution-matching heads, training objectives, and few-step inference procedure remain unchanged. The sliding-window latent reconstruction procedure in v2 Section 3.4 was already documented in v1 Appendix C.

P1.justification: v2 moves v1 Appendices A–C into Sections 4.1 and 3.4, reorganizes the remaining appendices, expands the mean-versus-mode explanation, and removes the duplicated contribution-introduction sentence. Most existing prose and the main section sequence remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds substantial tables for one-minute results and human ratings. Figure 4 is reorganized from two to three frames per scene and gains a LongLive row; Table 1 also gains that comparator and an expanded caption. Figures 1–3 and the ablation display are substantially retained.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds a substantial diffusion-distillation discussion covering trajectory regression, consistency methods, distribution matching, and hybrids. It explicitly positions the proposed global/local objective separation against approaches blending objectives on one output. Publication-year and title updates to retained references do not constitute additional research changes.

T1.justification: The mathematical objectives and numbered equations remain unchanged. Section 3.3 expresses the existing conditional-mean versus mode-seeking motivation using explicit optimum notation and explanatory qualifications, without adding a substantive derivation, theorem, or proof.

improvement.justification: v1's minute-scale claims relied mainly on 30-second automatic evaluation. v2 directly strengthens their empirical basis with 60-second results and human judgments of quality, consistency, and static artifacts, while adding concrete planning limitations. This substantially improves validation and qualification of the central contribution. The longer-horizon comparison still lacks SFT-only baselines, and the human ratings lack uncertainty estimates, limiting the strength of comparative conclusions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, references, and appendices support comparison, including matching material relocated between sections.

after.justification: v2 retains these experiments and adds LongLive comparisons, 60-second generation results, and a 31-participant user study.

before.justification: v1 reports original quantitative video-generation comparisons, qualitative examples, and component ablations in Tables 1–2 and Figures 3–4.

results.title: Mode Seeking meets Mean Seeking for Fast Long Video Generation

C1.justification: The central novelty, backward-stability principles, and quality-recovery claims are retained. The abstract, introduction, and conclusion extend the efficiency contribution to implemented datacenter kernels and up to 1.74x acceleration over FA4 on GB300, replacing the earlier future-work status.

C2.justification: v3 substantially expands the interpretation of efficiency limits: softmax throughput and scale computation can negate FP4 GEMM benefits, explaining PV slowdowns and hardware-dependent gains. It adds paged-attention and MXFP8 configuration limitations, training-cost tradeoffs, and a hypothesis that QAT improves robustness to quantization noise without substantially changing attention-logit distributions.

D1.justification: v3 adds detailed datacenter kernel instructions, tile and memory layouts, synchronization scheduling, quantization backends, and training-overhead accounting. It supplies code-access links and reports released kernels where v1 promised future release. Most original training hyperparameters are retained in Appendix C, relocated from Appendix B.

E1.justification: The video-generation and language-model datasets and tasks remain unchanged, including VBench, C4, Dolci-Instruct, and the retained language benchmark suites. The new kernel experiments vary hardware, tensor configurations, and precision within attention benchmarking; they do not introduce different represented data or task requirements.

E2.justification: v3 adds evaluated BF16 FlashAttention-4 comparisons in the datacenter kernel benchmarks; v1 only discussed FA4 as a future implementation basis. The original model-quality comparator sets and RTX 5090 comparisons against FlashAttention2 and SageAttention3 are retained.

E3.justification: v3 adds noncausal B200/GB300 benchmark protocols with multiple precision combinations, tensor configurations, and cosine/max/mean error measurements against BF16 (Figure 6, Tables 6–7). Figure 6 uses 32 heads on B200 and 24 on GB300. Appendix C.2 also changes the stated Qwen continued-pretraining model from 8B to 14B, aligning with the retained main text without establishing a rerun.

E4.justification: v3 adds substantial analyses of block-scaled PV slowdowns, numerical fidelity across precision combinations and tensor shapes, and training computation/memory/time overhead (Appendices B–C). These examine operating limits and implementation tradeoffs absent from v1. The original backward-design and outlier-mitigation ablations remain unchanged.

E5.justification: Neither version supplies repeated-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests for the reported comparisons. The new mean/max absolute errors quantify kernel discrepancies, not statistical uncertainty; the human-evaluation reporting is retained.

E6.justification: All numerical scores in Tables 1–4 and the original quantitative plots are unchanged. v3 adds substantial kernel results: NVFP4 QK plus FP8 PV reaches 2026 TFLOPS on B200 and 2677 TFLOPS on GB300, reported as 1.31x and 1.74x over their respective BF16 FA4 comparisons. Tables 6–7 add latency/error results, and Appendix C.1 reports approximately 1.2x–2x training slowdown.

M1.justification: v1 leaves datacenter inference kernels as future work. v3 introduces a CuTe-DSL implementation with mixed-precision QK/PV paths and a TMEM overlap schedule (Section 2.5, Appendix B). This substantially extends inference procedures, while the core QAT training algorithm remains unchanged.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained. v3 corrects grammar, terminology, and cross-references, revises the conclusion and part of related work, adds disclosures, and inserts a kernel appendix while moving the training setup to Appendix C.

P2.justification: New throughput plots, the TMEM scheduling diagram, and hardware/latency/error tables substantially expand the visual explanation of implementation and performance tradeoffs (Figure 6, Figure 10, Tables 5–7). Existing displays are rearranged; the qualitative examples remain the same and are renumbered from Figures 6–8 to Figures 7–9.

R1.justification: v3 develops the relationship to FA4 from a planned implementation basis into an implemented extension and discussion of asymmetric hardware scaling. It adds CuTe-DSL and kernel-resource citations and refines the fused-attention motivation; the broader PTQ/QAT positioning remains stable.

T1.justification: The quantization definitions, STE equations, softmax-gradient derivation, and auxiliary-output identity are retained. Corrections to indexed variables in Algorithms 1–2 and an algorithm-line reference fix notation and cross-referencing without changing the mathematical reasoning.

improvement.justification: v3 turns the explicitly deferred datacenter kernel into a documented and evaluated component, with numerical-fidelity checks and negative latency results that clarify when low precision helps or hurts. Added training-cost accounting and code-access information substantially strengthen practical validation and reproducibility information. Downstream accuracy evidence remains unchanged, and the headline datacenter gains use NVFP4 QK with FP8 PV; the improvement rests on stronger implementation evidence and clearer tradeoffs.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Attn-QAT work. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite additions and relocation.

after.justification: v3 retains those original results and adds B200/GB300 throughput measurements, kernel latency and numerical-error comparisons, and training-overhead findings.

before.justification: v1 reports original video-generation and language-model experiments, training ablations, a 99-prompt human evaluation, and RTX 5090 kernel benchmarks.

results.title: Attn-QAT: 4-Bit Attention With Quantization-Aware Training

It also qualifies transfer to SD v3.0: memorization is weaker on the reused benchmark, and the U-Net mechanistic analysis may not transfer directly. The added full-500 evaluation changes filtering within the existing benchmark; SD v3.0 changes the evaluated model rather than introducing a new dataset or task.

Newly added comparisons use narrower selections: SD v3.0 Table 9 includes RTA, Wen, and Han but explicitly excludes Ren as inapplicable, while the CFG-scale-1 comparison in Table 4 includes only Wen and no mitigation. No new mitigation baseline family is introduced.

It also evaluates all 500 prompts and introduces SD v3.0 testing on 39 prompts selected using SSCD > 0.3. These substantially expand the evaluation protocols while retaining the original filtered experiments.

E4.justification: The existing attention-block, head, timestep, positive-target, and non-memorized-input analyses are retained. New Section A.6 tests the complete CA-in-GUARD method's sensitivity to inference choices; Sections A.7.3–A.7.4 examine dependence on the similarity metric and prompt filtering. Figures 5 and 14 add qualitative case comparisons.

E5.justification: Both versions specify four generated images per prompt and report means with 95% confidence intervals for SSCD and CLIP, without FID intervals. Additional result rows use the existing uncertainty-reporting style; no changed run count, seed policy, significance test, or estimation procedure is documented.

E6.justification: The original main and detailed result tables retain their numerical values. v2 adds substantial results, including full-benchmark CA-in-GUARD SSCD scores of 0.201 and 0.137 for SD v1.4/v2.0, and SD v3.0 SSCD of 0.168 versus Han's 0.200. DINO, inference-ablation, memory, and qualitative findings are also new. These are additional evaluations, not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The GUARD guidance equation, statistical spike detector, attention-logit attenuation, and batched inference procedure are unchanged. The SD v3.0 evaluation does not document a new algorithmic component or a changed mitigation procedure.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained. v2 groups the original block/head/timestep analyses under A.5, adds subsections for new evaluations, moves the impact statement before the references, adds acknowledgements, and updates the publication footer. This is localized reorganization rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands and reorganizes the displays: the framework diagram moves into the main text, Figure 1 changes from a single row to a larger 2-by-2 arrangement, and several appendix plots are enlarged. New qualitative and robustness figures and new evaluation tables are added. The runtime table is redesigned around per-example time and memory; retained plot contents are unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds Jeon et al. (2025) and discusses its complementary probability-landscape perspective, and adds Caron et al. (2021) for DINO evaluation. It also introduces the SD v3.0 evaluation novelty claim. The broader positioning against training-time, unlearning, and inference-time approaches remains stable.

T1.justification: The mathematical method definitions and equations are retained, with no new theorem, proof, or formal assumption. The added CFG discussion restates the existing guidance equation and interprets its behavior.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the empirical support for the paper's robustness claims. The new inference ablations, DINO evaluation, and unfiltered benchmark results directly test dependencies on the default sampler configuration, similarity metric, and prompt selection that v1 left largely unresolved. Qualitative comparisons and memory measurements improve practical assessment. The SD v3.0 evidence remains limited to 39 prompts and lacks detailed transfer implementation, but the broader validation provides a substantial net improvement while preserving the original evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GUARD work. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and corresponding equations, tables, and figures can be matched despite relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds inference-setting ablations, DINO retrieval measurements, full-benchmark evaluation, SD v3.0 results, and GPU-memory measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original Stable Diffusion experiments, including memorization and image-quality measurements, component ablations, non-memorized prompt evaluation, and runtime results.

results.title: You Don’t Need All That Attention: Surgical Memorization Mitigation in Text-to-Image Diffusion Models

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction add the claim that the same pipeline generalizes to MNIST classification beyond robotics. The three principal contributions and the existing architecture-generation and robotic-control claims remain intact.

C2.justification: New discussion argues that the performance advantage persists beyond top-10 selection and connects task tolerances to weight-generation precision. Appendix C interprets permutation failure as dependence on spatial ordering; Appendix H acknowledges the current input-scale constraint requiring PCA. These refine the existing account without replacing it, and Section 7's limitations remain substantively unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 documents MNIST's training-split PCA reduction from 784 to 32 dimensions and network filtering, and newly specifies robotics success tolerances. Existing dataset-generation and diffusion hyperparameters are retained in relocated Tables 7 and 8; the PDFs do not establish changes to those settings.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates robotic control on three ManiSkill3 tasks. v2 retains these and adds MNIST classification with inputs reduced to 32 dimensions by PCA, substantially extending empirical coverage into supervised image classification (Appendix H).

E2.justification: Table 2 retains SANE and D2NWG for both seen and unseen architectures, and the alignment comparison retains GHN and SGD. Added analyses reuse existing comparison methods; the permutation condition is an ablation of NNiT.

E3.justification: v2 substantially extends evaluation with CKA measurements, function-preserving permutation controls, 80-policy mean and worst-architecture summaries, and MNIST accuracy evaluation using PCA fitted on the training split. The original 64/8 architecture split, 50-episode evaluation, and top-10-from-100 protocol remain stated. The relationship between the new 80-policy analysis and that 100-sample protocol is unexplained.

E4.justification: New Appendix C tests representational diversity and whether destroying alignment prevents successful generation. Appendix F examines selection effects through unselected and worst-architecture performance, while Appendix I quantifies architecture diversity under unconditional sampling. These substantially extend v1's heatmaps, parameter-distance analyses, and illustrative rollouts.

E5.justification: The existing seed counts and uncertainty reporting remain unchanged. New CKA entries use the already present mean-plus/minus format without introducing a defined uncertainty estimator, confidence interval, significance test, or additional replication protocol. Generated-policy counts concern evaluation sampling rather than repeated training runs.

E6.justification: Tables 1–4 retain their results. New Table 9 reports NNiT mean success of 78.8%, 74.7%, and 54.9% versus D2NWG's 15.6%, 60.0%, and 12.2% on PickCube, PushCube, and StackCubeEasy. Additional findings include the permutation ablation's 78.8%-to-0% contrast, CKA scores, 96.1% mean MNIST accuracy, and 53 unique architectures among 100 joint samples. These are added results, not improvements to the retained scores.

M1.justification: The GHN/CNN weight generator, patch tokenization, architecture tokens, transformer backbone, MoNL objective, and inference procedure remain unchanged. MNIST applies the existing pipeline to another task; the permutation experiment ablates its training data.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized language and heading edits, adds acknowledgements and appendix cross-references, and reorganizes existing supplementary sections. MoNL moves earlier, dataset generation moves later, and implementation details become a separate appendix. The main narrative is largely preserved.

P2.justification: v2 adds the CKA and full-distribution tables, relocates existing appendix displays, and swaps the numbering of the anchoring heatmaps and diversity histograms. The histogram display is more compact, while existing diagrams, heatmaps, rollouts, and main result-table structures are retained.

R1.justification: The reference lists contain the same works, and the substantive positioning relative to weight-generation methods, GHNs, and diffusion transformers is retained.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation and Equations 1–5 are substantively unchanged. The MoNL derivation moves from Appendix C to Appendix A. New empirical analyses introduce no theorem, proof, or revised formal assumption.

improvement.justification: v1 supported alignment mainly through visualizations and parameter diversity, and emphasized selected top-10 performance. v2 adds a controlled permutation ablation, representational-diversity evidence, and unselected and worst-architecture results (Appendices C and F), substantially strengthening support for the central mechanism and making performance reporting more informative. MNIST provides additional cross-domain evidence. The unexplained 80-versus-100 sampling relationship and absence of MNIST comparators limit completeness, but do not outweigh these substantial evidentiary gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same NNiT work and contain readable main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices. Retained material can be matched despite appendix reorganization and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds permutation, representational-similarity, performance-distribution, MNIST classification, and joint-sampling analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original ManiSkill3 policy-generation experiments, GHN-versus-SGD comparisons, weight-diversity analyses, and simulated policy rollouts.

results.title: NNiT: Width-Agnostic Neural Network Generation with Structurally Aligned Weight Spaces

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution statements and conclusion retain the same claims about projection energy, dual-subspace LoDA, GAO, closed-form recalibration and empirical superiority. The appendix adds evidence and extensions without revising those headline claims.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive explanations of hyperparameter failure regimes, rank saturation and the larger gains on smaller models. Appendix B.4 connects GAO's resistance to future interference to a conditional gradient-cone model, while C.3 discusses preservation of pretrained CLIP representations. These extend v1's existing sharing-versus-isolation interpretation.

D1.justification: Algorithm 1 newly documents feature caching, zero initialization, cumulative-statistic updates and disabling the isolated branch on the first task. Appendix C.3 explains CLIP prototype construction and score fusion. The existing optimizer, training budget and hardware disclosures remain; the new fusion coefficient alpha is not assigned a value.

E1.justification: V2 retains the five original downstream datasets and adds UCF101 action classification, Aircraft recognition and Cars recognition in Tables 8–9. These extend the represented tasks and visual categories beyond the original evaluation; changing pretrained backbones is assessed separately under E3.

E2.justification: Tables 8–9 introduce evaluated comparators including CoOp, ZS-CLIP, SimpleCIL, RAPF and PROOF without experience replay. Table 10 adds LAE and HiDe-Prompt, while Table 7 expands the overhead comparison with CODA, SLCA and SSIAT. Original comparison memberships remain intact; Seq-LoRA corresponds to the existing sequential LoRA baseline.

E3.justification: The original settings remain, while new evaluations introduce LAION-400M-pretrained CLIP, alternative initial/incremental class splits, DINO/iBOT initialization, different ViT sizes, rank and hyperparameter sweeps, and two-dimensional loss-plane testing. One new protocol is internally ambiguous: Appendix C.3 specifies a 100-class UCF subset, but Table 8 includes a B100 Inc20 setting.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained component and merging ablations, v2 adds GAO loss trajectories, broader hyperparameter sensitivity, rank/resource analysis, and comparisons across pretraining methods and model sizes. Figures 11–12 examine both general and isolated update directions in two-dimensional loss landscapes, extending v1's one-dimensional general-direction analysis.

E5.justification: The retained experiments preserve their three-seed averaging and uncertainty entries. Figure 8 extends the existing practice with three-seed means and error bars. No increased run count, new uncertainty-estimation procedure, confidence interval or significance test is reported.

E6.justification: Tables 1–6 retain their numerical results, while Tables 7–10 and Figures 7–12 add substantial new findings. For example, Table 10 newly reports LoDA last accuracies of 73.66 with DINO and 76.83 with iBOT. An added entry is inconsistent: Table 7 gives VPT-NSP 75.69 versus 76.13 in retained Table 6 under the same stated 20S-ImageNetR setting.

M1.justification: The original LoDA procedure remains unchanged, but Appendix C.3 introduces a substantial CLIP adaptation. It combines a frozen CLIP model with a prototypical classifier and a separately LoDA-tuned model trained with an image–text matching loss. Prediction uses weighted score fusion between both models in Eq. C.3.1, extending the original single-backbone inference procedure.

P1.justification: The existing narrative, section order, abstract and conclusion are retained. V2 organizes new material into Appendices A–C, repairs the unresolved 'Appx.??' reference to 'Appx.B.2', and updates the date. There is no extensive rewriting or reorganization of the existing text.

P2.justification: V2 adds the staged Algorithm 1 display, Tables 7–10 and Figures 7–12, including sensitivity plots, model-size comparisons and loss-landscape panels. Existing main-text displays are largely retained; Figure 4 corrects update labels to include w_G. The new visual evidence substantially expands the presentation.

R1.justification: Section 2 and the original novelty positioning remain unchanged. The appendix adds focused positioning against CLIP prompt learning, head adaptation and feature replay, with additional references for CLIP, SimpleCIL, RAPF, PROOF, self-supervised pretraining and the new datasets.

T1.justification: Appendix B adds proofs of Theorems 3.1 and 3.3 and a derivation of the general-subspace solution in Eq. 4. Section B.4 additionally develops a gradient-alignment expansion and a future-loss bound using a newly stated gradient-cone assumption with bounded residual. These substantially expand the formal analysis.

improvement.justification: Appendices A–C address substantial gaps in v1 by supplying missing derivations, making the training pipeline explicit, and extending limited sensitivity and backbone evidence with controlled analyses. This materially improves the method's inspectability and empirical support. New reporting inconsistencies remain, including the VPT-NSP discrepancy between Tables 6–7 and the UCF split mismatch, and the GAO argument is conditional on its cone assumption. These limitations temper, but do not outweigh, the substantial gains in explanation and validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LoDA research work and provide readable text, equations, tables and figures. V1 ends after its references; v2 retains the main study and adds Appendices A–C. The added appendix is a substantive addition, not an extraction gap.

after.justification: V2 retains those experiments and adds original sensitivity studies, CLIP evaluations, backbone and model-size comparisons, and loss-landscape analyses in its appendices.

before.justification: V1 reports original continual-learning experiments on five datasets, component ablations, projection-energy analyses and computational comparisons in Tables 1–6 and Figures 3–6.

results.title: Task-Driven Subspace Decomposition for Knowledge Sharing and Isolation in LoRA-based Continual Learning

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction recast the contribution as an operational, answer-level uncertainty framework. The claim of independent reasoning superiority over single-agent RL is replaced by a claim about post-debate performance and peer-information utilization. This materially narrows what the framework and training results are claimed to establish.

C2.justification: v2 expands the earlier proxy caveats, distinguishing latent beliefs, answer-level diagnostics, and training signals. It explicitly limits the heterogeneity theorem to information potential, acknowledges that the stronger agent is not uniformly improved, and discusses compatible model pairings. Appendix J adds substantive limits concerning mathematical tasks, answer equivalence, and extension beyond exact-match verification.

D1.justification: v2 adds a source-code location, documents the Single-GRPO training budget and AIME length exceptions, and changes the computational-resources training group size from 16 to five, matching Table 2 in both versions. Existing pseudocode, prompts, hardware information, and most hyperparameters are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions train on MATH and evaluate on MATH500, GSM8K, AMC23, AIME24, and AIME25. The homogeneous and heterogeneous Qwen/Llama diagnostic coverage is retained. The new ablations use existing tasks and model pairings.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains Zero-Shot MAD and Standard IPPO. New Table 3 adds independently trained Single-GRPO Pair agents and Intrinsic-only and NLL-only variants, substantially extending the comparisons needed to distinguish debate co-training from standalone training and individual uncertainty components.

E3.justification: For AIME, v2 increases response/prompt limits from the previously stated 2,048/5,120 tokens to 4,096/9,216, materially changing evaluation conditions. The new Single-GRPO baseline receives 15 training epochs versus UMAD's retained two. Section 3.2 also changes the stated rollout count from 16 to five, although Appendix D.5 retains 16; the actual diagnostic sampling protocol remains inconsistent.

E4.justification: New Appendix E.1 and Table 3 separately test the intrinsic reward and NLL weighting and examine whether standalone GRPO training explains the gains. Conversely, v1's two dialogue case studies illustrating homogeneous failure and heterogeneous success are removed. The existing uncertainty trajectories, flipping analysis, and longer-debate evaluation remain.

E5.justification: v1's Table 1 provides point estimates without evaluation seed counts or uncertainty estimates. v2 adds uncertainty throughout Table 1 and specifies five evaluation seeds, while Table 3 reports three-seed means and standard deviations. Identical UMAD entries appear in both tables despite these differing seed descriptions, leaving their statistical provenance unclear.

E6.justification: Table 1 substantially revises AIME results and heterogeneous UMAD scores. At T=5, UMAD's heterogeneous agent averages change from 50.6/57.7 to 66.5/65.8; the stronger agent now trails IPPO's 67.4 average. Table 3 adds component and GRPO comparison results. These are revised reports under changed AIME budgets and seed reporting, not demonstrated same-setting performance improvements.

M1.justification: UMAD retains the same GRPO-based training procedure, standardized NLL advantage weighting, and peer-correctness intrinsic reward. Algorithm 2 is unchanged. The revised descriptions of these signals as operational proxies do not establish a procedural change.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, theoretical exposition, method explanation, and results discussion are extensively rewritten. Related work is condensed in the main text and reorganized into Appendix A; limitations move from Section 8 to Appendix J. Dialogue examples are removed, an ablation appendix is introduced, and author/publication information is updated.

P2.justification: Table 1 is regrouped by debate round and gains comparison coloring and an expanded caption; Table 3 is added and the dialogue-example boxes disappear. All six figures retain the same underlying graphics, with localized caption and placement changes. The overall visual format remains stable.

R1.justification: v2 adds discussion of identity-aware debate, ModeX, and Tang et al.'s uncertainty-driven policy optimization, plus a Llama reference. It removes the Kadavath and Tomov references and the earlier first-work assertion. Most other bibliography changes concern the same works' publication metadata; the principal research positioning remains uncertainty analysis coupled with MARL.

T1.justification: v1's Theorem 3.3 claims a marginal information-gain ordering from a conditional novelty assumption, while its proof compares message pairs. v2 replaces it with homogeneous saturation Assumption 3.3 and Theorem 3.4, explicitly bounding the joint-information advantage by Delta, with a matching proof in Appendix B.3. The earlier individual-agent entropy/KL derivation is also removed.

improvement.justification: v2 corrects the central heterogeneity theorem's statement–proof mismatch, better distinguishes operational proxies from Bayesian quantities, and adds previously missing component and standalone-RL controls in Table 3. These changes substantially strengthen the paper's theoretical validity and empirical argument. Conflicting seed and rollout descriptions still limit reproducibility, and dialogue examples are lost, but these drawbacks do not outweigh the substantive improvements.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same UMAD research. Their main text, appendices, equations, algorithms, tables, and figures are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial rewriting and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical analyses, revises Table 1 results, and adds component ablations and a Single-GRPO Pair comparison in Table 3.

before.justification: v1 reports original debate experiments, uncertainty and answer-flipping analyses, and UMAD training results, including Table 1 and Figures 1–6.

results.title: Epistemic Gain, Aleatoric Cost: Uncertainty Decomposition in Multi-Agent Debate for Math Reasoning

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims about universal robustness asymmetry, its memorization connection, RA-Det, and detection superiority. The abstract's 7.81% improvement claim is unchanged; additional experiments support existing claims rather than redefine them.

C2.justification: Appendix D.2 reclassifies epoch-based evidence as a training-stage trend rather than a validated monotonic memorization proxy and interprets the new AMS associations as more direct support. V2 also discusses training-source independence, learned-probe necessity, inference overhead, and the limitations of single-generator training for real-world distributions. However, a retained paragraph and Figure 6's caption still describe epochs as a memorization proxy.

D1.justification: Appendix A newly identifies LSUN and AIGIBench/GenImage provenance and gives training-source sample counts. The stated hardware changes from four NVIDIA 4090 GPUs to eight H200 GPUs, and Table 5 reports compute, parameters, memory, and latency. Core training hyperparameters and the code link remain unchanged; the hardware revision alone does not establish reruns.

E1.justification: Table 4 adds seven generator columns: SDXL, SDv3.5, FLUX, FLUX1-dev, MJ-v6, Infinity, and VAR. This extends evaluation to newer synthesis systems and autoregressive generation. Appendix A also introduces diffusion-source and mixed-source training using SDv1.4 data from AIGIBench/GenImage. The original benchmark and CelebA-HQ study remain.

E2.justification: C2P-CLIP, previously discussed only in related work, becomes an evaluated efficiency comparator alongside UniFD in v2 Table 5. The detector membership in Table 1 and the JPEG/blur comparisons is unchanged.

E3.justification: V2 adds SDv1.4-only training with 52,922 real/72,000 fake images and mixed-source training with 72,000/72,000, alongside the retained ProGAN 360,000/360,000 setting. It introduces fixed-probe controls, a five-value margin sweep, AMS-based evaluation, and matched-hardware efficiency measurements. Appendix D.2 also changes the stated epoch-analysis aggregation from epsilon values generally to small-epsilon values; the PDFs do not establish that the retained plots were recomputed.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained backbone, loss, branch, and post-processing analyses, v2 tests learned probing against Gaussian noise, Gaussian blur, and resize residuals; examines margin sensitivity and training-source dependence; and analyzes computational cost. Appendix D.2 adds AMS-based validation of the memorization relationship, addressing a question previously investigated only through training epochs.

E5.justification: V1 Figure 6 already reports linear fits with slopes and R-squared values. V2 applies this estimation approach to AMS in Table 6, adding point-estimate results rather than a new uncertainty-reporting practice. Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: Table 1 and the retained ablation scores are unchanged, including RA-Det's 93.47% ACC/97.00% AP. V2 adds substantial results: for example, ProGAN-trained RA-Det scores 57.19%/61.50% on FLUX in Table 4, fixed-probe variants achieve 86.11–87.07% ACC in Table 3, and AMS regressions have positive slopes with R-squared values of 0.59–0.73. Efficiency results are new, and Figure 2 replaces the CLIP similarity distribution.

M1.justification: The frozen encoder, conditional-UNet probing module, semantic/discrepancy/residual branches, fusion, and composite loss remain unchanged. Alternative probes and contrastive margins are experimental controls, not revisions to the proposed detector.

P1.justification: The overall narrative and most introductory, methodological, theoretical, and concluding text remain intact. V2 locally rewrites ablation, robustness, and epoch-validation discussions; adds generality and efficiency subsections, acknowledgements, and an impact statement; updates the publication header; and reorganizes the appendices around the additions.

P2.justification: V2 adds four tables covering training-source summaries, detailed generator results, efficiency, and AMS regression, and expands/regroups the original ablation table. Figure 2 replaces the CLIP histogram and fixes panel labels; Figure 4 gains a detailed caption. Figures 5 and 6 are relocated, with their original plotted results retained.

R1.justification: V2 adds citations for new generators and data sources, including Infinity, VAR, SDXL, FLUX, LSUN, AIGIBench, and GenImage. The appearance-versus-behavior positioning remains intact. Publication updates to existing references and consolidation of the duplicated Hounie citation do not represent newly introduced works.

T1.justification: V2 removes Appendix B.2's explicit inequality asserting that SIDE divergence strictly decreases with training epochs and withdraws its claimed theoretical justification. The central definitions, Assumption 4.1, Lemma 4.2, Theorem 4.3, and their proofs remain unchanged in Section 4 and the relocated Appendix D.1.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation of the central mechanism: v1 lacked fixed-probe controls and relied on an asserted epoch-to-memorization relationship; v2 adds probing controls and AMS-based evidence. Training-source and contemporary-generator tests, together with measured computational costs, also improve assessment of applicability. These address important evidential gaps. The gains are tempered by Table 4's unclear averaging scope and the contradictory epoch-proxy wording retained in Figure 6.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RA-Det work. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support comparison. The original appendices are retained as Appendices C and D in v2, alongside new material.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds training-source comparisons, recent-generator evaluations, further ablations, efficiency measurements, and AMS-based memorization analysis.

before.justification: V1 reports original cross-generator detection results, component ablations, JPEG/blur robustness experiments, and DDPM feature-shift experiments in Appendix B.

results.title: RA-Det: Towards Universal Detection of AI-Generated Images via Robustness Asymmetry

C1.justification: The benchmark and method contributions and the 10-of-13-task claim remain. V2 narrows the novelty assertion to systematic study of an interactive agent task, presents FT-Agent as a strong initial baseline, and removes the conclusion's claim that it uniquely achieves nonzero AIME accuracy.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly states that the constrained Manual SFT comparison is not an expert upper bound and limits model-generalization conclusions to tested 3B/7B settings. It interprets the extended-budget result as evidence of a diagnostic bottleneck. Existing causal-reasoning and planning limitations remain.

D1.justification: V2 adds an implementation repository link and the AIME judge prompt, and clarifies per-method sample budgets, Manual SFT's lack of LLM assistance, and OpenHands' shared wrappers. Appendix A.5 corrects the AIME split prose to 15/15, matching v1's Table 1 rather than establishing a changed split.

E1.justification: Table 1 and Appendix A retain the same 13 tasks, five domains, and training/evaluation resources. The additional comparisons reuse the existing five-task ablation subset; no new dataset or task scenario is evaluated.

E2.justification: V2 substantially expands the focused comparisons with Codex using GPT-5.2, Claude Code using Sonnet-4.6-thinking, and LLM-assisted Manual SFT (Tables 4 and 6). The original base-model, Manual SFT, and OpenHands comparisons remain.

E3.justification: V2 adds a 24-hour OpenHands setting and two open-source planner configurations while retaining the main 12-hour, 2,000-sample protocol. Appendix A.1.1 revises AIME's stated evaluator from MATHVerify to symbolic verification with a GPT-5 fallback; this establishes a reporting revision, without establishing that earlier experiments were rescored.

E4.justification: V2 substantially broadens analyses of comparison fairness and generality: open-source planner sensitivity, the effect of giving manual practitioners LLM assistance, and whether doubling OpenHands' time budget improves AIME performance (Figure 3b; Appendices B.1.3 and B.4). Existing data-scaling, target-size, and failure-case analyses remain.

E5.justification: V1 reports point scores without run counts or uncertainty estimates. V2 reports FT-Agent mean and standard deviation over three independent initializations for test and validation results (Tables 2 and 11), explicitly identifies comparison baselines as single-run results, and reports two runs for the extended-budget check.

E6.justification: Table 2 replaces FT-Agent point estimates with three-run summaries: Visualization changes from 36.00 to 29.33±6.11 and PI4PC from 44.00 to 49.00±4.36; validation summaries also change. New results include frontier-agent/backbone scores, 20.00% AIME accuracy for assisted Manual SFT, and no improvement from the extended OpenHands budget. These are new or aggregated results, not demonstrated improvements to the method.

M1.justification: The three-stage FT-Agent procedure, experience and best-configuration tracking, progressive validation, and prompt architecture remain unchanged (Section 3.2; Appendix G). Added planning backbones test the same procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract, conclusion, and selected experimental and baseline paragraphs are rewritten. Focused-comparison and evaluator subsections and a conflict-of-interest disclosure are added, while the overall section order and most method and appendix prose are preserved.

P2.justification: V2 adds comparison Tables 4 and 6, redraws Figure 3 with additional planner bars and revised labels, and reformats the main and validation tables to accommodate uncertainty reporting. Other figures and appendix tables are largely retained with relocation and renumbering.

R1.justification: Section 5 adds Gome, cited as Zhang et al. (2026), and briefly discusses diagnostic reasoning beyond scalar-score tree search. V2 also refines its novelty positioning around systematic interactive fine-tuning evaluation; the existing related-work categories and other cited works remain.

T1.justification: The task objective, proposal equation, best-configuration update, and split-allocation formula are retained. Repeating the existing split formula in the main text adds no mathematical definition, assumption, derivation, or proof.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the evidence behind v1's broad superiority claims through FT-Agent uncertainty reporting, frontier-agent and assisted-human comparisons, and budget checks, while narrowing conclusions accordingly. Evaluator and baseline clarifications also improve transparency. Single-run comparators and older point estimates retained in Appendix C remain limitations, but the gains substantially improve the evaluation's credibility.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FT-Dojo/FT-Agent study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A-G are readable, and retained content can be matched across additions, relocation, and renumbering.

after.justification: v2.pdf reports original benchmark experiments, three-run FT-Agent statistics, additional agent and assisted-human comparisons, and a budget-sensitivity experiment.

before.justification: v1.pdf reports original fine-tuning experiments across 13 tasks, validation/test results, ablations, and agent decision traces.

results.title: FT-Dojo: Towards Autonomous LLM Fine-Tuning with Language Agents

C1.justification: The central claims about exponential context savings and optimality among recursive agentic systems remain. The abstract and conclusion replace their SAT-focused emphasis on a 3B model outperforming frontier LLMs with claims spanning SAT fine-tuning and Go training from scratch. The introduction additionally claims improved length generalization against matched Go baselines.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly distinguishes long computation from long-input access, using Needle-in-a-Haystack to explain an applicability boundary. It acknowledges storage and transfer costs outside the local-space measure and warns that correct Go labels can arise through shortcuts or invalid traces. Conversely, v1's explicit question-preservation limitation for shallow recursion is reduced to an appendix pointer without the same explanation.

D1.justification: New Appendix C documents Go trace generation and filtering, trace renderings, data splits, evaluation subsets, architecture, optimizer settings, precision, and attention masks. Section 5 adds a code-repository pointer and explains that scaffold-inserted tokens are excluded from the training loss. These substantially expand reproducibility information; Appendix B's SAT settings remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates SAT only. v2 retains SAT and adds 4x4 placement-Go position evaluation using exact-solver proof traces, with IID and longer-search test scenarios. Appendix C restricts supervision to finite traces querying Win/Lose states. This substantially expands the evaluated domain and reasoning requirements.

E2.justification: The SAT comparator roster in Table 1 is unchanged. v2 adds trained CoT and PENCIL comparators for Go, using the same small Transformer and proof supervision as the recursive model. These introduce direct comparisons against flat reasoning and single-context compression that were not experimentally evaluated this way in v1.

E3.justification: The SAT protocol is unchanged. The new Go protocol matches 3.18M-parameter models and 64K training updates, introduces IID and length-selected splits, and evaluates teacher-forced trace exact match on 1K roots per split, IID rollout metrics on 256 roots, and context lengths on 10K roots. Sections 5.2 and C.4 describe strict rollout validation, although the appendix does not explicitly enumerate the main text's child-label and parent-decision checks.

E4.justification: v2 adds length-OOD tests of extrapolation to longer searches, training-convergence comparisons in Figure 3, and rollout-validity diagnostics distinguishing correct binary answers from valid reasoning traces. It also compares context requirements across the three Go methods. The existing SAT context-efficiency analysis is retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental run or seed counts, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The new Go learning curves and accuracy entries do not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: SAT Table 1 is unchanged, including recursive-model accuracies of 98%, 95%, and 64%. Appendix D adds cross-size and out-of-distribution robustness tests and runtime analyses. These investigate substantial additional questions beyond v1's retained architectural and transfer ablations.

For example, Table 10 reports MaxClique sizes of 2.82 ± 0.01 for fully fine-tuned unified-MDS transfer and 4.34 ± 0.01 for MTL with graph statistics. Further additions quantify size transfer, inference times, and DIMACS performance.

M1.justification: Section 3.1 changes the stated encoder activation from leaky ReLU to GELU, also specified in v2's Table 8. The GCON backbone approach, objectives, and transfer framework remain intact. Expanded decoder documentation does not establish an additional procedural change.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and most prose remain. v2 consolidates the former related-work appendix into Section 2, clarifies reducibility versus transferability, edits the abstract and results discussion, and adds an impact statement. P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 8–15 and Algorithm 1, substantially expanding the presentation of settings, reduction comparisons, generalization results, and runtimes. Figure 1 is enlarged and several existing tables move with the revised layout. Figure 2 and the original numerical tables retain their substantive displays.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the visual presentation with a full-width method diagram, prompt-decomposition and diagnostic tables, a two-panel KL-drift illustration, and additional boxed examples. Universal-head filtering also remains. Additional implementation explanations and alternative-ablation experiments do not establish a revised identification method.

P1.justification: The seven-section main structure and much existing prose remain. Local revisions qualify the abstract and conclusion, consolidate related-work headings, separate the Results subsection and expand discussion subsections. Appendix A becomes a procedural guide, and an impact statement and conference header are added.

The retained WMDP plots are resized, arranged side by side and renumbered; original appendix tables are retained under new numbers.

The added explanation limiting approximate additivity to task-specific heads clarifies the existing assumption; no new formal result, proof or substantive derivation appears.

These defects limit precision but do not outweigh the substantial gains.
