Shaded uncertainty bands already appear in v1. v2 introduces no new stated uncertainty-estimation procedure, significance test or increased run count.

E6.justification: All matched entries in the original ROC-AUC and single-table result tables remain unchanged. v2 adds extensive results for stronger baselines, PR-AUC, adaptation, support scaling and ablations; Table 17 reports average ROC-AUC of 0.7342 for target-task fine-tuning and 0.7261 for cross-task fine-tuning under those new conditions. Efficiency reporting also changes, including RDB-PFN's parameter count from 2.64M to 0.7M while retaining its 34-second timing.

M1.justification: Section 5.1.3 changes the specified feature decoder from Gaussian/Softmax sampling to clipping/normalization and discretization/binning. Appendix D.2 adds optional gradient adaptation and chunked-support probability averaging. The three-stage prior and main Transformer architecture remain; revised parameter counts alone do not establish an architecture replacement.

P1.justification: Targeted paragraph rewrites clarify assumptions, attention terminology, efficiency and transfer interpretations, and remove duplicated implementation prose. Section 7 becomes Conclusion and Limitations, and a new experimental Appendix D precedes the retained, renumbered proof and raw-results appendices. The main narrative structure remains recognizable.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is redrawn with revised resource values and axis labels; Figure 6 becomes a two-panel baseline comparison. New Figures 8–10 display PR-AUC, adaptation, context scaling and ablations. Table 4 and Tables 12–30 add substantial new displays, while existing relational result tables gain comparator rows. These exceed simple relocation or renumbering.

R1.justification: The bibliography is unchanged. Sections 6.1 and B.3 refine positioning relative to Griffin and RT by explicitly treating them as contextual relational references and distinguishing RT's local graph-conditioned label access from RDB-PFN's fixed global support. The broader positioning against real-data pretraining and privacy-oriented generators remains.

T1.justification: The completeness and universality definitions, assumptions, theorems and proofs are unchanged after matching v1 Appendix D to v2 Appendix E. Assumption 4.2 replaces generic value/rest notation with explicit attribute and conditioning notation without changing the locality condition.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical scrutiny of the central design choices through component and backbone ablations, DFS sensitivity, stronger baselines and PR-AUC checks, addressing important gaps in v1's evidence. Clearer protocol boundaries and more accurate speedup summaries also improve interpretation. The reduced 20k-RDB ablation budget limits conclusions about the full training pipeline, but the added controls and explicit limitations provide a substantial overall quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RDB-PFN study and provide readable text, equations, figures, tables and appendices. Existing proofs and experiments can be matched despite appendix renumbering and added analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds stronger-baseline comparisons, PR-AUC evaluation, adaptation experiments, context scaling and component ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on 19 relational prediction tasks and 23 single-table datasets, including model comparisons, pretraining comparisons and inference timing.

results.title: Relational In-Context Learning via Synthetic Pre-training with Structural Prior

C1.justification: The introduction and conclusion now claim demonstrated advantage-aware extensibility while preserving log-space symmetry, replacing a future direction in v1. The central Gaussian-weighting, replay-utilization and theoretical-guarantee claims remain.

C2.justification: Section 4.3 replaces the claim that vanishing sigma recovers a purely on-policy gradient with a conservative, biased near-on-policy interpretation. Advantage-sign agnosticism becomes a limitation addressed through an evaluated variant, with environment-specific gains discussed in Appendix D.3. Physical-robot validation remains future work.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-repository link in the abstract, reports explicit advantage-dependent scale pairs and clarifies shared GAE construction. Existing hardware, optimizer, learning rates and Meta-World/LIBERO training configurations remain. Detailed configurations for the new control benchmarks are not supplied.

E1.justification: v2 expands Meta-World evaluation from three displayed tasks to a ten-task study and adds four Classic Control tasks and ten MuJoCo tasks in Appendix D. These substantially broaden discrete and continuous control coverage; LIBERO and GridWorld remain.

E2.justification: PPO/PPO-Clip, SAPO and No-Clip retain their roles in the corresponding original comparisons. The added benchmarks reuse PPO and SAPO. Advantage-Aware GIPO is introduced as a proposed-method variant and ablation, rather than a new baseline.

E3.justification: v2 adds cross-task evaluation using normalized-score IQM, final training-rollout returns for Classic Control, and comparisons across unified and advantage-dependent damping configurations. Sections 3.4, 4.4 and C.1 also revise V-trace descriptions toward GAE. Because v1 already specified GAE in C.2, this establishes a reporting revision, not that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Tables 1, 6 and 7 add substantive comparisons of unified versus advantage-aware damping, including targeted HalfCheetah, Ant and Hopper ablations addressing v1's stated future direction. Existing utilization diagnostics, GridWorld analysis and unified-scale sensitivity remain. v1's brief description of a V-trace-combination check is removed.

E5.justification: v1 explicitly presents single-run learning curves; its regime table reports variation across tasks. v2 adds five-seed evaluations, including 400 Meta-World training runs, and reports seed-level means and standard deviations in Tables 3, 5 and 6. Original curves remain single-run, and the new IQM rankings have no confidence intervals.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive numerical results. Table 1 reports Meta-World IQM scores of 0.730 for GIPO (1.0, 1.0), 0.412 for SAPO and 0.180 for PPO; Table 7 reports MuJoCo scores of 0.606, 0.413 and 0.119 for its leading GIPO configuration, SAPO and PPO. These are newly reported evaluations. Original figures and regime statistics remain unchanged; v1's qualitative V-trace-combination finding is omitted.

M1.justification: v2 introduces an Advantage-Aware GIPO variant that selects different Gaussian damping scales for positive and negative advantages, such as sigma_neg = 0.5 × sigma_pos. This changes sample weighting but is a limited extension of the retained Gaussian surrogate and Algorithm 1.

P1.justification: Changes include localized contribution and conclusion rewrites, a compressed related-work opening, an experiment roadmap, Appendix D, and updated author, affiliation and publication text. Section 6.2 also corrects Figure 2's orientation description. The existing narrative and section order remain largely intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds substantial tabular presentation through aggregate rankings, per-task return tables and an ablation table, numbered 1 and 3–7. The original regime table becomes Table 2. All nine original figures are retained, with several relocated through appendix reflow and new page breaks.

R1.justification: v2 adds the GAE citation and replaces the criticism that SAPO's advantage asymmetry lacks justification with a comparison emphasizing GIPO's compatible advantage-aware weighting and log-space symmetry. TRPO, ACER and SCAPPO reference updates concern already cited works.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions, performance and concentration bounds, and Appendix B derivations are retained. No new formal result or proof accompanies the advantage-aware extension; the revised small-sigma discussion concerns interpretation.

improvement.justification: The five-seed, ten-task Meta-World study and seed-level variability reported across additional control tasks substantially strengthen v1's predominantly single-run empirical support. The advantage-aware ablations also directly investigate a previously unresolved limitation. New benchmark settings and score normalization remain underspecified, IQM confidence intervals are absent, and LIBERO remains single-run. These limitations temper the claims, but the broader replicated evidence provides a substantial overall quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GIPO research. Their complete text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable matching, including the additional Appendix D in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds five-seed Meta-World, Classic Control and MuJoCo evaluations, including advantage-aware ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original Meta-World and LIBERO training results, GridWorld bias–variance calculations and replay-utilization diagnostics in Appendix C.

results.title: GIPO: Gaussian Importance Sampling Policy Optimization

C1.justification: The central contributions and instructed-versus-open performance gap remain. However, v2 corrects v1's introductory claim of single-digit alignment even with oracle support: below 8% is now explicitly restricted to Direct mode, while oracle-supported alignment reaches 20.6%. This materially qualifies the headline claim without redefining the contribution.

C2.justification: The new Limitations section explicitly addresses small-sample comparisons, uneven language coverage, valid refactorings outside the original human choice, and possible LLM-construction bias. Appendix A.6 also uses the new control to favor poorer candidate-plan quality over judge bias as an explanation for Sonnet's Multiplan decline. These substantially expand the boundaries and interpretation of the evaluation.

D1.justification: v2 identifies Gemini 3.1 Pro for rule filtering, documents MiniMax's configuration, and reports releasing 150 additional commits with descriptions and rule sets. Most environment specifications and prompts are retained. Conversely, Section 4.1 drops the explicit harness-version listing, including Qwen Code v0.6.2.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate 100 refactoring instances from 87 repositories across the same six programming-language categories and the same tracks. The language breakdown analyzes retained coverage. v2 explicitly distinguishes its additional 150 released commits from the instances evaluated in the paper.

E2.justification: v2 adds MiniMax M2.7 to the four retained agents: GPT-5.2, GPT-5.1 Codex Mini, Sonnet 4.5, and Qwen3. Its results appear in the Instructed Track and all three Open Track modes, establishing an actual comparator addition.

E3.justification: The rule filter changes the scoring criteria throughout evaluation, reducing mean additive rules from 29.66 to 17.94. Section 4.1 revises the reported precision calculation and specifies filtered line sets for precision and patch size. New protocols include a 30-rule human audit and randomized six-plan judge control. These are substantive evaluation revisions; they do not establish that retained agent executions were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained mode comparisons and case studies, v2 adds an expert audit of restrictive rules, a control investigating oracle-selection bias, and performance breakdowns by language (Appendices A.3, A.6, and A.7). These substantially extend analysis of measurement validity and possible explanations for the results.

E5.justification: v1 already reports 95% confidence intervals and five test-suite calibration runs. v2 adds paired sign-flip permutation tests with 100,000 permutations and Benjamini–Hochberg correction, language-level standard errors, and Cohen's kappa for the human audit. This substantially expands statistical assessment without establishing additional repeated agent runs.

E6.justification: v2 broadly updates alignment, precision, and edit-size results and adds MiniMax and validation results. GPT-5.2 Open Track alignment changes from 7.7/14.1/19.4% to 7.9/15.1/20.6% across Direct/Plan/Multiplan; its instructed precision changes from 56.2% to 48.4% (v1 Tables 4–5; v2 Tables 5–6). These accompany revised scoring and should not be interpreted as same-setting performance gains. Some case-study scores also change.

M1.justification: Section 3.4 adds a post-generation filter that removes additive rules enforcing arbitrary implementation choices; Appendix A.3 identifies Gemini 3.1 Pro as the classifier. This extends the existing benchmark-construction method, while the refactoring agents' Direct, Plan, and Oracle Multiplan procedures remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The main text undergoes extensive rewriting and explanatory restructuring: static-rule formalization moves into Section 2.1, construction steps receive clearer organization, and the introduction and conclusion are substantially revised. A dedicated Limitations section is added. The case-study and prompt appendices remain largely intact apart from corrections and updated references.

P2.justification: v2 redraws the pipeline and rule illustrations, reformats the instance-statistics display, relocates the metric diagram, and expands result displays. Figure 8 replaces the Open Track PASS panel with alignment, changes the IFR axis range, and adds MiniMax. New tables present benchmark comparisons, the human audit, language results, and significance summaries.

R1.justification: v2 adds a structured comparison of seven prior benchmarks in Table 1 and supporting citations concerning refactoring, static analysis, code benchmarks, and the new model. Most compared benchmarks were already discussed in v1, and the positioning around large, multilingual, human-intent refactoring remains. Bibliographic updates to existing works do not constitute new research coverage.

T1.justification: Section 4.1 corrects reductive precision to intersect removed lines with rule coverage in the original repository R, rather than the patched repository. The symbolic-propagation example also corrects its witness enumeration. Most other definitions are retained or relocated, and no new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v1 acknowledges arbitrary naming requirements as a scoring concern; v2 directly addresses them through filtering and an expert audit reporting 80% agreement (Appendix A.3). Together with the corrected precision definition, controlled judge analysis, significance testing, and explicit limitations, this substantially strengthens the central evaluation's validity and interpretability. The audit remains small and the oracle control has unexecuted alternatives, while some harness-version detail is lost, but these limitations do not outweigh the gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CodeTaste and provide readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–D. Corresponding material can be matched across revisions, renumbering, and relocation.

after.justification: v2 reports original evaluations of five coding agents and adds a human rule audit, oracle-judge validation, language-level analysis, and significance tests.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of four coding agents on CodeTaste, including alignment, instruction following, functional correctness, precision, costs, and case studies.

results.title: CodeTaste: Can LLMs Generate Human-Level Code Refactorings?

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same headline contributions: perfect HSL equivariance through double-cover lifting, improved robustness and predictive performance, and applicability to RGB and scale transformations. The added experiments do not replace these core contribution statements.

C2.justification: Beyond v1's computational-cost, large-cardinality, and lifting-degeneracy discussions, v3 explains two substantive applicability boundaries. Invariant classification pooling can suppress label-relevant color, while reduced filter width can hurt performance without sufficient distribution shift. Section 5.5 connects these mechanisms to the new experiments and explicitly identifies the conditions favoring T3CEN.

D1.justification: v3 adds measured memory and training throughput, identifying nvidia-smi and tqdm and specifying that the first 100 iterations are discarded before averaging the next 100. It also supplies training budgets for the new failure-condition experiments. Existing hardware descriptions and the main hyperparameter table remain essentially unchanged; the new experiments are not documented comprehensively.

E1.justification: v3 adds KUTomaData tomato-ripeness classification, where absolute color predicts the label, and controlled MNIST scenarios with identical or mildly shifted train-test hue distributions. These extend evaluation to important task conditions beyond v1's disjoint-hue MNIST experiment and nuisance-color robustness emphasis. Existing dataset coverage is retained.

E2.justification: Compared with v1 Table 5, v3 Table 6 adds ResNet-AugMix and ResNet-DeepAug to both saturation and luminance comparisons, and Planckian jitter, labeled ResNet-Plackian, to saturation comparisons. This substantially expands evaluated augmentation alternatives across six datasets. The existing ResNet-aug row is renamed ResNet-Jitter, rather than constituting another added comparator.

E3.justification: Appendix D.6 changes the reported Camelyon17 train/validation/test hospitals from 1,2,3/4/5 to 0,3,4/2/1; unchanged result values do not establish reruns. New protocols include 200-epoch KUTomaData training, 1,000-iteration MNIST comparisons at 0, 5, 10, and 15 degrees of shift, and ResNet18 resource measurements after 100 warm-up iterations. Most retained training settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New Section 5.5 directly tests failure when color identifies the class and when distribution shift is absent or small. Appendix C.4 measures how frequently redundant lifting occurs across six datasets, whereas v1 only analyzed its mathematical occurrence. Appendix D.8 adds measured computational scaling. Existing cardinality, coverage, and equivariance-error analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Appendix D retains the stated three-seed and five-seed protocols and the existing parenthesized variability reporting. Added augmentation rows follow that practice; the new failure-condition tables provide point results without introducing explicit seed counts, confidence intervals, or significance procedures. Changed parenthesized values are result changes.

E6.justification: New results include KUTomaData errors of 31.75 for T3CEN-H4 versus 19.13 for ResNet18, MNIST accuracy across shift magnitudes, augmentation comparisons, redundancy percentages, and resource measurements. Retained rows also change: saturation-shifted CIFAR-100 T3CEN-S4 error changes from 44.27 (1.70) to 41.35 (1.27), its CIFAR-10 entry from 11.59 (1.33) to 11.59 (1.39), and luminance-shifted Caltech-101 ResNet-aug/Jitter error from 30.82 to 57.03. The PDFs do not explain these revisions.

M1.justification: The double-cover lifting, discretized HSL groups, group convolutions, and classification pooling are retained. RGB and scale extensions already appeared in v1; their relocation to v3's Discussion does not introduce a method component.

P1.justification: Most existing prose remains close to v1. Local edits replace degenerate-lifting terminology with redundant representations, move RGB and scale applications into a separate Discussion, and add impact and acknowledgement sections. Section 4 is retitled Background, duplicating Section 3's heading. These are limited editorial and structural changes.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to two-column layout, several comparison tables are transposed, and Figure 1 is redrawn as lifting and cyclic-permutation diagrams. RGB and scale panels are separated, while dataset-example figures are merged. New failure-condition, redundancy, and computation tables and tomato examples substantially extend the displays.

R1.justification: v3 adds references for KUTomaData, Planckian jitter, Özmen's Deepaugment, and tqdm. The related-work discussion and positioning against earlier color-equivariant methods remain substantially unchanged. Publication updates for existing references, including Adam and Polar Transformer Networks, are not new cited works.

T1.justification: The existing equations, group constructions, and Appendix B proofs are retained. New Appendix C.4 refines the redundancy definition by explicitly distinguishing fully redundant inputs at 0.5 from partially redundant inputs at 0.25 or 0.75. No new equivariance proof or revised derivation accompanies this limited addition.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens empirical scrutiny and practical applicability guidance: it directly demonstrates important failure conditions, broadens augmentation comparisons, and replaces a generic computational-cost warning with measurements. These address important gaps in v1's evaluation. The gains outweigh remaining reporting problems, including sparse details for new experiments and the unexplained Camelyon17 split revision. The broad superiority wording also needs qualification: v3 Table 6 reports saturation-shifted Caltech-101 error of 35.53 for AugMix versus 40.02 for the best listed T3CEN variant.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same T3CEN research, with matching authors, core construction, and retained experiments. All 24 pages of v1 and 20 pages of v3, including figures, tables, equations, and Appendices A-D, support comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds augmentation comparisons, tomato-ripeness and MNIST failure-condition experiments, redundancy measurements, and computational benchmarks.

before.justification: v1 reports original equivariance-error measurements and classification experiments on synthetic shapes, natural images, small NORB, and Camelyon17, plus MNIST analyses in the appendix.

results.title: A Hypertoroidal Covering for Perfect Color Equivariance

C1.justification: The abstract and principal contributions retain the same claims: sparse adaptive warps suffice for strong PDE solvers, connect to three physical perspectives, scale to 3D and compete with larger foundation models. The additional experiments support these claims without redefining them.

C2.justification: Section 5.1 replaces largely unexplained diffusion and Helmholtz performance with proposed kinetic-collision and frequency-domain ray interpretations, explicitly qualified as heuristic. It adds structured-grid and boundary-condition limitations and revises the assessment of rollout quality. Figure 13 further qualifies interpretability as clearest in laminar, transport-dominated regimes.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-access link, specifies bilinear sampling, and explains periodic wrapping, zero-valued out-of-domain sampling and mixed boundary handling. Table 5 supplies learning rates for the added PDEGym tasks. The new parameter-count table mainly consolidates information already stated in v1.

E1.justification: Table 1 expands from 16 to 18 datasets by adding PDEGym CE-RM and Wave Layer, extending the existing flow-and-wave coverage. The earlier datasets, conditioned tasks, scaling benchmark and Helmholtz evaluation remain.

E2.justification: Table 3 adds a non-learned, randomly initialized warp control to the comparison with the full model. The external comparator sets remain unchanged: FNO, CNextU-Net/CNUNET and scOT in benchmarking, and POSEIDON-L in the scaling study.

E3.justification: v2 substantially extends evaluation design through a 21:60 rollout window and training-data sweeps at 5%, 10%, 20%, 50% and 100% on three datasets. These are added protocols; the retained experiments keep their stated metrics, model configurations, learning-rate search and training budgets.

E4.justification: Beyond the new random-warp control, Appendix A.4.1 tests data efficiency, Table 9 extends the existing single-scale ablation from Rayleigh-Benard to three additional datasets, and Figure 13 examines multiple learned heads across three problems. These substantially broaden evidence about adaptivity, data requirements, multiscale structure and interpretability.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-seed accuracy estimates, confidence intervals or significance tests. Throughput error bars remain standard deviations across datasets in v1 Figure 7 and v2 Figure 8; the added experiments introduce no new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Existing Table 1 next-step and 1:20 scores are unchanged, but v2 adds substantial results for longer rollouts, PDEGym, data efficiency and ablations. New long-rollout findings include FNO outperforming FLOWERS on supernova simulations at steps 21–60: 1.6350 versus 2.0709 VRMSE. The non-learned-warp control reports 0.2190 next-step and 0.4138 rollout VRMSE.

M1.justification: The pointwise displacement predictor, multihead pullbacks, value projections, residual blocks and multiscale architecture are unchanged. Bilinear interpolation and boundary handling receive additional documentation. Non-learned warps are introduced as an experimental control, not as a revision to the proposed method.

P1.justification: The introduction and limitations are substantially rewritten, Section 3.3's kinetic explanation is condensed, and the former convolution appendix becomes main-text Section 3.1.1. New appendix subsections and consistent SELFWARP terminology further reorganize the narrative beyond simple additions of results.

P2.justification: v2 expands and reformats Table 1, adds the data-efficiency figure/table and multihead visualizations, restructures the single-scale results table and adds a parameter-count summary. Figures 1–2 are refined and several displays relocated. The redundant Helmholtz table is removed while its results remain in Table 4.

R1.justification: v2 adds focused connections to multigrid/AMG, latent encoder-decoder operator learning and kinetic interpretations of attention, with corresponding references. The central positioning of adaptive pullbacks relative to Fourier, convolution and attention methods remains. Numerous other bibliography edits update publication metadata rather than introduce different works.

T1.justification: The characteristic expansion, kinetic-limit derivation and wave parametrix are retained. v1 Appendix C's convolution argument moves into v2 Section 3.1.1, with its finite-head sum made explicit. This restatement and the characteristic derivative-notation clarification do not substantively change the mathematics; the new mechanism discussion remains heuristic.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the central adaptive-warp idea: the random-warp control tests whether learning the displacements matters, while data-efficiency and longer-rollout evaluations probe robustness and reveal additional exceptions to FLOWERS' advantage. Explicit boundary/grid limitations and code-access information improve transparency. These gains address important evidential gaps in v1, although the expanded physical explanations remain heuristic and accuracy uncertainty is still unreported.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FLOWERS research work. Their text, equations, tables, figures and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material moved or renumbered between versions.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds benchmark results, longer-rollout evaluations, data-efficiency experiments and further architectural analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original PDE prediction experiments, autoregressive rollouts, model-scaling results and architectural ablations, with additional conditioned-prediction and Helmholtz results in the appendices.

results.title: Flowers: A Warp Drive for Neural PDE Solvers

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the headline claims: unequal channel rates, the 0.255-bit information-theoretic gap, potentially unbounded GPTQ suboptimality, and state-of-the-art Llama/Qwen performance over 1–4 bits. The added experiments do not revise these central claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations of Gaussian applicability and query/key deviations, calibration-distribution mismatch, corpus-dependent fine-tuning benefits, and calibration-context tradeoffs. Fine-tuning is removed from the future-work discussion, although statements restricting the work to layerwise optimization and small-to-mid-sized models remain outdated.

D1.justification: v2 adds an implementation link and detailed fine-tuning instructions: AdamW settings, learning-rate schedule, four epochs, checkpointing, CPU caching, streamed integer codes and rescaler precision handling. It also reports four H100 GPUs for Llama-3-70B and documents the revised rate-search procedure. The linked resource's availability cannot be verified from the PDFs alone.

E1.justification: v1 uses WikiText-2 for calibration and perplexity evaluation alongside downstream benchmarks. v2 adds C4 perplexity evaluation, RedPajama calibration, and C4/RedPajama fine-tuning, substantially expanding corpus coverage and testing transfer beyond the calibration distribution. Existing downstream tasks remain.

E2.justification: The original comparison sets are retained. New longer-context comparisons include reported results for AQLM, DB-LLM, PV-Tuning, YAQA-B and QuIP (Tables 10 and 13). The new Llama-3-70B comparison additionally includes PB-LLM and OstQuant (Table 14); these are actual comparison entries, not merely citations.

E3.justification: v2 supplements the retained 2048-token evaluations with 4096- and 8192-token protocols, compares 1024 versus 2048 calibration contexts, and evaluates Llama-3-70B. It introduces fine-tuning budgets and controlled corpus comparisons using matched sequence counts. Appendix D also changes the reported mixing-search budget from 15 to 10 iterations.

E4.justification: The original component ablations remain. v2 adds Gaussian-versus-Laplace weight-distribution diagnostics (Figure 11), calibration-context sensitivity (Table 12), and calibration/fine-tuning corpus analyses across rates (Tables 15–16 and Figure 15). These test theoretical applicability and distribution sensitivity absent from v1.

E5.justification: Appendix E introduces distribution-fitting statistics: Kolmogorov–Smirnov distances to fitted Gaussian and Laplace distributions, averaged across layers with closer-fit counts. This adds statistical estimation and reporting, but neither version reports repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals or formal significance tests.

E6.justification: Most original benchmark entries remain, while v2 adds extensive fine-tuned, C4, longer-context and 70B results. For example, Table 2 retains Qwen3-8B WaterSIC perplexity 11.37 at 2.125 bits and adds 10.18 for the separately trained WaterSIC-FT configuration. Figure 5 also changes its reported rate-distribution statistics.

M1.justification: Section 4 adds WaterSIC-FT, which freezes integer codes and trains continuous rescalers using teacher-student distillation. Rate assignment changes from binary search to a secant method, and Appendix D now matches the target rate at each adaptive-mixing candidate instead of reusing an initially selected scale.

P1.justification: v2 expands the introductory explanation, revises procedural prose, adds acknowledgements, and separates supplementary model evaluations into Appendix F while moving zero-shot evaluations to Appendix G. Most existing exposition, theory and prior-work text remains substantially unchanged.

P2.justification: The model-size plot moves from v1 Figure 3 to v2 Figure 1 with a logarithmic size axis and additional curves. Main comparison plots become side-by-side displays; algorithms and appendix tables are relocated and compacted. New diagnostic figures and experimental tables substantially revise the presentation beyond renumbering or numerical updates.

R1.justification: v2 adds positioning through prediction-based Gaussian rate-distortion theory (Zamir et al., 2006), outlier-safe pretraining (Park et al., 2025), and a source for 70B comparisons (Huang et al., 2024). The prior-work review is largely retained; most other reference edits update publication metadata.

T1.justification: v2 corrects the rate definition by adding 1/n, fixes the matrix-factor placement in Appendix B Equation (35), and restores the addition sign in Appendix C's regularized objective. The principal theorem, assumptions and proof strategy remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical assessability through cross-corpus controls, matched-context comparisons with stronger methods, and 70B evaluation, addressing gaps explicitly deferred in v1. Fine-tuning documentation and mathematical corrections also help. These gains outweigh reporting weaknesses, but reconciliation is needed: 1-bit Llama-3.2-1B fine-tuned perplexity is 30.47 in Table 1 versus 32.85 in Tables 7 and 16, and broad SOTA and scope statements are not fully aligned with the expanded evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same WaterSIC research. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices support comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds fine-tuning, cross-corpus, calibration-sensitivity and larger-model experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original WaterSIC perplexity, zero-shot accuracy, component ablations and compression measurements.

results.title: WaterSIC: information-theoretically (near) optimal linear layer quantization

C1.justification: The three principal contributions remain, but the abstract, introduction, and conclusion explicitly scope the guarantees to a minimal stylized model and describe larger-model evidence as qualitative agreement. The claimed empirical reach extends from 1.5B to 8B parameters.

C2.justification: v3 explicitly states that the short-prompt construction abstracts away discourse, positional structure, and long-range dependencies, and positions deep linear networks as a limited illustration. It changes the depth interpretation from monotonic increase to approximate non-decrease and adds an explanation involving task-irrelevant shared components for Qwen-3-8B's weak raw feature separation.

D1.justification: Unlike v1 Appendix N.2, v3 Appendix O.2 specifies 10 fine-tuning epochs, per-device batch size 16, learning rate 1e-5, zero weight decay, and FP16 training. Section 8.2 also specifies the 20% activation-retention diagnostic. Existing synthetic hyperparameters are unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same synthetic analogy/two-hop tasks, generated natural-language entity-category dataset, and orthogonal-input depth experiment. Qwen-3-8B extends model scale on retained coverage; renaming the natural-language experiment does not introduce a new dataset or task.

E2.justification: The joint-training, similarity-first, attribution-first, and identity-bridge controls remain in their corresponding experiments. Qwen-3-8B is an additional architecture tested under the existing curricula, rather than a newly evaluated competing reasoning method.

E3.justification: v3 introduces an 8B model configuration and a feature diagnostic retaining the top 20% of MLP activations at relational tokens. Earlier experimental settings are otherwise retained; the newly stated natural-language fine-tuning hyperparameters do not establish that earlier settings changed.

E4.justification: Section 8.2 adds a Qwen-3-8B diagnostic examining whether shared representation components obscure feature alignment, reporting weak separation with full representations and using filtered activations. Existing end-to-end/ReLU, premise-frequency, and layer-depth analyses remain unchanged.

E5.justification: Both versions report means and standard deviations for synthetic experiments and point estimates for natural-language results. v3 adds no repeated-run counts, seed information, confidence intervals, or significance-testing procedure.

E6.justification: New Table 3 reports Qwen-3-8B feature similarity/success of 0.3785/84% for joint training, 0.3757/75% for late attribution, and 0.2704/34% for late similarity. Existing main and appendix numerical results and Figure 1 are retained. These are additional-model results, not same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The attention/value block, linear feature layer, cross-entropy training, curricula, and identity-bridge construction remain. Renaming the linear MLP and correcting cumulative training-time indices reconcile descriptions with the existing theoretical procedure; they do not establish a different core method.

P1.justification: The abstract, introductory framing, model description, experimental narrative, conclusion, and impact statement undergo substantial rewriting. Terminology is standardized around a minimal transformer-style block and feature layer, and a proof roadmap organizes the appendix arguments. Citation style, headings, and front matter also change.

P2.justification: v3 adds the compact Qwen-3-8B Table 3, corrects Table 1's two-hop success column from A to R, and fixes the one-layer-only appendix table caption. The unchanged Figure 1 moves beside its discussion. Existing table structures and plot design are largely preserved despite document reflow.

R1.justification: v3 adds focused deep-linear-network context in Appendix A, citing Saxe, Kawaguchi, Laurent and Brecht, Hardt and Ma, and two Arora papers. It also connects the analogy definition to Gentner's structure-mapping theory and refines the comparison with Huang et al.; the central research positioning remains.

T1.justification: The supporting mathematics is substantially revised. Theorem 6 replaces the 0.8 alignment lower bound with Omega(1), while Section 7 makes random orthonormal inputs independent of labels explicit. Its appendix proof revises Lemma 18, stage indexing, error bounds, and the previously omitted input residual. Other appendices restore missing representation-decomposition terms, revise the joint-training alignment bound, and replace the no-alignment derivations for Propositions 8 and 9 with inner-product bounds.

improvement.justification: The decisive gain is improved mathematical consistency in this theory-centered paper: v3 replaces problematic no-alignment derivations, restores omitted representation terms, and revises the deep-linear proof and its overly specific 0.8 guarantee. Narrower assumptions and claims trade breadth for better alignment between statements and supporting arguments. The proof roadmap and disclosed fine-tuning settings further improve assessability. The added 8B experiment remains limited by filtered feature measurements and point estimates; it is supplementary to the substantial theoretical corrections.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Feature Resemblance study. Their main text, equations, tables, figure, and complete appendices support comparison, including matching content across appendix and table renumbering.

after.justification: v3 retains these original experiments and adds Qwen-3-8B results and an activation-based feature diagnostic in Section 8.2 and Table 3.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic-data experiments, natural-language fine-tuning results, curriculum and identity-bridge comparisons, and appendix analyses of feature alignment.

results.title: Feature Resemblance: Towards a Theoretical Understanding of Analogical Reasoning in Transformers

C1.justification: The introduction and conclusion more explicitly center the contribution on multi-chunk KV reuse where full-context prefilling remains feasible but redundant. Information flow is qualified as operational rather than formal causal analysis. The central attention-selection, positional-alignment, and reordering contributions remain.

C2.justification: v2 substantially refines applicability and interpretation: it qualifies information-flow claims, limits the motivation when exact prefilling is already cheap, and distinguishes attention fidelity from generation-oriented selection. Section 6.3 corrects the VLM budget interpretation and acknowledges the OCRBench exception, 842 versus CacheBlend's 845 at k=2. Section 8 also frames latency comparisons as implementation-dependent measurements rather than ideal compute costs.

D1.justification: v2 explicitly documents the common 15% recomputation budget, global first-stage selection without per-chunk quotas, normalized chunk scoring, and stable ordering of ties. It clarifies that VLM k denotes visual chunks and identifies FlashInfer-style kernels for irregular attention. These refine implementation and experiment documentation without establishing changed underlying settings.

E1.justification: Appendix C adds the LongBench v2 short-question subset, comprising 180 examples with reported context lengths of 10k-210k. The original four LongBench datasets, five VLM benchmarks, and Needle-in-a-Haystack evaluation remain. This extends coverage within the existing long-context QA focus.

E2.justification: Tables 7, 8, 10, and 11 add evaluated comparisons with KVLink5, TurboRAG, PCW, BM25 Recompute, PyramidKV, SnapKV, and StreamingLLM. This substantially broadens comparison beyond the original recomputation baselines to training-based cache reuse, retrieval, and compression or eviction methods.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include a Llama-3-3B comparison, accuracy evaluation on the selected 180-example LongBench v2 subset, attention-matrix MSE averaged across layers on 100 HotpotQA examples, and an ascending-versus-descending ordering control. These substantially expand the evaluation protocol. Explicitly stating the existing experiments' 15% recomputation budget does not establish that those experiments changed or were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendices D.3, E, and G add tests of full-context attention recovery, sensitivity to chunk-order direction, and component-level runtime overhead. These provide substantial new mechanism and efficiency analyses. The original RoPE, Needle-in-a-Haystack, and layer-selection analyses remain; Figure 4's corrected caption does not constitute a new experiment.

E5.justification: Both versions report median latency over 10 independent runs. v2 adds no accuracy confidence intervals, significance tests, seed information, or revised repeated-run practice. The new evaluation sample counts and averaged metrics do not provide uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Tables 7-14 add substantial results for new comparators, longer contexts, and diagnostic analyses. For example, Table 9 reports accuracy of 0.2889 for Our, 0.2611 for CacheBlend, and 0.2056 for EPIC. Among retained results, Table 3 changes the LLaMA fixed-chunk NarrativeQA baseline from 0.1623 to 0.1862. Most original scores remain unchanged; Table 6's conversion from percentages to fractions is equivalent.

M1.justification: Attention-mass top-k selection, global RoPE reconstruction, full-layer KV recomputation, and two-pass chunk reordering are retained. Section 4.3 makes the global selection budget, normalized chunk score, and tie handling explicit. Figure 1 already depicts reordering by selected-token ratio in v1, supporting clarification rather than an established algorithm change.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and most existing prose remain. v2 adds targeted explanations, revises terminology and section titles, updates author/affiliation and publication-header text, and reorganizes the expanded appendices, moving the original implementation appendix from B to F. This is not a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: Tables 7-14 substantially expand the presentation of comparisons and diagnostic evidence. Existing displays also change: Figure 2 receives new colors and marker styling, Tables 5-6 are restructured, and several captions and highlights are revised. Figure 4's erroneous heatmap caption is corrected while its actual plot remains unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations to SnapKV, KVLink, TurboRAG, and PCW, plus a RAG subsection explaining that the method operates after retrieval. Appendices B and D expand positioning relative to trained cache-reuse methods, passage retrieval, and complementary KV compression, while retaining the original training-free recomputation positioning.

T1.justification: The existing KV, RoPE, positional, and attention-selection mathematics is retained apart from notation clarification. Equation 9 expresses the selected-token-ratio reordering rule already depicted in v1 Figure 1. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs, and v2 adds no substantive mathematical derivation.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for the central selection and efficiency claims through broader comparator families, attention-recovery and reversed-order controls, and longer-context evaluation. It also corrects misleading VLM interpretations and the Figure 4 caption, while clarifying application boundaries and experimental budgets. Some added baseline settings remain underspecified and accuracy uncertainty is still absent, but the targeted validation and correction of misleading explanations provide a substantial overall quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same InfoFlow KV work and provide readable text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices. The original implementation appendix B is retained as appendix F in v2; relocated content can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains the original empirical evaluations and adds baseline comparisons, LongBench v2 results, attention-recovery measurements, a reordering ablation, and a latency breakdown.

before.justification: v1 reports original LLM and VLM benchmark results, positional ablations, retrieval and layer-selection analyses, and inference-latency measurements.

results.title: InfoFlow KV: Information-Flow-Aware KV Recomputation for Long Context

Appendix E also explains the new baselines' failure mechanisms and describes text alignment as competitive rather than universally best. Original comparators remain; the change from '2D Edit' to 'SDXL' in Table 2 identifies the existing baseline more explicitly.

Additional comparison protocols introduce video/multi-view generation followed by reconstruction and direct text-image fusion. Original benchmark settings, metrics, defaults, and user-study design are retained.

Figures 9–11 add diagnostic case studies of alternative pipelines' branch misalignment, reconstruction inconsistency, and attribute leakage; Table 6 adds computational-cost analysis.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-seed counts, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests for the empirical comparisons. The new 100-case evaluation and 10-sample timing subset concern evaluation sample sizes, not repeated runs or uncertainty estimation.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and section organization are retained. Changes include grammar fixes, a clearer Section 5.4 title, affiliation and publication-status updates, acknowledgements, an impact statement, and a new Appendix E with subsequent appendix renumbering.

P2.justification: Figures 2–3 and the visual ablation are reformatted as larger, full-width displays. v2 adds dataset galleries in Figures 7–8, baseline visualizations in Figures 9–11, and Tables 3–6. Existing supplementary figures are retained and relocated, with extensive reflow of the surrounding layout.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for Wan, MV-Adapter, Nano Banana Pro, and additional completion, affordance, and visual-token research, while extending discussion of alternative conditioning routes. The central novelty argument remains unchanged. Interp3D and optimal-transport bibliographic updates refer to already cited works.

T1.justification: Section 3 and Appendix A retain the same mathematical definitions, spectral assumptions, stability analysis, and Wasserstein bounds and proofs. Typographical corrections and an optimal-transport citation update do not change the mathematical reasoning.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical credibility through four additional comparison families and evaluation beyond the original 21 manually curated ambiguity cases. It also corrects the unsupported negligible-overhead assertion with measured costs and exposes text-alignment tradeoffs. Missing uncertainty estimates and incomplete new configuration details remain limitations, but the broader validation and more accurate account of practical costs resolve important weaknesses in v1.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe RelaxFlow. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, a 100-case evaluation, and runtime and memory measurements in Appendix E.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark results, component and sensitivity ablations, qualitative experiments, and a 32-participant user study in Section 5 and the appendices.

results.title: RelaxFlow: Text-Driven Amodal 3D Generation

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions, and conclusion retain the same training-free caching claim, two core mechanisms, and headline of up to 3.7× acceleration while preserving 98% quality. New evidence does not redefine these central contributions.

It also specifies failure conditions involving rapid camera motion, complex textures, and abrupt geometry changes, explicitly acknowledging that CAS cannot eliminate the speed-versus-drift trade-off.

New Tables 7–9 reuse subsets of existing methods: HERO is absent from these additions, and DuCa is also absent from Table 9; neither is removed from the original comparisons.

E3.justification: Appendix D introduces LingBot-14B evaluation at two resolutions with 49 frames and 70 steps, Voyager evaluation at 30 and 70 steps, and LingBot evaluation at 81 and 161 frames. It also adds control-time and context-dependent memory profiling. The original evaluation settings remain intact.

E4.justification: New analyses test whether caching advantages persist across backbones, resolutions, denoising schedules, and longer contexts, and examine control overhead and memory scaling. These substantially broaden robustness and efficiency analysis. Tables 5–6 contain unchanged ablations moved from the appendix into the main text.

E5.justification: Both versions retain the statement that latency is averaged over multiple trials after warm-up. The additions introduce no seed or repetition counts, confidence intervals, significance tests, or new uncertainty-reporting procedures.

E6.justification: Tables 1–6 retain identical results, while Tables 7–11 add substantial numerical evidence. Examples include Voyager PSNR 25.49 and 4.09× speedup at 70 steps, control overhead of 0.047–0.060%, and extra memory of 0.02–0.03 GB. These are additional measurements under specified settings, not improvements to the unchanged 50-step results.

M1.justification: The curvature calculation, token partitioning, reuse/linear/damped predictors, accumulated drift trigger, and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged. The added mathematical justification does not alter the caching procedure.

P1.justification: Changes include localized expansion of the curvature explanation and ablation discussion, additional appendix organization, and updated author order, affiliations, publication text, and acknowledgements. Most existing prose and the main narrative structure are retained.

P2.justification: Five new tables present configuration studies and resource profiling, and existing Tables 5–6 move into the main text. Appendix figures are regrouped and repositioned, including paired qualitative comparisons. This substantially expands and redistributes the displayed evidence while retaining the original figure content.

R1.justification: v2 adds the LingBot reference and several survey and quantization references, and corrects Voyager attribution by removing the HunyuanVideo citation. HiCache's updated publication information refers to the same work. The related-work taxonomy and novelty positioning remain largely unchanged.

T1.justification: v1's Appendix A contains the normalization theorem and proof. v2 adds reuse and linear-prediction error bounds, a curvature-based error bound, finite-difference consistency, and a hard-token dilution proposition, with explicit smoothness and speed assumptions. The original normalization theorem is retained as Theorem A.5.

improvement.justification: Appendix D substantially strengthens validation beyond v1's default configurations and directly measures control and memory costs. Added local error analysis and concrete failure conditions also improve the explanation and applicability assessment. Statistical reporting remains limited, and Eq. (19)'s single-point Taylor remainder is not generally valid for vector trajectories, but that localized proof issue does not outweigh the broader empirical and explanatory gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe WorldCache and contain readable text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices. The original method, experiments, and supplementary analyses can be matched reliably despite additions and relocation.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds LingBot evaluations, sampling and rollout-length studies, and control-overhead and memory measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original generation experiments on Voyager and Aether, Sintel depth and camera-pose evaluation, caching ablations, and runtime measurements.

results.title: WorldCache: Accelerating World Models for Free via Heterogeneous Token Caching

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution list retain the same central claims: a first any-to-any masked-discrete-diffusion model, joint multimodal token modeling, specialized training and inference techniques, and competitive multimodal performance. The shortened conclusion does not materially change these claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations linking the new ablations to image quality and avoidance of overly brief spoken responses, and argues for reduced-step efficiency relative to autoregressive baselines. New Appendix C identifies instruction-based visual editing as a future extension through data and model scaling.

D1.justification: Appendix A newly discloses a training batch size of 128 and replaces the fixed position-penalty value with an index-dependent decay description. The batch-size disclosure does not establish a changed training setting. Existing optimizer settings, learning rates, sequence length, dataset quantities, and project-access information are retained.

E1.justification: Appendix B adds DPG-Bench image-generation evaluation and a spoken version of MME using synthesized questions. These extend benchmark coverage within already demonstrated task families; the training datasets in Table 4 and existing evaluation coverage are retained.

E2.justification: The original comparator sets in Tables 1–2 remain unchanged. New Table 7 compares against SD v1.5, SD v2.0, and Show-o. Tables 8–9 additionally introduce latency comparisons against Emu, NExT-GPT, and GLM-4-Voice, previously compared on quality metrics.

E3.justification: v2 substantially expands evaluation procedures with measured image-generation time and TTS real-time factor, quantitative MME comparisons across text and synthesized-speech inputs and outputs, DPG-Bench category scores, and component-removal controls. Appendix A also revises the stated position-penalty setting. The PDFs do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond retaining the sampling-step analysis and inpainting examples, Appendix B.2 adds the first targeted ablations of position penalty and special-token pre-infilling. These test image-generation scores and spoken-response brevity, respectively. Appendix B.4 also extends efficiency analysis to measured latency against autoregressive baselines.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or statistical significance tests for its experiments. The new average latency measurements do not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 and the quality scores in Table 3 are retained unchanged, but substantial results are added. Table 3 reports 28.57 versus 1.29 seconds for 256 versus 10 text-to-image steps; this is a newly reported step comparison, not a version-to-version performance gain.

M1.justification: The reported position-penalty rule changes: v1 specifies a fixed factor of 0.5, whereas v2 specifies a factor decreasing with token index to a minimum of 0.5 (Section 3.4 and Appendix A). The backbone, tokenizers, training objective, training stages, and other inference components remain unchanged.

P1.justification: v2 makes scattered grammar and terminology corrections, expands related-work explanations, shortens the conclusion, and adds impact and acknowledgment sections. Appendix B becomes an experimental section with subsections, retaining the original image gallery in B.5, followed by a new limitations appendix. The main narrative organization is preserved.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the displayed evidence with spoken-VQA, ablation, DPG-Bench, and latency tables, plus a side-by-side pre-infilling ablation figure. Table 3 gains a latency column and an expanded caption. Earlier image galleries are retained as Figures 9–10 rather than removed or replaced.

R1.justification: The positioning against NExT-Omni is substantively revised. v1 describes it as having a text-only backbone and requiring additional generation models; v2 removes that characterization and instead distinguishes flow matching from masked diffusion through training targets and decoding updates. Section 2 also adds CoDi and expands coverage of flow-based and masked-diffusion research, including Fudoki.

T1.justification: The masked-token loss and entropy-based confidence equations remain unchanged. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs. The added diffusion-versus-flow discussion is conceptual, and the standard real-time-factor formula serves an empirical timing metric.

The improvement concerns supporting evidence rather than higher headline scores. Its strength remains limited by missing timing hardware details, absent uncertainty estimates, and very small numerical effects in the position-penalty ablation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Omni-Diffusion, and their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support comparison. Retained content can be matched despite pagination changes and figure renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains these results and adds original spoken-VQA evaluation, component ablations, DPG-Bench results, and latency measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original ASR, TTS, visual understanding, image-generation, sampling-step, and qualitative multimodal results in Section 4 and Appendix B.

results.title: Omni-Diffusion: Unified Multimodal Understanding and Generation with Masked Discrete Diffusion

C1.justification: Section 1.1 narrows the explicit minimax-optimality contribution from the methods in Sections 3 and 4 to those in Section 3, withdrawing the corresponding claim for process-reward PG. The central base-model-barrier and adaptive-SGD claims remain.

C2.justification: Section 3.2 newly interprets the Qwen3 curves as suggesting that post-training did not extend the base model's support. Appendix A.6 removes the claim that clipping affects only iteration complexity under best-of-m exploration, consistent with the revised reward-query bound. Existing concluding limitations remain.

D1.justification: V2 documents the new evaluation's model identities, completion count, likelihood estimator and decoding parameters, and clarifies online query reuse. Synthetic implementation settings and the code-access link are unchanged.

E3.justification: The added Math-500 evaluation uses two 8B models, 64 completions per problem, temperature 0.7, top-p 0.95 and top-k 50. This introduces a new generation-based evaluation protocol; the retained synthetic experiments have unchanged reported settings.

E4.justification: Figure 2a adds a real-model diagnostic case study of the base-model barrier through likelihood-quantile curves before and after post-training. The synthetic off-support and training-trajectory analyses remain; no new component ablations or sensitivity studies appear.

E5.justification: Section 6 adds statistical estimation of per-problem success probability using the fraction of correct answers among 64 completions, whereas the retained synthetic curves use directly computed model likelihoods. No confidence intervals, significance tests or training-seed variability are added.

E6.justification: Figure 2a adds Qwen3 likelihood-quantile results: both models have lower-tail estimated zeros, the post-trained model is higher through much of the middle range, and the curves cross toward the upper range. The synthetic results are retained without changed findings or values.

M1.justification: The PG-OR/PG-PR updates, adaptive learning rates and best-of-m exploration are retained. Algorithm 2 makes the base/uniform sampling mixture explicit, while the new Section 3.1 footnote explains prediction-query reuse within the existing exploration framework.

P1.justification: The section and appendix organization remains stable. V2 adds an experimental paragraph and explanatory footnote, locally rewrites proof passages, and corrects wording, notation and bibliographic details without broadly restructuring the narrative.

P2.justification: Figure 2 replaces the synthetic CDF panel with the Qwen3 comparison, retains the synthetic quantile panel, and adds panel labels, a model legend and a revised caption. Figure 1 is visually unchanged; the remaining layout differences mainly reflect text reflow.

R1.justification: V2 adds the Qwen3 technical report and Let's Verify Step by Step in connection with the new experiment. Most other reference edits update publication metadata or authorship; the substantive related-work positioning is retained.

T1.justification: Assumption 1 now bounds features for all sequences, and new Assumption 2 strengthens Corollary 7's conditions. Theorems 10–12 and Appendix C substantially revise hard-instance constructions, parameter restrictions and lower bounds. Theorem 11's mistake bound changes from Omega(k^N/gamma^2) to Omega(k^N/(N gamma^2)); Theorem 12 restricts outputs to autoregressive linear models and uses new Lemma 28. Appendix A also changes Proposition 20's min to max and adds a zeta-squared factor to Corollary 24's reward-query bound.

Appendix C replaces position-independent constructions used for arbitrary target sequences with constructions that explicitly support the margin condition, while Assumption 2 supplies conditions needed for Corollary 7's equal-token-likelihood argument. Together with corrected complexity bounds, these substantially improve theoretical reliability despite narrower guarantees. The Math-500 illustration adds practical context, although zero successes among 64 completions cannot establish zero probability or unchanged support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, figures, algorithms, equations and Appendices A–C are readable and support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains the original synthetic experiments and adds an original evaluation of Qwen3-8B-Base and Qwen3-8B on Math-500, reported in Figure 2a.

results.title: Post-Training with Policy Gradients: Optimality and the Base Model Barrier

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution statements, and conclusion retain the same central claims about reverse-KL diversity degradation, entropy-guided forward-KL augmentation, uncertainty transfer, and efficient distillation. The headline gains across model sizes are unchanged; new experiments support these retained claims.

Appendix A explains the sources of computational overhead. The placement discussion also qualifies random selection as underperforming on 'most' rather than 'all' benchmarks.

D1.justification: v2 adds a stated public-code location, discloses a four-A100-80GB setup, and documents computational profiling. P1.justification: v2 lightly revises the abstract and introduction, adds comparison subsections, moves the threshold discussion to Appendix I, and corrects cross-references and terminology. P2.justification: Five new tables present GKD, objective comparisons, adaptive-KL baselines, coefficient sensitivity, and top-k sensitivity. The threshold table moves to Appendix I, and main-text figures and tables are rearranged. results.title: Entropy-Aware On-Policy Distillation of Language Models

C1.justification: The central claims about sparse differentiable routing, exact rule extraction, and performance-complexity tradeoffs remain. The introduction and contributions additionally claim zero operator-gradient variance and that TT-SPARSE uniquely supports all three task types natively within one interpretable rule-learning architecture.

It also adds substantive explanations concerning post-hoc sparsification failures, separate mapping weights, don't-care simplification, and operator memory/noise costs. These considerably expand the explanation and qualification of the design.

These materially expand reproducibility documentation without establishing changes to retained experiments.

E3.justification: v2 adds a GPU/float32/batch-64 operator benchmark averaged across ten configurations, regularization sweeps with a shared QMC extraction pipeline and extractability-based comparison, and exhaustive Boolean-function fitting. It adds operator cost/noise diagnostics, per-node complexity with and without don't-care terms, tests of structural sparsity and learned routing, and standard-versus-deep expressivity analyses in Section 4.1 and Appendices H.1–I.

E5.justification: The new operator comparison reports gradient variance and loss standard deviation, with Perturbed results distinguished by 32 versus 256 Monte Carlo samples. The existing five-seed benchmark protocol, standard-error reporting, and Friedman-rank reporting remain unchanged; no increase in benchmark repetitions is established.

P1.justification: v2 separates Soft TopK and LTT components into numbered subsections, clarifies mathematical terminology, rewrites extraction explanations, consolidates contributions, and condenses experiment and future-work prose. Figure 4 is corrected, and several existing illustrations are relocated or rescaled. The original benchmark tables and empirical plot images are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for straight-through estimation, DILP, L0 regularization, threshold logic, and interpretable clinical prediction, and introduces the claim of unique native support across three task types. The existing related-work categories and most research positioning remain intact.

T1.justification: v2 adds a Sperner-based bound on threshold-node prime implicants and explicit characterization of standard versus deep-node expressivity. It corrects Figure 4's inconsistent weights and Boolean formula. The Soft TopK optimization and gradient derivations retain their substance, with notation and indexing refinements.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important gaps in support for the central design through sparsification controls, operator measurements, and direct testing of the threshold-node expressivity restriction. It also fixes the worked rule-extraction example and supplies essential preprocessing and training details. Figure 17 introduces aggregation and color-label inconsistencies, but these limited defects do not outweigh the substantial gains in evidence and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TT-SPARSE research. Their main texts, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds operator measurements, sparsification comparisons, per-node complexity analyses, and synthetic and tabular expressivity experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original predictive-performance and complexity results on 28 datasets in Tables 1–3, alongside component and hyperparameter ablations.

results.title: TT-Sparse: Learning Sparse Rule Models with Differentiable Truth Tables

results.title: Decoupling Reasoning and Confidence: Resurrecting Calibration in Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims about encoded absences, limitations of standard explanations, complementary explanation methods, and absence-aware debiasing. Additional experiments support these existing claims.

Appendices A.4–A.5 discuss transformer applicability and positive-potential stability under sparse inputs. It also clarifies the distinction between formal pattern families and semantic interpretations, while retaining the earlier intervention-approximation caveat.

D1.justification: V2 adds a code repository address on the first page and technical information for the new experiments, including token aggregation, measured layer locations, InputXGradient channel selection, and eight-patch and ten-image selection procedures. Existing training hyperparameters and hardware disclosures are retained.

E1.justification: The synthetic motion, colored-pixel, ImageNet-1k, and ISIC tasks remain. Appendix B.4 adds an ISIC scenario described as having weaker spurious correlations. The added ViT evaluations extend model configurations rather than introducing another dataset or task.

E2.justification: The most-activating-patch control already appeared at the default CNN setting in v1 Appendix B.3. V2 extends it across the existing hyperparameter comparisons in Table 3 and displays it in Table 1. Logical-NOT and debiasing comparator sets are otherwise retained.

E3.justification: V2 adds substantial evaluation protocols: ViT-B/16 measurements using minimum activation over tokens, earlier-layer measurements, prediction-flip tests with a suppression-only control, and attribution evaluation on selected ten-image subsets. It also introduces weaker-bias training and quantitative controlled-versus-patch interventions. These supplement the retained original protocols.

E4.justification: New analyses test where inhibition occurs across layers, whether it affects ImageNet predictions independently of increased activations, whether selective attribution computation remains informative, and whether debiasing survives weaker correlations. Appendix B.5 adds quantitative validation of patch interventions against data-generation-based interventions; v1 had only the qualitative controlled-intervention examples.

E5.justification: V2 adds standard deviations for the previously reported most-activating-patch control. However, Appendix B.3 removes the explicit SciPy independent t-test description and aggregate CNN p-values while retaining significant-channel counts. The existing five-run disclosures and other standard-deviation reporting remain.

E6.justification: V2 adds ViT, layer-wise, prediction-flip, attribution-subset, weaker-bias, and quantitative intervention results. Examples include suppression-only flip rates of 8.2% versus 3.5% for random patches, and weaker-bias inverse accuracies of 0.64 versus 0.46 for presence-only debiasing. Figure 4 also changes activation labels, including 2.9 to 3.2 and -7 to -6.9. Original CNN Table 1 and ISIC Table 2 scores remain unchanged.

M1.justification: Non-target attribution, activation-minimizing feature visualization, and the presence-plus-absence debiasing losses remain unchanged. V2 experimentally implements the attribution-subset selection strategy already suggested in v1 Section 6; this does not establish a new method component.

P1.justification: V2 adds localized explanatory paragraphs and appendix subsections, including A.5, while preserving the main section sequence and most existing prose. Author-affiliation and publication text are updated. This is an expansion within the existing narrative structure rather than an extensive rewrite.

P2.justification: Table 1 gains a ViT column and most-activating row; Table 3 gains a control column. New Tables 4, 6, and 7 present supplementary analyses using the existing visual style. Existing figures are largely preserved with reflow, and v1 Table 4 becomes v2 Table 5.

R1.justification: Section 3 adds positioning against concept-discovery approaches, including WWW and CLIP-Dissect. New references also support the ViT, GeLU, and Swish discussions. The Walter et al. reference changes title and publication information while retaining its role in the argument.

T1.justification: Sections 2.1 and A.2 newly specify the concept underlying the formal definition as a family of input patterns sharing a neuronal effect, explicitly excluding semantic coherence as a formal requirement. The encoded-absence inequalities, constructive existence argument, feature-direction definition, and loss equations remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: V1's ImageNet evidence centered on neuron activations, and its controlled-intervention check was qualitative. V2 adds a suppression-only prediction test and quantitative controlled-versus-patch comparisons, substantially strengthening the links to decisions and intervention validity. ViT and weaker-bias experiments further support generality. These gains outweigh the loss of explicit t-test details, although the new suppression-only procedure remains briefly specified.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and Appendices A–B are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: V2 retains those original experiments and adds transformer evaluations, layer-wise analyses, prediction-intervention tests, and further debiasing and intervention results.

before.justification: V1 reports original synthetic motion and toy-model experiments, ImageNet activation interventions, and ISIC debiasing results, with supplementary analyses in Appendix B.

results.title: What is Missing? Explaining Neurons Activated by Absent Concepts

C1.justification: v2 adds public dataset and code release as an explicit third contribution, replacing v1's promise of a future dataset release. The central claims about the arena, model rankings, domain-dependent preferences and inadequate professional finance quality remain.

C2.justification: v2 qualifies expert-arena agreement because independent rubric ratings and pairwise choices use different elicitation procedures. It also interprets the new correlations as arena blind spots, acknowledges that many domain effects fail multiple-testing correction, and discusses computational costs. These refine the retained overall interpretation.

D1.justification: v2 supplies concrete dataset and code access links instead of a future release promise. It adds prompt-source distributions, detailed expert-review instructions including shuffled presentation, batching and review duration, and per-model token usage, providers and API costs. The smaller finance-study sample changes sampling within existing coverage.

E2.justification: The same 16 models participate in the arena comparisons, and comparator membership in the academic and finance ranking tables is unchanged. Newly cited finance and spreadsheet systems are discussed as related work, not evaluated as additional baselines.

E3.justification: The finance study changes from 52 battles and 104 spreadsheets, mostly rated once, to 25 battles and 50 spreadsheets each rated by all five experts: 134 versus 250 evaluations. v2 also adds a circulation question and a blinded pairwise follow-up in which five experts each assess 25 battles. Generation temperatures and token limits remain unchanged.

These substantially extend the retained diagnostic analyses.

E5.justification: v2 adds leaderboard error bars and 95% bootstrap Elo and analytic Bradley-Terry intervals (Figure 1, Table 9), Benjamini-Hochberg and Benjamini-Yekutieli corrections, a pooled-versus-domain likelihood-ratio test, and correlation significance tests. Expert reliability is now assessed across all 50 spreadsheets rather than only 15 multiply rated cases.

E6.justification: The main leaderboard and failure-tag rates are unchanged, but finance results are replaced under the revised design: overall mean 2.87 to 2.86 and expert-arena agreement 42.3% to 56.0%. v2 newly reports 66.4% agreement in the pairwise follow-up, 16.1% circulation acceptance, correlation results and $1,244.10 cost across 9,647 generations. M1.justification: The single-pass SheetSpec generation approach, matching algorithm, feature-augmented Bradley-Terry model, 29 features and failure-tagging pipeline are retained. The generation schema and judge prompt are unchanged; relocated explanations and revised evaluation studies do not establish a method change.

P1.justification: v2 extensively compresses and rewrites the abstract, background and analysis narrative, moves domain discussions and failure-judging details into reorganized appendices, and incorporates much of the former conclusion into an expanded Impact Statement. Conflict-of-interest and funding disclosures are also added.

P2.justification: v2 adds correlation, prompt-distribution, confidence-interval and resource-use tables, introduces error bars in Figure 1, and removes v1's expert-agreement scatterplot. It relocates the academic ranking table and substantially regroups appendix displays. The spreadsheet example images themselves are retained.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially expands positioning through a finance-task evaluation discussion covering works such as BloombergGPT, FinGPT, FinQA, TAT-QA, PIXIU and FinBen. It also expands spreadsheet-specific comparisons, explicitly distinguishing declarative workbook synthesis from manipulation tasks with predefined gold answers.

Section 3 replaces the explicit standard cross-entropy expression with equivalent MLE prose; no substantive theory or proof change is introduced.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SpreadsheetArena study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material relocated between sections.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion extend the claimed empirical scope to SE(3) robotic grasping. The central contributions—intrinsic average-velocity modeling, practical tangent-space supervision, conflict-aware optimization, and CFG—retain their previous meaning.
