The SE(3) discussion distinguishes distribution fitting from physical grasp feasibility, while Appendix G interprets capacity and limited-data findings as lacking a consistent memorization signature and explains the omitted torus nearest-neighbor diagnostic.

These substantially broaden task and domain coverage beyond the retained spherical, torsion-angle, rotation, and synthetic hypersphere experiments.

Tables 15–17 investigate capacity reduction, performance with limited training data, and possible memorization through train-generated versus test-generated nearest-neighbor comparisons. These substantially extend the retained gradient-conflict, CFG, and hypersphere analyses.

The existing five-seed means and NLL standard deviations are retained; no increase in repeated-run counts is reported.

E6.justification: Matched pre-existing numerical results are unchanged, but substantial new results appear. Table 4 reports one-step grasp success of 65% for RMF, 60% for G-LSD, and 3.2% for RFM; Table 7 reports RMF DNA MSE 0.030 and k-mer correlation 0.94. New KLD scores, sampling curves, and capacity/data-fraction results further expand the evidence.

M1.justification: Section 3 and Algorithm 1 retain the same transported average velocity, geodesic interpolation, JVP target, decomposed objective, PCGrad updates, and CFG formulation. The new applications and surrogate-error analysis do not document a changed algorithm or new method component.

P1.justification: v2 expands the probability-path background and experimental discussion, inserts the curvature-analysis appendix and proof subsection, and makes localized wording and heading corrections. P2.justification: New Tables 4, 7, and 12–17 add application comparisons, KLD, capacity disclosures, and statistical diagnostics; new Figure 7 provides a substantial multipanel sampling-step comparison. improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for the paper's efficiency and applicability claims: Figure 7 directly tests sampling-budget tradeoffs, Tables 15–17 examine capacity and limited-data behavior, and the grasp and DNA experiments extend practical validation. Detailed configurations for the new applications remain sparse, but the broader validation and clearer limitations provide a substantial net quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Riemannian MeanFlow work. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable, and retained content can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds grasp generation, promoter DNA generation, sampling-step comparisons, and capacity, limited-data, and memorization experiments.

results.title: Riemannian MeanFlow for One-Step Generation on Manifolds

Some AREW and proxy entries in Tables 3 and 5 reproduce earlier results.

P2.justification: v2 adds telecom and robustness plots and Tables 3–5, and splits the old Figure 5 between Figure 6 and the relocated, reformatted Figure 9b. The intervention panel is correctly relabeled MediQ. New Figures 8 and 9a nevertheless contain misleading axis labels.

R1.justification: Appendix A substantially expands positioning relative to on-policy distillation and direct intermediate-reward shaping, distinguishing their feedback sources and objectives. New citations cover distillation, telecom evaluation, tool agents, and credit assignment; the earlier related-work discussion is largely retained.

Appendix A also adds mathematical comparisons with on-policy distillation and direct reward shaping. These exceed notation changes.

A1.justification: Both PDFs are complete, readable versions of the same SeL/AREW study. Text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices can be matched despite substantial expansion and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds telecom tool-use experiments, robustness tests, reward-shaping comparisons, and rubric-based evaluations.

results.title: On Information Self-Locking in Reinforcement Learning for Active Reasoning of LLM agents

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion broaden the stated empirical scope from three to five foundation models. The central claims—a unified online-learning framework, a formal regret–acceleration connection, three principal instantiations and up to 24% speedup—remain substantively unchanged.

C2.justification: New Appendix E qualifies the experiments as adaptation from drafts trained from scratch, rather than released checkpoints, and emphasizes framework contributions over benchmark-specific gains. v2 also interprets the new scaling and warm-up findings, revises the theoretical discussion to describe saturation, and corrects Appendix C.1's explanation from small to high acceptance rate for an accurate draft.

D1.justification: New disclosures include draft architecture and parameter counts for Hydra, EAGLE and EAGLE-3 (B.7), TPS aggregation as the mean of per-question throughput (B.10), and from-scratch initialization (E). E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same seven benchmarks: GSM8K, MATH, the mathematical MMLU subset, Code-Search-Python, Spider, MBPP and Alpaca-finance. Ens-Hydra is also added as an alternative comparator in Tables 4 and 9. The comparator sets in retained Tables 1 and 2 are unchanged.

E3.justification: The evaluation configurations expand from three to five target models through Vicuna-13B and Qwen3-32B, with Qwen3-1.7B drafting for the latter. New protocols sweep 500, 1000 and 1500 warm-up samples and approximate environmental variation using consecutive prompt-embedding distances. These substantially extend the evaluation design; retained experiments keep their documented settings.

E4.justification: v2 adds warm-up sensitivity (Table 8), ensemble-versus-optimistic updating for Hydra (Tables 4 and 9), and an empirical illustration of theoretical trends (Figure 11). E5.justification: Table 2's caption changes from results averaged over three runs 'with standard deviations' to simply averaged over three runs. Neither version displays standard deviations in that table, so this corrects the reporting description rather than removing uncertainty values. Three-run reporting and the uncertainty entries in the other retained tables remain unchanged.

E6.justification: Numerical results in Tables 1–2, the original hyperparameter and overhead tables, and the existing plots are retained. results.title: Deep Learning for BioImaging: What Are We Really Learning?

C2.justification: Section 3.5 corrects the earlier Short SQuAD K=1 superiority claim and qualifies larger-K gains as task-dependent, including no bAbI improvement. The retained SQuAD scores are 38.1 for K=1 versus RMT's 42.6, with 54.9 at larger K. New appendices explain memory bottlenecks, qualify input-memory advantages when per-layer capacity increases, and acknowledge unequal comparator state sizes and coarse reconstruction-capacity estimates.

D1.justification: Appendix B adds detailed per-model settings and total memory-state sizes in Table 6, clarifies WRITE-head initialization and curriculum stabilization, and specifies previously unspecified larger-K settings. Appendix K supplies Algorithm 1 and minimal PyTorch-like code. These substantially expand reproducibility documentation; the repository was already linked in v1.

E3.justification: New protocols sweep memory size and WRITE steps, vary Mamba state configurations, and compare input-level versus per-layer memory under matched and enlarged budgets. Added latency tests use larger models, 4k–16k contexts, and batch size 1. PG19 evaluation introduces reconstruction-capacity thresholds over 8–64-token sequences. These extend evaluation design rather than establish reruns of the retained experiments.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained WRITE-step extrapolation, meta-learning ablation, and reconstruction-loss analyses, v2 adds memory-size sensitivity tests in Appendix F, constrained-state Mamba comparisons in G, and memory-placement ablations in J. Appendix D extends latency scaling analyses. These directly probe memory bottlenecks, parameter efficiency, and compute amortization.

E5.justification: The existing mean-and-standard-deviation reporting over three runs is retained. Table 8 additionally reports LaCT's best of three runs alongside its mean and standard deviation because of high variability. This changes the reported summary practice without establishing increased run counts for existing experiments.

E6.justification: Table 1's scores are unchanged, while Table 2 fills the previously missing higher-K GradMem language-modeling result with 2.91±0.01 cross-entropy. Tables 7–9 and Figures 8, 10, and 11 add substantial comparison, capacity, latency, and ablation results. Appendix D's new latency prose conflicts with Figure 8, limiting exact timing interpretation.

Appendix I adds an adaptation using learned LoRA adapters during WRITE with a frozen, adapter-free READ model. Appendix J also tests directly optimized per-layer KV memory as an alternative parameterization.

P1.justification: The main section order and most existing prose are preserved. v2 makes targeted language corrections, clarifies memory initialization and second-order ablation terminology, updates author/publication information, and adds an impact statement, acknowledgements, and appendix contents guide. Figure 3 moves, Figure 6 is reflowed, and captions are refined, producing a substantial expansion of visual and technical presentation.

R1.justification: Appendix A adds LaCT/TTT Done Right and Nested Learning references and expands the existing TTT discussion with Table 4's comparison against Titans, Atlas, and LaCT. This sharpens distinctions in memory level, update granularity, and objectives while retaining the original research positioning. Other bibliography changes largely update publication metadata.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation through previously missing TTT comparisons and controlled memory-budget and placement analyses, while expanded settings and pseudocode improve reproducibility. results.title: GradMem: Learning to Write Context into Memory with Test-Time Gradient Descent

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and discussion retain the same central contributions: MSIS variance reduction, efficient shared-orbital Excited Pfaffians, generalization across structures and compounds, and many-state calculations. C2.justification: The ethylene state-swap explanation changes from self-reinforcing overlap-penalty ordering in v1 Appendix J to a Rydberg–valence crossing and a parameter-similarity hypothesis in v2 Appendix L. v2 also interprets the C2 swap as an avoided crossing, explicitly excludes transfer to unseen structures, and adds qualifications concerning conical intersections and residual spin-state mixtures.

D1.justification: New Appendix O.2 states that the implementation is publicly available and supplies a code link. The added comparisons disclose hardware, determinant constraints and NES pretraining requirements. E1.justification: Both versions cover the same Li–Ne atoms, 12 molecules, 33-state beryllium calculation, carbon-dimer dissociation and crossing geometries, and ethylene torsion and pyramidalization. The added analyses reuse this coverage; their different model configurations and compute budgets do not introduce new tasks or populations.

Appendix N also includes Szabo et al. (2024) in the expanded runtime comparisons, whereas v1 Appendix L's compute estimates focused on NES. Existing accuracy comparators remain.

The reported VMC learning-rate schedule also changes from 0.02/(1+1/10000) to 0.02/(1+t/10000), without establishing that existing experiments were rerun.

Existing parenthesized energy uncertainties remain unchanged, and neither version documents an increased seed or repeated-run count.

E6.justification: The original energy values in v1 Tables 4–8 are retained in v2 Tables 9–13. Substantial new results include normalized effective sample sizes, architecture convergence and optimizer-dependent timings: Table 5 reports cumulative C2 speedups of 208 times with Adam and 46 times with KFAC versus SPRING. New Table 6 reports a first excitation of 1.3817 eV for budget-limited NES versus 0.4294 eV for the proposed method. These are added comparisons, not improvements to the retained energy results.

M1.justification: The architecture, sample-pooling strategy and spin snapping remain. However, the written computational specification changes: Eq. 7 uses squared overlap, the normalizer and bridge-system expressions are revised, and the pretraining Procrustes rotations are corrected. These are limited formula-level corrections; the PDFs do not establish an implementation change or rerun.

P1.justification: The six-section main narrative and most prose remain. Changes include localized background and limitations edits, rewritten compute-time and ethylene explanations, inserted appendix sections, and corrected terminology, affiliation/contact text and conference footer. The additional scientific content does not entail wholesale narrative restructuring.

P2.justification: v2 adds substantial quantitative displays: Figures 11, 12 and 17 show effective sample size, architecture convergence and runtime scaling, while Tables 2–6 present sample counts, timings and budget-limited excitation energies. Original figures are retained and relocated or renumbered; Figure 2's caption is shortened and several table captions are corrected.

These refine selected connections to prior work without substantially changing the overall research positioning.

These repair or narrow the existing mathematical treatment without introducing a new theoretical framework.

Effective-sample-size diagnostics, mathematical corrections and a code-access statement further improve assessability. A material qualification remains: Table 5 supports 208 times faster C2 steps with Adam but 46 times with KFAC versus SPRING, so the retained headline speedup needs clearer optimizer qualification. Nevertheless, the added evidence substantially improves the paper's support for its efficiency claims.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Excited Pfaffians and Multi-State Importance Sampling work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching across the revision.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds effective-sample-size measurements, an architecture comparison, expanded runtime measurements and a compute-budget-matched NES experiment.

before.justification: v1 reports original VMC calculations for second-row atoms, 12 molecules, carbon-dimer and ethylene potential energy surfaces, and 33 beryllium states, together with runtime measurements and ablations.

P2.justification: v2 adds a correctness-versus-time plot, benchmark-characterization plots, a timeout-sweep figure, and an Easy-split table. Existing result tables expand, the case-study figure is redesigned, the raw-invariant example moves into the introduction, baseline plots are combined, and algorithms and hyperparameter tables are reformatted.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same WONDA research. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, allowing equations, algorithms, experiments, tables, and figures to be matched across revisions.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds model-family comparisons, Easy-split results, benchmark characterization, and a timeout sensitivity analysis.

before.justification: v1 reports original fine-tuning experiments, verification results, pipeline-stage ablations, and curated-dataset statistics, including Tables 3–4 and the appendices.

results.title: Not All Invariants Are Equal: Curating Training Data to Accelerate Program Verification with SLMs

The code-access claim is documented in the PDF, without external verification.

The added simulation-based-inference citation is not an evaluated baseline.
