These include 50,000/10,000/10,000 training/validation/test splits, label normalization, generated-output clamping, and benchmark-specific architectures and training schedules. Appendices D, E, and H additionally specify surrogate perturbations, nine ODE solver configurations, OOD distance bands, and physical OOD tests using 1,000 in-distribution and 1,000 OOD samples.

E4.justification: New Appendix D tests sensitivity to surrogate-output noise and nine independently trained Unifoil evaluators. Appendix E tests Euler, RK4, and adaptive Dopri5 integration. Appendix H adds OOD-distance sweeps and physical/conditioning-shift stress tests. These substantially expand the robustness evidence beyond v1's retained permutation, accuracy-conditioned diversity, and original OOD analyses.

E5.justification: The original five-run reporting practice remains. New Table 8 specifies averaging over five noise seeds and reports means and ranges across nine Unifoil surrogates trained using three architectures and three seeds each. These add variability estimation for the robustness experiments without establishing an increased run count for the original experiments.

E6.justification: Original result-table entries are retained. New Tables 4 and 5 report Diag-CFM round-trip errors of 2.247e-2 on thin films and 9.15e-3 on FashionMNIST, lowest among the three methods in each setting. Further tables add surrogate, solver, and OOD findings. The select-best improvement range is corrected from 13–31% to 5–31%, and Zero-Deviation rejection improvement from 10–27% to 8–27%, matching existing tables. New Table 13 reports gas-turbine hard-OOD AUC 0.773, while retained Figure 8 shows 0.754; this discrepancy is unexplained.

M1.justification: The zero-anchored states, flow-matching objective, and uncertainty algorithms remain unchanged. V2 adds a task-specific architectural extension for FashionMNIST: a U-Net-style CNN with skip connections, FiLM conditioning, and bottleneck self-attention that predicts image and label velocities (Appendix F.7). V1 used MLP velocity networks.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the overall narrative structure are retained. V2 inserts two experimental subsections and two robustness appendices, updates cross-references and appendix labels, adds code availability and acknowledgements, and makes localized abstract, conclusion, bibliographic, and publication-footer edits.

P2.justification: V2 substantially expands the tabular presentation with benchmark Tables 4–5, mathematical-definition Table 7, surrogate/solver Tables 8–9, and OOD Tables 13–14. The original Figures 1–10 and earlier result tables are retained, with changed placement and table numbering. The general main-text and appendix layout styles remain.

R1.justification: Section 2.2 adds Wildberger et al. on flow matching for simulation-based inference and distinguishes conditional posterior sampling from the paper's bidirectional mapping. New citations to Luce, Ma, and Xiao support the added benchmarks. Most research positioning remains unchanged; consolidation of Lipman's preprint and publication references does not remove a distinct prior work.

T1.justification: Propositions 4.1–4.2 and their Appendix A proofs are unchanged. Appendices C.4–C.5 add mathematical specifications of the new forward problems, including layer transfer matrices and the five image-statistic functions in Table 7. This is a limited addition of formal definitions, without new theoretical guarantees.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation missing in v1: surrogate and solver checks directly probe dependence on evaluation approximations, while physically motivated OOD tests and two exact-forward benchmarks strengthen evidence for reliability and broader applicability. Added technical documentation and code-access information improve reproducibility. These gains outweigh reporting weaknesses: the gas-turbine AUC discrepancy between Table 13 and Figure 8 remains unexplained, and Table 14 includes an ensemble win despite retained blanket UQ-superiority claims.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Diagonal Flow Matching research. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching across additions, relocation, and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds thin-film and FashionMNIST experiments, surrogate and solver robustness checks, and additional OOD evaluations.

before.justification: V1 reports original model comparisons on gas turbine, Unifoil, and DTLZ datasets, plus permutation, diversity, and uncertainty-quantification experiments in Section 5 and the appendices.

results.title: Generative Inverse Design with Abstention via Diagonal Flow Matching

C1.justification: The abstract and central claims about structured environments, accessibility, and competitive protein design remain unchanged. The introduction and conclusion modestly broaden the explicit performance-parity claim from ProteinMPNN to ProteinMPNN and BoltzGen.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands interpretation and limitations: it identifies self-correction loops, explains how TRF insertion can relocate the protein core, and discusses smaller-model failures. The conclusion explicitly limits evidence to RosettaScripts and a few structures and conditions expected generalization on scientific knowledge and structured interfaces. A new impact statement addresses misuse and confidently wrong designs.

D1.justification: v2 adds a project-code link and a detailed MD appendix specifying OpenMM 8.2, VMD 1.9.3, CHARMM36, solvation and ion settings, integration parameters, and equilibration procedures. It also discloses OpenRouter provider selection and clarifies model sizes. Existing prompts, XML templates, preprocessing descriptions, and TRF parameters are retained.

E1.justification: The same eight canonical-design backbones and four TRF-insertion proteins are retained. New Appendix C expands diagnostic task coverage to custom score functions, sequence extraction, per-residue energy reporting, and cavity-volume/radius-of-gyration calculations under differing prompting support.

E2.justification: v2 adds BoltzGen and a randomized scripted policy to the canonical-design comparisons, retaining ProteinMPNN, both fixed human protocols, and the existing naive policy. Appendix E.5 additionally evaluates two manual revisions of the human protocol on 9KGY and 9C14. These substantially broaden the comparison methods.

E3.justification: Section 3.2 replaces the reported 128-design comparator trials with matched total budgets of approximately 2048 candidates and removes the stated pLDDT >=85 filtering rule. v2 also evaluates Qwen3 30B, introduces canonical-design AF3 validation of selected top-10 designs, and adds 1-microsecond MD validation protocols. These are reported protocol changes, without establishing that every retained experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds prompt-only environment ablations, an experiment withholding ESMFold metrics from Qwen3 235B, iterative human-protocol analysis, and MD stability checks for both protein-design tasks. The ESMFold ablation reports changes below 0.1 angstrom RMSD and 1% pLDDT. These substantially extend the investigation of environment necessity, feedback dependence, and design stability.

E5.justification: The existing 16-trial, 1000-bootstrap, best-of-eight reporting remains. v2 adds three independent MD replicates with different initial velocities, MD confidence intervals, and paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with family-wise error control at 0.05. This introduces inferential testing beyond v1's descriptive uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Canonical results are revised under changed protocols: aggregate GPT-5 RMSD changes from 639 to 608 milliangstroms and ProteinMPNN from 570 to 581 (v1 Table C.2; v2 Table E.3). New results include ablations, comparators, and MD outcomes, including NCAA median RMSD of 2.6 versus 3.1 angstroms for GPT-5 and the human baseline. Original NCAA AF3 scores are retained. The narrative changes its win count from five to four backbones, although v2 Table E.2 still shows an agent variant leading on five.

M1.justification: The proposed interaction loop, three action types, simplified syntax, Pareto selection, prompts, and action templates are retained. The smaller LLM evaluation and withholding of ESMFold feedback are experimental variants; no revision to the proposed framework is established.

P1.justification: The main narrative and most appendix prose are retained. v2 edits comparison and evaluation passages, separates the NCAA comparison/evaluation discussion, adds an impact statement and dedicated ablation/MD appendices, and updates affiliations and model terminology. The changes do not amount to a wholesale language or structural rewrite.

P2.justification: v2 redraws Figure 1, separates and resizes previously paired main-text figures, reorganizes the canonical trajectory grid, and changes table ordering and column structure. New displays include the environment-ablation table, MD summary table, and three MD trajectory figures. These substantially revise the visual presentation.

R1.justification: The introduction newly distinguishes low-level scientific-software integration from high-level orchestration, including ProtAgents and Agent Laboratory. References add BoltzGen and MD-related works and remove the mixed-chirality macrocycle paper. Appendix A's broader positioning remains largely unchanged; bibliographic metadata expansions do not constitute new research coverage.

T1.justification: Neither version develops formal theorems or proofs, and the retained method and syntax descriptions introduce no changed mathematical reasoning. The new stability measurements and statistical tests are evaluation additions.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence behind the original claims through environment and feedback ablations, broader comparisons, matched candidate budgets, canonical AF3 validation, and replicated MD checks for both design tasks. These address important weaknesses in v1's validation and controls. Small protein sets, limited human iteration, and the inconsistent backbone win-count summary remain weaknesses, but do not outweigh the gains. The added stability evidence remains computational rather than experimental validation of synthesized proteins.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Agent Rosetta work and contain readable text, figures, tables, and appendices. Retained appendix material can be matched across renumbering; no material reading gaps prevent comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds environment ablations, expanded baseline comparisons, and molecular-dynamics simulation outcomes.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on composition-penalty generation, canonical protein sequence design, and TRF insertion, including numerical results in its appendices.

results.title: Protein Design with Agent Rosetta: A Case Study for Specialized Scientific Agents

C1.justification: The central cached-retrieval and beyond-log-probability claims remain. v3 explicitly extends the conclusion to reasoning models and qualifies cached retrieval as the dominant rather than sole pathway in the tested settings. These refine the scope and exclusivity of the original contribution.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive interpretations of answer-colon inactivity and Magistral's null PANL ablation, attributing the latter to redundant confidence information across reasoning traces. It newly identifies untested paraphrases and persona framing as limitations. It also introduces an OOD-artifact exclusion interpretation, although Table 1 does not support the assertion that all reported shifts lie within its natural percentile ranges.

D1.justification: C.4 adds substantial Magistral reproducibility information: checkpoint, attention implementation, decoding limit, filtering to 4998 trials, stratified activation collection, calibration selection, and trace-position extraction. C.1.9 newly specifies the three regression fits, feature combinations, and Ridge regularization of 1.0. These document the added analyses rather than demonstrate changes to previously stated settings.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates factual question answering on TriviaQA. v3 adds mathematical problems from BigMath and multiple-choice questions from MMLU, plus a TriviaQA scenario with explicit reasoning traces preceding answers. These substantially broaden task and input-context coverage (2.9; Figures 25–28).

E2.justification: The central variance-partitioning comparison expands beyond mean answer log-probability to include minimum, maximum, variance, first-token, and last-token log-probabilities, individually and jointly. These are evaluated comparators with reported results, substantially broadening the tested alternatives to activation-based confidence prediction (C.1.9, D.3; Figure 14).

E3.justification: v3 introduces distinct protocols for Magistral, including two-phase reasoning/confidence prompts, a 1024-token generation limit, and stratified sampling. New controls additionally corrupt the answer-colon position and share its selected probe regularization across positions; steering sensitivity tests add strengths 1 and 10. These extend the evaluation design without establishing reruns of retained experiments.

E4.justification: New analyses test whether the pre-answer answer-colon position causally contributes to confidence, whether conclusions survive alternative log-probability summaries, and whether intervention shifts resemble natural activation variability. v3 also adds steering-strength sensitivity and decoding across reasoning-trace positions (Figures 13–14, 26, 29; Table 1).

E5.justification: Table 1 newly reports empirical 5th–95th percentile reference ranges for natural cosine similarities and norm ratios using 3000 activation trials. Existing SEM reporting and fivefold cross-validation remain. Neither version documents an increase in repeated runs or seeds.

E6.justification: Original results are largely retained. New results include BigMath accuracy of 40.2%, MMLU accuracy of 76.8%, and Magistral's null PANL-noising effect despite effective patching. The expanded baseline analysis reports combined-baseline R² = 0.100 and additional PANL R²unique = 0.38 (D.3). These are added findings under new analyses or settings, not same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The intervention and probing framework is retained, with limited procedural adaptations for reasoning traces. Magistral patching corrupts the question and full reasoning/answer block instead of only answer embeddings, and donor matching uses reasoning-trace length instead of answer length (C.4).

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the overall narrative are retained. v3 inserts dedicated OOD and answer-colon subsections, reorganizes the variance-partitioning methods, expands the generalization and conclusion passages, and adds limitations and an impact statement. These are targeted structural edits accompanying new content rather than a wholesale rewrite.

P2.justification: v3 substantially expands the visual presentation with an experiment roadmap, answer-colon and baseline-analysis plots, reasoning prompts and results, additional dataset panels, a steering sensitivity figure, and Table 1. Original figures are largely retained and renumbered; Figure 2 is redrawn with revised typography and tick labeling while preserving its plotted results.

R1.justification: v3 adds BigMath and MMLU references, Yang et al. on verbalized confidence, Teplica et al. on shared uncertainty circuits, and Kumaran et al. on error detection. The latter two provide additional positioning, while the main relationship to prior mechanistic and neuroscience work remains intact.

T1.justification: The existing intervention and metric equations are preserved in substance. The newly explicit variance-partitioning formula explains an existing empirical analysis; it does not introduce new theoretical reasoning. Neither version supplies formal theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v1's broad mechanism account relied on TriviaQA without explicit reasoning and a single log-probability summary. v3 substantially strengthens its evidential basis through additional task types, a reasoning model, answer-colon controls, and broader baselines, while acknowledging alternative pathways and prompt limitations. A material weakness remains: the new OOD discussion claims all shifts fall within natural ranges, although Table 1 lists scale-5 cosine similarities of 0.992–0.995 below the corresponding lower bounds of 0.997–0.998. This weakens that particular argument but does not outweigh the substantial gains in controlled evidence and demonstrated applicability.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study, How do LLMs Compute Verbal Confidence? Their main text, equations, figures, and appendices support comparison. Retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering, with no essential reading gaps.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and adds BigMath, MMLU, Magistral reasoning-model experiments, and further control and robustness analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original calibration, activation intervention, probing, and attention-blocking experiments on Gemma 3 27B and Qwen 2.5 7B using TriviaQA.

results.title: How do LLMs Compute Verbal Confidence?

C1.justification: The generator and benchmark contributions remain central. The introduction and conclusion extend the prompt-optimization claim to domains outside the optimization distribution and explicitly emphasize validation of task-difficulty controls. The advertised billions-scale task space was already documented in v1 Appendix C.

C2.justification: For the revised benchmark, v2 replaces v1's strong All-Edit model-ranking statement with caution about low success rates. It interprets baseline initialization as easier but liable to preserve the initial implementation, and explicitly identifies prompt-only optimization and limited model/scaffold coverage as remaining limitations.

D1.justification: v1 Appendix O's extensive domain, dataset, and module prompt specifications are removed and replaced by repository access guidance in v2 Appendix D.1. The documented five-task learned prompt also changes, without explaining whether this is a correction or a new run. v2 adds MARL's four-GPU requirement and updates estimated total compute from 23,000 to 35,000 GPU-hours.

E1.justification: Evaluated coverage expands from ten to fourteen domains, adding neural cellular automata, offline RL, on-policy MARL, and trajectory prediction. These were described but not evaluated in v1. v2 includes their DiscoBench results and uses them for explicitly held-out-domain prompt evaluation.

E2.justification: The three LLM-backed agents and all-fixed DiscoBench baseline are retained. However, v2 Appendix J.9–J.10 adds all-fixed baseline references to per-task comparisons of tuned prompts; v1's corresponding prompt-tuning results compared the four task-count conditions without that reference.

E3.justification: v2 adds evaluation on four domains outside the retained ten-domain prompt-training distribution. The module sweep expands from 15 configurations of four modules to 63 configurations of six modules. The new initialization experiment controls starting code across eight selected domains using DeepSeek-v3.2. Existing benchmark action budgets and dataset splits are retained.

E4.justification: Section 8.2 adds an empty-versus-baseline initialization ablation and qualitative examination of resulting algorithms. Section 8.1 substantially expands v1 Appendix G's module sweep, while dropping its detailed maximum-score summary. Section 7 adds an explicit analysis of generalization beyond the prompt-training domain distribution.

E5.justification: Both versions specify three meta-seeds, additional attempts until three successful runs where feasible, and 95% Elo intervals from 100 bootstrap rounds. Per-task stratified bootstrap intervals and interquartile means are retained, as are eight-inner-seed means and standard errors for the single-task prompt-tuning curves.

E6.justification: Benchmark aggregates, success@3 values, and numerous per-task results change. For example, DeepSeek's Single-Edit success rate changes from 80.0% in v1 Table 2 to 71.3% in v2 Table 3 on expanded coverage, not a comparable-setting decline. New results include held-out-domain prompt scores and initialization success rates of 92.4% versus 75.4% in Section 8.2.

M1.justification: The task generator, two-stage meta-train/meta-test construction, MLGym scaffold, and Claude/DeepSeek prompt-tuning procedure remain unchanged. The additional domains and on-policy target/activation modules emphasized in v2 were already specified in v1 Appendices B–C.

P1.justification: The document is substantially reorganized: design analyses gain a main-text section, domain appendices are consolidated, successful-run results move out of the main comparison, and the task-prompt appendix is removed. Method and research-direction passages are condensed, and evaluation terminology and section titles are revised.

P2.justification: v2 adds the benchmark-property table, restructures main result tables, replaces module-summary tables with Figure 2, and extensively expands appendix plots. Some presentation becomes less specific: many combination panels in Figures 32–39 use 'OnPolicyRL all' instead of v1's explicit module-combination labels.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to ProgramBench, Hyperagents, and process reward models, and presents benchmark positioning in a new property-comparison table. The underlying related-work argument remains stable; most other bibliographic revisions update publication metadata rather than introduce different works.

T1.justification: The task-count formula, its inclusion-exclusion derivation, the model-unlearning extension, and Elo equations are unchanged between v1 Appendices E–F and v2 Appendices C–D. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v1's empirical validation covered ten domains and pooled prompt-tuning performance. v2 evaluates the four previously untested domains, explicitly separates transfer beyond the training-domain distribution, and adds controlled initialization comparisons and broader module ablations. These address important gaps in validating diversity, generalization, and controllable difficulty. The gains outweigh reduced self-contained prompt documentation and less informative combination-plot labels.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DiscoGen/DiscoBench work and provide readable main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices. Reordered sections and previously documented capabilities can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and reports expanded domain evaluations, held-out-domain prompt performance, and an initialization ablation.

before.justification: v1 reports original DiscoBench evaluations of three LLM-backed agents, prompt-tuning experiments, module-combination analyses, and discovered algorithms.

results.title: Procedural Generation Of Algorithm Discovery Tasks in Machine Learning

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list and conclusion retain the same central claims: adapting diffusion LLMs through a unified delimiter-based corpus and domain adaptation, followed by SFT and RL, achieves strong small-data BBO performance. The added experiments support these existing claims without materially redefining them.

C2.justification: V2 broadens interpretation through the matched-backbone results, GP-prior sensitivity, mixed RNA findings and pretraining-knowledge audit. It explicitly acknowledges that unavailable pretraining data prevent an exact overlap audit. Section 4.6 also narrows the earlier interpretation about avoiding 'prompt hacking' to robustness under natural paraphrases that preserve task semantics and output format.

D1.justification: V2 newly documents stage-specific optimization steps and processed sample counts, inference-context resampling, single-pass greedy token filling, and duplicate rejection until 128 unique valid candidates are obtained. It adds representative paraphrases, GP implementation information and the ranking-probe procedure. The abstract's code hyperlink changes from an anonymous repository to the named DiBO GitHub repository; these are documented access instructions, not independently verified availability.

E1.justification: V2 retains the four original Design-Bench tasks and adds RNA-A/B/C from BootGen, involving length-14 RNA sequence optimization (Appendix A.6, Table 11). This substantially extends biological task coverage beyond the original DNA and robot-morphology evaluations.

E2.justification: V2 adds a matched LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct autoregressive comparator across all four original tasks and all three training stages (Table 2), providing a substantial new comparison against the diffusion backbone. The main table's named comparator set is retained. Inference-only dLLM with MCTS was excluded from quantitative comparisons in both versions; its discussion was moved.

E3.justification: V2 introduces matched-backbone controls, random versus evenly spaced pool sampling, Top-5/10/20 metrics, and ranking probes using 500 groups per task for K=2–5. It adopts dimension-scaled GP priors and changes the stated continuous-task DA learning rate from 1e-4 to 1e-5. That reported setting revision does not establish that retained experiments were rerun; newly disclosed training budgets and decoding details are documentation additions.

E4.justification: V2 adds analyses testing the backbone's contribution, sensitivity to offline-pool sampling, the effect of GP priors, and possible pretrained design-label knowledge (Tables 2, 6, 8 and 12). These address important questions absent from v1. The delimiter, training-stage, context-similarity and hyperparameter analyses are largely retained.

E5.justification: Both versions specify eight random seeds and mean ± standard deviation for optimization results. V2 introduces no new confidence intervals, significance tests or changed repeated-run counts. Additional result rows and the ranking probe's sample size do not establish a change in uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: DiBO's four headline maximum scores remain unchanged, but GP results and rankings change under revised priors; for example, Grad-EI's TF Bind 8 maximum changes from 0.673 to 0.864. DiBO's TF Bind 8 median changes from 0.599 in v1 Table 5 to 0.473 in v2 Tables 9–10, although v2 Table 8 retains 0.599. Numerous new results include mixed RNA outcomes: DiBO leads maximum scores on RNA-A/C but trails both comparators on every reported RNA-B metric.

M1.justification: Equation (3) revises the stated domain-adaptation loss indicator to include prompt masking alongside response masking. This is a localized loss-expression change: both versions already describe joint prompt-response reconstruction, so an implementation change is not established. The backbone, corpus construction, DA–SFT–RL pipeline and reward remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The main section order and most existing prose remain intact. V2 makes targeted wording changes, expands implementation and appendix explanations, rewrites the prompt-robustness discussion and conclusion, and moves the inference-only comparison into Section 4.4. Author/affiliation and proceedings-header text also change; there is no wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: V2 adds substantial displays for the matched backbone comparison, pool sampling, prompt paraphrases, GP-prior comparisons, Top-K performance, RNA results and ranking audit. Existing ablation tables are regrouped and renumbered, and Figure 2 is relocated with a shorter caption. The two existing figures retain essentially the same visual content.

R1.justification: V2 adds literature supporting high-dimensional GP calibration and implementation, including Hvarfner, Binois and Wycoff, Garnett and BoTorch, plus BootGen and additional BBO/multimodal citations. The central positioning relative to autoregressive optimization and inference-only diffusion remains intact. Publication updates for existing works and removal of a duplicate ICT reference do not constitute new research positioning.

T1.justification: Equation (3) adds a prompt-mask condition to the formal loss indicator, changing its mathematical expression rather than merely its typography. The other training objectives and similarity definition are retained, and neither version supplies theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: The matched trained autoregressive control and calibrated GP comparisons substantially strengthen evidence for DiBO's advantages beyond v1's comparisons. Explicit training budgets and inference procedures resolve important reproducibility gaps, while RNA evaluations and a narrower paraphrase interpretation better expose applicability boundaries. These gains outweigh a material reporting defect: v2 gives conflicting TF Bind 8 medians, 0.599 in Table 8 versus 0.473 in Tables 9–10. The improvement concerns stronger evaluation and documentation, not increased headline DiBO scores.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DiBO research work. The full main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching material that was moved or renumbered.

after.justification: V2 retains original experiments and adds a matched autoregressive comparison, GP-prior and sampling analyses, RNA evaluations and a pretraining-overlap probe.

before.justification: V1 reports original optimization experiments on four Design-Bench tasks, component ablations, hyperparameter sensitivity studies and appendix median results.

results.title: Training Diffusion Language Models for Black-Box Optimization

C1.justification: The core contribution remains discounted historical reward estimation for sample-efficient RLVR. The abstract and conclusion qualify lower MSE by mild non-stationarity, while the introduction adds an appropriate-discount-factor qualification and claims statistically significant superiority over a broader baseline set.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands explanations of how nonzero advantages on all-correct/all-incorrect groups affect exploration and why DBB needs wider clipping. It adds interpretations of prior sensitivity, preservation of useful diversity, model-dependent discount selection and the tuning-versus-MSE tradeoff with empirical Bayes. Suggested settings for 30B+ models are explicitly extrapolations.

D1.justification: Appendix C clarifies clipping conventions and per-method settings and adds implementation guidance for GRESO and DAPO. Appendices H–I specify EMA initialization and online method-of-moments fitting for the empirical-Bayes prior. Existing hardware, data filtering, optimizer settings and framework links are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions train on DAPO-Math-17k and retain the same six mathematical and three general-reasoning evaluation benchmarks. The additional 0.6B model uses existing benchmarks; continuous and dense rewards are discussed only as future work.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds evaluated GRESO and DAPO baselines alongside GRPO and RePO. Appendices H–I additionally compare DBB with per-prompt EMA, Laplace smoothing and empirical Bayes on estimation MSE. These substantially broaden the comparator set.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include testing both GRPO and DBB under two clipping ranges, prior-parameter sweeps, Best@8 evaluation and a discount-factor search on Qwen3-0.6B-Base. The expanded main comparison explicitly matches total rollout budgets. Existing Table 5 training settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New Appendices D–I investigate whether clipping explains the gains, sensitivity to prior strength, whether lower entropy harms useful response diversity, model-scale dependence of the optimal discount factor, and whether simpler estimators suffice. These address substantial questions beyond v1’s existing discount-factor, MSE and Dr.GRPO analyses.

E5.justification: v1 reports scalar benchmark scores without stated replication or significance tests. v2 reports four independent evaluation seeds, means and standard deviations, and one-sided paired t-tests over per-prompt accuracies in Table 1. Appendix C clarifies that these are evaluation repetitions, not four independent training runs.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces earlier scores with four-evaluation-run summaries. Reported DBB-minus-GRPO gains for 1.7B/8B change from 3.22/2.42 to 3.43/2.32 points in distribution and from 12.49/6.92 to 10.05/8.34 out of distribution. These are revised estimates, not demonstrated improvements from a changed method. New baseline, clipping, Best@8, prior-sensitivity and estimator-comparison results substantially expand the findings.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1, the discounted posterior updates, initialization and GRPO/Dr.GRPO integration remain unchanged. The wider DBB clipping range was already disclosed in v1; v2 investigates it without changing the proposed procedure.

P1.justification: Targeted rewrites expand the abstract, experimental discussion and Sections 5.1–5.2, with terminology and cross-reference corrections. v2 adds acknowledgements, updates affiliation/publication text and appends new analyses, while retaining the main section order and most methodological exposition.

P2.justification: Table 1 is substantially expanded with additional baselines, uncertainty values and significance rows. v2 adds Figures 4–8 and Table 6, providing new diagnostic plots, a prior-sensitivity heatmap and estimator comparisons. Figure 6 redisplays existing Mean@8 curves alongside newly reported Best@8 curves.

R1.justification: Section 5.3 and Appendices H–I newly position DBB against simpler shrinkage and shared-prior estimators. Section 6 and the cited-work set otherwise remain essentially unchanged; the Gelman reference switches editions of the same book rather than introducing a different work.

T1.justification: Appendices H–I add formal definitions and conditional MSE expressions for EMA, Laplace smoothing and empirical Bayes, including EMA’s historical weights. The original DBB equations and Appendix B derivation remain unchanged; the mathematical additions support the new comparator analyses.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation by addressing v1’s limited comparator set and absent uncertainty reporting. Appendix D directly tests the important clipping-range confound, while prior-sensitivity, Best@8 and alternative-estimator analyses better support the central argument. Replication covers evaluation randomness rather than training variability, and reporting inconsistencies remain, such as Appendix G claiming six benchmarks while Table 6 lists five. These limitations do not outweigh the substantial evidential gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DBB reward-estimation work. All pages, including figures, tables, equations and appendices, are readable and support comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, evaluation statistics, clipping controls, prior sensitivity and supplementary estimator analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original Qwen3 training and benchmark results, discount-factor ablations, training dynamics and empirical reward-estimation error analyses.

results.title: Discounted Beta–Bernoulli Reward Estimation for Sample-Efficient Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion retain the same scientific claims. The introduction's fourth numbered contribution becomes a separate paragraph with unchanged meaning. Additional experiments support the existing efficiency and generative-quality claims without redefining them.

C2.justification: v2 adds diversity-loss and model-strength hypotheses for high-step degradation, attributes the text-to-image oracle advantage to distribution shift, and explicitly identifies the mixed schedule as heuristic. One interpretation is overstated: Appendix C.1 claims the gamma = 0.5 variant beats SiD2 at every step count, but Table 4 gives FID 2.99 versus 2.96 at 128 steps.

D1.justification: v2 documents text-conditioning architecture, sampler dimensions and hyperparameters, additional FiLM/guidance explanations, parallel RAPSD preprocessing, TPU hardware, and training/inference timings. It also revises the class-sampler settings. Reproducibility information expands substantially, although the text-training dataset remains identified only through the SiD2 reference.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates class-conditional ImageNet generation. v2 adds text-conditioned training on the dataset described as SiD2's, zero-shot MS-COCO evaluation at 512 × 512, and unconditional ImageNet generation at 256 × 256. These substantially broaden task and distribution coverage.

E2.justification: The original class-conditional comparator sets remain unchanged. New comparisons include published SiD text-to-image results in Table 3 and ADM unconditional results in Table 5, alongside SiD2.

E3.justification: v2 adds zero-shot text evaluation, baseline sampling sweeps extending to 4096 steps, a gamma = 0.5 sampling control, and timed hardware comparisons. Appendix D.2 also revises the reported class-conditional sampler from 3 to 5 mixture components and learning rate 0.001 to 0.01. The PDFs do not establish whether retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix C.1 newly investigates high-step degradation using multiple metrics, extended SiD2 sampling, and increased sampling noise. Section 5.5 adds a text-to-image oracle-spectrum comparison, while Appendix C.2 demonstrates contrast manipulation previously only described. Original schedule, conditioning, and hyperparameter ablations are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report averaging the main ImageNet results over five generation sets with different seeds. v2 introduces no new repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty-estimation practices.

E6.justification: All original table entries and Figure 3 curves are retained. New results include MS-COCO FID 7.08 at 96 steps versus reproduced SiD2's 7.56 at 160 steps, and unconditional ImageNet FID 16.8 at 256 steps versus 17.2 at 512 steps. Table 4 adds degradation and noise-control results; Appendix E adds measured runtime results. These are newly reported comparisons, not improvements over v1 under unchanged settings.

M1.justification: The core spectral schedules and training/sampling algorithms remain unchanged. v2 implements text conditioning through T5-XXL embeddings, pooled FiLM conditioning, and transformer cross-attention, with an attention-pooling/MLP spectrum sampler (Sections 4.4, 5.5, and D.2). These are adaptations of the retained method.

P1.justification: v2 locally clarifies schedule construction, spectrum manipulation, and conditioning, and corrects wording. It adds Section 5.5 and an impact statement, subdivides Appendix C, and inserts a computational-cost appendix. Most existing prose and the main narrative structure remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds dedicated text-to-image, high-step degradation, and unconditional comparison tables, plus contrast-control and text-to-image sample grids. Existing displays are retained, with Table 1 highlighting and some relocation. Original appendix Tables 3–5 become Tables 6–8, and the original sample Figure 6 becomes Figure 7.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for ADM, MS-COCO, attention pooling, and T5, supporting its new experiments and implementation. The main positioning against global noise schedules and earlier spectral approaches remains unchanged. The Ramesh citation-year correction concerns the same work.

T1.justification: The spectral bounds and closed-form schedule derivations are retained. Added substitution steps and the explicit least-squares objective elaborate existing computations. The expectation qualification was already present in v1's derivation, and the Parseval explanation formalizes its existing spectrum–variance connection rather than introducing a substantive new theoretical result.

improvement.justification: v1's empirical support was confined to class-conditional ImageNet and left high-step deterioration unexplained. v2 substantially strengthens the paper through cross-task validation, diagnostic experiments testing a mitigation for that deterioration, and measured runtime evidence supporting practical efficiency. Incomplete text-data disclosure, unexplained revisions to sampler settings, and the overstated all-step comparison limit reproducibility and interpretation, but do not outweigh these substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same spectrally guided diffusion work. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support comparison, including matching retained material across renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original text-to-image, unconditional generation, high-step degradation, contrast-control, and computational-cost results.

before.justification: v1 reports original ImageNet generation experiments, comparisons with reproduced SiD2 models, sampling-step evaluations, and ablations.

results.title: Spectrally-Guided Diffusion Noise Schedules

C1.justification: The abstract and headline contributions remain the finite-horizon control formulation, three-regime betting theory, and a universal DQN that improves deadline power and confidence sequences while preserving validity. The expanded experiments primarily provide additional support for these retained claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations of reward tradeoffs, optimization difficulty with larger action spaces, transfer beyond training distributions, and use of the Type-I error budget. It explicitly limits real-data evidence to resampled marginal distributions and adds an interpretability limitation. The conclusion replaces the Beta-only experimental limitation with broader remaining distributional questions.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-repository link, GEO sample identifiers, humidity station/date information, humidity normalization and resampling instructions, and specifications for the new policy variants. The original implementation descriptions, architecture, hardware information, and Table 1 hyperparameters remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained Beta/Beta-mixture experiments, v2 evaluates transfer to logit-normal distributions and six real-data sources: three DNA methylation samples and three relative-humidity stations. It also adds Bernoulli-family training and evaluation, using a separately trained policy.

E2.justification: The external comparator set remains empirical Kelly, Linear-ε, Hedge, STaR-Bets, and STaR-Hoeffding. Figure 6 adds DQN-EB and DQN-U as internal comparators in the retained Beta-mixture setting, and Figure 15 compares the original DQN with its nine-action variant.

E3.justification: v2 adds empirical-distribution resampling protocols with N=100 and null controls, a matched-budget action-space comparison, evaluation at N=250, 300, and 350, and retraining/evaluation at α=0.01. These substantially extend the evaluation design; the original experiments and main training settings remain intact.

E4.justification: Appendix F adds reward-function and action-space ablations, distribution-transfer tests, deadline and significance-level sensitivity experiments, and explicit Type-I error checks. These address design choices and robustness questions beyond v1's training curves and qualitative trajectories, which are retained.

E5.justification: The new real-data curves use the existing practice of estimating frequencies over 5,000 trials. Neither version reports confidence intervals, significance tests, or variability across independently trained DQN seeds. The fixed-seed checkpoint evaluation remains unchanged; null-calibration curves are new outcomes, not uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Existing results are retained, while Figures 6–18 add substantial new findings. These include improved power on additional distribution families, the highest deadline rejection probability in five of six real-data cases, earlier rejection versus terminal-power tradeoffs from reward shaping, and no overall improvement from nine actions.

M1.justification: The main three-action DQN and its architecture remain unchanged. Sections 4.4 and F.1 add trained DQN-EB and DQN-U variants with early-rejection rewards, while F.4 tests an expanded nine-action policy. These are limited extensions of the existing learning procedure.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized wording edits, expands Section 4.4, adds an Impact Statement, and organizes Appendix F into nine subsections. The original training and trajectory subsections move to F.8–F.9. Most existing prose and the overall section structure are retained.

P2.justification: v2 adds thirteen multipanel figures, Figures 6–18, displaying new comparisons, data histograms, calibration curves, and ablations. Original Figures 1–5 remain, while v1 Figures 6–9 become Figures 19–22. Table 1 is retained.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds Koning and Van Meer (2026), discussing their Doob-martingale construction and distinguishing this paper's restriction to multiplicative betting processes. Other reference changes largely update metadata for existing works rather than introduce new research positioning.

T1.justification: Equation 1 generalizes deadline power to expected utility E[u(τ)1{τ≤N}] for nonnegative, nonincreasing u, with an expected-wealth constraint at bounded stopping times. The subsequent analysis specializes to u=1. The Bellman recursion, principal theoretical results, and Appendix A–B proofs are retained.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's explicit Beta-only validation limitation through transfer tests on logit-normal and six real empirical distributions, alongside separately trained Bernoulli experiments. Reward/action ablations and null-calibration checks also make the design choices and empirical behavior better supported. Real-data evidence remains limited to i.i.d. resampling, but the broader validation materially strengthens the paper while retaining its original theory and results.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, Learning to Bet for Horizon-Aware Anytime-Valid Testing. Their main text, equations, figures, table, and Appendices A–F are readable and support comparison, including matching retained material across renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those results and adds original distribution-transfer experiments, real-data evaluations, ablations, sensitivity tests, and null-calibration results.

before.justification: v1 reports original dynamic-programming calculations, DQN training, Monte Carlo rejection probabilities, confidence-sequence experiments, and betting trajectories in Section 4 and Appendix F.

results.title: Learning to Bet for Horizon-Aware Anytime-Valid Testing

C1.justification: Both versions claim improved block-factorized modeling, a compact soft-conditioned AR component, better code-generation accuracy–latency tradeoffs, approximately twofold dynamic-decoding speedup, and preserved bidirectional capabilities. V2 explicitly names infilling and planning in the contribution list, but the added evidence principally substantiates the existing capability claim.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations that improvements do not depend on strong standalone AR coding ability, global EOS penalties overcome the need for local scoping, generation becomes less left-to-right, and batching amortizes AR overhead. Some interpretations overreach: Appendix B.1 calls full soft-conditioning strictly Pareto-optimal, although Table 4 gives Top-5 higher HumanEval accuracy at B=4, 56.1% versus 51.8%, at the same reported throughput.

D1.justification: Most original Appendix A implementation details remain. V2 adds a code-access statement and extensive instructions for new configurations, including infilling entropy weight 0.5 and fallbacks, waiting-line disagreement penalty 1.0, and graph-model architecture and training epochs. These materially expand reproducibility information; the PDF establishes the repository disclosure, not its external availability.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates code generation on HumanEval, MBPP, their enhanced test suites, and BigCodeBench. V2 retains these and adds HumanEval-Infilling, ParallelBench waiting-line tasks, and graph-traversal planning, including task-specific training. Missing-span generation with surrounding context and synthetic planning substantially broaden task coverage.

E2.justification: The original Dream-Coder and ADJUST comparisons remain. V2 adds standalone Qwen3-0.6B results and comparisons against DreamOn, Dream-Instruct-7B, and MGDM in the added tasks. Table 2 also includes Deepseek-Coder-6.7B, Seed-Coder-8B, and Qwen2.5-Coder-7B reference scores, explicitly attributed to Wu et al. rather than newly run experiments.

E3.justification: Section 4.2 changes controlled masking from 8-token to 32-token segments and extends tested block sizes to 16 and 32, making the training-loss plots different-setting results. New experiments vary AR size, batch size, and blocks decoded per iteration, introduce a code-extraction-failure metric, and specify additional task-specific training and decoding protocols. The original code-generation configurations in Table 3 remain.

E4.justification: V2 retains the Top-1 conditioning and local-horizon analyses while adding Top-3/Top-5 conditioning, boundary-token removal, AR-size controls, global EOS penalization, one-versus-two-block decoding, generation-order correlations, batching, and code-extraction error analysis. These investigate substantial additional questions about mechanism, decoding flexibility, and efficiency.

E5.justification: Both versions specify a single-sample, fixed-seed evaluation in Appendix A.2. Neither introduces repeated-run uncertainty estimates, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The new Spearman correlations analyze generation order rather than uncertainty in reported performance.

E6.justification: Figures 4–5 and the original conditioning and scope results are retained. Numerous new results appear: v2 Table 2 reports 62.5% infilling accuracy at 1.3 tokens/step versus DreamOn's 62.5% at one token/step; Table 9 reports 63.1% versus 52.6% waiting-line accuracy at K=8. Graph-traversal and additional ablation results also appear. Table 6's one-block HumanEval values conflict with Table 4, preventing a reliable interpretation of those entries as same-setting updates.

M1.justification: V2 adds an AR verification mode that penalizes disagreement with DLM predictions, plus global decoding with EOS penalties (Section 3.5). Appendix C introduces mixed-entropy infilling with fallback rules and graph-traversal verification through remasking. These substantially extend inference procedures; the original soft-conditioning architecture and training objective remain.

P1.justification: V2 makes localized rewrites to generation strategies and experimental narration, reorganizes ablations into Appendix B, and moves proofs to Appendix D. Most introduction, theoretical, and related-work prose remains. Author contribution markings and publication information also change; much of the additional text documents new scientific content rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: Figure 3 is redrawn for five block sizes, and Figures 6–7 add multipanel AR-size and decoding-scope comparisons. New tables display errors, infilling, planning, ordering, batching, and multiple-block results. V1 Table 1 becomes the expanded v2 Table 4; the original scope table becomes Table 5, and Figure 5 moves unchanged. These substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: V2 adds references for InCoder, the evaluation harness, DreamOn, diffusion-based planning, and Swordsman. The related-work positioning otherwise remains substantially unchanged. DiffuCoder's change from a 2025 preprint citation to a 2026 conference citation represents the same work, not an added research comparison.

T1.justification: Theorems 3.2–3.3 and their proofs remain unchanged after relocation from Appendix B to D. Section 3.5 makes a limited mathematical correction: the partial-block entropy domain changes from k≤L/B to k≤B, and full-block entropy is evaluated at B instead of L/B.

improvement.justification: V1 largely supports preserved non-causal capabilities through architectural arguments; v2 directly tests infilling and planning and adds controls examining AR capacity, global decoding, and computational overhead. This closes an important empirical gap and substantially improves understanding and reproducibility. The gains outweigh localized reporting weaknesses, particularly the Table 4 Pareto overclaim and Table 6 inconsistencies. Unchanged uncertainty reporting still limits confidence in small measured differences.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CoDiLA research. Their text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material relocated between versions.

after.justification: V2 retains these empirical results and adds original infilling, waiting-line planning, graph-traversal, and ablation results in Section 4 and Appendices B–C.

before.justification: V1 reports original training-loss measurements, code-generation accuracy and throughput, and conditioning and candidate-scope ablations in Section 4 and Appendix A.

results.title: Locally Coherent Parallel Decoding in Diffusion Language Models

C1.justification: The central post-training claim becomes more specific: v4 attributes emergence to contrastive preference optimization, with standard SFT insufficient, rather than broadly to post-training. This algorithm-level conclusion enters the abstract, introduction, and discussion. The main claims about behavioral robustness, distributed detection mechanisms, and underelicited capacity are retained.

C2.justification: Appendix S substantially narrows the interpretation of learned-vector improvements: they do not transfer to broader self-knowledge, and shorter, more assertive responses accompany degraded faithfulness and prefill detection. v4 also qualifies zero-FPR findings to trial numbers 1-10, reports confabulation outside that range, and explicitly acknowledges that the mechanism of post-training emergence remains unidentified.

D1.justification: v4 supplies detailed LoRA hyperparameters, optimizer and schedule settings, preference-data access information, and an abliterated-model link. It clarifies model-matched concept vectors, shared transcoder usage, intervention token positions, and logit-based estimators. Some information is lost: v1's explicit refusal-ablation region boundaries and optimization search bounds are omitted.

E1.justification: v4 adds preference training using Dolci-Instruct-DPO and downstream evaluation on HaluEval, JailbreakHub, MMLU/GPQA-based chain-of-thought faithfulness tasks, and 1,900 self-written-versus-prefilled response examples. These substantially extend the represented data and task requirements beyond v1's concept-injection and generic-prompt evaluations.

E2.justification: v4 introduces comparisons among standard, reference-free, shuffled, and reversed DPO; chosen/rejected-response SFT; SFT with KL; margin-plus-KL training; and DPO without prior SFT (Table 3). Cross-model refusal experiments also add magnitude-matched random-direction controls. These are evaluated comparators absent from v1.

E3.justification: v1 aggregates OLMo results over layers 25, 32, 38, 45, and 51; v4 reports layer-specific evaluations at 19, 22, and 25 on 50 concepts. New experiments introduce controlled LoRA training, TPR-minus-FPR comparisons, and logit-based refusal-ablation evaluation. The attention-probe target also changes in the prose from steered/unsteered activations to successful/failed concepts, although v4 Figure 27 retains the old caption.

E4.justification: v4 adds training-objective and data-domain ablations, DPO beta sweeps, norm/unembedding controls, binary-classification analysis, trial-number sensitivity findings, and cross-model refusal controls. It also investigates downstream side effects. Conversely, the PLS2 steering analysis and v1 Figure 14b-d's circuit-importance analyses disappear; Figure 14a is retained as v4 Figure 33.

E5.justification: v4 newly specifies the existing 100 injection trials as 10 trial numbers with 10 samples each and discusses sampling and judge variability (Appendix B.3); this does not establish additional runs. Appendix H adds correlations controlling for other vector properties. Existing confidence-interval and cross-validation reporting largely persists, without new training-seed information.

E6.justification: Substantial new results include TPR-minus-FPR of +14.4 percentage points for standard DPO versus -13.5 for chosen-response SFT (Table 3). Newly reported downstream comparisons show MMLU faithfulness falling from 37.5% to 21.5% and prefill detection from 36.3% to 16.1% with the bias vector. These are new evaluations; the retained concept-injection gains are unchanged. OLMo results are replaced under revised settings.

M1.justification: The learned steering vector, renamed a bias vector, retains its training procedure. v4 adds a procedural variant for cross-model refusal ablation: a uniform per-model projection weight selected by a minimum-effective-dose rule (Appendix C.2), alongside the original approach using optimized regional weights.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, mechanistic explanations, and discussion receive extensive editing. Section 4 is reframed, Section 6 distinguishes the learned bias from injected concept vectors, related work is reorganized, and limitations become a separate section before discussion. The appendices are substantially reorganized, beyond simple renumbering.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redesigned, gate panels from v1 Figures 10-12 are consolidated into v4 Figure 11, and positive-attribution displays are regrouped in Appendix L. The circuit-distribution panel moves to Appendix O while other circuit-importance panels disappear. Layer-specific OLMo plots, new diagnostic figures, and multiple experimental tables substantially change the presentation.

R1.justification: v4 adds substantive comparisons with Pearson-Vogel et al., Lederman and Mahowald, and Rivera and Africa, relating cached-representation detection, probability matching, latent capacity, and trained steering awareness to its findings. Benchmark and faithfulness references also expand. This materially broadens the research positioning beyond v1's discussion.

T1.justification: The auxiliary circuit-importance definition, gate attribution multiplied by steering projection, is removed with the corresponding analysis. The central steering-attribution mathematics, including complete-cut conditions and Equations 1-3, remains unchanged between v1 Appendix M and v4 Appendix Q.

improvement.justification: v1 mainly associated introspection with checkpoint stage and assessed broader learned-vector effects through response style and length. v4 adds controlled training comparisons that substantially strengthen the preference-training explanation, and downstream tests expose important limits and adverse effects previously untested. Geometric controls further strengthen the mechanistic evidence. These gains outweigh the removal of some circuit-importance evidence and reporting inconsistencies, including Table 9's caption conflicting with the domain-sufficiency interpretation in Section 3.3.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study, Mechanisms of Introspective Awareness. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable, allowing additions and removals to be distinguished from relocated material.

after.justification: v4 retains those empirical results and adds preference-training experiments, cross-model refusal-ablation tests, geometric controls, and downstream evaluations.

before.justification: v1 reports original concept-injection experiments, causal interventions on model components, feature analyses, and learned-vector training results.

results.title: Mechanisms of Introspective Awareness

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central claims: IQ-Learn reduces to BC, Dual Q-DM is equivalent to AIL, and Bellman constraints enable generalization and mitigation of compounding errors. The value-flow framing emphasizes propagation already claimed in v1.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the added experiments as demonstrating superior demonstration efficiency and broad hyperparameter robustness, while acknowledging extreme-setting failures on Humanoid. The universal superiority wording in Section 6.2 is too strong: Figure 3 shows LS-IQ above Dual Q-DM on Hopper with one demonstration. The underlying propagation explanation is retained.

D1.justification: v2 supplies a Dual Q-DM implementation link and adds ReCOIL's source information and hyperparameters in Table 9. Appendix F.2 documents the new offline procedures and sweep ranges. Existing hardware, architectures, and Tables 3-8 remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds a Gridworld generalization case in Figure 1 and an explicit offline scenario for IQ-Learn variants on the retained MuJoCo tasks. The original hard tabular instance and all five MuJoCo tasks remain; demonstration-count sweeps do not add datasets.

E2.justification: ReCOIL joins the MuJoCo comparisons in Figures 2-3. Its underlying work was discussed in v1 but was not an evaluated comparator there. The existing MuJoCo and hard-instance comparator sets are otherwise retained.

E3.justification: v2 substantially expands evaluation design with 1, 3, 5, and 7 demonstration trajectories, offline training using expert initial states and expert-only regularization, and Bellman-bound and penalty-coefficient sweeps. These are additional protocols; the original task-specific demonstration counts, listed hyperparameters, and ten-rollout evaluation procedure remain.

E4.justification: New analyses test several previously unexamined questions: Gridworld visualizes action selection outside demonstrations; Figure 3 tests demonstration efficiency; Figure 6 examines removing online interactions; and Figure 7 tests sensitivity to constraint bounds and penalty strength on HalfCheetah and Humanoid.

E5.justification: Both versions generally specify three independent seeds. v2 newly identifies Figure 6 as means with standard deviations over five seeds. This adds explicit uncertainty reporting for the offline experiment, but conflicts with the blanket three-run statement and does not establish increased runs for retained experiments.

E6.justification: v2 adds ReCOIL returns, demonstration-count results, Gridworld Q-value patterns, offline learning curves, and sensitivity results. New findings include poor offline performance for all three tested methods and sensitivity to extreme settings on Humanoid. The original hard-instance compounding-error trend remains; these additions are not evidence of a version-to-version performance gain.

M1.justification: The core constrained objective, Bellman penalty, architectures, and Algorithms 1-2 are retained. Value flow names the propagation mechanism already described in v1. The discounted theoretical formulation and experimental bound sweeps do not establish a replacement of the implemented base method.

P1.justification: The subtitle and mechanistic terminology shift to value flow. Section 3.2 moves the reparameterization argument before Theorem 1, Section 4.2 expands its explanatory narrative, and an impact statement is added. Appendices are renumbered and experimental details subdivided, while the main section sequence and much existing text remain.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column conference layout for the main text and references, with revised typography and running headers. It adds four figures and the ReCOIL hyperparameter table, updates comparison legends, and relocates existing displays. The original hard-instance plot and illustrative MDP become Figures 4 and 5.

R1.justification: Related work adds discussion of importance-weighted BC from imperfect demonstrations and further references on AIL with function approximation and reward generalization. The central positioning against IQ-Learn and primal-dual IL remains. The stage-coupled AIL reference changes from its preprint to publication rather than becoming a new work.

T1.justification: New Appendix D develops the stationary discounted setting, including occupancy-flow constraints and discounted objectives. Theorems 3-4 and Propositions 4-5 extend the IQ-Learn/BC reduction and Dual Q-DM/AIL equivalence with proofs. The original finite-horizon results and technical lemmas are retained.

improvement.justification: Appendix D addresses v1's finite-horizon restriction, while evaluating the closely related ReCOIL addresses an important comparison gap. The new generalization, offline, demonstration-count, and sensitivity experiments materially strengthen assessment of the proposed mechanism and practical behavior. The implementation link also improves reproducibility information. These gains outweigh localized weaknesses, including the overstated universal superiority claim in Figure 3's discussion and inconsistent three-run/five-seed reporting.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Dual Q-DM and the same analysis of IQ-Learn. Their complete main texts and appendices support reliable comparison despite the changed subtitle, conference formatting, and renumbering. Figures, tables, equations, and retained proofs can be matched.

after.justification: Original tabular and MuJoCo results remain, supplemented by Gridworld, demonstration-count, offline-training, and hyperparameter-sensitivity results in the main text and Appendix F.2.

before.justification: Section 6 reports original experiments on the hard tabular instance and five MuJoCo tasks, with results in Figures 1-2.

results.title: Non-Adversarial Imitation Learning Provably Free of Compounding Errors: The Value Flow Mechanism

C1.justification: V2 narrows the introduction and conclusion's broad first-targeted-attack claim to CoT-based targeted behavior hijacking in reasoning VLAs. It also claims visually plausible physical patches. The central contribution—redirecting actions through adversarial manipulation of CoT without changing user instructions—remains intact.

C2.justification: V2 replaces the claim that object keywords alone trigger attacks with a context-dependent interpretation and adds hypotheses about reasoning format and CoT-to-action coupling. It interprets camouflage/effectiveness tradeoffs and occlusion sensitivity, and replaces the unaddressed-stealth limitation with transferability limitations. These substantially refine the account of practical applicability and failure conditions.

D1.justification: V2 documents physical content/TV weights of 1.5 and 100, an annealed DIP regularization strategy, global/local CLIP processing, and the larger tablecloth dimensions. It adds a project-page link advertised as hosting videos. Existing hardware and calibration-network details remain; v1's explicit randomized-homography EoT description is shortened.

E1.justification: SimplerEnv, LIBERO and their curated tasks are retained. Coverage expands to simulated patch occlusion, physical tablecloth deployments with objects covering the patch, lighting and clutter variations, and a mouse-to-scissors physical scenario. V2 also evaluates the distinct task of detecting instruction–CoT inconsistency.

E2.justification: The main attack comparator set is unchanged: Action-Only becomes Action Attack, and CoT-Only becomes TRAPCoT-only. V2 adds GPT-5 as an evaluated comparator for the lightweight defenses in Table 6 and introduces a physical PGD-versus-DIP comparison.

E3.justification: V2 introduces center/edge occlusion tests at 10%, 25% and 50%, a TV-weight sweep, a 57 × 43 cm physical tablecloth setting, and defense metrics for benign consistency, attack rejection and latency. Table 9 revises and expands each instruction-variant set from four prompts to five. The stated 175-rollout unit changes from per VLA to per task; this does not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New analyses examine occlusion location and severity, PGD versus DIP camouflage, CLIP-guided textures, TV-weight sensitivity, and physical robustness to layouts, distractors and lighting (Appendices C.4, C.6 and D.3–D.5). The universal-patch study, latent-feature analysis and original failure cases are retained through relocation or renumbering.

E5.justification: V2 specifies 50 trials per optimizer for the new object-occluded physical comparison, supplementing the unchanged 15-trial original test and five simulation repeats. This adds trial-count information for a distinct experiment, rather than documenting increased repetitions of the old study. Table 1 dispersion reporting is unchanged, with no new confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: Table 3 and the original physical outcomes remain unchanged. Table 4 replaces instruction-variant results under revised prompts: paraphrasing ASR changes from 53.6% to 70.6% for MolmoAct and 15.7% to 25.1% for InstructVLA, so these are not same-setting gains. New physical results report 19/50 successes for PGD and 17/50 for DIP; defense, occlusion and TV-regularization results substantially expand the evidence.

M1.justification: V2 adds reference-image content regularization, CNN-based Deep Image Prior patch generation, and a CLIP-guided alternative (Section 5.3 and Appendix C.6). Section 7 implements format-specific consistency defenses where v1 only proposed a detector. These substantially extend the method; TV regularization, homography, color calibration and the core CoT/action losses already existed.

P1.justification: V2 polishes terminology and prose, regroups method subsections into attack effectiveness and stealthiness, moves universal-patch analysis to Appendix C.5, and separates physical deployments into dedicated subsections. The principal section sequence and much existing exposition are retained; the expansion primarily adds scientific content.

P2.justification: V2 replaces the opening threat cartoon with a detailed framework overview, revises the physical-deployment figure, and adds optimizer, CLIP, deployment-variation and hazardous-task illustrations. New defense, occlusion and TV tables substantially expand the displays. Existing distribution, latent-feature, calibration and physical-result figures are retained and relocated.

R1.justification: V2 adds Deep Image Prior and TPatch citations, removes the Qi et al. visual-jailbreak reference, and narrows novelty positioning to CoT-based behavior hijacking. The pi0.5 and VLA-OS reference changes concern the same works with updated bibliographic information, rather than new research coverage.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation expands the optimization objective and defines reference-feature and CLIP alignment losses (v2 Equations 4, 9 and 13). Existing CoT/action losses, homography and trajectory-score definitions remain substantively unchanged. Neither version provides theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: V1 explicitly left stealth unaddressed and only suggested a countermeasure. V2 substantially strengthens practical validation through patterned patches tested under physical occlusion, quantified sensitivity analyses, and an implemented defense comparison (Sections 5.3, 6.5 and 7; Appendices C–D). Revised instruction prompts also remove task-changing examples. Camouflage assessment remains largely visual and defense implementation details are limited, but the additions address important gaps in applicability and mitigation evidence without depending on higher headline scores.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TRAP research, with matching authors, core attack framework and principal experiments. The complete main texts and Appendices A–D support comparison, including figures, tables and equations.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds occlusion experiments, camouflage analyses, physical deployment tests and a defense evaluation.

before.justification: V1 reports original intervention experiments, simulated attacks on three VLAs, transferability and robustness analyses, and 15 physical robot trials.

results.title: TRAP: Hijacking VLA CoT-Reasoning via Adversarial Patches

C1.justification: The central contributions remain native CAPTCHA solving, automated reasoning-action data, and self-correction training. V2 narrows the performance message to strong overall synthetic results and mixed real-world transfer, and replaces the conclusion's lower-latency claim with fewer interaction steps. General GUI preservation is also qualified.

C2.justification: V2 substantially expands interpretive boundaries: frontier agents remain competitive, real-world transfer does not establish uniform superiority, and interaction steps do not establish full latency performance. Appendix A newly distinguishes answer-conditioned supervision from verified faithful explanations and identifies missing evaluations. Appendix E interprets failures as perception and recovery bottlenecks and discusses data-scale saturation.

D1.justification: Appendices E.1 and E.3 supply previously missing action/executor specifications and training details, including coordinate mapping, parsing, four B200 GPUs, full-parameter SFT, ZeRO-2, precision, sequence length, batching, optimizer, learning rate, and warmup. UI-Vision prompts are also supplied. These materially improve reproducibility documentation; the code/model/data access link is unchanged.

E1.justification: V2 adds UI-Vision element-grounding and layout-grounding evaluation, extending coverage to harder desktop interfaces and functional-region localization. The seven synthetic CAPTCHA types, 26 real-world types, training data sources, and three previous GUI benchmarks remain.

E2.justification: Tables 1 and 7 add Qwen3-VL-8B/32B-Instruct, GPT-5.4, and Gemini-3-Flash-Preview to CAPTCHA comparisons. Table 3 adds the Instruct baselines and removes its OpenAI CUA column. These changes substantially strengthen and broaden the evaluated comparator set; Oedipus remains unevaluated.

E3.justification: Added experiments introduce Instruct configurations, a 4B capacity check, and 50%/100%/150% CAPTCHA-data conditions. UI-Vision uses custom output parsing, disabled thinking, element accuracy, and layout mean IoU. Existing CAPTCHA sample counts and interaction budgets remain stated as before; newly disclosed training settings are not evidence that earlier protocols changed.

E4.justification: Appendix E adds a data-scale saturation study, a 4B ScreenSpot-V2 capacity check, and qualitative inspection of OCR, interaction-sequence, and recognition failures. Section 3.2 also newly reports manual trace inspection. The original reasoning/self-correction ablations and Appendix B case studies are retained unchanged.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. V2 continues the same point-estimate reporting practice.

E6.justification: V2 adds extensive results: dynamic CAPTCHA success is 78.60%/84.20% for the new Instruct variants, with GPT-5.4 at 56.80% and Gemini at 59.90%. Original Thinking scores, real-world rows, and main ablations remain unchanged. New UI-Vision, real-world, scale, and capacity results broaden the findings; Gemini leads the full real-world comparison on average. V1's under-three-second execution claim is removed.

M1.justification: Section 3.3 changes the written loss from normalization by total token count to separately normalized reasoning and action losses, changing their relative weighting. Section 4.1 also adapts Instruct models using thinking tags. The core generation and self-correction pipeline remains intact; the PDFs do not establish whether the loss revision reflects an implementation change or a documentation correction.

P1.justification: V2 makes targeted rewrites to the abstract, related work, results discussion, conclusion, and limitations; distinguishes Thinking/Instruct terminology; shortens the running title; and adds acknowledgments and Appendix E. The original section sequence and most pipeline, prompt, and case-study text remain intact.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn with new model curves and GUI benchmark axes. Table 1 expands substantially, Table 3 gains grouped model columns and UI-Vision rows, and the original real-world comparison becomes part of expanded Table 7. New action-space, training-configuration, and data-scale tables further expand the displays. Figures 2–8 retain their imagery.

R1.justification: V2 adds references including GUI-Actor, GUI-Libra, Reasoning under Vision, STaR, and UI-Vision, and revises descriptions of existing CAPTCHA solvers. It repositions existing CAPTCHA resources as evaluation-oriented rather than primarily insufficiently diverse. The overarching positioning around native GUI-agent learning remains.

T1.justification: The Section 3.3 loss formula is mathematically revised: separate division by reasoning/action token counts replaces division by their combined count. With the stated equal coefficients, these objectives are not equivalent; v2's formula supports the intended group balance. No theorems or proofs are added.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses important weaknesses through stronger measured baselines, broader GUI evaluation, and substantially fuller reproduction details. It retains earlier results while acknowledging competitive frontier performance and narrowing transfer and latency claims. The corrected loss specification and explicit rationale-faithfulness limitation improve scientific clarity. Missing uncertainty estimates and unresolved implementation history remain, but the overall gains in evidential credibility and reproducibility are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ReCAP research. Their full text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable, and retained content can be matched reliably across relocation and model renaming.

after.justification: V2 retains these original results and adds Instruct-model evaluations, frontier-model comparisons, UI-Vision results, and data-scale and capacity analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original synthetic and real-world CAPTCHA evaluations, general GUI benchmark results, reasoning and self-correction ablations, and qualitative case studies.
