C1.justification: v1 presents covariate-adjusted variance reduction as a practical contribution in its abstract, introduction, and conclusion. v2 limits the directly observable method covered by its theory to IPW, retains AIPW as an oracle characterization, and defers practical variance reduction to future work. Its conclusion also strengthens the asymptotic width comparison beyond the earlier special cases.

C2.justification: v2 explains that nontrivial event-time augmentation generally requires unobserved counterfactual event times and that entry-frozen augmentation introduces error outside the current argument. Section 4.3 explicitly identifies the variance-upper-bound curve as a benchmark rather than a valid confidence-sequence boundary. Section 4.2 also acknowledges degenerate exceptions to the nonmartingale obstruction.

D1.justification: v2 specifies the new never-event probabilities but omits v1's simulation mixture tuning value eta-squared = 1/16 and shock widths 0.5 and 0.3. These omissions reduce reproducibility detail; they do not establish that the omitted parameter values changed. No code or data access resource is added.

E1.justification: Dataset 5.1 now includes units whose events never occur, with probabilities 0.20 under control and 0.35 under treatment. This revises the simulated population beyond delayed finite events. The delayed-reward task and OOM telemetry dataset remain; moving the latter into Section 6 adds no dataset.

E2.justification: The empirical IPW-versus-event-time-AIPW comparison in v1 Table 2 is removed, leaving IPW alone in the main simulation. Classical pointwise intervals, the variance-upper-bound benchmark, and the Lindon and Kallus (2025) Poisson comparison remain.

E3.justification: Section 5 narrows the reported evaluation from IPW and running-mean AIPW, each with oracle and estimated variance coverage, to one IPW coverage assessment. The retained design still resamples assignments with fixed potential outcomes, using 500 units, Uniform(0,10) entry times, balanced randomization, and the same nominal coverage levels.

E4.justification: The central augmentation analysis testing whether running-mean adjustment reduces interval width while preserving coverage is withdrawn, along with the explicit oracle-versus-estimated variance coverage comparison. The reward–time dependence analysis, resampled trajectories, martingale-violation example, and OOM case study remain despite relocation and redrawing.

E5.justification: v2 explicitly states 200 assignment resamples for its coverage estimates; v1 does not specify the replication count underlying Table 2. This is newly reported run information, not an established increase: the 100 paths in v1 Figure 2 are retained as 100 paths in v2 Figure 4. Neither version reports Monte Carlo confidence intervals for coverage rates.

E6.justification: v1 Table 2 reports estimated-variance IPW coverage of 96.8%, 97.9%, and 99.7% for control, treatment, and their difference; v2 Section 5 reports 96.0%, 97.0%, and 99.0%. These replace results under a changed synthetic population, so they do not establish same-setting deterioration. AIPW coverage results and the reported 86%, 76%, and 83% width reductions are removed. Synthetic plots change, while the OOM findings remain.

M1.justification: The IPW/AIPW formulas and normal-mixture union-bound construction remain unchanged; identifying AIPW as generally oracle changes its applicability claim rather than its algorithm. Corollary 4.10 makes a limited inference-output correction by explicitly returning p = 1 when the inversion set is empty.

P1.justification: The title and abstract are rewritten, Section 4 substantially expands and reorganizes the filtration explanation, the simulation description becomes a structured list, and the conclusion is extensively rewritten. The OOM case study moves from Appendix C into its own main-text section, while its Poisson comparison remains in the appendix.

P2.justification: The two-column main text becomes single-column, with extensive reflow and resized displays. Table 2 is removed, synthetic figures are redrawn with changed axes and trajectories, and several displays move between the main text and appendices. The reward-dependence and OOM figures move into the main text, while the sample-path boundary comparison moves to Appendix B.

R1.justification: The cited works and substantive positioning relative to design-based inference, survival analysis, and counting-process methods are retained. The logrank reference changes from its 2020 preprint to the 2024 publication of the same work; other reference changes are bibliographic corrections or formatting.

T1.justification: Theorem 4.4 changes from a cumulative-process equivalence to a unit-level characterization with explicit predictability and conditional-propensity assumptions, with a revised Appendix A.1 proof. Lemma 4.5 changes its boundedness condition to residual jumps and strengthens the stated approximation remainder. Proposition 4.12 and Appendix A.5 generalize two special variance regimes to arbitrary limiting variance shares, proving a limiting relative width at most one.

improvement.justification: v2 resolves an important practical overclaim: v1 promotes and quantifies usable AIPW variance reduction, whereas v2 explains its dependence on unavailable counterfactual event times and limits practical guarantees to IPW. It also clarifies the benchmark's inferential status and supplies a more general relative-width theorem and proof. Although some simulation specifications are lost, the clearer separation of implementable inference from oracle results substantially improves the paper's scientific reliability.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same design-based inference framework despite the changed title. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–C are readable, and relocated material can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 reports simulation coverage across 200 treatment-assignment resamples in Section 5 and retains the OOM telemetry analysis in Section 6.

before.justification: v1 reports original Monte Carlo coverage and variance-reduction results in Section 5 and Table 2, plus an analysis of production OOM telemetry in Appendix C.

results.title: Design-Based Anytime-Valid Inference for Randomized Experiments with Delayed Outcomes and Staggered Entry

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same claims about distributional output-length prediction, log-t modeling, risk-aware TIE scheduling, and online/offline performance and generalization. Additional experiments support those retained contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds a consistency–robustness interpretation of expectation/CVaR, explains classical scheduling assumptions that fail in LLM serving, and discusses training-cost amortization, temperature degradation, noise tolerance, and preemption overhead. The training-data limitation itself is retained from v1's Appendix E and moved into Section 7.

D1.justification: v2 adds an explicit TIE repository link, specifies single-GPU deployment for OpenPanGu, and identifies Qwen3-32B in thinking mode as the prompt classifier. These improve access and implementation documentation without establishing changes to the retained method or deployments.

E1.justification: Both versions use LMSYS-Chat-1M, ShareGPT, and Alpaca for online chatbot serving and offline synthetic data generation. New prompt-family diagnostics reuse existing samples, while sensitivity tests vary configurations within retained coverage. OpenPanGu results already appeared in v1.

E2.justification: v2 newly evaluates TRAIL against TIE in Appendix D.8, Table 11; v1 only discussed TRAIL. The main FCFS, SSJF, and LTR comparator set and existing distribution/score ablation variants are retained.

E3.justification: Appendices D.4–D.9 add substantial experimental protocols: prompt classification, training-data budget controls, training at temperature 0.7 with evaluation at 0.4–1.6, fixed-beta comparisons across loads, and multiplicative sigma perturbations. These extend evaluation rather than revise the original benchmarks' stated settings.

E4.justification: v2 adds prompt-family tail diagnostics, training-scale sensitivity, temperature generalization, adaptive-versus-fixed-beta comparisons across loads, and prediction-noise robustness. These substantially broaden analysis beyond v1's distribution/score ablations, repetition-count and degrees-of-freedom studies, and scheduling heatmaps.

E5.justification: Existing repeated-generation fitting and KS testing are retained. v2 introduces no new repeated-evaluation counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance-testing procedures. The new generations-per-prompt settings concern training-data budgets.

E6.justification: Tables 7–12 add extensive diagnostic and sensitivity results while retaining earlier benchmark values, including relocated OpenPanGu results. For example, Table 11 reports TIE/TRAIL latency of 0.67/1.41 s/token at 100 RPS; Table 12 shows TIE at 1.66 versus LTR at 1.55 under maximum sigma noise at 100 RPS.

M1.justification: The DeBERTa predictor, log-t parameterization, training strategy, censored expectation/CVaR score, adaptive beta, starvation prevention, and asynchronous scheduling procedure remain unchanged. New experiments test existing components.

P1.justification: Localized structural edits remove the introductory existing-solutions paragraph, add Discussion and Acknowledgements, revise the impact statement, move limitations into the main text, and consolidate OpenPanGu material. Most existing technical prose remains unchanged.

P2.justification: Six new appendix tables provide substantial new diagnostic and sensitivity displays. v1's separate OpenPanGu Tables 7–8 are merged into Tables 5–6. The ten existing figures and main Tables 1–4 are retained, with only minor positioning and pagination changes.

R1.justification: v2 expands the existing SEPT connection through a stochastic-scheduling paragraph and adds learning-augmented-algorithm positioning with new references. It also adds model and contextual citations and removes the TensorRT-LLM reference. These are focused extensions of the retained LLM-scheduling positioning.

T1.justification: Assumption 3.1, Theorem 3.2, the method equations, and the proofs and censored-distribution derivations in Appendices A–B are unchanged. The new learning-augmented discussion is conceptual and adds no formal theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: v1 discussed preemption costs without evaluating a preemptive comparator and acknowledged training-data costs without an end-to-end data-efficiency study. v2 directly addresses both gaps through Tables 8 and 11, alongside substantial robustness validation. The results expose useful boundaries, including TRAIL's advantage at 30–40 RPS and TIE's loss to LTR under maximum noise. These gains outweigh a limited editorial regression: Section 2 still references the deleted introductory baseline discussion.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TIE scheduler. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching, including relocated material.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds prompt-family diagnostics, sensitivity experiments, prediction-noise tests, and a TRAIL comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original distribution-fitting results, online and offline scheduling benchmarks, ablations, and additional-model experiments.

results.title: Scheduling LLM Inference with Uncertainty-Aware Output Length Predictions

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and discussion retain the same central contributions: a clarified and extended count-diffusion design space, transferred guidance and attrition mechanisms, and competitive generation and biological imputation. Expanded evidence and revised result interpretations do not redefine these core claims.

C2.justification: Section 5.3 now distinguishes pointwise prediction from distributional fidelity and acknowledges stronger pointwise competitors. It attributes foundation-model success on low-biased MNAR data to miscalibration, without testing the proposed high-biased counterexample. New Section 8 explicitly discusses sampling speed, limited exploration of design choices, restricted gene coverage, and unexplored biological adaptations.

D1.justification: V2 replaces the anonymous reviewer-code disclosure with a public repository link and expands Appendix D.3 substantially. It documents PyTorch GAIN/HI-VAE implementations, GAIN activation handling, a 100,000-step CountsDiff/ReMDM budget, scIDPM epoch counts within the retained 150-hour budget, and ED/MMD/SWD computation. Newly disclosed details do not by themselves establish changed experiments.

E1.justification: Both versions use synthetic count vectors, CIFAR-10, CelebA, and the fetal and heart cell atlases. The fetal 50% MCAR and 25% low-biased MNAR tasks, heart 50% MCAR task, and fetal 40% MCAR ablations are retained. No additional evaluated dataset or missingness scenario is documented.

E2.justification: Tables 2, 3, and 10 add scGPT trained from scratch and pretrained, xTrimoGene, and Blackout to the full imputation comparisons. HI-VAE is now evaluated with both Poisson and Gaussian likelihoods. Blackout previously appeared in other experiments, but its participation in these comparisons is new; RAW is simply renamed Zero imputation.

E3.justification: The imputation benchmarks expand from four metrics to include ED, MMD, and SWD, with R-squared, MAE, and Pearson correlation added in Appendix E.6. GAIN's reported training budget changes from 50 epochs to 10,000 iterations. The splits and gene panels remain unchanged. V2 also inconsistently describes toy SWD as both Wasserstein-1 and Wasserstein-2, leaving any actual implementation change there unclear.

E4.justification: V1's scIDPMs comparison with and without catastrophic outliers disappears from Tables 3 and 10. V2 adds a limited scratch-versus-pretrained scGPT comparison. The rounding checks, schedule/guidance/attrition/sampling-step sweeps, and downstream classifier evaluation remain; the classifier study moves from Appendix E.6 to E.7.

E5.justification: Both versions report mean and standard error using ten resamples of 50,000 fetal or 20,000 heart data points; v2 explicitly calls these bootstrap resamples. No additional runs, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance-testing procedure are reported. Changed uncertainty values and display precision do not establish a new statistical procedure.

E6.justification: Tables 2, 3, and 10 revise numerous imputation scores and add substantial comparator and metric results. For fetal MCAR, single-sample CountsDiff RMSE changes from 1.401 to 1.42; GAIN changes from 51.163 to 1.87 alongside its revised reported setup. Newly added pretrained scGPT achieves MNAR RMSE 0.24. Toy, image, and existing ablation results are retained, apart from rounding.

M1.justification: Sections 3.1-3.6 and Algorithms 1-2 retain the same forward process, weighted objective, attrition mechanism, guidance, stochastic rounding, and RePaint-based imputation. Expanded explanations and baseline implementation disclosures do not establish changes to CountsDiff itself.

P1.justification: The overall narrative and section order remain recognizable. V2 makes localized explanatory edits, numbers the experiment subsections, rewrites the imputation discussion, reorganizes Appendix D.3, and adds a dedicated limitations section. Affiliations and the publication header also change; most method and proof prose is retained.

P2.justification: The principal imputation tables are substantially redesigned with additional columns, pointwise/distributional headers, method groups, and within-group highlighting. V2 adds full-metric Tables 14-16, compresses Table 1, and integrates Figures 7-11 beside their appendix discussions instead of leaving them at the document's end. These relocated figures retain their content.

R1.justification: V2 adds positioning around scGPT, xTrimoGene, and few-step samplers, plus FID/IS references, while removing examples such as scVAE, AdImpute, and scDesign3. The central relationship to Blackout and JUMP remains unchanged. Numerous publication-year and venue updates refer to the same previously cited works.

T1.justification: Propositions 3.1, 3.2, and B.1 and the derivations in Appendix B are retained. Changes to mathematical presentation concern notation, punctuation, and typesetting, including explicit probability symbols in B.9, rather than new assumptions, proofs, or mathematical reasoning.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the central biological evaluation through stronger comparators and multiple distributional metrics, reducing reliance on scFID and making CountsDiff's pointwise weaknesses explicit. Expanded implementation information, the public-code disclosure, and concrete limitations improve reproducibility and interpretation. These gains outweigh remaining shortcomings: the new foundation-model settings are sparsely documented, and the explanation of their MNAR advantage remains untested.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CountsDiff. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A-F are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated figures and renumbered tables.

after.justification: V2 retains these original experiments and reports expanded imputation comparisons and additional evaluation metrics in Tables 2, 3, 10, and Appendix E.6.

before.justification: V1 reports original synthetic-count experiments, CIFAR-10 and CelebA generation results, and fetal and heart scRNA-seq imputation experiments, including appendix ablations and classifier evaluations.

C1.justification: The abstract narrows forecasting superiority from 'outperforms strong specialized baselines' to 'achieves competitive performance against' them. The central contributions—shared tokenization, self-supervised pretraining, forecasting/decoding support, and interpretable representations—remain unchanged.

C2.justification: Section 7 explains that trial alignment supplies temporal regularity that may not transfer to spontaneous activity or less structured pseudo-trials. Broader downstream applications are explicitly qualified as untested possibilities. Appendix D newly interprets smoothing sensitivity as affecting reconstruction and forecasting more strongly than decoding.

D1.justification: v3 fills important reproducibility gaps by specifying EMA smoothing with alpha = 0.15, training-split normalization, added dataset selection/windowing, and revised TCN implementation and training details. The abstract replaces a promised code release with a reported release and repository address. The preprocessing additions document previously unspecified procedures; they do not establish that the original experiments changed.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained simulations and Tseng mouse recordings, v3 evaluates Sun's cue-delay-choice mouse dataset and Atanas's spontaneous activity recordings from freely moving C. elegans. Tables 1–5 add forecasting and position, velocity, and head-angle decoding evaluations, substantially extending populations, recording conditions, and behavioral targets.

E2.justification: The comparator roster is retained, but Appendix B revises the decoding TCN from four causal convolutional layers to four residual blocks containing two weight-normalized convolutions each. This revised comparator appears in Figure 4B and Table 17. Added datasets use the existing POCO and POYO+ comparators.

E3.justification: Added protocols include 64-point Sun trials and a 10/3 mouse split, plus 80-point C. elegans pseudo-trials, a 60/20-session split, and a stated 40-point forecast horizon. TCN decoding changes from 100 to at most 200 epochs, adding early stopping and expanding the weight-decay grid. The smoothing experiment adds controlled preprocessing settings. Appendix B's generic 24-point POCO horizon leaves its C. elegans protocol ambiguous.

E4.justification: Appendix D adds a focused smoothing sensitivity experiment: Table 12 varies EMA alpha across 0.15, 0.60, and 1.00 and measures reconstruction, CalM/POCO forecasting, and decoding. Existing component ablations and PCA/LDA/shuffle analyses are retained; the representation study moves from Appendix E to F.

E5.justification: v1 already includes graphical error bars, some appendix mean-plus-minus values, and shuffle analyses. v3 adds explicit numerical standard deviations for the principal experiments and Wilcoxon tests for multi-session comparisons in Appendix E. These distinguish significant decoding differences from nonsignificant held-out forecasting, with p = 0.3684. No increase in repeated runs or seeds is established.

E6.justification: Tables 1–5 and 12 add results for new datasets and smoothing conditions; for example, held-out Sun position-decoding R2 is 0.9581 for CalM and 0.8870 for POYO+. Figure 4B replaces TCN pitch/roll/yaw R2 values of 0.4930/0.4188/0.3097 with 0.6217/0.6007/0.6076 under the revised comparator and training settings. Existing CalM benchmark means are retained.

M1.justification: The NQ tokenizer, dual-axis transformer, embeddings, training objectives, regularizers, and linear/nonlinear decoding heads remain unchanged in Section 3 and Appendix C. Expanded descriptions and additional dataset evaluations do not establish a change to CalM's algorithm.

P1.justification: The title now names CalM, headings and grammar are polished, the discussion is expanded, and acknowledgements are added. A numerical-results appendix is inserted and the representation appendix relabeled. The main section sequence and most existing prose remain intact.

P2.justification: v3 substantially expands result presentation with main-text benchmark Tables 1–5, smoothing Table 12, and numerical/statistical Tables 15–19, including difference, p-value, and significance rows. Existing figures are largely retained or relocated. Ablation headers now explicitly identify removed components, and Figure 2's caption is expanded.

R1.justification: v3 adds Sun et al. (2025) and Atanas et al. (2023) as dataset sources. Section 2 and the substantive positioning relative to neural foundation models, population dynamics models, and decoding methods remain essentially unchanged.

T1.justification: Equations 1–19, including the simulation dynamics, quantization and loss definitions, decoding equations, and d-prime definition, are retained. No mathematical assumptions, derivations, theorems, or proofs are added or substantively revised.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens evidence that previously relied on one real dataset, documents consequential preprocessing, tests smoothing sensitivity, strengthens the TCN comparison, and adds statistical assessment of central results. The narrower abstract and expanded limitations better calibrate the claims. The unresolved C. elegans forecasting-horizon description limits that comparison, but the broader validation and improved transparency provide a substantial net quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CalM and retain matching core methods and experiments. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite the revised title and added material.

after.justification: v3 retains those original results and adds evaluations on another mouse dataset and C. elegans recordings, preprocessing sensitivity results, and statistical analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulation and mouse forecasting/decoding experiments, tokenizer evaluation, component ablations, and representation analyses.

results.title: CalM: A Self-Supervised Foundation Model for Population Dynamics in Calcium Imaging Data

C1.justification: Both versions retain the same two central contributions: a direct analysis of belief-dependent rewards accounting for belief estimation, and a staged strategy with sublinear high-probability regret for directly state-dependent rewards. The principal rates and novelty claims remain; the simulations provide supporting evidence.

C2.justification: v2 qualifies the staging-related regret penalty as a feature of the current method, explicitly noting that staging might be avoidable and that no matching lower bound is provided. It adds practical interpretations of tuning and staging, while explaining that the simulation parameters are not market-calibrated and the empirical evidence is illustrative.

D1.justification: Appendix F adds data preprocessing and feature construction, HMM and reward parameters, implemented confidence bonuses, tuning grids, hardware and runtime information, and a code-repository link. These substantially extend v1's pseudocode and brief planned postprocessing description. Some XGBoost configuration details are delegated to a cited paper.

E1.justification: v2 adds the first evaluated dataset and application: a semi-synthetic credit-marketing task derived from UCI Default of Credit Card Clients. Three contact actions are evaluated under two latent economic regimes affecting both client profiles and rewards; v1 evaluates no dataset or scenario.

E2.justification: v1 has no empirical comparator. v2 evaluates Plain LinUCB against the belief-aware strategies in Section 5 and Appendix F. Other cited latent-bandit algorithms are discussed as possible alternatives but are not evaluated.

E3.justification: Appendix F introduces an experimental protocol with 50,000 rounds, a 250-round random-action warm start, specified context and reward generation, and pseudo-regret evaluation using true beliefs unavailable to the learner. It also specifies stage lengths and regularization/exploration grids, with displayed configurations selected in hindsight. These are new experiments, not revisions of earlier experimental settings.

E4.justification: New analyses disentangle update frequency from confidence-bonus design by comparing two bonus forms across stage lengths 1, 15, 37 and 224. Figures 3–4 and Tables 4–6 additionally examine exploration and regularization sensitivity. v1 contains no corresponding empirical analyses.

E5.justification: v2 introduces empirical uncertainty reporting: 100 independent runs with seeds 1951–2050, means, and bands or table entries representing plus or minus two standard errors. v1 reports no experimental runs or empirical uncertainty.

E6.justification: All simulation outcomes are new. At 50,000 rounds, Tables 4–5 report hindsight-selected results of 754 ± 16 for Plain LinUCB and 246 ± 9 for LinUCB-Belief-Complex with stage length 37, where uncertainties are twice the standard error. The curves and grids also report sensitivity to bonus design and tuning; there are no v1 scores for a before-and-after performance comparison.

M1.justification: The core staged LinUCB algorithm is retained. Appendix F.3 introduces practical variants with approximated, tuned confidence bonuses and extends simplified-form bonuses to staged updates. Box C also corrects the emission-matrix output from the transpose of the estimated O matrix to that matrix itself.

P1.justification: The abstract and introductory motivation are rewritten, Section 2 is reorganized around both reward models and regret definitions, and much of the former Challenges Overcome section moves into an expanded Appendix B. Algorithms and bounds appear earlier, followed by the new simulation section. This substantially changes the narrative organization.

P2.justification: v2 adds Figures 1–4, Tables 1–6 and baseline pseudocode in Box D. These introduce regret curves, uncertainty bands, sensitivity panels, simulation-parameter tables and full result grids where v1 had no empirical displays. Existing algorithm boxes are retained and reflowed.

R1.justification: v2 adds Hong et al.'s Latent Bandits Revisited and distinguishes its constant-state setting from the retained Non-stationary Latent Bandits reference, now labeled 2020b. It also adds application, dataset and XGBoost references and clarifies prior alignment work. The central positioning against Nelson et al. remains.

T1.justification: The principal T^(3/4) and T^(7/8) guarantees and their assumptions remain. Section 2.3 and new Appendix E.3 define actual regret explicitly and add a proof sketch giving an order T^(5/8) connection at fixed confidence, sharpening v1's informal Remark 2.4. The main proof sketch also corrects the second-moment order from s times stage length to s squared times stage length.

improvement.justification: v2 replaces a promised experiment with a documented 100-run comparison and sensitivity study that examines the value of belief estimates and the practical role of staging. Together with uncertainty reporting, implementation information, the sharper actual-regret argument and clearer organization, this substantially improves support and reproducibility. The empirical evidence remains limited to one semi-synthetic scenario using hindsight tuning and heuristic confidence bonuses.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching models, algorithms and theoretical appendices. Their text, equations and visual material support reliable comparison. The numerical-simulation appendix in v1 is explicitly a placeholder, not an extraction gap.

after.justification: Section 5 and Appendix F report original simulations using UCI-derived client profiles, including comparisons and sensitivity analyses averaged over 100 runs.

before.justification: v1 contains theoretical results and algorithm descriptions but no original empirical outcomes. Appendix F explicitly postpones numerical simulations to version 2.

results.title: A Direct Approach for Handling Contextual Bandits with Latent State Dynamics

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same contributions and central claim: few-step MeanFlow policies enable competitive performance with reduced computational cost through likelihood approximation and adaptive velocity estimation. Adding HumanoidBench to the supporting experiment list does not redefine that claim.

C2.justification: Appendices E.5–E.6 add explanations involving GMM component selection, normalizing-flow architectural constraints, SAC's unimodality and BPTT's entropy-free mode collapse. The new impact statement discusses prospective robotics benefits. The existing limitation that strong performance requires two sampling steps remains.

D1.justification: The advertised code location changes from MFPolicy/MFPO to dongxiaoyi-xyz/MFPO. Appendix D adds SAC-Flow's implementation link, framework and hyperparameters, and explicitly describes batch-size harmonization. These are limited additions to the existing implementation documentation.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained MuJoCo, DeepMind Control Suite and toy coverage, v2 adds three HumanoidBench tasks—Sit Simple, Crawl and Balance Simple—and AntMaze-v1, v3 and v4. These extend evaluation to additional high-dimensional control tasks and multi-goal navigation.

E2.justification: SAC-Flow joins the existing MuJoCo and DeepMind Control Suite comparisons. New appendix comparisons evaluate SAC-GMM with 4 and 16 components, MEow, and a BPTT-trained MeanFlow policy. FPMD and RFM are discussed but are not reported as evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: v2 adds progressive component timing controls, real-task likelihood evaluation against a 1000-step Euler reference, GMM component-count comparisons, and AntMaze trajectory evaluation after 100k interactions. Table D1 becomes Table 2 and changes DIME's reported target-smoothing coefficient from 0.005 to 1; whether retained experiments were rerun is unspecified.

E4.justification: New Appendix E.2 measures the incremental cost and benefit of MeanFlow, ADN and adaptive velocity estimation. E.3 adds training-time likelihood-error and estimator-variance diagnostics, while E.6 examines multimodal exploration using AntMaze trajectories and entropy-related controls. Existing ablations and hyperparameter analyses are retained under new numbering.

E5.justification: Comparable benchmark curves retain means over five random seeds with standard-deviation shading, and the added benchmark comparisons use the same convention. No increased run count, new confidence-interval procedure or significance testing is reported.

E6.justification: v2 adds HumanoidBench returns, SAC-Flow results, GMM/MEow comparisons, AntMaze trajectories and ADN-error findings. Table 3 reports component results ranging from 2.45 hours and 0.52 normalized return for the diffusion-policy control to 2.81 hours and 1.00 for full MFPO. Table 1 adds SAC-Flow's 0.96 ms inference latency, and Figure 2 lowers the final MaxEntDP Humanoid-v3 points.

before.justification: V1 reports original generation experiments on Earth/climate data, meshes, SO(10), alanine dipeptide and robot trajectories, including quality, runtime and constraint-violation results.

These are substantive repairs to the approximation proofs, although theorem statements and approximation constants remain unchanged.

This substantially strengthens the paper's main theoretical contribution. The introductory guarantee is also made consistent with Section 5. The efficiency revisions remain unexplained, and Figure 1's new logarithmic-scale caption overgeneralizes beyond its query panels, but these limitations do not outweigh the theoretical repair.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same BFM-SWM and BFM-VM research. The main text, algorithms, equations, three figures, and Appendices A–D are readable and can be matched across versions despite reflow.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments on both applications and reports revised efficiency measurements for influence maximization.

before.justification: Section 6 and Appendices C–D report original experiments on influence maximization and CIFAR-10 crowdsourcing, including objective values, oracle-query counts, and running times.

results.title: Budget-Feasible Mechanisms for Submodular Welfare Maximization in Procurement Auctions

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion broaden the performance claim from state-of-the-art EDL methods to second-order predictors generally, and the introduction explicitly includes LLM uncertainty quantification. The central contributions of possibilistic projection, tractable Dirichlet approximation, and computational efficiency remain the same.

C2.justification: v2 adds focused explanations connecting the regularizer to minimum commitment and suppression of unsupported class evidence. It acknowledges that the parameterization precludes exact uninformative initialization, explains ordinary random initialization, and discusses reduced applicability in low-capacity settings. These qualify and elaborate the existing interpretation without replacing it.

D1.justification: Appendix C and Table 7 newly disclose warmup and linear regularization schedules, alongside retained coefficient values; this does not establish that earlier experiments changed. v2 also supplies new dataset/model configurations, baseline-tuning information, and V100 hardware details for timing. The abstract changes code availability from promised to reported available.

E1.justification: v2 adds TinyImageNet as a supervised 200-class task, beyond its existing OOD role, and adds ImageNet classification. It also extends evaluation to Mistral-7B on OpenBookQA, with ARC-Challenge, ARC-Easy, and CommonsenseQA as OOD datasets. MNIST and CIFAR-10-C remain present in Appendix E.

E2.justification: The CIFAR comparison adds DUQ, KL-PN, RKL-PN, PostNet, NatPN, RSNN, and ensembles. The fine-grained comparison adds DUQ, KL-PN, RKL-PN, PostNet, and NatPN. IB-EDL participates in the new LLM comparison. These substantially broaden evaluated comparators; MC Dropout/MC Drop and RS-NN/RSNN are matched as renamed methods.

E3.justification: New protocols include TinyImageNet training with a 95/5 split, ImageNet evaluation using frozen MAE ViT-B/16 features and a trained classifier, and Mistral-7B fine-tuning with ECE, NLL, and OOD AUROC reporting. Appendix F introduces a separate batch-128 runtime comparison. Retained experiments' stated splits and budgets remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds reliability diagrams testing calibration on CIFAR-10 and Stanford Dogs, regularizer ablations on CIFAR-10-LT and CIFAR-100, and memory/runtime comparisons testing efficiency. Existing regularization sensitivity, training-size, evidence-distribution, corruption, and leave-one-out approximation analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report predictive results as mean ± standard deviation over five random seeds. Added predictive experiments retain this practice, while cost measurements are averaged over five runs. No revised run count for existing experiments, new uncertainty estimator, confidence interval, or significance-testing procedure is reported.

E6.justification: Matched original table entries remain numerically unchanged, but v2 adds extensive results for new comparators, tasks, calibration, ablations, and efficiency. Examples include 89.47±0.6 OpenBookQA accuracy and 63.43±0.1 ImageNet accuracy. Added CIFAR ensemble rows exceed single-model DAPPr accuracy; on OpenBookQA, DAPPr's ECE of 3.11 exceeds IB-EDL's better 2.27.

M1.justification: The posterior projection, Dirichlet approximation, closed-form maximizer, softplus-plus-one parameterization, regularizer, uncertainty scores, and loss pseudocode remain unchanged. New experimental backbones and newly documented regularization schedules do not establish a revision to the proposed algorithm.

P1.justification: The introduction and portions of Sections 4.1–4.4 receive localized rewriting and explanatory expansion. MNIST and corruption discussions move into Appendix E, and appendix headings become more specific. The main six-section narrative and much of the existing prose remain unchanged.

P2.justification: v2 adds an overview diagram, a pipeline diagram, reliability plots, and tables for new benchmarks, ablations, and efficiency. Existing comparison tables expand, Table 6 is transposed into a compact layout, and MNIST and corruption tables move to the appendix. These substantially change the visual presentation beyond renumbering.

R1.justification: v2 adds foundational possibility-theory references and citations supporting the new LLM, dataset, and MAE experiments. It explicitly positions DAPPr as building on Hieu et al.'s possibilistic foundation, already cited in v1, and expands the EDL comparison in Appendix B. The main related-work taxonomy and novelty positioning remain intact.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions, high-capacity approximation, Proposition 1, and Appendix A proof are retained. Changes to conditioning notation and added explanations of Bayesian prediction, initialization, and applicability do not introduce a new formal result or substantively revise the derivation.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for the paper's generality, calibration, and efficiency through broader comparator families, larger-scale classification, LLM evaluation, reliability diagrams, and measured computational costs. Newly disclosed schedules and implementation details also improve reproducibility. Some prose remains overbroad, such as the unqualified best-CIFAR-accuracy statement despite higher ensemble scores in Table 1, but this limited issue does not outweigh the substantial gains in validation and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DAPPr research work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching across the expanded and reorganized later version.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds classification and question-answering experiments, calibration analyses, further ablations, and computational-cost measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original DAPPr classification, uncertainty estimation, OOD detection, regularizer ablation, and approximation-validation results, alongside attributed baseline results.

results.title: Possibilistic Predictive Uncertainty for Deep Learning

C1.justification: The abstract and contributions change the central claim from a formal causal-inference framework to SCM-inspired dependency-graph reasoning, explicitly excluding interventions and counterfactual semantics. Claims of robust generalization and logical consistency give way to structural traceability, although benchmark-superiority claims remain.

C2.justification: v3 removes v1's assertion that topological ordering guarantees hallucination-free reasoning and limits the benefit to structural transparency and fewer unsupported steps. It adds interpretations of reward instability and inference-cost tradeoffs, and corrects the appendix's claim that a linear relationship implies exponential complexity growth. Dependence on teacher data and unverified generalization beyond four hops remain acknowledged.

D1.justification: v3 specifies the teacher, the 60% training-query seed subset, 10,539 generated candidates, and rejection counts. Appendix A supplies a prompt and output template; Section 3.5 explains tokenized length and training-data-based interval estimation. Tables 3-4 disclose 1,700 RL steps and concrete reward and length settings that v1 leaves unspecified.

E1.justification: Both versions cover HoVer 2-4-hop and EX-FEVER 2-3-hop verification in Table 1 and retain Figure 1's 1-3-hop analysis. Additional model scores and reward experiments do not introduce another dataset, domain, or task scenario.

E2.justification: v3 adds ProgramFC to the Qwen3-8B comparison in Table 1; v1 reports ProgramFC only in the GPT-3.5 block. The other named comparators remain. Decoding-time length penalties and reranking are discussed without reported comparative evaluations.

E3.justification: v3 substantially extends evaluation design through reward-removal controls and sweeps over correctness rewards, reward weights, and token-length intervals in Tables 2 and 4. Appendix C adds a whole-chain DAG and parent-validity metric, and Table 1 adds the matched-backbone ProgramFC evaluation. Newly disclosed settings for retained experiments do not establish that those experiments changed.

E4.justification: v1 compares SFT, CPO, and GRPO and analyzes structural correlations. v3 retains these analyses while adding tests of individual reward contributions, hyperparameter sensitivity, training instability, and structural faithfulness. These directly investigate the proposed reward design and its failure conditions.

E5.justification: Table 3 newly reports a training-reward dispersion statistic, 'Reward last std.' of 0.259. This does not establish repeated-run uncertainty. The existing significance tests and correlations in Figure 6 remain unchanged, and neither version reports benchmark confidence intervals or repeated-run counts.

E6.justification: v3 fills missing Qwen EX-FEVER scores and adds Qwen3-8B ProgramFC results averaging 64.31%. New reward experiments report 0.7544 accuracy with full rewards, 0.7427 without Rs, and 0.6433 without Rl; Appendix C reports structural faithfulness above 95%. SCM-GRPO's main-table average remains 71.02%, and the original optimization and structural-analysis results are retained.

M1.justification: Both versions retain teacher-distilled structured chains, parent-before-child graph construction, SFT, and GRPO with the same correctness, structure, and length rewards in Equations (1)-(8). The SCM-inspired reframing and newly specified implementation details do not establish a changed algorithm.

P1.justification: v3 edits terminology and passages across the abstract, introduction, methods, results, and conclusion while retaining the main section order and much of the original prose. It organizes the expanded appendix into A-D and adds acknowledgements and an impact statement. Author, affiliation, correspondence, and running-header text also change.

P2.justification: The compact optimization-only Table 2 becomes a full-width, grouped ablation table with a training-status column, supplemented by new stability and sensitivity Tables 3-4. Figure 1 is redrawn with clearer labels and a substantially expanded caption. Figures 2-7 retain their underlying graphics but are repositioned and receive caption revisions.

R1.justification: v3 adds Graph of Thoughts and Verify-and-Edit, replaces citations to different works with HoVer, EX-FEVER, Search-o1, and Qwen3 source papers, and removes several infrastructure and other references. It also substantially narrows the novelty positioning from causal inference to explicit structural dependencies. Metadata updates to retained works are separate from these substantive changes.

T1.justification: The model tuple, DAG construction constraint, and mathematical objectives in Equations (1)-(8) are unchanged. No theorem, proof, or derivation is added. The causal-to-structural reframing changes interpretation, while the new faithfulness evaluation applies existing graph-validity constraints.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially improves claim-evidence alignment by replacing unsupported causal and hallucination-free guarantees with a bounded structural interpretation. The matched-backbone comparison, reward-component tests, and concrete implementation disclosures address important weaknesses in v1's validation and reproducibility. Main accuracy scores do not improve, and the new faithfulness result still lacks a stated sample size and uncertainty, but these remaining gaps do not outweigh the substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SCM-GRPO work, with readable text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices. The original Appendix A is retained as Appendix D in v3; the additional material can be distinguished reliably from relocated content.

after.justification: v3 retains these empirical results and adds reward ablations, sensitivity and training-stability results, and a structural-faithfulness evaluation.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark accuracies, an optimization-strategy ablation, and empirical analyses of generated reasoning structures in Appendix A.

results.title: Grounding Multi-Hop Reasoning in Structural Causal Models via Group Relative Policy Optimization

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion extend the central efficiency claim from attention-kernel acceleration to measured full-model decode-latency acceleration of up to 1.25x in batched generation. The original sampling and kernel-speedup claims remain, but the claimed practical benefit now covers a substantially broader execution scope.

C2.justification: Section 3.5 develops explanations of bandwidth shares and how batching, context length, weight quantization, and KV quantization affect benefits. Section 6 qualifies untested cache-method combinations and MLA applicability. Appendix U adds interpretations of diffuse attention and small tiles as sources of approximation error, motivating future tile-aware allocation.

D1.justification: v2 documents the new generation configuration, LongBench truncation, HumanEval grading, and fidelity-measurement procedure. Appendix R revises the reported flash-attn version from 2.7.3 to 2.7.1. Existing kernel pseudocode, detailed microbenchmark instructions, and repository access information are otherwise retained.

E1.justification: v2 adds LongBench v2 long-context reasoning evaluations (Section 3.4 and Appendix I) and HumanEval code generation (Appendix T). These substantially broaden task coverage beyond the retained GSM8K, MMLU, and RULER evaluations.

E2.justification: The existing SDPA, top-k, FlashInfer, and FlashDecoding comparisons are retained. FlashAttention-2, used for the new end-to-end comparison, already appears as FlashDecoding in v1's microbenchmark. LongBench v2 and HumanEval reuse SDPA; ShadowKV, OmniKV, and DuoAttention are discussed but not evaluated.

E3.justification: New protocols include batched generation with six 30k-token prompts and 2048 generated tokens, HumanEval greedy pass@1 evaluation, and controlled fidelity measurements over 40 prompts per task and 32 decoding steps. LongBench v2 introduces 32k truncation. The stated microbenchmark flash-attn version also changes from 2.7.3 to 2.7.1, without establishing that retained timings were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix U adds controlled comparisons of sparse and dense outputs at identical decode states, attention-support analysis across tiles, and a tile-size sweep. Tables 28–30 investigate approximation errors and failure conditions beyond the retained variance, one-hot-layer, and learned-budget analyses.

E5.justification: v2 adds repetition and aggregation specifications for new experiments: three LongBench v2 runs and end-to-end timing averages over nine batches. The existing 95% bootstrap-CI practice and retained experiments' repetition information remain unchanged; no increase in runs for existing results is established.

E6.justification: Retained numerical results and plotted findings are unchanged. New Table 3 reports decode times of 101.22 seconds per batch for FlashAttn-2, 80.97 for S2ANTA-flash, and 82.36 for S2ANTA-prop, yielding 1.250x and 1.229x speedups. LongBench v2, HumanEval, and fidelity/sensitivity tables add substantial new outcomes rather than same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The sampling rules, prop/flash kernels, Bernoulli query sampling, mean-group-query estimator, and reinforcement-learning budget allocation are retained. Algorithms 1–8 are unchanged. Section 3 adds an explanation of the kernels' relationship to systematic sampling, not a procedural revision.

P1.justification: v2 locally rewrites the abstract, conclusion, and Section 4 introduction, clarifies kernel terminology, standardizes headings, and adds acknowledgments and conference publication text. References move before the appendices. Most existing exposition and the overall method-to-evaluation structure remain unchanged.

P2.justification: Seven new tables provide LongBench summaries and sweeps, end-to-end timings, HumanEval results, and three fidelity/sensitivity displays (Tables 2, 3, 18, and 27–30). This substantially expands the displayed evidence. Existing Figures 1–10 are retained, while existing tables and figures are repositioned through page reflow.

R1.justification: Section 6 extends the existing complementarity argument through discussion of ShadowKV, OmniKV, DuoAttention, MLA/DeepSeek-V2, and stochastic spiking attention. References for LongBench v2, HumanEval, and FlashAttention-2 are also added. The overall positioning as value-stage sparsification complementary to cache management remains intact.

T1.justification: The estimator definitions, unbiasedness and variance proofs, Bernstein bound, and operation-count analyses are retained. Section 3.5 adds a limited quantitative bandwidth-model calculation: approximately 15 GB of weight traffic and 24 GB of KV traffic, combined with a 1.5x kernel gain, predict a 1.26x decode speedup. v1 only discussed the Amdahl constraint qualitatively.

improvement.justification: v1 demonstrated kernel acceleration without measuring full-model decode savings. v2 closes that important validation gap with Table 3's batched decode measurements, reporting prefill separately. LongBench v2 and HumanEval broaden accuracy evidence, while Appendix U identifies conditions affecting kernel fidelity. Together these substantially strengthen practical validation and applicability guidance, although measured speedups remain limited to Llama 8B on RTX 6000 Ada.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SANTA study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, algorithms, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison after matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds LongBench v2, HumanEval, end-to-end decoding measurements, and kernel-fidelity analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original kernel timings, GSM8K, MMLU and RULER evaluations, numerical experiments, layer ablations, and learned sampling-budget results.

results.title: Stochastic Sparse Attention for Memory-Bound Inference

C1.justification: The central factor-isolated editing contribution and DFS headline results remain. v3 corrects and emphasizes the full-suite CLRS contribution, qualifies comparable compute as model-level MACs, and adds a conclusion that SPARK improves or matches OpenEvolve across five additional benchmarks.

C2.justification: The new Limitations section explicitly acknowledges transfer failures on BFS, Floyd–Warshall, and KMP, additional search-time LLM costs, and dependence on manually defined factors. Appendix A.4 interprets the new controls as evidence that tags alone are insufficient. These additions substantially strengthen qualifications and mechanism interpretation.

D1.justification: v3 adds a SPARK code-repository link, cost-accounting definitions, and wall-clock and per-candidate training times in Table A.5. These improve access information and resource disclosure, while the existing pseudocode and listings remain unchanged. Detailed training and implementation recipes for the new benchmarks are still sparse.

E1.justification: v3 adds evaluations on MNIST-1D, 20News, CartPole-v1, Mice Protein Expression, and Breast Cancer Wisconsin, substantially extending coverage beyond algorithmic reasoning. All 30 CLRS tasks were already present in v1's Table A.1; their increased prominence is not new coverage.

E2.justification: Table A.2 adds a focused comparison with diagnostic methods such as Random-Scope SAR, Fixed-OP SAR, and Fixed-ACT SAR. The main external comparator set—OpenEvolve, EvoPrompting, FunSearch, and EoH—remains unchanged; reusing these methods on additional benchmarks does not itself expand that set.

E3.justification: The added experiments introduce four MNIST-1D backbone configurations, classification accuracy/loss and reinforcement-learning return metrics, and search-cost measurements. Table A.5 specifies 100 proposed candidates for OpenEvolve, EvoPrompting, and SPARK versus 400 for EoH and FunSearch. These are additional protocols; the existing CLRS search-and-transfer protocol is retained.

E4.justification: Appendix A.4 substantially expands the ablations to test whether region tags alone suffice, whether random or fixed scope selection works, and whether RC directives provide additional benefit. These controls extend the earlier ASR-versus-RC+SAR comparison. Existing search-dynamics analyses and evolution traces remain.

E5.justification: Both versions report the same five-seed trajectories with means and min–max shading in Figure A.1. v3 adds no new repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests for its additional result tables.

E6.justification: Original CLRS table values and plotted results are unchanged. New results include MNIST-1D average accuracy of 95.99% for SPARK versus 70.25% for OpenEvolve, and DFS accuracy of 50.27% for Random-Scope SAR versus 80.50% for full SPARK. v3 also reports full-suite means and replaces the erroneous 18-task conclusion summary with 21/30 and 19/30 wins, consistent with the retained Table A.1.

M1.justification: The ASR–RC–SAR procedure, OPERATOR/ACTION regions, feasibility checks, and archive-based search remain unchanged. Algorithms 1–2 and all six program listings are retained. The new execution example and additional evaluations do not document a changed method.

P1.justification: v3 revises experimental summaries, clarifies terminology, corrects CC to SCC, updates authorship and publication text, and adds Limitations and Acknowledgement sections. The appendix receives clearer subsection organization, but most existing prose, the main narrative sequence, and code listings are retained.

P2.justification: v3 substantially expands the tabular presentation with main-text Table 2 and appendix Tables A.2–A.5, covering controls, an execution example, benchmark scores, and costs. Existing algorithms and Figure 2 are repositioned, and the former Table 2 becomes Table 3. The original figure images and code-listing displays remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v3 adds references supporting the five new benchmarks and removes peripheral citations previously attached to appendix interpretations, including Fu et al. (2019) and Qi et al. (2026). The related-work discussion and positioning relative to NAS, iterative refinement, and structured editing remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Equations (1)–(4), the factor-local feasible-set definition, and the heuristic feasibility argument remain unchanged. Appendix A.3 explains metric bookkeeping without adding mathematical results, substantive derivations, or proofs.

improvement.justification: Table A.2 directly tests whether tags alone explain SPARK's gains, substantially strengthening evidence for the central mechanism beyond v1's limited component ablation. Broader evaluations and explicit cost, transfer, and factorization limitations improve validation and transparency. New-benchmark protocols and uncertainty remain underreported, and Table A.4's Base and EoH averages disagree with its displayed scores. These weaknesses limit precision but do not outweigh the substantial gains in experimental support and qualification.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SPARK and provide readable text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices. The original experiments and code listings can be matched reliably despite additions and relocation in v3.

after.justification: v3 retains the original empirical results and adds scope-control experiments and evaluations on five non-CLRS benchmarks.

before.justification: v1 reports original SPARK evaluations on CLRS, component ablations, five-seed search trajectories, and evolved architecture examples, including appendix results for 30 tasks.

results.title: Structured Progressive Knowledge Activation for LLM-Driven Neural Architecture Search

C1.justification: The central continual-learning thesis and three desired properties remain unchanged. The abstract, contribution list and conclusion now explicitly claim natural-language validation on Skill-Mix, while the abstract identifies the earlier demonstration as a controlled synthetic task.

C2.justification: The discussion replaces the synthetic-only applicability caveat with a remaining limitation concerning fuzzy definitions of skills and their compositions. The noise study adds a concrete qualification concerning annotation quality. Existing limitations concerning dataset construction, soft-token optimization and computational cost remain.

D1.justification: v3 adds code repository links and substantial Skill-Mix reproduction information in Appendix D.3: training-data construction, hyperparameters, inference and grading prompts, and insertion examples. Appendix D.2.1 newly discloses random padding within a 128-token limit for existing pretraining; this does not establish that the procedure changed between versions.

E1.justification: Section 6 adds natural-language generation on Skill-Mix, targeting modus ponens and statistical syllogism and mixing them with other language skills during training. This substantially extends coverage beyond the retained binary-operation and synthetic digit-transformation tasks.

E2.justification: The new Skill-Mix comparison includes an unadapted Llama3.2-3B-Instruct reference in Figure 7. LoRA and prompt tuning are reused comparators; their extension to Skill-Mix is not itself a baseline addition. Comparator membership in the original experiments, including the ICL comparison, remains unchanged.

E3.justification: Skill-Mix introduces a distinct protocol using Llama3.2-3B-Instruct, 300 GPT-5-generated training examples per target skill, 50 joint-skill test queries and GPT-5 grading. The noise experiment adds controlled corruption of training skill labels. Previously reported synthetic-task splits and budgets are retained.

E4.justification: Section 5.3.3 and Appendix A.6 add a bounded sensitivity study asking how inaccurate skill labels affect learning and composition: INV-POL, held-out ADD and five soft tokens, with varying corruption levels. The existing length, composition-complexity and initialization ablations are retained.

E5.justification: The existing binomial standard errors and standard deviations across held-out configurations or ICL example-count settings remain unchanged. The added Skill-Mix and noise plots introduce no repeated-seed information, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: Figure 7 adds natural-language results, including approximately 70% joint-skill success with combined neologisms versus 6% for the unadapted model. Figure A4 adds evidence that composition deteriorates under label noise, even while single-operation performance remains comparatively robust. These are new experiments; the earlier numerical results are retained unchanged.

M1.justification: The frozen-model procedure, skill-centered training, vocabulary-integrated soft tokens and optimization objective remain unchanged in Section 3 and Algorithm 1. Skill-Mix uses the previously described word-replacement insertion mechanism rather than introducing a new method component.

P1.justification: v3 makes widespread but limited copyedits, standardizes terminology, distinguishes algorithmic and natural-language experiments, and consolidates experimental details under Appendix D. It also corrects the Appendix A.5 heading and adds impact and acknowledgment sections. Most existing exposition remains intact.

P2.justification: v3 adds Figure 7, Figure A4 and prompt listings, removes the redundant hyperparameter-summary Table E7, and relocates existing displays. Original graphics remain unchanged. Caption corrections include removing Figure 2's reference to a nonexistent panel D.

R1.justification: The cited works and substantive novelty positioning are retained. Citations and behavioral-alignment context added to the main discussion were already present in v1 Appendix B. Author, venue and publication-year corrections concern the same referenced works.

T1.justification: The closed-form assumption, compositional notation, Definitions 3.1–3.2 and training objective are unchanged. No new theorem, proof or substantive mathematical derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: The natural-language experiment substantially strengthens the central composition claim beyond v1's explicitly acknowledged synthetic-only demonstration. The noise analysis tests an important practical vulnerability, and detailed prompts and settings improve reproducibility. The gains remain bounded: Skill-Mix covers one model, two target skills and 50 GPT-5-graded queries without uncertainty estimates, so broader continual-learning generality remains unestablished.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Skill Neologisms research. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices support comparison, including matching content across appendix reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds natural-language Skill-Mix experiments and a skill-label-noise analysis.

before.justification: v1 reports original XOR/XNOR experiments, synthetic digit-operation learning and composition results, and ablations in Section 5 and Appendix A.

results.title: Skill Neologisms: Towards Skill-based Continual Learning

C1.justification: Both versions retain the central contributions: generation-aligned understanding through three tasks, two-stage transfer to synthesis, strong results across 22 synthesis tasks, and the SynerMed release. The new evaluations support these contributions without redefining them.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the new VQA results as preserving general medical understanding and potentially improving fine-grained representations, and the segmentation results as evidence of useful tumor-related cues. The conclusion explicitly identifies the current framework's 2D scope and proposes 3D volumetric modeling as future work.

D1.justification: Section 4.2 newly documents slice-wise inference, reconstruction of volumes in original slice order, and volume-level metric computation for all methods. The project link changes from Mhilab/SynerMedGen to piooip/SynerMedGen; the PDFs do not establish whether resource availability changed.

E1.justification: Appendix B.2 adds evaluation on VQA-RAD, SLAKE, OmniMedVQA, and MMMU-Med, extending understanding evaluation beyond the constructed generation-aligned tasks. Appendix B.4 adds brain tumor segmentation on the already-used BraTS dataset. Existing synthesis and generalization coverage is retained.

E2.justification: Table 9 introduces InternVL2 as an evaluated comparator alongside Bagel and HealthGPT. Existing synthesis and generation-aligned understanding comparator sets remain unchanged. Figure 15 adds qualitative comparisons with Pix2Pix, BBDM, and SynDiff, which were already quantitative baselines.

E3.justification: The new segmentation evaluation specifies 100 BraTS cases, a 70/10/20 train/validation/test split, nnU-Net, DSC, and three input conditions. Additional task combinations are evaluated after Stage I and Stage I+II. The new volume-level synthesis evaluation description discloses previously unspecified settings without establishing that existing experiments changed or were rerun.

E4.justification: v1's progressive CTS-to-CTS+MI-to-full ablation is supplemented by all individual and paired task combinations at both training stages in Table 10. Table 11 tests whether synthetic T1CE helps tumor segmentation, and Figure 15 adds qualitative comparisons with dedicated synthesis methods. The existing K-sensitivity and generalization analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Existing plotted error bars are retained. No run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or statistical tests are added; new Tables 9-11 report point estimates.

E6.justification: Original Tables 1-8 and the K-sensitivity results are unchanged. New results include VQA-RAD scores of 61.3 for SynerMedGen versus 60.1 for Bagel, MI-only ablation SSIM of 50.72/83.34 after Stage I/Stage I+II, and segmentation DSC of 56.25 without T1CE, 62.48 with synthetic T1CE, and 64.83 with real T1CE. Figure 15 adds qualitative synthesis outputs.

M1.justification: The Bagel-based architecture, CTS/MI/TIA tasks, objectives, and two-stage GAU/UCG procedure are unchanged. The added nnU-Net experiment evaluates generated images downstream; it does not modify SynerMedGen.

P1.justification: v2 makes limited abstract and conclusion edits, adds an evaluation-protocol paragraph and appendix subsections, removes an unresolved reference marker, and adds acknowledgements and conference publication text. The main narrative and section organization remain substantially intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds three compact result tables and Figure 15 with magnified qualitative comparisons, plus running headers and local layout changes. Existing displays are retained: v1 Table 9 becomes Table 12, and appendix example Figures 15-27 become Figures 16-28.

R1.justification: The related-work sections and reference list are unchanged, as is the positioning around misalignment between medical understanding and generation. New benchmarking does not revise the claimed novelty or relationship to prior approaches.

T1.justification: The mathematical task definitions and loss equations (1)-(6) are unchanged. No theoretical assumptions, propositions, proofs, or derivations are added or revised.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the central understanding-generation premise. Compared with v1's task-aligned understanding tests and progressive ablation, Tables 9-10 provide external VQA checks and isolate individual and paired task contributions. Table 11 adds downstream evidence of tumor-relevant usefulness beyond image-fidelity scores and visual inspection. These address important evidential gaps, while the volume-level evaluation description and explicit 2D limitation improve interpretability. New experiment settings remain sparsely documented and uncertainty reporting is still limited, but the overall evidential gains are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SynerMedGen work. All pages, including Appendices A-E, are readable, and corresponding equations, tables, figures, and renumbered appendix content can be reliably matched.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds standard medical VQA evaluations, additional task ablations, and downstream brain tumor segmentation results.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthesis and understanding evaluations, component ablations, and generalization experiments in Section 4 and the appendices.

results.title: SynerMedGen: Synergizing Medical Multimodal Understanding with Generation via Task Alignment

C1.justification: Section 1.2 drops the assertion that the greedy optimization guarantee also translates into prediction risk, consistent with the deletion in Section 3.1. The abstract, contribution bullets, and central claims about coupled training and negative transfer otherwise remain unchanged.

C2.justification: Appendix B.3 now explicitly states that Theorem 3.1 concerns selection-stage iterates, not the post-selection refit or its test metrics. It also removes the explanation that refitting reduces greedy-stage shrinkage. The broader limitations and negative-transfer interpretations remain.

D1.justification: B.3 explicitly distinguishes the internal AFS iterates, separately trained teacher, and final ridge predictor, specifying that only the selected deployment span is retained. V1 already documented the labeled-only teacher and refit penalty of 0.001; v2 resolves ambiguity about their roles.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same synthetic linear and logistic scenarios and the same Parkinson’s, Bank Marketing, and PneumoniaMNIST tasks, with unchanged deployment and privileged-feature coverage.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is unchanged: labeled-only and Two-Stage models, generalized distillation and Vapnik SVM+ for Bank Marketing, and the linear, kernel, and CNN comparisons for PneumoniaMNIST. B.3 clarifies the existing Two-Stage comparison.

E3.justification: The reported splits, preprocessing, sample sizes, training budgets, tuning grids, and metrics remain unchanged. PneumoniaMNIST’s post-selection ridge refit was already documented in v1; v2 makes the evaluated predictor explicit.

E4.justification: The same privileged-signal, nuisance-dimension, unlabeled-sample-size, and coupling-parameter analyses remain. The Parkinson’s eight-split robustness check and synthetic classification diagnostic are also retained without new analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original synthetic experiments and evaluations on Parkinson’s Telemonitoring, Bank Marketing, and PneumoniaMNIST, including appendix results.

These substantially expand the paper's visual presentation.

The stricter downstream budget is a material tradeoff whose utility consequences are not measured in either PDF.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with the same title, authors, and buffering–aggregation framework. Their main text, appendices A–G, equations, algorithms, figures, and tables support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 likewise contains theoretical results without original experimental, simulation, or data-analysis outcomes. Experiments are referred to [CSZZ26]; Appendix E.1's probability tables remain a mathematical counterexample.

before.justification: V1 reports theoretical constructions, proofs, and an analytically calculated counterexample, but no original empirical outcomes. References to accuracy and delay experiments do not supply results; Section 1 directs readers to [CSZZ26].
